title: Laboratory Capacity, Diagnostic Performance, and Operational Barriers in Conflict-Affected Yemen: A Cross-Sectional Study from Al-Dhalea and Radfan Districts
description:
This project contains all data, materials, and analysis scripts for the research study: "Laboratory Capacity, Diagnostic Performance, and Operational Barriers in Conflict-Affected Yemen: A Cross-Sectional Study from Al-Dhalea and Radfan Districts."

Study Overview

A comprehensive cross-sectional assessment of diagnostic laboratory services in two conflict-affected districts of Yemen (Al-Dhalea and Radfan), conducted from July to December 2025. The study evaluated 20 laboratories, interviewed 60 laboratory personnel, and analyzed 700 patient samples to assess operational capacity, diagnostic accuracy (malaria RDTs and CBC), and identify barriers to reliable service delivery.

Key Findings

· Malaria RDTs demonstrated high accuracy (sensitivity: 95.4%, specificity: 94.5%)
· Significant operational barriers: reagent stockouts (40% of labs), intermittent electricity (30%), staff training gaps (45% untrained)
· Mean turnaround time: 2.1 days, with only 26.7% of results reported within 24 hours
· Overall error rate: 5.0%, primarily from RDT-microscopy discordance

title: Identifying and Supporting Children and Families Experiencing Housing Instability and Homelessness in a Head Start Program
description:
Nearly half of children experiencing homelessness in the U.S. are five years old or younger, meaning that over 1 million children experience severe housing instability during a critical developmental period. During this time, access to high-quality learning opportunities and support for family needs are paramount. Head Start has identified children experiencing homelessness as a priority population for enrollment, because a crucial component of Head Start’s model involves connecting families to wraparound services (e.g., food and housing assistance programs, other social services) that could provide the critical support these families need. However, there are no validated screening tools to assist Head Start Family Service Workers, the primary liaisons between programs and families, to identify families experiencing housing instability and homelessness. Further, the research on children and families experiencing housing instability and homelessness overwhelmingly focuses on the negative impacts of homelessness. This approach further marginalizes a population that has its own strengths and assets. Limited extant research has attempted to identify the strengths of families experiencing homelessness, and no research to date has explored whether these strengths, as well as access to wraparound services offered through Head Start, buffer children and families from the challenges associated with housing instability and homelessness. Our objectives are to 1) validate a screening tool that Head Start Family Service Workers use to identify families experiencing housing instability and homelessness; 2) identify the personal strengths of families experiencing housing instability and homelessness, and 3) understand whether family assets and wraparound services can buffer children and families from the stress of housing instability and homelessness.

To meet our objectives, we will use quantitative analytic techniques to validate an existing screening tool used by Head Start, the Quick Risks and Assets for Family Triage–Early Childhood (QRAFT-EC) with children enrolled in Head Start programs and their families. In a three-part analytic strategy, we will 1) conduct a psychometric analysis of the QRAFT-EC to assess its dimensionality, validity, reliability, sensitivity, and specificity; 2) use a latent profile analysis, a person-centered analytic approach, to identify family assets; and 3) conduct a longitudinal analysis investigating whether and how family assets and wraparound services can buffer children and families experiencing homelessness. We will draw on the QRAFT-EC screening data and intake forms, child development assessments, and other routinely collected data sources through a partnership with the Alliance for Community Empowerment, a Head Start grantee in Bridgeport, Connecticut. 

The findings of this study will establish the validity of the QRAFT-EC screening tool for assessing family homelessness and related needs and strengths. Findings will also illuminate overlooked assets among families experiencing housing instability and homelessness that can be elevated in strengths-based case management and supports.

title: Evidential Deep Learning derived risk of Schizophrenia based on structural MRI and its relation to genetic risk factors
description:
For many years, Machine Learning Algorithms have been employed in an effort to accurately detect, classify and predict psychologic disorders using a wide range of variables, from clinical measurements, over electrophysiologic data (Rahul et al. 2024) to structural imaging. 

One of the most researched topics hereby is the classification of Schizophrenia using sMRI / fMRI images, where throughout the last decade, Neural Networks have gained increasing popularity, (Sadeghi et al. 2022) and regularly obtain better performances (Di Camillo et al. 2024).

However, there are several prevalent issues inhibiting the practical use of Deep Learning and the interpretability of its results. Most notably, many studies suffer from extremely small sample sizes, sometimes well below 100 MRI scans in total, which is arguably not sufficient for a Deep Learning Task, especially one so complex. Furthermore, only a handful of studies examine the performance of their classifier on unseen data from different acquisition sites (Cui et al. 2022, Wang et al. 2024, Vieira et al. 2019), which however is crucial for determining the generalizability of the trained model, as otherwise it can not be ensured that the model is not overfitting on sample-specific markers. This often leads to studies reporting impressive accuracies (or similar metrics such as AUROC, Sensitivity, Specificity) far beyond 0.9 - but it is highly questionable if those models could reach even remotely comparable performances on scans from independent acquisition sites. (Di Camillo et al. 2024) 

Beyond issues centring around the lack of data, neural networks itself suffer from multiple shortcomings, such as being a “black-box”, making it difficult to know which information a network utilizes for its prediction – though several approaches tackling this have been successfully implemented over the years -, and to interpret the results beyond the classification.

Another problem is the inability of a standard neural network classifier to express confidence in its prediction – for example an image classifier trained entirely on pictures of cats and dogs would classify an image of an horse as either of the former two, with no way to indicate that there even is the chance of the image not belonging to either class. To address this, multiple methods have been introduced over the years, such as Bayesian Neural Networks, Deep Ensembles (Lakshminarayanan et al. 2016), Monte Carlo Dropout (Gal and Ghahramani 2015) and Evidential Deep Learning (Sensoy et al. 2018). 

This work tries to address these issues sequentially. 
First, a Evidential Deep Learning Classifier will be trained, as a computationally efficient alternative to Deep Ensembles, BNNs and MCD, capable of expressing confidence not only in the form of predictive variance, but as both vacuity (from here on referred to as uncertainty) and dissonance, whilst ideally rivalling a Neural Network trained as a current state-of-the-art softmax classifier in performance.

As Evidential Deep Learning – to the best of our knowledge – has not yet been applied to any 3D neuroimaging task, with the most similar application being the classification of chest radiography scans (Ghesu et al. 2020), a comparison of multiple EDL Loss functions, as well as other methods of estimating confidence/uncertainty will be carried out, and potential hybrid use cases examined.


Second, the trained classifier will be applied to the UK Biobank, and its results will be linked to the genetic profiles of the subjects in two distinct ways. This makes it possible to make inferences on the “type” of information our classifier extracts from structural MRI Scans to make its classifications. Whilst this won’t allow inferences on the relation between specific brain structures and genetic risk variants, it is feasible to draw tentative conclusions if the classification corresponds to specific genetic risk for Schizophrenia, a general genetic risk for psychopathology, no genetic risk at all, or potentially novel genetic risk variants, which yields crucial insights for the potential of connecting structural MRI measures to genetic risk, facilitated through Neural Networks.

Results of this work may have substantial implications for future research; to note some:
1) Use of EDL as assisting Tool in psychiatric Diagnostics and screening – a computationally efficient classification that can express its confidence, thereby making its predictions more trustworthy, might prove to be useful tool for making diagnostics more accurately and quicker.
2) Intersection of structural neuroimaging and genetic risk – currently there is a large gap between our knowledge of the existence of varying genetic risk factors, their functional outcomes and their impacts on different scales, from molecular circuits to large structural variations. This approach may result in a novel point of view to research genetic risk.

title: Evaluation of Diagnostic Tests for Canine Ehrlichiosis in Latin America: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis (2010–2025)
description: Canine ehrlichiosis is a disease caused by Gram-negative, obligate intracellular bacteria, primarily transmitted by the tick Rhipicephalus sanguineus (Vieira et al., 2011). Ehrlichia canis infection can occur in dogs regardless of sex or age; however, some studies suggest a predisposition in certain breeds, as well as greater susceptibility in immunocompromised individuals, such as puppies and geriatric animals (Jane E. Sykes, 2023). This systematic review aims to evaluate the sensitivity and specificity of the main tests used for the diagnosis of E. canis in dogs, based on studies that adopt a reference standard. To date, there are no published systematic reviews on the diagnostic accuracy of this disease, particularly in the context of Latin America. This systematic review will follow the PRISMA-DTA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses of Diagnostic Test Accuracy Studies) guidelines (McInnes et al., 2018; Salameh et al., 2020), with a focus on diagnostic accuracy studies. The eligibility criteria were defined based on the PICOS framework (Population, Index test, Comparator, Outcome, Study design). The search will cover studies addressing diagnostic methods for canine ehrlichiosis in Latin American populations. Reviewers will conduct a systematic search in relevant databases. Study selection, screening, and data extraction will be performed using the Rayyan QCRI tool. The methodological quality of the included studies will be assessed using the QUADAS-2 (Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies) tool, as recommended for systematic reviews of diagnostic accuracy(Whiting et al., 2011). Extracted data will be analyzed and synthesized descriptively, aiming to map existing evidence and highlight gaps in the literature. The results will be presented through infographics, tables, and charts to facilitate visualization of the findings

AI in Facial Trauma management
description:
This research project is a scoping review that examines the current role of artificial intelligence (AI) and digitally assisted technologies in the diagnosis, prediction, and surgical management of facial trauma. The study was developed in response to the increasing use of AI-related technologies in healthcare and surgery, particularly within craniofacial and maxillofacial reconstruction. Although artificial intelligence has demonstrated promising diagnostic and predictive capabilities in several medical specialties, its effectiveness and true clinical application in facial trauma surgery remain unclear. Existing literature frequently describes advanced digital surgical technologies as “AI,” despite many systems functioning primarily as computer-assisted tools rather than autonomous machine learning or deep learning models. This project therefore aims to critically evaluate the available evidence and clarify the current state of AI integration in facial trauma management.

The primary purpose of the study is to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy and predictive performance of AI-based models and computer-assisted technologies used in facial trauma surgery, and to compare these approaches with conventional clinical and radiological assessment methods. The review also seeks to determine whether current technologies truly incorporate artificial intelligence capable of autonomous analysis and prediction, or whether they mainly provide digitally guided support for surgical planning and reconstruction.

title: Diagnostic accuracy of agitated saline-enhanced ultrasound for confirmation of central venous catheter placement in the emergency department of a tertiary care hospital in Mexico
description:
This is a prospective, observational diagnostic accuracy study designed to evaluate the performance of agitated saline-enhanced ultrasound compared with chest radiography for detecting malposition of central venous catheter (CVC) tips placed in the emergency department.
Consecutive adult patients (≥18 years) with a clinical indication for CVC placement will be included. Patients with femoral access or procedures performed by services other than Internal Medicine will be excluded.
CVCs will be inserted under aseptic conditions using ultrasound guidance and the Seldinger technique. Immediately after catheter placement, a transthoracic ultrasound evaluation with an agitated saline (microbubble) test will be performed. A total of 10 mL of agitated saline (90% saline and 10% air) will be injected through the distal lumen while obtaining a subcostal or apical four-chamber view.
Time to the appearance of hyperechoic contrast in the right atrium will be recorded. A positive test will be defined as delayed (>1 second) or absent visualization of microbubbles in the right atrium.
Operators will document and interpret ultrasound findings immediately after the procedure and prior to obtaining chest radiography.
Subsequently, all included patients will undergo chest radiography, interpreted by radiology residents blinded to ultrasound results. Chest radiography will serve as the reference standard for confirming catheter tip position.
Diagnostic performance will be assessed by calculating sensitivity, specificity, and predictive values.
The study is considered minimal risk, and all data will be handled confidentially and anonymized.

title: Utilization of Reticulocyte Hemoglobin Equivalent (Ret-He) in Pregnant and Postpartum Women: A Protocol for Scoping Review
description:
During pregnancy, iron requirements increase substantially due to fetal growth, expansion of maternal plasma volume, and placental metabolism. Maternal iron deficiency during the perinatal period has been suggested to be associated with increased risks of preterm birth, low birth weight, and postpartum depression. Proper management of iron status is therefore essential for maternal and child health.
Reticulocyte hemoglobin equivalent (Ret-He) reflects the hemoglobin content of reticulocytes and serves as a sensitive marker of short-term iron status. Ret-He is less affected by blood dilution and inflammation, which are common in pregnancy, and can be measured simultaneously with a complete blood count by automated hematology analyzers. Ret-He may detect iron deficiency more sensitively than conventional indicators such as ferritin and mean corpuscular volume (MCV), and has gained attention as a useful parameter for diagnosing iron deficiency anemia and monitoring therapeutic response. Despite these advantages, few studies have examined its utility specifically in pregnant or postpartum women. In addition, the existing studies vary widely in their evaluation criteria for diagnostic accuracy. Given the limited number of studies and the heterogeneity in assessment methods, a scoping review was deemed more appropriate than a systematic review. This approach enables us to comprehensively map the current landscape of Ret-He usage and to identify evidence gaps that may inform future research.
This review aims to comprehensively evaluate the utility of Ret-He in the clinical care of pregnant and postpartum women.

title: Is Shear Wave Elastography non-inferior to Transient Elastography for non-invasive diagnosis of Hepatic Fibrosis: Systematic review and Meta-analysis.
description:
The care for patients with risk factors for liver cirrhosis involves accurate diagnosis and staging of hepatic fibrosis. Despite liver biopsy being the gold standard, non-invasive sonographic modalities have increasingly been incorporated in the care of patients with suspected fibrosis. These modalities include shear wave elastography (SWE) and transient elastography (TE). This systematic review and meta analysis aims to investigate the diagnostic accuracy of SWE and TE among adult patients with suspected liver fibrosis. 
A systematic search from Cochrane Library, Embase, Google Scholar, Ovid Medline, PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science, identified studies investigating diagnostic modalities for staging liver fibrosis, and used histologic assessment as the gold standard. We collected data on study participants, demographics, etiology of liver disease whereas our outcomes of interest included diagnostic accuracy reflected by the area under the curve (AUCs). Pooled AUCs for any fibrosis (≥stage 1), significant fibrosis (≥stage 2), advanced fibrosis (≥stage 3), and cirrhosis (stage 4) were meta-analyzed through a random effects model and have been expressed as cumulative effect size and 95% confidence interval (ES(95%CI)).

title: Novel Transient elastography devices for detecting liver fibrosis in patients with multiple etiologies. Systematic review and diagnostic accuracy meta analysis
description:
Background
Liver fibrosis is a key precursor to cirrhosis and liver cancer, making early and accurate diagnosis essential. Non-invasive tools like Fibroscan, which uses transient elastography, have transformed fibrosis detection. A newer device, Fibrotouch, has emerged, claiming superior diagnostic accuracy.
Objective
This meta-analysis compares the diagnostic performance of Fibrotouch and Fibroscan across multiple liver disease etiologies, including Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C, alcoholic liver disease, and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease.
Methods
A systematic search of PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science databases was conducted up to March 1, 2025. Studies reporting sensitivity and specificity for detecting fibrosis stages (F2: significant fibrosis, F3: advanced fibrosis, F4: cirrhosis) were included. Quality was assessed using the QUADAS-2 tool. Pooled sensitivity, specificity, AUROC, diagnostic odds ratio, and likelihood ratios were calculated using a random-effects model. Analyses were performed in STATA.
Results
The meta-analysis included 9 studies on Fibrotouch (1,563 patients) and 32 on Fibroscan (6,034 patients). Fibroscan consistently outperformed Fibrotouch in diagnostic accuracy across all fibrosis stages. For instance, AUROC values for F2, F3, and F4 were higher for Fibroscan (0.91, 0.95, and 0.96) compared to Fibrotouch (0.81, 0.92, and 0.89), indicating superior diagnostic performance.
Conclusion
While Fibrotouch provides comparable diagnostic data, Fibroscan consistently outperforms it, especially in terms of AUROC values. These findings reinforce Fibroscan as the preferred non-invasive tool for accurate liver fibrosis staging across various liver diseases.

title: Behavioral Biometrics for Continuous Authentication on Mobile Devices: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Recognition Performance Across Modalities

title: Clinical Applications of Artificial Intelligence in Periodontology: A Systematic Review of the Literature
description:
Introduction

Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming various fields of medicine, including dentistry. AI applications in periodontology hold promise for improving diagnosis, treatment planning, and patient care. This protocol outlines a systematic review to evaluate the current evidence on clinical applications of AI in periodontology.


Research Question

What are the clinical applications of artificial intelligence in periodontology, and what is the evidence for their effectiveness and impact on patient outcomes?


PICO Question

Population: Patients with periodontal diseases

Intervention: Artificial intelligence applications (e.g., diagnosis, risk assessment, treatment planning, outcome prediction)

Comparison: Traditional methods or other AI applications

Outcome: Diagnostic accuracy, treatment efficacy, patient-reported outcomes


Inclusion Criteria

Study Design: Clinical trials, cohort studies, case-control studies, cross-sectional studies

Population: Patients with any type of periodontal disease (gingivitis, periodontitis)

Intervention: Any AI application used for diagnosis, risk assessment, treatment planning, or outcome prediction in periodontology

Outcomes: Diagnostic accuracy, treatment efficacy, patient-reported outcomes

Language: English


Exclusion Criteria

Study Design: Case reports, case series, reviews, editorials, letters to the editor, conference papers/presentations

Population: Animal studies, in vitro studies

Intervention: AI applications not directly related to periodontology

Outcomes: Not relevant to clinical practice or patient care

Language: Non-English



Search Strategy


Databases: PubMed, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, Scopus, Web of Science™ Core Collection, ProQuest Dissertations and Theses Global

Keywords: AI, Artificial Intelligence, machine learning, deep learning, neural network, convolutional network, Periodontology, periodontics, periodontal disease, periodontitis, periodontium, periodontal

Boolean Operators: AND, OR


Study Selection

Title and Abstract Screening: Two reviewers will independently screen titles and abstracts for eligibility.

Full-Text Review: Full texts of potentially eligible studies will be retrieved and reviewed independently by two reviewers.

Disagreement Resolution: Any disagreements will be resolved through discussion or consultation with a third reviewer.

Data Extraction

Study Characteristics: Study design, population, intervention, comparison, outcomes, follow-up period

AI Model Details: Type of AI algorithm, input data, training data, performance metrics

Outcome Data: Diagnostic accuracy (sensitivity, specificity, AUC), treatment efficacy, patient-reported outcomes

Quality Assessment

Risk of Bias: The risk of bias in included studies will be assessed using appropriate tools (e.g., Cochrane Risk of Bias tool, Newcastle-Ottawa Scale).

Data Synthesis

Narrative Synthesis: A narrative synthesis will be conducted to summarize the findings of the included studies.

Meta-Analysis: If appropriate, a meta-analysis will be performed to pool the results of studies with similar interventions and outcomes.

title: MICRORNAs POTENTIAL AS DIAGNOSTIC BIOMARKERS FOR HEART FAILURE: A SCOPE REVIEW
description: This scope review project aims to analyze the current evidence regarding the role of microRNAs (miRNAs) as potential biomarkers for the early diagnosis of heart failure (HF). HF is a serious cardiovascular disease with high prevalence and mortality, and early diagnosis is crucial for improving prognosis. title: A meta-analysis to determine the predictive accuracy of biomarkers for the anemia therapy response in the chronic kidney disease patients undergoing hemodialysis.
description:
Title
A meta-analysis to determine the predictive accuracy of biomarkers for the anemia therapy response in the chronic kidney disease patients undergoing hemodialysis. 

Anupriya, Naushaba Ahmad, Pragya Pant, Manoj K Prasad, Anupa Prasad, Ankita Tandon, Amit Kumar

 Introduction and Background
Anemia is a common complication in chronic kidney disease (CKD), particularly in patients on maintenance hemodialysis. It adversely affects quality of life, increases hospitalization rates, and contributes to cardiovascular mortality. Erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (ESAs) and intravenous iron are the cornerstones of anemia therapy in CKD. However, variability in response remains a significant challenge in clinical practice. Blood biomarkers offers valuable insights for prediction of anemia therapy response in patients with CKD undergoing hemodialysis. This study will examine the role of biochemical parameters to predict anemia therapy response in CKD patients undergoing hemodialysis.


Inclusion Criteria
● Studies reported age between 18 and 75 years
● Studies reported diagnosis with CKD Stage 5 and on maintenance hemodialysis for ≥3 months
● Studies reported data for responder and non-responder biomarkers for the anemia therapy 
● Published as full text article



Methodology
Search: Two independent reviewers will search the articles using the online databases PubMed, Embase, Web of Sciences for obtaining the relevant articles from the literature. Last search will be considered on 05 September 2025. Articles published in English language and human subjects will be considered. 

Search terms: Following search terms will be used for obtaining the relevant articles from the literature. Query('dialysis'/exp OR 'dialysis') AND ('anemia'/exp OR 'anemia') AND ('erythropoietin'/exp OR 'erythropoietin' OR 'iron'/exp OR 'iron') AND ('response'/exp OR 'response') AND ('anemia'/dm OR 'chronic kidney failure'/dm OR 'end stage renal disease'/dm OR 'iron deficiency'/dm OR 'iron deficiency anemia'/dm OR 'kidney disease'/dm OR 'kidney failure'/dm) AND 'human'/de AND ('article'/it OR 'review'/it) Mapped termsn/a

Search Screening : We will screen the search results obtained from different databases using COVIDENCE platform. Any discrepancy will be resolved by the consensus. 


Data Extraction
Two reviewers will extract the data independently in the data collection form. The following relevant data will be extracted True positive, true negative, False Positive, False Negative, Specificity, sensitivity, total of subjects, cut off value, total number of responder and non-responders in the study, country, authors name, publication year. 

Statistical Analysis
Pooled sensitivity and specificity with 95% confidence interval will be computed using the random effects model. sROC curve will be computed for determining the discriminatory power of each of reported biomarkers (Ferrtin, IRON, TIBC, TSAT, Hepcidin, STFR). Forest plot will be computed for pooled effect size. Heterogeneity will be examined by the I2 statistic and meta-regresssion and subgroup analysis will be done for the exploration of heterogeneity. All the statistical analysis will be completed in the software using STATA version 18. 

Outcome
The study will determine the prognostic accuracy of the biomarkers ((Ferrtin, IRON, TIBC, TSAT, Hepcidin, STFR ) for anemia therapy response in the CKD patients undergoing hemodialysis.

title: FRESQUE Study
description:
Title: Prospective validation of Fresno-Quebec rule to identify patients not requiring a radiograph before shoulder dislocation reduction

Rationale:
- Anterior shoulder dislocations are frequent in the emergency department (ED). Although the diagnosis can usually be made clinically, radiographs are often ordered prior to reduction to rule out concomitant fractures. Around 20% of dislocations are associated with fractures, "clinically relevant" in around 10%. Systematic radiographs expose patients to radiation, prolong ED stay and pain, and increase healthcare costs.
- The Fresno-Quebec clinical decision rule, developed in 2018 in North America, aims to safely identify patients who do not require a pre-reduction radiograph. Its retrospective validation in France in 2023 suggested that unnecessary radiographs could be reduced without impacting patient outcomes. However, prospective validation is still lacking.

Objectives:
- The primary objective is to prospectively assess the diagnostic performance of the Fresno-Quebec rule in identifying patients without clinically relevant fractures among adults presenting with anterior shoulder dislocation.
- Secondary objectives include assessing a modified version of the rule and the physician’s clinical impression, and describing time intervals in patient management in the ED (time to X-ray, time to reduction, total ED length of stay).

Design and methods:
- Prospective, multicenter, observational study
- Adults ≥18 years with clinical anterior shoulder dislocation (trauma <12h) will be screened.
- All patients will receive usual care. Radiographs will be performed at the discretion of the treating physician according to standard practice.
- The Fresno-Quebec rule will be calculated using clinical data prospectively collected.
- The rule will then be applied retrospectively to the data for validation purposes.

Outcomes:
- Primary: proportion of clinically relevant fractures among patients with a negative rule result (false negatives, 1–NPV).
- Secondary: diagnostic performance of the modified rule, diagnostic accuracy of physician impression, and time intervals in ED management.

Sample size:
Based on prior studies, we estimate that 240 patients will be required to obtain adequate precision, accounting for an expected 35% rule-negative rate and ≤5% loss to follow-up, for a final target of 252 patients across 7 centers. Analyses will include sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, and 95% confidence intervals.

Ethics:
- The study is non-interventional, complies with the French MR-004 framework and GDPR regulations,, and has obtained ethical approval from Sorbonne University Ethics Committee.
- Patient participation will be based on informed non-opposition.
- Data will be anonymized and securely stored, with long-term archiving planned according to institutional requirements.

Expected outcomes and impact:
- If validated, the Fresno-Quebec rule could safely reduce the number of unnecessary pre-reduction radiographs, improving patient comfort, reducing exposure to radiation, shortening ED stays, and optimizing resource use. This would benefit both individual patients (less pain, faster care, fewer tests) and healthcare systems (improved patient flow, reduced costs).
- The study could support future guideline development for the management of shoulder dislocations in the ED.

title: RELIABILITY, APPLICABILITY AND EXPANSION OF ACCESS TO DIAGNOSIS THROUGH TELECONSULTATION IN STOMATOLOGY: a scoping review
description: Teledentistry comprises several modalities of remote dental care, notably teleconsultation—defined as the exchange of clinical information among healthcare professionals—and telediagnosis, which involves issuing diagnostic reports. However, the impact of teleconsultation on the early diagnosis of oral lesions remains uncertain. This study aims to synthesize the available evidence and provide a comprehensive overview of the reliability, applicability, and potential to expand access to the diagnosis of oral lesions, including malignant and potentially malignant disorders, through teleconsultation in oral medicine. A systematic search was conducted in MEDLINE/PubMed, Cochrane Library, EMBASE, LILACS, and gray literature up to January 2025, with no language restrictions. Methodological quality and risk of bias were assessed using specific tools: Newcastle-Ottawa (cohort studies), JBI (cross-sectional studies), QUADAS-2 (diagnostic accuracy studies), and GRADE (certainty of evidence). A narrative synthesis was performed. A total of 25 observational studies (cross-sectional, cohort, and diagnostic accuracy) were included, involving 8,746 patients assessed via teleconsultation, although not all studies reported the exact number of participants. Among the evaluated cases, 612 were confirmed as malignant. Diagnostic agreement between general practitioners and specialists ranged from 60% to 100%, being higher in studies with standardized protocols, prior training, or those conducted by specialists. Remote diagnostic accuracy reached up to 97% compared to the gold standard. Overall satisfaction with the service was high (96.5%), and 75% of patients reported the procedure as comfortable. Some studies demonstrated that teleconsultation contributes to expanding access to diagnosis in oral medicine, as reflected in an increase in referrals. Despite promising findings, the high methodological heterogeneity (>85%) among studies precluded a robust meta-analysis and limited the generalizability of results.

title: Use of Artificial Intelligence to Identify the Risk of Adverse Drug Events in Clinical Pharmacology: A Scoping Review
description:
This project is a comprehensive scoping review of the global literature on the application of artificial intelligence (AI) to predict or detect adverse drug reactions (ADRs). Its overarching goal is to map and synthesize the spectrum of AI methodologies in pharmacovigilance, assess their performance, and identify gaps that will guide future research and implementation.

Purpose and Aims

Landscape Mapping: Systematically identify all published studies (2000–2025) in which AI techniques—machine learning, deep learning, knowledge graphs, natural-language processing, or hybrid approaches—have been applied to clinical or real-world data for ADR risk prediction.

Characterization of Methods: For each study, detail the type of AI model, data source, sample size, predictor variables, validation strategy, and performance metrics (AUC, sensitivity, specificity, F1-score, etc.).

Performance Synthesis: Compare and contrast model performance across algorithms and data environments, highlighting which approaches achieve the highest discrimination and calibration in different clinical settings.

Evidence Gaps & Recommendations: Identify under-studied areas (e.g., lack of external validation, limited use of explainable AI), and propose methodological best practices for future studies.

Project Overview

Search & Selection: We will run structured Boolean queries in major bibliographic databases and IEEE Xplore, screen ~2,270 records, and include 35 studies after duplicate removal and full-text review.

Data Extraction: Using a dual-reviewer process and a standardized template, we will extract study descriptors, AI model details, performance metrics, and authors’ stated limitations.

Synthesis Approach: Findings will be organized by AI methodology (e.g., tree-based vs. neural networks), validation type (internal vs. external), and data source (EHR vs. claims vs. spontaneous reports). We will present summary tables of counts, medians, and ranges of key performance indicators.

Optional Meta-analysis: If a homogeneous subset of ≥5 studies reports comparable AUCs, we will perform an exploratory random-effects meta-analysis and meta-regression to quantify pooled discrimination performance and explore moderators such as AI type.

Expected Outcomes

A comprehensive inventory of AI methods used in ADR prediction, with clear reporting of their strengths and limitations.

Benchmark performance metrics that researchers and clinicians can use to gauge the maturity of different AI approaches.

A structured set of recommendations—including a proposed checklist for model development, validation, and reporting—that will help standardize future AI-driven pharmacovigilance research.

Identification of critical gaps, such as the need for more external validation, incorporation of covariates, and adoption of explainable AI, which will inform funding priorities and collaborative initiatives.

By delivering both a broad overview and focused insights into AI’s role in drug‐safety monitoring, this scoping review will serve as a reference point for researchers, regulators, and health-system leaders seeking to harness AI for safer medication use.

title: Application of Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma (FAST) in Resource-Limited Areas: A Scoping Review
description: Trauma ranks among the leading causes of death and disability worldwide. According to World Health Organization (WHO) data, 4.4 million people die annually from injuries resulting from accidents or violence. This burden is particularly pronounced among individuals aged 15 to 44, with low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) bearing the primary impact—accounting for over 90% of these global trauma-related deaths. In these resource-constrained regions, relatively weak infrastructure, scarce medical resources, and inadequate emergency response systems compound frequent trauma incidents. Costs associated with readmissions, surgical interventions, and mortality rates rise significantly, placing immense pressure on medical resources and overwhelming healthcare systems. Patients often fail to receive timely diagnosis and treatment due to lack of imaging examinations and sufficient medical resources, posing severe challenges to trauma management. Currently, routine trauma imaging examinations commonly include computed tomography (CT) and ultrasound imaging. Although CT offers high sensitivity and specificity in trauma detection and diagnosis, concerns persist regarding its high cost and radiation exposure. Furthermore, the inability to move critically ill patients limits CT application in resource-constrained settings [1]. Ultrasound examinations can be performed at the bedside, but conventional ultrasound imaging is time-consuming. Compared to CT and conventional ultrasound, Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma (FAST) is the current primary diagnostic tool for trauma patients. First proposed by Rozychi et al. and widely recognized at an international conference in 1996, FAST is a bedside ultrasound method for rapidly assessing visceral hemorrhage in trauma patients. Its application has since expanded to include acute abdominal conditions such as abdominal aortic aneurysms and gallbladder stones. The FAST examination typically covers the subxiphoid region, right upper quadrant, left upper quadrant, and pelvis. It examines the hepatic-renal and splenic-renal spaces, the rectovesical pouch (uterovesical pouch), and the pericardial cavity for free fluid, determining the presence of hemorrhage in the abdominal cavity, pelvic cavity, and pericardial cavity. As a simple, low-cost, non-invasive imaging modality, FAST is particularly well-suited for resource-limited settings, especially those lacking advanced imaging equipment. It has become an indispensable alternative for managing trauma patients, effectively enhancing the timeliness and efficacy of trauma care. However, despite FAST's significant potential in resource-limited settings, current research predominantly focuses on trauma populations outside these regions and is often limited to single-center studies with small sample sizes. Therefore, this study systematically reviews the literature on FAST application in trauma care within resource-limited settings. The aim is to provide evidence-based guidance for trauma care practices and personnel training in such regions, while analyzing implementation barriers and strategies for adaptive improvements.

title: Eye Tracking during Visual Paired-Comparison Tasks for Detecting Cognitive Decline
description:
To provide a more comprehensive understanding of the capability of this assessment tool, the present systematic review and meta-analyses aim to evaluate the effectiveness and usefulness of paired visual comparisons based on eye tracking movement as a tool for assessing memory deficits in individuals with age-related cognitive changes.

2 Methods
2.1 Study protocol
This systematic review followed the “Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis” (PRISMA) guidelines (see the PRISMA checklist).18 A predefined protocol was developed and is available upon request from the corresponding author. The inclusion criterion for this systematic review was the participation of impaired memory participants and/or healthy participants, with a focus on evaluating recognition memory using VPC with ETM. Key outcomes are novelty preference scores, percent looking time at novel images, total looking time, and total fixations. Both observational and experimental studies will be considered.
2.2 Eligibility criteria
Studies including participants classified as healthy and with impaired memory, where their memory was assessed based on the VPC task, which has been published or accepted for publication in peer-reviewed journals and written in any language, were considered. No restrictions were applied in terms of study design, setting, country, or time frame. Descriptive or review articles, conference proceedings, and articles for which the full text was unavailable were excluded. Only studies that included assessments of novelty preference scores based on the VPC task were included.
2.3 Search strategy
Six electronic databases, namely, PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, Scopus, SportDiscuss, ProQuest, and the OpenGrey, were searched from inception to November 2023, without applying any time limits or filters. The research strategy employed appropriate Boolean operators (AND, OR, and NOT) to combine the relevant keywords. Additionally, field tags, wild-card options (such as truncated words), and Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) terms were used where applicable. Additionally, to minimize the risk of missing relevant publications, the reference lists of the included manuscripts and related citations from other journals identified via Google Scholar were reviewed. Furthermore, a search of personal files was also performed. The full research strategy and keywords used are presented in Table S1.
2.4 Selection process
The process used for selecting articles is outlined in Figure 1. EndNote software (version 20) was used to remove duplicate articles recorded in the initial search results. Titles and abstracts of all unique hits were screened by the first two authors (MAB and KT) for eligibility, and disagreements were resolved by consensus. The full texts of the selected studies were subsequently screened for eligibility, and disagreements were resolved by consensus. The reasons for excluding an article during the abstract and full-text screening were recorded.
2.5 Data extraction
Using a pilot-tested extraction form, the two first authors (MAB and KT) independently collected the data and resolved disagreements by consensus. The extracted data included participant characteristics (number of participants, age, educational level), study characteristics (country, methodology), and key outcomes, and the results are presented in Table 1.
2.6 Quality assessment
Two examiners independently assessed the methodological quality of the studies using the Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies (QUADAS-2) tool.19 The tool evaluates the methodological quality of diagnostic accuracy studies in four domains: patient selection, index test, reference standard, and flow and timing. It assesses bias within each domain and examines the applicability of findings in the first three domains. Independent evaluators assigned assessments of "low", "high", or "unclear" risk of bias to each guiding question within the domains.
2.7 Statistical analysis
The random-effects model was constructed using the restricted maximum likelihood estimation with the Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman (HKSJ) method20 to determine the effect size of the VPC and its pooled sensitivity and specificity. Three studies were considered the minimum number of studies needed to be included in the meta-analysis. The standardized mean difference (SMD) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated to investigate whether differential effects existed between the nap and control groups/interventions for declarative memory across all studies. The SMD (Hedges’ g) was used to measure effect size and was considered small at g < 0.5, moderate at 0.5 < g < 0.8, and large at g > 0.8.21 Forest plots were generated to illustrate point estimates of Hedges’ g and 95% CIs. The between-study variance tau-square (Tau2) test was used for heterogeneity, and the I2 statistic was used to assess the heterogeneity among studies; I2 statistics were considered low at I2 < 50%, moderate at 50%< I2 < 75%, and high at I2 > 75%.22 The 95% prediction interval for the true outcomes was calculated.23 As indicated by Rothstein et al.,24 funnel plots of potential asymmetries were constructed, and Begg and Mazumdar’s rank correlation test,25 Egger’s linear regression test,26 and Duval and Tweedie’s trim and fill method27 were used to identify publication bias. Outliers were assessed using the “dmeta” package (version 0.0.9000);28 after all outliers were retrieved, a second random effects meta-analysis was performed. The stability of each study’s pooled SMD was assessed via leave-one-out sensitivity analyses involving the removal of individual studies from the analysis and computing the excluded study’s impact on the overall effect estimate. The statistical significance level was set at p < 0.05 for all analyses. This meta-analysis was conducted using the R programming language (version 4.2.3)29, 30 with the “metafor” package (version 3.8.1).31

title: Accuracy of urine dipstick test for UTI early diagnosis: a systematic review
description: Approximately 130–175 million urinary tract infections (UTIs) occur worldwide each year. It is estimated that more than 80% of women will experience at least one episode of this infection during their lifetime, and among these, 30% will present with recurrent UTIs. According to the 2023 Practical Approach to Care Kit (PACK) guidelines, the management of patients with urinary symptoms who do not require urgent attention involves requesting urinalysis, urine culture, and antimicrobial susceptibility testing, in addition to prescribing empirical treatment, with clinical reassessment once results are available. This approach, however, demands significant time from both the physician and the patient, and could potentially be optimized by using urine dipstick tests in the outpatient setting. Urine dipstick testing is already recommended as a first-line diagnostic tool in several established clinical guidelines, including the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines for urinary tract infections in adults, which advocate dipstick testing prior to urine culture in non-pregnant women presenting with urinary symptoms in primary care. Similarly, the European Association of Urology (EAU) Guidelines on Urological Infections recommend urine dipstick analysis as an initial diagnostic step in uncomplicated UTI. Urine dipsticks assess leukocyte esterase and nitrite, among other parameters, and have demonstrated high specificity for bacteriuria confirmed by urine culture in several primary studies. Therefore, this study aims to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of urine dipstick tests for urinary tract infections in symptomatic adult women, including pooled sensitivity and specificity, through a systematic review of diagnostic test accuracy studies. The structured research question is: "What is the accuracy of urine dipstick testing in the diagnosis of urinary tract infection in symptomatic adult women compared with urine culture as the reference standard?" The Evidence Synthesis methodology will include systematic database searching, independent duplicate quality appraisal using QUADAS-3, and statistical synthesis using bivariate and HSROC models. Findings will be discussed in the context of their applicability to the Brazilian Unified Health System (SUS), considering local prevalence estimates and the potential impact on urine culture utilization and cost-effectiveness. It is expected that this research will strengthen evidence-informed clinical decision-making and support policy recommendations for primary care settings.

title: Evaluation of Diagnostic Imaging and Histological Analysis in the Detection of Myofascial Trigger Points: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
description:
This project consists of a systematic review and meta-analysis aimed at evaluating the diagnostic accuracy of imaging techniques and histological analysis in the detection of myofascial trigger points (MTrPs). Myofascial pain syndrome is one of the most prevalent musculoskeletal disorders in clinical practice and is commonly associated with localized pain, hypersensitivity, reduced function, and impaired quality of life. MTrPs are considered the main clinical feature of this condition and have traditionally been identified through manual palpation based on the presence of taut bands, hypersensitive nodules, and referred pain responses.
Despite their widespread clinical use, the diagnostic criteria and pathophysiological basis of MTrPs remain controversial. Manual palpation continues to be the most frequently used diagnostic approach; however, previous studies have demonstrated substantial variability in both inter- and intra-examiner reliability. Furthermore, the lack of internationally standardized diagnostic criteria has contributed to considerable heterogeneity across clinical and research settings, limiting reproducibility and diagnostic consistency.
In response to these limitations, increasing attention has been directed toward objective diagnostic methods capable of identifying MTrPs through structural or mechanical tissue alterations. Among these approaches, ultrasound imaging and elastography have emerged as promising non-invasive techniques for visualizing focal hypoechoic regions and alterations in tissue stiffness associated with MTrPs. Additionally, histological analysis through biopsy has been proposed as a method for investigating the microscopic structure of affected muscle tissue, including potential sarcomere contracture, inflammatory changes, fibrosis, or other structural abnormalities.
However, current evidence regarding both imaging and histological findings remains heterogeneous and, in some cases, contradictory. While several studies suggest that ultrasound and elastography may objectively identify MTrPs and distinguish them from healthy muscle tissue, other investigations question the specificity and consistency of these findings. Similarly, histological studies have reported variable results concerning muscle fiber morphology, inflammatory processes, and tissue composition.
The purpose of this systematic review is therefore to critically synthesize the available evidence regarding the diagnostic utility of ultrasound imaging, elastography, and histological analysis in the evaluation of MTrPs. The review will specifically examine the diagnostic accuracy, reliability, sensitivity, specificity, and clinical applicability of these methods compared with the current clinical standard based on manual palpation. In addition, the study aims to summarize the histological characteristics described in the literature and assess whether these findings support the existence of reproducible tissue alterations associated with MTrPs.
This project is expected to provide a comprehensive overview of current diagnostic approaches for MTrPs, clarify the strengths and limitations of imaging and histological methods, identify gaps in the literature, and contribute to improving diagnostic standardization in myofascial pain research and clinical practice.

title: Perceptions of Perinatal Distress: The Impact of Parent Gender, Symptom Presentation, and Mental Health Literacy on Future Psychology Professionals’ Responses
description:
This research project investigates how future healthcare professionals, particularly psychology students, recognise and respond to symptoms of perinatal psychological distress in mothers and fathers. Despite growing awareness of maternal perinatal mental health, paternal distress remains under-recognised and undertreated, partly due to stigma, gender role ideologies, and limited mental health literacy. The present study aims to examine whether recognition accuracy, confidence in clinical judgement, and stigma vary based on the parent's gender, symptom presentation, and birth context.

The study employs a 2 (parent gender: mother vs. father) × 2 (symptom type: depressive vs. irritable presentation) × 2 (birth complications: complications vs. no complications) between-subjects experimental design using vignette methodology. Participants will be randomly assigned to read one of eight case vignettes depicting a distressed parent and will then respond to measures assessing their recognition of symptoms, perceived competence in working with the parent, and attitudes towards the parent (i.e., stigma). Mental health literacy will be assessed as a moderator, based on its known influence on diagnostic accuracy and stigma reduction. Additionally, socially desirable responding will be measured and controlled for as a covariate to account for potential response bias in self-report data.

The study hypothesises that paternal distress, particularly when expressed as irritability rather than depressive symptoms, will be less accurately recognised, elicit higher stigma, and reduce confidence in professional engagement relative to maternal distress. It is also expected that higher mental health literacy will predict greater recognition accuracy and lower stigma, particularly in response to vignettes involving fathers. The results are anticipated to inform educational interventions aimed at improving gender-inclusive mental health training and reducing diagnostic biases in perinatal care.

title: Validating Medical Pictograms for Diagnostic Communication in Low-Literacy Regions
description:
This study aims to validate the effectiveness of medical pictograms as an alternative communication tool for diagnostics and patient interaction in low-literacy settings in the United States and Ghana. The research compares pictogram-based within healthcare applications to determine which approach most accurately supports patient comprehension, diagnostic accuracy, and task efficiency.

Conductbed within the framework of Mary Global Health’s AI-powered Patient Access Terminal (PAT) initiative, an ongoing program designed to reach and serve over 35,000 patients across multiple underserved communities in the United States, this study focuses on improving the quality and accessibility of diagnostic communication for populations with limited health literacy.

By analyzing real user interactions, the study will assess whether pictogram interfaces can improve diagnosis accuracy, reduce time to understanding, and enhance patient satisfaction compared to conventional methods.

Upon completion of the project, we are expected to have an evidence-based recommendations for implementing inclusive, low-literacy-friendly AI healthcare interfaces at scale, supported by statistical validation of accuracy, usability, and patient outcomes. title: Artificial Intelligence in hospital malnutrition: A systematic Review
description:
Hospital malnutrition is an increasingly prevalent condition in healthcare, posing a significant challenge to both patients and healthcare systems globally. It affects approximately 30% to 50% of hospitalized patients, with higher rates observed in medicine care units and geriatrics. A significant proportion of hospitalized patients experience some form of malnutrition, which often remains undiagnosed or inadequately treated. This condition not only detrimentally impacts patient health but also contributes to rising healthcare costs, extended hospital stays, and an increased risk of severe complications. The causes of hospital malnutrition are multifactorial, including clinical, therapeutic, environmental, and nutritional factors. Vulnerable patients, such as those with chronic illnesses like cancer, cardiovascular and renal diseases, as well as post-major surgery patients, elderly individuals, and those with acute conditions impairing normal food intake or nutrient absorption, are particularly at risk. Hospital malnutrition can arise from several factors, including reduced availability of nutrients, damage to vital organs that disrupt metabolism and nutrient absorption, and interventions such as pharmacological treatments or surgeries that alter normal bodily functions. Furthermore, hospital environmental factors, such as the absence of a homelike environment or inadequate nutritional support, contribute to the onset of malnutrition. When present, hospital malnutrition can lead to severe complications, including increased mortality and morbidity, prolonged hospital stays, weakened immune responses, and a heightened risk of nosocomial infections. Wound healing may be delayed, and patients’ recovery capacity can be compromised, increasing the likelihood of developing additional complications during hospitalization. These complications not only reduce the quality of life for patients but also impose an economic burden on healthcare systems, accentuating the need for preventive and timely interventions.
In this context, artificial intelligence (AI) technologies emerge as a promising tool to enhance healthcare management and optimize hospital processes. AI has become an integral part of various healthcare domains, where it is used to analyze vast amounts of clinical data and assist in diagnosing and treating diseases. AI can examine complex clinical variables, including vital signs, laboratory results, and diagnostic imaging, aiming to identify patterns that may elude human assessment. Consequently, the use of AI in healthcare can improve diagnostic accuracy, personalize treatments based on patients' specific characteristics, and reduce overall costs by optimizing resource utilizatio. The impact of AI in healthcare extends beyond clinical performance improvements; it also involves the reorganization of hospital processes, enabling more effective resource management, reducing medical errors, and enhancing the quality of care provided.

title: The Clinical Learning Environment as a Structural Determinant of Empathy and Burnout in Medical Trainees: A Scoping Review
description:
Empathy is a foundational clinical competency with well-documented associations with patient outcomes, diagnostic accuracy, therapeutic alliance, adherence to treatment, and overall patient satisfaction. However, a consistent body of empirical evidence demonstrates that empathy declines significantly across the trajectory of medical training, most markedly during the clinical years, when direct patient contact is greatest and empathic engagement is most professionally demanded. This paradox — that the environment most requiring empathy is the one most associated with its erosion — has not been adequately explained by the existing literature, which has focused predominantly on intervention efficacy rather than on environmental determinants.

Concurrent with documented empathy erosion, learner burnout has reached epidemic proportions in medical education globally. Prevalence estimates range from 37% to over 80% depending on the measurement instrument, training stage, and geographic context. Burnout and empathy erosion are not independent phenomena: depersonalization, a relational withdrawal component of the Maslach burnout construct, is mechanistically and conceptually proximate to empathy decline. Yet the literature has historically treated these as parallel rather than interacting constructs, studying them in largely separate research streams.

The clinical learning environment (CLE) which encompasses supervisory relationships, workload structures, institutional culture, hidden curriculum transmission, peer dynamics, psychological safety, and the organizational characteristics of clinical training settings, is increasingly recognized as a primary contextual determinant of both trainee wellbeing and professional identity formation. Despite this recognition, no scoping review has systematically mapped the evidence on how specific, measurable dimensions of the CLE relate to both empathy trajectories and burnout outcomes simultaneously in medical trainees.

Existing reviews have addressed adjacent territory: the causes of empathy decline (qualitatively), the efficacy of empathy-training interventions, or burnout prevalence and correlates in isolation. What remains unmapped is the intersection, specifically, how the structural features of clinical training environments function as determinants of both empathy and burnout, and what this implies for educational reform. This represents a significant and consequential gap, with direct implications for curriculum design, accreditation standards, supervisory practice, and institutional wellbeing policy.

Furthermore, the existing literature on both empathy and burnout in medical education is geographically skewed toward high-income, predominantly English-speaking contexts. The extent to which findings are transferable to low- and middle-income country (LMIC) settings — where the majority of the world's physicians are trained — remains largely unexplored. This scoping review will explicitly map the geographic distribution of evidence as a dimension of its synthesis

title: POCUS Use and Impact in Adult Outpatient Primary Care: A Scoping Review
description:
Point of Care Ultrasound (POCUS) is used by physicians of many different specialties to bring advanced imaging to the bedside and to improve patient care. POCUS is the practice of clinicians using an ultrasound during the patient encounter to guide clinical decision making by narrowing differentials, reducing uncertainty, and guiding therapies. It is a real-time focused assessment at the bedside of patients with suspected pathology. It differs from consultative imaging in that the examination is hypothesis-driven and meant to answer a binary or graded clinical question that could immediately impact care. And lastly, it is the treating clinician who performs the POCUS exam and then uses the answers to guide care. 
Currently, this tool is used by some adult primary care physicians to narrow differential diagnoses in several common outpatient concerns, including evaluating for the cause of chest pain, shortness of breath, joint pain, and abdominal pain. Using POCUS for this purpose remains an emerging field and there are many questions regarding whether POCUS can improve diagnostic accuracy, reduce morbidity/mortality, reduce costs, and improve patient and provider satisfaction. Through this scoping review, we will investigate the different uses of POCUS in the adult outpatient setting, how physicians are utilizing this tool in adult primary care worldwide, how primary care physicians are being trained and evaluated for competency, and whether impact on patient care has been demonstrated. 
A preliminary search for existing systematic or scoping reviews on the topic was conducted. One systematic review (Sorensen B, Hunskaar S. Point-of-care ultrasound in primary care: a systematic review of generalist performed point-of-care ultrasound in unselected populations. Ultrasound J. 2019 Nov 19;11(1):31. doi: 10.1186/s13089-019-0145-4) evaluated the efficacy of different POCUS applications that primary care physicians could perform. Our scoping review instead will focus on the extent to which POCUS is being used in adult primary care settings and how physicians are being trained and evaluated for competency. Additionally, we will attempt to ascertain whether there are any studies that describe patient-related outcomes in the adult primary care population. 
Another systematic review (Andersen CA, Holden S, Vela J, Rathleff MS, Jensen MB. Point-of-care ultrasound in general practice: a systematic review. Ann Fam Med. 2019;17(1):61-69. doi:10.1370/afm.2330) evaluated the use and impact of point-of-care ultrasound in the family medicine setting but was not inclusive to other primary care physicians, such as general internal medicine. Lastly, these reviews are older than five years, and therefore, there is likely additional evidence since they were completed.

title: MRD/PET-CT Concordance and Prognostic Value in Multiple Myeloma: Systematic Study-Level Analysis
description:
Objectives
- Quantify agreement between MRD and PET-CT at the same timepoint using κ statistics.
Evaluate the prognostic significance of dual negativity vs other categories (MRD−/PET+, MRD+/PET−, MRD+/PET+). 
- Explore heterogeneity by risk of bias, detection method, and study design.

Eligibility Criteria
- Population: Adults with multiple myeloma after therapy assessment.
- Interventions/exposures: MRD (flow or NGS, any sensitivity) and PET-CT performed within ±30 days.
- Outcomes: Concordance (2×2 tables) and time-to-event (PFS/OS) per dual-negativity status.
- Study types: Prospective or retrospective studies with ≥10 paired patients.
- Time frame: January 1, 2015 – June 30, 2025. The original systematic search covered publications up to April 30, 2025; two additional eligible studies published in May–July 2025 were identified through manual surveillance of recent issues and conference proceedings before database lock.
- Exclusions: Reviews, abstracts without extractable data, and studies with non-overlapping timepoints.

Information Sources and Search Strategy
PubMed and Cochrane CENTRAL: (Multiple Myeloma"[MeSH Terms] OR "multiple myeloma"[All Fields]) AND ("Neoplasm, Residual"[MeSH Terms] OR "residual disease"[All Fields] OR MRD[All Fields]) AND ("Positron-Emission Tomography"[MeSH Terms] OR "PET"[All Fields] OR "PET-CT"[All Fields] OR "FDG-PET"[All Fields]). Manual addition of cited or related studies. Full strings included in Supplement Material.

Data Extraction and Items
Extract: study ID, n, MRD method, imaging modality/criteria, 2x2 concordance data, HRs or KM curves, follow-up, ASCT status, risk of bias. Two reviewers independently cross-checked entries.

Risk of Bias Assessment
Concordance outcomes: QUADAS-2
Prognostic outcomes: QUIPS
Each domain judged Low / High / Unclear; disagreements resolved by consensus.

Statistical Analysis Plan
Agreement metrics: observed proportion, Cohen’s κ (and AC1 sensitivity).
Random-effects pooling (REML + Hartung-Knapp), report τ², I², 95 % PI.
Directional discordance model (MRD-/PET+ vs MRD+/PET-).
Prognosis: log-HR pooling for dual-negativity; include reconstructed HRs if needed.

Sensitivity analyses:
Exclude high-risk or misaligned studies.
Alternative continuity corrections.
Subgroup/meta-regression by MRD method or imaging criteria.
Publication bias: Egger’s test, contour funnel plots.

All code executed in R (4.4+) with meta/metafor; scripts deposited in Github.

Deviations from PROSPERO Policy
Because initial data extraction had begun before we learned of PROSPERO’s requirement for prospective registration, this project is retrospectively registered on OSF instead.

Data Availability
Screening logs, extraction sheets, and analytic code are uploaded as read-only CSV/R files; patient-level data are not included.

Funding and Conflict of Interest
None
