title: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence on American and Canadian Hospitals' Internal Functioning and Patient Outcomes: A Systematic Review
description:
Primary purpose: This systematic review aims to synthesize the available evidence on artificial intelligence (AI) initiatives implemented in American and Canadian hospitals between September 2022 and August 2024, and to assess the impact of these initiatives on hospitals' internal functioning and patients' medical outcomes.

Why this is needed:
Three gaps in the existing literature motivated this review. First, no systematic review has compared AI implementation across the United States and Canada simultaneously, despite both countries being global leaders in healthcare AI adoption—the US as the largest investor and patent holder (GlobalData, 2024), and Canada as the first country with a national AI strategy affecting healthcare (Radu, 2021). Second, prior systematic reviews on AI in healthcare (Meskó et al., 2018; Choudhury & Asan, 2020; Obermeyer & Emanuel, 2016) predate the 2022 peak in FDA-approved AI/ML medical devices (Joshi et al., 2024) and therefore do not capture the current regulatory and deployment landscape. Third, the specific impact of AI on hospitals' internal functioning—as opposed to patient outcomes alone—has not been systematically examined as a primary outcome domain.Specific objectives:

Objective Description
Objective 1 Identify and categorize the main AI-based initiatives implemented in US and Canadian hospitals (diagnostic, predictive, administrative, clinical decision support)
Objective 2 Quantitatively synthesize reported impacts on hospital efficiency (diagnosis time, resource allocation, cost reduction, workflow optimization)
Objective 3 Quantitatively synthesize reported impacts on patient medical outcomes (mortality, readmission, complication rates, treatment success)
Objective 4 Identify and systematically catalog challenges to AI integration into clinical workflows (generalisability, equity, ethics, privacy, provider resistance)
Objective 5 Compare US and Canadian AI adoption patterns, priorities, and reported barriers
Research questions (exact wording):

RQ1: What are the main artificial intelligence-based initiatives that American and Canadian hospitals have implemented to improve their internal processes between September 2022 and August 2024?

RQ2: How have these artificial intelligence-based initiatives impacted hospitals' performance (efficiency, resource allocation, clinical decision-making) and patients' medical outcomes (diagnostic accuracy, mortality, readmission, quality of life)?

PICo framework:

Component Definition
Population (P) Hospitals located in the United States or Canada (all types: academic, tertiary, community, rural, teaching, for-profit, non-profit)
Phenomenon of Interest (I) Artificial intelligence-based initiatives, including but not limited to: machine learning, deep learning, convolutional neural networks, natural language processing, large language models, generative AI, computer vision, clinical decision support systems, predictive analytics, robotic surgical systems, wearable-integrated AI, and administrative automation tools
Context (Co) Hospital internal functioning, defined as clinical workflows (diagnosis, treatment, monitoring), administrative processes (scheduling, documentation, billing), resource allocation (staffing, bed management, equipment), and clinical decision-making pathways during the period September 1, 2022 to August 31, 2024
2. Background and Rationale
Why US and Canada together?
The United States and Canada share a geographic region and have highly interconnected healthcare research ecosystems, yet their healthcare systems differ fundamentally in financing (private insurance–dominant in US vs. single-payer in Canada), regulation (FDA vs. Health Canada), and AI governance approaches (Radu, 2021; Hummelsberger et al., 2023). Comparing these two countries allows the review to identify whether AI adoption patterns and impacts differ by healthcare system type—a question with implications for other countries considering national AI strategies.

Why September 2022 to August 2024?
This 24-month window was selected for three reasons. First, 2022 marked the peak year for US Food and Drug Administration approvals of AI- and machine learning-enabled medical devices, with more devices approved in 2022 than in any prior year (Joshi et al., 2024). Second, the rapid emergence of generative AI and large language models (e.g., GPT-3.5/4) in late 2022 fundamentally changed the landscape of clinical and administrative AI applications (Waisberg et al., 2023; Zaretsky et al., 2024). Third, a focused two-year window ensures the review captures the most current evidence, which is critical for a rapidly evolving technology field where studies older than 24–36 months may describe obsolete AI architectures.

What is already known: prior systematic reviews

Review Focus Key finding Gap this review addresses
Meskó et al. (2018) mHealth Digital health transformation Identified medical imaging and decision support as primary AI domains Predates 2022 FDA approval surge; no US-Canada comparison
Choudhury & Asan (2020) JMIR Med Inform AI safety in clinical settings Emphasized algorithmic bias and data quality risks Did not assess hospital internal functioning as outcome
Obermeyer & Emanuel (2016) NEJM Big data and machine learning Identified potential for AI to exacerbate inequities Conceptual, not empirical synthesis
Yin et al. (2021) J Med Internet Res AI in US hospitals Mapped early adoption patterns Single country; predates 2022–2024 LLM era
What remains unknown (gap statement):
No prior systematic review has: (1) simultaneously compared US and Canadian hospital AI implementations using a standardized methodology; (2) restricted to the post-2022 FDA approval peak period; (3) operationalized "hospital internal functioning" as a distinct outcome domain separate from patient outcomes; (4) applied GRADE certainty assessment to AI hospital implementation evidence; or (5) systematically cataloged implementation challenges (generalisability, equity, ethics, provider resistance) as a primary synthesis outcome rather than a secondary mention.

Expected contribution:
This review will produce the first systematically synthesized, GRADE-assessed evidence base on AI in US and Canadian hospitals for the 2022–2024 period, usable by hospital administrators, health technology assessment agencies (e.g., CADTH in Canada, ICER in the US), and policymakers developing national AI governance frameworks.

3. Methods Overview
Study design: Systematic review following PRISMA 2020 guidelines (Page et al., 2021). No meta-analysis planned a priori due to anticipated heterogeneity; narrative synthesis using Synthesis Without Meta-Analysis (SWiM) framework (Campbell et al., 2020).

Eligibility criteria (summary):

Inclusion: Peer-reviewed publications, English/French, AI in hospitals, US or Canada, September 2022–August 2024, quantitative component

Exclusion: Non-hospital settings, no quantitative analysis, unpublished/preprint, full text unavailable

Information sources:

PubMed (biomedical literature, primary tool)

Scopus (broad interdisciplinary coverage)

Google Scholar (comprehensive coverage, used alongside standard databases)

Search date: September–October 2024

Outcome measures (extracted):

Diagnostic accuracy (sensitivity, specificity, AUC, accuracy, F1-score)

Time-based efficiency (diagnosis time, treatment delay, length of stay)

Clinical decision metrics (treatment selection, resource allocation, triage accuracy)

Patient outcomes (mortality, readmission, complication rates, functional status)

Implementation barriers (generalisability, equity, ethics, privacy, cost, provider resistance)

Risk of bias assessment:

QUADAS-2 for diagnostic accuracy studies (10 expected)

PROBAST for prediction model studies (9 expected)

ROBINS-I for non-randomized intervention studies (9 expected)

RoB 2 for randomized controlled trials (1 expected)

Dual independent assessment by two reviewers; conflicts resolved by third reviewer

Certainty assessment: GRADE framework (Guyatt et al., 2011) applied to each major finding

Synthesis method: Narrative synthesis with studies grouped into outcome domains identified during data extraction (expected domains: case detection efficiency, clinical decision-making impact, integration challenges)

4. Expected Outcomes
Primary expected outcomes (findings the review is designed to produce):

Outcome category Expected finding type How it will be reported
Diagnostic AI performance Ranges of sensitivity/specificity/AUC across studies Table with study-level values; narrative summary with median and range
Time efficiency improvements Reported time savings (minutes, hours, days) Narrative summary; no pooling expected due to heterogeneity
Clinical decision support Proportion of studies reporting improved decisions Counts (k/X studies) with examples
Implementation challenges Frequency of each challenge type across studies Categorized count table (e.g., "generalisability: k=19 studies")
US vs. Canada comparison Differences in AI application focus and reported barriers Descriptive comparison; statistical testing not planned due to small Canada sample (k≈8)
Secondary expected outcomes (exploratory):

Identification of AI applications with consistent positive results across ≥3 independent studies

Identification of AI applications with mixed or negative results

Gaps in the literature where prospective multi-site trials are absent

What this review will NOT produce:

Pooled meta-analytic estimates (heterogeneity is expected to be too high; meta-analysis would be misleading)

Causal conclusions about AI effectiveness (observational and retrospective designs dominate; causality cannot be inferred)

Cost-effectiveness analysis (insufficient cost data expected in included studies)

Recommendations for specific commercial AI products (the review synthesizes evidence by AI type, not brand)

Uncertainty to be reported:
The certainty of evidence for each major finding will be reported using GRADE (High/Moderate/Low/Very Low). Given the anticipated predominance of retrospective, single-institution validation studies without external validation, the review expects to rate most findings as Low or Very Low certainty. This will be stated transparently as a finding in itself—not a failure of the review—highlighting the gap between AI research volume and research quality.

5. Practical and Scientific Significance
For hospital administrators and clinicians:
This review will provide an evidence map showing which AI applications have demonstrated reproducible benefits in real-world hospital settings versus those still confined to research validation. Administrators can use this to prioritize AI investments with stronger evidence bases.

For health technology assessment agencies:
CADTH (Canada) and ICER (US) require systematic evidence synthesis for technology coverage decisions. This review will provide a high-level evidence inventory specific to each country's context.

For policymakers:
The review's findings on implementation challenges—particularly equity concerns (Zink et al., 2024; Guni et al., 2024) and algorithmic bias (Kiyasseh et al., 2023b)—will inform AI governance and regulation, including potential requirements for equity monitoring and model auditing in hospital settings.

For researchers:
By systematically cataloging study designs, risk of bias profiles, and missing evidence (e.g., prospective multi-site trials, equity-stratified analyses), this review will identify priority areas for future primary research.

Relationship to Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs):
This review is relevant to SDG 3 (Good Health and Well-Being) by synthesizing evidence on AI's potential to improve healthcare quality and efficiency, and to SDG 10 (Reduced Inequalities) by systematically identifying and reporting equity concerns in AI deployment (Zink et al., 2024; Guni et al., 2024).

6. Limitations of This Review (Acknowledged in Advance)
Limitation Mitigation strategy
Retrospective registration Fully disclosed in registration; all protocol deviations documented in supplementary file
Two-year time window (2022–2024) Justified by FDA approval peak and LLM emergence; longer-term trends cannot be assessed
English/French language restriction Acknowledged as language bias; French Canadian studies explicitly included to mitigate
Grey literature excluded Acknowledged as potential publication bias toward positive findings; peer-reviewed focus maintains quality floor
No meta-analysis (likely) SWiM framework used; meta-analysis feasibility assessed and reported; heterogeneity explicitly described
Google Scholar reproducibility limits Search parameters documented; limitations acknowledged; used only alongside reproducible databases
Small Canada sample (k≈8 expected) US-Canada comparison descriptive only; no statistical inference between countries
No patient/public involvement Acknowledged as limitation; not within scope of this review

title: Validation of an Agentic-Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Model System for Dermatology Decision Support
description:
Dermatology presents significant diagnostic complexity, with unevenly distributed specialist access. Decision support tools that surface traceable evidence at the point of care represent a high-value intervention if they can demonstrably improve physician accuracy.

Existing RAG evaluations rely on automated benchmarks and do not assess clinical evidence trustworthiness, answer grounding, or impact on physician decision-making. This study addresses these gaps through a physician reader study.

Large language models (LLMs) have emerged as a transformative technology in medical question answering, demonstrating the ability to process complex clinical narratives and generate clinically relevant responses, with leading systems approaching or exceeding physician-level performance on standardized assessments such as the USMLE. Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) systems employing iterative gap-aware retrieval loops represent a further extension, with preliminary evidence suggesting improved evidence coverage on complex queries.

In the dermatology domain, in silico studies have shown that LLMs can match or outperform dermatologists in diagnostic accuracy across a range of skin conditions. However, no study has evaluated a RAG system via a physician reader study in dermatology, and no prior work has assessed evidence grounding of RAG outputs using physician judgement. This study addresses both gaps. For the specific system evaluated here automated MCQ accuracy on the a dermatology-relevant subset of the MedQA dataset constructed for this study was assessed during development and serves as the pre-clinical evidence base. No prior clinical validation has been conducted for this system configuration.

title: Abstract
description:
Sepsis is a leading cause of global morbidity and mortality, requiring early recognition to improve clinical outcomes. Current biomarkers such as procalcitonin (PCT) and C-reactive protein (CRP) show limited specificity. Pancreatic stone protein (PSP) has emerged as a promising early biomarker due to its rapid rise during infection and cellular stress. However, evidence across studies is inconsistent. This systematic review and meta-analysis will synthesize diagnostic and accuracy data for PSP in ED settings. 

This protocol follows PRISMA-P guidelines. We will search MEDLINE, Embase, PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science and Cochrane CENTRAL from inception to September 2025. Eligible studies include cross-sectional diagnostic accuracy studies, prospective cohort studies, and nested case-control studies measuring PSP at the time of presentation (0–6 hours) to distinguish sepsis from infected or non-infected. Diagnostic outcomes include sensitivity, specificity, and AUROC. QUADAS-2 will assess the risk of bias. Random-effects models will be used for all meta-analysis.

Only published data will be used; ethics approval is not required. Findings will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publications and conference presentations. 

This will be the first systematic review to focus on the diagnostic accuracy of pancreatic stone protein for sepsis in emergency department populations. Heterogeneity may arise from differences in PSP assays and sepsis definitions across studies.

title: Automated Scoring of Drawings from a Tablet-Based Complex Figure Copy task
description:
Objective 
Complex Figure Copy Tasks are one of the most commonly employed neuropsychological tests. However, manual scoring of this test is time-consuming, requires training, and can then still be inconsistent between different examiners. We aimed to develop and evaluate a novel, automated method for scoring a tablet-based Figure Copy Task. 

Method 
A cohort of 261 healthy adults and 203 stroke survivors completed the computerised Oxford Cognitive Screen – Plus Figure Copy Task. Responses were independently scored by two trained human raters and by a novel automated scoring program.  

Results 
Overall, the Automated Scoring Program was able to reliably extract and identify the separate figure elements (sensitivity and specificity of 92.10% and 90.20% respectively) and assigned total scores which agreed well with manual scores (ICC = .83). Receiver Operating Curve analysis demonstrated that, compared to overall impairment categorisations based on manual scores, the Automated Scoring Program had an overall sensitivity and specificity of 80% and 93.40% respectively (AUC = 86.70%). Automated total scores also reliably distinguished between different clinical impairment groups with acute stroke survivors scoring significantly worse than longer term survivors, which in turn scored worse than neurologically healthy adults.  

Conclusions 
These results demonstrate that the novel automated scoring algorithm was able to reliably extract and accurately score Figure Copy Task data, even in cases where drawings were highly distorted due to comorbid fine-motor deficits. This represents a significant advancement as this novel technology can be employed to produce immediate, unbiased, and reproducible scores for Figure Copy Task responses in clinical and research environments.

title: Clinical Utility of Plasma p-tau217 Dual-Threshold (Rule-in/Rule-out) Strategies for Reducing Confirmatory Amyloid Testing in Alzheimer's Disease: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
description:
To systematically evaluate, along two distinct dimensions, the (1) diagnostic performance and (2) clinical 
utility of plasma p-tau217 dual-threshold strategies for reducing confirmatory amyloid positron emission 
tomography (PET) or cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) testing in adults being evaluated for Alzheimer's disease. 
Diagnostic performance is operationalized as rule-out sensitivity and rule-in specificity, while clinical utility 
is operationalized as the gray-zone proportion and the proportion of participants in whom confirmatory 
testing is avoided. The research question for this review is structured according to the PIRD framework (Population, Index 
test, Reference standard, Diagnosis/Target condition), which is the framework recommended by the 
Cochrane Handbook for diagnostic test accuracy reviews.
Primary outcomes comprise two distinct dimensions, consistent with the primary objective: 
(1) diagnostic performance, comprising rule-out sensitivity and rule-in specificity, and (2) clinical utility, 
comprising the gray-zone proportion and the proportion of participants in whom confirmatory testing is 
avoided. Positive and negative predictive values are reported as primary outcomes supporting the 
diagnostic performance dimension. The full set of primary outcomes is as follows: Sensitivity of the rule-out threshold (and, where reported, overall algorithm sensitivity) — diagnostic performance. Specificity of the rule-in threshold (and, where reported, overall algorithm specificity) — diagnostic performance. Positive predictive value (PPV) — diagnostic performance. Negative predictive value (NPV) — diagnostic performance. Proportion of participants classified into the gray zone — clinical utility. Proportion of participants in whom confirmatory PET or CSF testing is avoided — clinical utility. Secondary Outcomes compromise area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). Positive and negative likelihood ratios. Diagnostic odds ratio. Reported rule-in and rule-out cutoff values, and the method by which they were derived. Performance of sequential or two-step algorithms incorporating plasma p-tau217 in

title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE APPLICATIONS IN VETERINARY ANTIMICROBIAL RESISTANCE DIAGNOSTICS AND SURVEILLANCE IN SRI LANKA: A SYSTEMATIC REVIEW
description:
Title: Artificial Intelligence Applications in Veterinary Antimicrobial Resistance Surveillance: A Systematic Review of Potential for Sri Lanka

Introduction and Objectives: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a critical One Health crisis in Sri Lanka, contributing to an estimated 2,610 attributable and 10,000 associated deaths in 2021. Within the veterinary sector, progress is constrained by limited laboratory capacity and fragmented surveillance. This systematic review evaluates the current and potential applications of artificial intelligence (AI) in veterinary AMR diagnostics and surveillance to identify viable solutions for the Sri Lankan context.

Methods: Following PRISMA guidelines, a systematic review of peer-reviewed literature (2015–May 2026) was conducted using PubMed and Web of Science. The study synthesized AI methodologies applicable to low-resource settings, focusing on diagnostic accuracy and surveillance integration.

Results: AI methodologies, including machine learning (e.g., Random Forests) and deep learning, are increasingly utilized for automated antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) and genomic interpretation. In Sri Lanka, critical data gaps exist in the poultry and dairy sectors, where recent 2025-2026 findings highlight a 75% resistance rate to tetracycline in biofilm-forming Escherichia coli. National isolates are further dominated by fluoroquinolone resistance, correlated with heavy veterinary enrofloxacin use. Our findings identify that AI-driven, smartphone-based computer-vision models for high-throughput AST screening can bypass laboratory infrastructure limitations by providing remote, standardized data interpretation.

Conclusions: AI presents an immediate opportunity to integrate fragmented farm data and antibiotic sales to enhance national surveillance. AI-augmented diagnostics can significantly improve veterinary AMR control; however, success requires sustained investment in digital infrastructure and cross-sector One Health collaboration.

title: Protocol for a scoping review on the use of transcranial doppler in cardiac, aortic and carotid surgery
description:
Cardiac, aortic, and carotid surgery are medical procedures at high risk for neurological complications; these include the occurrence of stroke, cognitive-behavioral alterations, disorders of consciousness, and focal neurological deficits [1–3]. The incidence of stroke in cardiac surgery is significant in about 1-5% of cases, whereas in aortic surgery is relevant in 7-10% of cases [4]. Perioperative stroke is also an important complication of carotid endarterectomy and its risk is around 2% [5].
The neurological complications following cardiovascular surgery are part of a series of alterations included in the definition of Post Operative Cognitive Dysfunction (POCD) [6], which have been classified into two types by the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association: type 1 includes major focal neurological deficits, stupor, and coma; type 2 includes milder deficits, without focal deficits, such as delirium or decline in cognitive function in one or more domains [7]. The diagnosis of POCD requires evidence of a decline in cognitive function from preoperative to postoperative, exclusion of postoperative delirium, abrupt onset, temporal correlation with surgery, exclusion of other neurological conditions, present prior to surgery, that may explain the neurocognitive deficits, and adequate neuropsychological evaluation to test all cognitive domains involved in the neurological dysfunction (i.e. attention, language, memory, executive functions) which is carried out by means of specific neuropsychological tests [6]. 
The pathophysiological mechanisms underlying POCD have long been debated and many risk factors have been linked to its onset, such as advanced age, hypertension, atherosclerosis, a previous stroke and diabetes, but two of the main etiopathogenetic mechanisms considered are embolization and hypoperfusion [8,9]. There are two kinds of emboli, gaseous and solid; the latter in turn can be divided into macroemboli and microemboli. Gaseous emboli are related to macroscopic or microscopic air bubbles that may be present in the cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) circuit [6], whereas solid emboli are related to parts of atheromatous plaques and cell aggregates, or inorganic parts of the CPB circuit, which may embolize into the central nervous vessels during surgical manipulation of the cardiovascular system [10]. Many Authors studied the correlations between microembolization and the occurrence of POCD; some findings reveal that the intraoperative embolic amount (measured with transcranial Doppler ultrasonography, TCD) correlates with the likelihood of postoperative cognitive decline [11,12], whereas other studies didn’t find such a correlation [13,14]. The nature of the emboli is also relevant in determining neurocognitive impairment: late POCD seems to depend more on gaseous microemboli than on solid ones [15]. As mentioned above, intraoperative TCD is a useful tool for the detection of emboli and it is possible, thanks to the multifrequency TCD instrumentation, to discriminate between solid and gaseous emboli [16]. 
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is a useful tool for the detection of brain lesions due to cardiac surgery. Focal neurological deficits appear in almost 3% of patients undergoing cardiac surgery in the early postoperative period [17], however, some of these patients present with lesions on MRI without clinical evidence of neurological deficits; the limitations of this method are that it is not always possible to prove that the lesions revealed post-operatively are not pre-existing at the time of surgery, as a pre-operative examination is not always available for comparison [18]. There are many types of MRI sequences useful for studying post-operative brain lesions, including diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI), fluid-attenuated inversion recovery sequencing (FLAIR), proton density-weighted, and T2 [19–22]. Lesions visualized with FLAIR sequences remain evident indefinitely. At the same time, those detectable at DWI typically appear within 2 hours of the injury event and disappear after about 2 weeks, making it easier to identify any lesions that may have arisen in conjunction with cardiac surgery [19,20] and making them particularly suitable for the study of this type of lesions. 
As neurological outcomes in cardiac surgery are still a clinical challenge, but their correlation with intraoperative embolic events and cerebral perfusion is still unclear, and as the use of TCD as intraoperative monitoring is not yet an established clinical practice in all cardiac surgery centers, this scoping review aims at an overview of the available direct and indirect evidence on the potential benefits of the use of intraoperative TCD, during cardiac and vascular surgery, on post-operative cognitive outcomes.

title: Knowledge, Attitudes and Barriers to Colorectal Cancer Screening in Split, Croatia
description: Colorectal cancer (CRC) represents one of the most significant public health challenges worldwide. It is the third most commonly diagnosed cancer and the second leading cause of cancer deaths worldwide. Croatia launched its National Colorectal Cancer Screening Program in 2007, targeting citizens aged 50–74 years with a biennial guaiac-based fecal occult blood test (gFOBT) (6). Early program data revealed that uptake was worryingly low: of the 1,056,694 individuals invited to participate by 2011, only 210,239 (19.9%) returned completed tests. Croatia’s Ministry of Health decided to modernize the program by introducing the fecal immunochemical test (FIT) as the primary screening method starting in autumn 2025. FIT offers several advantages: it requires only a single stool sample, there are no dietary restrictions, and it uses antibodies specific to human hemoglobin, improving both sensitivity and specificity for lower gastrointestinal bleeding. This reduces the likelihood of false positives caused by diet and enhances detection of significant lesions. However, changing the test alone will not be enough to address the underlying participation problem. Research shows that many people lack basic knowledge about CRC and the purpose of screening. Fear of a cancer diagnosis, embarrassment, and misconceptions about the procedure are common reasons for not participating. In Split-Dalmatia County in Croatia, these challenges may be even more pronounced. Participation in the national program here has been among the lowest in the country despite the region’s high and rising CRC incidence. This study aims to examine knowledge levels, perceived barriers and socioeconomic factors affecting CRC screening participation in the Split population. By identifying the most important factors influencing participation, it will be possible to develop practical interventional strategies that will encourage more people to get tested and ultimately reduce the region’s CRC mortality rates.

title: Culture-Negative Infective Endocarditis Diagnosed by Molecular Methods in Sub-Saharan Africa: A Scoping Review (PRISMA-ScR)
description:
Rationale: Culture-negative infective endocarditis (CNIE) is under-characterized in sub-Saharan Africa, where rheumatic heart disease predominates and molecular diagnostics are unevenly available. This scoping review maps published cases in which a molecular method (targeted PCR/serology, 16S rRNA sequencing, or mNGS) contributed to diagnosis, to describe the regional evidence base, diagnostic methods used, and reported clinical impact.

Review Question: What is the reported diagnostic and clinical experience with molecular methods (targeted PCR/serology, 16S rRNA sequencing, mNGS) in culture-negative infective endocarditis across sub-Saharan African countries, as described in published case reports and case series?

Eligibility (PCC): Population - patients of any age diagnosed with possible or definite CNIE per (modified) Duke or 2023 Duke-ISCVID criteria, managed in a sub-Saharan African country. Concept - use of at least one molecular diagnostic method contributing to pathogen identification. Context - any healthcare setting in sub-Saharan Africa; publications from 2010-present.

Information Sources: PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, African Journals Online (AJOL), Google Scholar (grey literature), and manual reference-list screening.

Data Charting: Country, patient demographics, valve type, Duke-ISCVID category, molecular method and specimen type, prior antibiotic exposure, organism identified, turnaround time, whether the result changed management, and clinical outcome.

Synthesis: Descriptive summary (counts, proportions) by country, molecular method, and organism. No meta-analysis of pooled diagnostic accuracy is planned given expected heterogeneity of source literature.

title: Exploration of Differentially Expressed circulating microRNAs as Diagnostic Biomarkers for Primary Aldosteronism
description:
Primary Aldosteronism (PA) is the most common cause of secondary hypertension and is associated with significant cardiovascular morbidity when left undiagnosed. Despite its clinical importance, the condition remains underdiagnosed due to the lack of reliable, minimally invasive biomarkers that can effectively distinguish PA from primary (essential) hypertension (PH). The current diagnostic pathway relies on screening with aldosterone-to-renin ratio, confirmatory tests, and adrenal vein sampling, which are invasive, costly, and not widely available.

This project aims to explore circulating microRNAs (miRNAs) as potential diagnostic biomarkers for PA. miRNAs are small, non-coding RNAs that regulate gene expression and are increasingly recognized for their stability in blood and disease-specific expression patterns. Leveraging machine learning and bioinformatics approaches, we will analyze miRNA expression profiles obtained from plasma/serum samples of patients with confirmed PA compared to those with PH. Differential expression analysis will identify candidate miRNAs that show significant and reproducible differences between the two groups.

We will then employ supervised machine learning models (e.g., Random Forest, Gradient Boosting) to evaluate the discriminatory power of these candidate miRNAs. Feature selection methods will be used to derive a parsimonious diagnostic signature with optimal sensitivity and specificity. Cross-validation and independent validation subsets will be applied to minimize overfitting and assess generalizability.

The expected outcome of this research is the identification of a panel of circulating miRNAs that can serve as non-invasive biomarkers for distinguishing PA from PH. Such a biomarker panel could improve early diagnosis, reduce dependence on invasive procedures, and ultimately guide more targeted and effective management of patients with hypertension. Beyond diagnostic utility, this study may also provide insights into the molecular pathways underlying aldosterone excess and its cardiovascular consequences.

title: Data collection and analysis from the Informatics Department of the Unified Health System in Brazil, using open source programming languages: a scoping review
description:
1 INTRODUCTION
The consolidation of the Brazilian Unified Health System (SUS) brought with it the need to develop instruments capable of recording, organizing, and providing information to support health management (Lima et al., 2009). Since its creation, SUS has required information systems capable of consolidating data in a structured and standardized manner, supporting both epidemiological surveillance and health planning. In this process, the Department of Informatics of SUS (DATASUS) assumed a strategic role by gathering, processing, and providing nationwide data, becoming one of the main sources of information for managers, researchers, and health professionals (Brazil, 2020a).
The availability of reliable and accessible data is a central requirement for public policy formulation, indicator evaluation, and the development of research in public health (Costa et al., 2025). However, the use of these databases still faces challenges related to the decentralization of sources, heterogeneity of records, data quality, and periodic system updates, which may limit their applicability in more complex analyses (Brazil, 2020a).
To overcome these limitations, the National Health Information and Informatics Policy (PNIIS) and the Digital Health Strategy for Brazil 2020–2028 (ESD28) have established guidelines focused on information governance, interoperability, and strengthening the technological infrastructure of SUS (Brazil, 2020b).
Established in 2004, the PNIIS defined principles for the use of Information and Communication Technologies within SUS, emphasizing the integration of national information systems, improvement of data quality, and strengthening of health management (Brazil, 2004). These guidelines were later updated to incorporate goals related to interoperability and information governance (Brazil, 2021).
Among the structuring initiatives for the modernization of SUS, the National Health Data Network (RNDS) stands out as a central platform integrating information from different systems and levels of care, promoting interoperability and providing essential data to support decision-making. Other initiatives include SUS Digital, through the “Meu SUS Digital” tool, and the PQDAS Program, which standardizes and improves the quality of supplementary health data in alignment with SUS data (Brazil; Ministry of Health; Secretariat of Digital Health Information, 2024).
The adoption of digital technologies not only modernizes infrastructure but also transforms the interaction between citizens, professionals, and managers, increasing efficiency and integration of care. This approach represents the evolution of the concept of eHealth, expanding the use of digital resources beyond service informatization. Technologies such as artificial intelligence, big data, telemedicine, wearable devices, and mobile applications have been used to improve management, access, and quality of care (World Health Organization, 2021).
According to the Ministry of Health (Brazil, 2020a), DATASUS integrates systems covering various areas of health care, such as the Hospital Information System (SIH), Ambulatory Information System (SIA), Mortality Information System (SIM), Live Birth Information System (SINASC), and the Notifiable Diseases Information System (SINAN), among others.
Despite the breadth of these databases, challenges persist regarding data quality, updating, standardization, and interoperability, which may limit reliable analyses and evidence-based decision-making. Ensuring efficient integration among systems is essential so that managers and professionals have access to consistent and up-to-date information.
Data collection and management in Brazil are directly linked to PNIIS and ESD28. While PNIIS establishes standards for organization, integration, and governance of health information, ESD28 defines priorities for digital technology use, including interoperability, professional training, and innovation. The articulation between these initiatives allows DataSUS data to be used strategically at different management levels (Brazil, 2020b; Costa et al., 2025).
Access to public health data in Brazil has advanced significantly, even before the Access to Information Law (LAI) came into effect in 2012. Tools such as TabNet and TabWin, developed by DATASUS, enable the creation of tables, graphs, and indicators to support epidemiological analyses (Saldanha et al., 2019; Silva, 2009). TabNet allows quick tabulations from public data, while TabWin enables microdata import and spatial representations.
Despite their usefulness, these tools have operational limitations, require specific training, and demand repetition of procedures for each new period analyzed. In this context, programming code emerges as an alternative to automate, speed up, and standardize data collection and processing.
The increased availability of SUS microdata, combined with the expansion of digital health tools, has driven the adoption of open-source programming languages for data manipulation and analysis (Costa et al., 2025). These languages enhance scientific reproducibility, integration with public databases, and automation of complex analyses such as risk modeling and time series (Wilson et al., 2014).
Despite these advances, there is a knowledge gap regarding systematic mapping of the use of open-source programming specifically applied to DATASUS. While isolated studies exist, comprehensive discussions of methods and tools remain scarce. The scoping review by Restrepo et al. (2023) on open health datasets in Latin America highlights this gap.
Although DataSUS has consolidated itself as a national repository, challenges such as heterogeneity, lack of standardization, variable data quality, and integration difficulties between systems still limit reproducibility.
At the same time, there is growing use of open-source programming in health data science. However, a systematic mapping is needed to identify how these tools are applied to DataSUS, which methods are used, and which gaps remain.
The absence of this overview hinders the consolidation of best practices and the development of more accessible technological solutions. Therefore, conducting a scoping review to systematize existing knowledge is necessary to support open science, improve public health analyses, and strengthen evidence-based decision-making within SUS.

2 OBJECTIVE
To map the evidence in the scientific literature on the use of open-source programming for the collection and analysis of data from Brazilian Health Information Systems.

3 METHOD
3.1 Study Design
This study consists of a scoping review, characterized as applied research with a technological development approach. The review will be conducted in accordance with the recommendations of the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses – Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR), aiming to ensure methodological rigor, transparency, and greater detail in the conduct and reporting of the study.
3.2 Data Sources
The databases selected for this review are: PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, Scopus, IEEE Xplore, LILACS, BVS (Virtual Health Library), Google Scholar, and the Brazilian Digital Library of Theses and Dissertations (BDTD). 
The choice of these databases is justified by their relevance to the topic, coverage of high-quality journals, and multidisciplinary scope. While databases such as PubMed, Embase, and LILACS are specialized in health and biomedical sciences, Scopus and Web of Science provide a multidisciplinary perspective, and IEEE Xplore contributes the necessary technical focus for topics related to programming and data analysis. Searches will also be conducted in Google Scholar and BDTD to capture gray literature not indexed in journal databases.
3.3 Identifying the Research Question 
The first step consists of formulating a well-focused research question, with the objective of mapping what has already been published on the use of open-source programming languages and tools in the context of DATASUS, as well as identifying potential gaps in the existing literature. 
Research question: What evidence is available in the literature on the use of open-source programming languages for the collection, extraction, and analysis of DATASUS data? 
Based on this guiding question, it will be possible to identify the most commonly used open-source programming languages for the collection and analysis of DATASUS data, recognize the libraries, frameworks, or tools frequently employed in these processes, and understand the main methods and techniques used for data collection, extraction, and analysis. Moreover, through this scoping review, it will be possible to map the key challenges reported in the literature regarding the use of open-source programming for working with DATASUS data, thereby contributing to a broader understanding of the topic.
3.4 Identifying the Most Significant Terms in the Question
To identify the most relevant terms present in the research question, a concept mapping was carried out a structured methodology aimed at identifying and organizing the key elements of a research question. The objective of concept mapping is to translate the identified concepts into search terms (keywords and controlled descriptors), which will be used in databases. This approach is essential to ensure that the search strategy is comprehensive, precise, and aligned with the research objectives, being especially useful in systematic reviews, scoping reviews, and other types of literature reviews.
From this research question, the main elements identified were: terms related to open-source programming languages, data collection, extraction, analysis, and DataSUS. To structure the search strategy, the PCC (Population, Concept, and Context) framework was used, which best represents the components of the research. This structuring allows for a more targeted and efficient search, ensuring that the results obtained are aligned with the research objectives and cover the essential aspects of the investigated topic, as presented in Table 1 describing the PCC strategy.


The process of mapping and refining terms, using the main term and the translation of terms between DeCS (Health Sciences Descriptors) and MeSH (Medical Subject Headings), is a robust methodological approach to ensure that the search strategy is comprehensive and precise, facilitating the retrieval of articles in bibliographic databases. 
3.5 Search Strategy
The search terms will be defined based on subject descriptors from the databases using the Health Sciences Descriptors (DeCS) and Medical Subject Headings (MeSH). 
The search strategies were adapted for each database, using controlled descriptors (MeSH, DeCS) and Boolean operators (AND, OR). The construction of the search strategy was carried out in two steps: first, the terms related to each concept were combined using the Boolean operator OR (e.g., “Programming Languages” OR “Python Programming” OR “R Programming”) to ensure search comprehensiveness. Next, the groups of terms were combined with each other using the Boolean operator AND (e.g., [Group 1] AND [Group 2] AND [Group 3] AND [Group 4]), ensuring the precision and relevance of the results. The entire process was conducted using the PubMed Advanced Search tool (available at: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/advanced/). 
No restrictions were applied regarding language or publication date, in order to ensure broad and inclusive coverage of the literature. 
These strategies were adapted to improve the sensitivity and specificity of the searches while maintaining the same framework initially established in the strategy developed for PubMed. The combination of terms, based on controlled descriptors (MeSH, DeCS) and Boolean operators (AND, OR), resulted in the following search strategies for each database, as presented in the appendices of this work through Table 2: Search Strategy in Databases.


3.6 Selection Process
Publications identified through the descriptors will be exported to the Rayyan application for duplicate removal and selection of articles/documents based on eligibility criteria, followed by full-text review and data extraction.
Studies addressing the use of open-source programming languages for the collection, extraction, and/or analysis of DataSUS data will be included. Documents describing data extraction methods from other information sources or systems will be excluded from the sample.
3.7 Data Management and Analysis
Both the selection process through title and abstract screening and full-text review, and the data extraction will be carried out by two researchers. Discrepancies will be resolved by consensus.
Due to the heterogeneity of the documents to be analyzed, quality assessment will be performed only for scientific articles indexed in databases, using the AGREE II instrument.
Data will be stored using the Research Electronic Data Capture (REDCap) software.

3.8 Ethical Considerations and Conflicts of Interest
In accordance with Brazilian Resolutions No. 466 of December 12, 2012, and No. 510 of April 7, 2016, this study is exempt from review by a Research Ethics Committee (REC). There are no conflicts of interest in this protocol. 
4 EXPECTED RESULTS
The scoping review will comprehensively map the scientific production related to the use of open-source programming languages applied to DataSUS, identifying the state of the art in the collection, processing, and analysis of data from Brazil’s national health information systems. It is expected to characterize the types of published studies, application contexts, the most explored SUS information systems, and the predominant methodological approaches, providing a consolidated overview of current practices in the field. The use of open-source code enables researchers and developers to access and contribute to the improvement of tools. Well-developed code supports efficient data integration and analysis, accelerating the development of new solutions tailored to community needs.
In addition, the review will enable the identification of the main tools, languages, and libraries used to handle SUS microdata, including Python, R, and other open-source resources. This characterization will allow an assessment of the accessibility, documentation, and reproducibility of existing solutions, contributing to an understanding of how these technologies have been applied in research and health management.
The mapping process is also expected to reveal gaps in the literature, such as the lack of methodological standardization, limitations in interoperability between systems, scarcity of automated tools, and insufficient studies addressing integration across different DataSUS databases. Identifying these gaps will provide guidance for the development of new technological solutions and for shaping future research agendas.
The review will further systematize the methodologies employed in the analyzed studies, describing strategies for data collection, preprocessing, statistical analysis, modeling, and data visualization. This systematization will help compare manual and automated approaches, highlighting best practices, limitations, and opportunities for improvement in the use of public health data.
From the perspective of management and public policy, the expected results include demonstrating the potential of open-source tools to enhance transparency, efficiency, and reproducibility in epidemiological and administrative analyses. The review should show how automation in data collection and processing can support managers, researchers, and SUS professionals in evidence-based decision-making.
Finally, the study is expected to produce a consolidated, up-to-date, and replicable body of knowledge capable of supporting the development of new technologies, guiding training processes, and strengthening open science in the context of Brazilian public health.
In the future, it is expected that these tools will become more accessible, customizable, and user-friendly, increasing transparency in analyses. This will enable more robust studies aligned with the needs of health professionals and researchers. Additionally, new methodologies may be developed to handle large-scale data, optimizing the use of DataSUS for epidemiological analyses, outbreak prediction, and public policy evaluation using big data technologies.

title: Deep Learning-Enhanced PET Imaging for Intelligent Medical Diagnosis
description:
Abstract
Positron Emission Tomography (PET) is widely used in modern healthcare to analyze metabolic and biochemical processes within the human body. It is particularly valuable for the early detection and diagnosis of diseases such as cancer, neurological disorders, and cardiovascular conditions. However, PET imaging is often affected by challenges like image noise, low spatial resolution, and high computational demands, which can limit its diagnostic effectiveness. These limitations highlight the need for more advanced and efficient computational techniques to improve image quality and interpretation.
To overcome these challenges, this study proposes a deep learning-based approach for enhancing PET image analysis. The framework combines multiple advanced models to improve feature extraction and learning efficiency. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) are used to capture important spatial features from PET images, while Residual Networks (ResNet) enable deeper model training without performance degradation. In addition, Transformer-based models are incorporated to understand global patterns and long-range dependencies within the images. The integration of PET with complementary imaging techniques such as PET/CT and PET/MRI further strengthens diagnostic accuracy by combining functional and structural information.
The proposed method demonstrates improved performance in key clinical applications, including tumor detection, neurological disorder analysis, and cardiac assessment. It enhances image clarity, increases diagnostic accuracy, and reduces computational limitations compared to traditional approaches. Overall, this work highlights the potential of deep learning to make PET imaging more reliable and efficient. Future research will focus on real-time implementation, minimizing radiation exposure, and improving model transparency through explainable artificial intelligence techniques.
Keywords:Positron Emission Tomography (PET), Deep Learning, Medical Image Analysis, Disease Diagnosis, Artificial Intelligence.

title: Artificial Intelligence in School Health Services: A Scoping Review of Opportunities, Challenges, and Future Directions
description:
Background
Artificial intelligence is fundamentally transforming healthcare delivery, clinical decision-making, and health systems operations worldwide. AI technologies, including machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, computer vision, chatbots, large language models, and clinical decision support systems, have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in diagnostic accuracy, predictive analytics, and administrative automation across various healthcare settings (Topol, 2019; Davenport & Kalakota, 2019; Rajpurkar et al., 2022). Nursing, as the largest professional health workforce globally, is increasingly implicated in this transformation (Clancy, 2020; Booth et al., 2021; Ronquillo et al., 2021).

School health services occupy a critical yet under-resourced position in the broader public health infrastructure. School nurses must simultaneously manage soaring rates of adolescent mental health disorders, a growing chronic disease burden, escalating administrative demands, and a persistent shortage of qualified school nursing staff. The National Association of School Nurses recommends a maximum ratio of one registered nurse per 750 students, a standard that the majority of US school districts fail to meet (National Association of School Nurses, 2022; Willgerodt et al., 2018). Approximately 25% of school-age children in the United States have at least one chronic health condition requiring ongoing management during the school day (Crump et al., 2013). Rates of anxiety, depression, and suicidal ideation among adolescents have risen sharply over the past decade, with schools now widely recognized as the primary setting for mental health identification and intervention (Torous et al., 2021; Grist et al., 2019).

Despite the rapid expansion of AI applications in hospital nursing, primary care, pediatric medicine, and public health, school health services have remained largely outside the discourse of AI adoption and evaluation. To date, no published scoping review has specifically and comprehensively mapped the evidence base for AI applications within school health services and school nursing practice. This gap is significant: without a systematic understanding of what AI technologies have been studied in school settings, what outcomes have been measured, and what barriers to implementation have been identified, school health leaders, nursing professional organizations, policymakers, and researchers lack the evidence foundation needed to make informed decisions about AI adoption, governance, funding, and workforce development.

Purpose and Objectives
The purpose of this scoping review is to systematically map the existing and emerging evidence on AI applications within school health services.

The specific objectives are:

To identify and characterize the types of AI technologies that have been studied or implemented in school health settings, school-based health centers, and school nursing practice.

To map the health domains and student health conditions that have been the focus of AI applications in school health settings, including mental health, chronic disease management, vision and hearing screening, obesity and nutrition, infectious disease, immunization, health education, and emergency preparedness.

To synthesize the reported opportunities, benefits, and positive outcomes associated with AI applications in school health services, including improvements in screening accuracy, diagnostic efficiency, administrative burden reduction, access equity, and student health outcomes.

To identify and categorize the reported challenges, barriers, risks, and ethical concerns associated with AI implementation in school health settings, including algorithmic bias, data privacy, digital equity, workforce readiness, explainability, regulatory concerns, and governance gaps.

To delineate the implications of existing AI evidence for school nursing practice, education, policy, and leadership, with a focus on competencies, governance structures, and practice changes necessary for responsible AI adoption.

To identify gaps in the current evidence base and establish priority directions for future research on AI in school health services.

Methods
This scoping review follows the updated methodological guidance for conducting scoping reviews published by the Joanna Briggs Institute (Peters et al., 2020; Peters et al., 2015), as built on the foundational methodology originally proposed by Arksey and O'Malley (2005) and subsequently refined by Levac et al. (2010). Reporting adheres to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR; Tricco et al., 2018), supplemented by PRISMA 2020 reporting standards where applicable (Page et al., 2021).

Eligibility Criteria

Eligibility is determined using the Population-Concept-Context (PCC) framework as recommended for scoping reviews by JBI (Peters et al., 2020).

Population: School-aged children or adolescents (aged 5-18 years), school nurses, teachers, school counsellors, school health providers, or parents/caregivers in the context of school health services.

Concept: Any AI-based technology, including machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, computer vision, chatbots and conversational agents, predictive analytics, clinical decision support systems, large language models, generative AI, robotics, and wearable devices incorporating AI-based analysis.

Context: Primary and secondary schools (K-12 and international equivalents), school-based health centers, school nursing practice in any country, and telehealth or remote health services delivered within or directly to school health contexts.

Study Designs: All study designs are eligible, including randomized controlled trials, quasi-experimental and pre-post studies, cohort and cross-sectional studies, qualitative and mixed-methods studies, feasibility and pilot studies, implementation science studies, and secondary analyses. Systematic reviews and scoping reviews are included for evidence mapping. Editorials, opinion papers, conference abstracts without sufficient methodological detail, and letters without primary data are excluded.

Information Sources

Searches are conducted across eight electronic bibliographic databases: PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science (Core Collection), CINAHL (Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature), Embase, PsycINFO, ERIC (Education Resources Information Center), and IEEE Xplore. Grey literature searches target WHO reports, UNESCO publications, OECD reports, national nursing organization documents (including the National Association of School Nurses), and government health department websites. Reference lists of included studies and relevant systematic reviews are hand-searched. The search period spans from database inception to January 2025.

Study Selection

Following the removal of duplicates using Rayyan citation management software, two independent reviewers screen all titles and abstracts against the PCC inclusion criteria. Full-text articles are retrieved for all records meeting the inclusion threshold, and the same two reviewers independently assess full-text eligibility. Disagreements are resolved through structured discussion, with arbitration by a third senior reviewer where consensus cannot be reached. Inter-rater agreement is calculated using Cohen's kappa coefficient.

Data Extraction

Data extraction is conducted using a standardized, piloted charting form developed in accordance with JBI scoping review guidance (Peters et al., 2020). The form captures: author(s) and year; country; study design; AI technology type and specification; health domain and clinical condition; school level and country income classification; participant characteristics; outcome measures and key results; reported benefits; reported challenges; ethical concerns; and recommendations made. Extraction is conducted independently by two reviewers, with discrepancies resolved by discussion.

Data Analysis and Synthesis

Data analysis follows the approach recommended by JBI for scoping reviews (Peters et al., 2020; Levac et al., 2010). Quantitative description using descriptive statistics summarizes study characteristics including frequency distributions of AI technology types, health domains, study designs, geographic origins, and publication years. Findings are synthesized narratively across thematic categories corresponding to the review objectives. An evidence map visually represents the density of evidence across the matrix of AI technology types and health domains. Descriptive thematic analysis identifies recurring patterns related to opportunities, barriers, and contextual factors. Expected Outcomes
This scoping review is expected to produce the following outcomes:

Comprehensive Evidence Map: A systematic mapping of the existing literature on AI applications in school health services, including the types of technologies studied, health domains addressed, populations involved, and outcomes reported.

Synthesis of Opportunities: A narrative synthesis of the reported opportunities and benefits of AI in school health, including improved screening accuracy, enhanced mental health support, reduced administrative burden, and increased access equity.

Synthesis of Challenges: A narrative synthesis of the reported challenges, barriers, risks, and ethical concerns associated with AI implementation in school health, including algorithmic bias, data privacy, digital divide, workforce readiness, explainability, legal uncertainty, and governance gaps.

Practice Implications: A comprehensive set of actionable implications for school nursing practice, including recommendations for AI literacy development, governance participation, equitable implementation advocacy, and relationship-centered practice.

Policy Recommendations: Evidence-based policy recommendations for AI governance frameworks, student data privacy protections, equity-focused procurement standards, and liability clarity.

Research Priorities: Identification of critical research gaps and priority directions for future research, including the need for rigorous randomized controlled trials, implementation science studies, cost-effectiveness analyses, and equity-focused evaluations.

title: Meta-analysis of Diagnostic Test Accuracy of Pediatric Sleep Questionnaire and the OSA-18 Questionnaire in the Screening of Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea
description: While the gold standard for the diagnosis of obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) in children is an attended polysomnogram (PSG), it is a resource intensive procedure, costly and with limited availability in many settings. Consequently, several subjective tools have been developed to assist pediatricians in screening children who would benefit from a PSG. One of the most widely used is the Pediatric Sleep Questionnaire (PSQ). OSA-18 is another commonly used questionnaire which is a disease-specific quality-of-life questionnaire. In this meta-analysis we aim to meta-analyze the data on diagnostic accuracy of PSQ and OSA-18 in the screening for OSA.

title: Metagenomic Next-Generation Sequencing Technologies in Respiratory Critical Care: A Living Scoping Review Protocol
description: This living scoping review aims to comprehensively map and describe the use of metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) for diagnosing respiratory infections in critically ill patients. It will examine the sequencing workflows employed, their diagnostic accuracy, and how mNGS findings are integrated into clinical decision-making within intensive care units (ICUs). Following JBI and Cochrane methodologies, the review will systematically identify and synthesise studies that apply mNGS to lower respiratory tract samples from ICU patients, describing technologies used, diagnostic performance, and clinical impact. Updated regularly, the review will provide an evolving overview of mNGS applications in respiratory critical care, highlighting current practices, challenges, and evidence gaps to inform future research and guide the implementation of mNGS in clinical diagnostics.
