title: Grammatical Correction and Morphological Productivity Tasks as Potential Identifiers of Developmental Language Disorder in Spanish-Catalan Bilingual Children: A Pilot Study
description: A critical problem for Catalan-Spanish bilinguals is the lack of assessment tools to conduct valid and accurate oral language evaluations. The purpose of this study was to provide initial pilot data for a new assessment tool in Catalan. We examined the possibility that two novel tasks, a grammatical correction (GramCorr) and morphological productivity (MP; nonword and word subtasks), could differentiate between Catalan-speaking children with and without developmental language disorder (DLD) with good diagnostic accuracy. Twenty-seven school-aged children with DLD (Mage = 9;1 years) and twenty-seven age/sex-matched typically developing (TD) children (Mage = 9;0 years) participated in the study. Group differences and diagnostic accuracy analyses (sensitivity and specificity and likelihood ratios) were conducted. Results showed that the global percentage of correct answers of children with DLD was significantly poorer than that of the TD controls in the two tasks. The preliminary diagnostic accuracy results suggested that the overall test (GramCorr+MP) can be used as an accurate tool to discriminate between children with DLD and children with TD. In addition, the MPnonword subtask on its own seems to provide sufficient information to diagnose DLD. When GramCorr and MPword task are used together, they can serve as tool to rule out a language disorder. Finally, the nature of both tasks, their usefulness for practitioners and future steps in the design of valid tools for the identification of Catalan speaking children with DLD were discussed.

title: Predicting Three-Month Pain and Disability in Frozen Shoulder: Protocol for the Development and Internal Validation of a Clinical Prognostic Model
description:
Frozen shoulder (FS) is a pathological condition affecting the glenohumeral joint and its surrounding soft tissues, leading to severe pain, restricted range of motion (ROM), disability, and a diminished quality of life (1). In particular, patients frequently report severe, drug-resistant pain—both during the day and at night—which is typically exacerbated at end-range or by abrupt movements (2). This is accompanied by multiplanar active and passive ROM limitations, particularly in external rotation with the arm by the side (3). Additionally, compensatory scapular dyskinesia and muscle atrophy of the whole shoulder girdle may be observed, especially in the later stages of the condition (1).
Although FS has historically been recognized as a localized, joint-specific pathology, growing evidence indicates that it is a musculoskeletal epiphenomenon driven by metabolic, inflammatory, and systemic dysregulation, alongside a clear influence from the patient's psychological profile (4). Consequently, the therapeutic paradigm is evolving toward a comprehensive, multi-system approach that integrates sleep hygiene, nutritional strategies, and psychological support (4–6).
The prognosis of FS is often challenging. Although some authors have characterized FS as a self-limiting pathology , current evidence recognises that symptoms can persist for years after onset (7). Specifically, moderate-to-severe ROM limitation, moderate pain, and functional issues have been reported from two to seven years following symptom onset. Furthermore, at a two-year follow-up, one-third of patients with FS remained dissatisfied or very dissatisfied with their rehabilitation pathway (7).
Prognostic research in FS is extensive and focuses on a wide range of outcome measures. For instance, diabetes mellitus, bilateral presentation, and a longer duration of symptoms are strong prognostic factors for poorer outcomes, potentially identifying patients who require early surgical intervention (8); conversely, age below 60 has been linked to a favorable response to non-surgical treatment (9). Notably, more severe baseline pain and functional limitations have been reported as negative predictors for both functional recovery and mobility improvement (10). Furthermore, diabetes, thyroid dysfunction, and autonomic symptoms negatively impact the quality of life of patients suffering from FS (11).
In parallel, psychological factors such as kinesiophobia, catastrophizing, anxiety, depression, and low health-related quality-of-life scores have emerged as significant predictors of persistent pain and disability (12). Finally, higher levels of kinesiophobia and comorbidities are associated with poorer disability and quality-of-life recovery (13), while higher baseline anxiety is negatively associated with functional outcomes at a three-month follow-up (14).
In clinical practice, accurately estimating a patient's prognosis is essential for guiding clinical decision-making. Prognostic prediction models can support this process by integrating multiple patient characteristics to generate individualized risk or recovery predictions. Indeed, prognostic prediction models are algorithms that combine multiple variables to estimate the likelihood of a specific outcome of interest for an individual patient, typically developed using a specific dataset (15). These models can be integrated into clinical decision support systems or presented as (online) calculators that require clinicians to manually input the values for each predictor to obtain the final prognostic estimate (15). Specifically, by utilizing these tools, clinicians can input a priori selected patient information, which the model processes to generate an individualized probability of achieving or not achieving a clinical outcome.
To the best of the authors’ knowledge, within the international literature on shoulder disorders, there is currently only one prognostic model, which assesses which patients will not have repeat shoulder instability after first-time traumatic anterior dislocation (16). However, although prognostic research is increasingly identifying various variables that impact outcomes in patients with FS, no prognostic model has yet been developed for this pathology. Therefore, this study will aim to develop and internally validate a prognostic model for patients suffering from FS.
Having a methodologically robust prognostic model available could allow clinicians to accurately estimate a patient’s prognosis, thereby informing clinical decision-making. Moreover, this tool could improve tailored treatment strategies by identifying different risk gradients for individuals who may require either minimal or more intensive interventions to achieve a positive outcome. Prognostic information is also essential for managing expectations and communicating with patients about their likely clinical trajectory.

METHODS

Study Design and Setting

This study is a retrospective prognostic model development study using data from three prospective cohorts. This study will be reported according to the Transparent Reporting of a multivariable prediction model for Individual Prognosis Or Diagnosis with artificial intelligence (TRIPOD+AI) guidelines (17), which provide harmonised guidance for reporting prediction model studies.

Ethical approval

The dataset used to prepare the present prognostic model will be aggregated from three separate datasets derived from previously published prospective cohort studies (13,14,18). Ethics Committee of University of Molise (Italy) approved all studies (24/2024 on October 02, 2024; 06/2025 on June 19, 2025; 16/2025 on 05 November 2025). All study-related procedures will be performed in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki.

Setting and participants

Adult individuals meeting the eligibility criteria were recruited during their initial specialist consultation for FS across three private physiotherapy practices in Roma, Lecce and Genova (Italy). The recruitment period was from November 2024 to February 2026. All participants were recruited seeking their first physiotherapy consultation for FS and had the same diagnosis supported by the same diagnostic criteria (Figure 1). Moreover, in all centers, during the recruitment process, one expert physiotherapist with more than eight years of clinical practice focused on shoulder disorders screened the participants for inclusion in the study.
All eligible participants were provided with detailed information regarding the research aims and procedures. A comprehensive information letter with dedicated information was provided to any individual who expressed interest. All individuals who met the inclusion criteria and agreed to participate in the study provided written, voluntary informed consent, while individuals who declined to participate were directed to standard rehabilitation.
During the 12-week prospective follow-up period, participants received standardised rehabilitation. Specifically, all patients underwent identical clinical management throughout the study. Therefore, this clinical management was not considered an exposure of interest, but rather an usual physiotherapy care provided to all participants.
All participants attended an educational session featuring standardized content across centers. This session addressed the natural history of FS, predisposing and prognostic factors, management options, home exercise recommendations, and expected recovery timelines. After the initial consultation, participants were referred to a qualified clinician for pharmacological management. Physical therapy rehabilitation commenced within few days of the initial consultation and consisted of joint mobilization, exercise therapy, and stretching, complemented by detailed instructions for a daily 30-minutes home exercise program.
Supervised sessions lasted approximately 45 minutes and were scheduled twice weekly during the first 2 weeks, once weekly for the subsequent 6 weeks, and once every 2 weeks during the final month. In all clinical settings, care was delivered by physiotherapists with over 12 years of experience in shoulder pathologies.
Two hundred and eight-three participants met all inclusion criteria; in particular, 80 participants were recruited for the cohort 1 (13), 120 participants from the cohort 2 (14), and 83 participants from the cohort 3 (18).

Inclusion and exclusion criteria

Participants eligible for this study were adults with a diagnosis of unilateral FS. FS is defined as a restriction of external rotation of the affected shoulder exceeding 50% compared to the contralateral side, along with limitations of less than 25% in at least two additional planes of movement (19). Symptoms were required to be stable or progressively worsening over the previous month, in line with the criteria established by Kelly et al. (2013) (19). Eligible participants were also required to be proficient in Italian and have no contraindications to corticosteroid therapy.
Exclusion criteria encompassed a history of shoulder trauma or fracture within the past year, previous rotator cuff repair or other shoulder surgical procedures within the same timeframe, and recent shoulder dislocations. Individuals with serious, specific shoulder pathologies (such as tumors or infections), as well as those with severe neurological or psychiatric disorders that could potentially interfere with study participation, were also excluded. Additionally, a negative radiographic evaluation for significant glenohumeral osteoarthritis was mandatory; specifically, a grade of 2 or higher on the Kellgren–Lawrence scale (20) was classified as an exclusion criterion to ensure the sample was accurately representative of individuals with FS rather than joint degeneration. Finally, pain elicited or worsened by neck movement and positive Wainner cluster (21) results was applied as further exclusion criteria.

Variables included in the model

Outcomes of interest for the model: Pain and disability were assessed as dependent variables, as they are the major concerns for people suffering from FS.
These dimensions were assessed using the two Shoulder Pain and Disability Index (SPADI) subscores (22). The SPADI is a self-report questionnaire used to assess the severity of shoulder pain and its impact on daily activities, assessing the degree of pain and difficulty experienced by the individual when performing various shoulder-related tasks, such as reaching, lifting, and sleeping (23). The questionnaire consists of 13 items divided into a pain subscale (5 items) and a disability subscale (8 items). For each item, the patient must assign a score ranging from 0 to 10 points, where a higher score indicates a greater level of pain or disability (22). The total score of each subscore of the SPADI is calculated by adding the single-question score and then normalising to 100. This study used the Italian version of SPADI since it showed robust psychometric properties in subjects with FS (24).

Independent predictors included in the model: 

Baseline score for pain and disability (continuous variable). Baseline scores for pain and disability have been identified as prognostic factors across multiple studies (10,13,18) and will be incorporated into our predictive models. Specifically, the baseline pain score will be included in the pain model, whereas the baseline disability score will be included in the disability model.

Age (continuous variable). Age as a predictor of conservative treatment failure has yielded somewhat conflicting results in the literature. Levine et al. (2007) (25) found that younger patients were more likely to fail non-operative management, and Rill et al. (2011) (26) identified age as a strong predictor of progression to surgery. This latter finding was recently supported by Kingston et al. (2018) (27), who demonstrated that younger age was significantly associated with surgical intervention. Ages of 60 or over were a better prognostic factor for non-operative treatment for FS (9). Conversely, in a systematic review, Mertens et al. (2021) (10) concluded that there is Level 2 evidence regarding factors influencing treatment outcomes in patients with FS, indicating that younger age is actually associated with better overall functionality.

Daily pain intensity (continuous variable). Two studies investigated the association between daily pain and outcomes in FS patients. Results revealed that higher initial pain was associated with a worse final disability (10), and those patients with the most severe symptoms at onset carry the worst prognosis (28).

Comorbidities (Yes/no for diabetes and thyroid; dichotomous variable). Various studies found that patients with diabetes had worse results in range of motion and pain recovery than patients without diabetes after conservative treatment (29). Moreover, few studies found an influence of diabetes for lower final functionality after conservative treatment (26,29). Lastly, diabetes is a significant risk factor for undergoing shoulder arthroscopy for the diagnosis of FS (30). Patients with diabetes mellitus would benefit from early surgery (8), as diabetes was a poor prognostic factor for non-operative treatment for FS (9). Presence of diabetes and thyroid disorder at baseline emerged to be a negative prognostic factor for shoulder pain, disability and quality of life in patients with FS (11,13).

Symptoms onset (Two classes: < or >5months). Evidence suggests that duration of symptoms is predictive for change in SPADI after 8 weeks (31), with shorter duration predicting larger improvements in SPADI. In addition, shorter duration of symptoms predicted better final function (26) and successful treatment after a home-based exercise program (7). Lastly, patients who suffer from chronic symptoms would benefit from early surgery (8).
Sex (dichotomous variable). Female sex (specifically women>45 years old) was found as a significant risk factor for undergoing shoulder arthroscopy for the diagnosis of FS (30). 


Statistical analysis

Descriptive statistics will be used to summarise participant characteristics, candidate predictors, and outcome measures. Continuous variables will be reported as means and standard deviations or medians and interquartile ranges, as appropriate according to their distribution, while categorical variables will be summarised using frequencies and percentages. The extent and patterns of missing data will be explored for all candidate predictors and outcomes. Assuming that data are missing at random, missing values in candidate predictors will be handled using multiple imputation by chained equations (MICE) (32). The imputation model will include all candidate predictors and both outcome variables to maximise the plausibility of the MAR assumption. Parameter estimates obtained from analyses across the imputed datasets will be combined using Rubin's rules (33). Participants with missing outcome data will not contribute to the development of the corresponding prognostic model.
Separate multivariable linear regression models will be developed for the two prespecified continuous outcomes: SPADI Pain and SPADI Disability. Continuous predictors will be modelled using restricted cubic splines with three knots (34).
Model performance will be evaluated in terms of discrimination (i.e., area under the curve), calibration (i.e., calibration plot, calibration intercept, and calibration slope), and clinical utility (i.e., decision curve analysis) (35). 
Internal validation will be performed using 500 bootstrap resamples. A uniform shrinkage factor will be derived from the bootstrap calibration slope and applied to all regression coefficients to reduce overfitting. Following coefficient shrinkage, the model intercept will be re-estimated to ensure appropriate calibration of the final model (36). The final optimism-adjusted regression coefficients and model performance measures will be reported. 

Sample size calculation

As this is a retrospective study, the sample size was fixed by the number of eligible participants available in the study database and could not be determined a priori. Therefore, rather than estimating the required sample size, we assessed the maximum complexity of the prognostic models that could be reliably developed with the available data.
The allowable model complexity was estimated using the pmsampsize package in R (https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/pmsampsize/versions/1.1.3/topics/pmsampsize), following the methodology proposed by Riley and colleagues for the development of multivariable prediction models with continuous outcomes (37). This approach determines the maximum number of predictor parameters that can be estimated while minimising the risk of model overfitting and ensuring adequate model performance.
For the SPADI Pain outcome, assuming an anticipated model performance of R2 = 0.20, a mean follow-up score of 20.31, a standard deviation of 16.69, and the available sample size of 283 participants, the analysis indicated that a model containing up to 9 predictor parameters (regression coefficients) could be reliably estimated.
Similarly, for the SPADI Disability outcome, assuming an anticipated model performance of R2 = 0.20, a mean follow-up score of 18.85, a standard deviation of 19.87, and the same available sample size, up to 9 predictor parameters (regression coefficients) could be estimated.

OPEN SCIENCE POLICIES AND CORE OPEN SCIENCE PRACTICES IN MAJOR MEDICAL JOURNALS: DEVELOPMENT OF AN AUTOMATIZED TOOL BASED ON A LLM
description:
Open science policies and core open science practices in major medical journals: development of an automatized tool based on a LLM

GUILLAUME FREYERMUTH / CONSTANT VINATIER / GAUTHIER LE-BARTZ-LYAN / SARAH BUET / PERRINE LUNEL / NICOLAS ROBILLARD / GWENAEL DUMONT / FLORIAN NAUDET / MATHIEU ACHER

BACKGROUND

Monitoring the use and application of Open Science practices is key to fostering Open Science and to understanding barriers and facilitators of open science practices. Monitoring also aids in measuring the impact of open science policies and can serve as a possible intervention to improve transparency and reproducibility. For instance, the Hong Kong principles support the assessment of researchers on the use of Open Science practices. Open Science Monitoring is a key priority for organizations such as the UNESCO [and the G7. The scientific community is also beginning to agree on key indicators to measure. For instance, in biomedicine, a core set of 19 open science practices has been developed to monitor various open science practices such as preregistration, open data, open access, open code, conflict of interest statements etc. 

In recent years, biomedical journals have implemented some policies that promote open science practices. Most notably, the influential International Committee of Medical Journal Editors (ICMJE) made prospective registration a requirement to publish clinical trial results in 2005. In 2018, it required a specific data-sharing statement to be included in each newly submitted paper (and prespecified in study registration). The impact of these policies have been studied previously showing an major influence on trial registration practices, and mixed results regarding actual data sharing. 

Automatized options are being developed to track change within the biomedical literature. It is therefore useful to assess the impact of the various open science policies adopted by biomedical journals using those tools. 

OBJECTIVES
 
This aim of this study, targeting major medical journals, is three-fold:
1. to describe open science policies in these journals, 
2. to develop and validate automatic tools that can be used to monitor key transparency practices 
3. to describe retrospectively changes on open science and transparency practices for articles published in those journals.

METHODS

Selection criteria

We will include in our study a sample of 10 major medical journals. 

Population: We will include research studies published in 2020 or 2021 in journals of interest:
- Annals of internal medicine 
- BioMed Central Medicine 
- The British Medical Journal
- Canadian Medical Association Journal 
- Journal of the American Medical Association 
- JAMA Network Open 
- Lancet
- Nature Medicine 
- Public Library Of Science 

Study design: All types of research articles will be included with a proportional number of 1/RCTs, 2/ meta-analyses and 3/ other research articles. 

Data sources: 
All articles and supplementary materials will be extracted from Pubmed and from the journal website. If an article isn’t open access, academic access will be used to get it. 

Automatized tool

Here we want to develop a tool using machine learning and to explore the feasibility of a tool based on a large language model (LLM) such as Mixtral or llama to extract the presence and absence of open science practices inside. Ideally this tool should be automatized, open source (or failing that, open weights). and used locally to enforce reproducibility. It should be able to identify journal articles (either in XML or pdf format) and all supplementary material (in pdf format) and to extract core Open Science practices. The task of extracting content out of a scholar article with an LLM involves optional innovations to ensure accuracy, robustness, and efficiency, such as embedding of raw data into vector stores, refining the method of prompting the LLM, and employing techniques like retrieval augmented generation (RAG) or fine-tuning.

Creation of the validation database: 

Data collection occurred from February 25th to March 18th 2024, following a standardized approach. For each journal, a stratification about study type was realized to select 10 RCT, 10 meta research and 10 other research articles per journal. To perform article selection, 1/ the algorithm of research from PubMed was used as described in table 1. Then, in each journal/category, we randomly selected 10 articles. As it, the database is composed of 30 articles from each journal with an equal representation of the different type of study designs for a total of 300 articles. In case the required number of articles of a given type wasn’t available in a given journal, the total number of articles was completed by articles with the same study design published in other journals (that were each time from a different journal). This was done by a first group of master 1 students (SB, PL, NR).

Search strategy and article selection process
 
All articles were classified by the publication date, the latest will get the number 1 and the oldest the max. After assigning these numbers, for each journal and type of study, each was given a random number and eligibility of articles will be assessed – for each journal and type of study- using this random number and included if those are in line with our selection criteria (data and code available on the Open Science Framework). As soon as the target number of included articles was reached, the same selection process was applied for the next journal and type of study.

Table 1: research algorithm for each study type:

Each research algorithm was validated according to the PRESS guideline (1) by an information specialist (XCH). 

Description of tools’ performance

Development will use the validation database of 300 papers selected from articles published in the journals of interest during the year 2020-2021 (30 per journal).

Statistical analysis: 

Tool’s performance will be determined by the computation of metrics: sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPC and the F1 score and the plotting of the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC). 
As highlighted in the literature (2), any error may also come from human. For each disagreement, a manual verification of the result by an expert (CV or FN) will be done to determine if the LLM is truly false or not. 

Outcomes to be extracted both for training and validation

- Type of study (Randomized Control Trial, meta-analyses, network meta-analysis, Observational study)
- Pre-registration (Yes/No)
- Data sharing (fully open access, on request, not available)
- Open Access Publishing (Yes/No)
- Code Sharing (Yes/No)
- Publication of results within 1 year of study completion (RCT) (Yes/No)
- Materials sharing (STAP, Protocol) (Yes/No)
- Utilization of reporting guideline (Yes/No) + which reporting guideline is use
- Reporting the existence of a preprint (Yes/No)
- Authors contribution (Yes/No)
- COI statement (Yes/No)
- Reporting ORCID identifiers (Yes/No)
- Funding statement (Yes/No)

Implications 
We aim to develop automated tools to monitor open science practices at major generalist biomedical journals. This work will inform the development of a broader open science observatory of biomedical journals. The leading biomedical journals in this study will hence provide important information about these journals that are considered as trusted sources by the medical community. Last, by tracking the open science practices, we will be able to describe the impact of various ICJME policy changes on selected open science practices (clinical trial data sharing and registration). This project is part of OSIRIS (Open Science to Improve Reproducibility in Science), a European project.

title: BSc Projects 2021-22 - The Prevalence of Exercise Addiction: A New Measurement Tool
description:
Several new behavioural addictions have been proposed in the literature but the degree to which they meet the criteria of an addictive disorder, as defined in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-5), remains equivocal. Exercise behaviours have been widely questioned regarding their potential to adopt addictive attributes (e.g., Freimuth et al., 2011): despite the beneficial effects of regular physical activity, when done in excess, this may be detrimental to physical and psychological wellbeing (Landolfi, 2013). The APA acknowledge developments in the exercise addiction (EA) literature but report a continued lack of peer-reviewed evidence addressing prevalence rates and clarification regarding comorbidity with other disorders – in particular, eating disorders (Trott et al., 2020). As a result, aetiology remains unclear and there is a profound lack of support for the establishment of any diagnostic classification. At the root of this problem is the poor methodology and weak specificity of the existing scales used to measure exercise behaviours and their alignment with addiction criteria. Existing research has categorised people in terms of EA using an a-priori approach with the application of high cut off scores (e.g., Hausenblas & Downs, 2002). However, we cannot accurately take an a priori approach to classification for EA is likely to depend on conditional probabilities such as underlying motivational factors and comorbid disorders (Weinstein & Weinstein, 2014). Not everyone scoring highly on the EAI may necessarily be at risk of an EA due to neglect of this consideration. Consequently, existing measures may lack sensitivity, and poor specificity has the added implication of potentially pathologising recreational behaviours. This is reflected in the variability of prevalence rates reported for EA (Trott et al., 2020). 
The present research aims to create an improved measure of EA (the Exercise Addiction Severity Index, EASI) and to record the prevalence of these behaviours and the frequency with which they occur independently as well as alongside other substance and behavioural addictions, and eating and mood disorders. Moreover, we will also explore whether there is an association between childhood engagement in physical activity and EA later in life to potentially highlight an avenue for longitudinal research within this area in the future.

title: Diagnostic Performance of Circulating Cell-Free DNA 5-Hydroxymethylcytosine Signatures for Hepatocellular Carcinoma: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
description: Rationale for the Study Overview This systematic review and meta-analysis examine the diagnostic accuracy of circulating cell-free DNA 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (cfDNA 5hmC) signatures for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) detection. To our knowledge, this represents the first meta-analysis combining evidence from diagnostic accuracy studies to determine the clinical utility of cfDNA 5hmC profiling for HCC diagnosis and surveillance. Background and Purpose Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the most common form of liver cancer, accounting for approximately 90% of cases. The poor prognosis results primarily from late-stage diagnosis, as current surveillance methods using ultrasound and alpha-fetoprotein show suboptimal performance for early detection. This diagnostic challenge becomes particularly acute in high-risk populations with liver cirrhosis, where clinicians face difficulty distinguishing early HCC from underlying cirrhosis. cfDNA 5hmC signatures constitute a novel class of epigenetic biomarkers with tissue-specific properties. 5-Hydroxymethylcytosine, an intermediate in DNA demethylation pathways, preferentially localizes to transcriptionally active genomic regions and displays cancer-specific alteration patterns. The 5hmC-Seal methodology permits genome-wide profiling of these modifications in plasma samples. Individual studies investigating cfDNA 5hmC signatures for HCC diagnosis have reported area under the curve values exceeding 90%. However, studies differ in methodology, population characteristics, and performance metrics, requiring systematic synthesis for clinical translation. Objectives 1. Evaluate the diagnostic performance of cfDNA 5hmC in distinguishing early-stage HCC from liver cirrhosis 2. Assess diagnostic accuracy of cfDNA 5hmC in differentiating HCC (all stages) from liver cirrhosis 3. Determine overall diagnostic performance of cfDNA 5hmC in differentiating HCC from non-HCC populations 4. Compare the diagnostic utility of cfDNA 5hmC with alpha-fetoprotein across all comparisons Methodology Our methodology follows PRISMA-DTA guidelines for diagnostic test accuracy reviews. We will conduct comprehensive searches of major databases (PubMed, Embase, Web of Science) using structured search strategies combining terms for hepatocellular carcinoma, cell-free DNA, 5-hydroxymethylcytosine, and diagnostic accuracy. Two independent reviewers will screen titles, abstracts, and full-text articles for eligibility, extract data using standardized forms, and assess study quality using QUADAS-2 criteria. The statistical analysis employs bivariate random-effects models to pool sensitivity and specificity estimates, accounting for the correlation between these measures and between-study heterogeneity. We will generate summary receiver operating characteristic curves and calculate pooled diagnostic odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals. Subgroup analyses will explore sources of heterogeneity including study design characteristics, population demographics, and methodological variations. Publication bias assessment will use funnel plots and statistical tests when sufficient studies are available. Expected Outcome: This study will: • Provide pooled diagnostic performance estimates with confidence intervals for clinical decision-making and guideline development • Identify optimal approaches for cfDNA 5hmC testing standardization • Document current evidence limitations and priority areas for future research, including optimal cut-off values and standardization requirements • Deliver evidence-based guidance for incorporating cfDNA 5hmC testing into HCC surveillance programs, particularly for high-risk patients with liver cirrhosis This study will address a significant knowledge gap with a potential for improving patient outcomes through enhanced early detection capabilities in hepatocellular carcinoma.

title: Effectiveness of Multidisciplinary (MDT) Team Activation Models and Algorithms in Collaborative Care for Pediatric Cancer Patients in Hospital
description:
Multidisciplinary Teams (MDTs) have been widely recognized as a critical approach to improving the quality, safety, and overall outcomes of healthcare services, particularly in oncology (Prades et al., 2015; Soukup et al., 2018). However, the implementation of MDTs across hospital settings shows significant variation, particularly regarding team activation mechanisms (Lamb et al., 213; Taylor et al., 2019). Most existing literature focuses on MDTs as collaborative structures or discussion forums, while MDT activation mechanisms as systematic, protocol-driven decisions are rarely studied (Fleissig et al., 2006). In routine practice, MDT activation is often ad hoc, relying heavily on individual clinician experience without the support of standardized algorithms or decision rules. This situation has the potential to lead to inefficiencies, delayed decision-making, fragmented care pathways, and inconsistent adherence to clinical guidelines (Pillay et al., 2016).
Pediatric cancer care, in particular, requires highly coordinated efforts across multiple disciplines (e.g., oncology, surgery, nursing, pharmacy, and psychosocial support) to optimize diagnostic accuracy, reduce treatment delays, and enhance clinical outcomes (Pritchard-Jones et al., 2020). While MDTs or tumor boards are widely recommended in pediatric oncology guidelines, their activation in routine practice remains inconsistent. Many hospitals still rely on ad hoc consultations or rigid, fixed-schedule meetings, which may not align with the dynamic and urgent needs of pediatric patients (Hahlweg et al., 2 and Hong et al., 2014). Trigger-based activation models and clinical algorithms offer a systematic approach to mobilize MDT expertise precisely when clinical, pathway, or digital thresholds are met (Kawamoto et al., 2005; Sutton et al., 2020).
This review will generate evidence to inform the design of a context-adaptive MDT activation model for pediatric cancer care, with explicit relevance to both high-resource and resource-constrained hospital settings.

title: For Reaching Peak Potential Is It Better to Train Athletes for Altitude or Select Athletes from Altitude Natives: A Systematic Review
description:
Review Title and Timescale   
Review Title  
For Reaching Peak Potential Is It Better to Train Athletes for Altitude or Select Athletes from Altitude Natives: A Systematic Review 

Actual Start Date:   
July 21, 2025

Bond University, Gold Coast, Australia

Review Methods   
Rationale:   
Altitude training has been used as early as the 1950s to induce hypobaric hypoxia, a condition that can stimulate physiological adaptations to low-oxygen conditions found in high-altitude environments (Dorelli et al., 2025; Saunders et al., 2009). Exposure to hypoxic conditions puts increased demand on the respiratory and cardiovascular systems, which leads to a cascade of physiological effects that can improve performance capacity (Deng et al., 2025). This cascade of physiological adaptations includes mechanisms such as increased erythropoietin production, enhanced oxygen-carrying capacity, and improved efficiency of oxygen utilization at the muscular level (Saunders et al., 2009). More specifically, it is known that altitude training can change the quantity and quality of hemoglobin, thereby enhancing aerobic work capacity (Chen et al., 2023). Additionally, VO₂max has been shown to improve with altitude acclimatization and training, contributing to greater fatigue resistance and faster recovery (Chen et al., 2023). While elite and tactical athletes travel to altitude to experience these physiological effects, these changes are transient. In contrast, many populations native to high altitudes exhibit these adaptations permanently due to generations of exposure (Bingham & Lee, 2014). Native high-altitude populations possess innate physiological adaptations shaped by generations of life in hypoxic environments (Bingham & Lee, 2014). To compensate for decreased oxygen partial pressure, literature suggests that those native to high altitudes have increased hemoglobin concentrations, optimized oxygen delivery systems, and increased VO2max (Beall et al., 1998; Brutsaert, 2008).   

In both elite/tactical athletes and native highlanders at altitude, there are increases in hemoglobin and VO2max (Beall et al., 1998; Brutsaert, 2008; Chen et al., 2023), both of which are known performance indicators. Elevated hemoglobin increases arterial oxygen content, in turn improving the oxygen delivery to working muscles and higher VO2max expands the ceiling of aerobic energy production (Webb et al., 2022). This leads to an individual with the ability to perform at a high standard. Despite elite/tactical athletes only experiencing transient changes, it common for elite/tactical athletes to go to altitude to stimulate these adaptations, thereby enhancing their performance (Deng et al., 2025). What remains unclear, however, is how these transient adaptations compare to the permanent haematological and metabolic traits of native high-altitude populations.   

There is a gap in the literature of direct comparative analysis between the adaptations in elite and tactical athletes who go to altitude to acclimatize and train compared to those who are native to high altitude. This research is designed to compare these populations and their hematological and metabolic adaptations in comparison to native highlanders. The overall purpose is to synthesize existing literature on these populations and draw observational conclusions with a focus on physiological responses to hypobaric hypoxia and the implications for performance. Specifically, this review aims to determine whether recruiters should prioritize recruiting individuals from high-altitude environments or whether targeted altitude training can effectively develop similar physiological benefits in non-natives.  

Review Questions and Objectives:   
Research Question:    
Can the transient metabolic and haematological adaptations achieved through altitude training in elite or tactical athletes match the permanent physiological traits of native high-altitude individuals?  

Research Objective:   
The aim of this systematic review is to compare the metabolic and haematological profiles of native high-altitude individuals with those of acclimatized elite/tactical athletes, focusing on blood-based markers and VO₂. The purpose is to determine whether transient adaptations from altitude training can match the permanent physiological traits of native high-altitude populations, thereby guiding recruiters in deciding between training lowland athletes or selecting individuals born at altitude.  

Eligibility Criteria:   
Inclusion Criteria  
Articles that target healthy, human elite and/or tactical athletes or high-altitude native populations over the age of 18.   
Articles that contain information regarding high altitude training or high altitude living.  
Articles that assess the physiological impacts of altitude on the cardiovascular system due to hypobaric hypoxia (i.e., natural altitude).   
Hb count, Hb mass, haematocrit, RBC count and volume, plasma volume, WBC, VO2.  
Articles that are original research, full-text, and peer reviewed.  
Articles that published in English or are translatable to English.   
Articles that have been published in the last 20 years.  
Articles that include at least one metabolic and one haematologic measure.   

Exclusion Criteria  
Articles that focus on simulated altitude training. 
Articles that include ergogenic aids, and supplements (other than iron). 
Articles that are unable to be retrieved in full text. 
Articles that include drug/medicinal interventions. 
Articles that involve non-athlete, non-tactical, and/or non-high-altitude native populations. 
Review articles. 
Articles that focus on altitudes below 2,000m. 
Articles that include less than 3 weeks at altitude. 
Articles that do not assess Hb count, Hb mass, haematocrit, RBC count and volume, plasma volume, WBC, VO2. 

Participants / Population:   
Elite and/or tactical athletes.  

Intervention(s)/Exposure:   
Altitude acclimatization/training.  

Comparator(s)/Control(s):  
Native highlanders.  
Metabolic and haematologic measures.  

Context:  
Altitude (1200m+).  

Primary Outcome(s):  
Metabolic and haematologic measures.  
Hb count, Hb mass, haematocrit, RBC count and volume, plasma volume, WBC, and VO2.  

Secondary Outcome(s):   
Performance at sea level following high altitude living/training.  

Information Sources:   
An initial search of 1-2 databases (PubMed and Embase) enabled an analysis of text words contained in the abstract and title and of the index terms. A second comprehensive search was developed using the identified keywords and index terms for each database information source (PubMed, Embase, The Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature [CINAHL], Web of Science). This was completed in consultation with a librarian on August 6th, 2025. This search was divided into five concepts, the first consisting of high-altitude native populations and potential related terms such as “sherpas” or “highlanders”. The second concept consists of elite and tactical athletes and is inclusive of similar terms such as “athlete*” or “tactical athlete”, as well as specific occupations (e.g., “military”). The third concept refers to physiological adaptations and includes terms such as “evolutionary adaptations” and “acclimatization”. The fourth concept includes altitude conditions and utilizes related terms such as “high altitude” and “hypobaric hypoxia”. The fifth concept relates to cardiovascular adaptations and related terms such as “cardiovascular adaptations” and “haemoglobin”.  

Search Strategy:   
Where possible, filters were applied to limit research to human subjects, published in the English language, and published in the last 20 years. Below is an example of the search strategy for PubMed, Embase, CINAHL, and Web of Science.   The Boolean operators “AND” and “OR” were used to structure the query as below, and truncation (*) and phrase searching (“...”) were used to maximise sensitivity and specificity. 

Database

title: Completeness of Reporting in AI Diagnostic Studies for Skin Cancer: A Protocol for a Systematic Review of Adherence to CLAIM, TRIPOD-AI, and STARD 2015 Standards
description: This systematic review evaluates the completeness of reporting in AI diagnostic and classification studies for skin cancer against three established reporting checklists: CLAIM (42 items), TRIPOD-AI (27 items), and STARD 2015 (30 items). The primary outcome is checklist-specific adherence rates. Secondary outcomes include item-level and domain-level adherence, temporal trends in reporting completeness (pre-CLAIM 2010–2019, post-CLAIM/pre-TRIPOD-AI 2020–2024, post-TRIPOD-AI 2025–2026), and correlation between reporting completeness and methodological quality. The review will search PubMed (MEDLINE), Embase, Cochrane CENTRAL, and ClinicalTrials.gov from 1 January 2010 to 30 June 2026. Two reviewers will independently screen, extract data, and assess risk of bias using QUADAS-2. Adherence data will be synthesised descriptively with median and IQR per checklist, stratified by publication period, journal type, impact factor, geographic region, imaging modality, validation design, and public dataset use.

title: Accuracy of inflammatory biomarkers in assessing outcomes in Chagas disease: a scoping review
description: This scoping review aims to map and synthesize the existing literature on inflammatory biomarkers in Chagas disease (CD), focusing on identifying gaps in current knowledge and providing guidelines for future research. The main research questions include: (1) What does the literature reveal about the diagnostic accuracy of inflammatory biomarkers in patients with CD? (2) Which aspects of this area have not yet been sufficiently explored or understood? (3) What recommendations can be made to guide future investigations, with suggestions on priority areas for advancing knowledge in the field? The search strategies will be conducted in the MEDLINE, EMBASE, LILACS, and DITA (Diagnostic Test Accuracy Database) databases, with no restrictions on language or date. Search terms will include descriptors related to "Biomarkers," "Inflammatory Mediators," and "Chagas Disease." The retrieved references will be exported to the systematic review platform Rayyan, where two independent reviewers will screen titles and abstracts, as well as assess full-text eligibility. Studies that meet the inclusion criteria will be incorporated into the review, and any discrepancies between reviewers will be resolved by a third reviewer. Cross-sectional (diagnostic accuracy) and cohort studies will be considered, including individuals with CD in the indeterminate, digestive, cardiac, or mixed forms, of both sexes, regardless of age, and from any healthcare setting.

title: Artificial Intelligence for Detection, Characterisation, and Clinical Decision Support in Bone Metastases on MRI: A Systematic Review
description: Bone metastases are a manifestation of advanced cancer. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is highly sensitive for detecting bone marrow disease, but small or subtle metastases may still be overlooked. Image interpretation of multiple MRI images can be time-consuming. Artificial intelligence has emerged as a promising tool to assist radiologists in overcoming these challenges by improving lesion detection and classification. In this study, we systematically reviewed current research on artificial intelligence applications for identifying bone metastases on magnetic resonance imaging. Existing evidence suggests that these tools may enhance diagnostic accuracy and support clinical decision-making, including improved prediction of treatment response and complications. However, most studies remain limited in terms of generalisability, and further validation is needed before widespread clinical adoption. This work aims to clarify the current landscape and highlight future research priorities in MRI imaging of bone metastasis.

title: Methods of assessing perinatal anxiety (MAP): The acceptability, effectiveness and feasibility of different approaches
description: Background: Mental illness affects 1 in 5 women in pregnancy and after birth with a cost to society of £8.1 billion for every annual cohort of births. Anxiety is one of the most common mental illnesses, affecting around 15% of women, and is associated with increased risk of adverse outcomes for women and their children. Despite this, there is no validated method of screening or assessing anxiety to identify women who need treatment. To be useful, any assessment tool for antenatal anxiety must meet a number of criteria. It must be: (1) acceptable to women; (2) effective at identifying women who require treatment; (3) acceptable and feasible to use in different context of the NHS and other services across the UK; (4) acceptable and easy to use by health professionals. Aims: This study aims to identify the most effective, acceptable and feasible method for assessing anxiety in women during pregnancy and after birth. Methods: This will be achieved through 4 work packages (WP) that compare 4 different tools for assessing anxiety: 2 anxiety-specific measures and 2 mental health measures (GAD, SAAS, CORE-10, Whooley questions) selected on the basis of research and clinical evidence that suggest they may be effective. To ensure relevance to different UK health services the project will be conducted in NHS services in England and Scotland. WP1 will identify which assessment tools are acceptable to women using a purposive sample of 40 pregnant and postpartum women. Cognitive interviews and in-depth qualitative interviews will be used to determine which assessment measures are most acceptable, and obtain women's views and experiences of perinatal anxiety and mental health assessment. WP2 will identify which assessment tool best identifies women who need treatment, as well as the optimal time to assess women during pregnancy. A systematic sample of 1915 women will be recruited in pregnancy and complete assessment tools at 12 weeks, 22 weeks and 31 weeks gestation and 6 weeks postpartum. Effectiveness of measures will be examined in terms of identifying women with poor daily functioning, quality of life, or those who need treatment. Potential confounding factors such as psychological treatment will be controlled for. Diagnostic accuracy will be established using gold standard clinical interviews on a randomly selected subsample of 401 women who score positive or negative for perinatal anxiety. WP3 will determine which assessment tool is acceptable and feasible to use in health services by implementing anxiety assessment in 2 services and evaluating the acceptability and feasibility of use in these services. A theoretically-informed implementation guide will be developed, with targeted versions for maternity, psychological and primary care services to enable wide scale implementation of assessment of perinatal anxiety. WP4 is a study within a project which will examine anxiety during pregnancy and after birth in two regions with a high prevalence of mental health conditions in the general population. This will use data from WP2 to determine the prevalence of perinatal anxiety, key sociodemographic risk factors and need for treatment in these regions. Anticipated impact: This research will identify and implement evidence-based assessment of perinatal anxiety in health services, which is acceptable to women and health professionals. This will help identify women early, which will increase the chances for early intervention to improve maternal and child outcomes. This research was developed through our partnerships with women who have experience of perinatal mental illness, health professionals and service managers. They have identified this as a priority problem and will work with us through the project to ensure its relevance to women and families and the NHS

title: Diagnostic accuracy of artificial intelligence in detecting vertical root fractures: A systematic review and meta-analysis
description:
Vertical root fracture (VRF) is a challenging endodontic complication that frequently results in tooth extraction due to diagnostic difficulty and delayed detection. Conventional periapical radiographs and clinical examination demonstrate limited sensitivity because of anatomical superimposition and subtle fracture lines. Cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) improves visualization but is associated with artifacts, radiation exposure, and interpretation variability.
Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly deep learning and machine learning-based image analysis models, has recently been applied to dental imaging for automated fracture detection. Although numerous experimental and clinical studies report promising outcomes, the actual diagnostic accuracy remains uncertain due to methodological variability, dataset bias, and differences in imaging modalities. Therefore, a systematic synthesis of available evidence is required

title: A MultiModal GENSCORE Assessment for Depression Screening Among Nigerian Pidgin-Speaking Adults: A Protocol Study
description: Depression is a leading cause of disability worldwide, yet its detection in low-resource and linguistically diverse settings remains challenging. Conventional self-report measures, such as the PHQ-9, are widely used but may fail to capture culturally nuanced expressions of depressive symptoms, particularly in Nigerian Pidgin-speaking populations. Advances in digital and artificial intelligence technologies offer opportunities to integrate multimodal data, combining self-report responses with vocal biomarkers such as tone, pitch, and speech rate, to improve diagnostic accuracy. The GENSCORE assessment is a novel, culturally adapted, multi-modal tool designed to address these limitations by leveraging text- and audio-based inputs for depression screening. This randomized controlled trial aims to evaluate the diagnostic performance of GENSCORE against the clinical gold standard (SCID-5-CV) and the PHQ-9, and to determine whether the multimodal approach provides incremental value over traditional self-report methods in a Nigerian community setting.

title: Applications of three-dimensional scanning using mobile devices and artificial intelligence for preoperative planning and follow-up of patients with cleft lip and/or palate: a scoping review
description:
Introduction
Cleft lip and/or palate is one of the most frequent congenital craniofacial malformations and represents a condition of high clinical complexity because of its anatomical, functional, aesthetic and psychosocial impact. Its management requires early assessment, individualised planning and longitudinal follow-up by multidisciplinary teams. Traditionally, morphological assessment has relied on two-dimensional photographs, dental models and direct anthropometric measurements; however, these tools have limitations in accurately capturing the three-dimensional complexity of the oronasal region. In this context, three-dimensional scanning using mobile devices and artificial intelligence tools have emerged as technologies with the potential to improve clinical documentation, preoperative planning, facial analysis, outcome assessment, and the functional and aesthetic follow-up of these patients. Nevertheless, their degree of clinical validation, accuracy, reproducibility and applicability in real-world care settings has not yet been clearly established.
Objective
To map the available evidence on the use of three-dimensional scanning technologies, mobile devices and artificial intelligence in preoperative planning and in the follow-up of clinical, functional and aesthetic outcomes in patients with cleft lip and/or palate.
Methodology
A scoping review will be conducted following the methodology proposed by Arksey and O’Malley and the PRISMA-ScR guidelines. The search will be carried out in PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science and BIREME, including publications from 2010 to April 2026. Studies evaluating the use of three-dimensional scanning through mobile phones, smartphones or mobile devices, with or without associated artificial intelligence tools, for the assessment, preoperative planning or follow-up of patients with cleft lip and/or palate will be included. Records will be managed in Rayyan; three reviewers will independently screen titles, abstracts and full texts, with discrepancies resolved by a fourth reviewer. Data extraction will be performed in Microsoft Excel and will include bibliographic information, methodological design, population characteristics, technology used, type of artificial intelligence, clinical, functional, morphometric, aesthetic and diagnostic-accuracy outcomes, as well as the authors’ limitations and recommendations. The analysis will be descriptive and thematic.
Expected results
This review is expected to identify and organise the available evidence on the use of three-dimensional scanning, mobile devices and artificial intelligence in the assessment, preoperative planning and follow-up of patients with cleft lip and/or palate. The review will describe the technologies used, their clinical applications, the outcomes assessed, the degree of clinical validation, potential advantages and the main technical, methodological and ethical limitations. It is also expected to identify knowledge gaps related to the prospective validation of these tools, the standardisation of capture and analysis protocols, longitudinal outcome follow-up, comparison with reference methods and the applicability of these technologies in resource-limited clinical settings.

title: Protocol for a systematic review and prognostic accuracy meta-analysis of tests and prediction models in first-trimester threatened miscarriage
description:
This project is a systematic review and prognostic accuracy meta-analysis evaluating biochemical, ultrasound, clinical, and multivariable prediction models for women presenting with first-trimester threatened miscarriage and an ultrasound-confirmed viable intrauterine pregnancy. Threatened miscarriage is one of the most common obstetric emergencies worldwide, yet counselling is often based on experience rather than rigorously quantified risk. Over four decades, many individual tests and composite models have been proposed, but their true prognostic performance, risk of bias, and incremental value over routine assessment remain uncertain.
The primary objective is to identify and compare the accuracy of candidate prognostic markers and models for predicting subsequent miscarriage versus ongoing pregnancy or live birth in this high-risk group. We will include prospective or nested cohort studies and high-quality evidence syntheses that report first-trimester biochemical markers (for example, progesterone, hCG, CA-125), ultrasound parameters (such as fetal heart rate, crown–rump length, gestational sac morphology), clinical factors, or multivariable and machine-learning models. The review follows PRISMA 2020 and PRISMA-DTA guidance, and uses CHARMS for model framing, QUADAS-2 for study-level risk of bias, and PROBAST for prediction model appraisal. Where at least four comparable studies report a given threshold, we will use random-effects bivariate or HSROC models to estimate pooled sensitivity, specificity, and summary ROC curves; otherwise, accuracy will be synthesised narratively.
Expected outputs include: (1) a fully documented protocol and data extraction tools; (2) a curated dataset of study-level accuracy estimates and model characteristics; (3) reproducible analysis code for all meta-analyses and figures; and (4) a set of evidence-based recommendations for future large, multicentre, TRIPOD-compliant cohorts and model validation studies. By making these materials openly available on OSF, we aim to increase transparency, facilitate replication and extension of our work, and provide a robust evidentiary foundation for future clinical guidelines and decision-support tools for the millions of women worldwide who experience threatened miscarriage each year.

title: Alignment of Reporting Guidelines for Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare with Governance Principles by the World Health Organization: a Scoping Review
description:
In recent years, the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has been rapidly expanding across various fields, including healthcare. In this sector, AI can enhance the delivery of healthcare services and medical practice, contributing to equity in healthcare access. AI can improve diagnostic accuracy and clinical care, advance health research and drug development, and assist in the implementation of public health interventions such as disease surveillance and health systems management.
In 2021, the World Health Organization (WHO) issued guidance on governance principles to be followed in the development and use of AI within the healthcare sector. In 2024 the World Health Organization issued an update of the previous guidance to cover the specific issues raised by Large Multi-Modal Models. More recently, governance of AI has been addressed by specific legislation in several key jurisdictions, such as the European Union and the US.

AI is subject of active research. For the reporting of research outcomes, a set of reference guidelines is available to the scientific community. Yet, many of the existing reporting guidelines were first written before the WHO’s guidance was issued, raising the question on whether these guidelines call for sufficient detail to address the governance matters raised by the WHO.
This scoping review aims to gather existing literature on reporting guidelines for studies on AI in healthcare. Its objectives are to identify the reporting guidelines currently available to the scientific community and to assess the alignment of these guidelines with the governance principles set by the WHO. Other key legislation may be addressed where relevant.

title: Diagnostic Value of Three-Dimensional Vena Contracta Area in Assessing Mitral Regurgitation Severity: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
description: This systematic review and meta-analysis aims to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of three-dimensional vena contracta area (3D-VCA), assessed by transthoracic or transesophageal echocardiography, in identifying severe mitral regurgitation (MR) in adult patients. 3D-VCA has been proposed as a more direct and geometrically accurate measure of MR severity compared to conventional two-dimensional echocardiographic methods. This review will synthesize evidence from diagnostic accuracy studies comparing 3D-VCA to reference standards such as PISA-derived effective regurgitant orifice area (EROA), regurgitant volume, regurgitant fraction, or two-dimensional vena contracta width. Pooled estimates of sensitivity, specificity, and diagnostic performance will be calculated using a bivariate random-effects model and hierarchical summary receiver operating characteristic (HSROC) analysis. The protocol adheres to PRISMA-DTA guidelines and was registered prior to data extraction.

title: Non-physician performance and interpretation of lung ultrasound for tuberculosis screening and early diagnostic assessment: a scoping review protocol
description: This project is a scoping review protocol that aims to map and summarize the available evidence on the ability of non-physician providers to perform and/or interpret lung ultrasound, or related point-of-care ultrasound approaches, for tuberculosis (TB) screening and early diagnostic assessment. The review focuses on non-physician cadres such as nurses, community health workers, paramedics, clinical officers, medical assistants, trainees, and other frontline providers without formal specialist ultrasound qualifications. It will examine evidence on image acquisition, interpretation, agreement, diagnostic accuracy, feasibility, acceptability, workflow, and implementation, as well as training, supervision, quality assurance, and contextual factors relevant to practice. Particular analytical interest will be given to community, primary care, rural, remote, and other out-of-hospital settings. The review will be conducted using Joanna Briggs Institute methodology for scoping reviews and reported in accordance with PRISMA-ScR guidance. Expected outcomes include a structured map of the existing literature, identification of evidence gaps, and findings that may inform future research, training strategies, and implementation efforts related to task-shifted lung ultrasound for TB in resource-limited settings.

This study employs a quantitative bibliometric approach to objectively present the research hotspots and emerging trends in the global AI-driven mental health landscape (2016–2025), specifically capturing the post-2023 surge in generative AI.
Results: Research output followed an exponential trajectory, exhibiting continuous growth and surpassing 3,000 publications in 2025. The United States and China lead in productivity, with King’s College London as the top contributing institution. The identified research clusters encompass foundational AI methodologies and four main clinical domains: diagnosis (e.g., neuroimaging and stress detection), digital interventions (e.g., AI-driven chatbots and mHealth), targeted conditions (e.g., PTSD, postpartum depression, and military mental health), and suicide prevention. Recent keyword bursts indicate a strategic shift toward diagnostic accuracy, loneliness, and occupational burnout as emerging frontiers since 2023.

title: Evidence for electrocardiographic patterns identifying acute coronary occlusion in non–ST-elevation acute coronary syndromes: A scoping review
description:
Objective: This scoping review will identify and map existing primary studies examining non-ST-elevation electrocardiographic patterns associated with angiographically confirmed acute coronary occlusion in patients with suspected or confirmed non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndromes.
Introduction: Electrocardiographic ST-elevation criteria have limited sensitivity for detecting acute coronary occlusion, and approximately one quarter to one third of NSTEMI patients have completely occluded culprit arteries. Other ECG patterns may improve detection; however, this evidence is fragmented and rarely synthesized. A scoping review is needed to map how these patterns have been defined and evaluated before diagnostic test accuracy synthesis can be undertaken.
Inclusion criteria: Primary empirical studies examining associations between specific non-ST-elevation ECG patterns and angiographically confirmed acute coronary occlusion in patients with suspected or confirmed acute coronary syndromes in acute care settings. Case reports and case series will be excluded from extraction but used for citation tracking.
Methods: The review will follow JBI scoping review methodology and PRISMA-ScR reporting guidelines. Searches of MEDLINE (Ovid), Embase, Scopus, Cochrane Library, and grey literature sources will be conducted. Studies available in English or English translation will be included with no date limits. Two independent reviewers will screen and extract data using Covidence and a pilot-tested extraction tool capturing study design, population characteristics, index test definitions, reference standards, and outcomes. Results will be presented in tabular and narrative form, grouped by ECG pattern.

title: Can conversation analysis distinguish between persons with epilepsy and persons with functional seizures during Video-EEG monitoring without event? A comparative diagnostic accuracy study
description:
Figuring out whether a person presenting with seizures in a medical setting has epileptic or non-epileptic, functional seizures (ES vs FS, respectively) can be difficult, even for seasoned epileptologists. The gold-standard differential diagnostic test for epileptic versus functional events is Video-Encephalographic Monitoring (VEM) whereby a typical event is recorded and a diagnosis is made dependent on whether seizure activity in the brain is identified (epileptic) or not (functional). 

While VEM is the most accurate tool to establish a diagnosis of ES and FS, there are several aspects of VEM which have prompted calls for the development of additional diagnostic means. The issues concerning VEM are, (1) it is very cost- and resource-intensive, (2) it is not available in countries and regions where cost and resources are limiting factors, (3) it requires a highly specialised medical team, (4) in about 59% of patients, a seizure event is recorded within the first 24 hours of VEM, but for a considerable number of patients, events are too infrequent to be captured during VEM (Lobello et al., 2006), (5) for 14-24% of patients, no clear diagnosis can be reached with VEM (Noe & Drazkowski, 2009; Lobello et al., 2006), (6) VEM results may, in fact, introduce diagnostic uncertainty: 17% of patients with functional seizures were found to have interictal epileptic discharges (IEDs), while 12 % of people with epileptic seizures were found never to have IEDs during VEM (Friedman & Hirsch, 2009), (7) VEM is the end-of-the-line diagnostic procedure, and often occurs years after seizure-suppressive medication has first been prescribed. On average, the differential diagnosis of functional seizures is made after five to ten years, with 20% of patients receiving a correct diagnosis of FS after ten years or more (Bahrami et al., 2019; Kerr et al., 2021; Reuber et al., 2002). In this time, 70% of patients may unnecessarily be taking at least one antiseizure drug (Lobello et al., 2009). 

Recent research has attempted to deliver tools which may improve the diagnostic certainty (for an overview, see Rosenkoetter et al., in preparation), especially when VEM remains without captured clinical event. Their applicability in clinical practice is unknown and calibration in diverse clinical settings is required. 

Conversation analysis of the diagnostic interview as a diagnostic tool in the patients of interest has already been investigated in several studies with promising outcomes (Biberon et al., 2020, Cornaggia et al., 2012, Papagno et al., 2017, Reuber et al., 2009, Zinchuk et al., 2021). The analysis of such interviews, however, is currently done "manually" by trained linguists and is therefore laborious and time-consuming. Conducting the interviews, on the other hand, could easily be integrated into the clinical routine. The ease of use, in combination with promising prior research outcomes, begets the question whether technology may provide more efficient analytic tools in order to make the technique useful for clinical practice.

We propose to use and adapt machine learning-based deep neural network models that are pre-trained on huge document collections to detect relevant information from text. To combine the different input modalities in this project, convolutional neural networks (CNNs, Gu et al., 2018) might provide automatic feature extraction and selection. 

Data will be obtained from consenting patients at a tertiary Epilepsy Centre in Germany. First, linguistic features will be extracted from recorded structured interviews. Then, the diagnostic results (sensitivity and specificity) of the automated conversation analysis (ACA; index test) will be compared to the results of VEM with no event recorded during the first day of the patients' stay (VEMnE; reference test). Specifically, we will test whether ACA could be an add-on procedure to increase the diagnostic accuracy of VEM without event capture. Further, for those patients who receive a definitive diagnosis via VEM (with captured event after 2 or more days of VEM), both index tests will be compared against the gold standard.

Patients will also be invited to complete a battery of psychological questionnaires. These and any routinely collected clinical data may be used to develop a predictive model utilising those outcomes in addition to ACA results. Such a predictive model could contribute to the development of a clinical decision rule based on ACA and informative clinical variables. 

Ultimately, if the automated analysis of diagnostic interviews shows promise, its utility as a triage test in secondary and primary care can be investigated, with the goal of eventually reducing the time until correct diagnosis and appropriate referral, especially in people with functional seizures.

title: Image quality control programs and their contribution to reducing diagnostic errors in radiology: A scoping review.
description:
Diagnostic image quality is a critical determinant of accuracy, efficiency, and patient safety in radiology services. High-quality images support the detection, characterization, and monitoring of diseases, whereas inadequate image quality may contribute to diagnostic errors, repeated examinations, unnecessary radiation exposure, increased healthcare costs, and delays in clinical decision-making. Consequently, image quality control programs have become essential components of quality assurance systems, aiming to ensure the consistent performance of imaging equipment, optimize imaging processes, and support reliable diagnostic outcomes.

The objective of this scoping review is to systematically map and synthesize the available scientific evidence regarding image quality control programs implemented in radiology services and their contribution to reducing diagnostic errors. The review will be conducted in accordance with the methodological recommendations of the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) and reported following the PRISMA Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) guidelines.

The study will examine publications from the last ten years that address quality control initiatives in diagnostic imaging and evaluate their impact on image quality and diagnostic performance. The review will seek to identify the types of quality control programs currently employed, their implementation strategies, and the outcomes associated with their use across different radiological settings.

Particular attention will be given to outcomes related to diagnostic accuracy, reduction of image artifacts, decreases in repeat examinations, mitigation of technical errors, and reductions in diagnostic discrepancies. In addition, the review will explore how these programs contribute to broader quality assurance frameworks and compliance with regulatory requirements governing radiology services.

The expected outcome of this study is a comprehensive overview of existing image quality control practices in radiology and the evidence supporting their effectiveness in improving diagnostic performance. By identifying current approaches, reported benefits, and knowledge gaps in the literature, the review aims to provide valuable information for healthcare professionals, radiology departments, researchers, and policymakers seeking to strengthen quality assurance initiatives and enhance patient safety. Furthermore, the findings may support the development and implementation of evidence-based quality control strategies capable of reducing avoidable diagnostic errors and promoting excellence in radiological practice.
