title: Protocol
description:
systematic review protocol

Title
Deep Learning Methods for Breast Cancer Analysis Using MRI: A Systematic Review

Review Question
What deep learning methods have been applied to breast cancer detection, classification, and segmentation using MRI, and what are their reported performance characteristics and limitations?

Eligibility Criteria
The inclusion criteria were:
(1) studies applying deep learning (DL) models for breast cancer diagnosis or classification,
(2) the use of MRI-based imaging as the primary modality,
(3) evaluation using standard metrics (e.g., accuracy, AUC, sensitivity).
(4) availability of experimental design or dataset details.
(5) Written in English.
The exclusion criteria included:
(1) studies relying solely on machine learning (ML) without explicit comparison to or integration with DL models.
(2) imaging modalities other than MRI,
(3) papers lacking full methodological or evaluation details.
(4) studies focusing on other cancer types.
(5) Conference papers.

Information Sources
PubMed, Google Scholar, Web of Science

Search Strategy
The search was conducted using explicit Boolean strings for each database syntax: (“breast cancer” OR “breast tumour”) AND (“MRI” OR “magnetic resonance imaging”) AND (“deep learning” OR “convolutional neural network” OR “CNN” OR “YOLO”) AND (“classification” OR “segmentation” OR “detection”).

Study Selection
Titles/abstracts screened → full-text review → inclusion.
Following PRISMA 2020 framework to ensure reproducibility, transparency, and methodological rigor in the identification, screening, and study selection.

Data Extraction
MRI modality, metrics.

Risk of Bias / Quality Assessment
Qualitative methodological assessment (dataset size, validation strategy).
The reliability of the included studies evaluated based on different standards: Data integrity: where verified ground truth was met by utilizing trusted publicly available datasets (e.g., Duke, QIN-Breast, TCGA-BRCA). Imbalance Handling: where a key risk of bias in BC detection is the prevalence of imbalanced data, here specific techniques like balanced patch sampling were used to mitigate this effect. Clinical Transparency: due to the black box nature of DL models which could be considered as a limitation, studies combined XAI or heatmaps visualization to provide higher clinical utility.
Most studies showed solid methodological design, especially those utilized large datasets or multi-modal inputs of MRIs, however some sources of bias couldn’t be exempted including lack of external confidential validation and limited dataset sizes.

Data Synthesis
The review synthesized findings from 8 studies focusing on advanced DL architectures for breast MRI. Among the reviewed studies, hybrid and multi-modal models consistently outperformed single-modal, and YOLO-based detectors demonstrated higher real-time localization abilities. While diagnostic accuracy shown to remain above 90%, the evidence base remains geographically and institutionally narrow due to many reasons.
In terms of addressed challenges for the transition of these models into clinical routines, most studies relied on limited set of publicly available datasets (e.g. Duke, QIN Breast), suggesting that while the architecture is good, the evidence base still needed and validation is still required for clinical standards. Moreover, the high computational costs remain as a barrier to adopting real-world deployment, which raises the need for something like a lightweight model that can be integrated into existing radiology workstations. Furthermore, the transparency issue in AI-Assisted decision-making tools needs a collaborative effort to utilize high quality, annotated, and diverse MRI data to ensure generalizability and validated frameworks.
In conclusion, DL is showing great promise for transforming breast MRI analysis from early detection and segmentation to personalized treatment planning. The combination of data diversity, explainable models, and clinical settings will shape the next era of computer-aided BC diagnosis, ultimately reduce human tedious workload and improve patient outcomes, while considering the limitations and challenges addressed previously.

Timeline
Review conducted between [September 2025 – January 2026].

title: POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND FOR UNDIFFERENTIATED AND MUSCULOSKELETAL PRESENTATIONS IN UK PRIMARY CARE: A SCOPING REVIEW PROTOCOL
description:
Background:
Point-of-care ultrasound (PoCUS) is increasingly used internationally yet remains emergent in UK primary care. While momentum is growing, variation in application and infrastructure persists. Undifferentiated and musculoskeletal (MSK) symptoms, common and diagnostically complex in general practice, may particularly benefit from PoCUS. International evidence suggests PoCUS improves diagnostic accuracy, reduces referrals to specialist care and enhances patient satisfaction. However, UK-specific evidence on PoCUS use, clinician training, governance, and implementation is sparse. With national priorities shifting towards community-based, technology-enabled care, understanding current PoCUS use is increasingly important.

Aim:
This scoping review aims to systematically map the current use of PoCUS in UK primary care for undifferentiated and MSK presentations, identifying clinical applications, user profiles, implementation contexts, and gaps in the literature.

Design and Setting:
A scoping review of peer-reviewed and grey literature pertaining to UK primary and community care settings, including general practice, urgent care, community diagnostic hubs, and related contexts.

Method:
Following the Joanna Briggs Institute framework and PRISMA-ScR guidelines, comprehensive searches will be conducted across MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, Web of Science, and relevant grey literature sources. Eligible studies include those involving healthcare professionals using PoCUS in adult UK primary care. Data will be charted, synthesised descriptively and thematically, and findings presented narratively with visual mapping.

Expected outcomes:
This review will provide a comprehensive overview of PoCUS use in UK primary care, highlighting how and where it is applied, by whom and to what effect. The findings will offer practical insights to support implementation and shape future research and service development.

title: A protocol for a systematic review and meta-analysis of the diagnostic accuracy of pulse pressure variations (PPV), stroke volume variation (SVV) and pleth variability index (PVI) for prediction of fluid responsiveness in anesthetized and mechanically ventilated dogs
description:
Background
Intravenous fluid resuscitation plays a vital role for hemodynamic optimization both in the surgical setting and in the intensive care unit. It's important to note that both hypovolemia (insufficient fluid volume) and hypervolemia (excess fluid volume) can have negative consequences. Hypovolemia is associated with multiorgan failure, while hypervolemia can lead to acute renal injury.
Failure to achieve hemodynamic optimization has been linked to increased mortality rates in people with conditions such as sepsis and acute respiratory distress syndrome, as well as in dogs hospitalized in intensive care units. Therefore, it's crucial to assess and optimize fluid balance in critically ill patients.
Recent research indicates that dynamic variables such as SVV, PPV and PVI may have higher predictive capabilities for assessing fluid responsiveness compared to static variables such as central venous pressure (CVP). In the recent time, numerous studies have investigated the diagnostic accuracy of these variables in both clinical settings and experimental canine models.

Target condition being diagnosed.
According to Frank-Starling's law, as preload increases, the stroke volume of the left ventricle also increases (ascending limb of the end-diastolic volume vs stroke volume curve) until it reaches a point of maximum myocardial stretch (flattening of the curve). Fluid responsiveness typically refers to a 15% or greater increase in cardiac output following the administration of a fluid bolus to increase cardiac preload. Patients who exhibit an increase in cardiac output after receiving fluid bolus are categorized as fluid responsive, indicating that their hearts are operating on the ascending limb of the Frank-Starling curve. Conversely, patients who do not experience a rise in cardiac output following fluid administration are considered fluid unresponsive, suggesting that their hearts are functioning on the flat portion of the curve. Administering additional fluid bolus to these patients may lead to tissue edema and hypoxia without a corresponding increase in stroke volume. Hence, accurately predicting fluid responsiveness is crucial for distinguishing between patients who will benefit from fluid administration and those who will not.
Index tests
SVV, PPV, and PVI are dynamic hemodynamic parameters that have demonstrated utility in predicting fluid responsiveness in mechanically ventilated patients. The rationale is that, during positive pressure ventilation, insufflation decreases preload of the right ventricle. When transmitted to the left side, this induces a decrease in preload of the left ventricle. If left ventricular stroke volume changes in response to cyclic positive pressure ventilation, this indicates that both ventricles are preload dependent. Mechanical ventilation can be used as a provocative test to challenge the slope of the Frank–Starling curve at the bedside. 
Clinical pathway Assessing fluid responsiveness in mechanically ventilated dogs, whether in surgical settings or intensive care units, is essential for optimizing hemodynamics. Overly aggressive fluid administration has been associated with adverse outcomes in humans, especially in cases of acute kidney injury and acute respiratory distress syndrome. Likewise, studies have shown a correlation between fluid overload and in-hospital mortality in hospitalized dogs. Thus, utilizing tools to assess fluid responsiveness is critical for informed clinical management.

Prior tests
Role of index tests
Assessing PPV can be routinely conducted using readily available equipment and at a relatively low cost. It only necessitates the placement of an arterial catheter and a monitor capable of capturing a graphic record of invasive blood pressure. Moreover, PVI represents a dynamic variable that can be acquired non-invasively, automatically, and continuously, enabling the measurement of respiratory variations in the pulse oximeter waveform amplitude. On the contrary, SVV can be estimated by echocardiography or by more complex equipment (e.g. PiCCO). All these tools have proven to be useful for predicting response to fluids and optimizing hemodynamic management in human and veterinary patients. Employing these tests would facilitate the guidance of fluid therapy by predicting the fluid responsiveness status, thereby preventing the administration of fluid boluses to non-responsive patients.

Alternative tests
Historically, central venous pressure has been a common method for predicting fluid responsiveness. Its assessment involves placing a central vascular access, often in the external jugular vein in dogs. However, multiple studies, both in human and veterinary medicine, have highlighted the superiority of dynamic variables over central venous pressure in predicting fluid responsiveness. 

Rationale
There is a need for a reliable and accurate marker to predict fluid responsiveness in in anesthetized and mechanically ventilated dogs. Several studies have investigated the predictive abilities of PPV, PVI and SVV in various clinical and experimental scenarios under different conditions (e.g. different hemodynamic status, different tidal volumes). However, comprehensive systematic reviews and meta-analyses of these studies are currently lacking.

title: Prognostic value of procalcitonin for bacteremia in pediatric oncologic febrile neutropenia in a Peruvian population
description: This project evaluates the prognostic value of serum procalcitonin measured at hospital admission for the detection of bacteremia in pediatric oncology patients presenting with febrile neutropenia. Using a diagnostic test design nested within a retrospective cohort, the study analyzes the first episode of febrile neutropenia in hospitalized children with cancer between 2021 and 2025 at a specialized referral center in Peru. Clinical characteristics, admission procalcitonin levels, and blood culture results obtained within the first 48 hours are assessed. Diagnostic accuracy measures, including ROC curve analysis, sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, and likelihood ratios, are used to determine the optimal procalcitonin cutoff. This project aims to generate local evidence to improve risk stratification and support timely clinical decision-making in pediatric febrile neutropenia.

title: Impacts of Symptom Checker Apps and Similar Tools on Health Care Professionals in General Practice – A Scoping Review
description:
Introduction 
Patients evaluating symptoms and deducing the necessity and urgency of seeing a physician is a core moment in medical care. A novelty in this process is the plethora of artificial intelligence-based or algorithm-based tools such as symptom checker apps (SCA) that are spreading on the market. They might have the most immediate affect on emergency care and primary care as those parts of health services that are directly accessible for patients. To date, it remains unclear, how SCA and similar tools are transforming working worlds of health care professionals, which work-related psychosocial demands and resources (Bakker et al. 2003) are connected to this transformation and how this is related to perceived stress for health care professionals (GDA 2014). 

Objectives 
This scoping review aims to systematically explore the existing knowledge on the impacts of symptom checkers or similar services on health care professionals in general practice and to identify gaps in knowledge. The following question was formulated: What is known from the literature about the impact of SCA and similar tools on health care professionals in general practice, especially with regards to work content and work organization, professional-patient-interaction/relationship, their professional self-image, job satisfaction, and perceived stress?

Inclusion criteria 
Articles concerning the impacts of SCA and similar tools on health care professionals in general practice will be included. We will follow the PCC scheme (population – concept – context) (Peters et al. 2015) to define inclusion and exclusion criteria. 
Population: The relevant population of our scoping review is health care professionals, not patients, without focus on specific countries. 
Concept: We will apply “impact of symptom checkers and similar tools” as relevant concept. We will include studies that focus on any artificial intelligence-based or algorithm-based SCA or similar services and tools offering self-diagnosis/pre-diagnosis that were designed for (potential) patients. We will exclude all health apps/services that do not provide patients’ self-diagnosis such as diagnostics apps for clinicians, nurses and veterinary surgeons; diagnostics apps with scan-technology or sensors; non diagnostic m-health applications (e.g. symptom monitoring, self-management of conditions, disease-management, medical decision making, telemedicine, medical information and coaching; motivation, fitness). 
Impacts will not be restricted to but can include work content/work, organization/service use, job satisfaction of health care professionals, perceived stress of health care professionals, professional–patient relationship and communication, professional self-image. We will exclude studies e.g. regarding diagnostic accuracy or accuracy of disposition, costs and cost-effectiveness, clinical effectiveness, safety, or patients’ usage of new technologies.
Context: We will focus on general practice as relevant context. 
We will include empirical studies, reviews and publications that discuss the topic in general as well as discussion papers, editorials, book chapters etc. To be included in the scoping review, the publication should be published 2000-2021, should be in English, German, French, Turkish or Russian language, and the full text paper should be obtainable. 


Methods 
The proposed scoping review will be conducted in accordance with the JBI methodology for scoping reviews (Peters et al. 2015). As we expect limited research with regards to our specific research interest, we have conceptualized the search strategy rather open. The following databases will be searched as they showed to be the most promising after preliminary testing: PubMed (Medline) and CINAHL. Search strings consisting of search terms and MeSH terms will be built and the titles and abstracts in the respective databases will be searched accordingly. Titles and abstracts will be screened against the background of the inclusion criteria. The reference lists of sources included will be screened to identify additional literature. To ensure quality control, the whole process will be conducted and constantly discussed by two independent reviewers. Duplicates will be removed in the literature management programme Citavi and the software Rayyan will be used to screen the sources. Key information of the data will be charted and managed in Microsoft Excel and results will be synthesized in text, tables, and graphics. 

Conflict of Interest
The authors declare that there is no conflict of interest.

title: Efficacy of Primary Care Training Programs in Enhancing the Detection, Knowledge, and Referral Pathways of Paediatric Anxiety and Depressive Disorders: A scoping review
description:
This scoping review aims to examine the availability and effectiveness of training programs designed to support general practitioners (GPs) in the detection and management of anxiety and depressive disorders in children and adolescents. These conditions are highly prevalent and often emerge early in life, yet remain substantially underdiagnosed in primary care settings. Given that GPs are typically the first point of contact for young people experiencing mental health difficulties, their ability to recognise symptoms, initiate care, and facilitate appropriate referrals is critical to improving outcomes.
A range of educational interventions has been developed to enhance GP knowledge, diagnostic confidence, and clinical practice in paediatric mental health. However, existing evidence regarding their effectiveness is mixed, with uncertainty surrounding their impact on diagnostic accuracy, referral pathways, and patient outcomes. Additionally, broader systemic factors (such as time constraints, service availability, and referral infrastructure) may influence the translation of training into practice.
This review will map the types of training interventions currently available, synthesise evidence on their outcomes, and identify gaps in the literature. The findings will contribute to a clearer understanding of how GP training can support early identification and management of paediatric anxiety and depression, and will inform future research, policy, and intervention development in primary care mental health.

title: ⁠Effect of the use of Artificial Intelligence tools on the diagnostic accuracy of medical students during clinical rotations: A scoping review.
description:
Introduction: Medical education is at an inflection point due to the rapid technological evolution, marked by the emergence of Artificial Intelligence (AI). Tools such as Machine Learning and Large Language Models (LLMs) are being integrated into the medical and educational fields, offering promising applications such as virtual patient simulation, the creation of personalized learning platforms, and support for clinical decision-making. However, despite the great interest and potential of AI, its integration into the medical curriculum is still early and fragmented. There is a need for rigorous scientific literature that specifically evaluates the impact of using these tools on the clinical judgment and diagnostic accuracy of medical students during their clinical rotations. Therefore, conducting a scoping review is justified to synthesize the available evidence, identify knowledge gaps, and propose strategies for optimal AI integration into medical training.


Methodology: A scoping review will be conducted following the guidelines of the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) and the PRISMA Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR). The search will be performed in key electronic databases such as PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Bireme, complemented by a review of gray literature (government reports, theses). Search terms will be developed using controlled vocabulary (MeSH, DeCS) and related keywords, focusing on the intersection of "Artificial Intelligence", "Diagnostic Accuracy", and "Medical Students in Clinical Rotations". Scientific articles, reviews, and technical documents in Spanish, English, and Portuguese, published between January 2015 and November 2025, will be included. The study selection process will be managed with Rayyan software and will involve title and abstract screening, followed by full-text review by two independent reviewers, with a third for conflict resolution. Data extraction will focus on bibliographic information, study objectives, methodological design, population, the type of AI used, and the documented effects on diagnostic accuracy.


Expected Results: This scoping review is expected to provide a comprehensive overview of the current evidence, allowing for: Identification of the specific types of AI tools that have been used for educational purposes in medical students during clinical rotations. Analysis of the positive and negative effects of AI use on students' diagnostic accuracy, differentiating the clinical areas of greatest application, as well as examination of the ethical and pedagogical implications associated with incorporating AI into clinical training settings and proposal of a framework for integrating artificial intelligence into medical education that optimizes its use as a learning resource while minimizing its potential adverse effects. The results of this research will serve as a fundamental guide for trainees, educators, healthcare professionals, and educational policy makers, facilitating informed decision-making regarding the implementation of AI in the training of future physicians.

Exclusions: case reports and case series without control group,
in silico studies, purely analytical validation studies without
clinical cohort, canine olfaction studies (narrative discussion only),
studies on biological matrices other than urine (breath, sweat, tissue
headspace), editorials, letters, conference abstracts (unless full data
subsequently published in peer-reviewed article), reviews, non-human
studies.

OUTCOMES
Primary: sensitivity and specificity per study, with reconstructible
2×2 contingency table (TP, FP, TN, FN).
Secondary: AUC, positive and negative predictive values, diagnostic
odds ratio, positive and negative likelihood ratios, ROC curves when
available.
Studies without reconstructible 2×2 table: authors will be contacted
(initial request at day 0, follow-up at day 14, cutoff at day 21,
fully documented). If data cannot be obtained, studies will be
included in narrative synthesis only and excluded from quantitative
meta-analysis.

PRE-SPECIFIED ANALYSES
- Bivariate meta-analysis (Reitsma model) stratified by clinical
 context (primary detection / recurrence surveillance / screening).
 Feasibility threshold: n ≥ 4 studies per stratum. Narrative
 synthesis otherwise.
- Overall pooled estimate across all clinical contexts: reported
 for descriptive purposes only, explicitly framed as an upper bound
 of interpretability and not as a clinically generalizable
 performance estimator.
- Subgroup analyses (if corpus permits): by analytical technology
 (GC-MS vs eNose vs other), by tumor stage (NMIBC vs MIBC), by
 grade (low vs high), by presence/absence of ML classifier.
- Sensitivity analyses: exclusion of QUADAS-2 overall high risk of
 bias studies; exclusion of PROBAST high risk studies on Analysis
 domain for ML studies.
- Meta-regression on covariates: publication year, analytical
 technology, disease prevalence, sample size (if n ≥ 10 studies
 per model).
- Heterogeneity assessment: I², τ², prediction intervals.
- Publication bias: Deeks' test (DTA-specific), funnel plot of
 diagnostic odds ratios.

TEMPORAL AND LANGUAGE FRAME
No lower date limit (young field, early studies to be captured).
Search cutoff: to be fixed at OSF deposit.
Languages: English and French; other languages assessed case by case
subject to translation feasibility.
Peer-reviewed publications only. Preprints excluded from main corpus
but flagged to identify studies in pipeline (for discussion).

METHODOLOGICAL QUALITY ASSESSMENT
QUADAS-2 for all included studies.
PROBAST additionally applied to studies with ML component
(PROBAST-AI to be considered depending on publication status at time
of assessment).
Dual independent assessment for screening (title/abstract and
full-text), data extraction, and risk of bias assessment.
Disagreements resolved by consensus or third reviewer arbitration.

title: Accuracy of Intraoperative Surgical Margin Assessment Techniques in Veterinary Oncology
description:
Accurate determination of surgical margin status is fundamental for detecting residual microscopic residual cancer in patients, predicting clinical outcomes, and optimizing treatment planning. Postoperative histopathology following surgical tumor resection is considered the gold standard for margin evaluation; however, this process typically takes one or two weeks to obtain results and only a limited sample of the surgical margins are assessed. Consequently, this delay results in a missed opportunity to evaluate surgical margins in real time and to utilize that information for immediate intraoperative decision-making, which could improve patient outcomes. Several techniques are available for intraoperative surgical margin assessment, each with different levels of accuracy, including frozen tissue section biopsy, imprint cytology margin, near-infrared fluorescence imaging, and optical coherence tomography (OCT) which has the potential to guide surgical-decision making in real-time.

This review aims to compare the diagnostic accuracy of intraoperative surgical margin evaluation techniques as individual studies focus on the reporting of accuracy of one technique in comparison to histopathology. Only studies on canine cutaneous or subcutaneous tumors will be included in the review. 
The primary outcome of the review is comparison of diagnostic accuracy for detection of positive surgical margins in cutaneous and subcutaneous tumors across techniques.

title: Serum PSA and Urinary Biomarkers in the Diagnosis of Clinically Significant Prostate Cancer: A Systematic Scoping Review
description:
Prostate cancer remains one of the most commonly diagnosed malignancies among men worldwide. While prostate-specific antigen (PSA) has been the cornerstone of prostate cancer screening for decades, its limitations in specificity and ability to distinguish clinically significant from indolent disease have prompted extensive research into novel biomarkers.
Clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa) is generally defined as disease with Grade Group ≥2 (Gleason score ≥7) and/or tumor volume criteria that warrant treatment, distinguishing it from indolent disease that may be suitable for active surveillance. The ability to accurately identify csPCa is crucial for reducing overdiagnosis and overtreatment while ensuring timely intervention for aggressive disease.
Numerous serum PSA derivatives (PSA density, PSA velocity, free/total PSA ratio, isoforms) and urinary biomarkers (PCA3, SelectMDx, ExoDx, TMPRSS2:ERG fusion, Mi-Prostate Score) have been developed and evaluated. However, the landscape of available biomarkers is complex and rapidly evolving, with varying levels of evidence supporting their clinical utility.
A scoping review is particularly appropriate for this topic because it will:
• Map the breadth of available biomarkers and their diagnostic performance characteristics
• Identify the range of study designs and methodological approaches used in biomarker evaluation
• Highlight gaps in the current evidence base
• Inform future systematic reviews and meta-analyses focused on specific biomarkers
• Provide clinicians and researchers with a comprehensive overview of the current state of biomarker research in csPCa diagnosis

Primary Objective
To systematically map and describe the evidence on serum PSA-based tests and urinary biomarkers for the diagnosis of clinically significant prostate cancer.
Secondary Objectives
1. To identify and categorize the types of serum PSA derivatives and urinary biomarkers studied for csPCa diagnosis
2. To describe the study designs, settings, and populations in which these biomarkers have been evaluated
3. To summarize the definitions of clinically significant prostate cancer used across studies
4. To map the diagnostic performance metrics reported for each biomarker category
5. To identify knowledge gaps and areas requiring further research
Review Questions
1. What serum PSA-based tests and urinary biomarkers have been investigated for diagnosing clinically significant prostate cancer?
2. What are the characteristics of studies evaluating these biomarkers (design, setting, population, sample size)?
3. How is clinically significant prostate cancer defined across different studies?
4. What diagnostic accuracy metrics are reported for these biomarkers?
5. What are the gaps in the current evidence base regarding biomarker evaluation for csPCa?

title: The Chinese Postpartum Depression Screening Tool: Development and Psychometric Testing
description: The primary aim of the empirical work reported within this project is to develop a screening tool with items designed on Chinese-featured risk factors and items adapted from the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) that will be useful in the early detection of Postpartum depression (PPD)in the Chinese Population. An exploration of previous and contemporary approaches to PPD detection, particularly of the 10-item EPDS, and the foundation as to why the application of a screening tool with Chinese characteristic and featured risk factors for PPD symptoms might be an important contribution to healthcare practice in China are provided. The role of traditional cultures and customs of postpartum practice in the Chinese population is introduced as a context for understanding the complexities and approaches to etiologies and early identification of PPD in the Chinese population. A range of empirically based studies applied to the etiology and associated risk factors for PPD are reviewed, illustrative of the prominence of PPD screening tools within clinical practice. A 20-item self-reported scale and extensive pilot interviews will be carried out on pregnant women in China using the SCID-5 CV. The score of Chinese Postpartum Depression Scale will be compared with the SCID-5 CV of depression to determine the validation of scale in the identification of PPD samples, and additionally, to demonstrate satisfactory sensitivity and specificity, as well as, a sensitivity to change in the severity of depression over time.

title: DEEP LEARNING FOR AUTOMATED DETECTION AND CLASSIFICATION OF TEMPOROMANDIBULAR JOINT DISORDERS: A SCOPING REVIEW
description:
Title: Deep Learning for Automated Detection and Classification of Temporomandibular Joint Disorders: A Scoping Review

Temporomandibular Joint Disorders (TMDs) are a significant clinical challenge associated with pain, functional impairment, and reduced quality of life. Traditional diagnostic approaches—such as manual interpretation of MRI, CBCT, CT, or panoramic images—can be time-consuming, subjective, and affected by inter-observer variability. With recent advancements in artificial intelligence (AI), particularly deep learning (DL) techniques, automated detection and classification of TMDs has emerged as a promising solution to enhance diagnostic accuracy and efficiency.

This scoping review systematically maps current evidence on deep learning applications for diagnosing TMDs, including anterior disc displacement (ADD), osteoarthritis, condylar degeneration, and degenerative joint disease. Using PRISMA-ScR guidelines, a comprehensive search across PubMed, ScienceDirect, IEEE Xplore, Google Scholar, and Wiley identified 15 eligible studies published between 2015 and 2025.

Across these studies, models such as Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), U-Net, ResNet, VGG16, MobileNetV2, YOLO, and ensemble architectures demonstrated high diagnostic performance—achieving accuracy levels up to 99%, sensitivity up to 98%, and significant improvements in segmentation precision. Findings indicate that deep learning can reduce diagnostic time by up to 50%, standardize interpretation, and serve as an effective decision-support tool for clinicians.

Despite promising results, challenges remain related to dataset diversity, external validation, reproducibility, and clinical integration. Future research should focus on multi-center datasets, multimodal learning, standardized benchmarking, explainability methods such as Grad-CAM, and ethical frameworks for AI deployment in healthcare.

This review highlights the potential of deep learning to transform TMD diagnostics, contributing to faster, more accurate, and more consistent radiologic evaluation, ultimately improving clinical outcomes for patients.

title: A Virtual Reality setup for the combined assessment of behavioral and psychophysiological cue-reactivity in gambling disorder
description:
Healthy participants show an increased tendency to discount delayed monetary rewards (temporal discounting) in the presence of appetitive pavlovian stimuli (Kim & Zauberman, 2013; Wilson & Daly, 2004), which is seen as an indicator of impulsivity. Similarly, pathological gamblers show increased discounting of delayed monetary rewards when addiction related cues are present (Dixon, Jacobs, Sanders, & Carr, 2006; Miedl, Büchel, & Peters, 2014). The conditioned reactivity to addiction related cues is believed to be one of the main reasons addictions are maintained (Carter & Tiffany, 1999). The related incentive sensitization theory (Berridge & Robinson, 2016) postulates that brain regions mediating motivation and incentive value become over sensitized to stimuli predicting the occurrence of the addictive behavior or substance and thereby creating appetitive motivation. In addition to heightened impulsivity when faced with addiction related stimuli pathological gamblers show deficits in goal-directed learning and increased habit-like behavioral patterns, indicating compulsivity (Wyckmans et al., 2019). Elucidating the mechanism behind these abnormal behaviors and how they are influenced by addiction related cues may play a crucial role in preventing cue induced relapse as well as helping to increase diagnostic accuracy and treatment (Robbins, Gillan, Smith, Wit, & Ersche, 2012).
Therefore, the aim of this study is to explore addiction related cue reactivity on a behavioral, physiological and subjective level in pathological and frequent gamblers. Traditionally studies aiming to do so either employed field studies (Dixon et al., 2006) or simple picture stimuli (Miedl et al., 2014). To overcome the practical limitations of field studies and the ecological limitations of pictures we created a virtual reality (VR) application that enables us to present gambling related and neutral environments with a high ecological validity. Within these environments’ tasks assessing impulsivity and the balance between goal-directed and habitual learning are presented (behavioral cue-reactivity). Impulsivity will be probed using the Delay Discounting task (DD) (Mazur, 1987). Participants make repeated choices between an immediate monetary reward and a larger but delayed monetary reward. The balance between goal-directed and habitual learning will be probed using the Two-Step task (TS) (Daw, Gershman, Seymour, Dayan, & Dolan, 2011; Kool, Cushman, & Gershman, 2016), which is a multistage decision-making task. Since the study can take place within our lab, we are able to record physiological measures such as skin conductance and heart rate (physiological cue reactivity) while presenting highly controllable realistic gambling stimuli. Subjective cue reactivity is measured via subjective ratings.

title: Automated Detection and Classification of Oral Lesions Using Deep Learning: A Scoping review and Meta-analysis
description:
Introduction: Some oral diseases are a common and often serious health problem worldwide. Especially, malignant or potentially malignant lesions have to be detected and diagnosed very early for their effective therapy. In recent years, deep learning has emerged as a powerful tool for automated detection and classification of oral lesions. This research, by conducting a scoping review and a meta-analysis, aims to provide an overview of the progress and achievements in the field of automated detection and classification of oral lesions using deep learning.
Methods: A scoping review methodology was used to identify relevant studies published in the last five years (2018-2023). A comprehensive search was conducted using several electronic databases, including PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus. The search keywords included "oral lesions", "deep learning", "neural networks", "convolutional neural networks", "machine learning", "artificial intelligence", and "automated diagnosis". Two reviewers independently screened the titles and abstracts of the identified studies for eligibility. The full texts of eligible studies were then reviewed, and data were extracted using a standardized form. Additionally, a meta-analysis was conducted to synthesize the findings from these studies.
Results: A total of 14 studies were identified and included in the scoping review. These studies employed various deep learning algorithms, including convolutional neural networks (CNNs), recurrent neural networks, and deep belief networks, to detect and classify oral lesions by clinical images. Of these studies, three were included in the meta-analysis. The estimated pooled sensitivity was 0.86 (95%CI= 0.80-0.91) and the pooled specificity was equal to 0.67 (95%CI= 0.58-0.75). 
Conclusion: Automated detection and classification of oral lesions using deep learning has made significant progress in recent years. The studies reviewed in this meta-analysis demonstrate the potential of deep learning algorithms in improving the accuracy and efficiency of oral lesion diagnosis. Future research should focus on developing robust and validated deep learning algorithms for the automated diagnosis of oral lesions.

title: Clinical Utility and Necessity of Preoperative CT Imaging in Functional and Aesthetic Nasal Surgery: A Systematic Review
description:
Overview and rationale 
Rhinoplasty, septoplasty and septorhinoplasty are among the most frequently performed operations worldwide. With a wide variety of indications like external deformities and internal dysfunctions, preoperative evaluations are necessary to inform sound, patient oriented surgical decisions. As such a wide variety of preoperative assessment methods are used, most common of which are physical examination, rhinoscopy, nasal endoscopy and CT imaging. These operations are costly, and most insurance companies require patients to have CT-documentation for clinical justification to proceed with payment. While CT scans provide ample insight into anatomical structures of the sinonasal region to help make informed decisions, they could also harm patients if used frequently due to their utilization of ionizing radiation. And since they are costly procedures, frequent use would also force significant financial burden on healthcare systems. Consequently, some recent studies have advocated for its limited use in complicated cases to ensure patient safety and cost-effectiveness. This PRISMA-2020-conformant systematic review was designed to respond to these controversies and assess CT scans overall utility and necessity in comparison to other preoperative assessment methods. 
Objective 
The main objective of this study was to compare various preoperative assessment methods in patients undergoing rhinoplasty, septoplasty or septorhinoplasty, with a specific focus on the utilization of CT imaging. 
Methods 
Eligibility: studies with patients undergoing rhinoplasty, septoplasty and septorhinoplasty (any age/indication) that utilized preoperative assessment with direct comparisons (CT vs other modalities). Included studies where Randomized trials, cohort studies, case-control studies, case series or cross-sectional studies reporting comparative outcomes. case reports, animal/in vitro studies, reviews, editorials, conference abstracts without full data, or studies lacking direct comparison between CT and alternative methods where excluded. 
Search and databases: an initial search was performed on April 14th,2025 in PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science and Cochrane library using MeSH terms and keywords. An updated search was performed on November 8th,2025 with same queries to cover the time gap. Language and publication date were not restricted. Also, reference list of relevant articles and systematic reviews were hand-searched to limit potential article-misses. 
Study selection and data extraction: two independent reviewers screened and data extracted articles with a third reviewer to resolve any disagreements. extracted domains included author(s), country, year of publication, sample size, study design, objective, patient characteristics, preoperative assessment methods (including computed tomography (CT) and alternative assessment methods as comparators), surgery type, surgery indication, relevant outcomes (diagnostic or clinical) and limitations. 
Risk of bias: MMAT 2018 was implemented to do study appraisal and risk of bias assessment. Studies where qualitatively categorized (low, medium, high) and no numerical scoring was applied, per MMAT guidance. 
Synthesis and certainty: although meta-analysis was considered initially, narrative synthesis was done due to significant heterogeneity. Certainty was graded using GRADE. 
Transparency: complete search strategies, PRISMA flow, extractions, risk-of-bias justifications and summary will be provided on OSF project page. AI assistance (ChatGPT) was only used for translation of non-English articles for screening and data extraction, with translations manually checked by reviewers. AI was not used to generate scientific content, analysis or conclusion. 
Current status and preliminary evidence map: From 2,334 records, 29 studies were included. The evidence base comprised two parallel-group randomized controlled trials (RCTs); 23 cohort or cross-sectional clinical studies; one technical study; and three laboratory or cadaveric studies. Population included both adult and pediatric; with three studies addressing adult nasal fracture; one pediatric series addressing congenital nasal dermoids; one small prospective case series focusing on adults undergoing secondary rhinoseptoplasty, comparing 3D volume-rendered CT with standard clinical examination; and three cadaveric investigations simulating functional rhinoplasty interventions. most common included preoperative modalities were nasal endoscopy, anterior rhinoscopy, or plain radiography; outcome domains included diagnostic agreement/accuracy, detection of specific anatomic or pathologic findings, changes in surgical planning, and patient-reported outcomes (NOSE, ROE, VAS, SNOT-22).
Expected outcomes and contributions: 
Deliverables: PRISMA-2020 flow diagrams; study characteristics, surgery types, comparator modalities (CT vs alternative preoperative assessment methods), outcomes measured tables; risk of bias summary; GRADE-style summary of findings; SWiM compliant narrative synthesis
Knowledge gains: the study will lead to a clean and complete map of human studies involving comparison of preoperative assessment methods in nasal surgeries, with emphasis on preoperative CT imaging and how it measures up in comparison to other preoperative modalities. This will highlight CT imaging areas of necessity and areas of redundancy, providing a clear map guiding physicians on how and where to use it in their assessments to ensure patients safety. 
Impact: this will help committees to come up with necessary guidelines and protocols for CT usage, inform future study designs to derive deeper paradigms, guide relative regulatory bodies such as ethics committees and insurance companies on appropriate comparators and their use, and help guide physicians for possibly more appropriate choices of preoperative modalities to ensure patient safety
Limitations and Risk Management: possible anticipated limitations in studies are small sample size, unclear randomization and blinding methods, heterogenous study designs, inconsistent outcome definitions, limited objective statistical analysis. To address these, appropriate risk of bias tools, transparent use of GRADE for certainty evaluation and SWiM for narrative synthesis are utilized. 
Ethics, Roles, Dissemination: due to utilization of previously published human studies in this study, ethics approval was non-applicable. The study received no external funding. Team roles covered otolaryngologist, sinus and nasal surgery fellow, and biostatistician/methodologists. 
Corresponding author is Dr. Mehdi Bakhshaee (BakhshaeeM@mums.ac.ir; https://orcid.org/0000-0001-9590-4798)
Study findings will be shared through an open OSF repository (protocol, material, extracted datasets, risk of bias justifications where permissible) and submission to a peer-reviewed journal, summarizing what is known, what is uncertain and what would be the next helpful steps.

title: The implications of mammography screening on health care use and its associated financial costs
description:
Description: ¨
This study examines the changes in health care use as a consequence of mammography screening in Denmark and its associated financial costs. The data are from Danish administrative health- and social registers in the period 1995-2018. 

Hypotheses: 
1) Women are more likely to increase their health care use after receiving a false positive in mammography screening. We expect that women diagnosed with breast cancer have a higher use, and women with normal results have a lower use. 
2) We hypothesize that patterns in health care use change as a consequence of being invited to screening. The direction of such change might be both ways and differences can occur across types of health care services.

Introduction:
Denmark has one of the world’s highest incidence rates of breast cancer. In 2007, The Danish national mammography-screening program was implemented and by 2010, all women aged 50-69 years had been invited for at least one round of screening.
Breast cancer screening with mammography is not 100% precise. For example, if a woman participates in one round of screening, she has a 0.9-6.5% risk of having a false-positive test result, and the cumulative risk is 20 to 60% if a woman participates in ten screenings every second year from 50-69 years [1-5].
The World Health Organization stated, more than 30 years ago, that screening programs could have unintended negative psychosocial consequences. Notably for those women who receive a positive screening test result, but also the mere invitation to screening could raise feelings of anxiety. We previously showed that false-positive screening results are associated with psychosocial consequences in up to three years [6], and a follow-up study indicates that some of these might persist for up to 14 years (Gram et al. Long-term consequences of false positive screening mammography: a matched cohort study with 14-years follow-up. Submitted). 
When a person receives a false-positive result in a screening program for a potentially life-threatening disease, research suggests that this changes the person’s health(-seeking) behavior in the future [7, 8]. The same can happen from the mere invitation to screening [9]. Qualitative studies elaborate that this is due to medicalization and that people fear for their health and need medical intervention to confirm that they are well and not sick [10]. We identified two quantitative studies that show that women use more health care services as a consequence of a false-positive mammography screening test in the first year after the test [11, 12].We previously showed that this also was the case for heavy smokers who had a false-positive test in CT screening for lung cancer [13, 14]. However, no studies have studied the health care use effects of a false-positive screening test beyond a year after the test, and therefore we do not know for how long such an effect is present. 

Aim:
We aim to address whether breast cancer screening changes health-seeking behavior by analyzing health care use data with 14 years of follow-up. We will analyze patterns of use and how these vary by screening result, e.g., cancer diagnosis, normal, and false positives. We will also compare the health care use among screening participants to a sample of screening-naive women. 

Design plan:
Study type: This is an observational study based on patient registers. We present data from Danish registers from 1995-2018. 
Blinding: Data are from national registers where people are unaware of being included in research studies. Ecologically, participants in screening were not blinded. There was no relevant blinding in the conduct of this study. 
Study design and sample size: This is a survey study augmented by data from Danish national registers. 1318 women who underwent screening in 2004-2005 participated in a questionnaire survey [6]. Each of these women are matched with ten women each in age and living in an area of Denmark with the same population density, but where women were not invited for screening until 2007-2010; these controls are randomly sampled from registers. Both the screened cases and their matched controls are followed up on health care use until Dec 31st, 2018, or death or emigration whichever occurs first. 
Personal levels of health care use are accounted for by the use in the nine years before the matched case’s screenings date.
The two cohorts differ in screening introduction because Denmark introduced mammography screening in two geographical parts of Denmark as a trial in 1991, and then introduced it to the rest of the country in 2007. By the end of 2010, all Danish women aged 50-69 had been invited to the screening. We followed the women for several years before and after the screening, and to account for short-term trends but identify long-term trends. 
The 1318 women have responded to the Consequences of Screening – Breast Cancer (COS-BC) questionnaire at six times points since 2004 [6]. The COS-BC is a psychometrically validated questionnaire with high content validity and adequate measurement properties that measures the psychosocial consequences of screening [15, 16].

Sampling plan:
We will get access to registers with information about health care services and costs (only those who are reimbursed by the government) for the primary and secondary sectors. We will also access registers on sociodemographic factors. As of the date of submission, the data exist in registers but have not been accessed or analyzed by the researchers.
- Primary: general practitioners, private practitioners, specialist doctors, and prescription drugs.
- Secondary: hospital admissions, outpatient visits, hospital visits, and surgical- and non-surgical procedures. 
- For prescription drugs, we will use data on level four for ATC codes. 
List of registers: 
- Demographic characteristics: BEF, BEFBOP, DOD, DODSAASG, VNDS
- Job information: AKM
- Educational level: UDDA
- Income: FAIK, IND
- Primary sector: SYSI, SSSY
- Secondary sector: LPR_ADM, LPR_DIAG, LPR_BES, LPR_SKSOPR, LPR_SKSUBE, PRIV_ADM, PRIV_DIAG, PRIV_BES, PRIV_SKSOPR, PSYK_ADM, PRIV_SKSUBE, PSYK_DIAG, PSYK_PERS, PSYK_SKSOPR, PSYK_SKSUBE
- Public cost factors for health services: DRGSAMB, DRBPAMB, DRGSHEL, DRGPHEL, DRGPSYK_AMB, DRGPSYK_HEL
- Prescription drugs: LMDB

The quality of the register data is adequate for example because it is used to generate claims to facilitate reimbursement by the state, and to communicate across hospital sections, etc. Some data will also become available to the patient, and therefore registration will have to be accurate. Also, prescription drugs will have few missing data. However, the LMDB does only cover prescription drugs and not drugs administered at hospitals. A number of prescriptions is a proxy for intake, yet we do not know if the prescriptions are actually consumed [17].
In Denmark, The billed charges of health care services are defined by political decision and do not reflect the actual value of these services. Therefore, the costs associated to increased health-care use are difficult to interpret and relate to, as the direct cost is somehow arbitrary. The actual costs of, e.g., a mammogram may vary significantly over a short period of time, for example, due to changes in volume of provided mammograms. Further, billed charges do not represent costs in a broader sense, as people can have additional costs such as transportation, lost work, etc. 

Variables:
Primary health sector: 
- General practitioner [18] contacts 
- GP contacts out-of-hours 
- Primary care specialists other than general practitioners 
- GP costs: based on billed charges
Secondary health sector: both psychiatric and somatic:
- Days of hospitalization 
- Out-patient clinic visits 
- Emergency room visits
- Surgery
- Non-surgery procedures
- Mammographies and other radiology of mammae: in- and out-of-hospital
- Psychiatric and somatic diagnoses: summed and individually
- Drugs – at level four ATC codes
- Total costs: based on billed charges
For all these measures, we will count number of services provided or number of contacts. If subjects are registered with more than one admission, visits, or surgery per day, these will only be counted as one. Subjects can be registered with two units if these are transferred across hospital sections. 

Other variables: 
- Breast cancer diagnosis: as tests are registered for the sake of reimbursement and not research, we do not use working diagnosis but only diagnoses, as a test that was done to rule out cancer might carry the working diagnosis cancer even if the test was negative. 
- Socioeconomic status based on income, wealth, ad work status
- Sociodemographic factors: age, marital status, native country.
- Charlson’s comorbidity index 
For all variables, one author will determine register codes for measures but they will be reviewed and validated by a second author.

Analyses plan:
Statistical model:
Most health care use data is suitable for analysis in a two-part model. The first part analyses the probability that a person will use the respective service at all during a particular time period. This first part may typically be viewed as use of health care that happened on the initiative of the health care seeking person, and not that of the health care system. The second part analyses the level of use among those who use the respective service during the time period. This second part may be viewed as use of health care due to the health care system, e.g. treatment protocols. This separation is only approximate as research shows that one of the strongest predictors of behavior and referrals e.g., in general practice, is pressure from patients.
Part one is implemented as a Poisson regression model which estimates the relative risk of using a specific service for cases compared to controls [19]. We used the method of Generalized estimating Equations (GEE) to account for matching and repeated measurement (e.g. the evaluation of a sequence of periods for each woman), and to estimate the correct covariance matrix. We used an offset to adjust for differing follow-up times. 
Part two involves a gamma regression, a generalization of Poisson regression that has two parameters: one for the mean and one for the variance. The parameter estimates from this model are interpreted as rate ratios, i.e. the factor by which cases use the service more than their controls. Also here matching and repeated measurement are accounted for by GEE. 
The product of the estimates from the first and the second part model gives a measure for the overall increase in use for a particular service.
We adjust each analysis for previous use of health care services in the 10 years before the matched case’s screening date to tentatively account for the woman’s generic level of health care use. Furthermore, we adjust for health status at screening by Charlson’s Comorbidity Index; a strong predictor of future use [20] [21]. Other potential confounders we adjust for are: age, cohabitation, degree of urbanicity, working status, country of origin, education, and income.
Inference criteria: We will use a 1% significance level to alleviate multiple testing. 
Data exclusion and missing data: If a subject has missing values on 90% of background variables, these will be excluded from the analysis. The use of register data implies that there will be few missing values. Subjects for which there are missing values for some of the background variables are put in a separate missing category for these variables.

There will be two primary sets of analyses: 
1) Analyses that focus on the difference between the screening group and the un-screened matched control. This will be analyzed collectively and independently across screening groups and matches. This will show if women who are invited for screening (screened in 2004-2005) will use less or more health care services compared to women who are not invited yet; not screened before 2007-2010. 
2) Analyses that compare the screening groups, defined by the screening result: normal, false-positive, and cancer, to each other. We expect that those who had normal results will have the lowest use of health care services, those who had a false-positive will use more, but less than those that were diagnosed with breast cancer. 

Secondary analyses: 
Also the following analyses will be conducted.
- An historical cohort-analysis; how does the health care use pattern change as screening is introduced in the two cohorts.
- We want to examine whether there is a gradient in socioeconomic status and the health care use. We know that Danish women with high socioeconomic status are healthier, yet are more likely to use more health care services than women of low socioeconomic status. If screening changes health-seeking behavior, we might be able to evaluate if this change is beneficial. For example, if the women with low socioeconomic status are more likely to increase their use it might be beneficial for the health of the women. Contrarily, if women with high socioeconomic status increase their use, it might not be beneficial. 
- We want to examine whether there is a change in socioeconomic status as a consequence of screening and/or a specific screening result. For example, are women with a false-positive more likely to have a lower level of income, retire early, or change marital status after the screening result?
- The screening cohort completed a questionnaire that measures the psychosocial consequences of screening. We would like to examine whether there is an association between these consequences and health care use. This might hint to who use more/less health care services, and who to target in psychosocial interventions. 
- Further, we want to do a relative importance analysis to determine which factors are most important for an increased use of health care services. 
- What are the costs associated to being diagnosed with breast cancer compared to normal screening results? This is relevant because about 30% of women will receive a false positive and one in ten are overdiagnosed with breast cancer in mammography screening programs [22]. New methods have recently been introduced to quantify such costs, and therefore relevant to test in this Danish population [23].

title: Predictive Performance of Machine Learning Algorithms for Recurrent Lumbar Disc Herniation Following Discectomy: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
description: This systematic review and meta-analysis aims to evaluate the predictive performance of machine learning (ML) algorithms for recurrent lumbar disc herniation (rLDH) following lumbar discectomy. While traditional logistic regression-based risk models exist, ML algorithms offer the potential to capture non-linear interactions among larger predictor sets. The existing evidence has not yet been quantitatively synthesized to evaluate ML-specific predictive performance metrics for this outcome. This review will systematically identify, critically appraise, and synthesize evidence from observational and modeling studies evaluating ML algorithms beyond simple logistic regression for rLDH prediction. The primary synthesis will evaluate discrimination performance, focusing on pooled Area Under the Curve (AUC), sensitivity, and specificity. Methodological quality will be assessed using the PROBAST tool, and the certainty of evidence will be evaluated using the GRADE approach. The findings are intended to characterize performance variations across algorithm types and identify evidence gaps, highlighting the need for external validation prior to clinical implementation.
