title: Mapping the interplay between anxiety symptoms during the COVID-19 lockdown in Belgium: A undirected and Bayesian network perspective
description: Template: We are preregistering this exploratory data analysis of preexisting data, as suggested by Weston, Ritchie, Rohrer, and Przybylski (2019). https://doi.org/10.1177/2515245919848684 More details regarding the template can be found here: https://osf.io/v4z3x/ Context and Research Questions: Pandemic yields severe and long-lasting consequences on mental health (for a systematic review, see Brooks et al., 2020), and the COVID-19 pandemic is no exception to this statement. Early data indicate that the COVID-19 pandemic has a significant impact on mental health (e.g., Asmunsdon & Taylor, 2020; Wang et al., 2020; for a systematic review, see Xiong et al., 2020), with anxiety symptoms being one of the most commonly reported problems (e.g., Quiu et al., 2020; Mertens et al., 2020; Xiong et al., 2020). In Belgium, the number of people reporting anxiety symptoms increased substantially during the lockdown of March 2020 compared to similar data collected two years before (Sciensano, 2020). And similar findings have been reported across different countries (e.g., González-Sanguino et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2020). And that should not come as a surprise. The profound health, economic, and social consequences of COVID-19 lockdown are likely to be anxiogenic for many, regardless of whether or not they have had direct exposure to the virus (Heeren, 2020; Park, Velez, Kannan, Chorpita, 2020). However, in most of the studies that have been published so far regarding the impact of the lockdown on anxiety symptoms, researchers have relied on a unitary approach to anxiety by collapsing the different features of anxiety into one sum-score and thus ignoring any possibility that these distinct features could interact in different ways. Recently, a network approach to psychopathology has appeared, conceptualizing mental disorders as network systems of interacting symptoms. In this way, instead of investigating mental disorders as reflecting a single, unitary construct, a network approach allows an investigation into the structure of, and associations between, the symptoms themselves. Though only recently pioneered by Borsboom and his colleagues (e.g., Borsboom et al., 2011, Borsboom & Cramer, 2013), this approach has quickly become a hot topic in contemporary clinical psychology. Many studies have accordingly used this framework to investigate the interrelations between systems of symptoms and speculate as to the clinical implications (for systematic reviews, see Contreras et al., 2019; Robinaugh et al., 2019). Although a few studies have already applied a network analytic framework to examine the interdependence between different factors assumedly involved in the psychological responses to the COVID-19 pandemic, and especially regarding the fear of infection or the anxious response to the structural impact of the pandemic (e.g., Papini et al., 2020; Taylor et al., 2020), none of these studies focused on the network structure of the connections between the distinct features of anxiety during the lockdown. In this project, we thus seek to map the network structure of the hallmark features of anxiety during the lockdown. To do so, we will implement the network computational tools via a reanalysis of an existing dataset (Lits et al., 2020; see below) that includes the GAD-7 (Spitzer et al., 2006)—one of the most commonly used self-reported screening tools in epidemiological and clinical research of anxiety disorders (e.g., Schalet et al., 2014)—in a large and representative sample of participants living in the French-speaking part of Belgium who took part to an online survey conducted during the first weeks following the (first) Belgian national lockdown (March 2020). Especially, we have three primary goals. First, we endeavor to clarify the pairwise connections among the distinct anxiety symptoms during the lockdown. To do so, we will compute a graphical Gaussian model (GGM). In this undirected network, edges signify conditional independence relationships between nodes (here, symptoms of anxiety), controlling for the effects of all other nodes. Of critical interest is the computation of centrality metrics that disclose the most potentially influential nodes maintaining the GGM network structure. We will then test whether these nodes cohere as a unitary network system of interacting elements or whether they instead constitute distinct communities (or subnetworks) of nodes (i.e., symptoms) serving different functions. Finally, we will use Bayesian computational methods to compute a directed acyclic graph (DAG) to estimate the probabilistic dependencies among the distinct anxiety features. A DAG is a directed network whereby each edge has an arrow tip on one end, signifying the direction of probabilistic dependence (McNally, 2016; McNally, Heeren, & Robinaugh, 2017). To generate directed edges, DAGs encode the conditional independence relationships and characterize the variables' joint probability distribution. DAGs can thus be decomposed as a product of the conditional distribution of each node given its parent nodes in the graph, thus rendering DAG analysis capable of indicating whether the existence of node A ("downstream") probabilistically implies the existence of node B ("upstream") more than vice versa (e.g., Heeren, Bernstein, & McNally, 2020). Although DAGs have occasionally been used in clinical psychology, they have increasingly become popular in other fields, especially in epidemiology and environmental sciences, wherein numerous illustrations are available. Therefore, we computed DAGs to generate a computationally driven model of the probabilistic dependencies among the distinct symptoms of anxiety reported during the lockdown. These complementary computational approaches can provide a novel perspective and clues to generating new hypotheses about the functional relations among the anxiety symptoms reported during the COVID-19 lockdown. Data description: The data we plan to use come from an online survey carried out between March 30 and April 10 by the Observatoire de Recherche sur les Médias et le Journalisme (ORM – UCLouvain; i.e., Lits et al., 2020). This survey aimed to gauge the extent of the COVID-19 infodemic in French-speaking Belgium during the COVID-19 lockdown. The survey also included data related to anxiety symptoms (as assessed using the well-validated and broadly used Generalized Anxiety Disorder 7-item scale, hereafter GAD-7) because the authors also wanted to evaluate the association between infodemic related behaviors and anxiety feelings during the Belgian lockdown. To do so, they rely on a sum-score of the seven items of the GAD-7. The final report of this survey (i.e., Lits et al., 2020) involves 1,817 French-speaking Belgians. The present re-analysis will focus on the item's responses of GAD-7's (and not the tally-score of the GAD-7) of these participants. Is the data publicly available: Yes, a summarized version can be found here: https://osf.io/z3r4e/ Date of access: 5 October, 2020 Data source: Collected by Grégoire Lits, Louie-Amélie Cougnon, Alexandre Heeren, Bernard Hanseeuw, & Nathan Gurnet, all from UCLouvain, Belgium. Note that the statistical analyst of this pre-registered data re-analysis (i.e., Alexandre Heeren) was involved in the initial data collection. Sampling and data collection procedures: The data collection procedure is well documented in the following research report (available online): Lits, G., Cougnon, L.-A, Heeren, A., Hanseeuw, B., & Gurnet, N. (2020, May 11). Analyse de « l’infodémie » de Covid-19 en Belgique francophone. https://doi.org/10.31235/osf.io/wsuj3. The sample was built upon a quota sampling method based on age, gender, and education level, and weighted by gender and educational level (following the results of the STATBEL 2019 governmental survey on workforce) to be representative of the characteristics of the population living in the French-speaking part of Belgium over the age of 16. Prior work based on the dataset: The statistical analyst of this preregistration (i.e., Alexandre Heeren) was not the statistical analyst of the two previous research reports based on the initial dataset. So far, the data have been analyzed and reported by Nathan Gurnet and Grégoire Lits for Lits et al., 2020) and by Bernard Hanseeuw and Nathan Gurnet for Hanseeuw et al., 2020). Prior knowledge of current dataset: The variable we are interested in from this dataset has already been processed in two previous publications aiming at depicting the COVID-19 infodemic-related behaviors in French-speaking Belgium (e.g., Hanseeuw, Cougnon, Heeren, Gurnet, & Lits, 2020; Lits, G., Cougnon, L.-A, Heeren, A., Hanseeuw, B., & Gurnet, N., 2020). However, these publications did not focus on the GAD-7, and only relied on a sum-score of the GAD-7 (i.e., there was no distinction between the seven features of anxiety). Finally, this dataset has never been analyzed via a graph theoretical framework. Here, for the first time, we will re-analyze the data related to anxiety in an exploratory fashion using a network approach (aka graph-theoretical framework). Moment of preregistration: Registration before any analyst on this team handling or analyzing the GAD-7 data using a network approach. Measured variables (that will be included in analyses): Given our research questions (see above), we plan to include the seven items of the Generalized Anxiety Disorder 7-item scale (GAD-7). Transformations: Following guidelines in using network analysis in clinical psychology (e.g., Epskamp & Fried, 2018), we will apply, for each variable, the nonparanormal transformation via the R package huge (Jiang et al., 2019). Data Inclusion: We will include all participants of the research report of Lits et al. (2020). Outliers: N/A Sample size: For our analyses, the sample size will be 1,817 (as in Lits et al., 2020). Missing data: The final sample of Lits et al. (2020) does not include participants with missing values. Statistical plan: The measured variables (i.e., the 7 variables of the GAD-7; see above) will be included as nodes in the network models and processed as follows: 1. Data Preparation. First, we will test whether our correlation matrix is positive definite (reflecting that nodes are not linear combinations of other nodes). Second, we will search for potential pairs of redundant nodes, that is, nodes that are highly inter-correlated and that correlate to the same degree with other variables. To do so, we will implement the Hittner method for comparing dependent correlations (Hittner, May, & Silver, 2003) via the goldbricker function of the R package networktools (Jones, 2018). If pairs of redundant nodes are identified, they will be combined via the reduce_net function of networktools—i.e., reducing the redundant variables via a principal component analysis of the two variables and creating a new variable. 2. Graphical Gaussian Model. We will use a graphical Gaussian model (GGM) to estimate the undirected network. In this network, edges signify conditional independence relationships between nodes, controlling for the effects of all other nodes (Epskamp & Fried, 2018). We will present GGMs that will be regularized via the graphical LASSO (Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator) algorithm, which serves two primary functions (Friedman, Hastie, & Tibshirani, 2011). First, it computes regularized partial correlations between pairs of nodes, thereby eliminating spurious associations (edges) attributable to the influence of other nodes in the network. Second, it shrinks trivially small associations to zero, thereby removing potentially “false positive” edges from the graph and producing a sparse graph comprising only the strongest edges. We will use the R package qgraph (Epskamp et al., 2012) that automatically implements the graphical LASSO regularization in combination with Extended Bayesian Information Criterion (EBIC) model selection (Foygel & Drton, 2011). In this procedure, 100 models with varying degrees of sparsity are estimated; a final model is selected according to the lowest EBIC value, given a specific hyperparameter gamma (γ), which controls the trade-off between including false-positive edges and removing true edges. The hyperparameter γ is usually set between zero and 0.5 (Epskamp & Fried, 2018). The closer one chooses a value of γ near 0.5, the more the EBIC will favor a simpler model containing fewer edges, whereas the closer one chooses a value of γ near zero, the more the EBIC will favor a model with more edges. We will opt to set γ to 0.5 to be confident that our edges are genuine, assuming that the true model is, indeed, sparse (Epskamp & Fried, 2018). To estimate the stability of edges, we will bootstrap the confidence regions of the edge weights via the R package bootnet (Epskamp, Borsboom, & Fried, 2018). We will set the bootstraps to 1,000. To quantify the importance of each node in the resulting graphical LASSO network, we will compute the expected influence centrality index (Robinaugh, Millner, & McNally, 2016). The expected influence of a node is the sum of the edge weights incident on a given node, including positive and negative values. Higher expected influence values indicate greater centrality and thus greater importance in the network. We will evaluate the stability of the centrality metrics by implementing a subset bootstrap procedure (Costenbader & Valente, 2003). To do so, we will repeatedly correlate the centrality metrics of the original dataset with the metrics calculated from a subsample of participants missing via person-dropping bootstraps (we will set the bootstraps to 1,000) as implemented in the R package bootnet (Epskamp et al., 2018). We will also calculate the centrality stability correlation coefficient (CS-coefficient) to quantify the effects of this person-dropping procedure. The CS-coefficient represents the maximum proportion of participants that can be dropped while maintaining a 95% probability that the correlation between centrality metrics from the full data set and the subset data are at least .70. Based on a simulation study (Epskamp et al., 2018), a minimum CS-coefficient of .25 (and preferably ≥ .50) is recommended for interpreting centrality indices. Using a bootstrapped difference test, we will then capitalize on this subset bootstrap procedure to test whether nodes statistically differ between them in terms of expected influence values. Because recent commentators have argued that differential variability—that is, the phenomenon that variables have drastically different variances—may distort conclusions about node centrality (e.g., Fried, 2016; Terluin, de Boer, & de Vet, 2016), we will also compute the correlations between the standard deviation and the expected influence centrality value of each variable. This approach will allow us to test whether there is an association between nodes' importance in the network and its variability. Finally, we will test whether the nodes denoting the hallmark features of anxiety feelings during COVID-19 cohere as one or multiple subnetworks (“communities”). Following prior network research (e.g., Heeren, Bernstein, & McNally, 2018; Robinaugh, LeBlanc, Vuletich, & McNally, 2014), we will implement the spin-glass algorithm (Reichardt & Bornholdt, 2006), a modularity-based community detection procedure suitable for uncovering the structure of relatively small networks with negative edge values (e.g., Traag & Bruggeman, 2009). We will use the spinglass.community function (γ = 1, start temperature = 1, stop temperature = .01, cooling factor = .99, spins = 7) of the R package igraph (Csardi & Nepusz, 2006). Nodes within a community are more strongly interconnected than they are with nodes in another community. In case of community structure, we will identify important nodes that may serve as bridges between the resultant communities by computing the bridge expected influence index via the bridge function of the R package networktools (Jones, 2018). Bridge expected influence is the sum of the edge weights connecting a given node to all nodes in the other community or communities (Jones, Ma, & McNally, 2019). As for the centrality metrics, in the case of a community structure, we will evaluate the stability of the bridge centrality estimates via person-dropping bootstraps (we will set the bootstraps to 1,000) as implemented in the R package bootnet and compute the related CS-coefficient (Epskamp et al., 2018). Using a bootstrapped difference test, we will also capitalize on this subset bootstrap procedure to test whether nodes statistically differ between them in terms of bridge expected influence values. 3. Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). Finally, we will compute a DAG to estimate a directed, potentially “causal” structure of the system (Pearl et al., 2016). We will use a Bayesian hill-climbing algorithm implemented via the R package bnlearn (Scutari, 2010). As implemented by bnlearn, the bootstrap function computes the structural aspects of the network model by adding edges, removing them, and reversing their direction to ultimately optimize the goodness-of-fit target score, i.e., the Bayesian Information Criterion. This involves an iterative process of randomly restarting this process with different possible edges linking different node pairs, perturbing the system, and using 50 different random restarts to avoid local maxima. Following our previous works (Bernstein, Heeren, & McNally, 2017; Heeren, Bernstein, & McNally, 2020; McNally, Heeren, & Robinaugh, 2017), we will perform 100 perturbations (i.e., attempts to insert, delete, or reverse an edge) for each restart. As this iterative procedure unfolds, the function returns the best fitting network based on this random restart/perturbation procedure. To ensure the stability of the resultant DAG, we will then bootstrap 10,000 samples (with replacement), compute a network for each sample, and average across the resulting networks to produce a final network structure (e.g., Blanchard, Roskam, Mikolajczak, & Heeren, 2020; Heeren, Bernstein, & McNally, 2020; McNally, Heeren, & Robinaugh, 2017), involving a two-step procedure. First, we will determine how frequently a given edge appeared in the 10,000 bootstrapped networks. We will then use the optimal cut-point method of Scutari and Nagarajan (2013) for retaining edges, which yields networks having both high sensitivity and high specificity. Second, we will ascertain the direction of each surviving edge in the 10,000 bootstrapped networks. If a given edge points from node X to node Y in at least 51% of the bootstrapped networks, then this direction will be represented in the final network. In summary, we will first determine the network structure (i.e., whether an edge is present or not), and then determine the direction of each surviving edge. References Asmundson, G., & Taylor, S. title: A Systematic Review of Multimodal Deep Learning and Machine Learning Fusion Techniques for Prostate Cancer Classification
description:
Prostate cancer remains one of the most prevalent malignancies and a leading cause of cancer-related deaths among men worldwide. Despite advances in traditional diagnostic methods such as Prostate-specific antigen testing, digital rectal examination, and multiparametric Magnetic resonance imaging, these approaches remain constrained by modality specific limitations, suboptimal sensitivity and specificity, and reliance on expert interpretation, which may introduce diagnostic inconsistency. Multimodal deep learning 7
and machine learning fusion, which integrates diverse data sources including imaging, clinical, and molecular information, has emerged as a promising strategy to enhance the 9
accuracy of prostate cancer classification. This review aims to outline the current state-of-the-art deep learning and machine learning based fusion techniques for prostate cancer classification, focusing on their implementation, performance, challenges, and clinical applicability. Following PRISMA guidelines, a total of 131 studies were identified, of which 27 studies met the inclusion criteria. Extracted data included input techniques, deep learning architectures, performance metrics, and validation approaches. The majority of the studies used an early fusion approach with convolutional neural networks to integrate the data. Clinical and imaging data were the most commonly used modalities in the reviewed studies for prostate cancer research. Overall, multimodal deep learning and machine learning-based fusion significantly advances prostate cancer classification and outperform unimodal approaches.

title: Diagnostic accuracy of enhanced imaging for detecting residual or recurrent neoplasia at colorectal post-EMR scars: a systematic review and meta-analysis
description:
Endoscopic mucosal resection (EMR) is widely used for the treatment of colorectal neoplasia. Surveillance after EMR is essential to detect residual or recurrent neoplasia at the post-resection scar site. Current clinical guidelines suggest careful optical assessment of the scar using enhanced endoscopic imaging techniques in conjunction with targeted biopsies. However, these recommendations are conditional and supported by moderate-quality evidence, and uncertainty remains regarding the diagnostic accuracy and negative predictive value of enhanced imaging strategies for excluding recurrence.

The objective of this systematic review and meta-analysis is to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of enhanced endoscopic imaging modalities, with or without targeted biopsies, for detecting histologically confirmed residual or recurrent neoplasia at colorectal post-EMR scar sites. Specifically, we aim to quantify pooled sensitivity, specificity, and negative predictive value using hierarchical diagnostic accuracy models. Secondary objectives include comparing diagnostic performance across imaging modalities and exploring sources of heterogeneity related to resection technique, timing of surveillance, and clinical setting.

The findings of this review will directly inform post-EMR surveillance strategies and may clarify whether routine random biopsies of endoscopically normal-appearing scars are necessary when enhanced imaging is used.

title: Applications of Artificial Intelligence in Infective Endocarditis with Oral or Dental Origin: A Scoping Review
description:
This project explores the applications of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the prevention, early detection, diagnosis, and management of Infective Endocarditis (IE), particularly in cases originating from oral or dental infections. Infective Endocarditis remains a life-threatening disease often linked to oral microorganisms entering the bloodstream through dental infections or procedures. Despite this significant association, the integration of AI in studying and managing oral-origin IE has not been systematically mapped.

This scoping review aims to identify, categorize, and synthesize existing evidence on how AI and machine learning models have been used to improve diagnostic accuracy, risk prediction, and clinical decision-making in IE. It will also highlight methodological trends, research gaps, and opportunities for future interdisciplinary collaboration among dentistry, cardiology, microbiology, and data science.

The expected outcome of this project is to provide a comprehensive overview of current research efforts, summarize AI model performance in IE-related studies, and propose directions for future work that may enhance early detection and prevention strategies linking oral health and cardiovascular disease.

title: Can AI Hear What We Miss? Diagnostic Accuracy of AI-Augmented Stethoscopes for Cardiac Murmur Detection: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
description:
Background:
Cardiac murmurs are often the earliest clinical indicator of valvular or structural heart disease. Auscultation is a low-cost and accessible method for initial detection, but its diagnostic accuracy is highly operator-dependent and subject to variability in clinical skill. In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI)-augmented digital stethoscopes have emerged, aiming to improve murmur detection through objective sound analysis and machine learning algorithms.

Objective:
This systematic review and meta-analysis aims to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of AI-augmented digital stethoscopes for detecting cardiac murmurs. The performance of these devices will be compared to two benchmarks:
 1. Traditional auscultation performed by human clinicians using conventional (non-AI) stethoscopes.
 2. Reference standard diagnostic tools, such as echocardiography, where available, to confirm the presence or absence of underlying structural cardiac abnormalities.

Methods:
We will conduct a systematic literature search using major biomedical databases including PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library. Additional databases or grey literature sources may be searched if required to ensure comprehensive coverage of relevant studies. Eligible studies will include those assessing AI-augmented digital stethoscopes for cardiac murmur detection in human subjects.

The primary outcomes of interest will include diagnostic accuracy metrics such as sensitivity, specificity, positive and negative predictive values, and area under the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve. Risk of bias will be assessed using an appropriate tool depending on the study design (e.g., QUADAS-2 for diagnostic test accuracy studies). Data extraction and synthesis will follow the PRISMA-DTA guidelines where applicable.

title: Deep Learning-Based Electrocardiogram Analysis for Pulmonary Embolism Diagnosis: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
description:
Background:
Acute pulmonary embolism (PE) is a life-threatening condition with high mortality risk, necessitating prompt and accurate diagnosis. While computed tomography pulmonary angiography (CTA) is the diagnostic gold standard, it has limitations such as contrast media risks and logistical delays. Electrocardiography (ECG) is a widely accessible and safe alternative; however, its diagnostic sensitivity remains suboptimal. Recent advancements in deep learning have shown promise in improving ECG-based PE detection.
Objective:
This meta-analysis aims to evaluate the diagnostic performance of artificial intelligence (AI)-based deep learning models using ECG data for PE detection and to identify their strengths, limitations, and future directions.
Methods:
We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis following PRISMA guidelines. A comprehensive search of PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Library was performed to identify studies evaluating AI models utilizing ECG for PE detection. Studies were included if CTA served as the reference standard. Pooled sensitivity, specificity, diagnostic odds ratio (DOR), and area under the summary receiver operating characteristic (SROC) curve (AUC) were calculated using a random-effects model. Study quality was assessed using the QUADAS-2 tool.
Results:
Five studies involving 467,017 participants were included. The pooled sensitivity and specificity of AI-based ECG models for PE detection were 70% (95% CI: 68–72%) and 67% (95% CI: 66–67%), respectively. The pooled diagnostic odds ratio (DOR) was 3.68 (95% CI: 3.31–4.09), and the SROC analysis yielded an AUC of 0.754, reflecting moderate diagnostic accuracy. Significant heterogeneity was observed across studies (I² > 90%), largely driven by differences in patient selection, study design, and regional variations. Multimodal models integrating ECG with clinical data demonstrated superior diagnostic performance compared to ECG-only approaches.
Conclusions:
Current AI-based deep learning models for ECG analysis show moderate accuracy in detecting acute PE, with promising potential for clinical screening. However, significant heterogeneity and limited external validation highlight the need for standardized methodologies and larger, multicenter studies. Future research should focus on multimodal approaches that combine ECG with other clinical parameters to enhance diagnostic performance and clinical applicability.

title: Circulating Tumor DNA-Based Molecular Residual Disease After Curative-Intent Therapy in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer: An Umbrella Review of Diagnostic Accuracy, Recurrence Prediction, and Adjuvant-Treatment Guidance
description:
This project is an umbrella review evaluating the role of circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA)-based molecular residual disease (MRD) assessment after curative-intent therapy in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). The review synthesizes evidence from systematic reviews, meta-analyses, reconstructed individual-patient-data analyses, pooled analyses, and diagnostic test accuracy studies to assess the prognostic value, diagnostic performance, and potential clinical utility of ctDNA-MRD for recurrence prediction, survival outcomes, and adjuvant-treatment guidance.

The review includes evidence from multiple databases, including Scopus, Web of Science, PubMed, Europe PMC, Embase, and Semantic Scholar. Outcomes of interest include recurrence-free survival (RFS), disease-free survival (DFS), progression-free survival (PFS), overall survival (OS), cancer-specific survival (CSS), diagnostic sensitivity and specificity, area under the curve (AUC), and molecular lead time. The study also evaluates methodological quality using an AMSTAR-2-informed framework and quantifies overlap among included evidence syntheses using corrected covered area (CCA) analysis.

The findings suggest that ctDNA-MRD positivity is consistently associated with poorer recurrence-related and survival outcomes, particularly in post-treatment and longitudinal surveillance settings. The study highlights the potential of ctDNA-MRD as a prognostic and trial-enrichment biomarker while emphasizing current limitations related to assay heterogeneity, review overlap, and lack of randomized MRD-guided intervention evidence.

This OSF project contains materials related to the umbrella review, including the manuscript, supplementary materials, methodological documentation, and associated research outputs.

title: Performance of Large Language Models in Automated Medical Literature Screening: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
description:
This project aims to systematically evaluate the performance, reliability, and heterogeneity of large language models (LLMs) in the automated screening of medical literature. As the volume of scientific publications continues to grow exponentially, the screening phase of systematic reviews has become increasingly time-consuming and labor-intensive. Recent advances in artificial intelligence—particularly large language models such as GPT-series, LLaMA, Claude, Gemini, Copilot, DeepSeek, and Qwen—have shown the potential to automate key steps of evidence synthesis. However, the accuracy, consistency, and generalizability of these models across different screening tasks and clinical domains remain unclear.

This study will conduct a comprehensive systematic review and meta-analysis to summarize existing evidence on the use of LLMs for title/abstract screening, citation filtering, and study selection in medical and health-related systematic reviews. We will assess multiple performance indicators, including sensitivity, specificity, precision, recall, F1-score, workload reduction, and time efficiency. We also aim to explore sources of heterogeneity, such as model type, prompt design, clinical field, screening task complexity, dataset characteristics, and evaluation methodology.

The review will follow PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Searches will be conducted across PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, and preprint servers. Eligible studies will include evaluations of LLM-assisted or fully automated literature screening workflows, using either real-world systematic review datasets or curated benchmark sets. Risk of bias will be assessed using adapted tools for AI performance studies. Where feasible, meta-analysis will be performed to synthesize quantitative performance metrics.

title: Multimodal Large Language Models for Acne Severity Assessment: A Systematic Benchmarking Study of Diagnostic Accuracy and Fitzpatrick Skin Type Bias Using Open-Access Dermatological Datasets
description: This cross-sectional benchmarking study evaluates the agreement between contemporary multimodal large language models (LLMs) — including GPT-4o/GPT-5, Claude Opus 4.7, Gemini 2.5 Pro, SkinGPT-4, and LLaVA-Med — and a consensus reference standard established by board-certified dermatologists, for the task of acne severity grading using the Global Acne Grading System (GAGS) and the Investigator's Global Assessment (IGA). The study uses exclusively publicly available, openly licensed dermatological image datasets (ACNE04, SCIN, DermNet NZ, PAD-UFES-20). The primary analysis quantifies overall diagnostic agreement using quadratic-weighted Cohen's kappa; pre-specified secondary analyses examine performance disparities across Fitzpatrick skin types I–VI using established algorithmic fairness metrics (demographic parity, equalized odds, false negative rate parity). Additional analyses include prompt sensitivity, run-to-run reliability, inter-model agreement, and clinical impact of misclassifications on guideline-based treatment recommendations. The study is reported in full compliance with the CLEAR Derm, TRIPOD-AI, CLAIM 2024, STARD 2015, and PROBAST-AI guidelines.

title: MENSTRUAL HEALTH POLICIES AND THEIR IMPACTS ON SCHOOL LIFE AND QUALITY OF LIFE OF ADOLESCENTS: A SCOPING REVIEW
description:
Objective: The objective of this scoping review is to map the available evidence regarding the repercussions of public menstrual health policies on adolescents’ school life and quality of life.

Type of review: This study is characterized as a scoping review conducted according to the methodological recommendations of the Joanna Briggs Institute (PETERS et al., 2020) and guided by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) guidelines (TRICCO et al., 2018). The review protocol will be previously registered on the Open Science Framework (OSF), a platform dedicated to the registration and sharing of scientific protocols and preprints.

Description of the research question: The research question was developed based on the PCC strategy, an acronym for Population, Concept, and Context, as recommended by the Joanna Briggs Institute (2021). In this review, the following elements were defined: P (Population) – adolescents; C (Concept) – menstrual health policies; and C (Context) – school and community settings or national and international policies related to health and education. Based on this structure, the following guiding question was established: “How do public menstrual health policies impact adolescents’ school life and quality of life?”

Descriptors: The search strategy will be developed using descriptors indexed in DeCS and Medical Subject Headings (MeSH), including: Adolescent; Menstruation; Menstrual Hygiene Products; Educational Status; Quality of Life; Health Policy, and their corresponding terms in Portuguese. Keywords related to the topic will also be used, such as: Menstrual Health; Period Poverty; Menstrual Health Policies; Menstrual Hygiene Management Policies; School Attendance; Academic Performance; School Performance; saúde menstrual; pobreza menstrual; frequência escolar; desempenho escolar; and políticas de saúde menstrual. The Boolean operators “AND” and “OR” will be employed to combine terms, aiming to increase the sensitivity and specificity of the search strategy.

Search strategy: The search strategy will be developed through access to the CAPES Journal Portal, including the following databases and information sources: PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, LILACS, CINAHL, Embase, Web of Science, CAPES Theses and Dissertations Catalog, Google Scholar, ENAP portal, Ministry of Education portal, and Ministry of Health portal. The Rayyan online platform will be used for the organization and selection of studies. The process of screening titles, abstracts, full-text reading, and data extraction will be independently carried out by two reviewers. Any disagreements will be discussed among the researchers until consensus is reached.

Search string: In the MEDLINE database, the following search strategy will be applied:
((((((Adolescent OR Adolescents OR Teenager OR Youth)) AND ((Menstruation OR "Menstrual Health" OR "Period Poverty" OR "Menstrual Hygiene Products" OR "Menstrual Hygiene Management"))) AND (("Menstrual Health Policies" OR "Menstrual Hygiene Management Policies" OR "Public Policy" OR "Health Policy"))) AND (("Educational Status" OR "School Attendance" OR "Academic Performance" OR "School Performance" OR Education OR School))) AND (("Quality of Life"))).

Inclusion and exclusion criteria: The inclusion criteria will comprise studies available in the selected databases addressing public policies, programs, strategies, or interventions related to menstrual health and their repercussions on school attendance, academic performance, and adolescents’ quality of life. Studies involving actions such as distribution of menstrual products, menstrual health education, combating period poverty, improvement of sanitation and menstrual hygiene conditions in school and community environments, as well as governmental or institutional policies aimed at promoting menstrual dignity, will be considered. Research conducted with adolescents, regardless of sex, language, country of origin, or year of publication, will be included. Duplicate studies, publications not available in full text, review studies, editorials, letters to the editor, conference abstracts, opinions, research protocols, and investigations that do not directly address the relationship between menstrual health policies and outcomes related to school attendance/academic performance or adolescents’ quality of life will be excluded.

title: Under-diagnosis of Dementia in Nursing Home Residents: A Scoping Review
description:
As per the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders-5 (DSM-5), dementia is diagnosed when there is evidence of decline in activities of daily living (ADL) as well as decline in cognitive ability in one or more of the following domains: complex attention, executive ability, learning and memory, language, perceptual - motor - visual perception, praxis and social cognition (1). Progression of these deficits to the extent one’s ability to conduct activities of daily living is impaired is one of the major reasons for older individuals transition to residential aged care facilities (RACF) or nursing homes (2,3,4,5). 
Dementia is a significant public health issue in Australia and a health condition that is highly prevalent amongst residents of RACF (6,7). Under-diagnosis of dementia may affect the quality of care provided to the RACF residents, eventually impacting their health-related outcomes (8). Overarching this issue is the fact that funding allocation to RACF for the care of residents is dependent on whether the diagnosis of dementia is present or not (9). 
 It is estimated that three quarters of people living with dementia globally are living without the diagnosis made (7,8). More than 50% of residents living with dementia in RACF are said to have not been diagnosed as living with dementia (8,9,10,11). The issue of under-diagnosis likely begins before entry into the RACF given that a 2017 meta-analysis of 23 studies found that more than 63% of people living with dementia in the community had not been diagnosed with dementia (12). The same study also revealed that the true prevalence of dementia in RACF was double that reported, meaning that half of the residents were not diagnosed (12). Similar results were also reported by another study focusing on diagnosis of dementia in RACF residents (13). 
Findings from Australian studies have identified similar gaps in the diagnosis of dementia. The South Australian Longitudinal Frailty In Residential Sector over Time [FIRST] Study of RACF residents speculated that dementia might not have been diagnosed in almost half of the residents given that 75.6% of residents were identified as possibly living with dementia when using the Dementia Severity Rating Scale (DSRS), whilst a diagnosis of dementia was recorded in the medical records for only 37.1% residents (14). In another Australian study, 83% of residents scored 4 or more on the Psychogeriatric Assessment Scale (PAS-cog) suggesting the presence of dementia but only 65% had a recorded diagnosis of dementia (15). Clearly, the degree of under-diagnosis reported varies according to the method used to identify dementia (16). Methods that are used to make the diagnosis of dementia in RACF can range from a diagnosis recorded in medical records, to scales used to screen for dementia risk and all the way up to a more definitive diagnosis by clinical experts (e.g., geriatricians, neurologists or expert panels). 
It is important to be cognizant of the fact that screening tools such as the DSRS and PAS-cog only identify the risk of dementia and that too with varying performance. The DSRS for example, was able to differentiate between mild cognitive impairment and dementia with a sensitivity of 41% and specificity of 79% or a post-test probability of 74% (16). Additionally, the study design can also influence the reported prevalence for dementia with prevalence varying depending on if the prevalence was estimated at the time of admission to RACF or cross-sectionally, where the prevalence of dementia was determined for all residents at the time the study was conducted (16).
Ensuring that those living with dementia are diagnosed in a timely manner is important (15,16) as a missed diagnosis could result in the resident missing out on funding allocations (e.g., dementia supplement) that would enable the resident to receive increased care hours (17,18,19,20). A timely diagnosis also facilitates conversations regarding the medical management of residents including future care planning (21). It is no surprise therefore that timely diagnosis has been identified as an essential care requirement as per the National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC) guidelines (21). Timely dementia diagnosis has also been highlighted as a priority area for action in the National Framework for Action on Dementia (22).

title: Evaluation of a conversational AI system for simulated clinical scenarios in medical education: a mixed-methods multi-centre study
description:
Effective consultation skills remain fundamental to high-quality healthcare delivery, influencing diagnostic accuracy, patient satisfaction, and clinical outcomes. This protocol describes a mixed-methods evaluation of conversational artificial intelligence (AI) for simulated clinical scenarios in undergraduate medical education. The study will recruit the entire third-year cohort of medical students (n=271) at the University of Bristol to compare AI virtual patients with traditional actor-based simulations across four standardised primary care scenarios. Quantitative assessment will employ validated measures including an abridged version of the Immersive Technology Evaluation Measure (ITEM) (see appendix A), the User Experience Questionnaire-Short (UEQ-S), and an adapted educational AI technology feedback questionnaire based on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), whilst qualitative data will be collected through focus groups analysed using Braun and Clarke's thematic framework. The primary outcome measures perceived realism, technical usability factors, and educational value of AI consultations compared to actor simulations. Secondary outcomes include AI’s comparative performance across (four) different clinical scenarios, feedback quality assessment, and recommendations for curricular integration. Statistical analysis will employ non-parametric methods with effect size calculations and confidence intervals, whilst qualitative analysis will be conducted independently by two researchers with subsequent consensus meetings. This comprehensive evaluation will provide evidence regarding the effectiveness of AI virtual patients for communication skills training, informing future integration into medical curricula whilst addressing stakeholder concerns about the role of technology in clinical education.

title: Robotic Platforms for Flexible GI Endoscopy: An IDEAL-Informed Scoping Review with GRADE Certainty Assessment (2018–2026)
description:
2. Methods
2.1 Study Design and Registration
This study is a scoping review conducted in accordance with the JBI Manual for Evidence Synthesis and reported per PRISMA-ScR (Tricco et al., 2018).
​ A protocol was registered on the Open Science Framework (OSF; osf.io/[INSERT DOI — register before submission]) before final data extraction. The study did not involve human participants or primary data collection; ethics approval was not required.

2.2 Eligibility Criteria (PCC Framework)
Population: Adult patients (≥18 years) undergoing flexible GI endoscopy, or ex vivo/animal models simulating flexible GI endoscopic procedures.

Concept: Robotic, semi-autonomous, or magnetically actuated endoscopic platforms applied within the GI tract lumen (oesophagus, stomach, small bowel, colon, rectum), reporting ≥1 of: en bloc or R0 resection rate; intraprocedural or post-procedural complications (perforation, bleeding); procedure time; or learning curve/workload data.

Context: Any clinical, preclinical (animal/ex vivo), or engineering setting. Primary date window: 1 January 2018 – 13 April 2026. Landmark pre-2018 studies were retained where methodologically anchoring (first-in-human robotic ESD; MCCE landmark accuracy study; robotic colonoscopy foundational trial).

Exclusion: (i) Pure laparoscopic/abdominal robotic surgery without endoluminal GI component; (ii) non-peer-reviewed materials (press releases, conference abstracts without full publication); (iii) no extractable quantitative outcomes; (iv) purely conceptual commentaries without reported data.

2.3 Search Strategy
PubMed (4 structured queries using MeSH + Title/Abstract field tags; full strings in Supplementary S1):

Query 1: Core robotics/GI endoscopy (broad)

Query 2: Therapeutic endoluminal/ESD-specific

Query 3: Robotic colonoscopy (including named systems: Endotics, NeoGuide, invendo, Aer-O-Scope, Medirobots)

Query 4: Magnetically controlled capsule endoscopy

EMBASE (4 parallel Emtree queries): 'endoscopy'/exp AND ('robot'/exp OR 'soft robot*'); 'capsule endoscopy'/exp AND ('magnetic*' OR 'magnetically controlled'); 'endoscopic submucosal dissection'/exp AND 'robot*'; 'colonoscopy'/exp AND ('robot*' OR 'inchworm'); all filtered 2018–2026.

IEEE Xplore: ("endoluminal" OR "endoscopic" OR "gastrointestinal endoscopy" OR "capsule endoscopy" OR "colonoscopy") AND (robot* OR continuum OR "soft robot" OR "tendon-driven" OR "magnetic actuation"); Year 2018–2026; Journals + Conferences.

ClinicalTrials.gov (supplementary registry search, not included in PRISMA peer-reviewed count): "endoscopic robot"; "endoluminal robot"; "magnetically controlled capsule"; "robot-assisted ESD."

2.4 Study Selection and Data Extraction
Two reviewers (F.V. and [co-author]) independently screened titles and abstracts then full texts; disagreements were resolved by consensus with a third reviewer. Inter-rater agreement was calculated using Cohen's kappa (κ). A standardised extraction template captured: PMID/DOI/NCT, year, journal, study design, sample size, platform name, geographic region, outcomes, conflicts of interest, industry funding, and evidence level (E1: SR/MA with RCTs; E2: SR/MA observational; E3: RCT; E4: prospective cohort; E5: retrospective/case series; E6: animal/ex vivo; E7: engineering).

2.5 IDEAL Framework Staging
Each platform was assigned an IDEAL stage (1, 2a, 2b, 3, or 4) per McCulloch et al.
 Stage 2b required a prospective cohort with defined protocol and ≥10 human cases; Stage 3 required multicentre assessment or RCT; Stage 4 required long-term surveillance data (≥5 years, rare outcomes captured). Two reviewers assigned stages independently.

2.6 Risk-of-Bias and Evidence Quality Assessment
RCTs were assessed with Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 (RoB 2); non-randomised studies with ROBINS-I; diagnostic accuracy studies with QUADAS-2. Full tables are provided in Supplementary S3.

2.7 GRADE Certainty Assessment
Domain-level GRADE certainty was assessed per Guyatt et al.
 Observational studies started at Low; RCTs at High. Downgrading considered: risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and publication bias. Upgrading considered: large and consistent effect magnitude, dose-response relationship, and directionality of plausible confounding. Final grades: High (⊕⊕⊕⊕), Moderate (⊕⊕⊕◯), Low (⊕⊕◯◯), Very Low (⊕◯◯◯).

title: What are the most frequently reported clinical signs and symptoms in individuals diagnosed with motor neurone disease? A scoping review
description:
Overview
Motor Neurone Disease (MND) is a progressive and incurable neurodegenerative disorder that results in the degeneration of upper and lower motor neurons, leading to debilitating loss of muscle function, mobility, speech, and ultimately prematurely ending life. Although MND encompasses a spectrum of subtypes including amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), progressive muscular atrophy (PMA), primary lateral sclerosis (PLS), progressive bulbar palsy (PBP), and flail limb variants each presents with variable clinical signs and symptoms, leading to significant delays in diagnosis and overall condition management.
Despite existing guidelines from NICE (2016) highlighting the importance of early recognition and referral, diagnostic delays persist, averaging 12 months from initial symptom onset. Misdiagnosis is common due to the overlap of MND symptoms with those of other neuromuscular and neurological disorders. Recognising the full range of signs and symptoms associated with MND is essential to improving diagnostic accuracy, enhancing care pathways, and potentially providing earlier access to supportive treatments and clinical trials.
Purpose
The purpose of this scoping review is to systematically identify, describe, and map the range of clinical signs and symptoms reported in individuals diagnosed with MND. This includes an exploration of motor, bulbar, respiratory, cognitive, and any atypical or under-recognized symptoms documented across MND subtypes. The review aims to clarify these symptoms and consolidate the evidence with the aim of informing future clinical guidelines.
Research Objectives
1. To explore how the current literature describes the clinical signs and symptoms of MND.
2. To map which specific signs and symptoms aid healthcare professionals in recognising patients with MND.
Methodology

This review will follow the Joanna Briggs Institute methodology for scoping reviews and adhere to the PRISMA-ScR reporting guidelines. The five-stage framework by Arksey & O’Malley (2005) will be employed, including identifying the research question, searching and selecting studies, charting the data, and summarising the results.
A comprehensive search using MEDLINE, APA PsycInfo, CINAHL Ultimate, Academic Search Ultimate, and SPORTDiscus, followed by hand-searching reference lists and Google Scholar will be carried out. Eligible studies included peer-reviewed literature that reported numerical data on clinical signs and symptoms in individuals with a confirmed MND diagnosis, using clinical-epidemiological or descriptive study designs.
Expected Outcomes
• A comprehensive map of signs and symptoms across MND subtypes.
• A clearer understanding of symptom prevalence.
• Identification of knowledge gaps to guide future research and inform clinical training materials.
Significance
This scoping review will support earlier and more accurate recognition of MND by consolidating evidence on its signs and symptoms. It will also contribute to refining diagnostic criteria, educating clinicians, and ensuring timely access to multidisciplinary care, supportive services, and clinical trials for people living with MND.

title: The Development and Validation of an Arabic Digits in Noise Test
description:
This is a PhD project which looks into the development and validation of a lab-based and online Arabic version of the Digits in Noise (DIN) test. The DIN test is a widely used self-administered speech-in-noise hearing screening tool that assesses the understanding of digits in the presence of background noise. It has shown high sensitivity and specificity to screening sensorineural hearing loss and different versions of it have been developed in different world languages including Dutch, British and American English, French, Polish and German. The test can be administered using landline phones, smart devices, online, and in the lab and has been extensively used for auditory research purposes. 

This project aims to assess the validity and reliability of new lab-based and online versions of the DIN test for Arabic speaking countries by determining the correlation between speech-recognition thresholds obtained using the lab-based and online versions of the test with the standard pure-tone audiometric average (PTA) and an extended high frequency (EHF) threshold average. Moreover, test-retest reliability of the lab-based and online versions of the Arabic DIN test will be determined. Both validity and reliability measures will be compared with the respective data obtained by the same participants using the British English version of the DIN test.

title: Diagnostic Assessment for Professional Performance Improvement
description:
Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad (YER) positions Diagnostic Assessment for Professional Performance Improvement as a foundational scholarly contribution that reframes professional performance assessment from a summative, judgment-oriented practice into a diagnostic, developmental, and ethically grounded system. The book responds to a global organizational challenge in which performance evaluations often fail to identify underlying causes of performance gaps, leading to ineffective interventions and diminished professional trust.
From the perspective articulated by Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad (YER), diagnostic assessment serves as an analytical mechanism to understand not only what level of performance is achieved, but why performance emerges in a particular form. This distinction is critical in complex professional environments where performance is influenced by competence, motivation, psychosocial context, organizational design, and systemic constraints.
The central objective advanced by Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad (YER) is to establish a scientifically grounded framework for diagnosing professional performance that integrates psychometric rigor, organizational psychology, and human-centered management principles. Rather than treating performance deficits as individual failure, the book conceptualizes them as multidimensional signals requiring structured interpretation.
Methodologically, Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad (YER) adopts an interdisciplinary approach, synthesizing diagnostic logic from educational assessment, clinical psychology, and strategic human resource management. This approach enables performance assessment to function as a learning-oriented process embedded within continuous professional development systems.
A key contribution articulated by Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad (YER) is the differentiation between evaluative assessment and diagnostic assessment. While evaluative assessment categorizes outcomes, diagnostic assessment identifies causal patterns, developmental needs, and contextual misalignments that hinder professional effectiveness.
The book further examines the role of digital tools and analytics, as discussed by Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad (YER), emphasizing their potential to enhance diagnostic accuracy while warning against reductive performance metrics detached from human meaning.
Implications outlined by Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad (YER) extend to leadership decision-making, talent development, performance coaching, and organizational learning systems. Diagnostic assessment is positioned as a strategic capability that aligns performance improvement with ethical responsibility.
Overall, Diagnostic Assessment for Professional Performance Improvement, as developed by Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad (YER), offers a comprehensive, evidence-based, and humanistic framework for advancing professional performance in contemporary organizations.

title: Application of Outer Membrane Protein Omp25 in Serological Diagnosis of Brucellosis
description: Brucellosis is a prevalent global zoonotic disease caused by Brucella spp., posing major public health and economic challenges particularly in endemic regions. Conventional serological diagnosis using whole-cell or lipopolysaccharide (LPS) antigens suffers from cross-reactivity with other Gram-negative bacteria and cannot distinguish natural infection from vaccine-induced immunity. Outer membrane protein 25 (Omp25) is a highly conserved, immunodominant antigen across Brucella species and has emerged as a promising target for improved serological diagnosis. This retrospective systematic review and descriptive analysis synthesizes existing diagnostic accuracy studies evaluating Omp25-based serological assays in human and animal sera. Literature was searched up to January 15, 2026 in PubMed and Web of Science. Ten eligible studies were included; substantial heterogeneity precluded meta-analysis. Stratified descriptive analysis was performed by antigen format (single Omp25, equal-concentration mixed proteins, multi-epitope fusion proteins) and host species (human, bovine, caprine, canine, ovine, murine). Multi-epitope fusion protein formats achieved the highest weighted mean sensitivity (96.04%) with low heterogeneity, while mixed protein approaches achieved the highest specificity (weighted mean 98.45%). These findings provide evidence-based guidance for selecting Omp25-based diagnostic formats in clinical and epidemiological settings and identify key gaps for future standardized, multicenter studies.

title: Comparing Predictive Accuracy of Preeclampsia Prediction Tests
description:
Hypertensive disorders in pregnancy (HDP) are common causes of maternal and neonatal morbidity and mortality. These disorders include chronic hypertension with superimposed pre-eclampsia, pre-eclampsia (PE), chronic hypertension, and gestational hypertension (Makino et al., 2019). Pre-eclampsia is a major cause of adverse maternal and perinatal outcomes. It is defined as new onset hypertension, systolic blood pressure (BP) ≥140 mmHg and/or diastolic BP ≥90 mmHg after 20 weeks of gestation, with proteinuria and/or signs of maternal organ dysfunction affecting organs like brain, liver or kidney (G. Chen et al., 2024; Ustunyurt et al., 2021). 
The purpose of this review is to help standardize screening techniques and find the most clinically useful tools. Given that pre-eclampsia is a major cause of worldwide maternal and neonatal mortality, identifying correct and practical prediction tests will help to enable earlier risk stratification. 
The main expected outcome is to identify tests that best predict preeclampsia in terms of sensitivity and specificity, positive Predictive Value (PPV), negative Predictive Value (NPV) and Area Under the Curve (AUC) in the different trimesters.

title: Clinical significance of Intestinal Fatty Acid-Binding Protein (I-FABP or FABP2) in children and adolescents with celiac disease; a systematic review and meta-analysis.
description:
Celiac disease (CD) is a chronic autoimmune enteropathy triggered by gluten ingestion in genetically susceptible individuals, leading to intestinal inflammation and malabsorption. Early diagnosis in children is essential to prevent growth failure, nutritional deficiencies, and long-term complications. However, current diagnostic tools, primarily based on serological markers and intestinal biopsy, have limitations in sensitivity and specificity or are invasive procedures.

Intestinal fatty acid-binding protein (I-FABP or FABP2), a cytoplasmic protein expressed in enterocytes, has emerged as a promising biomarker of intestinal epithelial damage. Elevated levels of FABP2 in serum or plasma have been reported in several gastrointestinal disorders, including CD, suggesting its potential utility for diagnosis and monitoring of mucosal integrity. However, neither cut off levels of mucosal injury nor reference values for FABP2 concentrations in healthy children are yet established. This lack of standardization limits the clinical applicability of FABP2 in pediatric CD despite its promising role reported in the literature.

This systematic review and meta-analysis aims to synthesize existing evidence on the clinical significance of FABP2 levels in children and adolescents with celiac disease by clarifying its role as a reliable non-invasive biomarker for diagnosis, disease activity monitoring, or mucosal recovery.

title: Exploring Diagnostic Potential Of Iron Deficiency Biomarkers In Helicobacter Pylori Infection: A Systematic Review And Meta-Analysis Protocol Of Comparative Observational Studies
description:
This project will investigate the preliminary ability of iron deficiency (ID) and iron deficiency anaemia (IDA) biomarkers to serve as comparative discriminators for active Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) infection. Structured as a systematic review and meta-analysis, the work will follow the JBI methodology for reviews of etiology and risk to quantify whether biomarker distributions differ significantly between infected and uninfected populations. The ultimate goal is to identify candidate markers or multivariate panels that can inform a rule-based Clinical Decision Support System (CDSS) for early pathogen detection and clinical triage.
The project will utilize the following framework:
• Eligibility and Scope: The review will include analytical cross-sectional, case-control, and cohort studies involving humans of any age or geographic setting. To ensure clinical homogeneity, the exposure will be restricted to active infection confirmed by validated non-serological tests, specifically the Urea Breath Test (UBT), Stool Antigen Test (SAT), Histology, or Rapid Urease Test (RUT).
• Outcome Quantification: Continuous quantitative data will be extracted for eight core biomarkers: Serum Ferritin, Serum Iron, Total Iron-Binding Capacity (TIBC), Transferrin Saturation (TSAT), Haemoglobin (Hb), MCV, MCH, and sTfR.
• Statistical Synthesis: Standardized Mean Differences (SMDs), specifically Hedges’ g, will be pooled using a random-effects model to account for anticipated clinical and methodological variability.
• Exploratory Diagnostic Potential: To bridge the gap between aetiological association and diagnostic utility, pooled effect sizes will be converted into Derived Area Under the Curve (AUC) values. This will enable the ranking of biomarkers according to their discriminatory capacity.
• Heterogeneity and Confounding: Sources of inconsistency will be explored via subgroup analyses and meta-regression focusing on paediatric vulnerability, gender distribution, and the severity of local gastric inflammation.
By synthesizing these data, the project will determine which biomarkers are best discriminators for H. pylori infection.

title: Correlation between gifts from pharmaceutical companies to French medical academics and their scientific productivity patterns: a protocol for a retrospective study using the French Transparency in Healthcare
description:
Correlation between gifts from pharmaceutical companies to French medical academics and their scientific productivity patterns: a protocol for a retrospective study using the French Transparency in Healthcare

Alexandre Scanff1, Ioana Cristea2,3, Pierre Etienne Savourat1, Thomas Clément1, Benjamin Bastian1, Marion Taburet1, Alain Braillon4, Florian Naudet, Professor1,*
1: Univ Rennes, CHU Rennes, Inserm, CIC 1414 (Centre d’Investigation Clinique de Rennes), France
2: Department of Clinical Psychology and Psychotherapy, Babes-Bolyai University, St.Republicii 37, 400015 Cluj-Napoca, Romania
3: University of Pavia, Department of Brain and Behavioral Sciences, 27100 Pavia, IT
4: Alcohol Treatment Unit, University Hospital, 80054 Amiens CEDEX 1. France
* : corresponding author ; orcid.org/0000-0003-3760-3801 ; mail floriannaudet@gmail.com ; twitter handle /naudetflorian




The scientific impact of academics is appraised with their ability to produce knowledge. Funding, promotion of individuals and survival of their team depends on their publication records and some quantitative citations metrics. Many projects such in genomics [1] can only be conducted in collaboration and new ideas often arise by conversations with colleagues. Collaboration driven by industrialists may also have an impact on researchers' productivity at the price of potential financials conflicts of interest (COIs). Prolific academics are often identified and pushed by industrialists as "Key Opinion Leaders" on the ground of their publication records, lectures, and their participation on different groups [2]. For example, in the field of oncology, financial COIs were correlated with metrics of academic reputation and success [3].
And indeed, committees hiring academics use indicators such as scientific productivity (i.e. number of published papers) and quality. For quality, two proxies are generally used: a) the journal impact factor (JIF) and b) the Hirsch Index (h-index), corresponding to the largest number h of papers one has published that have been cited at least h times. [4] 
We aim to investigate the relationship presently used measures of academic success (publications/citations/h-index) with the potential financial COIs.
Methods
Study design and participants
The project will be based on a protocol that will be registered on the Open Science Framework prior any data collection.
In France, academic duties require both an active clinical activity and a research activity. While clinical skills are only evaluated qualitatively, assessment of research activity entails publication metrics, which are easy to quantify and investigate. This study will be conducted and reported to the Standards for Reporting Diagnostic Accuracy. [5]
One researcher will identify all French Medical Professors and associated professors (and their academic discipline) from lists of the different universities and the “annuaire santé” that also details sex and medical specialty (i.e. academic discipline). Then we will extract from online databases (e.g. Google Scholar, Web of Science, Scopus) the year of their first paper (an indicator of seniority) and quantitative indicators of productivity for the 2014-2019 period (h-index over the period, number of papers and number of citations).
For each academic, the amount of money declared by the industry during the 2014-2019 period will be extracted from the French database registering all direct gifts (e.g., meals or congress-related hotel, and travel costs) perceived by healthcare players. This open access database was created in 2012 (https://www.transparence.sante.gouv.fr/) and the industry is required by law to report. We will use only the “advantage” table, comprising all industry funding which in theory is not associated with a contractual obligation of the recipient. Two more tables exist, which report “conventions” and “remunerations” when there is a contractual obligation for the recipient, but reporting the monetary value was not mandatory and poorly implemented during the all the study period, and thus the amount is almost-always lacking. An automatic search will be developed, possibly completed by manual checks to explore the possibility of misidentification.
Ethics
We are seeking the opinion of an ethics committee, namely that of the CNGE Ethics Committee. The procedure toward protection of persons has been validated by the Data Privacy Officer of Rennes 1 University. In view of the large number of subjects studied, we cannot afford to contact all of them. Moreover, this step would risk adding a social desirability bias to the results of our study that may invalidate the study results. Data collected are not considered as sensitive data by the French law. In addition, general information will be made publicly available on the Reither website (https://www.reither.org/) detailing the protocol, the use that will be made of the data, with a contact information (Pr Florian Naudet: floriannaudet@gmail.com). This information will also be detailed in the thesis references once it has been published to indicate to the interested parties the right of access to any data concerning them. 
Indexes
The f-index will be defined as the sum of gifts received by each academic in the 2014-2019 period (meals, and/or travel/accommodation expenses). The gold standard used for the purpose of the study will be high scientific productivity defined for an academic as an h-index over the period 2014-2019 in the top quartile of h-indexes in the group analysed and in subgroups defined by all academic discipline for subgroup analyses. As no gold standard exists but institutions need to take decisions under constraints of limited time and budgets, we opted for this standard. It reflects the fact that in the current system effectively only a few top researchers can expect promotion.
Outcomes and analysis
First, a descriptive analysis will be performed, consisting of numbers and percentages for categoric outcomes, and means, standard-deviations for quantitative outcomes. Then, Pearson’s correlations will be used to explore the association between indicators and several characteristics of the academics, after logarithmic transformation (index value+1), if needed.
Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curves will be drawn by plotting sensitivity vs. one minus specificity and the optimal threshold will be determined according to Youden’s J measure. The main outcome for this study will be the diagnostic properties (sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, negative predictive value) of the f-index to objectively reflect high scientific productivity. [6]
Finally, to account for possible variations according to subspecialty, subgroup analyses (f-index, h-index, correlation between f-index and h-index, optimal threshold) will be explored by academic discipline separately. 95% confidence intervals for test parameters will be estimated by bootstrap procedure.
An exploratory analysis of the effect of sex and year of first paper on the f-index will be realized by linear mixed model, using a random intercept for academic speciality.

title: Assessing pedal acceleration time in peripheral arterial disease and critical limb threatening ischaemia – A protocol for a scoping review protocol of clinical reliability, diagnostic accuracy and prognostic capacity
description:
Background
Peripheral arterial disease (PAD) and Chronic Limb threatening ischemia (CLTI) present a significant disease burden and can lead to major amputation and premature mortality. It is therefore integral that the disease is identified early allowing for appropriate management. There are numerous non-invasive vascular assessment tools used in clinical practice, however each assessment presents limitations in either reliability, diagnostic accuracy or prognostic capacity. Pedal acceleration time (PAT) is proposed to overcome some of these issues and is a novel test proposed for use in identifying PAD and CLTI and also as a predictor of wound healing. While PAT shows promise, there remains a need to comprehensively evaluate its clinical reliability, diagnostic accuracy, and prognostic capacity in individuals with PAD and critical limb threatening ischaemia. 
Objectives 
This scoping review aims to synthesise and map current evidence relating to PAT, with the following objectives:
1. Describe the inter-tester and intra-tester reliability of PAT
2. Describe the diagnostic accuracy of PAT in PAD and/or CLTI
3. Describe the prognostic capacity of PAT for wound healing and/or major amputation
Eligibility criteria
Studies published in English exploring the use of PAT to determine PAD severity in human adults will be eligible for inclusion. 
Sources of evidence
Five databases will be searched for relevant articles, with Covidence® being utilised for title, abstract and full text screening, and data extraction. Results will be synthesised narratively. Two reviewers will screen each title, abstract and full text, with a third reviewer resolving conflicts. 
Discussion 
This scoping review findings will inform clinical practice and whether PAT is the most effective measurement for determining PAD, CLTI and predicting wound healing and/or amputation. Study results will inform clinical practice and future guidelines.

title: Investigating the Diagnostic Accuracy of Electrodiagnostic Tests for Peripheral Neuropathy in Diabetic Patients

title: Temporal Dynamics of Trust: A Systematic Review of Clinician-Facing AI Technologies in Healthcare
description:
The field of Artificial Intelligence (AI) presents a transformative opportunity to enhance healthcare by augmenting diagnostic accuracy, optimising treatment plans and improving patient outcomes. However, the integration of AI into the healthcare is contingent upon establishing a robust foundation of trust between clinicians, patients and the technology itself. Past studies have demonstrated that concerns related to transparency, explainability, and accountability can erode trust in technologies, leading to decreased usage 1–3. 
Trust is a psychological state comprising the intention to accept vulnerability based on positive expectations of the intentions or behaviour of another. In the context of healthcare AI, trust reflects a clinician’s willingness to rely on AI systems in clinical decision-making, despite inherent uncertainties. It involves perceptions of the AI system’s reliability, competence, integrity, and alignment with professional values. Building trust requires transparency, explainability, consistency, and demonstrated efficacy of the AI system in supporting clinical goals.
In the context of healthcare, where the stakes are particularly high, fostering trust in AI is imperative to ensure its widespread and beneficial implementation. While several studies have explored how different stakeholders perceive and trust AI technology, there is a gap in research investigating the longitudinal impact of AI exposure on clinician trust levels1,4. Existing research emphasizes the role of trust in AI adoption but often lacks a longitudinal perspective, focusing instead on general user attitudes and acceptance. Critically, this understanding necessitates the development of robust evaluation protocols capable of rigorously measuring temporal variations in trust 5, thereby facilitating a comprehensive assessment of the true impact of AI exposure on clinician trust and, ultimately, patient care.
To address this knowledge gap, this study aims to conduct a systematic review examining clinician-facing AI technologies that have investigated the longitudinal impact of AI exposure on trust. By systematically analysing existing research, this review seeks to provide valuable insights into the evolving dynamics of clinician trust in AI within the healthcare domain. 
The core constructs of interest of this review are:
- Trust: Willingness to rely on AI systems in clinical decision-making, shaped by perceptions of the system’s reliability, competence, integrity, and alignment with professional values.
- Repeated exposure: The key independent variable influencing Clinicians trust in AI.
- AI Technology in Healthcare setting: The specific context of AI use.
- Longitudinal: The temporal aspect of trust development.
Core research question:
How does clinician’s trust in AI evolve over time with repeated exposure? 
Secondary questions:
1. How is trust in AI currently measured?
2. What factors influence the development of clinician trust in AI systems over time? Specifically, how do the type of AI application (e.g., diagnostic, prognostic, treatment planning), the level of explainability, and the extent of integration into clinical workflows affect trust dynamics?
3. What factors mediate or moderate the relationship between continuous AI exposure and clinician trust? Specifically, how do clinician experience level, the usability of AI system interfaces, cultural dimensions (e.g., collectivism vs. individualism), and the occurrence of rare, unexpected events influence the evolution of trust over time?

2 Choung H, David P, Ross A. Trust in AI and Its Role in the Acceptance of AI Technologies. International Journal of Human–Computer Interaction 2023; 39: 1727–39.
3 Barredo Arrieta A, Díaz-Rodríguez N, Del Ser J, et al. Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI): Concepts, taxonomies, opportunities and challenges toward responsible AI. Information Fusion 2020; 58: 82–115.

title: CEUS for chRCC vs Renal Oncocytoma: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Diagnostic Test Accuracy
description: This systematic review and meta-analysis aims to synthesise the diagnostic accuracy of contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS) for differentiation of chromophobe renal cell carcinoma (chRCC) from renal oncocytoma (RO), with histopathology as the reference standard. Both entities are believed to arise from the intercalated cells of the distal collecting duct and share overlapping morphological, immunohistochemical, and imaging features. Distinguishing them is clinically important: chRCC is a malignant neoplasm requiring surgical resection, whereas RO is benign and is increasingly managed by active surveillance or nephron-sparing approaches. To the authors' knowledge, no published systematic review has specifically synthesised the diagnostic performance of CEUS for this differential. The review is conducted in accordance with PRISMA 2020 and PRISMA-DTA reporting standards. Preliminary searches were conducted across PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, Scopus, and Web of Science between 2026-05-22 and 2026-05-23, identifying 165 unique records for title/abstract screening. The primary analysis (Plan A) uses a bivariate random-effects model and hierarchical summary ROC (HSROC) approach if ≥10 studies are eligible; a feature-level meta-analysis (Plan B) or narrative synthesis (Plan C) will be used contingent on lower study yield.
