title: Real-time detection of eating behavior and meal consumption by commercial wrist-worn smartwatches: protocol for a systematic review and meta-analysis
description: Accurate assessment of dietary consumption and eating behavior is essential for understanding nutrition-health relationships, yet traditional dietary assessment methods are subject to recall bias, social desirability bias, and high participant burden. Commercial wrist-worn smartwatches provide a promising, unobtrusive platform for real-time detection of eating behavior by capturing hand-to-mouth movements and related intake gestures through embedded sensors in naturalistic settings. This systematic review protocol aims to synthesize the existing evidence on the diagnostic accuracy, analytical performance, and feasibility of commercial wrist-worn smartwatches for real-time detection of eating behavior and meal consumption. The review will be conducted in accordance with PRISMA 2020 guidelines, with additional adherence to PRISMA-DTA for diagnostic accuracy studies and PRISMA-P for protocol reporting. Findings will inform the translational potential of smartwatch-based approaches for applications in clinical nutrition, behavioral interventions, and public health monitoring.

title: Do differences in facial positioning influence the susceptibility of memory? An investigation into the misinformation effect and eyewitness misidentificatio. (Working Title).
description:
Reserach utilising the Misinformation Paradigm to examine eyewitness suceptibility to misinformation when exposed to different and similar facial positions at encoding and the misinformation phase. 

Full registration infromation is provided below and within the relevant heading boxes:

Have any data been collected for this study already? (optional)

No, no data have been collected for this study yet.

What's the main question being asked or hypothesis being tested in this study? (optional)

We have previously developed two mock-crime videos, each showing the same perpetrator committing the same crime (i.e., a robbery) following the same script. In one video, the perpetrator is shown in only frontal view, and in the other video, the perpetrator is shown only in profile view (i.e., only the right side of his face is shown). 

We have also developed a misinformation news video, which will contain an image of police suspect. The police suspect is not the real culprit (i.e. is misinformation), but the news report explains that a man has been apprehended by police in relation to a recent handbag theft in the area. The report will also explain that police officers reviewed CCTV of the event and looked like a local resident and this is the individual who has been apprehended. Participants will also be informed that the apprehended suspect is maintaining innocence. A headshot of the arrested suspect will then be shown on screen, followed by a request for members of the public to get in touch if they have any further information relating to the crime. 

For the mock-crime video, we have created a 6-person target-present lineup (which includes the perpetrator and 5 fillers) and a 6-person target-absent lineup (which includes the misinformation suspect and 5 fillers and does not include the perpetrator). Further, we have created four versions of the lineup: frontal pose with target present, frontal pose with target absent, profile pose with target present, profile pose with target absent. Frontal pose lineups show only the front of the face of each lineup member; profile pose lineups show only the profile pose (i.e., right side of the face) of each lineup member.

In this study, we are testing whether identification accuracy is better when the misinformation innocent suspect in the news report is presented in a different pose (e.g., front) to the perpetrator at encoding and lineup members at test (e.g., profile), compared to when the misinformation innocent suspect in the news report is presented in the same pose (e.g., front) to the perpetrator at encoding and lineup members at test (e.g., front). 

Specifically, we ask: 
RQ1: Is susceptibility to misinformation acceptance decreased (i.e., fewer innocent suspect IDs in TA lineup, and more correct guilty suspect identifications IDs in TP lineup) when the misinformation is presented in a different pose to the encoding event and test compared to when the misinformation is in the same pose? 

RQ2: Is discrimination accuracy better (as measured by pAUC) when misinformation is presented in a different pose to the encoded event and lineup test, compared to when misinformation is presented in the same pose as the encoded event and lineup test?

RQ3. Is discrimination accuracy higher when participants view a profile misinformation face when the encoding and test faces are frontal, compared to when participants view a frontal misinformation face when the encoding and test faces are profile. 

Hereafter, the same pose conditions include the conditions in which the encoding, misinformation and test poses were the same (i.e., Front encoding, Front misinformation, Front test, or Profile encoding, Profile misinformation, Profile test). Hereafter, the different pose conditions include the conditions in which the encoding and test poses matched and the misinformation was presented in a different pose (i.e., Front, Profile, Front or Profile, Front, Profile). 

(RQ1) We predict that the false alarm rate to the innocent suspect in the target-absent condition will be lower in the different-pose compared to same-pose misinformation condition, and the HR to the perpetrator in target-present lineups will be higher in the different-pose compared to same-pose misinformation condition. This is because the misinformation similarity literature (in which people are asked to correctly identify another individual), suggests that higher similarity between misinformation and the encoding event will lead to more identification errors. That is, increased similarity between stooges in the study led to increases in conjunction errors in which participants incorrectly associated a familiar actor with a familiar action that was actually performed by someone else (Earles, Kersten, Curtayne & Perle, 2008).

(RQ2) Because we predict the above patterns in the HR and FAR in the different-pose compared to same-pose misinformation condition, we predict that discrimination accuracy (ability to discriminate between innocent and guilty suspects) will be the better when participants are exposed to different-pose misinformation compared to same-pose misinformation.


(RQ3) We also predict discrimination accuracy will be higher when participants view a profile misinformation face when the encoding and test faces are frontal, compared to when participants view a frontal misinformation face when the encoding and test faces are profile. This is because faces encoded and tested from the front have been found to be more easily recognisable (Colloff et al., 2020). The possible reasons why front faces are more easily recognised may be explained by better holistic encoding when the face is viewed from the front (Taubert, Apthorp, Aagten-Murphy & Alais, 2011) and the importance of viewing important front facial features when encoding a face (McKelvie, 1976). Therefore, if the original encoding is strong (i.e., viewing the front of the face), but the misinformation is weaker (i.e., viewing the side of a face), then memory strength for the stronger facial position may mean participants are less likely to be misinformed. 

If different pose misinformation results in better discrimination accuracy than same pose, then we will conclude that individuals are less likely to be misinformed when misinformation is presented in a different facial position at misinformation than at encoding and test (RQ1-2). If discrimination accuracy is higher when profile pose misinformation is introduced to frontal encoding/test compared to frontal pose misinformation introduced during profile encoding/test, it can be concluded that a face presented in profile pose face is less likely to misinform participants than a face presented in frontal pose (RQ3).



Design:
A traditional Misinformation Paradigm will be used, consisting of an encoding event, misinformation exposure and a memory test. Therefore, I will use a 2 (perpetrator pose at encoding and test: front or profile) x 2 (Misinformation suspect pose: front or profile) x 2 (lineup condition: target absent or target present) between-subjects design. The facial positioning the participant views at encoding will always be matched at test (i.e. front facing at encoding = front facing at test, or profile facing at encoding = profile facing at test). 


Method:
Participants will watch a mock crime video depicting a theft. The perpetrator will be shown committing the theft in frontal pose only, or in profile pose only. After approximately 1 minute of completing a distractor task, participants will be shown a television style news broadcast discussing the theft. During the broadcast the innocent (misinformation) suspect will be shown either from a frontal or profile facial position. Participants will be told during the broadcast that the innocent suspect has been arrested in relation to the theft, however they are maintaining their innocence. After a further 1-minute distractor task, participants will be told that will be shown 6 photos and asked whether the perpetrator who they saw committing the crime in the video is present. They will be told that the perpetrator may or may not be present and so not identifying anyone might be the correct answer. Next, participants will be shown a 6-person simultaneous lineup, consisting of either the perpetrator and 5 fillers (target-present), or the innocent suspect with 5 fillers (target-absent). The participant may look at the lineup members for any length of time desired. The participant will be asked whether the perpetrator from the crime video was present in the lineup and asked to select the picture they believe is the perpetrator. Participants will also be given the option to select “I do not believe the criminal is present” if they do not believe the original perpetrator is present in the lineup. For participants who select a person from the lineup, they will be asked to provide a confidence rating regarding how confident they are in their decision. The scale will range from 50-100 ascending in 10 increments, with 50 being “guessing” and 100 being “completely certain the person IS the perpetrator”. If a participant selected that the perpetrator is not present, they will be told “Identify the person who is most likely to be the perpetrator” and asked to provide a confidence rating regarding how confident they are in their decision. The scale will range from 100-50 descending in 10 increments, with 100 being “completely certain the person is NOT the perpetrator” to 50 “guessing. Afterwards, participants will be asked a multiple-choice attention check about the content of the video (e.g., “what happened in the video that you watched”). Finally, Participants will be debriefed as to the aim of the study.


Describe the key dependent variable(s) specifying how they will be measured. (optional)

1) Identification responses: For each lineup condition, we will calculate the proportion of perpetrator (i.e., correct “yes” decisions, ‘hits’), filler (i.e., incorrect “yes” decisions) and reject (i.e., incorrect “no”) identification decisions in the target-present lineups, and we will calculate the proportion of innocent suspect (i.e., incorrect “yes” decisions, ‘false alarms’), filler (i.e., incorrect “yes” decisions) and reject (i.e., correct “no”) identification decisions in the target-absent lineups. For example, the proportion of perpetrator identifications is calculated by dividing the total number of correct perpetrator identification decisions by the total number of target-present lineups, the proportion of filler identification decisions in target-present lineups is calculated by dividing the total number of incorrect filler identifications by the total number of target-present lineups etc. 

2) Discriminability (atheoretical measure): We will calculate partial area under the curve (pAUC) values and CIs using the statistical package pROC (Robin et al. 2011). For our main analysis (RQ2), we will calculate pAUC for the same pose and different pose conditions. To answer RQ3, and check that the results are the same over front encoding and test conditions (i.e., FFF, FPF) and profile encoding and test conditions (i.e., FFF, FPF), we will also calculate pAUC for each of the 4 experimental conditions 2 (perpetrator pose during encoding and test: frontal or profile) x 2 (Misinformation suspect pose: frontal or profile). To calculate pAUC we will construct partial ROC curves. Each curve will plot the hit rate (HR) against the false alarm rate (FAR) over decreasing levels of confidence. HR will be the number of perpetrator IDs ÷ number of target-present lineups and FAR will be the number of innocent suspect IDs ÷ number of target-absent lineups. Confidence will be conceptualised on a single confidence scale (ranging from 100 ‘certain not the perpetrator’ to 50 (guessing not the perpetrator’ to 50 ‘guessing is the perpetrator’ to 100 ‘certain is the perpetrator’. Each curve will plot 12 HR-FAR pairs over decreasing levels of confidence, such that the left-most points of the curves show the HR and FAR at the highest level of confidence (i.e., when subjects reported that they were 100% certain that the person was the perpetrator); the second points on the curves show the cumulative HR and FAR for the two highest levels of confidence (i.e., 100% certain and 90% certain that the person was the perpetrator), and so forth. The right-most points of the curves show the HRs & FARs for all subjects who made an identification in that condition (see Colloff & Wixted, 2020; Mickes, Flowe, & Wixted, 2012). Specificity (1 – FAR) when calculating the pAUC will be set using the smallest FAR range, with the FAR range determined by the estimated innocent suspect ID FAR rate. 

3) Discriminability (theoretical measure): We will also fit a signal-detection process model to the data in each of the two (same pose, different pose) conditions (e.g., Wixted & Mickes, 2014). The model uses counts of perpetrator, foil and reject identification decisions made at different levels of confidence in target-present and target-absent lineups to estimate discriminability (i.e., ability to discriminate between innocent and guilty suspects) and a set of confidence criteria. The specific discriminability measure will depend on whether an equal-variance model, or an unequal-variance model provides the best fit to the data (as measured by chi-square goodness of fit test). If an equal variance model is used, the discriminability measure will be d'. If an unequal variance model is used and the magnitude of the unequal variance parameter does not vary across conditions, then the discriminability measure will be d (the distance between the means of the innocent and guilty distributions in units of σinnocent). If an unequal variance model is used and the magnitude of the unequal variance parameter does vary across conditions, then the discriminability measure will be da using the standard formula: (µguilty - µinnocent) / √[.5(σ2guilty + σ2innocent)]. Note that setting µinnocent = 0 and σinnocent = 1 by convention, the equation reduces to da = µguilty / √[.5(σ2guilty + 1)]. We will use the independent observation model (but we will explore the fit of other models, e.g., ensemble model, to see if the ensemble model improves the fit; see Wixted et al., 2018). We will run 1,000 iterations using fminsearch. 

How many and which conditions will participants be assigned to? (optional)

Subjects will be randomly assigned into one of the 8 experimental conditions (i.e., 2 perpetrator pose x 2 lineup conditions x 2 target present or absent lineup). Each experimental condition is depicted in the table 1. 

Table 1: Table to show Front (F), Profile (P), Target Present (TP) and Target Absent (TA) experimental conditions.

Front Front Front – Target Present FFF-TP
Front Front Front- Target Absent FFF-TA
Front Profile Front- Target Present FPF-TP
Front Profile Front- Target Absent FPF-TA
Profile Profile Profile – Target Present PPP-TP
Profile Profile Profile- Target Absent PPP-TA
Profile Front Profile- Target Present PFP-TP

Specify exactly which analyses you will conduct to examine the main question/hypothesis. (optional)
1. Identification Responses. For our main analysis we plan to collapse the data across “same misinformation pose” (i.e., FFF, PPP) and “different misinformation pose” (i.e., FPF, PFP) conditions. We will first test the difference in the HR across same vs different conditions, and FAR across same vs different conditions using pairwise z tests. This will answer RQ1.
 
2. Discriminability (atheoretical measure): To statistically compare the same vs different ROCs, we will use the statistical package pROC to make a pairwise comparison using D, which is the difference of the two pAUCs divided by the standard deviation of the difference estimated by bootstrapping (Robin et al. 2011). This will answer RQ2.

We also plan to repeat this same vs different analysis separately for the front encoding and test conditions (i.e., FFF, FPF) and then for the profile encoding and test conditions (i.e., PPP, PFP). This will allow us to check that the pattern of results is the same across two perpetrator pose at encoding and test conditions.

We will also compare ROCs for FPF with PFP using the statistical package pROC to make a pairwise comparison using D. This will answer RQ3.

3. Discriminability (theoretical measure): We will make a pairwise comparison (same pose, different pose). We will first fit a model with discriminability parameter free to vary over the two conditions being compared (full model). We will then fit a reduced model, which constrains the discriminability parameter to be the same across the two conditions. If the reduced model provides a significantly worse fit of the data than the full model (using chi-square test), then this suggests that there is a statistically significant difference in discriminability across the two conditions. Again, the manipulated categorical conditions are (same pose, different pose), whereas the dependent variable is discrimination accuracy (measured by d', d or da, as noted above). 





Any secondary analyses? (optional)
We will plot CACs (following Mickes, 2015) to examine proportion correct at each level of confidence in the experimental conditions.



How many observations will be collected or what will determine sample size? 

Based on the conventions used in the lineup literature, in each of the 8 conditions, we will aim to recruit a minimum of 250 participants, with the total number of participants in the experiment equal to at least 2,000 participants (i.e., 8 conditions x 250 = 2,000). Using the mean difference and standard deviations observed in Mickes, Flowe, and Wixted (2012) as a guide, a power analysis indicated that, with 250 subjects per between-subjects condition, power would exceed 80% (for RQ3). A further 25 participants will be recruited for each condition to mitigate the impact of incomplete data collection, repetition or participation (i.e., 8 conditions x 25 = 200). As such, the total number of participants to be recruited is 2,200. 


Anything else you would like to pre-register? (e.g., data exclusions, variables collected for exploratory purposes, unusual analyses planned?) (optional)

Data will be excluded if participants report technical problems after watching the mock-crime video, or if participants incorrectly answer the attention check question. If a participant has taken part more than once (e.g., there are repetitions of the same email address / ID code), only data from their first completion will be included in the data for analysis.

At present we expect to receive full funding to obtain the number of aforementioned participants. In the event that we receive less funding given the COVID-19 pandemic, we will amend the sample size accordingly and focus on collapsing data across same vs different misinformation pose (i.e., recruit at least 250 in the collapsed “same pose” and “different pose” conditions, which will give us sufficient power to address RQ2-the main RQ-but limited power to address RQ3 using ROC analysis).

title: Deep Learning for Whole-Slide Histologic Subtyping of Lung Cancer: A Systematic Review and Diagnostic Test Accuracy Meta-analysis
description:
This project is a systematic review and restricted exploratory diagnostic test accuracy meta-analysis evaluating deep learning models for whole-slide histologic subtyping of lung cancer using H&E-stained digital pathology images. The review focuses on clinically relevant classification tasks, including adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, small-cell carcinoma, and benign or histologic mimic categories. Seven electronic databases (Web of Science, Scopus, PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Online Library, Europe PMC, and Semantic Scholar) were searched through April 25, 2026.

The study synthesizes evidence regarding the diagnostic performance, methodological quality, and clinical applicability of artificial intelligence systems in computational pathology. Quantitative synthesis was restricted to clinically interpretable whole-slide, slide-, or case-level datasets with extractable 2 × 2 diagnostic accuracy data for adenocarcinoma versus squamous cell carcinoma. Secondary analyses summarize reported AUCs, likelihood ratios, diagnostic odds ratios, risk of bias, and evidence gaps across different diagnostic tasks.

This review highlights both the promise and current limitations of deep learning for lung cancer histologic classification and emphasizes the need for external validation, standardized reporting, clinically relevant operating thresholds, and pathologist-supervised implementation before routine clinical adoption.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Dermatology in Sub-Saharan Africa: A Scoping Review Protocol
description:
Background: Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) faces a critical shortage of dermatology specialists, with fewer than 1 dermatologist per 1 million people in some countries. Skin diseases, including Neglected Tropical Diseases (NTDs), fungal infections, and skin cancers, cause substantial morbidity, yet diagnostic capacity remains severely limited. Artificial intelligence (AI) technologies offer potential solutions through image-based diagnosis, but implementation in resource-limited settings faces unique challenges.
Objectives: This scoping review aims to map the current landscape of AI technologies applied to dermatology in SSA, identify implementation barriers and facilitators using the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR), and assess feasibility for deployment in resource-limited settings.
Methods: We will include original research (diagnostic accuracy studies, implementation studies, qualitative research, mixed methods, case studies) and systematic/scoping reviews published between January 1, 2018, and March 31, 2026, in English or French. Studies must evaluate AI-based dermatological tools in SSA settings and report performance metrics or implementation outcomes. We will search PubMed, IEEE Xplore, Google Scholar, and African Journals Online (AJOL), complemented by grey literature from WHO, WHO AFRO, KEMRI, and clinical trial registries. Two independent reviewers will screen titles/abstracts and full texts using Rayyan. Data extraction will use a standardized form capturing study characteristics, AI technology, disease focus, performance metrics, and implementation determinants mapped to CFIR domains. Data will be synthesized narratively following Synthesis Without Meta-Analysis (SWiM) guidelines.
Results: Findings will be presented as a narrative synthesis with descriptive mapping, CFIR-framed implementation analysis, feasibility assessment, and a practical implementation framework for AI dermatology deployment in SSA.
Conclusions: This review will synthesize evidence on AI dermatology in SSA, identify implementation barriers and facilitators, and provide guidance for responsible AI deployment in resource-limited settings

title: Artificial Intelligence for Diagnosis and Segmentation in Laryngoscopy: A Systematic Review
description:
Objective: To systematically evaluate the diagnostic performance of artificial intelligence (AI) in laryngoscopic imaging and to compare the diagnostic accuracy and clinical applicability across various imaging modalities and AI architectures.
Methods: Adhering to the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, a systematic search was performed across PubMed, ScienceDirect, and Web of Science databases for studies published between 2018 and 2025. Original research articles that applied AI to laryngoscopic images or videos for diagnosis, detection, or segmentation were included. Two reviewers independently conducted the literature screening and data extraction.
Results: A total of 42 studies were included. Deep learning models demonstrated diagnostic performance comparable to that of clinical experts in the identification of laryngeal lesions. Models utilizing NBI imaging demonstrated superior performance in the detection of early-stage laryngeal cancer compared with standard WLI models. However, the QUADAS-2 assessment revealed that 80% of the studies exhibited a high risk of bias in the "Patient Selection" domain, primarily attributed to the retrospective pre-selection of high-quality images with limited sample sizes.
Conclusion: AI holds significant potential in laryngeal lesion detection and can effectively augment clinicians workflows. However，despite the high-performance metrics reported, significant challenges persist . Future research should prioritize the development of high-quality datasets and facilitate the clinical translation of AI systems.

title: BipoSense Statistical Process Control Method
description: Early detection of emerging affective episodes is crucial in managing bipolar disorder (BD). Passive sensing - passive data collection via smartphone or wearable - offers a promising solution by potentially capturing altered activity, communication, and sleep patterns, indicative of manic and depressive episodes. Recently, statistical process control (SPC) has been introduced to psychopathology as a novel approach to identify out-of-control processes. However, its application to mobile sensing data and to bipolar disorder remains unexplored. To investigate SPC’s potential in detecting emerging affective episodes, we utilized the BipoSense study, which monitored patients with BD. The BipoSense data covers 12 months of continuously collected passive sensing data via smartphone app, daily e-diary data and bi-weekly expert interviews, i.e. 26 in a row, to assess the psychopathological status. Compliance was excellent. A total of 29 depressive and 20 (hypo)manic emerging episodes in 28 patients were included in the analyses. SPC charts and multilevel analyses revealed heterogenous results. Passive sensing, despite its potential as a low-burden, continuous measurement tool, did not demonstrate robust detection of affective episodes or prodromal states. Self-rated current bipolar mood, assessed via e-diary, outperformed passive sensing parameters in predicting current episodes, whereas predicting prodromal phases was also limited. Notably, SPC with personalized control limits did not surpass established clinical cut-off scores. Even after systematic optimization of SPC settings, the combination of detected emerging episodes in relation to false alarms was insufficient for clinical use. Future studies warrant mobile sensing parameters closer aligned to psychopathology, therewith increasing validity, sensitivity, and specificity.

title: Five Minute ASD Diagnostic Impressions
description:
“Frank autism” describes the distinct behavioral presentation of individuals with ASD, and is recognizable within minutes of meeting the individual. To date, clinicians use this term loosely to describe a wide range of behavioral presentations that do not necessarily correspond to overall level of functioning. In one study that aimed to better understand the utility of this phenomenon, licensed psychologists watched 10-minute video clips of another clinician administering the Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule (ADOS; Lord, Rutter, DiLavore, & Risi, 2002) to toddlers who had previously been flagged as possibly having ASD on a commonly used ASD screening tool (Gibrielsen, et. al., 2015). After watching the video, clinicians were instructed to indicate whether they would refer the child for a comprehensive ASD-specific assessment. Of the children that were observed, 61% were referred and ultimately diagnosed with ASD, 25% were referred but ultimately diagnosed with language delays, and 11% were referred but were ultimately found to be typically developing. The sensitivity and specificity of the referral process was 0.61 and 0.82, respectively. From the total sample of children observed, one-third of the children were ultimately diagnosed with ASD, one-third were ultimately diagnosed with a language delay but no ASD, and one-third were found to fall within the broad range of typical development. These findings suggest that trained clinicians are able to identify individuals with ASD and discern them from individuals who may have other developmental delays from behavioral observation alone. However, it also demonstrates that not all toddlers with ASD present with behavioral characteristics that are readily apparent, given that the children included in this sample were referred for further testing rather than given an initial diagnosis. 

Another recent study explored the diagnostic impressions of a trained clinician within the first five minutes of meeting a young child for an ASD evaluation (Wieckowski et. al., 2021). After five minutes of interacting with the child, clinicians were instructed to indicate whether or not they believed the child would meet criteria for ASD following the evaluation, and recorded their confidence in this initial impression. Results showed that 81% of initial clinical impressions matched with the final diagnosis, with 92% of the cases that were initially thought to have ASD meeting criteria. However, 24% of the cases that were initially thought not to have ASD ultimately met criteria for ASD at the end of the evaluation. Overall, clinicians were confident in their initial impressions, particularly for those cases where a child was thought to not have ASD. These results further highlight the ability of trained clinicians to detect ASD from behavioral observation alone, as well as underscores the fact that not all young children with ASD present with a “frank” phenotype. 

Despite clinical and empirical evidence suggesting that trained clinicians can discern ASD from non-ASD with good reliability after a brief behavioral observation, the factors that contribute to this impression have not been readily studied, and studies to date have focused on young children. The initial study proposing the Frank Autism construct surveyed 151 clinicians with ASD diagnostic expertise about their representation and usage of this “frank autism” phenomenon. Results showed that 97% of clinicians were familiar with the phenomenon and believed that they could determine whether or not an individual fit the phenotype of “frank autism” within roughly ten minutes of interaction or observation. Of those clinicians that were familiar with the phenomenon, they estimated that roughly 40% of the ASD population exhibited the “frank autism” phenotype. Clinicians also reported that the most specific behaviors associated with this phenotype included impaired reciprocity, atypical vocal prosody, poor quality eye contact, atypical motor mannerisms, and atypical gait or posture. These findings highlight some common variables that may impact initial impressions during ASD diagnostic decision making. However, no studies to date have empirically validated these anecdotal endorsements. 

Given that the phenomenon of “frank autism” is used widely in clinical practice, and likely has implications for who is ultimately diagnosed, it is important to empirically validate what behavioral factors commonly contribute to this impression. Understanding these factors has the potential to improve diagnostic classification by combining computational and clinical expertise to analytically identify key features that may be useful to predict ASD in young children (Corona et. al., 2021). Additionally, it may provide further clinical utility for identifying “frank” ASD symptoms in females, as it is well established that males and females with ASD present with varying behavioral characteristics and are perceived differently both by their peers and clinicians (Cola et. al., 2020). More broadly, this construct may be useful in addressing current controversies about the status of ASD as a biological entity (Mottron, 2021, Fein et. al. 2021, Eigsti et. al., 2022).

The current study aims to quantitatively assess what factors contribute to a clinician’s initial impression of ASD within the first five minutes of an evaluation. These factors include gesture, eye contact, motor mannerisms, prosody and vocalizations, facial expressions, focus/shifting of attention (including perseverative thinking and distractibility), social reciprocity (responses), and interactions with others (initiations). We also aim to replicate the findings of Wieckowski et. al., 2021 to assess the stability of five-minute impression status and ultimate diagnostic group classification, expanding these findings to adolescent and adult populations. In addition to assessing participant factors, we aim to evaluate clinician factors, such as background and years of experience, and their effect on initial impression accuracy.

title: Spectral imaging for in-vivo abdominal tumor detection
description: The research project will entail a systematic review of peer-reviewed studies assessing the in-vivo use of multispectral and hyperspectral imaging for tumor detection (and margin delineation) during surgery for abdominal / gastro-intestinal cancers. This review aims to quantify diagnostic accuracy (sensitivity, specificity, AUC...), to characterise workflow integration (acquisition time, processing latency), and to evaluate downstream impacts on surgical decision-making and outcomes. Spectral imaging setups in minimally invasive or open abdominal cancer surgery will be investigated on their ability to differentiate cancerous from normal tissue. Expected outcomes include a quantification of diagnostic performance, identification of optimal spectral bands, and recommendations for future clinical trials and algorithm development.

title: Ultrasound Assessment of the Perineal Body: A Scoping Review.
description:
This study aims to systematically review and map the current literature on ultrasound assessment of the perineal body (PB) in women. The PB is a complex fibromuscular structure critical for pelvic floor support, yet its anatomy and function remain incompletely understood. While MRI and cadaveric studies have provided valuable insights, ultrasound offers a dynamic, non-invasive, and accessible method for detailed evaluation.

We will conduct a scoping review following PRISMA-ScR guidelines, focusing on studies published between 1997 and 2025 that use ultrasound to visualize or measure the PB in clinical, diagnostic, or research settings. Key ultrasound parameters such as PB thickness, three-dimensional measurements, and elastography findings will be analyzed. The review will also examine methodological differences, ultrasound techniques, and emerging technologies like AI-based image analysis.

Expected outcomes include identifying knowledge gaps, standardizing ultrasound measurement approaches, and recommending optimal imaging protocols. Ultimately, this research will support improved diagnostic accuracy and understanding of the PB’s role in pelvic floor disorders, guiding future clinical and research applications.

title: Artificial Intelligence for Early Detection of Colorectal Cancers Using Capsule Endoscopy Data: A Scoping Review Protocol
description:
Colorectal cancer (CRC) continues to weigh heavily on public health worldwide, with the latest GLOBOCAN 2022 estimates pointing to 1.9 million new diagnoses and more than 900,000 fatalities in the last year, cementing CRC’s position as the third-most diagnosed cancer and the second-deadliest across the globe (6). Projections suggest that by 2040, the annual case load will swell to beyond 3.2 million, marking a 63% steep climb driven chiefly by aging populations, dietary choices, rising obesity rates, and related metabolic syndromes (6). Observers note that the increase is not confined to any single continent, surfacing in high Human Development Index (HDI) nations and spreading rapidly through many areas of Asia, with particular acceleration evident in North America, Australasia, and several Latin American nations (6). While screening technologies and therapeutic advances have improved, the stubbornly high death toll underscores the imminent requirement for more effective early-detection initiatives on a worldwide scale (6).

Capsule Endoscopy (CE) has transformed the assessment of the gastrointestinal tract by providing a comfortable, silent, and awake-viewed tour through the GI tract via a tiny wireless camera that patients simply swallow in a gel-encased pill. The pioneer of this approach, the PillCam (originally named M2A), first targeted the often-cryptic small bowel and achieved FDA clearance in the United States in August 2001 (4,12,13). Following this advance, the colon capsule innovation arose, offering a gentler second look at the colon for patients hesitant to endure the rigors of colonoscopy preparation or those whose index colonoscopy was incomplete. The PillCam Colon 2, developed by Given Imaging and later acquired by Medtronic, received de novo FDA clearance in November 2012 and was marketed in 2014 to address the clinical need for accurate polyp detection in carefully selected patients (1,4,12). Multiple studies and meta-analyses confirm that, with appropriate indications, colon capsule endoscopy (CCE) detects the majority of clinically relevant colonic polyps, showing 88–95% agreement for polyps ≥6 mm compared with standard colonoscopy (2,3,12).

Manual review of CCE data involves tens of thousands of images per procedure, which is labor-intensive and time-consuming. Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly deep learning using convolutional neural networks (CNNs), has emerged as a transformative tool to automate lesion detection, enhance diagnostic accuracy, and reduce interpretation time (1,4,14–17). Studies report AI polyp detection sensitivities of up to 98.1% in CCE datasets, with significant reductions in reading time by as much as 70% compared with expert human reviewers (1,4,14,15). Recent research also emphasizes the importance of developing explainable AI models to improve clinical acceptance and integrate trusted decision support into clinical workflows (5).

Despite the promising advances, the literature remains heterogeneous regarding AI algorithms, study methodologies, evaluated capsule platforms, target lesions (e.g., polyp size, dysplasia vs. carcinoma), and performance metrics (1–4,7,8,14,15,17). A comprehensive scoping review is therefore crucial to systematically map existing global evidence, classify AI and machine learning approaches applied to capsule endoscopy data for early CRC detection, synthesize diagnostic performance metrics, and identify current knowledge gaps and limitations. This will support future research planning, clinical translation, and deployment of AI-augmented capsule endoscopy as a scalable CRC screening tool. The purpose of the study is to identify and categorize artificial intelligence and machine learning approaches including deep learning, convolutional neural networks, and other AI algorithms applied to colon capsule endoscopy for the early detection of colorectal cancer and precursor lesions and to summarize and report diagnostic performance metrics (such as sensitivity, specificity, and diagnostic accuracy) and highlight key gaps, limitations, and challenges in the current evidence base to inform future research and clinical adoption.

title: The Expertize in Question Formulation: Homogeneity and Discriminability of Questions in the Concealed Information Test
description:
Factors related to questions that affect the accuracy (sensitivity and specificity) of CIT and the expertise in formulating a set of questions have become important topics. 
In CIT, it is essential for maintaining the specificity of CIT to choose the non-critical items so that the critical item is not made salient in question sets (i.e., homogeneity of items) because an outstanding critical item may bias an innocent examinee and increase their physiological response to the critical item (Ogawa et al., 2015). This could potentially cause false arrest or even prosecution. In fact, Japanese practitioners have been trained to formulate homogeneous questions for cases with different backgrounds to avoid the risk of such bias. Nevertheless, the relationship between homogeneity in question sets and the expertise in formulating questions has never been tested.
Another aspect, that may affect the sensitivity of CIT, is the selection of items that are likely to be recognized by examinees who encoded these critical items during crime commission (i.e., discriminability of items). The concreteness of items presented to examinees (Geven et al., 2019) has been identified as a factor in discriminability. For instance, a robber may encode that they used scissors in a broken-into house to threaten a victim but may not encode the type of scissors (e.g., kitchen scissors, fabric shears, and garden shears). In addition, even if the offender encoded a specific type of scissors, the retention and retrieval of that detail may become more difficult as a function of time. Therefore, it is ideal to formulate question sets using a higher level of category to achieve optimal discriminability of items.
Another factor related to the discriminability of question sets is to formulate them with few elements. When it comes to, for example, the cash being stolen from a velcro purse, the velcro purse can be used as a critical item consisting of two elements: "velcro," which is a type of opening and closing of a purse, and "purse," which is a type of container. In this case, since it is not necessary to discriminate all items by one type of element (e.g., the container of stolen money), it is possible to share the same cue (e.g., purse) among items by selecting an item such as “zipper purse” as a non-critical item. The sharing of the same element increases the probability that multiple elements ("purse" and "velcro") will be required to identify the critical item (i.e., the examinee needs to remember multiple elements to detect the critical item). It is more challenging for the examinees to remember more elements, and the difficulty of the retention and retrieval may increase over time similar to the items with a lower level of category. In the meantime, the above issue does not occur when formulating a set of questions with one type of element, such as "wallet" and "envelope." Formulating a set of questions with fewer elements encourages choosing items of higher category levels (e.g., the container of stolen money). Therefore, the number of elements can be considered as a factor of the discriminability of items closely related to the category level. However, the factors related to questions that affect the discriminability in CIT has just started being tested, and their relationship with expertise in formulating a set of questions has not been examined.
Therefore, we will compare question sets formulated by university students and CIT examiners by measuring the factors of the homogeneity and discriminability of these sets. In addition, we will examine if the expertise in question formulation makes a difference in perceived homogeneity evaluated by a sample that is not aware of the critical items (study 1) and in discriminability measured by a recognition test using a sample that encodes the critical items (study 2).

title: Links between Menopause, Depression, and Anxiety: A Systematic Review of Potential Psychological Factors and Cognitive-Affective Mechanisms
description:
With increasing life expectancy, women spend on average one-third of their lives in the climacteric (Yılmaz & Avci, 2022). Despite its obvious significance, the climacteric has received relatively little attention in both scientific research and public discourse, although public awareness has been increasing in recent years. The stages of climacteric have been defined by the World Health Organization (WHO), but the terminology has been updated according to the STRAW+10 criteria (Ambikairajah et al., 2022) and encompass the following stages: premenopause, early and late perimenopause, and postmenopause. The premenopausal phase extends to the start of the menopausal transition (early perimenopause), while the perimenopause covers the menopausal transition from the first persistent changes in menstrual cycle length until 12 months after the final menstrual period (FMP). The perimenopause (often used synonymously with menopausal transition) is therefore defined as the period of hormonal and cyclic fluctuations preceding menopause, including the first year thereafter, while menopause itself is retrospectively determined after 12 consecutive months without menstruation. Following the FMP, the postmenopausal period encompasses approximately the first five years (Ambikairajah et al., 2022; Greendale et al., 2020; Sherman, 2005). Over 80% of women experience climacteric symptoms, including vasomotor complaints (hot flushes, night sweats), sleep disturbances, brain fog (memory or attention problems), vaginal dryness, loss of libido, or joint pain, all of which are linked to hormonal changes (Gracia & Freeman, 2018; Stute, 2023). Psychosocial mechanisms such as role transitions and confronting the process of aging also play a role. Together these biological, psychological, and social transitions render the climacteric a “window of vulnerability” for the development of psychopathologies (Barth Olofsson & Collins, 2000; Sassarini, 2016; Soares & Zitek, 2007). Various studies indicate an increased risk of depression in women undergoing climacteric. A meta-analysis shows that the severity of symptoms and the risk of depressive symptoms in perimenopausal women are almost twice as high as in premenopausal women (De Kruif et al., 2016). Similarly, other studies suggest that the risk of depression and anxiety is particularly elevated during the menopausal transition, with anxiety symptoms potentially persisting into the postmenopausal period (Alblooshi et al. 2023).
Both depressive and anxious symptoms are influenced by a) cognitive-affective mechanisms and b) psychological vulnerabilities. Reward processing, as an important cognitive-affective mechanism, is necessary to anticipate pleasures or rewards and to develop the motivational behaviour required to pursue them. In this context, reward positivity (RewP) captures the neural response to reward feedback as an EEG measure (Proudfit, 2015). It has been shown that reduced RewP increases the risk of developing depression, and that depressive disorders are associated with deficits in reward processing (Proudfit et al., 2015). The increased vulnerability resulting from reduced RewP is more evident in depression than in anxiety disorders and occurs particularly when people are exposed to high levels of stress or stressful life events (Kujawa et al., 2014; Weinberg et al., 2022).
Another key cognitive-affective mechanism related to psychopathology is error processing, which is reflected by the neural marker error-related negativity (ERN), an event-related potential (ERP) component (Gehring et al., 1993). Internalising disorders are associated with increased sensitivity to errors, which manifests as heightened ERN amplitudes. This is partly evident in depression, but is more pronounced in anxiety disorders or in individuals showing high levels of anxiety and worry, amongst other factors. In externalising disorders, such as substance abuse, correspondingly reduced ERN amplitudes are observed (Olvet & Hajcak, 2008, 2012; Pasion & Barbosa, 2019). It was also demonstrated that individuals with obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) and anxiety disorders, as well as those with elevated subclinical symptoms in these areas, also exhibit increased ERN amplitudes (Riesel et al., 2019). These individuals have been robustly found to exhibit increased ERN amplitudes.
In addition to reward and error processing, fear conditioning also constitutes a potentially important cognitive-affective mechanism affecting psychopathological symptoms. In fear-conditioning paradigms, a previously neutral cue is repeatedly paired with an aversive unconditioned stimulus, leading it to elicit a conditioned fear response (CS+). A second stimulus is never paired with the aversive stimulus and is regarded as a safety signal (CS-). Meta-analyses show that individuals with anxiety disorders often exhibit stronger reactions to the CS+, which also last longer. Furthermore, they also frequently react to the CS- with increased fear, suggesting that there is only a slight differentiation between the CS+ and the CS-. They therefore have greater difficulty distinguishing between danger (CS+) and safety (CS-) and tend to generalise their fear more strongly (Duits et al., 2015; Lissek et al., 2005). 
Finally, emotion regulation also affects symptoms of anxiety and depression. Emotion regulation strategies influence how people cope with stress and, consequently, affect mood and susceptibility to depressive or anxiety symptoms, amongst others. Negative correlations are observed between adaptive strategies (e.g. reappraisal or acceptance) and depressive or anxiety symptoms, as adaptive regulation leads to a lower symptom burden. Maladaptive strategies (e.g., avoidance), by contrast, are positively associated with anxiety and depressive symptoms and are linked to increased vulnerability to anxiety disorders and depression (Aldao et al., 2010).
Apart from cognitive-affective mechanisms, individual differences in psychological vulnerabilities also play a key role in susceptibility to depression and anxiety. Individuals with a history of depressive or anxious episodes are more psychologically vulnerable to experience another episode later in life (Gracia & Freeman, 2018; Santoro et al., 2021). Similarly, early negative life events, such as childhood maltreatment, are associated with an increased risk of later anxiety or depressive disorders. (Macalli et al., 2021; Nikkheslat et al., 2020; Teicher & Samson, 2013). Irritability, a construct associated with depression, is accompanied by reduced emotional regulation and increased self-criticism. This can lead to an increased experience of negative affect and a reduced experience of positive affect, and to an overall increased susceptibility to environmental stressors and thus to depression. (Mauas et al., 2014). From a personality and temperament perspective, low self-esteem, perfectionism, dependency, pessimism, and rumination tendencies have been shown to be relevant to depressive or anxious symptoms (Bean & Ciesla, 2024; Doron et al., 2013; Hankin et al., 2004; Michl et al., 2013; Vink et al., 2008; Zou et al., 2025). Among the Big Five personality traits, individuals with higher levels of neuroticism and lower levels of extraversion are more prone to depressive or anxious symptoms (Clark et al., 2003; Olvet & Hajcak, 2012; Parker & Brotchie, 2010; Yılmaz & Avci, 2022). 
Taken together, various cognitive-affective mechanisms and psychological vulnerabilities play an important role in the manifestation of depressive and/or anxious symptoms. Furthermore, existing research indicates that the climacteric represents a window of vulnerability for depressive and anxious symptoms. Thus, an open question is whether these cognitive–affective mechanisms and psychopathological vulnerabilities contribute to the association between the climacteric and the increased incidence of anxiety and depressive symptoms.. Previous reviews have primarily focused on the increased prevalence of depression during this life stage, emphasizing psychosocial and hormonal factors (Alblooshi et al., 2023; Badawy et al., 2024; Brown et al., 2024; Jia et al., 2024). To date, no systematic review has examined the mechanisms underlying heightened depressive and anxious symptoms during climacteric by focusing on cognitive-affective mechanisms and psychological vulnerabilities.
The vulnerability-stress model explains the development of mental disorders through the interaction of individual vulnerabilities (e.g. biological, genetic, social) and stressful events, with psychological processes influencing symptom characteristics and their consequences (Wirtz, 2026). Applied to the climacteric, the model postulates a direct link (Figure 1) between climacteric symptoms – or the climacteric as a challenging context due to e.g. physical complaints and hormonal changes – and psychopathological symptoms (path a), in particular depressive and anxiety symptoms. The model proposed in this review suggests that this relationship is mediated by cognitive-affective mechanisms (path b), including impaired reward processing, error processing, fear conditioning and emotional regulation, which may explain how climacteric stressors translate into psychopathology. Psychological vulnerabilities such as personality traits (e.g., neuroticism) might moderate this mediation (path c) - meaning that higher levels of these moderators amplify the mediated path - and the link between climacteric symptoms and psychopathologies (path a) potentially resulting in more severe anxious and depressive symptoms during climacteric.

title: Advancements in Herpes Zoster Diagnosis, Treatment, and Management: A Systematic Review of Artificial Intelligence Applications
description:
This project is a systematic literature review that investigates the current landscape of artificial intelligence (AI) applications in the diagnosis, treatment, and management of herpes zoster (HZ), a viral infection caused by the reactivation of the varicella-zoster virus. The primary objective of this review is to synthesize existing advancements and provide a comprehensive overview of how AI is being utilized to enhance patient care in this domain.
Following PRISMA guidelines, a systematic search was conducted across three databases—PubMed, Web of Science Core Collection, and IEEE. Studies were included if they were research articles written in English, focused specifically on herpes zoster, and presented actual AI applications. Key data extracted included the types of AI tasks performed, algorithms used, data sources and types, and the clinical applications of AI in the context of herpes zoster. 
The findings are categorized into three main areas:
1. Diagnosis – AI techniques that improve diagnostic accuracy and efficiency through image analysis and deep learning.
2. Treatment – Predictive modeling to forecast treatment outcomes using multimodal clinical and imaging data.
3. Management – Applications that support epidemiological research, case identification, and risk analysis for complications such as post-herpetic neuralgia.

title: Genetics in the first tier of newborn screening: a scoping review.
description:
B. ABSTRACT

2. STRUCTURED SUMMARY 

Newborn screening (NBS) is one of the most successful worldwide healthcare interventions. In most countries, systematic biochemical screening at birth identifies pre-symptomatic infants with severe treatable conditions so that treatment can be started as early as possible, which prevents long-lasting disability. Genomic techniques are well established as second-tier confirmatory tests, but they are not presently used as first-tier tests, with the notable exception of spinal muscular atrophy (SMA). This limits the number of potential diseases for which it is possible to screen. In order to better understand the potential future of genetic NBS, we have conducted a scoping review (SCR) to identify pilot studies or well established programs applying genetic techniques as first-tier NBS. To our best knowledge there has been no previous review on the subject of molecular NBS, which has the potential to deeply impact the practice of all paediatricians by allowing for much broader NBS.

B. INTRODUCTION

3. RATIONALE
3.1 General information about newborn screening and the biochemical expanded profile of tandem mass spectrometry with molecular confirmatory tests.
3.2 So far, next generation sequencing (NGS) genomic techniques are only being used in second-tier confirmatory tests for biochemical screening.
3.3 However today several conditions, which are treatable can only be screened by genetic testing.
3.4 Despite the breakthroughs in genomic technology as applied to health and diagnostics, there are no routine programs with molecular first-tier NBS, with the exception of SMA. 
3.5 In this context, the authors review the existing literature and discuss if there is potential for a transition to include advanced genomic techniques as a first-tier method of molecular newborn screening.

4. OBJECTIVES
4.1 To review literature in order to assess previous pilots or experiences with molecular newborn screening as 1st-tier test.
4.2 To extract and summarize diagnostic approach and methodology included in the molecular newborn screening.

4.3 REVIEW QUESTIONS:
4.3.1 Are there any pilots and/or implemented molecular NBS programs as 1st tier test worldwide?
4.3.2 Which are the diseases already being screened by molecular NBS.
4.3.3 What techniques are being used? 
4.3.4 What are the challenges (ethical and parents acceptance) to move the genetic newborn screening forward?

C. METHODS
 5. PROTOCOL AND REGISTRATION

5.1 This protocol was created using the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-analysis Protocols (PRISMA-ScR), which was revised and approved by the research team.

5.2 The final protocol was registered in a progressive manner with the Open Science Framework on 8th of December 2021.

6. ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA

6.1 Inclusion: original, peer-reviewed full-text articles on genetic newborn screening as 1st-tier test, published between the period of 2016 - March of 2021, written in English involving human participants. 
6.2 Exclusion: studies with no available full-text. Abstracts, guidelines, commentaries, editorials, meetings or presentations, proceedings from symposiums, seminars, round table discussions, debates, post scripts, letters to the editors, patents, case reports, book chapters, dissertations or theses and systematic reviews. Genetic newborn screening applied as 2nd-tier test. Newborn screening of infectious diseases and COVID19 screening were excluded. 

7. INFORMATION SOURCES 

7.1 We have conducted the search using Ovid/MEDLINE, PubMed and Scopus databases. The search was limited to studies published from January 2016 to the present, due to the former date being the debut of the application of molecular techniques to the field of newborn screening. 

8. SEARCH 

8.1 The search was not restricted to any particular genetic disorder or metabolic disease, but primarily excluded the screening of infectious diseases. Our main search strategy was based on the selection of molecular genetic techniques applied as a first-tier test for NBS. In addition, databases were restricted to human-specific studies in the English language. We used the keywords ‘neonatal screening’, OR ‘newborn screening’, OR ‘Guthrie card’ AND ‘PCR’, AND ‘polymerase chain reaction’, OR ‘sequencing’, OR ‘mutation analysis’, NOT ‘infectious’, NOT ‘virus’, NOT ‘sepsis’, NOT ‘covid’. Additionally, we also performed an update of new strategic papers linked to the pilots we found in the last year. 

8.2 These is the search strategy used to search the databases mentioned above. The study has been structured according to the PICOS method. The PICO scheme you can see in the attached file (Figure 1).

8.3 MEDLINE/OVID

Search Strategy: it will be disclosed in details after publication.

9. SELECTION OF SOURCES OF EVIDENCE 

9.1 Our process will follow the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR). 

9.2 To increase consistency among reviewers, the two independent reviewers (Dr. Piazzon F. and Dr. Hovhannesyan K.) screened all the abstracts, in a second stage; all previously selected articles were fully reviewed by two investigators to determine if they met the eligibility criteria. We resolved disagreements on study selection and data extraction by consensus and discussion with the third reviewer (Prof Servais L) if needed.

10. DATA CHARTING PROCESS

10.1 A data-charting design was jointly developed by three reviewers to determine which variables to extract. Only two reviewers independently charted the data, after they discussed the results with the third reviewer and continuously updated the charts in an iterative process. All data were digitally registered using Microsoft Office Excel.

11. DATA ITEMS 

11.1 We resumed important data on articles (e.g., country of origin), engagement characteristics and contextual factors (e.g., name of the disease, genetic technique applied in the NBS, number of positive cases), barriers and challenges found in the screening programs (e.g., ethics and parent acceptance).

12. CRITICAL APPRAISAL OF INDIVIDUAL SOURCES OF EVIDENCE

Not applicable.

13. SYNTHESIS OF RESULTS

We grouped the studies by the type of diseases, and summarized the type of laboratory genomic techniques, populations and study designs, along with the measures used and broad findings. 

D. RESULTS

14. SELECTION OF SOURCES OF EVIDENCE

15. CHARACTERISTICS OF SOURCES OF EVIDENCE

15.1 Provide an overall summary in the text, with more details by disease screened and which techniques are used. Present all these data also in a table.

17. RESULTS OF INDIVIDUAL SOURCES OF EVIDENCE

18. SYNTHESIS OF RESULTS
18.1 Framework and diagram flow with all the process for the review. 

E. DISCUSSION

19. SUMMARY OF EVIDENCE

19.1 Critical review of the pilots 
Pilots bring different levels of evidence. We will critically review the impact of the different pilot studies and the potential feasibility at whole-population scale. We will identify diseases for which genetic NBS as first tier seems to be the most mature.

19.2 Critical discussion of ethical and parental acceptance issues
In this section, we will discuss the level of evidence for parental acceptability, as well as the main ethical issues that have been raised and how they have been assessed.

20: LIMITATIONS

Our scoping review has some limitations. To make our review more feasible, we were only able to include a structured search in dedicated databases of science as in the systematic reviews but we did not include the gray literature.

21. CONCLUSIONS

21.1 Proposal to improve the molecular NBS for treatable rare disorders.

21.2 We will propose a path for future development of genetic NBS

title: The Accuracy and Challenges of Virtopsy for Age Estimation: A Systematic review & Meta-Analysis in Forensic and Medico-Legal Investigation
description:
Overview:
This project explores the growing forensic utility of Virtopsy, a non-invasive imaging technique using modalities such as CT (Computed Tomography), MRI (Magnetic Resonance Imaging), and PMCT (Post-Mortem CT), for age estimation in both living and deceased individuals. The project critically evaluates its accuracy, reliability, and population-specific performance through a systematic review and meta-analysis, aiming to inform medico-legal investigations and forensic protocols.

Purpose:
The primary aim is to quantify the diagnostic accuracy and methodological consistency of Virtopsy-based age estimation techniques across diverse anatomical landmarks and demographic populations. It further investigates gender-specific performance and the influence of developmental stages on reliability.

Methodology:

A systematic literature review was conducted in accordance with PRISMA guidelines, covering peer-reviewed studies published between 2015 and 2025.

Databases searched included PubMed, Scopus, ScienceDirect, and Web of Science.

Studies were selected based on strict inclusion criteria and assessed using the QUADAS-2 tool to determine methodological quality and bias risk.

Extracted data included imaging modality, anatomical site, subject demographics, reliability indices, and diagnostic metrics such as accuracy, correlation coefficients, and mean absolute error (MAE).

A random-effects meta-analysis was conducted to pool results, with subgroup analyses exploring variation by population, age group, gender, and skeletal site.

Key Findings:

The overall pooled diagnostic accuracy of Virtopsy for age estimation was 77.01%.

The clavicle region showed the highest accuracy (90%) and lowest MAE (1.94 years), making it the most reliable anatomical marker.

Gender-specific analysis indicated slightly better performance in males (r = 0.887) than in females (r = 0.870).

Internal reliability was consistently high (κ > 0.7), but external reliability varied due to methodological heterogeneity across studies.

Accuracy decreased in older populations, and substantial variability was observed across anatomical sites and developmental stages.

Challenges Identified:

Lack of standardized imaging protocols and analysis frameworks.

Variations in anatomical development patterns across different populations.

Difficulty in interpreting age-related changes in older individuals due to reduced skeletal differentiation.

Limited integration of AI or machine learning in current assessment methods.

Conclusion and Implications:
Virtopsy represents a promising tool in non-invasive forensic age estimation, particularly effective in adolescent and young adult populations. However, to enhance its legal admissibility and cross-population utility, there is a pressing need for standardized protocols, AI-assisted diagnostics, and population-specific validation studies. The findings of this study support the inclusion of Virtopsy in forensic practice, while also highlighting areas needing further refinement and technological integration.

title: A scoping review protocol for cognitive bias in US and Canadian medical diagnosis: Current prevalence and management through education and policy
description:
In 2002, psychologist Daniel Kahneman’s received the Nobel Prize for his work on errors in judgement and decision-making. Kahneman’s and Amos Tversky’s collaboration, dating back to the 1990’s, with Canadian physician Donald Redelmeier, advanced work on cognitive biases in medical decision-making.
 In 2005, US and Canadian physicians began to publish regularly on cognitive bias in medical diagnosis. The literature through 2017 suggests missed or delayed diagnoses were implicated in 10-15% of cases, 17% of adverse events and 10% of deaths. Research also suggested cognitive bias was associated with 74% of missed or delayed diagnoses, regardless of whether a condition was rare or common or of the degree of confidence in the incorrect diagnosis. 
 Given the well-documented importance of reducing cognitive bias in order to promote medical diagnostic accuracy, the current scoping review will integrate the English language reviews and literature 2005 through 2020 based on vignettes, case-studies, surveys, and medical record searches as well as policy and theory. It is anticipated the scoping review will document prevalent and overlooked biases; include theory and findings about circumstances that promote bias; and align policy recommendations with interventions that have more or less robust evidence for their efficacy. Given the history of the field, the review concentrates on medical diagnosticians and their patients in the USA and Canada.

title: NyameriNet
description: The development of "Nyameri," a hypothetical next-generation mobile application for diabetic retinopathy (DR) image analysis, represents a synthesis of cutting-edge academic research and commercial product features into a cohesive, plausible technology. The core of the Nyameri system is its custom-designed Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), named NyameriNet. This architecture is engineered to deliver high diagnostic accuracy while operating efficiently on mobile devices without constant reliance on cloud connectivity. While specific architectural details like the exact number of layers are not provided in the source materials, the design philosophy aligns with state-of-the-art models known for their balance of performance and efficiency. For instance, NyameriNet's estimated size of approximately 40 MB is comparable to DRNet13, which was reported to be 35 MB. This suggests an architecture that may incorporate techniques such as depthwise separable convolutions or other forms of model optimization to maintain a small footprint. The primary function of NyameriNet is a five-class classification task: No DR, Mild, Moderate, Severe, and Proliferative DR. This multi-stage grading is a standard benchmark in the field, reflecting the clinical need for precise disease staging. The simulated performance of NyameriNet is projected to exceed current clinical standards, positioning it as a highly advanced tool. The model is expected to achieve an accuracy rate between 96% and 98%, a figure supported by numerous studies on complex CNN architectures. For example, a DenseNet-121 model using CLAHE and ESRGAN preprocessing on the APTOS 2019 dataset achieved 98.36% accuracy , while a hybrid Inception v3 model reached 98.7% accuracy on the same dataset. Similarly, a modified VGGNet-based transfer learning model trained on the Kaggle EyePACS dataset achieved 96.6% accuracy after extensive data augmentation. Sensitivity and specificity are critical metrics for any screening tool, and NyameriNet's projected values aim to surpass established benchmarks. An estimated sensitivity of 97-98% significantly outperforms the minimum requirements set by bodies like the British Diabetic Association (BDA) of 80%. This level of performance is consistent with top-tier models; for instance, a study on the Messidor-2 dataset achieved a sensitivity of 97.63% , and another model reached 99.21% on the Kaggle test dataset. Specificity is projected to be in the range of 95-97%, also exceeding the BDA's 95% minimum requirement. Models like DeB5-XNet have demonstrated 97.1% specificity on the DDR dataset , and a WFDLN model achieved 98.0% specificity on the Messidor dataset. These figures underscore the potential of modern deep learning to provide highly reliable screening results. The model's precision and F1-score are also projected to be very high, at 0.96-0.98, indicating a low rate of false positives and a strong balance between precision and recall.
