title: Giving Voice to the COVID Generation: Assessing Language Development and Risk for Impairments
description:
Children born during the COVID-19 pandemic (BDC) are now in preschool and have experienced unprecedented social and educational restrictions as well as reduced linguistic input during critical developmental years. The long-term consequences of these constraints on language acquisition remain critically understudied, creating an urgent need for research. This project undertakes the timely research endeavor of providing a systematic characterization of language development in BDC preschoolers, and developing an evidence-based, open-access multivariable risk calculator to estimate individual risk for language impairments.
Portugal, one of the EU countries that implemented the strictest COVID-19 measures, offers a unique setting to assess the impact of pandemic- related constraints on child development. Our previous research has highlighted significant developmental delays in BDC infants, toddlers, and preschoolers, reinforcing the importance of this project. By leveraging advanced statistical modeling and interdisciplinary expertise, this project will identify key predictors of language impairments and translate findings into a practical tool that enhances early identification and intervention.

Over 18 months, this project will follow a structured four-phase approach:

Phase 1 | Systematic Literature Review: A systematic literature review will synthesize quantitative findings to establish a comprehensive overview of the pandemic's impact on early language development. These findings will directly inform the design of the parental questionnaires used in the subsequent phase, ensuring that the study focuses on the most critical environmental and social factors.

Phase 2 | Longitudinal Study: This phase will include a large-scale longitudinal study with two cohorts of typically developing BDC children (4- year-olds with one year of pandemic exposure and 5-year-olds with two years of exposure, n=400). Data will be collected at two-time points, with a one-year interval between each collection. Caregivers will complete questionnaires based on the relevant findings from the systematic literature review conducted in Phase 1. Children will undergo individual standardized language assessments to evaluate their language skills. Data analysis will employ Structural Equation Modeling to uncover the direct and indirect effects of pandemic-related restrictions on language development, accounting for critical environmental and social factors.

Phase 3 | Development of a Multivariable Risk Model: Building on the findings from Phase 2, a predictive model will be developed to identify key risk factors, such as sociodemographic, environmental, and developmental variables contributing to language delays. Logistic regression will be employed to construct the model, estimating the likelihood of language impairments based on these factors. The model will output a probability score categorized into low, moderate, and high risk. Cross-validation will be performed to ensure model robustness using measures of sensitivity and specificity. Post-validation adjustments will refine the model based on data analysis.

Phase 4 | Creation of the Risk4LI Calculator: The model developed in Phase 3 will be used to create the Risk4LI calculator, implemented as a free interactive web-based form. This will ensure accessibility for professionals in education, healthcare, and related fields. The tool will allow personalized, real-time assessment of child-specific risk factors, facilitating referrals for more comprehensive assessments and early interventions before language difficulties escalate. By providing a free, user-friendly platform, this project bridges the gap between scientific research and practice, offering a solution with applicability beyond the scope of this study.

This research is both timely and critical. Language development is foundational for academic success and social integration, yet pandemic-born cohorts remain at risk for long-term difficulties. The project's interdisciplinary approach, integrating linguistics, psychology, education, speech therapy, clinical sciences, and informatics expertise, ensures a robust analysis of developmental trajectories while delivering tangible solutions for language assessments. The resulting research will have a lasting impact on scientific research and contribute to the development of educational and clinical policies.

Beyond its immediate impact, this project sets the stage for future advancements in early language screening. Risk4LI's framework can be adapted for other populations and enhanced using machine learning techniques to refine predictive accuracy. These potential applications position Risk4LI as a transformative tool in childhood research, education, and clinical practice, helping to identify and support children at risk of language delays, ultimately ensuring better outcomes for BDC children and future generations.

title: The Application of Artificial Intelligence Combined with Digital Biomarkers in the Prediction and Monitoring of Sarcopenia: A Scoping Review
description:
Sarcopenia is an age-related disorder characterized by loss of muscle mass and strength, accompanied by a decline in physical function. It is closely associated with multiple adverse health outcomes, including increased risk of falls, disability, prolonged hospitalization, and higher mortality. Studies have shown that sarcopenia affects approximately 10% to 27% of older adults worldwide. Therefore, early detection and continuous monitoring of sarcopenia are essential for promoting healthy aging. Emerging technologies, such as artificial intelligence (AI), have shown substantial potential across multiple domains of health management. However, AI approaches, particularly machine learning, often require large volumes of data. Conventional data collection still relies largely on manual measurements and self-reported questionnaires, which have several limitations, including low sensitivity, limited accessibility, high subjectivity, and an inability to capture dynamic changes in daily life. In addition, many patients seek medical help only when symptoms become severe, which hinders early intervention. Therefore, objective, quantitative, continuous, noninvasive, and convenient data on muscle health are urgently needed to address the limitations of traditional approaches. Digital biomarkers (DBs) are defined as objective, quantifiable physiological or behavioral data collected using wearable, portable, implantable, or ingestible digital devices. These data may support early prediction and screening of sarcopenia and facilitate proactive maintenance of muscle health, consistent with the latest 2025 Expert Consensus of the Asian Working Group for Sarcopenia. This shift may help advance a new era of muscle health that is quantifiable, predictable, and modifiable.
Although previous studies and reviews have examined the application of AI or machine learning techniques in the prediction, screening, and diagnosis of sarcopenia, important methodological and evidence synthesis gaps remain. First, prior reviews have mainly focused on the predictive performance, diagnostic accuracy, or pooled effect estimates of prediction models based on wearable devices. Few have systematically mapped, from a scoping review perspective, the distribution of evidence and research landscape regarding the combined use of AI/ML techniques and broadly defined DBs for sarcopenia prediction, screening, risk identification, and monitoring. Second, existing studies have insufficiently characterized the sources, types, and measurement dimensions of DBs, and relevant data sources should not be limited to wearable devices. In addition, reporting of digital data acquisition procedures and key AI/ML modeling workflows remains inadequate in many studies, limiting model reproducibility, generalizability, and clinical applicability. Meanwhile, the available evidence is highly heterogeneous in terms of participant characteristics, country or regional distribution, sarcopenia assessment methods, and diagnostic definitions.
This scoping review aims to systematically map the current evidence and emerging trends in the use of artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) techniques combined with digital biomarkers for the prediction, screening, and risk identification of sarcopenia. The specific objectives are to: (1) synthesize and summarize the types of digital devices, derived measurements, and digital biomarker characteristics commonly used in existing studies; (2) characterize sarcopenia assessment methods, definitions, diagnostic criteria, and participant characteristics; (3) summarize AI/ML algorithm categories, data processing workflows, feature engineering methods, validation strategies, and model performance metrics; (4) identify key limitations and challenges related to sample representativeness, data quality, standardized reporting, model generalizability, and clinical translation; and (5) explore future research directions for standardized digital biomarker acquisition, AI/ML model optimization, and continuous monitoring of muscle health.

title: Accuracy and reliability of artificial vision systems for measuring joint range of motion in individuals with musculoskeletal conditions or healthy participants: a scoping review
description: Artificial vision systems are emerging technologies that enable the assessment of human movement without physical contact or reflective markers. These systems have been increasingly applied in rehabilitation and physiotherapy to measure joint range of motion (ROM) and other kinematic parameters. However, the methodological quality and consistency of evidence on their measurement properties remain unclear. This scoping review aims to map and summarize the available scientific evidence on the validity and reliability of artificial vision systems applied to the measurement of joint range of motion in individuals with musculoskeletal conditions or in healthy participants. The review will follow the JBI Manual for Evidence Synthesis and the PRISMA Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) guidelines. The protocol will be registered in the Open Science Framework (OSF) prior to data collection. Searches will be conducted on December 15, 2025, in PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, Embase, CINAHL, SciELO, and LILACS without year restrictions. Eligible studies will include those assessing measurement properties—validity, reliability, measurement error, or responsiveness—of artificial vision systems used to quantify joint ROM. Two reviewers will independently screen titles, abstracts, and full texts using Rayyan, with agreement rates calculated for each phase. Data will be extracted using a pre-defined form and summarized descriptively in tables and narratives. The methodological quality of included studies will be evaluated according to the COSMIN guideline, with the QUADAS-2 tool considered for studies focused on diagnostic accuracy. The findings are expected to provide an overview of the measurement quality and applicability of artificial vision systems in clinical and research settings, identifying current evidence gaps and highlighting which technologies demonstrate sufficient validity and reliability for clinical use.

title: Probe-Based Confocal Laser Endomicroscopy for Real-Time Optical Diagnosis Along the Correa Cascade of Gastric Carcinogenesis: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Diagnostic Accuracy
description:
Gastric cancer develops through a well-defined stepwise pathological sequence — the Correa cascade — progressing from Helicobacter pylori-associated gastritis through atrophic gastritis, intestinal metaplasia, and dysplasia to invasive carcinoma. Early detection at precancerous stages is critical, yet current surveillance relies on random biopsy protocols that are limited by sampling error and inability to provide real-time histological information.
Probe-based confocal laser endomicroscopy (pCLE) enables real-time, in vivo optical biopsy at cellular resolution during standard endoscopy. Primary studies suggest high diagnostic accuracy across Correa cascade stages, but existing meta-analyses are fragmented — addressing only single stages, conflating pCLE with the discontinued eCLE platform, and omitting a large body of East Asian literature.
This study is the first systematic review and meta-analysis to evaluate pCLE diagnostic accuracy across the complete Correa cascade — from H. pylori gastritis to early gastric cancer — in a unified analytical framework. We will pool data using a bivariate random-effects model, assess evidence quality by GRADE, and conduct pre-specified subgroup analyses by geographic region, operator experience, and pCLE classification system. Both English and Chinese-language databases will be searched to minimise geographic bias.
Findings will provide the most comprehensive evidence base to date for pCLE-guided gastric surveillance, with direct implications for clinical guideline development and targeted biopsy protocol design.

title: Risk assessment in randomised controlled trials of interventions for youth depression: a scoping review.
description:
Main question: In young people (up to 18 years of age) who are receiving psychological or pharmacological treatment for depression in a randomised controlled trial, how is risk (e.g. risk of suicide, self-harm) assessed?

Background 

Suicide, the fatal act of self-harm with the intent to end one’s own life (Harding, 2020), is the leading cause of death globally in adolescents aged 15-19 (Asarnow and Mehlum, 2019). Relatedly, the prevalence of non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI) is increasing in adolescence and a major predictor of future death by suicide (Asarnow and Mehlum, 2019). NSSI is defined as the ‘deliberate, self-inflicted destruction of body tissue without suicidal intent and for purposes not socially sanctioned, includes behaviors such as cutting, burning, biting and scratching skin' (“International Society for the Study of Self-injury”, 2018). Mood disorders are a well-documented risk factor for attempting suicide (MacLean, 2011); with the incidence of depression occurring in half to two-thirds of individuals who were successful in their suicide attempts (Harwood et al., 2001). It is thought that approximately 90% of those who commit suicide or die from sudden death seek help from their healthcare system – mostly GPs in the 3 months leading to their death (De Leo et al., 2013), suggesting that primary care can play a major role in the identification and prevention of suicide risk. 

For researchers and clinicians, it is crucial to be able to identify risks in adolescents in order to reduce suicide attempts within this population. Instruments of risk assessment have evolved over the years, including clinical professional judgement, actuarial assessment and structured professional judgement. Currently, clinical guidelines in the UK dictate that following self-harm, all individuals should be offered psychosocial assessments (Murphy et al., 2010). This is in order to identify both the current and future risk of harm which is a key component in determining the best possible course of treatment and clinical management. Over time, psychosocial assessments have been developed and refined, yet classically have been designed to be conducted by psychiatrists. Since the 1970’s whereby it became more typical for mental health nurses to carry out risk assessments due to the spike in NSSI rates, a wider range of both clinical and non-clinical staff now conduct risk screenings. Research indicates that non-clinicians and cross-disciplinary clinical staff are as proficient as psychiatrists in carrying out risk assessments with regards to content, comprehensiveness and suitability of referrals for specialised clinical management (Murphy et al, 2010). It is less clear however, what risk assessments are commonly used in research settings and educational settings (which are increasingly the first contact with mental health services in the UK). For example, although greater awareness and understanding of mental health has been garnered in educational professionals, staff often feel unequipped with regards to the best course of action (Evans, 2018). Largely the use of risk assessments examining harm to self and others with adolescents with depression is under-documented, and there is a lack of understanding with regard to models of assessment for youth. Therefore, here we will outline the methods for a systematic scoping review in regard to how risk (to self and others) is assessed in young people with depression. Through understanding the variety of risk assessment tools, we aim to provide guidelines for assessing risk in young people with depression.

Inclusion Criteria 
The eligibility criteria for included studies are based on the PICOS framework [Methley, 2014].

Population (P): young people aged 18 and under experiencing depression, i.e. they were seeking help for symptoms of depression/depression diagnosis and/or were presenting with depression deemed to exceed a threshold for intervention pre-specified by the trial team. Studies where participants have comorbid psychiatric conditions will be included with the proviso that the intervention focus is on depression. Studies will be included when the reported mean participant age falls below 19 (e.g a mean that falls on 18.5 will be included).
Intervention (I): The trial intervention is designed primarily to decrease symptoms of depression. All treatment interventions for depressive symptoms, e.g psychological or pharmacological, will be eligible. Participants aged under 18 years are the direct recipients of the trial intervention (i.e. interventions targeted at parents will not be included).

Comparators (C): There will be no comparator restrictions.

Outcomes (O): This review plans to give an overview of the current tools and practices that are undertaken within Randomised Control Trials (RCTs) to assess risk to one’s self (e.g., self harm and suicide) and to others and whether there is change in level of risk reported during the trial. 

Studies (S): Studies will be eligible if they are RCTs published in English and refer to human subjects. Trials from any country and setting will be eligible, and no restrictions will be set on when the outcome was measured, including follow ups post-treatment. 

Search strategy 
We will conduct a systematic search of four electronic bibliographic databases (PsychINFO, Ovid MEDLINE, PsychARTICLES and Embase) using the database host Ovid. The search strategy applied has been developed collaboratively by three review team members with the overarching aim of conducting a comprehensive search of the relevant literature. To inform development of the search strategy, an informal search was undertaken. Here we examined text words contained in the title, abstract and keyword headings from a selection of relevant literature.

A preliminary search was conducted and analysis of text words contained in the title and abstract of retrieved records was carried out and a second search was undertaken to refine the proposed search terms. Our search will include the following terms: (Depress* OR dysthymi* OR persistent depressive disorder) AND (Youth OR young people OR teen* OR adolescen* OR child* OR paediatric OR juvenile OR under 18) AND (RCT OR Randomised Control* Trial OR Randomized Control* Trial).

Our search will be limited to RCTs which remain the gold-standard methodology for assessing psychological/pharmacological interventions within our chosen population (Emslie, Mayes, & Ruberu, 2005). Furthermore, we have chosen to limit our search to English language articles for feasibility and that pertain to human subjects, in line with our PICOS framework. 

This proposed search string was agreed on by three review team authors including a clinical psychologist. Two of the review team authors will perform the search, restricting the search using validated Ovid search filters to English language and human subjects. Additionally, we will utilise the validated search filters allowed by Ovid MEDLINE and PsycINFO to identify RCTs and exclude duplicates from the remaining records using the Ovid de-duplicating function.

Source of evidence 
Initial Screening
Papers retrieved from the initial database search will be uploaded into Mendeley. Records will initially be screened by title and then by abstract by two independent researchers in accordance with the research question and eligibility criteria. Discrepancies in agreement will be reviewed by a third researcher.

Full-Text Screening
Any full text articles deemed relevant will be reviewed by two researchers independently. Discrepancies will be discussed with a third reviewer. The final list of articles from the full text screening will be reviewed by a clinical psychologist.

Data Charting 
A data charting procedure will be applied to all studies included from full-text screening using an adapted charting template from the Joanna Briggs Institute Manual (Aromataris, 2020). The following data will be extracted and charted: publication characteristics (e.g. title, first author, year of publication, area of interest); sample demographics (e.g. sample size, age range, age mean, gender % female, ethnicity, country income level of publication); clinical characteristics (e.g. details of clinical diagnosis, depressive symptoms); measure(/s) of risk assessment (e.g. domains assessed, time points of assessment, number of items in tool, details of psychometric validation of tool; further risk assessment with multidisciplinary team; level of risk at each assessment time point; change in risk assessment outcome; intervention characteristics (e.g. psychological/pharmacological, intervention procedure, mode of delivery, context of delivery, experimental groups); primary outcomes (e.g. measurement instrument, outcome summary). Data charting will be performed by two trained review team members in continuous collaboration and consulting with a third review team member (clinical psychologist).

Analysis of evidence 
A PRISMA diagram will be made in order to detail the subsequent search strategy numbers at each step of the data collection and analyses. Analysis of data will involve the use of quantitative methods such as counts and frequencies to gain data on study and outcome characteristics (e.g., number of included papers, and the total number of varying risk assessment tools). These will be displayed in a table alongside qualitative data regarding how and when the risk assessment was conducted.

Risk of bias assessment or quality appraisal 
As this is a scoping review, we will not be conducting a risk of bias assessment or quality appraisal, in line with the Joanna Briggs Institute Manual (Aromataris, 2020).

The views expressed are those of the author(s) and not necessarily those of the NHS, the NIHR or the Department of Health and Social Care.

title: Coverage of the rapid molecular test for the diagnosis of Tuberculosis in different global contexts: scoping review protocol
description: Introduction: Tuberculosis (TB) is a disease that stands out for its prevalence in areas characterized by high social vulnerability and densely populated regions. title: Molecular detection methods for Yersinia pestis: a systematic review and exploratory meta-analysis of diagnostic accuracy and public health applicability
description:
This registration describes the protocol for a systematic review and exploratory meta-analysis of molecular detection methods for Yersinia pestis. The review will evaluate diagnostic accuracy evidence from human clinical samples and will also map evidence from animal, vector, environmental, spiked-sample, and analytical validation studies to clarify public health applicability.

The main human diagnostic accuracy question will focus on suspected plague patients or clinically relevant human specimens, molecular index tests including PCR, qPCR, LAMP, RPA/RAA, MIRA, CRISPR-based methods, digital PCR, sequencing, and other nucleic acid-based assays, and reference standards including culture, predefined independent composite standards, or independent confirmation by an authoritative laboratory. The main outcomes will be study-level sensitivity and specificity with 95% confidence intervals. Exploratory DOR meta-analysis and sensitivity analyses will be performed only when the data are sufficiently interpretable.

Animal, vector, environmental, spiked-sample, and analytical performance studies will not be combined with human clinical diagnostic accuracy data. These studies will be summarized separately as evidence for surveillance, analytical validation, technical maturity, and field applicability. Risk of bias for diagnostic accuracy studies will be assessed using QUADAS-2. The review will follow PRISMA-DTA and PRISMA-S reporting principles.

PROSPERO registration was attempted before formal screening, data extraction, risk-of-bias assessment, and final statistical analysis. However, the PROSPERO diagnostic test accuracy registration template was not available for selection at the time of submission. Therefore, this OSF registration is used to provide a public timestamped protocol record before formal review procedures proceed.

title: Comparative Diagnostic Accuracy of Artificial Intelligence–based Systems for Mental Health Screening: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
description:
This project consists of a diagnostic accuracy systematic review and meta-analysis examining the ability of artificial intelligence (AI) systems to perform mental health screening. Specifically, the study investigates how accurately AI-based systems can detect common mental health conditions when compared with validated reference standards, such as standardized self-report questionnaires or clinical assessments.

The first objective is to estimate the overall screening performance of AI-based systems across existing studies. The second objective is to estimate the screening performance of dialogue-based AI systems (i.e., conversational agents that interact directly with users through dialogue). In addition, moderator analyses will explore potential sources of variability in screening performance, including the mode of AI use (dialogue-based interaction versus non-dialogue classification approaches), the source and modality of input data analyzed by the system (e.g., user dialogue, social media text, clinical records, or audio input), and the underlying AI architecture (e.g., large language model–based versus non-LLM approaches).

The expected outcome of this study is a comprehensive synthesis of the current evidence regarding the accuracy of AI systems in mental health screening, with particular attention to whether dialogue-based AI systems may achieve higher screening performance due to their ability to capture richer contextual information during user interaction, which may be especially relevant in cases involving multiple or overlapping symptoms. Additionally, the study will explore whether differences in AI architecture are associated with variations in screening performance, with the expectation that large language model–based systems, given their extensive pre-training and capacity to process complex linguistic information, may demonstrate higher accuracy compared with non-LLM approaches. Overall, the findings aim to inform future research and support the development and evaluation of AI-based tools for psychological screening.

Detailed Description of Research Project

Title: Agentic AI in Medical Image Analysis: A Preliminary PRISMA-Guided Evidence Map of Large Language Models, Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Multi-Agent Systems, and Model Context Protocol Integration in Radiology and Pathology

Authors: Pedram M. Aghaei, Behnam Kiani Kalejahi, Kamila Khalimova, Mohammad Javad Rajabi Institution: Department of Computer Science and Biomedical Engineering, School of Engineering, Central Asian University, Tashkent 111221, Uzbekistan Corresponding author: p.aghaei@cau.uz Registration date: June 2026

1. Background and Motivation

Medical imaging generates more than one billion radiological examinations annually worldwide. Global radiologist supply is severely constrained — the World Health Organisation estimates that two-thirds of the global population lacks access to diagnostic imaging services, and in high-income countries radiologist workload has increased by approximately 40% over the past decade. These pressures are making AI-assisted workflow support increasingly important. At the same time, the complexity of clinical imaging decisions is growing: integration with genomic data, treatment planning systems, multi-disciplinary team inputs, and longitudinal patient histories demands a fundamentally different class of AI tool than the narrow classifiers developed over the past decade.

Deep learning transformed specific, well-defined imaging tasks — lesion detection, organ segmentation, cancer screening — with landmark studies achieving expert-level performance on narrow benchmarks. However, these systems operate in isolation. They process single inputs and return single outputs, cannot retrieve guidelines, cannot integrate clinical history or prior reports, provide no natural-language interface, and offer no mechanism for workflow integration beyond a single prediction score. Their clinical adoption has accordingly been limited relative to their technical performance.

A second, structurally distinct transformation is now underway. Large language models (LLMs) such as GPT-4 and vision-language models (VLMs) enable simultaneous reasoning over imaging data and clinical text. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), originally proposed for knowledge-intensive natural language processing, has been adapted to ground clinical AI outputs in retrieved guidelines, protocols, and domain-specific documents, with early evidence of substantially reduced hallucination rates. Agentic architectures — systems capable of planning multi-step tasks, invoking external tools, querying clinical databases, and coordinating specialised processing modules — represent an emerging layer that may enable dynamic, context-sensitive imaging workflow support. The recent standardisation of agent-infrastructure connectivity through protocols such as Anthropic's Model Context Protocol (MCP) further opens pathways to integration with DICOM/PACS servers, electronic health records, reporting templates, and clinical knowledge bases.

Together, these five architectural layers — passive LLMs/VLMs, RAG, agentic RAG, autonomous agents, multi-agent systems, and MCP-style integration — are creating an entirely new class of clinical AI. The published evidence on this transition is growing exponentially, concentrated almost entirely in 2025–2026. However, the evidence base is highly heterogeneous across architecture, task, modality, evaluation method, clinical domain, and deployment context, making narrative reviews unreliable and meta-analysis impossible without a preliminary systematic mapping exercise.

2. Knowledge Gap

Despite the rapid growth of published work, no PRISMA-guided systematic evidence map exists that comprehensively characterises the full architectural spectrum from passive LLMs through RAG, autonomous agents, multi-agent systems, and MCP-style integration infrastructure specifically within medical imaging. Several reviews address adjacent topics — RAG in radiology, foundation models in pathology, LLMs in healthcare broadly — but none maps the complete architectural landscape, proposes a unifying taxonomy, conducts comparative quality appraisal across tiers, or provides a structured governance and clinical readiness framework. This evidence map is designed to address that gap.

3. Purpose and Research Question

The primary purpose of this study is to produce a preliminary PRISMA-guided systematic evidence map of agentic AI architectures in medical image analysis — characterising the available evidence, proposing a unifying taxonomy, identifying research priorities, and establishing the methodological foundation for a completed systematic scoping review.

Primary research question: What LLM, VLM, RAG, autonomous-agent, multi-agent, and MCP-style architectures have been applied to radiology and pathology imaging workflows, and what evidence — at any maturity stage — exists for their design, performance, safety, governance, and deployment readiness?

Five specific objectives:

Provisionally characterise the medical imaging tasks, clinical domains, and imaging modalities addressed by agentic and foundation-model AI systems across radiology and pathology.
Propose and validate a novel six-tier architecture taxonomy (T0: Passive LLM/VLM → T1: RAG → T2: Agentic RAG → T3: Autonomous Agent → T4: Multi-Agent System → T5: MCP-style Integration) that organises the current evidence landscape and is designed to remain applicable as foundation model capabilities evolve.
Map data sources, clinical tools, and infrastructure connections (DICOM/PACS, EHR, clinical guidelines, WSI platforms, report templates) used by each architecture tier.
Assess, in a representative subsample, the evaluation methods, performance metrics, validation design, hallucination assessment approaches, and clinical readiness levels of identified systems.
Propose a governance and safety framework and a five-priority research agenda to guide both the completion of this review and the broader research field.
4. Study Design and Methods

This study is a preliminary PRISMA-guided systematic scoping review, following PRISMA 2020 for review reporting, PRISMA-ScR for scoping review extensions, and PRISMA-S for systematic search strategy documentation. A scoping design was selected because the evidence base is too heterogeneous in architecture, task, modality, evaluation method, and clinical context for meta-analysis to be appropriate or valid at this stage.

This work is explicitly a preliminary evidence map, not a completed systematic scoping review. Three major databases (Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library) have not yet been searched due to institutional authentication constraints, and human dual-review of the full 223-record eligible pool is underway. The present registration documents the protocol in its current state. The completed systematic review — incorporating all database searches, full human dual-review, complete data extraction, and comprehensive quality appraisal — is the planned final output.

Information sources and search strategy: Formal Boolean searches were executed in Scopus (330 records, official RIS export, 8 June 2026) and PubMed/MEDLINE (10 records, official NBIB export, 8 June 2026; note: this primary query is acknowledged as a likely undercount and will be supplemented with six broader queries covering report generation, digital pathology, multimodal AI, clinical decision support, agentic AI, and vision-language models). A peer-maintained grey-literature supplementary source was accessed (GitHub: Awesome-AI-Agents-for-Healthcare; 169 unique records after deduplication). Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, and ACM Digital Library were not searchable due to institutional access restrictions; all documented search strings for these databases are included in this registration and will be executed to complete the review. After cross-source deduplication, 500 unique candidate records were identified.

Selection process: Automated four-tier title/abstract classification was applied to all 500 records: P0 (core agentic/RAG/MCP + imaging domain confirmed — 126 records), P1 (LLM/VLM/FM + imaging confirmed — 97 records), P2 (uncertain — 172 records, retained for secondary consultation), P3 (excluded — 105 records). A total of 223 P0+P1 records were identified for full-text retrieval. Human dual-review of all 223 records with inter-rater reliability calculation (target Cohen's kappa ≥ 0.80) and conflict-resolution protocol is currently underway.

Representative subsample: To anchor the preliminary evidence map before full-text review is complete, a purposive representative subsample of 40 studies was selected across all six architecture tiers, prioritising peer-reviewed studies, maximising domain diversity (radiology: n = 22; pathology: n = 14; infrastructure/governance: n = 4), and including the five highest-cited or most recently published records per tier. Of these, 32 met final eligibility on full-text review and are reported in the evidence map tables.

Data extraction: For all 32 included subsample studies, data extraction covered: bibliographic identifiers; clinical domain and imaging modality; architecture tier assignment (T0–T5); specific model(s) and version; retrieval mechanism; tool specification; dataset; evaluation metrics with confidence intervals; validation design; human-in-the-loop status; hallucination assessment; governance features; and clinical readiness level (L0–L4). Full extraction will be applied to all final included studies in the completed review.

Quality appraisal: Applied to the 32-study subsample using: QUADAS-2 for diagnostic accuracy studies (n = 8); CLAIM for medical imaging AI papers (n = 18); DECIDE-AI for clinical decision support evaluation papers (n = 6); and a custom five-domain checklist for agentic/RAG/MCP papers not covered by existing instruments (n = 12), assessing retrieval source authority, tool-call reliability, output faithfulness and hallucination risk, auditability and explainability, and human oversight provision.

Evidence strength labelling: All cited studies carry evidence level labels applied consistently throughout: Peer-reviewed clinical (indexed clinical journal); Peer-reviewed benchmark (indexed CS/AI venue); Preprint (arXiv/bioRxiv/medRxiv, not yet peer-reviewed); Grey literature (technical specification, GitHub repository, or institutional documentation). This stratification ensures preprint results and grey literature are not inadvertently presented as peer-reviewed clinical evidence.

Synthesis approach: Narrative synthesis across six themes: architecture taxonomy, clinical domain and modality, evaluation methodology, clinical readiness, governance and safety, and deployment context. Quantitative meta-analysis is not attempted owing to fundamental heterogeneity.

5. Expected Outcomes

Primary deliverable — Preliminary evidence map (current): A preliminary PRISMA-guided evidence map providing the following original contributions: (1) a novel six-tier architecture taxonomy for agentic AI in medical imaging; (2) a comparative preliminary evidence synthesis across radiology (12 representative studies) and pathology (10 representative studies), stratified by evidence strength tier; (3) a clinical readiness distribution table mapping all architecture tiers to deployment levels L0–L4; (4) a governance and safety framework covering hallucination risk, auditability, human oversight, EU AI Act compliance, and FDA SaMD pathways; (5) a five-priority provisional research agenda: prospective RAG clinical validation, standardised agentic benchmarks, clinical governance infrastructure, agentic protocol-modification safety, and regulatory science engagement.

Secondary deliverable — Completed systematic scoping review (planned): Upon completion of the WoS, IEEE Xplore, and ACM Digital Library searches; expanded PubMed queries; human dual-review of all 223+ eligible records with kappa reporting; complete data extraction; comprehensive quality appraisal of all included studies; final PRISMA flow diagram with complete counts; and OSF registration identifier confirmed — the full systematic scoping review will supersede this preliminary evidence map. This completed review is expected to cover approximately 600–700 unique records after all database coverage is included, with an estimated 80–120 final included studies across all six architecture tiers.

Specific anticipated findings (provisional, subject to confirmation in completed review):

Within the representative subsample reviewed, RAG architectures (T1) appeared to be the most clinically mature tier, with seven peer-reviewed studies tentatively suggesting accuracy improvements of 6–22% over baseline LLMs in radiology QA tasks and consistent hallucination reduction — however, no prospective multi-centre clinical trial has been conducted for any RAG system. Pathology WSI foundation models (T0) appeared to be the most technically mature category, with several Nature-published models reporting AUROC > 0.90 on pan-cancer benchmarks with external validation, though prospective deployment data are absent. Multi-agent systems (T4) showed promising benchmark performance but uniformly lacked prospective validation and safety documentation. MCP-style integration architectures (T5) were at the conceptual and early prototype stage. All architecture tiers remained at clinical readiness Level 1–2 (retrospective, single-site validation); no agentic system in the representative subsample had completed prospective multi-centre clinical evaluation.

All findings are explicitly provisional and will be confirmed, extended, or revised in the completed systematic review.

6. Significance and Anticipated Impact

This evidence map is expected to make four specific contributions to the field. First, the six-tier architecture taxonomy provides a common language for researchers, clinicians, and regulators to describe and compare agentic AI systems in clinical imaging — a contribution designed to remain applicable as specific foundation models and commercial products evolve. Second, the governance and clinical readiness framework provides a practical tool for radiology departments, AI developers, and regulatory bodies to assess where specific systems stand in the deployment readiness spectrum and what steps are needed to advance. Third, the research priority agenda provides an evidence-based direction for funding bodies and research groups to invest effort most effectively. Fourth, the PRISMA-S documented search strings — including strings for WoS, IEEE, ACM, and four expanded PubMed queries — provide a replicable, extensible foundation that any research group worldwide can use to update or extend this evidence base.

The study builds directly on a progressive research trajectory from the authors' group in deep-learning medical imaging (bone tumour classification, brain tumour GAN segmentation, skin lesion synthesis, liver CAD systematic review, bone age estimation), and extends a companion PRISMA review of LLMs and generative foundation models in cloud-enabled IoMT medical imaging. Together, these works map the transition from narrow discriminative models through generative AI to the fully agentic, workflow-integrated systems characterised in the present evidence map.

7. Limitations Acknowledged at Registration

The following limitations are acknowledged in advance and documented transparently as required by good systematic review practice:

Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, and ACM Digital Library have not yet been searched — the primary coverage limitation of this preliminary map.
The primary PubMed query (n = 10) likely underestimates PubMed coverage; expanded queries are planned.
Human dual-review of the 223-record full-text pool is underway; results presented in the preliminary map are from an automated screening plus a 32-study purposive subsample.
Quality appraisal is indicative, applied to the 32-study subsample only.
OSF registration identifier is pending confirmation.
The evidence base is concentrated in English-language, North American and European, arXiv-published computer science literature — publication bias risk is high.
The field is growing so rapidly that additional relevant records will have been published between the search date (8 June 2026) and any future publication of this review.
8. Funding and Conflicts of Interest

This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sector. All authors declare no competing interests. No commercial AI products or platforms are endorsed by this evidence map.

title: Diagnostic value of copeptin combined with hypersensitive cardiac troponin T detection in early acute myocardial infarction: A protocol of randomized double-blind diagnostic trial
description:
Abstract
Background: The sensitivity and specificity of the routine detection of acute myocardial infarction(AMI) in early diagnosis are not high, which can not meet the clinical needs. Copeptin combined with hypersensitive cardiac troponin T(hs-cTnT) is a new detection scheme, and its value in the early diagnosis of acute myocardial infarction is still unclear. Accordingly, the aim of this study is to evaluate the diagnostic value of copeptin combined with hypersensitive troponin T detection in early acute myocardial infarction.
Methods: This is a prospective, randomized, double-blind diagnostic trial to investigate the diagnostic value of copeptin combined with hypersensitive troponin T detection in early acute myocardial infarction. Approved by the clinical research ethics of our hospital. Patients were randomly divided into one of two test protocols: (A) copeptin combined with hs-cTnT group and (B) cardiac troponin I (cTnI) group. Patients, doctors, nurses, inspectors, and data-gathering assistants were blinded to group allocation. We will focus on the sensitivity comparison of the two detection methods at different time periods and the sensitivity and specificity comparison of the two detection methods. Data were analyzed using the statistical software package SPSS version 25.0 (Chicago, IL). 
Discussion: The purpose of this study is to evaluate the diagnostic value of copeptin combined with hypersensitive cardiac troponin T detection in early acute myocardial infarction. The results of this study will establish clinical evidence for the detection of high sensitivity cardiac troponin T in the early diagnosis of acute myocardial infarction.

title: The Effect of Artificial Intelligence-Generated Feedback on ‎Clinical Reasoning in Medical Learners:‎ A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
description:
This systematic review and meta-analysis will examine the effect of AI-generated feedback on clinical reasoning performance in medical learners. Clinical reasoning is a core competency in medical education and includes processes such as diagnostic reasoning, differential diagnosis generation, history-taking, management reasoning, and decision-making under uncertainty. With the increasing use of artificial intelligence, including large language models and other AI-supported educational tools, there is a need to determine whether AI-generated feedback meaningfully improves learners’ clinical reasoning and under what conditions it may be most effective.

The primary purpose of this review is to estimate the effect of AI-generated feedback on clinical reasoning performance compared with any eligible control condition, including human expert feedback, standard curriculum, no feedback, or delayed feedback. Eligible participants will include medical learners across the training continuum, including undergraduate health care students, postgraduate trainees, residents, fellows, and practicing clinicians. Eligible interventions will include AI-generated feedback delivered either in real time or after completion of a clinical task, simulation, case, or educational encounter.

The primary outcome will be clinical reasoning performance measured using validated or clearly defined clinical reasoning instruments. Outcomes may include diagnostic accuracy, quality of differential diagnosis, management reasoning, history-taking quality, script concordance test scores, key-feature examination scores, or global clinical reasoning ratings. Secondary outcomes will include learner self-efficacy, feedback acceptance or uptake, knowledge retention, learning efficiency, and automation bias. Automation bias will be treated as a safety-relevant outcome and will refer to learners’ uncritical acceptance, adoption, or reliance on AI-generated output without adequate critical appraisal.

Where studies are sufficiently comparable, quantitative synthesis will be conducted using random-effects meta-analysis. Hedges’ g will be used as the primary effect size for continuous outcomes because studies are expected to use different scoring tools and assessment formats. Subgroup and moderator analyses will explore whether effects differ by learner level, AI system type and version, feedback timing, clinical specialty, comparator type, and outcome domain. Where meta-analysis is not appropriate because of limited study numbers or substantial heterogeneity, findings will be synthesized narratively.

The expected outcomes of this project are to clarify whether AI-generated feedback improves clinical reasoning performance in medical learners, identify the educational contexts in which AI feedback may be most effective, and highlight potential risks such as automation bias. The review will also assess the methodological quality, risk of bias, and certainty of the evidence using appropriate appraisal tools via MERSQI and GRADE. The findings are expected to inform educators, curriculum leaders, researchers, and clinical training programs about the responsible use of AI-generated feedback in clinical reasoning education and identify priorities for future primary research.

title: Examining the specificity of the relations between mindreading, social motivation, neurodiversity and mental health in adolescents and young adults: A transdiagnostic dimensional approach.
description:
Description
This is the pre-registration for the data collected for the Medical Research Council funded project (MRC Reference: MR/X002896/1) titled 'Developing a measure of social understanding for 15 – 24-year-olds that is appropriate, fair, valid, and theoretically motivated'.

Background
Mental health and neurodevelopmental conditions are leading causes of disability in adolescence and early adulthood (Kieling et al., 2024). Accumulating evidence suggests that mental health conditions and neurodevelopmental conditions are associated with differences in social experiences including loneliness and social isolation (Thompson et al., 2025). Remarkably, the social-cognitive processes underpinning these social outcomes remain poorly understood. The aim of the current study is to leverage a transdiagnostic dimensional approach to investigate the degree to which mental health symptoms and neurodevelopmental traits overlap and the extent to which difficulties with mindreading (the ability to reason about others’ mental states) and social motivation (the tendency to approach social situations) cross-cut traditional mental health and neurodevelopmental conditions in adolescents and young adults.

Dimensional Approaches to Mental Health and Neurodiversity
Unlike case-control studies comparing narrowly defined groups of participants with specific conditions, transdiagnostic dimensional studies harness normal variation in symptoms and traits in large community samples to identify spectra of mental health and neurodiversity that account for the co-occurrence of symptoms and traits (Astle et al., 2022; Gillan & Seow, 2020). The past decade has witnessed a rapid increase in the application of bifactor modelling to identify general cross-cutting factors that explain the co-occurrence of mental health symptoms, called the ‘P-factor’ (Caspi et al., 2024), and, more recently, the co-occurrence of neurodevelopmental traits, called the ‘N factor’ (Apperly et al., 2024). In these models, each symptom or trait is also explained, in part, by specific symptom or trait factors, called ‘P-Free’ factors (Caspi et al., 2024) to reflect the fact that these factors capture variance that is not shared with other symptoms or traits that load onto the general factor. This approach to modelling mental health and neurodiversity can provide new insight about the extent to which risk factors and outcomes are transdiagnostic or condition-specific (Apperly et al., 2024; Capsi et al., 2024).

While promising, key gaps in understanding the dimensional structure of mental health symptoms and neurodevelopmental traits exist. Attempts to model the dimensional structure of mental health have, until recently, overlooked neurodevelopmental traits (Michelini et al., 2024). Prominent mental health models, developed in adult samples, have identified three key ‘P-Free’ symptom dimensions alongside the P-factor: externalizing, internalizing, and psychosis (Caspi et al., 2014, 2024). Parallel work involving adults has examined the dimensional structure of neurodevelopmental traits and identified a general N-factor alongside four ‘N-free’ factors: autism, ADHD, cortical hyperexcitability, specific learning differences (dyslexia/dyspraxia) (Apperly et al., 2024). To date, there have been no formal attempts to investigate the links between P and N and the symptom/trait-specific factors. Emerging evidence from children and adolescents suggests that ADHD traits and autism traits are explained by both the P-factor and condition-specific factors (Harden et al., 2020). Alongside this work, evidence from meta-analyses indicate high levels of co-occurrence between neurodevelopmental conditions and mental health conditions (Lai et al., 2019; Njardvik et al., 2025). One possibility is that P and N represent distinct propensities to experience mental health difficulties on the one hand and neurodevelopment traits on the other. These factors may be correlated but they represent dissociable spectra. Alternatively, symptoms of mental health conditions and neurodevelopmental traits may co-occur because they can be explained by a single general transdiagnostic factor (e.g., Caspi et al., 2024; Apperly et al., 2024). The first aim of the current study was to examine the factor structure of traits associated with common neurodevelopmental conditions and symptoms of common mental health difficulties in a large sample of adolescents and young adults. We also sought to examine how fairly these dimensions capture mental health and neurodiversity across sex, age and ethnicity by assessing the resulting models for bias. 

To this end, we will examine the relations between neurodevelopmental traits and mental health symptoms by comparing a series of theory-driven models. We will first begin by testing the N+4 model in a large sample of adolescents and young adults. We will compare the N+4 model as specified in Apperly et al. (2024) with an alternative specification of this model where all indicators load onto both a specific and general factor (see Figure 1). In the original N+4 model, indicators related to Tics (i.e., obsessions, compulsions, motor tics and verbal tics) and sensory sensitivity loaded only onto the general factor (N), meaning that it was not possible to examine whether N-free variance in Tics was linked with any outcomes. We will test a model where the four Tics indicators load onto a specific ‘Tics’ factor and the sensory sensitivity indicators load onto the C factor (capturing cortical hyperexcitability). If each indicator loads onto a specific latent factor, then it will be possible to compare the bifactor model against a first-order five-factor model and a higher-order five-factor model. A first-order five-factor model will provide insight about the interpretability of the specific factors in the bifactor model (Caspi et al., 2024). For example, it will be possible to examine how first-order condition-specific factors are related to specific outcomes (e.g., mindreading, social motivation) and compare this with the N-free condition-specific factors.

Having established the best-fitting solution for the neurodevelopmental traits, we will next test theory-driven models for mental health based on existing literature (e.g., Caspi et al., 2024). Specifically, we will examine whether 10 indicators of internalizing, externalizing, and thought disorder (see Figure 2) are best explained by: (1) a one-factor model in which all indicators load onto a P factor; (2) a first-order three-factor model in which indicators load onto one of three correlated factors (i.e., internalizing, externalizing, and thought disorder); (3) a higher-order model in which the three first-order factors load onto a second-order P factor; (4) and finally a bifactor model in which every indicator loads onto both a general factor (P) and a specific orthogonal factor (i.e., P-free internalizing, P-free externalizing, and P-free thought disorder). Given that some indicators from the N+4 model may capture mental health rather than neurodevelopmental traits, we will re-run each of these models incorporating four additional indicators from the neurodevelopmental traits battery (i.e., obsessions, compulsions, aura-like hallucinations, impulsivity). Specifically, obsessions, compulsions and aura-like hallucinations will be permitted to load onto the P-free ‘Thought Disorder’ latent factor (e.g., Michelini et al., 2024) and the impulsivity indicator will be permitted to load onto the P-free ‘Externalizing’ latent factor (e.g., Michelini et al., 2024). 

The best-fitting models for neurodevelopmental traits and mental health symptoms will then be used to establish the relations between neurodevelopmental traits and mental health symptoms. To this end we will compare a two general factor bifactor solution in which neurodevelopmental traits are explained by both a general neurodevelopmental factor (‘N’) and specific N-free factors (e.g., A, B, C, D) and mental health symptoms are explained by a correlated but distinct general mental health factor (‘P’) and specific P-free condition factors (e.g., internalizing, externalizing, thought disorder). Figure 3 shows the alternative specifications for this model depending upon the results of the analysis of the best fitting model for N (Figure 3A-C and Figure 3D-F). Note that, we will test whether four key indicators (i.e., obsessions, compulsions, aura-like hallucinations, and impulsivity) are indicators of neurodevelopmental traits only (Figure 3A and Figure 3D), mental health symptoms only (Figure 3B and Figure 3E), or both by permitting cross-loadings (Figure 3C and Figure 3F). We will compare the best-fitting two general factor bifactor solution against a one general factor bifactor solution (Figure 3G-L).
When the best-fitting model for neurodevelopmental traits and mental health symptoms is identified, we will examine the validity of the model. Specifically, we will examine the validity of the general factor(s) using self-reported diagnoses of mental health and neurodevelopmental conditions. If a single general factor is the best fitting model, then those with a reported diagnoses of either a mental health condition or neurodevelopmental condition should have higher latent factor scores on the general latent factor. If a two general factor model is the best fitting model, then those with a reported neurodevelopmental diagnosis should have higher scores on the N factor than those without a diagnosis. Likewise, those with a reported mental health condition should have higher scores on the P factor than those without a diagnosis. 

Mindreading Difficulties as a Transdiagnostic Indicator
Early prominent accounts of autism implicated mindreading as a source of variation in differences between autistic people and neurotypical people in communication and social interaction (Baron-Cohen, 1995). Divergence in mindreading was initially viewed as a specific hallmark of autism (Baron‐Cohen, 1991) but subsequent research, using case-control designs, now points to differences in mindreading in children and adults with externalizing problems, internalizing problems and a wide range of neurodevelopmental conditions, implying that mindreading difficulties are transdiagnostic (Cotter et al., 2018).
Bifactor transdiagnostic models of mental health and neurodiversity make it possible to examine the degree to which phenotypes like mindreading are associated with specific symptom dimensions that do not overlap with other dimensions (e.g., psychosis-like symptoms or autism traits) or cut across mental health and neurodevelopmental conditions as evidenced by links with the general factor (Caspi et al., 2024). Recently, Devine et al. (under review) examined the specificity of the relations between the P factor and P-free factors and mindreading performance in a large sample of 8- to 13-year-old children in the UK. Supporting the transdiagnostic account, P-factor scores were more strongly related to mindreading than P-free symptom dimensions (i.e., capturing autism traits, ADHD traits, externalizing symptoms, and internalizing symptoms). In other words, once the general tendency to experience mental distress or neurodevelopmental traits (i.e., the P-factor) was considered, P-free symptom factors did not explain any unique variance in mentalizing. Building on this work, the second aim of the current study was to examine the specificity of the links between mindreading, mental health and neurodiversity using a transdiagnostic dimensional approach in adolescents and young adults. If the transdiagnostic account holds, any general factor (e.g., P- or N-factors) will be more strongly related with mindreading than any specific symptom dimension factor. In contrast, if the specificity account holds, then mindreading will show unique associations with specific symptom dimension factors, over and above any general factor (e.g., P- or N-factors).

Social motivation as Transdiagnostic Indicator
Social motivation refers to individual differences in the degree to which people show social interest, derive pleasure from social interactions, and show a willingness to build and maintain social bonds (Chevallier et al., 2012; Devine & Apperly, 2022). Social motivation is correlated with but distinct from mindreading in childhood and adolescence and uniquely contributes to success with social interactions with peers (Devine & Apperly, 2022). Meta-analyses of case-control studies suggest lower levels of social pleasure among people with depression and schizophrenia (Gandhi et al., 2022). Differences in social motivation have also been identified among autistic people (Chevallier et al., 2012; Han et al., 2019) and people with ADHD (Demurie et al., 2011). Together these findings suggest that low levels of social motivation may cut across a range of different mental health and neurodevelopmental conditions (e.g., Gerber et al., 2025). To date, the unique links between social motivation, mental health and neurodiversity have not been examined using a transdiagnostic dimensional approach. To address this gap, the third aim of the current study was to examine the specificity of the links between social motivation, mental health and neurodiversity using a transdiagnostic dimensional approach in adolescents and young adults.

title: Predictive performance of models for postoperative delirium in neurosurgery: A systematic review
description:
This systematic review aims to evaluate the predictive performance of clinical prediction models for postoperative delirium (POD) in adult patients undergoing intracranial neurosurgical procedures. Despite neurosurgery being associated with some of the highest rates of POD among surgical specialties, no systematic review has comprehensively evaluated the available prediction models in this population.
A comprehensive search will be conducted across PubMed, Embase, Web of Science and PubMed from inception to 31st March 2026. Studies will be eligible if they include adults undergoing intracranial procedures, evaluate POD as the primary outcome using a validated instrument (CAM, CAM-ICU, or DSM criteria), develop or validate a clinical prediction model, and report quantitative model performance metrics. Studies restricted to spinal surgery, review articles, conference abstracts, and studies without performance metrics will be excluded.
The primary outcome is model discriminative performance, reported as AUROC. Secondary outcomes will include pooled sensitivity and specificity, calibration, and Bayesian diagnostic metrics. Meta-analysis will be performed using a random-effects REML model, with heterogeneity assessed by I². Risk of bias will be assessed using PROBAST. This review will be reported in accordance with PRISMA 2020 guidelines.

title: Title :AI for Rotator Cuff Tears: A Diagnostic Accuracy Meta-analysis
description: This preregistered PRISMA-DTA meta-analysis evaluates the diagnostic accuracy of artificial intelligence (AI) for detecting rotator cuff tears across MRI, ultrasound, and radiographs. We will pool sensitivity, specificity, AUROC, and diagnostic odds ratio using bivariate random-effects and HSROC models, and synthesize paired AI-vs-human results when the same dataset is read by both. Prespecified subgroup and meta-regression analyses examine modality, AI architecture (CNNs, transformers, radiomics/hybrids), dataset size, external validation, and reference standard (surgery vs expert radiologist). Risk of bias will be assessed with QUADAS-2 and QUADAS-AI, with sensitivity analyses excluding high-risk or internal-only validations. Findings will contextualize AI performance against traditional imaging benchmarks
subjects: Orthopedics | Radiology | Medicine and Health Sciences | Medical Specialties

title: The Effectiveness of Deep Learning-Based Convolutional Neural Networks for Automated Detection of the Inferior Alveolar Nerve Canal on Cone Beam Computed Tomography (CBCT) Scans: A Systematic Review of Accuracy, Reliability, and Clinical Applicability
description:
Background:
Accurate identification of the Inferior Alveolar Nerve Canal (IANC) is crucial in dental sur-gical procedures to prevent complications such as nerve damage. Manual detection of the IANC on Cone Beam Computed Tomography (CBCT) scans is time-consuming and prone to operator variability. Deep learning-based Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) offer a promising alternative for automating this process, but their generalizability and clinical ap-plicability remain underexplored.
Objective:
To evaluate the effectiveness, reliability, and clinical applicability of CNNs in the automated detection of the IANC on CBCT scans, identify limitations in current approaches, and pro-pose directions for future research.
Methods:
A systematic review was conducted using databases including PubMed, Scopus, and IEEE Xplore. Inclusion criteria focused on studies employing CNNs for IANC detection, reporting key metrics such as accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity. Risk of bias was assessed using the RoB2 tool, and data on CNN architecture, dataset size, and performance were extracted.
Results:
Nine studies were included, employing architectures such as U-Net, ResNet, and DenseNet. CNN models demonstrated high accuracy (85%-97%), sensitivity (84%-95%), and specifici-ty (85%-96%), outperforming manual detection in consistency and reliability. However, lim-itations included small sample sizes, lack of dataset diversity, and overfitting risks, impact-ing generalizability across populations.
Conclusion:
CNNs exhibit significant potential for automating IANC detection on CBCT scans, improv-ing diagnostic precision and reducing variability. Addressing challenges such as dataset di-versity, standardization of evaluation metrics, and external validation is critical for clinical adoption.
