title: Does Increasing Ecological Validity Enhance Older Adults’ Gaze Following?
description:
Does Increasing Ecological Validity Enhance Older Adults’ Gaze Following?
Preregistration Document
22/02/2022

Others’ directional eye gaze confers substantial social information to the observer. Following others’ eye gaze and, in doing so, engaging in joint attention, is considered a critical and core component of human social cognition (Stephenson et al., 2021). In experimental studies, the extent to which an individual engages in gaze following upon the observation of others’ averted gaze has conventionally been measured using the gaze-cueing paradigm (Friesen & Kingstone, 1998). Within this task, individuals respond to targets that appear either at the left or right hand-side of the screen as quickly and as accurately as possible. Before each target is presented however, a centrally located face with averted gaze towards either the left or to the right hand-side of the screen is presented. Each target can therefore be categorized as being gaze-cued (appearing at the location the gaze cue looked towards) or gaze-miscued (appearing at the location the gaze cue looked away from). Gaze following – an attention shift via the gaze cue stimulus – is considered to have occurred when response times to gaze-cued targets are faster than response times to gaze-miscued targets. 

The gaze-cueing effect is highly robust in healthy adults (McKay et al., in press), but experimental evidence now indicates it may decline with age. Although older adults exhibit a gaze-cueing effect, relative to younger adults the magnitude of that effect is significantly reduced (McKay et al., under review). This age-related decline also emerges irrespective of whether gaze-cues are informative regarding the location of the upcoming target or not, indicating that both reflexive (emerging following non-predictive gaze cues) and volitional (emerging following predictive gaze cues) gaze-cueing is affected. However, the age effect for volitional gaze following was substantially larger, with the specific pattern of results suggesting that this was due to younger (but not older) adults exhibiting a boost in gaze-cueing following predictive gaze cues. 

The finding that predictive gaze cues seem to boost younger adults’ gaze-cueing is consistent with Olk and Kingstone’s (2015) proposal that volitional effects – arising from predictive cues that produce reflexive orienting in and of themselves – have an additive effect on attentional cueing. That is, across both predictive and non-predictive tasks, reflexive stimulus-driven attention should occur, given the presence of the stimulus in all trials, irrespective of predictiveness. However, when cues are predictive, additional volitional top-down orienting occurs which ‘boosts’ attentional cueing effects. The finding that this ‘boost’ is only seen for younger adults therefore aligns with the cognitive decline model of social cognitive ageing, which predict age-related reductions should particularly affect volitional processes.

However, all studies in this literature to date have used gaze-cue stimuli that have poor ecological validity. At most, illusory biological motion has been present via the presentation of multiple slightly different images wherein the gaze cue shifts from direct to averted across the trial (e.g., as in Dalmaso et al., 2015; Nagy et al., 2020; Slessor et al., 2008). Most studies, however, presented only a single static averted gaze cue (e.g., as in Bailey et al., 2014; Deroche et al., 2016; Gayzur et al., 2014; Slessor et al., 2016). These methodological approaches provide excellent laboratory control but raise obvious questions about whether the same age effects would emerge when more realistic stimuli and methods are used. 

Ecological validity is an important consideration in the study of almost all types of psychological phenomena, and for understanding people in general, but it assumes particular significance in any consideration of age effects. This is because the degree to which a task uses stimuli that are true-to life or ecologically valid is also likely to influence the extent to which that task assumes meaningfulness and relevance to the participant. Extensive literature reveals motivational shifts with ageing, whereby personally relevant and meaningful goals are increasingly prioritized with advancing age (see Carstensen, 2021). Rather than cognitive decline disrupting volitional gaze following, older adults may therefore not exhibit a boost for predictive gaze cues on conventional gaze-cueing tasks simply owing to a decreased motivation to engage with the standard task. By using a gaze-cueing task with greater ecological validity, this study will provide novel data that helps to differentiate these two competing possibilities. 

To achieve this goal, younger and older adults will be asked to complete two predictive gaze cueing tasks (in a counterbalanced order). One will closely follow a previously used paradigm with standard static face stimuli (Slessor et al., 2016 specifically). The other will be the same paradigm, but will use stimuli that have enhanced ecological validity. If age-related differences in motivation contribute to age-differences in volitional gaze-cued attention, the age-effect in gaze-cueing should be attenuated for the task that has enhanced ecological validity relative to the standard gaze-cueing task. Specifically, there should be a three way interaction between gaze cueing condition, age group, and ecological validity such that the effect of age-group (older adults’ reduced gaze cueing effect) on the effect of gaze cue type (faster response times on gaze-cued relative to gaze-miscued trials) will differ depending on the tasks’ ecological validity (the effect of age on the effect of gaze-cueing condition will be smaller when cues are more ecologically valid). 

Stimuli 

Examples of the gaze stimuli are shown in Figure 1. For the standard task, grey scale photographs of four actors (two males, two females) with neutral expressions will be used from the FEEST database (Young et al., 2002). The stimuli’s gaze was precisely manipulated by the study authors (Slessor et al., 2016), and we have acquired these stimuli from the study authors for use in the present study. For the enhanced ecological validity task, we will use naturalistic videos of four actors (two males, two females) shifting their gaze. For both types of stimuli, as in Slessor et al. (2016) the target will be an asterisk of approximately 1x1cms and the fixation cross will be a plus sign.

Predictive Gaze-Cueing Procedure

Number of trials. As in Slessor et al. (2016), there will be 96 trials for each gaze-cueing task. Two thirds of the trials (64 with 16 per actor and 32 left targets and 32 right targets) will be gaze-cued and one third (32 with 8 per actor and 16 left targets and 16 right targets) will be gaze-miscued. The 96 trials per task will be presented randomly within a single block. There will therefore be two blocks. The order of these two blocks will be counterbalanced randomly across participants with a one-minute break given in-between.

Instructions. Participants will be instructed to maintain fixation on the fixation cross as is typical for gaze-cueing tasks. As in Slessor et al. (2016) participants will perform a speeded localization task wherein they will be instructed to respond to whether the target asterisk appeared at the left or the right of the screen by making key presses. 

Trial series. The fixation cross will appear alone in the centre of the screen for 1000ms (as in Slessor et al., 2016). However, in contrast to Slessor et al. (2016), the fixation cross will remain on the screen throughout the entire trial series to facilitate gaze fixation. 

In the standard paradigm, the stimulus with direct gaze will then be presented for 80 ms. This will be done to equate the presence of prior direct gaze across the two tasks because the enhanced ecological validity stimuli have a direct gaze starting point. This will then be followed by the averted gaze cue stimuli for 220ms. 

In the enhanced ecological validity paradigm, the video of the face with eye gaze moving from direct to averted will be presented. The total length of the video is 300ms comprising 80ms of direct gaze, 32ms of shifting gaze, and 188ms of full averted gaze. Figure 1 shows a schematised examples of the respective stimuli across time. 

As in Slessor et al. (2016), following stimulus presentations, the face image or video will disappear, and the target stimuli will appear at either the left or right (approximately 10.5cm to the left or right of the centre of the fixation cross). The stimuli will remain on-screen until a response is executed. Thereafter, 500ms of noise will be presented as a mask to ensure that image aftereffects do not affect subsequent trial performance. 

Power Analysis

Slessor et al. (2016) Study 2 reported a significant gaze cue validity X age interaction (ηp2 = .18) in a predictive gaze-cueing task such that older adults exhibited reduced gaze-cueing relative to younger adults. We conducted an a priori power analysis in G*Power 3.0 using the default as in G*Power 3.0 effect size specification option. We determined that for an ANOVA with a within-between interaction, given  of .05, power of .90, two groups (i.e., young adults and older adults), two measurements (i.e., reaction times for direct gaze cued trials, reaction times for direct gaze miscued trials), the default repeated measures correlation of .50, and assuming the smaller of the previously uncovered partial eta-squared values of .18 for the interaction, a total sample size of 16 (8 participants per age group) would be required. Considering our plan to test for a higher-level interaction effect, as well as the potential for some data loss, we planned to recruit two times this amount for a sample size of 32 (16 participants per age group). 

Data Reduction and Preparation Plan

We will remove any participant with less than 50% accuracy overall, assuming such participants did not engage properly with the experimental task (e.g., due to misunderstanding of instructions, boredom, fatigue, etc.). For the remaining participants, we will remove response times associated with incorrect responses. We will also remove RTs < 100ms, as we assume that these represent responses that are not target driven (i.e., anticipation responses). Very slow responses will be characterised as those that are > 3500ms and these will be removed as is conventional in this field given these responses are not likely to be related to the previously presented probes and therefore aren’t a measure of the construct of interest in the experiment. The remaining RTs will be log-transformed as is standard for RT data given it is typically positively skewed. Each participant’s mean log-transformed RT in direct-gaze-cued and direct-gaze-miscued trials for the nonpredictive and predictive cueing blocks will then be calculated and compiled for use in analyses.

Analysis Plan

The central research question will be addressed using a 2 (gaze-cueing condition: gaze-cued, gaze-miscued) x2 (ecological validity: high, low) x 2 (age-group: young adult, older adult) mixed ANOVA. For descriptive purposes, we will also compare young and older adults on the following demographic and background measures using t-tests and chi-square tests as appropriate.

Demographic and Background Measures 

Ethnicity, Sex, and Age

In addition to sex and age, data on ethnicity will be collected. Prior studies have shown that direct gaze perception may be subject to a small other-race effect in which Asian and Caucasian participants show relatively suboptimal perception of other-race direct gaze cues relative to own-race direct gaze cues (Collova et al., 2017). Uono and Hietanen (2015) also found higher accuracy in gaze detection for own-race persons for Caucasian observers; however, in their study no own-race effect of gaze perception was uncovered for Asian observers. Nonetheless, given the possibility of an other-race effect in eye gaze perception, racial demographics will be collected. To this end, we will ask participants: ‘What do you consider to be your ethnic origin or affiliation?’ With response options ‘Caucasian’, ‘Asian’, ‘Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander’, ‘African’, ‘Pacific Islander’ or ‘other (please specific below)’. To record sex, participants will be asked ‘what is your gender?’ The options they can select from are ‘Male’, ‘Female’, ‘Other’, or ‘Prefer not to say’. To record age, participants will be asked ‘How old did you turn in years on your last birthday (e.g., 32, 26, 65)?’.

Edinburgh Handedness Inventory – Short Form

Handedness is an important consideration in any task where participants are making speeded manual responses as in reaction time tasks. The four-item short form Edinburgh Handedness Inventory (Veale, 2014) is an adapted and simplified version of the Edinburgh Handedness Inventory (Oldfield, 1971) developed using powerful confirmatory factor analysis techniques. It has good reliability ( = .93; Veale et al., 2014), and the four-item short form’s factor structure was found to be robust across adult age groups (see Veale, 2014).

Liebowitz Social Anxiety Scale – Self Report 

There is some evidence that social anxiety influences persons’ perceptions of eye gaze and responsiveness to gaze cues (Chen et al., 2017; although see Talipski et al., 2021). Here, we will assess social anxiety using the Liebowitz Social Anxiety Scale – Self-Report (LSAS-SR; Baker et al., 2002) to establish whether younger and older adults are matched in their social anxiety. This scale has been adapted from the original clinician administered version (Liebowitz, 1987), and measures fear and avoidance of 24 social situations via a Likert scale. It has been shown to have high internal consistency ( = .95; Baker et al., 2002). 

Autism Quotient 

Because Autism Spectrum Disorder and autistic traits have been linked to reduced performance in tasks requiring perception of and responsiveness to others’ direct gaze (e.g., see Madipakkam et al., 2019), we also aimed to quantify Autistic traits as a background characteristic. To this end, we will use the full Autism Quotient (AQ; see Baron-Cohen et al., 2001). The AQ comprises 50 questions. Participants rate their agreement (on a Likert scale) with 50 statements about themselves, each designed to tap into whether the individual has the Autistic trait or not across five symptom domains. Within each domain, the AQ has moderate to high internal consistency (s > .63; Baron-Cohen et al., 2001).

Intelligence, Education, and Cognition 

The National Adult Reading Test II (NART-II) will be administered to estimate full-scale IQ. Participants will also be asked to report their total years of full-time education (open response numerical with two examples supplied). The Mini-Addenbrooke’s Cognitive Examination (Mini-ACE) will be completed as a cognitive screening measure. The word-colour STROOP task will be used to index inhibitory control and Digit Span (Forwards and Backwards) to measure working memory. The Digit Span test is a subtest of both the Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale (WAIS) and the Wechsler Memory Scales (WMS). Subjects are read a sequence of numbers and asked to repeat the same sequence back to the examiner in order (forward span) or in reverse order (backward span). Forward span captures attention efficiency and capacity. Backward span is an executive task particularly dependent on working memory. The Trail Making Task will be administered to index psychomotor speed (Part A), and executive control (Part B).

Social Frailty Scale

The Social Frailty Scale (Pek et al., 2020) is an 8-item scale that indexes social frailty. This is a validated measure that assesses access to both general and social resources, as well as the fulfilment of basic social needs.

Visual Contrast Sensitivity 

We will compare younger and older adults in their visual contrast sensitivity using a Contrast Sensitivity Chart.

title: Neurobiological correlates of cognition in bipolar disorder and ADHD – enhancing diagnostic accuracy in women
description:
Bipolar disorder (BD) and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) are prevalent neuropsychiatric conditions with overlapping symptoms, leading to frequent misdiagnoses. These contribute to delayed or insufficient treatment, affecting daily and occupational functioning. Women with BD are more often misdiagnosed, and females with ADHD receive diagnosis and treatment years later than males. This study aims to improve diagnostic accuracy for women by identifying shared and disorder-specific neurocognitive profiles and associated neurobiological markers in female individuals with BD and ADHD.
The first aim is to identify differences in neurocognition between men and women across the BD-ADHD spectrum, focusing on executive function, working memory, attention, and processing speed. The second aim investigates neurobiological markers, such as cerebrospinal fluid biomarkers and MRI-derived brain metrics, specific to women with these conditions. 
By associating cognitive categories with neurobiological markers, the study aims to identify sex-specific profiles that enhance diagnostic precision. This research fills a critical gap, potentially improving tailored treatments for women, who have historically been underrepresented in clinical trials. Findings may also inform the development of AI-driven diagnostic tools for BD and ADHD.

Original student exam papers and identifiable data are not deposited, in accordance with the institutional ethics framework.

title: Mapping Regulatory Standards and Guidance for the Performance Evaluation of In Vitro Diagnostics: A Scoping Review Protocol
description:
In vitro diagnostic medical devices (IVDs) are essential tools in modern healthcare, enabling the detection, diagnosis, prognosis, prediction and monitoring of diseases from samples taken from the body such as blood, saliva, or tissue. The regulation of all health products, including IVDs, is guided globally by a set of underlying principles that ensure public and personal health protection while enabling innovation and access. Regulatory systems are developed to ensure that technologies on the market, be they established or novel, are safe, perform as intended and are reliable. These three characteristics underpin regulatory requirements and processes. Regulatory frameworks provide structured pathways for the development, assessment, and approval of IVDs, ensuring that rigorous standards are met before and after IVDs are introduced into clinical practice. Without clear regulatory guidance and standards, there is a risk that tests may not be developed with reference to the current state of the art, potentially leading to misdiagnosis, delayed treatment, or harm to patients or their users. For regulators, the term “state of the art” is generally considered to be the stage of technical capability at a given time as regards products, processes and services, based on the consolidated findings of science, technology and experience. It is an evolving concept, that acknowledges shifts in risks due to new developments in the clinical setting. 

IVD performance evaluation is the systematic process of assessing how well an IVD performs in terms of its accuracy, reliability, and clinical benefit over its lifetime. The Global Harmonization Task Force (GHTF) defines performance evaluation of an IVD medical device as “the assessment and analysis of data to establish or verify the performance of an IVD medical device” (GHTF/SG5/N6:2012). Performance evaluation is a cornerstone of regulatory authorisation and mature regulatory bodies (e.g. IMDRF members and WHO listed authorities) generally require comprehensive performance data before an IVD can be placed on the market. 
Under the global IVD regulatory model supported by international regulatory agencies (i.e. GHTF, IMDRF [International Medical Device Regulators Forum]), performance evaluation assesses 3 core pillars: 

1. Scientific Validity – Evaluates the link between the biomarker being measured and the clinical condition of interest, ensuring the test is based on sound scientific principles. GHTF defines scientific validity as “the association of an analyte to a clinical condition/physiological state” (GHTF/SG5/N6:2012).
2. Analytical Performance – Measures the technical accuracy of the test, including analytical sensitivity, specificity, precision, and limits of detection. GHTF defines analytical performance as “the ability of an IVD medical device to detect or measure a particular analyte” (GHTF/SG5/N6:2012).
3. Clinical Performance – Assesses how well the test performs in a clinical context, such as its ability to correctly identify or rule out a condition in the target population (e.g. clinical sensitivity and specificity, and predictive or likelihood values). GHTF defines clinical performance as “the ability of an IVD medical device to yield results that are correlated with a particular clinical condition/physiological state in accordance with target population and intended user” (GHTF/SG5/N6:2012).

In the UK, the Centres of Excellence for Regulatory Science and Innovation (CERSIs) are a nation-wide initiative launched by Innovate UK in partnership with the MHRA, the Office for Life Sciences, and the Medical Research Council (MRC). These centres, established in 2025, aim to transform how innovative medical products, such as diagnostics, digital health tools, and advanced therapies are evaluated and approved, ensuring they reach patients safely and efficiently. Among the seven established CERSIs, the Clinical Evaluation and Assessment for Regulation of Diagnostic Tests (CLEARED) centre is dedicated to improving the regulatory pathways for IVDs (www.cersi-ivd.com). Part of CLEARED’s mission is to develop robust regulatory guidance to help innovators and manufacturers navigate complex regulatory approval processes for IVDs. 
A specific objective of CLEARED is to draft a new, fit-for-purpose guidance document or international standard for the performance evaluation of IVDs. The current European Standard for performance evaluation of IVDs (BS [British Standard] EN 13612:2002) is outdated and lacks substantive guidance on key domains of performance evaluation. It does not address contemporary technologies, including IVDs incorporating artificial intelligence (AI) or genomics for example, nor does it reflect current regulatory expectations under the EU IVDR. 

The anticipated outputs of this project include:
1) A comprehensive mapping of current regulatory guidance and standards for IVD performance evaluation.
2) Identification of gaps, ambiguities, and inconsistencies across frameworks.
3) Clarification of how core performance domains are defined and operationalised.
4) Evidence to inform the drafting of a new, fit-for-purpose guidance document or international standard for IVD performance evaluation.
5) A methodological foundation to support regulators, manufacturers, and innovators in aligning future performance evaluation practices with contemporary scientific and regulatory expectations.

Ultimately, this work aims to strengthen regulatory science in diagnostics, improve clarity for innovators navigating regulatory pathways, and enhance patient safety by ensuring that IVD performance evaluation reflects current technological capabilities and methodological standards.

title: Prevalence of Myofascial Trigger Points in Patients with Low Back Pain: A systematic Review
description:
Low back pain is considered a symptom associated with various pathologies and is classified, according to scientific evidence, as either specific or non-specific depending on its underlying cause. Specific low back pain is linked to an identifiable pathoanatomical cause, which may include issues affecting structures outside the lumbar spine, specific disorders of the lumbar spine (such as epidural abscesses, compression fractures, spondyloarthropathies, neoplasms, or cauda equina syndrome), or conditions causing radicular pain, radiculopathy, or spinal canal stenosis. Although these conditions are clinically severe, prevalence studies indicate that only 5% of low back pain cases are attributed to specific causes, with 4% associated with compression fractures, 3% with spinal stenosis, and less than 1% with serious diseases such as tumors or infections.

Identifying cases of potentially serious low back pain relies on alarm signs, such as nocturnal pain or unexplained weight loss; however, these signs alone usually have low diagnostic accuracy. Therefore, a more effective diagnostic approach involves combining different clinical features to determine when further investigation is warranted.

Given that myofascial trigger points are considered clinically relevant sources of pain in individuals with low back pain, and considering the need to compile existing knowledge on the prevalence of active and latent trigger points associated with this type of pain, this study aimed to conduct a literature review on the prevalence of trigger points in patients with low back pain.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning in Breast Cancer Diagnosis: A Systematic Review
description:
Breast cancer remains one of the most prevalent cancers affecting women globally. Early and accurate diagnosis is critical for improving treatment outcomes and survival rates. In recent years, Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) have emerged as powerful tools in the field of medical diagnostics, particularly in oncology. These technologies have shown promise in enhancing diagnostic accuracy, reducing human error, and streamlining workflows in radiology, pathology, and genomic analysis.
This systematic review aims to comprehensively evaluate existing literature on the application of AI and ML techniques in breast cancer diagnosis. The review will focus on assessing the diagnostic performance (e.g., sensitivity, specificity, accuracy) of these models across various diagnostic modalities such as mammography, ultrasound, MRI, histopathological images, and genetic biomarkers.
The purpose of this review is to Synthesize evidence on how AI and ML are being utilized in breast cancer diagnosis, Identify which algorithms and datasets are most commonly used, Compare the performance of AI/ML models with conventional diagnostic methods, Highlight gaps in current research and provide recommendations for future studies, The expected outcomes include a detailed summary of current AI/ML technologies in breast cancer diagnostics, an evaluation of their diagnostic accuracy, and an identification of challenges and future opportunities for clinical implementation. This review will contribute to the body of knowledge that can inform clinicians, researchers, and healthcare policymakers about the readiness and reliability of AI-assisted diagnostic tools in breast cancer care.

title: The influence of a specific or a broad patient referral on diagnostic accuracy
description:
This study aims to determine whether clinical information causes cognitive errors in acute internal medicine and emergency cases. Specifically, we will study how the information presented in referral letters(as made by general practitioners) impacts the diagnostic performance of medical interns. We want to investigate the effect of a broad, a specific and correct, and a specific, but incorrect referral question on diagnostic performance. We expect that when a patient is referred with a specific question, this will influence the diagnostic hypothesis into the direction of the suggested diagnosis independent of whether this diagnosis is correct or not; conversely, we expect that referral with a broad question will not influence diagnostic accuracy. Furthermore, we expect that confidence in diagnosis might increase when the participants have the same hypothesis as the specific referral question suggests and we also expect participants will take less time to diagnose in such cases, compared to broad referral questions.

Keywords: diagnostic error, cognitive bias, clinical reasoning, patient safety

title: Development and Validation of Cognitive Tests for Essential Tremor: A Scoping Review
description:
This scoping review examines cognitive assessment tools used in essential tremor (ET), a common movement disorder which is being increasingly recognized for its neurocognitive impacts. The study aimed to identify neuropsychological measures developed or validated for use in ET, evaluate their measurement properties, and characterize the cognitive domains and diagnostic accuracy reported in the literature. Following PRISMA guidelines, a systematic search of four major databases yielded 15 eligible studies comprising cross-sectional and cohort designs involving predominantly older, highly educated adults (aged 60–85) often undergoing evaluation for surgical interventions. Results revealed that while 21 distinct instruments were identified, no ET-specific cognitive tools have been developed. ET was consistently associated with deficits in attention and executive function; for example, the Repeatable Battery for the Assessment of Neuropsychological Status (RBANS) Attention Index showed a large deficit (d=0.86,p<.001). Traditional screening measures, such as the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) and Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE), demonstrated poor predictive validity for longitudinal decline (AUCs of 0.65 and 0.63, respectively). Conversely, the Cerebellar Cognitive Affective Syndrome Scale (CCAS-S) showed strong sensitivity, identifying deficits in 65% of participants. Motor tremor was consistently found to have a cofounding effect on timed, manual-based tasks. Clinically, neuropsychologists should prioritize motor-minimized or motor-free assessment protocols and employ targeted batteries focusing on executive function and attention rather than relying on general screenings to accurately monitor cognitive progression in patients with ET.
Key words: Essential Tremor, cognitive, impairment, neuropsychological testing.

title: Overlapping Chest X-Ray Features of Pneumonia and Tuberculosis: A Literature Review of Radiographic Similarities and Misdiagnosis Rates
description:
Pneumonia and pulmonary tuberculosis (PTB) are two of the most common infectious diseases affecting the lungs, especially in low- and middle-income countries. Despite being caused by different pathogens and requiring distinct treatments, both diseases frequently present with overlapping radiographic findings on chest X-ray (CXR). These similarities can lead to substantial diagnostic uncertainty, especially in resource-limited settings where CXR remains the primary imaging tool.

This literature review aims to examine and summarize the radiographic similarities between pneumonia and pulmonary tuberculosis on plain chest radiographs. The study specifically focuses on identifying CXR features that are most frequently mistaken for one another and evaluating published evidence on how often pneumonia is initially misdiagnosed as TB, and vice versa.

The purpose of this project is to provide a comprehensive synthesis of current knowledge regarding:
(1) characteristic and overlapping radiographic findings of pneumonia and PTB on chest X-ray,
(2) the frequency and contributing factors of misdiagnosis between the two conditions, and
(3) the clinical consequences associated with these diagnostic errors, including delays in correct treatment or inappropriate therapy.

This research is expected to highlight the limitations of CXR interpretation in differentiating pneumonia from TB and to provide evidence-based insights that may help clinicians improve diagnostic accuracy. Ultimately, this review aims to support better clinical decision-making and reduce misdiagnosis rates, thereby improving patient outcomes in areas where reliance on chest radiography remains high.

title: Diagnostic Performance of Ultra-Low-Dose CT Compared to Standard CT in Detecting Pulmonary Nodules: A Systematic Review
description:
Pulmonary nodules are small growths in the lungs that may represent benign lesions or early-stage lung cancer. Early and accurate detection is crucial for timely intervention and improved patient outcomes. Standard-dose computed tomography (CT) is currently the gold standard for detecting pulmonary nodules; however, it involves exposure to ionizing radiation, which may pose long-term risks, especially in screening populations.
Ultra-low-dose CT (ULDCT) has emerged as a promising alternative imaging modality, offering substantial reductions in radiation exposure while maintaining diagnostic capability. The primary concern, however, is whether this reduction in dose compromises the ability to detect pulmonary nodules with the same sensitivity, specificity, and diagnostic accuracy as standard-dose CT.
This systematic review aims to critically evaluate and synthesize current evidence on the diagnostic performance of ULDCT compared to standard CT for detecting pulmonary nodules. We will examine key diagnostic metrics including sensitivity, specificity, area under the curve (AUC), positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), and inter-reader agreement. In addition, the review will assess how technical factors (e.g., scanner type, slice thickness, reconstruction algorithms) and patient characteristics influence diagnostic performance.
Expected outcomes of this review includes comprehensive summary of existing evidence comparing ULDCT and standard CT, Assessment of whether ULDCT provides a reliable and safe alternative for lung cancer screening or follow-up. Identification of gaps in current research to guide future studies and clinical guidelines.
Ultimately, this review will help radiologists, clinicians, and policymakers evaluate the feasibility of implementing ULDCT in routine practice for early lung cancer detection with minimized radiation exposure.

title: The Aggregation Fallacy: Beyond the Illusion of Precision in Forensic Violence Risk Assessment
description:
This project provides reproducibility and reporting materials supporting the manuscript “The Aggregation Fallacy: Beyond the Illusion of Precision in Forensic Risk Assessment.” The paper addresses a recurring problem in forensic mental health practice: multiple risk instruments are frequently “stacked” and narrated as convergent corroboration, even when instruments share constructs, inputs, and measurement error. In such cases, the appearance of increased confidence may not reflect increased evidentiary independence, and combination rules—especially implicit OR-logic (“high risk if any tool is high”)—may inflate false positives and distort proportionality in legal decision-making.

Purpose. The project operationalizes the manuscript’s core claims in a transparent, audit-ready way. It supplies (i) a dependence-sensitive benchmark demonstrating how OR-logic inflation changes under plausible inter-tool dependence, (ii) derived outputs (tables and figures) used in the manuscript, and (iii) drop-in LaTeX appendices and reporting scaffolds designed to improve courtroom literacy and contestability. The goal is not to produce field prevalence estimates, but to provide a clear structural demonstration of how base rates, redundancy, and integration rules jointly shape error burdens that are legally material.

Methods and contents. The repository includes a reproducible simulation benchmark (Box A) based on a latent-Gaussian threshold model with exchangeable inter-tool correlation (ρ). Parameters reflect an illustrative setting in which each tool has marginal false-positive rate α and sensitivity Se, and the OR-rule classifies as positive if any tool flags “high risk.” Monte Carlo simulations generate the reported false-positive and true-positive rates, confidence intervals, and fold-inflation relative to a single tool. The repository also contains scripts to regenerate the benchmark outputs and to recreate manuscript figures illustrating false-positive behavior under OR/AND rules and the break-even conditions under which OR-logic could be decision-rational given asymmetric error costs.

Expected outcomes. (1) A reproducible, dependence-aware benchmark that readers can rerun, adapt, and critique; (2) derived tables/figures that match the manuscript reporting; (3) LaTeX appendix material suitable for direct inclusion in journal supplements; and (4) audit scaffolding (assumptions and changelog) to support transparent scholarly and courtroom communication. More broadly, the project aims to promote Parsimonious Validity: anchoring evaluation on one best-fit instrument for the referral outcome/horizon and integrating genuinely orthogonal evidence (dynamic change, protective factors, and disconfirmatory information) with explicit uncertainty.

Ethics and data statement. This repository contains no identifiable human participant data. Examples are synthetic/illustrative. The simulation benchmark is a structural demonstration and should not be interpreted as a direct estimate of real-world violence risk or tool performance in any specific jurisdiction.

How to use. Users can reproduce the benchmark and regenerate outputs by installing dependencies listed in the repository and running the included pipeline script. Derived outputs are provided for convenience and traceability.

title: Machine Learning-Enhanced Echocardiography for the Detection of Coronary Artery Disease: A Scoping Review Protocol
description: Coronary artery disease (CAD) remains a leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide. Echocardiography is widely available and provides real-time structural and functional assessment, but diagnostic accuracy is limited by operator dependency. Machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) approaches have emerged as promising tools to enhance echocardiographic interpretation. This protocol outlines a scoping review to map the available evidence.

title: Diagnostic Accuracy of 99mTc-Pyrophosphate Scintigraphy for Transthyretin Cardiac Amyloidosis: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
description: This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluates the diagnostic accuracy of 99mTc-pyrophosphate (PYP) scintigraphy for detecting transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis (ATTR-CM). A comprehensive search of PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, CNKI, and Wanfang Data was conducted from database inception through December 2025. Fourteen independent studies comprising 2,433 patients (577 ATTR-CM positive, 1,856 negative) were included. Endomyocardial biopsy or validated clinical criteria served as the reference standard. Pooled estimates were derived using a bivariate mixed-effects model, and subgroup analyses compared 1-hour planar imaging versus 3-hour delayed imaging with SPECT/CT. The meta-analysis yielded a pooled sensitivity of 94.2% (95% CI: 89.8%–97.2%) and specificity of 97.4% (95% CI: 95.9%–98.5%), with an area under the SROC curve of 0.98. Specificity was significantly higher for 3-hour SPECT/CT protocols (98.0%) compared to 1-hour planar imaging (95.1%; p = 0.02). This registration documents the completed systematic review protocol, including search strategies, inclusion criteria, and statistical analysis plans. The study findings support the use of 3-hour delayed SPECT/CT imaging to optimize diagnostic specificity in clinical practice.

title: Monitoring of Open Science practices in major medical journals - a case study
description:
BACKGROUND

Monitoring (evaluating and quantifying) the use and application of open science practices is key to fostering open science and to understanding barriers and facilitators of open science practices. Monitoring also aids in measuring the impact of open science policies and can serve as a possible intervention to improve transparency and reproducibility. For instance, the Hong Kong principles (1) propose tracking open science practices as a key metric for researcher assessment. Open science monitoring is a key priority for organizations such as the UNESCO (2) and the G7 (3). The scientific community has begun to develop both principles covering which open science practices should be tracked (4) and how to monitor them. For instance, in biomedicine, a core set of 19 open science practices has been developed (5) covering areas such as preregistration, open data, open access and open code. 

Many biomedical journals have also begun to implement policies that promote open science practices. Most notably, the International Committee of Medical Journal Editors (ICMJE) made prospective registration a requirement to publish clinical trial results in 2005 (6). In 2018, it required a specific data-sharing statement to be included in each newly submitted paper (and prespecified in study registration) (7). The impact of these policies has been studied previously, showing a major impact on trial registration practices (8) and mixed results regarding actual data sharing (9)(10). Beyond the common policies set out by the ICMJE, there is variation across biomedical journals regarding other open science policies. In 2007, the Annals of Internal Medicine encouraged, without mandating, data-sharing practices (11). The BMJ encouraged data-sharing in 25 March 2009 (12), made it mandatory in 01 September 2013 for trials of drugs and devices (13) and in 01 July 2015 for all clinical trials (14). Starting in May 2024, all trials published in The BMJ will be required to share their underlying data (15). PLOS journals enforced clinical trial data-sharing in 03 March 2014 (16). This diversity in journals’ open science policies can be monitored by using the Transparency and Openness Promotion (TOP) factor (17), a metric proposed by the Center for Open Science (18) to assess journals’ open science policies. 

Various automated tools have been developed to track changes in behavior across the biomedical literature (e.g.(19)). These tools can be used to assess and monitor open science practices (20), and aid in developing an observatory of open science practices across scientific journals. If those tools are indeed able produce accurate and reproducible results, such an observatory could allow 1/ to determine the real percentage of open science practices, 2/ to assess whether changes in journal’s policies were followed by changes in published articles, and 3/ to point what needs to be improved by researchers and editors. 
 
OBJECTIVES
 
This aim of this study is three-fold:
 to set up a proof-of-concept observatory of major medical journals using automatic tools that can be used to monitor key transparency practices; 
 to describe open science policies in major medical journals;
 to describe retrospectively changes on open science and transparency practices for articles published in the major medical journals with a longitudinal description of registration and data sharing practices following major changes in their policies
METHODS

This protocol will be pre-registered on the open science Framework (link). 
Selection of journals 

Our study will assess a sample of major medical journals (Table 1). We will not rely on impact factor to select target journals as this metric has several limitations (21). Instead, we will focus on a purposeful sample of ten internationally recognized generalist medical journals (specialists medical journals will be excluded) with a majority of current (or former) members of the International Committee of Medical Journals Editors (ICMJE). Furthermore, two major open access journals in the field of medicine, JAMA Network Open and BMC Medicine (the flagship medical journal of the BMC series) will also be included.

Selection of articles 
Key transparency practices
In order to monitor key transparency practices in the target journals, we will include all research articles published in the 2020-2023 period. 
Registration practices for clinical trials following policy changes
We will retrospectively describe changes in registration practices for clinical trials, within our sample of journals by including all randomised controlled trials published in these journals between 2003-2010 (i.e. starting 2 years before the ICMJE policy mandating registration, and up to 5 years after implementation of this policy). 
Registration practices for clinical trials following policy changes
We will retrospectively describe changes in data-sharing practices for clinical trials. This will include extracting all randomised controlled trials published in a given journal from our sample from 2 years before a change in its data-sharing policy, and up to 2 years after implementation of the policy. Search strategies
All eligible articles from the target journals will be identified via searches on PubMed detailed in the following subsection for the articles used for the analysis of key transparency practices. These search strings have been validated according to the PRESS guideline (24) with a specific reviewing by an information specialist (it is the same search string as our study that aims to develop the LLM tool, available on the OSF at https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/3V6JW ). 
Research articles
We will use the following search string: ((2020:2023[Date - Publication]) AND "hasabstract" NOT ("comment"[Publication Type]) NOT ("letter"[Publication Type]) NOT ("editorial"[Publication Type]) NOT ("published erratum"[Publication Type]) NOT ("news"[Publication Type]) NOT ("introductory journal article"[Publication Type]) NOT ("biography"[Publication Type]) NOT ("portrait"[Publication Type]) NOT ("congress"[Publication Type]) NOT ("interview"[Publication Type]) NOT ("retraction of publication"[Publication Type]) NOT ("personal narrative"[Publication Type]) NOT ("retracted publication"[Publication Type]) NOT ("patient education handout"[Publication Type]) NOT ("lecture"[Publication Type]) NOT ("autobiography"[Publication Type]) NOT ("clinical conference"[Publication Type]) NOT ("classical article"[Publication Type]) NOT ("address"[Publication Type]) NOT ("legal case"[Publication Type]) NOT ("expression of concern"[Publication Type]) NOT ("festschrift"[Publication Type]) NOT ("overall"[Publication Type]) NOT ("bibliography"[Publication Type]) NOT ("corrected and republished article"[Publication Type]) NOT ("interactive tutorial"[Publication Type]) NOT ("duplicate publication"[Publication Type]) NOT ("directory"[Publication Type]) NOT ("newspaper article"[Publication Type]) NOT ("periodical index"[Publication Type]) NOT ("dictionary"[Publication Type]) NOT ("meta analysis"[Publication Type]) NOT ("randomized controlled trial"[Publication Type])) AND ("Annals of Internal Medicine"[Journal] OR "BMC Medicine"[Journal] OR "BMJ"[Journal] OR "CMAJ"[Journal] OR "JAMA"[Journal] OR "JAMA Netw Open"[Journal] OR "Lancet"[Journal] OR "Nat Med"[Journal] OR "N Engl J Med"[Journal] OR "PLOS Med"[Journal]). 
Randomised controlled trials
We will use the following search string: (2020:2023[Date - Publication] AND "hasabstract" AND randomizedcontrolledtrial[Filter] AND ("Annals of Internal Medicine"[Journal] OR "BMC Medicine"[Journal] OR "BMJ"[Journal] OR "CMAJ"[Journal] OR "JAMA"[Journal] OR "JAMA Netw Open"[Journal] OR "Lancet"[Journal] OR "Nat Med"[Journal] OR "N Engl J Med"[Journal] OR "PLOS Med"[Journal])). 

After further development we will also try to use a IA Tool that we are developing (refer to box 1 and to research protocol: https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/3V6JW ) to identify all RCTs in case it outperforms our search strategy.
Similar search strings adapted to the different journals and timeframe will be used for analyses of registration and data sharing practices following policy changes.
Systematic review and meta-analyses
We will use the following search string: (2020:2023[Date - Publication] AND "hasabstract" AND meta-analysis[Filter] AND ("Annals of Internal Medicine"[Journal] OR "BMC Medicine"[Journal] OR "BMJ"[Journal] OR "CMAJ"[Journal] OR "JAMA"[Journal] OR "JAMA Netw Open"[Journal] OR "Lancet"[Journal] OR "Nat Med"[Journal] OR "N Engl J Med"[Journal] OR "PLOS Med"[Journal])). 

After further development we will also try to use our IA Tool to identify all systematic review and meta-analyses in case it outperforms our search strategy.
Collection of relevant articles
We will use R [version 4.2.2 RRID:SCR_001905], and the packages rvest and RSelenium to create web scraping scripts that extract eligible articles (PDF) and any supplementary materials from the website of each of the ten journals included in our sample. Two main strategies will be adapted to each journal:
- A strategy for open access articles, as detailed with an example using articles from The BMJ (Appendix 1); 
- A strategy for articles under a paywall, that will require institutional access and the use of another method using RSelenium packages, as detailed with an example using articles from JAMA (Appendix 2). 
In addition, for each eligible article, the XML file will be extracted either from PubMed, PubMed Central, Unpaywall or Alexandria3k if available, or through the API of the respective journal if accessible.
In case no solution is found to retrieve the pdf, XML and/ or the supplementary materials, we will contact the different journals to ask for an access to all the needed documents. 
Manual extraction of data in research articles
In order to determine the diagnostic performance of each tool to detect each open science practice, we will use a manual extraction of open science practices as a gold standard. Therefore 3 distinct manual extractions will be performed for 1/ key transparency practices, 2/ registration practices for clinical trials following policy changes and 3/ data sharing practices for clinical trials following policy changes (see below for more details including sample size computations). Because of time constraint (availability of researchers in charge of data extraction) data extractions have started on 29/04/2024 prior the registration of the protocol and are being performed by two independent reviewers (MS, FJA), but no interventions began before it. The first 100 extracted articles will be triple checked by CV and disagreements identified in the following articles will be resolved by consensus with a third reviewer (FN or CV). About 150 articles were extracted by one researcher as of registration and extractions are still on going without any analysis being carried out when the protocol is registered. 
Identification of automatized tools
We will identify existing automatic tools that can monitor any of the previously established 19 core open science practices (5). Those tools will be searched by reviewing the ScreenIT pipeline (20) curated by the Automated Screening Working Groups and by contacting several public (e.g., Rtransparent and ODDPub) and private groups (e.g., SciScore and DataSeer) performing open science monitoring. Box 1 lists some tools/initiatives identified in preliminary searches. 

RTransparent: R package that automatically identifies and extracts indicators of transparency (data availability, code availability, statements of conflicts of interest, statements of funding, statements of protocol registration) from TXT and PMC XML versions of published research articles in biomedicine (https://github.com/serghiou/rtransparent). For data and code, rTransparent uses ODDPub effectively with only small adjustments. We will expand the code for registration to cover OSF and PROSPERO and if needed all other)*.
ODDPub: R package that facilitates detecting open data and open code (https://github.com/quest-bih/oddpub)**.
ctRegistries: Checking for registration statement for clinical trials (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/17407745221087456, https://github.com/maia-sh/trn-pop).*
DataSeer: Artificial Intelligence based tool that facilitates checking data sharing policies (https://dataseer.ai/).*
SciScore: Machine learning based tool to evaluate items in the MDAR checklist and use of key biological resources (https://sciscore.com/). 
ContriBOT: A R tool, that detects and extracts Author contribution statements and acknowledgements from scientific papers. (https://github.com/quest-bih/ContriBOT) **.
IA Tool: We are currently developing and IA tool (see our protocol for both development and validation https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/3V6JW ) based on a large language model (LLM) such as Mixtral to extract the presence and absence of open science practices inside medical journal articles. Ideally this tool will be automatized, open source (or failing that, open weights). It should be able to identify journal articles and supplementary material that is in .pdf format and to extract core open science practices. The task of extracting content out of a scholar article with an LLM involves optional innovations to ensure accuracy, robustness, and efficiency, such as embedding of raw data into vector stores, refining the method of prompting the LLM, and employing techniques like retrieval augmented generation (RAG) or fine-tuning*.

Outcomes 
Key transparency practices
For each open science practice (Table 3) in which an automated tool will be identified, we will use the tool on the sample of papers from 2020 to 2023 (included, Table 2). In case certain tools only apply to open access articles, we will restrict our analysis using those specific tools to those articles and document the number of open access articles used and the number of articles that were not used. We will therefore record the open access status of all research articles included in the study. In order to assess the diagnostic accuracy of the tools, we will randomly sample 10 articles from each articles type (RCT, meta-analysis or other research article) per journal for manual assessment (i.e. a total of 300 research articles) from 2022-2023. This sample size ensures a precision of ± 6% to estimate percentages in the worst-case scenario for precision estimations (i.e. if the percentage is 50%). These 300 articles will be manually extracted and will serve as the gold standard. This manual extraction will also be used to estimate how many papers retrieved using our search strategy are actually false positives (i.e. how many are not research articles). 
Registration practices for clinical trials following policy changes
In order to explore whether the tools are able to detect a change following the 2005 ICMJE policy that mandated registration, we will monitor registration practices for all available randomized control trials published 2 years before and 5 years after the policy (i.e. 01/07/2005) in all selected journals (when applicable), which means from 01/07/2003 to 01/07/2010 (Table 2). 
In order to assess the diagnostic accuracy of the tools, we will randomly select 15 articles per journal for manual assessment from 2003 to 2010. This sample size (150) ensures a precision of ± 8% to estimate percentages in the worst-case scenario for precision estimations (i.e. if the percentage is 50%). These 150 articles will be manually extracted and will serve as the gold standard. This manual extraction will also be used to estimate how many papers retrieved using our search strategy are actually false positives (i.e. how many are not randomised controlled trials). 
Data sharing practices for clinical trials following policy changes
In order to explore whether the tools are able to detect changes following implementation of the various data sharing policies, we will monitor data sharing practices for all available randomized control trials (RCT): 
- Published 2 years before and after the policy (i.e. 01/04/2007 (11)) that encouraged data sharing in Annals of Internal Medicine which means from 01/04/2005 to 01/04/2009;
- Published 2 years before and after the policies that encouraged (i.e. 25/03/2009 (12)), mandated for drug and devices (i.e. 01/01/2013 (13)) and then mandated for all trials (i.e. 01/07/2015 (14)), in The BMJ which means from 25/03/2007 to 01/07/2017;
- Published 2 years before and after the policy (i.e. 01/04/2014 (16)) that mandated data sharing in PLOS Medicine which means from 01/04/2012 to 01/04/2016;
- Published 2 years before and up to date after the ICMJE policy that encouraged data sharing (i.e. 01/07/2018 (7)), in all remaining journals which means from 01/07/2016 to 01/07/2020;
Longitudinal descriptions will be performed separately for each journal.
In order to assess the diagnostic performance of the tools, we will assess 50 articles randomly sampled articles from all 4 groups defined above (Annals, BMJ, PLOS, and ICMJE) over the selected period, i.e. a total of 200 articles. This sample size ensures a precision of ± 7% to estimate percentages in the worst-case scenario for precision estimations (i.e. if the percentage is 50%). These 200 articles will be manually extracted and will serve as the gold standard. This manual extraction will also be used to estimate how many papers retrieved using our search strategy are actually false positives (i.e. how many are not randomised controlled trials). 
Analysis
General approach
For each open science indicator and for each specific validation sample, we will use a 2x2 table (e.g. table 4) with the manual extraction as gold standard and the extraction by automatic tool as intervention. Due to the lack of consensus on a gold standard for automatic extraction, manual extraction is considered the most reliable method for obtaining information and will be regarded as the gold standard.

We will estimate the diagnostic accuracy of each tool by deriving sensitivity, specificity per indicator and F-score (25), by using the value identified by manual inspection as the gold standard. Systematic differences between journals will be explored by performing a subgroup analysis by journal. Estimated parameters will be presented with their 95% confidence intervals. Performance of different tools tracking the same open practices may vary because tools have been optimized on different training data and may also rely on different operational definitions of what is being tracked. If certain articles are unavailable, we maintain the predetermined power level by replacing them with alternative articles chosen at random from the same journal, or, if needed, from another randomly selected journal with a similar publication type.

Table 4: Describe of the performance of each automatic tool. 
 
Key transparency practices
A descriptive analysis of each of the parameters described above will be carried out by journal. Categorical variables will be described over the time period using number and percentages (with their 95% confidence intervals). For registration and data sharing, subgroup analyses will be specifically performed for clinical trials and for meta-analyses separately.
Registration practices for clinical trials following policy changes
A descriptive analysis of clinical trial registration will be carried for all journals around 01/07/2005. Categorical variables will be described over the time period using number and percentages for each year. This analysis will be descriptive with no specific strategy regarding statistical inference.

Data sharing practices for clinical trials following policy changes
A descriptive analysis of clinical trial data sharing will be carried for all journals around 01/07/2018. Categorical variables will be described over the time period using number and percentages for each year. This analysis will be descriptive with no specific strategy regarding statistical inference.

Exploratory analysis 
A secondary analysis will assess whether performance differs between pdf vs. XML files, for papers for which both are available in order to help to interpret data
PERSPECTIVES
Implications 
In this study, we will explore various automated tools to monitor open science practices at major generalist biomedical journals. This work will inform the development of a broader open science observatory of biomedical journals. The leading biomedical journals in this study will hence provide important information about these journals that are considered as trusted sources by the medical community. Last, by tracking the open science practices, we will be able to describe changes occurring around implementation of various policy changes on selected open science practices (clinical trial data sharing and registration). Finally, if the accuracy of the automatic tools is good, we will be able to expand the observatory to other journals to more holistically measure the landscape, depending validation. 
Limitations
Because it will be based on a selected sample of major journals, this study will lack external validity regarding core open science practices in other journals (including specialty journals) (10). But given the complexity of the task, it is important that, before further development of the observatory, we start with a small sample of journals. These journals were chosen as we are sure they publish all the different types of research articles that are targeted by the open science practices we are interested in monitoring. In addition, because some automated indicators only detect mention of a registration, or mention of data sharing, it is likely that we won’t be able to detect failure to comply with study registration and/or data sharing plans (26). Finally, because journals can change their reporting practices over time and software tools can improve, it is possible that the diagnostic properties assessed in our study will differ in the future evaluations. Regarding this specific point, the potential identification of challenges in line with reporting in our study may be useful to inform future journal policies in order to reach a better harmonization and to ease monitoring of core Open Science practices.

title: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of the Diagnostic Accuracy of the Papanicolaou Society of Cytopathology System of Reporting Pancreatic Cytology
description:
Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of the Diagnostic Accuracy of the Papanicolaou Society of Cytopathology System of Reporting Pancreatic Cytology

Collaborators
• Dr Sana Ahuja
• Dr Sufian Zaheer

Start date
15th March 2024

Expected date
30th April 2024

Stage of review as of 12th April 2024
Preliminary search

Review question
 Primary
What is the diagnostic accuracy of the Papanicolaou Society of Cytopathology System of Reporting Pancreatic Cytology in Diagnosing Malignancy?

 Secondary
What is the inadequacy rate of fine needle aspiration in pancreatic aspirates?

Sources
Pubmed, EMBASE

Search Strategy
Two main criteria, joined by AND Boolean operator. The OR operator will be used to expand the search within the criteria.
1. Pancreas (target organ)
2. Pancreatic aspirates (specimen)
3. Papanicolaou Society of Cytopathology System of Reporting Pancreatic Cytology
Example: (Pancreas) AND (Pancreatic aspirates) AND (Papanicolaou Society of Cytopathology System)
Only full text articles will be selected.
References of all the articles will be checked.


Population
Any female or male patient presenting with any pancreatic mass or detected incidentally on radiological investigations

Intervention
1. Intervention: Fine needle aspiration biopsy
2. Inclusion criteria: Any patient with pancreatic mass found suitable for fine needle aspiration biopsy on clinical/ radiological examination 
3. Fine needle aspiration biopsy reported according to the Papanicolaou Society of Cytopathology System of Reporting Pancreatic Cytology

Control
Patient having histopathological examination of the same pancreatic mass by core needle biopsy, incisional or excisional biopsy. However, clinical follow-up with no change in nature of swelling would be used in case of benign lesions diagnosed on fine needle aspiration cytology.

Outcome
 Primary outcome
Diagnostic accuracy in diagnosing:
1. Malignant disease including ductal adenocarcinoma, neuroendocrine carcinoma, mucinous cystadenocarcinoma
2. Benign diseases including chronic pancreatitis, tuberculosis, pseudocyst

Measures of effect: Sensitivity and specificity by bivariate analysis. Diagnostic Odds ratio will be done as a univariate analysis.

 Secondary outcome
Inadequate rate of pancreatic aspirates, reported as a proportion

Study selection
Two independent reviewers will screen studies for inclusion. The initial screening will be by the title followed by abstract and eventually through full text review. Any disagreements will be resolved by consensus among other team members. 
The studies will be entered in Microsoft excel and Rayyan software.

Data extraction
The information which will be extracted:
1. Type of study: Retrospective/ Prospective
2. Total number of patients who underwent fine needle aspiration biopsy and proportion categorised in each category of the Papanicolaou Society of Cytopathology System 
3. Number of patients who underwent biopsy (histopathological examination- reference test) in each category
4. The distribution of benign and malignant histological diagnosis among each category of the Papanicolaou Society of Cytopathology System where reference test was done
5. Patient flow

The data will be extracted by one investigator and checked and entered into Microsoft Excel spreadsheet by another investigator. Any disagreements will be resolved by consensus among other team members. 
The authors of the various studies included will not be contacted for any additional information and any lack of data will be evaluated while assessing the quality of the study.

Quadas-2

Four different cut-offs could be used for the diagnosis of malignant disease:
i. Atypical, Neoplastic, Suspicious for malignancy and Malignant categories were considered positive for malignancy
ii. Neoplastic, Suspicious for malignancy and Malignant categories were considered positive for malignancy

iv. Only cases under the Malignant category were considered positive for malignancy
3. The result of quality assessment using the Quadas 2 tool will be entered. 
4. The data will be analysed to get a pooled estimate of sensitivity and specificity along with their Forest plots.

title: Measurement properties of vaginal palpation for pelvic floor muscle function assessment
description:
Considering that vaginal palpation is the method most used by physiotherapists to evaluate pelvic floor muscle, demonstrating good psychometric/clinimetric properties of intra-examiner validity and reproducibility and that, to date, no systematic review has been found that investigates its diagnostic accuracy and compiles clinimetric properties, it is necessary a systematic review. 
The systematic review of existing studies will allow a synthesis of available evidence to elucidate the diagnostic accuracy and consistency of results obtained through vaginal palpation. Furthermore, it is expected to identify gaps in knowledge and recommend directions for future research that can support clinical practice regarding diagnosis through vaginal palpation as a clinical tool for assessing PFM and caring for women at risk of or with dysfunctions. of the pelvic floor installed, contributing to the professional practice of physiotherapists.
The questions of this systematic review are: 1. What are the clinimetric properties of vaginal palpation to assess PFM function in women?; 2. What is the quality of the evidence on the clinimetric properties of vaginal palpation to assess PFM function in women?
The objective of this review is to compile the clinimetric properties and quality of evidence from vaginal palpation to assess PFM.

title: Simulationen zur Förderung der diagnostischen Kompetenzen in der heil- und sonderpä-dagogischen Hochschulbildung: Strukturiertes Klickspiel oder Einsatz GPTAvatar - ein Vergleich mit Noviz:innen und Expert:innen
description:
Diagnostische Kompetenzen sind eine zentrale Qualifikation für heil- und sonderpädagogische Fachkräfte, um Kinder mit besonderem Förderbedarf frühzeitig zu erkennen und darauf aufbau-end passgenaue, datengestützte Fördermassnahmen zu planen und umzusetzen. Entsprechend bildet die Diagnostik einen Schwerpunkt in der heil- und sonderpädagogischen Aus- und Weiter-bildung. Dabei sind für die hochschulische Ausbildung unterschiedliche Kompetenzniveaus von Noviz:innen bis Expert:innen zu berücksichtigen.
Zur Förderung der diagnostischen Kompetenz werden in der Lehre derzeit Fachbücher und meist papierbasierte Fallvignetten eingesetzt. Zur Vertiefung eignen sich interaktive Simulatio-nen (Heitzmann et al., 2019), die anhand von Fallbeispielen den diagnostischen Prozess mit mehreren Entscheidungsmöglichkeiten spielerisch darstellen. Klickbasierte Simulationsspiele sind stark strukturiert. Freier sind hingegen KI-gestützte Avatare, die adaptiv auf die Person reagieren und Audio-, Bild- und Videodaten verarbeiten können. Dadurch unterstützen sie das Lernen, geben gezielte Hilfestellungen und fungieren als virtuelle Mentoren (Fink et al., 2024).
Fragestellung
In einem 2x2-Experiment wird ein strukturiertes Klickspiel mit dem GPTAvatar (Robinson, 2023) im Expert:innen-Noviz:innen-Vergleich untersucht. In beiden Spielen holen die Teilnehmenden Informationen über jeweils ein Kind mit Leseschwierigkeiten ein, treffen möglichst datengestütz-te und fundierte Förderentscheidungen und begründen diese. Der Avatar sichert das gesamte Gespräch in Logdaten und ist für das Spiel mit einem Fallbeispiel konfiguriert sowie mit Verhal-tensregeln versehen worden. Untersucht wird das diagnostische Vorwissen (DaKI; Jungjohann & Gebhardt, 2023), und der Einfluss der Selbsteinschätzung des Cognitive Load (Krieglstein et al.,2023) auf die Qualität diagnostischer Entscheidungen (Heitzmann et al., 2019). Die Fragestellung ist, ob sich die Noviz:innen von den Expert:innen in der Bearbeitung der beiden Simulatio-nen unterscheiden, gemessen an der kognitiven Belastung und der diagnostischen Qualität, und inwiefern sie unterschiedliche Begründungen für die Förderentscheidungen geben. 
Design und Methode
In die Studie werden N = 25 Noviz:innen und N = 25 Expert:innen der Heil- und Sonderpädago-gik aus Deutschland und der Schweiz einbezogen. Alle Teilnehmenden bearbeiten zwei diagnos2tische Fälle - einen im Klickspiel und einen mit dem GPTAvatar. Die Reihenfolge der Bearbeitung erfolgt randomisiert im Sinne eines 2 x 2-within-Designs mit Messwiederholung. 
Die Förderentscheidungen werden als Index auf Basis der diagnostischen Qualität nach Kriterien von Heitzmann et al. (2019) kodiert, auf einer Skala von (1) unpassend bis (3) ausreichend-datengestützt und passend zum Erwartungshorizont. Die abhängige Variable diagnostische Qualität der Förderentscheidung wird mit dem diagnostischen Vorwissen (Selbsteinschätzung DaKI) als Covariate und dem Einfluss der Reihenfolge der Bearbeitung in Beziehung gesetzt und im ANOVA-Modell analysiert.
Die Ergebnisse werden aufzeigen, inwiefern der Einsatz KI-gestützter Avatare im Vergleich zu strukturierten Klickspielen eine Förderung diagnostischer Kompetenzen ermöglicht. Weiter könnten die Ergebnisse genutzt werden, verschiedene Lernspiele für Noviz:innen und Ex-pert:innen zu entwickeln, um unterschiedliche diagnostischen Kompetenzniveaus zu adressieren.

title: Evidence Mapping of Imaging Biomarkers in Nonarteritic Anterior Ischemic Optic Neuropathy: A Scoping Review
description:
This registration covers a scoping review protocol that will systematically identify, chart, and map imaging biomarkers and imaging features investigated in patients with clinically diagnosed non-arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy (NAION). Eligible modalities include, but are not limited to, fundus photography; optical coherence tomography (OCT) (e.g., RNFL, GC-IPL/GCC); optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA) (e.g., peripapillary and macular vessel density, including the radial peripapillary capillary plexus); colour Doppler imaging/ocular ultrasonography; laser speckle flowgraphy (LSFG); fluorescein angiography (FA)/indocyanine green angiography (ICGA); magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), including fMRI and DTI when applied to NAION; adaptive-optics scanning laser ophthalmoscopy (AO-SLO); and imaging-derived artificial intelligence/deep-learning features.
Purpose: to describe which imaging modalities and specific biomarkers have been studied in NAION, for which clinical applications (diagnosis, differential diagnosis, prognosis, longitudinal monitoring, or disease characterisation), with which study designs, sample sizes, and comparator groups, and where evidence concentrates or is sparse on an evidence map of imaging modality × clinical application.
Methods: Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) guidance for scoping reviews; reporting according to PRISMA-ScR. Planned databases: PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science Core Collection, Cochrane Library, CNKI, WanFang Data, VIP, and SinoMed. Languages at screening: English and Chinese. Original clinical studies (case–control, cohort, cross-sectional, interventional trials, and case series with ≥3 participants) will be included. Two reviewers will screen independently after a calibration pilot targeting Cohen’s κ ≥ 0.80. Formal QUADAS-2 appraisal will not determine inclusion or weighting. No meta-analysis of diagnostic accuracy or treatment effects is planned.
Expected outcomes: a PRISMA-ScR flow diagram; descriptive tables of study and biomarker characteristics; a multi-modality evidence map; and a synthesis of consensus findings and research gaps to inform future study design and candidate imaging endpoints. This work is distinct from existing OCTA-focused systematic reviews/meta-analyses (e.g., Khalili et al.; Chou et al.): it is a multi-modality scoping evidence map, not an OCTA-only diagnostic-accuracy meta-analysis.
Stage at registration: protocol finalisation and planning of preliminary searches only. Formal dual screening and data charting have not started.

title: Managing communication challenges in mental healthcare using mobile translation applications: A simulation-based pilot study
description:
This pilot study explores the use of a mobile translation application in simulated mental healthcare consultations involving a language barrier. Twelve German-speaking mental healthcare providers, including both trainees and qualified professionals, will conduct simulated outpatient mental health assessments with Turkish-speaking standardised service users (SUs). Communication will be facilitated entirely through a mobile app offering text and voice translation.

The study aims to assess diagnostic accuracy, app usability, communication quality, translation errors, and non-verbal interaction. Data will be collected through recordings, app usage metrics, questionnaires, and optional interviews. The findings will inform the feasibility and design of a larger study and provide insight into the opportunities and limitations of translation technologies in multilingual mental healthcare.

title: Attitudes Towards Profiling Survey Study 3B
description:
This is an experimental moral psychological study on people's attitudes towards "pre-crime" profiling and pre-crime police work (that is, using profiling or other information to prevent people who may be about to commit a crime from doing so). The study uses the contrastive vignettes method, and has a 3 (information source: AI profiler, expert group, anonymous source; between-subjects) x 4 (type of crime: murder, credit fraud, cannabis growing, graffiti; within-subjects) x 2 (outcome: true positive, false positive; within-subjects) mixed design. This study is intended as a replication of a previous study (Study 3: https://osf.io/sfcxy/?view_only=6955471e082e44fb836281c71efeb9dd) with the same design, but with slight modifications to the vignettes, due to unexpected results in the previous study.

A result that had previously replicated across all prior experimental studies did not replicate in Study 3, namely, a main effect of the police's information source. In prior studies, participants' moral judgments were generally less negative when the police made an arrest based on an anonymous tip than when the police acted based on either purely AI-based profiling or profiling conducted by a group of experts.

The purpose of this study is to see whether the lack of a significant main effect of the information source could have stemmed from issues in the vignettes of Study 3. The vignettes in Study 3 were different in many ways from the vignettes used in prior studies: several changes were made to help keep the study relatively short to avoid exhausting participants, given the repetitiveness of the within-subjects conditions. Some changes to the vignettes were made to better align with the new design. Our concern is that some of these changes may have been detrimental to communicating what we wanted to communicate to the participants. In this study, we attempt to correct for possible mistakes in the vignettes.

(Study 3 was intended to expand on prior studies in this series by introducing several changes to the design. Studies prior to this had only focused on one type of crime to be prevented (cultivating cannabis), and all experimental manipulations were between subjects. In Study 3, we introduced other suspected "future crimes" (murder, credit fraud, graffiti), and made both the type of crime as well as the outcome of the arrest and investigation (true or false positive; the suspect either was or was not, in fact, about to commit a crime) into within-subjects factors. We were interested to see whether outcome biases observed in prior studies that included an outcome manipulation (Study 2a: https://osf.io/nhgc2/?view_only=f053c361e0fb4adc877ee7c427cfa73e ; Study 2b: https://osf.io/qhbd4/?view_only=25af6cdd494846ffa9bd7c5835ff7f3e) would replicate even when both potential outcomes were presented to the same person. Since the information source condition has remained a between-subjects manipulation throughout all studies, the lack of a main effect cannot stem directly from a different design between earlier studies and Study 3.)

title: STUDY PROTOCOL: Diagnostic Accuracy of Artificial Intelligence and Deep Learning Models in the Imaging Diagnosis of Adenomyosis
description:
This registration protocol details a systematic review and meta-analysis focused on the diagnostic performance of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Deep Learning models for detecting uterine adenomyosis. Adenomyosis is a prevalent gynecological condition often underdiagnosed due to significant interobserver variability in Transvaginal Ultrasound (TVUS) and Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI).

The primary objective is to provide a high-level quantitative synthesis of AI diagnostic accuracy, specifically focusing on Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Radiomics. Unlike previous qualitative reviews, this study will employ advanced Bivariate Mixed-Effects Models to calculate pooled sensitivity and specificity, overcoming the threshold effect inherent in computer vision algorithms.

Methodological quality will be assessed using QUADAS-2 and the PROBAST+AI tool to evaluate risk of bias and data leakage. The findings aim to establish clinical benchmarks for the integration of AI in precision gynecology, aligning with the "Office of the Future" framework for the SOGESP 2026 congress.
