title: Diagnostic Accuracy and Discriminative Validity of Clinician-Administered Physiotherapy Examination Tests in Adults With Nonspecific Neck Pain: A Systematic Review
description: The present systematic review will be undertaken to identify, appraise, and synthesize the evidence on the diagnostic accuracy and discriminative validity of clinician-administered physiotherapy examination tests used in adults with nonspecific neck pain. Specifically, the review will aim to synthesize two related but distinct evidence streams: (1) diagnostic-accuracy studies evaluating clinical tests against an explicit reference standard for identifying predefined clinically relevant target conditions or classification states, and (2) discriminative or known-groups studies evaluating whether clinical tests distinguish predefined clinically relevant patient groups when no accepted reference standard exists. For diagnostic-accuracy studies, emphasis will be placed on measures such as sensitivity, specificity, likelihood ratios, and diagnostic odds ratios. For discriminative studies, emphasis will be placed on measures of group discrimination and classification performance, as appropriate to the study design. A further objective will be to determine which tests, or prespecified test clusters, appear to offer the greatest potential clinical utility within their respective target constructs. In addition, the review will examine whether findings from studies at lower risk of bias are more consistent and clinically informative than those from studies at higher risk of bias, with risk of bias assessed separately according to study design.

title: A multiverse approach on skin conductance response quantification focusing on baseline-correction approaches and trough-to-peak scoring in human fear conditioning research
description:
Since the so-called “replication crisis”, the reproducibility of findings as a major quality criterion in natural science is the target of methodological discussions in many research areas (Munafò et al., 2017; Open Science Colloboration., 2015). To address this topic, the scientific community requires strategies to increase transparency. 

When preparing their data, researchers inevitably take more or less arbitrary decisions by picking a processing pipeline out of a large pool of (potentially) equally justifiable data processing and analysis choices (Brand, Dixon, & McBee, 2019). Usually there is more than one suitable path without a clear empirical evidence for the superiority of appropriateness of one specific path (Dragicevic, Jansen, Sarma, Kay, & Chevalier, 2019). These researchers’ degrees of freedom provoke a garden of forking paths (Gelman & Loken, 2014) which has been criticized in the current literature. Further, the lack of consensus about data processing and analysis pipelines used even within an area of research leads to difficulties in comparing findings across different studies. Consequently, the result of a single statistical model applied to a single data set generated via a specific preprocessing pipeline - as typically reported in research papers - is limited, since it doesn’t inform on the robustness of the result. 
To address the problem of choosing one data processing path while multiple suitable paths may exist, multiverse analysis has been proposed (Steegen, Tuerlinckx, Gelman, & Vanpaemel, 2016). Thereby researchers generate a ‘data multiverse’ from all or many possible decision paths in processing a single data set. The underlying idea of a data multiverse is that at every point the researchers have to take a decision, the multiverse grows by one more possible data set or by a whole branch of single data sets. This naturally leads to a multiverse of results based on this data multiverse even when applying an identical statistical model to all data sets (i.e., ‘data multiverse’). A similar approach is to set up a ‘model multiverse’ by applying different statistical models to a single data set (Donnelly, Brooks, & Homer, 2019; McBee, Brand, & Wallace E. Dixon, 2019; Patel, Burford, & Ioannidis, 2015). 
As a consequence, a data multiverse analysis illustrates the existence of possible outcomes based on equally justifiable choices within different preprocessing or transformation pipelines of a single data set (Stern, Arslan, Gerlach, & Penke, 2019). In case findings show homogeneity of results across the different forking paths, the robustness of an effect independent of the used preprocessing pipeline (for a data multiverse) or statistical pipeline (for a model multiverse), can be assumed. If inhomogeneity, however, is observed, this may inform us on potential boundary conditions (for instance inclusion of specific covariates).

In this sense, we want to address a topical problem concerning skin conductance response (SCR) quantification approaches which arises from recent methodological discussions about comparability of methods and procedures. 
In human fear conditioning research the most commonly used psychophysiological index to infer fear learning are SCR. In practice, different methods to quantify SCR exist:
First of all, the trough-to-peak (TTP) approach consists of quantifying the SCR amplitude as the difference of the peak score of the response and the preceding trough within specific time-windows and criteria (Boucsein, 1992). It can be conducted manually or semi-manually (i.e., computer-assisted) through trained raters and is supported in a fully computerized (though manually modifiable) way in the software Autonomate, which implements the TTP criteria (Boucsein, 1992) in computer-based algorithms (Green, Kragel, Fecteau, & LaBar, 2014). 
Second, computational approaches for SCR quantification exist with software programs such as Ledalab or PsPM providing computerized model-based SCR quantification (Bach, 2014; Staib, Castegnetti, & Bach, 2015).
A third SCR quantification approach is what we here refer to as baseline correction approach (Pineles, Orr, & Orr, 2009): The baseline of each SCR is defined as the mean in a pre-CS period (conditioned stimulus). This mean is subtracted from the subsequent peak response in a post-CS period. Of note, the pre- and post-CS periods vary in the literature.
In sum, there is no standard quantification approach for SCR, but all approaches mentioned are currently used interchangeably. 


As part of previous work, we conducted a systemic literature research (described in detail in: Lonsdorf et al., 2019) covering all publications (including e-pubs ahead of print) in PubMed from the 22nd September 2018 to the 22nd March 2019 to identify records which measure SCRs in human fear conditioning research. From 854 records identified through database searching, 50 records remained after the exclusion of review articles/ meta-analysis, rodent work, irrelevant topics, duplicates and no SCR measurement (for further information on screening and exclusion of records see the supplemental flow chart according to PRISMA guidelines (Liberati et al., 2009)). In these articles, TTP and baseline correction for SCR quantification were most common in the field with few studies employing computational approaches (an overview can be found in the additional bar chart). Yet, the “baseline correction category” is itself a particularly heterogeneous category as we identified 16 different ways to perform SCR quantification through baseline correction through our systematic literature search. These differed in the duration and length of the time windows used (yet, only partly explained by different experimental timings of the employed paradigm). Because TTP SCR quantification approaches are conducted semi-manually by independent raters they may be affected by the raters’ decision even with extensive rater-training.


Here, we aim to investigate whether differences in the operationalization of SCR quantification through baseline correction and semi-manual TTP scoring as used in the field (described in detail in: Lonsdorf et al., 2019) result in divergent or convergent outcomes. Hence, we employ these different definitions in a multiverse analysis by applying all of them to a single preexisting data set to generate a data multiverse. Beside the frequentist approach we implement a Bayesian inference approach and compute Bayes Factors. Bayes Factors quantify the evidence for the absence of an effect or the absence of evidence for or against an effect.

As our primary aim, we want to test for CS+/CS- discrimination within fear acquisition training (effect of main interest) as a prime example in this data multiverse based on different SCR quantification approaches.

Our secondary aim is to use trait anxiety, as assessed by the STAI-Questionnaire (Spielberger, Gorsuch, & Lushene, 1983), as a case example for individual differences in fear conditioning to test robustness of a possible association between CS+/CS- discrimination in fear acquisition training and trait anxiety regarding different baseline correction approaches and TTP scoring in a data multiverse approach. This is important as individual difference effects are much more subtle and hence potentially more susceptible to data processing differences (Eysenck, 1963; Lonsdorf & Merz, 2017; Naveteur & Freixa i Baque, 1987). Findings regarding the association between trait anxiety as a criterion variable and differential SCRs in fear conditioning research show inconsistent results and were mainly assessed in small samples fear conditioning experiments (Indovina, Robbins, Núñez-Elizalde, Dunn, & Bishop, 2011; Lissek et al., 2005; Mineka & Oehlberg, 2008; Plehn & Peterson, 2002; Torrents-Rodas et al., 2013; larger sample: Sjouwerman, Scharfenort, & Lonsdorf, preprint).

Hence we want to investigate the agreement between the baseline correction variants and TTP scoring from the multiverse approach using the Bland-Altman approach for method comparison (Bland & Altman, 1986, 1995).

title: Effects of the eGENA Decision Support System on Team Performance and Stress During High-Fidelity Simulated Surgical Emergencies in Anesthesiology
description:
Medical emergencies during surgical procedures place anesthesiology teams under extreme cognitive and emotional strain. Acute stress in these situations is associated with impaired attention, working memory, and decision-making, which in turn increases the risk of medical errors and compromises patient safety. At the same time, repeated exposure to high-stress situations contributes to long-term adverse mental health outcomes among anesthesiologists, including burnout, depression, and reduced job satisfaction. Decision support systems (DSS) and digital cognitive aids have been proposed as a promising approach to improve emergency performance while potentially reducing stress-related burden.

The present project investigates the effects of the digital decision support system eGENA (“electronic memory and decision support for emergencies in anesthesiology”) on team performance and stress responses during high-fidelity simulated anesthesiological intraoperative emergencies. eGENA is a progressive web-based application developed by the German Society of Anesthesiology and Intensive Care Medicine (DGAI) and the Professional Association of German Anesthesiologists (BDA). It provides structured, algorithm-based guidance for the diagnosis and treatment of intraoperative emergencies using checklists and decision pathways that can be flexibly adapted to patient characteristics and situational demands. Prior studies have demonstrated that eGENA improves protocol adherence, diagnostic accuracy, and overall emergency performance in simulated settings, while its effects on stress and strain remain largely inconclusive. 

Wiczorek_Revision

Building on this prior work, the current study aims to experimentally evaluate whether access to eGENA during emergency management leads to (a) improved team performance and (b) reduced subjective and psychophysiological stress in anesthesiology teams. The project follows a counterbalanced within-subjects design in which interdisciplinary teams consisting of anesthesiologists and anesthesia nurses manage two standardized, high-fidelity intraoperative emergency scenarios in a real operating room environment using a patient simulator (SimMan 3G). Typical scenarios include life-threatening complications such as pulmonary embolism or transfusion reactions. Each team completes one scenario with access to eGENA and one scenario without eGENA, with scenario order and eGENA availability counterbalanced across teams.

title: Primitives and outcomes in decision-making using immersive technology
description:
We conducted a systematic review following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. The review aimed to synthesize evidence on how immersive design primitives influence decision-making outcomes and the mechanisms by which these effects occur.
2.1. Search Strategy
Six electronic databases representing the biomedical, psychological, engineering, computer science, and interdisciplinary literature were systematically searched: Pub-Med, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, and ProQuest CENTRAL. The search was con-ducted on April 16th, 2026, and included studies published from database inception until the search date. The search strategy was organized around three core concepts: (1) immersive environments, (2) immersive design primitives, and (3) deci-sion-making.
Keywords within each concept (see Appendix 1) were combined using the Bool-ean operator “OR”, while the three concepts were combined using the operator “AND”. The search strategy was iteratively refined through preliminary searches and discussions among the authors to maximize sensitivity and specificity. All retrieved records were exported to EndNote 21 (Clarivate Analytics, Philadelphia, PA, USA) for duplicate removal and screening.
2.2. Eligibility criteria
Studies were eligible for inclusion if they met all of the following criteria: 1) In-vestigated immersive or semi-immersive technologies, including virtual reality (VR), augmented reality (AR), mixed reality (MR), or related immersive environments, 2) Examined at least one immersive design primitive, including embodiment, interactiv-ity, perceptual realism, temporal simulation, social presence, environmental structure, multisensory integration, or related primitive-level manipulations, 3) Included a deci-sion-making outcome, such as decision quality, choice behavior, preference for-mation, risk perception, risk-taking, trade-off evaluation, decision confidence, deci-sional conflict, or behavioral intentions, 4) Examined, tested, or theoretically linked mechanisms explaining how immersive primitives influenced decision-making out-comes (e.g., cognitive, perceptual, affective, motivational, social, and behavioral mechanisms), 5) Reported empirical findings through experimental studies, random-ized controlled trials, quasi-experiments, mixed-methods studies, or survey-based studies with clearly defined decision outcomes, 6) Were published in peer-reviewed journals or conference proceedings, and 7) Were written in English.
Studies were excluded if they: 1) did not involve immersive technologies, 2) fo-cused solely on technology development or usability without a decision-making out-come, 3) did not examine a design primitive or its influence on decision-making, 4) lacked empirical data, or 5) consisted of editorials, commentaries, opinion papers, ab-stracts, dissertations, or non-peer-reviewed publications.
2.3. Study Selection and Data Extraction
After removing duplicates, records underwent a two-step screening process. Ini-tially, titles and abstracts were evaluated for eligibility. Then, the full texts of studies deemed potentially relevant were independently reviewed for inclusion. Any disa-greements were resolved through discussion within the review team until agreement was achieved. This study selection process was documented with a PRISMA flow dia-gram, showing the number of records identified, screened, excluded, and included in the final analysis.
A standardized data extraction form was created in Microsoft Excel to ensure uni-form data collection across studies (Appendix 2). For each study, details were gathered on publication info, application domain, immersive technology, immersion level, de-cision-making context, decision type, immersive design primitives, how primitives were operationalized, manipulation strategy, mechanisms linking primitives to out-comes, study design, sample details, and decision outcomes. Special focus was on identifying how immersive primitives affected decision-making processes. These mechanisms were categorized into six families: cognitive, perceptual, affective, moti-vational, social-influence, and behavioral-heuristic. For each study, both the manipu-lated primitives and their effects on decision-making were recorded to support path-way analysis.

title: Age-Specific Optic Nerve Sheath Diameter Cut-Off Values for Detecting Raised Intracranial Pressure in Children: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
description:
This study aims to systematically evaluate the diagnostic accuracy and age-specific cut-off values of optic nerve sheath diameter (ONSD) measured using ultrasonography for detecting raised intracranial pressure (ICP) in pediatric populations. Raised ICP is a critical condition in children with neurological disorders, including traumatic brain injury, hydrocephalus, infections, and intracranial tumors. Non-invasive bedside techniques such as ONSD ultrasonography have gained increasing attention as potential screening tools for early ICP detection.

A systematic review and diagnostic meta-analysis were conducted following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. Multiple electronic databases were searched to identify relevant studies evaluating ONSD as a diagnostic marker for raised ICP in children. Eligible studies included pediatric participants aged 0–18 years and reported diagnostic accuracy data comparing ONSD measurements with reference standards such as invasive intracranial pressure monitoring, computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), or lumbar puncture.

Data extracted from included studies comprised study characteristics, participant demographics, diagnostic thresholds, and diagnostic accuracy parameters including sensitivity, specificity, true positives, false positives, true negatives, and false negatives. A hierarchical summary receiver operating characteristic (HSROC) model and random-effects meta-analysis were used to estimate pooled diagnostic accuracy.

The study also explores age-specific variations in ONSD cut-off values across pediatric age groups. The findings aim to support clinical decision-making and provide evidence for the use of ONSD ultrasonography as a non-invasive screening tool for raised intracranial pressure in children.

title: Diagnostic Accuracy of Wearable Technologies for Atrial Fibrillation Detection: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
description:
Abstract 
Background: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most common sustained cardiac arrhythmia and a major cause of stroke, heart failure, and mortality. Due to its often paroxysmal and asymptomatic nature, AF frequently remains undiagnosed using conventional short-term monitoring strategies. Wearable technologies have emerged as scalable tools for AF detection, but their overall diagnostic accuracy across platforms remains uncertain.
Objective: To systematically evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of wearable devices for detecting AF using a diagnostic test accuracy meta-analysis.
Methods: A systematic review was conducted following PRISMA-DTA guidelines. PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane Library databases were searched from inception to 25th February 2026. Prospective and retrospective diagnostic accuracy studies assessing wearable AF detection devices in adults. Eligible studies used electrocardiographic reference standards and reported sufficient data to estimate sensitivity and specificity. Devices were categorized into handheld ECG-based devices, smartphone-based photoplethysmography (PPG) applications, passive smartwatch monitoring systems, and prolonged monitoring devices. Pooled sensitivity and specificity were estimated using bivariate random-effects models.
Results: A total of 51 studies comprising 33,374 participants were included. Wearable devices demonstrated high diagnostic accuracy across all categories. Pooled sensitivity ranged from 92.5% to 96.8%, while specificity ranged from 93.6% to 98.0%. Smartphone-based PPG applications showed the highest sensitivity (96.8%), whereas passive smartwatch monitoring demonstrated the highest specificity (98.0%). Handheld ECG devices also showed strong performance with high sensitivity and low negative likelihood ratios. Moderate heterogeneity was observed across studies.
Conclusion: Wearable technologies demonstrate high diagnostic accuracy for atrial fibrillation detection, particularly in controlled and selected populations, and show promise for large-scale screening and monitoring.

title: Investigating GABA and Glx in Hypersomnolence Disorders: A Harmonized Spectroscopy Study
description:
Central disorders of hypersomnolence (CDH) are chronic neurological conditions characterized by excessive daytime sleepiness (EDS) and include narcolepsy type 1 (NT1), narcolepsy type 2 (NT2), and idiopathic hypersomnia (IH). NT1 is defined by cataplexy and low or absent cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) hypocretin levels, and both NT1 and NT2 typically show multiple sleep-onset REM periods (SOREMPs) on the Multiple Sleep Latency Test (MSLT). NT2, however, lacks cataplexy and presents with normal hypocretin levels. Differentiating NT2 from IH can be particularly challenging, as both lack clear biomarkers; however, IH is generally associated with prolonged nocturnal sleep or increased total sleep time, whereas SOREMPs are not typically observed (Bassetti et al., 2019; Fronczek et al., 2020; Lammers et al., 2020; Sateia, 2014). 

Despite overlapping symptoms, functional neuroimaging studies have revealed functional brain alterations in NT1, especially in default mode network (DMN) regions such as the medial prefrontal cortex and posterior cingulate (Drissi et al., 2016; Gool et al., 2019, 2020; Xiao et al., 2019). Activation across these regions is normally associated with EDS in these people (Horovitz et al., 2009). Studies assessing brain metabolism with fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (FDG-PET), consistently observed glucose hypometabolism in regions of the DMN in NT1 compared to NT2 and healthy controls (Huang et al., 2018; Joo et al., 2004). Emerging evidence also suggests that disruptions in DMN connectivity may contribute to EDS in IH compared to healthy controls. Specifically, IH has been associated with reduced functional connectivity in the anterior DMN and increased cortical thickness and volume in posterior DMN hubs like the precuneus (Pomares et al., 2019). 

While functional imaging has advanced our understanding of hypersomnolence disorders, fewer studies have examined neurochemical alterations in CDH. Metabolites such as gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), glutamate+glutamine (Glx), N-acetylaspartate (NAA), and choline can be non-invasively quantified using magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS). GABA and Glx are key indicators of excitatory–inhibitory balance and may reflect functional changes, while NAA and choline serve as markers of neuronal viability and membrane turnover, potentially indicating structural alterations.

Early studies reported altered NAA/creatine ratios in the hypothalamus of people with NT1, suggesting neurodegeneration (Lodi et al., 2004). Later work found elevated GABA levels in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) (Kim et al., 2008). A study by Gao et al. (2024) reported higher GABA/Glx ratios in the medial prefrontal cortex of people with NT1 during N2 sleep, primarily driven by increased GABA concentrations (Gao et al., 2024). This neurochemical imbalance was negatively correlated with cognitive performance and REM sleep latency, linking altered inhibitory-excitatory balance to cognitive dysfunctioning and increased REM propensity. Although MRS evidence is limited for NT2 and IH, in vitro studies show that CSF from individuals with these conditions, as well as NT1, enhances the effect of GABA on GABA-A​ receptors. This suggests a shared increase in inhibitory signaling across primary hypersomnias (Rye et al., 2012; Trotti et al., 2015). These findings may distinguish patient groups from healthy controls and support the hypothesis that NT2 and IH, like NT1, may be characterized by increased GABAergic tone despite normal hypocretin levels. Additional evidence from Poryazova et al. (2009) showed lower myo-inositol levels in the right amygdala and strong negative correlations between mI/Cr and NAA/Cr across the amygdala and hypothalamus. Given that myo-inositol is a glial marker involved in intracellular signaling and NAA reflects neuronal integrity, these findings support dysfunction in hypothalamo-amygdala pathways in narcolepsy (Poryazova et al., 2009).

However, prior studies were often limited by small sample sizes, restricting the ability to explore associations between neurometabolite levels and clinical variables such as sleep quality, EDS severity or medication use. Additionally, most focused primarily on NT1 compared to well-rested healthy controls, often excluding NT2 and IH. Crucially, few studies have addressed whether neurometabolic alterations reflect underlying pathology or are influenced by the acute or chronic experience of sleepiness. Research in healthy individuals suggests that short-term sleep deprivation can significantly impact neurometabolite levels, particularly GABA and Glx, resulting in impaired cognitive performance on behavioural tasks (Fan et al., 2024; Park et al., 2020; Yoon et al., 2024). This highlights the importance of disentangling disorder-specific alterations from state-dependent changes due to sleepiness, both in hypersomnolent populations and healthy controls. Given previous findings of DMN connectivity alterations in IH and possible disruptions in NT2, assessing neurometabolite levels across NT1, NT2, and IH may help identify subtype-specific neurochemical profiles. Comparing these groups to both well-rested and sleep-deprived healthy controls further allows us to differentiate trait-related alterations from state-dependent effects of sleep loss. 

Therefore, the primary aim of this study is to investigate neurometabolite levels using MEGA-PRESS spectroscopy in a well-characterized, multicenter sample of NT1, NT2, and IH patients, as well as healthy controls scanned following both a well-rested night and a night of partial sleep deprivation. We will focus on two DMN hubs, the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) and posterior cingulate cortex (PCC), to determine whether neurometabolite variations differentiate between groups and provide insight into the neurochemical basis of hypersomnolence. The inclusion of both rested and sleep-deprived healthy controls allows us to account for state-dependent sleepiness effects, which can confound comparisons between hypersomnolent patients and fully rested controls. Lastly, we will examine clinical variables such as subjective sleep quality, daytime sleepiness, insomnia severity, mood symptoms, and cognitive complaints in relation to neurometabolite levels to further characterize the clinical relevance and heterogeneity of hypersomnolence disorders. Identifying disorder-specific neurometabolic patterns may ultimately improve diagnostic accuracy across hypersomnolence subtypes.

title: Multiplex Testing for HIV, Viral Hepatitis, and STIs: A Scoping Review
description:
The global commitment to ending the HIV, viral hepatitis, and STI epidemics by 2030 has placed a strong emphasis on integrated testing services to improve early diagnosis and linkage to care. Expanding access to multiplex testing, which allows for the simultaneous detection of multiple infections, is a key strategy in achieving universal health coverage and improving public health outcomes. These tests are particularly important in addressing co-infections among priority populations, such as pregnant women, men who have sex with men (MSM), transgender individuals, and people at high risk for STIs and viral hepatitis. By enabling early diagnosis and timely treatment, multiplex testing plays an important role in reducing transmission rates and enhancing disease management at both individual and population levels.
Systematic reviews and meta-analyses are considered gold standards in evidence-based medicine, typically drawing from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) to guide clinical interventions. However, in public health research, where interventions often extend beyond controlled settings, scoping reviews have become a valuable approach to synthesizing evidence from a variety of study designs, including observational, qualitative, and grey literature sources. Scoping reviews allow for a broader examination of available evidence, capturing implementation challenges, policy gaps, and emerging innovations in disease prevention and control.
This scoping review integrates data from indexed scientific literature and grey literature sources (e.g., technical reports, conference abstracts, and dissertations) to provide a comprehensive understanding of the feasibility, usability, and diagnostic accuracy of multiplex testing for HIV, viral hepatitis (HBV, HCV), and STIs. The review examines studies published between 2019 and 2024, focusing on different types of multiplex tests, including molecular diagnostics, serology-based rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs), and self-testing platforms. Key outcomes include diagnostic performance, patient acceptance, and barriers to implementation across various healthcare settings.
By summarizing barriers, limitations, and successes of multiplex testing, this review aims to generate actionable evidence to inform public health policies, advocacy efforts, and the integration of multiplex diagnostics into routine healthcare services. Findings will provide insights into how multiplex testing can be optimized for different populations and settings, helping to advance evidence-based strategies for disease prevention, early detection, and linkage to care.

title: Diagnostic test accuracy of clinical examinations finding and patients' history features used for shoulder musculoskeletal disorders: An overview of systematic reviews
description:
This overview of systematic reviews aims to consolidate and critically appraise evidence on the diagnostic accuracy of clinical examinations and history-taking factors for Shoulder Musculoskeletal disorders. Shoulder pain is a common musculoskeletal complaint in primary care with significant impacts on quality of life, productivity, and healthcare costs. While several diagnostic tests exist, their accuracy varies widely, and no clear national guidelines currently exist for diagnosing shoulder disorders.
The study is designed according to Preferred Reporting Items for a Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Diagnostic Test Accuracy Studies (PRISMA-DTA) statement. A comprehensive search will be conducted in five databases (PubMed, EMBASE, CINAHL, Cochrane Database, and PEDro) from inception to present, supplemented by citation tracking and gray literature searches. Systematic reviews of diagnostic test accuracy that evaluate at least one diagnostic parameter for shoulder musculoskeletal disorders will be included.
Two independent reviewers will screen studies, extract data on diagnostic properties (sensitivity, specificity, likelihood ratios, etc.), and assess methodological quality using the University of Bristol's tool for assessing risk of bias in SRs (ROBIS). This overview will provide clinicians with synthesized evidence on the most accurate clinical tests for shoulder disorders, aiding in evidence-based diagnostic decision-making and potentially improving patient outcomes through more accurate and efficient diagnoses.

title: Large Language Model in Cardiovascular Emergency: A Scoping Review
description:
Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) persist as the foremost global health challenge, responsible for 17.9 million annual deaths (80% from acute coronary syndromes and cerebrovascular events). Projections suggest CVDs will maintain this position beyond 2050, having already contributed to 100 million disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) lost from 2000-2019. Out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) exemplifies critical unmet needs, with 90% mortality rates and frequent catastrophic neurological outcomes among survivors.

Contemporary cardiovascular emergency management spans a care continuum from prehospital response to post-discharge rehabilitation. While systemic improvements have elevated survival rates over the past decade, persistent gaps demand innovations to strengthen coordination among bystanders, EMS teams, clinicians, and rehabilitation specialists. The complexity of time-sensitive, multistakeholder interventions underscores the necessity for integrated solutions across the survival chain.

Digital health advancements present transformative opportunities. Artificial intelligence (AI) already augments ECG interpretation and clinical deterioration prediction, while machine learning enhances diagnostic accuracy and risk stratification. Natural language processing (NLP) reshapes clinical documentation and decision support, with large language models (LLMs) emerging as multimodal platforms capable of real-time clinical reasoning, data synthesis, and dynamic instruction generation.
Critical knowledge gaps persist regarding LLM deployment in acute cardiovascular settings. Existing research emphasizes medical knowledge assessments but neglects operational validation in resuscitation environments. The potential synergy between LLMs and conventional AI systems remains underexplored, particularly in first-response guidance, prognostic modeling, and adaptive medical education.

title: Future Pulse: Artificial Intelligence-Driven Diagnostics in Digital Health
description:
Rachmad, Yoesoep Edhie. 2021. Future Pulse: Artificial Intelligence-Driven Diagnostics in Digital Health. Book of Primary Care & Community Health Publishing, Thousand Oaks Special Issue, 2021. https://doi.org/10.17605/osf.io/87ahk



"Future Pulse: AI-Driven Diagnostics in Digital Health" by Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, published in 2021 by the Book of Primary Care & Community Health Publishing in Thousand Oaks, delves into the transformative role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in modern diagnostics. The book emerges from the need to explore how AI technologies can revolutionize healthcare, particularly in diagnostics, offering a more efficient, accurate, and personalized approach to medical care.
Definition and Basic Concepts
The book begins by introducing the fundamental concepts of AI and its application in healthcare. It outlines how AI has evolved over the years to become an integral part of modern medical diagnostics. AI is defined as a branch of computer science that develops algorithms and systems capable of performing tasks that typically require human intelligence, such as learning, reasoning, and problem-solving. In healthcare, AI is utilized to analyze complex medical data, aiding in diagnostics and treatment planning.
Underlying Phenomena
The motivation behind this book is the rapid advancement and integration of AI technologies in the healthcare sector. The author highlights the increasing volume of healthcare data, the demand for personalized medicine, and the need for more efficient diagnostic tools as key phenomena driving the exploration of AI in diagnostics. The book underscores the potential of AI to address these contemporary challenges and improve patient outcomes.
Problem Statement
The primary problem addressed by the book is the integration of AI into healthcare diagnostics. It examines the challenges and opportunities of incorporating AI technologies in medical diagnostics, aiming to understand how these technologies can be effectively utilized to enhance diagnostic accuracy and efficiency while addressing ethical and privacy concerns.
Research Objectives
The book aims to provide a comprehensive analysis of the role of AI in healthcare diagnostics, exploring its applications, benefits, and challenges. It seeks to outline strategies for successful implementation, emphasizing the importance of ethical guidelines and regulatory frameworks to ensure the responsible use of AI in diagnostics.
Indicators
Key indicators of successful AI integration in healthcare diagnostics, as identified in the book, include improved diagnostic accuracy, faster diagnostic processes, enhanced data analysis capabilities, and more personalized treatment plans. The book also considers the development of robust ethical and legal frameworks as critical indicators.
Operational Variables
Operational variables in the book include AI technologies such as machine learning algorithms, neural networks, and natural language processing tools. The book also explores variables related to healthcare outcomes, data management practices, and regulatory compliance.
Determining Factors
The determining factors for the successful implementation of AI in healthcare diagnostics include technological advancements, data availability and quality, regulatory environments, and healthcare professionals' readiness to adopt AI-driven tools. The author emphasizes the role of interdisciplinary collaboration in overcoming technical and ethical challenges.
Implementation and Strategy
The book outlines various strategies for integrating AI into healthcare diagnostics, such as investing in AI research and development, fostering collaboration between technology developers and healthcare professionals, and establishing comprehensive training programs for healthcare workers. It also highlights the need for continuous monitoring and evaluation to adapt to evolving technologies and healthcare needs.
Challenges and Supportive Factors
The book identifies several challenges, including data privacy concerns, algorithmic biases, and the potential for job displacement within the healthcare sector. Supportive factors include technological innovations, supportive regulatory policies, and public acceptance of AI in healthcare. The author calls for a balanced approach to address these challenges while leveraging supportive factors to maximize the benefits of AI.
Determining Factors of the Book
The relevance and impact of the book are determined by its timely exploration of emerging technologies, its comprehensive analysis, and its practical recommendations for healthcare professionals and policymakers. The book’s ability to address ethical considerations and propose actionable strategies also contributes significantly to its importance.
Research Findings
The book presents several case studies demonstrating successful AI applications in diagnostics. These include enhanced imaging analysis, personalized medicine through genetic profiling, and efficient epidemiological data analysis. These findings illustrate the tangible benefits of AI integration, providing evidence of its potential to transform healthcare delivery.
Conclusion and Recommendations
In conclusion, the book emphasizes the vital role of AI in modernizing healthcare diagnostics. It advocates for their ethical and responsible adoption, emphasizing the need for regulatory frameworks and continuous evaluation. The author recommends fostering interdisciplinary collaborations, investing in technological innovations, and developing comprehensive regulatory frameworks to ensure the successful integration of AI in diagnostics.
"Future Pulse: AI-Driven Diagnostics in Digital Health" offers a detailed exploration of how AI can enhance traditional diagnostic practices and pave the way for new approaches in healthcare. It underscores the importance of innovation, ethical responsibility, and strategic implementation to harness the full potential of these transformative technologies.

title: Diagnostic Performance of Competing Imaging Examinations for Pediatric VUR
description:
Diagnostic accuracy of Voiding Cystourethrogram (VCUG), Radionuclide cystogram (RNC) and contrast-enhanced voiding urosonography (ceVUS) in diagnosing any grade of vesicoureteral reflux (VUR) in the pediatric population: A systematic-review and meta-analysis.

title: Translation of oral health research priorities into research topics in an equity-based priority setting exercise
description: Background: In the context of research priority setting, participants express their research priorities and ideas in various forms, ranging from narratives to explicit topics or questions. However, the transition from these expressions to well-structured research topics or questions is not always straightforward. Challenges intensify when research priorities pertain to interventions or diagnostic accuracy, requiring the conversion of narratives into the PICO (Participant, Intervention, Comparator, Outcome) format. Scope and findings: This project aimed to understand the challenges of engaging a diverse, multilingual population in setting oral health research priorities. While not a comprehensive priority-setting effort, we modified James Lind Alliance's (JLA) methods and used thematic analysis to establish a list of priority research topics and questions. This was accomplished by conducting interviews with 40 community participants and 14 dentists from various ethnic backgrounds in Malaysia. The interview language depended on participant preferences, including English, Malay, and Mandarin, with translations handled collaboratively by bilingual research assistants. The process involved thematic analysis, discussion with a research committee, and necessary modifications. Our interpretations revealed distinct categories of participant statements: explicit, complicated, implicit, and incomplete. In this study, we identified a three-step approach to translate research ideas that are presented either as explicit statements or as complicated narratives.

title: The Application of Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning Techniques Combined with Digital Biomarkers in the Prediction and Monitoring of Sarcopenia: A Scoping Review
description:
Sarcopenia is an age-related disorder characterized by loss of muscle mass and strength, accompanied by a decline in physical function. It is closely associated with multiple adverse health outcomes, including increased risk of falls, disability, prolonged hospitalization, and higher mortality. Studies have shown that sarcopenia affects approximately 10% to 27% of older adults worldwide. Therefore, early detection and continuous monitoring of sarcopenia are essential for promoting healthy aging. Emerging technologies, such as artificial intelligence (AI), have shown substantial potential across multiple domains of health management. However, AI approaches, particularly machine learning, often require large volumes of data. Conventional data collection still relies largely on manual measurements and self-reported questionnaires, which have several limitations, including low sensitivity, limited accessibility, high subjectivity, and an inability to capture dynamic changes in daily life. In addition, many patients seek medical help only when symptoms become severe, which hinders early intervention. Therefore, objective, quantitative, continuous, noninvasive, and convenient data on muscle health are urgently needed to address the limitations of traditional approaches. Digital biomarkers (DBs) are defined as objective, quantifiable physiological or behavioral data collected using wearable, portable, implantable, or ingestible digital devices. These data may support early prediction and screening of sarcopenia and facilitate proactive maintenance of muscle health, consistent with the latest 2025 Expert Consensus of the Asian Working Group for Sarcopenia. This shift may help advance a new era of muscle health that is quantifiable, predictable, and modifiable.
Although previous studies and reviews have examined the application of AI or machine learning techniques in the prediction, screening, and diagnosis of sarcopenia, important methodological and evidence synthesis gaps remain. First, prior reviews have mainly focused on the predictive performance, diagnostic accuracy, or pooled effect estimates of prediction models based on wearable devices. Few have systematically mapped, from a scoping review perspective, the distribution of evidence and research landscape regarding the combined use of AI/ML techniques and broadly defined DBs for sarcopenia prediction, screening, risk identification, and monitoring. Second, existing studies have insufficiently characterized the sources, types, and measurement dimensions of DBs, and relevant data sources should not be limited to wearable devices. In addition, reporting of digital data acquisition procedures and key AI/ML modeling workflows remains inadequate in many studies, limiting model reproducibility, generalizability, and clinical applicability. Meanwhile, the available evidence is highly heterogeneous in terms of participant characteristics, country or regional distribution, sarcopenia assessment methods, and diagnostic definitions.

title: Association between the use of lisdexamfetamine, methylphenidate or atomoxetine during childhood or adolescence and development of substance use disorder: A scope review of in vivo studies.
description: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by persistent inattention and hyperactivity/impulsivity at excessive levels incompatible with the developmental period. Many patients are diagnosed during childhood, but the disorder can persist into adulthood. Treatment for ADHD also involves pharmacological interventions, in which the first-line options are central nervous system stimulants such as lisdexamfetamine and methylphenidate, while the second-line treatment includes non-stimulants such as atomoxetine. In recent decades, there has been an increase in ADHD diagnoses and the consequent increase in the use of such drugs. As a result, there is a concern and criticism regarding diagnostic accuracy, misuse, and the high number of prescriptions, especially of stimulants. However, the long-term consequences of these drugs and the impact they may have on public health in the future are still uncertain. It is important to emphasize that these drugs mimic the action of some drugs of abuse, that is, they are capable of activating brain reward pathways and producing feelings of pleasure. Continuous use can lead to the development of substance use disorder (SUD), which is characterized by stages of compulsion, withdrawal, and anticipation/preoccupation that are directly linked to brain neuroadaptations. Given this scenario, this scoping review seeks to investigate whether there is any correlation between the use of lisdexamfetamine, methylphenidate, or atomoxetine during childhood and adolescence and the development of SUD in adulthood by evaluating studies in vivo based on a systematic search in databases.

title: Diagnostic Performance of Artificial Intelligence Models in Differentiating Bacterial and Viral Pneumonia: A Meta-analysis
description:
Background: Accurate differentiation between bacterial and viral pneumonia is crucial for appropriate antimicrobial stewardship and clinical management. While artificial intelligence (AI) models, including deep learning and radiomics, have shown promise in medical imaging, their diagnostic performance varies across studies.
Objective: The primary objective of this systematic review and meta-analysis is to evaluate the overall diagnostic accuracy of AI models in distinguishing bacterial from viral pneumonia based on medical imaging (e.g., CXR, CT).
Methods: We will conduct a comprehensive search in databases including PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library. Studies reporting diagnostic performance metrics (sensitivity, specificity, AUC) of AI models for this specific differential diagnosis will be included. Quality assessment will be performed using the QUADAS-2 tool. Data synthesis will be conducted using bivariate random-effects models to generate pooled sensitivity, specificity, and summary receiver operating characteristic (SROC) curves.
Expected Results ： This study aims to provide high-quality evidence regarding the potential of AI as a non-invasive adjunctive tool for differentiating pneumonia pathogens, potentially reducing the misuse of antibiotics and improving diagnostic efficiency in clinical practice.
subjects: Medicine and Health Sciences

title: Plasma ctDNA Next-Generation Sequencing Versus Tissue Genotyping for Actionable Driver Detection in Advanced NSCLC: An Umbrella Review of Diagnostic Accuracy and Treatment-Decision Impact
description:
Description
This umbrella review evaluates the diagnostic accuracy and treatment-decision relevance of plasma circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) next-generation sequencing (NGS) compared with tissue genotyping for actionable driver detection in advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). The review synthesizes evidence from systematic reviews and meta-analyses assessing plasma-based liquid biopsy approaches for detecting actionable genomic alterations, including EGFR, KRAS, EGFR T790M, and broad multi-driver panels. Review-level evidence and exploratory occurrence-level diagnostic analyses were integrated to assess sensitivity, specificity, positive and negative predictive values, and likelihood ratios. Methodological quality, certainty of evidence, and overlap between included reviews were evaluated using AMSTAR-2, QUADAS-2, GRADE, and corrected covered area (CCA) analyses. The findings indicate that plasma ctDNA NGS demonstrates strong rule-in utility when positive actionable alterations are detected, but insufficient rule-out performance following negative plasma results. The review supports plasma ctDNA NGS as a complementary strategy alongside tissue genotyping rather than a replacement for tissue-based molecular testing in advanced NSCLC.

title: Evaluation of a conversational AI system for simulated clinical scenarios in medical education: a mixed-methods multi-centre study
description: Effective consultation skills remain fundamental to high-quality healthcare delivery, influencing diagnostic accuracy, patient satisfaction, and clinical outcomes. This protocol describes a mixed-methods evaluation of conversational artificial intelligence (AI) for simulated clinical scenarios in undergraduate medical education. The study will recruit the entire third-year cohort of medical students (n=271) at the University of Bristol to compare AI virtual patients with traditional actor-based simulations across four standardised primary care scenarios. Quantitative assessment will employ validated measures including an abridged version of the Immersive Technology Evaluation Measure (ITEM) (see appendix A), the User Experience Questionnaire-Short (UEQ-S), and an adapted educational AI technology feedback questionnaire based on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), whilst qualitative data will be collected through focus groups analysed using Braun and Clarke's thematic framework. The primary outcome measures perceived realism, technical usability factors, and educational value of AI consultations compared to actor simulations. Secondary outcomes include AI’s comparative performance across (four) different clinical scenarios, feedback quality assessment, and recommendations for curricular integration. Statistical analysis will employ non-parametric methods with effect size calculations and confidence intervals as well as group analysis, MMRM, mixed models outcomes and necessary post hoc analysis, whilst qualitative analysis will be conducted independently by two researchers with subsequent consensus meetings. This comprehensive evaluation will provide evidence regarding the effectiveness of AI virtual patients for communication skills training, informing future integration into medical curricula whilst addressing stakeholder concerns about the role of technology in clinical education.

title: Emergent applications of machine learning for diagnosing and managing appendicitis: a state-of-the-art review
description: Appendicitis is one of the most common surgically treated diseases, with more than 300,000 appendectomies being performed in the United States annually. Despite its common nature, appendicitis can be difficult to diagnose at times even with the established criteria of systems like the Alvarado Score. Atypical presentations and poor predictive value of laboratory tests complicate diagnoses and decisions for surgical intervention. CT imaging improves sensitivity and specificity of diagnoses, however this tool bears the drawbacks of high operator dependency and needless radiation exposure. The need for a framework that can inform the selective use of CT scans, especially for equivocally-scored cases of appendicitis, warrants the use of machine learning. Machine learning is a rapidly evolving field with increasing applications in healthcare at-large. This artificial intelligence approach uses historical data to train a model that captures existing patterns in data to predict outcomes. The aim of this review is to classify these novel uses of various machine learning algorithms in the context of appendicitis management and examine their potential to reshape pre-operative and post-operative decision-making.

title: Protocol: In multi-reader multi-case study designs, do AI-diagnostic tools improve accuracy outcomes for radiologists in cancer risk stratification?
description:
The use of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) techniques in healthcare has become a topic of significant discussion. Methods using such algorithms have demonstrated remarkable improvements in terms of accuracy and sensitivity in medical image recognition tasks1. In clinical practice, evidence has shown that AI technology can be used as a clinical decision tool to diagnose numerous diseases when using radiological techniques such as X-ray, CT, MRI, or ultrasound1. ML algorithms thus are seen as being able to efficiently provide diagnostically accurate data to patients on a shorter timescale. 

Challenges and complications
Although AI has been lauded as a revolutionary technique and can be suggested to perform better than humans in healthcare on several issues regarding their accuracy and utility in clinical practice, some of the main issues that have arisen are: 
• Algorithms are normally inputted with a specific output in mind while a doctor may be able to make a more flexible decision. For example, an AI tool that has been developed to consider lymph node metastasis in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma may be able to outperform radiologists2. However, this model will not be able to then make decisions that only a doctor can on the best course of action for the patient. 
• Overdiagnosis3: The algorithms from AI detect and diagnose conditions whether they cause harm for a patient or not. For example, if we consider a CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA) to detect pulmonary emboli (PE) in the lungs, this is usually an incidental finding and even when detected, PE only needs to be treated on a symptomatic basis. AI tools for CTPA may detect this at a much higher rate. Are smaller lesions therefore being detected with the extra sensitivity that are less harmful? The question then arises on how we should approach this data: who should be treated and who should not? 



AI application in medical imaging analysis
The future of AI seems to be as a diagnostic support tool integrated within a radiologist’s workflow, allowing an increase in efficiency and a reduction in errors1. Studies that thus compare AI models with radiologist or clinician-mediated diagnosis may not highlight the effects AI may have in a clinical setting and quantify the gain in accuracy from AI in reading images. 

More radiological test studies have thus shifted to implementing a multi-reader multi-case (MRMC) design4. This design is popular as once a radiologist has viewed twenty cases there is less information to be gained by asking them to view a further twenty than asking a different radiologist to view the same twenty5. The study design asks multiple radiologists to view the same cases and means that results can correlate within readers meaning that bootstrapping and modelling can account for these parameters to enhance statistical power. These studies’ primary outcome arises as a receiver operator characteristic (ROC) curve that describes a plot of sensitivity vs. 1-specificity for diagnostic tests6. The AUC can then be used as a measure to combine both sensitivity and specificity to compare diagnostic tools. 

In recent years, several systematic reviews regarding artificial intelligence and radiology have been published7,8. These have focussed on diagnostic performance and how AI models compare to a radiologist. Due to the heterogeneity of data across the field of AI tools these have often been narrative syntheses. By solely considering the MRMC study design this allows examination of a more homogenous dataset. The study design outlined above also will help interpretation of how AI-diagnostic tools may help optimise cancer management in healthcare. Studies using this as a primary outcome are often required by regulatory bodies for licensing new radiological devices9. Furthermore, by solely analysing MRMC studies this also will allow consideration of detailed methodological components across studies to consider data presentation and analysis within the field of AI and radiology. 

This systematic review thus aims to assess MRMC studies using ROC AUC outcome measures to consider whether AI-assisted clinician diagnosis may be beneficial. The review will also examine design, analysis, and reporting of MRMC studies regarding AI to consider how these may influence the data that is ultimately presented.

title: Leveraging AI-Driven Neuroimaging Biomarkers for Early Detection and Social Function Prediction in Autism Spectrum Disorders. A Systematic Review
description: This systematic review examines artificial intelligence (AI) applications in neuroimaging for autism spectrum disorder (ASD), addressing the critical need for objective biomarkers that could enable earlier detection and more accurate prediction of developmental outcomes. Methods: Following PRISMA guidelines, we conducted a comprehensive literature search across eight databases, yielding 146 studies from an initial 1,872 records. These studies were systematically analyzed to address key questions regarding AI-neuroimaging approaches in ASD detection and prognosis. Results: Neuroimaging combined with AI algorithms demonstrated significant potential for early ASD detection, with electroencephalography (EEG) showing promise. Machine learning classifiers achieved high diagnostic accuracy (85-99%) using features derived from neural oscillatory patterns, connectivity measures, and signal complexity metrics. Studies of infant populations identified the 9–12-month developmental window as critical for biomarker detection and preceding behavioral symptoms. Multimodal approaches integrating various imaging techniques substantially enhanced predictive capabilities, while longitudinal analyses showed potential for tracking developmental trajectories and treatment response. Conclusions: AI-driven neuroimaging biomarkers represent a promising frontier in ASD research, potentially enabling detection before behavioral symptoms manifest and providing objective measures of intervention efficacy. While technical and methodological challenges remain, advancements in standardization, diverse sampling, and clinical validation could facilitate translation into practice, ultimately supporting earlier intervention during critical developmental periods and improving outcomes for individuals with ASD.

title: Screening Cognition in Neuro-Oncology: Brief Bedside and App-Based Tools for Perioperative Brain Tumor Care — A Systematic Review
description: Cognitive dysfunction is a frequent and debilitating symptom in brain tumor patients, arising from tumor burden, treatment effects, and disruption of brain networks. Gold-standard neuropsychological assessments provide detailed evaluation but are impractical for routine perioperative care due to length and resource requirements. This systematic review evaluates brief, bedside-compatible, or app-based cognitive screening tools used pre- and post-operatively in adult brain tumor patients, assessing their feasibility, diagnostic accuracy, and clinical utility for longitudinal monitoring.

title: Diagnostic Accuracy of Large Language Models for Emergency Department Triage and Clinical Differential Diagnosis: A Systematic Review and DTA Meta-Analysis
description:
This study is a preregistered systematic review and diagnostic test accuracy (DTA) meta-analysis evaluating the performance of large language models (LLMs) in clinical differential diagnosis and emergency department triage.

The primary objective is to quantify the diagnostic accuracy of LLMs, including GPT-4–class models, ChatGPT-3.5, DeepSeek-R1, and multi-agent architectures, in identifying correct top-1 primary diagnoses and appropriate triage classifications when compared with physician panels or validated clinical reference standards.

A comprehensive literature search will be conducted across PubMed, Scopus, Embase, Web of Science, CINAHL, and the Cochrane Library from inception to March 2025. Additional sources will include Google Scholar (first 20 pages), citation tracking, and preprint servers (medRxiv, arXiv). Eligible studies will include those assessing LLM performance on clinical diagnostic or triage tasks with extractable accuracy metrics.

The primary outcomes will be:
(1) Proportion of correct top-1 primary diagnosis
(2) Proportion of correct or appropriate triage classification

Secondary outcomes include top-3 differential diagnosis inclusion, unsafe triage rates, and comparative performance against physicians or validated symptom checkers.

Random-effects meta-analysis using DerSimonian–Laird estimation will be performed, with heterogeneity assessed using I² and Tau² statistics. Prediction intervals will be reported to reflect expected variability across clinical contexts. Subgroup analyses will be conducted based on clinical setting, LLM architecture, case source (real patients vs vignettes), and task type.

Methodological quality will be assessed using the QUADAS-2 tool adapted for LLM diagnostic accuracy studies, and certainty of evidence will be evaluated using the GRADE framework.

This study aims to provide the first comprehensive synthesis of LLM diagnostic and triage performance within a formal DTA framework, with a specific focus on patient safety implications, including unsafe triage rates in real-world emergency settings.

The findings are expected to inform clinicians, researchers, and policymakers regarding the safe and appropriate integration of LLMs as clinical decision support tools, while explicitly evaluating their readiness—or lack thereof—for autonomous clinical deployment.

title: Improving cut-off determination of Neuropsychological tests: a Bayesian approach
description:
Traditional validation approaches in neuropsychology typically rely on normative data from healthy individuals to establish cut-off scores. While this method provides estimates of specificity, it does not inform sensitivity, and the resulting cut-off is generic rather than pathology-specific. This limitation becomes critical when assessing clinical populations, as neuropsychological tools are often validated on very small patient samples. Such constraints make it difficult to apply standard Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) analyses, which require sufficiently large and balanced datasets to produce reliable estimates.

To address this issue, we propose a Bayesian adaptation of the ROC framework. The rationale behind this approach is that Bayesian methods naturally incorporate uncertainty arising from sample size, allowing for more robust inference even when patient data are scarce. Unlike simple simulation techniques, Bayesian modeling provides posterior distributions for key parameters, enabling credible intervals for cut-off scores, sensitivity, and specificity.

In our conceptual example, we consider a dataset with 200 healthy controls and only 10 patients. Using Bayesian regression, we estimate model parameters and generate simulated datasets from posterior distributions. For each simulated dataset, we compute ROC curves and derive credible intervals for diagnostic metrics. This approach leverages prior assumptions about the relationship between patients and controls and models data distributions using Student’s t-distribution, which accounts for heavier tails and greater variability in small samples. Consequently, the Bayesian framework offers a principled solution for neuropsychological validation in contexts where traditional ROC analysis is impractical.

title: Artificial intelligence in optical coherence tomography and magnetic resonance imaging for optic neuropathies: Scoping Review
description: Introduction: Optic neuropathies are diseases that affect the optic nerve and cause visual loss of varying degrees. Among the most common are glaucoma and non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, both major causes of irreversible blindness worldwide. Early diagnosis depends on imaging techniques such as optical coherence tomography (OCT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), which allow precise evaluation of structural and functional changes in the optic nerve. In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a promising tool in neuro-ophthalmology, capable of processing large volumes of images with high diagnostic accuracy. However, the rapid expansion of scientific evidence calls for a review that synthesizes current advances, applications, and limitations of this technology. Methodology: A scoping review will be conducted of studies published between 2015 and 2025 on the use of AI models applied to the analysis of OCT and MRI in optic neuropathies. The search will include databases such as PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, SciELO, and BIREME, using MeSH and DeCS descriptors related to artificial intelligence, deep learning, and optic neuropathies. Grey literature will be included, and the snowball technique will be applied. Expected results: It is expected to generate an updated overview of the evidence on AI in the diagnosis of optic neuropathies, identifying the most used models, their benefits, limitations, and perspectives for clinical integration in neuro-ophthalmology.

title: Comparison of different methods for the meta-analysis of diagnostic test accuracy studies – a simulation study
description: Meta-analysis of diagnostic test accuracy (DTA) studies is, due to its co-primary endpoint of sensitivity and specificity, methodologically more challenging than its univariate counterpart in intervention studies. In medical practice, methods for the meta-analysis of DTA studies often do not distinguish between diagnostic thresholds in the primary studies and only use information from a single threshold per study. In contrast, more recent approaches incorporate all available information by considering all diagnostic thresholds and can express summary estimates depending on the threshold. We will systematically compare eleven methods for the meta-analysis of DTA studies, five of which consider a single diagnostic threshold per study, while the other six consider all available thresholds. Using simulation scenarios that resemble realistic meta-analysis datasets, we will investigate the methods’ bias, empirical coverage and convergence behavior for diagnostic tests on both the continuous and ordinal scale. Our aim is to detect situations in which certain methods are superior or inferior to others and thus aiding practitioners in an adequate choice of method when performing meta-analysis in a specific setting.

title: TMS-derived markers (NoMEPs_Clin_study1)
description:
TMS of the motor cortex has a well-established role in clinical neurophysiology and is used worldwide to assess the conduction of cortico-spinal connections. Changes in motor activation and excitability can be readily assessed by recording the responses induced in the muscles when stimulating the primary motor cortex (M1). Neurophysiological measures, such as resting motor threshold (rMT), motor evoked potential (MEP) amplitude and latency, Cortical Silent Period (CSP) duration, Short-latency afferent inhibition (SAI) and MEP recruitment curves, can be used to provide evidence of disease-related changes in cortical motor output in patients. 

TMS derived measures show high variability that introduces some uncertainty and reduces potential applications in clinical practice (Neva et al., 2017; Christie et al., 2007; Goldsworthy et al., 2016; Koski et al., 2005; Malcolm et al., 2006; Terao & Ugawa, 2002). Within individuals, trial-to-trial variability of TMS derived measures is probably a consequence of intrinsic fluctuations of the excitability of cortical and spinal neurons. To reduce the impact of this variability, multiple measures are usually collected and averaged to obtain individual values. However, this variability may still affect the precision of measurement by introducing measurement noise. Additionally, TMS derived measures are highly variable between individuals. A recent big collaborative study has shown that this variability is higher across individuals of the same study than between studies suggesting that it is not explained by the use of different TMS devices and procedures (Corp et al., 2020). The conventional methodology to measure TMS-derived responses from one muscle only, i.e. the target muscle, may contribute to variability of measures. It is indeed known that the TMS induces muscle contraction in more than one muscle at the same time. This is possibly due to 1) overlapping cortical muscle representations centrally (Lotze et al., 2003; Wassermann et al., 1992), 2) low focality of TMS which activates surrounding non-target cortical regions (Rothwell, 1991; Thielscher & Kammer, 2004), 3) and the organization of muscles in synergies, such that stimulating one muscle can also activate its associated muscles (Melgari et al., 2008). When only one muscle is recorded, it is assumed that the muscle represents the corticospinal excitability and that responses in other muscles would only provide redundant information. However, other muscles respond to TMS pulses given to the target muscle chosen as the hotspot, and such responses are not correlated with each other. Preliminary unpublished data from our lab revealed a significant error rate of the first dorsal interosseous muscle (FDI) and the adductor pollicis brevis (APB) muscular responses (error is defined as instance when the target muscle fails to elicit a MEP, but at least one other recorded muscle does). Hence, we believe that relying solely on the conventional method of muscle registration from a single target muscle could also significantly contribute to the variability of TMS-induced measures. Furthermore, our results also showed that combining the target muscle with one or two other muscles consistently reduced this error observed in monitoring the single target muscle. Specifically, co-registering FDI, APB, and the common extensor of the fingers (EDC) has shown to be the most effective combination in reducing the error rate compared to monitoring FDI alone. Neglecting the responses that occur in other muscles may lead to an error in estimating corticospinal excitability, both in terms of rMT and in terms of MEP amplitude and SAI. So, this study includes a pilot experiment, which allows for the optimization of measurement of TMS-derived indices, and a main experiment, which tests the diagnostic accuracy of the new indices in AD. 

Aim: 
This experiment aims to quantify the advantages of co-registering responses from multiple muscles derived from TMS, specifically from three muscles of the right upper limb: the first dorsal interosseous muscle (FDI), the adductor pollicis brevis (APB), and the common extensor of the fingers (EDC). We expect that recording TMS from multiple muscles will lead to an improvement in the reliability and accuracy of TMS measurements. In particular, it will allow for a reduction of variability in rMT estimation between subjects. Also, there will be less variability in MEP and SAI measurements, both within and between subjects. This will provide information about the reliability, the internal and external variability of the study and the accuracy of the considered measurements, in order to ensure quality and robustness of the experiment results. 

Specifically, the project aims to explore: 
If considering TMS responses from multiple muscles can reduce the variability of resting motor threshold (rMT) between subjects.
If considering TMS responses from multiple muscles can reduce the variability of MEPs trial by trial, between subjects and sessions. 
If considering TMS responses from multiple muscles can reduce the variability of short-latency afferent inhibition (SAI) trial by trial, between subjects and sessions.

title: Which cognitive screening tool is most accurate for detecting mild cognitive impairment in cognitively unimpaired Parkinson’s Disease patients? A systematic review and meta-analysis.
description:
Rationale 

Mild cognitive impairment (MCI) is frequent in Parkinson’s Disease (PD) patients and may represent an intermediate state preceding dementia. Early and accurate identification of MCI in PD is essential for prognostic and therapeutic interventions. However, it remains unclear which cognitive screening tools best detect MCI in cognitively unimpaired PD patients. 

Objectives 

To systematically evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of cognitive screening tools in detecting MCI among cognitively unimpaired patients with Parkinson’s Disease compared with formal neuropsychological assessment (gold standard).

title: Machine Learning for Automated Classification of Abnormal Lung Sounds obtained from Public Databases: A Systematic Review
description:
Background: Pulmonary auscultation is essential to identifying abnormal lung sounds in at initial physical assessment. However, auscultation is highly operator-dependent and is subject to significant inter-observer variability. To aid in identifying abnormal lung sounds, automatic classi-fication using machine learning (ML) models arises as an alternative. Training ML models require large amounts of data and creating public databases intends to solve this issue. Objective: To per-form a systematic review of abnormal lung sound classification with ML models and recordings derived from public databases to compare differences in characteristics, diagnostic accuracy, con-cerns, and data sources. Methods: A comprehensive literature search in MEDLINE, Embase, CEN-TRAL, Web of Science, and Scopus was performed from Jan 1990 to Dec 2022. A complementary search using references to the included papers was conducted. Abstracts and titles were screened, and selected articles underwent full-text review and data extraction. Quality assessment was ac-complished using a modified QUADAS-2 tool. Results: We included 62 studies that used both an ML model and a public-access database to classify abnormal lung sounds. Artificial neural networks (ANN) and support vector machines (SVM) were the most frequently used ML classifiers. Accuracy ranged between 49.43% and 100% for the discrimination of abnormal sound types and 69.40% and 99.62% for classification of sounds by disease class. Seventeen public databases were identified. Notably, the majority (66%) of studies used the ICBHI 2017 database as one of their data sources. Most studies had a high risk of bias and concerns regarding patient selection and reference standard domains. Discussion: ML models can consistently learn to classify abnormal lung sounds from pub-lic data sources. Inconsistent reporting of performance and methods are major limitations in the currently available literature. Although essential for the evolution of the field, public databases should adhere to a standard recording and labeling methodology.

title: The Oxford Digital Multiple Errands Test (OxMET): Validation of a Simplified Computer Tablet Based Multiple Errands Test
description:
Impairments in executive functioning are common following Acquired Brain Injury, though there is a lack of screening tools which present both a time efficient and ecologically valid approach to assessing the consequences of executive impairments. We present the Oxford Digital Multiple Errands Test (OxMET), a novel and simplified computer-tablet version of a Multiple Errands Test.
We recruited 124 neurologically healthy controls and 105 stroke survivors to complete the OxMET task. Normative data and internal consistency were established from the healthy control data. Convergent and divergent validation was assessed in a mixed subset of 158 participants who completed the OxMET and the OCS-Plus. Test-retest reliability was examined across a mixed subset of 39 participants. Finally, we investigated the known-group discriminability of the OxMET.
The OxMET demonstrated very high internal consistency, and stable group level test-retest performance as well as good convergent and divergent validity. The OxMET demonstrated high sensitivity and good specificity in overall differentiation of stroke survivors from controls. Stroke survivors made significantly more errors than healthy controls, as well as being less accurate and slower to complete the task. 
This paper presents the Oxford Digital Multiple Errands Test as a brief, easy to administer tool, designed to quickly screen for potential consequences of executive impairments in a virtual environment shopping task on a computer tablet. Initial normative data and validation within a chronic stroke cohort is presented.
