title: Examining the Effect of the Language Pathway Test in Latine Dual-Language Learners' Performance
description:
Being a DLL is a cognitive benefit that should be celebrated. Nonetheless, we are still relying on academic assessments designed for monolingual children, and DLL performance is still being appraised based on English monolingual norms (Mancilla-Martinez et al., 2020). Gaps between DLL and monolingual English-speaking children have been reported at kindergarten entry, and many of those children are classified as long-term English learners, having less access to the general curriculum in the upper grades (NASEM, 2017). The approach of measuring DLLs' knowledge by comparing their performance with their monolingual peers, using assessments that had been designed for and normed on English-monolingual learners, has led to a deficit perspective.
It is widely recognized that not only assessments in one language do not accurately capture DLLs' academic abilities, but those assessments are influenced by cultural factors (Thordardottir et al., 2006). Culture shapes child development and cultural practices of the dominant group; in this case, English-monolingual children had been taken as the norm (Gutiérrez & Rogoff, 2003). However, approximately 33% of preschool-age children in the U.S. are DLL (Migration Policy Institute, 2021), with Spanish being the most common home language (Park et al., 2018). Latine children are the fastest-growing population in the U.S. (U.S. Census Bureau, 2019), and although, as López and Foster (2021) argue, not all Latine children are considered DLL, one in four are Latine, and one in three are DLL. For this project, we will refer to Latine DLLs, given that our sample is children who speak Spanish at home and parents report being Latine.
The development of educational processes within Latine DLL is not homogeneous. The framework of the Integrated Model for the Study of Developmental Competencies in Minority Children (Coll et al., 1996) helps understand the intragroup academic variability of Latine DLLs. For example, there is variability within this group regarding English proficiency, Spanish proficiency, and years of instruction in their first or second language (e.g., August & Shanahan, 2006). López and Foster (2021) state that language proficiency is essential in developing academic trajectories within and across languages. This argument is based on the Interdependence Theory of Language Development of Cummins (1979), who highlights the interdependence of language skills. The revised hierarchical model by Kroll and Stewart (1994) states that the two languages, in this case, Spanish and English, share a conceptual system, meaning that children’s experiences with each language influence their proficiency in those languages. Thus, it is crucial to consider both languages (i.e., Spanish and English) when assessing young Latine DLL. Espinosa & García (2012) argue that valid and appropriate assessments for DLL are critical for ECE programs to provide the necessary educational services.

The most comprehensive way to assess Latine DLLs' skills, using standardized designed measures, is to utilize conceptual scoring rather than assessments normed on and for English monolingual children. Conceptual scoring focuses on children's knowledge, taking into consideration the Spanish and English languages simultaneously (Mancilla-Martinez et al., 2020). Despite the extent of literature on the utility of conceptual scoring to better assess DLLs (e.g., NASEM, 2017), most of the research has focused on the area of literacy, leaving the examination of other domains, such as mathematics, highly unexplored even though early numeracy is the most predictive skill for long-term academic achievement (Mix, 2019; Nguyen et al., 2016). Examining how DLLs perform in different domains is crucial, given that assessing children's school readiness progress helps teachers identify individual needs to prepare each child to be ready for school (U.S. Department of Health & Human Services, 2022). 

The call for using conceptual scoring measures is not new. Unfortunately, academic assessments designed for monolingual students are commonly used with Latine DLLs in Spanish or English. As Mancilla-Martinez et al. (2020) stated, "DLLs have typically been treated as two monolinguals in one person" (p.3085). The common practice is to use single-language assessments that have been adapted from existing measures normed on English monolingual students and use those to interpret DLLs' academic abilities, which may need to be revised
The proposed study seeks to address the need for a more equitable understanding of Latine DLLs' academic development by examining study the effect of the English ‘proficiency’ test (i.e., preLAS test) on Latine DLLs’ performance in different school readiness domains (e.g., math, science, literacy).

title: Near-Infrared Spectroscopy (NIRS) coupled with machine learning/chemometrics for screening pesticide residues in whole fruits and vegetables: systematic review of performance, chromatographic reference standards, and deployment readiness (2016–2026).
description: This protocol outlines a systematic review to evaluate the performance of near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) combined with machine learning/chemometrics for the detection, classification, and/or quantification of pesticide residues in whole fruits and vegetables. We will include peer-reviewed primary studies published in English between 01 Jan 2016 and 10 Feb 2026 that use validated chromatographic methods (GC/LC, with MS when applicable) as the reference standard. Searches will be conducted in Scopus, Web of Science, Embase and ScienceDirect, followed by study selection by two independent reviewers with adjudication by a third reviewer. Start will be used for reference management, deduplication, screening, and data extraction. Primary outcomes will be sensitivity/specificity and AUC (classification) and RMSEP and predictive R² (regression). Risk of bias will be assessed using QUADAS-2 for classification studies and PROBAST for regression/predictive modeling studies. Evidence will be synthesized narratively, with meta-analysis performed when data are sufficiently comparable, and will include assessment of operational deployment readiness (e.g., portability, time-to-result, and feasibility for food safety monitoring).

title: Diagnostic accuracy of diffusion-weighted imaging for differentiating between postoperative recurrence of glioma and radiation-induced brain injury: A protocol for systematic review and meta analysis
description: Current treatments for glioma include surgery, radiotherapy, and chemotherapy. For such patients, it is difficult to completely remove the tumor part by surgery, resulting in easy recurrence after surgery, and chemoradiotherapy will cause radiation-induced brain injury in patients. Glioma recurrence and radiation-induced brain injury are similar in clinical manifestations as well as imaging, so it is difficult to differentiate in clinical practice. In recent years, it has been found that magnetic resonance diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) can be used in the differential diagnosis between glioma recurrence and radiation-induced brain injury, but there is a lack of relevant evidence-based medical evidence. The aim of this study was to investigate the value of DWI in differentiating glioma recurrence from radiation-induced brain injury by systematic review.

title: STAndards for ReporTing Equality, Diversity and Inclusion (START-EDI)
description: START-EDI reporting guidelines will provide a list of minimum items that should be reported by healthcare researchers, ensuring that diversity is incorporated in essential areas such as research design, data collection, public involvement, dissemination and impact. These reporting guidelines will be a universal, generic toolkit which can be adopted for clinical prediction model studies, diagnostic accuracy and efficacy/effectiveness studies. We anticipate that the guidelines will promote greater transparency and completeness in research and therefore benefit clinicians, journal editors, patients, healthcare providers, policymakers and other key stakeholders.

title: Use and appropriateness of Reporting Guidelines in physical therapy research: a protocol for a meta-research study
description:
INTRODUCTION: Problems about reporting of a scientific study can affect dissemination of research in different manners. It is known that study methods are frequently not described in adequate detail and that results are presented ambiguously or selectively. To overcome these problems, reporting guidelines (e.g. CONSORT, PRISMA, STARD and STROBE statements) have been developed to increase the transparency of research. While recent evidence suggested that these guidelines are frequently used inappropriately in studies published in the major medical journals, the extent and appropriateness of use in physical therapy research has not been systematically evaluated. The aim of this meta-research study will be to evaluate the frequency of using reporting guidelines and their appropriate use in physical therapy published research.
METHODS: A cross-sectional analysis is planned on a random sample of 200 studies published in the last ten years (2010-2019) in the five generic rehabilitation journals with the highest 5-year impact factor. Randomization will be stratified for publication date to include an equal number of studies from 2010 to 2014 (n=100), and from 2015 to 2019 (n=100). Randomised controlled trials, systematic reviews, diagnostic accuracy studies and observational studies will be included. Crude prevalence estimates with 95% confidence intervals of using and appropriateness of using will be estimated. A bivariate analysis will assess the relationship between the use of reporting guidelines and the year of publication.
DISSEMINATION PLANS: Several studies have shown the positive influence of reporting guidelines on the completeness of research reporting but no one investigated the use and the appropriateness of reporting guidelines in physical therapy research. Therefore, this study will add relevant knowledge that may contribute to improve further the reporting of rehabilitation research. The results of this research will be published in a peer-reviewed journal and will be presented at relevant (inter)national scientific events.

title: Use of Radiomics through Magnetic Resonance Imaging in the Diagnosis of Prostate Cancer Prior to Biopsy: a Scoping Review
description: Radiomics has emerged as a diagnostic tool in response to the increasing incidence of prostate cancer and the need to implement non-invasive methods for its detection. The growing workload in the medical field and the demand for precise diagnoses justify this research, which focuses on analyzing the diagnostic utility of radiomics prior to biopsy. The study includes data from patients with confirmed prostate biopsy results, regardless of cancer stage, and who underwent Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) as the primary imaging technique. The objective of this research is to evaluate the diagnostic performance of MRI-based radiomics in detecting prostate cancer before biopsy, through sensitivity and specificity analysis

title: FACTORS AFFECTING HEALTHCARE PROVIDERS IN THE IMPLEMENTATION OF PREGNANCY TERMINATION POLICIES: A SYSTEMATIC INTEGRATIVE REVIEW PROTOCOL
description: AUTHORS Authors Ms Bielka Carvajal. Division of Nursing, Midwifery & Social Work, The University of Manchester. Departamento de Promoción de la Salud de la Mujer, Universidad de Chile. Dr Helen White. Division of Nursing, Midwifery & Social Work, The University of Manchester. Dr Jane Brooks. Division of Nursing, Midwifery & Social Work, The University of Manchester. Prof Ann Thomson. Division of Nursing, Midwifery & Social Work, The University of Manchester. Dr Alison Cooke. Division of Nursing, Midwifery & Social Work, The University of Manchester. BACKGROUND The cessation of a pregnancy before the foetus is ready to survive outside the womb can occur due to several causes, including an abnormal embryo, a woman's medical condition or her choice (1,2). Although the result in these three scenarios is the same, there has been a need from the general population and medical staff to differentiate the 'spontaneous' loss from the deliberate act to terminate a pregnancy. Therefore, terms such as spontaneous abortion, medical abortion, medical termination, induced abortion, miscarriage, pregnancy loss, pregnancy termination and others have been used, often inconsistently, to describe these differences (3). While some of these terms could help to diminish women's sorrow after the loss (4), some others are considered to increase discrimination and fear of punishment, especially in contexts where induced abortions are against the law (5). In particular, this review will refer to the active process of ending a gestation before foetal extrauterine viability (6–8) as the termination of pregnancy (TOP). As in any other healthcare policy, the implementation of pregnancy termination services involves law enactment, developing new staff skills, creating new guidelines and protocols, and acquiring equipment (9). Additionally to these, this process is also profoundly affected by what individuals believe to be right and wrong (10,11), which in the case of TOP is grounded in people's beliefs about human life and women's rights (12). Healthcare providers are an essential factor when implementing any policy; moreover, they are considered de facto policymakers because their actions and attitudes shape policies (13). For example, healthcare professionals could decide to be less compliant with clinical guidelines if they perceive them as a threat to their clinical autonomy (14) or too complicated (15). This autonomy or discretion can also be used against procedures or regulations that providers consider to be immoral, thus affecting the availability of certain services. Healthcare providers are usually allowed to abstain from participation in activities against their moral or religion, known as conscientious objection (16). This permission is generally given in TOP cases, where the abstention could differentiate between causes and include different professionals who are allowed to object (17). Moreover, these differences about what is considered immoral could extend to emergency contraception, which some argue affects the implantation process (18–20). Regarding conscientious objection, balancing the provider's right to object with women's right to choose can be challenging and affect patient referrals, especially in places where the objection rate is high (21–23). Furthermore, the referral process itself must be planned meticulously, or non-objectors could face a heavier workload than those who object (23). Beyond the impact of conscientious objection, providers could set other potential barriers when sexual and reproductive policies are being implemented, affecting access and healthcare provision (12,24–30). Therefore, this review aims to explore the facilitators and barriers affecting healthcare providers when implementing pregnancy termination (including emergency contraception) policies. INTEGRATIVE REVIEW Successful implementation of healthcare policies can be a complex issue; thus, it is best studied using a broad range of research (31–33). Considering the growing volume of evidence in all subjects, reviews stand as a strategy that allows the synthesis of a large portion of evidence while making recommendations or providing an overview of the studied topic. It is possible to identify several types of review that respond to different aims (34,35). Considering this review aims to explore the TOP policy implementation process, an integrative review can be particularly useful as they include findings from quantitative, qualitative and unpublished literature to provide an insight into the studied topic (36–38). In Cronin and George’s (38) words, integrative reviews integrate communities of practice 'who study similar topics using different paradigms, conceptual language, and research traditions, even in their metatheoretical analyses' (p.2). Accomplishing the integration of different evidence types is not exempt from challenges, especially when trying to ensure rigour in the process (38,39). Thus, Whittemore and Knafl (2005) defined five stages that this integrative review will follow to ensure it is being developed correctly and systematically. METHODS AND ANALYSIS Problem Identification As stated in the introduction of this review, healthcare personnel actions and attitudes can affect medical care provision, affecting the implementation of policies and/or guidelines. Therefore, this review aims to explore facilitators and barriers to healthcare personnel's participation in the implementation of pregnancy termination (including emergency contraception) policies. Hence, the research question of this integrative review will be: 'What are providers' experiences and attitudes in implementing emergency contraception and pregnancy termination policies?' Secondary questions for this review will address two different implementation aspects: i) how patient referral is addressed in conscientious objection cases? and ii) how the healthcare team manages conscientious objection? Additionally, in the cases where conscientious objection is not part of these policies, it is expected to explore i) what are the perceptions of this situation among the healthcare team? ii) how do healthcare personnel who consider themselves objectors deal with the situation? iii) how does the healthcare team balance 'protection' of the objector's position while providing care? Literature Search A good literature search strategy in a review should ensure that all relevant studies/documents are retrieved. Furthermore, when the search fails to do so, the chances of bias increase and the results become less trustworthy (40). In this review, the eligibility criteria to select the literature will be the following: Inclusion Criteria Participants For studies to be eligible in this review, they must include healthcare providers as research participants. The concept 'healthcare providers' will be understood as the personnel directly involved in the prescription or provision of emergency contraception or those who perform pregnancy terminations or provide medical care before, during or after this procedure. Type of studies This review will include quantitative, qualitative and mixed-method primary research focused on exploring healthcare providers' experiences. Therefore, the three types of studies will be eligible for inclusion providing that they are focused on providers' experiences while implementing emergency contraception and pregnancy termination policies. No literature will be excluded based on the study's subtype (quasi-experimental, non-experimental, and others), methodology (phenomenology, grounded theory and others), gender or ethnicity of the participants, the country of origin of the publication, or when the article was published. Unpublished articles will also be eligible in this review (such as congress abstracts). In these cases, attempts will be made to contact the authors to retrieve more information about the study. Policy reports aimed to describe TOP or emergency contraception policies will also be included in this review. Phenomenon of Interest The phenomenon of interest in this review is the implementation of pregnancy termination policies. Although emergency contraception is not abortive, some providers recognise it as an action against 'human' life; hence, it will be studied as part of the pregnancy termination phenomenon. Exclusion Criteria A flow diagram using the recommendations made by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) will be created describing the reasons for excluding articles in this review (41). The exclusion criteria for this review will be: i) Studies not focused on providers' experiences when implementing policies or where their experiences/attitudes could not be isolated from the article ii) Studies where providers were not included as participants iii) Articles focused on miscarriages, ectopic pregnancy, pregnancy loss or any other unprovoked pregnancy termination iv) Personal opinions, such as commentaries and editorials v) Articles where the full text version cannot be accessed by the research team (attempts will be made to obtain these from the authors) vi) Articles where the full text is in a language different from English or Spanish Search Strategy This review will use a three-step search strategy to maximise the retrieval of literature. The first step will be focused on searching electronic databases using PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcome) (42) and SPIDER (Sample, Phenomenon of Interest, Design, Evaluation and Research type) (43) strategies. Considering that PICO is more focused towards quantitative literature and SPIDER is more specific to qualitative studies, it is expected that by using both most of the existing literature in both paradigms is retrieved (43,44). The second step will be a hand search of the references mentioned in international reports related to the topic and a hand search using the reference lists of all selected articles. Finally, the third step will be to contact authors who are prolific in the topic area to identify any unpublished 'grey' literature. Electronic Searches The search of the literature will be conducted in the following medical and social science databases: The Cumulative Index of Nursing and Allied Health Literature (CINAHL) Plus, the British Nursing Index, Medical Literature Analysis and Retrieval System Online (Medline), the Psychological Information Database (PsycINFO), the Applied Social Sciences Index Abstracts (ASSIA), the Social Science database. Furthermore, to ensure retrieving literature from low and middle-income Spanish speaking countries the search will also be conducted in the Scientific Electronic Library Online (SciELO), and the Latin American and Caribbean Health Sciences Literature (LILACS). These databases include literature related to healthcare from Latin American countries and hold the largest volume of literature available in the subject area. The searches will use the keywords described in Appendix 1. The research team will agree on the final search strategy to ensure that the process is rigorous. The final search strategy will be published in detail, along with the results of the review. Other searches The hand search of relevant literature will be conducted using the list of references of international and congress reports related to the studied subject made by the United Nations Fund for Population Activities (UNFPA), the Guttmacher Institute, the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG), the International Confederation of Midwives (ICM), the International Council of Nurses (ICN), the International Federation of Gynaecology and Obstetrics (FIGO), the International Pharmaceutical Federation (FIP) and the World Health Organization (WHO). The reference lists from selected articles will also be screened to identify any study not retrieved in the electronic searches. A list of authors will be created, and prolific authors in the topic area will be approached to enquire about any unpublished evidence related to the topic. DATA EVALUATION Selection of Studies The selection of eligible studies will be conducted in two consecutive steps: i) reviewing titles and abstracts retrieved, and ii) reviewing the full-text version of the articles considered eligible using the inclusion and exclusion criteria. For this, a screening tool developed by the research team following the recommendations of Polanin et al. (45) will be used (see Appendix 2). This tool will be piloted and adapted (if necessary) using 20 articles retrieved in the search to ensure questions are appropriate (45). For this, the first author (BC) will screen articles using the tool to determine if they should be included in the study. After completing this process, the same articles will be read in full, and a decision for its inclusion will be made accordingly. After both processes are completed, the decisions made using both techniques will be contrasted. The whole process will be monitored and reviewed by two other authors in the research team (HW/AC). In the cases where a discrepancy is found, the research team will analyse which aspects of the articles lead to the disagreement and the tool will be edited to ensure this situation is resolved. If the screening tool requires amendment, the revised tool will be piloted using another 3 articles from the search. All references will be managed using EndNote©. Once the electronic search is complete duplicate articles will be removed using this software. After this process, the first author will review all titles and abstracts of articles resulting from the searches using the inclusion and exclusion criteria. This process will be monitored and reviewed by two other authors in the research team (HW/AC). When the article's exclusion raises concerns, the paper will be considered by the research team to reach a consensus on inclusion or exclusion. The full-text version of all articles considered eligible will be downloaded, and the first author (BC) will conduct an assessment for their inclusion. Two other members of the research team (HW/AC) will monitor and review these articles to ensure rigour. When a full-text version cannot be secured, the publication's authors will be contacted to obtain it. Those articles where the full-text version cannot be obtained from the authors will be excluded from the review. Once article selection is complete, their reference list will be screened to ensure all relevant literature is included. The same process will be conducted with reference lists from international reports. The whole research team will approve the final body of literature for review. Data Extraction and Quality Assessment The tool that will be used in this review for the data extraction process (see Appendix 3) is an adaptation of the data collection form for intervention reviews for randomised controlled trials (RCT) and non-RCTs published by the Cochrane Collaboration (46,47). The form will be piloted and adapted (if necessary) using the first 20 articles retrieved in the search to ensure it is appropriate, using the same rigorous process and members of the research team outlined in the ‘Selection of Studies’ section. If a situation raises concern during the data extraction process, the research team will discuss and resolve it. Irrespective of the results of their quality assessment, all studies will undergo data extraction. A quality appraisal will be conducted for each selected article using the Mixed Method Appraisal Tool (MMAT) version 2018 (48). This tool allows assessment of the quality of primary research using qualitative, quantitative (randomised controlled trials, non-randomised and descriptive studies) or mixed-method methodology (Appendix 4). To incorporate the quality appraisal of policy reports and guidelines the research team included a modification in the MMAT tool (see Appendix 4), with consideration to the policy process cycle (49). Part six of this tool includes the dimensions for assessing a report as 'good', which are: a clear aim, have used appropriate evidence to its formulation, addressing cultural differences in the implementation process, including information about the evaluation process of the policy and a conflict of interest statement. The appraisal tool will be piloted using the first 20 policy documents retrieved in the search, using a rigorous process with three members of the research team as outlined in the ‘Selection of Studies’ section. This pilot test will aim to determine if it is possible to answer the questions using the data in the reports, otherwise the questions will be reformulated to obtain information about the dimensions proposed in this tool. A growing number of authors have started to discourage calculating overall quality scores for appraised articles (50–53). Their main arguments for doing so are focused on the insufficient information provided by a 'score number' and the problems of assigning weight (importance) to the criteria used to evaluate quality. Therefore, and following MMAT suggestions (48), no article will be scored nor excluded from this synthesis. The quality appraisal findings will be incorporated in the results section of this review emphasising which dimensions were most likely to be accomplished and missed. DATA ANALYSIS, CONCLUSION DRAWING AND VERIFICATION To be rigorous when managing data extracted from very different types of studies, the data will be analysed following Whittemore and Knafl’s (2005) recommendation for integrative reviews. This process includes data reduction, data display and data comparison (38). For this, each study will be read to extract the results. Results will later be compared within and against the rest of the studies to address differences and similarities. Data will be grouped and described into types of designs and relevant categories related to the studied topic. In each group, literature will be read and re-read to identify common themes and patterns which will later be used to create a conceptual model (54). Once the conceptual model is created, it will be verified against the primary data sources to ensure confirmability (55). Conflicting evidence that cannot be included in the model will be reported as part of the narrative synthesis. Data results will be displayed in tables and diagrams to improve comprehension of the process undertaken. The first author will keep a reflective journal throughout the review process, and a reflexivity section will be incorporated as part of the final review. title: Cliniflow: Effects of AI, Human, and Hybrid Diagnostic Advice (and Advice Timing) on Physicians’ Diagnostic Decisions
description: This preregistration covers a randomized experiment on the Human Diagnosis Project (Human Dx) platform. Physician participants diagnose internal medicine case vignettes and receive diagnostic advice from either (i) a 4-LLM ensemble, (ii) a 4-physician ensemble, (iii) a hybrid collective (2 physicians + 2 LLMs), or (iv) no advice (control). Advice is presented either early (together with case details and before a diagnosis is made) or late (after all clinical findings are shown and participants made their initial diagnosis). Outcomes include diagnostic accuracy (top-1/top-3/top-5 and mean reciprocal rank (MRR), of the correct diagnosis), advice uptake (similarity to advice and change after advice), and diagnostic confidence. Analyses will use hierarchical Bayesian models with varying intercepts by case.

title: Differential diagnosis checklists reduce diagnostic error differentially: a randomized experiment
description:
Introduction Wrong and missed diagnoses contribute substantially to medical error. Can a prompt to generate alternative diagnoses (prompt) or a differential diagnosis checklist (DDXC) increase diagnostic accuracy? How do these interventions affect the diagnostic process and self-monitoring?
Methods Advanced medical students (N = 90) were randomly assigned to one of four conditions to complete six computer-based patient cases: Group 1 (prompt) was instructed to write down all diagnoses they considered while acquiring diagnostic test results, and to finally rank them. Groups 2 and 3 received the same instruction plus a list of 17 differential diagnoses for the chief complaint of the patient. For half of the cases, the DDXC contained the correct diagnosis (DDXC+) and for the other half, it did not (DDXC-; counterbalanced). Group 4 (control) was only instructed to indicate their final diagnosis. Mixed-effects models were used to analyze results.
Results Students using a DDXC that contained the correct diagnosis had better diagnostic accuracy, mean (standard deviation), 0.75 (0.44), compared to controls without a checklist, 0.49 (0.50), P < 0.001, but those using a DDXC that did not contain the correct diagnosis did slightly worse, 0.43 (0.50), P = 0.602. The number and relevance of diagnostic tests acquired were not affected by condition, nor was self-monitoring. However, participants spent more time on a case in the DDXC-, 4:20 minutes (2:36), P ≤ 0.001, and DDXC+ condition, 3:52 minutes (2:09), than in the control condition, 2:59 minutes (1:44), P ≤ 0.001.
Discussion Being provided a list of possible diagnoses improves diagnostic accuracy compared with a prompt to create a differential diagnosis list, if the provided list contains the correct diagnosis. However, being provided a diagnosis list without the correct diagnosis did not improve and might have slightly reduced diagnostic accuracy. Interventions neither affected information gathering nor self-monitoring.

title: Topical diagnostic agents for identifying head and neck cancers of unknown primary: a systematic review across aerodigestive tract specialties
description:
Topical contrast agents have been explored for decades as adjuncts in the detection of malignant and premalignant disease of the upper aerodigestive tract (UADT). Applied directly to the epithelium, these dyes enhance visual discrimination between normal and abnormal tissue, guide biopsy selection, and assist in delineating resection margins. Their appeal lies in their low cost, ease of application, and immediate visual feedback, making them suitable for both outpatient and intraoperative use.

Agents trialled include non-fluorescent dyes such as toluidine blue (TB), Lugol’s iodine (LI), methylene blue (MB), and acetic acid (AA). Fluorescent probes, most notably 5-aminolevulinic acid (5-ALA), allow fluorescence-guided assessment under specialised illumination. Despite widespread use, uptake has been uneven, with diagnostic performance varying by agent, method of application, and anatomical site. Concerns about false positives and specificity have limited broader acceptance.

Newer optical imaging modalities, such as narrow-band imaging, autofluorescence, and chemiluminescence, are often promoted as alternatives. However, these require costly equipment and have shown variable accuracy, limiting uptake, particularly in low-resource settings. By contrast, topical dyes remain inexpensive, pragmatic tools that can augment mucosal assessment.
The aim of this systematic review was to evaluate the diagnostic performance of topical dyes, both fluorescent and non-fluorescent, in the assessment of UADT lesions. Specifically, we examined their utility in detecting malignant and dysplastic change and in delineating surgical margins, with the goal of providing a comprehensive overview of their clinical value across subsites.
To address this aim, we undertook a systematic literature search and critical appraisal of published studies, followed by quantitative and descriptive synthesis of the available evidence.

title: Comparative Prognostic Accuracy of 19 Biomarkers for Mortality Prediction in Adult Sepsis: A Bayesian Diagnostic Test Accuracy Network Meta-Analysis
description:
Background and rationale:
Sepsis remains a leading cause of mortality among critically ill patients worldwide, with in-hospital death rates ranging from 25% to over 50% in patients progressing to septic shock. Numerous circulating biomarkers have been proposed for predicting sepsis-related mortality, including conventional markers such as procalcitonin (PCT), C-reactive protein (CRP), and blood lactate, as well as novel analytes such as mid-regional proadrenomedullin (MR-proADM), soluble urokinase plasminogen activator receptor (suPAR), presepsin, and interleukin-6 (IL-6). However, the vast majority of existing studies have evaluated only one or two biomarkers in isolation, and systematic reviews to date have adopted pairwise designs that do not permit simultaneous cross-biomarker comparison. Consequently, no unified ranking framework exists to guide clinicians and guideline developers in selecting the most accurate prognostic biomarker for sepsis mortality prediction.

Diagnostic test accuracy network meta-analysis (DTA-NMA) offers a principled statistical framework to address this gap by synthesising both direct and indirect evidence across a connected network of biomarkers, enabling simultaneous comparison and probabilistic ranking even in the absence of head-to-head studies.

Objectives:
The primary objective of this systematic review is to simultaneously compare the prognostic accuracy of 19 pre-specified circulating biomarkers for predicting all-cause mortality in adult patients with sepsis, severe sepsis, or septic shock using a Bayesian DTA-NMA framework.

Secondary objectives include:
(1) To rank all 19 biomarkers according to their overall discriminative ability using the surface under the cumulative ranking curve (SUCRA) and pairwise posterior superiority probabilities;
(2) To identify which biomarkers offer the best "rule-in" value (highest positive likelihood ratio) and "rule-out" value (lowest negative likelihood ratio);
(3) To explore whether clinical setting (ICU vs. emergency department), sepsis definition (Sepsis-1/2 vs. Sepsis-3), mortality endpoint, and cut-off derivation method modify biomarker performance.

Study design:
This will be a systematic review and Bayesian diagnostic test accuracy network meta-analysis. The review will be conducted and reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Diagnostic Test Accuracy studies (PRISMA-DTA) and its network meta-analysis adaptation (PRISMA-NMA).

Search strategy:
A comprehensive literature search will be conducted in PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, the Cochrane Library, and Web of Science from database inception through December 2024, supplemented by manual reference screening. No language or publication-type restrictions will be applied.

Eligibility criteria:
Studies will be included if they: (a) enrol adult patients (≥18 years) with sepsis, severe sepsis, or septic shock; (b) evaluate one or more of 19 pre-specified biomarkers for all-cause mortality prediction; and (c) report sufficient data to reconstruct a 2×2 diagnostic contingency table. Paediatric/neonatal studies, conference abstracts without full data, studies reporting only AUROC without 2×2 data, and animal studies will be excluded.

Index tests (19 biomarkers):
PCT, CRP, blood lactate, presepsin, MR-proADM, suPAR, IL-6, IL-8, sST2, PTX3, NT-proBNP, sTREM-1, galectin-3, TNF-α, heparin-binding protein (HBP), human epididymis protein 4 (HE4), oxygenation index (OI), PCT clearance, and lactate clearance.

Reference standard:
All-cause mortality at a defined time point (in-hospital, 28-day, 30-day, 90-day, or ICU mortality).

Data extraction and quality assessment:
Two reviewers will independently perform study selection, data extraction, and risk-of-bias assessment using the QUADAS-2 tool. Disagreements will be resolved by a third reviewer.

Planned statistical analysis:
The primary analysis will employ a Bayesian bivariate hierarchical model that jointly estimates logit-transformed sensitivity and specificity across all biomarkers within a network framework, implemented via Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) simulation in JAGS. Weakly informative priors will be used. Summary measures will include pooled sensitivity, specificity, diagnostic odds ratio (DOR), positive and negative likelihood ratios, and SROC curves. Rankings will be quantified using SUCRA values, rankograms, and pairwise posterior superiority probabilities. Pre-specified meta-regression and subgroup analyses will examine sources of heterogeneity. Sensitivity analyses will include leave-one-out analysis, alternative prior specifications, and restriction to biomarkers with ≥3 studies. Publication bias will be assessed using Deeks' funnel plot asymmetry test and comparison-adjusted funnel plots.

Software: R (version 4.3.x), JAGS (version 4.3.1), R2jags, mada, ggplot2, coda.

Expected timeline:
Literature search and screening: January–March 2025
Data extraction and quality assessment: March–May 2025
Statistical analysis and manuscript drafting: May–August 2025

title: Adaptation, external validation and refinement of two children’s homes Swiss-French topic search filters on RERO DOC
description:
Abstract
Objectives:
To adapt, validate and refine topic search filters meant to retrieve Swiss social work bachelor theses focusing on children’s homes written in French and indexed in RERO DOC
Study design:
Search filter external validation, refinement and internal validation
Methods:
Full-text assessment of all 385 bachelor theses published by HETS Valais students and indexed in RERO DOC, extraction of titles and assessment of whether they focus or not on children’s homes. Adaptation of the two previously built filters for RERO DOC, measurement of their performances on this new dataset. Development of three new 
Results:
Performances of the original topic search filters dropped significantly when applied to this external validation set. The highly sensitive children’s homes search filter performance went from 79.45%/95.12% sensitivity/specificity to 66.32%/78.89% and the highly specific search filter performance went from 69.86%/98.37% sensitivity/specificity to 54.74%/83.39% when tested on the RERO DOC dataset. Reasons included: a lower prevalence of specific keywords within children’s homes titles (now out of date or highly canton-specific) and limited functionality of searches making use of character accentuations.
A highly sensitive (“exhaustive”), a highly specific (“focused”) and a balanced (“best trade-off”) RERO DOC specific search filters were developed iteratively using a search simulator. The “exhaustive” search filter achieved 87.37% sensitivity and 71.88% specificity. The “focused” search filter achieved 62.11% sensitivity and 93.40% specificity. And the “best trade-off” filter achieved 74.74% sensitivity and 84.38% specificity.
Novel keywords included in these filters include: reference, fugue, mineur, rupture, plainte and St-Raphael/Saint-Raphael.
Limitations:
The RERO DOC search filters were used without using data from abstracts or the full extent of advanced search features available and could be improved further. The new search filters should be used with caution on different databases, if used to search works from non-Swiss settings (for instance works from France), if used to search for works published prior to 1980/1990 or if used to search for works published in the following decades.

title: Digital neuropsychological assessments for neurocognitive disorders - a Scoping Review
description:
Research regarding digital neuropsychological tests and screenings has been growing steadily for the past years. More and more existing assessments have been digitally adapted and supplemented by additional parameters (such as linguistic analyses), which are possible to record due to digitization. Overall, there appear to be major differences between the digital assessments with regard to quality criteria (including validation), normative data, but also their applicability in the context of neuropsychological diagnostics of neurocognitive disorders (NCD).
We will conduct a systematic and sensitive search on the platform PubMed with search and MeSH terms of three contentual clusters: neurocognitive disorder (NCD), digital technology and neuropsychological assessment. First, the titles and abstracts of the articles will be checked for inclusion (e.g. digital cognitve assessements) and exclusion criteria (e.g. cognitive training, age of participants <18 years) and then full-text analyses will be conducted. The analyses will focus on the following points: Existence of validation and standardization as well as sensitivity and specificity measures for MCI or NCD.
The aim of the described scoping review is to provide an up-to-date overview of digital neuropsychological methods for the diagnostics of neurocognitive disorders and to point out their quality and applicability.

title: Identification of new spectral signatures associated with dengue virus infected sera
description: In a quest to use Raman spectroscopy as an optical diagnostic tool, we recorded Raman spectra of 32 dengue virus (DENV)-infected and 28 healthy sera samples in the near-infrared spectral range (540 to 1700 cm−1) using laser at 785 nm as the excitation source. We observed clear differences in the Raman spectra of DENV-infected sera as compared with those of healthy individuals. Here, as a result of our study, we report 12 unique Raman bands associated with DENV-infected sera that are not reported earlier. After applying analysis of variance and t-test (p < 0.05) on these 12 bands, six Raman bands at 630 (N-acetylglucosamine), 883 (in-plane bending (ring) of deoxyribose), 1218 (amide III–β conformation from C6H5–C stretching vibrations of tryptophan and phenylalanine), 1273 (amide–III), 1623 (tryptophan) and 1672 cm−1 (ceramide) were found only in the DENV-infected sera. The remaining six Raman bands at 716 (lipids), 780 (Uracil-based ring breathing mode), 828 (ring breathing tyrosine), 840 (α-anomers), 1101 (ν(C–N) of lipids and DNA) and 1150 cm−1(glycogen/carotenoids) were only found in healthy sera. Two types of classification models, principal component analysis and linear discriminant analysis, were employed to develop principal component analysis–linear discriminant analysis model that has provided diagnostic accuracy 96.50%, sensitivity 93.44%, and specificity 100%. This indicates that these 12 Raman bands have the potential to be used as biomarkers for optical diagnosis of DENV infection. This study provides a new insight for future research in the field of optical diagnosis using Raman spectroscopy.

title: Clinical Governance, Quality Management, and Radiation Protection in Diagnostic and Interventional Radiology: A Scoping Review within the Italian National Health Service (SSN), 2016–2026
description:
TITLE:
Clinical Governance, Quality Management, and Radiation Protection in Diagnostic and Interventional Radiology: A Scoping Review within the Italian National Health Service (SSN), 2016–2026

DESCRIPTION / ABSTRACT:
Background:
In modern healthcare settings, radiological departments face growing organizational and regulatory complexity. Ensuring high standards of diagnostic accuracy while minimizing clinical risk and patient radiation exposure requires a multi-professional and integrated governance strategy. However, Clinical Governance, Quality Management Systems (QMS), clinical risk management, and Radiation Protection are often addressed as separate domains, potentially limiting the development of coordinated quality and safety strategies. This scoping review maps the available evidence, regulatory frameworks, and operational models supporting their integration within the Italian National Health Service (SSN).
Objectives:
1. To identify and map organizational models integrating Clinical Governance, Quality Management, clinical risk management, and Radiation Protection across Diagnostic Imaging and Interventional Radiology services.
2. To examine the relationship between relevant Italian legislative requirements (e.g., Legislative Decree 101/2020 on radiation protection and Law 24/2017 on patient safety) and international quality standards (ISO 9001:2015 and ISO 7101:2023).
3. To synthesize operational strategies addressing safety checklists, Diagnostic Reference Levels (DRLs), Radiation Dose Monitoring Systems (RDMS), contrast media safety, digital workflows, and Artificial Intelligence (AI) integration.
4. To identify existing Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) and propose an integrated KPI framework for evaluating the performance of multidisciplinary radiology teams.
Methods & Eligibility Criteria (PCC Framework):
This scoping review was conducted in accordance with the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology and the PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews) guidelines.

Eligibility criteria were structured according to the PCC framework:

-Population (P): Diagnostic Imaging and Interventional Radiology services and their multidisciplinary healthcare teams, including Radiologists, TSRM/Radiographers, Medical Physicists, and Nurses.
-Concept (C): Clinical Governance models, Quality Management Systems (ISO 9001:2015 and ISO 7101:2023), Clinical Risk Management (patient safety, safety checklists, contrast media safety), Radiation Protection (Diagnostic Reference Levels [DRLs], Radiation Dose Monitoring Systems [RDMS], optimization, and justification), and digital innovation, including Artificial Intelligence (AI).
-Context (C): Public and accredited private healthcare facilities operating within the Italian National Health Service (SSN).
Sources published between January 1, 2016 and July 31, 2026 were eligible for inclusion.

Results & Corpus:
A structured search of PubMed and Scopus, supplemented by Google Scholar and targeted searches of institutional and professional sources (AGENAS, SIRM, FNO TSRM-PSTRP), identified a final corpus of 67 unique sources. Thematic analysis mapped these sources across three primary operational pillars: (1) Quality Management Systems & Standards; (2) Clinical Risk Management & Safety Checklists; and (3) Radiation Protection, Optimization & Dose Monitoring. The three categories were not mutually exclusive, with individual sources contributing to more than one thematic domain. Overall, the 67 sources generated 72 thematic assignments, corresponding to 24 assignments per pillar.
Significance:
This study provides an evidence-informed framework for healthcare managers, clinical leaders, and radiology professionals to support the integration of Clinical Governance, Quality Management, Clinical Risk Management, and Radiation Protection, bridging regulatory requirements with continuous quality improvement in Diagnostic Imaging and Interventional Radiology.

title: Clinical Utility of Plasma p-tau217 Dual-Threshold Strategies for Reducing Confirmatory Amyloid Testing in Alzheimer's Disease: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
description:
Purpose

This project is a systematic review and meta-analysis examining whether "dual-threshold" blood testing strategies using plasma p-tau217 — a biomarker of tau pathology — can safely reduce the need for expensive, invasive confirmatory testing (amyloid PET scans or lumbar puncture/CSF analysis) in patients being evaluated for Alzheimer's disease.

Rather than using a single cutoff value to classify patients as amyloid-positive or amyloid-negative, dual-threshold approaches set two cut-points: a lower threshold below which amyloid pathology can be confidently ruled out, and a higher threshold above which it can be confidently ruled in. Patients falling between these thresholds occupy an indeterminate "gray zone" and still require confirmatory imaging or CSF testing. In principle, this allows roughly half to two-thirds of patients to be triaged with a simple blood draw, concentrating scarce and costly diagnostic resources on the smaller subset of ambiguous cases.

While a substantial body of individual studies has evaluated such strategies across memory clinics, population cohorts, and multicenter validation settings, no prior systematic review has specifically synthesized this dual-threshold literature as distinct from single-cutoff diagnostic accuracy studies. This review fills that gap.

Approach

The protocol follows PRISMA-P 2020, PRISMA-DTA, and Cochrane diagnostic test accuracy methodology:

Search strategy: Comprehensive searches of PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and Scopus (no date restriction, English-language only), supplemented by reference screening and forward citation searching.
Eligibility: Studies must evaluate plasma p-tau217 using a genuine dual-threshold, rule-in/rule-out, or gray-zone framework (not a single cutoff), validated against amyloid PET and/or CSF reference standards.
Screening & extraction: Independent, duplicate screening and data extraction (Rayyan platform), with disagreements resolved by a third reviewer; inter-rater agreement quantified via Cohen's kappa.
Risk of bias: Assessed using QUADAS-2 across four domains (patient selection, index test, reference standard, flow/timing).
Statistical synthesis: Random-effects and bivariate models (R packages: mada, meta, metafor, diagmeta) to pool sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, gray-zone proportion, and proportion of confirmatory testing avoided, with HSROC/SROC curves, heterogeneity assessment (I², τ², Cochran's Q), pre-specified subgroup and sensitivity analyses, and Deeks' test for publication bias where applicable.
Evidence certainty: Graded using GRADE-DTA.

Expected Outcomes

The review aims to produce pooled, quantitative estimates of dual-threshold diagnostic performance — rule-out sensitivity, rule-in specificity, predictive values, gray-zone size, and the realistic proportion of PET or CSF testing that can be avoided — along with an understanding of how these estimates vary by assay platform (immunoassay vs. mass spectrometry), reference standard, and clinical setting. The findings are intended to give clinicians, health systems, and guideline developers a rigorous evidence base to inform the design and adoption of blood-based, dual-threshold diagnostic pathways for Alzheimer's disease in routine practice, with results disseminated via peer-reviewed publication and conference presentation, and registered prospectively on OSF.

Planned analyses will explore heterogeneity according to model type, input features (e.g., clinical, laboratory, imaging, or multimodal data), joint type, reference standard, study design, and validation approach. This review aims to provide an evidence-based assessment of the current accuracy, robustness, and clinical applicability of machine learning–based models for diagnosing PJI and to identify priorities for future research.

title: CANINE EQUINOCOCOCOSIS: Diagnostic tests used in environmental surveillance for cystic echinococcosis.
description:
Cystic echinococcosis (CE) is a chronic parasitic zoonosis caused by the larval stage of Echinococcus granulosus, a cestode that inhabits the small intestine of dogs and other canids. It is a neglected disease, usually asymptomatic, of fortuitous diagnosis, and whose diagnostic confirmation requires sequential tests (imaging, ELISA and Western blot); it is usually treated surgically (Rojas-Pincheira et al., 2022). 
Although man is only an accidental host, the diagnostic difficulties, surgical treatment and its complications; added to the increasing close relationship with pets; the absence of symptomatology in parasitized dogs; allow people to assume a lower perception of the risk of acquiring zoonotic diseases and, therefore, facilitate the perpetuation of the disease. 
Worldwide, 2,225 lives are lost due to QS, with a mortality rate of 0.007 x 100,000 population; and a loss of years due to illness, disability or premature death of 184,000 (World Health Organization, 2016). Most cases are diagnosed in adults due to the slow growth of the parasite, and only 10-20% of cases are diagnosed in children under 16 years of age(Moro & Schantz, 2009; Salazar-Mesones et al., 2022). Therefore, identifying a parasitized dog and treating it will always be the most economical, rapid and practical prevention intervention under the One Health strategy.
For the identification of E. granulosus in dogs, copro-ELISA presents sensitivity and specificity values of 92.6% and 86.4% respectively; and other authors with 38.3% sensitivity and 59.2% respectively (Isabel Jercic et al., 2019; Lahmar et al., 2007; Morel et al., 2013). Copro-PCR a sensitivity and specificity of 78% and 93% respectively; and like the previous case, a sensitivity and specificity of 35.6% and 75.5% respectively (Isabel Jercic et al., 2019; Oba et al., 2016). These values generate diagnostic uncertainty, questioning whether the differences are due to limitations of the diagnostic test, to factors associated with the sample or to variability in parasitic dissemination. 
Therefore, the objective of this study is to analyze the available evidence of the accuracy of diagnostic tests used in canine echinococcosis through a systematic review.

title: Autism Traits & Lived Experience Scale (ATLES): A Community-Developed Autism Questionnaire for Diagnosing and Screening Adults
description:
The current study seeks to refine and validate the ATLES, a novel adult autism self-report questionnaire designed to address longstanding gaps in ASD assessment. Although increasing numbers of adults are seeking evaluations, existing measures were developed for children, validated in narrow samples, or based on outdated diagnostic criteria. To improve diagnostic accuracy and reduce missed or delayed identification, our long-term goal is to disseminate a psychometrically sound, gender inclusive, neuroaffirming instrument that can be used as both a screening tool and diagnostic aid in real-world clinical settings.
The objective of this project is to evaluate and optimize the measure using the DSM-5-TR criteria, a gender-balanced, diverse national sample, and recruitment from outpatient clinics specializing in differential diagnosis. Guided by strong preliminary data, our central hypothesis is that the questionnaire will demonstrate robust psychometric properties and function equivalently across gender groups.
Building on preliminary work developed collaboratively with autistic and neurodivergent researchers, this study will assess item performance, internal consistency, factor structure, convergent validity, and diagnostic accuracy using both Classical Test Theory and Item Response Theory. We will also examine gender related differences and test measurement invariance across adults assigned female and male at birth. Recruitment from outpatient diagnostic clinics will enhance generalizability and allow evaluation of the measure’s utility in distinguishing ASD from other psychiatric conditions.
We expect the measure to show strong internal consistency, acceptable convergent validity, and adequate sensitivity and specificity. We also anticipate significant differences between ASD and non ASD groups, no significant gender differences, and no autism by gender interaction. The outcome will be a refined, validated questionnaire supported by rigorous psychometric evidence and ready for broader clinical and research use.
Ultimately, this project will advance the field by providing the first adult autism self-report measure developed by autistic individuals, aligned with DSM 5 TR, gender inclusive, neuroaffirming, and validated in real-world diagnostic settings. By improving the accuracy and equity of adult ASD identification, this work has the potential to reduce misdiagnosis, expand access to services, and meaningfully enhance the lives of autistic adults.

title: Emotion Regulation in Clinical and Non-Clinical Adolescents: An Exploratory Integration of Self-Report Profiles and Frontal Alpha Asymmetry
description:
This study is a post-hoc secondary analysis examining emotion regulation in adolescents aged 13 to 18 years across clinical and non-clinical groups. Data were not collected as part of a single unified study; the healthy control sample and the clinical samples were recruited and assessed in separate research projects, and the present analysis integrates these datasets for comparative purposes. Accordingly, all findings should be interpreted within the constraints of a post-hoc, cross-sectional design.
Adolescence represents a period of heightened emotional reactivity and concurrent maturation of prefrontal regulatory circuitry, making it a developmentally sensitive window in which individual differences in emotion regulation carry demonstrable consequences for later psychopathology trajectories. Despite a growing literature linking disruptions in both behavioural emotion regulation and neural indices of frontal activity to internalising disorders in young people, most studies examine these levels in isolation and within non-clinical samples. The present study addresses this gap by integrating self-report measures of emotion regulation strategy use and regulation difficulties with resting-state frontal alpha asymmetry (FAA) as a neurophysiological index, assessed in diagnostically confirmed clinical groups alongside a healthy comparison group.
Three groups are included: a healthy control group (HC), a group meeting diagnostic criteria for Major Depressive Disorder (MDD), and a group meeting criteria for an Anxiety Disorder (ANX). Clinical diagnoses were confirmed via the Mini-DIPS structured clinical interview. Healthy control eligibility and dimensional symptom severity across all participants were assessed using the DISYPS-III (Döpfner & Görtz-Dorten, 2017). The final analytic sample comprises 103 participants (HC: n = 25, MDD: n = 53, ANX: n = 25).
The primary self-report instrument is the FEEL-KJ (Grob & Smolenski, 2005), which assesses adaptive and maladaptive emotion regulation strategies across anger, sadness, and fear contexts. Secondary self-report measures are the Emotion Regulation Questionnaire (ERQ; Abler & Kessler, 2009), the Difficulties in Emotion Regulation Scale (DERS), and the Affective Style Questionnaire for Youth (ASQ-Y; Graser et al., 2019). Resting-state EEG was recorded to derive FAA as a neurophysiological complement to the self-report battery.
One hypothesis is designated confirmatory. It predicts disorder-congruent emotion-context specificity on the FEEL-KJ, tested via a Group x Emotion Context interaction in a linear mixed model, with a pre-specified crossover contrast serving as the directional confirmation endpoint. All remaining hypotheses are exploratory, addressing FAA group differences, associations between FAA and self-reported regulation difficulties, dimensional severity associations, diagnostic classification accuracy, and cross-instrument convergence across the self-report battery. Given the post-hoc nature of the study and the separate origins of the datasets, no findings from the exploratory analyses are intended to be interpreted as confirmatory evidence.
The study aims to contribute to a sparse literature on cross-level emotion regulation research in diagnostically confirmed adolescent samples, to evaluate whether FAA meaningfully differentiates clinical from non-clinical adolescents, and to examine whether disorder-specific patterning in emotion regulation emerges or whether clinical-versus-control differences are broader and less diagnostically differentiated than theoretical models predict.

title: Epidemiology of Orofacial Clefts in East Africa: a Systematic Review
description:
This research project is a systematic review designed to provide an epidemiological mapping of Orofacial Clefts (OFCs) across eleven East African nations: Uganda, Rwanda, Burundi, Tanzania, Kenya, South Sudan, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Ethiopia, Eritrea, Djibouti, and Somalia. Its primary purpose is to address the critical "data gap" regarding the prevalence and etiology of cleft lip and palate in East Africa. While surgical interventions have increased across the region, public health policy remains hampered by fragmented data. Currently, estimates of OFC prevalence vary wildly due to inconsistent reporting methods, ranging from community-based surveillance to localized hospital registries.

This project seeks to synthesize literature published between 2011 and 2025 to achieve three core objectives:
1. To determine the pooled prevalence of OFCs, distinguishing between birth incidence and the "surgical backlog" of untreated cases.
2. To evaluate how these anomalies are distributed by sex, phenotype (isolated vs. syndromic), and laterality.
3. To investigate the correlation between OFCs and regional specificities, such as consanguinity, nutritional deficiencies (folic acid), and environmental exposures like biomass fuel smoke.

To ensure the highest level of academic rigor, the project will utilize a multifaceted search strategy across six major databases (PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Google Scholar, AJOL, and WHO Global Index Medicus). The study will employ a unique "Tiered Evidence Approach," stratifying data into population-based, hospital-based, and service-based categories. This methodology will allow the research to account for selection bias and provide a more nuanced understanding of the regional burden. Data synthesis will be performed using STATA (v17.0), utilizing a random-effects model to manage the anticipated heterogeneity of the East African healthcare landscape.

The findings of this systematic review are expected to serve as a foundational evidence base for several key stakeholders:
1. Public Health Policy: By identifying high-risk regions and specific environmental triggers, the study will provide a roadmap for primary prevention strategies and maternal-fetal health interventions.
2. Healthcare Planning: Accurate prevalence data will assist Ministries of Health and NGOs in optimizing resource allocation for surgical missions and multidisciplinary cleft care centers.
3. Clinical Counseling: Identifying the prevalence of associated malformations will improve the diagnostic accuracy and prenatal counseling provided to families.
4. Scientific Contribution: This study will be registered with Open Science Frame, contributing a standardized, peer-reviewed dataset to the global body of epidemiological research, specifically highlighting the unique challenges faced by the East African population.

title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN THE DIAGNOSIS AND TREATMENT OF CHILDHOOD HANDWRITING DISORDERS: A SCOPING REVIEW
description:
This protocol outlines a scoping review on the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in the diagnosis and treatment of childhood handwriting disorders, such as dysgraphia and difficulties with spelling, grammar, punctuation, or text composition. Handwriting is a complex skill that develops progressively from early childhood and may reflect underlying neurodevelopmental disorders when impaired. Despite advances in traditional interventions, diagnostic and therapeutic challenges persist—particularly in socioeconomically disadvantaged settings.
 In this context, AI emerges as a promising tool to enhance diagnostic accuracy and personalize interventions. Previous studies have successfully used algorithms to detect graphic behavior patterns and adapt to individual needs through intelligent applications. However, AI use in the field of childhood handwriting remains limited, with many studies still in the experimental phase.
 The review will follow the methodological framework proposed by Arksey and O’Malley, complemented by the Joanna Briggs Institute and PRISMA-ScR guidelines. Relevant databases such as PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar will be searched, including literature without language or date restrictions. Data will be analyzed using narrative synthesis and thematic qualitative analysis.
 The ultimate aim is to synthesize current knowledge, establish an open-access categorized database, and provide evidence-based recommendations to guide the safe and effective use of AI in addressing these disorders. In addition, expert consultation will be included to integrate clinical and technological perspectives.

title: Role of natriuretic peptides in the early identification of heart failure in patients with type 2 diabetes: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
description:
Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) affects approximately 1 in 9 adults and has reached a pandemic-level burden worldwide. In 2021, an estimated 529 million individuals of all ages were living with diabetes, 90% of whom had T2DM. This figure is projected to increase by 59.7% by 2050, rising from a prevalence of 6.1% in 2021 to 9.8% (1). T2DM is a leading global cause of disability and mortality. In 2021, diabetes-related complications accounted for 41.4 million years lived with disability (YLDs), 79.2 million disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) and over 6.7 million deaths (1,2). 
T2DM is also a primary risk factor for incident heart failure (HF), and all patients with T2DM are now considered at high risk of developing HF (3). In 2021, HF affected more then 55.5 million people globally -more than the double the prevalence in 1990- and its incidence continues to rise, particularly in low- and middle-income regions (4). HF is often secondary to other chronic conditions and is associated with significant morbidity, including fatigue and functional limitations. It accounted for over 5.3 million YLDs globally; with an estimated all-cause mortality rate of 20% at one-year and 50% at five-years following the diagnosis (5). 
Among individuals with T2DM, HF is the most common fatal cardiovascular complication (6). Having T2DM confers a 2- to 5-fold higher risk of developing HF, and approximately 22% of T2DM patients are living with HF (6,7). The prevalence of both conditions is increasing globally, underscoring the need for early screening and timely intervention to reduce their combined burden (8). The coexistence of HF and T2DM lead to an amplified clinical and economic burden (7), characterized by more frequent hospitalizations, poorer quality of life, and higher mortality; more than twice the rate observed in patients with HF without T2DM (9). 
Despite this shared burden, HF often remains underdiagnosed in individuals with T2DM, particularly in its early or asymptomatic stages (10). Early detection is critical, as T2DM accelerates cardiac remodeling and dysfunction, even before clinical signs emerge. Delayed diagnosis typically results in patients presenting with advanced HF, which is associated with poorer outcomes, increased hospitalizations, lower quality of life, and higher mortality (11). This also imposes a greater economic burden on healthcare systems due to the need for more intensive therapies and prolonged care (12). As such, a proactive approach – incorporating routine screening and cardiovascular risk stratification in patients with T2DM, essential to reduce adverse outcomes. 
Natriuretic peptides (NP) are cardiac-derived hormones essential for maintaining cardiovascular homeostasis. B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) and N-terminal pro-BNP (NT-proBNP) are key biomarkers for evaluating cardiac function. Importantly, NP levels can become abnormal before the onset of HF symptoms or the appearance of significant echocardiographic changes (13,14). Their inclusion in cardiovascular risk stratification may therefore facilitate earlier detection and treatment of HF in patients with T2DM. 
The American Diabetes Association (ADA) now recommends annual measurement of BNP or NT-proBNP in adults with diabetes to enable early intervention and prevent progression to symptomatic (stage C) HF (15). Elevated levels (BNP ≥50 pg/mL, NT-proBNP ≥125 pg/mL) are associated with increased risk of HF, hospitalization, and mortality (15). A comprehensive meta-analysis evaluating prognostic markers for cardiovascular outcomes in T2DM patients, identified NT-proBNP as the strongest predictor (16). Elevated NP can reflect underlying cardiac stress in patients with T2DM and should prompt further cardiovascular evaluation (17). 
Clinical trials such as PONTIAC and STOP-HF have demonstrated the prognostic utility of NPs and support their role in guiding early pharmacological interventions aimed at reducing HF progression (18,19). However, despite this growing body of evidence and guideline recommendation, NP-based screening remains uncommon in routine care for patients with T2DM (20). 
While progress has been made, important evidence gaps and challenges remain regarding the optimal implementation of NP based screening strategies. Notably, there is no consensus on optimal cut-off values for NP levels in the context of screening asymptomatic HF in T2DM, and threshold vary across studies. This lack of standardization introduces heterogeneity and complicated the interpretation of diagnostic accuracy across populations. 
Two recent systematic reviews have explored related topics. Ahmad et al. evaluated a wide variety of biomarkers and risk models for predicting cardiovascular outcomes in individuals with T2DM. They concluded that NT-proBNP is the strongest prognostic marker in this population, reinforcing its potential value for early risk stratification. However, this review did not assess the diagnostic performance of NP testing for early HF detection (16). In contrast, Goyder et al. conducted a systematic review focused on the diagnostic accuracy of NPs in detecting asymptomatic HF. Their results showed that NT-proBNP-based screening had better diagnostic performance than BNP (sensitivity 87%, specificity 85% vs. sensitivity 75%, specificity 78%), but they noted significant heterogeneity due to the lack of agreement on optimal cut-off values (21). 
To our knowledge, no previous study has comprehensively evaluated the diagnostic performance of natriuretic peptides as a screening tool for early heart failure specifically in adults with T2DM. This systematic review and meta-analysis aim to address this gap by synthesizing the available evidence on NP-based screening in this high-risk population. Our objective is to determine whether NP testing can facilitate earlier detection and prompt intervention, ultimately reducing HF-related morbidity and mortality in individuals with T2DM.

title: Diagnostic Performance of Artificial Intelligence Models Using Complete Blood Count Parameters for Anemia Diagnosis and Classification: A Systematic Review and Diagnostic Accuracy Meta-Analysis
description:
Background

Anemia affects over 1.6 billion people globally, with disproportionate burden in low- and middle-income countries where advanced diagnostic tests are unavailable. Differential diagnosis between iron deficiency anemia, thalassemia, and other hemoglobinopathies remains challenging, particularly in resource-limited settings. Artificial intelligence models using routine complete blood count parameters have emerged as promising, cost-effective diagnostic tools. However, their overall diagnostic accuracy, generalizability, and clinical applicability remain uncertain.

Objectives

Primary Objective: To evaluate the pooled diagnostic accuracy (AUC, sensitivity, specificity, and diagnostic odds ratio) of artificial intelligence and machine learning models using complete blood count parameters for anemia diagnosis and classification.

Secondary Objectives:

1. To synthesize feature importance from explainable AI studies (SHAP, LIME) to identify the most consistently influential CBC parameters
2. To compare AI model performance against traditional discriminant indices (Mentzer, RDWI, CRUISE, and others)
3. To evaluate the added value of CBC-derived hematological indices to AI performance via meta-regression
4. To identify the minimum CBC parameters required for high accuracy and propose an evidence-based minimal panel
5. To explore heterogeneity sources through subgroup analyses and meta-regression

Methods

Study Design: Systematic review and diagnostic accuracy meta-analysis

Protocol Registration: PROSPERO CRD420261451245

Search Strategy: Systematic search of MEDLINE (PubMed), Embase, Scopus, Cochrane CENTRAL, IEEE Xplore, and Web of Science from inception to July 14, 2026, supplemented by Google Scholar and citation tracking.

Eligibility Criteria:

· Population: Human participants of any age with any type of anemia
· Intervention: AI/ML models using CBC parameters for anemia diagnosis or classification
· Comparator: Clinical reference standard (serum ferritin, hemoglobin electrophoresis, HPLC, genetic testing, bone marrow examination, or clinical diagnosis by hematologist)
· Outcomes: Sensitivity, specificity, AUC, diagnostic odds ratio
· Study Design: Cross-sectional, retrospective cohort, prospective cohort, case-control, and diagnostic accuracy studies

Data Extraction: Two reviewers independently extracted data using a standardized, piloted form.

Risk of Bias Assessment: PROBAST-AI and QUADAS-2 tools.

Data Synthesis: Bivariate random-effects meta-analysis using the Reitsma approach and HSROC model. Subgroup analyses, meta-regression, and sensitivity analyses were performed. Feature importance was synthesized from XAI studies.

title: Mapping Global Evidence on HPV and Cervical Cancer Screening Methods, Limitations, and Emerging Point-of-Care Technologies: A Scoping Review Protocol
description:
Mapping Global Evidence on HPV and Cervical Cancer Screening Methods, Limitations, and Emerging Point-of-Care Technologies: A Scoping Review Protocol
