ABSTRACT
Introduction: Human Papilloma Virus (HPV) is a sexually transmitted agent. HPV is the causative agent of Cervical Cancer (CC) and 5.2% of all cancers globally. Despite the presence of several CC screening tests, there is still limited knowledge on which cost-effective commercial CC screening tests including technologies under Research and Development (R&D) that are currently available for use within Low- and Middle-Income Countries (LMICs). Here, we outline a protocol for a scoping review, aiming at mapping literature on the screening methods for HPV and CC, their limitations and the point of care (POC) tests under R&D.
Methods: We will undertake a scoping review of literature on the prevailing HPV and CC screening methods including those under R&D to identify screening gaps. We will search MEDILINE, Web of Science, EMBASE, CINAHL (EBSCO), Google scholar to obtain evidence on the HPV and CC screening methods. We will consider studies published between January 2016 and January 2026. The scoping review will be developed according to Arksey and O’Malley and Levac et al and guided by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR). Equally searched will be grey literature (dissertations/theses, conference proceedings, websites of global bodies like the WHO, and applicable government reports) publishing evidence on HPV and CC screening among women. 
Ethics and dissemination
No ethical approval is required since no human participants or animals will be part of this study. The results of this Scoping review will be disseminated electronically in peer-reviewed journals, in-print and via conference presentations. 

Open Science Framework Registration number:

Strengths and Limitations of this study
• This review will consider females of 25 years and above and may miss data about screening in those less than 25 years of age
• This review will consider articles published in English only and may miss information from articles published in other languages
• The pipeline for data extraction was generated by highly experienced librarians and therefore robust enough to capture sufficient information about HPV and CC screening
• Four leading public health databases (EMBASE, Ovid MEDLINE, WEB OF SCIENCE CINAHL) with extensive information about HPV and CC will be searched to provide sufficient information
• This study is anticipated to yield data about existing gaps in HPV and CC screening globally
Keywords: Human Papilloma Virus; Cervical Cancer; Screening; Research and Development; Limitations

Introduction 
Human Papillomavirus and Cervical Cancer
Human Papillomavirus, a member of the Papillomaviridae family1 is a very diverse virus with over 200 genotypes2. The Alpha-papilloma genera of Firstpapillomavirinea are the most medically important as they cause anogenital, oral mucosa, and head and neck carcinomas. Alpha-papilloma viruses cause 40% of oral cancers3. 
HPV infection is the most common sexually transmitted infection (STI) worldwide, and most sexually active persons acquire it at some point in their lifetime4,5. Women get infected by men who carry HPV (HPV infection reservoirs), who are a critical source of hrHPV that causes CC6,7. Also, many anogenital as well as upper aero-digestive tract carcinomas, plus their precancerous lesions in men, are currently known to stem from HPV infection that is sexually acquired8,9. Infection with HPV does not always translate into cancer; however, a small percentage (10%) of persistent infections progress to cancer. Following a silent incubation period ranging from 10–20 years, hrHPV transforms the squamous epithelial or glandular cells, leading to invasive CC10,11,12. Oncoprotein E6 targets p53 for breakdown through the ubiquitin pathway, hence averting apoptosis13,14 and allowing continuous replication. On the other hand, E7 oncoprotein breakdown of pRb results in spontaneous entry into the cell cycle S phase15 which subsequently stimulates cell proliferation. The incidence of viral integration increases with the severity of the precancerous lesions of the cervix and in the cervical epithelium, the resulting premalignant alterations or squamous cell dysplasia are together termed cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN). The exfoliated epithelial cells released at the end of the life cycle contain several biomarkers (viral particles, DNA, mRNA, and viral proteins) detectable in cervico-vaginal swabs or urine. The cytopathic effects of the virus on the epithelial cells are also identifiable through cytological methods. 
Based on the life cycle and carcinogenesis, a number of viral targets have been identified for diagnostic use. These include the genetic regions of L1, E6/E7 DNA, E6/E7 mRNA, viral proteins such as the E6/E7 oncoproteins as well as the antibodies to viral proteins. These HPV diagnostic targets are currently detected through use of both conventional and contemporary methods with several newer tests under R&D. Conventional tests are the traditional or ordinary tests that have existed for a long time and bear long sample to result times (>1hour), require complex laboratory infrastructure as well as highly trained personnel. Examples include; Cobas HPV (Roche Molecular Systems, Inc.), Abbott RealTime High Risk HPV (Abbott GmbH) and Aptima HPV test (Hologic). Conversely, contemporary or modern tests are those newly developed tests that have short sample to result times, little or no need for a complex laboratory and highly trained laboratory staff and are mostly deployable as POC tests. Examples include; Xpert HPV, careHPV Test, OncoE6™ Cervical assay among others. 

Global Burden of Cervical Cancer
According to the WHO, the majority (94%) of global CC-related mortality occurred in LMICs in 202216. A significant variation in national rates of new cases and deaths exists among countries17, possibly explainable by the differing prevalence of hrHPV strains, and disproportionate accessibility to countrywide screening programs18,19. For instance, the top five countries with the highest global age-standardized mortality rate per 100,000 women (ASMR) are all African countries: Eswatini (ASMR 64.3), Malawi (ASMR 54.1), Zambia (ASMR 49.4), Zimbabwe (ASMR 47.9), and Lesotho (ASMR 42.3). On the other side, the five countries with the least global age-standardized rates for mortality per 100,000 women in descending order were: Switzerland (ASMR 1.1), Syrian Arab Republic (ASMR 1.3), Saudi Arabia (ASMR 1.3), Finland (ASMR 1.3), Malta (ASMR 1.4), and Australia (ASMR 1.4)20. A 10-fold difference in the new CC cases and death rates exists, with sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) and Melanesia registering the highest regional rates21. This high burden, especially in SSA, could partially be attributed to the synergistic epidemic comprising HPV and Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) since the risk of developing CC is 6-times greater in HIV positive than in the HIV negative women22. As a result, out of all the cancers, CC accounts for close to 2.4 million years of life lost among females in the age range of 15 and 59. Cervical cancer is also blamed for 22% of the years of life lost in low-income countries (LICs), 10% in middle-income countries (MICs), and 5% in HICs23. As per the WHO predictions, CC attributable deaths will rise to 443,000 annually worldwide by 203024 with >98% taking place in LMICs and the greatest proportion in SSA25. Despite the WHO projections, CC elimination remains difficult because of poor health and social systems, absent basic screening tools besides inadequate CC awareness and education in SSA countries26. 
Several reviews on HPV/CC screening methods have already been performed by different researchers. For instance, a systematic review and meta-analysis done by Magdi et al 202127 only covered diagnostic accuracy of HPV tests for the screening of CC in low-resource settings. Then Karisani et al 202428 conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to evaluate the accuracy of screening CC tests as alternative standalone methods. In 2023, Kundrod and the team29 performed a review on CC screening in general. In 2025, Amit et al30 carried out a systematic review and meta-analysis to evaluate different CC screening methods for women living with HIV while excluding those without HIV. In 2025, Ruchika Gupta et al31 conducted an updated and comprehensive summary of the sensitivity and specificity of three HPV POC tests (careHPV™, oncoE6™ cervical test, Xpert® HPV) to guide resource-constrained countries for their implementation in CC screening. However, the rest of the POC tests were not included and significant inter-study heterogeneity that could be attributed to the HPV prevalence in the populations included in these studies was noted. They also reported the publication bias among the studies on careHPV™ and oncoE6® cervical test and those on physician-collected samples for Xpert® HPV assay. Jennifer Pillay et al32 in 2021 undertook a systematic review to inform an update to recommendations by the Canadian Task Force on Preventive Health Care which was only limited to Canada. As indicated, several studies have been conducted to identify gaps in HPV and CC screening. However, no existing review has simultaneously: compared i) all HPV/CC screening methods, ii) synthesised limitations iii) mapped emerging POC technologies globally.
There is a need to map existing evidence on the HPV and CC screening methods, their limitations and the POC tests for HPV that are still under R&D by synthesising both quantitative and qualitative data as well as studies that employ a mixed-methods approach. Therefore, the purpose of this scoping review is to map the literature evidence on the HPV and CC screening methods, their limitations and the POC tests for HPV that are under R&D globally by synthesising data from quantitative and qualitative studies. It is anticipated that findings from this study will enable the researchers to identify research gaps and guide future research towards improved diagnostics for women in CC screening programmes. The results of this study will also guide policymakers in designing CC screening programmes based on HPV and CC diagnostics that are more accessible to end-users to increase the uptake of CC screening services globally. 
A preliminary search of PROSPERO, MEDLINE, the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews and the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) Database of Systematic Reviews and Implementation Reports was conducted. No current or in progress scoping reviews or systematic reviews on the topic were identified that assessed the HPV and CC screening methods, their limitations and the POC tests for HPV that are still under R&D. The objective of this scoping review is to assess the extent of the literature on the HPV and CC screening methods, their limitations and the POC tests for HPV that are still under R&D. We will conduct a scoping review to identify gaps in HPV and CC screening. Results from an updated review will inform implementation strategies for improving the accessibility of diagnostics that can be used in the primary care setting to increase rates for both HPV and CC screening and potentially reduce disparities. 

METHODS AND ANALYSIS
The scoping review will be developed according to Arksey and O’Malley33 and Levac et al34 and guided by the PRISMA-ScR checklist35 (supplementary file 1). Following the search, all identified citations will be collated and uploaded into the EndNote 21 Reference Management Software36 and deduplicated. The full text of selected citations will be assessed in detail against the inclusion criteria by two independent reviewers. Reasons for exclusion of sources of evidence at full text that will not meet the inclusion criteria will be recorded. Any disagreements that arise between the reviewers at each stage of the selection process will be resolved through discussion, or with an additional reviewer. The results of the search and the study inclusion process will be presented in a PRISMA flow diagram (figure 1).
 
Figure1: PRISMA flow diagram of the study selection procedure. PRISMA is denoted as Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta Analysis

Review objectives and Questions

Main objective
The main objective of this review will be to map the available evidence on screening methods for human papillomavirus and cervical cancer, including their limitations and emerging point-of-care technologies under research and development. 

Specific objectives 
1. To describe the characteristics of existing HPV and cervical cancer screening methods. 
2. To identify reported limitations of current screening approaches. 
3. To summarize, emerging point-of-care HPV screening technologies under development.

Review questions
1. What are the characteristics of the current HPV and Cervical cancer screening methods?
2. What are the reported limitations of the current HPV and Cervical cancer screening methods?
3. What are the emerging point of care HPV screening technologies under Research and Development?


Table 1: PCC for assessing research question eligibility
Population Women ≥ 25 years
Concept HPV and Cervical cancer screening methods, limitations, and POC Technologies

Context
 Global (with emphasis on LMIC if relevant)

Types of sources
This scoping review will consider both experimental and quasi-experimental study designs including randomized controlled trials, non-randomized controlled trials, before and after studies and interrupted time-series studies. In addition, analytical observational studies including prospective and retrospective cohort studies, case-control studies and analytical cross-sectional studies will be considered for inclusion. This review will also consider descriptive observational study designs including case series, individual case reports and descriptive cross-sectional studies for inclusion. Qualitative studies will also be considered that focus on qualitative data including, but not limited to, designs such as phenomenology, grounded theory, ethnography, qualitative description, action research and feminist research. In addition, systematic reviews that meet the inclusion criteria will also be considered, depending on the research question. Text and opinion papers will be considered for inclusion in this scoping review.

Search strategy for relevant studies
The search strategy will aim at locating both published and unpublished studies. A three-step search strategy will be utilized in this review. First an initial limited search of MEDLINE (PubMed) and Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature (CINAHL) (EBSCO) will be undertaken to identify articles on the topic. The keywords contained in the titles and abstracts of relevant articles, and their synonyms will be used to develop a full search strategy for review (Appendix I for a detailed search strategy). The search strategy will be adapted for each included database and information source. The reference list of all included sources of evidence will be screened for additional studies. The search string will include the following terms: HPV, Cervical cancer and screening and their synonyms. Studies published in English language as appropriate will be included. While performing the search, the Boolean terms AND/OR will be employed to separate the key words. Studies published between January 2016 and 11th March 2026 will be included to capture recent advancements in HPV screening technologies. All information sources (eg, electronic databases, conference proceedings, websites, search engines or other online sources, contact with study authors) will be included. Other sources of information such as grey literature will also be searched for additional studies.


Selection of eligible studies 

Data available for this study will be selected based on the following criteria

Inclusion criteria
The following will be included; studies published on HPV and CC screening methods in women 25 years and older, studies on POC technologies under development, articles published on limitations of HPV and CC screening, articles published between 2016-2026, and studies published in English. 


Exclusion criteria
The following will be excluded from the review; articles published on HPV and CC screening in women under 25 years, articles published on CC diagnosis in women, articles published before 2016, non-English literature, articles that cannot be digitally accessed, articles that need to be peer-reviewed, including preprints and abstracts
Data extraction
Data will be extracted from included studies by independent reviewers using a data extraction tool developed by the reviewers. The data extracted will include specific details about the participants, concept, context, study methods and key findings relevant to the review question/s. A draft extraction form (Appendix II) will be employed. Any disagreements that arise between the reviewers will be resolved through discussion, or with an additional reviewer. Where required, authors of inaccessible papers will be contacted for additional data. 

Charting the data
A data charting form (appendix II) will be developed for capturing data from each selected study using Microsoft. Prior to the start of the review, two reviewers (FJ and MT) will pilot the data charting form and their experiences with the form will guide any modifications from time to time within the review period. As a pilot, FJ and MT will test the data charting tool with 10 included studies. Key variable for extraction will include; study population, country, sample size, age range, study design, intervention, narrative findings and quantitative findings. Following the pilot phase, FJ will capture all the data which will then be reviewed by MT to ensure all the data are fully and correctly captured.

Data analysis and presentation 
The STATA V.17(StataCorp LLC Texas USA) statistical software will be employed for the extraction of themes from the selected studies. The attributes of eligible studies will be shown inform of a descriptive numeral summary. Findings consistent with the objectives of the review will be displayed in form of tables and figures. Descriptive summary will be presented inform of counts, frequencies, percentages, tables and charts. The screening methods (e.g., cytology, HPV DNA, VIA, POC) will be categorized according to type. We will undertake the thematic analysis for limitations, barriers and emerging technologies. Subgroup summaries will be made for LMIC verses HIC and HIV verses non-HIV populations. Through a narrative account of our results, we will present the key concepts from the selected articles consistent with our research questions. The gaps identified in this review consistent with the current HPV and CC screening will be highlighted to guide future research into diagnostics for HPV and CC especially in resource constrained settings.

Quality Appraisal
To determine the quality of the eligible studies, selected JBI quality appraisal tools37 will be employed. The JBI appraisal method is advantageous in that it is applicable to a variety of studies such as Cross-sectional studies, Cohort studies, Prevalence studies, Systematic Reviews and Case control studies among others. The number of studies found to be showing poor quality will be harmonized by FJ and MT. Eligible studies will be separately evaluated by the two reviewers and any discrepancies will be harmonized via discussions. Articles with poor quality will be considered for mapping evidence from the analysis.

Ethics and dissemination
Ethical approval is not required as this uses publicly available data. The results of this Scoping review will be disseminated electronically in peer-reviewed journals, in-print, policy briefs and through local or international conference presentations.

Patient and public involvement
This scoping review protocol has not involved any patients and the public in the design, conduct, reporting and dissemination plans of this research.

title: Thoracoscopy versus closed pleural biopsy with Cope needle in undiagnosed exudative pleural effusions: systematic review
description: This systematic review aims to compare thoracoscopy with closed pleural biopsy using a Cope needle in adults with undiagnosed exudative pleural effusions following thoracentesis and initial pleural fluid analysis. Pleural effusion is a common clinical condition associated with diverse pulmonary and systemic diseases, and accurate etiological diagnosis is essential for appropriate management and prognosis. When initial investigations are inconclusive, pleural biopsy becomes a critical diagnostic step. Closed pleural biopsy with a Cope needle remains widely used, particularly in resource-limited settings, due to its low cost and accessibility, although its diagnostic yield is variable. In contrast, medical thoracoscopy (pleuroscopy) enables direct visualization and targeted biopsies, offering higher diagnostic accuracy, especially for malignant pleural disease, albeit with greater infrastructure requirements. This review will systematically evaluate and synthesize available evidence on the overall diagnostic yield and safety profile of these procedures. Secondary outcomes will include diagnostic yield by etiology (malignancy and tuberculosis), complication rates, need for additional diagnostic procedures, and length of hospital stay. The study will follow PRISMA 2020 guidelines, assess methodological quality using validated tools, and evaluate the certainty of evidence using the GRADE approach. By providing a comprehensive and methodologically rigorous comparison, this review aims to inform clinical decision-making and optimize diagnostic strategies, particularly in diverse healthcare settings, including low- and middle-income countries.

title: Introduction
description:
Sepsis is defined as life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection (1). Recent global estimates suggest approximately 166 million cases and 21.4 million deaths each year, making sepsis a major contributor to morbidity and mortality worldwide (2). Early recognition is essential for improving outcomes yet remains clinically challenging. 

The current Sepsis-3 definition uses the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score to identify organ dysfunction, with qSOFA as a simplified bedside tool. However, qSOFA’s sensitivity and specificity vary widely across studies (3). Biomarkers such as procalcitonin (PCT) and C-reactive protein (CRP) are commonly used but have limited diagnostic accuracy with AUROC reported between (4). 

Pancreatic stone protein (PSP), also known as regenerating islet-derived protein 3β (REG3B), is a secreted protein involved in innate immune responses, epithelial barrier integrity, and cellular stress signaling. PSP production is rapidly upregulated in pancreatic acinar and intestinal epithelial cells in response to microbial products and early inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6 and IL-22. These upstream triggers are reported to occur earlier in the host response than the hepatic pathways that drive CRP or the hormonal pathways that drive PCT, leading to PSP levels rising sooner in the course of infection. This early release has motivated interest in PSP as a diagnostic biomarker for identifying sepsis at the time of clinical presentation (5). However, existing studies report inconsistent findings, with substantial heterogeneity in patient populations, timing of PSP measurement, sepsis definitions, and assay methodologies. 

Pancreatic stone protein (PSP) is the secreted protein product of the REG1A gene, which is primarily expressed in pancreatic acinar cells, pancreatic ductal epithelium, and intestinal epithelial cells (6). Although PSP has gained attention for its potential role in early sepsis identification, its biological functions extend beyond infection. Under physiological conditions, PSP contributes to maintenance of gut mucosal integrity, supports epithelial repair following tissue injury, and participates in innate immune defense by limiting bacterial adhesion and translocation (6). PSP expression also increases in response to pancreatitis, trauma, and other forms of cellular stress, reflecting its role as a general stress-response and regeneration-associated protein. These broader functions highlight that PSP is not solely a sepsis biomarker, but part of an epithelial defense and repair network shaped by inflammation, microbial interactions, and tissue injury (6).

title: Protocol for a Scoping Review on the Diagnostic Performance of the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) in Individuals With or At Risk of Alcohol-Related Brain Damage (ARBD)
description:
This scoping review aims to map the existing literature on the use and reported diagnostic performance of the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) in adults with or at risk of Alcohol-Related Brain Damage (ARBD). ARBD refers to a spectrum of cognitive impairments resulting from chronic alcohol misuse and is frequently underdiagnosed, especially in its early stages. The MoCA is a widely used cognitive screening tool across clinical and research settings; however, its specific application, strengths, limitations, and reported diagnostic accuracy (including sensitivity and specificity) within ARBD populations remain unclear. The primary objective of this review is to systematically identify and examine published and grey literature that discusses the MoCA’s use in this population, its diagnostic performance, and contextual factors that may influence test results, such as cognitive domains assessed, test versions, and patient characteristics.
A comprehensive literature search will be conducted across multiple bibliographic databases (PsycINFO, PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science) and grey literature sources (Google Scholar, OpenGrey, ProQuest Dissertations). Literature published in English from 2005 to 2025 will be included, reflecting the timeline since the MoCA's development. Title and abstract screening, followed by full-text review, will be carried out in Covidence by two independent reviewers using predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria. Data will be charted in Excel or Google Sheets using a structured extraction form piloted on a subset of included studies. Extracted information will include study design, sample characteristics, MoCA versions, domains tested, comparator tools, diagnostic outcomes, and key conclusions.
Findings will be synthesized narratively and presented in summary tables, a PRISMA flow diagram, and, if appropriate, a conceptual map. This review is expected to provide a comprehensive overview of how the MoCA has been applied in populations affected by alcohol misuse, where evidence is concentrated or lacking, and what methodological or contextual factors shape its reported effectiveness. By consolidating this information, the review will inform future research, clinical screening practices, and the development of early intervention strategies for cognitive impairment related to alcohol use.

title: Spectrum of Movement Disorders Presenting to the Emergency Department: A Systematic Review
description:
Title: Spectrum of Movement Disorders Presenting to the Emergency Department:
 A Systematic Review
 
 Purpose: Synthesize global evidence on type, frequency, etiology, and clinical
 outcomes of movement disorders presenting to emergency departments (ED). No
 prior systematic review exists on this topic.

 Background: Single-center studies (Dallocchio 2018, Italy; Bhoyar 2022, India;
 Yoon 2008, Korea) report movement disorder ED frequency of 0.07–0.09% of
 visits, with wide variation in dominant phenotype by geography and referral
 pattern. Existing narrative reviews (Gandhi 2020) do not provide pooled
 estimates. Gap impedes ED preparedness, training, and resource planning —
 especially in low/middle-income settings.

 Methods: Systematic review following PRISMA 2020. Databases: PubMed, CENTRAL,
 Embase, Semantic Scholar. Population: adults ≥18y presenting to ED with any
 movement disorder. Study types: observational studies (cross-sectional,
 cohort, case series ≥5 patients). No date restriction; English only. Dual
 independent screening and extraction (Shardul Bhattarai + Sharthak Bhattarai).
 Narrative synthesis by disorder category; pooled prevalence meta-analysis if
 ≥3 studies report same outcome.

 Expected outcomes:
 - Comprehensive map of movement disorder spectrum in ED globally
 - Pooled prevalence estimates by disorder type where data permit
 - Summary of diagnostic accuracy and time-to-diagnosis data
 - ED disposition and short-term outcomes by phenotype
 - Identification of evidence gaps to guide future prospective studies

title: Establishing an updated consensus across experts within research and practice on the conceptual definition of Making Every Contact Count (MECC) across the UK and Ireland: A Delphi Study
description:
The current pre-registration contains a protocol for a Delphi study to explore the consensus conceptual definition of Making Every Contact Count, and if considered appropriate, an operational definition too.

Making Every Contact Count (MECC) is broadly defined as an opportunistic approach to health promotion and prevention by making use of the thousands of conversations service providers have with service users each day. NICE guidelines on public health interventions require that they focus on ‘clearly circumscribed and defined actions’ relating to health promotion or prevention. However, the definition of MECC is vague and lacking clarity, indicated by the variation in how it has been interpreted and implemented by both researchers and in practice. For example, since the MECC consensus statement was released in 2016, MECC has specified into topic areas such as mental health, been applied to group activities, become divided into sub-types (e.g Healthy Conversation Skills), and expanded into various sectors including the public and third sectors. Additionally, the official definition of MECC does not specify the behaviour change techniques utilised within the brief health conversation, providing little guidance or consistency in how it is applied. Overall, the application of MECC has diverged and developed considerably since the release of the consensus statement in 2016, indicating a need to revise the current definition and increase its sensitivity and specificity. 
There are various consensus group methods, however the Delphi methodology is able to coordinate a large group of experts and retain their anonymity, vastly reducing any effects of power dynamics. This attribute is especially important given that key experts involved in MECC include both researchers and coordinators of public health and healthcare. Therefore, the current study will utilise a Delphi methodology, namely an online survey of at least three rounds, to attain a detailed consensus definition of MECC that clearly specifies what it does and does not describe. The resulting consensus definition for MECC will provide strong utility for both research and practice, to ensure all stakeholders are communicating around the same concept when they use the term MECC.

title: A scoping review on adenomyosis and artificial intelligence
description: This scoping review aims to explore the intersection of adenomyosis and artificial intelligence (AI) in medical research and practice. Adenomyosis is a gynecological condition characterized by the presence of endometrial tissue within the uterine muscle, often causing pain and heavy menstrual bleeding. Despite its prevalence, the diagnosis and management of adenomyosis remain challenging due to its complex presentation and the limitations of traditional imaging techniques. The integration of AI, including machine learning and deep learning algorithms, has the potential to enhance diagnostic accuracy, personalize treatment plans, and predict patient outcomes. This review will systematically map the existing literature to identify how AI is being utilized in the study of adenomyosis, highlight gaps in current research, and propose directions for future studies. By synthesizing available evidence, this review seeks to provide a comprehensive overview of the role of AI in advancing the understanding and management of adenomyosis.

title: Prescription Medications with ADHD Symptoms as a Potential Adverse Effect
description:
Source of Data. We analyzed Micromedex data (Truven Health Analytics) for the 200 most commonly prescribed medications in the United States based on the most recent ClinCalc DrugStats Database (2022 data released in 2024), which utilizes data from the annual Medical Expenditure Panel Survey (MEPS) conducted by the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ) (ClinCalc DrugStats Database, August 2024). We chose to focus on these medications for our initial analyses as they are the most likely to be encountered by primary care and specialty-care physicians and thus may have generalizable clinical impact. Micromedex is a suite of databases (e.g., DRUGDEX, Index Nominum, MARTINDALE, POISONDEX, TOMES, REPROTEXT, REPROTOX, TERIS, Shepard’s Catalog of Teratogenic Agents, DISEASEDEX, and Identidex) offering comprehensive drug, disease and toxicology oriented information for health care professionals and patients. Micromedex incorporates peer reviewed, evidence-based drug information including, but not limited to, data derived from the US Food and Drug Administration’s labeled adverse drug effects that serves as a frequently used industry standard. It has strong sensitivity and specificity (Barrons, 2004; Cheng et al., 2010). We extracted terms related to core ADHD symptoms and potential ADHD symptom mimics (defined below), listed in both quick and in-depth answers, under adverse effects, black box warnings, medication counseling, or patient handouts.

Defining ADHD Symptom Effects. An operationalized codebook defined words that indicated the presence of core ADHD symptoms. The codebook also included words or terms that indicated symptoms and conditions that potentially mimic ADHD symptoms that might lead a clinician to incorrectly suspect ADHD-like symptoms are present. Coding both core ADHD symptoms and potential mimics of ADHD symptoms allows us to place an upper and lower bound on the likely interpretations of clinicians. For core symptoms, there were two sources for the codebook’s exemplar word bank: (1) DSM-5-TR ADHD symptom terminology (e.g., forgetfulness, inattention, distractibility, hyperactivity, restlessness) and (2) terms extracted from 18 prescription drug labels of medications expected to have side effects or adverse reactions that could mimic ADHD symptoms (e.g., albuterol, atorvastatin, gabapentin). After 18 drug labels, full saturation of the word bank was reached. Trained bachelor’s level research coders were instructed to indicate the presence of individual core symptoms of ADHD detected in Micromedex data. Inter-rater reliability for core ADHD symptom coding will be calculated.
We also developed a codebook of symptoms (e.g. cognitive slowing, activation, anxiety) or conditions (e.g. hypothyroidism, hyperthyroidism, hypomania, insomnia) that could reasonably lead a clinician to suspect ADHD in the absence of additional history or workup, which might present with symptoms which could reasonably be misinterpreted as ADHD core symptomatology but are temporally and etiologically distinct from ADHD. This word bank was derived through review of the 18 prescription drug labels selected for creation of the initial core symptoms codebook and supplemented via expert consensus by an interdisciplinary team of physicians representing the fields of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry, Pediatrics, Pediatric Neurology and Internal Medicine-Pediatrics. For example, if a medication is associated with anxiety, the individual might appear inattentive or have difficulty concentrating. Similarly, if a medication is associated with activation, the individual might appear restless, hyperactive, or impatient. Coders were bachelor’s level, trained research assistants who were instructed to indicate the presence of individual mimic symptoms of ADHD detected in Micromedex data. In cases of uncertainty, examples were brought for review to the physician panel. Inter-rater reliability for mimic ADHD symptom coding will be calculated.
The coding process involved 4 coders assigned specific drug labels who coded both the ADHD core symptoms and the mimics for each assigned label. A weekly coding meeting was held in which coders could bring rare or difficult examples to the expert panel for feedback and discussion. When rare or difficult examples occurred, these were documented in a Redcap text box for review at the coding meeting. 

AI Coding. 
We also used AI to screen for core and mimic symptoms that may have been missed by the manual coding. To do so, we pulled the AI response from DeepSeek using the prompt adapted from the codebook with the goal to extract ADHD core symptoms and mimic symptoms along with direct quotes from the label – a similar process as a human coding. Results are organized in spreadsheets. After filtering out the pairs of symptoms that had been identified as completely identical between AI and human coder, a research assistant flags anything that AI picked up and human coders didn’t (or vice versa). A second-level review will be conducted by at least one practicing clinician (e.g., child and adolescent psychiatry fellow). If further review is required after the practicing clinician's review, consensus discussion will be held with the team to gather multidisciplinary perspectives. A panel of clinical experts will discuss flagged items and reach clinical consensus for additional mimic symptoms to be included. Codebook and AI prompt will be revised accordingly.

All findings will be summarized descriptively in order to comprehensively map and raise clinician awareness of medications that may commonly mimic ADHD symptoms. Implications for ADHD diagnosis, particularly in settings that may not have direct access to patient medical records or by providers who may be unfamiliar with non-psychiatric prescription medication effects, will be discussed.

title: Comparison of bedside lung ultrasonography versus chest radiography for diagnosis of respiratory distress syndrome in preterm neonates: A systematic review and Diagnostic test accuracy meta-analysis
description:
1. Anticipated or actual start date.
1 February 2026
2. Anticipated completion date.
 31 December 2026
3. Review question
What is the diagnostic accuracy of lung ultrasonography, as compared to chest radiography, for the diagnosis of respiratory distress syndrome in preterm neonates?
4. Searches
 a) The key databases for search will include the Cochrane Library (present version), MEDLINE via PubMed (1966 to present), Embase (1974 to present), and Web of Science (1900 to present). 
b) Also, the reference lists of the included studies will be explored for backward citation search.
c) No language restrictions will be applied while searching.
d) Studies reported only as abstracts will be eligible if sufficient information is available from the report or contact with the authors to fulfil the inclusion criteria. 
e) We will also search the cross-references in relevant narrative or systematic reviews for additional studies. 
6. Condition or domain being studied.
Respiratory distress syndrome(RDS)
Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome is a disease of the lung that primarily affects preterm neonates, secondary to surfactant deficiency. Surfactant is a lipid-protein substance produced by type II alveolar cells that reduces surface tension, enabling alveoli to stay open and facilitating effective gas exchange. In preterm infants (especially those <34 weeks), insufficient surfactant leads to alveolar collapse, impaired oxygenation, and respiratory failure shortly after birth. RDS typically presents within the first hours of life and is characterized by: tachypnea, grunting, nasal flaring, chest retractions, increased oxygen and ventilatory requirement. The risk and severity of RDS increase with lower gestational age and birth weight. 
Traditionally, diagnosis combines clinical signs with chest radiography (CXR) showing diffuse reticulogranular (“ground-glass”) opacities and reduced lung volumes. and air bronchograms. Chest X-rays have been the reference standard because they have been part of long-established diagnostic algorithms.However, concerns about ionizing radiation exposure, especially with multiple serial X-rays in fragile neonates.
 The Characteristic features of Lung Ultrasonography (LUS) include: Diffuse bilateral “white lung” pattern, Coalescent B-lines, Thickened and irregular pleural line, Absence of spared areas. There are many scoring systems used to diagnose the severity of RDS; among them, BRAT’s score is the most commonly used. LUS provides a radiation-free, bedside modality, increasingly used in NICUs. 
For this review, studies including any of the commonly used LUS scoring systems (Brat’s, Raimondi’S or Rodrigues’s) for RDS and having cases with any of the following findings on LUS in the absence of “double lung point” sign or alveolar-interstitial syndrome, shall be included:
● Absent A-lines and “white lung” appearance
● Lung consolidation (irregular hypoechoic areas separate from surrounding pulmonary tissue) with air bronchograms 
● “lung pulse” sign
● “Snowflake” sign (no significant hepatization but air-bronchograms present)
● Absence of spared areas 

For the review, the following clinico-radiological diagnosis of RDS will be considered: 
ALL of the following:
● Preterm neonates <35 weeks of gestation
● Requirement of positive end expiratory pressure (PEEP) of at least 6 cm H2O immediately after birth,
● Continued need for any respiratory support beyond the first 12 hours of life,
● Chest X-ray suggestive of any of the following: 
● Stage 1 RDS: fine granular pattern with few air-bronchograms
● Stage 2 RDS: distinct granularity and excessive air-bronchograms 
● Stage 3 RDS: increased opacity with reduced air-bronchograms
● Stage 4 RDS: diffuse bilateral opacified lung (white-out) with lack of cardiac borders and loss of all air-bronchograms
● With or without the need for surfactant administration
● Without any pre-existing lung malformation or pulmonary disorder

7. Participants/population

Inclusion: Preterm neonates (gestational age <35 weeks) presenting with clinical features of respiratory distress in the early neonatal period (≤72 hours of life), admitted to neonatal intensive care units with or without the need for surfactant.

Exclusion: Neonates with the following conditions shall be excluded:
a) Any major congenital malformation
b) Chromosomal abnormality
c) Congenital lung malformation

8. Index test
Lung ultrasonography (LUS) performed at bedside for the radiological diagnosis of neonatal respiratory distress syndrome (RDS).

9. Reference standard
 Chest radiography (CXR) is used for the radiological diagnosis of neonatal RDS in clinically suspected cases.

10. Context
 Lung ultrasound is increasingly studied and used for neonatal respiratory evaluation due to several important advantages:
a. Radiation-free: Unlike chest X-ray, LUS avoids ionizing radiation, which is critically important in preterm neonates who are more susceptible to DNA damage and long-term cancer risk from radiation. 
b. Bedside and Repeatable: LUS can be performed at the bedside in the neonatal ICU, enabling real-time assessments and serial monitoring of lung status without having to transport unstable infants to radiography.
c. High Diagnostic Accuracy: Multiple studies and reviews show that LUS has sensitivity and specificity comparable to or exceeding chest X-ray for diagnosing RDS in preterm neonates:
Studies report LUS showing specific findings like pleural line abnormalities(thickened pleura, irregular pleura, etc.), “white lung,” B-lines, and subpleural consolidations, which correlate with RDS and disease severity. In one study, LUS scores were better predictors of the need for surfactant therapy compared with chest X-ray scores.
d. Quantitative and Severity Assessment: LUS scoring systems (e.g., 6- or 12-zone lung scores) can quantify lung aeration and disease severity, helping clinicians assess progression or improvement in a more objective way than standard CXR patterns.
e. Differentiation of Causes of Neonatal Respiratory Distress: Emerging evidence shows that LUS can differentiate RDS from other causes of neonatal respiratory distress, such as transient tachypnea of newborn (TTN), using characteristic signs (e.g., double lung point for TTN vs. consolidation patterns in RDS)

11. Primary outcome(s). 
Diagnostic test accuracy measures:
● HSROC
● Sensitivity
● Specificity
● Positive predictive value
● Negative predictive value
● Diagnostic odds ratio

12. Additional outcome(s)
a. Time to diagnosis (minutes)
b. Adverse effects (hypothermia, acute deterioration following procedure)

title: A mobile-health smartphone application shows high diagnostic accuracy for malignant skin lesions in a Latin American population: a prospective diagnostic accuracy study
description:
This research project is a diagnostic accuracy study designed to evaluate the performance of an artificial intelligence (AI)-based smartphone application for the detection and triage of malignant skin lesions in a Colombian population with broad ethnic diversity and a predominance of Fitzpatrick skin phototypes III–VI. The project was developed in response to the increasing global burden of skin cancer and the growing need for accessible, scalable strategies that facilitate early detection and timely referral to dermatologic care, particularly in regions with limited specialist access.

Globally, skin cancer represents one of the most common malignancies and continues to rise in incidence. Although melanoma accounts for most skin cancer-related deaths, non-melanoma skin cancer (NMSC), including basal cell carcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma, contributes substantially to morbidity and overall mortality due to its very high incidence. In Colombia, melanoma exhibits distinct epidemiologic characteristics compared to high-incidence countries, including a predominance of acral lentiginous melanoma and a high proportion of advanced-stage diagnoses. Mortality-to-incidence ratios are nearly twice those observed in many high-income countries, reflecting delays in diagnosis and barriers to specialized care. At the same time, artificial intelligence tools for skin lesion classification are rapidly expanding, yet most available algorithms have been trained and validated using datasets derived predominantly from European, North American, and Oceanian populations, with minimal representation of darker skin phototypes or Latin American populations. This lack of demographic diversity raises concerns regarding the generalizability and equity of AI-assisted dermatologic tools.

The primary purpose of this project is therefore to determine the sensitivity and specificity of a mobile-health application that integrates a convolutional neural network with optional dermatologist review for identifying malignant skin lesions in real-world clinical settings involving ethnically diverse populations. The study also aims to evaluate the application’s performance in detecting premalignant lesions and specific skin cancer subtypes, including basal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and melanoma. In addition, subgroup analyses according to Fitzpatrick phototype were conducted to explore whether diagnostic performance varies across different skin types.

The study was conducted at the Dermatology Unit of San Ignacio University Hospital (HUSI) in Bogotá, Colombia, and complemented by three rural and underserved community health brigades in Mahates (Bolívar), Buenaventura (Valle del Cauca), and Leticia (Amazonas). These regions were intentionally selected because they include Afro-descendant, Indigenous, and mixed Hispanic populations with higher frequencies of darker skin phototypes and historically limited access to dermatologic services. By incorporating participants from both tertiary urban care centers and remote underserved regions, the project seeks to improve representation of populations traditionally excluded from AI validation studies in dermatology.

Eligible participants included adults attending dermatologic consultation who presented with at least one cutaneous lesion suitable for photographic assessment. After informed consent, lesions underwent standardized evaluation including sociodemographic characterization, Fitzpatrick skin phototype classification, dermatologist clinical assessment, and image capture using the smartphone application. The application generated an AI-based risk classification and, when necessary, incorporated remote review by a dermatologist panel. Dermatologists performing the clinical evaluations were blinded to the application results. Lesions suspicious for malignancy underwent biopsy for histopathological confirmation, while benign and premalignant lesions were classified using predefined clinical and histopathologic criteria. Data were collected and managed using REDCap, ensuring secure storage and standardized data acquisition across both urban and remote settings.

The primary expected outcome of this project is to provide robust evidence regarding the diagnostic performance of AI-assisted mobile applications in populations that have been historically underrepresented in dermatologic AI research. Specifically, the study seeks to determine whether this technology maintains acceptable sensitivity and specificity in individuals with darker skin phototypes and diverse ethnic backgrounds. Secondary expected outcomes include generating data on the performance of the application across different lesion categories and cancer subtypes, as well as identifying potential disparities in algorithmic accuracy between phototype groups.

More broadly, this project aims to contribute to the development of more equitable and generalizable AI systems in dermatology. The findings may help inform future validation studies, support safer integration of AI-assisted triage tools into clinical practice, and encourage the inclusion of ethnically and phenotypically diverse populations in dermatologic machine learning datasets. The project also seeks to explore the potential role of smartphone-based AI technologies as accessible screening and referral-support tools in low-resource settings where access to dermatologists is limited.

title: Comparative Assessment of Endoscopic Ultrasound-Guided vs. Percutaneous Biopsy in Pancreatic Lesions: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Diagnostic Performance
description:
Introduction: Pancreatic cancer ranks as the fourth deadliest form of cancer. However, it's essential to note that not all pancreatic masses signal primary malignancy. Therefore, it is imperative to establish the correct differential diagnosis, a process further supported by pre-operative biopsy procedures. This meta-analysis aims to compare the diagnostic performance of two minimally invasive biopsy approaches for pancreatic tissue sampling: percutaneous biopsies guided by CT or ultrasound, and transduodenal biopsies guided by endoscopic ultrasound.
Methods: A systematic literature search will be performed on the MEDLINE and Scopus databases using predefined search terms. The selected studies will undergo analysis to evaluate the diagnostic performance of the two biopsy methods. Additionally, they will be assessed for potential bias utilizing the Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies 2 (QUADAS-2) tool. Statistical analysis will be conducted using RevMan and MetaDisc software.

title: Optimizing Sudden Cardiac Death Prevention in STEMI
description: Despite considerable progress in managing ST‐elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), sudden cardiac death (SCD) remains a major clinical challenge, contributing to 14.8% of deaths within 30 days and 2.2% within the first year post‐MI. Although implantable cardioverter‐defibrillator (ICD) therapy—guided primarily by left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF)—has been proven to reduce mortality in landmark trials (e.g., MADIT, MUSTT, MADIT-II), the modest sensitivity and specificity of LVEF limit its utility as a sole risk stratifier. Emerging clinical trends highlight the progression from traditional LVEF‐based models to more comprehensive risk assessment strategies. This review critically examines additional modalities.

title: Diagnostic Accuracy of AI-Enabled Handheld Echocardiography by Novice Healthcare Workers for Detection of Left Ventricular Systolic Dysfunction: A Protocol for Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
description:
This study is a systematic review and meta-analysis designed to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy and clinical utility of artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled handheld echocardiography performed by novice healthcare workers for the detection of left ventricular systolic dysfunction (LVSD).

Background and Rationale

Left ventricular systolic dysfunction is a major contributor to heart failure, a condition associated with significant global morbidity and mortality. Early and accurate detection of LVSD is essential for timely intervention and improved patient outcomes. However, access to expert echocardiography is limited in many healthcare systems due to shortages of trained sonographers and cardiologists.

Recent advances in artificial intelligence have enabled handheld echocardiography devices to assist users in both image acquisition and interpretation. These systems provide real-time feedback, automated view recognition, and automated or semi-automated assessment of cardiac function. As a result, they may allow healthcare workers with limited echocardiography training (e.g., nurses, medical students, paramedics, and community health workers) to perform clinically meaningful cardiac assessments.

Despite promising findings from individual studies, the overall diagnostic performance of AI-assisted handheld echocardiography in novice users remains uncertain, with variability across study designs, AI systems, operator types, and clinical settings.

title: Meta-analysis of prion disease biomarkers
description:
This meta-analysis will be focused on the role of the most commonly used cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) biomarkers in the diagnosis of human prion diseases. The selected CSF biomarkers are: 14-3-3, total-tau, tau ratio, RT-QuIC and alpha-synuclein. The prion diseases included in the scope of the study are: sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, genetic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, Gerstmann–Sträussler–Scheinker syndrome and fatal familial insomnia.
The search will be performed in PubMed under pre-defined search strategy and inclusion criteria, following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) recommendations. Selected papers will be evaluated with the QUADAS-2 tool for the quality assessment of diagnostic accuracy studies. Main data will be collected, including study type, participants involved, sample size and biomarker test results in the study population. Paper evaluation and data collection will be performed by two independent researchers, and discrepancies will be discussed in person.
Data analysis will be carried out in R following standard procedures for diagnostic test accuracy meta-analyses, including, but not limited to, estimation of pooled effects, heterogeneity quantification and publication bias.

title: A Randomized Controlled Trial on the Efficacy of DeepSeek-R1 in Assisting Clinicians with the Differential Diagnosis of Gliomas
description:
Background
Gliomas are rapidly progressing intracranial tumors with a poor prognosis, making early and accurate diagnosis crucial for treatment decisions. Although pathological biopsy remains the diagnostic gold standard, it is invasive and time-consuming, creating a clinical need for non-invasive and efficient auxiliary diagnostic tools. Furthermore, gliomas, solitary brain metastases, and primary central nervous system lymphoma (PCNSL) share highly similar clinical symptoms and imaging manifestations, posing significant challenges for differential diagnosis. In recent years, reasoning-based large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated potential in differential diagnosis within medical fields such as emergency medicine and ophthalmology. However, their efficacy in glioma differential diagnosis lacks systematic evaluation.

Objective
This study employs a prospective randomized controlled trial design to evaluate the diagnostic performance of the DeepSeek-R1 model in assisting clinicians with differentiating gliomas, solitary brain metastases, and primary central nervous system lymphoma.

Methods

Design: A multicenter, randomized controlled trial conducted across five tertiary Grade A hospitals nationwide.
Participants: Twenty neurosurgeons with ≤4 years of experience (resident physicians or attending physicians) will be recruited and randomly assigned to either the DeepSeek-R1-assisted group (experimental group) or the conventional diagnosis group (control group).
Case Source: A total of 240 cases will be included, comprising 120 cases from published typical case reports in international journals (e.g., The New England Journal of Medicine) within the last two years, and 120 cases from patients pathologically confirmed with the three target diseases at Peking University Shenzhen Hospital over the past seven years.
Outcome Variables:
Primary Outcome Variable: Top 1 diagnostic accuracy (i.e., the accuracy of the initial diagnosis).
Secondary Outcome Variables: Diagnostic time (in minutes), diagnostic quality score (using a Likert scale), LLM hallucination rate (frequency of erroneous or irrelevant content in model output), and a physician usability questionnaire (using a Likert scale).
Statistical Analysis: Chi-square tests will be used to compare categorical variables between groups. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis will assess diagnostic performance. The Mann-Whitney U test will be employed for non-normally distributed continuous variables.
Expected Results and Significance
This study anticipates demonstrating that DeepSeek-R1 can significantly improve the differential diagnostic accuracy of junior physicians for gliomas while optimizing diagnostic efficiency. The findings will provide high-level evidence-based medical evidence for the application of LLMs in the field of neuro-oncology, thereby promoting the clinical translation of artificial intelligence-assisted diagnostic tools.

title: Artificial Intelligence Applied to Endoscopic and Laryngoscopic Imaging for the Detection of Head and Neck Cancer: A Systematic Review
description: Retrospective registration of a completed systematic review (PRISMA 2020) evaluating artificial-intelligence, machine-learning, and deep-learning models applied to endoscopic and laryngoscopic imaging for the detection, diagnosis, or malignant-versus-benign classification of head and neck cancer. Six databases (PubMed/MEDLINE, OpenAlex, IEEE Xplore, Scopus, Embase, Web of Science) were searched for 2015-2025; 101 primary studies met eligibility. Diagnostic accuracy and methodological quality (QUADAS-2-style risk of bias) were appraised, with narrative synthesis and exploratory random-effects pooling. The review was registered retrospectively at the point of manuscript submission; the full protocol, search strategy and run log, included-studies dataset, and PRISMA 2020 checklist are attached as supplementary files.

title: Diagnostic Accuracy of Artificial Intelligence for Pulmonary Hypertension Detection: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis across Multiple Input Modalities
description:
Study Description
Pulmonary hypertension (PH) carries a median diagnostic delay of 2 to 3 years, and its gold standard confirmatory test -- right heart catheterization -- is invasive and unsuitable for population-level screening. Over the past decade, artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) applied to routine clinical data have emerged as candidate non-invasive case-finding tools, with published systems spanning ten distinct input modalities: electrocardiogram (ECG), echocardiography, chest X-ray (CXR), cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMR), computed tomographic pulmonary angiography (CTPA), electronic health records (EHR), auscultation or phonocardiography, photoplethysmography (PPG), omics (proteomics, lipidomics, miRNA, gene expression), and multimodal combinations.
Despite this rapid accumulation of single-modality reports, no systematic synthesis has quantified AI diagnostic accuracy for PH across modalities under a common analytic framework, nor have any primary studies performed within-subject head-to-head comparisons between modalities.
This study is a systematic review and meta-analysis of diagnostic test accuracy studies evaluating AI- or ML-based PH detection. We searched PubMed, Embase, Cochrane CENTRAL, and Web of Science from inception to March 31, 2026 (with a final update on April 30, 2026). Fifty studies published between 2016 and 2026, covering all ten input modalities, met inclusion criteria. Diagnostic accuracy was pooled using a bivariate random-effects model (mvmeta package in R) for studies with complete 2x2 contingency table data (k = 32), and AUROC was pooled separately on the logit scale (k = 41). Pre-specified subgroup analyses by input modality and meta-regression with modality as a covariate were conducted. Risk of bias was assessed using QUADAS-2. Two pre-specified sensitivity analyses evaluated the influence of extreme-performing studies and a population-level screening cohort.
The pooled sensitivity was 0.873 (95% CI 0.823-0.910), pooled specificity 0.823 (95% CI 0.776-0.863), and pooled AUROC 0.897 (95% CI 0.870-0.919), with substantial heterogeneity (I² = 99.3%). Meta-regression identified AI input modality as a significant predictor of specificity (P = 0.007). Chest X-ray-based AI ranked highest by predicted operating point but was heavily influenced by a single high-performing study. EHR-based and multimodal AI achieved the highest pooled AUROCs in smaller subgroup pools. The absence of within-study head-to-head modality comparisons precluded a formal diagnostic test accuracy network meta-analysis, necessitating an indirect comparison approach.
This is the first systematic review and meta-analysis to pool AI diagnostic test accuracy for PH across all input modalities. The findings support the potential utility of AI-based PH case finding while highlighting the need for prospective head-to-head modality comparisons conducted under TRIPOD-AI reporting standards and threshold-recalibration at primary-care prevalence levels.

title: Depression in Older Residents Permanently Residing in Nursing Homes: A Scoping Review Protocol
description:
Depression presents with symptoms such as sadness, loss of interest or pleasure, and tiredness that lasts more than two weeks and impairs an older person’s ability to engage in their activities of daily living.[1] Depression is common in nursing home residents with one systematic review reporting the prevalence to be as high as 18.9% (95% CI 14.8-23.8%).[2] The true prevalence, however, is likely higher with half of the cases un-detected, with under-diagnosis common.[3, 4] Failure to detect depression when it is there can result in detrimental health consequences for the resident. Furthermore, the reported prevalence of depression likely varies depending on how depression is defined and measured.

Given population ageing globally, and with the number of older people aged 65 years and over expected to more than double between 2020 and 2050,[5] there is likely to be increased demand for nursing home places because older age is associated with nursing home admission.[6] It follows that as a result of increasing numbers of nursing home residents, depression will be encountered more often in that care setting, making it essential that aged care staff and health practitioners are better equipped to identify and manage this health condition. Depression has longer-term health consequences such as increased mortality risk.[7] However, more research to better understand these consequences is still necessary. For example, little is known about the effects of depression on other outcomes such as frailty or hospitalisation.

Screening for depression is possible using validated clinical scales. Screening can detect risk, leading to timely diagnosis and management. It also leads to increase awareness and makes education of residents, their carers and staff possible. A recent systematic review and meta-analysis identified 23 validated scales that are used to screen for depression in nursing homes.[8] Consisting of 15 questions, the Geriatric Depression Scale (GDS-15)[9] has been most commonly referenced in the literature. Furthermore, the Nursing Homes Short Depression Inventory (NH-SDI)[10] had the best diagnostic test accuracy whilst the Cornell Scale for Depression in Dementia-4 Item Version (CSSD-4)[11] was the best for those with dementia in that study.[8] 

Health care staff may prefer briefer and less time-consuming tools given their busy daily care for the residents. Brief instruments to screen for depression exist but are yet to be validated with nursing home residents. Patient Health Questionnaire-2 (PHQ-2)[12] is one such item. It is a validated two-item screening tool for depression and a brief version of the nine-item Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-9)[13], with questions relating to depressed mood and loss of anhedonia. The Patient Health Questionnaire-4 (PHQ-4)[14] combines the PHQ-2 with the two-item Generalized Anxiety Disorder Scale (GAD-2)[15], screening simultaneously for both depression and anxiety.
 
Following the identification of risk, it is important to identify risk factors that might be treatable. Cognitive, functional impairment, and baseline depression scores have been identified as risk factors for depression amongst nursing home residents.[16] Therefore, interventions aimed at enhancing cognitive and physical function might be treatment options for residents of nursing homes. Non-pharmacological interventions such as psychotherapy may benefit some patients.[17, 18] Pharmacological approaches, whilst potentially beneficial, could also result in adverse reactions (e.g. sedation and falls) because of the frailty seen in nursing home residents.[19] 

Developing an overview of the current literature on this health topic is important as it allows identification of the current literature gaps in understanding and would help inform the planning for future research to address any identified gaps.

title: A Systematic Review on Novel Diagnostic Biomarkers of Endometriosis in Association with Moderate-to-Severe Disease
description:
Endometriosis is a chronic, estrogen-dependent gynecological condition affecting approximately 11% of reproductive-aged women. It is characterized by ectopic implantation of endometrial-like tissue, causing pelvic pain, infertility, and systemic symptoms that severely impact quality of life. Currently, diagnosis relies on laparoscopic visualization, leading to prolonged diagnostic delays averaging 6.7 years. Given the limitations of imaging techniques such as MRI and transvaginal ultrasound (TVS) in detecting deep and superficial lesions, research efforts have focused on identifying novel non-invasive biomarkers. While CA-125 has been widely studied, it lacks specificity, limiting its diagnostic utility. Recent discoveries, including neutrophil gelatinase-associated lipocalin (NGAL), endocan, and tRNA-derived small RNAs (tsRNAs), show potential for early and accurate detection, particularly in advanced-stage disease (Stage III/IV). This systematic review aims to synthesize existing evidence on novel biomarkers associated with moderate-to-severe endometriosis, evaluating their diagnostic accuracy, clinical applicability, and potential for replacing invasive diagnostic methods.
Expected Outcomes:
- Comprehensive Analysis – Identification and classification of emerging biomarkers that differentiate Stage III/IV endometriosis from minimal disease.
- Diagnostic Performance Evaluation – Assessment of biomarker sensitivity, specificity, and predictive value, compared to existing modalities.
- Clinical Implications – Discussion on biomarker integration into routine diagnostics, aiming to reduce diagnostic delays and improve patient outcomes.
- Future Research Directions – Highlighting gaps in biomarker research and proposing key areas for further investigation in translational medicine.

title: A Hybrid AI-Meta-Analysis Framework for Irritable Bowel Syndrome Diagnosis: Development and Conflict-Zone Validation of a Low-Cost CBC-Based Tool
description:
This repository contains all data, code, and supplementary materials for the study "A Hybrid AI-Meta-Analysis Framework for Irritable Bowel Syndrome Diagnosis." This work addresses the critical global need for affordable, non-invasive diagnostic tools for Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS), especially in low-resource and conflict-affected settings.

The study employs a novel three-phase hybrid design:
1. Phase 1 - Meta-Analysis: A comprehensive, PRISMA-compliant meta-analysis of 110 studies (n=43,250 participants) was conducted to establish the diagnostic utility of Complete Blood Count (CBC)-derived inflammatory markers (Neutrophil-to-Lymphocyte Ratio (NLR), Mean Platelet Volume (MPV), Platelet-to-Lymphocyte Ratio (PLR)) in IBS, revealing significant subtype-specific effects.
2. Phase 2 - AI Model Development: An interpretable machine learning model (XGBoost) was developed on the harmonized global dataset, achieving an AUC of 0.89. Model interpretability was achieved using SHAP values, identifying NLR as the dominant predictor.
3. Phase 3 - Conflict-Zone Validation: The AI tool was prospectively validated in an independent cohort from Yemen (n=142), a active conflict zone, maintaining an AUC of 0.82. The study introduces and validates malaria-adjusted thresholds, achieving 88.6% specificity in endemic conditions, and demonstrates a 92% reduction in cost compared to colonoscopy.

This project provides one of the first diagnostically validated, conflict-resilient, and cost-effective diagnostic solutions for IBS, designed for deployment in the world's most challenging healthcare environments.

Keywords: Irritable Bowel Syndrome; Neutrophil-Lymphocyte Ratio; Artificial Intelligence; Low-Resource Settings; Meta-Analysis; Diagnostic Tool; Conflict Zones; Global Health.

title: Comparative Analysis of Consequences Associated with Posterior-Type Ankyloglossia in infants
description:
This study aims to analyze the clinical manifestations associated with different posterior types of ankyloglossia in infants, according to the FreLac classification system. Ankyloglossia is a congenital condition characterized by a restrictive lingual frenulum that may interfere with oral function, particularly during breastfeeding. While anterior forms have traditionally received greater clinical attention, posterior forms are increasingly recognized as potentially relevant contributors to breastfeeding difficulties and early orofacial development.
The primary objective of this research is to compare the prevalence of breastfeeding-related symptoms and early functional orofacial alterations among infants presenting with different posterior types of ankyloglossia (mixed, posterior, and mucosal). The study specifically evaluates maternal symptoms (such as nipple pain, fissures, and mastitis), infant feeding-related signs (including aerophagia, regurgitation, choking, and clicking sounds), and early indicators of altered orofacial development (such as high-arched palate and mandibular retrognathia).This is a prospective observational clinical study including 285 infants aged between 0 and 6 months, evaluated between 2023 and 2024 in a level IV hospital in Barcelona (Spain). Infants were classified according to the FreLac classification and assessed through standardized clinical evaluation. Descriptive and inferential statistical analyses were performed to identify differences between groups.
The working hypothesis of this study is that posterior and mucosal forms of ankyloglossia are associated with a higher prevalence of breastfeeding difficulties and functional alterations compared with mixed forms, due to their greater restrictive effect on the posterior portion of the tongue and its role in generating intraoral vacuum and coordinated swallowing.
Expected outcomes include the identification of specific clinical patterns associated with posterior-type ankyloglossia, which may support improved diagnostic accuracy and earlier recognition of functionally significant cases. The findings are intended to contribute to a better understanding of the role of posterior tongue mobility in breastfeeding and early orofacial development, and to inform clinical decision-making and multidisciplinary management strategies.
This study was retrospectively registered in the Open Science Framework (OSF) to ensure transparency and reproducibility of the research process.
