title: Systematic Review and Diagnostic Test Accuracy Meta-analysis of Artificial Intelligence Models for Classification of Cervical Cytology Images
description:
Systematic Review and Diagnostic Test Accuracy Meta-analysis of Artificial Intelligence Models for Classification of Cervical Cytology Images 

This study is designed as a systematic review and diagnostic test accuracy (DTA) meta-analysis to evaluate the pooled performance of artificial intelligence (AI) models for the classification of cervical cytology images. The protocol is developed in accordance with the PRISMA-DTA statement for reporting systematic reviews of diagnostic test accuracy studies (McInnes et al., 2018) and follows established methodological recommendations for DTA meta-analyses (Reitsma et al., 2005; Deeks et al., 2005; Whiting et al., 2011). 

Cervical cytology remains a cornerstone of cervical cancer screening worldwide. However, its diagnostic performance is affected by inter- and intra-observer variability, workload burden, and limited access to expert cytopathologists in resource-constrained settings. In recent years, machine learning and deep learning models have been increasingly applied to automated cytological image analysis. Although individual studies report high diagnostic performance, results vary substantially across datasets, validation strategies, and AI architectures. A quantitative synthesis of diagnostic accuracy using appropriate bivariate modeling is therefore required. 

The primary research question is: what is the pooled sensitivity and specificity of artificial intelligence-based models for detecting abnormal cervical cytology compared with expert cytopathological interpretation and/or histopathological confirmation? 

The review follows a Population–Index test–Reference standard–Target condition (PIRT) framework appropriate for DTA studies. The population includes cervical cytology images derived from Pap smear or liquid-based cytology samples obtained from women undergoing screening or diagnostic evaluation. The index test consists of artificial intelligence models designed for automated image classification, including traditional machine learning algorithms (e.g., support vector machines, random forest, gradient boosting methods) and deep learning architectures (e.g., convolutional neural networks, residual networks, EfficientNet, Vision Transformers, hybrid CNN–Transformer systems). The reference standard includes expert cytopathologist interpretation, typically based on the Bethesda System, and/or histopathological confirmation where available. 

The primary target condition will be defined as abnormal cytology versus normal cytology (NILM). Where studies report multi-class Bethesda categories, data will be harmonized to a binary framework. The preferred primary threshold will be ASC-US or higher versus NILM, reflecting screening-relevant abnormality detection. If harmonization to ASC-US+ is not feasible due to reporting structure, abnormal versus normal classification as defined by study authors will be used. A predefined sensitivity analysis will evaluate alternative thresholds (e.g., HSIL+ versus <HSIL) where sufficient data are available. 

Eligible studies include original diagnostic accuracy investigations evaluating AI-based models for classification of cervical cytology images and reporting sufficient information to derive 2×2 contingency tables (TP, FP, FN, TN), either directly or via sensitivity and specificity with class distribution. Only peer-reviewed journal publications in English will be included. Studies focused exclusively on HPV testing, colposcopy, or histological image analysis without cytological imaging will be excluded. Prognostic models, treatment-response prediction models, reviews, editorials, conference abstracts lacking full methodological detail, animal studies, and studies without extractable diagnostic performance metrics will also be excluded. Restriction to English-language peer-reviewed publications may introduce language and publication bias and will be acknowledged as a limitation. 

A systematic literature search will be conducted in PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Google Scholar from database inception to 31 August 2025. Search strategies will combine cervical cytology–related terminology with artificial intelligence–related terminology, including controlled vocabulary and free-text terms. For Google Scholar, searches will be conducted on a single predefined date using fixed query strings, and screening will be limited to the first 300 results sorted by relevance to enhance reproducibility. Reference lists of eligible articles will be manually screened for additional studies. 

Study selection will be performed independently by two reviewers. Titles and abstracts will be screened first, followed by full-text evaluation against predefined eligibility criteria. Discrepancies will be resolved through discussion and consensus. 

Data extraction will be conducted independently by two reviewers using a standardized extraction form. Extracted variables will include author, year, country, study design, dataset type (public versus proprietary), validation strategy (cross-validation, hold-out, external validation), analytical level (image-level, slide-level, or patient-level classification), AI model architecture, reference standard, decision threshold (if reported), and diagnostic performance metrics. 

When TP, FP, FN, and TN values are not explicitly reported, contingency tables will be reconstructed only if sensitivity, specificity, and class distribution (N_positive and N_negative) are clearly provided or can be unambiguously derived from the article. Reconstruction will follow the formulas: TP = round(Sensitivity × N_positive); FN = N_positive − TP; TN = round(Specificity × N_negative); FP = N_negative − TN. Nearest-integer rounding will be applied. Internal consistency checks will ensure agreement between reconstructed and reported performance metrics. Studies lacking sufficient information for reliable reconstruction will be excluded from quantitative synthesis and, if relevant, described narratively. Sensitivity analyses will assess the impact of reconstructed data on pooled estimates. 

Methodological quality and risk of bias will be assessed using QUADAS-2 (Whiting et al., 2011) across four domains: patient selection, index test, reference standard, and flow and timing. Each domain will be evaluated for risk of bias and applicability concerns. 

For statistical synthesis, a bivariate random-effects meta-analysis based on the Reitsma model (Reitsma et al., 2005) will be used to jointly synthesize logit-transformed sensitivity and specificity while accounting for their correlation. Pooled sensitivity and specificity with 95% confidence intervals will be estimated. A summary receiver operating characteristic (SROC) curve with confidence and prediction regions will be constructed. Diagnostic odds ratios and positive and negative likelihood ratios will also be calculated. Between-study heterogeneity will be primarily assessed using τ² estimates and prediction intervals; I² statistics for sensitivity and specificity will be reported as supplementary descriptive indicators. The expected range of diagnostic performance in future clinical settings will be quantified through prediction intervals. 

Predefined subgroup analyses will explore potential sources of heterogeneity, including dataset type (public versus proprietary), validation strategy (cross-validation versus external validation), analytical level (whole slide image versus patch-based analysis), and model category (machine learning versus deep learning). Meta-regression will assess the influence of continuous moderators such as sample size and year of publication. Publication bias will be evaluated using Deeks’ funnel plot asymmetry test (Deeks et al., 2005), recognizing its limitations in DTA meta-analyses. 

All statistical analyses will be conducted in R using established packages for diagnostic meta-analysis, including mada, meta, and metafor. Statistical significance will be defined as p < 0.05. 

At the time of registration, study identification, data extraction, and statistical analyses have been completed. The protocol is registered prior to journal submission to ensure methodological transparency and reproducibility. 

McInnes MDF et al. PRISMA-DTA Statement. JAMA. 2018. 

Reitsma JB et al. Bivariate analysis of sensitivity and specificity. J Clin Epidemiol. 2005. 

 Deeks JJ et al. Evaluating diagnostic tests in meta-analysis. BMJ. 2005. 

 Whiting PF et al. QUADAS-2 tool. Ann Intern Med. 2011.

title: Diagnostic Accuracy of Infrared Thermal imaging for detecting Diabetic Peripheral Neuropathy: A Systematic Review and Meta Analysis
description:
Diabetic peripheral neuropathy is one of the most common microvascular complications of diabetes mellitus, leading to pain, numbness, increased risk of falls, and foot ulcers that may progress to amputation. Early diagnosis is essential to prevent these severe outcomes. Conventional diagnostic methods for DPN - such as nerve conduction studies, monofilament testing, and clinical scoring systems have limitations in terms of invasiveness, cost, accessibility, and operator dependency.
Infrared thermal imaging has emerged as a promising, non-invasive, and contact-free diagnostic modality that can detect subtle changes in skin temperature distribution to autonomic and small fiber dysfunction, which occur early in DPN. Several studies have evaluated the diagnostic accuracy of IRT for detecting DPN, but their findings are scattered, heterogenous, and sometimes inconclusive. Moreover, with recent advances, machine learning based image analysis methods have been applied to IRT data, potentially improving diagnostic performance compared to conventional interpretation.
PURPOSE: The purpose of this Systematic review and Meta-analysis is to comprehensively evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of infrared thermal imaging for detecting diabetic peripheral neuropathy, using established reference standards like nerve conduction studies, clinical scores). This review will:
1. Synthesize evidence on the sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), and area under the ROC curve (AUC) of IRT in diagnosing DPN.
2. Compare diagnostic performance between conventional human interpretation of thermograms and machine learning -based approaches, if sufficient studies are available.
3. Assess sources of heterogeneity such as imaging protocols, thermal parameters, patient populations, and reference standards.
4. Evaluate methodological quality and risk of bias of included studies using a validated tools like QUADAS-2
EXPECTED OUTCOMES : 
1. Pooled diagnostic accuracy: Produce a pooled estimate (sensitivity, specificity, AUC) for IRT in detecting DPN.
2. Determine if ML-based IRT analysis shows better diagnostic performance than conventional interpretation.
3. Highlight gaps in the current literature, such as small sample sizes, inconsistent methodologies, or lack of external validation.
4. Give pragmatic guidance for clinical use and outlie priorities for future research 
5. Assess the potential of IRT to help distinguish DPN - related changes from the other causes of diabetic foot ulcer, such as peripheral arterial disease or ischemia

title: Rapid Geriatric Screening Tools in Primary Health Care: Protocol for a Scoping Review with a Focus on Low- and Middle-Income Countries
description:
This project is a scoping review protocol designed to identify, map, and synthesize the available evidence on rapid geriatric screening tools and risk stratification strategies used for older adults in primary health care settings. The review focuses on tools intended to support the early identification of frailty, functional decline, cognitive impairment, vulnerability, loss of intrinsic capacity, multimorbidity, and other geriatric risks among adults aged 60 years or older, with particular attention to low- and middle-income countries.

Population ageing is increasing the demand for accessible, efficient, and context-sensitive approaches to geriatric assessment in primary health care. Although Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment is considered a reference standard for multidimensional evaluation of older adults, it is often difficult to implement in routine primary care because it requires substantial time, trained personnel, and specialized resources. Rapid screening tools may offer a pragmatic alternative by helping primary care teams identify older adults at higher risk and guide appropriate care planning, referrals, and follow-up. However, the evidence on which tools are available, which domains they assess, how they perform psychometrically, and how feasible they are in real-world primary care settings remains fragmented.

The main purpose of this scoping review is to characterize rapid geriatric screening tools and risk stratification strategies used in primary health care and community-based settings worldwide. The review will place special emphasis on evidence from low- and middle-income countries, where primary care services often face resource constraints and limited access to specialist geriatric care. The review will also describe reported psychometric properties, including validity, reliability, sensitivity, specificity, and area under the ROC curve when available. In addition, it will examine evidence on feasibility, acceptability, barriers, facilitators, and contextual adaptations related to implementation in primary health care.

The review will follow established methodological guidance for scoping reviews, including the Joanna Briggs Institute framework and the PRISMA extension for Scoping Reviews. Eligible studies will include observational studies, diagnostic accuracy studies, randomized and non-randomized trials with a screening tool component, implementation studies, and mixed-methods studies published from 2010 onwards in English, Portuguese, or Spanish. The review will include studies conducted in primary health care and community-based settings and will exclude studies focused exclusively on hospital inpatient, emergency, or long-term institutional care settings.

Definitive searches will be conducted in PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Embase, Web of Science, and LILACS after prospective registration on the Open Science Framework. Pilot searches were previously conducted only to calibrate and refine the search strategies. Retrieved records will be managed using Rayyan, with independent title and abstract screening by two reviewers, followed by duplicate full-text eligibility assessment. Data will be extracted using a standardized charting form covering study characteristics, country and World Bank income classification, population, tool characteristics, domains assessed, administration time, mode of application, psychometric properties, outcomes, feasibility, acceptability, implementation barriers and facilitators, and methodological quality.

Given the expected heterogeneity of tools, populations, study designs, and health system contexts, no quantitative meta-analysis is planned. Instead, findings will be synthesized through descriptive mapping and narrative synthesis. The expected outcomes of this project include a comprehensive overview of rapid geriatric screening tools used in primary health care, a classification of the main domains assessed by these tools, a summary of reported measurement properties and implementation evidence, and identification of evidence gaps, especially in low- and middle-income countries.

The results are expected to inform clinical practice, primary care organization, future research priorities, and the development or adaptation of rapid multidimensional assessment strategies for older adults. This review is also linked to the broader PRIME research programme, which aims to strengthen evidence on rapid instruments for multidimensional evaluation of older adults in primary care. Since this study will synthesize data from previously published literature and will not involve primary data collection from human participants, ethical approval is not required.

title: Diagnostic Accuracy of Placental Growth Factor Alone Versus the sFlt-1/PlGF Ratio for Predicting Preeclampsia During the Second Trimester: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
description:
Preeclampsia is a major cause of maternal and perinatal morbidity and mortality worldwide. Early identification of women at risk during pregnancy is essential to facilitate timely monitoring and intervention. Placental Growth Factor (PlGF) and the soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 to Placental Growth Factor ratio (sFlt-1/PlGF ratio) are among the most widely investigated biomarkers for the prediction of preeclampsia. However, uncertainty remains regarding whether PlGF alone or the combined sFlt-1/PlGF ratio provides superior diagnostic performance during the second trimester of pregnancy.

This systematic review and meta-analysis aims to synthesize available evidence on the diagnostic accuracy of PlGF alone and the sFlt-1/PlGF ratio for predicting preeclampsia during the second trimester. Eligible studies will include observational and diagnostic accuracy studies reporting sufficient data to calculate sensitivity, specificity, or related diagnostic performance measures. Pooled estimates of sensitivity, specificity, diagnostic odds ratio, positive likelihood ratio, negative likelihood ratio, and summary receiver operating characteristic curves will be generated. The findings are expected to clarify the comparative predictive value of these biomarkers and support evidence-based clinical decision-making for the early detection of preeclampsia.

title: Validation of multiplex bead-based assay biomarkers for integrated multi-pathogen serosurveillance: a scoping review protocol
description:
Objective: 
The objective of this scoping review is to map the methods and test performance characteristics of validated antigen markers used to measure IgG antibody responses to infectious pathogens using Luminex multiplex bead assay (MBA) platforms for serosurveillance.

Introduction: 
Serosurveillance can complement traditional infectious disease surveillance by identifying prior pathogen exposure or immunity, including infections missed because of mild or asymptomatic presentation or limited diagnostic performance. Luminex MBA platforms enable simultaneous measurement of multiple antibody responses from a single sample and have demonstrated comparable sensitivity and specificity to conventional serological assays in several studies. MBA platforms also improve efficiency and scalability for integrated serosurveillance. However, there remains limited systematic documentation of validated antigen markers and validation approaches for measuring pathogen exposure and immunity using Luminex MBA platforms.

Eligibility criteria:
This review will include primary studies that quantify IgG antibodies to infectious pathogens in human serum, dried blood spot, or saliva specimens using Luminex MBA platforms. Studies that are conducted in non-humans, use exclusively specimen types other than venous blood, capillary blood, or saliva for antibody detection, and are not available in English will be excluded.

Methods: 
This scoping review will follow the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodological guidance for evidence synthesis. We will search the PubMed database using predefined pathogen-specific search terms. Two reviewers will independently screen titles, abstracts, and full texts according to the eligibility criteria. Data extraction will be conducted using a customized and pretested extraction tool. Data will be summarized narratively and presented in tabular and graphical formats.

title: The ability of paramedics to predict disposition from the emergency department, and the impact of confidence on their prediction: a cross-sectional diagnostic accuracy study
description:
The proposed research will attempt to answer the question “What is the ability of paramedics to predict their patient’s final disposition from the emergency department?” Additionally, and unique from previous research, this study seeks to ask the question “what is the ability of paramedics to predict their patient’s final disposition from the emergency department when they are confident in their prediction?” 

This study will take place in a single regional Emergency department in British Columbia, Canada. 

Participants will be asked to select predetermined binary choices on a questionnaire, with these choices compared to actual disposition from the emergency department. 

All paramedics and Emergency Medical Responders (EMRs) transporting adult patients to North Island Hospital – Comox Valley (CVH) will be approached for enrolment in the study on a consecutive basis. 

Paramedics and EMR transporting patients from other Island Health facilities through the patient transfer network (PTN) will be excluded. Study team members will also be excluded from participating. Paramedics with patients requiring immediate resuscitation will not be excluded, however will be directed to complete the study questionnaire after clinical handover. This will be defined by either a Canadian Emergency Department Triage and Acuity Scale (CTAS) classification of 1 or paramedics bypassing triage and delivering patients directly to a resuscitation bay. 
Patients who leave the emergency department against medical advice will be excluded from data analysis; however their information will be recorded, and the gross number of events will be reported. Patients who die in the ED will be included in the “admitted” category.
Consistent with the majority of diagnostic accuracy studies, the proposed study does not have an identified null hypothesis, therefore a power calculation specific to this study cannot be accurately obtained. In order to ensure sufficient data is collected however, power calculations for a null hypothesis of “no difference from a coin flip,” representing sensitivities and specificities of 50% have been conducted, utilising a hospital admission rate of 39%. This results in a required sample size of at least 246 patients admitted and 157 discharged, a figure which will be greatly exceeded with the expected sample size of 700-1000. Previous studies, as identified in appendix 1 have ranged from sample sizes of 261 to 932. If at the end of the two-month data collection period less than 246 admissions have occurred, less than 157 discharges have occurred, or a total sample size of less than 700 has been captured, the data collection period will be extended for an additional month.

title: Role of Artificial Intelligence in Detecting Alveolar Bone Loss on Panoramic Radiography
description:
Main Goals: To find, review, and summarize all the recent scientific studies that test how well AI can detect alveolar bone loss on panoramic radiographs.

Based on the methodology and the preliminary findings from the included studies, this systematic review is expected to yield the following specific results and outputs:

1. A Critical Appraisal of Evidence Quality
A key result will be the classification of the included studies by methodological rigor. The application of the CASP checklist is expected to output a clear distribution, likely showing that a portion of the studies are of high quality, while others may have moderate or low scores due to common limitations like small sample sizes, lack of external validation, or retrospective design. This appraisal is a crucial output that contextualizes the reported performance metrics.

2. A Qualitative Synthesis of Diagnostic Performance
The primary output will be a consolidated narrative and tabular summary of the diagnostic accuracy of AI models for detecting periodontal bone loss. This will clearly present some key performance metrics, including Sensitivity, Specificity, Accuracy, Area Under the Curve (AUC), and F1-scores, reported across the eligible studies. The expectation is to confirm the trend of high performance, with metrics such as AUC values frequently exceeding 0.90, demonstrating the strong technical capability of these systems.

3. Identification of AI Model Evolution and Clinical Readiness
The review is expected to output a clear analysis of how AI applications have evolved, from initial binary classification tasks to more advanced, clinically relevant functions like tooth-level segmentation and automated staging. This output will map the technological progression and highlight the most promising architectures (e.g., U-Net, YOLO variants) for specific diagnostic tasks.

4. A Defined Set of Research Gaps and Future Directions
A major output will be a clearly articulated list of critical limitations and unanswered questions in the current evidence base. This is expected to include gaps such as the need for large-scale, prospective clinical trials; the importance of multi-center external validation to ensure generalizability; and the lack of studies evaluating AI integration into real-world clinical workflows and its impact on treatment decisions and patient outcomes.

5. Evidence-Based Conclusions and Recommendations
The final, synthesized output will be a set of concise, evidence-based conclusions stating the current state of AI for this diagnostic purpose. Furthermore, the review will output practical recommendations for two key audiences: researchers (e.g., to adopt standardized reporting and focus on translational studies) and clinicians (e.g., that AI shows high potential as a decision support tool but requires further validation before routine independent use).

title: Diagnosis of ADHD in Preschool Children: A Scoping Review
description: This scoping review aims to systematically map the existing literature on the diagnostic approaches used to identify Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) in preschool-aged children (below 6 years of age). Early identification of ADHD is critical, as timely diagnosis can facilitate earlier interventions and potentially improve developmental and behavioral outcomes. The review will focus on the range of diagnostic tools, methods, and strategies currently employed, including standardized checklists, observational assessments, and parent/teacher reports. In addition to evaluating the diagnostic accuracy (e.g., sensitivity, specificity) of these methods, the review will explore related outcomes such as parental satisfaction and access to early intervention services. A comprehensive literature search will be conducted across three databases—PubMed, EMBASE, and Web of Science—using a structured search strategy based on Boolean operators and relevant Medical Subject Headings (MeSH). Studies eligible for inclusion will encompass observational research, clinical trials, psychometric studies, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and consensus guidelines published in English. The review will follow the PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews) guidelines. Data will be synthesized using thematic analysis to identify key themes related to diagnostic practices, challenges, population-specific considerations, and evolving tools such as technology-based assessments.

title: Integrating Objective Measures in ADHD Assessment: Using Online Eye-Tracking and Continuous Performance Test in Adults
description: Attention-Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is typically assessed using subjective measures like interviews, behavioural observations, self-reports, and clinician-administered rating scales, such as the Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (ASRS; Kessler et al., 2005). While these methods are widely used, they can be influenced by biases and inconsistencies (Faraone et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2024). Recent technological advances have expanded assessment options, especially through eye-tracking and Continuous Performance Tests (CPTs), which provide objective, neurological, and quantifiable data on attention and inhibitory control (Lee et al., 2021). This study investigates whether combining subjective measures (ASRS scores), behavioural performance on the CPT Non-X task (commission and omission errors, mean reaction time and d prime), and neurological behavioural data (webcam-based eye-tracking metrics of fixation duration, fixation count, and scanpath length) can accurately differentiate adults with ADHD from those without (Lev et al., 2022; Conrad et al., 2023; Dziemian et al., 2024; Kessler et al., 2005; RealEye, 2024). Data collection will be conducted remotely using participants' own devices, removing barriers such as travel, costs, or location. In a cross-sectional design, group differences in eye-tracking metrics, ASRS scores, and CPT results will be compared. Correlations between ASRS scores and objective neurological measures will be examined to assess convergent validity, and hierarchical logistic regression will evaluate predictive models—initially using CPT alone, then CPT + eye-tracking, and finally CPT, eye-tracking, to CPT + Eye-tracking + ASRS and objective neurological measures to determine the most accurate method for ADHD diagnosis. By integrating subjective, objective, and neurological data, this multimodal approach aims to create a more scalable and reliable ADHD assessment tool that reduces biases found in subjective evaluations and enhances remote accessibility (Faraone et al., 2021; Lee et al., 2021), ultimately improving diagnostic accuracy beyond reliance on a single measure (Andreou & Argatzopoulou, 2025).

title: Real-World Evaluation of GPT-4 Turbo Vision for Dermoscopic Skin Cancer Detection
description:
Background: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) models, such as ChatGPT and Gemini, are increasingly being integrated into dermatology for skin cancer detection, despite limited validation. This study simulates real-world primary care workflows to bridge the gap between AI innovation and clinical application. The findings will determine whether integrating generative AI into dermatologic triage is feasible, particularly in underserved settings with limited specialist access. Additionally, diagnostic uncertainty metrics will identify areas that require human-AI collaboration. This protocol adheres to the latest Standards for Reporting Diagnostic Accuracy Studies (STARD 2015) and Transparent Reporting of a Multivariable Prediction Model for Individual Prognosis or Diagnosis – Artificial Intelligence Extension (TRIPOD-AI) guidelines.
Methods and analysis: In this retrospective, cross-sectional diagnostic accuracy study, 750 prospectively curated dermoscopic images (533 benign, 217 malignant/precancerous) from validated repositories (International Skin Imaging Collaboration Archive, DermNet New Zealand, dermatology textbooks) will be analyzed. Lesions spanned melanocytic, non-melanocytic, keratinocyte-derived, and vascular tumors, reflecting real-world diagnostic diversity. The latest publicly available versions of ChatGPT-4 Turbo with Vision (OpenAI) and Gemini 1.5 Pro (Google) - or their successor models - will provide diagnoses via standardized, clinician-mimicking prompts without clinical metadata. The reference standard consists of histopathologically or expert- confirmed diagnoses. Primary outcome: overall diagnostic accuracy. Secondary outcomes: model comparison, diagnostic certainty (re-prompting frequency, unclassifiable responses), lesion-specific sensitivity/specificity, triage performance (benign, precancerous, malignant), explainability, and management suggestions.

title: Investigating the contribution of different cortical areas and layers to consciousness and its signatures
description: Several theories of consciousness agree about a key role for the cerebral cortex but disagree on which cortical areas and layers are critical. These mechanistic questions are best investigated in animal models, but the lack of reliable measures of consciousness in such models has so far hampered research. Here we propose, first, to validate in freely moving mice and rats a measure of consciousness—PCI—that has shown high sensitivity and specificity in humans. This measure reliably infers the level of consciousness by analyzing the complexity of the cortical response to a brief stimulation. To do so, we will employ in rodents an adaptation of PCI (PCIst) obtained by electrically and/or optogenetically stimulating different cortical areas and layers and simultaneously recording with high-density probes (such as Neuropixels) from hundreds of cortical and subcortical neurons to shed light on the cellular and network mechanisms of consciousness. As indicated by preliminary results, we will confirm that in rodents PCIst reliably distinguishes among conscious and unconscious states– waking, NREM sleep, REM sleep, anesthesia—just as it does in humans. We will then use PCIst to test whether some cortical areas and/or cortical layers more reliably track consciousness levels. This analysis will provide critical new data to understand the mechanisms of consciousness and unconsciousness and help adjudicate among competing theories.

title: Accuracy of CRISPR/Cas-based nucleic acid detection for HIV: A systematic review and meta-analysis
description:
Background: Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) remains a major global public health burden, with approximately 39 million people living with HIV worldwide. Early and accurate diagnosis is critical for effective treatment and prevention of transmission. However, conventional nucleic acid testing methods such as RT-qPCR require expensive equipment, trained personnel, and long turnaround times, limiting their use in resource-limited settings.

The CRISPR/Cas system (particularly Cas12a and Cas13a) has emerged as a promising diagnostic platform due to its unique trans-cleavage activity, enabling rapid, sensitive, and portable nucleic acid detection. Numerous studies have applied CRISPR-based tests for HIV detection, but the overall diagnostic accuracy has not been systematically evaluated.

Purpose: This systematic review and meta-analysis aims to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of CRISPR/Cas-based nucleic acid detection tests for HIV. Specifically, we will pool sensitivity, specificity, positive/negative likelihood ratios, diagnostic odds ratio, and summary receiver operating characteristic (SROC) curve with area under the curve (AUC).

Methods: We will search PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, Embase, Cochrane Library, and CNKI from 2017 to present. Studies using CRISPR/Cas technology for HIV nucleic acid detection with RT-qPCR as reference standard will be included. Two reviewers will independently screen studies, extract data, and assess methodological quality using the QUADAS-2 tool. A bivariate random-effects model will be used to pool diagnostic accuracy estimates. Subgroup analyses and meta-regression will be conducted to explore potential sources of heterogeneity.

Expected outcomes: This study will provide the first comprehensive evidence on the diagnostic accuracy of CRISPR/Cas technology for HIV detection, informing clinical practice and guiding future research in point-of-care testing.

title: Accuracy of the Autism Spectrum Quotient in Identifying Autism
description:
The Autism Spectrum Quotient (AQ) is recommended by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) for use in screening and as part of the assessment process for adults suspected of being autistic. However, most psychometric evidence for the 50‑item AQ and its shorter forms comes from case–control studies, in which autistic and non‑autistic participants are recruited in advance based on known diagnostic status. This design inflates estimates of sensitivity, specificity, and overall diagnostic accuracy, because the contrast between groups is artificially maximised and does not reflect the uncertainty present in real clinical pathways.

To inform policy and clinical practice more reliably, there is a need to evaluate the AQ in clinically relevant study designs, where diagnostic status is not known at the point of questionnaire completion, and where participants more closely resemble those encountered in primary care, mental health services, or specialist autism referral pathways. This systematic review and meta-analysis will synthesise psychometric evidence under these conditions to provide a more accurate understanding of how well different AQ versions perform when used for screening in routine practice.

title: Comparative Diagnostic Accuracy of S100B, GFAP, and UCH-L1 for Predicting Neurosurgical Intervention in Traumatic Brain Injury: A Scoping Review Protocol
description:
Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a major global health burden, with millions of emergency department visits annually. A critical clinical challenge is determining which patients with mild-to-moderate TBI require neurosurgical intervention. Current practice relies heavily on CT imaging, which is resource-intensive, costly, and exposes patients to ionising radiation. Blood-based biomarkers have emerged as potential triage tools to complement or reduce reliance on CT, with three candidates—S100B, GFAP, and UCH-L1—receiving regulatory approval in Europe and the United States.
Despite growing literature, the evidence base has notable limitations. First, most meta-analyses use CT positivity as the primary outcome, which does not directly reflect neurosurgical need. Second, biomarker performance is biologically influenced by age, yet few studies stratify results across paediatric, adult, and elderly populations. Third, sex-specific differences in biomarker release and diagnostic accuracy remain largely unexplored, despite plausible biological mechanisms and emerging evidence in concussion research.
This scoping review will systematically map the existing evidence on the diagnostic accuracy of S100B, GFAP, and UCH-L1 for predicting neurosurgical intervention in TBI. Using the PCC framework, we will include studies across all ages and settings, focusing on neurosurgical outcomes as the primary endpoint, while also capturing secondary outcomes such as CT positivity, clinically important TBI composites, functional outcomes, and mortality.
The purpose of this project is to provide a comprehensive overview of the current evidence landscape, identify the extent to which age and sex stratification have been 
addressed, and highlight head-to-head comparisons of biomarkers where available. Expected outcomes include:
- A mapped summary of studies reporting biomarker accuracy for neurosurgical intervention.
- Documentation of whether and how age and sex differences are considered.
- Identification of evidence gaps and methodological limitations.
- A proposed research agenda to guide future primary studies and meta-analyses.
By clarifying what is known and unknown, this review will inform clinicians, researchers, and policymakers about the readiness of blood-based biomarkers for clinical triage in TBI, and provide a foundation for more targeted systematic reviews and evidence-based practice.

title: Evaluating Large Language Models as Classifiers (LLM-as-rater) for Hospital Incident Reports
description:
This research project evaluates the capability of five frontier Large Language Models (LLMs)—ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, DeepSeek, and Mistral—to act as blinded classifiers ("LLM-as-rater") for hospital Incident Reporting (IR). The primary purpose is to assess whether these models can accurately replicate the classification tasks typically performed by human raters, relying exclusively on free-text narrative descriptions (e.g., "Where", "What happened", "How and why it happened", "Description") without access to prior structured human classifications.
The study is designed as an observational, retrospective agreement study based on a source dataset of 1,988 incident reports collected at the Policlinico di Bari (Italy) and its affiliated facilities between 2015 and 2025. To ensure robust evaluation on clinically and medico-legally relevant scenarios, the analysis is conducted on an extended sample of 824 cases. This sample combines a "discriminating core" of 624 difficult cases (which includes all severe harm events, deaths, and cases with inter-rater disagreement or reclassification) and a "population anchor" of 200 random, straightforward cases. Post-stratification weights are then applied to these strata to re-anchor the performance estimates to the real-world population distribution.
The project focuses on three main comparative evaluations:
AI vs. Expert Gold Standard: Measuring the agreement between the model's classification and the final expert consensus.
AI vs. Human Benchmark: Comparing the model's performance against the initial classification provided by the front-line professional who reported the event.
Algorithmovigilance (AI vs. AI): Analyzing cross-model agreement to determine if different models share the same systematic biases or correlated errors, effectively agreeing with each other more often than they agree with human experts.

The primary outcome is the level of agreement on the severity of harm, which is measured on a five-level ordinal scale. Secondary outcomes include:
Accuracy in identifying the specific event type across 16 controlled categories.
Triage capability, measured by the model's sensitivity and specificity in predicting whether a review of the Electronic Health Record (EHR) is necessary.
Confidence calibration, evaluated via the Expected Calibration Error (ECE) to see if a model's stated confidence aligns with its actual accuracy.
An indirect knowledge cutoff probe, testing whether models correctly apply an updated (July 2024) 23-item list of sentinel events from the Italian Ministry of Health instead of the legacy 16-item list.
Expected outcomes include a comprehensive framework for understanding LLM reliability in clinical risk management. The study aims to map specific AI failure modes—such as chronic overconfidence, over-reliance on medical records, or failure to update domain knowledge—and to provide empirical evidence on the phenomenon of "shared bias" among frontier models in a specialized medico-legal context.

title: Potential for use of point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) in primary care – benefits, harms, diagnostic accuracy and education opportunities: an umbrella review
description:
Abstract

Background: One of the greatest challenges in primary care is to make rapid decisions in an unfiltered patient population with usually little technical equipment. Point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) is a relatively new development where the clinician directly performs a focused sonographic examination with a specific question in mind. This could be a valuable adjunct to the clinical examination and could replace other imaging in some situations. 

Objectives: The purpose of this umbrella review is to evaluate benefits, harms, diagnostic accuracy and education opportunities of point-of-care ultrasonography (POCUS) in primary care.

Methods: First, a study protocol with preliminary search terms and eligibility criteria has been created. The study protocol will be registered in the Open Science Framework platform (osf.io). Database search will be conducted in MEDLINE (Ovid) the Cochrane Library (Wiley), epistemonikos.org and Scopus (Elsevier) etc. in September-October 2022. The search will be limited to systematic reviews published since 2012 to 2022 (last 10 years). For searching and reporting, the PRISMA guidelines and the Cochrane Handbook will be taken into consideration.

Significance for public health: The main object of this umbrella review is to draw attention to the potential of point-of-care ultrasound in primary care and to elicit deficits and disadvantages. In addition, current training programs will be evaluated. In this way, areas of application can be meaningfully expanded and future training programs can be etablized to further improve health care in the primary care sector.

title: Problem Representation, Metacognition, and the Limits of Diagnostic Self-Critique in Frontier Language Models
description:
Large language models are increasingly capable diagnosticians, yet they are deployed using simple single-pass prompts that offer no mechanism for self-correction or uncertainty monitoring. A natural intuition, asking the model to critique and revise its own answer, has been shown to degrade rather than improve reasoning performance. This raises a fundamental question: is reflective prompting inherently counterproductive, or does the cognitive structure of the reflection determine whether it helps or hurts?

This preregistered study tests whether prompt architecture, specifically, the presence of problem representation as a structured intermediate reasoning step, determines the direction and magnitude of diagnostic self-correction in frontier language models. We compare three conditions across 50 complex clinical cases from the New England Journal of Medicine Clinical Pathological Conference series: (1) a standard single-pass diagnostic prompt, (2) an adversarial self-critique prompt that asks the model to argue against its own leading diagnosis before revising, and (3) a structured reflection prompt grounded in the Assessment of Reasoning Tool framework, which requires the model to first distill the case into a one-sentence problem representation using semantic qualifiers before conducting a balanced reassessment.

Five frontier models (GPT-5.4, GPT-5.2, Claude Opus 4.5, Claude Sonnet 4.5, and Gemini 3 Pro) are evaluated across all three conditions, yielding 750 model-case-condition observations. The primary outcome is top-1 diagnostic accuracy assessed via an LLM-based scoring system with synonym resolution. Secondary outcomes include confidence calibration (Expected Calibration Error, Brier score with Murphy decomposition), diagnostic switch rates (rescues versus sabotages), and confidence shift directionality between initial and revised assessments.

We hypothesize that adversarial self-critique will reduce diagnostic accuracy relative to baseline by destabilizing correct initial diagnoses, while structured reflection with problem representation will improve accuracy by anchoring downstream reasoning on discriminating clinical features. We further hypothesize that structured reflection will improve confidence calibration and that textual features of the self-critique phase will predict diagnostic switches. Exploratory analyses examine whether reflection benefits scale with model capability, whether baseline confidence moderates the reflection effect, and whether structured prompting improves anchoring resistance on difficult cases.

This work bridges the gap between the general self-correction literature, which has shown that prompted LLMs cannot reliably self-correct without external feedback, and the clinical reasoning literature, which identifies problem representation as the cognitive step that most distinguishes expert from novice diagnosticians. By testing whether transplanting this cognitive structure into a prompt architecture changes the outcome of self-correction, the study offers both a practical contribution (a prompting strategy for clinical AI deployment) and a theoretical one (evidence on whether structured intermediate representations can substitute for the external feedback that self-correction typically requires).

title: Diagnostic Utility of Ultrasound in Peroneal Compression Neuropathy - A Scoping Review
description:
Peroneal compression neuropathy is an increasingly recognized condition that affects gait, balance, and contributes to falls. Despite its clinical significance, there is currently no validated, standardized diagnostic tool comparable to the CTS-6 for carpal tunnel syndrome. This diagnostic gap means many patients with treatable peroneal neuropathy go unidentified and remain at continued risk of morbidity.
Diagnosis relies on a combination of assessments, each with important limitations:
• Physical examination techniques are not widely performed outside of specialist centres
• Gait laboratory analysis is costly and has low accessibility in most clinical settings
• Electrodiagnostic testing (EMG/NCS) is painful, costly, and lacks sensitivity for early-stage compression
Ultrasound (US) has emerged as a promising diagnostic modality for peripheral nerve assessment. It is non-invasive, widely available, inexpensive, and can provide real-time structural information about the nerve including cross-sectional area (CSA), echogenicity, and fascicular architecture. However, the diagnostic accuracy, parameters, and utility of ultrasound specifically for peroneal compression neuropathy have not been systematically mapped.

The primary objective of this scoping review is:
• To map the existing evidence on the diagnostic utility of ultrasound for peroneal compression neuropathy at the fibular head in adults

title: Machine Learning Algorithms for Predicting Outcomes and Complications After Reverse Shoulder Arthroplasty: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
description:
This systematic review and meta-analysis aims to comprehensively evaluate the application of machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI) algorithms for predicting outcomes and complications following reverse shoulder arthroplasty (RSA). Despite the increasing prevalence of RSA in orthopedic practice, predicting individual patient outcomes remains challenging due to complex interactions between patient factors, implant design, surgical technique, and rehabilitation protocols. Traditional statistical methods have demonstrated inherent limitations in capturing these complex, non-linear relationships that influence clinical outcomes.
The primary objective of this study is to systematically evaluate the performance of ML/AI algorithms in predicting complications (instability, infection, notching, loosening) after RSA. Secondary objectives include: (1) assessing predictive accuracy metrics (AUC, sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV) of various ML/AI models; (2) evaluating the generalizability of these models across different populations and healthcare settings; and (3) identifying novel predictive factors not captured by traditional statistical methods.
Adhering to PRISMA guidelines, we will conduct a comprehensive search of electronic databases (PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, Web of Science) from inception to present. The review will include studies applying ML/AI techniques to predict outcomes after RSA, encompassing development and validation studies, comparative algorithm studies, and external validation studies. Two independent reviewers will screen studies, extract data, and assess risk of bias using appropriate tools (PROBAST for prediction model studies).
The investigation will compare different ML/AI algorithms (supervised learning algorithms such as random forests, support vector machines, and neural networks; unsupervised learning algorithms including clustering techniques; deep learning approaches; natural language processing of clinical notes; and computer vision analysis of radiographic images) and their predictive performance, contrasting them with traditional statistical methods. Furthermore, we will evaluate ML/AI models across different patient populations, surgical indications, and data sources (registry data, electronic health records, imaging).
Meta-analysis will be performed for comparable algorithms and outcomes where appropriate. Subgroup analyses will be conducted based on algorithm type, data source, and prediction target. Narrative synthesis will be employed to compare implementation approaches and identify best practices for ML/AI application in RSA outcome prediction.
This represents the first systematic review specifically focusing on ML/AI applications for outcome prediction after RSA. The findings will guide researchers and clinicians in selecting optimal ML/AI approaches for different prediction tasks, identify key data elements needed for accurate prediction, and highlight implementation challenges and solutions. By improving outcome prediction, this work could facilitate more personalized surgical planning, implant selection, and postoperative management, potentially enhancing patient outcomes and optimizing resource utilization. Additionally, the review will establish a roadmap for future ML/AI research in shoulder arthroplasty by identifying knowledge gaps and methodological limitations in existing studies.

title: Plasma p-tau217 and Aβ42/40 in Cognitively Unimpaired Asian Individuals by Amyloid PET Status: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
description:
This project is a systematic review and meta-analysis examining plasma biomarkers in relation to amyloid positron emission tomography (PET) status in cognitively unimpaired Asian individuals. The primary purpose of this study is to clarify the diagnostic utility of plasma p-tau217 and Aβ42/40 for identifying amyloid PET positivity in this population. Secondary objectives are to evaluate between-group differences in biomarker levels according to amyloid PET status and to assess the performance of composite biomarker models, including p-tau217/Aβ42 and combined p-tau217 and Aβ42/40 models.

This project addresses an important evidence gap. Blood-based biomarkers are increasingly recognized as less invasive and more scalable alternatives to amyloid PET for detecting early Alzheimer’s disease pathology. However, most available evidence has been generated in predominantly non-Asian populations, and the performance of these biomarkers in cognitively unimpaired Asian individuals has not yet been comprehensively synthesized. In addition, the currently available literature is methodologically heterogeneous, including not only diagnostic accuracy studies reporting area under the curve (AUC) values, but also studies that permit only group-comparison analyses using standardized mean differences (SMDs). A systematic synthesis is therefore needed to clarify the current evidence base and to identify important sources of between-study variability.

Registration in PROSPERO had originally been planned. However, at the time of protocol development, the public PROSPERO registration system was not accepting new submissions under the diagnostic test accuracy review category. Therefore, this protocol was registered in OSF.

A systematic literature search will be conducted in CENTRAL, PubMed, and CINAHL from database inception to March 25, 2026, without language restrictions. Both published studies and gray literature will be considered. Studies will be considered eligible if they include cognitively unimpaired individuals from Asian populations, determine amyloid status using amyloid PET, and report plasma p-tau217, Aβ42/40, p-tau217/Aβ42, and/or composite biomarker models with sufficient data for quantitative synthesis. Both interventional and observational studies will be eligible; however, for interventional studies, only baseline data collected before treatment initiation will be used. Studies will be excluded if they include mixed populations without separate data for cognitively unimpaired individuals, use cerebrospinal fluid biomarkers only, report only covariate-adjusted diagnostic models without unadjusted performance metrics, include 20 or fewer cognitively unimpaired participants, or primarily enroll participants with major psychiatric, neurologic, or systemic disorders unrelated to cognitive impairment. Studies investigating the prognostic performance of plasma biomarkers for predicting future amyloid PET status will also be excluded, because the review focuses on cross-sectional diagnostic accuracy. When overlapping cohorts are reported across multiple publications using the same assay method, only the most comprehensive dataset will be retained. If the same cohort is evaluated using different assay platforms, each relevant dataset will be included.

Data extraction and risk of bias assessment will be performed by I.T. and independently checked by W.K. Any discrepancies will be resolved through discussion. Extracted variables will include author, publication year, country, cohort name, sample size, age, biomarker assay method, study setting, amyloid PET positivity criterion, area under the curve (AUC), 95% confidence interval (CI), standard error (SE), and summary statistics required for the calculation of standardized mean differences (SMDs). Sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, and negative predictive value will not be quantitatively synthesized because these metrics are strongly influenced by threshold selection and assay variability and are therefore expected to show substantial heterogeneity. Accordingly, AUC will be used as the primary measure of diagnostic performance. When required data are missing, corresponding authors will be contacted by email. If no reply is received within 1 week, SEs for AUC values lacking reported 95% CIs will be estimated using the method of Hanley and McNeil, and 95% CIs will subsequently be calculated as AUC ± 1.96 × SE. When the mean and standard deviation needed for SMD analyses are unavailable, they will be estimated from the median and interquartile range using the methods proposed by Luo et al. and Wan et al.

Because the literature relevant to this clinical question is limited, studies that are not designed as pure diagnostic accuracy studies, as well as studies that do not report AUC and are therefore eligible only for the SMD analysis, may still be included. For this reason, risk of bias will be evaluated using the AXIS tool, which is suitable for a broader range of observational studies, rather than QUADAS-2, which is designed specifically for diagnostic accuracy studies. AXIS has also been used in previous meta-analyses of plasma biomarkers.

Data will be synthesized using frequentist random-effects meta-analysis with the “meta” and “metafor” packages in R (version 4.2.5). Pooled AUC analyses will be conducted to assess the ability of plasma biomarkers to distinguish amyloid PET-positive individuals from amyloid PET-negative individuals. The primary analyses will consist of separate meta-analyses of plasma p-tau217 and Aβ42/40. Secondary analyses will include pooled standardized mean differences between amyloid-positive and amyloid-negative groups for p-tau217 and Aβ42/40, together with pooled AUC analyses of composite biomarkers, including p-tau217/Aβ42 and combined p-tau217 and Aβ42/40 models. For SMD analyses, Hedges g will be used as the effect size. Subgroup analyses will consist of separate pooled AUC analyses for p-tau217 and Aβ42/40 according to assay platform, country, amyloid PET positivity definition, and study setting, provided that at least two studies are available within each subgroup. Statistical heterogeneity will be quantified using the I² statistic. Publication bias will be assessed when at least 10 studies are available for a given analysis.

The expected outcomes of this project are a quantitative summary of the diagnostic accuracy of plasma p-tau217 and Aβ42/40 for amyloid PET status in cognitively unimpaired Asian individuals, an estimate of between-group biomarker differences according to amyloid PET status, and an assessment of the performance of relevant composite biomarker models. More broadly, this project is expected to clarify the current evidence base in Asian populations, identify important sources of heterogeneity across studies, and provide useful information for the design of future validation studies and potential clinical implementation of blood-based biomarkers for preclinical Alzheimer’s disease.

title: SALIVARY BIOMARKERS OF DISEASE PROGRESSION IN SJÖGREN’S SYNDROME: A SCOPING REVIEW
description: This protocol details a scoping review aimed at mapping and synthesizing the available scientific evidence on salivary biomarkers associated with disease progression in Sjögren's Syndrome (SjS). SjS is a complex systemic autoimmune exocrinopathy characterized by progressive lymphocytic infiltration of the exocrine glands, which causes glandular hypofunction and debilitating oral and ocular dryness. While clinical monitoring has traditionally depended on invasive minor salivary gland biopsies, saliva serves as a promising, non-invasive biological matrix capable of providing real-time molecular insights into SjS activity and damage trajectories. Following the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology and PRISMA-ScR reporting guidelines , the review utilizes a strict PCC strategy targeting patients with primary or secondary SjS (Population), salivary biomarkers associated with disease activity and progression (Concept), and any clinical or laboratory setting (Context). Primary observational and experimental human studies published in English, Portuguese, or Spanish will be included , whereas letters, editorial opinions, reviews, in vitro or animal models, and studies focusing solely on initial diagnostic accuracy without progression data will be excluded. Systematic literature searches will be executed across major databases, including PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, LILACS, Cochrane Library, and Google Scholar. Two independent reviewers will handle study selection and data extraction using Rayyan software, with any discrepancies resolved by a senior third reviewer. Finally, the extracted data will undergo both qualitative and quantitative synthesis using descriptive statistics to effectively highlight current research trends, and the clinical translational potential of these salivary biomarkers from the laboratory bench to point-of-care applications.

title: Diagnostic Accuracy of Digital Scanning Compared to Traditional Methods in Dental Alignment Assessment: A Systematic Review
description:
PROBLEM FORMULATION

This study aims to answer the following question, structured by PICO: In patients 
requiring dental alignment assessment (P), is the use of digital scanning (I) more 
accurate in assessing dental alignment compared to traditional methods, such as 
physical impressions and clinical examinations (O), when considering diagnostic 
accuracy (O)?

HYPOTHESIS

The hypothesis of this study is that the digital scanning method will demonstrate 
superior diagnostic accuracy in assessing dental alignment compared to traditional methods such as physical impressions and clinical examinations. It is assumed that digital scanning will provide a more precise and detailed assessment of dental alignment, resulting in more accurate diagnoses for patients.

OBJECTIVE

This study aims to investigate, through a systematic review of the literature, the 
diagnostic accuracy of digital scanning compared to traditional methods in the 
assessment of dental alignment. The systematic review will seek to compare the 
effectiveness of using digital scanning with traditional methods, such as physical molds and clinical examinations, in patients who require dental alignment 
assessment, with emphasis on diagnostic accuracy.

METHODS

The systematic review will be conducted according to the PRISMA 2020 statement (Page et al., 2021). The PICOT elements defined for this study are: population, patients requiring dental alignment assessment; intervention, use of digital scanning for dental alignment assessment; comparison, traditional methods of dental alignment assessment, such as physical impressions and clinical examinations; outcome, diagnostic accuracy in dental alignment assessment; and study type, clinical trial.
The study design will include conducting a systematic search of international 
databases to identify relevant studies published to date. Clear inclusion and 
exclusion criteria will be defined to select studies that meet the objectives of the 
review. Retrieval and extraction of detailed information and data from the included studies will be performed using standardized data collection criteria.
The synthesis of the main findings of the included studies will be performed using 
qualitative methods as appropriate. The results will be summarized following the 
PRISMA guidelines. This method will ensure a rigorous and comprehensive 
assessment of the diagnostic accuracy of digital scanning compared to traditional 
methods in the assessment of dental alignment.

ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA

Only clinical trials that compare digital planning with analogue planning in the 
assessment of dental alignment will be included. Descriptive studies, systematic 
reviews, case reports and in vitro studies will be excluded. In addition, studies that do not use traditional methods of dental alignment assessment, such as physical molds and clinical examinations. Studies investigating alternative technologies or methods that are not directly related to digital or analog planning will also be excluded. The search will be restricted to articles published in English, available in full, with no date limit.

SEARCH

A systematic literature search will be performed in the following databases: 
MEDLINE/PubMed, EMBASE, Cochrane Library and SciELO. Grey literature will also be considered by searching Google Scholar. The search strategy will be based on MeSH terms from PubMed and adapted for other databases. Rayyan software (Rayyan Systems Inc., Cambridge, MA, USA) will be used for the systematic search. Four independent researchers (FMM, GSEC, IBAQ and LFA) will screen the records (titles/abstracts) and select studies that meet all eligibility criteria for full-text reading. Discrepancies will be resolved through discussion or by the opinion of a fifth reviewer (NSF).

DATA EXTRACTION

Four authors (FMM, GSEC, IBAQ and LFA) used a spreadsheet to extract the methodological data of the study. The extracted variables included: author, year of publication, details of the digital scanning procedure (type of scanner, software used), details of the traditional evaluation methods (type of physical mold, clinical examinations) and outcome (diagnostic accuracy).

QUALITY ASSESSMENT AND RISK OF BIAS

The methodological quality and risk of bias of the included studies will be assessed using the adapted Newcastle-Ottawa scale, whose evaluation criteria will include the adequacy of randomization, allocation concealment, and population characterization at selection; comparability of groups at baseline and control of confounding factors in comparability; and blinding of outcome assessment, adequate outcome measurement, and complete follow-up at outcome. Each criterion will be scored, and studies will be classified as high, moderate, or low risk of bias based on the total score, with a score of 7 to 9 points considered low risk of bias, a score of 4 to 6 points considered moderate risk of bias, and a score of 0 to 3 points considered high risk of bias.

title: Early prognostication after severe traumatic brain injury: a multicenter reader study of physician accuracy
description: Decisions to withdrawal life-sustaining treatment following severe TBI are often made within the first 72 hours post-injury. These decisions are typically based on the treating physician's subjective assessment of the likelihood of meaningful neurological recovery. However, the accuracy of such predictions remain poorly validated. We will conduct a multicenter, multireader diagnostic accuracy study using deidentified patient cases from a Level 1 trauma center. We anticipate that physician accuracy will be modest, with substantial variability between readers and potential bias toward early pessimism.

title: From Saliva to Diagnosis: A Scoping Review of Conventional and Biosensor-Based Methods for Salivary Biomarkers in Chronic Kidney Disease
description: This project aims to comprehensively map the available evidence on the use of salivary biomarkers for the detection and monitoring of chronic kidney disease (CKD), comparing their diagnostic performance to conventional blood and urine tests. The project also explores emerging biosensor-based technologies that may enable non-invasive, point-of-care CKD diagnostics. We systematically searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, and Cochrane Library up to July 1, 2025, without language or year restrictions. Eligible studies included adult CKD patients and healthy controls, assessed salivary biomarkers against validated reference standards, and reported diagnostic accuracy measures. Data synthesis highlights creatinine and urea as the most validated salivary biomarkers, with novel candidates such as TMAO, cystatin C, and specific amino acids showing promise for early detection. Findings underscore the need for standardization, broader clinical validation, and integration into dental workflows for effective CKD screening.

Emerging home-based sleep apnea testing, wearable sensors, non-contact monitoring, and artificial intelligence-enabled diagnostic algorithms may support lower-burden diagnosis, triage, or follow-up in children. This systematic review will synthesize the patient-level diagnostic accuracy of AI-enabled, home-based, wearable, and other low-burden objective diagnostic technologies for pediatric obstructive sleep apnea compared with polysomnography. title: Feasibility and Clinical Utility of Quantitative EEG (qEEG) in Paediatric Intensive Care: A Scoping Review
description:
Monitoring brain function in critically ill children is an essential yet complex component of pediatric intensive care. EEG provides real-time insight into cerebral electrical activity and helps clinicians detect seizures, assess background patterns, and guide neurologic management. Standard EEG offers only a brief snapshot. Continuous EEG (cEEG) extends monitoring over hours or days, increasing detection of non-convulsive seizures and evolving injury.

Quantitative EEG (qEEG) advances this further by transforming raw EEG signals into simplified trends using automated algorithms. This allows clinicians to evaluate frequency bands, symmetry, suppression patterns, sleep–wake cycling, and potential seizure activity at the bedside. qEEG has also been used to guide therapeutic goals such as achieving burst suppression during anticonvulsant therapy.

Although pediatric data remain limited, early studies suggest qEEG can support seizure detection, prognostication, and neurological monitoring across a range of PICU populations, including hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy and post–cardiac arrest care. Successful implementation requires structured training, particularly in artifact recognition, but when used appropriately qEEG offers strong sensitivity and specificity for seizure detection and meaningful real-time information.

A major consideration is feasibility. The value of qEEG depends on whether it can be integrated into busy PICU workflows, interpreted reliably by frontline staff, and used to guide actionable clinical decisions. Current studies vary in design, sample size, qEEG modalities, and analytic approaches, making a comprehensive evidence map essential.

This scoping review aims to synthesize existing evidence on qEEG feasibility, clinical utility, and outcomes in the PICU, providing practical guidance for teams—including those without on-site neurophysiology support—seeking to enhance neurological monitoring.

Review Question:

What evidence exists on the feasibility, clinical utility, and outcomes of quantitative EEG in pediatric intensive care patients aged 0–18 years?

PCC Framework:

Population: 
Children aged 0–18 years cared for in a PICU. Studies involving NICU-only infants, adults, or non-PICU settings will be excluded. Any diagnosis is eligible as long as qEEG is used during critical illness.

Concept:
Quantitative EEG used for neurological monitoring, seizure detection, background assessment, or clinical decision-making. qEEG modalities may include spectral analysis, amplitude-integrated EEG, seizure detection algorithms, asymmetry indices, suppression assessment, and similar tools. Studies must report feasibility, clinical utility, or patient outcomes.

Context:
The PICU clinical environment. Studies must involve real-world or clinically relevant qEEG use. Research conducted outside PICU settings, in outpatient clinics, or for elective neurophysiology or psychiatric purposes will be excluded.

Types of Evidence:
Eligible sources include randomized trials, quasi-experimental studies, cohort studies, case–control studies, cross-sectional studies, case series, case reports, qualitative studies, systematic reviews, and text or opinion papers addressing qEEG in the PICU.

Timeframe:
Studies published between 2015 and 2025, in English or with English abstracts, will be included.

Outcomes:
Feasibility (training, implementation, workflow integration), clinical utility (seizure detection, background interpretation, prognostication), and any impact on clinical decision-making or patient outcomes.

Methods:

This scoping review will follow the JBI methodology, which includes defining the research question, aligning inclusion criteria, and outlining the planned approach to searching, selecting, extracting, and presenting evidence. Once the review begins, the remaining steps will include conducting the search, screening evidence, extracting data, analyzing and mapping results, and summarizing key findings.

If the protocol is formally registered (e.g., OSF), the registration details will be provided to ensure transparency.

Search Strategy:

A comprehensive search strategy was developed with a professional medical librarian. Searches were conducted on November 11, 2025, in:

Ovid MEDLINE

Embase and Embase Classic

Cochrane CENTRAL

APA PsycInfo

SCOPUS

WHO Global Index Medicus

Searches used controlled vocabulary and keywords and were limited to English-language publications from 2015–2025. A full strategy will be included in the Appendix.

Study Selection:

All search results will be imported into Covidence for deduplication and screening. Titles and abstracts will be reviewed independently by two reviewers. Full texts of potentially relevant studies will then be assessed. Disagreements will be resolved by discussion or a third reviewer. Reasons for exclusion will be documented, and a PRISMA diagram will summarize the selection process.

Data Extraction:

A structured extraction form will be developed and piloted. Extracted information will include:

Study characteristics

Patient population

qEEG modality and variables

Purpose and timing of monitoring

Outcomes related to feasibility, clinical utility, or patient care

Key findings and limitations

One reviewer will review all the data and then two reviewers will extract data independently. Any revisions to the extraction tool will be reported.

Data Analysis and Presentation

Data will be synthesized narratively and visually (figures and summary sections). Findings will highlight feasibility, clinical utility, workflow integration, patient outcomes, and gaps in the current evidence base.

title: Use of non-mainstream features across contexts: changes across early elementary school
description:
Developmental Language Disorder (DLD) is one of the most common learning disorders
and affects between 7% and 9% of children (Tomblin, et al., 1997). DLD is often under-identified in children who speak a mainstream dialect, but both false-positives and false negatives are common in children who speak non-mainstream dialects, such as African
American English (AAE) (Green, 2011). This leads to a serious problem in potentially
misallocated resources (Green, 2011). Recent research suggests that diagnostic
accuracy can be improved if we compare language use to that of typically-developing
peers who speak the same dialect (Oetting & Newkirk, 2008; Oetting, 2018). This
Disorder within Diversity Framework requires an in-depth understanding of language use
by typically developing children as their language use is the benchmark for determining
whether children have DLD. There has been an increase in the number of studies on
NMAE, including research from diverse fields such as linguistics (e.g., Van Hofwegen &
Wolfram, 2010), education (e.g., Terry, Connor, Thomas-Tate, & Love), and
communication sciences (Oetting, Lee, & Porter, 2013). Yet implementing within-dialect
comparisons remains difficult due to the limited research on NMAE use, specifically how
use changes across development and contexts, and the factors related to the individual
differences in use of NMAE features.
The project addresses two specific aims 1) determine the frequency of
use of NMAE features by typically developing children across conversational contexts
and grades and 2) determine the factors relating to the use of NMAE features in school
contexts.

title: Comparison of Clinical Test Findings and Arthroscopic Findings in Frozen Shoulder: A Scoping Review
description:
Purpose and Scope
This scoping review aims to map and synthesize the existing body of literature exploring the relationship between physical/clinical examination findings and arthroscopic observations in patients with Frozen Shoulder (Adhesive Capsulitis).

While physical examination is the clinical cornerstone for diagnosis—typically focusing on global restrictions in active and passive range of motion (ROM)—there is a recognized diagnostic gap. Current evidence suggests a potential lack of high predictive value in these clinical tests when compared to the "gold standard" of arthroscopy. This review will specifically investigate how clinical markers (such as the Coracoid Pain Test and specific ROM patterns) correlate with intra-articular pathological changes (such as capsular thickening, synovitis, and fibrosis of the rotator interval).

Methodology
Following the JBI Manual for Evidence Synthesis and the PCC (Population, Concept, Context) framework, this review will include:

Population: Adults (≥18 years) with a clinical diagnosis of Frozen Shoulder.

Concept: The correlation between non-invasive physical maneuvers and invasive arthroscopic findings.

Context: Clinical and surgical settings globally.

A systematic search will be conducted across PubMed, Scopus, Cochrane Library, and Google Scholar for studies published from the year 2000 onwards. Data selection and extraction will be performed by three independent reviewers to ensure high reliability and transparency.

Expected Outcomes
The primary outcome of this research is to produce a comprehensive map of diagnostic accuracy. Specifically, the study expects to:

Identify High-Value Clinical Markers: Determine which physical tests (e.g., loss of external rotation vs. coracoid palpation) show the strongest correlation with arthroscopic evidence of disease.

Highlight Knowledge Gaps: Identify inconsistencies in current diagnostic protocols where clinical findings may fail to predict surgical reality.

Refine Diagnostic Pathways: Provide a synthesis that aids clinicians in making more accurate, evidence-based diagnoses without immediate reliance on invasive procedures or expensive imaging.

Significance
By validating the diagnostic value of clinical tests against arthroscopic findings, this study seeks to improve cost-effectiveness and patient outcomes in the management of Adhesive Capsulitis, particularly in resource-limited settings where advanced imaging is unavailable.
