title: Scoping Review Protocol on blood-based diagnostic biomarkers in borderline ovarian tumors (BOT) and stage I ovarian cancer
description:
The present scoping review aims to identify and map existing evidence on blood-based biomarkers that have been studied for their diagnostic or predictive value in borderline ovarian tumors (BOT) or stage I invasive ovarian cancer. We will include all observational studies and/or randomized controlled trials (RCT), investigating blood-based biomarkers used for diagnostic purposes in patients with BOT or stage I invasive ovarian cancer. Biomarkers must be measured in blood-derived samples such as serum, plasma, whole blood, or circulating nucleic acids (e.g., miRNA, cfDNA), regardless of diagnostic confirmation
method or study design.

We will consider all studies with available data, such as specificity, sensitivity, and area under the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve. We will also include case reports and conference presentations if available. 
Studies will be excluded if they evaluate biomarkers derived from non-blood sources (e.g., tumor tissue, ascitic fluid), focus on prognostic or therapeutic monitoring rather than diagnostic purposes, or investigate advanced-stage ovarian cancer (FIGO stage III–IV) unless included solely as a comparator group.

Data will be extracted on biomarker type, detection method, study design, tumor stage, and diagnostic metrics. Risk of bias will be assessed using QUADAS-2. No meta-analysis will be performed; instead, a descriptive synthesis will summarize biomarker types, diagnostic performance, and methodological variability. Subgroup analysis will explore biomarker categories (e.g., protein, miRNA, cytokine) and histological subtypes (e.g., serous, mucinous).

title: Eye-Tracking in Attachment and Trauma Disorders: A Scoping Review
description:
This scoping review aims to map and synthesise the existing literature on the use of eye-tracking technology as a diagnostic aid for trauma- and stressor-related disorders, specifically Reactive Attachment Disorder (RAD), Disinhibited Social Engagement Disorder (DSED), Acute Stress Disorder (ASD), and Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD). Misdiagnosis between these disorders is common due to overlapping symptoms, subjective clinical judgment, and a lack of objective biomarkers. Eye-tracking, which measures visual attention patterns such as fixations, saccades, and gaze aversion, may offer a non-invasive, quantifiable tool to improve diagnostic accuracy.

Following PRISMA-ScR and JBI guidelines, we will systematically search six major databases and Google Scholar for empirical studies using eye-tracking in individuals with a primary diagnosis of RAD, DSED, ASD, or PTSD. Data will be extracted in duplicate, coded in ATLAS.ti, and synthesised thematically to identify the scope, methodological trends, and potential diagnostic indicators emerging from the literature.

Expected outcomes include:

- A comprehensive overview of how eye-tracking has been applied in these disorders.

- Identification of methodological strengths and gaps in the existing research.

- Preliminary insights into whether eye-tracking measures can help differentiate between attachment- and trauma-related disorders.

- The findings will inform future research design and may contribute to the development of more objective, reliable diagnostic tools in child and adolescent mental health.

title: Evaluation of Diagnostic Tests for Canine Ehrlichiosis in Latin America: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis (2010–2025)
description: Canine ehrlichiosis is a disease caused by Gram-negative, obligate intracellular bacteria, primarily transmitted by the tick Rhipicephalus sanguineus (Vieira et al., 2011). Ehrlichia canis infection can occur in dogs regardless of sex or age; however, some studies suggest a predisposition in certain breeds, as well as greater susceptibility in immunocompromised individuals, such as puppies and geriatric animals (Jane E. Sykes, 2023). This systematic review aims to evaluate the sensitivity and specificity of the main tests used for the diagnosis of E. canis in dogs, based on studies that adopt a reference standard. To date, there are no published systematic reviews on the diagnostic accuracy of this disease, particularly in the context of Latin America. This systematic review will follow the PRISMA-DTA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses of Diagnostic Test Accuracy Studies) guidelines (McInnes et al., 2018; Salameh et al., 2020), with a focus on diagnostic accuracy studies. The eligibility criteria were defined based on the PICOS framework (Population, Index test, Comparator, Outcome, Study design). The search will cover studies addressing diagnostic methods for canine ehrlichiosis in Latin American populations. Reviewers will conduct a systematic search in relevant databases. Study selection, screening, and data extraction will be performed using the Rayyan QCRI tool. The methodological quality of the included studies will be assessed using the QUADAS-2 (Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies) tool, as recommended for systematic reviews of diagnostic accuracy(Whiting et al., 2011). Extracted data will be analyzed and synthesized descriptively, aiming to map existing evidence and highlight gaps in the literature. The results will be presented through infographics, tables, and charts to facilitate visualization of the findings.

title: Systematic Review on Sexual Dimorphism by Tomographic Analysis of the Orbital Region
description:
This systematic review protocol aims to evaluate the presence and degree of sexual dimorphism in the orbital region through morphometric and morphological analyses obtained from computed tomography (CT) images. The orbital cavity is increasingly being investigated in forensic anthropology due to its resistance to trauma and its potential to exhibit sex-based anatomical variations.
The review will include cross-sectional studies that assessed adult individuals using CT imaging, reporting either linear orbital measurements (e.g., height, width, interorbital distance) or morphological descriptors relevant to sex estimation. When available, measures of diagnostic accuracy—such as sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, and area under the ROC curve—will be extracted and synthesized. Odds ratios (ORs) will be used as the primary effect measure for associations between orbital metrics and sex classification.
A comprehensive search will be conducted in eight international databases and grey literature sources. Risk of bias will be assessed using the AQUA tool (Anatomical Quality Assessment). Where feasible, a meta-analysis will be performed using a random-effects model, and heterogeneity will be explored through subgroup analyses, particularly considering sex, age group, and population.
This protocol was developed following best practices for systematic reviews and incorporates key methodological refinements based on existing high-impact literature in forensic and anatomical sciences. The findings are expected to contribute robust evidence for the development of sex estimation models based on orbital morphology and morphometry.

title: Advancing Diagnostic Accuracy: Conceptual and Operational Definitions of “Ineffective Breathing Pattern” (00032) in Cardiac Surgery Recovery
description: This project represents the first phase of a methodological study aimed at developing conceptual and operational definitions for the defining characteristics and related factors of the NANDA International nursing diagnosis Ineffective Breathing Pattern (00032) in patients recovering from cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass. This phase consists of a scoping review conducted according to PRISMA-ScR guidelines, which identified 12 relevant studies. The findings highlight common postoperative respiratory changes and support the development of population‑specific definitions, while also revealing important gaps that justify expert validation and future clinical research.

title: Differences in Intraoperative Management of Patients with a Diagnosis versus Misdiagnosis Related to Heart Failure
description: Single-center observational study of patients undergoing major non-cardiac surgery with general anesthesia. A clinical diagnosis of heart failure was determined by diagnosis codes and keywords within the anesthesiology history and clinical examination. An adjudicated diagnosis of heart failure was determined by a panel of physicians routinely involved in the care of patients with heart failure (cardiologists, cardiac anesthesiologists, intensivists). Practice patterns and outcomes were studied among patients in whom an accurate diagnosis of heart failure (clinical diagnosis = adjudicated diagnosis) versus those with a misdiagnosis (clinical diagnosis >< adjudicated diagnosis).

title: Hearing screening in older adults with diabetes: identifying the most reliable methods
description: This project is a systematic review aimed at identifying, describing, and comparing hearing screening methods used in older adults with diabetes mellitus, assessing their diagnostic accuracy and effectiveness for early detection of hearing loss. Hearing loss is a common yet often underdiagnosed condition among older adults with diabetes, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. Given the association between diabetes and microvascular and neuropathic changes that affect auditory function, effective screening is essential for timely intervention and improved quality of life. The review will follow strict eligibility criteria and draw on multiple databases (including PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and LILACS), with methodological quality assessed using the QUADAS-2 tool. The findings are expected to support the identification of the most reliable and feasible hearing screening methods for this specific population, contributing to improved auditory health care practices.

title: Scoping Review Protocol: Evidence and Gaps in the Interpretation of Patch Test Results for Allergic Contact Dermatitis in Skin of Colour
description:
Allergic contact dermatitis (ACD) is a common inflammatory dermatosis with substantial effects on patient quality of life and healthcare systems. Patch testing is the diagnostic gold standard for identifying causative allergens. Interpretation of patch test reactions is guided by recommendations from the International Contact Dermatitis Research Group (ICDRG), which rely primarily on visual assessment of erythema, infiltration, papulation and vesiculation, together with consideration of temporal evolution and clinical relevance.
However, existing interpretive frameworks are largely derived from studies conducted in predominantly White populations. Individuals with skin of colour (SOC) are underrepresented in foundational patch testing literature, educational resources and consensus statements. Morphological expressions of inflammation differ in more heavily pigmented skin, where erythema may be subtle or violaceous, vesiculation less conspicuous, and lichenification, induration or post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation more prominent. These differences may complicate grading and risk misclassification or underdiagnosis.
Compounding this challenge is the inconsistent definition of “skin of colour” in the literature. Studies variably use race, ethnicity, geographic ancestry or Fitzpatrick phototype to classify participants. The Fitzpatrick skin type scale, originally developed to predict sunburn risk and guide phototherapy dosing, does not reliably correlate with race and has recognised limitations. The use of social constructs as proxies for pigmentation introduces methodological and interpretive ambiguity.
The existing literature addressing patch test interpretation in SOC is limited and heterogeneous, including observational studies, reviews, guidelines and expert opinion. The scope, characteristics and methodological approaches of this evidence base have not been comprehensively mapped.
The purpose of this scoping review is to systematically identify, characterise and synthesise the available literature on the interpretation of patch test results for ACD in individuals with SOC. Specifically, this review aims to:
1. Examine how SOC is defined and operationalised in studies addressing patch test interpretation.
2. Describe the clinical features, morphological descriptors and grading systems used in interpreting patch test reactions in SOC.
3. Identify reported diagnostic challenges, limitations or proposed adaptations.
4. Characterise study designs, populations, clinical settings and geographic distribution of the literature.
5. Map evidence gaps and areas requiring further research.

The review will follow guidance from the Joanna Briggs Institute and will be reported in accordance with the PRISMA extension for scoping reviews (PRISMA-ScR). A comprehensive search will be conducted across MEDLINE (via PubMed), Embase, Scopus and CINAHL, supplemented by reference list screening and targeted grey literature searches. Quantitative, qualitative and mixed-methods studies, as well as reviews and consensus statements, will be eligible. No date restrictions will be imposed; English-language publications will be included.
Findings will be synthesised descriptively and presented in narrative and tabular formats to map conceptual approaches, areas of consensus and variability, and methodological patterns. No formal critical appraisal will be undertaken, consistent with scoping review methodology.
This review seeks to provide a structured overview of the evidence base, clarify conceptual ambiguities and inform future research, education and guideline development aimed at improving diagnostic accuracy and equity in dermatologic care.

title: Comparison of echocardiography and CT angiography for detection of cardiac thrombi in ischemic stroke: A protocol for systematic review and meta-analysis
description: Investigation of potential embolic sources is an important diagnostic step in managing patients with acute ischemic stroke. However, the diagnostic yield and diagnostic accuracy of cardiac CT angiography (CTA) for detection of cardiac thrombi in stroke patients, compared to echocardiography remains controversial. Our aim was to study the diagnostic yield and diagnostic accuracy of CTA for detection of cardiac thrombi in stroke patients, compared to two dimensional echocardiography, by performing a protocol for systematic review and meta-analysis.

title: Validez diagnóstica de las pruebas diagnósticas para porfirias hepáticas: Revisión de alcance
description:
Purpose
Acute Hepatic Porphyria (AHP) is a group of rare, often underdiagnosed, metabolic disorders that can cause severe neurological complications (such as neurovisceral pain, seizures, and paralysis) if not diagnosed and treated promptly.

In emergency or inpatient settings, rapid diagnosis is a challenge. Qualitative rapid urine tests, such as the Watson-Schwartz test and the Hoesch test, have historically been used as initial screening tools, especially in low-resource settings. However, there is considerable uncertainty about their reliability, and some guidelines (such as the British and Irish Porphyria Network) do not recommend them due to reports of low sensitivity and specificity.


The purpose of this project is to conduct a scoping review to identify and describe the available scientific evidence on the diagnostic validity (sensitivity and specificity) of these rapid qualitative tests.


Research Description
This study is a Scoping Review that will follow the methodology proposed by the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI).

The general objective is to describe the internal and external validity characteristics of rapid qualitative tests used for the detection of acute hepatic porphyrias in adult patients (18 years or older). The review will focus on studies conducted in the context of emergency departments, hospital admission, and intensive care units (ICUs).

A systematic and comprehensive search of the literature published in the last 10 years will be conducted in databases such as MEDLINE, Embase, LILACS, Cochrane Database, and SCOPUS, as well as grey literature (Google Scholar) . Three independent reviewers will perform the screening and data extraction.


Expected Outcomes
The results of this review are expected to provide a clear synthesis of the current evidence on the reliability of rapid qualitative tests. Specifically, the outcomes will allow for:

Synthesizing Diagnostic Validity: To understand and summarize the reported data on sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), and negative predictive value (NPV) of the tests (e.g., Hoesch, Watson-Schwartz).

Informing Clinical Practice: To establish with greater reliability whether the use of these tests is justified in emergency services to confirm or rule out the clinical suspicion of AHP.

Identifying Knowledge Gaps: To determine if the validity of these tests has been adequately studied in the relevant clinical contexts (emergency, ICU) or if the current evidence is limited, inconsistent, or outdated.


Guiding Future Research: If it is confirmed that the validity of current tests is not as expected, the results will "open a door to generate the need to establish new initial diagnostic tools" that offer greater reliability, with the ultimate goal of reducing the high morbidity and mortality associated with undiagnosed acute porphyria attacks.

title: Accuracy of the Autism Spectrum Quotient in Identifying Autism
description:
The Autism Spectrum Quotient (AQ) is recommended by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) for use in screening and as part of the assessment process for adults suspected of being autistic. However, most psychometric evidence for the 50‑item AQ and its shorter forms comes from case–control studies, in which autistic and non‑autistic participants are recruited in advance based on known diagnostic status. This design inflates estimates of sensitivity, specificity, and overall diagnostic accuracy, because the contrast between groups is artificially maximised and does not reflect the uncertainty present in real clinical pathways.

To inform policy and clinical practice more reliably, there is a need to evaluate the AQ in clinically relevant study designs, where diagnostic status is not known at the point of questionnaire completion, and where participants more closely resemble those encountered in primary care, mental health services, or specialist autism referral pathways. This systematic review and meta-analysis will synthesise psychometric evidence under these conditions to provide a more accurate understanding of how well different AQ versions perform when used for screening in routine practice.

Diagnostic Accuracy of Digital Scanning Compared to Traditional Methods in Dental Alignment Assessment: A Systematic Review
description:
PROBLEM FORMULATION

This study aims to answer the following question, structured by PICO: In patients 
requiring dental alignment assessment (P), is the use of digital scanning (I) more 
accurate in assessing dental alignment compared to traditional methods, such as 
physical impressions and clinical examinations (O), when considering diagnostic 
accuracy (O)?

HYPOTHESIS

The hypothesis of this study is that the digital scanning method will demonstrate 
superior diagnostic accuracy in assessing dental alignment compared to traditional methods such as physical impressions and clinical examinations. It is assumed that digital scanning will provide a more precise and detailed assessment of dental alignment, resulting in more accurate diagnoses for patients.

OBJECTIVE

This study aims to investigate, through a systematic review of the literature, the 
diagnostic accuracy of digital scanning compared to traditional methods in the 
assessment of dental alignment. The systematic review will seek to compare the 
effectiveness of using digital scanning with traditional methods, such as physical molds and clinical examinations, in patients who require dental alignment 
assessment, with emphasis on diagnostic accuracy.

METHODS

The systematic review will be conducted according to the PRISMA 2020 statement (Page et al., 2021). The PICOT elements defined for this study are: population, patients requiring dental alignment assessment; intervention, use of digital scanning for dental alignment assessment; comparison, traditional methods of dental alignment assessment, such as physical impressions and clinical examinations; outcome, diagnostic accuracy in dental alignment assessment; and study type, clinical trial.
The study design will include conducting a systematic search of international 
databases to identify relevant studies published to date. Clear inclusion and 
exclusion criteria will be defined to select studies that meet the objectives of the 
review. Retrieval and extraction of detailed information and data from the included studies will be performed using standardized data collection criteria.
The synthesis of the main findings of the included studies will be performed using 
qualitative methods as appropriate. The results will be summarized following the 
PRISMA guidelines. This method will ensure a rigorous and comprehensive 
assessment of the diagnostic accuracy of digital scanning compared to traditional 
methods in the assessment of dental alignment.

ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA

Only clinical trials that compare digital planning with analogue planning in the 
assessment of dental alignment will be included. Descriptive studies, systematic 
reviews, case reports and in vitro studies will be excluded. In addition, studies that do not use traditional methods of dental alignment assessment, such as physical molds and clinical examinations. Studies investigating alternative technologies or methods that are not directly related to digital or analog planning will also be excluded. The search will be restricted to articles published in English, available in full, with no date limit.

SEARCH

A systematic literature search will be performed in the following databases: 
MEDLINE/PubMed, EMBASE, Cochrane Library and SciELO. Grey literature will also be considered by searching Google Scholar. The search strategy will be based on MeSH terms from PubMed and adapted for other databases. Rayyan software (Rayyan Systems Inc., Cambridge, MA, USA) will be used for the systematic search. Four independent researchers (FMM, GSEC, IBAQ and LFA) will screen the records (titles/abstracts) and select studies that meet all eligibility criteria for full-text reading. Discrepancies will be resolved through discussion or by the opinion of a fifth reviewer (NSF).

DATA EXTRACTION

Four authors (FMM, GSEC, IBAQ and LFA) used a spreadsheet to extract the methodological data of the study. The extracted variables included: author, year of publication, details of the digital scanning procedure (type of scanner, software used), details of the traditional evaluation methods (type of physical mold, clinical examinations) and outcome (diagnostic accuracy).

QUALITY ASSESSMENT AND RISK OF BIAS

The methodological quality and risk of bias of the included studies will be assessed using the adapted Newcastle-Ottawa scale, whose evaluation criteria will include the adequacy of randomization, allocation concealment, and population characterization at selection; comparability of groups at baseline and control of confounding factors in comparability; and blinding of outcome assessment, adequate outcome measurement, and complete follow-up at outcome. Each criterion will be scored, and studies will be classified as high, moderate, or low risk of bias based on the total score, with a score of 7 to 9 points considered low risk of bias, a score of 4 to 6 points considered moderate risk of bias, and a score of 0 to 3 points considered high risk of bias.

title: Data collection and analysis from the Informatics Department of the Unified Health System in Brazil, using open source programming languages: a scoping review
description:
1 INTRODUCTION
The consolidation of the Brazilian Unified Health System (SUS) brought with it the need to develop instruments capable of recording, organizing, and providing information to support health management (Lima et al., 2009). Since its creation, SUS has required information systems capable of consolidating data in a structured and standardized manner, supporting both epidemiological surveillance and health planning. In this process, the Department of Informatics of SUS (DATASUS) assumed a strategic role by gathering, processing, and providing nationwide data, becoming one of the main sources of information for managers, researchers, and health professionals (Brazil, 2020a).
The availability of reliable and accessible data is a central requirement for public policy formulation, indicator evaluation, and the development of research in public health (Costa et al., 2025). However, the use of these databases still faces challenges related to the decentralization of sources, heterogeneity of records, data quality, and periodic system updates, which may limit their applicability in more complex analyses (Brazil, 2020a).
To overcome these limitations, the National Health Information and Informatics Policy (PNIIS) and the Digital Health Strategy for Brazil 2020–2028 (ESD28) have established guidelines focused on information governance, interoperability, and strengthening the technological infrastructure of SUS (Brazil, 2020b).
Established in 2004, the PNIIS defined principles for the use of Information and Communication Technologies within SUS, emphasizing the integration of national information systems, improvement of data quality, and strengthening of health management (Brazil, 2004). These guidelines were later updated to incorporate goals related to interoperability and information governance (Brazil, 2021).
Among the structuring initiatives for the modernization of SUS, the National Health Data Network (RNDS) stands out as a central platform integrating information from different systems and levels of care, promoting interoperability and providing essential data to support decision-making. Other initiatives include SUS Digital, through the “Meu SUS Digital” tool, and the PQDAS Program, which standardizes and improves the quality of supplementary health data in alignment with SUS data (Brazil; Ministry of Health; Secretariat of Digital Health Information, 2024).
The adoption of digital technologies not only modernizes infrastructure but also transforms the interaction between citizens, professionals, and managers, increasing efficiency and integration of care. This approach represents the evolution of the concept of eHealth, expanding the use of digital resources beyond service informatization. Technologies such as artificial intelligence, big data, telemedicine, wearable devices, and mobile applications have been used to improve management, access, and quality of care (World Health Organization, 2021).
According to the Ministry of Health (Brazil, 2020a), DATASUS integrates systems covering various areas of health care, such as the Hospital Information System (SIH), Ambulatory Information System (SIA), Mortality Information System (SIM), Live Birth Information System (SINASC), and the Notifiable Diseases Information System (SINAN), among others.
Despite the breadth of these databases, challenges persist regarding data quality, updating, standardization, and interoperability, which may limit reliable analyses and evidence-based decision-making. Ensuring efficient integration among systems is essential so that managers and professionals have access to consistent and up-to-date information.
Data collection and management in Brazil are directly linked to PNIIS and ESD28. While PNIIS establishes standards for organization, integration, and governance of health information, ESD28 defines priorities for digital technology use, including interoperability, professional training, and innovation. The articulation between these initiatives allows DataSUS data to be used strategically at different management levels (Brazil, 2020b; Costa et al., 2025).
Access to public health data in Brazil has advanced significantly, even before the Access to Information Law (LAI) came into effect in 2012. Tools such as TabNet and TabWin, developed by DATASUS, enable the creation of tables, graphs, and indicators to support epidemiological analyses (Saldanha et al., 2019; Silva, 2009). TabNet allows quick tabulations from public data, while TabWin enables microdata import and spatial representations.
Despite their usefulness, these tools have operational limitations, require specific training, and demand repetition of procedures for each new period analyzed. In this context, programming code emerges as an alternative to automate, speed up, and standardize data collection and processing.
The increased availability of SUS microdata, combined with the expansion of digital health tools, has driven the adoption of open-source programming languages for data manipulation and analysis (Costa et al., 2025). These languages enhance scientific reproducibility, integration with public databases, and automation of complex analyses such as risk modeling and time series (Wilson et al., 2014).
Despite these advances, there is a knowledge gap regarding systematic mapping of the use of open-source programming specifically applied to DATASUS. While isolated studies exist, comprehensive discussions of methods and tools remain scarce. The scoping review by Restrepo et al. (2023) on open health datasets in Latin America highlights this gap.
Although DataSUS has consolidated itself as a national repository, challenges such as heterogeneity, lack of standardization, variable data quality, and integration difficulties between systems still limit reproducibility.
At the same time, there is growing use of open-source programming in health data science. However, a systematic mapping is needed to identify how these tools are applied to DataSUS, which methods are used, and which gaps remain.
The absence of this overview hinders the consolidation of best practices and the development of more accessible technological solutions. Therefore, conducting a scoping review to systematize existing knowledge is necessary to support open science, improve public health analyses, and strengthen evidence-based decision-making within SUS.

2 OBJECTIVE
To map the evidence in the scientific literature on the use of open-source programming for the collection and analysis of data from Brazilian Health Information Systems.

3 METHOD
3.1 Study Design
This study consists of a scoping review, characterized as applied research with a technological development approach. The review will be conducted in accordance with the recommendations of the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses – Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR), aiming to ensure methodological rigor, transparency, and greater detail in the conduct and reporting of the study.
3.2 Data Sources
The databases selected for this review are: PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, Scopus, IEEE Xplore, LILACS, BVS (Virtual Health Library), Google Scholar, and the Brazilian Digital Library of Theses and Dissertations (BDTD). 
The choice of these databases is justified by their relevance to the topic, coverage of high-quality journals, and multidisciplinary scope. While databases such as PubMed, Embase, and LILACS are specialized in health and biomedical sciences, Scopus and Web of Science provide a multidisciplinary perspective, and IEEE Xplore contributes the necessary technical focus for topics related to programming and data analysis. Searches will also be conducted in Google Scholar and BDTD to capture gray literature not indexed in journal databases.
3.3 Identifying the Research Question 
The first step consists of formulating a well-focused research question, with the objective of mapping what has already been published on the use of open-source programming languages and tools in the context of DATASUS, as well as identifying potential gaps in the existing literature. 
Research question: What evidence is available in the literature on the use of open-source programming languages for the collection, extraction, and analysis of DATASUS data? 
Based on this guiding question, it will be possible to identify the most commonly used open-source programming languages for the collection and analysis of DATASUS data, recognize the libraries, frameworks, or tools frequently employed in these processes, and understand the main methods and techniques used for data collection, extraction, and analysis. Moreover, through this scoping review, it will be possible to map the key challenges reported in the literature regarding the use of open-source programming for working with DATASUS data, thereby contributing to a broader understanding of the topic.
3.4 Identifying the Most Significant Terms in the Question
To identify the most relevant terms present in the research question, a concept mapping was carried out a structured methodology aimed at identifying and organizing the key elements of a research question. The objective of concept mapping is to translate the identified concepts into search terms (keywords and controlled descriptors), which will be used in databases. This approach is essential to ensure that the search strategy is comprehensive, precise, and aligned with the research objectives, being especially useful in systematic reviews, scoping reviews, and other types of literature reviews.
From this research question, the main elements identified were: terms related to open-source programming languages, data collection, extraction, analysis, and DataSUS. To structure the search strategy, the PCC (Population, Concept, and Context) framework was used, which best represents the components of the research. This structuring allows for a more targeted and efficient search, ensuring that the results obtained are aligned with the research objectives and cover the essential aspects of the investigated topic, as presented in Table 1 describing the PCC strategy.


The process of mapping and refining terms, using the main term and the translation of terms between DeCS (Health Sciences Descriptors) and MeSH (Medical Subject Headings), is a robust methodological approach to ensure that the search strategy is comprehensive and precise, facilitating the retrieval of articles in bibliographic databases. 
3.5 Search Strategy
The search terms will be defined based on subject descriptors from the databases using the Health Sciences Descriptors (DeCS) and Medical Subject Headings (MeSH). 
The search strategies were adapted for each database, using controlled descriptors (MeSH, DeCS) and Boolean operators (AND, OR). The construction of the search strategy was carried out in two steps: first, the terms related to each concept were combined using the Boolean operator OR (e.g., “Programming Languages” OR “Python Programming” OR “R Programming”) to ensure search comprehensiveness. Next, the groups of terms were combined with each other using the Boolean operator AND (e.g., [Group 1] AND [Group 2] AND [Group 3] AND [Group 4]), ensuring the precision and relevance of the results. The entire process was conducted using the PubMed Advanced Search tool (available at: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/advanced/). 
No restrictions were applied regarding language or publication date, in order to ensure broad and inclusive coverage of the literature. 
These strategies were adapted to improve the sensitivity and specificity of the searches while maintaining the same framework initially established in the strategy developed for PubMed. The combination of terms, based on controlled descriptors (MeSH, DeCS) and Boolean operators (AND, OR), resulted in the following search strategies for each database, as presented in the appendices of this work through Table 2: Search Strategy in Databases.


3.6 Selection Process
Publications identified through the descriptors will be exported to the Rayyan application for duplicate removal and selection of articles/documents based on eligibility criteria, followed by full-text review and data extraction.
Studies addressing the use of open-source programming languages for the collection, extraction, and/or analysis of DataSUS data will be included. Documents describing data extraction methods from other information sources or systems will be excluded from the sample.
3.7 Data Management and Analysis
Both the selection process through title and abstract screening and full-text review, and the data extraction will be carried out by two researchers. Discrepancies will be resolved by consensus.
Due to the heterogeneity of the documents to be analyzed, quality assessment will be performed only for scientific articles indexed in databases, using the AGREE II instrument.
Data will be stored using the Research Electronic Data Capture (REDCap) software.

3.8 Ethical Considerations and Conflicts of Interest
In accordance with Brazilian Resolutions No. 466 of December 12, 2012, and No. 510 of April 7, 2016, this study is exempt from review by a Research Ethics Committee (REC). There are no conflicts of interest in this protocol. 
4 EXPECTED RESULTS
The scoping review will comprehensively map the scientific production related to the use of open-source programming languages applied to DataSUS, identifying the state of the art in the collection, processing, and analysis of data from Brazil’s national health information systems. It is expected to characterize the types of published studies, application contexts, the most explored SUS information systems, and the predominant methodological approaches, providing a consolidated overview of current practices in the field. The use of open-source code enables researchers and developers to access and contribute to the improvement of tools. Well-developed code supports efficient data integration and analysis, accelerating the development of new solutions tailored to community needs.
In addition, the review will enable the identification of the main tools, languages, and libraries used to handle SUS microdata, including Python, R, and other open-source resources. This characterization will allow an assessment of the accessibility, documentation, and reproducibility of existing solutions, contributing to an understanding of how these technologies have been applied in research and health management.
The mapping process is also expected to reveal gaps in the literature, such as the lack of methodological standardization, limitations in interoperability between systems, scarcity of automated tools, and insufficient studies addressing integration across different DataSUS databases. Identifying these gaps will provide guidance for the development of new technological solutions and for shaping future research agendas.
The review will further systematize the methodologies employed in the analyzed studies, describing strategies for data collection, preprocessing, statistical analysis, modeling, and data visualization. This systematization will help compare manual and automated approaches, highlighting best practices, limitations, and opportunities for improvement in the use of public health data.
From the perspective of management and public policy, the expected results include demonstrating the potential of open-source tools to enhance transparency, efficiency, and reproducibility in epidemiological and administrative analyses. The review should show how automation in data collection and processing can support managers, researchers, and SUS professionals in evidence-based decision-making.
Finally, the study is expected to produce a consolidated, up-to-date, and replicable body of knowledge capable of supporting the development of new technologies, guiding training processes, and strengthening open science in the context of Brazilian public health.
In the future, it is expected that these tools will become more accessible, customizable, and user-friendly, increasing transparency in analyses. This will enable more robust studies aligned with the needs of health professionals and researchers. Additionally, new methodologies may be developed to handle large-scale data, optimizing the use of DataSUS for epidemiological analyses, outbreak prediction, and public policy evaluation using big data technologies.

title: Scoping Review of Risk Prediction Models for Acute Kidney Injury Following Cardiac Arrest Resuscitation
description:
This scoping review aims to systematically map the existing evidence on risk prediction models for acute kidney injury (AKI) in adult patients following successful resuscitation from cardiac arrest (including both out-of-hospital cardiac arrest [OHCA] and in-hospital cardiac arrest [IHCA]).
Cardiac arrest survivors are at high risk of developing AKI, which is strongly associated with increased mortality, prolonged hospital stay, and poor neurological outcomes. In recent years, several risk prediction models (such as nomograms, logistic regression-based scores, and machine learning models) have been developed to predict AKI occurrence, progression, or severity in this population. However, the evidence remains sparse, fragmented, and has not yet been systematically synthesized or critically appraised.
The objectives of this scoping review are:
(1) to identify all published and unpublished studies that have developed, validated, or updated risk prediction models for AKI after successful cardiac arrest resuscitation;
(2) to summarize the key characteristics of these models, including study design, sample size, predictors, performance metrics (e.g., AUC/C-index, calibration, sensitivity, specificity, decision curve analysis), and validation approaches (internal/external);
(3) to assess the methodological quality of the included models using the PROBAST tool; and
(4) to highlight current evidence gaps and provide clear directions for future research and clinical application.
This scoping review will follow the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology for scoping reviews and the PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews) checklist. Comprehensive searches will be performed in PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, CNKI, Wanfang, VIP, and other relevant databases, with no language or publication date restrictions.
The findings of this review will provide clinicians, researchers, and guideline developers with a clear overview of the current state of AKI risk prediction modeling in post-cardiac arrest patients and serve as a foundation for the development of more robust, externally validated, and clinically implementable prediction tools.

title: Protocol for supporting hypertensive disorders of pregnancy research with systematic evidence mapping--a novel biomarker characterization tool
description:
This systematic evidence map aims to identify and categorize biomarkers in pregnant women that can be used to evaluate, diagnose, or predict hypertension in pregnancy in animal models and to inform research that can investigate the impact of environmental exposures on those biomarkers as a predictive tool for cardiovascular disease risk in women. Under the current criteria, diagnosis in the latter half of pregnancy merely confirms the presence of disease. While diagnosis may allow for intervention in severe cases of HDP, the window for prevention has passed (Von Dadelszen and Magee 2016). Early diagnosis and timely intervention are imperative to improving pregnancy outcomes in cases of HDP. Current research on the various types of HDP focuses on identifying predictive methods with high sensitivity and specificity to allow for necessary care. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) recognizes that predictive biomarkers are integral to early detection and targeted therapy of HDP; however, there is a scarcity of biomarkers approved for clinical prediction of these disorders (Roberts et al. 2013). The identification of novel biomarkers that can be used in clinical settings to quickly and accurately detect early PE or predict those at highest risk for HDP are needed to improve pregnancy outcomes, potentially by allowing additional time for intervention. Some animal models of hypertension in pregnancy are available and have been used to assess aspects of these diseases; however, the etiologies of HDP and how mechanisms in these models may differ from that in humans are not well understood. Therefore, given the importance of biomarkers in the prediction of these diseases, an important consideration is whether these biomarkers translate across species and if new or existing animal models can be used to further elucidate mechanisms and predict diseases, especially mechanisms that may be affected by environmental exposures.
Currently the extent, availability, utility, and human relevance of biomarkers and mechanisms of HDP that are studied in animal models is unclear. In addition, the extent to which environmental exposures impact these biomarkers and mechanisms is critical to understanding the role of environment in the development and exacerbation of HDP, yet the impact of many environmental exposures on HDP in both humans and animal models also remains unclear. The resulting SEM will serve as a findable and accessible resource that can be used to inform future primary research as well as literature-based evaluations.

title: A systematic review and meta-analysis of the diagnostic accuracy of the Queen of Hearts (PMcardio) AI-ECG algorithm for detection of acute coronary occlusion compared to conventional ECG interpretation methods
description:
This registration documents the protocol for a systematic review and meta-analysis evaluating the diagnostic test accuracy of the Queen of Hearts (QoH) artificial intelligence algorithm for detecting acute coronary occlusion on 12-lead electrocardiograms.

BACKGROUND: Acute coronary occlusion requires urgent reperfusion therapy, yet conventional STEMI criteria miss a substantial proportion of patients. The Queen of Hearts algorithm, a neural network-based ECG interpretation tool deployed via PMcardio, has been evaluated in approximately 13 studies across 40,000 patients in multiple countries.

OBJECTIVES: To systematically synthesize all available evidence on QoH diagnostic accuracy, pool sensitivity and specificity using bivariate meta-analysis, generate hierarchical summary ROC curves, compare QoH performance against conventional ECG interpretation methods (STEMI millimeter criteria, ECG machine algorithms), and explore heterogeneity by clinical setting, algorithm version, and reference standard.

METHODS: Comprehensive search of PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, and Cochrane Library using hybrid product-specific and technology-focused search strategy. Dual independent screening and quality assessment using QUADAS-2 adapted for AI diagnostic studies. Bivariate random-effects meta-analysis with HSROC curves. Pre-specified subgroup analyses by clinical setting, QoH version, comparator type, and reference standard hierarchy.

EXPECTED OUTCOMES: Pooled estimates of QoH diagnostic accuracy, comparative performance versus conventional methods, identification of sources of heterogeneity, and GRADE evidence certainty ratings.

REGISTRATION RATIONALE: PROSPERO does not currently accept diagnostic test accuracy systematic reviews. This OSF registration provides transparent, timestamped pre-specification of all methods prior to literature screening.

PROTOCOL PUBLICATION: This protocol will be submitted to Systematic Reviews journal for peer review and publication.

title: Sepsis and Metabolic Stress Response in Critically Ill Patients with Diabetic Ketoacidosis: A Scoping Review.
description:
This registration documents the protocol for a systematic scoping review titled "Sepsis and Metabolic Stress Response in Critically Ill Patients with Diabetic Ketoacidosis: A Scoping Review."

Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) represents a severe acute metabolic emergency in intensive care units (ICU). DKA per se frequently induces a profound systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS)—characterized by severe leukocytosis, tachycardia, and tachypnea—which closely mimics sepsis. This clinical overlap creates a diagnostic dilemma that often leads to delayed initiation of targeted antimicrobial therapy or, conversely, excessive unneeded empirical broad-spectrum antibiotic use.

This scoping review systematically maps and synthesizes literature published between 2015 and 2025 evaluating the clinical, laboratory, microbiological, and prognostic intersection between sepsis and metabolic stress in adult DKA patients. The synthesis is structured across five core analytical domains:

1. Epidemiological Profile & Precipitants: Prevalence of confirmed infection as the primary precipitating factor in critical DKA compared to non-infectious causes (e.g., insulin omission or new-onset diabetes).
2. Diagnostic & Discriminative Biomarkers: Evaluation of diagnostic accuracy, Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC-ROC), sensitivity, specificity, and optimal cut-off points for cellular ratios and inflammatory markers (Neutrophil-to-Lymphocyte Ratio [NLR], Monocyte-to-Lymphocyte Ratio [MLR], Procalcitonin [PCT], Interleukin-6 [IL-6], and C-Reactive Protein [CRP]) to differentiate true sepsis from pure metabolic stress.
3. Risk & Association Measures: Quantitative synthesis of reported Odds Ratios (OR) and Relative Risks (RR) for acute clinical complications, including septic shock, severe DKA, and Acute Kidney Injury (AKI).
4. Microbiological Profiling: Distribution of infectious foci (respiratory, urinary, abdominal, bloodstream) and characterization of invasive or opportunistic Gram-negative pathogens (e.g., Klebsiella pneumoniae invasive liver abscess syndrome, Serratia rubidaea).
5. Resource Utilization & Special Subgroups: Comparative analysis of vasopressor reliance, ICU/hospital length of stay, and the emergence of SGLT2 inhibitor-associated euglycemic DKA during septic episodes.

The review strictly follows the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology for scoping reviews and the PRISMA Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) guidelines.

title: Game Design and Player Experience in Games for Assessing Mild Cognitive Impairment: A Systematic Review
description:
This systematic review investigates the design and player experience of games developed for assessing mild cognitive impairment (MCI). MCI, a transitional stage between normal cognitive aging and dementia, requires early detection to enable timely intervention. Traditional screening tools such as the MMSE and MoCA have limitations in sensitivity and specificity, prompting exploration of game-based approaches as alternative or complementary assessments.

The review aims to synthesise existing literature on serious games and gamified applications for MCI assessment, with a focus on:

Transparency of game artefact reporting – evaluating how clearly and completely games are described in publications.

Implementation of formal game design elements – assessing game structures using frameworks such as Fullerton’s Formal Elements and Schell’s Elemental Tetrad.

Design philosophy – distinguishing between serious games built for assessment and gamified adaptations of traditional tests.

Role of older adults in the design process – applying Druin’s typology to examine participatory design practices.

Evaluation of user and player experience – mapping how usability, accessibility, human factors, and hedonic engagement are assessed.

A comprehensive search will be conducted in Scopus, IEEE Xplore, and ACM Digital Library. Eligible studies must be peer-reviewed, focus on MCI assessment, and use an electronic game or gamified system. Data will be extracted and analysed thematically, guided by the ENTREQ framework to ensure rigour and transparency. The findings will provide a consolidated view of current practices, identify gaps in game design and reporting, and offer recommendations for designing effective and engaging game-based assessments for older adults.

title: Offline-First Mobile OCR and FHIR Interoperability for Bedside Vital Sign Digitisation in Geriatric Care under Power and Network Constraints: A Ghanaian District Hospital Study
description:
# Offline-First Mobile OCR and FHIR Interoperability for Bedside Vital Sign Digitisation in Geriatric Care under Power and Network Constraints: A Ghanaian District Hospital Study

**Author:** Titus Afeo Azure Aduku, BSN, RN 
**Affiliation:** Department of Nursing, Tatale District Hospital, Ghana Health Service, P. O. Box YD 9, Tatale, Northern Region, Ghana 
**Corresponding Email:** titusafeoazureaduku@gmail.com 

---

## Abstract

### Background
Manual transcription of bedside vital signs in resource-limited district hospitals across Sub-Saharan Africa is slow, error-prone, and burdensome for health personnel. Although digital health platforms offer potential solutions, existing cloud-based artificial intelligence (AI) and optical character recognition (OCR) systems consistently fail in remote border facilities due to frequent power blackouts, cross-border network dropouts, high API costs, and strict data privacy regulations (e.g., Ghana's Data Protection Act, 2012 [Act 843] and Cybersecurity Act, 2020 [Act 1038]). Furthermore, human expert usability testing of mobile health (mHealth) applications remains unscalable due to severe clinical workforce shortages.

### Objective
To design, benchmark, and validate an offline-first mobile clinical OCR pipeline that digitizes paper-based vital sign charts on low-cost commodity hardware into standardized Health Level Seven Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (HL7 FHIR R4) `Observation` payloads mapped to Logical Observation Identifiers Names and Codes (LOINC), and to evaluate its interface usability using a local, automated Large Language Model (LLM)-as-a-Judge framework.

### Methods
We benchmarked an edge-computing OCR pipeline (combining local OpenCV image filtering and Google ML Kit text recognition) on physical bedside tablet hardware (Samsung SM-X210: Qualcomm Snapdragon 695 5G, 4 GB RAM) and a throttled single-core ARM Cortex-A53 virtual device emulator representing entry-level smartphones ($\le \$130\text{ USD}$). Diagnostic accuracy was evaluated across a validated dataset of $N = 250$ distorted clinical vital sign charts derived from the open-access VitalDB repository. Extracted parameters (blood pressure, heart rate, respiratory rate, temperature) were converted into HL7 FHIR R4 JSON payloads, bound to standard LOINC codes, and validated using the HAPI FHIR Engine. User interface usability was evaluated locally using an offline quantized model (Llama-3-8B-Instruct) scored against Jakob Nielsen’s 10 Usability Heuristics and validated against gold-standard expert human benchmarks. Resilience to power outages was tested across 50 off-grid "Ward-to-OPD" deferred batch-synchronization scenarios using 256-bit AES-encrypted local SQLite queues.

### Results
The on-device OCR pipeline achieved a mean processing latency of $120.30\text{ ms}$ ($\text{SD} = \pm 24.16\text{ ms}$) on physical tablet hardware and $243.80\text{ ms}$ ($\text{SD} = \pm 54.39\text{ ms}$) under single-core emulation. Automated OCR charting significantly outperformed manual keyboard entry speed ($t_{249} = 103.50, p < 0.001$; Wilcoxon $W = 31380, p < 0.001$). The pipeline yielded an overall Character Error Rate (CER) of $0.8\%$ ($0.008$), with minimal Mean Absolute Errors:

* **Systolic BP MAE:** $0.428\text{ mmHg}$
* **Diastolic BP MAE:** $0.288\text{ mmHg}$
* **Heart Rate MAE:** $0.192\text{ bpm}$
* **Respiratory Rate MAE:** $0.116\text{ breaths/min}$
* **Temperature MAE:** $0.015^\circ\text{C}$

All generated JSON payloads ($250/250, 100.0\%, p = 1.000$) achieved full HL7 FHIR R4 schema compliance and correct LOINC terminology bindings. The local Llama-3-8B judge model demonstrated strong agreement with human expert ratings ($r = 0.840, p < 0.001$), achieving $87.20\%$ classification accuracy ($\text{F1} = 0.729$, Cohen’s $\kappa = 0.645$, Krippendorff’s $\alpha = 0.646$, $\chi^2_1 = 104.60, p < 0.001$). Over off-grid blackout periods averaging $12.15\text{ hours}$ (accumulating up to 115 queued records per device), the physical deferred sync protocol achieved a $100.0\%$ record preservation rate ($0\%$ data loss) with a mean batch upload latency of $3.738\text{ seconds}$.

### Conclusions
On-device OCR combined with local rule-based FHIR parsing enables rapid, highly accurate, and fully offline bedside vital sign digitization on commodity mobile hardware, eliminating transcription errors while maintaining interoperability with central electronic medical record systems. Executing all computations on-device bypasses electrical grid and network failures, eliminates recurring mobile data fees, and guarantees statutory data sovereignty under national cybersecurity and privacy laws. Furthermore, localized LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation provides a zero-cost, privacy-preserving, and human-aligned software quality auditing mechanism for continuous mHealth optimization in resource-constrained healthcare environments.

---

title: How Artificial Intelligence Innovations Create Value in Health Systems: A Systematic Review of Randomized Controlled Trials Assessing Effectiveness, Efficiency, Equity, and Responsiveness
description:
Artificial Intelligence (AI) is rapidly emerging as a disruptive force within health systems, with innovations being applied in nearly every facet of healthcare delivery (Rajpurkar et al., 2022). Over the past decade, Health AI innovations have been developed to enhance diagnostic accuracy, optimize treatment decisions, enable predictive modeling, and improve system-level functions such as resource allocation (Alowais et al., 2023; Olawade et al., 2024). As health systems face growing pressure to deliver higher-value care, Health AI has gained traction for its potential to address challenges at the patient, provider, and system levels.

Integration of technology into healthcare is not new. Earlier waves of innovations (i.e. including electronic medical records, virtual care platforms, and remote monitoring) were similarly promoted as solutions to longstanding system inefficiencies (Ezeamii et al., 2024; Haleem et al., 2021). Despite widespread uptake, however, many of these technologies have failed to generate clear evidence of value. Challenges included unclear definitions of “value,” inadequate measurement of outcomes before and after implementation, and a lack of evaluation of broader system-level trade-offs.

AI carries both greater opportunity and greater risk compared to earlier technologies given its ability to rapidly augment changes (i.e. ranging from missed implementation benefits to direct patient harm). There is, hence, an urgent need to assess how Health AI innovations are being implemented across care settings (e.g., primary, tertiary, long-term care) and system levels (e.g., departmental, institutional, regional, national), and examine the value these tools intend to create and whether this happens in practice.

The objective of this review is to systematically evaluate AI innovations that have been studied using randomized controlled trials (RCTs) to determine how they have improved health system outputs and outcomes. In relation to the system Outputs (public health and personal healthcare services), the produced value can be categorized across four domains (effectiveness, efficiency, responsiveness, and equity) that collectively reflect the performance of a high-value health system. In relation to system Outcomes, value is generated with improvements in health, financial and user satisfaction. We focus on RCTs, because of their ability to identify cause- and-effect relationships on specific outcomes. This will make quantifying effects of the AI intervention on specific outcomes more plausible. 

The review will synthesize data from eligible RCTs in relation to it’s health system value. We acknowledge that there will be significant heterogeneity of study protocols, outcome measures and innovations examined (i.e. where they are deployed, how they were deployed, and outcomes of interest). Therefore this will be a systematic mapping review, that will inform for future work on where intervention systematic reviews and meta-analysis may be conducted for specific use-cases.

title: Biometric Data in PTSD Detection: A Scoping Review of Digital Applications
description:
Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) is frequently under-diagnosed due to the limitations of self-reported symptoms and clinical interviews, which can be subjective and delayed. Recent developments in biometric data—such as heart rate variability (HRV), EEG, voice patterns, and skin conductance—offer more objective and scalable approaches to PTSD detection, particularly when integrated into digital health platforms like mobile apps, wearable sensors, and AI-based systems.

However, existing research in this area is fragmented. Many studies focus on a narrow range of biometric signals, and few incorporate sex-based differences in PTSD presentation, which may affect diagnostic accuracy. In addition, some promising biometric markers remain underexplored, and the role of machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI) in enhancing detection is inconsistently applied.

This scoping review aims to map the current landscape of biometric data used in PTSD detection, assess their integration into digital tools, and identify underutilized modalities and methodological gaps. Special attention will be given to the inclusion of sex-related features in AI/ML models.

The review will result in a comprehensive synthesis of existing knowledge, highlight opportunities for innovation, and offer practical recommendations for developing inclusive and effective PTSD detection systems using biometric technologies.

title: Artificial Intelligence versus Endoscopists in Endoscopic Ultrasound-Guided Diagnosis of Pancreatic Lesions: Does AI Bridge the Expertise Gap? A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
description:
Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) is the most sensitive imaging modality for the detection and characterization of pancreatic lesions, offering spatial resolution superior to computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging for lesions smaller than 2 cm. Despite its diagnostic primacy, EUS interpretation remains profoundly operator-dependent. The learning curve for pancreatic EUS is among the steepest in interventional endoscopy: acquiring competence in pancreatic station recognition, lesion characterization, and differentiation of malignant from benign conditions—particularly distinguishing pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) from chronic pancreatitis (CP), autoimmune pancreatitis (AIP), and pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (PNETs)—typically requires several years of supervised training and exposure to high procedural volumes. This expertise gradient creates a systemic inequity: diagnostic quality is concentrated in high-volume tertiary centers, while patients managed at lower-volume institutions or by less experienced endosonographers face a measurably higher risk of missed or delayed diagnosis.
Artificial intelligence (AI) systems—encompassing convolutional neural networks (CNNs), deep learning (DL) architectures, artificial neural networks (ANNs), support vector machines (SVMs), and hybrid multimodal models—have been applied to EUS image analysis, EUS video processing, and EUS-guided fine-needle aspiration/biopsy (EUS-FNA/B) cytological evaluation across a growing body of single-center studies. Multiple systematic reviews and meta-analyses published between 2022 and 2023 have reported pooled sensitivities and specificities exceeding 90% for AI-assisted EUS in the diagnosis of pancreatic malignancy. However, these analyses share a critical limitation: they evaluate AI diagnostic performance in isolation, without systematically addressing the clinically decisive question of how AI performs relative to human endoscopists of varying experience levels. The question of whether AI can functionally bridge the expertise gap—elevating the diagnostic performance of novice or intermediate endosonographers to approach that of recognized experts—has not been answered by any existing meta-analysis.
This systematic review and meta-analysis is designed to address this evidence gap directly. The review will comprehensively identify, appraise, and synthesize studies reporting the comparative diagnostic performance of AI systems and human endoscopists in EUS-based evaluation of pancreatic lesions, including solid masses (PDAC, CP, AIP, PNET) and cystic lesions (intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasms [IPMNs], mucinous cystic neoplasms [MCNs]). The primary analysis will generate pooled estimates of sensitivity, specificity, and area under the summary receiver operating characteristic curve (SROC-AUC) for AI versus endoscopist performance. A pre-specified expertise gap analysis will quantify the magnitude of diagnostic performance difference between novice and expert endosonographers in the absence of AI assistance, and examine whether this gap is attenuated or eliminated with AI support. Subgroup analyses will be performed by AI architecture type, pancreatic lesion category, EUS modality (B-mode, contrast-enhanced EUS, elastography, EUS-FNA/B cytology), and validation strategy (internal versus external). Methodological quality will be assessed using the QUADAS-2 framework, and the bivariate random-effects model will serve as the primary statistical approach.
The expected outputs of this review are threefold. First, a rigorous, updated quantitative synthesis of AI diagnostic performance in pancreatic EUS, extending beyond the literature cutoffs of prior meta-analyses to include high-quality studies published through mid-2025, including the first randomized crossover trial in this field (Cui et al., JAMA Network Open, 2024). Second, the first pooled quantitative estimate of AI's capacity to reduce the endoscopic expertise gap in pancreatic EUS diagnosis—a finding with direct implications for clinical training program design, AI deployment policy, and the equitable distribution of diagnostic capability. Third, a structured identification of methodological gaps in the existing literature, including the near-universal absence of prospective external validation and the inconsistent reporting of endoscopist experience levels, which will inform the design of future multicenter prospective trials.

title: Protocol for a systematic review of prognostic models for predicting individualized risk of cervical cancer occurrence in screened women
description:
Cervical cancer is the fourth most common cancer among women worldwide, and it remains the most frequent cancer affecting the female reproductive system, with approximately 660.000 new cases and 350,000 deaths reported in 2022 worldwide (1). Traditional screening methods use a one-size-fits-all approach, typically recommending that individuals begin screening at age 21 and undergo testing every three to five years, regardless of their personalized risk (3). However, this strategy may lead to high cost per identified case and cause harm, as frequent screening in low-risk population is likely to result in higher number of false positive tests (5). Additionally, a frequent number of false positive tests expose women to unnecessary potentially harmful follow up procedures, such as conization, which carries risks including bleeding, infection, cervical stenosis, and increased risk of preterm birth (6, 7). To enhance accuracy and efficiency of cervical cancer screening, artificial intelligence and prognostic modeling have been proposed (8). Prognostic models, which estimate the risk of future clinical outcomes based on clinical and non-clinical variables, offer potential for enhancing the diagnostic accuracy of cervical cancer screening. Recent studies have investigated the use of machine learning to support cancer screening, including automating cytology analysis, predicting disease progression, and personalizing screening intervals (11, 12). However, it may take time before prognostic models reach their full potential, as challenges in implementation and validation hinder widespread adoption (8). 

This study aims to systematically review and evaluate prognostic models developed for use in predicting cervical cancer among women in a cervical cancer screening program. We will describe the model’s characteristics, compare performance and assess methodological quality in model development and evaluation. If feasible, predictive performance measures will be pooled in a meta-analysis to provide a summary of model performance and explore heterogeneity, i.e., if model performance varies by e.g., case mix variation or outcome definition.

title: Serum and Cerebrospinal Fluid NLRP3 Inflammasome-Related Cytokines (IL-1β and IL-18) as Diagnostic and Prognostic Biomarkers in Traumatic Brain Injury: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
description:
This research project systematically investigates the role of NLRP3 inflammasome-related cytokines, specifically interleukin-1 beta (IL-1β) and interleukin-18 (IL-18), as diagnostic and prognostic biomarkers in traumatic brain injury (TBI). TBI remains a major global cause of mortality, neurological disability, and long-term cognitive impairment, yet reliable molecular biomarkers capable of accurately reflecting injury severity and predicting outcomes remain limited in routine clinical practice. Neuroinflammation is increasingly recognized as a central driver of secondary brain injury, with activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome pathway playing a pivotal mechanistic role in post-traumatic neuronal damage.

The primary purpose of this systematic review and meta-analysis is to synthesize current evidence regarding serum and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) levels of IL-1β and IL-18 in patients with TBI compared with healthy or non-TBI controls. The project quantitatively evaluates biomarker elevation, diagnostic discrimination, and prognostic associations across diverse clinical settings and biological sample types. By integrating findings from multiple observational studies, the research aims to clarify whether these inflammasome-associated cytokines can serve as clinically meaningful biomarkers for injury detection, severity stratification, and neurological outcome prediction.

The study employs rigorous systematic review methodology in accordance with PRISMA 2020 and MOOSE reporting standards. Comprehensive database searches, structured quality assessment, subgroup analyses, sensitivity analyses, and random-effects meta-analytic models are used to ensure methodological robustness. The project additionally explores how biomarker performance varies according to sample matrix (serum versus CSF), traumatic brain injury severity, timing of sample collection, and assay platform.

Expected outcomes of the project include identification of pooled effect sizes for IL-1β and IL-18 elevation in TBI, evaluation of their diagnostic accuracy using area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) metrics, and characterization of their relationship with clinical severity scores and long-term neurological outcomes. The study is expected to demonstrate that IL-18, particularly in CSF, possesses stronger diagnostic and prognostic potential than IL-1β, while both biomarkers reflect activation of the NLRP3-driven neuroinflammatory cascade following traumatic injury.

Beyond biomarker evaluation, the project seeks to contribute to translational neurotrauma research by establishing a mechanistic link between inflammasome activation and clinical disease progression. The findings may support the future development of rapid point-of-care diagnostic tools, targeted anti-inflammatory therapeutic strategies, and biomarker-guided management approaches in TBI care. The research also highlights the broader relevance of neuroimmune pathways in acute neurological injury and emphasizes the importance of integrating molecular diagnostics into modern neurocritical care practice.

title: Diagnostic Accuracy and Additive Diagnostic Yield of Xpert MTB/RIF and Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra Compared with Conventional Diagnostic Modalities on Thoracoscopic Pleural Biopsy Specimens for Pleural Tuberculosis: A Retrospective Study
description:
Tuberculous pleural effusion (TPE) is one of the commonest forms of extrapulmonary tuberculosis, and microbiological confirmation remains difficult because of the paucibacillary nature of pleural disease. Conventional diagnostic methods such as acid-fast bacilli (AFB) smear microscopy, mycobacterial culture, and histopathology each have inherent limitations. GeneXpert MTB/RIF and the newer GeneXpert MTB/RIF Ultra assay have improved the diagnosis of tuberculosis; however, comparative evidence regarding their performance on thoracoscopic pleural biopsy specimens remains limited.

This retrospective diagnostic accuracy study aims to compare the diagnostic performance of GeneXpert MTB/RIF and GeneXpert MTB/RIF Ultra performed on thoracoscopic pleural biopsy specimens using a Composite Reference Standard (CRS). The study will also compare these molecular assays with conventional diagnostic modalities, including AFB smear microscopy, mycobacterial culture, and histopathological examination, and evaluate their additive diagnostic yield.

The findings are expected to provide evidence regarding the optimal diagnostic approach for pleural tuberculosis in routine clinical practice, particularly in tuberculosis-endemic settings.

title: AI stridor analysis
description:
Objective: This review examines artificial intelligence (AI) applications in analyzing respiratory sounds, specifically stridor, to address limitations in traditional, operator-dependent diagnostic methods. 

Data Sources: A structured search across PubMed, Scopus, and Ovid was conducted, focusing on studies from 2010 to 2024 relevant to AI and stridor detection. 

Review Methods: The review synthesizes findings from studies employing machine learning (ML) models like Artificial Neural Networks (ANN), Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN), and Support Vector Machines (SVM) to enhance stridor diagnosis by analyzing respiratory sound patterns. 

Results: The reviewed studies demonstrate high diagnostic accuracy, with models such as Quadratic Discriminant Analysis (QDA) and Personalized Federated Learning with Self-Distillation (PFL-SD) achieving accuracies up to 100% and 96.1%, respectively. AI techniques showed potential to classify stridor types, identify anatomical locations of obstructions, and guide clinical decision-making, particularly in pediatric cases requiring prompt intervention. 

Conclusion: AI-driven respiratory sound analysis offers promising advancements in stridor diagnosis through improved accuracy and early detection, though limitations in data standardization and underexplored pediatric applications present challenges and opportunities. Future research on larger, standardized datasets could expand the potential of AI tools in this critical clinical setting.
