title: ML-Based Cardiovascular Risk Prediction in Inflammatory Rheumatic Diseases: A Scoping Review Protocol
description:
1. Background
Individuals with inflammatory rheumatic diseases (IRDs) - such as rheumatoid arthritis (RA), systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), psoriatic arthritis (PsA), ankylosing spondylitis (AS), and similar conditions- have a much higher risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD) and related deaths than the general population. Chronic systemic inflammation accelerates atherosclerosis through both unique and shared pathways with traditional cardiovascular risk factors.

Widely used cardiovascular risk prediction tools like the Framingham Risk Score, SCORE2, QRISK3, and ACC/AHA Pooled Cohort Equations were developed for the general population. These tools often underestimate cardiovascular risk in IRD patients, even when using disease-specific adjustments such as the EULAR-recommended 1.5x multiplier for RA. As a result, more research now uses machine learning (ML) methods, including random forest, gradient boosting, LASSO, support vector machines, neural networks, and others, to create risk prediction models adapted to IRD patients. These models usually include disease-specific attributes like autoantibodies, inflammatory markers, and disease activity scores along with traditional risk factors.

Existing systematic reviews in this space have focused either on the performance of traditional (non-ML) risk algorithms in IRDs, or on ML for CVD risk prediction in the general population. No review has systematically mapped the specific literature on ML-based cardiovascular risk prediction among inflammatory rheumatic diseases as a group. Given the heterogeneity in disease types, algorithms, outcome definitions, and assessment measures used across this emerging body of research, a scoping review is the most suitable methodology to comprehensively map the breadth and characteristics of existing evidence prior to conducting more targeted syntheses.

2. Research Question (PCC Framework)
Population: Adult patients (≥18 years) diagnosed with an inflammatory rheumatic disease (RA, SLE, PsA, AS, or related systemic autoimmune rheumatic diseases).
Concept: Development, validation, or comparative evaluation of machine learning–based models for predicting cardiovascular risk or cardiovascular events.
Context: Any clinical, registry-based, or EHR-derived research setting, in any country or healthcare system.
Review question: What is the nature and extent of the evidence on machine learning–based cardiovascular risk prediction models in patients with inflammatory rheumatic diseases?

3. Objectives
1. To map which inflammatory rheumatic diseases have been studied in the context of ML-based CV risk prediction.
2. To identify which ML algorithms have been applied and how their performance has been evaluated.
3. To catalogue which predictor variables (traditional CV risk factors vs. disease-specific variables) are most commonly used.
4. To identify which CV outcomes are predicted (e.g., composite MACE, myocardial infarction, stroke, subclinical atherosclerosis).
5. To evaluate the extent of external validation and comparison against traditional risk scores.
6. To identify gaps in the current evidence base to guide future primary research and inform the feasibility of a future systematic review/meta-analysis.

4. Eligibility Criteria
Inclusion criteria:
- Studies involving adult patients with a diagnosed inflammatory rheumatic disease (RA, SLE, PsA, AS, systemic sclerosis, vasculitides, or mixed/overlap IRD populations)
- Studies developing, validating, or comparing a machine learning model, defined as any supervised or unsupervised algorithm beyond a single unpenalized logistic regression model used as a standard scoring system. Penalized regression methods (LASSO, Ridge, Elastic Net) are explicitly counted as ML for this review, given their use as feature-selection as well as regularization tools in the included primary literature. Studies using unpenalized logistic regression alongside other ML methods for comparison are included.
- The outcome must be cardiovascular risk, cardiovascular events, or a CV-related surrogate (e.g., subclinical atherosclerosis, arterial stiffness) predicted via the ML model.
- Original research articles, including retrospective and prospective cohort studies
- Peer-reviewed publications in English

Exclusion criteria:
- Studies in pediatric/juvenile-onset IRD populations only
- Studies focused solely on rheumatic heart disease (post-streptococcal), which is etiologically distinct.
- Studies using only traditional risk scores without any ML component
- Conference abstracts without full text, editorials, commentaries, case reports
- Studies where CV outcome data cannot be isolated for the IRD population (e.g., mixed autoimmune cohorts without disease-specific subgroup results)

5. Search Strategy
Databases: MEDLINE (PubMed), Embase, Web of Science, Scopus, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library
IEEE Xplore and ACM Digital Library are included in addition to clinical databases because applied ML research in healthcare is frequently first published in computer science or bioinformatics conference proceedings before appearing in clinical journals. Limiting the search to medical databases alone risks missing methodologically relevant studies at an earlier stage of dissemination.

Search concept blocks (to be combined with AND):
1. Inflammatory rheumatic disease terms: rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, psoriatic arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, spondyloarthritis, systemic sclerosis, vasculitis, inflammatory arthritis
2. Machine learning terms: machine learning, artificial intelligence, deep learning, random forest, gradient boosting, neural network, predictive model, risk prediction model
3. Cardiovascular terms: cardiovascular disease, cardiovascular risk, myocardial infarction, stroke, atherosclerosis, major adverse cardiovascular events, MACE
Search date range: Inception to present (database search date to be recorded at time of execution)
Other sources: Manual reference list screening of included studies; forward citation searching via Google Scholar; grey literature search (preprint servers: medRxiv, bioRxiv) to capture recent unpublished work given the fast-moving nature of this field.

6. Study Selection
Two independent reviewers will screen titles and abstracts, followed by full article texts, according to the eligibility criteria using a reference management or screening tool (e.g., Rayyan or Covidence). Discrepancies will be resolved through discussion or by consulting a third reviewer. The selection process will be documented using a PRISMA-ScR flow diagram.

7. Data Charting
A standardized data extraction form will capture: author, year, country, IRD studied, sample size, study design, ML algorithm(s) used, comparator (if any, e.g., Framingham/QRISK3), predictor variables included, CV outcome definition, follow-up duration, performance statistics (AUC/C-statistic, sensitivity, specificity, calibration), internal vs. external validation, and key findings.

In addition, given the ML focus of this review, the following model-building characteristics will be extracted for each study:
- Class imbalance handling: method used to address the typically low prevalence of CV events relative to non-events (e.g., SMOTE, class weighting, undersampling), or none reported
- Missing data strategy: method used (e.g., multiple imputation, mean/median imputation, k-NN imputation) vs. complete-case analysis
- Explainability/interpretability: whether the study used feature-importance or explainability methods (e.g., SHAP, LIME, partial dependence plots) or presented the model as a “black box” without interpretability analysis
- Adherence to ML reporting standards: whether the study references or follows a structured ML model reporting guideline (e.g., TRIPOD+AI, TRIPOD-ML, MI-CLAIM), charted descriptively as an indicator of reporting quality in the field rather than as a formal risk-of-bias judgment

The charting form will be piloted on 3–5 included studies and refined iteratively, consistent with JBI scoping review guidance.

8. Synthesis of Results
Findings will be presented in tabular or graphical formats, such as by disease, algorithm type, by outcome, and temporal trends, in accordance with scoping review methodology. Consistent with PRISMA-ScR guidance, no formal risk-of-bias or quality appraisal will be performed, as the principal purpose is to map the existing evidence rather than assess its certainty. However, reporting-quality indicators, including adherence to TRIPOD+AI or equivalent ML reporting guidelines, use of explainability methods, and approaches to class imbalance and missing data, will be charted and summarized descriptively to support the identification of methodological gaps for future research.

9. Reporting
This review will be reported according to the PRISMA extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) checklist.

10. Registration
This protocol will be registered prospectively on the Open Science Framework (OSF) before commencing the literature search.

title: Automated Data Extraction from PDFs Using a Multi-Stage, Large Language Model-Enabled Process: A Proof-of-Concept Study
description:
Objective
The objective of this study is to compare automated data extraction using a multi-stage, LLM-enabled process with a conventional, human-led data-extraction approach. Specifically, we aim to evaluate the accuracy metrics and error types associated with each process.
Research Questions
1. What is the comparative accuracy of an automated, multi-stage, LLM-enabled evidence extraction process versus a conventional, human-only data extraction approach?
2. How do types and distribution of errors compare between the two approaches?
Methods 
Study design: We will use a validation study design within a diagnostic test accuracy framework to evaluate the performance of a multi-stage, automated, LLM-enabled evidence extraction process against a reference standard.
Sample size: Our study sample will consist of randomized and nonrandomized studies drawn from three rapid reviews. Because this is an exploratory study, we will not conduct a formal sample size calculation.
Selection of source studies: To avoid any risk of data contamination, we will use three rapid reviews, which have been completed but not yet published. The topics of the rapid reviews focus on 1) the efficacy and harms of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) vaccines[8], 2) the efficacy and harms of coronavirus disease (COVID)-19 vaccines[9], and 3) values and preferences of patients receiving pharmacologic and psychologic treatments for chronic insomnia.[10] Together, these rapid reviews encompass a broad range of study designs (e.g., randomized trials, nonrandomized studies of interventions, qualitative studies) and outcomes (e.g., categorical, continuous, patient-reported measures). 
Conventional human-led data extraction [Refence Standard]: Data for the rapid reviews were extracted by a single investigator and checked for correctness and completeness by a second, senior reviewer. Data elements include 1) Study characteristics (e.g., registration number, first author); 2) Characteristics of study participants (e.g., mean age, inclusion/exclusion criteria); 3) Numerical data related to participant flow (e.g., number of randomized individuals overall and per study group); 4) Outcome data (e.g., the proportion of individuals experiencing an event, or rankings of values and preferences).
Automated data extraction: 
For automated data extraction, we will use a 6-step multi-stage, LLM-enabled evidence extraction process. It begins by using an external parsing service, Landing AI (https://landing.ai/), to parse Portable Document Format (PDF) files of study publications (Step 1), then employs an LLM—specifically Google Gemini 3 Pro, though the architecture supports other models—to extract data and information from a study report (i.e., the main study reporting article or ‘index’ article) and any associated study supplements, appendices, and related companion articles (i.e., publications or study registrations reporting information related to the index article) (Step 2). The system links these supplementary data to the main index article (Step 3) and, to improve recall, conducts multiple runs of the extraction step (Step 4). Step 5 uses a voting algorithm to identify the most frequent value extracted for each data point across the multiple data extraction runs, and exports these values into the final dataset for comparison with the reference standard (Step 6).
Data management: A data manager will oversee the data collection process. The data manager will receive completed tasks, verify data completeness, perform data cleaning as needed, and organize outputs into standardized formats to enable comparison between data extraction approaches. We will store data electronically in Excel datasheets. All investigators will have access to the data. The final LLM prompts, model configuration settings, and human- and model generated data extractions will be saved and shared as part of dissemination. Likewise, we will make the final data available upon request. 
Adjudication panel: The data manager will compile a single standardized sheet containing the outputs of both data extraction approaches, with group identifiers removed, and submit it to the adjudication panel. The credibility of any validation study depends on the quality of its reference standard. Because human data extraction is error-prone, an adjudicated ground truth is required. The adjudication panel will resolve disagreements between automated and human data extraction to determine the most accurate information for each data point. This adjudicated reference standard will then serve as the ground truth for calculating performance metrics.
To avoid bias for or against the automation tool, the adjudication process will be blinded. The panel will include senior members of the team who were not involved in conducting the rapid reviews. Adjudication panelist tasks will first assess whether data are concordant between the two approaches. We define concordance as ‘the proportion of data items that are factually congruent between the two methods, regardless of differences in style or presentation’.[11] Data elements that are concordant will be assumed to reflect accurately extracted data compared with the ground truth. Next, panelists will adjudicate discordant data elements between the two approaches by consulting the original source documents to establish the ‘ground truth’. Both data extractions will then be recompared against the ground truth to determine whether an error is present. Lastly, the panelists will judge the severity of errors in terms of their potential impact on review results and conclusions. A second adjudicator will review any discordances flagged by the first adjudicator and will either accept the first adjudicator’s determinations or engage in dialogue to come to a consensus determination. Every final decision about the presence and severity of an error, together with the supporting rationale, will be documented to ensure a transparent and auditable trail. 
Performance Metrics: Outcomes of interest include:
• Accuracy metrics (accuracy, recall, precision, F1-score). In the context of data extraction, accuracy refers to the proportion of data items that are either correctly extracted or correctly identified as unavailable. To calculate these performance metrics, we will use the ground truth as the reference standard.
• Concordance. We will use percent agreement rather than kappa statistics, as chance agreement is minimal when extractors rely directly on source material.
• Error Analysis. We will determine the types of errors (e.g., missed data, unsupported data) and the potential severity of errors. 

Ethical and Privacy Considerations. 
The study is solely aimed at advancing knowledge and understanding in the field of AI-based data extraction, without involving any human subjects or sensitive data. Therefore, ethical considerations and associated procedures are not applicable for this research. We will use an LLM that does not train on uploaded PDFs or user interactions unless explicitly permitted, ensuring that the intellectual property rights of copyrighted study reports are fully respected.

title: Are basophil activation test (BAT) and IgE levels useful tools in confirming penicillin allergy? Novel diagnostic approach in beta-lactams hypersensitivity reactions
description:
Background:
Penicillin allergy is one of the most commonly reported drug allergies worldwide. However, numerous studies have demonstrated that a substantial proportion of patients labeled as penicillin-allergic are not truly allergic when evaluated with validated diagnostic procedures. Misdiagnosis may lead to the use of broader-spectrum antibiotics, increased healthcare costs, antimicrobial resistance, and suboptimal clinical outcomes. Traditional diagnostic methods, including skin testing and drug provocation testing, have limitations related to sensitivity, specificity, accessibility, and patient safety. In recent years, laboratory-based diagnostic tools such as the Basophil Activation Test (BAT) and measurement of penicillin-specific Immunoglobulin E (IgE) antibodies have emerged as potential adjuncts in the diagnostic workup of beta-lactam hypersensitivity.
Objective:
This systematic review aims to evaluate the diagnostic utility of the Basophil Activation Test (BAT) and serum specific IgE measurements in confirming penicillin allergy and other beta-lactam hypersensitivity reactions. The review will assess the sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, and overall clinical applicability of these tests compared with established reference standards, including skin testing and drug provocation testing.
Research Question:
Among patients with suspected penicillin or beta-lactam allergy, how accurately do BAT and specific IgE testing identify true hypersensitivity reactions compared with conventional diagnostic methods?
Methods:
A systematic literature search will be conducted in electronic databases including PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library. Studies involving human participants evaluated for suspected penicillin or beta-lactam allergy using BAT and/or specific IgE testing will be considered for inclusion. Eligible study designs will include prospective and retrospective cohort studies, diagnostic accuracy studies, case-control studies, and relevant clinical investigations.
Two independent reviewers will perform study selection, data extraction, and quality assessment. Discrepancies will be resolved through discussion or consultation with a third reviewer. Risk of bias will be assessed using appropriate methodological tools, such as QUADAS-2 for diagnostic accuracy studies.
Outcomes:
The primary outcomes will include sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, negative predictive value, and likelihood ratios of BAT and specific IgE assays. Secondary outcomes will include comparison of diagnostic performance across different beta-lactam agents, patient populations, clinical phenotypes of hypersensitivity reactions, and laboratory methodologies.
Significance:
This review seeks to provide a comprehensive synthesis of current evidence regarding novel in vitro diagnostic approaches for beta-lactam hypersensitivity. The findings may contribute to improved diagnostic pathways, reduction of unnecessary penicillin allergy labels, optimization of antibiotic stewardship, and enhanced patient safety.

title: Innovation in Obstetric Diagnosis: The Emerging Role of Magnetic Resonance Imaging in the Placenta Accreta Spectrum: An Integrative Literature Review.
description:
This is an integrative literature review of descriptive and qualitative character. The integrative review refers to a theoretical and analytical approach to published collections aimed at updating a given subject, enabling the researcher to obtain multiple types of information from existing works for theoretical grounding, characterized by guiding questions.
The search was conducted during the first semester of 2025, including studies published within the last five years, in the following databases: PubMed, SciELO, ScienceDirect, and LILACS.
As a first step, the PICO strategy was employed, which considers the deepening of clinical approaches as a means of formulating research questions.
As an acronym, the present study represents: P (Population): Pregnant women with clinical suspicion or confirmed diagnosis of PAS (accreta, increta, or percreta). I (Intervention): Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) as a diagnostic imaging tool for Placenta Accreta Spectrum. C (Comparison): Ultrasound (grayscale and Doppler), the current standard diagnostic method in obstetric practice. O (Outcomes): Diagnostic accuracy of MRI, assessed through sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, and negative predictive value in the detection and classification of Placenta Accreta Spectrum. Based on this strategy, the following research question was formulated: How has magnetic resonance imaging been consolidating itself as an innovative and emerging tool in the precise diagnosis of placenta accreta spectrum, and what are its impacts on specialized obstetric practice concerning this twenty-first-century pathology?

title: Dried blood spot proteomics in newborn screening: a scoping review of its complementarity to metabolomic and genomic strategies
description:
Background. Dried blood spot (DBS) sampling underpins newborn screening (NBS) worldwide, where it is used chiefly for metabolite, enzyme-activity, and nucleic-acid testing. Proteomic analysis of DBS — the direct measurement of proteins and peptides — has emerged more recently as a candidate modality, but the extent, diversity, and maturity of this work, and its relationship to established metabolomic and emerging genomic strategies, have not been systematically mapped.
Purpose. This scoping review aims to map the range and nature of proteomic approaches applied to neonatal DBS in a screening context, and to characterise their positioning within the screening pathway relative to metabolomic and genomic strategies. The guiding question is: which proteomic approaches (protein/peptide measurement) have been applied to DBS in a neonatal screening population, on which analytical platforms, for which target conditions, and in what role — first-tier, second-tier confirmatory, genomic interface/variant resolution, panel extension, or discovery?
Methods. The review follows the framework of Arksey & O'Malley, refined by Levac et al., and is reported in accordance with PRISMA-ScR. Eligibility requires three cumulative criteria: (i) a proteomic measurement, (ii) the DBS matrix (whole blood dried on filter paper), and (iii) an effective neonatal screening population. Records are identified across six sources (PubMed/MEDLINE, ScienceDirect, Cochrane Library, OpenAlex, Embase, and citation-tracking) over 2010–2026, deduplicated, and screened in two stages (title/abstract, then full text with coded exclusion reasons). Data are charted on ~30 variables, including analytical platform, sample preparation, target condition, population and design, pathway positioning, reported performance, stability, throughput, prematurity interactions, conflicts of interest, and programme links. Study appraisal is interpretive and design-driven — QUADAS-2 for diagnostic-accuracy studies, a CLSI-anchored analytical grid for validation/feasibility/discovery studies, and AMSTAR-2 for included reviews — and is not used for scoring, exclusion, or weighting, consistent with PRISMA-ScR. Findings are synthesised narratively by thematic cluster, without meta-analysis.
Expected outcomes. An evidence map of platforms, target conditions, and pathway positioning; identification of the most mature and reproduced application areas; and characterisation of remaining gaps — including neonatal reference values and the prematurity axis — supporting an articulation of DBS proteomics as a complement and bridge between metabolomic and genomic newborn-screening strategies.

title: Clinical Progress in Breast Propagation-Based Imaging (PBI): A 10-Year Scoping Review of Technological and Diagnostic Advances
description:
Propagation-based imaging (PBI) is an emerging x-ray phase-contrast technique that has seen notable technological progress and growing interest in its clinical application for breast imaging. Advancements over the past decade include improvements in x-ray sources, detector sensitivity, imaging parameters, phase retrieval methods, and reconstruction algorithms.
This scoping review aims to answer the following question: What are the key technological developments and clinical implications of PBI for breast imaging over the past ten years, and how does it compare to standard breast imaging modalities in terms of diagnostic performance and clinical readiness?

To address this, the review will:

1. Catalogue recent technological advancements in breast PBI, covering both hardware (x-ray sources, imaging parameters, detectors and patient positioning) and software (image reconstruction and phase retrieval) proponents.
2. Assess the diagnostic performance of PBI in breast imaging, focusing on image quality, lesion detectability and radiation dose.
3. Compare breast PBI with established imaging techniques such as digital mammography, tomosynthesis, ultrasound, and MRI, in terms of diagnostic accuracy, feasibility, and clinical integration.
4. Identify current limitations and outline future directions for clinical adoption.

By clarifying the status of PBI, this review aims to inform future research and development and support its potential integration into routine breast cancer screening and diagnosis.

title: The EVIDENCE Framework: A Pre‑registered Protocol for Detecting and Preventing Evidence Recycling in AI‑Assisted Systematic Reviews and Meta‑Analyses
description:
Purpose: The EVIDENCE Framework is an eight domain editorial checklist (Evaluation of originality, Verification of sources, Integrity in synthesis, Diversity of data, Ethical AI use, Novel contribution, Contextual relevance, Editorial responsibility) designed to detect evidence recycling – the AI driven paraphrasing of existing research findings that creates an illusion of novel evidence without new data. This pre registered protocol outlines the prospective validation of the framework.
Methods: We will conduct a diagnostic accuracy study using 100 systematic reviews or meta analyses that declared use of generative AI. Two independent reviewers will apply the EVIDENCE Framework (index test) blinded to a reference standard. The reference standard consists of a three expert panel manually auditing all sources for evidence recycling using semantic similarity tools. Primary outcomes are sensitivity, specificity and inter rater reliability (Cohen’s κ). Secondary outcomes include feasibility (median completion time) and positive/negative predictive values.
Expected outcomes: We anticipate that the EVIDENCE Framework will demonstrate high sensitivity (>80%) and substantial inter rater reliability (κ > 0.7) for detecting evidence recycling. The protocol includes pre specified editorial action thresholds (e.g., any “Not met” on Verification of sources triggers mandatory dependency matrix submission). Results will inform journal policies on AI assisted evidence synthesis.
Data sharing: De identified dependency matrices, EVIDENCE scores and reference standard judgments will be deposited on OSF with a CC BY license upon publication.

title: The experiences of artificial intelligence utilization in healthcare services and healthcare professionals workloads: a scoping review
description: In recent years, the landscape of healthcare services has undergone transformative changes with the incorporation of Artificial Intelligence. (AI). AI encompasses a range of technologies including, but not limited to, machine learning, natural language processing, and deep learning, which have been progressively employed to optimize healthcare services and manage workloads effectively. The penetration of AI in healthcare is premised on its potential to automate routine tasks, offer decision support systems, and enhance diagnostic accuracy, thereby ostensibly reducing the workloads of healthcare professionals and enhancing efficiency. Therefore, evaluating the impacts of AI utilization in healthcare services on the workloads of healthcare professionals becomes imperative to delineate the nuanced implications it harbors for the healthcare workforce.

title: Development and internal validation of a search filter meant to identify Swiss graduate theses focusing on children’s homes written in French
description:
Abstract
Background and rationale:
Swiss social work students from higher education universities (HETS Lausanne, HETS Fribourg, HETS Valais and HETS Genève) have published over 4000 theses from 2008-2018, many of which report primary qualitative research (mainly interview studies). The current number of social work theses (thousands), variation in indexing, terminology and keywords used by students (foyer, maison, home, lieu de vie, institution, etc.) (or used in different universities) and database limitations (no abstracts available online for almost all theses) has made it difficult for to find Swiss works focusing on this topic. Children’s home research not identified by end-users and stakeholders are unlikely to be read, could be unnecessarily undertaken again and may therefore contribute to research waste. Neglecting children’s home research found in graduate theses also means that children in care and care workers would have given their time to contribute to research that may end up having little to no impact. A well-developed topic search filter meant to help identify children’s home research could prove to be a useful tool to limit research waste in this context.
Objective:
To develop and validate search filters meant to retrieve Swiss social work graduate theses focusing on children’s homes (topic search filter) written in French and indexed in Swissbib.
Study design:
Search filter development study and internal validation of the filters on one (1) dataset of relevant records and one (1) dataset of irrelevant records
Methods:
First, consecutive theses published by HETS Lausanne social work students from 1960-2015 were manually sought and assessed until 10 children’s home theses were found for each decade. Based on a brief assessment of their contents, 73 theses were deemed to focus on children’s homes and 123 to focus on other topics (“irrelevant theses”). The titles of the 73 included theses constituted the development set. The development set was analyzed using the Systematic Review Accelerator word frequency analyzer tool and the most commonly found 1 or 2 words keywords were extracted to an Excel document. Each keyword’s ability to correctly identify relevant theses (sensitivity) and correctly exclude irrelevant theses (specificity) was then calculated by emulating Swissbib’s exact keyword search and wildcard searches functions with imbricated COUNTIF().Two search filters were iteratively developed by subjectively selecting and combining keywords with the highest specificity and/or the highest sensitivity. The best “OR” keyword combinations were then sought through trial and error using the dynamic Excel search emulator, trying as best as possible to select keywords leading to inclusion of relevant records only. For all relevant theses titles which could not be found I tried to identify which missing keyword(s) combination(s) could have been used to include them without also including too many irrelevant titles too.
Results:
The highly sensitive search filter achieved 79.45% sensitivity and 95.12% specificity. This search filter found 58 out of 73 (79.45%) relevant theses and adequately excluded 117 out of 123 (95.12%) irrelevant records. The most effective highly specific search filter achieved 69.86% sensitivity and 98.37% specificity. This search filter found 51 out of 73 (69.86%) relevant theses and adequately excluded 121 out of 123 (98.37%) irrelevant records. It is meant to adequately exclude as many non-children’s homes theses as possible. Although a few additional relevant theses with uninformative titles could have been found with children’s homes non-specific keywords this was deemed to be inadequate for this would likely negatively affect the filter performances when/if used in a different dataset or database.
Limitations:
Search filter performances could therefore be slightly different in Swissbib. These search filter performances in other databases including French literature is currently unknown. The performance of a search filter is bounded by the limitations of the data (titles and abstracts) on which it is based; in the current context it is difficult to achieve higher sensitivities when a substantial portion of titles provide little information on the study focus and no abstracts are available. These search filter performances may vary over time if a) keywords in use change or b) graduate theses titles become more or less informative. These search filters are meant to identify children’s homes theses published from 1960 to 2015.A number of French keywords specific to children’s homes such as “foyer de jeunesse” (Canada), “home d’enfants”, “établissement dépositaire”, “Serix” and “maison d’éducation à caractère social (MECS)” (France) were not identified within children’s home theses, which suggests relevant titles can still be missed by these search filters and performances will vary if they are used to search non-Swiss theses. A sample of n=73 children’s homes theses was not enough to identify the full breadth of children’s homes keywords in use in Switzerland from 1960 to 2015. Identifying theses whose focus were children’s homes involved a level of subjectivity, particularly for institutions with mixed populations (children and adults) and other authors may differ with some of the judgements made.
Discussion:
The performances of the two search filters developed in this study should be tested (external validation) in other Swiss databases such as RERO Explore or Renouvaud prior to a more widespread use. HETS Lausanne’s librarians may encourage social work students to use these search filters to identify Swiss children’s homes theses and the Excel search simulator could also be used (and improved) to teach about developing effective search strategies.
HETS students and higher education students could be given more or better guidance on how to make their theses titles more informative to future potential readers if they wish for others to benefits from insights emerging from their work. Swiss social work higher education schools should consider also including theses abstracts in electronic databases to help users identify works they may be interested in. PDF versions of graduate theses would also massively increase their accessibility and both national and international visibility.

No funding was received for this work.
Registration: Not done, previous report versions nevertheless available at https://osf.io/dc6xy/files .
Data and materials: See https://osf.io/dc6xy/files. All other data is otherwise included within this manuscript.

title: RELIABILITY, APPLICABILITY AND EXPANSION OF ACCESS TO DIAGNOSIS THROUGH TELECONSULTATION IN STOMATOLOGY: a scoping review
description: Teledentistry comprises several modalities of remote dental care, notably teleconsultation—defined as the exchange of clinical information among healthcare professionals—and telediagnosis, which involves issuing diagnostic reports. However, the impact of teleconsultation on the early diagnosis of oral lesions remains uncertain. This study aims to synthesize the available evidence and provide a comprehensive overview of the reliability, applicability, and potential to expand access to the diagnosis of oral lesions, including malignant and potentially malignant disorders, through teleconsultation in oral medicine. A systematic search was conducted in MEDLINE/PubMed, Cochrane Library, EMBASE, LILACS, and gray literature up to January 2025, with no language restrictions. Methodological quality and risk of bias were assessed using specific tools: Newcastle-Ottawa (cohort studies), JBI (cross-sectional studies), QUADAS-2 (diagnostic accuracy studies), and GRADE (certainty of evidence). A narrative synthesis was performed. A total of 25 observational studies (cross-sectional, cohort, and diagnostic accuracy) were included, involving 8,746 patients assessed via teleconsultation, although not all studies reported the exact number of participants. Among the evaluated cases, 612 were confirmed as malignant. Diagnostic agreement between general practitioners and specialists ranged from 60% to 100%, being higher in studies with standardized protocols, prior training, or those conducted by specialists. Remote diagnostic accuracy reached up to 97% compared to the gold standard. Overall satisfaction with the service was high (96.5%), and 75% of patients reported the procedure as comfortable. Some studies demonstrated that teleconsultation contributes to expanding access to diagnosis in oral medicine, as reflected in an increase in referrals. Despite promising findings, the high methodological heterogeneity (>85%) among studies precluded a robust meta-analysis and limited the generalizability of results.

title: Bias in Healthcare AI and its Implications for Clinical Decision-Making: A Scoping Review
description: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly being integrated into various domains of healthcare. These technologies are transforming healthcare by exhibiting compelling diagnostic accuracy, rivalling that of human experts and reducing diagnostic errors (The American Journal of Managed Care 2025). However, AI systems can also perpetuate and reinforce existing biases, thereby, producing undesirable effects on clinical decision-making (Cross et al. 2024). Biases can compound over time, further worsening the healthcare delivery for marginalized communities and making bias in Healthcare AI a pressing ethical concern to be addressed. The aim of this scoping review is to conceptually analyze bias in healthcare AI, as bias itself is a layered concept and carries different senses across disciplines and contexts. Understanding how bias is conceptualized is essential because such conceptualizations shape what is identified as problematic and, consequently, what is considered in need of mitigation. This review therefore seeks to examine how bias in healthcare AI is understood in existing literature, the different types and sources of bias identified, and the factors contributing to the emergence of bias in clinical decision-making. Additionally, the review aims to explore the implications of bias on clinical decision-making and critically analyze the observable limitations of current bias mitigation strategies proposed in healthcare AI.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Detecting Neurological and Psychiatric Comorbidities Through Orofacial Biomarkers: A Rapid Systematic Review
description:
Background and Rationale
The orofacial region provides a direct, accessible window into central nervous system function. Measurable biological outputs—specifically jaw muscle activation (electromyography), salivary biomarkers, and microscopic facial kinematics—frequently alter in the early stages of major neurological and psychiatric disorders. Conditions such as Parkinson’s disease, major depressive disorder, generalized anxiety, and schizophrenia present distinct orofacial signatures.

While dental clinicians interact with these exact biological signals during routine appointments, they currently play no role in frontline neurological screening. Machine learning architectures have recently demonstrated the capacity to map these complex, non-linear orofacial patterns with high diagnostic accuracy (historically ranging from 72% to 99% in isolated datasets). However, the literature remains fragmented. No comprehensive review has yet synthesized the diagnostic accuracy of these varied AI frameworks specifically for neuro-psychiatric screening, leaving a critical gap between advanced computational models and practical dental clinical applications.

Objectives
This rapid systematic review aims to systematically map and critically evaluate the current state of AI applications using orofacial data for neuro-psychiatric detection. The primary objectives are to:
 • Evaluate the diagnostic accuracy (sensitivity, specificity, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve) of existing AI models across distinct orofacial modalities.
 • Determine whether multimodal AI integrations (e.g., combining salivary chemistry with dynamic kinematics) yield superior predictive power compared to standalone single-biomarker models.
 • Identify the methodological barriers preventing the translation of these diagnostic tools from engineering laboratories into physical dental operatories.

Methodology
This study will follow a streamlined rapid review framework adapted from the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) guidelines to ensure structural transparency:
 
Search Architecture:
We will execute a systematic search strategy across PubMed, Google Scholar, and Semantic Scholar targeting peer-reviewed literature published between 2015 and 2026.

Eligibility Criteria:
Included studies must utilize machine learning or deep learning algorithms to evaluate human orofacial data (saliva, facial video, or jaw muscle mechanics) for the primary purpose of identifying or tracking a neurological or psychiatric condition. Studies focusing solely on local dental pathologies (e.g., localized temporomandibular joint disorders) or relying purely on standard neuroimaging protocols (such as fMRI) will be excluded.

Data Extraction & Quality Assessment: 
Data regarding model architecture, sample sizing, biomarker categories, and accuracy metrics will be rigorously extracted into a centralized matrix. Risk of bias will be evaluated by assessing study design limitations, sample sizes, and validation methods to contextualize the strength of the current data.

Clinical Significance:
By establishing a clear, evidence-based assessment of AI capabilities in this domain, this review aims to challenge the traditional boundary between dental medicine and neurology. Proving the viability of AI-driven orofacial screening could ultimately allow the routine dental chair to serve as an opportunistic, non-invasive frontline for early neurodiagnostic intervention—a pivot that could fundamentally improve long-term patient prognoses.

title: Intersectional Minority Stress and Mental Health
description:
Background: 
Black sexual and gender minoritized (BSGM) individuals in the United States experience pervasive stigma and systemic discrimination that contribute to significant mental health disparities. The scope of escalating systemic discrimination remains alarming and is particularly impactful for BSGM individuals. This study applied two foundational frameworks, Minority Stress Theory and Intersectionality, to understand these experiences. Minority Stress Theory, which identifies the experience of identity-based distal stressors (e.g., discrimination, violence) and proximal stressors (e.g., internalized stigma, identity concealment) faced by marginalized populations. Next, intersectionality describes the multiplicative effect of minority stress among those with multiple marginalized identities. BSGM individuals experience intersectional stress from both their racial and gender/sexual identities. The chronic experience of pervasive discrimination influences cognitions, emotions, and behaviors, and contributes to significant psychological distress and impairment. 

The pervasive impact of intersectional stress may systematically bias the measurement of distress and impairment in psychopathology, and particularly personality disorders (PDs). Current diagnostic systems fail to adequately account for socio-contextual factors that contribute to distress and impairment, such as intersectional stress. For example, categorical PD nosology attributes distress and impairment to internal deficits. Dimensional models, while empirically derived, still lack guidance for distinguishing between pathology and intersectional stress responses. The conflation of intersectional stress and pathology can not only distort psychopathological assessment but may also increase mental health disparities. For example, BSGM individuals may avoid seeking mental health services due to emotional barriers such as distrust in the healthcare system or previous experiences of stigma from providers. 

Aims: 
The present study aims to enhance current understanding of the impact of intersectional minority stress on BSGM individuals and its implications on personality pathology measurement. Specifically, dimensional nosologies remain limited in their ability to disentangle behaviors explained by underlying personality pathology from those influenced by socio-contextual factors, such as proximal and distal stressors. Additionally, this study will contribute to the current mental health disparities literature by examining how intersectional minority stress contributes to emotional barriers that may deter BSGM individuals from utilizing mental health services. 

Expected Outcomes 
This project aims to advance the discussion on the impact of socio-contextual factors on psychopathological assessment in marginalized populations (i.e., BSGM individuals). By employing an intersectional minority stress-informed lens, we seek to establish preliminary evidence for more equitable diagnostic practice considerations that distinguish pathology from adaptive responses to intersectional minority stress. Our work contributes to a growing foundation for context-informed personality measurement, with important implications for improving diagnostic accuracy, guiding individualized treatment planning, and ultimately promoting long-term mental and physical health outcomes for Black sexual and gender minoritized individuals.

title: Performance of the SpO₂/FiO₂ ratio as a surrogate for the PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio in adults with acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS): a protocol for a systematic review and meta-analysis
description:
Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) remains associated with high mortality, yet nearly half of affected patients are not recognized in clinical practice. The PaO₂/FiO₂ (P/F) ratio has long served as the cornerstone of ARDS definitions, but arterial blood gas analysis is invasive and resource-intensive. The SpO₂/FiO₂ (S/F) ratio, derived from pulse oximetry, offers a non-invasive alternative and has been incorporated into recent ARDS definitions. However, reported sensitivities and specificities of S/F-based definitions vary considerably across studies, and it remains unclear whether the S/F ratio can reliably substitute for the P/F ratio in ARDS. This systematic review and meta-analysis will evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of the S/F ratio as a surrogate for the P/F ratio in adults with ARDS.

We will include prospective or retrospective observational studies and randomized controlled trials reporting both S/F and P/F ratios in adults with ARDS or acute lung injury. Searches were performed in PubMed, EMBASE, CENTRAL, and Web of Science from inception to 13 August 2025, and will be updated on 11 April 2026. Study screening and data extraction will be conducted independently by three reviewers. The primary outcome is the diagnostic performance (sensitivity and specificity) of the S/F ratio compared with a P/F threshold of 300 mmHg. Secondary outcomes include accuracy for other P/F thresholds (200 and 100 mmHg), correlation coefficients between S/F and P/F. Pooled estimates will be obtained using the bivariate random-effects model (Reitsma). Heterogeneity will be assessed using Cochran’s Q test, and its magnitude will be quantified using the I² statistic, and risk of bias will be assessed using the QUADAS-2 tool.

title: The Relational Calculus for Green AI
description:
This project is the public home of Relational Calculus, a meta‑mathematical framework that replaces the brute‑force logic of absolute‑scale computation with dimension‑less, capacity‑anchored blueprints. At its heart lies a simple but radical axiom: every system possesses an intrinsic maximum—a “North Star”—and by expressing all observations as fractions of that limit, complexity collapses, efficiency soars, and transfer across domains becomes automatic.

The collection gathers the complete stack: the foundational theoretical paper, a ready‑to‑run Relational Decoder (an open‑source algorithm that probes any black‑box function and extracts its dimensionless template), and five applied case studies that prove the principle in wildly different arenas—number theory (deterministic prime pair lattices), symbolic artificial intelligence (a geometric chess engine that exhibits emergent strategy with zero domain knowledge, gaining 90%+ efficiency), high‑energy physics (scale‑invariant jet tagging that transfers zero‑shot across collision energies with +14.5% AUC), quantum chemistry (80% error reduction in cross‑molecule transfer), and precision oncology (a lightweight XGBoost that achieves 98.4% cross‑species diagnostic accuracy under a 70% hardware‑signal collapse, completely erasing batch effects). A companion paper extends the logic to large language models, proposing Relational‑CoT as a drop‑in replacement for resource‑intensive chain‑of‑thought reasoning.

Every work converges on the same empirical signature: >90% reduction in computational cost, genuine zero‑shot generalization across scales and species, and the proof that Green AI is not an aspiration but an engineering reality. An integrated STEM curriculum for ages 10–14 ensures that the relational lens is taught before the continuous one, inoculating the next generation against the wasteful “math of deviation.”

All code, data, and executable papers are open‑source. The project is intended not as a scholarly gesture but as an enablement instrument for the industrial shift from the Age of Fire—where more compute meant more extraction—to the Era of Relation, where measuring how full a system is replaces the endless pursuit of how much.

title: Association of early parathyroid hormone level and calcium with chronic hypoparathyroidism in patients following total thyroidectomy: a systematic review and meta-analysis
description:
Total thyroidectomy, the major cause of permanent hypoparathyroidism, can permanently damage the parathyroid glands, the structures responsible for producing parathyroid hormone (PTH), and thus result in postoperative hypoparathyroidism. Most patients whose PTH decreases post-operatively experience transient hypoparathyroidism and recover within 6 months; 0.2%-3% will, however, develop chronic hypoparathyroidism and require long-term calcium and/or vitamin D supplementation. Chronic hypoparathyroidism is associated with nephrocalcinosis, renal insufficiency, seizures, arrhythmia, ischemic heart disease, depression, and cataract, and with hospitalization for depression and affective disorders.

Aiming to minimize complications and avoid overtreatment, investigators have tried to predict both transient and chronic postsurgical hypoparathyroidism. Responding to a survey of American and European Endocrine Societies, 30% of American and 41% of European society respondents reported routine use of PTH assays after thyroidectomy. 

Most diagnostic test accuracy studies have suggested that low PTH and serum calcium level in the early postoperative period may predict transient hypocalcemia and chronic hypoparathyroidism after thyroidectomy, but the reported diagnostic performance varied among studies. A systematic review reported 89% median accuracy, 88% median sensitivity, and 90% median specificity of measuring early PTH for predicting temporary postoperative hypocalcemia.14 Another prior review addressed the possible predictive value of early measurement of PTH and calcium for long term hypoparathyroidism but included only one study. After this review, investigators have published several new diagnostic test accuracy studies addressing prediction of long-term hypoparathyroidism. 

Owing to substantial variation among studies regarding timing of measurement, PTH/calcium thresholds to predict chronic hypoparathyroidism, sensitivity, specificity, prevalence, the value of PTH and calcium measurements to predict chronic hypoparathyroidism remain uncertain. To address the remaining uncertainties, we aim to undertake a systematic review and a meta-analysis of studies evaluating the use of PTH/calcium levels to predict chronic hypoparathyroidism after total thyroidectomy.

title: Diagnosing self regulation in students – The use of diagnostic and non-diagnostic cues across 4 countries
description: Self regulated learning is a key competence in education (Dent & Koenka, 2016). However, many students have problems to learn self-regulated (Karlen, 2016). Strategies of self-regulated learning are not regularly part of school lectures (Dignath & Veenmann, 2021) and many teachers are also not competent to induce self-regulated learning (Karlen et al., 2020; Michalsky, 2017). One key component of this teacher competence is to first diagnose the pre-exsting ability of students to learn self-regulated in order to be able to choose adequate induction strategies. The present study focuses on the utilization of cues in order to diagnose self-regulated learning. Therefore, we manipulate the availability of cues. Pre- and inservice teachers are presented with diagnostic cues only or both, non-diagnostic cues and diagnostic cues. A third group of participants recived both diagnostic and non-diagnostic cues and was additionally informed about the diagnosticity of the presented cues and told to ignore the non-dagnostic ones. Diagnostic accuracy as well as the use of cues is measured. Additionally the influence of teacher experience, knowledge, beliefs and attitudes is tested.

Assessing the Diagnostic Yield of Post-Mortem Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) for Detecting Cardiac Anomalies in Fetal and Perinatal Deaths: Protocol for a Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
description:
Cardiac anomalies represent one of the most common categories of congenital malformations, affecting approximately 8-12 per 1000 live births, and are a leading cause of fetal and perinatal mortality. In this context, accurate diagnosis of cardiac anomalies is crucial for genetic counselling, recurrence risk assessment, and parental understanding. Conventional autopsy, though considered the gold standard, faces challenges such as parental refusal and limited availability of paediatric pathologists. Post-mortem imaging, including magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), computed tomography (CT), and ultrasound, often termed "virtopsy," is increasingly proposed as a non-invasive alternative. However, its diagnostic yield specifically for cardiac anomalies in fetal and perinatal deaths remains to be systematically evaluated. 
Despite increasing use of post-mortem imaging, there is limited comprehensive evidence regarding its diagnostic yield specifically for cardiac anomalies in fetal and perinatal deaths. This systematic review and meta-analysis aims to synthesize available evidence to determine the diagnostic accuracy of various post-mortem MRI for detecting cardiac anomalies in this population. The findings are anticipated to have significant clinical implications by contributing to the development of clinical practice guidelines for the use of post-mortem imaging in the evaluation of cardiac anomalies. The findings are expected to inform clinical guidelines, support healthcare policy and resource planning, enhance family counselling practices, and highlight the need for specialized training in post-mortem imaging interpretation.

title: The SPECTRA Evidence Stack: An Auditable Neuroaffirmative Framework for Integrating Multi-Source Evidence in Adult Neurodivergence Assessment
description: This methods paper introduces the SPECTRA Evidence Stack, a transparent, neuroaffirmative framework for integrating multi-source evidence in adult neurodivergence assessment. The framework structures data from self-report, informant-report, and performance or observational measures through three layers—Response Quality, Multi-source Convergence, and Confidence Synthesis—preserving discrepancies as clinically interpretable signals rather than treating them as noise. We present the conceptual architecture, theoretical rationale, illustrative clinical vignettes, and a formative synthetic stress test of rule behavior. This work does not validate diagnostic accuracy, clinical effectiveness, or real-world utility; it establishes a methodological foundation for future empirical and clinical evaluation.

title: Protocol for a Systematic Review: Quantitative Assessment Methods and Biomarkers in Progressive Ataxias
description:
This registered protocol outlines the methodology for a systematic review evaluating quantitative assessment tools and biomarkers in progressive ataxias. Progressive ataxias are a heterogeneous group of neurodegenerative disorders characterized by cerebellar dysfunction and progressive motor impairment. Early and objective quantification of disease progression remains a clinical challenge, and validated biomarkers are urgently needed for clinical trials and personalized management.

The review will address the following research question using the PECO framework:
• Population: Adults and children diagnosed with progressive ataxias (e.g., spinocerebellar ataxias, Friedreich's ataxia, multiple system atrophy–cerebellar type)
• Exposure: Application of quantitative assessment methods (e.g., wearable sensors, motion capture, digital biomarkers, neuroimaging metrics) and/or molecular/cellular biomarkers
• Comparison: Conventional clinical scales (e.g., SARA, BARS) or absence of quantitative assessment
• Outcomes: (1) Psychometric properties (validity, reliability, responsiveness); (2) Correlation with disease severity/progression; (3) Feasibility and clinical utility

Eligible study designs include observational studies (cross-sectional, longitudinal), validation studies, and clinical trials reporting quantitative outcomes. No language restrictions will be applied. The literature search will be conducted across PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, and EMBASE from inception to February 2026.

Data extraction will include study characteristics, ataxia subtype, assessment methods, biomarker types, and outcome metrics. Risk of bias will be assessed using appropriate tools (e.g., QUADAS-2 for diagnostic accuracy studies, NIH Quality Assessment Tool for observational studies). Given expected methodological heterogeneity across studies, a narrative synthesis will be performed without meta-analysis.

This protocol was registered prior to data extraction to ensure methodological transparency and minimize reporting bias.

title: The Digital Twin Landscape in Medical Diagnosis: A Scoping Review and Bibliometric Analysis of Emerging Applications, Translational Challenges, and Future Theranostic Potential
description:
Amid the growing global demand for precision medicine and personalized healthcare, traditional medical diagnostic models face significant challenges [1, 2]. Current diagnostic methods often rely on empirical judgment and population-based reference data, struggling to capture the dynamic changes and heterogeneous characteristics of individual physiological systems. This leads to frequent issues such as delayed early disease warnings, limited diagnostic accuracy for complex conditions, and suboptimal treatment plan adaptability, which collectively represent critical bottlenecks in improving healthcare quality and efficacy [3-5]. To address these challenges, academia and industry are actively exploring the deep integration of cutting-edge engineering technologies with clinical medicine. Among these, digital twin technology, a hallmark of the Fourth Industrial Revolution, is driving profound transformations in medical diagnostics due to its unique value [6, 7].

Originating from industrial manufacturing, digital twin technology creates digital replicas of physical entities to enable dynamic mapping and optimized control throughout their lifecycle [8, 9]. In recent years, advancements in the Internet of Medical Things, high-precision medical imaging, biosensing technologies, and artificial intelligence algorithms have facilitated the penetration of digital twins into the medical field [10]. The core of this approach lies in integrating multidimensional data—such as genomics, proteomics, imaging, and physiological signals—to construct highly accurate digital twin models of the human body or specific organs. These models enable real-time monitoring, simulation, and precise prediction of physiological states and pathological changes [11]. Compared to industrial applications, medical digital twins must address the complexity and dynamism of biological data, ensuring real-time performance and high fidelity to support precise diagnostics [12].

The primary advantage of digital twins in medical diagnostics lies in their ability to shift from passive diagnosis to proactive prediction and from population-based generalizations to individualized precision [6, 13]. By constructing digital twin models synchronized with patients in real time, clinicians can simulate pathophysiological processes in a virtual environment, avoiding the risks and invasiveness of traditional diagnostic procedures (e.g., biopsies or contrast imaging) [14]. For instance, cardiovascular digital twin models have demonstrated their ability to monitor myocardial electrophysiological activity in real time, not only pinpointing myocardial infarction lesions with precision but also detecting subtle conduction abnormalities early, providing diagnostic evidence for occult pathologies [15]. Moreover, digital twin technology significantly enhances diagnostic workflows and decision-making efficiency. Through virtual simulations, clinicians can pre-optimize diagnostic pathways and parameters before complex procedures or identify early-stage lesions imperceptible to the naked eye by deeply analyzing imaging data [16, 17]. In oncology, digital twins can dynamically track the microscopic evolution and biological behavior of tumors, accurately determining their malignancy, invasion scope, and subtype [12, 18, 19]. Figure 1 illustrates a feedback control system centered on a patient’s digital twin, demonstrating how it achieves precise diagnostics through multisource data integration, with detailed mechanisms discussed further in the main text.

In recent years, medical digital twin technology has shown immense potential in clinical areas such as cardiovascular diseases [17, 20-23], oncology [16, 18, 24, 25], and neurological disorders [26-29]. However, as an emerging interdisciplinary technology, its application in medical diagnostics remains in the early stages of rapid development, facing multiple challenges. For example, the lack of data standardization and sharing hinders the integration of heterogeneous multisource data, limiting model generalizability [30-32]. Incomplete ethical and regulatory frameworks may impede the widespread adoption of digital twins in clinical trials [5, 33]. Additionally, issues such as model accuracy and interpretability, high computational demands, and substantial maintenance costs represent critical barriers to technology translation [34, 35]. Currently, there is a lack of systematic reviews in academia that comprehensively outline the application status, core technologies, research hotspots, and future directions of this field.

Therefore, this study employs a combination of scoping review and bibliometric analysis to systematically examine the global literature on digital twins in medical diagnostics, aiming to address the following core questions:

From the perspectives of global research distribution, international collaboration, core funding, and interdisciplinary integration, what are the macroscopic characteristics of the research landscape in this field?

What are the key data sources, core modeling techniques, and algorithms used to construct digital twin models for diagnostics?

In which disease contexts are digital twins currently applied in medical diagnostics, and at what stage of technological maturity are these applications?

What are the systemic bottlenecks in data, modeling algorithms, and clinical translation that hinder the transition from theory to application, and what are the key future research directions?

Through systematic analysis of these questions, this paper aims to map the global landscape of digital twin applications in medical diagnostics and outline its future development directions. This work seeks to inspire innovative thinking and foster interdisciplinary collaboration to advance this transformative technology toward maturity.

title: How Are AI-Assisted Systematic Reviews Evaluated in Evidence-Based Healthcare? A Scoping Review
description:
This scoping review aims to map and characterize the indicators used to evaluate the performance, reliability, efficiency, validity, or impact of artificial intelligence–assisted systematic review processes in health research. Artificial intelligence technologies, including machine learning, natural language processing, and large language models, are increasingly being applied to different stages of the systematic review process, such as literature searching, deduplication, screening, data extraction, risk of bias and meta-analysis. However, the methods and indicators used to evaluate these applications remain heterogeneous.
The review will include empirical studies that assess the use of artificial intelligence in one or more stages of a systematic review conducted in a health-related field. The included studies shall compare AI-assisted methods with previously published systematic reviews. Data will be charted on the type of AI technology, stage of the review process, comparator or reference standard, and reported performance and quality indicators.
The review will identify commonly used measures, such as sensitivity, specificity, precision, recall, accuracy, F1 score, agreement statistics, workload reduction, time savings, reproducibility, reliability, usability, and transparency. It will also examine gaps in current evaluation practices and areas in which standardized indicators may be needed. The findings are expected to support the development of more consistent and transparent approaches for evaluating AI-assisted systematic reviews in health research.

title: Artificial Intelligence for Reporting Quality: Validation of an LLM-Based Tool to Assess STARD 2015 Compliance in Imaging Research
description:
Background: Incomplete reporting in diagnostic accuracy research limits the ability to assess risk of bias, judge clinical applicability, and integrate findings into evidence syntheses. Although the Standards for Reporting Diagnostic Accuracy Studies (STARD) 2015 guideline provides a 30-item checklist to guide transparent reporting, adherence remains suboptimal in imaging research despite widespread endorsement, publication of explanatory materials, and dissemination of author checklists. Existing approaches to improving compliance have yielded only limited and inconsistent improvements, and the editorial infrastructure required to verify adherence at scale is often lacking. Large language models (LLMs) have recently shown promise for automated reporting guideline assessment, achieving approximately 90% accuracy against human ratings for CONSORT and other guidelines. However, no studies have evaluated whether LLMs can reliably assess adherence to STARD 2015.

Purpose: To evaluate whether AutoReporter, an LLM-based reporting guideline assessment tool, can reliably assess adherence to the STARD 2015 checklist in diagnostic accuracy studies, using previously published human reference ratings as the reference standard.

Methods: This validation study will apply AutoReporter, using the reasoning model o3-mini in a zero-shot, non-retrieval configuration, to two previously published cohorts of imaging-focused diagnostic accuracy studies with available item-level human STARD adherence ratings: Hong et al. (n=41) and Al-Ghita et al. (n=126), yielding a combined dataset of 167 studies. Full-text articles will be acquired from PubMed Central or institutional repositories and preprocessed using XML parsing or PDF-to-text conversion. AutoReporter outputs will be compared against human reference labels, which were assigned in duplicate and resolved by consensus. Binary classification metrics, including accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, F1 score, and Cohen's kappa, will be calculated per checklist item and at the article level, with 95% confidence intervals. Systematic disagreements between AutoReporter and human ratings will be reviewed by the research team to characterize the nature and sources of discordance.

title: Meta-analysis of prion disease biomarkers
description:
This meta-analysis will be focused on the role of the most commonly used cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) biomarkers in the diagnosis of human prion diseases. The selected CSF biomarkers are: 14-3-3, total-tau, tau ratio, RT-QuIC and alpha-synuclein. The prion diseases included in the scope of the study are: sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, genetic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, Gerstmann–Sträussler–Scheinker syndrome and fatal familial insomnia.
The search will be performed in PubMed under pre-defined search strategy and inclusion criteria, following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) recommendations. Selected papers will be evaluated with the QUADAS-2 tool for the quality assessment of diagnostic accuracy studies. Main data will be collected, including study type, participants involved, sample size and biomarker test results in the study population. Paper evaluation and data collection will be performed by two independent researchers, and discrepancies will be discussed.
Data analysis will be carried out in R following standard procedures for diagnostic test accuracy meta-analyses, including, but not limited to, estimation of pooled effects, heterogeneity quantification and publication bias.

title: The dimensionality of proposed DSM-5 PTSD symptoms in trauma-exposed young children
description: Objective. A subtype of the posttraumatic stress disorder diagnosis for children 6 years and younger (PTSD-6Y) was introduced in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual, Fifth Edition (DSM-5). However, the latent structure of PTSD symptoms in this age group has not been previously investigated. The present study therefore utilized confirmatory factor analytic (CFA) techniques to evaluate the proposed DSM-5 PTSD-6Y factor structure and criterion and convergent validity against competing models. Method. Data for N=284 (3-6 years) trauma-exposed young children recruited following a variety of traumas in New Orleans were examined. We compared the DSM-5 PTSD-6Y model to DSM-IV, and alternate 1- 2- and 4-factor models. Convergent validity was established aganst the Child Behaviour Checklist (CBCL). Criterion related validity was established by comparing each model to a categorical rating of impairment. Results. In terms of symptom structure, the Dysphoria and PTSD-6Y models offered the better accounts, although neither satisfied minimum requirements for a good fitting model. These two models also only showed small levels of convergence with CBCL dimensions. With respect to patterns of criterion validity, the 1-factor model offered the most compelling balance of sensitivity and specificity, with the 2-factor model and the Dysphoria model following closely behind. Conclusions. There is little support for the symptom cluster instantiated in DSM-5 PTSD-6Y. Although a 4-factor Dysphoria model offers a better overall account of clustering patterns, alongside acceptable sensitivity and specificity for detecting clinical impairment, it also falls short of being an adequate model in this younger age group.

title: Diagnostic Accuracy of CEUS LI-RADS for HCC in Non-Cirrhotic At-Risk Patients (NAFLD/MASLD Population): a systematic review and meta-analysis
description:
This systematic review and meta-analysis aims to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of Contrast-Enhanced Ultrasound Liver Imaging Reporting and Data System (CEUS LI-RADS) for the detection of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) in non-cirrhotic individuals at risk due to metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), formerly known as non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD). As the epidemiology of HCC shifts toward metabolic liver disease, an increasing number of HCC cases are being reported in patients without established cirrhosis, creating challenges for early diagnosis and surveillance.

The review will systematically identify and synthesize evidence from studies assessing the performance of CEUS LI-RADS categories for differentiating HCC from other focal liver lesions in non-cirrhotic MASLD/NAFLD populations. Diagnostic accuracy measures including sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, negative predictive value, likelihood ratios, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) will be extracted and pooled where appropriate using meta-analytic methods.

The expected outcome is to provide comprehensive evidence regarding the utility and reliability of CEUS LI-RADS in this emerging at-risk population, identify current evidence gaps, and inform future clinical practice, surveillance strategies, and diagnostic guidelines for HCC in non-cirrhotic MASLD/NAFLD patients.

title: Providing a More Nuanced View of Depression Diagnosis through Weighting Depression Items using IRT
description: Traditionally through the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Text Revision (DSM-5-TR), clinicians would make diagnoses for Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) through counting the number of expressed symptoms until a threshold is reached. Either the patient exceeds the threshold and has the disorder, or they do not pass the threshold and are not considered to have the disorder. This current system does not take symptom severity into account and weighs all symptoms equally when tallying the expressed symptoms to reach the diagnostic threshold. By utilizing Item Response Theory (IRT) this study will examine the item severity and discriminability of the Patient Health Questionnaire – 9 (PHQ-9) and A clinically useful depression outcome scale (CUDOS) to determine the latent trait score for each participant’s profile of MDD symptoms. Using the latent trait score, this study will examine if certain participants who didn’t reach the diagnostic threshold still exhibit as high or higher levels of the underlying depression or anxiety construct than participants who do meet the diagnostic threshold for a diagnosis. Additionally, this study will examine how sensitivity and specificity differ based on symptom counts from PHQ-9 only, CUDOS only, PHQ-9 and CUDOS together, or from the latent score from the combined PHQ-9 and CUDOS together.

title: Diagnostic accuracy and clinical utility of circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) vs. traditional biopsy in monitoring Minimal Residual Disease (MRD) in Hematologic Malignancies
description:
In the evolving landscape of precision oncology, the detection of Minimal Residual Disease (MRD) has become the "Gold Standard" for predicting relapse and guiding therapeutic decisions. However, the traditional method for monitoring MRD in hematological malignancies—the bone marrow biopsy—is inherently invasive, painful for patients, and often subject to spatial heterogeneity (the "sampling bias").

The current synthesis aims to critically evaluate a transformative alternative: Circulating Tumor DNA (ctDNA). This "liquid biopsy" approach offers a non-invasive, real-time snapshot of the tumor’s genetic landscape from a simple blood draw. While the potential of ctDNA is widely discussed, there remains a critical gap in clinical consensus regarding its diagnostic accuracy and clinical utility compared to traditional biopsies across the diverse spectrum of blood cancers.
