title: Understanding the Cultural Adaptation and Validation of Depression Screening Tools for South Asians: A Scoping Review
description:
Depression is a leading cause of global disability, affecting approximately 280 million people worldwide. The prevalence of depression in South Asia is notably higher than the global average, at around 3.9%, compared to the global rate of 3.8% and the UK's rate of 3.3%. Cultural, social, and linguistic factors significantly shape how depression is perceived and expressed among South Asians. However, existing depression screening tools, developed primarily in Western contexts, may not fully capture the cultural nuances of South Asian communities, underscoring the need for adaptation and validation of these tools to improve diagnostic accuracy and treatment outcomes.

This scoping review aims to identify depression screening tools that have been developed, culturally adapted, and validated specifically for South Asians. It also seeks to examine the strategies and processes used in the development, cultural adaptation, and validation of these tools, and to map the available evidence on these processes and the effectiveness of the adapted tools. The review will include studies involving South Asians from countries like India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Nepal, Afghanistan, Bhutan, and the Maldives, as well as South Asian diaspora communities globally. It will focus on cultural adaptation and validation strategies for depression screening tools within clinical, community, and research settings. Eligible sources will include peer-reviewed journal articles and grey literature such as book chapters, conference papers, theses, dissertations, reports, and guidelines from recognized institutions or governmental bodies, published in English.

A systematic search of databases such as Ovid, PsycINFO, MedLine/PubMed, Web of Science, CINAHL, Scopus, and EMBASE will be conducted, supplemented by hand-searching key journals and reference lists of identified articles. The search strategy will use specific terms related to the population, concept, and tools, employing Boolean operators and truncations to ensure comprehensive coverage. Screening and selection of studies will be managed using Rayyan Citation, with at least two reviewers evaluating full-text eligibility. Data extraction will involve thematic headings and pilot testing for comparability, focusing on study information, population characteristics, and key information on cultural adaptation and validation of depression screening tools. 

Descriptive quantitative analysis and qualitative narrative synthesis will be used to analyze the data. The review will answer research questions regarding the characteristics, strategies, and evidence of culturally adapted depression screening tools for South Asians. This review is crucial for informing future research, guiding clinical practice, and shaping mental health policies to improve the diagnosis and treatment of depression among South Asians and the diaspora, addressing a significant gap in mental health care.

title: Information Sources, Search Strategy, Study Selection and Data Extraction
description:
Information sources and search strategy
The following databases will be searched:
• PubMed/MEDLINE
• Embase
• CINAHL
The search strategy will combine terms for inflammatory bowel disease, malnutrition or nutritional risk, nutritional screening tools, and the selected reference standards. The PubMed strategy will be adapted for Embase and CINAHL using database-specific subject headings and syntax.
Search filters will include humans, publication date from 1 January 2020 to July 2026, and English language or English translation available.
The PubMed search strategy is provided in Appendix 1.
Study selection
Search results from PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase and CINAHL will be imported into Zotero, where duplicates will be removed. The deduplicated records will then be imported into Rayyan for screening.
Titles and abstracts will be screened by one reviewer against the predefined PICO criteria. Records will be classified as include, exclude or maybe. All records marked include or maybe will proceed to full-text review. A second reviewer will check all records marked include or maybe and a sample of excluded records, using every tenth excluded record.
Full-text screening will be performed against the same eligibility criteria, and each study will be classified as included or excluded. Reasons for exclusion at full-text stage will be recorded. Any disagreements or uncertainties will be resolved by discussion.
The study selection process will be reported using a PRISMA flow diagram.
Data extraction
Data will be extracted into a standardised Excel workbook after full-text review. Each included study will be assigned a study ID using the first author, publication year and a key word from the title.
Study-level data will include basic study details, population demographics, IBD type, clinical setting, nutritional screening tools assessed, comparator used, comparator definition, screening tool cut-off, and whether complete or reconstructable 2 x 2 data are available.
Diagnostic accuracy data will be extracted at the study-screening tool-comparator level. Extracted data will include number analysed, reported sensitivity and specificity, TP, FP, FN and TN where available or derivable, and calculated PPV, NPV, accuracy and kappa.
For each study-screening tool-comparator row, it will be recorded whether a complete 2 x 2 table is reported or can be reconstructed. Rows with complete or reconstructable 2 x 2 data will be included in the structured diagnostic accuracy synthesis. PICO-eligible studies without sufficient 2 x 2 data will be summarised narratively as supportive evidence.
Extracted rows will be organised by comparator first and then by nutritional screening tool, for example MUST versus GLIM, SaskIBD-NR versus GLIM, and equivalent groups for ESPEN criteria and SGA where available.

title: Investigating the Prevalence and Profile of ADHD and the Effectiveness of the CPT-3 Attention Deficit Assessment Tool, in Children and Young People with Sturge-Weber Syndrome.
description:
Secondary Data Analysis

This project aims to investigate the prevalence and profile of ADHD symptoms in CYP with SWS. Existing, anonymised clinical data on ADHD, ASD, Epilepsy and Intellectual Disability diagnoses, ADHD questionnaire scores, cognitive assessment scores, ASD questionnaire scores, as well as ADHD scores on a computerised assessment, will be analysed. These data originate from the Sturge-Weber and Neurocutaneous Disorders (SWANS) clinic, in Great Ormond Street. It is hypothesized that there will be a high prevalence of ADHD in CYP with SWS, and it will be higher than the reported prevalence of ADHD in the general population. It is also predicted that the profile of ADHD in the SWS population will indicate more symptoms of inattention than hyperactivity in CYP with SWS. Findings will highlight the importance of ADHD assessments for CYP with SWS in clinical settings to facilitate much needed timely support and treatment for this population. A secondary aim is to explore the sensitivity and specificity of the Conners’ Continuous Performance Test (3) (Conners CPT 3; Conners 2014), as a diagnostic tool for ADHD within this population. The CPT-3 is a computerised assessment of attention-related difficulties, used in the SWANS Clinic at GOSH, in individuals aged 8 years old and older. This part of the study will shed light on the effectiveness of this assessment tool for use in CYP with SWS within clinical settings.

title: Artificial Intelligence for Dyslexia Detection: A Systematic Review of Multimodal Diagnostic Accuracy (2019–2025)
description: This systematic review archives the methodology and outcomes of a comprehensive investigation into Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) techniques for dyslexia detection. Covering studies from 2019 to 2025, the review benchmarks the diagnostic performance of various algorithmic architectures (including SVM, CNN, RNN, and hybrid models) across multiple data modalities: EEG, eye-tracking, speech, and digital handwriting. The synthesis evaluates model accuracy and generalizability while documenting the current technical challenges, data preprocessing standards, and the transition of experimental prototypes into practical screening tools.

title: Prognostic accuracy of the pulmonary embolism severity index, the simplified pulmonary embolism severity index, and the Bova score in patients with a confirmed pulmonary embolism: a systematic review and meta-analysis
description:
Pulmonary embolism (PE) is a common and potentially life-threatening condition that continues to pose challenges in emergency care, particularly in identifying which patients are at low risk and suitable for outpatient management versus those at risk of clinical deterioration who may require escalation of therapy. Early and accurate risk stratification is essential, as it directly informs decisions around disposition, monitoring, and advanced interventions.

Several clinical tools are used to support this process, including the Pulmonary Embolism Severity Index (PESI), the simplified PESI (sPESI), and the Bova score. While PESI and sPESI are widely used to estimate short-term mortality risk, the Bova score is designed to identify patients at intermediate risk of early hemodynamic decompensation. Despite their widespread adoption and guideline support, uncertainty remains regarding their comparative and overall prognostic accuracy, particularly in the emergency department setting.

The purpose of this research project is to conduct a systematic review and meta-analysis evaluating the cumulative sensitivity, specificity, and predictive value of the PESI, sPESI, and Bova score for predicting short-term mortality and clinical deterioration in adult patients with acute PE diagnosed in the emergency department. By synthesizing data from observational cohort studies, this study will generate pooled estimates of prognostic performance and assess the reliability of these tools in real-world practice.

The expected outcomes include a clearer understanding of how well these risk stratification tools perform and where their limitations lie. These findings aim to inform clinical decision-making regarding patient disposition and therapeutic escalation, optimize resource utilization, and identify gaps for future research to improve risk stratification strategies in acute PE.

title: Treatment of premenstrual dysphoric disorder and perinatal depression
description:
Treatment of premenstrual dysphoric disorder and perinatal depression – A systematic review and meta-analysis
Sinha Engel, Stephanie Haering, Isabella Hebel, Cornelia Weise & Lars Schulze

Research Question
Premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD) and perinatal depression (PND) are highly prevalent and debilitating mental disorders. Among women of childbearing age, 2-6% suffer from PMDD (Sveindóttir & Bäckström, 2000; Wittchen et al., 2002), and 29% from its mild form, the premenstrual syndrome (Borenstein et al., 2003). Among pregnant women about 15% of pregnant women fulfill the criteria of a major antenatal depression (Yin et al., 2021) and after childbirth, about 17% of women develop postnatal depression (Wang et al., 2021). While it is widely acknowledged that both sex- and gender-related factors determine reproductive mental health (Helpman, 2023), affective sensitivity to female sex hormones, especially estradiol and progesterone, represents a central etiological mechanism underlying PMDD and PND (Peters et al., 2025; Soares & Zitek, 2008). Multiple treatment options for PMDD and PND exist, particularly antidepressant psychopharmacological treatment and cognitive-behavioral psychotherapy. For PMDD, antidepressants can be administered continuously, or exclusively during the luteal phase. The suppression of menstrual cycle-related hormonal fluctuations, e.g. through hormonal contraceptives, is another treatment option. While there are systematic reviews and meta-analyses that confirm the effectiveness of these treatments (Brown et al., 2021; Cuijpers et al., 2023; Ford et al., 2012; Kleinstäuber et al., 2012), a direct meta-analytical comparison of the three main options – psychotherapeutic, psychopharmacological and, for PMDD, hormonal treatment, is still lacking. To address this gap, we aim to provide an up-to-date review on the effectiveness of existing treatments for PMDD or PND, with a particular focus on comparing their relative efficacy by means of network meta-analyses. 
Therefore, the planned project aims at…
 systematically describing all randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that evaluated psychotherapeutic, psychopharmacological or hormonal treatment for PMDD or PND.
 analyzing the effectiveness of these treatment options compared to waiting lists, placebo treatments, care-as-usual, or alternative treatments, separately for PMDD and PND.
 analyzing the comparative effectiveness of these treatment options, including a ranking of these treatment approaches, separately for PMDD and PND.
 studying the effects of potential confounding variables 

Study Design
We will conduct a systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs that compared the effectiveness of psychotherapeutic, psychopharmacological or hormonal treatment to a control group in patients with PMDD and/or PND. This systematic review and (network) meta-analysis will be conducted in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 guidelines (Page et al., 2021) and the PRISMA extension for network meta-analyses (Hutton et al., 2015). 


Study Objectives
Previous systematic reviews and meta-analyses confirm the effectiveness of psychotherapeutic and psychopharmacological (including hormonal) treatments for PMDD or PND. In this study, however, we aim to provide an up-to-date review, including a direct comparison of these specific treatment approaches. 

Participants/Population
Studies that investigated adults (mean age >18 years) with PMDD or PND, as defined by the DSM-5 or former versions (American Psychiatric Association, 2013) will be eligible. Studies with self-reported diagnoses or diagnoses via clinical cut-offs of self-report instruments are excluded. 
PMDD has been included as a diagnostic entity in the DSM-5, but was not listed in previous versions. Therefore, studies relying on former versions of the DSM will be considered only if they studied patients with a severe premenstrual syndrome, as determined by prospective symptom tracking over two consecutive menstrual cycles. 
According to the DSM-5, PND patients are to be diagnosed with a major depressive disorder and the specifier “with peripartum onset”, if the episode started during pregnancy or within the first four weeks postpartum. However, evidence shows that the risk of a depressive episode is increased up to one year postpartum (Gaynes et al., 2005). Thus, we decided to extend this time criterion by including depressive episodes during pregnancy and up to one year postpartum. 

Interventions
Eligible studies must evaluate the effects of psychotherapeutic, psychopharmacological or hormonal treatments. Stand-alone psychotherapeutic methods that were not integrated into a broader psychotherapeutic framework (e.g., behavioral activation only), and alternative treatments, including lifestyle interventions, complementary therapies (e.g., music therapy, art therapy), counseling, or dietary supplements are not regarded as eligible psychotherapeutic, psychopharmacological or hormonal treatment. There will be no restriction regarding the publication year. 

Comparators
Eligible studies must include a control group. It can be expected that most studies will provide comparisons between psychotherapeutic, psychopharmacological or hormonal treatments and control groups such as waiting lists, placebo treatments, care-as-usual, or alternative treatments. However, studies that provide direct comparisons between psychotherapeutic, psychopharmacological or hormonal treatments will be included as well. Thus, we will incorporate both a) comparisons between our treatment approaches of interest (i.e., direct comparisons of psychotherapy vs. psychopharmacological vs. hormonal treatment) as well as comparisons of b) psychotherapeutic, psychopharmacological or hormonal treatments vs. other control groups like waiting groups, or placebo conditions. 




Main Outcomes
Studies are required to assess the symptoms detailed below at least once after treatment. If multiple post-treatment assessments are reported, we will extract the values closest to the primary post-treatment timepoint.

In accordance with the diagnostic criteria, we defined the following outcome measures. 
PMDD: 
 Primary outcome will be the severity of premenstrual dysphoric symptoms, for example assessed through ratings of the daily record of severity of problems during the premenstrual phase (Endicott et al., 2006).

PND: 
 Primary outcome measure will be the severity of depressive symptoms. The Edinburgh Perinatal Depression Scale (Cox et al., 1987) will be prioritized as the main outcome, given its widespread use and specificity for PND. If data from this scale is unavailable, alternative measures such as the Beck Depression Inventory (Beck et al., 1996) or the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (Kroenke et al., 2001) will be considered. 

Study Design
Studies are eligible if they report the results of a RCT investigating at least two different arms in individuals with PMDD and/or PND. We will not include observational studies without randomization to treatment arms.

Data Collection Procedures

Literature Search
We searched the following electronic databases (03/04/2025): PubMed, Web of Science, PsycInfo, PsycArticles and PSYNDEX, using terms related to the study design (e.g. RCT and variations) AND terms related to PMDD OR PND AND terms related to Psycho(pharmaco)therapy. The full electronic search strategy is documented in the appendix. 
We applied snowball search methods by checking relevant systematic reviews and/or meta-analyses about intervention studies in PMDD and PND (Brown et al., 2021; Busse et al., 2009; Cuijpers et al., 2023; Ford et al., 2012; Kleinstäuber et al., 2012). 
 
Data Extraction (Selection and Coding)

Abstract and Title Screening
This step will be supported by an open source machine learning software (ASReview; van de Schoot et al., 2021). This software utilizes active learning to sort and resort the identified records by prioritizing the most relevant records based on the user’s inclusion and exclusion decisions. The sorting algorithm thus brings forward the most relevant records to be screened next by the researcher. It has been demonstrated that most eligible records will be identified after screening between 8% and 33% of the records (van de Schoot et al., 2021). 
 Two trained researchers will screen abstracts and titles as follows: One trained researcher will screen title and abstracts until a) ASReview and this researcher have identified 50 consecutive non-relevant records and b) at least 33% of the studies have been screened. The second trained researcher will then screen the final 50 non-relevant consecutive records in duplo. In case of discrepancies, a consensus will be reached between both researchers to clarify who is right. If this is the second researcher, the screening of the first reviewer will continue until 50% (66%, 80%, and 100%) of all records have been checked. Again, the final 50 records will be double-checked. 

Exclusion criteria for this step are: a) language other than English or German b) no original study (e.g., meta-analyses, reviews, pre-registration), c) case study, d) no peer-reviewed article (e.g., conference abstract only), e) non-human sample (e.g., cells, animals), f) non-adult sample, g) no psychotherapeutic, psychopharmacological or hormonal randomized controlled treatment trial, h) no participants with PMDD and/or PND included - prevention studies are excluded for this reason, as well. 

Full-text Screening
Potentially relevant articles will be retrieved in full-text and further screened for eligibility, in duplo by two independent researchers. In addition to the criteria outlined above, the following exclusion criteria will be used for the full-text screening:
• No random assignment of participants to the psycho(pharmaco)therapy and/or control arms
• Neither PMDD (diagnostic criteria DSM-5/ severe premenstrual dysphoric syndrome with prospective daily ratings), nor PND (DSM criteria for depressive episode and occurrence during pregnancy up to one year postpartum)
• No psychotherapeutic, psychopharmacological or hormonal treatment (e.g. only stand-alone psychotherapeutic method, lifestyle intervention, complementary therapy, counselling, or food supplements) 
• No assessment of relevant outcome measures (after treatment)
• Complete sample is already included in another publication included in this review
 
Data Extraction
A standardized extraction sheet (see attachments) will be implemented in Covidence. Trained researchers will independently extract all data. In case of discrepancies, an additional independent researcher will decide about the data extraction. The coded information will include: 
 Bibliographic information
 Sample characteristics (e.g., age)
 Eligibility criteria (e.g. suicidality, comorbidities)
 Treatment characteristics (e.g. treatment duration, number of sessions/ dose)
 Study design (e.g. timing of post treatment assessment)
 Outcome assessments
 Risk of bias (based on RoB2) 

Study authors will be contacted if primary outcome data is missing.

 
Strategy for Data Synthesis

Qualitative Synthesis
We will evaluate the above-mentioned clinical and methodological features of the included studies that could affect the size of the effect. For instance, we will examine whether patients across the different treatment options are comparable in terms of psychopathological characteristics. Significant variation in these effect modifiers indicates intransitivity. If intransitivity is suspected, a quantitative synthesis (see below) may not be appropriate. 

Quantitative Synthesis
Pairwise comparisons
First, we will conduct pairwise random-effects meta-analyses based on the calculation of Hedges’ g as effect size. These pairwise comparisons will be calculated for all directly compared intervention categories (e.g., hormonal treatment vs. waitlist; psychotherapy vs.waitlist). Heterogeneity of effect sizes will be tested with an overall Q-statistic. We will explore heterogeneity with different moderator analyses using potential effect modifiers. Publication bias will be assessed through funnel plot asymmetry and statistical tests (e.g., Egger’s test). 

Network model
For this model, the reference treatment will be the most commonly used comparator across included studies, ensuring meaningful comparisons between treatments. We expect this to be either waitlist or placebo conditions. We expect to include the following nodes:
 Placebo pill
 Wait list 
 Care-as-usual
 Psychotherapy
 Psychopharmacological treatment
 Hormonal treatment 
 Combined approach

 If enough data is available, we will evaluate the statistical agreement between direct and indirect comparisons (i.e. consistency). If inconsistency is detected, we will explore potential effect modifiers and conduct sensitivity analyses, such as excluding studies contributing to inconsistency.

Risk of Bias Assessment
The risk of bias for included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) will be assessed using the Revised Cochrane Risk of Bias Tool (RoB-2; Sterne et al., 2019). Studies with high risk of bias will be examined in sensitivity analyses to assess their impact on the results.

title: Benefits and Drawbacks of Modern Educational Approaches Compared with Traditional Teaching Methods for Electrocardiogram Education Among Anesthesia Learners: A Systematic Review
description:
Electrocardiogram (ECG) interpretation is a core skill for anesthesia trainees and plays an important role in intraoperative patient assessment, detection of cardiac arrhythmias, hemodynamic monitoring, and clinical decision-making during anesthesia. Inadequate ECG interpretation skills may lead to delayed diagnosis and inappropriate management and potentially life-threatening complications for patients.
Traditionally, traditional ECG education has historically relied on passive hub-based instruction such as lecture-based, face-to-face classroom instruction, and printed instructional materials that have only been able to transmit information from the instructor to the learner. However, advances in educational technologies have led to the emergence of innovative instructional approaches, including simulation-based learning, e-learning, web-based learning, mobile applications, gamification, flipped classrooms, case-based learning, problem-based learning, virtual reality (VR), augmented reality (AR), and artificial intelligence (AI)-based instructional systems.
Although these educational approaches are increasingly implemented in the education of healthcare professionals and contribute to better education of learners by creating an active and engaged learning environment, a comprehensive review of these methods and their advantages and disadvantages in creating an overall perception has been less discussed and concluded. Modern educational methods may improve knowledge acquisition, diagnostic accuracy, overall engagement, confidence, and long-term retention, but they may also increase educational costs, implementation complexity, technological requirements, and cognitive workload.
Therefore, we as a research team concluded that a comprehensive synthesis of available evidence is needed to determine the advantages and disadvantages of modern educational approaches compared to traditional educational methods for ECG training among anesthesia trainees.

title: Comparative Assessment of Endoscopic Ultrasound-Guided vs. Percutaneous Biopsy in Pancreatic Lesions: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Diagnostic Performance
description:
Introduction: Pancreatic cancer ranks as the fourth deadliest form of cancer. However, it's essential to note that not all pancreatic masses signal primary malignancy. Therefore, it is imperative to establish the correct differential diagnosis, a process further supported by pre-operative biopsy procedures. This meta-analysis aims to compare the diagnostic performance of two minimally invasive biopsy approaches for pancreatic tissue sampling: percutaneous biopsies guided by CT or ultrasound, and transduodenal biopsies guided by endoscopic ultrasound.
Methods: A systematic literature search will be performed on the MEDLINE and Scopus databases using predefined search terms. The selected studies will undergo analysis to evaluate the diagnostic performance of the two biopsy methods. Additionally, they will be assessed for potential bias utilizing the Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies 2 (QUADAS-2) tool. Statistical analysis will be conducted using RevMan and MetaDisc software.

title: Clinical indicators of the nursing diagnosis Impaired Psychological Comfort in postpartum women: A diagnostic test accuracy systematic review protocol
description:
Background: Early and precise identification of the Nursing Diagnosis Impaired Psychological Comfort in postpartum women is critical for clinical decision-making and maternal mental health care. However, the diagnostic accuracy of its clinical indicators requires synthesis based on robust evidence. Objective: To analyze the clinical indicators of the Nursing Diagnosis Impaired Psychological Comfort in postpartum women reported in the literature. Methods: This diagnostic test accuracy systematic review protocol follows Cochrane recommendations and PRISMA-DTA reporting guidelines. Searches will be conducted across eight databases (MEDLINE/PubMed, Cochrane Library, EMBASE, LILACS, CINAHL, Scopus, Web of Science, and PsycINFO) without language or publication year restrictions. Inclusion criteria: full-text studies addressing, defining, describing, associating, or validating clinical indicators, signs, symptoms, or emotional/behavioral manifestations related to Impaired Psychological Comfort or clinically related phenomena in postpartum women. Exclusion criteria: (1) editorials, abstracts, letters to the editor, theses, dissertations, book reviews, and theoretical/reflection papers; (2) studies addressing exclusively causal factors, social determinants, or risk factors without analyzing clinical manifestations; and (3) unretrievable studies, those not answering the research question, or those with low methodological quality. Two reviewers will independently screen studies via Rayyan and extract data, consulting a third reviewer to resolve discrepancies. Methodological quality will be appraised using QUADAS-2; studies with high risk of bias (<50% "yes" responses) will be excluded. Results will be synthesized through a PRISMA-DTA flowchart, summary tables, and narrative description, including diagnostic accuracy metrics when available.

title: AI-Enabled EEG for Epilepsy Diagnosis Compared With Clinical Experts: Systematic Review and Diagnostic Test Accuracy Meta-Analysis
description:
Background: Electroencephalography (EEG) interpretation for epilepsy diagnosis faces persistent challenges including specialist shortages, variable interpretation accuracy, and limited accessibility. Artificial intelligence (AI)-based automated interpretation systems promise to address these limitations, yet their diagnostic performance compared to clinical experts remains incompletely characterized.
Objective: To systematically evaluate and meta-analyze the diagnostic accuracy of AI-enabled EEG interpretation compared with human clinical experts for epilepsy detection.
Methods: We conducted a systematic review following PRISMA-DTA and Cochrane MECIR standards, searching PubMed, Scopus, IEEE Xplore, and Google Scholar through June 2025. Studies directly comparing AI algorithms with human expert interpretation using identical EEG datasets were included. Quality assessment employed QUADAS-AI criteria. Bivariate meta-analysis was performed to estimate pooled sensitivity, specificity, diagnostic odds ratios, and likelihood ratios.
Results: Three studies encompassing 9,775 EEG examinations met inclusion criteria. AI demonstrated superior pooled sensitivity (0.83–0.85 vs. 0.77–0.80) and specificity (0.83–0.85 vs. 0.72–0.75) compared to human experts. The diagnostic odds ratio for AI was approximately double that of humans (12–13 vs. 6–7). AI exhibited consistently narrower confidence intervals, indicating greater interpretive reliability. For normal versus abnormal EEG classification, AI achieved 86–90% sensitivity with enhanced consistency compared to human evaluators. However, substantial heterogeneity (I²>75%) and methodological limitations were identified across studies.
Conclusions: AI-based EEG interpretation demonstrates diagnostic performance equal or superior to human experts with enhanced consistency, supporting potential implementation as clinical triage tools. However, limited transparency, patient selection bias, and deployment feasibility constraints warrant further investigation before widespread clinical adoption.

title: A collaborative rat functional MRI multi-center study.
description:
In this international collaborative project, we seek to gather the rodent imaging community toward performing a rat fMRI multi-center comparison, within the same template as Grandjean et al. NIMG 2020. We want to examine functional connectivity (FC) parameter distribution at the population level within key networks (somatosensory and default-mode network) of the rat brain, as well as establish connectivity sensitivity and specificity in the collected datasets. To do so, we will gather rat BOLD fMRI datasets from individual labs (n=10, any protocol).
In a desire to push further, we seek to obtain additional datasets pertaining to within-laboratory test-retest (i.e. scans that were collected in the same control animals within a period of 6 months or less), as well as datasets in sensory-stimulation fMRI (limb or whisker stimulation). Finally, we would like to organize a standardized data collection arm of this study for laboratories interested. This would include the de-novo acquisition of a dataset (n=10) using predefined, mutually-agreed, and standardized parameters consistent across all participating laboratories.
The end-goal is to make this as an available resource to researchers and to publish an extensive description of the collective dataset in a peer-reviewed journal.

title: Using an ICF-based framework to analyse the components evaluated in standardised measures of motor control and movement quality: A scoping review protocol
description:
Introduction:
Low back pain (LBP) is a heterogeneous and multifactorial condition that represents a major health concern.[1,2] Motor control dysfunction is thought to play a significant role in the persistence of pain for a substantial subgroup of LBP patients.[3–5] In fact, the quality of movement of people with LBP differs significantly from that of people without LBP,[6] and accordingly, the examination of lumbopelvic motor control and movement quality serves as a basic component of the physical examination for all patients with LBP.[7–9]
Although there are several clinical test batteries and observation lists available to assess motor control and movement quality,[10–14] there is currently no consensus on a standardized and validated approach in clinical practice. To effectively incorporate these aspects into the management of LBP, clear guidance on measurement is needed. Given the absence of a criterion standard method, content validity must be prioritized to ensure that assessment tools comprehensively capture all relevant dimensions.[15] This requires fostering a shared understanding of these constructs to enable rigorous content validity research, avoiding incomplete or misguided treatment interventions. 

Therefore, this proposed review aims to answer the following research question:
What components of lumbo-pelvic motor control and movement quality are included in standardized measures whose validity and reliability have been established in adult populations in the context of LBP?

Previous reviews in this area have primarily focused on reliability and construct validity,[10,13,16–18] with little attention given to content validity. Using a newly developed ICF-based framework,[19] this review will be the first to identify existing validated standardized measures and determine which components of MC and MQ are captured by each tool. This structured overview aims to highlight knowledge gaps in the current understanding of these measures and provide a foundation for future research to develop more comprehensive and valid assessment tools.

Methods:
The proposed scoping review will be conducted in accordance with the JBI methodology for scoping reviews and will follow the PRISMA-ScR guidelines.[20,21]
Eligibility criteria:
The PCC framework has been used to develop eligibility criteria. At level 1 (title and abstract screening), screening criteria will include descriptive studies (1) focussing on direct measurement of lumbopelvic MC or MQ, (2) in an adult population with NSLBP and (3) published in English or German language (for feasibility reasons).
At level 2 (full-text screening), the following more specific criteria will be used for screening:
Types of evidence sources: In accordance with Sibley and colleagues,[22] we will be searching for each index publication – a measure’s first publication presenting its development and/or initial psychometric evaluations.
Participants/Population: Only studies including adult participants with chronic/recurrent LBP (or pain developers in longitudinal studies) will be considered for inclusion. Studies assessing patients with relevant systemic, neurologic and/or psychiatric diseases will be excluded.
Concept: Descriptive studies, having a stated objective or commonly used tool to directly assess lumbo-pelvic MC or MQ, having (1) both a standardized testing protocol and standardized evaluation criteria, and (2) a minimum of 1 psychometric property (validity or reliability) evaluated (for quality assessment purposes, as argued by Sibley and colleagues[22]).
Context: The clinical setting is of interest for this review. No methods for long-term measurement of continuous movement and posture behaviour in daily life will be considered. 

Search strategy & information sources:
As recommended, the general search strategy will consist of three steps.[20] After an initial preliminary search of the databases MEDLINE (PubMed) and CINAHL, a second search will then be undertaken across four relevant databases (MEDLINE (Pubmed), CINAHL, Web of Science, Scopus). Thirdly, the reference lists of identified reports and articles will be searched for additional sources. In addition, a hand-search of the reference lists of relevant systematic reviews in the field [10,13,16–18,23] and a Google Scholar search using modified search terms (by screening the first 200 results) will be conducted. If further clarification or information is required, the authors will be contacted. Search dates will be documented as well as any contact with authors of the chosen studies. 

Source of evidence selection:
Following the search, titles/abstracts and full-texts will be independently screened in two steps by two reviewers (GP and MK, with conflicts resolved by discussion / a third reviewer). The inclusion criteria at each stage will be pilot tested on a random sample using the online tool “Cadima”, which will aid the entire selection process. The names of all measures identified at abstract screening stage will be recorded for manual cross-checking and hand search for the index publication. At the stage of full-text screening, the reasons for the exclusion of articles will be stated. 

Data extraction
A preliminary draft of a charting table has been created, which will be subjected to a pilot test on a randomly selected sample of five articles. The results of this test will be used to inform any necessary revisions to the table. It includes
1) Name of measure
2) Reference
3) Preliminary psychometric properties evaluated
4) Stated purpose of measure
5) Components of MC/MQ purportedly assessed
6) Development methods
7) Target population
8) Number of items
9) Evaluation parameters
10) Brief description of measurement procedure
11) ICF based components of MC & MQ
 a) MC functions (MCF)
 b) MCF specified
 c) MQ domains

Analysis and presentation of results
The components of MC and MQ evaluated in each measure will be explored by coding the individual items and tasks of the respective measure according to a newly developed ICF-based framework.[19] Two investigators will independently review the tasks and scoring criteria of each measure and will identify on a binary scale (yes/no) which components of motor control (“motor control functions”) and which components of movement quality (“movement quality domains”) are included in each measure. Individual components will be defined as included if they are inherent to task performance, even if not explicitly part of the measure’s evaluation criteria. Disagreements will be resolved through consensus discussion or a third reviewer.
The extracted data will be synthesised and integrated into a series of visual outputs (tables and figure of framework), which will present a comprehensive overview of the standardised MC and MQ measures and their respective components.

title: A Scoping Review Protocol: Best Practices for Improving Nucleic Acid Quality from FFPE Samples
description:
Background: Formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissues constitute vast biorepositories for molecular research, yet the fixation process significantly compromises nucleic acid integrity. While technological advances have improved extraction methods, systematic evaluation of optimization strategies across tissue types and preservation conditions remains limited. This scoping review aims to comprehensively map evidence on methodologies for maximizing DNA and RNA quality from FFPE specimens to enhance their utility in molecular diagnostics and research applications.

Methods: This scoping review, following PRISMA-ScR guidelines and the Joanna Briggs Institute methodology for scoping reviews, will systematically evaluate FFPE nucleic acid optimization approaches. We will search molecular pathology and bioanalytical databases (PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, bioRxiv) and technical literature from manufacturers to identify relevant studies published from 2015 to 2025. The review will quantitatively assess: 1) extraction methodologies that demonstrably improve nucleic acid recovery across different tissue types and preservation conditions; 2) quantifiable impacts of pre-analytical variables on DNA and RNA quality metrics; and 3) performance parameters of innovative extraction protocols. Data extraction will utilize standardized assessment tools including DIN (DNA Integrity Number), RIN (RNA Integrity Number), Ct values from qPCR, and MIQE (Minimum Information for Publication of Quantitative Real-Time PCR Experiments) guidelines for reporting PCR data. Quality assessment will employ the QUADAS-2 tool for diagnostic accuracy studies and STARD guidelines, adapted for reporting diagnostic evaluations. Data synthesis will include forest plots for comparing extraction efficiencies, and regression analyses examining relationships between pre-analytical variables and nucleic acid quality, following Annual Review of Pathology standards for quantitative evidence synthesis.

Discussion: This review will establish evidence-based recommendations for optimizing FFPE nucleic acid quality, addressing variability across tissue types and preservation conditions. Results will guide standardization of pre-analytical handling, extraction protocols, and quality assessment methods, ultimately improving reproducibility and success of molecular analyses using archived FFPE specimens in pathology and precision medicine.

BACKGROUND

Formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue specimens represent one of the most valuable and extensive biospecimen resources in pathology and biomedical research1. These preserved tissues enable retrospective studies linking molecular findings with clinical outcomes, creating unparalleled opportunities for translational research and precision medicine2. The global repositories of FFPE samples, containing millions of specimens with associated clinical data, constitute an irreplaceable resource for investigating disease mechanisms and identifying biomarkers3.

Despite their widespread availability and historical significance, FFPE tissues present substantial challenges for molecular analyses4. The formalin fixation process, while excellent for preserving morphology, creates extensive DNA-protein crosslinks, introduces base modifications, and causes nucleic acid fragmentation5. These chemical alterations significantly impact the quality and quantity of nucleic acids that can be extracted from FFPE tissues, often limiting their utility in advanced molecular applications such as next-generation sequencing (NGS), digital PCR, and transcriptomic analyses6.

The optimization of nucleic acid extraction from FFPE samples has become increasingly critical as molecular diagnostic techniques continue to evolve and expand in clinical practice. Researchers and clinicians face numerous challenges when working with these specimens, including nucleic acid fragmentation and chemical modifications that impact amplification efficiency, variable extraction yields dependent on tissue type and preservation conditions, and the presence of PCR inhibitors that interfere with downstream applications. Additional concerns include inconsistent performance across different extraction methodologies, limited reproducibility between laboratories and protocols, significant degradation of RNA integrity affecting gene expression analyses, and persistent difficulties in recovering sufficient high-quality DNA for comprehensive genomic profiling7.

Recent technological and methodological advances have demonstrated considerable progress in addressing these limitations8. Innovations in tissue processing, deparaffinization techniques, enzymatic treatments, and purification methods have significantly improved nucleic acid recovery from FFPE tissues9. Studies have shown that optimized extraction protocols can increase DNA yields by 50-300% and improve amplifiable fragment length by up to 70% compared to conventional methods10. Similarly, specialized RNA extraction approaches have enhanced the recovery of intact RNA molecules suitable for transcriptomic analyses11.

Despite these advances, there remains significant heterogeneity in methodological approaches and success rates across different laboratories and tissue types12. The field lacks a comprehensive synthesis of evidence regarding optimal extraction methods across diverse FFPE sample types, a clear understanding of how pre-analytical variables impact extraction efficiency, systematic evaluation of emerging technologies, and standardized quality assessment metrics for FFPE-derived nucleic acids.13

This scoping review aims to address these gaps by systematically mapping and synthesizing the existing evidence on optimization methods for improving nucleic acid quality from FFPE samples. Specifically, we will explore current best practices in extraction methodology, evaluate the impact of pre-analytical variables, identify innovative approaches showing promise for enhancing nucleic acid integrity, and synthesize evidence on quality assessment metrics for downstream applications.

title: Optimizing “Continuous Psychophysics” for Rapid Assessment of Visual, Motor, and Cognitive Function in Clinical Populations
description: In this research, we aim to adopt the novel psychophysics paradigm as a clinical and cognitive assessment tool for visual, motor, and cognitive functions. Existing diagnostic methods generally take a lot of time and effort, making them difficult and sometimes impossible to use with certain clinical patient groups or children. This research will address this issue by employing the continuous psychophysics method. This is a new psychophysical experiment paradigm utilizing a simple target-tracking task. Despite its simplicity, this method is robust, reliable, and can accurately measure perception and cognition, providing insights into visual function within minutes. Our main goal is to determine whether continuous psychophysics can efficiently diagnose the differences between various sensory, motor, and cognitive deficits in patients. The research will unfold in three stages, first by using computer simulations, we will test the method's sensitivity and accuracy under controlled conditions. Secondly we will conduct control experiments with healthy participant using simulated cognitive or visual disparities will be introduced to validate the method's effectiveness in real-world scenarios. Finally with patient testing; we will test the method on patients suffering from Macular Degeneration, Glaucoma, and Cranial Nerve Palsies, further refining its application for clinical use. Beyond the original target-tracking experiment, we will also simulate visual deficiencies through reduced contrast and higher target uncertainty and utilize alternative response mechanisms, such as eye-tracking and tactile tracking. In conclusion, if successful, this research would significantly improve diagnostic accuracy and could be used in hospitals as a tool for visual and motor disorders. It offers a faster and more efficient assessment method, potentially leading to earlier treatment and better patient outcomes. This innovation holds the potential to facilitate earlier treatment and improve patient outcomes. Beyond the development of diagnostic tools, this project aims to enhance our understanding of neuro-ophthalmological conditions, ultimately contributing to an improved quality of life for millions of affected individuals worldwide.

title: The Metric Blind Spot in Deep Learning Brain MRI Reconstruction: A Systematic Review and Causal Safety Framework
description:
A systematic review of how the safety, artifacts, and fidelity of deep-learning brain MRI reconstruction are evaluated, following PRISMA 2020.

Deep neural priors can shorten brain MRI acquisition four- to tenfold, but the same priors can erase or invent diagnostic detail without disturbing the numbers used to certify them. Seven databases were searched to July 2026 for primary studies of human brain MRI reconstruction reporting fidelity, artifact, robustness, or observer outcomes. From 27,327 records identified and 26,924 after deduplication, 220 primary studies published between 1995 and 2026 were included.

The review asks three questions: (RQ1) how far do pixel-wise fidelity metrics diverge from radiologist judgement; (RQ2) what mechanisms explain that divergence; and (RQ3) what evaluation paradigms could establish reconstruction safety before deployment. Risk of bias in the diagnostic-accuracy and reader-study subset was appraised with QUADAS-2; the remaining algorithmic studies were appraised on reproducibility and robustness.

REGISTRATION STATUS: This is a RETROSPECTIVE registration. The review was completed before this registration was created. The protocol was fixed in the project repository on 2026-07-23, before screening began on 2026-07-27, but that timestamp rests on filesystem metadata rather than an independent registry, and is therefore not offered as proof of prospective registration. Protocol deviations are documented in full in the registered amendments log.

This review was not registered with PROSPERO, which does not accept reviews without a direct clinical health outcome.

title: GP AI Skin Cancer Portal Study
description:
This study examines how artificial intelligence (AI) decision-support influences general practitioners’ (GPs) treatment management decisions for suspicious skin lesions. The primary objective is to assess whether AI assistance can improve triage efficiency in primary care by reducing unnecessary consultations for benign lesions without compromising patient safety.

Although AI-based dermatological tools show promising diagnostic performance, their impact on GP decision-making in realistic clinical workflows remains insufficiently understood.

The study will evaluate how different levels of AI assistance affect diagnostic judgments, treatment decisions, and related outcomes in clinical-like conditions. Outcomes include referral behaviour, diagnostic accuracy, decision quality, and related behavioural measures.

The study is preregistered to ensure transparency and reproducibility by specifying hypotheses, design, and analysis procedures in advance.

Does an Interactive Frequency-Format Outcomes Simulator Improve Bayesian Statistical Reasoning about Mass Screenings? A Pilot Test of Rarity Roulette 2.0 with Frequency Tree Visualization
description:
This second pilot study tests whether an interactive frequency-tree visualization improves Bayesian statistical reasoning about mass screenings for low-prevalence problems, compared to probability-format text explanations.

Background: Mass screenings for rare conditions (e.g., medical tests, security checks, content moderation) generate overwhelmingly false positives even when accuracy is high — a problem to which people are blind due to base rate bias. Gigerenzer and Hoffrage (1995) showed that frequency format improves Bayesian reasoning. Sedlmeier and Gigerenzer (2001) demonstrated this can be taught in under two hours using frequency representations with visualizations. Recent research (Binder et al., 2021; Böcherer-Linder & Eichler, 2019) indicates frequency trees produce superior "diagnostic efficiency" (accuracy ÷ time) compared to tables alone.

Changes from Pilot 1: Based on Pilot 1 findings (N=76, inconclusive results with wide CIs), we revised the experimental condition to use frequency trees rather than frequency tables, following literature suggesting trees make nested-set structure more graphically transparent. We also tightened data quality criteria: explicit 15-minute minimum completion time, two embedded attention checks, and self-reported effort questions.

Current Study: We developed Rarity Roulette, an interactive online simulator using frequency trees and natural language summaries. This pilot (N=60) randomly assigns participants to either: (1) read probability-format explanations, or (2) interact with Rarity Roulette's frequency-tree-based tool. After the intervention, all participants complete 5 Bayesian inference problems.

Primary hypothesis: Participants in the Rarity Roulette condition will use Bayesian algorithms more often than those in the probability-format condition.

Expected outcomes: Results will inform whether frequency trees improve upon Pilot 1's uncertain findings, and guide development of a larger preregistered study.

description: This registration describes a systematic review and diagnostic test accuracy meta-analysis evaluating clinical metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) and microbial cell-free DNA sequencing for invasive fungal disease (IFD) among immunocompromised high-risk hosts, including hematologic malignancy and hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT/HCT) patients. title: Diagnostic Accuracy and Psychometric Validation of Motion Sickness Assessment Tools: A Scoping Review
description: Motion sickness is a frequent condition resulting from conflicting sensory signals between the eyes, vestibular system, and body, leading to symptoms like nausea, vomiting, dizziness, headache, sweating, pallor, drowsiness, and increased salivation. Although tools such as the Motion Sickness Susceptibility Questionnaire (MSSQ), Simulator Sickness Questionnaire (SSQ), and the Motion Sickness Assessment Questionnaire (MSAQ) are widely used. Most available tests rely on subjective symptom reports, which impacts diagnostic accuracy across diverse populations. This scoping review aims to summarize clinical diagnostic criteria and psychometric properties (reliability, validity, sensitivity, and specificity) of motion sickness assessment tools. Following the PCC framework (Population: individuals with motion sickness; Concept: diagnostic tools/criteria; Context: psychometric properties), search was conducted between 2015 -2025 in databases like PubMed, Scopus, Cochrane, and Science Direct. A total of 17,295 articles were identified and after duplicate removal, 5,527 articles remained for title and abstract screening. Out of these, 5,500 were excluded, leaving 27 for full-text review. Ultimately, 8 studies met the inclusion criteria. The review was compiled in accordance to PRISMA extension for scoping review (PRISMA-ScR) Guidelines. MSSQ (Cronbach's alpha 0.86, test-retest correlation > 0.8, high sensitivity 78-90%, moderate specificity 70-85%, good predictive validity r=0.45); SSQ (high levels of alpha 0.85+, valid nausea/oculomotor/disorientation subscores, good sensitivity post-VR, specificity less well established); and VIMSSQ (high alpha 0.86-0.92, ICC 0.83-0.90, age/sex effects sensitivity, good convergent validity r 0.62-0.76). MSSS, FMSQ, MSAQ insufficient specificity/sensitivity information available for full validation SWID and VIC some alpha but inadequate sensitivity/specificity. Current tools reliably identify at-risk individuals and measure severity but may overestimate susceptibility, highlighting the need for standardized diagnostic criteria and physiological markers to improve specificity and adapt to emerging technologies.

title: Human–Machine Symbiosis Theory
description:
In the trajectory of human civilization, the relationship between humans and technology has continuously evolved from simple tools that extended physical capabilities to complex systems that augment cognitive processes and decision-making. In the contemporary digital era, this relationship has reached a critical turning point, where the boundaries between human agency and machine intelligence are increasingly intertwined. It is within this transformative context that Human–Machine Symbiosis Theory, originally conceptualized by Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad (YER) in 2016, emerges as a conceptual framework to understand, interpret, and navigate the deepening integration between human beings and intelligent systems.
The year 2016 represents a pivotal moment in technological development, marked by the acceleration of artificial intelligence, the proliferation of data-driven platforms, and the increasing reliance on algorithmic systems across diverse domains of life. During this period, machines were no longer confined to executing predefined instructions; they began to learn, adapt, and interact in ways that closely resemble human cognitive functions. This shift raised fundamental questions about the nature of human–machine interaction: Are machines merely tools, or are they becoming collaborative agents? How does human identity, autonomy, and decision-making evolve in the presence of increasingly intelligent systems? And most importantly, how can a balanced and mutually beneficial relationship between humans and machines be conceptualized?
Human–Machine Symbiosis Theory was developed as a response to these questions. Rather than framing the relationship between humans and machines as one of competition or replacement, this theory proposes a model of symbiosis an interdependent relationship in which both entities contribute to and benefit from each other’s capabilities. In this framework, humans and machines are not opposing forces but complementary systems, each enhancing the strengths and compensating for the limitations of the other.
At the core of this theory lies the concept of co-evolution. Human capabilities and machine intelligence do not develop independently; they evolve together through continuous interaction. As humans design and interact with machines, they influence the development of technological systems. At the same time, these systems reshape human behavior, cognition, and social structures. This reciprocal relationship creates a dynamic cycle of adaptation and transformation, in which both humans and machines are continuously redefined.
Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad (YER), through his 2016 conceptual foundation, identifies three primary dimensions that characterize human–machine symbiosis: cognitive augmentation, adaptive interaction, and systemic integration. These dimensions provide a structured framework for understanding how symbiotic relationships are formed and sustained.
Cognitive augmentation refers to the enhancement of human intellectual capabilities through machine assistance. Technologies such as artificial intelligence, data analytics, and decision-support systems enable individuals to process information more efficiently, make more informed decisions, and extend their cognitive reach beyond natural limitations. In this sense, machines act as amplifiers of human intelligence, enabling new forms of creativity, problem-solving, and innovation.
Adaptive interaction highlights the evolving nature of communication between humans and machines. Unlike traditional tools, which require users to adapt to predefined interfaces, modern intelligent systems are designed to learn from user behavior and adapt accordingly. This creates a more intuitive and personalized interaction, where machines respond to human needs in real time. The adaptive nature of this interaction fosters a sense of collaboration, blurring the distinction between user and system.
Systemic integration, the third dimension, emphasizes the embedding of human–machine relationships within broader socio-technical systems. Symbiosis does not occur in isolation; it is part of a larger ecosystem that includes organizational structures, cultural norms, and technological infrastructures. This dimension highlights the interconnectedness of human and machine activities, demonstrating how symbiotic relationships influence and are influenced by the systems in which they operate.
Together, these dimensions illustrate that human–machine symbiosis is not a static condition but a dynamic and evolving process. It is characterized by continuous feedback loops, where human input shapes machine behavior, and machine output influences human decision-making. This process creates a hybrid form of intelligence one that combines human intuition, creativity, and ethical judgment with machine precision, speed, and analytical capability.
One of the most significant contributions of Human–Machine Symbiosis Theory lies in its humanized perspective. While much of the discourse surrounding artificial intelligence focuses on technological advancement, this theory emphasizes the importance of maintaining a human-centered approach. It recognizes that technology should not only enhance efficiency but also support human values, well-being, and autonomy.
From this perspective, symbiosis is not merely about integration but about alignment. The effectiveness of human–machine relationships depends on the extent to which technological systems are designed to complement human needs and aspirations. This requires a deep understanding of human behavior, cognition, and emotion, as well as a commitment to ethical principles such as transparency, accountability, and inclusivity.
The theory also addresses common concerns about the potential displacement of human roles by machines. Rather than viewing automation as a threat, Human–Machine Symbiosis Theory reframes it as an opportunity for transformation. As machines take over routine and repetitive tasks, humans can focus on activities that require creativity, empathy, and critical thinking. This shift has the potential to redefine the nature of work, education, and social interaction, creating new possibilities for human development.
However, the realization of this potential is not automatic. It requires careful design, governance, and continuous evaluation of human–machine systems. Without these considerations, the integration of technology may lead to unintended consequences, such as loss of autonomy, increased dependency, or reinforcement of existing inequalities. The theory therefore emphasizes the importance of proactive and responsible approaches to technological development.
In addition to its theoretical contributions, Human–Machine Symbiosis Theory has significant practical implications across various domains. In healthcare, for example, symbiotic systems can enhance diagnostic accuracy and patient care by combining human expertise with machine analysis. In education, adaptive learning systems can personalize instruction and support diverse learning needs. In business and marketing, data-driven insights can inform strategy while maintaining a human-centered approach to customer engagement.
These applications illustrate the versatility of the theory and its relevance to contemporary challenges. They also highlight the importance of interdisciplinary collaboration, as the successful implementation of symbiotic systems requires expertise from multiple fields, including technology, social science, and ethics.

From the earliest mechanical inventions to the sophisticated digital systems of the present era, technology has functioned as both an extension of human capability and a catalyst for societal transformation. Yet, as we advance further into the twenty-first century, the nature of this relationship is undergoing a profound and unprecedented shift. Technology is no longer merely a passive instrument; it is becoming an active participant in cognitive processes, decision-making structures, and social interactions. This work emerges not only as a theoretical contribution but also as a reflective inquiry into one of the most critical questions of our time: how can humans and machines form a relationship that is not defined by competition or domination, but by mutual enhancement and sustainable coexistence?
The year 2016 represents a significant milestone in the trajectory of digital transformation. This work seeks to bridge that gap by emphasizing the relational, psychological, and ethical dimensions of human–machine interaction.
Human–Machine Symbiosis Theory is structured around three core dimensions: cognitive augmentation, adaptive interaction, and systemic integration. These dimensions provide a comprehensive framework for analyzing how symbiotic relationships are formed, sustained, and evolved.
Cognitive augmentation refers to the enhancement of human intellectual capabilities through the integration of machine intelligence. In contemporary digital environments, individuals are increasingly supported by systems that provide real-time information, predictive insights, and decision-making assistance. These systems extend the boundaries of human cognition, enabling individuals to process complex information and solve problems more effectively. However, cognitive augmentation is not merely about increasing efficiency; it is about expanding human potential. The goal of symbiosis is not to create systems that replace humans, but to develop systems that enhance human capabilities while respecting human autonomy, dignity, and well-being.

title: Effect of risk expression using likelihood ratios or natural frequencies in Bayesian inference tasks
description:
Transparent, unbiased and evidence-based communication of risks of medical procedures is an integral component of shared decision making, empowering patients to make choices in accordance with their own values (IQWIG – Allgemeine Methoden, S. 136, 2022; Elwyn, 2012). There is ample evidence that risk communication using natural frequencies rather than conditional probabilities facilitates Bayesian Reasoning, improving participants' performance in Bayesian textbook inference tasks such as the interpretation of diagnostic or screening test results (Akl, Oxman, 2011; McDowell and Jacobs, 2017). Consequently, the German "Good-Practice"-Guideline on health communication advocates the use of natural frequencies in patient guidelines (GPGI, 2015).
However, approximately 3 out of 4 people fail to correctly determine the positive predictive value of a test when sensitivity, false-positive rate and prevalence are given in the natural frequency format (McDowell and Jacobs, 2017).


Alternatively, odds and likelihood ratios (LR) can be used to calculate the risk of having a disease given a positive or negative test result.
The pre-test odds represent the ratio of the number of people with the disease to the number of people without the disease. To calculate the post-test odds of having the disease, the pre-test odds are multiplied by the positive or negative likelihood ratio (LR) of the diagnostic test used. The LR is a compound indicator of test accuracy, calculated by the sensitivity and specificity of a diagnostic test (Grimes & Schulz, 2005).

Calculating the post-test odds requires explicit acknowledgement of the base rate. Thereby, insight into the influence of the base rate on post-test probabilities and its computation in the setting of varying base-rates might be facilitated. In contrast, in the natural frequency format, the base-rate has already been broken down into its individual components and can thus be disregarded.

The evidence on the use of odds and LR as an alternative to conditional probabilities or natural frequencies remains scarce. However, some studies suggest that risk expression using odds and LR could also facilitate Bayesian reasoning compared to conditional probabilities (e.g. Juslin, 2011). It is still unclear whether odds and LR could be an alternative to the established risk communication formats, and to our knowledge, no head-to-head trial comparing natural frequencies with likelihood ratios in Bayesian inference tasks has been conducted to date.

Thus, in an randomized repeated-measures trial, we assess the performance of participants in the calculation of post-test probabilities and post-test odds when presented with either natural frequencies or odds and likelihood Ratios.

title: Method
description:
This is a study protocol for a rapid review of diagnostic accuracy. The acronym Population, Index Test, Reference Standard, and Outcome (PIRO) was used to describe the components related to the identification of the problem and the development of the research question: "Does the detection of galactomannan antigen in serum compared to the gold standard tests of lung histopathology/cytopathology and/or lung biopsy aid in the speed of diagnosis of invasive pulmonary aspergillosis?". The acronym was defined as follows: P - samples from patients with invasive pulmonary aspergillosis; I - Galactomannan antigen detection in serum; R - Lung histopathology/cytopathology examination or lung biopsy; O - Sensitivity and Specificity, Accuracy, Positive Predictive Value, and Negative Predictive Value.
The bases used in the search were: BVS Sáude, PubMed, Cochrane, Embase, and Scopus. The descriptors used in the search were: "Invasive Pulmonary Aspergillosis," "galactomannan," "Sensitivity and Specificity," "Data Accuracy," "Systematic Review," "Validation Study," "Evaluation Study." Mendeley software was used to manage the references and remove duplicates.
The first stage of study selection will be performed by two independent reviewers using RAYYAN software to read the titles and abstracts. Next, the selected studies will be read in full and selected according to the study eligibility criteria. The inclusion criteria for the studies are diagnostic tests with galactomannan antigen, serum as the biological investigation material, lung histopathological/cytopathological examination, or lung biopsy as the gold standard comparators. Exclusion criteria are galactomannan antigen as diagnostic of other fungal diseases, other investigational biological materials, and other diagnostic tests. A third reviewer will be consulted for the discussion of disagreements.
The following variables from the selected articles will be extracted into an Excel spreadsheet for data analysis: author, year, source, study type, sample size, sample type, study objective, intervention, comparators, primary and secondary outcomes, study limitations, and authors' conclusion. If feasible, a descriptive analysis of the data found and a meta-analysis will be performed using RevMan software.
The instrument chosen to assess the quality of the studies was the AMSTAR-2 conducted by two independent reviewers. The methodological quality of selected studies will be assessed by the AMSTAR-2 tool conducted by two independent reviewers. Disagreements between reviewers will be resolved by consensus or through discussion with a third author.

title: Association between maternal pelvic outlet dimensions and self-reported anal incontinence symptoms after vaginal childbirth.
description:
Vaginal childbirth can predispose to a variety of pelvic floor dysfunction symptoms, both in the early postpartum period (1) and later in life (2–4). During the 2nd stage of labour, particularly during crowning of the fetal head, the maternal pelvic floor muscles, ligaments, and nerves are subject to extensive stretching (5–7), which can result in irreversible structural damage (8) and subsequent functional loss (2–4).
 
Anal incontinence encompasses the involuntary loss of feces or flatus and is generally regarded as the most bothersome dysfunction (9–11). Within one year after childbirth, it has been reported to affect 19% of women who delivered vaginally (12). Instrumental vaginal birth and obstetric anal sphincter injuries (OASIS) are important predictors (13). The latter is defined as a perineal tear extending into the anal sphincter complex during vaginal childbirth (14). Although relatively common (15), many women reporting AI after delivery did not have evidence of structural anal sphincter trauma at the time of delivery (16).
 
To date, few studies have investigated the interplay between maternal pelvic outlet dimensions, vaginal childbirth-related pelvic floor trauma and related dysfunction symptoms. During the expulsive phase of labor, the fetal head is bounded by the pubic symphysis and inferior pubic rami on one side, and the U-shaped puborectalis and pubovisceralis part of the levator ani muscle on the other side (5). In a biomechanical model study, Tracy et al. demonstrated that maternal pelvic characteristics (e.g., levator ani loop length, subpubic arch angle, levator origin separation distance) contribute more to the probability of sustaining levator ani muscle trauma compared to fetal characteristics (e.g., head circumference) (17). 

The subpubic arch angle (SPAA) is defined as the angle between the joining of the two inferior pubic rami at the level of the pubic symphysis. Several studies have demonstrated an association between the maternal SPAA and the course of labour, e.g., the occurrence of occiput posterior presentations (18), duration of the 2nd stage (19), or the need for operative obstetric intervention by either cesarean section or assisted vaginal birth (20,21). In a prospective observational cohort study, Frudinger et al. demonstrated that a narrow SPAA was associated with postpartum AI symptoms in nulliparous women (22). Angles were estimated through clinical examination of the pelvis at the time of routine antenatal visits during the third trimester of pregnancy, with subsequent dichotomization into “narrow” or “broad” categories at a 90° cut-off (22). Under the influence of ovarian and placental hormones, the maternal pubic symphysis undergoes important changes throughout pregnancy (23), with wider SPAA observed with increasing gestational age (24). The presence of concomitant anal sphincter injury was assessed through clinical examination of the perineum at the time of delivery (22). Several studies have shown that this method often lacks both sensitivity (15,25,26) and specificity (27).
 
In conclusion, this study aims to investigate the association between the maternal SPAA, measured before the 2nd stage of labour using volumetric trans-perineal ultrasound, and self-reported anal incontinence symptoms after delivery. Structural pelvic floor trauma will be assessed remotely from childbirth using the gold standard technique of pelvic floor ultrasound.
