title: Perceptual sensitivity and grammar processing in individuals with ASD and LAD
description:
Authors: Larson, C., Canale, R., Magnuson, J., Stevens, M. C., & Eigsti, I.

Background 

Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a highly prevalent condition that is characterized by social communication difficulty and restricted and repetitive behaviors and interests (APA, 2013). Other key features of ASD include enhanced perceptual sensitivity (i.e., hypersensitivity) at the behavioral (Heaton et al., 2008; Ralli et al., 2018) and neural (O’Connor, 2012; Sapey-Triomphe et al., 2019) levels, and structural language deficits, particularly in grammar, relative to NT peers (Eigsti & Bennetto, 2009; Wittke et al., 2017). Some work has identified links between perceptual sensitivity and ASD symptomology and other complex skills in ASD (Coffey-Corina et al., 2008; Jaffe-Dax & Eigsti, 2020; Jones et al., 2009; Schwartz et al., 2020; but see Constantino et al., 2006), such as between pitch discrimination and early language developmental milestones in ASD (Eigsti & Fein, 2013). However, the developmental relationship between perceptual and language skills remains unclear, and no prior work has examined the relative role of perceptual versus language skills during information processing.

Approximately 9% of individuals who receive an ASD diagnosis in childhood go on to no longer meet criteria for an ASD diagnosis later in development, referred to by our group as Loss of the Autism Diagnosis (LAD; Fein et al., 2013; see also Anderson et al., 2014; Mukaddes et al., 2014). By the time they reach adolescence, individuals with LAD perform similarly to neurotypical (NT) peers on perceptual (e.g., face recognition) and language tasks (e.g., vocabulary; Fein et al., 2013). 

There is evidence of subtle differences in perceptual sensitivity in LAD relative to NT peers, such as enhanced pitch discrimination in easy, but not hard, conditions (Eigsti & Fein, 2013). In this study, performance on a pitch discrimination task was associated with current levels of ASD symptomology and onset of first words (i.e., a measure of early language development) across LAD, ASD, and NT groups. However, there was no association between pitch discrimination and current language skills across these groups (Eigsti & Fein, 2013). These findings suggest that perceptual sensitivity of pitch and ASD features are associated early in development (e.g., https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28632303/); limited work has examined how perceptual sensitivity to pitch and language skills, are associated later in development. 

The measures used by Eigsti and Fein (2013), including Clinical Evaluation of Language Fundamentals-4 Core Language composite standard scores and Peabody Picture Vocabulary Test standard scores, may be insufficiently sensitive to concurrent relationships between perceptual sensitivity of pitch and language in verbally fluent individuals of school age and beyond. For instance, group averages on CELF Core Language in the 2013 study were all in the average or above average range, suggesting limited range on this measure in this high-achieving sample of adolescents. Additionally, although there were significant group differences in language ability, within-group relationships between language and perceptual sensitivity of pitch were not examined. Thus, nuance in language skills may have not been captured in this prior study. Examining language with an experimental task may allow us to better understand the relationship between perceptual and language skills, and examining within-group relationships between language and perceptual sensitivity may allow us to determine the degree to which this relationship may differ between LAD, ASD, and NT groups. 

It is possible that enhanced perceptual sensitivity diminishes the degree to which linguistic processes relative to perceptual processes are recruited during language processing. Enhanced sensitivity to low-level perceptual features of linguistic input (e.g., pitch, voice onset time) may lead to slower or less accurate language processing (e.g., grammaticality judgment; Eigsti & Bennetto, 2009; Heaton et al., 2008; Ralli et al., 2018). However, examining low-level features of linguistic input may represent a confound given that the perceptual features examined are perceptual features related to language. The current study makes use of a task that aims to reduce the confound of having perceptual features related to language present in the perceptual task. The Click Task (Fodor & Bever, 1965) represents a test that juxtaposes perceptual sensitivity and linguistic sensitivity. In this task, a nonlinguistic “buzz” or “click” sound is superimposed on spoken sentences in a variety of locations vis a vis clausal boundaries: within the boundary, or displaced from clausal boundaries. Participants are asked to identify where in the sentence the click occurred. Accurate identification of click location when the click is displaced from clausal boundaries suggests enhanced perceptual sensitivity to this nonlinguistic click sound relative to linguistic sensitivity. Specifically, “natural breaks” in sentences occur at clausal boundaries, and should therefore be more perceptually salient as a segmentation point than other points in a sentence (e.g., within words, between subjects and verbs). As a result, an individual drawing upon linguistic processes is more likely to place the click at a clausal boundary whereas an individual drawing upon perceptual processes is more likely to place the click in the veridical location. In an alternative explanation, as we process linguistic information, processing resources may be more available when there is a natural break in the stream of incoming information, freeing up processing resources to perceive and mark the location of a nonlinguistic sound. For individuals who are less efficient or robust in processing linguistic information, the distinction between the pause and the non-pause location might be more salient, leading to much greater inaccuracy of location marking for clicks outside the clausal boundary. Thus, this task tests the degree to which perceptual versus linguistic processes are drawn on during processing.

It is also possible that the Click Task measures attentional processes, such as attention to novelty (Reber & Anderson, 1970). In this task, linguistic information is presented before perceptual information and becomes predictable as the sentence unfolds whereas the “click,” or perceptual information, is less predictable and is anticipated by participants. In the competition for attention, the “click” may, therefore, receive more attention than clausal boundaries due to novelty and response bias effects (West, Huedo-Medina, Magnuson, & Eigsti, in prep). It is possible that attentional competition and response bias explain performance on the Click Task to a greater degree than the relative roles of perceptual versus linguistic processes, and this experimental paradigm may not rule out this possibility. However, there is evidence suggesting that performance is influenced by clausal boundaries (i.e., linguistic information) over and above response bias (e.g., slower reaction time in more versus less syntactically complex sentences; Cohen & Mehler, 1996; Dalrymple-Alford, 1976) and the Click Task includes an ungrammatical-sentence control condition which eliminates linguistic predictability. Additional work examining clinical populations may provide further evidence as to the role of attention versus perceptual/linguistic processes in this task. 

In the only study to date using the Click Task with a clinical population, Daughtry (1982) showed enhanced perceptual relative to linguistic sensitivity on the Click Task in a group of children with fluency disorders. Findings revealed that children with dysfluent speech were able to identify the location of a click in a sentence more accurately than peers without dysfluent speech, suggesting enhanced perceptual relative to linguistic sensitivity in this clinical group. Note that this pattern of results is the reverse of what is generally observed in a clinical population. This study showed that, in a group defined by disrupted linguistic processes but not disrupted attentional processes, there was a diminished influence of linguistic processes in favor of perceptual processes during combined linguistic and perceptual processing. However, this study had a limited sample size (n = 10 per group); accordingly, these results require replication. 

Importantly, there is heterogeneity in language ability in ASD (Kjelgaard & Tager-Flusberg, 2001; Wittke et al., 2017) and preliminary evidence of heterogeneity in language ability in LAD (Fein et al., 2013; Larson et al., in prep). Enhanced perceptual sensitivity may explain some of the variance in language ability observed in ASD and LAD, such as if enhanced perceptual sensitivity were to diminish the degree to which linguistic processes are recruited during language processing (e.g., based on evidence of an association between early language milestones and pitch discrimination; Eigsti & Fein, 2013). For instance, perceptual resources may capture attentional resources to a greater degree than linguistic processes in individuals who accurately identify click location. Thus, the current study will examine the role of perceptual linguistic sensitivity during the Click Task (i.e., click location identification + sentence comprehension; Fodor & Bever, 1965) in ASD and LAD versus NT peers, as well as in how perceptual linguistic sensitivity during the Click Task relates to language processing.

At the neural level, there is also evidence of enhanced perceptual sensitivity in ASD relative to NT peers (e.g., Baum et al., 2015; Jassim et al., 2021; Marco et al., 2011). Jassim et al.’s (2021) meta-analysis of perceptual-task based fMRI studies on ASD showed greater activation in several perceptual-related brain regions in ASD relative to NT peers, such as in the primary somatosensory cortex on simple perceptual tasks and in the secondary somatosensory cortex on complex perceptual tasks. However, to our knowledge, there are no studies that use fMRI examine the relationship between perceptual sensitivity at the neural level and language skills at the behavioral level. Two studies have used evoked potentials to examine this relationship, showing that the latency and amplitude of responses predicted language skills (Bruneau et al., 2003; Oram Cardy et al., 2008). Additionally, Schwartz et al. (2020) used event-related potentials to show that relatively greater amplitude of neural response to nonspeech sounds (i.e., mismatch neural response) was associated with relatively higher rates of atypical auditory behaviors (e.g., covering ears, using objects to make noise repetitively). This finding provides evidence of a link between enhanced perceptual sensitivity at the neural and behavioral level. This study also showed that relatively poorer language was associated with relatively higher rates of atypical auditory behaviors. However, they did not test the relationship between neural response to nonspeech sounds and language skills. There are calls to expand this upon work, such as using fMRI to improve the spatial specificity of neural activity and using additional measures of language performance (Baum et al., 2015). 

We will examine perceptual-related neural activation via task-based fMRI, using the control condition of the semantic-adaptive matching paradigm (Wilson et al., 2018). In this visual-symbol condition, participants are asked to identify matching (e.g., Xαση, Xαση) versus non-matching (e.g., ηασ¥ϟ, ηασδϟ) symbol pairs. In the semantic condition of this task, participants are asked to identify matching (e.g., day, night) versus non-matching (e.g., apple, door) word pairs. The condition contrast isolates language-related neural activation from nonlinguistic neural activation. By controlling for language-related neural activation associated with the semantic condition, we will isolate nonlinguistic neural activation, or perceptual-related neural activation, associated with the control condition. We will examine the degree who which this perceptual-related neural activation is associated with ASD, LAD, and NT group status, as well as the degree to which perceptual-related neural activation is associated with behavioral language performance. Thus, we are adopting a two-fold approach to testing the relationship between enhanced perceptual sensitivity and language in ASD and LAD relative to NT peers by examining this relationship at the neural and behavioral level. 

Our research questions are:

1) Does perceptual sensitivity, as measured by Click Task accuracy, differ in ASD, LAD, and NT peers?
2) Does Click Task accuracy correlate on an individual level with performance on a grammaticality judgment task?

3) To what extent is neural activation during a perceptual task associated with grammatical processing on a grammaticality judgment task in ASD, LAD, and NT peers? b) Does this relationship differ in individuals with versus without language difficulties?

title: DIAGNOSTIC ACCURACY OF BIOMARKERS FOR LATENT AUTOIMMUNE DIABETES IN ADULTS: AN INTEGRATIVE REVIEW
description:
Diabetes Mellitus Type LADA (Latent Autoimmune Diabetes in Adults) represents a peculiar form of diabetes that combines features of Type 1 Diabetes and Type 2 Diabetes. This condition is notable for the presence of autoantibodies directed to pancreatic beta cells, suggesting an underlying autoimmune etiology. According to the United Kingdom Prospective Diabetes Study (UKPDS), a significant proportion of patients with DM (Diabetes Mellitus) diagnosed in adulthood (up to 12% of cases) have slowly progressive autoimmune diabetes, a type of diabetes known as LADA, with prevalent underdiagnosis in many instances, often attributed to its clinical presentation, which resembles Type 2 diabetes, leading to underestimation of the autoimmune component. Understanding the differences in pathophysiology between these forms of diabetes is essential for the development of accurate diagnostic strategies. Traditional biomarkers used in the diagnosis of type 1 diabetes, such as the presence of autoantibodies against pancreatic beta cells, may be useful in identifying LADA. However, it is important to consider that the progression of beta cell destruction in LADA is slower than in type 1 diabetes, and typical features of type 2 diabetes, such as insulin resistance, may also be present. Despite the similarities with type 1 diabetes, LADA usually manifests in adults and its progression is gradual and slower, often being confused with the diagnosis of type 2 diabetes. Manisha et al. established a worldwide prevalence of LADA of 5.1% among patients with T2DM and showed the role of the autoantibody GAD in the screening of LADA, also bringing awareness to the measurement of antibodies in the identification of the disease. From this perspective, the differential diagnosis of LADA is often challenging, due to the overlapping characteristics with other forms of diabetes, leading to misdiagnosis and delay in appropriate treatment. According to the guidelines of the Brazilian Diabetes Society (SBD), the diagnostic criteria for LADA type diabetes are: (1) age at diagnosis <30 years, (2) patients who present slow and progressive destruction of ? cells, presenting positive antibody dosage, and (3) patients who do not require insulin therapy during the first 6 months after diagnosis. Furthermore, Sia et al. found BMI <23 kg/m2 to be the most significant clinical predictive factor for distinguishing between type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (DM) and autoimmune DM in adults (>20 years) with newly diagnosed DM, followed by serum triglycerides <98 mg/dL, HDL >46 mg/dL, and HbA1c >8.6%. Therefore, analyzing the accuracy of LADA diagnostic biomarkers is essential for determining the appropriate therapeutic management and optimizing the patient's prognosis, understanding their diagnostic importance. By assessing them, it is possible to identify which tests or combinations of tests are most effective in distinguishing between LADA, type 1 and type 2 diabetes, allowing an early and accurate diagnosis, initiating appropriate treatment from the onset of the disease. This is essential to ensure an appropriate and personalized therapeutic approach, which takes into account the complexity of LADA's pathophysiology and its similarities and differences with other types of diabetes. Conduct an analysis of the literature regarding the accuracy of the main diagnostic biomarkers applied in the identification of Latent Autoimmune Diabetes in Adults (LADA). An integrative review on this topic is crucial to identify accurate diagnostic biomarkers that can distinguish LADA from other forms of diabetes, such as type 1 and type 2. Thus, such identification will not only help in the implementation of appropriate treatments from the beginning, improving clinical management and health outcomes for patients, but will also make it possible to avoid ineffective and potentially detrimental treatments to a better prognosis. This is a qualitative research of the integrative review type to identify productions on topics associated with the accuracy of diagnostic biomarkers of Latent Autoimmune Diabetes in Adults (LADA). The integrative review provides the synthesis of knowledge and the applicability of significant studies in practice and is indicated as an important tool in the health field. To construct this research, the PICO strategy will be used as a basis for structuring a clear and targeted research question. PICO is an acronym that stands for: patient, problem or population of interest (P); intervention (I); comparison ©; and result, from the English “outcome” (O). This makes it easier to search for relevant evidence and analyze the results. The search for articles will be carried out in the following databases: PubMed, BVS, Scielo, Google Scholar.
The search for articles will be carried out in the following databases: PubMed, BVS, Scielo, Google Scholar. The research will follow the following inclusion criteria: a) be a research article; b) be available in full text; c) studies available in Portuguese, English or Spanish; d) have been published between 2014 and 2024; e) articles that address the theme (biomarkers for the diagnosis of LADA-type Diabetes Mellitus). As exclusion criteria, texts that were not related to the theme and/or presented duplicates, in addition to those that fit into case reports, were disregarded. The aim is to identify knowledge gaps regarding the accuracy of diagnostic biomarkers of latent autoimmune diabetes in adults.

title: Comparison of the Diagnostic Efficacy of Conventional, Serological, and Molecular Methods for Human and Animal Sporotrichosis: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
description: This project is a systematic review with meta-analysis aimed at comparing the diagnostic efficacy of conventional, serological, and molecular methods for detecting sporotrichosis in humans and animals (particularly cats and dogs). Sporotrichosis, caused by the Sporothrix spp. complex, is an emerging zoonosis with increasing impact on public and veterinary health, especially in tropical regions. Given the limitations of conventional diagnostic methods—such as culture, histopathology, and cytology, which have low sensitivity in atypical presentations and require weeks to yield results—this study evaluates faster and more promising alternatives, including serological tests (ELISA, Western blot, immunodiffusion) and molecular techniques (PCR, qPCR, LAMP, NGS). The research aims to provide a robust quantitative synthesis of diagnostic accuracy, stratified by species, clinical form, disease stage, and geographic region. In addition to estimating sensitivity and specificity for each technique, the study will apply meta-regression and sensitivity analyses, assess risk of bias using QUADAS-2, and evaluate evidence quality with GRADE. The results are expected to support practical recommendations for standardizing diagnostic protocols in both clinical and veterinary laboratories, enhancing clinical decision-making and informing public health policies. The project will follow PRISMA-DTA guidelines, with a preregistered protocol on a recognized platform (e.g., PROSPERO), and an extensive search strategy covering major scientific databases and grey literature. Findings will be disseminated through scientific publications, conference presentations, and informational materials for health surveillance institutions.

title: The diagnostic accuracy of SARS-CoV-2 nasal rapid antigen self- test: a systematic review and meta-analysis
description:
Introduction: Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) is the cause of corona virus disease (COVID-19), a disease that quickly spread into a pandemic. So, reliable diagnostic tests for SARS-CoV-2 are vital for the management of COVID-19 pandemic. The gold standard for the diagnosis of SARS-CoV-2 is the molecular detection test using the reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction technique (rt-PCR), which is characterized by various disadvantages in contrast to the self-taken nasal rapid antigen tests which give results faster, have lower costs and do not require specialized personnel. Therefore, the usefulness of self-taken rapid antigen tests is indisputable in disease management, facilitating both the health system and the examinees. Our systematic review aims to access the diagnostic accuracy of the self-taken nasal rapid antigen tests.
Methods: This systematic review conducted following the PRISMA guidelines and the Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies 2 (QUADAS-2) tool was used to assess risk of bias in the included studies. All the studies included in this systematic review were found after searching the 2 databases Scopus and PubΜed. Anything but original articles were excluded from this systematic review while all the studies concerning self-taken rapid antigen tests with a nasal sample and using rt-PCR as a reference test were included. Meta-analysis results and plots were obtained using RevMan software and the MetaDTA website.
Results: All 22 studies included in this meta-analysis demonstrated a specificity of self-taken rapid antigen tests greater than 98%, which exceeds the minimum required yield for the diagnosis of SARS-CoV-2, according to WHO. However, the sensitivity varies (from 40% to 98.7%), which makes them in some cases unsuitable for the diagnosis of positive cases. In the majority of the studies, the minimum required performance set by the WHO, is achieved, which is 80% compared to the rt-PCR. In this meta-analysis the pooled sensitivity of self-taken nasal rapid antigen test was calculated 91,1% and the pooled specificity 99,5%.
Conclusion: In conclusion, self-taken nasal rapid antigen tests have many advantages over rt-PCR, such as those related to the rapid reading of the results and their cheap cost. They also have considerable specificity and some self-taken rapid antigen tests kits also have remarkable sensitivity. Consequently, self-taken rapid antigen tests have a wide range of utility, but are not able to completely replace rt-PCR tests.

title: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Large Language Models for Rare Genetic Disease Diagnosis
description:
Large language models (LLMs) have emerged as a potentially transformative technology for clinical diagnostics. Foundation models such as GPT-4, Claude, Gemini, and DeepSeek-R1 demonstrate broad biomedical knowledge, can process unstructured clinical text, and exhibit emergent reasoning capabilities. A landscape analysis of 17 primary studies (conducted as part of protocol development) reveals a rapidly maturing but heterogeneous field with several key findings:

Agentic systems dramatically outperform standalone LLMs. Multi-agent architectures with tool access achieve 55-78% Recall@1 (e.g., LA-MARRVEL: 78%, DeepRare: 57-71%, RareAgents: 76.7%), whereas standalone LLM prompting yields only 12-33% Recall@1 (Kim et al. 2024: 17% top-50; Chimirri et al. 2025: 19.9% across 10 languages).
LLM-as-reranker outperforms LLM-as-solver. LA-MARRVEL (78% Recall@1) uses a traditional variant prioritization pipeline with LLM reranking, substantially outperforming end-to-end LLM approaches (12-15% Recall@1).
Genetic data substantially boosts performance. DeepRare HPO-only: 46.8% Recall@1 vs. HPO+VCF: 70.6% Recall@1, a 23.8 percentage point improvement.
Full EHR text outperforms HPO-only input. RareSeek R1 achieves 68.4% Recall@1 with full clinical narratives vs. 19.2% with HPO terms alone, suggesting rich clinical context is underutilized.
A real-world performance gap persists. Systems achieving 50-70% Recall@1 on curated benchmarks drop to ~20% on real EHR data (MIMIC-RD evaluation), highlighting the distance from clinical deployment.
Benchmark heterogeneity limits direct comparison. Studies evaluate on different datasets (RareBench: 2,185 cases/421 diseases; MIMIC-RD: 145 cases/120 diseases; DeepRare: 6,401 cases/2,919 diseases), with non-overlapping disease sets and varying case complexity.

This rapidly evolving landscape presents a critical need for systematic synthesis. The field currently lacks:

A comprehensive quantitative synthesis of LLM diagnostic accuracy across studies, architectures, and input modalities -- our landscape analysis identified ~13 studies with Recall@K metrics but no existing synthesis has pooled or systematically compared them
Standardized comparison between standalone LLM approaches, agentic LLM systems, and traditional bioinformatics baselines -- the 4-5x performance gap between standalone and agentic architectures is a central finding that requires formal meta-analytic confirmation
Assessment of clinical utility beyond accuracy metrics -- including reasoning quality, time-to-diagnosis impact, and clinical actionability
Identification of failure modes including hallucination rates, reference accuracy (DeepRare reports 95.4% citation accuracy, but this is one study), and performance disparities across disease prevalence tiers, medical specialties, and patient populations
Evidence-based guidance for clinical implementation of LLM-based diagnostic tools in rare disease settings

No existing systematic review comprehensively addresses LLM-based approaches to rare genetic disease diagnosis. Prior reviews (e.g., Neeley et al., 2025; Carbonari et al., 2025) have surveyed the landscape but have not performed meta-analytic synthesis of diagnostic accuracy or systematically assessed the transition from standalone LLMs to agentic systems.

title: Diagnosis and Classification of Different Machine Learning methods for Knee Osteoarthritis: a systematic review and meta-analysis
description:

With the evolution of deep neural network architectures, new strategies are emerging for image classification. Many deep learning models have been developed to diagnose kOA. Its trending and increasing applications, ML remains an emerging field with incredible potential. However, the diagnostic test accuracy of different machine learning methods is still controversial. Therefore, this study was to gather the existing research on the use of machine learning methods and assess its application for detection in screening patients with KOA.

title: Emergent applications of machine learning for diagnosing and managing appendicitis: a state-of-the-art review
description: Appendicitis is one of the most common surgically treated diseases, with more than 300,000 appendectomies being performed in the United States annually. Despite its common nature, appendicitis can be difficult to diagnose at times even with the established criteria of systems like the Alvarado Score. Atypical presentations and poor predictive value of laboratory tests complicate diagnoses and decisions for surgical intervention. CT imaging improves sensitivity and specificity of diagnoses, however this tool bears the drawbacks of high operator dependency and needless radiation exposure. The need for a framework that can inform selective use of CT scans, especially for equivocally-scored cases of appendicitis, warrants the use of machine learning. Machine learning is a rapidly evolving field with increasing applications in healthcare at-large. This artificial intelligence approach uses historical data to train a model that captures existing patterns in data to predict outcomes. The aim of this review is to classify these novel uses of various machine learning algorithms in the context of appendicitis management and examine their potential to reshape pre-operative and post-operative decision-making.

title: Clinical Translation of Artificial Intelligence in Musculoskeletal Care: A Systematic Review of Current Applications, Evidence Gaps, and Implementation Readiness
description:
Background Musculoskeletal (MSK) disorders affect approximately 1.71 billion people worldwide and are a leading cause of disability, with care dependent on imaging interpretation. Diagnostic variability, workload, and limited quantitative biomarkers challenge current practice. Artificial intelligence (AI) can address these issues by improving diagnostic accuracy and efficiency, but clinical readiness and real-world impact are not yet established. This review critically evaluates AI applications in MSK imaging, emphasizing clinical validation and workflow integration, and proposes a framework for translating AI into practice.
Methods A systematic search was conducted across PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, and arXiv for studies published between January 2022 and December 2025. A total of 1,245 records were identified, 892 records were screened after duplicate removal, and 123 full-text reports were assessed for eligibility. Study quality, risk of bias, and implementation readiness were evaluated using criteria adapted from CLAIM, CONSORT-AI, QUADAS-2, PROBAST, and FDA AI/ML SaMD guidance.
Results Of 123 full-text reports assessed, only three studies met the strict criteria for formal imaging-based AI synthesis requiring quantitative, imaging-based validation. All three formally included studies were exclusively focused on MRI, with formal evidence limited to MRI-based segmentation and quantitative biomarker extraction. Although these systems demonstrated promising technical performance under controlled conditions, clinical evidence remained limited by single-center designs, lack of external validation, absence of cost-effectiveness analysis, and lack of patient-centered outcome assessment.
Conclusions AI has strong potential to improve diagnostic consistency, quantitative assessment, and clinical decision support in MSK care. However, the current formal evidence base remains technically promising but clinically under-validated and does not yet support widespread clinical adoption. Future research should prioritize multi-center prospective validation, workflow integration, patient-centered outcomes, cost-effectiveness, and post-deployment monitoring.

title: The Use of AI-Assisted Digital Otoscopes for Evaluating Pediatric Patients in Rural Settings: A Scoping Review
description:
Introduction: Otitis media (OM) is one of the most prevalent infectious diseases in childhood and represents a significant public health problem due to its association with hearing loss, developmental complications, and frequent antibiotic use. In this context, Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative technology for evaluating the tympanic membrane using digital otoscopes, showing great potential for improving diagnostic accuracy and expanding access to specialized care in rural settings. However, the implications of these technologies extend beyond their diagnostic performance and include aspects related to their implementation, feasibility, acceptance, and applicability in resource-limited settings. Therefore, the objective of this project is to map the available evidence on the use of AI-assisted digital otoscopes for the evaluation of the tympanic membrane in pediatric patients, identifying their applications, benefits, limitations, challenges, and future opportunities.
Objective: To map and synthesize the available evidence on the use of AI-assisted digital otoscopes for evaluating the tympanic membrane in pediatric patients in rural settings
Methodology: A scoping review will be conducted following the methodology of the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) and the PRISMA-ScR guidelines. Databases such as PubMed, 


Scopus, Web of Science, LILACS, and BIREME will be searched using MeSH and DeCS terms related to AI, digital otoscopy, and middle ear pathology in pediatrics. Scientific articles, reviews, and technical and institutional reports published between 2015 and 2025 will be included.
Expected results: The study aims to generate a comprehensive mapping of the available evidence on the characteristics and diagnostic performance of AI-assisted digital otoscopes in the pediatric population; the types of devices and AI systems used; the reported diagnostic performance indicators; the contexts of use and the feasibility of implementation in rural settings; as well as the advantages, barriers, and challenges to their adoption. The results will provide relevant evidence for educators, clinicians, health policy makers, and researchers interested in the digital transformation of pediatric care in rural areas.

Findings will undergo narrative synthesis, and diagnostic meta-analysis may be considered if sufficient clinically and methodologically homogeneous data are available.

This project also includes structured extraction databases, screening workflows, and methodological documentation developed for the review.

title: TITAN SR vs ChatGPT 4.1 for Abstract Screening.
description: Background and motivation. Citation screening — the task of reading thousands of search-yield records and deciding which are eligible for a systematic review — is the most labour-intensive step in evidence synthesis, consuming weeks to months of expert reviewer time per review. Recent work has demonstrated that large language models (LLMs) can automate this task with high accuracy: Cao et al. (2025) reported that GPT-4.1 with an optimized "ScreenPrompt" prompt template achieved 96.6% sensitivity and 93.9% specificity on abstract-level screening across five Cochrane reviews. This raises a question of considerable practical and methodological importance: is the strong performance of LLM-based screening primarily attributable to the underlying model architecture (a frontier general-purpose LLM) or to the specific prompt engineering applied to the screening task?The distinction matters. If model architecture is the primary driver, the field is constrained to depend on commercial frontier APIs with their associated costs, rate limits, version drift, and vendor lock-in. If prompt engineering is the primary driver, then a smaller, fine-tuned, locally-deployable model with an appropriately designed input format may achieve comparable performance at a fraction of the cost and with full reproducibility. Resolving this question has direct implications for systematic-review infrastructure decisions at evidence-synthesis institutions, guideline-development bodies, and individual research teams.Project design. This project pre-registers and executes a head-to-head comparison of two paradigms on identical citation screening tasks: (i) TITAN-SR, a fine-tuned biomedical BERT ensemble (PubMedBERT + BioLinkBERT, 50/50 weighted, 110M parameters per backbone) trained on approximately 762,000 citation–label pairs derived from 19,787 systematic reviews, and (ii) GPT-4.1 (model version gpt-4.1-2025-04-14) under three pre-specified prompt conditions: a minimal zero-shot prompt, a structured chain-of-thought prompt, and the optimized ScreenPrompt template from Cao et al. (2025). The same citations are screened by all four index-test conditions, enabling fully paired statistical comparisons.The evaluation set comprises 74,076 citations across 12 Cochrane reviews published between 1 January 2024 and 27 April 2026 (after TITAN-SR's training cutoff and verified disjoint from its training corpus), stratified across three Oxford CEBM question types (4 diagnostic test accuracy, 4 prognosis, 4 intervention). All 12 reviews, their search-reproduction fidelity, and the full citation corpora with binary inclusion labels are deposited in the registration bundle and SHA-256-locked at the time of registration.Pre-specified hypotheses. The primary hypothesis (H1) is that TITAN-SR is non-inferior to GPT-4.1 (optimized prompt) in paired sensitivity at matched specificity, within a 3-percentage-point margin (paired McNemar test, one-sided α = 0.025). Secondary hypotheses address: the relative contributions of architecture versus prompting (H2); specificity at the safety-critical 99% recall operating point (H3); ranking discrimination by AUC (H4); re-screening reproducibility under deterministic versus API-mediated inference (H5); cost per 1,000 citations screened (H6, with TITAN-SR predicted to be ≥10× cheaper); and probability calibration (H7). Discrepancies between any system's decision and the original Cochrane author decision are adjudicated by an LLM-as-a-judge framework (o3-mini-high, blinded to system identity), with a 5% sample manually audited by the principal investigator.Expected outcomes and contributions. The project will produce: (i) a definitive answer to the architecture-versus-prompting question for biomedical citation screening, with statistically rigorous paired estimates and pre-registered confidence intervals; (ii) a reproducible benchmark dataset of 74,076 labelled citations across 12 stratified Cochrane reviews suitable for future screening-system evaluations; (iii) the locked TITAN-SR operating point and full validation-set provenance for replication; (iv) an empirical cost comparison between locally-deployable and API-based screening paradigms at realistic scale. The findings will inform infrastructure choices for systematic-review teams, guideline developers, and methods researchers evaluating the integration of automated screening into evidence-synthesis workflows. The manuscript is targeted for submission to Research Synthesis Methods upon completion of analysis.

title: On the Overlap of Human and Machine Explanations in Melanoma Diagnosis from Dermoscopic Images
description: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems, specifically deep neural networks (DNNs), are becoming increasingly popular in medical image analysis. A substantial hurdle for their application in a clinical setting is their inherent intransparency – DNN models are in the vast majority of cases black boxes. One possible solution to this issue is the use of explainable artificial intelligence (XAI). While XAI algorithms are already readily applied in skin cancer detection, it is unclear to which extent human and machine reasoning overlap and how much physicians trust support systems based on explainable artificial intelligence. Therefore, we evaluate the influence of AI support that includes XAI (based on heatmaps and on an explanatory ontology) on the diagnostic accuracy, confidence, and trust in the support system of dermatologists. Additionally, we evaluate whether more human-like explanations - measured by quantifying the overlap between human and machine explanations - correlate with higher trust of users of XAI-based support systems.

title: Protocol for Systematic Review on Secondary Immunodeficiency
description:
Protocol for a Systematic Review on Secondary Immunodeficiency: Definitions, Diagnostic Frameworks, and Management Strategies Across Clinical Contexts
1. Background and Rationale
Secondary immunodeficiency (SID) represents an increasingly recognized and clinically significant condition characterized by impaired immune function arising from extrinsic causes rather than inherited defects. Unlike primary immunodeficiencies, which are genetically determined, SID develops as a consequence of infections, malignancies, metabolic disorders, malnutrition, pharmacologic immunosuppression, transplantation, aging, or systemic inflammatory diseases. The expanding use of immunomodulatory and immunosuppressive therapies, combined with demographic aging and global infectious disease burdens, has led to a substantial increase in individuals at risk of immune compromise. Despite this growing prevalence, diagnostic definitions, immunological thresholds, screening pathways, and management strategies for SID remain heterogeneous across specialties and healthcare systems.
The clinical consequences of SID are substantial. Patients frequently experience recurrent or severe infections, poor vaccine responses, prolonged hospitalizations, antimicrobial resistance, and increased mortality. In addition to infectious susceptibility, immune dysregulation may contribute to malignancy progression, autoimmune complications, and impaired recovery from systemic illness. Although immunoglobulin replacement therapy, antimicrobial prophylaxis, vaccination strategies, and immune monitoring are widely used in specific populations, their indications and timing differ significantly between hematology, oncology, rheumatology, transplant medicine, and infectious disease practice.
Current literature addressing SID is fragmented across disease domains. Studies evaluating hypogammaglobulinemia in hematological malignancies differ methodologically from those assessing HIV-related immune suppression or post-transplant immunocompromise. Furthermore, laboratory criteria for defining clinically meaningful immunodeficiency vary widely, with inconsistent immunoglobulin thresholds, lymphocyte count cutoffs, and vaccine response criteria. The absence of standardized definitions complicates comparative evaluation of interventions and impedes evidence synthesis.
Although systematic reviews have examined immunoglobulin replacement in specific malignancies or prophylaxis in particular populations, no comprehensive review has integrated diagnostic frameworks, etiologic categories, immune assessment strategies, and therapeutic approaches across the full spectrum of secondary immunodeficiency. Given the clinical and public health implications of inconsistent practice, a structured synthesis of existing evidence is warranted.
This protocol outlines the methodology for a systematic review designed to synthesize evidence from 100 eligible journal articles examining secondary immunodeficiency across multiple etiologists. The review aims to evaluate definitions, diagnostic criteria, infection risk patterns, immunologic markers, and intervention strategies. By applying transparent search methods, standardized appraisal tools, and structured narrative synthesis in accordance with PRISMA and SWiM guidance, this review seeks to provide a reproducible and decision-oriented synthesis to inform clinical practice and future research.
2. Objectives
Primary Objective
To systematically evaluate how secondary immunodeficiency is defined, diagnosed, and managed across clinical conditions, and to assess the evidence supporting interventions aimed at reducing infection-related morbidity.
Secondary Objectives
1. To identify and compare diagnostic thresholds used to define clinically significant immune compromise.
2. To assess the relationship between laboratory immune parameters and clinical infection outcomes.
3. To evaluate evidence supporting immunoglobulin replacement therapy, antimicrobial prophylaxis, vaccination strategies, and immune monitoring.
4. To determine methodological quality and risk of bias across included studies.
5. To grade certainty of evidence for major outcome domains.
3. Eligibility Criteria (PICOS Framework)
Population
Adults and children with secondary immunodeficiency resulting from:
• Hematological malignancies
• Solid tumors
• HIV infection
• Post-transplant immunosuppression
• Autoimmune or inflammatory diseases
• Metabolic or systemic disorders
• Drug-induced immunosuppression
• Aging-associated immune decline
Primary immunodeficiencies will be excluded unless clearly distinguished from secondary causes.
Intervention/Exposure
Studies evaluating:
• Diagnostic criteria or immune assessment frameworks
• Immunoglobulin replacement therapy
• Antimicrobial prophylaxis
• Vaccination strategies
• Immune monitoring protocols
• Predictive tools or biomarkers
Comparator
Comparators may include:
• Standard care
• No intervention
• Alternative therapeutic strategies
• Different diagnostic thresholds
• Pre- and post-intervention comparisons
Outcomes
Primary outcomes:
• Incidence of serious or recurrent infections
• Infection-related hospitalization
• Infection-related mortality
Secondary outcomes:
• Immunoglobulin levels and immune cell markers
• Vaccine response rates
• Antibiotic usage patterns
• Adverse effects of interventions
Study Design
Eligible designs:
• Randomized controlled trials
• Non-randomized interventional studies
• Cohort studies
• Case-control studies
• Cross-sectional studies
• Systematic reviews
• Diagnostic accuracy studies
• Clinical guidelines
Exclusions:
• Case reports
• Editorials
• Conference abstracts without full text
• Non-peer-reviewed publications
Only English-language studies will be included.
4. Databases and Search Strategy
The following databases will be searched:
• PubMed/MEDLINE
• Scopus
• Web of Science
• Cochrane Library
• Embase
• ClinicalTrials.gov
Searches will cover January 2004 to December 2024.
Core PubMed Search String
("secondary immunodeficiency" OR "secondary immune deficiency" OR "acquired immunodeficiency" OR "immunosuppression")
AND
("diagnosis" OR "diagnostic criteria" OR "immune monitoring" OR "immunoglobulin" OR "hypogammaglobulinemia" OR "vaccine response")
AND
("infection" OR "infectious complications" OR "prophylaxis" OR "immunoglobulin replacement therapy" OR "IgRT")
AND
("clinical outcomes" OR "mortality" OR "hospitalization")
Database-specific adaptations using controlled vocabulary (e.g., MeSH, Emtree) will be applied.
Reference lists of included articles will be manually screened.
5. Screening Process
All identified records will be imported into reference management software and duplicates removed.
Stage 1: Title and Abstract Screening
Two independent reviewers will screen titles and abstracts against eligibility criteria. Studies will be coded as include, exclude, or unclear.
Stage 2: Full-Text Screening
Full texts of potentially eligible articles will be independently assessed by the same two reviewers.
Disagreements will be resolved through discussion. If consensus cannot be reached, a third reviewer will adjudicate.
Reasons for full-text exclusion will be documented.
A PRISMA flow diagram will summarize selection.
6. Data Extraction Plan
A standardized data extraction form will be developed and piloted.
Extracted variables will include:
• Study characteristics
• Population demographics
• SID definition criteria
• Immune markers measured
• Intervention details
• Outcomes reported
• Follow-up duration
• Funding sources
Two reviewers will independently extract data from a subset of studies to ensure consistency. Remaining studies will undergo single extraction with independent verification.
Missing or unclear data will prompt attempts to contact authors when feasible.
7. Risk of Bias Assessment
Risk of bias will be assessed using design-specific tools:
• RoB 2 for randomized trials
• ROBINS-I for non-randomized interventional studies
• Newcastle-Ottawa Scale for observational studies
• QUADAS-2 for diagnostic accuracy studies
• AMSTAR 2 for systematic reviews
• AGREE II for guidelines
Two reviewers will independently assess risk of bias. Discrepancies will be resolved by consensus.
Results will be presented in tabular and graphical formats.
8. Synthesis Plan
Given expected heterogeneity in populations and outcomes, a meta-analysis will only be conducted if at least three studies demonstrate sufficient clinical and methodological comparability.
If meta-analysis is not appropriate, synthesis will follow SWiM guidance.
Studies will be grouped by:
• Etiologic domain
• Diagnostic approach
• Intervention type
• Outcome category
Direction-of-effect synthesis will be used where quantitative pooling is not feasible.
Evidence tables will summarize findings.
9. Certainty Assessment Plan
The GRADE framework will be applied to major outcome domains:
• Infection incidence
• Hospitalization
• Mortality
• Vaccine response effectiveness
• Benefit of immunoglobulin therapy
Certainty will be rated as high, moderate, low, or very low based on:
• Risk of bias
• Inconsistency
• Indirectness
• Imprecision
• Publication bias
Summary of Findings tables will be generated.
10. Timeline
Protocol finalization and registration: Month 1
Search execution and deduplication: Month 2
Screening process: Months 2–3
Data extraction and risk of bias: Months 3–4
Synthesis and certainty assessment: Months 4–5
Manuscript revision and submission: Month 6
11. Amendments Policy
Any modifications to eligibility criteria, search strategy, outcomes, or analytic approach will be documented in a dated amendments log within the registration platform.
If protocol registration occurs after partial review completion, deviations will be transparently described, including stage of completion at time of registration and justification for any changes.
No post hoc outcome switching will occur. All amendments will be clearly reported in the final manuscript.

title: Toward a Universal Diagnostic Score for Inflammatory Bowel Disease: A Systematic Review, Meta-analysis, and Evidence-Based Score Development Study
description:
Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), comprising ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease, lacks a universally applicable, inexpensive, and noninvasive diagnostic model. Although numerous biomarkers and clinical predictors have been individually investigated, no single parameter demonstrates universal diagnostic utility. This study aims to systematically evaluate the diagnostic performance of routinely available biomarkers and clinical features for differentiating IBD from non-IBD conditions, including irritable bowel syndrome and infectious colitis.

A systematic review and meta-analysis will be conducted in accordance with PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Electronic databases including PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library will be searched. Eligible diagnostic studies, cohort studies, case-control studies, and cross-sectional studies reporting the diagnostic performance of fecal calprotectin, C-reactive protein, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, albumin, hemoglobin, red cell distribution width, platelet count, neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio, platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio, systemic immune-inflammation index, and relevant clinical predictors will be included.

The primary outcomes will include sensitivity, specificity, diagnostic odds ratio, likelihood ratios, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve. Risk of bias will be assessed using QUADAS-2, and certainty of evidence will be evaluated using the GRADE approach. Random-effects meta-analysis will be performed where appropriate.

Using pooled evidence from published studies, an evidence-based framework for a universal diagnostic score for inflammatory bowel disease (EVIDENCE-IBD Score) will be proposed. The study utilizes exclusively published aggregate data and does not involve human participants or individual patient-level information; therefore, ethical approval is not required.

title: Development of a Short Symbol-Based Screening Instrument for Internet Gaming Disorder: The Inclusion of Videogame in the Self (IVS) Scale for Children and Adolescents
description:
Accurate screening for Internet Gaming Disorder (IGD) in children and adolescents remains a challenge in routine clinical settings. This study evaluated the psychometric properties and diagnostic utility of the Inclusion of Videogame in the Self (IVS) scale, a brief pictorial tool assessing the perceived fusion between self and video game. A clinical sample of 189 children and adolescents (M = 13.0 years, SD = 3.2) completed the IVS, IGD, and Social Media Disorder (SMD) measures. While the five-item scale showed a solid factor structure and reliability, diagnostic accuracy was limited. A single item assessing the “relationship” with the favourite game emerged as a strong screening proxy, correlating with IGD and minimally with SMD. A cut-off score of 3 or higher yielded 100% sensitivity and a 45% false-positive rate. The Single-Item IVS shows promise as a quick, developmentally appropriate screening tool to identify youth at risk for IGD, warranting further validation in broader samples. More generally, the IVS is the first attempt to conceptualise inclusion of self in an activity (the game) rather than in a group or other person.

Note: To protect participant confidentiality, descriptive sociodemographic variables except age and gender were removed from the dataset.

title: DIAGNOSTIC ACCURACY OF BIOMARKERS FOR LATENT AUTOIMMUNE DIABETES IN ADULTS: AN INTEGRATIVE REVIEW
description:
Diabetes Mellitus Type LADA (Latent Autoimmune Diabetes in Adults) represents a peculiar form of diabetes that combines features of Type 1 Diabetes and Type 2 Diabetes. This condition is notable for the presence of autoantibodies directed to pancreatic beta cells, suggesting an underlying autoimmune etiology. According to the United Kingdom Prospective Diabetes Study (UKPDS), a significant proportion of patients with DM (Diabetes Mellitus) diagnosed in adulthood (up to 12% of cases) have slowly progressive autoimmune diabetes, a type of diabetes known as LADA, with prevalent underdiagnosis in many instances, often attributed to its clinical presentation, which resembles Type 2 diabetes, leading to underestimation of the autoimmune component. Understanding the differences in pathophysiology between these forms of diabetes is essential for the development of accurate diagnostic strategies. Traditional biomarkers used in the diagnosis of type 1 diabetes, such as the presence of autoantibodies against pancreatic beta cells, may be useful in identifying LADA. However, it is important to consider that the progression of beta cell destruction in LADA is slower than in type 1 diabetes, and typical features of type 2 diabetes, such as insulin resistance, may also be present. Despite the similarities with type 1 diabetes, LADA usually manifests in adults and its progression is gradual and slower, often being confused with the diagnosis of type 2 diabetes. Manisha et al. established a worldwide prevalence of LADA of 5.1% among patients with T2DM and showed the role of the autoantibody GAD in the screening of LADA, also bringing awareness to the measurement of antibodies in the identification of the disease. From this perspective, the differential diagnosis of LADA is often challenging, due to the overlapping characteristics with other forms of diabetes, leading to misdiagnosis and delay in appropriate treatment. According to the guidelines of the Brazilian Diabetes Society (SBD), the diagnostic criteria for LADA type diabetes are: (1) age at diagnosis <30 years, (2) patients who present slow and progressive destruction of ? cells, presenting positive antibody dosage, and (3) patients who do not require insulin therapy during the first 6 months after diagnosis. Furthermore, Sia et al. found BMI <23 kg/m2 to be the most significant clinical predictive factor for distinguishing between type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (DM) and autoimmune DM in adults (>20 years) with newly diagnosed DM, followed by serum triglycerides <98 mg/dL, HDL >46 mg/dL, and HbA1c >8.6%. Therefore, analyzing the accuracy of LADA diagnostic biomarkers is essential for determining the appropriate therapeutic management and optimizing the patient's prognosis, understanding their diagnostic importance. By assessing them, it is possible to identify which tests or combinations of tests are most effective in distinguishing between LADA, type 1 and type 2 diabetes, allowing an early and accurate diagnosis, initiating appropriate treatment from the onset of the disease. This is essential to ensure an appropriate and personalized therapeutic approach, which takes into account the complexity of LADA's pathophysiology and its similarities and differences with other types of diabetes. Conduct an analysis of the literature regarding the accuracy of the main diagnostic biomarkers applied in the identification of Latent Autoimmune Diabetes in Adults (LADA). An integrative review on this topic is crucial to identify accurate diagnostic biomarkers that can distinguish LADA from other forms of diabetes, such as type 1 and type 2. Thus, such identification will not only help in the implementation of appropriate treatments from the beginning, improving clinical management and health outcomes for patients, but will also make it possible to avoid ineffective and potentially detrimental treatments to a better prognosis. This is a qualitative research of the integrative review type to identify productions on topics associated with the accuracy of diagnostic biomarkers of Latent Autoimmune Diabetes in Adults (LADA). The integrative review provides the synthesis of knowledge and the applicability of significant studies in practice and is indicated as an important tool in the health field. To construct this research, the PICO strategy will be used as a basis for structuring a clear and targeted research question. PICO is an acronym that stands for: patient, problem or population of interest (P); intervention (I); comparison ©; and result, from the English “outcome” (O). This makes it easier to search for relevant evidence and analyze the results. The search for articles will be carried out in the following databases: PubMed, BVS, Scielo, Google Scholar.
The search for articles will be carried out in the following databases: PubMed, BVS, Scielo, Google Scholar. The research will follow the following inclusion criteria: a) be a research article; b) be available in full text; c) studies available in Portuguese, English or Spanish; d) have been published between 2014 and 2024; e) articles that address the theme (biomarkers for the diagnosis of LADA-type Diabetes Mellitus). As exclusion criteria, texts that were not related to the theme and/or presented duplicates, in addition to those that fit into case reports, were disregarded. The aim is to identify knowledge gaps regarding the accuracy of diagnostic biomarkers of latent autoimmune diabetes in adults.

title: Human papillomavirus genotyping for the detection of cervical precancer and cancer in women living in sub-Saharan Africa: a scoping review protocol
description:
More than 200 human papillomavirus (HPV) genotypes exist, each with varying transforming potential 1, 2. The incidence and mortality of cervical cancer are highest in low-to-middle income countries, such as sub-Saharan Africa. 3, 4 South Africa has the highest burden of HIV globally, and women living with HIV (WLWHIV) are at an increased risk of HPV infection and progression to cervical dysplasia and cervical cancer. 5-7
zur Hausen demonstrated the oncogenic role of HPV in cervical cancer pathogenies which subsequently shifted the diagnostic focus to detecting high-risk HPV. 8, 9 This has led to the introduction of HPV DNA testing to screen women for the presence of high-risk HPV types, such as types 16 and 18. 10 HPV DNA testing has superior sensitivity compared to cytology, and does not require speculum examination which risks inter-observer variability. 10 For HPV DNA testing, signal amplification or nucleic acid amplification with polymerase chain reaction (PCR) can be performed on cervical specimen which was either collected by a health-care worker or through self-sampling. 11, 10
Due to the varying risk associated with HPV types, genotyping allows for the identification of high risk types which aids in risk stratification and triaging. 1 The presence of an HPV infection alone does not result in cervical cancer; thus, histology is reference standard in the detection of cervical cancer. 
Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) is a diagnosed through histology, that clears in most cases but can also develop into precancer and cancer 12.. CIN 1 related cellular changes are usually limited to 1/3 of the thickness of the epithelium being affected and CIN 1 cells rarely present with atypical nuclei. 12 CIN 2 affects the lower 2/3 of the epithelium, disturbing cellular maturation and leading to cells presenting as atypical upon histological investigation. 12 The most severe dysplasia occurs when more than 2/3 of the epithelium is affected, classified as CIN 3. 12 Histology results are classified as CIN 1, CIN 2 or CIN 3, with cytology HSIL results usually being classified as either CIN 2 or CIN 3. 13
In 2022, a scoping review was conducted focusing on HPV genotypes in an HIV setting in Botswana, however, the study was focused on examining the prevalence of HPV and how it is essential for HPV vaccination policies.14 There are no scoping reviews published to date that focused on performance of HPV genotyping to detect cervical precancer, thus to the best of the authors’ knowledge this scoping review will be the first.

Aim and objective:
To provide a comprehensive overview of HPV genotyping for the detection of cervical advanced transforming lesions, the aim of this scoping review is to identify, collate and present published data regarding the performance of these molecular assays and related characteristics in women living in sub-Saharan Africa. 

Review questions:
• How did authors define precancer?
• What was the endpoint? (CIN2, CIN3, Ca)
• How did these assays perform in detecting Precancer/CIN2+/malignancy? (Sensitivity and specificity) Performance difference between WLWHIV and HIV-negative women?
• What were the characteristics of the study populations? (location (country), symptomatic or asymptomatic? etc) ?
• How many studies included PLWHIV? 
• Characteristics of the assays – what genotypes did they detect and did the assay discriminate? Or just hrHPV? Or just (for example) 16/18/45?
Eligibility criteria: 
Studies determining/evaluating the performance of HPV genotyping for the detection of cervical precancer
Population 
• Women living in sub-Saharan Africa
• WLWHIV or HIV-negative 
• Cervical histology available in study or precancer/malignancy diagnosed clinically or cytologically 
Concept:
Studies that evaluate the performance of hrHPV nucleic acid assays as a modality to detect cervical cancer or precancer as part of screening or diagnosis in women living in Sub-Saharan Africa. 

The use of HPV genotyping assays has been recommended as a cervical cancer screening or diagnostic modality. However, data describing the performance of these assays in a setting of high-HPV prevalence setting such as sub-Saharan Africa remain scarce. 

Context:
This is a scoping review to map the performance of HPV genotyping assays as cervical cancer screening or diagnostic modality in studies performed in women living in Sub-Saharan African countries from 2010- 2024

Study source/ evidence selection:
Two study members will select publications using a two-tiered screening method. 
After the relevant databases are searched with the specified keywords and results obtained, publications with titular and abstract keywords congruent with the search terms of this protocol will be selected. Once selected, the publications will undergo a full-text review to ascertain relevance to the scoping review. A senior member of the study team will then cross-check the screened publications to confirm eligibility. 
Disagreements amongst or between the study team members involved in screening and cross-checking will be resolved by a fourth senior study member. title: Application and Expansion of a Data-Driven Algorithm Predicting ADHD and Impairment to a Nationally Representative Sample
description:
Current diagnostic protocols for ADHD suffer from a number of limitations. First, ADHD has a relatively large number of conceptually overlapping symptoms, with a striking lack of robust and standardized methodology for incorporating relevant factors, like executive function, SCT, and impairment into the diagnostic process. Second, despite prior work suggesting variations in core ADHD symptoms and impairment based on age and gender, such differences are generally overlooked by diagnostic protocols. 

To begin addressing this issue, one recent study used machine learning to develop an algorithm encompassing eight ADHD symptoms that predicted ADHD diagnosis with greater sensitivity and specificity than current screening tools. Additionally, the eight symptoms predicted academic and global impairment just as well as or better than all 18 symptoms. However, this study used data from a sample of children over-recruited for ADHD, so it remains unknown whether findings can be generalized to community samples. 

The current study aims to replicate findings in a nationally representative sample of children with and without ADHD, and the examine whether the abbreviated algorithm's accuracy for predicting ADHD diagnosis, symptom sum scores, and impairment levels can be improved by incorporating executive function, SCT, impairment, gender, and age.

title: Artificial Intelligence for Lung Cancer Classification in Cytology Specimens: A Systematic Review and Diagnostic Test Accuracy Meta-analysis of Benign–Malignant Diagnosis and ADC/SCC/SCLC Subtyping
description:
This registration contains the protocol and planned methodology for the systematic review and diagnostic test accuracy meta-analysis entitled *“Artificial Intelligence for Lung Cancer Classification in Cytology Specimens: A Systematic Review and Diagnostic Test Accuracy Meta-analysis of Benign–Malignant Diagnosis and ADC/SCC/SCLC Subtyping.”* The study evaluates the diagnostic performance of artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning, and deep learning models applied to lung cancer cytology specimens for benign–malignant classification and histologic subtyping, including adenocarcinoma (ADC/LUAD), squamous cell carcinoma (SCC/SQCC), and small-cell lung cancer (SCLC).

The review follows PRISMA-based reporting principles and includes comprehensive searches of multiple electronic databases. Eligible studies are assessed using QUADAS-2 adapted for AI diagnostic studies. Meta-analyses are performed using bivariate random-effects models to estimate pooled sensitivity, specificity, likelihood ratios, diagnostic odds ratios, and summary receiver operating characteristic (SROC) curves. Additional analyses include heterogeneity assessment, threshold-effect testing, publication-bias evaluation, and Fagan nomogram analysis.

The objective of this registration is to ensure methodological transparency, reduce selective reporting bias, and provide a publicly accessible record of the study design, eligibility criteria, planned analyses, and outcomes before publication.

title: Diagnostic Accuracy of Delirium Screening Tools in the Emergency Department: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis
description:
Background
Few studies have directly compared the diagnostic accuracy of different tools for detecting delirium in the emergency department.

Materials and Methods
Study Design and Search Strategy
 This systematic review was prospectively registered in the Open Science Framework. This study was conducted and reported in strict accordance with the Preferred reporting items for systematic review and meta-analysis of diagnostic test accuracy studies (PRISMA-DTA) [18]. The PRISMA-DTA checklist is provided in eTable 1 in Supplement 1. We conducted searches in EMBASE, Medline, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) databases until March 20 2026 to identify studies assessing the diagnostic accuracy of delirium screening tools in the ED. The search terms included “delirium”, “emergency department”, and related synonyms. We also performed hand searching of references and backward/forward citation chasing

Study Selection
 We included studies that met the following criteria: (1) observational studies utilizing a cross-sectional or cohort design; (2) adult patients (≥18 years) presenting to the emergency department; (3) application of any structured delirium screening tool for diagnosis or screening; (4) use of standard operationalized diagnostic criteria (eg, DSM-III through DSM-5, ICD-10, Feighner, or Research Diagnostic Criteria) as the reference standard; and (5) reported sufficient data to calculate diagnostic accuracy. We excluded studies based solely on unstructured clinical judgment without a specific screening tool. Two reviewers (Y.C.L. and W.T.C.) independently screened articles for inclusion. Any discrepancies were resolved through discussion or consultation with a third reviewer (C.S.L.). 

Data Extraction and Quality Assessment 
 Two reviewers (Y.C.L. and W.T.C.) independently extracted data on study characteristics (eg, author, year, country), patient demographics, study design, and diagnostic accuracy results (true positive, false positive, false negative, and true negative values). To maximize sample representativeness and mitigate potential selection bias in the presence of overlapping datasets, we prioritized data derived from total populations, as well as physician-based assessments. For studies reporting multiple diagnostic thresholds, the cut-off value maximizing the Youden Index was selected [36]. Risk of bias was assessed using the Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies 2 (QUADAS-2) tool [19]. Any discrepancies were resolved through discussion or consultation with a third reviewer (C.S.L). 

Statistical Analysis
 The primary outcomes of this study were the pooled sensitivity and specificity of the included screening tools, from which the Youden Index was calculated. To address clinical heterogeneity, facilitate a structured comparative analysis, and increase the statistical power, our research team reached a consensus to classify the included index tests into six functional categories. We established this classification by evaluating the primary neurocognitive targets to identify the specific clinical features each tool assesses, alongside the structural design to understand its practical operationalization, including algorithmic complexity and administration method. First, the Assessment of Arousal and Sedation (ArouSed) category targeted the altered level of consciousness, which included the Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale (RASS) and the modified RASS (m-RASS) [20-22]. Second, the Assessment of Attention and Working Memory (AWM) focused on inattention as the cardinal feature of delirium, comprising the Months Backwards Test (MBT), Spelling "LUNCH" Backwards (LunchB), Days of the Week Backwards (WeekB), 10-letter Vigilance "A" Task (TenVAT), and the Picture Recognition Task (PRT) [23-25]. Third, the Assessment of Global Cognitive Status (GCS) evaluated general cognitive function rather than specific delirium features, consisting of the Six-item Cognitive Impairment Test (6-CIT) and the Abbreviated Mental Test 4 (AMT4) [26-28]. Fourth, the Composite Delirium Diagnostic Algorithms (CDDA) represented multicomponent tools employing hierarchical algorithms to evaluate multiple neurocognitive domains, encompassing the Confusion Assessment Method (CAM) [29], CAM for the ICU (CAM-ICU) [25], Modified CAM for the Emergency Department (mCAM-ED)[30], 4 'A's Test (4AT) [31, 32], Nursing Delirium Screening Scale (Nu-DESC)[33], the Brief CAM (bCAM) [24], and modified bCAM (m-bCAM)[34]. Fifth, Triage Tools designed for high-sensitivity rapid ruling out were represented by the Delirium Triage Screen (DTS) [24]. Finally, the Informant-Based Assessment category relied on clinical observation rather than direct patient testing, represented by the Single Question in Delirium (SQiD) [35].

We conducted a Bayesian bivariate random-effects network meta-analysis to jointly synthesize sensitivity and specificity[37, 38]. Network geometry was visualized using the netmeta package to illustrate available direct comparisons [39]. Posterior distributions were estimated via Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) simulations[40-42]with minimally informative priors [43], implemented in Just Another Gibbs Sampler (JAGS). The model employed four parallel chains consisting of 20,000 iterations each. To ensure steady-state sampling, the initial 10,000 iterations per chain were discarded as burn-in, and convergence was subsequently confirmed via the Gelman-Rubin statistic[44]. Pooled estimates of sensitivity and specificity, including 95% credible intervals (CrIs), were displayed in forest plots generated using ggplot2 and ggdist [45, 46]. Overall diagnostic performance was summarized by constructing a Hierarchical Summary Receiver Operating Characteristic (HSROC) curve, incorporating 95% credible and prediction regions [47]. 

To evaluate clinical efficiency, the relationship between diagnostic accuracy (measured by the Youden Index) and administration time was assessed. Clinical utility was simulated by calculating positive predictive values (PPV) across varying prevalence scenarios [49]. Publication bias was examined using Deeks’ funnel plot asymmetry test [50, 51], where a P-value < .05 indicated potential bias [50]. All statistical analyses were performed using R software, version 4.5.1 [52].
