title: Machine Learning-Based Prognostic Prediction Models for Post-operative Rehabilitation Outcomes in Elderly Hip Fracture Patients: A Scoping Review and Evidence Map
description:
Background
Hip fracture is one of the most severe musculoskeletal injuries in older adults, associated with high mortality, functional decline, and substantial healthcare burden. Globally, the incidence of hip fracture is projected to increase dramatically with population aging, with estimates suggesting over 6 million cases annually by 2050. Despite surgical intervention, post-operative rehabilitation outcomes remain highly variable, with approximately 50% of patients failing to recover pre-fracture functional levels. Accurate prognostic prediction of rehabilitation outcomes is critical for individualized treatment planning, resource allocation, and shared decision-making between clinicians, patients, and families.
In recent years, machine learning (ML) methods — including random forest, gradient boosting (XGBoost/LightGBM), support vector machines, artificial neural networks, and deep learning — have been increasingly applied to clinical prognostic prediction, demonstrating advantages over traditional statistical models in handling high-dimensional, nonlinear data. However, the application of ML-based prognostic models in elderly hip fracture rehabilitation remains fragmented, with considerable heterogeneity in algorithms used, outcomes predicted, and methodological quality reported. No comprehensive evidence synthesis has systematically mapped this body of literature.
Objectives
This study aims to conduct a scoping review and evidence map to systematically identify, describe, and visualize the existing evidence on ML-based prognostic prediction models for post-operative rehabilitation outcomes in elderly hip fracture patients. The specific objectives are:
To identify the volume, scope, and characteristics of published studies in this field;
To describe the distribution of ML algorithms, predicted outcomes, model performance metrics, and key predictive features;
To assess the risk of bias of included studies using the Prediction model Risk Of Bias ASsessment Tool (PROBAST) and reporting completeness using the Transparent Reporting of a multivariable prediction model for Individual Prognosis Or Diagnosis (TRIPOD) checklist;
To generate evidence maps (bubble chart and heat map) visualizing the density and gaps of evidence across ML algorithm types and rehabilitation outcome categories;
To identify research gaps and priorities to guide future high-quality ML prediction model development in this domain.
Methods
This scoping review and evidence map will be conducted in accordance with the JBI methodology for evidence mapping and reported following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) checklist.
Eligibility criteria: Studies will be included if they: (1) enrolled elderly patients (aged ≥60 years) with hip fracture (femoral neck fracture, intertrochanteric fracture, or subtrochanteric fracture) undergoing surgical intervention; (2) developed or validated a prognostic prediction model using ML methods (including but not limited to logistic regression as baseline comparator, decision tree, random forest, support vector machine, XGBoost/LightGBM, artificial neural network, or deep learning); (3) predicted at least one post-operative rehabilitation-related outcome, including functional recovery (e.g., Barthel Index, FIM score, ADL), mortality, readmission, complications, length of hospital stay, discharge destination, or quality of life. All study designs will be considered, including model development studies, validation studies, and systematic reviews. No restrictions will be applied to publication date or language (English and Chinese).
Search strategy: A systematic search has been conducted across six electronic databases: PubMed, Web of Science (Core Collection), Scopus, Embase, Cochrane Library, and CINAHL. The search was completed on December 12, 2025.
Study selection: Two independent reviewers will screen titles and abstracts, followed by full-text assessment of potentially eligible studies. Discrepancies will be resolved through discussion or arbitration by a third reviewer.
Data extraction: Standardized data extraction will be performed independently by two reviewers, capturing study characteristics (author, year, country, sample size), population characteristics (age, fracture type, surgical approach), ML model features (algorithm type, number and category of predictors, feature selection method, missing data handling), predicted outcomes (outcome type, definition, follow-up time point), model performance metrics (AUC/C-index, sensitivity, specificity, calibration), validation strategy (internal/external), model interpretability (SHAP values, feature importance), and clinical translation (decision curve analysis, web calculator).
Quality assessment: Risk of bias will be assessed using the PROBAST tool across four domains (participants, predictors, outcome, analysis), yielding domain-specific and overall risk of bias ratings (low/high/unclear). Reporting completeness will be evaluated using the TRIPOD checklist.
Evidence mapping: A bubble chart (ML algorithm type × outcome category, with bubble size representing study count) and a heat map (evidence density matrix) will be generated to visualize the distribution of evidence and identify research gaps.
Registration Note
Database searches were completed on December 12, 2025. Title and abstract screening has been completed prior to this registration. This registration is submitted during the full-text screening phase, before data extraction, quality assessment, or any form of evidence synthesis has been initiated. No outcomes or patterns within the data have been observed or analyzed at the time of registration.
Expected Outcomes
This study is expected to produce the first comprehensive evidence map of ML-based prognostic prediction models for post-operative rehabilitation in elderly hip fracture patients. Key outputs will include: a characterization of the current evidence landscape (study volume, geographic distribution, algorithm types, outcome coverage); an assessment of overall methodological quality and reporting standards in this field; visual evidence maps identifying areas of concentrated research and critical evidence gaps; and a research agenda highlighting priorities for future model development, external validation, and clinical implementation studies. Findings will be submitted for publication in a peer-reviewed journal focused on evidence synthesis or clinical prediction modeling.

title: Neonatal jaundice in Global Majority babies: A Scoping Review of diagnostic and management practices in Western healthcare systems
description:
Rationale for scoping review vs. systematic review
For the chosen research question, a systematic review may be considered inappropriate as the literature is heterogenous and potentially underdeveloped conceptually (Munn et al., 2018). Additionally, as the research question is broad and exploratory, key concepts, especially surrounding how individuals are racialised within society are not clearly established. In contrast to a systematic review, a scoping review allows researchers to examine how a topic has been studied within literature, which populations have been included and also where gaps in literature exist (Arksey and O’Malley, 2005; Peters et. al. 2020). 
As the aim of this literature review is not to infer causality of an intervention relative to an outcome, a scoping review is preferred, as opposed to a systematic review where evidence synthesis may be the final output. The heterogeneity of the available evidence base in terms of study design e.g. grey literature, qualitative studies, policy documents and observational research may mean that a scoping review design is preferable. This is also due to the permission of the inclusion of multiple methodologies without requiring formal quality appraisal or meta-analysis processes (Levac, Colquhoun and O’Brien, 2010). What is more, scoping reviews identify research gaps and concepts which could justify a subsequent systematic review, which could then in turn synthesise existing evidence to inform policy changes (Tricco et al., 2018). 
As the research question focuses on perceptions and experiences as opposed to objective outcomes alone, a scoping review is preferred and commonplace within health service research in investigating how care is delivered in different population groups (Peters et al., 2020). A systematic review may not describe the nuance of social or institutional factors affecting healthcare delivery and experiences of clinicians.
Research question: 
How do UK clinicians approach diagnosis and management of neonatal jaundice in global majority babies? A mixed methods study. 
Stage 1: Identification of the research question
The objectives of this scoping review are to:
1. Map the existing evidence on how neonatal jaundice is diagnosed and managed in global majority babies within Western clinical settings.
2. Identify and describe clinical approaches, tools, and guidelines used by clinicians based in Western healthcare settings when assessing and managing neonatal jaundice in global majority infants.
3. Explore clinicians’ experiences, perceptions, and decision-making related to diagnosing and managing neonatal jaundice in global majority babies.
4. Identify reported challenges, uncertainties, and inequities in the diagnosis and management of neonatal jaundice affecting global majority babies.
5. Highlight gaps in the evidence base to inform future research, clinical guidance and policy development aimed at improving equity in neonatal jaundice care.
Informed by the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology for scoping reviews, these objectives align closely with the PCC framework to ensure methodological rigour (Peters et. al., 2020).

To explore concepts, contexts, varying evidence and populations, a broad research question is chosen using the PCC (Population, Concept, Context) framework to adhere to methodological consistency (Peters et. al., 2020): 

‘Neonatal jaundice in Global Majority babies: A Scoping Review of diagnostic and management practices in Western healthcare systems’

PCC Framework Application
Population (P)
• Global majority babies/neonates 
(may also be described in the literature as infants from Black, Asian, and other racially minoritised groups)
Concept (C)
• Diagnosis and management of neonatal jaundice
• Clinical approaches, assessment methods (visual assessment, transcutaneous bilirubinometry, serum bilirubin testing) and management strategies following diagnosis by a health care professional/clinician 
Context (C)
• Western healthcare settings 
• Clinical settings where neonatal care is provided (e.g. labour wards, birth centres, postnatal wards, neonatal units, transitional care units, community midwifery services)
• Healthcare delivered within healthcare settings in North America, Australia, Western Europe

PCC Inclusion and Exclusion Criteria
Population
Inclusion
• Neonates (≤28 days of age) described as global majority babies, including but not limited to infants identified in the literature as:
o Black, Asian, African, Caribbean, Middle Eastern, Mixed groups or other racially minoritised groups
• Studies involving clinicians (e.g. midwives, neonatal nurses, paediatricians, neonatologists, general practitioners) providing care to global majority neonates
Exclusion
• Studies exclusively involving white infants with no disaggregated data for global majority babies
• Studies focused on older infants or children (>28 days)

Concept
Inclusion
• Clinical diagnosis of neonatal jaundice, including:
o Visual assessment
o Transcutaneous bilirubin measurement
o Serum bilirubin testing
o Use of clinical guidelines or decision-making tools
• Management of neonatal jaundice, including:
o Phototherapy
o Exchange transfusion
o Monitoring, follow-up, and referral pathways
• Clinicians’ knowledge, attitudes, experiences, or decision-making relating to neonatal jaundice in global majority babies
• Identification of barriers, facilitators, or uncertainties in diagnosis and management
Exclusion
• Studies focusing solely on biochemical mechanisms, pathophysiology or genetics without clinical application
• Studies addressing jaundice secondary to non-neonatal conditions (e.g. congenital liver disease beyond the neonatal period)
• Intervention studies unrelated to diagnosis or management (e.g. parental education only)

Context
Inclusion
• Studies conducted in Western healthcare settings 
• All Western healthcare settings providing neonatal care, including:
o Neonatal units
o Transitional care units
o Labour wards
o Birth centres
o Postnatal wards
o Community midwifery or health visiting services
o Primary care settings
Exclusion
• Studies conducted outside Western healthcare settings 
• Non-clinical settings or care provided by non-clinicians 

Types of Sources
Inclusion
• Quantitative, qualitative and mixed methods studies
• Clinical guidelines, audits and service evaluations
• Grey literature (e.g. NHS reports, professional body guidance, theses, NGO reports)
Exclusion
• Opinion pieces without empirical or policy basis

Stage 2: Identification of relevant studies

A comprehensive search strategy will be adopted to capture the full scope of appropriate literature using multiple databases, grey literature sources and secondary references lists (Levac et al., 2010). As researcher familiarity with the existing literature improves, the search strategies may be refined throughout the review process, demonstrating the iterative nature of scoping reviews (Arksey and O’Malley, 2005). Searches will be conducted across databases including; MEDLINE, CINAHL, PsycINFO using terms; ‘neonatal jaundice’, ‘hyperbilirubinaemia’, ‘race’, ‘ethnicity’, ‘disparities’, ‘diagnosis’, ‘diagnostic accuracy’, ‘disparities’, ‘disparity’, ‘clinic decision making’, ‘escalation.’ Inclusion criteria for studies include; qualitative, quantitative, policies, peer-reviewed, published 2000-2025, English language, addressing behaviour of clinicians, race, ethnicity and neonatal care. Exclusion criteria include publications without racial analysis or without clinical context. 
Stage 3: Study selection

Against the predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria, titles and abstracts will be screened, followed by a review of the full text. Due to the limitations of the Professional Doctorate, the screening will only be conducted by the primary researcher, which will minimise methodological rigour, however this is due to the small funding capabilities of the research (Peter et. al., 2020). Using the PRISMA-ScR flow diagram, the study selection processes will be clearly documented and reported (Tricco et. al., 2018). 
Stage 4: Charting data
Key data and information are extracted systematically by data charting from the studies included within the scoping review. This can include key concepts, population characteristics, author, study design and country where the research was conducted (Arksey and O’Malley, 2005). To improve rigour, transparency and findings credibility, a data extraction form will be piloted for 5 studies from the scoping review study selection and refined iteratively by the reviewer (Levac et. al., 2010). 

Stage 5: Collating, summarising and reporting results
Data extracted from stage 4 will be synthesised by thematic analysis to present an overview of the themes within the existing evidence and to identify gaps within the literature, as opposed to assessing methodological quality via critical appraisal tools or synthesise new evidence for example with pooled effect estimates (Arksey and O’Malley, 2005; Peters et. al., 2020). Findings will be reproducible and directly related to the research question. 
Stage 6: Consultation with relevant stakeholders

To attempt to ensure that missing evidence is added to the scoping review or to inform the interpretation of the studies, stakeholder consultation can be added as a final optional stage if it is within the scope of a Professional Doctorate (Arksey and O’Malley, 2005). If appropriate, clinicians, patients, policymakers and families of babies racialised as belonging to Global Majority groups can be approached to consult on the scoping review (Levac et. al., 2010).

title: Diagnosing Quark–Gluon Entanglement Beyond Spatiotemporal Separation: A Sensitivity–Specificity Framework
description: Quantum entanglement is conventionally identified through spatiotemporal separation and the violation of Bell-type inequalities. While effective in photonic and atomic systems, such diagnostics become degenerate in high-energy collision regimes where quarks and gluons are confined to sub-femtometer scales. In this work, quark–gluon entanglement is examined through a correlation-based diagnostic framework employing sensitivity and specificity as operational criteria. Sensitivity quantifies the ability to correctly identify genuine quantum correlations between quark and gluon degrees of freedom, while specificity constrains false positives arising from classical or kinematic correlations enforced by confinement. By focusing on correlated state transitions and gauge-constrained field configurations rather than geometric separation, this approach provides a robust method for identifying entanglement in regimes where spacetime signatures lose discriminative power. The framework clarifies the interpretation of collision experiments and supports a regime-aware understanding of entanglement as constrained correlation rather than spatial distance

title: SYSTEMATIC IDENTIFICATION OF P48 AS AN ADVANTAGEOUS DIAGNOSTIC PROTEIN FOR MYCOPLASMA BOVIS INFECTIONS: A LITERATURE SURVEY AND COMPUTATIONAL INSIGHT
description:
This study investigates the diagnostic potential of the P48 protein as a highly specific biomarker for Mycoplasma bovis infections. M. bovis is a major cattle pathogen responsible for respiratory disease, mastitis, and arthritis, leading to severe economic losses in the livestock industry. Current diagnostic tools lack adequate sensitivity and specificity, necessitating the identification of reliable molecular targets for improved detection methods.

Through a systematic literature review and computational analysis, this research evaluates the physicochemical properties, structural stability, and immunogenic potential of P48, comparing it with other candidate biomarkers such as Variable Surface Proteins (VSPs), MbovP proteins, and MilA. Computational assessments reveal P48’s superior stability (instability index: 23.64), thermostability (aliphatic index: 83.40), and moderate hydrophilicity (GRAVY score: -0.349), supporting its use in serological assays.

The findings confirm P48 as a promising diagnostic protein for biosensor and immunoassay development, highlighting its potential application in cost-effective and rapid M. bovis detection. This research advocates for further experimental validation and the integration of P48-based diagnostics into routine veterinary testing to improve disease management and control strategies.

title: Current and Emerging Applications of Artificial Intelligence in the Clinical Management of Burn Patients: A Scoping Review.
description:
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
Introduction:
Artificial Intelligence (A I) is considered an emerging tool within computer sciences, using logic processes, algorithms, machine learning, and deep learning to simulate human mind functions such as intelligence, reasoning, and information processing [1].. This tool has had a significant impact in healthcare, notably in the creation and use of applications for diagnostic support and medical/surgical decision-making in various clinical settings. These applications have enabled healthcare professionals to improve diagnostic accuracy, prevent and anticipate possible complications, and personalize and adjust treatment according to each patient's needs [1]..
In plastic and reconstructive surgery, there is growing interest in using these tools for the care and management of burn patients, as well as for optimizing rehabilitation processes and preventing chronic sequelae[2].
This scoping review aims to explore the current and emerging applications of AI in the comprehensive management of burn patients, identifying benefits, limitations, and possible future recommendations.

Methodology: A scoping review will be conducted of observational studies, original and scientific articles, meta-analyses, systematic or scoping reviews, and gray literature published between 2010 and 2025, in English or Spanish. A comprehensive search will be performed in electronic databases such as PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, SciELO, and LILACS, using MeSH descriptors related to AI and its application in plastic surgery and burn patient management. As a complementary strategy, the snowball technique will be applied to the bibliographic references of selected articles to identify additional relevant studies not retrieved in the initial search.

Expected Results: The results are expected to provide a comprehensive view of current AI uses in plastic and reconstructive surgery focused on burn patient management, identifying especially successful cases, possible obstacles encountered, and recommendations for the potential application of this tool in the field. The findings will be aimed at researchers, healthcare professionals, or anyone interested in AI applications for burn patient care.

title: Use of Artificial Intelligence Platforms in Enhancing Learning and Research Skills Among Postgraduate Medical Trainees: A Systematic Review and Qualitative Meta-Synthesis
description:
This systematic review examines how postgraduate medical trainees (residents and fellows) use artificial intelligence platforms, particularly large language models like ChatGPT and GPT-4, for learning and research. 

PURPOSE: To synthesize evidence on AI adoption patterns, perceived benefits and challenges, and ethical concerns in postgraduate medical education following the November 2022 release of ChatGPT—a transformative moment that enabled individual trainees to access AI tools without institutional gatekeeping.

METHODS: Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, we searched three databases (SciSpace, Google Scholar, PubMed) for studies published January 2023-December 2024. Two independent reviewers screened 2,847 records, extracting data from 24 eligible studies involving 2,897 trainees across 15 countries. Quality appraisal used the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. Reflexive thematic analysis synthesized qualitative findings.

EXPECTED OUTCOMES: 
1. Comprehensive mapping of AI use patterns across specialties, training levels, and geographic contexts
2. Identification of six key themes: cognitive scaffolding, efficiency gains, research productivity, critical evaluation needs, ethical concerns, and equity implications
3. Assessment of evidence quality—revealing that all studies rely on self-reported perceptions without objective outcome validation
4. Policy recommendations for residency programs addressing academic integrity, diagnostic accuracy concerns, and equitable access
5. Research agenda highlighting critical gaps: need for objective learning outcome studies, longitudinal competency assessments, and patient care impact evaluations

This review addresses an urgent knowledge gap as AI tools fundamentally reshape medical training, informing evidence-based educational policy development.

title: T Cell Activation Mechanism
description:
The “TCR complex” is located in the membrane of T lymphocytes and is composed of, among other proteins, the TCR itself, CD3 and CD247. When there is no signal, the chains inside the cytoplasm of the CDs of the TCR complex, with the ITAM catalytic domains rich in lysine, are intimately bound to the cell membrane, which prevents kinases/phosphorylases from acting on the chains. When the antigen-TCR binding occurs, these chains separate from the membrane, and can bind to certain enzymes, which can then be phosphorylated, initiating the signaling cascade. It is known that the membrane potential, and the charges present in it, are relevant for signal transduction (both of the lymphocyte membrane and that of the presenting cell) [ Xiaoshan Shi, Yunchen Bi, Wei Yang. Ca2+ regulates T-cell receptor activation by modulating the charge property of lipids. Nature, 2013, 493, 111-115]. The lipids in this membrane are peculiar, such as phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) and phosphatidylinositol 3,4,5-trisphosphate (PIP3), with three and four phosphate groups, respectively, and are relevant for the transmission of the signal between the TCR and CD3. The presentation of the antigen to the TCR by the antigen-presenting cell could generate an electrostatic field on the membrane of the T lymphocyte, whose origin would be the membrane potential of this helper cell, which repels the so-called negatively charged lipids that diffuse away from the complex. These lipids kept the lysine-rich chains of the CDs in the membrane. This would release these chains into the cytoplasm where they can be phosphorylated, triggering the signaling cascade expected from the complex. That is, the signal would be electrostatic in nature. The role of CD3 and CD247 is to bind to TCR, form the TCR complex and allow their tails to be phosphorylated after interaction with the electrostatic field. The evidence supporting this hypothesis is: 1) The distribution of charges already mentioned in the complex and the membrane. 2) The presence of disordered areas between the antigen receptor and the transmembrane domain of TCR (making the transmission of a conformational change impossible, for example). 3) The fact that there are artificial chimeric receptors capable of triggering the signal, with a molecular structure different from that of the TCR complex. 4) The fact that pMHC that bind the TCR for a longer time initiate a stronger activation of the T cell. 5) The antigen alone is not able to activate the lymphocyte. 6) Only one interaction is enough to activate the T-cell. 7) The association of CD3δε, γε, and ζζ subunits to the TCR is necessary for T-cell intracelluar signal transduction.

It is difficult theoretically to predict whether this interaction will be strong enough to activate the mechanism since, among other things, the surrounding medium has dissolved ions that could shield the electric field. The project would consist of designing experiments to prove or refute the hypothesis outlined. For example:

1) T cell + APC with MHC but depolarized: Bring a depolarized presenting cell to the receptor: See if the interaction would occur in the case of an APC with a depolarized cell membrane, and see how this can be achieved. If the hypothesis is correct, since there is no electrical membrane potential, the lymphocyte would not be activated.

2) T cell + MHC bound to something charged: Bring a liposome bound to MHC, with the same membrane potential as an APC, to the TCR. If the hypothesis is correct, activation would occur.

3) T cell + something that carries a negative electrostatic charge and can be brought to the receptor by some means, without interaction with MHC, for example, if we subject the T cell to a negative electrostatic field with the TCR complex oriented towards it and the cell is activated, this would corroborate the hypothesis

4) Visualize anionic lipid movement using fluorescent lipid analogs (e.g., NBD-PS).

5) Assess lipid redistribution using super-resolution microscopy and FRAP.

The Electrostatic Switch: A Unified Biophysical Theory of Lymphocyte Activation

Executive Summary
We propose a universal mechanism for Antigen Receptor (TCR/BCR) triggering based on Electrostatic Lipid Sequestration. In the resting state, the signaling domains (ITAMs) of the receptor are electrostatically "locked" against the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane by anionic lipids ($PIP_2$, $PIP_3$, SAPI33). Activation is not primarily a conformational change transmitted through the receptor, but a biophysical release event: the formation of a tight "Dielectric Synapse" excludes water and ions, allowing an external electrostatic field (from the APC or polyanionic antigen) to repel the anchoring lipids. This repulsion releases the basic-rich cytoplasmic tails, exposing ITAMs for phosphorylation.
1. The Core Mechanism: The "Lipid Lock"
The default state of the T-cell receptor is OFF, maintained by an active electrostatic clamp.
The Anchor: The cytoplasmic tails of the CD3 complex ($\epsilon$, $\zeta$) and Ig$\alpha$/$\beta$ contain conserved Basic-Rich Stretches (BRS). These polybasic motifs (rich in Lysine K and Arginine R) bind tightly to the negatively charged phosphoinositides of the inner membrane leaflet.
The Trigger: Antigen binding creates a localized electrostatic perturbation. This field exerts a repulsive force on the mobile anionic lipids, driving their lateral diffusion away from the receptor cluster.
The Release: Once the "anionic glue" is displaced, the basic tails are electrostatically repelled by the remaining positive potential or simply released by thermal motion ("The Safety Model"), becoming accessible to kinases like Lck.
2. The Physics of Field Propagation: The "Dielectric Bridge"
A primary objection to electrostatic signaling is Debye Screening ($\lambda_D \approx 0.8$ nm in physiological saline). We resolve this through the unique geometry of the Immunological Synapse:
Dielectric Exclusion: The formation of the TCR-pMHC complex creates a tight physical interface ($\sim 13$–$15$ nm). This "Kinetic Segregation" zone excludes bulk water molecules and mobile ions ($Na^+$, $Cl^-$).
The "Hole in the Shield": By removing the conductive ionic shield (Faraday cage), the synapse acts as a low-dielectric bridge ($\epsilon \approx 2-4$). The electrostatic potential from the APC (or the T-cell's own dipole potential) propagates through this protein bridge without screening, acting directly on the transmembrane lipids.
Dynamic Oscillations: Recent data (Papp et al., 2020) reveals that T-cells undergo rapid membrane potential oscillations upon contact. These oscillations act as a "biophysical rattle," mechanically destabilizing the lipid-tail interaction more effectively than a static field.
3. Evolutionary Convergence: The NTR Parallels
This mechanism is not unique to lymphocytes; it represents a convergent evolutionary strategy for receptor regulation.
Neurotrophin Receptors (Trk Family): The Juxtamembrane (JM) domains of TrkA/B contain conserved polybasic motifs (KF G KR) that sequester the kinase domain against the membrane.
Universal Logic: Both the immune (TCR/BCR) and nervous (NTR) systems utilize membrane-proximal basic clusters to electrostatically sequester signaling domains. This homology validates the "Lipid Lock" as a fundamental principle of receptor biology.
4. Experimental Validation: The "Inverse Proofs"
A. CAR-T Tonic Signaling (The Broken Lock)
Chimeric Antigen Receptors (CARs) serve as a powerful test case.
Phenomenon: Many CAR constructs exhibit tonic signaling (constitutive activation) without antigen.
Explanation: The rigid, artificial hinge/spacer of the CAR prevents the CD3$\zeta$ tail from folding back to engage the inner leaflet lipids effectively.
Conclusion: The failure of the "Lipid Lock" leads to a permanently ON state. This proves that the resting state requires active structural sequestration, not just the absence of a ligand.
B. Superantigens (Forced Dielectric Stabilization)
Superantigens (e.g., SEB) bypass peptide specificity but still trigger the TCR.
Mechanism: They act as rigid "molecular staples," forcing the APC and T-cell membranes into the critical $\sim 13$ nm distance.
Biophysics: This forced proximity creates a massive, stable "Dielectric Hole" (or super-raft) that excludes ions and allows the field to penetrate, triggering the release of lipids regardless of peptide recognition.
C. T-Independent B-Cell Activation (The Pure Field)
TI-2 antigens (e.g., S. pneumoniae polysaccharides) activate B-cells without T-cell help.
Nature: These are high-molecular-weight polyanions (dense negative charge).
Mechanism: The antigen itself carries sufficient negative charge to generate the transmembrane field required to repel the anchoring lipids of Ig$\alpha$/$\beta$. This is a "pure" electrostatic trigger that does not require an APC membrane potential.
5. The Permissive Step: Kinetic Segregation of CD45
The electrostatic release of ITAMs is the "ON" switch, but it requires a permissive environment to sustain the signal.
Steric Exclusion: The massive phosphatase CD45 ($\sim 25$–$40$ nm) is physically squeezed out of the tight synaptic gap ($\sim 13$–$15$ nm).
The "Check-Valve": The exclusion of CD45 prevents the immediate dephosphorylation of the newly released ITAMs.
Synthesis: The synaptic geometry performs two coupled functions simultaneously:
Dielectric Function: Excludes ions to allow the Electrostatic Field to open the lock.
Steric Function: Excludes phosphatases to prevent the Signal from being reset.
6. Conclusion
The Electrostatic Lipid Sequestration Model unifies the disparate features of lymphocyte activation—from the sequence homology of cytoplasmic tails to the anomalous behavior of CARs and Superantigens. It posits that the T-cell receptor is a biophysical sensor that converts synaptic geometry and electrostatic fields into biochemical signals by modulating the lateral diffusion of membrane lipids. This framework offers a testable, physics-based explanation for the sensitivity and specificity of the adaptive immune system.

title: Shared Errors or Corrective Insight? Investigating Teamwork as a Strategy to Improve Diagnostic Accuracy in Challenging Diagnostic Situations
description: This experimental study investigates how teamwork in different team compositions affects medical residents’ diagnostic accuracy in challenging diagnostic situations. In phase 1, participants evaluate diagnoses from one of two sets of six clinical cases individually. In phase 2, they assign diagnoses for eight further cases, four of which are similar to cases encountered in phase 1, but another diagnosis is correct for these cases (critical cases). An availability bias arises when clinicians are influenced by recent cases making them more likely to assign a familiar but inappropriate diagnosis to similar subsequent cases (Mamede et al., 2010). The study design is intended to induce this form of bias and thus represents a challenging diagnostic situation. In phase 3, participants work on four cases from phase 2 again, either individually or in pairs. In pairs, the cases are either critical for both members (homogeneous pairs; same cases in phase 1) or for one of the members (heterogeneous pairs; different cases in phase 1). Heterogeneous interactive pairs and homogeneous interactive pairs will be compared to each other as well as to their corresponding nominal pairs to (A) investigate whether a heterogeneous composition can decrease the assignment of a biased diagnosis and enhance diagnostic accuracy, and (B) determine the influence of real interaction as opposed to mere aggregation of individual perspectives.

title: Artificial Intelligence for Coronary Artery Disease Prediction Using ECG and CCTA: A Systematic Review
description:
Coronary Artery Disease (CAD) is the leading cause of death worldwide, highlighting the need for more reliable and efficient diagnostic tools beyond conventional methods. Artificial Intelligence (AI), particularly Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL), has shown strong potential for detecting obstructive CAD by learning complex patterns from Electrocardiogram (ECG) and Coronary Computed Tomography Angiography (CCTA) data. This rapid systematic review assesses and compares the diagnostic performance and methodological quality of AI models built for CAD prediction using ECG and CCTA data. A systematic search following PRISMA 2020 guidelines was conducted for primary
studies published between 2021 and 2025. Eleven studies were included, six using ECG data and five using CCTA data. Methodological quality was evaluated using the PROBAST+AI tool. ECG-based models achieved AUC (0.72–0.961) and CCTA-based models showed slightly stronger top-end performance, with AUC (0.77–0.97). External validation was uncommon in both groups, applied
in only 40% of CCTA studies and 33% of ECG studies, so neither modality demonstrated clearly greater validation maturity. Despite these strong results, PROBAST+AI assessment revealed a high risk of bias in 90.9% of the included studies, largely due to weaknesses in the analysis domain, including poor handling of missing data and the absence of model calibration reporting. AI models
show strong diagnostic accuracy for CAD across both modalities, although external validation was limited and applied in a minority of studies. However, the widespread methodological bias means these tools should currently support clinical decision-making rather than replace standard diagnostic methods. Future studies should focus on prospective multicentre validation and the use of
multimodal data.

description: This project is a systematic review and diagnostic test accuracy meta-analysis evaluating artificial intelligence (AI)-based classification of lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) growth patterns on hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) whole-slide images. title: AI-Driven Speech Biomarkers for Parkinson's Disease: A Systematic Review of Explainable Machine Learning, Multimodal Fusion, and Longitudinal Validation
description:
This systematic literature review examines the current state of evidence for artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) frameworks that utilize speech signals as digital biomarkers for Parkinson's disease (PD) diagnosis, progression tracking, and treatment response monitoring. The review places particular emphasis on explainable AI (XAI) methods ( including SHAP, LIME, and GradCAM ) and their integration into clinically interpretable diagnostic pipelines.
Background
Parkinson's disease affects approximately 10 million people worldwide and is projected to double in prevalence by 2050. Current diagnostic and monitoring practice relies on episodic clinical assessments and subjective rating scales such as MDS-UPDRS-III, which have limited capacity to capture early-stage symptoms, real-world fluctuations, and treatment response dynamics. Speech is an early and sensitive marker of PD-related neuromotor deterioration, and the ubiquity of smartphones makes remote speech-based monitoring a scalable and cost-effective alternative. Despite substantial growth in AI-based PD speech research, the field is constrained by three persistent gaps: dominance of cross-sectional study designs, opacity of deep learning models, and insufficient cross-linguistic and multimodal validation.
Purpose
The purpose of this review is to:

Synthesize current evidence on AI/ML frameworks applied to PD speech biomarkers published between 2020 and 2026
Evaluate the quality and consistency of reported diagnostic accuracy metrics across studies
Map the landscape of XAI methods applied to PD speech and assess the degree to which explanations have been clinically validated
Identify confirmed evidence gaps — particularly in longitudinal validation, cross-linguistic robustness, multimodal fusion with XAI, federated learning, and digital twin architectures — to justify and inform the subsequent doctoral research work packages (WP2–WP5)

Methods
The review follows PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Four Boolean search strings were deployed across PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, and Web of Science, restricted to English-language peer-reviewed publications from 2020 to 2026. Screening is conducted in Rayyan. Quality assessment applies QUADAS-2 for diagnostic accuracy studies and TRIPOD-AI for ML model development studies. Synthesis is narrative, organized thematically by speech feature domain. Meta-analysis was not planned due to anticipated methodological heterogeneity.
Expected Outcomes

A comprehensive narrative synthesis of AI/ML approaches to PD speech biomarkers organized by phonatory, articulatory, prosodic, linguistic, and multimodal domains
A structured evidence gap map identifying underexplored areas for future research
A formal confirmation of research gaps in XAI clinical validation, longitudinal study design, and cross-linguistic robustness
A peer-reviewed systematic review manuscript

title: The em—ergence of the em—dash: a population-level rise in medRxiv Discussion sections (2020–2025) compatible with increasing LLM-assisted writing
description:
# OSF Registration: Stage 2 confirmatory analysis

**Title:** The em—ergence of the em—dash: a population-level rise in medRxiv Discussion sections (2020–2025) compatible with increasing LLM-assisted writing

**Principal investigator:** Przemysław Czuma, MD, ORCID 0009-0009-8235-2053
Poland; Polish Association: AI in Medicine

**OSF project (umbrella):** https://osf.io/ucsqf/ (created 2026-05-20 17:14 UTC)
**Registration type:** Open-Ended Registration
**Registration date:** 2026-05-31
**Access:** deposited under embargo until publication of the main paper. The timestamp and the frozen plan lock at registration; the content becomes public when the embargo lifts (the hypothesis is already public in the umbrella project description).

> **Note on what is and is not deposited here.** This registration freezes the *analysis plan* only. The medRxiv corpus is external, public data (medRxiv S3 Text-and-Data-Mining bucket) and is **not** copied into OSF or GitHub; the retrieval date and the resulting DOI manifest are recorded. No results exist at registration time. Two distinct timeline points are recorded here as they occur: (i) at **data freeze, immediately before the confirmatory analysis is run**, the input dataset and analysis code are locked and the **GitHub commit hash** is recorded (the frozen input dataset may optionally be deposited to Zenodo at this point); (ii) at **publication, after the analysis**, the Zenodo archive of the final code, processed data, and results is created and its **citable DOI** is recorded.

---

## 1. Background and relationship to prior exploratory work

Prior exploratory analysis on a sample of medRxiv preprints (1,941 DOIs collected from deposits between 2019 and 2025, of which 1,873 passed the length filter and were analysed, via an HTML-based extraction pipeline) indicated a marked post-ChatGPT increase in em-dash prevalence in Discussion sections. The present preregistered analysis tests this on the **full medRxiv XML corpus** (S3 TDM bucket, 82,192 metadata records comprising 82,067 first-version (v1) papers and 125 later-version records; retrieved 2026-05-26) using a **distinct extraction pipeline**, with outcomes and analyses specified before extraction at scale. Of the 1,941 exploratory DOIs, 1,926 (2.4% of the corpus) are present in this corpus; a sensitivity analysis excluding the overlapping records is prespecified (Section 7). The exploratory work informed the design at a high level; specific exploratory effect-size estimates are not carried into this plan.

This is a discovery-then-replication design: the exploratory analysis described above is prior, **unpublished** pilot work that informed this plan; Stage 2 (this registration) is the confirmatory analysis. The exploratory results are not released as a preprint.

## 2. Research question and hypotheses

**Primary hypothesis (H1).** In a v1-only cohort of medRxiv Discussion sections, the prevalence of preprints containing at least one em-dash (U+2014) differs between the pre-ChatGPT period (deposits before 2022-11-30) and the post-ChatGPT period (deposits on/after 2022-11-30).

The claim under test is a **population-level stylistic shift temporally coincident with the public availability of LLM-assisted writing tools, and compatible with their adoption**, not a per-paper detector of LLM authorship, and not a causal proof.

## 3. Data source and corpus

- **Source:** medRxiv S3 Text-and-Data-Mining bucket (full-text JATS XML), public external data; retrieved 2026-05-26 (82,192 metadata records = 82,067 v1 papers + 125 later-version records). The corpus is not redistributed.
- **Units:** preprints (one record per DOI after the v1 restriction below).
- **Deposit date:** from JATS ``, with fallback to DOI date parsing.

## 4. Cohort definition (inclusion / exclusion)

- **Temporal scope (primary):** deposits 2020-01-01 to 2025-12-31 (six full years). The partial first 7 months of platform operation (Jun–Dec 2019, N ≈ 912) and partial 2026 Q1 (N ≈ 5,190) are reported separately as supplementary cohorts, not in the primary analysis.
- **Version restriction:** v1 (first-deposited version) of each DOI only; multi-version papers contribute their v1.
- **Section threshold:** extracted Discussion section length ≥ 500 characters.
- **Extraction:** manual-validation-passed JATS extraction (Section 10).
- **Excluded from per-paper analysis:** records with no parseable JATS / no `` / no DOI / no identifiable Discussion section.

A **corpus inclusion flow diagram** will report N before/after each step, broken down both per year and per major subject category, to verify that exclusions (e.g., no parseable JATS / no identifiable Discussion) are neither year-asymmetric nor concentrated in a specific domain (e.g., physics/math preprints with non-standard formatting). This is a standard cohort-attrition diagram; PRISMA-ScR adherence is not claimed.

## 5. Variables

- **Primary outcome:** binary `HasEm`, Discussion section contains ≥ 1 em-dash (U+2014).
- **Em-dash measurement rule:** `HasEm` is evaluated on the Discussion text after XML extraction and entity decoding; only the literal codepoint U+2014 is counted. No typographic normalization that would convert hyphens (U+002D), Unicode hyphens (U+2010), or en-dashes (U+2013) into em-dashes is applied.
- **Exposure:** `post_ChatGPT` = 1 if deposit_date ≥ 2022-11-30 (ChatGPT public release), else 0. No wash-out period.
- **Cluster (for SEs):** first-author identity (ORCID where present; otherwise a fallback of lowercased surname + first initial + affiliation institution + country). Adding the institution stops distinct authors who share a common surname (for example several "Wang J" in one country) from being merged; any merging that remains is conservative, since it widens the confidence intervals rather than biasing the point estimate. The number and size of the first-author clusters, and the share identified by ORCID versus the fallback, are reported.
- **Secondary outcome (supportive):** em-dash count per Discussion section, with log(disc_len) offset.

## 6. Primary analysis and reporting hierarchy

**Model:** logistic GLM, `logit(P(HasEm)) = β₀ + β₁·post_ChatGPT`, with **first-author cluster-robust (sandwich) standard errors**. α = 0.05, single primary hypothesis (no multiplicity correction needed).

**Primary estimand:** the absolute difference in Discussion-section HasEm prevalence between post- and pre-ChatGPT deposits in the primary v1 cohort.

**Reporting (explicit interpretive hierarchy):**
1. Per-era HasEm% with counts and 95% Wilson CIs (descriptive).
2. **Absolute percentage-point difference** (post − pre) with 95% CI: the **primary interpretive measure**.
3. Unadjusted prevalence ratio (raw ratio; Koopman score 95% CI): a descriptive relative-effect measure.
4. Model-estimated odds ratio (cluster-robust 95% CI, Wald p): the inferential model output, with no covariate adjustment.

**Pre-specified magnitude interpretive scale** (bound to absolute pp difference): ≥ 5 pp → "substantial"; 2–5 pp → "moderate"; < 2 pp → "trivial, regardless of statistical significance". Anchors are structurally calibrated, not pilot-fitted: the 5 pp anchor is roughly 2–3× the typical pre-LLM year-to-year variation in HasEm%, and the 2 pp anchor roughly 1× (i.e., the within-baseline noise floor).

**Minimum detectable effect:** at α = 0.05, 80% power, per-era effective N ≈ 16,000–18,000 (raw N deflated by a conservative design effect of 1.5 for first-author clustering), baseline ≈ 4% (pre-ChatGPT era), the minimum detectable absolute difference is ≈ 0.4–0.6 pp. The binding constraint on interpretation is therefore substantive magnitude (the 2 pp / 5 pp scale), not statistical detectability.

## 7. Analysis hierarchy (three tiers; no formal α-spending)

**Supportive analyses** (pre-registered, reported regardless of the primary p-value):
- Em-dash **count density**: a robust Poisson GLM (log(disc_len) offset, first-author cluster-robust SE), reporting the IRR with 95% CI.
- **Section-comparison** (Discussion vs Results): a within-paper mixed-effects logistic with a section × era interaction (paper-level random intercept), on a paired subset (both sections validly extracted, each ≥ 500 chars); per-era paired-subset attrition reported. Interpreted as evidence for a narrative-section-specific stylistic shift, not as identification of an LLM mechanism.
- **Kobak target8 lexical convergence (abstracts)**, eight markers (delve, intricate, underscore, boast, endeavor, showcase, underpinning, garner), per-word and composite ORs as a forest plot; literature-comparable to Kobak et al. (2025). *(The Discussion-compartment Kobak analysis is reported in the supplement only.)*
- **Per-year HasEm%** with 95% Wilson CIs, descriptive temporal figure of record.
- **Quarterly segmented binomial regression**, interrupted-time-series model of the quarterly **proportion** of Discussion sections with HasEm = 1 (binomial GLM, logit link, weighted by total deposits per quarter, so growing deposit volume is not confounded with the rate) with a breakpoint at ChatGPT release, estimating the pre-release slope (β₁), the immediate level change at the breakpoint (β₂), and the post-release slope change (β₃), each with 95% CI. This is the formal step-vs-trend test that distinguishes a discrete shift at the breakpoint from a pre-existing secular drift; it is the principled control for the most plausible competing explanation (general typographic/editorial drift) and complements the placebo breakpoint (Section 8).
- **Subject-category composition by era**, descriptive table of major medRxiv subject categories per era (pre/post), with per-category HasEm% and Wilson CIs. Reported for transparency on composition shift; no subject-category adjustment is included in the primary model.

**Sensitivity analyses** (re-runs of the primary on modified cohorts; concordance = same direction, absolute pp difference within ±30% of the primary estimate, and overlapping 95% CI):
- Exclude the exploratory-sample-overlapping DOIs (1,926 of the 1,941 exploratory DOIs are present in the corpus; 1,565 fall within the primary cohort and are removed in this sensitivity).
- Latest-version cohort instead of v1.
- Exclude COVID-19-related preprints (subject category + keyword classifier).
- Alternative disc_len thresholds (≥ 250 and ≥ 1,000 characters).
- Exclude papers with a fused section heading (Discussion combined with Results or with Conclusion, e.g. "Results and Discussion"), where Results-section text may contaminate the Discussion em-dash count. Such fusions are 3.9% of the primary cohort and asymmetric by era (5.4% pre vs 2.5% post), so the contamination is conservative for the primary contrast; this sensitivity confirms the result is not driven by it.
- Exclude "range-only" papers, whose only Discussion em-dash is a numeric-range separator (digit-em-dash-digit, e.g. "1934-1971", "10-20 g"). A pre-registered diagnostic found these are 0.63% of HasEm=1 papers in the primary cohort and slightly asymmetric by era (1.36% pre vs 0.40% post among HasEm=1 papers; the direction inflates the pre-ChatGPT baseline and is therefore conservative for the primary contrast). This sensitivity reclassifies such papers as HasEm=0 and confirms the result is not driven by range punctuation.

## 8. Falsification, placebo breakpoint

Restricted to the **pre-LLM-only sub-cohort** (2020-01-01 to 2022-11-29), refit the primary model with a placebo cutoff at **2021-06-30**. Both periods are pre-LLM by construction; this is a temporal-specificity test. Pre-specified decision rule:

| Outcome | Interpretation |
|---|---|
| Real ≥ 5 pp (substantial) AND placebo < 2 pp | Primary contrast is temporally specific to the ChatGPT window. |
| Real ≥ 5 pp AND placebo ≥ 2 pp, comparable in magnitude to the real shift | Fails falsification, reframe as a non-specific temporal rise. |
| Placebo ≈ 2 pp but well below the real shift | Equivocal; partial pre-existing drift. |

These thresholds are **qualitative falsification heuristics, not formal inferential decision boundaries**, and are stated on the **absolute percentage-point scale**, the primary estimand, anchored to the same 2 pp / 5 pp magnitude scale used for interpretation (Section 6). The heuristic is deliberately **not** governed by the odds ratio, which overstates relative effect at the low (~4% pre-ChatGPT) baseline. Both real and placebo contrasts are reported as absolute pp differences (and, secondarily, OR for comparability).

**Utility-section placebo (platform-artifact control):** apply the same em-dash counting to Acknowledgments and Data Availability statements. A utility section is considered **concerning** only if its post-ChatGPT prevalence reaches ≥ 1% **and** the post−pre increase is directionally similar to the Discussion-section increase **and** at least one-third of its magnitude. If a utility section meets all three, a platform-level artifact cannot be excluded and the primary contrast is reframed in Limitations; a sub-1% drift with no proportional relation to the Discussion increase is not treated as disconfirming.

## 9. Historical reference and comparator

No external comparator corpus is used. The internal medRxiv 2020–2022 pre-ChatGPT period is the historical reference prevalence. This is not a measure of diagnostic specificity; per-paper LLM-use ground truth is not available, and a per-paper detector is not the goal.

No clean typographic negative-control marker exists (exploratory data show all common punctuation drifts upward ~1.13×–1.29× in this corpus). Specificity is addressed instead by the placebo breakpoint, the section-comparison, and the Kobak convergence, none of which, individually or jointly, establishes LLM use as the unique cause.

## 10. Extraction validation (before primary analysis)

The validated constructs are **objective and deterministic**, presence of the literal character U+2014 in a text span, and identification of the Discussion section boundary against the source JATS XML, not subjective coding. Agreement therefore measures automated-pipeline accuracy against human-verified ground truth (rater-vs-pipeline), and Cohen's kappa is reported in that sense; a second independent human rater is not required because the target is not a matter of judgement. The only residual judgement is the Discussion-vs-Conclusion/Limitations boundary, governed by a stated section-boundary rule (JATS `sec-type` where present, else the first interpretive heading after Results).

Two pre-specified manual-review samples, drawn and reviewed **before** the primary analysis runs:

- **Sample A (section extraction, random):** n = 200 (100 pre-, 100 post-ChatGPT), stratified by year; verifies section identification and scope. Metric: % agreement with 95% Wilson CIs.
- **Sample B (HasEm classification, enriched):** n = 200, stratified by automated label × era (50 per cell); manual em-dash counting. Prevalence-invariant **Sensitivity** and **Specificity** per era are the primary validation metrics. Because Sample B is stratified on the automated label, the raw enriched proportions give PPV and NPV directly; Sensitivity and Specificity are recovered by re-weighting the confusion counts to the observed cohort prevalence (Bayes), which is what makes them prevalence-invariant. PPV and NPV are reported descriptively only.

Acceptance thresholds: Sample A section-ID and scope ≥ 90%. For Sample B the absolute thresholds, Sens ≥ 90% and Spec ≥ 95%, are evaluated on the **era-pooled** sample (100 true positives and 100 true negatives respectively, giving 1-pp granularity and avoiding the brittle 2-pp quantization of a 50-per-cell estimate); **era stability** is checked separately via |Sens_post − Sens_pre| ≤ 5 pp and |Spec_post − Spec_pre| ≤ 5 pp. **Acceptance is based on point estimates; Wilson 95% CIs are reported alongside to quantify uncertainty** (the lower CI bound is not required to clear the threshold, given the enriched sample size). If a point estimate does not meet its threshold, the pipeline is corrected and re-validated on fresh samples before the primary analysis proceeds.

## 11. Stopping rule and deviations

The confirmatory analysis is run **once** on the frozen Stage 2 dataset after retrieval and validation complete. No interim analyses; no adaptive stopping. Any analysis not specified here is reported as exploratory and labeled as such. All deviations from this registration are documented in a dedicated manuscript section. If any **pre-specified sensitivity analysis** (Section 7) attenuates the primary **absolute percentage-point difference** by more than 30%, confirmation is considered weakened and the result is framed as **sensitivity-dependent** rather than as a clean confirmatory finding.

## 12. Analyses explicitly NOT pre-registered as confirmatory

To keep the confirmatory core lean, the following are **not** part of this registration; they may be reported as clearly-labeled exploratory analyses, in the supplement, or deferred to follow-up work:
- ESL/NES first-author language stratification (exploratory / follow-up only).
- Kobak target8 in Discussion sections (supplementary).
- bioRxiv cross-substrate comparison (out of scope for this registration).
- Cross-model LLM emission audit (out of scope).

## 13. Software, code, and data availability

- **Analysis software:** Python 3.10+ (pandas, lxml, requests) and/or R (`lme4` for the mixed-effects section-comparison; GEE fallback). Scripts are idempotent and emit timestamped manifests.
- **Code:** public GitHub repository (`em-ergence-em-dash`). Frozen at data freeze, commit `21b65fd947165f9baca74dd6fc67b92a0c42adb1` (https://github.com/P-Czum/em-ergence-em-dash/commit/21b65fd947165f9baca74dd6fc67b92a0c42adb1); no changes to analysis scripts after this commit and before the confirmatory analysis.
- **Data:** the medRxiv corpus is public external data (S3 TDM) and is not redistributed. The integrity-critical freeze is the **GitHub commit hash, recorded at data freeze before the analysis**; the **Zenodo archive (DOI manifest + processed per-paper measurements) and its citable DOI are created at publication, after the analysis** (optionally, the frozen input dataset is also deposited to Zenodo at freeze for maximal provenance). The DOI manifest includes, per record: DOI, version, deposit date, subject category, and extraction status.

## 14. AI-assisted analysis disclosure

AI tools (Claude, Anthropic) were used for code generation, statistical-analysis assistance, and editorial review. They did not formulate the research question, choose the corpus, or independently make scientific decisions. Full disclosure appears in the manuscript.

## 15. Competing interests

The author declares no competing financial interests. Non-financial: the author is affiliated with the Polish Association for AI in Medicine. No external funding supported this work.

## 16. Pre-specified contingencies

Operational fallbacks fixed in advance, so that hitting them does not force an undocumented ad-hoc decision. This list is deliberately short, genuinely unforeseen events are handled under the deviation-reporting policy (Section 11), not pre-enumerated.

- **Validation cannot reach threshold.** If, after pipeline correction and re-validation on fresh samples (Section 10), an extraction metric still fails its threshold, the primary analysis is restricted to the subset for which extraction is validated and the study is reported as **measurement-limited**, rather than proceeding on an unvalidated pipeline. The restriction and its effect on N are reported.
- **Missing version metadata.** Papers whose deposit version cannot be parsed from the MECA `manifest.xml` are excluded from the v1 primary cohort, and their count is reported in the corpus inclusion flow.
- **Model non-convergence.** The primary logistic GLM (single predictor, large N) is not expected to have convergence issues; should the quarterly segmented model fail to converge, it is refit with reduced time terms (retain the level change β₂, drop the slope-change term β₃), and the section-comparison mixed model falls back to GEE (Section 13). Any fallback actually used is reported as such.

title: Applications of artificial intelligence in endobronchial ultra-sound for lung cancer diagnosis and staging: a scoping review
description: This scoping review evaluated the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in endobronchial ultrasound (EBUS) for lung cancer diagnosis and staging. A total of 26 studies published between 2015 and 2026 were included, with most employing deep learning–based models. The main clinical application was diagnostic classification of malignancy, followed by segmentation, cytological analysis, anatomical navigation, and multimodal predictive models. Most studies used EBUS-derived images or videos from both Convex Probe-EBUS and Radial Probe-EBUS procedures. Although findings highlight the growing potential of AI to improve diagnostic accuracy and image analysis, current evidence remains limited by retrospective designs, small sample sizes, and single-center studies.

title: Visual Attention and Decision Deliberation in AI-Driven Dermatology: The Role of Case Complexity and AI Accuracy
description:
Project Description
Skin cancer is the most common type of cancer in the Netherlands and many other countries, and the number of patients visiting general practitioners (GPs) for suspicious skin lesions continues to rise each year. Artificial intelligence (AI) tools have shown promise in matching the diagnostic accuracy of trained dermatologists for skin lesion assessment. However, integrating AI into clinical practice has been challenging, in part because clinicians and AI tend to make different types of errors, and doctors often do not fully trust or know how to use AI outputs in their decision-making.
This study aims to provide new insights into how clinicians use and respond to AI advice when diagnosing skin lesions as malignant (melanoma) or benign (nevus). Using webcam-based eye-tracking technology, we will observe where and how long doctors look at different parts of the screen—including the AI’s advice—while they review photos of skin lesions and make diagnostic decisions. Given that cases can vary in difficulty, and even AI makes mistakes, we are interested in understanding how doctors deal with cases with inherent uncertainty, as well as when the AI advice provides misleading advice. Therefore in this study, we will systematically vary the difficulty of the cases and the accuracy of the AI advice (correct vs. incorrect).

Exploratory sub-analyses will compare responses across clinicians with different levels of experience (GPs, dermatologists, and residents), among other factors.
Study procedure:
Participants will complete the study online, reviewing a set of 49 clinical photographs of skin lesions. For each photo, they will use a slider to indicate how likely they believe the lesion is benign or malignant, expressing both their diagnostic decision and their confidence. The study uses a within-subjects design: The AI advice will sometimes be correct and sometimes intentionally incorrect, allowing us to see how doctors respond to both helpful and misleading AI. Benign cases will include subjectively difficult cases, objectively difficult cases, and objectively easy cases. The Malignant cases will also be dividing into easy, medium and difficult.

We will collect detailed eye-tracking data—such as the number and duration of fixations on the AI output or the skin lesion, the order in which different screen elements are viewed, and regressive fixations—to measure visual attention and cognitive processing. We will also record reaction times and confidence ratings. 

Main research questions:

How do case difficulty and AI advice accuracy, influence decision-making processes while diagnosing skin lesions?

Expected outcomes:
We expect that doctors will pay more attention to AI advice and deliberate longer (as shown by more fixations and longer reaction times) when cases are difficult and when the AI advice is wrong.

title: Diagnostic Test Accuracy of Artificial Intelligence–Based Assessment of Chest Radiographs for Osteoporosis: An Updated Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
description:
This project aims to evaluate the diagnostic test accuracy of artificial intelligence–based assessment of chest radiographs for detecting osteoporosis.
The systematic review and meta-analysis will update previous evidence by including newly published studies and applying a standardized methodology.
The expected outcome is to provide an up-to-date summary of diagnostic performance, identify sources of heterogeneity, and offer guidance for future AI-based osteoporosis screening research.

title: Prehospital evaluation of confidence and practice in treatment of out of hospital cardiac arrest across Australia, UK and New Zealand
description:
Introduction 

Cardiac arrest defined as loss of mechanical activity of the heart confirmed by the absence of signs of circulation [1]. Out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) is defined as cardiac arrest occurring outside of hospital. It has an annual incidence of 65.4-to-108.9/100,000-person year globally [2] and 108.9 per 100,000-person year in Australia, according to the Australasian Resuscitation Outcomes Consortium (Aus-ROC) epistry [3]. This registry compiles data from all regional emergency medical services (EMS) across Australia and New Zealand, underscoring the significant morbidity and mortality associated with OHCA—fewer than 1 in 8 (11%) patients survive to hospital discharge [3]. Globally, this pattern is echoed. A large systematic review and meta-analysis of international OHCA registries found rates of return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) and survival to hospital admission to be 29.7% and 22.0%, respectively [4]. Despite advancements in prehospital care, survival rates have not significantly improved over the past three decades. 

 

The Resuscitation Council UK and the International Liaison Committee on Resuscitation (ILCOR) recommend consideration of eight reversible causes of cardiac arrest, commonly referred to as the "4 Hs and 4 Ts" i.e., hypoxia, hypothermia, hypo/ hyperkalemia, hypovolemia, tamponade, tension pneumothorax, thrombosis and toxins [5]. These recommendations are based largely on expert consensus mostly drawn from in-hospital cardiac arrest (IHCA) data [6]. There is a notable lack of robust literature on the causes of OHCA. Much of the existing data stems from patients who survive to hospital admission [7], introducing survivor bias. Furthermore, registry data regarding arrest aetiology are often incomplete or inconsistently reported [8]. In the resource-limited prehospital setting, it is often not feasible to reliably identify or exclude these causes, potentially impacting OHCA outcomes compared to IHCA. 

In recent decades, critical care capabilities have expanded into the prehospital setting worldwide [8]. This includes the use of mechanical cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) devices [9], point-of-care (PoC) diagnostics [10], and extracorporeal CPR (eCPR) [11]. Across Australia, UK and New Zealand, some EMS have incorporated advanced diagnostics and highly trained personnel into OHCA management, potentially contributing to regional differences in outcomes [12]. 

 
Identifying the underlying cause of OHCA is crucial. While literature suggests that approximately 60% of OHCAs are presumed to be of cardiac origin [7], there is limited data detailing the remaining 40% of cases. Timely identification and treatment of the underlying cause is critical to achieving meaningful outcomes and may be a key factor in the lack of progress in OHCA survival rates [13]. 


To date, no study has evaluated prehospital clinicians’ confidence in identifying the underlying cause of OHCA. This cross-sectional survey aims to describe the current landscape of OHCA management across EMS in Australia, UK and New Zealand, including team composition, clinician experience, use of critical care resources and diagnostic adjuncts, clinician confidence in identifying arrest aetiology, and perceived barriers to improving OHCA outcomes. 

Background and literature review . 

 

Change in Use of Equipment for OHCA 

Outcomes for Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest (OHCA) have stagnated at a low survival rate of approximately 13% over the last three decades [1]. While treatment algorithms for OHCA have not undergone major changes, there have been significant advancements in the use of technology and clinical expertise, which have the potential to improve these outcomes. 

Key advancements include: 

Mechanical Compression Devices: These devices, introduced in the early 2000s, have enabled prolonged and effective resuscitation, especially in cases where manual compressions may be inadequate or difficult to sustain [14]. 

Specialized Ventilators: Newer ventilators designed specifically for use during cardiac arrest have improved the management of respiratory support during resuscitation efforts [15]. 

Point-of-Care Diagnostics: The improvement in diagnostic technology, particularly portable devices, allows for immediate clinical decision-making and better-targeted interventions in the prehospital setting [16]. 

Critical Care Clinicians: The integration of specialized paramedics and physicians into emergency medical services has shown promise in improving patient outcomes. Evidence suggests that these critical care teams may have a positive impact on OHCA survival rates [17]. 

Despite these advancements, there remains a significant gap in the literature regarding the composition of cardiac arrest teams in various countries, as well as the use of different adjuncts and technologies during resuscitation. Understanding the global variation in OHCA management is essential for identifying best practices. 

 

Confidence in Ruling In/Out the 4Hs and 4Ts 

The International Liaison Committee on Resuscitation (ILCOR) recommends that clinicians consider the “4Hs and 4Ts” as reversible causes of cardiac arrest. These include: 

4Hs: Hypoxia, Hypovolemia, Hypo/ Hyperkalemia, Hypothermia 

4Ts: Tension Pneumothorax, Tamponade, Toxins, Thrombo-embolism 

ILCOR also suggests that the treatment algorithm should be adapted based on the underlying reversible cause. However, diagnosing these causes in the prehospital environment, often with minimal information and without detailed medical histories, remains a challenge. 

While this issue has not been directly studied, some indirect evidence suggests that physical examination alone is insufficient for diagnosing the underlying cause in critically ill patients [18]. Most current OHCA registries record the presumed cause of death by clinicians rather than post-mortem confirmation [6], which means that clinicians' confidence in ruling in or out these causes is not well documented. 

 

The Role of Prehospital Clinicians' Perspectives 

While there is considerable literature focusing on improving OHCA outcomes from the perspectives of academics, resuscitation societies, and hospital clinicians, less attention has been paid to the perspectives of prehospital clinicians [19]. This is an important gap in understanding, as the barriers faced by paramedics, emergency medical technicians (EMTs), and critical care paramedics may differ significantly from those identified in hospital-based studies. 

Understanding the specific challenges faced by prehospital clinicians, such as time constraints, limited diagnostic tools, and the lack of definitive diagnostic information in the field, could yield important insights into how to improve OHCA outcomes. Their perspectives may also uncover additional barriers not previously identified by hospital-based clinicians or resuscitation experts. 

 

Key Areas for Future Research 

This study is part of a bigger project looking into gaps in current management strategy of OHCA with aim to idenitify the gaps and then provide information to fuel future research in improving the outcomes of OHCA. 

Global Comparison of OHCA Resuscitation Teams: Investigating how different countries structure their OHCA resuscitation teams and utilize adjuncts like mechanical compression devices or specialized ventilators can provide valuable insights into optimizing resource allocation and clinical practice. 

Clinician Confidence in Diagnosing Reversible Causes: Research focused on prehospital clinicians' confidence in identifying the 4Hs and 4Ts could help refine training and improve diagnostic accuracy in the field. 

Prehospital Clinician Barriers to Improving OHCA Outcomes: Understanding the challenges faced by prehospital clinicians can inform future interventions, training programs, and policy changes to improve OHCA survival rates.

Aims 

To understand, the confidence of clinicians to diagnose the underlying cause of OHCA and barriers to improvement in its management. 

The current composition of teams responding to out of hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) in prehospital services across Australia, UK and New Zealand 

This study is part of a bigger project looking into gaps in current management strategy of OHCA with aim to identify the gaps and then provide information to fuel future research in improving the outcomes of OHCA. 

 Objectives 

The investigators will do a cross-sectional survey study of prehospital clinicians across the prehospital services in Australia, UK and New Zealand and assess the current composition of teams, use of adjuncts, standard operating procedure for managing OHCA of the service, confidence of clinicians in ruling in/out the 4Hs and 4Ts using a Likert scale and perceived barriers to improving OHCA management. 

Expected outcomes 

The study will inform the current practice for management of OHCA across prehospital services in Australia, UK and New Zealand. It will inform us about the confidence of clinician in ruling in/out the 4Hs and 4Ts and the perceived barriers in improving outcomes of OHCA

Rationale / justification 

This survey will inform us about the current management practices for OHCA, application of ILCOR guidelines and clinicians' confidence in the use of the guidelines. It will also inform us clinicians' perception about barrier to improvement in OHCA management.

We are aiming to have all the prehospital primary response sites involved in the study. This will be co-ordinated through Australasian Resuscitation Outcomes Consortium (AUS-ROC) for Australia and New Zealand and through National HEMS research and audit forum (NHRAF) and National Ambulance Service Research Steering Group for the UK. The survey will be distributed by the site champions through a survey links/ QR codes and posters containing both. Email links and QR codes will be sent though departmental emails and posters will attached at various places in their departments. The survey will also be advertised through social media.
