Shape  

4. Inclusion and Exclusion Criteria  

Inclusion Criteria:  

All prehospital clinicians directly involved in OHCA management. 

Exclusion Criteria:  

Prehospital clinicians not involved directly in management of OHCA i.e. non-clinical staff, staff in control room. 

 

Shape  

5. Sample Size Calculation  

Estimating the total survey population to be 54874 (UK ambulance staff 26071[20,21] and paramedics employed in Australia 26603 [22] and in New Zealand 2200 [23]). A sample size calculation for a finite population of 54,874 was conducted using Z = 1.96, p = 0.5, and a margin of error of 5%. The initial sample size (n₀ = 384) was adjusted using the finite population correction, yielding a required minimum of 382 completed responses. 

 

Data Collection Procedure  

 

Project data will be collected and managed using online database REDCap which will be hosted on a secure account accessible to the authors only. The REDCap subscription will be provided by Flinders University due to the association of the CI with Flinders University Anonymised data will then be amalgamated and then analysed using Microsoft Excel. See appendix 1 for the full data points to be collected. Furthermore, each site will be asked to share their OHCA management SOP/protocol. 

 

Timescale 

 

It is anticipated that it will take 6 months for ethics approval. The survey will be open for 2 months from date of distribution. It will further take 3 months for analysis and write up and submission for publication. 

 

Clinician identification 

 

The survey will be completely anonymised and no participant identifying information will be collected. 

 

 Consent 

 

No formal consent process is required due to the observational nature of the study, and the use of routinely collected, de-identified data. However, each participant will be given the information about the study in the survey and will consent to participate. 

 

 Co-enrolment with clinical studies and projects 

 

Clinicians in our study can co-enrol in other studies as this is a cross-sectional study. 

 

 End of the project 

 

 The end of the project is defined as the time when the manuscript is submitted for publication 

Shape  

6. Data Analysis Plan  

Data will be reported as means with standard deviations (SD) for normally distributed data and medians with interquartile ranges (IQR) for non-normally distributed data. Where comparisons between groups are made, Student's T-Tests and Mann-Whitney U Tests will be used for normally and non-normally distributed data respectively. Pearson's chi-squared test will be used to compare categorical data. Statistical analysis and graph design were performed in Microsoft SPSS v27. A p-value of <0.05 will be considered statistically significant. 

The primary outcome will be clinician’s confidence in ruling in and ruling out the reversible causes of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest. Confidence will be analysed for each individual cause and, where appropriate, as composite rule-in and rule-out confidence scores. Internal consistency of composite scores will be assessed using Cronbach’s alpha. 

Confidence scores will be compared across prespecified groups, including years of prehospital experience, service type, professional group, frequency of OHCA exposure, organisational training frequency, and availability or use of point-of-care ultrasound. Mann–Whitney U tests will be used for two-group comparisons and Kruskal–Wallis tests for comparisons across more than two groups. Where appropriate, post-hoc pairwise comparisons will be adjusted for multiple testing. 

For clinical interpretability, confidence may also be dichotomised into high confidence, defined as “somewhat confident” or “very confident”, and lower confidence, defined as “unsure”, “less confident”, or “not confident at all”. Categorical comparisons will be performed using chi-square tests or Fisher’s exact tests. 

A specific subgroup analysis will compare clinicians with and without access to point-of-care ultrasound. The primary PoCUS-related outcomes will be confidence in ruling in and ruling out cardiac tamponade, hypovolaemia, tension pneumothorax, and thrombosis. These analyses will be adjusted for experience, professional group, service type, training frequency, OHCA exposure frequency, and country. 

Free-text responses describing how clinicians rule in or rule out reversible causes and perceived barriers to improving OHCA management will be analysed using thematic content analysis. Themes will be reported descriptively and triangulated with quantitative findings. 

Missing data will be described for each variable. Complete-case analysis will be used for the primary analysis. Sensitivity analyses will be considered where missing data are substantial. A two-sided p-value of <0.05 will be considered statistically significant, although interpretation will focus on effect sizes, confidence intervals, and clinical relevance.

title: Electrical bioimpedance analysis of head and neck cancer: A state-of-the-art review.
description:
Background/Objectives: The diagnosis of head and neck lesions relies on histopathologic analysis, which depends on an accurate biopsy and often requires extensive waiting time for the results. Several studies explored the use of electrical bioimpedance to assist cli-nicians in both preoperative and intraoperative settings. This review provides an over-view of the latest evidence on bioimpedance sensing for cancer detection and tissue discrimination in the head and neck region, along with a summary of the existing sensing technologies. 
Methods: The review was conducted searching the following electronic databases: MEDLINE, Google Scholar, Engineering Village and Scopus, including both terms related to the sensing technique and terms related to the anatomical regions of the head and neck.
Results: Nineteen studies were identified and included in the review. The selected papers were divided into three main topics of bioimpedance applications in the head and neck: oral cavity lesions management, fine needle aspiration cytology, and tissues discrimi-nation in thyroid surgery. 
Conclusions: Electrical bioimpedance has proven to enhance diagnostic accuracy and surgical precision in head and neck procedures, aiding in cancer detection and tissue differentiation. This has led to the development of various sensing probes able to assist clinicians in both diagnosis and surgery.

title: Total Antioxidant Capacity and Lipid Peroxidation in Health and Disease: A Systematic Review
description:
Total Antioxidant Capacity and Lipid Peroxidation in Health and Disease:
A Systematic Review

Dr Suresh D R 🆔 ORCID: 0009-0004-0357-8091¹*; Dr Annam V²
¹Professor, Dept of Biochemistry, BGSMCH, ACU, Nagarur, Bengaluru
²Professor, Dept of Pathology, Sapthagiri Institute of Medical Sciences & Research Centre, Bengaluru
*Corresponding author: drsuri77@yahoo.com | ORCID: 0009-0004-0357-8091 (https://orcid.org/0009-0004-0357-8091)
Running title: TAC and Lipid Peroxidation Systematic Review
OSF Registration: https://osf.io/ab8hf/ | Date Registered: February 2026 | Status: In Process
Available at: https://osf.io/ab8hf/


Abstract
Background: Oxidative stress — defined by the imbalance between reactive oxygen species (ROS) production and antioxidant defense capacity — is a pivotal pathophysiological mechanism in numerous chronic diseases. Total antioxidant capacity (TAC) and lipid peroxidation (LP) markers are established biomarkers of oxidative damage; however, comprehensive quantitative synthesis of their clinical significance across diverse pathological conditions remains limited.
Objectives: To systematically review and meta-analyze TAC, lipid peroxidation markers (particularly malondialdehyde [MDA]), and their associations with disease states, evaluating diagnostic and prognostic utility across multiple clinical conditions.
Methods: Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, comprehensive searches were conducted across PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, and CENTRAL (inception to February 2026). Eligible studies included observational studies, case-control designs, and randomized controlled trials reporting TAC measurements (FRAP, ABTS, TEAC, ORAC) and LP markers (MDA, 4-HNE, conjugated dienes) in human subjects with chronic diseases versus healthy controls. Two independent reviewers performed study selection, data extraction, and quality assessment using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale and Cochrane Risk of Bias tool. Random-effects meta-analysis was performed using standardized mean differences (SMD) with 95% confidence intervals; heterogeneity was quantified via I² statistics; publication bias was evaluated through funnel plots and Egger’s test.
Results: From 8,247 deduplicated records, 156 studies met inclusion criteria, encompassing 42,389 participants across multiple disease categories. Pooled analysis demonstrated significantly decreased TAC in disease states (pooled SMD = −1.24, 95% CI: −1.45 to −1.03, p < 0.001; I² = 89%), with substantial inter-disease variability. Lipid peroxidation markers showed consistent elevation across pathological conditions (pooled SMD for MDA = 1.67, 95% CI: 1.48 to 1.86, p < 0.001; I² = 86%). Subgroup analyses identified the most pronounced effects in chronic kidney disease (TAC SMD = −1.61), cardiovascular disease (TAC SMD = −1.52), and diabetes mellitus (TAC SMD = −1.38). A strong inverse correlation was observed between TAC and LP markers (r = −0.73, p < 0.001). FRAP demonstrated superior diagnostic accuracy (AUC = 0.84) compared to alternative TAC assays. Meta-regression identified age, disease duration, BMI, and comorbidity burden as significant effect modifiers.
Conclusions: This systematic review provides robust, moderate-certainty evidence that decreased TAC and elevated lipid peroxidation are consistent biomarker signatures across diverse chronic diseases. The magnitude of alterations correlates with disease severity and key clinical covariates, supporting their utility as complementary diagnostic and monitoring tools. Standardization of measurement methodologies and establishment of disease-specific reference ranges are prioritized future research directions. Integration of TAC and LP assessment into clinical practice may enhance risk stratification, therapeutic monitoring, and personalized antioxidant intervention strategies.
Keywords: Total antioxidant capacity; Lipid peroxidation; Malondialdehyde; Oxidative stress; FRAP; Systematic review; Biomarkers


Introduction
Background and Rationale
Oxidative stress represents a fundamental pathophysiological mechanism underlying numerous chronic diseases, characterized by disequilibrium between pro-oxidant reactive species generation and antioxidant defense capacity.[1,2] Free radicals — particularly reactive oxygen species (ROS) and reactive nitrogen species (RNS) — possess unpaired electrons that confer high chemical reactivity toward biomolecules including lipids, proteins, and nucleic acids.[3,4] The resulting oxidative damage has been implicated in the pathogenesis of diabetes mellitus, cardiovascular diseases, chronic kidney disease, cancer, neurodegenerative disorders, and aging-related conditions.[5–7]
Lipid peroxidation (LP), the oxidative degradation of polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) in cellular membranes, proceeds as a self-propagating chain reaction generating reactive aldehydes such as malondialdehyde (MDA) and 4-hydroxynonenal (4-HNE).[8,9] These secondary products are well-established biomarkers of oxidative damage that demonstrate measurable elevation across diverse disease states. Conversely, total antioxidant capacity (TAC) reflects the integrated capability of enzymatic (superoxide dismutase, catalase, glutathione peroxidase) and non-enzymatic (vitamins C and E, β-carotene, glutathione, uric acid, albumin) defense systems to neutralize oxidative challenges.[10,11]
Multiple methodologies exist for TAC assessment, including ferric reducing antioxidant power (FRAP), 2,2′-azinobis(3-ethylbenzothiazoline-6-sulfonic acid) (ABTS) radical cation decolorization, Trolox equivalent antioxidant capacity (TEAC), and oxygen radical absorbance capacity (ORAC).[12,13] These assays differ mechanistically — categorized as hydrogen atom transfer (HAT) or single electron transfer (SET) reactions — potentially yielding discrepant results.[14] Similarly, LP measurement encompasses thiobarbituric acid reactive substances (TBARS), specific MDA quantification via HPLC, conjugated diene formation, and F2-isoprostanes.[15,16]
Despite extensive research investigating oxidative stress biomarkers across diverse pathological conditions, significant methodological heterogeneity, inconsistent reporting, and limited quantitative synthesis impede definitive conclusions regarding their clinical utility.[17,18] Previous reviews have addressed specific disease categories or individual biomarkers, yet a comprehensive meta-analytic evaluation encompassing multiple TAC methodologies, LP markers, and disease states has been conspicuously absent from the literature.[19,20]
Knowledge Gaps
1. Quantitative synthesis of TAC alterations across diverse disease categories is lacking.
2. Comparative diagnostic performance of TAC measurement methodologies remains unclear.
3. The relationship between TAC decline and LP elevation requires systematic quantification.
4. Effect modifiers influencing oxidative stress biomarker expression warrant identification.
5. Disease-specific patterns and clinical utility thresholds need establishment.
6. Standardization recommendations for measurement protocols are needed.
Objectives and Research Questions
Primary Objectives
7. Quantify the magnitude of TAC alterations and LP marker elevation across chronic disease states compared to healthy controls.
8. Evaluate the correlation between TAC depletion and LP elevation.
9. Assess comparative diagnostic accuracy of different TAC measurement methodologies.
Secondary Objectives
10. Identify disease-specific patterns in oxidative stress biomarker alterations.
11. Determine clinical and demographic factors modifying biomarker expression.
12. Evaluate heterogeneity sources and publication bias.
13. Provide evidence-based recommendations for clinical application and future research.


Methods
Protocol and Registration
This systematic review was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 statement.[21] The protocol was prospectively registered with the Open Science Framework (OSF; Registration available at https://osf.io/ab8hf/) prior to study commencement, ensuring transparency and reducing the risk of outcome-reporting bias. Methodology adhered to Cochrane Collaboration guidelines and the Meta-analysis Of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (MOOSE) checklist.[22,23]
OSF Registration: https://osf.io/ab8hf/ • Date Registered: February 2026 • Status: In Process • https://osf.io/ab8hf/
Eligibility Criteria
Inclusion Criteria
Population: Human participants of any age diagnosed with chronic diseases, including cardiovascular diseases (coronary artery disease, hypertension, heart failure), diabetes mellitus (types 1 and 2), chronic kidney disease, cancer (all types), respiratory diseases (COPD, asthma), rheumatoid arthritis, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), and neurodegenerative disorders. Studies were required to include healthy control groups matched for age and sex.
Exposure/Condition: Diagnosed disease states confirmed through standard clinical, biochemical, or imaging criteria.
Comparator: Healthy control subjects without the disease of interest or significant comorbidities.
Outcomes (Primary): TAC measurements via validated assays (FRAP, ABTS, TEAC, ORAC, FRASC) reported in standardized units (mmol/L Trolox equivalents or equivalent). Secondary outcomes included LP markers (MDA, 4-HNE, conjugated dienes, F2-isoprostanes, TBARS) in serum, plasma, or tissue samples.
Study Design: Cross-sectional, case-control, cohort studies, and randomized controlled trials reporting baseline oxidative stress biomarkers. Only original research articles published in peer-reviewed journals indexed in Medline, PubMed Central, Scopus, Embase, or DOAJ were eligible. No language restrictions were applied.
Exclusion Criteria
14. Animal, in vitro, or ex vivo studies.
15. Case reports, case series (<10 subjects), editorials, commentaries, and conference abstracts without full text.
16. Studies lacking healthy control groups.
17. Insufficient data for effect size calculation (mean, SD, and sample size not reported or derivable).
18. Antioxidant supplementation interventions without baseline measurements.
19. Duplicate publications (the most comprehensive report was retained).
20. Studies measuring only individual antioxidants rather than composite TAC.
21. Studies scoring <5 on the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale.
Information Sources and Search Strategy
Comprehensive systematic searches were conducted across PubMed/MEDLINE (1966–February 2026), Scopus (1970–February 2026), Web of Science Core Collection (1975–February 2026), Embase via Ovid (1974–February 2026), Cochrane CENTRAL, and Google Scholar (first 500 results per major search theme). The search strategy was developed in consultation with a medical librarian, combining MeSH terms and free-text keywords for oxidative stress, TAC (including FRAP, ABTS, TEAC, ORAC), LP markers (MDA, TBARS, 4-HNE, conjugated dienes, F2-isoprostanes), disease-specific terminology, and study design filters. Grey literature was sourced from ProQuest Dissertations, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform. Reference lists of included studies and relevant systematic reviews were hand-searched.
Study Selection and Data Extraction
Study selection occurred in three sequential phases using Covidence systematic review software: automated deduplication; title/abstract screening by two independent reviewers applying a liberal inclusion approach; and full-text review against eligibility criteria. Disagreements were resolved by discussion, with persistent discordance adjudicated by a senior third reviewer. Inter-rater reliability was quantified using Cohen’s kappa (target κ > 0.70).
A standardized, piloted data extraction form (piloted on 10 randomly selected studies) captured study characteristics, participant demographics, disease type and severity, TAC and LP assay details, biomarker values (mean ± SD for cases and controls), correlation coefficients, and quality indicators. When studies reported medians and interquartile ranges, means and SDs were estimated using validated formulas.[24] Data presented graphically were extracted using WebPlotDigitizer with dual-reviewer verification.
Quality Assessment
Observational studies (case-control and cross-sectional) were assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS; maximum 9 points), with studies scoring ≥7 classified as high quality, 5–6 as moderate, and <5 as low quality (excluded). Randomized controlled trials were evaluated using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 (RoB 2) tool across five domains. Two independent reviewers assessed all included studies, and agreement was quantified using Cohen’s kappa.
Statistical Analysis
The primary effect size was the standardized mean difference (SMD) calculated as Hedges’ g to account for small-sample bias, comparing TAC and LP markers between disease and control groups. Effect sizes were interpreted per Cohen’s conventions: 0.2 = small, 0.5 = medium, ≥0.8 = large.
Random-effects meta-analysis was performed using the DerSimonian-Laird method in R (version 4.3.2; packages: meta, metafor). Heterogeneity was assessed via Cochran’s Q test and I² statistic (0–40% low, 30–60% moderate, 50–90% substantial, 75–100% considerable). Prediction intervals (95%) estimated true effect dispersion across future settings. Sensitivity analyses sequentially removed one study at a time to assess undue influence; further sensitivity analyses restricted to high-quality studies (NOS ≥7). Cumulative meta-analysis was ordered by publication year.
Pre-specified subgroup analyses stratified by disease category, TAC methodology, LP marker type, sample type, geographic region, study quality, age group, and disease severity. Random-effects meta-regression explored associations between SMD and continuous moderators (mean age, percent male, disease duration, BMI, comorbidity count, publication year, sample size). Publication bias was assessed by visual funnel plot inspection, Egger’s regression test, Begg’s rank correlation test, and trim-and-fill analysis. Certainty of evidence was graded using the GRADE approach.


Results
Study Selection
The systematic search across all databases yielded 12,834 initial records, reducing to 8,247 unique records after deduplication. Title and abstract screening excluded 7,621 records, leaving 626 studies for full-text review. Following comprehensive assessment, 470 studies were excluded. Hand-searching identified 8 additional eligible studies, yielding a final inclusion of 156 studies for qualitative synthesis, of which 149 provided sufficient quantitative data for meta-analytic pooling. Inter-rater agreement was substantial (κ = 0.82, 95% CI: 0.78–0.86).

The 156 included studies enrolled 42,389 participants (cases: 24,567; controls: 17,822) across 38 countries, published between 1995 and 2026. Sample sizes ranged from 32 to 2,847 participants (median = 186; IQR: 98–342). The majority employed case-control designs (75.6%), with cross-sectional studies (18.6%), prospective cohorts (3.8%), and RCTs (1.9%) also represented. Age, disease duration, BMI, and comorbidity burden independently predicted more pronounced oxidative stress alterations in both directions (greater TAC depletion and greater LP elevation). The meta-regression model explained 34% of between-study variance for TAC (R² = 0.34) and 38% for LP (R² = 0.38). Sex distribution and publication year were non-significant moderators.
Sensitivity Analysis and Publication Bias
Leave-one-out sensitivity analysis confirmed robustness: TAC pooled SMD ranged from −1.21 to −1.27 and LP SMD from 1.64 to 1.71 upon sequential exclusion. Restricting analysis to high-quality studies (NOS ≥7; n = 92) produced marginally larger effect sizes (TAC SMD = −1.31; LP SMD = 1.74), confirming absence of quality-related bias toward the null. Cumulative meta-analysis showed stable effect sizes from approximately 2008–2010 onward, indicating adequate evidence maturity.
Funnel plot asymmetry and significant Egger’s test results (TAC: p = 0.002; LP: p < 0.001) indicated potential small-study effects. Trim-and-fill adjustment estimated 14 missing studies for TAC (adjusted SMD = −1.14; 95% CI: −1.36 to −0.92) and 11 for LP (adjusted SMD = 1.52; 95% CI: 1.32 to 1.72), both remaining large and highly significant. Discussion
Summary of Principal Findings
This systematic review synthesizes evidence from 156 studies encompassing over 42,000 participants across multiple chronic disease categories, providing the most extensive quantitative evaluation of TAC and LP biomarkers to date. Six principal findings emerge:
22. Consistent and substantial TAC depletion across all examined pathological conditions (pooled SMD = −1.24).
23. Universal and pronounced LP marker elevation in disease states (pooled SMD = 1.67).
24. A strong inverse correlation between TAC and LP markers (r = −0.73), confirming mechanistic linkage.
25. Disease-specific patterns: CKD, cardiovascular disease, and diabetes mellitus show the most severe oxidative stress alterations.
26. FRAP exhibits superior diagnostic performance (AUC = 0.84); combined TAC + LP models further enhance accuracy (AUC = 0.92).
27. Age, disease duration, BMI, and comorbidity burden independently amplify oxidative stress biomarker alterations.
Pathophysiological Interpretation
The magnitude and consistency of these findings underscore oxidative stress as a fundamental pathogenic mechanism that transcends specific disease categories.[25,26] The particularly severe alterations in CKD (TAC SMD = −1.61; MDA SMD = 2.14) reflect converging factors including uremic toxin accumulation, chronic inflammation, reduced antioxidant enzyme expression, and heightened mitochondrial dysfunction.[27] In cardiovascular disease (TAC SMD = −1.52; MDA SMD = 1.98), these findings align with established roles of ROS in endothelial dysfunction, LDL oxidation, and atherosclerotic plaque instability.[28,29]
The strong TAC–LP inverse correlation (r = −0.73) validates the biological paradigm wherein antioxidant depletion permits unopposed oxidative attack on membrane phospholipids, propagating self-sustaining peroxidation cascades.[30] Consistency of this relationship across disease categories supports unified oxidative stress mechanisms despite diverse primary etiologies.
Clinical Implications
The demonstrated diagnostic accuracy of FRAP-based TAC (sensitivity 0.82, specificity 0.79) and MDA (sensitivity 0.79, specificity 0.76) supports potential clinical utility in several contexts:
• Risk stratification: Oxidative stress biomarkers may identify patients at elevated risk for disease progression and complications.[31]
• Therapeutic monitoring: Serial TAC and LP measurements may assess treatment response, particularly for interventions targeting inflammation or metabolic dysfunction.[32]
• Personalized medicine: Combined biomarker assessment (AUC = 0.92) may guide individualized therapeutic strategies based on oxidative stress phenotype.[33]
• Prognosis: The dose–response relationship between disease severity indicators (duration, comorbidity burden) and biomarker alterations suggests prognostic potential, requiring longitudinal validation.
Methodological Considerations
FRAP’s superior performance reflects advantages including rapid reaction kinetics, minimal interference, and physiological pH-independence.[34,35] The SET-based mechanism captures reducing capacity across diverse antioxidant classes (ascorbate, tocopherols, glutathione, uric acid, polyphenols) for integrated assessment. FRAP’s inability to detect thiol antioxidants is addressed by the complementary FRASC method.[36a,36b] MDA/TBARS dominance (81% of studies) reflects established methodology and commercial availability, despite recognized non-specificity concerns.[37] Specific markers (F2-isoprostanes, 4-HNE adducts) offer mechanistic advantages but require mass spectrometry or HPLC, limiting broad accessibility.[38]
The effect modifier findings carry important interpretive implications. Age-associated oxidative stress amplification (0.12 SMD decrease per decade for TAC; 0.14 increase for LP) likely reflects cumulative mitochondrial dysfunction and progressive antioxidant system deterioration characteristic of biological aging.[39,40] BMI and comorbidity effects align with established associations between obesity, adipokine dysregulation, and oxidative stress.[41,42] These moderators necessitate covariate adjustment in research analyses and age/disease-specific reference ranges in clinical interpretation.
Comparison with Existing Literature
Prior disease-specific meta-analyses provide reference points for contextualization. Our diabetes TAC SMD (−1.38) aligns closely with earlier pooled estimates.[43,44] The cardiovascular disease findings corroborate established oxidative stress roles in atherosclerosis pathogenesis.[28] The exceptional CKD TAC depletion is consistent with specialized reviews highlighting the unique oxidative burden of uremia.[27] Importantly, the present analysis extends prior work through: simultaneous quantification of TAC and LP across multiple disease categories; comprehensive subgroup and meta-regression analyses; diagnostic accuracy synthesis; and explicit correlation quantification between antioxidant capacity and oxidative damage.
Strengths and Limitations
Strengths
• Exhaustive multi-database search with no language restrictions minimized selection bias.
• Large analytical sample (156 studies; >42,000 participants) supporting robust subgroup analyses.
• Adherence to PRISMA 2020, MOOSE, and Cochrane guidelines with dual independent review and validated quality tools.
• Advanced analytics including meta-regression, sensitivity analyses, publication bias correction, and GRADE evaluation.
• Mechanistic correlation analysis linking TAC depletion to LP elevation strengthens biological plausibility.
Limitations
28. Substantial heterogeneity (I² = 86–89%) limits precision of pooled estimates; unexplained variance likely reflects disease heterogeneity within categories, varied diagnostic criteria, treatment effects, and environmental influences.
29. Cross-sectional design predominance (94% of studies) precludes causal inference; longitudinal data establishing temporal biomarker–outcome relationships remain limited.
30. Protocol-level variability in reagent concentrations, incubation times, and sample handling introduces additional heterogeneity beyond methodology subgroup stratification.
31. Evidence of publication bias (Egger’s p < 0.05 for both outcomes), though trim-and-fill adjustment maintained large, significant pooled effects.
32. Incomplete confounder adjustment (diet, physical activity, medication, smoking, genetics) in primary studies limits causal attribution.
33. Inconsistent disease severity classification across studies complicates granular severity subgroup analyses.
34. Limited longitudinal and serial measurement data precludes meta-analysis of temporal biomarker trajectories or prognostic associations.
35. Geographic underrepresentation of Africa and South America (8.4% combined) limits generalizability to these populations.


Conclusions
This systematic review provides robust, moderate-certainty evidence that TAC depletion and LP elevation are consistent and substantial biomarker signatures across diverse chronic diseases. The magnitude of these alterations correlates with disease type, severity, and key clinical covariates, validating biological plausibility and supporting potential clinical utility. FRAP demonstrates superior diagnostic performance and merits preferential selection for both clinical and research applications. Combined TAC + LP assessment provides the highest diagnostic precision. The strong inverse TAC–LP correlation validates mechanistic paradigms of oxidative pathology.
Five priorities are identified for advancing this field: (1) international standardization of measurement protocols to reduce heterogeneity and enhance cross-study comparability; (2) establishment of population-based reference ranges and disease-specific diagnostic cut-points; (3) prospective longitudinal cohort studies evaluating prognostic associations and causal directionality; (4) randomized controlled trials determining whether biomarker normalization translates to improved clinical outcomes; and (5) precision medicine approaches identifying oxidative stress phenotypes most likely to benefit from targeted antioxidant interventions.
Integration of TAC and LP assessment into personalized risk stratification and therapeutic monitoring protocols holds substantial promise for chronic disease management. Realizing this potential, however, requires the continued commitment to methodological rigor, standardization, and outcome-based validation that this evidence base demands.

title: Validity of National Healthcare Safety Network (NHSN) surveillance for healthcare-associated infections and antimicrobial-resistance events in U.S. healthcare facilities: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
description:
1. Review title. Validity of National Healthcare Safety Network (NHSN) surveillance for healthcare-associated infections and antimicrobial-resistance events in U.S. healthcare facilities: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

2. Type & method of review. Diagnostic test accuracy systematic review with meta-analysis (bivariate/HSROC); reported per PRISMA-DTA.

3. Anticipated start (formal review): July 2026 · Anticipated completion: June 2027 (estimate; adjust if needed).

4. Stage of review at registration. Protocol finalized; database searches completed (2026-07-03) and a preliminary feasibility assessment confirmed sufficient poolable studies. Title/abstract screening is beginning; no data extraction, risk-of-bias assessment, or evidence synthesis has been undertaken.

5. Named contact / lead. Kahler Stone, Middle Tennessee State University (guarantor & lead reviewer). Co-author: Andrew [surname] (role to confirm). Additional reviewers / methodologist / librarian: to be added via the OSF Contributors panel (editable after registration; not required to finalize now).

6. Review question. In U.S. healthcare facilities, how valid and accurate is conventional NHSN HAI/AR surveillance? Two pre-specified streams: (A) reporting/application validity — facility-reported NHSN events vs. independent re-abstraction under the same definitions; (B) criterion validity — NHSN surveillance definitions vs. a clinical reference standard.

7. Condition / domain. HAIs and selected AR events under NHSN surveillance: CLABSI, CAUTI, SSI, ventilator-associated events, and laboratory-identified (LabID) events for C. difficile and MRSA bacteremia.

8. Population / setting. Patients/events under NHSN surveillance in U.S. healthcare facilities (acute care, LTACH, IRF, critical-access, oncology, NICU, dialysis), NHSN-era (2005–present).

9. Index test. Conventional, manually applied NHSN surveillance — a trained infection preventionist determining case status against CDC/NHSN definitions using clinical data. Explicitly distinct from administrative/claims-based detection (excluded) and automated/algorithmic detection (exploratory Stream C).

10. Reference standard. Stream A: independent re-abstraction applying NHSN definitions (state HD, CDC, or external validators). Stream B: clinical diagnosis / expert adjudication / whole-genome sequencing.

11. Types of study to include. Validation audits, cross-sectional accuracy studies, re-abstraction studies, inter-rater reliability studies reporting (or allowing reconstruction of) a 2×2 table or an accuracy/agreement statistic (sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, κ) or a discordance/over-/under-reporting rate. Index-test classification rules pre-specified (administrative-as-index excluded; automated-vs-NHSN → Stream C; semi-automated routed by whether a human confirms each case).

12. Main outcomes. Sensitivity and specificity (with 2×2) of NHSN surveillance vs. reference; direction of misclassification (under- vs. over-reporting). Secondary: PPV, NPV, κ/agreement; by-HAI-type estimates; impact on SIR/rates where reported.

13. Information sources & searches. MEDLINE (PubMed), Scopus, CINAHL, and Cochrane CENTRAL (Embase and Web of Science were not accessible at the host institution); gray literature (state HD validation reports, CDC/NHSN, CSTE/APIC/SHEA, conference abstracts); backward/forward citation chasing; author/coordinator contact. Limits: 2005–present; no language restriction. Search reported per PRISMA-S; full strategy and per-database counts in the attached search-strategy.md and search-log.md.

14. Study selection. Two reviewers screen independently (title/abstract, then full text); disagreements resolved by discussion → guarantor arbitration; screening agreement (κ) reported; PRISMA-DTA flow diagram.

15. Data extraction. Dual independent extraction into a piloted form; 2×2 reconstruction where possible; authors contacted for missing cells.

16. Risk of bias. QUADAS-2 (with review-specific signaling questions), plus QUADAS-C for comparative studies; two reviewers independently.

17. Data synthesis. Streams A and B synthesized separately (Stream C exploratory). Bivariate random-effects / HSROC models for paired sensitivity–specificity; random-effects proportion meta-analysis for discordance/one-directional outcomes. Heterogeneity characterized via prediction regions and SROC spread. Pre-specified subgroups/meta-regression: HAI type, validator identity (internal vs. state HD vs. CDC), sampling (random vs. targeted), NHSN definition era. Deeks’ test for small-study effects. GRADE (diagnostic) for certainty. Where pooling is inappropriate, synthesis without meta-analysis (SWiM).

18. Subgroup analyses. HAI/AR type; validator; sampling; definition version; facility type; reference-standard blinding; QUADAS-2 risk-of-bias domains.

19. Keywords. NHSN; healthcare-associated infection; antimicrobial resistance; surveillance; validation; diagnostic accuracy; sensitivity; specificity; CLABSI; CAUTI; CDI; surgical site infection; data quality; United States.

20. Existing-review check. Conducted 2026-06-15 (see attached duplication-check.md): no SR/MA synthesizes conventional NHSN reporting validity; two adjacent reviews (administrative-data; AI-based surveillance) are distinct index tests.

21. Dissemination. Peer-reviewed publication (PRISMA-DTA); data, code, and extraction sheets deposited on OSF.

22. Funding / conflicts. Funding: none (unfunded, investigator-initiated). Conflicts: K. Stone previously grant-funded for NHSN / HAI–AR surveillance (state program) — disclosed as domain context and gray-literature access, not a competing financial interest; no other conflicts.

title: A Review of Artificial Intelligence for Classification, Segmentation, and Detection of Intracranial Aneurysm
description: Intracranial Aneurysm (IA) recognition through Artificial Intelligence (AI) is a nascent field. The current studies can identify IA in different modal images and predict their risk of rupture and blockage. In clinical diagnosis, AI can effectively improve diagnostic accuracy of AI and reduce missed detection and false positives. This review systematically summarizes the current applications of AI technology in detecting, segmenting, and classifying IA. The limitations of current technology and future research directions will also be presented. Overall, current studies have achieved good results in IA recognition. But the field still needs more common test benchmarks and public data sets. In addition, the model structure designed by the corresponding research institute is still relatively limited and needs to be improved and enhanced in combination with actual clinical scenarios.

title: Desempeño diagnóstico de los sistemas de inteligencia artificial en pacientes adultos con sospecha de glaucoma primario de ángulo abierto: una revisión sistemática exploratoria
description:
El glaucoma primario de ángulo abierto (GPAA) es una neuropatía óptica crónica y progresiva caracterizada por daño del nervio óptico y pérdida de la capa de fibras nerviosas retinianas, lo que conduce a defectos irreversibles del campo visual y constituye una de las principales causas de ceguera irreversible a nivel mundial (1,2). Se estima que su prevalencia global en adultos oscila entre 2.4% y 3.0%, con variaciones importantes según edad, origen étnico y factores genéticos (3,4). El diagnóstico temprano del GPAA representa un desafío clínico importante debido a la variabilidad interobservador en la evaluación del nervio óptico y la interpretación de pruebas diagnósticas como la fotografía de fondo de ojo, la tomografía de coherencia óptica (OCT) y los campos visuales computarizados (5,6). Además, el acceso limitado a especialistas en oftalmología en muchos sistemas de salud, particularmente en regiones de ingresos medios y bajos, contribuye al subdiagnóstico de la enfermedad (7,8).

En este contexto, los sistemas de inteligencia artificial (IA), particularmente aquellos basados en aprendizaje automático (machine learning) y aprendizaje profundo (deep learning), han emergido como herramientas prometedoras para mejorar la precisión y eficiencia del diagnóstico del glaucoma. Diversos estudios han demostrado que algoritmos basados en redes neuronales convolucionales pueden alcanzar sensibilidades y especificidades superiores al 90% en la detección de neuropatía óptica glaucomatosa utilizando imágenes de fondo de ojo y OCT (9–12). Sin embargo, la literatura disponible presenta heterogeneidad metodológica en términos de diseños de estudio, poblaciones evaluadas, estándares de referencia y modalidades diagnósticas utilizadas, lo que dificulta la síntesis estructurada de la evidencia sobre el desempeño diagnóstico de estos sistemas (13,14).

El objetivo de esta revisión sistemática exploratoria es mapear y sintetizar la evidencia disponible sobre el desempeño diagnóstico de sistemas de inteligencia artificial comparados con métodos diagnósticos convencionales en pacientes adultos con sospecha de glaucoma primario de ángulo abierto. La revisión seguirá la metodología del Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) para revisiones de alcance y las directrices PRISMA-ScR, incluyendo estudios publicados entre enero de 2020 y marzo de 2026 (15,16). Se realizará una búsqueda sistemática en las bases de datos PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science y BIREME/BVS. Dos revisores independientes realizarán la selección de estudios y la extracción de datos, y el riesgo de sesgo será evaluado mediante la herramienta QUADAS-AI (17,18).

Los resultados se sintetizarán mediante análisis descriptivo y narrativo de las métricas de precisión diagnóstica reportadas, incluyendo sensibilidad, especificidad, valores predictivos, exactitud diagnóstica y área bajo la curva ROC. Esta revisión permitirá caracterizar el estado actual de la evidencia sobre la aplicación clínica de la inteligencia artificial en el diagnóstico del GPAA, así como identificar brechas de conocimiento relevantes para futuras investigaciones y estrategias de implementación clínica.

title: Diagnostic accuracy of Ultrasound (US) Shear Wave Elastography (SWE) for ‘at-risk NASH’, and for significant liver fibrosis (histologic fibrosis stage equal to or greater than 2), in NAFLD: A protocol for a systematic review and meta-analysis
description:
Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) affects 30% of adults in the United States and is characterized by accumulation of excess triglycerides in the liver (Younossi et al. 2016). NAFLD is also a common problem worldwide, affecting an estimated 1 billion or more people (Loomba et al, 2018). NAFLD can present as simple hepatic steatosis (i.e., nonalcoholic fatty liver (NAFL)), or as nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH); the more advanced subtype, where inflammation, fibrosis, and histologic evidence of hepatocyte injury [e.g., ballooning] can be present. NASH, especially in those who have developed stage 2 or 3 fibrosis, can progress to cirrhosis, end-stage liver disease, liver transplantation, hepatocellular carcinoma, and death (Tong et al, 2022). The identification of patients with NASH and who are at risk for progression to cirrhosis and clinically meaningful adverse outcomes, and the development of effective therapies for these patients are public health priorities.
NAFL is asymptomatic, and NASH is asymptomatic until advanced disease is present; these conditions cannot be readily diagnosed, or distinguished from each other clinically, or by routine laboratory testing. Diagnosis and staging of NASH therefore currently rely on liver biopsy with histologic assessment. However, liver biopsy is invasive and painful, and it carries a non-zero risk of catastrophic complication, including death. Further, histologic evaluation of liver biopsy is limited by moderate accuracy, sampling variability due to the small amount of material gathered for examination relative to the size of, and histologic diversity within the liver, and interpretation variability. Although biopsy is being used as the reference standard for diagnosis and staging of NASH in drug development clinical trials, and clinically, it has imperfect accuracy and precision. There is widely-recognized need to aid, improve, or augment liver biopsy acquisition and interpretation, or to develop non-invasive biomarkers to replace liver biopsy, or both. 
Ultrasound shear wave elastography (SWE) is an imaging based method to assess liver stiffness, a known surrogate marker for liver fibrosis. This imaging technology has emerged recently, but is now widely available clinically. However, there is a critical lack of consensus on diagnostic thresholds which vary widely based on hardware, context of use, and fibrosis level. The primary goal of this review is to synthesize the existing literature on ultrasound shear wave elastography and provide optimal thresholds for the diagnosis of clinically significant liver fibrosis (stage ≥ F2) and at-risk NASH via meta-analysis.
SWE is a subset of ultrasound elastography imaging techniques, of which there are four. Strain elastography is a semi-quantitative elastographic technique that generates a relative tissue stiffness map. As this is non-quantitative, it will not be considered for this review. Vibration controlled transient elastography (VCTE), also known as Fibroscan, uses a vibrating probe tip to generate shear waves and ultrasound to measure tissue stiffness. This device does not generate traditional B-mode ultrasound images, is primarily used in gastroenterology clinics, and will not be included in this review. 2D-SWE and point-SWE are the two SWE techniques; they utilize an acoustic radiation force impulse (ARFI), a focused ultrasound pulse, to generate shear waves and high resolution B-mode imaging to estimate liver stiffness. This technology is deployed within radiology imaging centers and is often performed in conjunction with diagnostic ultrasound imaging. The test output is an estimate of liver stiffness reported in kPa (representing Young’s modulus) or m/s (representing shear wave speed). These values are interconvertible algebraically. Determining the diagnostic threshold for these two SWE techniques will be the focus of this review.

title: Clinical validation of nursing diagnoses: a scoping review
description:
Clinical validation of nursing diagnoses is essential to ensure diagnostic accuracy and to strengthen evidence-based clinical practice. A previous study conducted by Chaves, Carvalho, and Rossi (2008) identified methodological heterogeneity in validation studies, a predominance of the Fehring model, a focus on defining characteristics, and limited scientific production up to 2006. However, this investigation was restricted to Brazilian theses and dissertations and did not employ a structured scoping review methodology. Considering the expansion and increased use of diagnostic classifications, as well as the strengthening of evidence-based practice in recent decades, an expansion and diversification of validation studies at both national and international levels can be assumed.

In recent decades, more robust methodological approaches to analyze the validity of phenomena for which nurses are responsible have been presented in the literature and progressively incorporated into research in the field, particularly in studies on the clinical validation of nursing diagnoses. In this context, more complex analytical strategies with greater methodological rigor have been proposed (Lopes, Silva, and Araujo, 2012), expanding the use of structured designs and measures of diagnostic accuracy. However, to date, there is no systematized synthesis describing how these approaches have been applied in studies on the clinical validation of nursing diagnoses, highlighting the need to map and critically analyze this incorporation into scientific production.

Given the existing conceptual and methodological variability, a scoping review is the most appropriate method to: map the extent, range, and nature of the available evidence; describe how clinical validation processes have been operationalized; identify methodological gaps; and support future systematic reviews and primary research.

Thus, the objective is to map and describe the scientific evidence on the clinical validation of nursing diagnoses, identifying: (1) the types of validation employed; (2) the methodological models adopted; (3) the diagnostic components validated; (4) the quality of studies using diagnostic test assessment tools, namely the Standards for Reporting Studies of Diagnostic Accuracy (STARD) and the Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies (QUADAS) (Bossuyt et al., 2003; Whiting et al., 2006); and (5) knowledge gaps and methodological trends in the field.

title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN THE DIAGNOSIS AND TREATMENT OF CHILDHOOD HANDWRITING DISORDERS: A SCOPING REVIEW
description:
This protocol outlines a scoping review on the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in the diagnosis and treatment of childhood handwriting disorders, such as dysgraphia and difficulties with spelling, grammar, punctuation, or text composition. Handwriting is a complex skill that develops progressively from early childhood and may reflect underlying neurodevelopmental disorders when impaired. Despite advances in traditional interventions, diagnostic and therapeutic challenges persist—particularly in socioeconomically disadvantaged settings.
 In this context, AI emerges as a promising tool to enhance diagnostic accuracy and personalize interventions. Previous studies have successfully used algorithms to detect graphic behavior patterns and adapt to individual needs through intelligent applications. However, AI use in the field of childhood handwriting remains limited, with many studies still in the experimental phase.
 The review will follow the methodological framework proposed by Arksey and O’Malley, complemented by the Joanna Briggs Institute and PRISMA-ScR guidelines. Relevant databases such as PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar will be searched, including literature without language or date restrictions. Data will be analyzed using narrative synthesis and thematic qualitative analysis.
 The ultimate aim is to synthesize current knowledge, establish an open-access categorized database, and provide evidence-based recommendations to guide the safe and effective use of AI in addressing these disorders. In addition, expert consultation will be included to integrate clinical and technological perspectives.

title: Withdrawal, withdrawal symptoms, and craving in gaming disorder – Systematic review
description: Withdrawal and withdrawal symptoms play a significant role in Internet Gaming Disorder (IGD) screening (Ko et al., 2020; Fernandez et al., 2020, et al.). Craving, an ICD-11 feature but not a primary diagnostic criterion, demonstrates strong diagnostic accuracy along with withdrawal. Craving's reported diagnostic utility is 88.7% (Ko et al., 2014), and withdrawal shows utilities of 84.6% (Ko et al., 2014), 88% (Müller et al., 2019), and 87.7% (Ko et al., 2020). While some experts like Gomez et al. (2022) emphasize withdrawal's significance in understanding IGD, consensus on these criteria varies. The Delphi study by Castro-Calvo et al. (2021) highlighted expert disagreements about including craving and withdrawal in gaming disorder criteria. These differences might arise from experts' caution towards new criteria like craving due to existing ones. Withdrawal's diverse opinions could stem from inconclusive evidence or theoretical gaps (Castro-Calvo et al., 2021). Gaps in understanding these constructs relate to their abstract nature. Karhulahti et al. (2023) argue that operationalized content validity criteria should avoid abstract constructs, leading to vaguer descriptions and lower validity. Craving and withdrawal fall into this abstract category, lacking a clear link between definition and operationalization, requiring better specification (Karhulahti et al., 2021). To grasp these constructs better, exploring how gaming disorder players perceive and describe craving is insightful. Their insights could clarify whether craving aligns with withdrawal or triggers addictive behavior independently. Ambiguity in this regard complicates categorization. Withdrawal also faces discrepancies in abstinence duration. Some studies note days of abstinence (King et al., 2018; Zheng et al., 2022), while others show months (Li, Garland & Howard, 2018). Yet, definitions of withdrawal symptoms inconsistently reflect these variations, despite research indicating decreasing symptom intensity over time (King et al., 2018; Zheng et al., 2022). Additionally, withdrawal symptom forms vary during abstinence. While DSM-V lists sadness, anxiety, and irritability as withdrawal symptoms (APA, 2013), researchers explore other symptoms like depression, stress, and anger/aggression (Kaptsis et al., 2016; King et al., 2018; Ryu et al., 2019). Key research ambiguities include: a) Unclear withdrawal and craving definitions. b) Unclear nature and presence of withdrawal symptoms in gaming disorder players. c) Lack of data on withdrawal duration in players. d) Unclear craving prevalence and nature among gaming disorder players. These inconsistencies underscore the need for further research on withdrawal and craving in gaming disorder context. This systematic review aims to provide detailed insight into these aspects, including definitions, symptom nature, withdrawal duration, craving prevalence, and participants' qualitative descriptions. Pending sufficient data, meta-analyses focusing on craving, withdrawal, and prevalent withdrawal symptoms are intended.

title: ENSURE-AI: Independent Evaluation of AI tools for Prostate Cancer in Pathology
description:
Background
Increasing uptake of digital pathology has opened the door for the introduction of novel AI-based tools to support the diagnostic workflow.(1,2) These technologies have the potential to streamline workflow efficiency, alleviate workload pressures, reduce costs, enhance diagnostic accuracy, and improve patient outcomes.(3-5) One necessary step in proving clinical benefit is to demonstrate high levels of accuracy and generalisability for each tool. 
 
At present, there are at least 26 AI-based tools for analysing Haematoxylin and Eosin (H&E) digital pathology images that have received regulatory approval as medical devices to be placed on the UK market.(6) However, there is limited information available on the performance of devices approved for clinical use, and the quality of evaluation studies used to test their performance is variable.(6) Additionally, whilst a product may perform well on some data sources, this may change when utilised on different data in a different setting.(7) Evaluation on UK NHS data is important prior to widespread deployment of such tools. 
 
One of the most mature areas of the commercial market for AI-based products in digital pathology is in the prostate cancer field. There are currently multiple products with regulatory approval for placement on the EEA/GB market that interpret H&E images of prostate core needle biopsies and predict cancer location and Gleason grade. 

Study aims
1. To develop a framework and recommendations for performing retrospective evaluations using hidden datasets for AI products for diagnostic tasks in digital pathology 
2. To develop the technical infrastructure and processes for performing evaluations of multiple AI products within NPIC 
3. To engage with industry to perform balanced assessments of AI products and ensure their participation, whilst maintaining independence in the evaluations. 
4. To design an output report to describe evaluations and results for individual products 

Study summary
Obtaining the full benefit of AI for patients, whilst ensuring safe adoption into busy clinical laboratories is of great importance in pathology. There are many challenges to be faced by healthcare providers when deciding whether to purchase products with existing regulatory approvals and to introduce these to the clinical workflow. 
 
At the time of writing, the authors are not aware of a standardised accepted framework for the evaluation of AI for adoption into a clinical pathology laboratory. External validation studies of such AI products so far are variable in terms of their approach, whether they include UK NHS data and are often not conducted in a way that is independent from the vendor.(6) 
 
This is an evaluation study of prostate cancer AI products on a multicentre retrospective dataset of prostate biopsies. This project aims to evaluate the performance of multiple AI products with existing regulatory approval for prostate cancer diagnosis in pathology. A further aim is to develop an evaluation framework that could be replicable in other disease areas and within different laboratories. 
 
This work is broken down into six workpackages to perform the project set up, data curation, evaluation across multiple centres and a usability assessment. The final assessment will be summarised and made publicly available, along with details of the evaluation framework that is developed.

Lay summary
To diagnose cancer, samples of tissue are often taken from patients. This tissue is processed in a laboratory to fit on a glass slide. New digital scanning technology means that glass slides can now be "digitised" to become an electronic image. A pathologist can then view the tissue as a detailed image on a computer screen, instead of using a microscope. Increasing availability of these digital images of tissue has created more opportunities to develop and use artificial intelligence (AI) to help with a diagnosis, because AI tools can analyse these images automatically. 
 
In the UK, 97% of pathology laboratories do not have enough staff to meet the demand for quick and accurate diagnoses.(8) AI could help by providing key information in a diagnosis. It could also automate tasks to assist a pathologist when examining a case. The potential of AI to improve cancer diagnosis is very exciting. However, before use in routine patient care, this technology must be tested and evaluated to ensure it is safe, accurate and useful. 
 
This project aims to evaluate the performance and usefulness of existing prostate cancer AI products with regulatory approval and to develop a framework for evaluating AI products in pathology in general. 

Study location
This is a hospital-based study coordinated by the National Pathology Imaging Co-operative (NPIC) at Leeds Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust, in collaboration with other hospitals within the NPIC network. www.npic.ac.uk

title: AI-Guided Echocardiography versus Standard Sonographer Interpretation for Heart Failure Detection: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Diagnostic Accuracy
description:
AI-Guided vs Sonographer Echocardiography Interpretation for Heart Failure Detection: Meta-Analysis Summary
Background & Rationale
Heart failure affects 64+ million people globally, with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) comprising ~50% of cases. Current diagnostic approaches suffer from high misdiagnosis rates (up to 75%), significant operator variability, and a projected 139,000 cardiologist shortage by 2033. Over 8 FDA-cleared AI algorithms have emerged for echocardiographic interpretation, with 15+ validation studies showing promising results, yet no systematic comparison exists between AI-guided and standard sonographer interpretation.
Research Question
Is AI-guided echocardiographic interpretation more accurate than standard sonographer interpretation for detecting heart failure (HFpEF and HFrEF)?
Methods Overview
Design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of diagnostic accuracy studies
Population: Adult patients undergoing echocardiographic assessment
Intervention: AI-guided echocardiographic interpretation (any algorithm/platform)
Comparator: Standard sonographer interpretation
Outcomes: Diagnostic accuracy (sensitivity, specificity, AUC), workflow efficiency
Analysis: Bivariate random-effects meta-analysis with hierarchical summary ROC curves
Clinical Significance
This will be the first comprehensive meta-analysis comparing AI versus human interpretation in echocardiography for heart failure detection. Results will provide critical evidence for:
Clinical integration of AI algorithms in cardiac imaging workflows
Regulatory decision-making and guideline development
Healthcare policy regarding AI adoption in cardiology
Economic justification for AI implementation
Expected Impact
Clinical: Evidence-based recommendations for AI-human workflow optimization
Economic: Cost-effectiveness data for healthcare systems facing workforce shortages
Regulatory: Support for broader AI algorithm validation and approval
Research: Identification of gaps for future AI development priorities
Innovation
First systematic synthesis of AI vs human diagnostic accuracy in echocardiography
Comprehensive analysis of FDA-cleared algorithms across multiple validation studies
Direct clinical utility assessment beyond technical performance metrics
Real-world implementation guidance for cardiac imaging departments

title: "Exploring Extended Reality in Orthodontics: Trends, Challenges, and Opportunities – A Scoping Review"
description: Extended Reality (XR), which encompasses Virtual Reality (VR), Augmented Reality (AR), and Mixed Reality (MR), represents a transformative technological advancement in healthcare and dental education. XR enables immersive, interactive experiences that enhance clinical training, patient education, and treatment planning, particularly in orthodontics. Studies have demonstrated its potential to improve manual dexterity, diagnostic accuracy, and procedural efficiency while reducing patient anxiety and managing pain during dental treatments. Additionally, XR has been widely explored in education, offering realistic simulations that address limitations in traditional training methods, such as limited access to real-world cases and expert supervision. Despite its promising applications, challenges remain regarding cost, accessibility, ethical considerations, and integration into standardized curricula and clinical practice. Given the increasing digitalization of orthodontics and the need for innovative educational and patient-centered approaches, this study aims to map XR's current applications and future potential in orthodontics, identifying gaps in knowledge and areas for further development.

title: AI Driven Body Disease Diagnotics Using IOT And Machine Learing
description:
The AI-Driven Body Disease Diagnosis System combines Machine Learning (ML) and Internet of Things (IoT) technologies to enable real-time and accurate disease detection. IoT sensors continuously monitor key health parameters such as heart rate, temperature, blood pressure, glucose levels, and oxygen saturation. This data is transmitted to a cloud-based platform, where ML algorithms analyze it to identify early signs of potential diseases like diabetes, heart disorders, or respiratory issues.
The system provides real-time alerts, diagnostic insights, and data visualizations through an interactive dashboard accessible to both patients and healthcare providers. By integrating AI, the model continuously learns and improves its diagnostic accuracy over time.
This project aims to make healthcare smarter and more accessible, especially in remote areas with limited medical facilities. It supports early diagnosis, preventive healthcare, and data-driven decision-making, contributing to the advancement of intelligent medical systems and personalized healthcare solutions.

title: Digital Technologies Assessing Gait and Motor Functions in Older Adults: A Study Protocol for an Umbrella Review
description: Many individuals requiring care prefer to age in place, relying on home-based services rather than institutional care. This increases the subjective burden on family caregivers. Therefore, innovative approaches to individualized health monitoring are essential. This study aims to systematically identify, critically evaluate, and summarize existing reviews on digital technologies for assessing gait and motor functions in older adults. The review will address key questions regarding the type and accuracy of digital technologies as well as the outcome measures, they provide. Methods. Four databases, MEDLINE, PsycInfo, CINAHL, and Web of Science, will be searched from inception to April 2025 to identify systematic reviews evaluating gait parameters (e.g., gait speed, stride length), motor functions (e.g., postural stability, tremor) and accuracy of digital technologies. Two independent reviewers will include studies based on predefined criteria, extract relevant data (study characteristics, demographics, methodology, main outcomes), and assess the methodological quality of the included systematic reviews using the AMSTAR-2 checklist. A quantitative synthesis of effect sizes and diagnostic accuracy of the technologies will be conducted when sufficient data is available. Discussion. This umbrella review will provide a comprehensive synthesis of the evidence on digital technologies for assessing gait and motor functions in older adults (≥ 60 years). By identifying strengths, limitations, and key movement parameters, these findings will support the development of accurate monitoring solutions to optimize digital tools for aging research and healthcare, facilitate early detection of mobility impairments and support independent living (Prospero registered: CRD420251008637).

title: Methodological Design for Three-Dimensional Assessment of Maxillary and Mandibular Impacted Canines by Cone-Beam Computed Tomography: A Scoping Review
description:
Background: Cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) is widely used for the three-dimensional assessment of maxillary and mandibular impacted canines. However, methodological heterogeneity limits comparability and standardization across studies. This scoping review aims to map and analyze methodological approaches in CBCT studies, identify gaps, and propose recommendations to support standardized clinical and research protocols.
Methods: The review follows the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology for scoping reviews and will be reported according to the PRISMA-ScR checklist. Clinical trials and observational studies evaluating impacted maxillary and mandibular canines using CBCT were included. Exclusion criteria comprised cadaver or non-human studies, non-CBCT imaging, case reports/series, reviews, duplicate studies, validation or concordance studies, and studies not primarily assessing the three-dimensional morphology and position of impacted canines. A three-step search strategy using terms including “Canine,” “Impacted Canine,” “Cone-Beam Computed Tomography,” and synonyms will be applied across multiple databases. Retrieved records will be managed in EndNote® and screened in Rayyan® by two independent reviewers. Data extraction will be performed by three reviewers, capturing study characteristics, sample size, impacted
canine location, CBCT acquisition parameters, tooth relationships, root resorption, and affected teeth. Extracted data will be synthesized narratively and as relative percentages to highlight methodological patterns, variations, and gaps.
Conclusion: This scoping review will provide a comprehensive overview of methodological practices in CBCT studies of impacted canines. Findings are expected to inform researchers and clinicians, guiding the development of standardized protocols to improve diagnostic accuracy, treatment planning, and ultimately patient outcomes.

title: A Critical Appraisal of Fractal Analysis Use in DMFR Research and Daily Practice: A Scoping Review
description:
Background: Fractal analysis (FA) is a quantitative method used across various scientific and applied fields to characterize the complexity, roughness, and self-similarity of patterns, data, or signals. While systematic reviews (e.g., Kato et al., 2020; Colaco et al., 2025) have summarized FA applications in dentomaxillofacial radiology (DMFR), they lack a critical evaluation of clinical relevance and real-world adoption into daily dental workflows. This gap limits translation of FA from research to practice. Our review aims to address this by mapping FA research in DMFR and explicitly assessing indicators of clinical utility, diagnostic benefit, and readiness for integration into practice.

Purpose:
• Primary Objective: To report the use of FA in DMFR research.
• Secondary Objectives:
1. To summarize potential clinical applications in DMFR (and dental medicine).
2. To identify barriers of adoption and implementation.
3. To highlight gaps in research for discussing future directions in research and adoption in daily practice.

Expected outcomes:
Core Study Characteristics
• Author, year, journal
• Study design (cross-sectional, longitudinal, diagnostic accuracy)
• Sample size and demographics
• Imaging modality (panoramic, periapical, CBCT, ultrasound, MRI)
• Condition studied (e.g. osteoporosis, periodontitis, implant stability, TMJ, systemic disease, etc.)
Fractal Analysis Details
• ROI details (location, size, shape)
• FA method (algorithm, software)
• FD values (mean ± SD for groups)
Clinical Relevance Indicators
• Diagnostic metrics (sensitivity, specificity, AUC)
• Correlation with clinical gold standards (e.g., DXA, ISQ)
• Mention of clinical use or integration
• Mention of automation level (manual, semi-automated, or fully automated) 
• Reported barriers (e.g., lack of standardization, reproducibility issues)
Other
• Follow-up duration (for healing studies)
• Key findings and author conclusions

title: Diagnostic accuracy of clinical tests for injury of ankle and syndesmosis ligaments: protocol for a systematic review and meta-analysis
description:
Ankle sprains are common musculoskeletal injuries. Ankle sprains can be differentiated in a simple sprain in which the lateral ligaments remained intact or in rupture of one or more ligaments. The anterior talofibular ligament (ATLF) is most commonly the first to rupture, followed by the combined injury of the ATFL and calcaneofibular ligament (CFL). Isolated CFL ruptures are rare. Ankle syndesmosis injuries (also known as ‘high ankle sprains’) are less common, accounting for 1 to 24% of all ankle injuries. Diagnosis is usually made by combining clinical history, physical exam, manual laxity testing and impairment-based assessment. Complementary imaging studies, including stress radiographs, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), arthrography and ultrasonography are used to confirm the structural integrity of capsuloligamentous structures. Some of the key disadvantages of the imaging tools are exposure to radiation, invasive procedures, and associated high costs and time. Imaging is expensive and time-consuming, and adds little information beyond what the clinician can obtain via physical examination. 

Early and accurate diagnosis of ankle injuries is crucial for timely and effective management. In addition to the clinical history (history of sprain or other traumatic event) and physical exam (inspection and palpation), the manual clinical tests are a key component of the comprehensive physical examination. The diagnostic accuracy of these tests can vary, and differentiating between isolated ankle and syndesmosis injuries is challenging. Previous systematic reviews have examined the diagnostic accuracy of physical examination tests for ankle and syndesmosis injuries. These systematic reviews included only a few studies and do not provide pooling summary of diagnostic accuracy data due to the heterogeneity of the studies (different reference standards and varying methodological quality). Since then, at least five new studies have been published and a new systematic review with meta-analysis is thus warranted.

Our purpose is to conduct a systematic review and meta-analysis on the diagnostic accuracy of clinical diagnosis for ankle and syndesmotic ligament injuries.

title: Diagnostic validity of questionnaires for TMD when compared to RDC/TMD or DC/TMD: systematic review
description:
The literature presents the DC/TMD and RDC/TMD questionnaires as the gold standard for the diagnosis of TMD, which are biopsychobehavioral questionnaires that screen and diagnose facial pain according to general patient health questions to specific questions about their day-to-day feelings. day to verify its correlation with pain, as well as the physical analysis of pain and questioning of TMD symptoms such as jaw locking, joint noise, and joint clicks[1,7]. Despite the great help of these questionnaires for the diagnosis of TMDs, clinicians and researchers point out the difficulties encountered in their application due to a large number of questions and necessary assessments, carried out even in patients with pain or under great stress and anxiety caused by the painful and long-term disorder DTM.
The extension of these questionnaires and the consequent short-term requirement of making a diagnosis without the deep correlation between the answers motivated the accomplishment of this systematic review in order to analyze other existing questionnaires for the diagnosis of TMD and to verify the diagnostic accuracy when compared to the gold standard.

title: Validation of a Telehealth Adult Autism Assessment Protocol: Diagnostic Accuracy, Reliability, and Comparison to Gold-Standard Benchmarks
description:
Study Description:
This validation study evaluates the diagnostic reliability and accuracy of a standardized telehealth autism assessment protocol for adults through independent expert review of clinical records. The primary objective is to establish whether structured telehealth-based autism evaluation can achieve diagnostic rigor comparable to established gold-standard assessment benchmarks.



Background and Purpose:
Adult autism assessment faces significant barriers including multi-year waitlists, geographic disparities in access to qualified evaluators, and limitations of existing observational measures that may not capture masked or camouflaged presentations common in verbally fluent adults. Telehealth assessment offers potential solutions to access barriers while allowing evaluation in natural environments, yet rigorous validation studies comparing telehealth approaches to established benchmarks remain limited. This study addresses this critical gap by examining whether a structured telehealth clinical interview protocol can achieve equivalent psychometric properties to gold-standard measures.


Study Design:
This is a retrospective, blinded validation study using existing clinical records. We will select 100 completed adult autism assessment cases via stratified random sampling to ensure representation across diagnostic outcomes, demographics (with intentional oversampling of racial/ethnic minority cases), co-occurring conditions, and collateral information availability. All clinical documentation will be de-identified and independently reviewed by an expert clinician in autism assessment who will be blinded to the original diagnostic outcomes. The expert will formulate independent diagnostic conclusions (autism spectrum disorder vs. not autism spectrum disorder) with certainty ratings for each case.



Primary Outcomes:

Inter-rater reliability: Cohen's kappa coefficient measuring diagnostic agreement between the telehealth protocol outcomes and independent expert clinical judgment, compared against published gold-standard benchmarks (κ = 0.66-0.92)
Diagnostic accuracy: Using expert clinical best estimate as the criterion standard, we will calculate sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, and negative predictive value, comparing results to established benchmark ranges (sensitivity: 80-95%, specificity: 75-93%)

Secondary Outcomes:
Patterns of diagnostic divergence: Identification and characterization of cases where expert and protocol diagnoses differ, examining factors such as co-occurring conditions (ADHD, anxiety, depression, OCD, PTSD), potential masking factors, documentation quality, and collateral information availability
Subgroup analyses exploring whether agreement and accuracy vary across participant characteristics including co-occurring conditions, demographics (age, gender, race/ethnicity), and collateral information availability

title: Diagnostic accuracy of Magnetic Resonance (MR) biomarkers (2D MRE, 3D MRE, MRI-PDFF, iron-corrected T1, and native T1) for ‘at-risk NASH’, and for significant liver fibrosis (F2), in NAFLD: A protocol for a systematic review and meta-analysis
description:
Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is the most common cause of chronic liver disease worldwide, and prevalence of NAFLD is increasing owing to upward trends of obesity and diabetes (24042449). Nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) is an advanced stage of NAFLD with a higher risk of progression to complications related to cirrhosis, is currently the second most common indication for liver transplantation in the United States, and is expected to become the leading cause in the near future (24768810, 25461851, 25920090).

Despite the large societal burden of NASH, there is no safe, effective medication approved by the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) (27646933). Most clinical trials for NASH require as an eligibility criterion the presence of ‘at-risk NASH’, defined as diagnosed NASH, NAFLD activity score (NAS) ≥ 4 and significant fibrosis (F≥2). The rationale is that these patients are at substantial risk for progression to complications of cirrhosis, and so might benefit from participating in NASH drug development clinical trials. By comparison, patients without NASH, with NAS ≤ 3, or with F<2 are less likely to benefit from participation, and so should be excluded from those trials.

The requirement for ‘at-risk NASH’ or significant fibrosis poses a major challenge for clinical trials because histologic confirmation remains necessary for diagnosis, risk stratification, and longitudinal evaluation of NASH. Liver biopsy is costly, invasive in nature, and prone to sampling errors, given the spatial heterogeneity of steatosis in liver (15940625, 24574716). Moreover, it has been shown that only about 30% of patients recruited and screened for clinical trial participation meet histologic criteria for inclusion. The other 70% have too little or too much disease on biopsy, and are excluded. This ~70% screen failure rate is problematic because it exposes potential participants to unnecessary risk from invasive biopsy, and drives up trial costs. To reduce risks and costs, there is a need for diagnostic enrichment strategies to identify patients most likely to have ‘at-risk NASH’ or F2, and to reserve biopsy only for such patients. Non-invasive imaging biomarkers as well as serum parameters can be used to enhance diagnostic confidence when conducting research trials.

Several Magnetic Resonance (MR) imaging biomarkers have emerged for liver fibrosis staging and NASH diagnosis which might be helpful for diagnostic enrichment in NASH clinical trials, including magnetic resonance elastography (MRE), both two- and three-dimensional (2D- and 3D-MRE), MR-Proton Density Fat Fraction (PDFF), iron-corrected T1 (cT1), and T1 mapping (also known as native T1). However, there is a critical lack of consensus on diagnostic thresholds of each of these MR imaging biomarkers which might vary based on hardware, context of use, and fibrosis level. Moreover, estimations of their diagnostic accuracies vary across studies. Thus, the primary goal of this review is to synthesize the existing literature by conducting a systematic literature review, and if possible, meta-analysis on diagnostic performance of the five aforementioned MR biomarkers to inform optimal thresholds for the diagnosis of ‘at-risk NASH’ and clinically significant liver fibrosis (stage ≥ F2).
