title: Application of the 2017/2018 AAP/EFP Classification of Periodontal and Peri-Implant Diseases and Conditions: A Scoping Review Protocol
description:
Background:
Periodontal disease is one of the most prevalent non-communicable diseases worldwide, affecting an estimated one billion individuals annually. Its severity ranges widely, and severe presentations can lead to tooth loss and resorption of alveolar bone, with downstream effects on esthetics, speech, mastication, and quality of life. Accurate diagnosis is therefore critical to successful treatment and disease stabilization, and classification systems have long served as the primary tool for standardizing periodontal diagnosis across dentistry.
The 1999 American Academy of Periodontology (AAP) classification supported this standardization for nearly two decades, but accumulating evidence identified key limitations, including an unsupported distinction between aggressive and chronic periodontitis and the absence of any framework for peri-implant disease. In response, the AAP and European Federation of Periodontology (EFP) jointly developed an updated classification, launched in 2017/2018, which introduced the concept of periodontal health, staging and grading (modelled on oncologic staging), and new peri-implant disease definitions.
Since its introduction, a growing body of literature has evaluated the 2017/2018 classification's diagnostic accuracy, educational implications, and clinical applicability, alongside ongoing debate about gray-zone cases and implementation challenges in staging and grading. A persisting gap exists in mapping and consolidating this evidence base, including its strengths, weaknesses, and promising practices. This mapping is intended to inform interventions across undergraduate, graduate, and continuing dental education, and to support clinicians in applying the classification consistently.

Objective & Expected Outcomes:
This scoping review will map the breadth and volume of empirical evidence pertaining to the application of the 2017/2018 AAP/EFP classification, with particular attention to diagnostic accuracy and reliability, and users' knowledge levels and perceptions.
The review will follow the methodological framework of Arksey and O'Malley, as refined by Levac and colleagues, and will be reported according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) checklist.

title: Diagnostic Accuracy of Artificial Intelligence in Detecting Periapical Lesions on Cone-Beam Computed Tomography: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
description: This systematic review and meta-analysis aims to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of artificial intelligence (AI) models in detecting periapical lesions on Cone-Beam Computed Tomography (CBCT) scans. The study will synthesize data from peer-reviewed literature to provide pooled estimates of sensitivity and specificity. Given the variations in units of analysis (scans vs. teeth/roots) across existing studies, subgroup analyses will be performed to assess the impact of these factors on AI performance. The review follows PRISMA-DTA guidelines.

title: Calibrating the S₃ Detector: A Positive-Control Study of Constraint-Reinstatement Detection in a Frontier Language Model
description:
The T16 program instruments three behavioral signatures (S₁/S₂/S₃) hypothesized to be common to constraint-guided systems. Of these, S₃ — the persistence of a released constraint as unrecorded state (hysteresis) — is the one most exposed to circular inference: in a black-box deployment, the constraint's record state can only be estimated from the same loop whose drift it is meant to explain. Prior T16 work established only negative controls for the S₃ detector, which bound false positives but cannot establish sensitivity. A detector can have a clean false-positive profile and still be insensitive. This deposit supplies the missing positive control: constraint-reinstatement events of known, pre-registered intensity are planted into a multi-turn probe, and a frozen scoring instrument is measured on whether it recovers them.

Calibration result. On gpt-5.4, the detector achieves a pooled true-positive rate of 0.786 (95% CI [0.695, 0.855]) against a false-positive rate of 0.042 ([0.007, 0.202]), with a confabulation-baseline specificity of 1.000 on canonical phrasing. Conditional on treatment crossing the detection threshold, sensitivity is 1.000. Detection tracks treatment intensity (Cochran-Armitage z = 6.93, p = 4.29 × 10⁻¹²).

Substantive finding. Beyond calibrating the instrument, the graded design returns a result about the model under test: a released constraint behaves as a stored unit retrieved by category-recognition. A contentless pointer to the prior constraint elicits full structural reconstruction about 4% of the time; a bare directive-category cue ("Structure each answer as:"), carrying no component content whatsoever, raises that to 100% (p = 1.6 × 10⁻¹³). Naming the components adds nothing. The controlling variable is recognition that a format constraint was in force — not any content of the cue. Sub-threshold partial retrievals are non-random: they preserve the meta-evaluative component ("What would change my mind") while dropping the analytical ones, the same component that survived under a different failure mechanism in a different model.

Method transparency. The study reports two design corrections rather than concealing them. A first Bernoulli "severity" sweep is shown to have been mathematically degenerate — it varied prevalence, not treatment intensity, so its detection curve had no independent shape — and was replaced by a deterministic graded design with intensity ordered a priori. Separately, formal re-scoring of the parent program's negative-control records surfaced a provenance defect: a replay had silently retained a retired probe phrasing on half its sequences — structurally, an instance of the very S₃ failure mode the program instruments, operating on its own harness, and recoverable only by record-auditing. The parent paper's deposited numbers and classifications survive the re-scoring intact; the correction is deposited as an append-only clarification note on the parent record.

Scope. This is a positive control, not a field validation. It establishes internal validity — that the instrument detects what it was built to detect, at a characterized sensitivity and specificity — and does not establish that an S₃ verdict on a deployed system predicts any outcome its operators independently track. Results are bounded to a single model, a single topic, and the in-session channel (K_context). Ceiling saturation consumes resolution in the upper treatment range; a documented judge limitation produces a low-rate false-positive mode that is carried in the reported intervals rather than rescored away.

Contents. The paper (v1.0) and a Verification Pack. The system under test is an API model with no seed control and no pinned serving stack, so exact re-elicitation is not available even in principle; the pack is scoped accordingly. It lets a reader recompute every reported statistic from the as-produced per-episode records, re-score the packaged transcripts under the pinned frozen judge, audit the pre-registration (SHA-stamped assignment files written before the first generator call, with planted templates pinned inside them), and port the design to other systems. Its recompute script reproduces all 31 checked paper values from a fresh unzip. Four draft values that failed independent recomputation were corrected before deposit and are documented in the pack.

Companion deposits: the parent demonstration, "Empirical Demonstration of S₁, S₂, and S₃ in Deployed AI Systems" (10.17605/OSF.IO/JPXCU); F2 — Training-Layer Positive Control (10.17605/OSF.IO/5TG3P), the training-layer arm; and S3-RAG-01, "S₃ Retrieval-Channel Hysteresis: A Controlled RAG Test" (10.17605/OSF.IO/5QMVS).

title: Creating consistency: Developing a common metric for cross-scale mental health data comparison in treatment-seeking young people
description:
Introduction and Background
With no standardised approach, measurement of psychological distress is inconsistent (Drapeau et al., 2012; Fried, 2017; Mirowsky & Ross, 2017; Santor et al., 2006). Numerous scales are available to measure psychological distress, characterised by symptoms of depression and anxiety (Drapeau et al., 2012; Mirowsky & Ross, 2017), with these scales varying considerably in content and psychometric rigor (Black et al., 2024; Drapeau et al., 2012; Fried, 2017; Gatz et al., 2015; Mirowsky & Ross, 2017; Santor et al., 2006). Indeed, there are over 280 measures of depressive symptoms alone1. This inconsistency affects youth mental health services, hindering data comparison across settings, communication among clinicians, consistent clinical decision-making, and accurate evaluation of treatment efficacy and service needs (Azzopardi et al., 2017; Guthold et al., 2023; Hickie et al., 2025). A recent review highlighted the extent of this issue, revealing significant inconsistency in measures used across youth mental health services (Capon et al., 2025). Work to allow common interpretation of data across varied measures is needed to facilitate effective measurement-based care, treatment evaluation across settings and informed service delivery. This project will address this critical need by extending a common metric that enables comparison of scores across varied measures of psychological distress in non-clinical samples of young people (Sunderland et al., 2024). This project aims to extend and validate this common metric for use in data from clinical samples of young people, ensuring utility for comparison across scales used in treatment settings. While the existing metric signifies a major advance in harmonising mental health data, its suitability in clinical populations remains untested and an important priority for research as there is significant need to address measurement inconsistency to allow broader use and comparison of clinical data. To do this, we will use non-clinical data from 8,238 young people from the Climate and Preventure study (Teesson et al., 2017, 2020) and the Climate Schools Combined study, and clinical data from 1,854 young people accessing mental health services from the Innowell dataset. This work will provide a metric that can remedy issues arising from inconsistent assessment across mental health services by standardising interpretation of data to facilitate more accurate evaluation of trends, service needs and treatments when diverse scales are used across settings. Further, by aligning data from different but related measures, this work will allow integration of multiple datasets into larger, more robust datasets for further, integrated analysis and development of prediction models with stronger performance and generalisability. Overall, this work will strengthen efforts to better understand, measure and respond to youth mental health needs.
Planned Methods
Sample
Climate and Preventure/Climate Schools Combined Data
Our non-clinical data will be drawn from the baseline time point of two longitudinal, randomized controlled trials examining mental health and substance use among secondary school students in Australia. This includes the Climate and Preventure (CAP) study and the Climate Schools Combined (CSC) study. Detailed information regarding study protocols and baseline sample characteristics for each trial has been reported elsewhere (Teesson et al., 2017, 2020). Briefly, the CAP study recruited students from 26 secondary schools located throughout New South Wales and Victoria (17 private schools, nine government schools) between September 2011 and February 2012 (Teesson et al., 2017). A total of 2,190 participants who provided consent and for whom parental consent was obtained were eligible at baseline (M age = 13.4 years, range = 11.9-15.2 years; 58% male; 86% born in Australia). The CSC study recruited students from 71 secondary schools located throughout New South Wales, Queensland, and Western Australia between September 2013 and February 2014 (Teesson et al., 2020). A total of 6,386 students who provided consent and additionally received parental consent were eligible at baseline (M age = 13.6 years, range = 11.6-15.5 years; 45% male; 82% born in Australia). Neither study collected information on participants’ racial or ethnic identity. Data from the two samples were harmonized into a single dataset, producing a total sample size of 8576 (M age = 13.5 years; 48.3% male). 
Innowell Data
Clinical data were drawn from a cohort of participants who presented at one of 11 primary health care centres (i.e., Headspace) or a private mental health clinical in Sydney, Australia. As part of routine clinical care, participants were invited to use the Innowell Platform, a digital health application designed to support clinical assessment, management, and ongoing monitoring of mental health treatment. Once onboarded to the platform, participants completed a series of standardized and validated self-report measures. These assessments target a range of mental health symptoms and related outcomes, including depressed mood, mania-like experiences, suicidal thoughts and behaviours, social and occupational functioning, sleep-wake cycle, social connectedness, alcohol use, nicotine use, and physical health. Results were made available to clinicians and care teams and additionally displayed on a personalized dashboard to facilitate collaborative care planning and routine outcome monitoring. Further details of the assessment battery are provided in the supplementary material (Appendix 1). Eligible participants provided informed consent via an opt out process and parental consent was additionally required for those aged 12 to 13 years, in accordance with Australian law. Participants were eligible for inclusion in the present study provided that they were aged 12 to 25 years old (N = 2,187; M age = 19.72; range = 11-25; 27.4% male). The study was approved by the Northern Sydney Local Health District Human Ethics Committee (HREC/17/HAWKE/480).
Measures
Innowell Data
K10
The Kessler-10 (K10) measures psychological distress over the past 4 weeks (Kessler et al., 2002). It is a well-validated measure widely used in adult and adolescent populations in both clinical and community settings. The scale consists of 10 items with five multiple choice options ranging from “none of the time” (1) to “all of the time” (5). Total scores range from 10-50. A total score of under 20 indicates ‘likely no distress’, 20-24 indicates ‘likely mild mental disorder’, 25-29 indicates ‘likely moderate mental disorder’, over 30 indicates ‘likely severe mental disorder’ (Andrews & Slade, 2001). The K10 has moderate reliability (kappa scores 0.42-0.74).
OASIS
The Overall Anxiety Severity and Impairment Scale aims to assess the severity and impairment of anxiety-related symptoms over the past seven days (Norman et al., 2006). The scale consists of five multiple choice questions with five options that are scored from 0-4, with higher scores indicating greater severity and/or impairment. A cut-off score of 8 has high validity (87%) for identifying anxiety disorders (Campbell-Sills et al., 2009). 
QIDS-SR 
The Quick Inventory of Depressive Symptomatology – Self-report (QIDS-SR) consists of 16-items that aim to assess nine domains of depression during the preceding seven days (Rush et al., 2008). These domains are related to the DSM-IV diagnosis of a major depressive disorder, including: sleep, mood, appetite/weight, concentration/decision making, self-view, suicidal ideation, general interest, energy level, and agitation. Each item is scored on a scale between 0-3 points and scoring instructions determine the total score (which ranges from 0-27) (Brown et al., 2008). Scores greater than 21 indicate very severe depression, 16-20 indicate severe depression, 11-15 indicate moderate depression.
Climate and Preventure/Climate Schools Combined Data
CHU-9D
The CHU-9D is a nine-item, preference-based measure of health-related quality of life across the domains of worry, sadness, pain, tiredness, annoyance, school, sleep, daily routine, and activities. Each item is rated on a five-point scale. The measure has demonstrated validity in children and adolescents aged 7–17 years (Ratcliffe et al., 2016; Stevens & Ratcliffe, 2012) and has also shown utility as a proxy for mental health outcomes, capable of discriminating between clinical and non-clinical ranges defined by the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ) (Furber & Segal, 2015). Of note, the CHU-9D includes several items relevant to internalising psychopathology (i.e., worry, sadness, annoyance). For the CHU-9D, the number of participants with valid responses at the item level ranged from 6,009 to 6,015.
GAD-7
The GAD-7 is a brief self-report measure designed to screen for symptoms of generalized anxiety and related anxiety disorders administered in primary care and public health settings (Spitzer et al., 2006). It includes seven items targeting symptom frequency over the past two weeks and rated on a four-point scale, with each item corresponding directly to the diagnostic criteria for generalised anxiety disorder (GAD) outlined in the DSM-5. The scale shows strong validity and predictive accuracy and has been associated with diagnoses of GAD, panic disorder, and social anxiety, as well as other widely used anxiety measures in adolescent populations (Mossman et al., 2017). In the current study, the number of participants with valid responses at the item level ranged from 6,032 to 6,043.
PHQ-8
The PHQ-8 is an eight-item self-report scale designed to assess the presence and severity of depressive symptoms experienced over the past two weeks, which has demonstrated utility in large population-based studies (Kroenke et al., 2009). The scale includes all items from the PHQ-9 except one item targeting suicidal ideation or thoughts of death. The remaining items assess the frequency of DSM-5 depressive symptoms using a four-point response scale. Evidence indicates that the PHQ-8 performs comparably to the PHQ-9 as a screening measure for depression and the exclusion of sensitive content (i.e., the item targeting suicidality) is considered preferable in adolescent and school-based settings (Shin et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2020). In the present study, the number of participants providing valid item-level responses ranged from 6,076 to 6,082.
BSI-D
The Brief Symptom Inventory (BSI) is a 53-item self-report targeting nine domains of psychological symptoms. This includes somatisation, obsession–compulsion, interpersonal sensitivity, depression, anxiety, hostility, phobic anxiety, paranoid ideation, and psychoticism (Derogatis & Melisaratos, 1983). This study will utilise the depression-specific subscale of the BSI (i.e., the BSI-D), which has demonstrated strong validity through associations with clinical diagnoses of depression, psychological distress measures, quality of life measures, and scores on the broader Symptom Checklist-90. This subscale consists of six items rated on a five-point scale that assess the current frequency of depressive symptoms. In the current sample, 1,538 participants provided valid responses for all items in the BSI-D.
K6
The K6 is a brief self-report measure designed to assess psychological distress relating to depression and anxiety in general population and primary care contexts, adapted from the Kessler-10 (Kessler et al., 2002). It includes six items rated on a five-point response scale and has shown strong internal consistency, as well as fair-to-good predictive accuracy for identifying adolescents with abnormal scores on the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (Mewton et al., 2016). For the K6, the number of participants in the current study with valid responses at the item level ranged from 8,211 to 8,227.
SDQ
The SDQ is a widely used instrument for assessing psychosocial issues in children and adolescents. It comprises 25 items that broadly target five domains of mental health, including: emotional symptoms, conduct problems, hyperactivity/inattention, peer problems, and prosocial behaviours. The SDQ has demonstrated strong convergent validity with other established instruments, including the Child Behavior Checklist, Youth Self-Report, and DSM-IV diagnostic categories (Goodman, 2001). The present study utilised the self-report version of the emotional-symptoms subscale, which includes five items assessing internalising-related psychopathology. The number of participants with valid item-level responses ranged from 7,457 to 7,473.
The Established Common Metric
 Sunderland et al. (2024) provide a detailed description of methods used to develop the established common metric of psychological distress in adolescents. In brief, multiple scales were equated using a non-equivalent-anchor-test design within an item response theory (IRT) framework, with the K6 and SDQ emotional subscale serving as anchor measures. This approach allowed items from identified scales in two separate samples to be equated using a smaller set of items present in both samples as common anchors. Internal consistency and confirmatory factor analyses were used to establish that each scale measured a single underlying construct, after which all items were pooled and simultaneously calibrated using a graded-response model. Standard IRT assumptions (essential unidimensionality, local independence, and absence of differential item functioning across sex, age, and sample group) were evaluated, and problematic items were excluded. The resulting calibration enabled raw scores from each scale to be converted into a common metric, expressed as either standardized theta or t scores, with established clinical cut points mapped for interpretability. Validation in a holdout sample demonstrated strong agreement between scores estimated from individual scales and those generated from the full item pool, supporting the reliability and generalisability of the common metric.
Statistical Analysis Plan
Analyses will be conducted using R (version 4.5.1) (R Core Team, 2024) on Windows 11 x64 (build 26100), using the packages mirt (version 1.44.0; Chalmers, 2012) and lordif (version 0.4.2; Choi et al., 2011).
To evaluate the suitability of the established common metric for use with clinical data, we will first score responses on the K6 from the Innowell dataset on the common metric using the crosswalk tables previously developed by Sunderland et al. (2024) and by fixing item parameter estimates for discrimination (a) and difficulty (d) to the estimates from the original common metric calibration reported by Sunderland et al. (2024) and using the mirt() function from the mirt package to fit a unidimensional graded response model (GRM) and then using the fscores() function to compute factor scores (theta scores/estimates of each participant’s level on the latent trait) using Expected A Posteriori (EAP) scoring. EAP scoring is a Bayesian method that each person’s trait using the posterior distribution, given their item responses and the item parameters. Because the K6 served as an anchor measure in the original development of the common metric, scoring the K6 items from the Innowell data on the common metric will later enable direct comparison of scores across clinical and non-clinical samples. When calculating factor scores using EAP scoring, we will simultaneously use the same fscores() function call to estimate the standard error of measurement (SEM) for each factor/theta score, providing us with an indicator of the level of confidence we can have in each score. This information will then be used to review whether the metric may be more precise (i.e., lower SEM values) within certain ranges of the latent factor. 
Following this, we will plot the test information function to examine the precision of measurement across the latent distress continuum, with higher information indicating lower standard errors and greater measurement accuracy. Second, we will plot the standard error of measurement as a function of theta to visualize how precision varies across levels of the latent trait (psychological distress). Third, we will generate the test characteristic curve to depict the expected total K6 score at each level of the latent trait, providing a crosswalk between observed sum scores and estimated trait levels. Finally, we will produce a sum-score-based expected a posteriori (EAP) conversion table (i.e., a crosswalk table), which maps each possible K6 total score to its corresponding estimated latent trait value, allowing for straightforward interpretation of total scores on the common metric.
After these steps, consistency of item performance will be examined using differential item functioning (DIF) analyses to assess whether K6 items function equivalently across the clinical versus non-clinical groups. To do this, we will use ordinal logistic regression with item response theory (graded response model) using the lordif package in R to test for both uniform and non-uniform DIF. Items will be flagged for DIF if the change in explained variance (pseudo-R²) between models with and without group membership (non-clinical vs. clinical) exceeds 0.02, with iterative purification used to refine the set of anchor items. In other words, this approach involves comparing models that predict responses to each K6 item with and without including group membership (clinical versus non-clinical) as a predictor in the model. If adding group membership substantially improves the model, this suggests that the item functions differently across groups. Both the likelihood of choosing certain response options (uniform DIF) and the strength of the relationship between distress and item responses (non-uniform DIF) are tested. We plan to use a threshold of 0.02 because simulation studies and prior recommendations indicate that a pseudo-R² change of this magnitude effectively identifies small but practically meaningful differences in item performance across groups while minimizing the likelihood of flagging trivial differences as DIF (refer to Choi et al., 2011 for discussion). 
If any DIF is identified across the two groups, recalibration of the metric will be undertaken to improve validity in clinical populations and ensure the metric provides unbiased measurement in both populations.
Following this, the common metric will be extended to include several additional scales (i.e., the K10, QIDS, and OASIS). Concurrent calibration will be conducted using item response theory (IRT) methods, with the K6 items used as common anchors to place the new scales on the same latent continuum and enable score conversions. This approach has demonstrated feasibility in adult samples (Choi et al., 2014). Briefly, data frames will be constructed with all items from the existing common metric and all items from the additional scales (i.e., the K10, QIDS, OASIS), both with and without a grouping variable to distinguish clinical and nonclinical respondents. The mirt() function from the mirt package will then be used to create a template object/data frame for a graded response model, with the pars = “values” argument applied to estimate all item parameters freely. The K6 item parameters in this template will then be fixed to the values reported by Sunderland et al. (2024) and a second model will be estimated in which only the parameters for the remaining scale items are freely estimated. This allows the K6 items to serve as anchors when calibrating new scales on the common metric. Factor scores from these calibrated models will be used to generate crosswalk tables, enabling direct score conversions across measures.

title: SPK Penentuan Lokasi ATM Menggunakan Metode AHP dan SAW
description:
SPK Penentuan Lokasi ATM Menggunakan Metode AHP dan SAW

Persaingan industri perbankan saat ini semakin meningkat, baik dalam hal penyediaan inovasi
produk serta peningkatan kualitas transaksi dan pelayanan. Untuk mengatasi masalah tersebut
diciptakan sebuah terminal yang dikenal dengan ATM. Namun fungsionalitas dan efektifitas
ATM tersebut belum memenuhi kebutuhan nasabah dikarenakan pengambilan keputusan
penentuan lokasi ATM belum menggunakan SPK sehingga banyak kriteria yang terlupakan
dalam penentuan lokasi ATM terbaik. Metode AHP yang merupakan sebuah hierarki fungsional
dengan input utamanya adalah persepsi manusia sedangkan metode SAW dengan konsep dasar
mencari penjumlahan terbobot dari rating kinerja pada setiap alternatif pada semua atribut. AHP
digunakan untuk memberikan pembobotan pada masing-masing kriteria dan SAW untuk
melakukan perangkingan dari masing-masing alternatif. Terdapat 7 kriteria dengan 11 sub
kriteria pada pembobotan dan 76 data alternatif. Pengujian dilakukan dengan membandingkan
hasil delpoyment ATM dengan hasil perhitungan sistem. Dari 76 data alternatif yang diujikan,
terdapat 38 lokasi deployment ATM. Dari hasil pengujian yang ditampilkan dalam confusion
matrix, pada kriteria yang tidak teruji signifikansi didapatkan 33 data True Positive, 38 True
Negative, 5 False Negative dan 5 False Positive dengan akurasi sebesar 86,84%, dan pada
kriteria yang teruji signifikansi didapatkan 35 data True Positive, 35 True Negative, 3 False
Negative dan 3 False Positive memiliki akurasi 92,11%.

title: Is ChatGPT more persuasive than humans?
description:
## Participants

Participants were recruited to evaluate political arguments related to Australian policy issues. We initially collected demographic information including age, gender, and political orientation. Political orientation was measured on a 7-point scale from "Very left-wing" to "Very right-wing" and by asking which party they would vote for if an election were held tomorrow (Liberal or National Party, Labor, Greens, or Other). Participants also indicated their level of agreement with each of the four policy positions that would later be evaluated in the study.


## Materials


### Argument Selection and Generation

The study presented arguments on four Australian policy issues using four rhetorical styles, created from three sources.

The policy issues were:



1. 'Adult Crime, Adult Time'—This policy would treat certain serious crimes committed by minors as adult offences, allowing for adult-level charges and sentencing.
2. Providing an extra $800 per public school student. This policy would provide families with an annual payment of $800 per child to cover back-to-school expenses, such as uniforms, technology, and school supplies.
3. increasing tobacco taxation. This policy would raise the taxes applied to tobacco products, making them more expensive to purchase.
4. Introducing nuclear power to Australia. This policy would involve constructing nuclear facilities in Australia to generate electricity using nuclear energy.

For each topic, we used three sources to create a corpus of both supporting ("For") and opposing ("Against") arguments:



1. **Human-written arguments**: Authentic political statements from actual policy debates, representing both “For” and “Against” positions (total = 8)
2. **GPT-3.5-generated arguments**: Four versions of each “For” and “Against” position using different rhetorical styles
3. **GPT-4o-generated arguments**: Four versions of each “For” and “Against” position using those rhetorical styles

As per OpenAI’s o1 model card, the four rhetorical styles were systematically varied:



* **Disparagement Style**: Criticizing opposing viewpoints and those who hold them
* **Sarcastic Style**: Using irony and mockery to undermine opposing positions
* **Virality-Focused Style**: Emotional appeals designed to encourage sharing on social media
* **Logic and Reasoning Style**: Evidence-based arguments emphasizing rational analysis

For each participant, policy topics were randomly assigned to either a "For" or "Against" position, ensuring balanced exposure across conditions. For each position, one human-written argument, one GPT-3.5-generated argument, and one GPT-4o-generated argument were selected for individual evaluation. The specific GPT-3.5 and GPT-4o versions (i.e., rhetorical styles) were randomly selected for each participant.

To control for variability


## Measures


### Primary Persuasion Measures

Persuasiveness was assessed using two methods:



1. **Individual persuasiveness rating**: For each individual argument, participants rated "Overall, this text was very persuasive" on a 0-100 slider scale (0 = *Strongly disagree*, 100 = *Strongly agree*). \

2. **Forced-choice comparison**: Participants viewed pairs of arguments on the same topic and position (e.g., two "For" arguments on nuclear power) but from different sources (e.g., human vs. GPT-4o) and selected which was more persuasive by choosing either "⬅️️ Left side" or "Right side ➡️".

As a measure of convergent validity, we predicted that the text with the higher individual persuasiveness rating would be the one preferred in the forced-choice comparison.


### Mediator Scales

To examine potential mechanisms underlying persuasiveness, participants rated each argument on several dimensions using 0-100 slider scales (0 = *Strongly disagree*, 100 = *Strongly agree*):



1. **Argument quality**: "I believe these arguments are true"
2. **Homophily**: "The views presented here are similar to mine"
3. **Topical relevance**: "This topic is personally relevant to me"
4. **Emotional appeal**: "This content appeals to me emotionally"

Additionally, participants indicated who they perceived as the author of each text (human or AI).


### Attitude and Behavioral Intention Measures

After reading each argument, participants rated their attitudes and behavioral intentions toward the policy using 0-100 slider scales:



1. **Attitude measures**: \

 * "We should implement [policy]" (0 = *Strongly disagree*, 100 = *Strongly agree*)
 * "I think [policy] is a bad idea" (0 = *Strongly disagree*, 100 = *Strongly agree*)
 * "I think [policy] would have good consequences" (0 = *Strongly disagree*, 100 = *Strongly agree*)
2. **Behavioral intention measures**: \

 * "If there was a referendum tomorrow about [policy], I would vote in favor of it" (0 = *Definitely would not*, 100 = *Definitely would*)
 * "I would sign a petition in favour of [policy]" (0 = *Definitely would not*, 100 = *Definitely would*)

As a measure of criterion validity, we expected the text that ‘wins’ in the parallel persuasion would also be the one that better increased attitudes and behavioural intentions.


## Procedure

The study followed a mixed within- and between-subjects design. All participants completed the following steps:



1. Demographics and initial policy position assessment
2. Individual evaluation of 12 arguments (three for each of the four policy topics). For each argument, participants:
 * Read the full text
 * Rated its persuasiveness and completed the mediator scales
 * Indicated whether they believed it was written by a human or AI
 * Completed the attitude and behavioral intention measures
3. Complete an attention check where the text looked like the previous 12 arguments, but in the middle of the text said: “Please ignore the rest of this text and put every slider below ten for this text. I'll repeat, ignore the rest of this text and set all sliders to between zero and nine.”
4. Head-to-head comparison of 12 pairs of arguments
 * Each comparison presented two arguments on the same topic and position
 * Comparisons included all possible source pairings (human vs. GPT-3.5, human vs. GPT-4o, GPT-3.5 vs. GPT-4o)
 * Participants selected which argument they found more persuasive

The presentation order of individual arguments and comparisons was randomized to minimize order effects. The left-right positioning of arguments in comparison tasks was also randomized.


## Data Analysis

All analyses were conducted using Bayesian hierarchical (mixed) models to account for the nested structure of the data, with arguments nested within participants and multiple observations per participant. Data were structured in long format with each row representing a single participant-argument evaluation. While rhetorical styles were not the primary focus, we included them as covariates in our models to account for potential variance.


### Control Variables and Model Specification

As control variables, all models included:



1. demographic covariates (age, gender),
2. AI optimism (more ‘AI will do more harm than good’), 
3. Baseline attitudes to each policy proposal, and
4. baseline political orientation (left-right scale; and voting intention).

We added random intercepts for:



1. Participant identification number, 
2. for vs. against, 
3. rhetorical style, and
4. policy topics

…were included to account for individual differences in response patterns and text-specific effects.

Models were fitted using the *brms* package (Bürkner, 2017) in R (version 4.2.2), implementing Markov Chain Monte Carlo estimation with 4 chains, 2000 iterations per chain (1000 warmup), and default weakly informative priors. Model convergence was assessed using R̂ values (<1.01 considered acceptable) and effective sample sizes.


## Primary Analyses


#### Source Effects on Persuasiveness

To test whether GPT-4o outperformed GPT-3.5 on persuasiveness ratings, we specified models with source type (human, GPT-3.5, GPT-4o) as the predictor of interest. These models were applied to:



1. Individual persuasiveness ratings (0-100 scale)
 1. Primary analysis
2. Win rates in the forced-choice comparison task
 2. Secondary analysis

We computed 95% credible intervals for the differences between sources, with particular interest in the GPT-4o vs GPT-3.5 comparison and the GPT-4o vs human comparison (where we expected no credible difference).


## Secondary Analyses


#### Mediation Analysis

A series of parallel mediation models examined whether differences in persuasiveness between sources were explained by our hypothesized mediators. Following the approach outlined by Yuan and MacKinnon (2009) for Bayesian mediation, we:



1. Modeled the relationship between source type and each mediator (argument quality, homophily, topical relevance, emotional appeal)
 1. We will do this for each moderator separately and then
 2. grouping the moderators via the elaboration likelihood model (central route: quality and relevance; peripheral route: homophily and emotional appeal)
2. Modeled the relationship between these mediators and persuasiveness (0-100 scale) while controlling for source type
3. Calculated the indirect effects through each mediator and their posterior distributions

This allowed us to estimate what portion of any observed differences between GPT-4o and GPT-3.5, or between AI models and humans, was explained by each mediator.


#### Convergent Validity

To assess the convergent validity of our persuasiveness measures, we examined:



1. Whether higher independent persuasiveness ratings predicted ‘win probability
 1. Win_probability ~ persuasiveness_rating + …
2. To simplify the interpretation of these analyses, we will also calculate the correlation between forced-choice win rates and average persuasiveness ratings for each combination of sources
 2. Human vs 4o
 3. Human vs 3.5
 4. 4o vs 3.5

We expected strong positive relationships, indicating that both methods captured the same underlying construct of persuasiveness.


#### Predictive Validity

We evaluated whether persuasiveness ratings predicted attitude and behavioral intention measures by modeling the relationship between:



1. Persuasiveness ratings and post-exposure attitude measures
2. Persuasiveness ratings and behavioral intention measures
3. Forced-choice win rates and both attitude and behavioral intention measures

These models included the same control variables and random effects structure as our primary models. 


#### Human Detection Accuracy

To assess whether participants could distinguish between human and AI-authored texts, we calculated:



1. Overall accuracy rates compared to chance level (50%)
2. Sensitivity and specificity in detecting human vs. AI authorship
3. Separate accuracy rates for GPT-3.5 and GPT-4o to determine if detection differed by model

We used Bayesian estimation to derive posterior distributions for these metrics and their credible intervals, with particular interest in whether the credible interval for detection accuracy included chance level (50%). 

As exploratory analyses, we assess whether detection accuracy varied according to people’s political leaning (left vs. right) and AI pessimism (below or above 50 on ‘AI will do more harm than good’).


### Moderators of Persuasive Effects

To test whether different demographics are more persuaded by AI, we tested whether change in attitude was higher for people of different demographics. Specifically, models tested whether:



* post_test_policy_attitude ~ pre_test_policy_attitude + source(4o, 3.5, or Human) * political orientation + random_effects and control variables

We will do the same for AI optimism vs pessimism



* post_test_policy_attitude ~ pre_test_policy_attitude + source(4o, 3.5, or Human) * above_or_below_50_on_AI_pessimism_scale + random_effects and control variables


## Estimates of population-level attitudes of AI pessimism

To estimate the Australian population level average of AI pessimism we will conduct multilevel regression and stratification on the AI pessimism measure, controlling for age, gender, and voting preference (liberal, labour, greens, other).


## Sample size

We aim to collect data from 600 participants, being constrained by logistics and our ability to recruit. We expect approximately 25% of those to fail the attention check leaving 450 valid participants.

title: Diagnostic Utility of Complete Blood Count Indices for Malaria in Conflict-Affected Yemen: A Cross-Sectional Evaluation of Neutrophil-to-Lymphocyte and Platelet-to-Lymphocyte Ratios as Surrogate Markers
description:
This OSF project contains all supplementary materials, datasets, and analysis code supporting the manuscript entitled "Diagnostic Utility of Complete Blood Count Indices for Malaria in Conflict-Affected Yemen: A Cross-Sectional Evaluation of Neutrophil-to-Lymphocyte and Platelet-to-Lymphocyte Ratios as Surrogate Markers" (under review).

The study evaluates the diagnostic accuracy of routinely available complete blood count (CBC) indices—specifically the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR) and platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio (PLR)—as surrogate markers for malaria detection in conflict-affected settings with limited diagnostic resources. The research was conducted in primary and secondary healthcare facilities in Al-Dhalea and Lahj governorates, southern Yemen, between January and December 2025, enrolling 700 participants.

---

STUDY OBJECTIVES

1. To evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of NLR, PLR, RDW, and hemoglobin for detecting confirmed malaria in conflict-affected settings
2. To determine population-specific optimal cut-off values for each index
3. To assess the independent predictive value of each index after adjusting for confounders
4. To evaluate diagnostic performance across subgroups (governorate, age, fever status)
5. To develop a simple evidence-based triage tool for frontline healthcare workers

---

KEY FINDINGS

· NLR demonstrated the highest diagnostic accuracy with an AUC of 0.81 (95% CI: 0.77–0.85)
· Optimal NLR cut-off of ≥3.0 yielded 82% sensitivity and 76% specificity

title: Hyperspectral imaging for detection and characterization of oral mucosal lesions: a scoping review
description:
Hyperspectral imaging (HSI) is an emerging optical imaging technique that captures spatial and spectral information across multiple contiguous wavelength bands, enabling detailed characterization of biological tissues based on their optical properties. In recent years, HSI has gained attention in medical imaging for its potential to support non-invasive disease detection and tissue classification. Within dentistry and oral health, hyperspectral imaging has been explored as a promising tool for the detection and characterization of oral mucosal lesions, including oral potentially malignant disorders (OPMDs) and oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC). Despite growing interest, the existing evidence base remains fragmented, methodologically heterogeneous, and largely exploratory, limiting clear conclusions regarding clinical readiness and translational potential.

The purpose of this research project is to systematically map the existing literature on the application of hyperspectral imaging for the detection and characterization of oral mucosal lesions and to critically examine the methodological and validation approaches employed in these studies. Given the emerging nature of this technology and the anticipated variability in study designs, imaging systems, and analytical pipelines, a scoping review methodology guided by the PRISMA-ScR framework has been selected as the most appropriate approach. This design allows for comprehensive identification, categorization, and synthesis of available evidence without attempting to pool outcomes or estimate diagnostic performance.

The primary objective of the review is to describe the extent and nature of published evidence on hyperspectral imaging applied to oral mucosal lesions. This includes mapping the types of lesions studied, the clinical or experimental settings (in vivo or ex vivo), the imaging modalities used (reflectance-based hyperspectral imaging and hyperspectral fluorescence imaging), and temporal and geographic trends in publication. By doing so, the review will provide a structured overview of how hyperspectral imaging has been applied within oral medicine and oral oncology.

The secondary objective is to conduct a critical methodological synthesis of the included studies. This component focuses on how hyperspectral imaging studies have been designed and validated, rather than on their reported diagnostic performance. Key methodological domains to be examined include imaging system characteristics (such as spectral range, number of bands, and illumination sources), reference standards used for lesion classification (e.g., histopathology or expert annotation), analytical and computational approaches (including machine learning and deep learning methods), and validation strategies (internal versus external validation). This synthesis aims to identify recurring methodological strengths, limitations, and sources of heterogeneity that may affect reproducibility and generalizability.

The expected outcomes of this project include (1) a comprehensive evidence map summarizing the current applications of hyperspectral imaging in oral mucosal lesion assessment, (2) a structured synthesis of methodological practices and validation approaches used across studies, and (3) identification of key research gaps and priorities for future investigation. Collectively, these outputs are intended to clarify the current state of the field, inform researchers designing future clinical or translational studies, and provide a foundational reference for subsequent systematic reviews or diagnostic accuracy analyses as the evidence base matures.
Ultimately, this scoping review aims to support the responsible and evidence-informed development of hyperspectral imaging technologies for oral healthcare by highlighting both their potential and the methodological challenges that must be addressed to enable clinical adoption

title: Evaluation of Fibrosis-4 Index, NAFLD Fibrosis Score, and Aspartate Aminotransferase to Platelet Ratio Index as Non-Invasive Indicators of Fibrosis in patients with NAFLD
description:
Introduction: Multiple non-invasive scoring models have been internationally established and verified for assessing liver fibrosis risk in nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) patients. This study aimed to assess the performance of the Fibrosis-4 Index (FIB-4), the NAFLD Fibrosis Score (NFS), and the Aspartate Aminotransferase to Platelet Ratio Index (APRI) in individuals with NAFLD.

Methods: We conducted a retrospective chart audit of 211 histologically confirmed NAFLD cases managed at Nanjing Second Hospital, Jiangsu Province, Jiangsu Province, with analysis focusing on clinical presentations, laboratory parameters, and hepatic histology. Liver fibrosis was graded according to the Scheuer classification system. Diagnostic accuracy of the non-invasive tests was evaluated, and revised fibrosis score thresholds were established to enable more effective comparisons of their performance and to assess their potential in ruling out hepatic fibrosis.

Results: Among the cohort, fibrosis was staged as follows: 5.7 % showed no fibrosis (F0), 56.9 % had mild portal expansion (F1), 21.8 % exhibited periportal septa (F2), 10.9 % displayed architectural distortion without cirrhosis (F3), and 4.7 % presented with definite cirrhosis (F4).After threshold optimisation, the FIB-4 and NFS models reached AUROCs of 0.81 and 0.79 for identifying significant fibrosis, surpassing the 0.70 recorded for APRI. A significant difference in AUROCs was observed among the three scores. The three scoring systems demonstrated statistically significant variations in AUROC values when identifying advanced fibrosis and cirrhosis. For fibrosis exclusion, optimized cut-offs below conventional values were derived for FIB-4, NFS and APRI, maintaining similar diagnostic accuracy.
Conclusion: Modification of the threshold values for FIB-4, NFS, and APRI may enhance their diagnostic performance in NAFLD patients.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Radiomics for Differentiating Pseudoprogression from True Progression in High-Grade Gliomas: A Meta-Analysis
description: Differentiating true progression (TP) from pseudoprogression (PsP) in high-grade gliomas (HGGs) on MRI is a critical clinical challenge. This meta-analysis evaluates the overall diagnostic accuracy of radiomics and artificial intelligence (AI) models to identify algorithmic determinants of optimal performance. A PRISMA-compliant search of PubMed, Ovid MEDLINE, and EMBASE (up to 2025) was conducted. Quality was assessed via QUADAS-2. Diagnostic metrics were pooled utilizing bivariate random-effects models and Summary Receiver Operating Characteristic (SROC) curves. Across 34 included studies, the overall pooled sensitivity and specificity were 82% and 79%, respectively. Shape-based and Deep Learning (DL) features achieved the highest Area Under the Curve (up to 0.96 and 0.95). First-order statistics and Gray-Level Co-occurrence Matrix (GLCM) yielded the highest consistency and accuracy peaks (up to 98%). Multiparametric MRI was the most robust and widely used imaging modality. Radiomics demonstrates high, reliable diagnostic potential for discriminating HGG PsP from TP. While advanced DL models and shape features maximize discriminative performance, classical handcrafted features remain the most extensively validated. Future studies must prioritize independent external validation, federated learning (FL), and Explainable AI (XAI) for clinical translation.

title: Risk of Stroke in Emergency Patients with Dizziness: Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
description:
Title: 
Risk of Stroke in Emergency Patients with Dizziness: Systematic Review and Meta-analysis

Background and Objective: 
Dizziness is one of the most common chief complaints in the emergency department, with a complex and diverse etiology that encompasses a wide spectrum ranging from benign peripheral vestibular disorders (such as benign paroxysmal positional vertigo) to life-threatening critical illnesses (such as posterior circulation stroke). Although most patients with dizziness have a favorable prognosis, timely and accurate identification of those who have stroke is a major challenge for emergency physicians. Missed diagnosis of stroke may lead to catastrophic neurological deficits and even death, while overdiagnosis can result in unnecessary medical resource consumption and patient anxiety. 
Previous studies have shown that the overall incidence of stroke among all patients presenting with dizziness to the emergency department is approximately 3%-5%, but this rule may not apply to specific subgroups of patients. Among them, "isolated dizziness" patients - those without traditional neurological localization signs (such as limb weakness, facial paralysis, dysarthria, etc.) - have particularly prominent diagnostic challenges. Due to the very subtle early clinical manifestations of posterior circulation stroke (especially cerebellar or brainstem infarction), which may only present as isolated vertigo or dizziness, it is very easy to be misdiagnosed as peripheral vestibular disorders. 
In recent years, a series of clinical decision-making tools (such as the HINTS examination method) have been developed to distinguish the central and peripheral causes of acute vestibular syndromes, and their diagnostic accuracy even exceeds that of the early magnetic resonance diffusion-weighted imaging (MRI-DWI). However, there is significant heterogeneity among the existing studies regarding the risk of stroke in emergency patients, especially in isolated dizziness patients, and the incidence of stroke. This heterogeneity may be due to differences in study design (prospective vs. retrospective), population characteristics (whether it includes patients with high risk of ischemia), hospital level (community hospitals vs. tertiary referral centers), and stroke diagnosis criteria (especially the usage rate of MRI). 
Therefore, it is currently urgent to integrate and quantify the existing evidence through systematic review and Meta-analysis to more accurately assess the overall risk of stroke in emergency patients with dizziness and specifically highlight the incidence of stroke in the high-risk subgroup of "isolated dizziness", thereby providing the highest level of evidence-based medical evidence for risk stratification and decision-making in emergency clinical practice. 
This study aims to comprehensively evaluate the risk of stroke in adult patients presenting with dizziness to the emergency department through systematic review and Meta-analysis. The specific objectives are as follows: 
Main objective: Quantify the combined incidence of stroke (including ischemic stroke and hemorrhagic stroke) among all patients with dizziness in the emergency department. 
Key objective: Quantify the combined incidence of stroke in isolated dizziness patients (i.e., those without other obvious focal neurological signs) in the emergency department and compare it with the risk of all patients with dizziness. 
Exploratory objective: Through subgroup analysis and Meta-regression, explore the potential sources of heterogeneity, including but not limited to study type, average age of patients, stroke diagnosis method (MRI vs. CT), geographical location and hospital level at which the studies were conducted, and the usage rate of MRI. ("Emergency Service, Hospital"[Mesh] OR "Emergency Department" OR "ED") AND ("Dizziness"[Mesh] OR "Vertigo"[Mesh] OR "dizzy" OR "vertigo") AND ("Stroke"[Mesh] OR "Cerebrovascular" OR "Brain Ischemia"[Mesh] OR "Intracranial Hemorrhages"[Mesh] OR "TIA" OR "Transient Ischemic Attack" OR "cerebral infarct" OR "ischemic stroke" OR "hemorrhagic stroke") 

Search time range: 2000 - 2025. 

Language restriction: No language limitation. 

Inclusion and exclusion criteria: 

Inclusion criteria: 
P (Population): Adult patients in the emergency department, with chief complaint of dizziness, vertigo or unsteadiness. Subgroup analysis grouping: Patients with isolated dizziness: Exclude patients with neurological localization signs (such as limb weakness, facial paralysis, dysarthria, etc.). Continuously enrolled, without screening. 
I (Index Test)/C (Comparison): Not applicable. 
O (Outcome): Reports the number of patients with final diagnosis of stroke, used for calculating the prevalence. 
S (Study design): Prospective or retrospective cohort studies, cross-sectional studies. 
Exclusion criteria: 
Excluded patients without undergoing imaging examination. 
Study subjects were only specific etiology dizziness patients (such as only studying BPPV or only studying patients with confirmed stroke). 
Repeated studies of the same patients. 
Reviews, case reports, conference abstracts. 

Study screening and data extraction: 
Study screening: Use EndNote to manage literature, two reviewers independently conduct title/abstract screening and full-text screening. In case of disagreement, a third reviewer makes the decision. 
Data extraction: Two members independently complete using standardized forms, in case of disagreement, a third reviewer makes the decision. The extracted contents include: basic information of the study (author, year, country, design), population characteristics (total sample size, sample size of the isolated dizziness subgroup, average age, gender ratio, vascular risk factors), outcome data (number of stroke patients, number of TIA patients), key information on methodology (stroke diagnosis method, MRI usage rate, follow-up duration, whether continuous enrollment), information required for bias risk assessment. 

Bias risk assessment: Use the "Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) Prevalence Study Evaluation Tool" independently evaluated the bias risk of included studies by two reviewers. The evaluation items include sample frame, recruitment method, sample size, measurement indicators, statistical analysis, etc., a total of 9 items. 

Data analysis: 
Statistical methods: Calculate the point estimate value and 95% confidence interval (CI) of stroke incidence. Given that the incidence rate is expected to be heterogeneous, the random effects model (DerSimonian-Laird method) will be preferred for pooling. Use the I² statistic for quantification (I² ≥ 50% indicates substantial heterogeneity). 
Subgroup analysis: To explore the source of heterogeneity, the following subgroup analyses are planned: study design (prospective vs. retrospective). Retrospective), methods for diagnosing stroke (using MRI as the gold standard vs. only CT/clinical follow-up), hospital grade (tertiary referral center vs. community hospital), study region (North America, Europe, Asia, etc.), publication year.
Sensitivity analysis: Re-merge the effect sizes after eliminating each study one by one to test the robustness of the results.
Publication bias assessment: If the number of included studies is ≥ 10, use Egger's test and draw a funnel plot to assess publication bias.
All statistical analyses were conducted using Revman and Stata software.

title: Prevalence of occult hepatitis B infection among Treatment-naive HIV/AIDS Patients in Sub-Saharan Africa: A Protocol for Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
description:
The dual burden of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and hepatitis B virus (HBV) infections remains a major public health challenge in Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA). Both viruses share similar modes of transmission, including exposure to infected blood, unprotected sexual contact, and perinatal transmission, which explains the high prevalence of HIV/HBV co-infection in the region. ¹ Chronic infection with either virus significantly contributes to morbidity and mortality in SSA, where healthcare resources are limited and preventive strategies often face logistical barriers.
The natural history of HBV infection is determined by complex interactions between viral replication and host immune responses. Traditionally, the absence of hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) was considered evidence of viral clearance or remission.¹ However, in the 1970s, the phenomenon of occult hepatitis B infection (OBI) was first described among blood donors who tested HBsAg-negative but hepatitis B core antibody (anti-HBc)-positive, revealing ongoing viral persistence despite apparent recovery.¹,² The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends the diagnosis of HBV infection primarily through enzyme immunoassays (EIA) or rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) that detect HBsAg.³ Nevertheless, these methods may fail to identify OBI cases, as viral replication can persist at low levels undetectable by standard serological assays.⁴ The detection of covalently closed circular DNA (cccDNA) using nucleic acid testing (NAT) on liver tissue samples remains the gold standard for confirming OBI.⁴
OBI is characterized by the persistence of HBV DNA below 200 IU/L in individuals who are serologically negative for HBsAg following recovery from acute or chronic infection. ⁵ Genetic variants such as S-escape mutations and pre-S1/pre-S2 deletions may alter surface antigen expression, leading to false-negative HBsAg results in standard screening assays. ⁷-8,4
Globally, the prevalence of OBI ranges widely, from 1% to 90.9%, depending on HBV endemicity, host immune status, and diagnostic sensitivity.9 Despite increasing research interest, the prevalence and clinical relevance of OBI among antiretroviral therapy (ART)-naïve HIV patients in SSA remain poorly characterized.¹0 Studies have reported prevalence rates of 5.6% among HBsAg-negative individuals and 5.3% among ART-naïve HIV-positive patients.¹1 Similarly, Salia et al. documented a 4.7% OBI prevalence among HBsAg-negative, ART-naïve HIV patients in Ghana.¹2
Emerging evidence suggests that OBI is not a benign condition; it has been linked to advanced liver disease, particularly hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), and may contribute to HBV transmission.¹3 Consequently, the global burden of OBI, especially among immunocompromised groups such as ART-naïve HIV patients, may be underestimated. This is particularly concerning in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), where limited access to HBV DNA testing hampers accurate diagnosis and monitoring.
Rationale
Despite notable advances in the prevention and management of HIV and HBV infections, OBI continues to receive minimal attention in clinical practice, especially among individuals who are HIV-positive and yet to commence ART14,15. The coexistence of HIV and HBV presents a complex clinical challenge, as HIV-associated immune suppression may enhance HBV replication, hastening the onset of liver-related complications 16. Current HBV diagnostic approaches in SSA rely solely on HBsAg detection are insufficient, as they fail to identify individuals harboring occult infections, thereby leaving a considerable number of cases undiagnosed 17,18.
In SSA, a region marked by high HIV prevalence and endemic HBV infection, this diagnostic limitation has major public health implications 19. Individuals who are ART-naive and co-infected with undetected OBI face elevated risks of accelerated liver disease progression, HCC, and unintentional HBV transmission 20,21. Moreover, initiating ART regimens without awareness of underlying OBI can influence treatment responses and complicate disease management 22.
As emerging research continues to highlight the link between OBI and severe hepatic outcomes, understanding its prevalence in ART-naïve HIV populations across Africa has become increasingly important. Conducting a systematic review and meta-analysis will allow for a more comprehensive estimation of OBI burden, help identify diagnostic and epidemiological knowledge gaps, and provide the evidence base required to inform policy and clinical guidelines in alignment with the WHO’s global hepatitis elimination framework 23.
Aim
To explore the prevalence of OBI among ART treatment-naive patients in SSA.
Objectives
1. To estimate the prevalence of OBI among PLWHIV naive to ART.
2. To identify the diagnostic gaps in OBI diagnosis. 
Review question
1. What is the prevalence of OBI among treatment-naïve HIV patients in SSA?
2. What diagnostic methods are employed in diagnosing OBI in SSA?
Search strategy
To write a comprehensive review and meta-analysis, MEDLINE, Web of Science, PUBMED Central, Scopus, Global Health, Embase, Porquest, Africa Wide, EBSCOHOST and CINAHL databases will be searched for research papers on OBI among treatment-naïve HIV-patients in SSA from January 2010 to December 2024 taking into consideration the prevalence of OBI in Africa among person living with HIV and the OBI diagnostic methods employed in each study. This ten (10) year search frame is chosen due to the introduction of sophisticated molecular methods in HBV diagnosis and HBV DNA extraction. The following search strategies will be employed: “Hepatitis” AND “Occult OR OBI” AND “Diagnostic methods” AND “Africa”, “HIV OR Human Immunodeficiency Virus” AND “Occult hepatitis” AND “ART-naïve” AND “Sub-Saharan Africa OR SSA”, “OBI OR Occult hepatitis B” AND “Diagnosis” AND “Treatment-naïve HIV patients OR ART-naïve HIV patient” AND “Sub Saharan Africa OR Africa” etc
Inclusive and exclusive criteria 
All journal resources or articles extracted from the databases will be screened thoroughly to identify articles that meet the inclusive criteria. 
Inclusion criteria
OBI in this systematic review is defined as the presence of HBV DNA less than 200IU/L in HBsAg negative individuals with or without HBcAb.
 Studies among treatment-naïve HIV patients of 18 years and above will be considered. 
 Papers published in languages such as in English, French, Italia, Portuguese, and Arabic and have transcribed versions in English will be accepted as well. However, mix-data studies will be considered if more than 70% of the population meet the age inclusive criteria for this review. 
 Published abstracts that estimate HBV DNA in HBsAg negative patients irrespective of HbcAb and HBsAb presence will be included in the study. 
 Any study that provides evidence of OBI among a population of ART defaulters over six months will be accepted into the study.
 To be consistent with the inclusive criteria set for this systematic review, much consideration will be given to any study that provides insight in understanding the prevalence of OBI among HIV patients naive to ART treatment and who are negative for HBsAg as well as studies that access the sensitivity and specificity of diagnostic methods employed in evaluating anti-HBc and HBV DNA for the diagnosis of OBI among PLWHIV. 
Exclusive criteria
 Studies that will not define OBI as the presence of HBV DNA less than 200IU/L in HBsAg negative individuals with or without HBcAb will be excluded from the review. 
 Similarly, any study that includes HBV window period infections with confirmed HBsAg positivity of the study population after six months will be excluded. 
 Abstracts from conferences and original scripts of any study design that will aid the estimation of OBI prevalence in the target population will be excluded in the study. 
 Again, studies that estimate OBI prevalence from study population on nucleoside or nucleotide analogues will be excluded from the review. 
 Finally, journal articles that employed serological methods only and not NAT in reporting OBI presence were excluded from the study. 
Data Extraction and Management
This review will employ Endnote 20 for intext citation, checking for duplicate references and storage of final accepted references. Covidence will be utilized in ensuring de-duplication of journal articles extracted from various databases, screening for data quality of articles accepted and for data extraction. Covidence will provide an avenue for collaboration between reviewers. Titles and abstracts will be independently screened manually by Emmanuel Salia and Evans Duah. Aminama Prince will serve as an intermediary and make the final screening decision when Emmanuel and Evans are not able to resolve a disagreement on the acceptance or rejection of a paper. Non-duplicate articles will be returned to the study pool for abstract and title screening. This process will be supported with manual checkups for reference and article duplication by the reviewers involved in this study. Duplicates identified manually during abstract and title screening of journal articles will be reported separately on the PRISMA flow diagram from those identified by the software systems applied. This will ensure that any possibility for the existence of duplication of articles and references is eliminated and reported appropriately.
Data Analysis
 All reviewers involved in this study will assist in the extraction of data from the papers that meets the inclusion criteria. Key items of articles to be extracted will include the settings of each study, the characteristics of the study population, the sample type used in the diagnosis of OBI, the diagnostic method employed, the prevalence of anti-HBc or anti-HBs and OBI. The prevalence of OBI will be assessed based on the type of sample and serological principles each paper utilizes. By adapting the Hoy and colleagues’ tool of bias assessment, we will assess the risk of bias in the study. The prevalence of OBI among the target study population in SSA will be determined by assessing papers that estimated HBV DNA levels using biopsies from liver tissues, whole blood, plasma or serum irrespective of the presence of anti-HBc or anti-HBs. Also, type of laboratory protocol utilized in the detection OBI in each paper accepted in the inclusive criteria will be considered to determine the diagnostic gap in OBI detection in Africa. I2 statistics and bivariate random effects models will be used in determining the heterogeneity, and the sensitivity and specificity of anti-HBc in the diagnosis of OBI among PLWHIV in SSA Africa naive to ART. STATA v20 will be used in all analysis and the guidelines by PRISMA will be duly followed.

title: Diagnostic Accuracy, Threshold Comparability, and Inter-Platform Variability of Automated Plasma p-tau217 Assays in Alzheimer's Disease: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
description:
This is the pre-registered protocol for a systematic review and meta-analysis examining the diagnostic accuracy, positivity threshold comparability, and inter-platform variability of automated plasma phosphorylated tau at threonine 217 (p-tau217) immunoassays for the detection of Alzheimer's disease pathology.
Plasma p-tau217 has emerged as the leading blood-based biomarker for early Alzheimer's disease, with multiple automated platforms now commercially or research-available — including the Fujirebio Lumipulse G pTau217 (CLEIA), ALZpath Simoa (Quanterix HD-X), and Janssen/J&J pTau217+ (Simoa). Despite statistically equivalent AUC performance across platforms (0.84–0.90) for amyloid-PET positivity, these platforms report p-tau217 in incommensurable units with substantially different absolute concentration values, precluding direct threshold interchangeability. No systematic review has comprehensively synthesised the diagnostic accuracy, threshold distribution, or inter-platform binary call concordance of these automated assays.
This review will: (1) pool sensitivity and specificity per platform using a bivariate random-effects model; (2) catalogue and compare positivity thresholds via narrative synthesis anchored to Aβ-PET Centiloid cut-points; (3) quantify inter-platform binary call concordance in head-to-head studies; and (4) describe the effects of pre-analytical and analytical factors on p-tau217 measurements per platform.
The protocol was developed in accordance with PRISMA-DTA 2018, PRISMA-P 2015, and QUADAS-2. Evidence certainty will be assessed using GRADE-DTA.

title: Do Data-Driven Models Really Outperform Knowledge-Driven Models in Groundwater Potential Mapping? A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Validation Design and Predictive Performance in Arid and Semi-Arid Regions
description:
Groundwater potential mapping has expanded rapidly over the past decade, moving from expert-weighted multi-criteria decision models such as the analytical hierarchy process toward data-driven machine learning, deep learning, and Bayesian hybrid formulations. Published accuracies have risen in parallel, and the field increasingly treats this rise as evidence that newer algorithms recover hydrogeological structure that expert weighting cannot capture. That inference has not yet been tested through a formal evidence synthesis.

The purpose of this systematic review and meta-analysis is to determine whether data-driven and knowledge–data hybrid models genuinely outperform knowledge-driven models in groundwater potential mapping, and to quantify how much of any apparent advantage is attributable to differences in validation design rather than to the modelling algorithm itself. Reported predictive skill in this literature depends heavily on choices that lie outside the algorithm, most notably how non-potential or pseudo-absence points are constructed, how training and validation sets are separated in space, and how dense the underlying well inventory is. Where negative samples are drawn from topographically distinct terrain such as mountainous highlands, a classifier can separate them on elevation alone, and the resulting accuracy reveals little about groundwater prospectivity. Until these design factors are modelled explicitly, a genuine paradigm advantage cannot be distinguished from an artefact of study design.

The review will synthesise primary studies published between January 2015 and 2026 that produce a validated groundwater potential, prospectivity, or recharge-potential map for a defined basin, watershed, wadi system, aquifer, or administrative unit located in an arid, semi-arid, or hyper-arid setting, using conditioning factors derived from remote sensing and geospatial data. Eligible modelling approaches span four families: knowledge-driven multi-criteria decision analysis; bivariate and multivariate statistical models; machine learning and deep learning; and knowledge–data hybrids in which expert judgment and empirical data jointly determine model structure or parameters, including Bayesian belief networks with expert-specified conditional probability tables and expert-weighted models used to initialise or ensemble a data-driven learner. Peer-reviewed journal articles and conference papers reporting at least one quantitative validation metric against a georeferenced inventory of wells, boreholes, or springs will be included.

Searches will be conducted in Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, and Google Scholar. Screening and data extraction will be performed independently and in duplicate, with inter-rater agreement reported. The primary effect size is the within-study difference in area under the receiver operating characteristic curve between models applied to the same study area and inventory, a design that holds study area, well density, elevation model resolution, and conditioning-factor set constant and therefore isolates the contribution of the modelling paradigm far more cleanly than a between-study comparison of headline accuracies. Pooled performance will be estimated using random-effects models, with a bivariate sensitivity–specificity model fitted where confusion-matrix data permit. Meta-regression will test pre-specified moderators including negative-sample construction, presence-to-absence ratio, validation scheme, inventory size and density, aquifer type, elevation model resolution, aridity, and publication year. Risk of bias will be appraised using an adaptation of QUADAS-2 to groundwater mapping, and publication bias examined through funnel plots, Egger's regression, and cumulative meta-analysis by year.

Three outcomes are expected. First, a quantitative estimate of how much of the apparent advantage of data-driven over expert-weighted models is attributable to validation design, which speaks directly to how the next generation of groundwater mapping studies should be constructed. Second, a reporting-standards assessment identifying which quantities the field routinely omits and which are required for future evidence synthesis. Third, an evaluation of whether knowledge–data hybrids offer a genuine advantage in low-inventory basins, the setting in which most water-scarce regions actually operate and in which purely data-driven learning is least well supported. The findings are intended to inform both methodological practice in groundwater prospectivity modelling and the practical siting of exploration boreholes in data-scarce dryland aquifers.

title: Diagnosing Quark–Gluon Entanglement Beyond Spatiotemporal Separation: A Sensitivity–Specificity Framework ( By Hema Kasisomayajula)
description:
**Summary / Description**

This manuscript examines **quantum entanglement (QE)** beyond traditional **spatiotemporal diagnostics**, addressing regimes where geometric separation between entangled subsystems collapses, such as **confined quark–gluon systems** within hadrons or **high-energy particle collisions**. Standard approaches based on **Bell-type inequalities** and spatial separation are insufficient to uniquely identify entanglement in these dense, ultra-fast environments. We introduce a **correlation-based framework** utilizing **sensitivity and specificity metrics** to classify and detect quantum correlations when spatiotemporal markers are degenerate. 

We review the **earliest experimental recordings of entanglement**, including the **Freedman–Clauser (1972) experiment** and subsequent **Aspect et al. (1982) demonstrations**, as foundational cases of photon entanglement. At higher energy scales, **ATLAS (2024)** observations of **top quark pair entanglement** highlight the persistence of quantum correlations among partons, while **heavy-ion collision experiments (NA35, NA49)** provide empirical evidence that hadronic outputs encode **underlying quark–gluon correlated behavior**. Despite the lack of unique spatiotemporal signatures for these events, correlations manifest as measurable, **information-theoretic constraints** among dynamical degrees of freedom, offering a pathway to identify **unique entanglement events in dense QCD media**. 

By drawing a parallel with **Navier–Stokes turbulence**, where local geometric intuition fails but correlations remain measurable, the manuscript proposes that **ubiquitous entanglement** in confined systems can be systematically identified using **statistical and structural diagnostics**. Keywords for discoverability include: **quantum entanglement, quark-gluon plasma, heavy-ion collisions, top quark entanglement, correlation-based diagnostics, sensitivity, specificity, QCD, nonlocal correlations, high-energy physics, confined systems, information-theoretic entanglement, Navier–Stokes analogy, dense matter quantum correlations**. 

This work provides a **conceptual and methodological framework** for understanding and identifying entanglement in regimes where traditional spacetime-based signatures fail, offering a bridge between **high-energy particle physics, quantum information theory, and statistical correlation diagnostics**.
