title: Comparative Prognostic Performance of Oxygenation Indices for Mortality in Adult ARDS: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
description:
Background: Oxygenation indices such as the PaO₂/FiO₂ (P/F) ratio are central to the classification and severity assessment of acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). However, alternative indices — including the SpO₂/FiO₂ (S/F) ratio, Oxygenation Index (OI), and Oxygen Saturation Index (OSI) — are increasingly reported in clinical studies and may differ in their prognostic performance for mortality.

Objective: To systematically review and quantitatively compare the prognostic performance of multiple oxygenation indices (P/F, S/F, OI, OSI) for predicting in-hospital and 28-day mortality in adult patients with ARDS.

Methods: We will conduct a PRISMA-compliant systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis of observational cohort studies. Adjusted association measures (e.g., OR, HR) and discrimination metrics (e.g., AUC, sensitivity, specificity) will be extracted where available. Between-study heterogeneity will be assessed using I² and τ², with predefined subgroup and sensitivity analyses.

Significance: While previous meta-analyses have evaluated the prognostic value of individual oxygenation indices (e.g., PaO₂/FiO₂ alone), no comprehensive synthesis has compared multiple indices within a unified meta-analytic framework. This study aims to clarify the relative prognostic utility of commonly used oxygenation metrics in ARDS, informing clinical interpretation and future research.

title: Resting-State Functional Connectivity Heterogeneity in Adult ADHD: Protocol for a Systematic Review of Methodological and Clinical Contributors and Implications for Neuropsychological Assessment
description: This registration describes the protocol for a systematic review of resting-state functional connectivity in adults aged 18 years or older with clinically diagnosed attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). The review will synthesise case-control, subgroup, and within-ADHD dimensional evidence; characterise the anatomical and neural-network distribution of connectivity findings; and examine methodological and clinical characteristics that may contribute to between-study heterogeneity. Prespecified methodological factors include acquisition parameters, resting-state instructions, preprocessing, head-motion control, nuisance and global signal regression, parcellation, connectivity estimation, and statistical correction. Clinical factors include ADHD presentation, symptom severity, medication status, psychiatric comorbidity, age, and sex or gender. Associations between resting-state functional connectivity and objective neuropsychological performance will be synthesised separately from symptom ratings and subjective cognitive measures. The primary approach will be structured synthesis without meta-analysis, with quantitative pooling undertaken only for sufficiently comparable independent samples. This is not a diagnostic-test-accuracy review and will not evaluate resting-state fMRI as a replacement for clinical diagnosis.

title: Application of Artificial Intelligence in the Diagnosis of Arbovirus-Related Diseases: A Scoping Review
description:
Introduction: Arboviral diseases represent an expanding global health challenge, particularly in tropical and subtropical regions affected by climate change, urbanization, and vector proliferation. Dengue, chikungunya, Zika, and yellow fever share overlapping clinical manifestations that hinder early differential diagnosis and may delay appropriate management. Conventional diagnostic methods are limited by cross-reactivity, cost, infrastructure requirements, and narrow diagnostic windows. In this context, artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a promising tool to enhance diagnostic accuracy and support clinical decision-making through the integration of clinical, laboratory, imaging, and epidemiological data. However, the existing evidence remains dispersed and methodologically heterogeneous. Therefore, this scoping review aims to map the available scientific evidence on the application of AI in the diagnosis and clinical decision-support of arboviral diseases.
Methodology: A scoping review will be conducted following the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) framework and reported in accordance with PRISMA-ScR guidelines. Studies published between 2016 and 2026 in English or Spanish will be included. A comprehensive search will be performed in PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and ScienceDirect, complemented by gray literature and snowballing strategies. Two independent reviewers will screen titles, abstracts, and full texts, with disagreements resolved by a third reviewer. Extracted data will include arbovirus type, AI methodology, diagnostic setting, and reported outcomes. Findings will be synthesized through descriptive and thematic analysis.
Expected Results: The review is expected to provide a systematic mapping of AI-based diagnostic applications for arboviral diseases, identify prevailing algorithms and data sources, and examine their contributions to early diagnosis and clinical decision-making. It will also highlight methodological limitations, implementation challenges, and knowledge gaps to guide future research and strengthen arboviral surveillance and diagnostic strategies.

title: Artificial Intelligence in the Diagnostic Imaging of Bone Tumours: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
description:
Background
Primary bone tumours are rare, accounting for approximately 0.2% of all malignancies, with osteosarcoma, chondrosarcoma, and Ewing sarcoma representing the most common entities. Bone metastases occur in up to 70% of patients with advanced breast, prostate, and lung cancers, making them a far more common clinical challenge. Accurate and timely radiological diagnosis is critical: delays in diagnosis of primary bone sarcomas are associated with larger tumour volume at presentation, higher rates of amputation, and worse overall survival.
Conventional imaging interpretation relies on radiologists' expertise in recognising subtle radiographic features. However, the rarity of primary bone tumours means that most general radiologists encounter fewer than five cases per year, contributing to a reported misdiagnosis rate of 15%–30% on initial radiography. Even for experienced musculoskeletal radiologists, differentiating benign from malignant lesions on MRI or CT remains challenging.
Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly deep learning using convolutional neural networks (CNNs), has demonstrated expert-level performance across a range of diagnostic imaging tasks in oncology. In musculoskeletal radiology, AI models have been developed for bone tumour detection, segmentation, and classification across multiple imaging modalities, with reported performance comparable to subspecialist radiologists in selected studies.
Several narrative reviews have summarised the applications of AI in bone and soft-tissue tumour imaging. However, these are susceptible to selection bias and do not provide pooled quantitative estimates of diagnostic performance. Prior systematic reviews have addressed narrow aspects of the topic — radiomics in chondrosarcoma, deep learning for pulmonary metastasis detection in osteosarcoma, machine learning for bone metastasis detection — but a comprehensive meta-analysis encompassing all imaging modalities and all tumour types is lacking. With the marked increase in AI bone tumour imaging studies published since 2021, a quantitative synthesis is urgently needed to establish benchmark performance metrics, identify sources of heterogeneity, and evaluate the readiness of AI models for clinical translation.
Purpose
The purpose of this systematic review and meta-analysis is to evaluate the diagnostic performance of AI models for the imaging-based detection, classification, and characterisation of primary bone tumours and bone metastases, including pre-specified subgroup analyses by imaging modality, tumour type, and model architecture.
Primary Research Question
What is the diagnostic performance (sensitivity, specificity, and AUROC) of artificial intelligence models for the detection, classification, and characterisation of primary bone tumours and bone metastases across radiography, CT, MRI, PET/CT, and bone scintigraphy?
Methods
Search strategy: A comprehensive search was conducted across PubMed, Ovid MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library from January 2015 to August 2025. MeSH terms and free-text terms were combined across three concept groups: (a) bone tumour, (b) imaging modality, and (c) artificial intelligence. Reference lists of all included studies and relevant review articles were screened manually.
Inclusion criteria: (1) original research studies evaluating AI-based models for diagnostic imaging of primary bone tumours or bone metastases; (2) studies using radiography, CT, MRI, PET/CT, or bone scintigraphy; (3) studies reporting at least one quantitative performance metric (sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, AUROC, F1 score, or precision); (4) human participants; (5) full-text availability in English; (6) minimum sample size of 50 patients.
Screening: Two reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts, followed by full-text evaluation. Discrepancies were resolved by consensus discussion with a third reviewer.
Data extraction: Two reviewers independently extracted data using a standardised, piloted extraction form. Extracted data included: first author, publication year, country, study design, sample size, tumour type, imaging modality, AI model architecture, reference standard, and all reported performance metrics.
Risk of bias assessment: Methodological quality was assessed using QUADAS-2, adapted for AI-based diagnostic studies. Two reviewers independently assessed each study, with disagreements resolved by consensus.
Statistical analysis: Bivariate random-effects meta-analysis using the DerSimonian–Laird method was performed for sensitivity, specificity, and AUROC, with pooled estimates calculated after Freeman–Tukey double arcsine transformation. Between-study heterogeneity was assessed using the I² statistic. Pre-specified subgroup analyses were performed by: (a) imaging modality, (b) tumour type, (c) model architecture, and (d) study design. Sensitivity analyses were performed excluding studies with a high overall risk of bias. Publication bias was assessed using Deeks' funnel plot asymmetry test. All analyses were conducted in R (version 4.3.0).
Expected Outcomes
1. Pooled diagnostic performance estimates — We expect AI models to achieve pooled sensitivity and specificity exceeding 85%, with pooled AUROC exceeding 0.90, providing the first comprehensive benchmark across all imaging modalities and tumour types.
2. Modality-specific performance differences — We anticipate that MRI-based models will demonstrate the highest pooled diagnostic accuracy, given the superior soft-tissue contrast provided by MRI, followed by CT-based and radiographic models.
3. Identification of key methodological limitations — We expect to find that most studies are single-centre, retrospective designs with limited external validation, inconsistent adherence to standardised reporting frameworks (CLAIM, FUTURE-AI), and considerable between-study heterogeneity.
4. Evidence-based recommendations — The review will identify the highest-priority gaps in the current evidence base, including the near-total absence of prospective validation studies and the need for multi-reader multi-case study designs, and provide actionable recommendations for future research and clinical translation.

title: Mapping Artificial Intelligence-Mediated Nursing Processes in Intensive Care Units for Critically Ill Oncology Patients: A Scoping Review Protocol
description:
This scoping review protocol maps the current state of literature on Artificial Intelligence (AI)-mediated Nursing Processes (Sistematização da Assistência de Enfermagem – SAE) in Intensive Care Units (ICUs) for critically ill oncology patients. The review focuses specifically on how AI technologies — including Large Language Models (LLMs) and Clinical Decision Support Systems (CDSS) — integrate with standardized nursing taxonomies (NANDA-I, NOC, and NIC), and on the validation metrics used to assess these systems, namely diagnostic accuracy, Content Validity Index (CVI), and Kappa coefficient.
The purpose of this review is twofold. First, it addresses a genuine gap in the literature: preliminary searches across PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, ScienceDirect, and OSF Registries confirmed that no existing scoping review or registered protocol simultaneously covers the intersection of AI-mediated Nursing Process, the ICU context, and the critically ill oncology population evaluated through these specific validation metrics. Related reviews exist for AI in nursing decision-making broadly, AI in critical care nursing, AI in oncology nursing, and computerized decision-support systems built on NNN taxonomies — but none combine all three elements together. Second, the review responds to a practical need in critical care nursing: as AI tools increasingly assist nurses in formulating diagnoses, predicting outcomes, and selecting interventions in high-acuity settings, the validity, safety, and clinical reliability of these AI-generated outputs must be systematically understood before broader adoption.
Following the JBI methodology for scoping reviews (Peters et al., 2020/2024) and reported according to the PRISMA-ScR checklist (Tricco et al., 2018), the review will search PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, CINAHL, LILACS, Google Scholar, and ProQuest Dissertations and Theses for quantitative, qualitative, and mixed-methods studies — including grey literature — addressing AI-driven nursing systems in adult ICUs, with a specific focus on oncology patients. Two independent reviewers will conduct title/abstract and full-text screening, followed by structured data extraction covering study metadata, population/setting, AI technology type, taxonomy use, validation metrics, and key findings.
Expected outcomes include: a comprehensive map of how AI technologies are currently being integrated into the Nursing Process for critically ill oncology patients; a characterization of the methodological approaches used to validate these AI systems (particularly diagnostic accuracy, CVI, and Kappa agreement); identification of technological and methodological gaps in the field; and a narrative synthesis highlighting clinical benefits, ethical considerations, and implementation challenges. These findings are intended to guide future empirical research and inform the responsible development of AI-assisted nursing tools in high-acuity oncology critical care settings.

title: Current Trends in Food Adulteration and Emerging Analytical Techniques for Food Authentication: A Systematic Review
description: Food fraud and adulteration present significant economic and public health risks within the global supply chain. This systematic review and meta-analysis investigates current trends in food adulteration practices and evaluates the efficacy of emerging analytical technologies for robust food authentication. Specifically, the review focuses on the application of rapid, non-destructive, and high-throughput techniques such as near-infrared (NIR) spectroscopy, mass spectrometry, and portable biosensors combined with advanced chemometric modeling (e.g., PCA, LDA, PLSR) and machine learning algorithms. The primary objective is to synthesize existing literature to assess the sensitivity, specificity, and limits of detection of these methodologies across complex food matrices including dairy, oils, spices, and meat. Furthermore, this project aims to identify existing technological gaps and provide a standardized framework for the future implementation of these analytical tools in routine food safety and quality monitoring.

title: Steerable guidewireless microcatheter systems for neurointerventions: a systematic rapid review
description:
This study aims to appraise evidence of steerable guidewireless microcatheter systems for neurointerventions. Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines were used to conduct and report this systematic review. A systematic search was conducted across MEDLINE (via PubMed), Cochrane Registry (via Cochrane Library), U.S. National Institutes of Health Ongoing Trials (via clinicaltrials.gov), World Health Organisation International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (via trialsearch.who.int) and IEEE (via IEEE XPLORE) databases for published articles before 5th of October, 2024. Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies 2 (QUADAS-2) and Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology assessments were used to offer appraisal towards study designs and evaluation of index (test) models in the context of the current review. 7 articles were included in this review after screening in two phases by three board certified clinicians against pre-piloted eligibility forms; three studies were of clinical study design with the remaining four reporting ex-vivo with/without in-vivo experiments. 38 patients were enrolled across the clinical designs who received the index (test) model with only one multi-centre non-randomised trial included in this study. No reports of adverse clinical outcomes or mortality outcomes related to the usage of index devices was reported. Across all the 38 clinical interventions reported; microguidewire free guidance was demonstrated in 14 (36.84) clinical interventions conducted with procedural deficiencies reported among 14 cases (36.84). Technical description of developmental index models been tabulated with novel findings discussed with neurovascular navigation demonstrated among 3 such models (75.0). Only two commercially available minimally invasive microcatheter platforms are available with design specificity and literature evidence for use in neurointerventions as informed by our systematic search; however due to lack of reference standards or case-control study designs across the included records, we did not offer comparisons of these systems against currently available gold standard microcatheters and/or robotic endovascular surgical systems. Developmental efforts in this context shows evidence of grade 4 technological readiness suggested by the sample included in this study. Despite evidence for ease of navigation with these systems in complex anatomical geometries in endovascular workflows, long term follow-up studies and association with better functional and/or clinical outcomes are unavailable. Future research should consider randomised case control study designs to establish associations and accelerated clinical translation of in-vivo and/or ex-vivo index models will offer expansion of the endovascular surgical toolkits to improve neurosurgical outcomes in minimally invasive microcatheter surgeries.

description: This study seeks to identify a salivary diagnostic panel for the assessment of periodontal disease. Saliva specimens from a single visit will be analyzed for seven host response proteins and six specific oral bacteria for their potential as a panel to yield high sensitivity and high specificity for discriminating periodontitis from health and gingivitis. The primary outcome is the reproducibility of a salivary diagnostic panel and/or risk calculator that contains the fewest number of analytes that can discriminate health and gingivitis from periodontal disease with >95% sensitivity and >95% specificity.

title: Effectiveness of Multidisciplinary (MDT) Team Activation Models and Algorithms in Collaborative Care for Pediatric Cancer Patients in Hospital
description:
Multidisciplinary Teams (MDTs) have been widely recognized as an important approach to improving the quality and safety of healthcare services. However, the implementation of MDTs across hospital settings shows significant variation, particularly in aspects of team activation, when MDTs are activated, who is involved, and based on what criteria.
Most of the literature focuses on MDTs as collaborative structures or forums, while MDT activation mechanisms as systematic decisions are rarely studied. MDT activation is often ad hoc, relying on individual experience, without the support of standardized algorithms or decision rules. This situation has the potential to lead to inefficiencies and inconsistent collaboration.
Pediatric cancer care requires highly coordinated across disciplines (oncology, surgery, nursing, pharmacy, psychosocial support), to optimize diagnostic accuracy, reduce delays in treatment, enhance clinical outcomes
While MDTs or tumor boards are widely recommended, their activation in routine remains inconsistent. Many hospitals rely on ad-hoc consultations or fixed-schedule meetings, leading to delayed decision-making, fragmented care pathways, and variable guideline adherence. Trigger-based activation models and clinical algorithms offer a systematic approach to mobilize MDTs expertise precisely when clinical, pathway, or digital thresholds are met. However, evidence on their effectiveness in pediatric oncology remains fragmented across clinical, informatics, and implementation science literatures. Moreover, evidence regarding which models are most effective, what components drive success, and how algorithms are implemented remains fragmented. No systematic synthesis has evaluated how structured activation mechanisms impact process efficiency, clinical safety, family-centered outcomes, or resource utilization. 
This review will generate evidence to inform the design of a context-adaptive MDT activation model for pediatric cancer care, with explicit relevance to both high-resource and resource-constrained hospital settings.

title: Diagnostic Accuracy of Circulating Myostatin for Sarcopenia: A Systematic Review and Diagnostic Test Accuracy Meta-Analysis
description:
This project is a systematic review and diagnostic test accuracy meta-analysis evaluating circulating myostatin for detecting sarcopenia in adults, The review will compare serum or plasma myostatin measurements with established sarcopenia criteria such as EWGSOP2 or AWGS.
Relevant databases will be searched systematically, Two reviewers will independently screen studies, extract diagnostic accuracy data and assess methodological quality using QUADAS-2. When sufficient data are available, pooled sensitivity, specificity, likelihood ratios, diagnostic odds ratio and the summary ROC curve will be calculated using appropriate random effects models.
The review aims to determine whether circulating myostatin has adequate diagnostic performance for clinical use and to identify sources of heterogeneity, research gaps and the need for standardized thresholds and prospective validation.

description: This project contains the protocol and materials for a scoping review mapping the landscape of artificial intelligence (AI)-enhanced point-of-care (POC) diagnostic technologies for infectious diseases in resource-limited settings. The review addresses which diseases and diagnostic modalities have been targeted, what AI techniques and deployment platforms are used, where studies have been conducted, what diagnostic accuracy is reported, and what barriers to implementation exist. title: Hematoxylin-eosin histochemistry for identification of dermatophytosis: A diagnostic accuracy study
description:
The goal of this study is to determine the diagnostic accuracy of routine Hematoxylin-eosin (H&E) histochemistry for identification of dermatophytosis in skin biopsies. The index test will be H&E stained slides and the gold standard diagnosis will be the final pathology report diagnosis. To do this, we will obtain a consecutive series of H&E slides from skin biopsies where periodic-acid Schiff histochemistry was performed to test for dermatophytosis, accruing cases from July 1, 2023 until September 30, 2024 . 

The slides will be evaluated by four observers at different levels of training. Each observer will rate the H&E slide as positive or negative for dermatophytosis. The observers will be blinded to the diagnosis and all clinical information. After a wash-out period of at least one week, the observers will review a teaching PowerPoint on clues to diagnosis of dermatophytosis, and then re-score the cases as positive or negative for dermatophytosis. Statistical analysis will be performed to identify diagnostic accuracy measures, pre- and post-course differences in accuracy, differences in accuracy by training level, and diagnostic accuracy of "clues" to dermatophytosis.

title: Validity and reliability of the assessment and diagnosis of musculoskeletal conditions using telemedicine: A systematic review
description:
RESEARCH OBJECTIVE 
To conduct a systematic review to assess the validity and reliability of the assessment and diagnosis of musculoskeletal conditions using synchronous telemedicine compared to standard in-person clinical assessment and diagnosis. 

METHODS
The protocol for this systematic review will be registered with the Open Science Framework (OSF) Registries. 

ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA
Population:
This systematic review will target studies of individuals of all ages (general and athletic populations) who present for the clinical assessment or diagnosis of a musculoskeletal (MSK) condition. The International Classification of Diseases lists MSK conditions as a diverse group of over 150 diagnoses that affects the locomotor system: specifically, muscles, bones, joints, tendons, and ligaments(1). MSK conditions are commonly described by their anatomical location and through their association with pain and impaired physical function despite their variability with regard to pathophysiology(1). Furthermore, MSK conditions can vary from those of acute onset and short duration to lifelong disorders(1). Examples of MSK conditions included in this systematic review include low back and neck pain, arthritis, musculoskeletal injury sequelae, and fractures. Patients with neurological conditions such as traumatic brain injury, spinal cord injuries, headaches (e.g. migraine, tension-type, cluster, cervicogenic, etc.) and movement disorders (e.g. Parkinson’s Disease, multiple sclerosis, muscular dystrophy, cerebral palsy, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, etc.) will be excluded from this study.

Exposure: 
The exposure is the clinical assessment and diagnosis (of risk factors for serious pathology, pain, function, barriers to recovery) of MSK conditions by synchronous, or real-time, telemedicine delivered by any healthcare provider. A clinical assessment includes the combination of a detailed patient history and physical examination to establish a correct clinical diagnosis(2). Studies assessing only single components of a clinical assessment (e.g. range of motion, strength, visual inspection, orthopedic or functional test etc.) will be excluded from this review. Telemedicine is defined by the World Health Organization as “the delivery of health care services, where distance is a critical factor, by all health care professionals using information and communication technologies for the exchange of valid information for assessment and diagnosis, treatment and prevention of disease and injuries, research and evaluation, and for the continuing education of health care providers, all in the interests of advancing the health of individuals and their communities”(3). Studies of clinical assessments or diagnoses using telemedicine with a completely asynchronous component will be excluded from this review. 

Comparator: 
The comparator is the clinical assessment, including a health history and physical examination (of risk factors for serious pathology, pain, function, barriers to recovery) of individuals with musculoskeletal conditions by standard care (e.g., in-person visits) by any healthcare provider.

Outcome: 
The outcomes are the reliability and validity of clinical assessments and diagnoses of individuals with musculoskeletal complaints by healthcare providers. Reliability is defined as the extent to which repeated measurements of a stable phenomenon by different people and instruments at different times and places produce similar results(4). Validity is defined as the degree to which the results of a measurement match to the true state of the phenomenon being measured(4). 

STUDY DESIGN/CHARACTERISTICS
Eligible studies must meet the following criteria 1) articles published in English in peer-reviewed journals (to increase feasibility) Unpublished manuscripts, letters, guidelines, commentaries, conference proceedings, editorials, theses, books, meeting abstracts, lectures, consensus development statements and other descriptive publications will be excluded. A list of potentially relevant articles in other languages will be included as an appendix in the final manuscript.

INFORMATION SOURCES AND SEARCH STRATEGY
MEDLINE, CINAHL, EMBASE, PsycINFO, and SPORTDiscus will be searched from inception to the proposed search date (to be determined a priori). The search strategy will be developed following consultation with an experienced health sciences librarian and will be reviewed by a second librarian using the Peer Review of Electronic Search Strategies Checklist(5,6) (see Appendix). The search strategy will be developed in MEDLINE and adapted to the other bibliographic databases. Search terms will include subject headings (e.g., MeSH in MEDLINE) for each database and free text words for the key concepts of telemedicine, clinical assessment, in-person assessment, and validity and reliability. EndNote will be used to delete duplicate references electronically across databases and record the number of duplicates identified. 

DATA COLLECTION AND ANALYSIS
Study Selection:
A two-phase (titles and abstracts; full-text articles) screening process will be used to select eligible studies. In phase I screening, pairs of independent reviewers will screen citation titles and abstracts to determine the eligibility of studies (categorizing studies as possibly relevant or irrelevant). Pairs of independent reviewers will screen possibly relevant studies in full text during phase II screening to determine eligibility and document reasons for exclusion. Reviewers will meet to discuss disagreements and reach consensus on study eligibility. A third reviewer will be involved provided consensus cannot be reached. Study authors will be contacted for additional information as needed when screening, assessing risk of bias, and conducting data extraction.

Data items and data collection process: 
The lead author will extract data from eligible studies to build evidence tables (see Appendix). A second reviewer will independently extract study results (e.g., reliability and validity measures, 95% CI) and any disagreements will be discussed to reach consensus. For all other data items a second reviewer will verify by checking the extracted data to minimize error.

From each study, extracted data will include author, publication year, study design, setting and participant characteristics(e.g., sample size, mean age, sex, and MSK condition), definition of exposure (characteristics of the clinical assessment delivered through telehealth), validity (index test, reference standard, and Chronbach’s alpha) and/or reliability (intraclass correlation efficient) outcomes, and 95% confidence intervals. 

Methodological quality and risk of bias appraisal:
Pairs of trained reviewers will critically appraise eligible studies using the Quality Appraisal Tool for studies of diagnostic Reliability, or QAREL, to assess the methodological quality of the reliability studies6. To assess the methodological quality of the validity studies, pairs of trained reviewers will critically appraise eligible studies using the Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies-2, or QUADAS-27. Reviewers will meet to reach consensus on the risk of bias of studies and a third independent reviewer will be involved to resolve any disagreements. 

Evidence Synthesis:
We will use the best evidence synthesis methodology and qualitatively synthesize the data from acceptable quality (low risk of bias) studies(10, 11). This type of synthesis not only allows conclusions to be provided based on the best available evidence, it also can report an insufficient level of evidence to make any conclusions(10). We will use evidence tables to create summary statements. We will stratify our synthesis by musculoskeletal regions of complaint (e.g. low back pain, neck pain, headache, etc.) and type of evidence (reliability and/or validity).

Following appraisal, studies that are considered adequate for low risk of bias will be classified according to the classification system described by Sackett and Haynes(9). This system is designed to classify diagnostic studies for the potential clinical utility and usefulness of a test in clinical practice(9). Studies in Phase I assess differences in the results of the diagnostic test between patients with a known condition and healthy individuals. Studies in Phase II assess the association between test results compared to a reference standard in patients diagnosed with the condition. Phase I and II studies identify the clinical utility of a diagnostic test(9). Phase III studies assess the ability of a test to perform in a population with the suspected condition(9). Phase IV studies examine the outcomes of patients who were assessed with the test compared to untested individuals(9). Phase III and IV studies identify the usefulness of a test in clinical practice(9).

title: Differences Between Parent and Child Reports in Disordered Eating Behaviours and Cognitions
description:
Disordered eating behaviours and cognitions in children and adolescents are often assessed using both self-report and parent-report tools. These perspectives can diverge significantly, affecting diagnostic accuracy and treatment planning. Despite the clear need for early intervention, assessing youth for eating disorders (identifying behaviours and cognitions) can be challenging. Children may have difficulty identifying internal symptoms and describing their mental state due to their developing cognitive capacities (Mariano et al., 2013). Moreover, many adolescents with eating disorders are ambivalent about treatment and may deny, distort, and/or downplay their symptoms (Fisher et al., 2001). A multi-informant approach may facilitate a more accurate assessment of eating disorder psychopathology in children and adolescents (Swanson et al., 2014). This systematic review will look into current literature to explore the nature and implications of discrepancies between parent and child reports.

References: 
1.Mariano, P., Watson, H. J., Leach, D. J., McCormack, J., Forbes, D. A. (2013). Parent–child concordance in reporting of child eating disorder pathology as assessed by the eating disorder examination. International Journal of Eating Disorders, 46, 617–625.
2. Fisher, M., Schneider, M., Burns, J., Symons, H., Mandel, F. S. (2001). Differences between adolescents and young adults at presentation to an eating disorders program. Journal of Adolescent Health, 28(3), 222–227. 
3. Swanson, S. A., Aloisio, K. M., Horton, N. J., Sonneville, K. R., Crosby, R. D., Eddy, K. T., Field, A. E., Micali, N. (2014). Assessing eating disorder symptoms in adolescence: Is there a role for multiple informants? International Journal of Eating Disorders, 47(5), 475–482.

title: Wireless versus Conventional Cardiofetal Monitoring in the Early Detection of Fetal Abnormalities: A Systematic Review Protocol
description: This systematic review protocol aims to evaluate the efficacy and safety of wireless fetal cardiotocography (wCTG, telemetry, wearables, TAfECG) compared to conventional wired monitoring in the early detection of fetal abnormalities in high- and low-risk pregnant women. Fetal monitoring is crucial for maternal and infant health, but conventional CTG restricts maternal mobility, negatively impacting the birth experience. Wireless technology promises greater comfort and autonomy, with the potential to improve maternal and neonatal outcomes. Using the PIRO strategy, this protocol details the methodology for identifying, selecting, evaluating, and synthesizing evidence from randomized clinical trials and observational studies. The primary outcome will be diagnostic accuracy in detecting fetal cardiotocography abnormalities. Secondary outcomes include maternal satisfaction, mobility, cesarean section rates, neonatal asphyxia, and cost-effectiveness. Risk of bias assessment will be performed using RoB 2 and ROBINS-I, and confidence in the evidence will be assessed using the GRADE system. The estimated timeline is 16 months, with prospective enrollment in OSF and PROSPERO. The results of this review will provide robust evidence to inform clinical practice and future research, aiming to optimize prenatal and intrapartum care.

title: Strategies for Assessing Post-Hospitalization Outcomes in Trauma Survivors and their Feasibility of Implementation: A Scoping Review Protocol
description:
ABSTRACT

Background: Each year, physical trauma affects over one billion people worldwide, generating a substantial burden in terms of mortality, disability, and productivity loss. The period following hospital discharge, encompassing the transition to home as well as outpatient and community-based follow-up care, represents a critical phase in the recovery process for individuals who have experienced traumatic injuries. Yet, this phase remains poorly documented. 

Objective: We aim to 1) map data on assessment strategies for various outcomes among trauma survivors after hospital discharge, including the tools and administration methods used, as well as the resources required, the perceived relevance of these strategies, and the barriers and facilitators to their implementation, and 2) compare the assessment strategies and the feasibility of their implementation in terms of response rates, resource use, costs, and sustainability or continuation beyond the study period.

Methods: We will conduct a scoping review using Joanna Briggs Institute methodology. We will search MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, Scopus, and PsycINFO for studies published since 1990 to reflect the evolution of contemporary follow-up practices, including the emergence of Patient-Reported Outcome Measures (PROMs) and digital tools. There will be no language restrictions. We will consider studies involving any trauma survivors, focusing on the evaluation of post-discharge health indicators. The period following hospital discharge, including the transition to short-term stays in rehabilitation facilities, the return home, and long-term outpatient or community-based follow-up care. Two independent reviewers will screen studies and extract data on population characteristics, assessment strategies, and feasibility dimensions. Results will be analyzed thematically and presented narratively. Counts and proportions of assessment strategies, their characteristics and associated barriers and facilitators will be presented. We also plan to conduct subgroup analyses according to clinical and social determinants and contextual factors. This protocol has been registered on the Open Science Framework.

Expected Results: This review will provide an overview of current practices regarding outcome assessment strategies for trauma patients after hospital discharge. It will provide data on the resources needed and contextual factors influencing the implementation of each assessment strategy. Findings will inform the design of sustainable strategies for monitoring long-term outcomes in trauma populations.

Keywords: (trauma survivors, post-discharge care, health indicators, patient-reported outcomes, feasibility.)

CONTEXTE
Each year, more than one billion people experience traumatic injuries worldwide [1]. Although recent advances in trauma care have significantly reduced post-trauma mortality, survivors still face a substantial ongoing burden [2]. Traumatic injuries are among the leading causes of disability [1, 3, 4], and account for the highest number of productive years of life lost [4].

The period following hospital discharge, including the transition to short-term stays in rehabilitation facilities, the return home, and long-term outpatient or community-based follow-up care, represents a critical phase in the recovery process for individuals who have experienced traumatic injuries. Yet, this continuum of care remains poorly documented.[5-8]. Trauma patients are at risk of developing long-term complications such as a decline in function, persistent pain, and reduced quality of life [9]. These risks may be exacerbated in the absence of appropriate, coordinated post-discharge support, increasing the strain on health systems and society [10]. In this context, the development of integrated, patient-centered models for follow-up outcome assessment, which are distinct from the provision of long-term-care is essential to better capture the functional, psychological, and social recovery of survivors [1, 4, 11].

Current quality of care assessment methods, such as trauma registries, typically focus on health outcomes during hospitalization or in the short term, thus neglecting patients’ long-term continuum of care [12, 13]. Furthermore, follow-up assessments rely primarily on objective health outcomes (e.g. mortality rate, readmissions) or administrative outcomes (service use, costs) [14, 15]. While these dimensions are important, they capture only a limited part of the patient’s long-term lived experience [13, 16]. In this regard, Patient-Reported Outcome Measures (PROMs) can serve as valuable complementary tools, enabling patients to assess their own health status at specific timepoints [17]. When combined with objective health outcomes, they offer a more comprehensive and nuanced view of recovery trajectories [18].

Despite their recognized value, the use of PROMs following trauma care remains inconsistent across jurisdictions. Some trauma systems, such as those in Australia [19] and the Netherlands [13] have successfully integrated longitudinal PROMs collection into routine practice. However, many other regions continue to face significant challenges that lead them to focus on isolated outcome assessment strategies rather than a comprehensive or integrated approach. [18]. Likewise, variability in administration methods (e.g., self-administration vs. professional-led, timing of assessments, type of personnel involved), heterogeneity in the tools used, and multiple barriers associated with data collection processes (e.g., required human and material resources, low patient response rates) have been described [20, 21]. Nonetheless, several facilitating factors have been identified, including the integration of outcome assessment strategies into routine care, the engagement of patients and their families, and the use of new technologies such as digital tools like mobile health applications, web-based monitoring platforms and electronic symptom trackers [7, 17, 19, 22-25]. 

To develop more coherent, accessible, and sustainable long-term outcome assessment strategies in trauma survivors, it is crucial to map existing health outcome measurement tools. Furthermore, describing the resources mobilized for their implementation after discharge, along with barriers and facilitators to their feasibility, will inform future models for follow-up outcome assessment [7, 26, 27]. Ultimately, effective implementation of such models can enhance continuity of care and support long-term recovery for trauma survivors.

METHODOLOGY
We will conduct a scoping review based on the methodological framework developed by Arksey and O’Malley (2005), structured into six stages: (1) identifying the research question, (2) identifying relevant studies, (3) study selection, (4) data extraction and analysis, (5) collating, summarizing, and reporting the results, and (6) stakeholder consultation to enrich or validate the findings [28, 29].

This protocol was developed in accordance with the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) guidelines for scoping reviews (JBI Scoping Review Methodology) [30, 31], and the results will be reported following the PRISMA-ScR checklist [30, 32]. This protocol has been pre-registered on the Open Science Framework (OSF).

STEP 1: Identifying the Research Question
This scoping review aims to map the nature and extent of available data on strategies used to measure outcomes in survivors of traumatic injuries following hospital discharge. It will focus specifically on outcome measurement, such as PROMs and other types of clinical, functional, psychological, social, or administrative indicators, obtained from routinely collected data or obtained directly from patients. This review will not address follow-up care delivery, but rather how outcomes are captured and assessed post-discharge.

More specifically, this review seeks to identify:
1) The outcome assessment strategies used to evaluate the long-term outcomes of trauma survivors, including the tools and instruments employed (including, but not limited to, PROMs);
2) The characteristics of these assessment strategies (e.g., type of outcome measured, mode of administration, timing within the care trajectory, frequency and duration of follow-up, individuals responsible for data collection);
3) The human resources involved (e.g., clinical staff, researchers and data analysts, administrative personnel, healthcare professionals or information systems technicians) and material resources required (e.g., standardized measurement tools, data collection software, administrative or clinical databases, computer equipment, remote communication tools) required to implement these strategies;
4) The barriers and facilitators to the implementation of the outcome assessment strategies, including their perceived relevance and the extent to which these strategies are adapted to patients’ needs;
5) The costs associated with their implementation.
6) The sustainability or continuation of the assessment strategies beyond the study period.

Eligibility Criteria
The inclusion and exclusion criteria are based on the population/concept/context framework for scoping reviews, as recommended in the methodological guidelines of the JBI [33]. 

Population: We will include all studies reporting outcome assessment strategies for adult or pediatric patients who have sustained traumatic injuries (i.e., traumatic brain injury, spinal cord injury, visceral organ injuries, orthopaedic injuries) requiring hospitalization, regardless of injury mechanism. Studies must clearly specify that participants were hospitalized due to physical traumatic injuries. Studies focusing exclusively on patients with burns will be excluded because these patients are often managed by specialized teams distinct from general trauma care. 

Concept: We will focus on structured strategies to assess in the post-discharge period following hospitalization for trauma. Studies must address concrete modalities of health data collection after hospital discharge, whether administered in person, by telephone, electronically, or through alternative patient-centered approaches (e.g., mailed surveys, proxy interviews, community-based assessments). We will include studies that report proxy PROMs (e.g., completed by caregivers or family members) when patients are children or adults physically or cognitively unable to complete them themselves, whether due to injury-related impairment (e.g., severe TBI) or pre-existing conditions (e.g., dementia, intellectual disability) [34-37] 

The types of outcomes/tools considered include (but are not limited to):
• Patient-Reported Outcome Measures (PROMs);
• Health indicators (e.g., pain, medical complications);
• Functional indicators (e.g., mobility, autonomy, performance-based measures);
• Psychological indicators (e.g., anxiety, depression, post-traumatic stress);
• Social indicators (e.g., social reintegration, return to work/school);
• Administrative indicators (e.g., use of healthcare services, hospital readmissions).

This classification draws on trauma research and health services evaluations, which highlight the need to consider both clinical outcomes and the broader psychosocial and functional dimensions of recovery [15, 18, 38, 39].

To be eligible, studies must document at least one of the following elements:
• Health follow-up outcomes or PROMs assessed post-hospital discharge;
• Detailed information on the outcome assessment strategies used to evaluate the long-term outcomes of trauma survivors (e.g., biological or functional measures, medical examinations, structured interviews, validated or non-validated questionnaires);
• Documentation of data collection modalities (e.g., timing within the care trajectory, frequency, duration, mode of administration [online, paper-based, phone], location);
• Description of the individuals involved in data collection (e.g., healthcare professionals, researchers, clinicians, administrative staff);
• Presentation, where applicable, of the material and human resources mobilized to collect the data;
• Reporting, when available, of:
o The feasibility and perceived relevance of the outcome assessment strategy;
o Response or participation rates;
o Barriers and facilitators;
o Sustainability or continuation of the strategy beyond the study period;
o Adaptation or adjustment strategies based on patients’ needs;
o Costs associated with the implementation of the assessment strategy.

Context: We will include all studies conducted after hospital discharge, across various post-discharge follow-up settings, whether clinical (e.g., outpatient visits, specialized trauma clinics, rehabilitation centers), community-based (e.g., community support services, home care organizations, trauma survivor support groups), or home-based (e.g., home visits by healthcare professionals, telephone follow-up, telemedicine, or digital self-assessment platforms). All geographic locations and models of care will be considered, as long as post-hospital outcomes are documented.

We will exclude studies without a follow-up period after hospital discharge, conducted exclusively in military settings with no intent for generalization, and reporting follow-up conducted solely as part of a research project, without any aim of organizational or systemic integration into a trauma care program. 

We will include publications from 1990 onward to reflect the evolution of contemporary follow-up practices, including the emergence of PROMs and digital tools, such as mobile health applications, web-based monitoring platforms and electronic symptom trackers [40]. There will be no language restrictions. Articles published in languages, other than that of the research team members, i.e. English, Arabic, Dutch, French, Italian, Portuguese, will be translated using the DeepL Translator tool. [41].

Source of evidence selection: All study designs will be considered, including quantitative, qualitative, and mixed-methods studies, provided they explicitly document the assessment of outcomes from a perspective applicable to a healthcare system. We will exclude single case studies and conference abstracts (i.e., abstracts without a full article available) and research protocols.

STEP 2: Identifying Relevant Studies

Databases
We will search for relevant studies in the following databases: MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, Scopus, and PsycINFO. Additionally, we will explore dissertations, theses, and academic reports via ProQuest. To ensure comprehensive coverage, we will also screen the reference lists of all included articles, dissertations, and theses to identify any additional eligible studies.

Search Strategy
In accordance with the Peer Review of Electronic Search Strategies (PRESS) guidelines [42], a rigorous systematic search strategy will first be developed in collaboration with an information specialist. The strategy will then undergo an independent peer review by a librarian. Our search strategy will be based on a combination of free-text terms and controlled vocabulary, including terms such as: trauma, injury, follow-up, PROMs, feasibility, barriers, and facilitators.
We will begin with a pilot search in MEDLINE (via PubMed) and Embase (via Ovid) to identify additional relevant keywords. Key terms extracted from the titles, abstracts, and full texts of selected studies will be collected and integrated into the final strategy. This enriched strategy will then be applied across all selected databases to ensure comprehensive coverage.

To ensure the sensitivity, specificity, and overall effectiveness of the search strategy, we will use a predefined set of eligibility criteria to select a group of sentinel studies (see Appendix 1). These studies represent a benchmark to evaluate the performance of the strategy. Sensitivity will be assessed by confirming that all sentinel studies meeting the criteria were successfully retrieved. Specificity will be considered by examining whether the strategy avoids retrieving an unmanageable volume of irrelevant citations, which could compromise the feasibility of the screening process. A preliminary version of the search strategy is available in Table 1.

STEP 3: Study Selection
We will use EndNote (version X9.3.3, New York City: Thomson Reuters, 2018) for citation management. Duplicate records will be identified and removed using both automated and manual methods.

Two reviewers (MLS, MAG) will independently screen the titles, abstracts, and full texts of the studies. To ensure the reliability and reproducibility of the selection process, they will follow a systematic and iterative approach, testing the screening process on random samples of 250 citations. This process will be refined until an acceptable level of inter-rater agreement is achieved, based on methodological standards (kappa > 0.8) [43].

In case of disagreements, a senior member of the research team (MB) will be consulted to resolve conflicts. Finally, we will document the search strategy, selection process, and reasons for exclusion in detail using a PRISMA flow diagram [44] to ensure transparency and traceability throughout the study selection process.

STEP 4: Data Extraction
We have developed a standardized data extraction form using the JBI template with Microsoft Excel (version 16.0, Redmond, WA: Microsoft Corporation, 2018), available in Appendix (X). This form will be iteratively tested by two reviewers (MLS, MAG) with both methodological and subject-matter expertise. The test will be conducted on a random sample of five studies representing the diversity of included studies, and the form will be refined until an acceptable level of inter-rater agreement is reached, in line with methodological standards (kappa > 0.8) [43]. Data will be extracted from the original publications along several key dimensions by two reviewers (MLS, MAG). Any discrepancies will be resolved through discussion or consultation with a third team member (MB or LM), if needed.

Regarding the study context, the following information will be collected: country, year of publication, funding source, research design, and the level of implementation (e.g., trauma system, provincial or national health authority, hospital-based, community-based). As for the study population, reviewers will extract the total number of participants and their distribution across various variables: sex, gender, age group, type and severity of trauma, place of residence (urban or rural), ethnocultural background, and socioeconomic status. We will also document the characteristics of the outcome/tool used after hospital discharge. This will include the nature of the indicators assessed, the PROMs used, the timing and frequency of assessments, the mode of administration (in-person, virtual, hybrid), the location where questionnaires were administered (e.g., home, outpatient clinic), as well as any specific adaptations made to meet patients’ particular needs.

In addition, the interventions’ feasibility analysis will be guided by Proctor’s Implementation Outcomes (PIO) framework. Accordingly, the following elements will be extracted: required infrastructure and resources (both human and material), response rate (the proportion of eligible patients who completed the questionnaires), institutional adoption rate, identified barriers and facilitators, as well as associated direct costs (e.g., staff salaries, equipment purchases, software licenses, training expenses) and indirect costs (e.g., time required from clinical personnel, workflow disruptions, or productivity losses related to implementation). The sustainability of the implemented assessment strategies will also be examined [45]. We will extract data aligned with the conceptual domains identified in recent sustainability models, including organizational capacity, ongoing learning, monitoring and feedback, alignment with broader systems, staff engagement, and community involvement. [46] Finally, we will collect information on patient engagement strategies and any equity-related considerations regarding the implementation of the assessment strategies, as well as social determinants that may affect response rates (e.g., sex, age, ethnocultural background, and socioeconomic status)[47]. Where available, we will examine stratified response rates to identify differential participation across subgroups. Particular attention will be given to populations at increased risk of being excluded from follow-up care, such as individuals with no fixed address or those living with mental health or substance use disorders. This will help highlight the barriers faced by these groups and how intersecting determinants influence their experience within the healthcare system.

Any disagreements between reviewers will be resolved through consensus-based discussion. In the event of persistent disagreement, a senior member of the research team (MB or LM) will be consulted to arbitrate the decision. If essential information is missing or unclear, we will contact the first, second, and last authors of the corresponding study, sending up to three emails to request clarification.

STEP 5: Collating, Summarizing, and Reporting the Results
The findings of this scoping review will be compiled, synthesized, and presented using both descriptive and analytical methods, in accordance with the guidelines of the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) and the PRISMA-ScR reporting framework. As previously mentioned, once study selection is complete, data will be extracted and organized into a summary table structured according to the type of health indicator/tool (e.g., clinical indicators, PROMs, functional, psychological, social, and administrative measures), follow-up modalities, implementation strategies, feasibility factors, and reported outcomes.

The results will be synthesized using a descriptive and thematic approach, highlighting overall trends, variations observed across the included studies and research gaps. To improve the interpretability of the findings, we will construct a mapping table that links the types of outcome assessed (e.g., PROMs, clinical, functional, psychological, social, administrative) and the other modalities involved (e.g., the mode of administration, frequency of assessments) with key feasibility elements such as response rates, timing of follow-up, resources mobilized, and reported costs. This cross-classification will support the identification of patterns between various follow-up indicators and tools, and help compare the feasibility of their implementation.

In addition to this mapping and thematic analysis (qualitative analysis), we will record the frequency of specific characteristics related to the outcomes/tools and the barriers and facilitators associated with their implementation using counts and proportions. This will support a more precise understanding of the key issues to consider in their implementation.

Subgroup analyses will be conducted, data permitting, to explore variations in follow-up strategies and feasibility dimensions across different participant-related and contextual factors. These factors will include the type of trauma, participant age group, mode of administration of the assessment tools (e.g., in-person, online, hybrid), and healthcare system context (e.g., low, middle, and high-income countries). This stratified synthesis will help identify whether certain strategies are more feasible, acceptable, or sustainable depending on the setting and population characteristics, thereby enhancing the contextual relevance and transferability of the findings.

The results will be presented in various formats to support interpretation and dissemination. Descriptive tables will summarize the characteristics of the studies and strategies, their feasibility, and key findings, while figures and graphs will provide a clear illustration of trends and comparisons across strategies.

STEP 6: Stakeholder Consultation
An advisory committee was consulted for the development of this protocol, to ensure the relevance and applicability of the findings. This committee include experts from high-, middle-, and low-income countries representing various disciplines involved in trauma care and post-discharge follow-up, including epidemiology, health data protection and enhancement, trauma surgery, nursing, rehabilitation, psychology, social work and primary care. We have also involved individuals with lived experience as well as healthcare decision-makers and administrators. 

The consultation process aimed to: 1) identify any additional references that could enrich the analysis; 2) gather feedback on elements to include, as well as on the presentation and interpretation of the findings; 3) explore opportunities for knowledge mobilization and practical application of the results in clinical practice and health policy.
To optimize collaboration, we will schedule periodic meetings (in person or virtual) with the members of the advisory committee at key milestones of the review process. These meetings will include structured group discussions and facilitated feedback sessions. In addition, we will use online tools such as questionnaires, shared documents and electronic surveys to systematically collect comments, suggestions, and evaluations. This mixed-methods approach will help capture both individual and collective perspectives and ensure their integration at different stages of the scoping review. This approach is aligned with best practices in stakeholder engagement during knowledge synthesis, which recommend combining synchronous and asynchronous data collection methods to ensure broad participation and integration of diverse perspectives [31, 48, 49].

LIMITATIONS AND MITIGATION STRATEGIES
This scoping review presents certain methodological limitations inherent to its design and the range of studies targeted. In accordance with the methodological recommendations for scoping reviews [28, 30, 33, 44] and due to the wide variety of study designs, we will not conduct a critical appraisal of the methodological quality of included studies. This will limit our ability to assess the strength of individual findings. However, this is in line with recommendations, and we will apply a rigorous selection and evaluation process, including independent dual screening and calculation of inter-rater agreement, ensuring consistency in the application of inclusion and exclusion criteria and maximizing the reliability of the review process.

Secondly, unlike systematic reviews, scoping reviews do not aim to estimate the effectiveness of an intervention, therefore, there will be no meta-analysis. As a result, we will not be able to determine the overall strength of the evidence. While this limits our ability to draw conclusions about the long-term impact of the health indicators/tools assessed, the clear structure of the review, according to the JBI and PRISMA-ScR guidelines, will ensure that findings are presented in a transparent and rigorous manner, thereby maximizing their usefulness for future research and decision-making, including future phases aimed at evaluating the effectiveness of long-term outcome assessment strategies in improving patient outcomes.

Third, the anticipated variability in the health assessment strategies and the methods used may limit comparability across studies. To address this, a standardized data extraction form will be developed based on predefined variables and analytical categories and refined through expert consultation. This process will help identify the key elements to be extracted and validate the analytical framework, thereby strengthening the rigor of the synthesis.

Fourth, the lack of standardization in health indicators and PROMs used across studies may complicate the assessment of post-discharge follow-up feasibility and limit the conclusions that can be drawn. To mitigate this issue, we will develop a mapping table linking the types of indicators assessed with feasibility elements (e.g., response rate, timing of evaluation, resources mobilized), which will contribute to a more structured and effective interpretation of the findings.

Finally, considering the inconsistencies in health assessment follow-up methods across healthcare contexts and systems, some results may not be generalizable to all clinical settings or to less-developed countries. To put this limitation into perspective, we plan to conduct subgroup analyses, when data is available, based on variables such as World Bank country income categories. This will help contextualize the findings according to specific settings.
In addition, an advisory committee composed of healthcare professionals, policymakers, and individuals with lived experience will be involved throughout the process to ensure the relevance and applicability of the findings, thereby enhancing the transferability of knowledge to clinical practice and health policy.

DISCUSSION
The results of this scoping review will provide an up-to-date and structured overview of strategies to assess outcomes in trauma survivors after hospital discharge. By identifying the strategies employed, their characteristics, the resources mobilized, as well as the barriers and facilitators to their implementation, this synthesis will offer an essential knowledge base to support the development of more integrated, accessible, and sustainable long-term assessment tools within trauma care systems.

The expected impacts extend to both research and clinical practice. This review will help inform methodological choices for future evaluation and interventional studies, while also guiding clinicians and decision-makers on favorable conditions for the integration of outcomes and assessment tools into post-trauma care pathways. The findings will also highlight current gaps in the literature, helping to prioritize areas that require further research efforts.

title: Leveraging AI-Driven Neuroimaging Biomarkers for Early Detection and Social Function Prediction in Autism Spectrum Disorders. A Systematic Review
description: This systematic review examines artificial intelligence (AI) applications in neuroimaging for autism spectrum disorder (ASD), addressing the critical need for objective biomarkers that could enable earlier detection and more accurate prediction of developmental outcomes. Methods: Following PRISMA guidelines, we conducted a comprehensive literature search across eight databases, yielding 146 studies from an initial 1,872 records. These studies were systematically analyzed to address key questions regarding AI-neuroimaging approaches in ASD detection and prognosis. Results: Neuroimaging combined with AI algorithms demonstrated significant potential for early ASD detection, with electroencephalography (EEG) showing promise. Machine learning classifiers achieved high diagnostic accuracy (85-99%) using features derived from neural oscillatory patterns, connectivity measures, and signal complexity metrics. Studies of infant populations identified the 9–12-month developmental window as critical for biomarker detection and preceding behavioral symptoms. Multimodal approaches integrating various imaging techniques substantially enhanced predictive capabilities, while longitudinal analyses showed potential for tracking developmental trajectories and treatment response. Conclusions: AI-driven neuroimaging biomarkers represent a promising frontier in ASD research, potentially enabling detection before behavioral symptoms manifest and providing objective measures of intervention efficacy. While technical and methodological challenges remain, advancements in standardization, diverse sampling, and clinical validation could facilitate translation into practice, ultimately supporting earlier intervention during critical developmental periods and improving outcomes for individuals with ASD.

title: Data Analysis and Outcome reporting
description:
Primary outcome
The primary outcome will be the diagnostic performance of predefined nutritional screening tools for identifying GLIM-defined malnutrition in adults with IBD.
Performance will be assessed using study-level sensitivity, specificity and diagnostic odds ratio where complete or reconstructable 2 x 2 data are available.
Secondary outcomes
1. Diagnostic performance of the predefined nutritional screening tools against ESPEN criteria and SGA, analysed separately from GLIM-based evidence.
2. The proportion of study-screening tool-comparator rows meeting the predefined screening benchmark of sensitivity >=80%.
3. Supportive diagnostic measures, including PPV and NPV, where available or calculable.
4. Narrative summary of PICO-eligible studies that report relevant performance, agreement or association data but do not provide sufficient data to reconstruct a 2 x 2 table.
Kappa and accuracy may be reported descriptively as supplementary measures but will not be used as primary measures of screening performance.
Data synthesis and analysis
The main synthesis will focus on predefined nutritional screening tools assessed against GLIM-defined malnutrition. Studies using ESPEN criteria or SGA as comparators will be analysed separately and will not be combined with GLIM-based evidence.
Studies with complete or reconstructable 2 x 2 data will be included in the structured diagnostic accuracy synthesis. Each row will represent one nutritional screening tool assessed against one comparator within one study.
For each study-screening tool-comparator row, sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV and diagnostic odds ratio will be calculated where sufficient data are available. Wilson 95% confidence intervals will be calculated for sensitivity and specificity. Diagnostic odds ratios will be presented with 95% confidence intervals. Where zero cells are present, a 0.5 continuity correction will be applied. A diagnostic odds ratio confidence interval excluding 1 will be interpreted as evidence that the screening tool shows discriminatory ability in that cohort.
Results will be presented in structured tables. The primary table will show study-level performance of each nutritional screening tool against GLIM. A secondary table will show performance against ESPEN criteria and SGA.
For each nutritional screening tool against GLIM, results will be summarised descriptively using the median and range of sensitivity and specificity, PPV and NPV ranges, kappa range, the number of studies in which the diagnostic odds ratio confidence interval excludes 1, and the number of rows meeting the predefined sensitivity benchmark of >=80%.
Kappa and accuracy may be reported descriptively as supplementary measures but will not be used as primary measures of screening performance.
Forest plots will be used to display study-level sensitivity and specificity estimates with 95% confidence intervals. No pooled estimate will be calculated.
Formal meta-analysis is not planned. PICO-eligible studies without complete or reconstructable 2 x 2 data will be summarised narratively as supportive evidence only.
Exploration of variation
Where necessary, variation in diagnostic performance will be explored descriptively in relation to population demographics, disease activity and clinical setting.
Because the number of studies per nutritional screening tool is expected to be small, formal subgroup analysis, meta-regression and pooled sensitivity analysis are not planned.

title: Diagnostic accuracy of metagenomic next-generation sequencing for osteomyelitis: a systematic review and meta-analysis
description: Osteomyelitis is a common and severe infectious disease in orthopedics. Traditional diagnostic methods primarily rely on microbial culture; however, these methods exhibit low positive rates (approximately 30–50%) and prolonged turnaround times (7–14 days), leading to diagnostic challenges and delayed clinical treatment. Metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS), as an unbiased pathogen detection technology, has demonstrated significant potential in the diagnosis of infectious diseases in recent years. Previous studies have indicated that mNGS exhibits high detection rates in bone and joint infections, yet a systematic evaluation specifically focusing on the diagnostic accuracy of mNGS for osteomyelitis remains lacking.

title: Scoping Review of Risk Prediction Models for Acute Kidney Injury Following Cardiac Arrest Resuscitation
description:
This scoping review aims to systematically map the existing evidence on risk prediction models for acute kidney injury (AKI) in adult patients following successful resuscitation from cardiac arrest (including both out-of-hospital cardiac arrest [OHCA] and in-hospital cardiac arrest [IHCA]).
Cardiac arrest survivors are at high risk of developing AKI, which is strongly associated with increased mortality, prolonged hospital stay, and poor neurological outcomes. In recent years, several risk prediction models (such as nomograms, logistic regression-based scores, and machine learning models) have been developed to predict AKI occurrence, progression, or severity in this population. However, the evidence remains sparse, fragmented, and has not yet been systematically synthesized or critically appraised.
The objectives of this scoping review are:
(1) to identify all published and unpublished studies that have developed, validated, or updated risk prediction models for AKI after successful cardiac arrest resuscitation;
(2) to summarize the key characteristics of these models, including study design, sample size, predictors, performance metrics (e.g., AUC/C-index, calibration, sensitivity, specificity, decision curve analysis), and validation approaches (internal/external);
(3) to assess the methodological quality of the included models using the PROBAST tool; and
(4) to highlight current evidence gaps and provide clear directions for future research and clinical application.
This scoping review will follow the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology for scoping reviews and the PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews) checklist. Comprehensive searches will be performed in PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, CNKI, Wanfang, VIP, and other relevant databases, with no language or publication date restrictions.
The findings of this review will provide clinicians, researchers, and guideline developers with a clear overview of the current state of AKI risk prediction modeling in post-cardiac arrest patients and serve as a foundation for the development of more robust, externally validated, and clinically implementable prediction tools.

title: Processo de validação de instrumentos de autoavaliação da voz: Uma revisão de Escopo
description:
Informações sobre a avaliação da validade, confiabilidade e responsividade nos instrumentos de autoavaliação de pacientes com disfonia são importantíssimos, visto que os principais objetivos do tratamento são melhorar a função vocal dos pacientes e seu bem-estar. Este tipo de estudo permite a otimização e o direcionamento das avaliações na prática clínica, diminuindo a sobrecarga ao paciente e ao terapeuta. A responsividade dos testes tem sido realizada nos últimos dez anos, apontando um interesse maior das pesquisas na criação de instrumentos mais sensíveis, para utilização na prática clínica e nos ensaios clínicos.
Portanto, para uma melhor utilização dos protocolos de autoavaliação vocal no diagnóstico ou acompanhamento terapêutico, faz-se necessário compreender as evidências científicas que respaldam a sua utilização, bem como todo o processo de validação que esse instrumento obedeceu. Acredita-se que essas informações auxiliarão o clínico na tomada de decisão de escolha do protocolo especifico a ser utilizado com cada paciente com base em evidências científicas. Desta forma, essa pesquisa propõe mapear o processo de validação de instrumentos de autoavaliação vocal, utilizados em pacientes disfônicos adultos, bem como fornecer a pesquisadores e clínicos evidências sobre a qualidade e utilidade clínica dos instrumentos de avaliação da voz utilizados na prática clínica no Brasil.
