title: Implementation of Focused Lung Ultrasound (FLUS) among geriatricians in a medical department: a prospective implementation study (GERI-FLUS Study)
description:
This study aims to implement focused lung ultrasound (FLUS) in a medical department among geriatricians and to evaluate both the implementation process and its outcomes in clinical practice.

FLUS is a bedside ultrasound technique that can assist in the assessment of common conditions such as dyspnoea, pneumonia, pleural effusion, and heart failure, potentially improving diagnostic accuracy and reducing the need for additional imaging. Despite its clinical relevance, FLUS is not routinely used in many geriatric settings, and structured implementation is required to support uptake.

The study will be conducted as a prospective observational implementation study at the Department of Medicine, Regional Hospital Randers, Denmark. The implementation process will be guided by the Knowledge to Action Framework. Initially, barriers and facilitators to implementation will be identified using selected constructs from the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR) through a questionnaire distributed to physicians in the department. Identified barriers will be discussed and prioritised in a structured consensus process, and implementation strategies will be selected based on the Expert Recommendations for Implementing Change (ERIC) taxonomy.

The selected strategies will be applied in clinical practice over a 12-month period. Use of FLUS will be monitored continuously through a structured log, capturing information on indication, supervision, findings, and impact on clinical decision-making. Competency development will be assessed based on achievement of independent practice.

The primary outcome is adoption, defined as the proportion of physicians achieving independent practice in FLUS. Secondary outcomes include competency development, distribution of FLUS use among physicians, sustainment over time, and implementation outcomes such as acceptability, feasibility, and self-efficacy.

The study is exploratory in nature. It is expected that the implementation process will lead to increased use of FLUS, improved physician competency, and identification of key barriers and facilitators relevant to future implementation efforts. The findings may inform how similar point-of-care ultrasound interventions can be implemented in comparable clinical settings.

Testing Human Anxiety Associations of Genes Previously Implicated by Mouse Anxiety Models
description: Anxiety disorders are some of the most common mental health disorders in the United States, with an estimated 31.1% of the population experiencing an anxiety disorder at some point in their life (National Institute of Mental Health, 2017). Some anxiety disorders, particularly generalized anxiety disorder (GAD), have been associated with the overuse of primary care medical services (Peter P. Roy-Byrne & Wayne Katon, 1997), but low rates of professional treatment, with only approximately half receiving professional help (Wang et al., 2005). Anxiety disorders are moderately heritable with an estimated 30-40% of phenotypic variance being caused by additive genetic variance based on twin studies (Hettema et al., 2001). However, genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have reported SNP heritabilities between 8% and 10% and identified numerous genome-wide significant associations with small effect sizes (Levey et al., 2020; Otowa et al., 2016), indicating that anxiety disorders are highly polygenic and genetic variance is made up of many common variants with small phenotypic effects. A more complete understanding of the genetics of anxiety disorders is needed in order to improve diagnostic accuracy, develop novel treatments, and clarify causes of these disorders. Mouse models of anxiety-like behaviors have implicated hundreds of genes potentially related to different aspects of human anxiety, and are an appealing study system because of the well-characterized mouse genome, controlled experimental settings, and established paradigms of anxiety-like behaviors. Established behavioral paradigms used to model anxiety-like behavior in mice include the light-dark box, elevated plus-maze, open-field test, and the zero maze, among others. These tests have been used to evaluate the effectiveness of anti-anxiety drugs (anxiolytics) and to identify genes that are associated with anxiety-like behaviors (Fonken et al., 2016, Henderson et al., 2004, Heredia et al., 2013, Hovatta et al., 2005). Research by Philip et al. (2010) evaluated anxiety phenotypes across 63 BXD recombinant inbred strains and found that no strain consistently exhibited high or low anxiety-like behavior across a range of behavioral paradigms, raising questions about how different behavioral paradigms reflect genetic factors of anxiety. We aim to investigate whether human orthologs of genes previously implicated in mouse anxiety-like behaviors also contribute to human anxiety phenotypes, and whether this relationship is affected by the human phenotype considered, or mouse behavior test or analysis conducted.

title: Accuracy of Immediate Postpartum Ultrasound Measurements in Predicting Expulsion and Displacement of Post-Placental Intrauterine Devices Inserted During Cesarean Delivery: A Prospective Observational Study
description:
This project is a prospective, single-arm observational study evaluating whether immediate postpartum ultrasound can predict expulsion or displacement of post-placental Copper T380A IUDs inserted during cesarean delivery.

Pregnant women at ≥37 weeks undergoing elective cesarean delivery received a Copper T380A IUD immediately after placental delivery through the hysterotomy incision. Ultrasound was performed within 12 hours postpartum to measure the fundus-to-IUD distance and IUD-to-internal cervical os distance. Follow-up ultrasound was performed at 6 weeks and 3 months to assess IUD position, displacement, or expulsion.

The primary aim is to determine the diagnostic accuracy of these immediate postpartum ultrasound measurements using ROC analysis, sensitivity, specificity, and optimal cutoff values. Secondary outcomes include expulsion rate, displacement rate, follow-up attendance, and complications such as bleeding, pain, infection, and thread-related symptoms.

The expected outcome is to identify ultrasound-based predictors that may support risk-stratified follow-up after cesarean post-placental IUD insertion. This registration is retrospective and is intended to document the study design, objectives, outcomes, and analysis plan transparently. Ethical approval was obtained from the Research Ethics Committee, Faculty of Medicine, Cairo University, code MS-191-2024.

title: Diagnostic accuracy of MTAP immunohistochemistry for CDKN2A homozygous deletion and for distinguishing mesothelioma from reactive mesothelial proliferations: a systematic review and bivariate meta-analysis
description:
This OSF project (DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/M9PTK) hosts the supplementary materials for a systematic review and bivariate / HSROC meta-analysis of the diagnostic accuracy of MTAP immunohistochemistry (a) as a surrogate for CDKN2A homozygous deletion and (b) for distinguishing mesothelioma from reactive mesothelial proliferations. The review is reported to PRISMA-DTA 2020 standards, with risk of bias assessed by QUADAS-2.

The frozen pre-registration is held separately at OSF Registries, DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/S7YW4, and is preserved exactly as registered. The controlling methods-of-record for the completed review is protocol amendment v5 (19 June 2026), as amended by protocol amendment v6 (6 August 2026) for changes made in response to peer review; both are deposited here. Between them they document every deviation from, and correction to, the registered plan with its rationale and impact. The primary review questions and the reference standards are unchanged from registration.

REVIEW QUESTIONS

(a) Primary question: What is the diagnostic accuracy of MTAP immunohistochemistry, used alone, for detecting CDKN2A homozygous deletion in pleural mesothelioma, taking dual-colour CDKN2A FISH (or an equivalent CNV / NGS reference) as the gold standard? Peritoneal mesothelioma is addressed separately, as a pre-specified and independently reported stratum, and is not pooled with the pleural primary analysis.

(b) Secondary question: What is the diagnostic accuracy of MTAP immunohistochemistry for distinguishing histologically or cytologically confirmed mesothelioma from reactive mesothelial proliferations, taking the integrated clinical-radiological-pathological diagnosis as the reference? Peritoneal cohorts are likewise reported separately from the pleural-main secondary pool.

POPULATION AND SPECIMENS

Adult patients with suspected mesothelioma (pleural as the primary target; peritoneal as a pre-specified, separately reported subgroup) undergoing diagnostic biopsy or pleural / peritoneal effusion cytology, in whom MTAP IHC has been applied as part of the ancillary diagnostic workup.

INDEX TEST

MTAP immunohistochemistry on formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tissue or cell block. Pre-specified primary loss definition: complete cytoplasmic loss with positive internal control. Pre-specified sensitivity-analysis convention: each study's own threshold including broader patterns (nuclear loss, focal loss, >=30% cells lost). Antibody clone recorded as a pre-specified subgroup variable (2G4 reference clone; mAb1813; EPR6893; 2B1G6; polyclonal / unspecified).

REFERENCE STANDARD

Primary: CDKN2A homozygous deletion by dual-colour FISH (>=10% nuclei threshold standard). CNV array and targeted NGS panels with explicit CDKN2A copy-number calls are accepted equivalents.

Secondary: integrated clinical-radiological-pathological diagnosis per IMIG 2017 / WHO 2021 with at least 12 months follow-up for benign controls. Incorporation bias is acknowledged and addressed in QUADAS-2 domain 3.

OUTCOMES

Primary: pooled sensitivity, specificity, positive and negative likelihood ratios, diagnostic odds ratio (all with 95% CI); summary HSROC curve with 95% confidence and prediction regions.

Secondary: between-study heterogeneity (tau^2, I^2); pre-specified subgroup pooled estimates by antibody clone and specimen format; pooled proportion of uninterpretable MTAP IHC results.

SEARCH (as executed)

PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, and a Google Scholar top-up, from inception to 18 June 2026. A single index-test-agnostic concept pair was applied at the database stage — (MTAP OR methylthioadenosine phosphorylase) AND (mesothelioma OR mesothelial); restriction to the MTAP-IHC index test and to an admissible reference standard was performed by manual screening. Per-source yields: PubMed 153, Web of Science 217, Scopus 194, Google Scholar 1, citation tracking 0 — 565 records identified, 20 studies included. The registered protocol named PubMed and Embase to 2 June 2026; Embase access lapsed at the re-run and was replaced by Web of Science, Scopus and Google Scholar, with the cut-off extended to 18 June 2026. This deviation, and the correction of the earlier two-strand / IHC-term search description to the single executed concept pair, are documented in amendment v5 and in the deposited search log (MTAP_search_strategy_log.md).

DATA EXTRACTION AND VERIFICATION

Two reviewers — V. Tayade (Grant Government Medical College & Sir J.J. Group of Hospitals, Mumbai) and G. Singh (AIIMS Rajkot) — extracted each included study independently from the source articles, and discrepancies between the two independent extractions were resolved by consensus to form the locked dataset. Every 2x2 cell (TP, FP, FN, TN) is transcribed verbatim from the source; no value is fabricated, approximated, inferred, or back-calculated, and manuscript point estimates are drawn only from the locked analysis output (mtap_dta_analysis_FINAL.R -> MTAP_R_output.txt). The locked extraction is deposited as MTAP_2x2_dataset_locked.csv and, in formatted form, as MTAP_Supplementary_Table_S1_2x2.xlsx; MTAP_2x2_dataset_v6.csv supersedes it, carrying the same counts with columns marking which arms contribute to a pooled stratum. (The registered record's description of the second-reviewer step is corrected in amendment v5; see that document.)

RISK OF BIAS

QUADAS-2 (Whiting 2011): four risk-of-bias domains (patient selection, index test, reference standard, flow and timing) and three applicability domains, scored per study. Tally across the 20 included studies: Low 85, High 24, Unclear 31. Workbook deposited as MTAP_QUADAS2_workbook.xlsx.

DATA SYNTHESIS

Bivariate random-effects meta-analysis (Reitsma 2005 / Rutter-Gatsonis HSROC) using the mada package in R, with logit-transformed sensitivity and specificity jointly modelled. Where a pool's specificity is at or near 100% (most or all false positives = 0), the pre-specified summary is the univariate random-effects pooled sensitivity (logit, DerSimonian-Laird), with specificity described as at/near 100%. Peritoneal cohorts are reported separately from the pleural pools, and the Fukuoka University representatives are entered sensitivity-only. Reproducible analysis code is deposited as mtap_dta_analysis_FINAL.R with its output log MTAP_R_output.txt; the SROC plots and the PRISMA-DTA study-flow diagram are deposited as PDF and PNG. The computational environment, and a cross-version check confirming the estimates reproduce under mada 0.5.12 and meta 8.5-0, are recorded in MTAP_sessionInfo.txt.

Pool composition as registered (20 studies / 22 two-by-two tables / five strata):
- Primary, pleural-main (k = 7): Chapel 2020, Chapel 2021, Vrugt 2023, Febres-Aldana 2024, Seker 2026, Broggi 2024, Brcic 2023.
- Primary, peritoneal, reported separately (k = 1): Quaranta 2025 (1% cutoff).
- Secondary, MTAP-alone, pleural-main (k = 9): Berg 2018 (tissue), Berg 2020, Chapel 2022, Lynggard (histology), Lynggard (cytology), Seker 2024, Hiroshima 2021, Amacher 2023, Aoe 2026.
- Secondary, peritoneal, reported separately (k = 2): Alsugair 2022 (biopsy), Quaranta 2025 (secondary).
- Fukuoka University series, sensitivity-only (k = 3): Kinoshita 2020 (tissue), Kinoshita 2021 (cytology), Sa-ngiamwibool 2022.

Pool composition after peer review (19 studies / 21 two-by-two tables; amendment v6): Alsugair 2022 was withdrawn from quantitative synthesis, both arms, because it scored MTAP loss by absent nuclear staining rather than the complete-cytoplasmic-loss convention applied throughout, and therefore does not read the same index test. Peritoneal data are no longer pooled: the k = 2 secondary peritoneal estimate is withdrawn and Quaranta 2025 is reported descriptively, as is the primary peritoneal arm. Three strata are pooled (primary pleural k = 7, secondary pleural-main k = 9, Fukuoka sensitivity-only k = 3) and two peritoneal strata (k = 1 each) are descriptive. Twenty reports remain in the flow diagram and in the study-characteristics table as identified and eligible. No 2x2 cell value changed, and no pooled pleural estimate changed.

PRE-SPECIFIED SENSITIVITY ANALYSES

(i) Exclude Seker 2024 from the secondary main pool. (ii) Stratify by specimen (tissue versus cytology) — performed; see SUBGROUP ANALYSES below. (iii) Stratify by clone (2G4 versus other) — performed; see below. (iv) Primary-pool sensitivity with each study's own threshold; the substituted counts are recorded in amendment v5 §8 and in the deposited dataset, and threshold-substituted re-fits were not performed. (v) Sa-ngiamwibool ID-handling variant. (vi) Lynggard cytology-only sensitivity to bound the effect of the shared TN = 20 reactive mesothelial controls used in both Lynggard arms; the drop-one-arm analyses are deposited as SROC_SECONDARY_drop_Lynggard_cyto.pdf and SROC_SECONDARY_drop_Lynggard_histo.pdf.

SUBGROUP ANALYSES

Performed and reported: specimen format (tissue k = 4 versus effusion cytology k = 5) and antibody clone (2G4 k = 3 versus other k = 6), both within the secondary pleural-main pool. Neither showed a difference in sensitivity. Outputs are deposited as SROC_SECONDARY_specimen_cytology.pdf and SROC_SECONDARY_clone_other.pdf; no SROC is produced for the tissue or 2G4 subgroups, in which every contributor returned zero false positives, so a bivariate model is not applicable and the pre-specified univariate summary applies. Because the single false-positive contributor in the whole pool is simultaneously the cytology arm, a non-2G4 clone and the broader loss threshold, specimen format, clone and threshold are mutually confounded at this number of contributors; both comparisons are therefore descriptive and neither is a test of difference.

Planned but not performed, the number of contributing studies being insufficient to support them: histologic subtype (epithelioid versus sarcomatoid including desmoplastic versus biphasic versus mixed); anatomic site (pleural versus peritoneal) as a pooled comparison; reference-standard modality; and time period (pre-2020 versus 2020 onward).

STATUS

The search, data extraction, QUADAS-2 assessment, and synthesis are complete. The manuscript was submitted to Cancer Cytopathology in June 2026, received a major revision decision in August 2026, and the revision was submitted on 14 August 2026. The registered protocol's status note originally read "synthesis completed; deviations nil"; amendment v5 corrects this to record that deviations and corrections were identified and are documented in full — that is, not nil — superseding the earlier "nil deviations" declaration. Amendment v6 records the further changes made in response to peer review.

FUNDING AND CONFLICTS

No external project funding. The reviewers declare no conflicts of interest, and no relationship with the manufacturer of any antibody clone or FISH-probe vendor.

title: Diagnostic Performance of Intravoxel Incoherent Motion MRI Parameters in Differentiating Malignant from Benign Breast Lesions: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
description:
This study is a PRISMA 2020-compliant systematic review and meta-analysis evaluating the diagnostic performance of intravoxel incoherent motion (IVIM) magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) parameters for differentiating malignant from benign breast lesions. IVIM enables simultaneous assessment of tissue diffusivity and microvascular perfusion without contrast administration, offering potential as a non-invasive imaging biomarker.

A comprehensive search of PubMed, Scopus, Embase, and Web of Science will be conducted from inception to January 2025. Eligible studies include those reporting IVIM-derived parameters (true diffusion coefficient [D], perfusion fraction [f], pseudo-diffusion coefficient [D*], and apparent diffusion coefficient [ADC]) with histopathological confirmation of breast lesions. Study selection, data extraction, and risk of bias assessment (QUADAS-2) will be performed independently by two reviewers.

Diagnostic accuracy will be synthesised using bivariate random-effects and hierarchical summary receiver operating characteristic (HSROC) models to estimate pooled sensitivity and specificity. Quantitative parameter differences will be analysed using standardised mean differences (Hedges g). Heterogeneity will be explored using I² statistics, subgroup analyses, and meta-regression. Publication bias will be assessed using Deeks' funnel plot asymmetry test.

This study aims to provide robust evidence on the clinical utility of IVIM MRI parameters, identify sources of heterogeneity, and inform future standardisation and integration of IVIM into breast imaging workflows. The findings are expected to support the development of contrast-free diagnostic strategies and guide future research, including AI-augmented IVIM modelling.

title: Out-of-hosptial management of tachycardia by paramedics: A scoping review
description:
Introduction: There are ten jurisdictional ambulance services (JASs) within Australia and New Zealand, each with their own set of clinical practice guidelines (CPGs). The management for out-of-hospital tachycardia is different in each CPG, pointing towards a potential knowledge gap in the literature. The objective of this scoping review is to understand the extent and type of evidence in relation to the out-of-hospital management of tachycardia by paramedics.
Methods: EBSCOhost, Scopus, MEDLINE, ProQuest, and Ovid were systematically searched on 10 March 2023. Inclusion criteria encompassed articles examining the management of tachycardia in paramedicine contexts. Following the removal of duplicates, two independent reviewers conducted screenings in JBI SUMARI. Exclusion reasons were documented, presented in a PRISMA flow diagram. Data extracted by reviewers were organised into a characteristics table and subjected to thematic analysis, with identified concepts documented in a concept table. Results were graphically presented in a Venn diagram, highlighting key concepts within three main themes.
Results: From 723 initially retrieved articles, 19 were ultimately included in the scoping review. Three main themes emerged from the data analysis: safety, efficacy, and further education. Concepts such as diagnostic accuracy, adverse events, and paramedic knowledge contributed to the safety theme. The evidence supporting the efficacy of paramedic tachycardia treatment was substantial, also addressing the need for CPG revision to enhance safety in supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) treatment. Exploring further education revealed new treatment options, treat-and-release protocols, and epidemiological insights into tachycardia within paramedicine.
Conclusions: The majority of literature supports the safety and efficacy of tachycardia treatment by paramedics, with only one article reporting adverse events. Innovative treatment options and treat-and-release protocols have proven successful, improving reversion rates, and reducing hospital admissions. These findings could significantly contribute to standardising out-of-hospital tachycardia treatment and potentially pave the way for paramedics to treat and release patients at home.

title: Deconstructing Automated Variant Interpretation: A Multi-Modal Ablation Study Comparing LLM Reasoning, Adversarial Agents, and Gradient Boosting in Inherited Cardiac Conditions
description: This study will employ a six-condition ablation design to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy, safety characteristics, and underlying cognitive mechanisms of three AI architectures in cardiogenetics: (1) Single-Agent Large Language Models (LLMs), (2) Adversarial Multi-Agent LLMs employing Critic–Arbitrator loops (GPT-5.1), and (3) a feature-based machine learning model (CatBoost). Each architecture will be evaluated under two information states—Baseline (ClinVar-blinded) and Enriched (ClinVar-available)—to isolate the effects of deep phenotypic reasoning versus external knowledge retrieval. This factorial framework is designed to test whether advanced reasoning architectures will yield measurable advantages over standard prompting and statistical pattern recognition, and to quantify the degree to which these systems will operate as independent diagnostic reasoners versus consensus-driven decision engines.

title: Biomarkers for the diagnosis and prognosis of patients with disorders of consciousness: a systematic review
description: Disorders of consciousness (DoC) are severe clinical conditions resulting from significant brain injuries and are characterized by varying degrees of impaired behavioural and cognitive responsiveness. In recent years, advances in neuroimaging, electrophysiology, and molecular techniques have led to the identification of potential biomarkers, offering promising avenues for improving diagnostic accuracy and prognostic prediction in DoC patients. This systematic review aims to evaluate the current landscape of biomarker research in DoC and to highlight the diagnostic, prognostic, and therapeutic implications of these developments. A structured search for studies on DoC and biomarkers was undertaken following PRISMA guidelines. The search was conducted across PubMed, Scopus, Cochrane Library, and Web of Science databases, focusing on studies published between 2014 and 2025. Out of 1,566 identified articles, 25 met the inclusion criteria and were analysed. The findings underscore the growing utility of biochemical biomarkers (e.g., neurofilament light chain, tau protein), electrophysiological (e.g., EEG, TMS-EEG), and neuromodulatory (e.g., TMS, tDCS and rTMS) and across different stages of DoC. Several studies also point to the potential of multimodal approaches combining these biomarkers to enhance the accuracy of diagnosis and prognosis. While promising, further research is needed to standardise protocols, validate findings in larger cohorts, and better tailor interventions based on individual patient profiles.

title: EUS elastography as an adjunct for the diagnosis of solid pancreatic masses and chronic pancreatic: A systematic review and meta-analysis
description:
The diagnosis of solid pancreatic masses and chronic pancreatitis (CP) remains challenging. Endoscopic ultrasound elastography (EUS-E), a non-invasive technique that measures tissue stiffness, has shown promising results for both conditions. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the diagnostic performance of EUS-E for solid pancreatic masses and CP.

A comprehensive search of multiple databases will be conducted. All published studies of adult participants who underwent EUS elastography for the diagnosis of pancreatic masses and CP will be included. Two reviewers independently will screen the studies, extract data, and evaluate the risk of bias. Statistical analyses will be performed utilizing the metandi and midas packages. A bivariate meta-analysis of sensitivity and specificity will be performed, accounting for the correlation between these two measures.

title: Machine learning models for predicting contraceptive discontinuation among reproductive-age women: A systematic review and meta-analysis
description:
This research project is a systematic review and meta-analysis that aims to evaluate the predictive performance of machine learning (ML) models for identifying contraceptive discontinuation among reproductive-age women. Contraceptive discontinuation remains a major public health challenge because it contributes to unintended pregnancies, unmet family planning needs, and adverse maternal and reproductive health outcomes. Early identification of women at high risk of discontinuation may support targeted counseling and personalized reproductive health interventions. In recent years, ML approaches have increasingly been applied to predict contraceptive discontinuation using large demographic and health datasets; however, evidence regarding their overall predictive accuracy and reliability has not been comprehensively synthesized.

The primary purpose of this study is to systematically identify, critically appraise, and quantitatively synthesize published studies that developed and/or validated ML-based prediction models for contraceptive discontinuation. The review will assess pooled predictive performance measures, including sensitivity, specificity, diagnostic odds ratio (DOR), and area under the summary receiver operating characteristic curve (SROC-AUC). The study will also evaluate heterogeneity across studies and explore differences in predictive performance according to ML algorithms, study settings, predictor variables, and validation methods.

A comprehensive literature search will be conducted in PubMed, Cochrane Library, Scopus, Wiley Online Library, and ProQuest for studies published up to August 31, 2025. Eligible studies will include original research involving reproductive-age women and reporting sufficient data on ML model performance. Two independent reviewers will conduct study selection, data extraction, and risk of bias assessment using the PROBAST tool.

The expected outcomes of this research include a pooled estimate of the predictive accuracy of ML models for contraceptive discontinuation and identification of factors contributing to variability in model performance. The findings are expected to provide evidence regarding the clinical and public health utility of ML-based prediction tools in family planning services. Additionally, the study may inform future research on predictive modeling and support the development of more robust and generalizable ML approaches for reproductive health applications.

title: Diagnostic Performance of Artificial Intelligence Algorithms for the Differentiation of Colorectal Liver Metastases from Benign Hepatic Lesions on CT: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
description: This study evaluates the diagnostic performance of artificial intelligence (AI) algorithms—encompassing deep learning and radiomics-based machine learning—in differentiating colorectal liver metastases (CRLM) from benign hepatic lesions on contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT). Following PRISMA-DTA guidelines, a systematic literature search was performed across PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, EMBASE, and IEEE Xplore for original diagnostic accuracy articles published between 2015 and 2026. Methodological quality was evaluated using the QUADAS-2 tool. A bivariate random-effects model was used to pool sensitivity and specificity from five eligible studies containing a total of 1,545 lesions (698 CRLM events and 847 benign controls). The pooled sensitivity was 86.4% (95% CI: 78.3–91.7%) and pooled specificity was 75.8% (95% CI: 60.9–86.3%). The findings show that while AI serves as an effective screening safety net due to high sensitivity, its diagnostic specificity remains variable, and performance drops significantly for sub-centimeter lesions (<10 mm).

title: eNose Technologies in the Detection of Cancer
description:
Early detection of cancer remains a critical goal in public health. This systematic review evaluates the diagnostic efficacy of electronic noses (eNoses) for detecting various cancer types using breath, urine, and other human biological samples.

This review aims to clarify the performance of eNoses across a broad range of cancers and sample types, while also evaluating how eNose device characteristics, such as sensor types and the number of sensors utilized, affect diagnostic accuracy. Additionally, we evaluate the current state of the field and identify key directions for future research.

title: Radiomics in Contrast-Enhanced Mammography for Breast Cancer Diagnosis and Characterisation: A Scoping Review

Radiomics, the extraction of high-dimensional, quantitative features from medical imaging, has emerged as a powerful tool in breast cancer imaging. Contrast-enhanced mammography (CEM) is an evolving modality that offers functional imaging capabilities comparable to MRI, yet with greater accessibility and reduced cost. CEM has demonstrated promise in lesion detection and characterisation, but its interpretation remains predominantly qualitative and reliant on radiologist expertise.
Radiomics applied to CEM may enhance diagnostic accuracy, reduce unnecessary biopsies, and enable noninvasive tumour characterisation. Preliminary evidence suggests that CEM radiomics can differentiate benign from malignant lesions, infer molecular subtypes, and predict nodal metastasis or prognosis. However, existing studies are methodologically heterogeneous, and no synthesis has yet mapped the scope and quality of current research.

title: Examining the Implications of Early Experiences of Stress and Parenting Quality for Infants’ Cortisol Responses during the Still-Face Paradigm
description:
The hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenocortical (HPA) axis is part of a complex stress response system that works in tandem with the autonomic nervous system to promote survival and aid in the management of stress (for in-depth reviews of the neurophysiology of the HPA axis, see Gunnar & Quevedo, 2007, Koss & Gunnar, 2018, and Lupien et al., 2009). Briefly, when signals of threat to one’s psychological or physical self are detected, the hypothalamus triggers a cascade of hormones eventually resulting in the production of cortisol in humans. Cortisol has an impact on the brain, behavior and cognition, and abnormally high or low levels can disrupt developmental trajectories in infancy and early childhood.

The Still-Face Paradigm (SFP) is a laboratory procedure that is widely used to assess infants’ socioemotional regulation strategies and abilities in the context of a period disruption in parent-infant interactions (Tronick, Als, Adamson, Wise, & Brazelton, 1978). The standard SFP consists of three episodes structured in an A-B-A sequence (Mesman et al., 2009; Tronick et al., 1978). The first episode is a play interaction in which parents are instructed to play with their infants as they normally would in other settings. The second episode is the still face in which parents are instructed to maintain neutral facial expressions and not respond to their infants’ cues. The third episode is a reunion period in which the parents are instructed to soothe their infant as they normally would while the infant remains seated in a high chair. Meta-analytic findings indicate that the experimental manipulation of parents’ psychological availability and responsiveness via the SFP is effective at eliciting a mean-level increase in infants’ cortisol levels (Provenzi et al., 2016). This finding is consistent with the notion that the functioning of the HPA axis is shaped by early experiences during parent-child interactions.

From a theoretical perspective, parental warmth and responsivity appear to closely align with the stress response system by signaling to the infant that they are safe. Studies examining the associations between parenting behavior and infants’ HPA axis responses to the SFP have produced inconsistent results. Some studies have provided evidence that sensitive responsiveness is associated with high infant cortisol responses, some have provided evidence that sensitivity is associated with low infant cortisol responses, and others indicate there is not a significant association between responsiveness and infant cortisol responses during the SFP (Grant et al., 2009; Martinez-Toreteya et al., 2014, 2015; Montirosso et al., 2013; Muller et al., 2015). A recent meta-analysis supported these conflicting findings by identifying no significant overall association between parental warmth/responsiveness and children’s HPA axis reactivity during the SFP (Hackman et al., 2018).

Hackman and colleagues’ (2018) meta-analytic study did provide evidence that the direction of the association between sensitive responsiveness and children’s cortisol reactivity may depend on contextual sources of stress. Specifically, high levels of parental warmth/responsiveness were associated with low HPA axis reactivity for children whose families had a middle to high socioeconomic status (SES). Conversely, high levels of parental warmth/responsiveness were associated with high HPA axis reactivity for children living in low SES environments. This finding is consistent with the biological sensitivity to context model, which suggests that early life experiences of stress and support have non-linear associations children’s physiological stress responses (Boyce & Ellis, 2005). That said, the meta-analytic findings were based on a single dichotomous measure of SES. Thus, additional research is needed examining a wider range of contextual challenges. Indeed, Hackman and colleagues’ 2018 study recommended that future research “clarify the nature and specificity of moderation by examining a broader range of environmental risks and supports that may buffer or exacerbate parenting behaviors’ impact on HPA axis functioning” (p. 1499). 

As highlighted by Hackman et al. (2018), socioeconomic hardship is one form of early adversity that may impact the early development of children’s stress response systems. Indeed, children raised in impoverished, single-parent family environments tend to exhibit elevated cortisol responses to stress (Blair et al, 2011; Evans, 2003; Lupien, King, Meaney, & McEwen, 2001; Provenzi, Giusti, & Montirosso, 2016; Repetti, Taylor, & Seeman, 2002; Martinez-Torteya et al., 2014). These results highlight the potential significance of families’ socioeconomic environments in shaping the development of children’s HPA axes. However, SES represents a wide range of challenges and lack of supports in children’s environments, which is not comprehensively captured by a dichotomized measure of low versus moderate/high SES.

Psychosocial stress is another potential marker of early experiences that may contribute to the development of the HPA axis. Indeed, various indices of psychosocial conditions—such as maternal mental health or marital status—have been found to be associated with infant cortisol reactivity during the SFP (Provenzi et al., 2016). For example, infants of depressed mothers are especially likely to exhibit a heightened cortisol response during the SFP (Brennan et al., 2008; Feldman et al., 2009; Martinez-Torteya et al., 2014). A limitation of the research in this area is the inconsistency in defining and operationalizing parents’ experiences of psychosocial stress. As a result, the current body of research limits our ability to understanding the full breadth of adversity and support necessary to examine the association of psychosocial stress on infants’ HPA axis reactivity.

title: Validation of the Obsessive Compulsive Eating Scale in Pregnancy
description:
This study will validate a novel measure of food cravings in pregnancy. Food cravings are strong urges for specific foods that are subjectively difficult or impossible to resist and often result in consumption. Food cravings are very common in pregnancy and have been linked to a significantly increased risk of excess gestational weight gain, which can cause a range of complications and short- and long-term health problems in pregnancy, delivery, and the postpartum. To date, existing measures of food cravings have not been validated specifically in pregnancy. This study will administer three measures of food cravings to a sample of 100 individuals in the second or third trimester of pregnancy, when cravings are typically most frequent and intense. These measures include two relatively novel measures of food cravings that are consistent with current models of food cravings as being cognitive-affective states (the Obsessive Compulsive Eating Scale and the Food Craving Acceptance and Action Questionnaire) as well as a well-established measure of food cravings that has substantial evidence base in the literature (the Food Craving Questionnaire-Trait-reducted). We will examine the psychometrics of these measures, along with their relationship to weight-related thoughts, behaviors, and outcomes, including symptoms of disordered eating and weight gain in pregnancy.

Participants who are eligible to participate will be invited to complete the following measures:

The Obsessive Compulsive Eating Scale (OCES): The OCES is a 14-item self-report questionnaire based on the well-established Obsessive Compulsive Drinking Scale that quantifies the cognitive underpinnings of food cravings. Items are rated on a scale of 0 to 4 and quantify the “obsessive” (e.g., frequency of thoughts) and “compulsive” (e.g., impaired functioning resulting from avoiding craved foods) tendencies of thoughts underlying specific food cravings. Higher scores indicate increased distress and interference of thoughts related to cravings.

Food Craving Acceptance and Action Questionnaire (FAAQ): The FAAQ is a two-factorial measure that quantifies “acceptance” of eating craved food and the “willingness” to control eating behavior despite cravings. Items are rated on a Likert-type scale, ranging from 1 = “very seldom true” to 6 = “always true.” Higher scores signify greater acceptance of motivations to eat craved foods. 

Food Craving Questionnaire- Trait, Reduced (FCQ-T-r): The FCQ-T-r is a 15-item questionnaire (adapted from the original 39-item version by selecting the 15 items with the highest item-total-correlations) assessing the behavioral, cognitive, and physiological aspect of food cravings. The FCQ-T-r asks about perceived lack of control over eating, thoughts or preoccupation with food, intentions to consume food, emotions before or during cravings, and cues that may trigger food cravings. The FCQ-T-r is scored on a Likert-type scale, ranging from 1 = “strongly disagree” to 5 = “strongly agree.” The measure has a one-factorial structure and high internal consistency.

Prenatal Eating Behaviors Screening tool (PEBS): The PEBS is a 12-item screening tool for eating disorders specifically in pregnancy that has been shown to perform with high sensitivity and specificity.

Participants will also be asked to provide information on their pregnancy (weeks pregnant, expected due date, prior pregnancies) and weight history (current weight, weight just prior to pregnancy, and highest and lowest adult weights).

title: Evidence on the utility of artificial intelligence in the interpretation of diagnostic radiological images in low and middle-income countries: a scoping review
description:
Background: In low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), access to diagnostic imaging remains limited due to scarce equipment, geographic barriers, inadequate digital infrastructure, and a shortage of trained personnel. Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a promising tool to address these gaps by enhancing diagnostic accuracy, supporting non-specialist health workers, and optimizing workflows. However, the evidence remains fragmented.
Objective: This scoping review aimed to identify and synthesize available evidence on the utility of AI in the interpretation of radiological diagnostic images in LMICs.
Methods: A scoping review was conducted in July 2025 following Arksey and O’Malley’s framework and reported according to the PRISMA-ScR guidelines. Searches were performed in PubMed, Scopus, and Clinical Key for studies published between 2000 and July 2025 in English and Spanish. Eligible studies included clinical applications of AI in radiological imaging within LMICs, reporting diagnostic accuracy, workflow impact, user perception, or implementation factors.
Results: From 620 records, 51 studies met the inclusion criteria, representing 33 LMICs. The majority were published between 2022 and 2025 and focused on ultrasound, X-ray, and computed tomography. Across these modalities, AI consistently improved diagnostic sensitivity, specificity, and clinical applicability, particularly for tuberculosis, pneumonia, obstetric care, and oncological screening. Evidence on magnetic resonance imaging was promising but mainly experimental, while mammography research remained scarce. Common limitations included small sample sizes, single-center designs, reliance on public datasets, and limited multicentric validation.
Conclusions: AI demonstrates significant potential to enhance radiological diagnostics in LMICs, particularly in ultrasound, X-ray, and computed tomography. Nevertheless, methodological heterogeneity, infrastructural challenges, and regulatory gaps underscore the need for larger multicenter studies, international collaboration, and context-adapted implementation strategies to ensure sustainable integration.

title: Complementary Vulnerabilities: A Systematic Review Comparing Reasoning Failures in Human and LLM Clinical Decision-Making
description:
Authors and Affiliations

Mohsen Amoei. McGill University, Montreal, Quebec, Canada / Mila - Quebec AI Institute, Montreal, Quebec, Canada

Elena Guadagno. Harvey E. Beardmore Division of Pediatric Surgery, The Montreal Children's Hospital, McGill University Health Centre, Montreal, Quebec, Canada

Dr Dan Poenaru. Harvey E. Beardmore Division of Pediatric Surgery, The Montreal Children's Hospital, McGill University Health Centre, Montreal, Quebec, Canada

Review Question
What are the distinct reasoning failure patterns exhibited by human clinicians and large language models (LLMs) in clinical decision-making, how do these failure patterns compare across both systems, and to what extent are they complementary, redundant, or orthogonal?

Methods
Searches

Scientific Literature
A medical librarian searched the following databases from January 2018 onward: PubMed, MEDLINE (Ovid), Embase (Ovid), and Scopus. The search employed a three-arm strategy: Search A targeted human clinical reasoning errors using terms related to cognitive biases, diagnostic errors, heuristics, and clinical decision-making failures; Search B targeted LLM clinical reasoning evaluation using terms related to large language models, medical benchmarks, AI hallucination, and reasoning failures; Search C targeted direct human-LLM comparative studies using combined terms from both domains. The search strategy used variations in text words found in the title, abstract or keyword fields, and relevant subject headings to retrieve articles examining reasoning failures in clinical decision-making by either human clinicians or large language models.

Grey Literature
arXiv was searched for preprints related to LLM clinical reasoning evaluation and AI cognitive biases in healthcare. Forward and backward citation searching (snowballing) will be conducted on all included studies. Conference proceedings and dissertation databases will also be searched.

Domain Being Studied
This systematic review examines clinical reasoning failures in both human clinicians and large language models performing healthcare decision-making tasks. The domain encompasses diagnostic reasoning, treatment planning, triage, and clinical judgment across all medical specialties. Human reasoning failures include cognitive biases (anchoring, confirmation bias, availability heuristic, premature closure), fatigue-related errors, and experience-dependent failures. LLM reasoning failures include hallucination, prompt sensitivity, context window limitations, training data biases, and non-reproducibility. The review specifically focuses on how and why reasoning fails (failure mechanisms) rather than aggregate performance metrics alone.

Inclusion and Exclusion Criteria
Studies were included if: (1) the study examined clinical reasoning or diagnostic decision-making by human clinicians (physicians, nurses, medical trainees) or large language models (GPT-4, Med-PaLM, LLaMA, and similar); (2) the study analyzed reasoning failures, errors, cognitive biases, or error mechanisms rather than reporting only accuracy metrics; (3) the study was published in English from January 2018 onward; (4) the study was a primary research article, including empirical studies, benchmark evaluations, randomized experiments, observational studies, cross-sectional surveys, or retrospective analyses; (5) for LLM studies, the system evaluated was a transformer-based large language model.

Studies were excluded if: (1) the study focused exclusively on non-clinical AI applications (e.g., administrative, scheduling); (2) the study involved only rule-based or traditional machine learning systems without large language models; (3) the study reported only aggregate accuracy, sensitivity, or specificity without characterizing specific failure types or reasoning mechanisms; (4) the study was an editorial, opinion piece, letter, commentary, or conference abstract without primary data; (5) the study was a case report describing individual diagnostic errors without systematic analysis of reasoning mechanisms.

Main Outcome(s)
The outcomes of this study will focus on (1) developing a unified taxonomy of clinical reasoning failure types classified as human-unique, LLM-unique, or shared between both systems, with characterization of underlying mechanisms for each failure type; (2) assessing the degree of complementarity between human and LLM reasoning failures, measured by the proportion of failure types that are unique to each system versus shared; (3) determining the prevalence of each failure type reported as the percentage of included studies documenting each reasoning failure; and (4) identifying clinical domains and task types most susceptible to each category of reasoning failure.

The unified taxonomy refers to a comprehensive classification framework that maps all identified reasoning failure types into three mutually exclusive categories based on convergent evidence from multiple studies. Complementarity will be assessed by examining whether systems show strengths where the other shows weaknesses, supporting collaborative deployment models.

Measures of Effect
This review uses qualitative thematic synthesis rather than quantitative meta-analysis. The primary measure is the classification of each reasoning failure type into one of three categories: human-unique, LLM-unique, or shared. For each failure type, prevalence will be reported as the percentage of included studies documenting that failure. For shared failures, mechanistic differences between human and LLM manifestations will be described qualitatively. The degree of complementarity will be expressed as the ratio of unique-to-shared failure types across both systems.

Additional Outcome(s)
These outcomes will explore the broader implications and applications of the comparative failure taxonomy:

Mitigation Strategy Effectiveness: Evaluating the effectiveness of reported mitigation strategies (e.g., structured reasoning prompts, cognitive debiasing techniques, retrieval-augmented generation, chain-of-thought prompting) for reducing reasoning failures in each system, and identifying which strategies show cross-system applicability.

Complementarity Thesis Evidence: Assessing evidence for or against the complementarity thesis, specifically whether human and LLM reasoning strengths and weaknesses are inversely correlated, supporting collaborative deployment over substitution models in clinical settings.

Domain-Specific Vulnerability Mapping: Mapping failure types to specific clinical specialties and task complexity levels to identify which clinical contexts are most and least suitable for human-AI collaborative decision-making.

Data Extraction
Data will be extracted using a standardized extraction form. The extraction form will be pilot-tested on a sample of 20 studies to ensure clarity and consistency before proceeding with full data extraction. Extracted data will include: standard bibliographic information (author(s), title, year, journal, DOI/PMID), study design, clinical domain and medical specialty, population characteristics (clinician type, experience level, or LLM model evaluated), reasoning failure types identified with definitions provided by the study authors, failure mechanisms described, prevalence or frequency data where reported, mitigation or debiasing strategies evaluated and their effectiveness, and study limitations. Data will be extracted by one reviewer and verified by a second reviewer. Any disagreements will be resolved through discussion or consultation with a third reviewer. A Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) Flow Diagram will be created to detail the number of records identified, screened, included, and excluded, as well as the reasons for exclusions.

Strategy for Data Synthesis
For this systematic review, data from the included studies will be synthesized using thematic synthesis following the approach described by Thomas and Harden (2008). The synthesis proceeds in three stages: (1) line-by-line coding of extracted data to identify reasoning failure types reported in each study, (2) organization of codes into descriptive themes representing distinct failure categories, and (3) generation of analytical themes through cross-domain comparison of human and LLM failure patterns.

Failure types will be classified as human-unique, LLM-unique, or shared based on convergent evidence from multiple studies. For shared failure types, the underlying causal mechanisms in humans versus LLMs will be compared to determine whether failures arise from analogous or distinct processes. Quantitative descriptive statistics will summarize the frequency of each failure type across studies, the distribution of studies across clinical domains, the proportion of studies supporting each taxonomy category, and study quality ratings. No statistical meta-analysis of effect sizes is planned due to the heterogeneity of study designs and outcome measures. Results will be presented using narrative synthesis supplemented by summary tables and a taxonomy visualization diagram. The synthesis findings will be reported in accordance with the PRISMA guidelines.

Analysis of Subgroups or Subsets
Subgroup analyses will be conducted to explore variation in reasoning failure patterns across the following dimensions:

(1) Clinical domain: Comparing failure patterns across specialties (e.g., emergency medicine, oncology, radiology, primary care, surgery) to identify domain-specific vulnerabilities in both human and LLM reasoning.

(2) LLM model type: Analyzing whether different model architectures (e.g., GPT-4, Med-PaLM, LLaMA, Claude) exhibit different failure profiles, and whether newer models show improvement on specific failure types.

(3) Task complexity: Examining whether failure patterns differ across simple diagnostic tasks (e.g., single-condition identification) versus complex multi-step clinical reasoning (e.g., differential diagnosis with comorbidities).

(4) Study design: Comparing findings from controlled experimental studies versus observational analyses versus benchmark evaluations to assess whether methodology influences reported failure patterns.

(5) Clinician experience level: Assessing whether reasoning failure patterns differ between medical trainees and experienced clinicians, and how these compare to LLM failure profiles.

A sensitivity analysis will examine whether excluding low-quality studies alters the taxonomy structure or key conclusions.

Quality Assessment
Study quality will be assessed using a custom adapted quality assessment framework evaluating three dimensions: methodological rigor (study design appropriateness, sample size adequacy, statistical methods), sample characteristics (population representativeness, clinical scenario realism), and reporting quality (transparency of methods, completeness of results, acknowledgment of limitations). Studies will be rated as high, medium, or low quality. Quality assessment will be conducted by one reviewer and verified by a second reviewer. Any disagreements will be resolved through discussion. A sensitivity analysis will be performed to determine whether excluding low-quality studies affects the overall findings or taxonomy structure.

Dissemination Plans
Results will be submitted for publication in a peer-reviewed journal and presented at relevant conferences including the AMIA 2026 Annual Symposium. The completed taxonomy, extraction data, and analysis code will be made publicly available through this OSF project. An arXiv preprint will be posted to ensure open access to findings prior to journal publication.

Registration
This review is registered on PROSPERO (submitted February 2026, registration pending).

title: JCAE Ablation Study
description:
# Pre-Registration: JCAE Ablation Study

**Title:** Causal Evaluation of Judgment-Conditioned Agentic Ecosystem Components: A Hybrid Controlled-Observational Ablation Study

**Authors:** Juan David Zuluaga-Monroy, Diego Fernando Zuluaga-Monroy

**Pre-registration date:** 2026-05-12
**OSF DOI:** [TO BE ASSIGNED ON OSF UPLOAD — pending]
**Status:** FROZEN — data collection may begin after OSF DOI is confirmed

---

## 1. Background and Motivation

The Judgment-Conditioned Agentic Ecosystem (JCAE) [Zuluaga-Monroy &
Zuluaga-Monroy 2026] introduces two pre-dispatch gates that classify
the epistemic state of a research claim (Gate 1: STABLE / AMBIGUOUS /
MISSING_EVIDENCE / CONTRADICTORY / HIGH_RISK / UNANSWERABLE) and evaluate
the expected value of stabilisation (Gate 2: EV > sum of costs). A
retrospective ablation on N=134 dispatches from one research project
suggests that these gates increase specialised subagent use from ~40% to
70% and triple the formation of multi-step reasoning chains, but the
retrospective design cannot establish causation.

This study tests whether the two gates **causally** improve six
pre-defined outcome measures across 30 standardised research tasks
under random condition assignment.

## 2. Research Questions and Hypotheses

### Primary hypotheses (Bonferroni-corrected α = 0.01)

**H1 (Citation correctness).** Condition A (JCAE Full) produces outputs
with higher citation correctness than Condition D (Baseline LLM), with
Cohen's d ≥ 0.5 and p < 0.01.

**H2 (Verification gate violations).** Condition A produces fewer
unverified completion claims per output than Condition D, with d ≥ 0.5
and p < 0.01.

**H3 (Calibration).** Condition A's stated confidence aligns more
closely with empirical correctness than Condition D, measured by absolute
calibration error (|stated − actual|), d ≥ 0.5 and p < 0.01.

### Secondary hypotheses (Bonferroni-corrected α = 0.0125)

**H4 (Gate 1 specific).** Condition A produces higher specialised
subagent dispatch rate than Condition B (No Gate 1), with d ≥ 0.4 and
p < 0.0125.

**H5 (Gate 2 specific).** Condition C (No Gate 2) shows higher dispatch
count and higher latency than Condition A, with d ≥ 0.4 and p < 0.0125.

**H6 (Frontier detection).** Condition A correctly classifies
UNANSWERABLE tasks at higher rate than Condition D (precision ≥ 0.7 vs
≤ 0.3), tested by exact binomial test.

**H7 (Ecological validity).** *DEFERRED to Phase 2.* This hypothesis
required parallel observational data and is removed from confirmatory
analysis under Tier 2 scope. The observational arm protocol remains
documented for potential future activation.

### Exploratory analyses

- Per-task-category effect heterogeneity
- Interaction effects (judgment-state × condition)
- Latency-quality tradeoff curves
- Inter-rater reliability between automated metrics, LLM-as-judge, and
 human evaluation on the validation subset

## 3. Study Design Overview

### Single-arm controlled design (Tier 2 scope)

**Controlled arm:** 30 standardised tasks × 4 conditions × 1 run
each = 120 task executions in a controlled harness using the Anthropic
API directly with explicit system-prompt manipulation.

**Note on scope.** This pre-registration covers the controlled arm
only. A complementary observational arm (real-research dispatches with
granular condition tagging) is designed and documented at
`observational/protocol.md` but is **deferred** to a Phase 2
investigation, to be activated only if reviewers explicitly request
ecological-validity evidence beyond what the controlled arm provides.
This deferral is a deliberate scoping decision, not an omission.

The controlled arm establishes causal effects under random assignment
within a well-defined task domain. Limitations of single-arm controlled
design (reduced ecological validity) are explicitly acknowledged in §11
of the paper.

### Random assignment (controlled arm)

Each task is run under all four conditions in randomised execution
order (24 random orderings sampled without replacement, then re-sampled
to fill 30 tasks). Run order is balanced to detect any time-of-day or
warm-up effects on the underlying API.

### Blinding

The LLM-as-judge sees only the output text, never the condition label.
Outputs are anonymised by stripping any system-prompt-revealing tokens
prior to judging.

## 4. Task Suite

Thirty standardised tasks distributed across six categories of
research-relevant work, five tasks per category. All tasks are drawn
from or constructed for the Tensegrity research project so that ground
truth is verifiable against existing artifacts (EXPERIMENTS-LOG.md,
paper drafts, results JSONs).

| Category | Tasks | Expected judgment state distribution |
| ----------------------------- | ----- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| Literature claim verification | 5 | 3 STABLE, 2 CONTRADICTORY |
| Cross-paper consistency check | 5 | 2 STABLE, 3 CONTRADICTORY |
| Provenance verification | 5 | 4 STABLE, 1 MISSING_EVIDENCE |
| Hypothesis design | 5 | 5 AMBIGUOUS / MISSING_EVIDENCE |
| Frontier detection | 5 | 3 transitional, 1 methodological, 1 undecidable |
| Section drafting | 5 | mixed |

Each task has:

- Task description (≤ 100 words, identical across conditions)
- Expected judgment state (for H6 evaluation only — never shown to system)
- Ground truth (for automated metrics) or rubric (for LLM-judge metrics)
- Source corpus (the documents the system is given access to)

The full task list with ground truths is committed to
`tasks/task_suite.json` and SHA-256 hashed for the pre-registration
freeze.

**Draft SHA-256 (2026-05-07, pre-freeze):**
`d8ca0900762b2b2459dc1de2b1fbd2e4816eef37867f6d83b1a664e599899540`

**Distribution deviation note (logged pre-freeze):**
CAT1 target was 3 STABLE / 2 CONTRADICTORY; actual is 2 STABLE /
3 MISSING_EVIDENCE. Deviation reason: Ingber 2003, Friston 2010, and
Papyan 2020 PDFs are absent from ARTICULOS BASE, making source-absent
verification the most natural and testable scenario. This is a more
demanding test than contradictory-claim detection.
CAT2 target was 2 STABLE / 3 CONTRADICTORY; actual is 1 STABLE (with
protocol note) / 4 CONTRADICTORY. Minor deviation.

## 5. Condition Specifications

Each condition is fully defined by its system prompt and dispatch
configuration, both committed to `conditions/`.

### Condition A — JCAE Full (control)

- Full constitutive disposition (soul) + dispatch protocol
- Gate 1 epistemic state classification active
- Gate 2 EV formula active
- All 27 subagents available
- Hooks active (PostToolUse, SubagentStop, Stop, SessionStart)

### Condition B — No Gate 1

- Full disposition + dispatch protocol
- Gate 1 disabled — system is instructed to dispatch by task type only
- Gate 2 active (operates on task-type signal instead of judgment state)
- All 27 subagents available

### Condition C — No Gate 2

- Full disposition + dispatch protocol
- Gate 1 active (judgment state classified)
- Gate 2 disabled — system dispatches whenever Gate 1 returns non-STABLE
 without cost-benefit evaluation
- All 27 subagents available

### Condition D — Baseline (vanilla LLM)

- Minimal system prompt: "You are a helpful research assistant. Answer
 the user's question."
- No constitutive disposition, no dispatch protocol, no subagents
- Direct single-turn response

All four conditions use identical model (Claude Sonnet 4.6), identical
temperature (0.0 for reproducibility), and identical max_tokens.

## 6. Outcome Measures

### Primary outcomes (automated)

**O1 — Citation correctness.** For tasks involving citation, percentage
of citations that (a) refer to a real source, (b) accurately reflect
what that source claims. Verified mechanically against the project's
ARTICULOS BASE corpus and EXPERIMENTS-LOG.md.

**O2 — Verification violations.** Count of completion-claim patterns
("done", "passes", "fixed", Spanish equivalents) emitted without a
verification action in the same response. Measured by the existing Stop
hook script applied to each output.

**O3 — Calibration error.** Absolute difference between the system's
stated confidence (extracted from hedge markers via NLP regex pipeline)
and the empirical correctness rate (from O1, O4, O6).

### Secondary outcomes (automated)

**O4 — Provenance match rate.** Percentage of provenance verification
tasks where the system's claim about source matches ground truth.

**O5 — Frontier detection accuracy.** For frontier detection tasks,
binary correctness of UNANSWERABLE classification + correct frontier_type.

**O6 — Process metrics.** Number of dispatches, total latency, total
tokens used per task.

### Tertiary outcomes (LLM-as-judge)

**O7 — Quality rubric score.** For section drafting and hypothesis
design tasks, a 1–5 score on each of: completeness, clarity, hedging
calibration, and operational specificity. LLM judge:
`meta/llama-3.3-70b-instruct` via NVIDIA NIM API (smoke-tested
2026-05-07; JSON rubric output validated, 216 tokens/call). This model
is architecturally distinct from the system under test (Meta Llama
family vs Anthropic Claude), satisfying the anti-self-evaluation
requirement. Fallback if NIM unavailable:
`mistralai/mistral-large-2-instruct` via NVIDIA NIM (same API key,
same base_url); second fallback: Claude Opus 4.5 from a separate
API key with structured anti-bias prompting (condition labels stripped).

### Validation outcome (human-rated subset)

**O8 — Human rubric.** 10 randomly-selected (task, condition) pairs
across all 30 tasks scored by one human evaluator (the senior author)
blind to condition. Used to validate LLM-judge against human judgment;
inter-rater agreement reported via Cohen's kappa.

## 7. Sample Size Justification

For α = 0.01 (Bonferroni-corrected for 3 primary hypotheses),
power = 0.80, and Cohen's d = 0.5 (medium effect), the required N per
group from a two-sample t-test is approximately n = 51.

We use a within-task repeated-measures design (each task run under all
4 conditions), so the relevant N is 30 paired observations per
between-condition contrast. Mixed-effects model accounts for
within-task correlation.

For Cohen's d = 0.5 detection in a paired design, N = 30 yields power
≈ 0.81 — adequate for primary hypotheses. Effects smaller than d = 0.5
may not be detectable; we will not interpret null results as evidence
of no effect.

## 8. Statistical Analysis Plan

### Primary analyses (pre-registered)

For each primary outcome (O1, O2, O3):

1. Fit mixed-effects model: outcome ~ condition + (1 | task)
2. Extract pairwise contrasts (A vs D, A vs B, A vs C) with Bonferroni
 correction
3. Report point estimate, 95% bootstrap CI (10 000 iterations), Cohen's d

For H6:

4. Exact binomial test of UNANSWERABLE classification accuracy under A vs D

### Triangulation analysis

*DEFERRED to Phase 2.* See §3 scoping note.

### Robustness checks (exploratory, not pre-registered as confirmatory)

- Sensitivity to LLM-judge: rerun O7 with a second judge model
- Effect heterogeneity across task categories
- Effect of run order
- Effect of token budget / latency

## 9. Stopping Rules and Exclusions

**No stopping rule** — we run all 120 controlled-arm tasks before any
analysis. Observational arm continues for 14 weeks regardless of
controlled-arm results.

**Pre-registered exclusions:**

- Runs where the API returns an error (re-run once; exclude if
 persistent)
- Runs where output is < 50 tokens (treat as system failure, re-run)
- Tasks where ground truth itself is contested in the project (mark and
 exclude post-hoc with explicit justification)

The authors developed the JCAE system under evaluation. To mitigate
self-evaluation bias:

title: Accuracy and Reliability of Wearable and Clinical-Grade Devices for Vital Sign Monitoring: Evidence from a Scoping Review of Validation Studies
description:
This scoping review aims to systematically map and critically appraise existing evidence on the accuracy and reliability of wearable (commercial) and clinical-grade devices for vital sign monitoring. The study focuses on commonly measured physiological parameters heart rate, respiratory rate, blood pressure, oxygen saturation, and body temperature and compares device performance against established clinical standards.

The review follows the methodological framework of the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) and adheres to the PRISMA-ScR reporting guidelines. Electronic databases including PubMed, Scopus, EBSCOhost, and ScienceDirect will be searched for validation or comparative studies published between 2015 and 2025. Eligible studies include those evaluating wearable or portable devices in healthy or clinical populations, using reference standards such as electrocardiography, pulse oximetry, or manual sphygmomanometry.

Data extraction will capture study characteristics, participant demographics, device types, measurement contexts (rest, motion, clinical use), statistical indicators of accuracy (bias, limits of agreement, MAE, RMSE), and reliability metrics. Methodological quality will be assessed using the COSMIN checklist for measurement properties and the QUADAS-2 tool for diagnostic accuracy studies.

The expected outcomes are to identify which classes of wearable devices achieve clinically acceptable accuracy compared to medical-grade instruments, highlight methodological and reporting gaps in current validation research, and provide guidance for future device development and regulatory evaluation in telemedicine and digital health contexts.

title: Circulating Tumor DNA-Based Molecular Residual Disease After Curative-Intent Therapy in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer: An Umbrella Review of Diagnostic Accuracy, Recurrence Prediction, and Adjuvant-Treatment Guidance
description: This umbrella review evaluates the current evidence on circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA)-based molecular residual disease (MRD) assessment after curative-intent therapy in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). The review synthesizes evidence from systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and pooled analyses regarding the diagnostic accuracy of ctDNA-MRD testing, prediction of recurrence and survival outcomes, and its potential role in guiding adjuvant treatment decisions. title: Evaluation of an intensive training course on chest x-ray interpretation and competence among trainee radiologists using eye tracking
description:
Visual search is a fundamental behaviour underpinning medical image perception (Brams et al., 2020). Radiologists perform many intricate visual search tasks daily to identify, stage, and diagnosis disease (Treviño et al., 2022). Yet, despite extensive training and clinical experience, reporting clinicians remain vulnerable to error. Error primarily stems from inefficient or incomplete searching and are perceptual in nature, rather than as a result deficient medical knowledge (Bruno et al., 2015), highlighting the need for a deeper understanding of how radiologists conduct visual search. Perceptual errors can be further exacerbated by the presence of multiple targets in an image (Kim & Mansfield, 2014), and whilst conventional approaches, such as verbal reports or annotations of search order attempt to address this problem, these self-reports can be unreliable due to discrepancies with actual search behaviour (Martinez et al., 2025). 

Eye tracking offers an objective, quantitative method to explore radiologists’ search patterns and underlying cognitive processes during image perception. While numerous studies have compared the diagnostic performance and eye movements of novices with experts cross-sectionally (van der Gijp et al., 2017; Waite et al., 2019; Wu & Wolfe, 2019), little is known about the within-participant improvements in visuospatial attention that may result from structured training interventions. To this end, the current study aims to examine first-year trainee radiologists performing a chest X-ray task before and after an intensive two-day training course. Assessment of changes in diagnostic accuracy and scan paths can provide insights into the ways in which targeted education can shape perceptual search strategies in one of the most widely used, yet error-prone, imaging modalities.

title: Extracellular Vesicles as Biomarkers for the Diagnosis of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
description: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) is an autoimmune inflammatory disease with a multifactorial etiology, primarily affecting women of childbearing age. It presents as a multisystemic condition, potentially involving the skin, kidneys, and heart. Diagnosis is based on clinical and immunological criteria, such as those established by SLICC and ACR/EULAR; however, it is often delayed due to the complexity of symptoms. A particular group of vesicles, known as extracellular vesicles (EVs), has shown relevance in the diagnosis and treatment of autoimmune diseases, representing a potential diagnostic method that is faster and more accurate for SLE. In this context, this study aims to analyze, through a systematic review, the use of EVs in the diagnosis of SLE, compared to currently available testing methods. The study will be conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. The electronic literature search will be conducted until June 2025 using the PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Cochrane Library databases to answer the PICO question: “Are extracellular vesicles effective as biomarkers for the diagnosis of systemic lupus erythematosus?” Diagnostic accuracy will be considered the primary outcome. The ideal biological material for EV collection and the biomarker detection method will be included as secondary outcomes. After article selection and data extraction, the data will undergo bias assessment and meta-analysis. It is expected that this study will determine the biomarker potential of EVs for the diagnosis of SLE.

title: AI in Precision Oncology: A Systematic Review of Somatic Genomics and Molecular Diagnostics in Solid Tumors
description:
Context: Next-generation sequencing (NGS) and digital droplet PCR (ddPCR) are central technologies in precision oncology for solid tumours. Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) tools are being developed at every stage of the molecular diagnostic pipeline from pre-analytical quality control and tumour cellularity estimation, through somatic variant calling and clinical annotation, to pan-tumour biomarker computation (TMB, MSI, HRD), liquid biopsy analysis, automated reporting, therapeutic matching, and laboratory information system (LIS) integration.

Gap: Despite the rapidly growing body of primary studies, no existing systematic review covers the full molecular diagnostic pipeline in a transversal (pan-cancer), multi-layer approach. Published reviews focus on isolated applications. None addresses the complete chain from sample QC to regulatory compliance. One PROSPERO-registered meta-analysis (CRD420251163071) partially overlaps with our layer E (AI + liquid biopsy) but does not cover the remaining six layers.

Aims: (1) To systematically identify and evaluate AI/ML tools applied to the seven functional layers (A–G) of the clinical NGS/ddPCR diagnostic pipeline in solid tumours. (2) To assess their diagnostic performance (sensitivity, specificity, AUC, concordance) against recognised gold standards. (3) To characterize the level of clinical maturity (research prototype vs. clinically validated vs. operational) and regulatory status (CE-IVDR, FDA SaMD, RUO/LDT). (4) To identify unresolved bottlenecks and gaps in clinical implementation.

title: Use of Salivary ATR-FTIR Spectroscopy in the Screening and Diagnosis of Systemic Diseases: A Scoping Review Protocol
description:
Abstract
Objective: This scoping review aims to map and synthesize the existing evidence on the use of salivary ATR-FTIR spectroscopy, alone or in combination with other analytical techniques, for the screening or diagnosis of systemic diseases in human studies.
Methods: The data sources included several databases, such as MEDLINE (PubMed), Excerpta Medica Database (EMBASE), The Cochrane Library, Livivo, LILACS, Web of Science, Scopus, Epistemonikos, and Google Scholar (gray literature), to identify articles on the topic. The electronic search was conducted on November 24, 2025, with an update performed on December 24, 2025. No language or publication period restrictions. Two independent researchers will apply eligibility criteria and select studies for inclusion in the scoping review, with a third specialist resolving discrepancies. Data extraction and review will also be conducted by two independent researchers, which will then be analyzed by the third expert researcher in scoping reviews to resolve any potential divergences. Data will be tabulated in an Excel spreadsheet; no specific software will be used for data extraction and management.
Inclusion criteria: Studies involving human participants, conducted in clinical, hospital, laboratory, or outpatient settings, that use salivary samples analyzed by ATR-FTIR spectroscopy, either alone or in combination with other analytical techniques, for the purposes of screening or diagnosis of systemic diseases. Original studies such as clinical trials, observational studies (cross-sectional, cohort, or case-control), pilot studies, diagnostic accuracy research, or methodological validation studies will be considered, with no restriction on language or publication period.
Exclusion criteria: Studies will be excluded if they do not use human saliva as the biological matrix, if they employ spectroscopic methods other than ATR-FTIR, or if they are conducted exclusively in animal models, cell cultures, or other experimental settings without direct clinical applicability. Studies addressing conditions restricted to the oral cavity, such as oral cancer, burning mouth syndrome, oral lichen planus, periodontal disease, gingivitis, dental caries, and other purely local oral disorders, will also be excluded, as these conditions do not reflect systemic diseases. Editorials, letters, protocols without data, guidelines, case reports, case series, reviews, book chapters, theses or dissertations, and full conference abstracts will likewise be excluded.
