title: Reliability and Validity of Straight Leg Raise Test in Individuals with Radicular Pain
description:
Background: The Straight Leg Raise (SLR) test is a widely used neurodynamic assessment tool for diagnosing radicular pain, yet questions persist regarding its reliability and validity across different populations and clinical contexts. Despite its widespread clinical application, there remains inconsistency in diagnostic accuracy and standardized testing protocols.
Objective: This scoping review aimed to systematically evaluate the reliability and validity of the Straight Leg Raise test in individuals with radicular pain, examining psychometric properties including sensitivity, specificity, and inter-rater reliability across diverse clinical populations.
Methods: A comprehensive search was conducted across four electronic databases (Scopus, PEDro, Cochrane Library, and PubMed) from 2015 to 2025, following PRISMA-ScR guidelines. Studies evaluating SLR test reliability and/or validity in individuals with radicular pain were included. Data extraction focused on sensitivity, specificity, reliability coefficients, and diagnostic accuracy measures. From a total of 1247 studies, Nine articles met the inclusion criteria following systematic screening and comprehensive analysis of complete texts.
Results: Most of the studies that were reported, according to the research, concluded that the SLR test demonstrated high sensitivity (77-97%) but limited specificity (25-81%) for detecting lumbar nerve root involvement. Inter-rater reliability was significantly enhanced by standardized testing protocols incorporating structural differentiation maneuvers, achieving excellent kappa values up to 0.87. Diagnostic accuracy varied dramatically across demographics, with individuals over 60 years showing notably reduced sensitivity of 33%.Combined testing approaches integrating SLR with supplementary tests like Bragard or slump tests enhanced both sensitivity and negative predictive values.
Conclusion: The SLR test remains an effective screening instrument for diagnosing radicular pain when used as part of comprehensive neurodynamic assessment batteries rather than as a standalone diagnostic tool. Future research should focus on developing standardized testing protocols, validated test combinations, and age-specific modifications to optimize diagnostic accuracy across diverse clinical populations with suspected radicular pain.

title: Accuracy of Intraoperative Surgical Margin Assessment Techniques in Veterinary Oncology
description:
Accurate determination of surgical margin status is fundamental for detecting residual microscopic residual cancer in patients, predicting clinical outcomes, and optimizing treatment planning. Postoperative histopathology following surgical tumor resection is considered the gold standard for margin evaluation; however, this process typically takes one or two weeks to obtain results and only a limited sample of the surgical margins are assessed. Consequently, this delay results in a missed opportunity to evaluate surgical margins in real time and to utilize that information for immediate intraoperative decision-making, which could improve patient outcomes. Several techniques are available for intraoperative surgical margin assessment, each with different levels of accuracy, including frozen tissue section biopsy, imprint cytology margin, near-infrared fluorescence imaging, and optical coherence tomography (OCT) which has the potential to guide surgical-decision making in real-time.

This review aims to compare the diagnostic accuracy of intraoperative surgical margin evaluation techniques as individual studies focus on the reporting of accuracy of one technique in comparison to histopathology. Only studies on canine cutaneous or subcutaneous tumors will be included in the review. 
The primary outcome of the review is comparison of diagnostic accuracy for detection of positive surgical margins in cutaneous and subcutaneous tumors across techniques.

title: A mobile-health smartphone application shows high diagnostic accuracy for malignant skin lesions in a Latin American population: a prospective diagnostic accuracy study
description:
This research project is a diagnostic accuracy study designed to evaluate the performance of an artificial intelligence (AI)-based smartphone application for the detection and triage of malignant skin lesions in a Colombian population with broad ethnic diversity and a predominance of Fitzpatrick skin phototypes III–VI. The project was developed in response to the increasing global burden of skin cancer and the growing need for accessible, scalable strategies that facilitate early detection and timely referral to dermatologic care, particularly in regions with limited specialist access.

Globally, skin cancer represents one of the most common malignancies and continues to rise in incidence. Although melanoma accounts for most skin cancer-related deaths, non-melanoma skin cancer (NMSC), including basal cell carcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma, contributes substantially to morbidity and overall mortality due to its very high incidence. In Colombia, melanoma exhibits distinct epidemiologic characteristics compared to high-incidence countries, including a predominance of acral lentiginous melanoma and a high proportion of advanced-stage diagnoses. Mortality-to-incidence ratios are nearly twice those observed in many high-income countries, reflecting delays in diagnosis and barriers to specialized care. At the same time, artificial intelligence tools for skin lesion classification are rapidly expanding, yet most available algorithms have been trained and validated using datasets derived predominantly from European, North American, and Oceanian populations, with minimal representation of darker skin phototypes or Latin American populations. This lack of demographic diversity raises concerns regarding the generalizability and equity of AI-assisted dermatologic tools.

The primary purpose of this project is therefore to determine the sensitivity and specificity of a mobile-health application that integrates a convolutional neural network with optional dermatologist review for identifying malignant skin lesions in real-world clinical settings involving ethnically diverse populations. The study also aims to evaluate the application’s performance in detecting premalignant lesions and specific skin cancer subtypes, including basal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and melanoma. In addition, subgroup analyses according to Fitzpatrick phototype were conducted to explore whether diagnostic performance varies across different skin types.

The study was conducted at the Dermatology Unit of San Ignacio University Hospital (HUSI) in Bogotá, Colombia, and complemented by three rural and underserved community health brigades in Mahates (Bolívar), Buenaventura (Valle del Cauca), and Leticia (Amazonas). These regions were intentionally selected because they include Afro-descendant, Indigenous, and mixed Hispanic populations with higher frequencies of darker skin phototypes and historically limited access to dermatologic services. By incorporating participants from both tertiary urban care centers and remote underserved regions, the project seeks to improve representation of populations traditionally excluded from AI validation studies in dermatology.

Eligible participants included adults attending dermatologic consultation who presented with at least one cutaneous lesion suitable for photographic assessment. After informed consent, lesions underwent standardized evaluation including sociodemographic characterization, Fitzpatrick skin phototype classification, dermatologist clinical assessment, and image capture using the smartphone application. The application generated an AI-based risk classification and, when necessary, incorporated remote review by a dermatologist panel. Dermatologists performing the clinical evaluations were blinded to the application results. Lesions suspicious for malignancy underwent biopsy for histopathological confirmation, while benign and premalignant lesions were classified using predefined clinical and histopathologic criteria. Data were collected and managed using REDCap, ensuring secure storage and standardized data acquisition across both urban and remote settings.

The primary expected outcome of this project is to provide robust evidence regarding the diagnostic performance of AI-assisted mobile applications in populations that have been historically underrepresented in dermatologic AI research. Specifically, the study seeks to determine whether this technology maintains acceptable sensitivity and specificity in individuals with darker skin phototypes and diverse ethnic backgrounds. Secondary expected outcomes include generating data on the performance of the application across different lesion categories and cancer subtypes, as well as identifying potential disparities in algorithmic accuracy between phototype groups.

More broadly, this project aims to contribute to the development of more equitable and generalizable AI systems in dermatology. The findings may help inform future validation studies, support safer integration of AI-assisted triage tools into clinical practice, and encourage the inclusion of ethnically and phenotypically diverse populations in dermatologic machine learning datasets. The project also seeks to explore the potential role of smartphone-based AI technologies as accessible screening and referral-support tools in low-resource settings where access to dermatologists is limited.

title: An exploratory cross-sectional study of the association between characteristics, physical activity and perceived health motivation and the prevalence of patellofemoral pain in students aged 18-40 in a UK university.
description:
Patellofemoral pain (PFP) is considered one of the most prevalent musculoskeletal (MSK) conditions facing primary healthcare (Crossley et al., 2016). Characterised by pain in the anterior aspect of the knee along the patella, it is usually aggravated by movements that load the patellofemoral joint, such as squatting, running, climbing stairs, and sitting for prolonged periods (Gaitonde et al., 2019). Given the chronic trajectory of this condition with 50%-57% of individuals reporting persistent symptoms 5-8 years after the incidence (Lankhorst et al., 2016), it creates a considerable financial burden on healthcare systems (Willy et al., 2019). In the United Kingdom, it is estimated that PFP accounts for 100,000 visits per year, representing a significant economic challenge for the National Health Service (Garza-Borjón et al., 2024).
 
A systematic review by Smith et al. (2018) demonstrated that the prevalence of PFP in the general population is approximately 22.7%, rising to 28.9% in young adults aged 15–24. The majority of epidemiological studies focus on adolescents, military personnel, or the general active population, meaning the university student population, both active and sedentary, is under-represented in the literature.
 
Despite these high estimates, research describing PFP’s longitudinal pattern in university cohorts remains scarce, particularly in the UK. This is important, as the university student population is a uniquely high-risk cohort. The academic lifestyle is inherently sedentary, often requiring prolonged periods of sitting for lectures and study that frequently exceed the 10-hour daily threshold associated with increased risk of chronic knee pain (Hanna et al., 2019; Lee et al., 2019). The link between prolonged sitting and PFP is well established, with Collins et al. (2016) finding that 80% of the PFP population experience anterior knee pain when sitting for a long time. While Bhatti et al. (2022) discovered an association between prolonged sitting and PFP in a university environment, their cohort included staff over the age of 40. This inclusion introduces diagnostic confounding, as PFP symptoms often overlap with patellofemoral osteoarthritis (PFOA) in older cohorts Crossley et al., 2016). By limiting this study to students typically below 40, a more homogenous sample is ensured, reducing the risk of degenerative changes skewing results.
 
A significant limitation in existing literature is the implementation of non-validated measurement instruments, mainly relying on subjective history (Smith et al., 2018), leading to the potential over or underestimation of prevalence. To address this, recent studies have implemented the Survey Instrument for Natural History, Aetiology and Prevalence of Patellofemoral Pain Studies (SNAPPS). Developed by Dey et al. (2016), the SNAPPS utilises a knee pain map and clinical feature questions to differentiate PFP from other injuries with high sensitivity (92%) and specificity (94%).
 
The SNAPPS has been successfully utilised in various global contexts. Xu et al. (2018) found a PFP prevalence of 20.7% in a Chinese community sample, while Akodu and Nwakalor (2018) observed a 45.3% prevalence among amateur runners in Nigeria. 
Only once has the SNAPPS been used in the general university setting by Ibeachu et al. (2019). However, the study looked at general knee pain and not PFP specifically. Furthermore, Yusuf et al. (2021) validated an electronic version (eSNAPPS), demonstrating excellent agreement with the paper version (ICC: 0.99 95% CI 0.99 — 1.00, p < 0.0001). This study will utilise the eSNAPPS to provide a standardised methodology. The benefit of using a validated tool in research to diagnose PFP is providing a standardised methodology to minimise heterogeneity. This will provide more accurate results and allow data from different studies to be pooled and compare the prevalence from different studies (Migliavaca et al., 2020). The use of such tools enhances the reliability of meta-analyses, especially when addressing the complexities of prevalence studies and their inherent heterogeneity (Migliavaca et al., 2022). However, it is noted that as a retrospective self-reported questionnaire, recall bias remains a limitation.
 
While PFP limits physical activity, with 74% of sufferers reducing or stopping sports participation (Heintjes et al., 2003), evidence also suggests that activity behaviours themselves impact knee symptoms. Ibeachu et al. (2019) linked knee symptoms to activity behaviours in UK students, suggesting that both sedentary and highly active lifestyles may influence joint loading and symptom development.
 
To categorise these levels, the International Physical Activity Questionnaire (IPAQ) is widely used in epidemiological studies. Craig et al. (2003) established the IPAQ as a reliable and valid tool for large-scale population studies. Although recent validation studies point out limitations in agreement with device-based measurements in some clinical groups, its usefulness in adult populations remains generally supported for observational cohort studies.
 
A cross-sectional study was done by Varela-Mato, Victor et al. [A10] (2012) in Spain to investigate the lifestyle habits and physical activity levels of university students. The search involved undergraduate students across various academic fields. The data were gathered using the International Physical Activity Questionnaire to evaluate physical activity, recording weekly engagement in vigorous activity, moderate exercise, and walking. This questionnaire enabled the researchers to determine physical activity levels in Metabolic Equivalent in Task (MET)- minutes per week and categorise participants into low, moderate, or high physical activity levels based on IPAQ scoring guidelines. The findings revealed that a significant number of students failed to meet the recommended physical activity levels, with lifestyle behaviour differences identified between male and female students (Varela-Mato, Víctor et al., 2012).
 
It is important to understand how patients feel about their health and what motivates them to take care of it, which may be associated with physical activity and PFP "Health styles" describe how people interact with their health through choices, actions, and motivations. Davies and Goodwin (2024) stressed the need to assess these traits, as they affect how people respond to treatment, comply with rehabilitation, and deal with symptoms over time.
 
Population segmentation methods have been employed to classify individuals into distinct health profiles based on patterns such as diet, smoking, mental health, and alcohol consumption (Bareham et al., 2012). Wolff et al. (2010) validated a model for health consumer segmentation, revealing that these behavioural profiles were linked to preventive health practices. In the UK, La Placa et al. (2014) categorised individuals into five behavioural segments, emphasising that health behaviours are significantly affected by personal motivations and social contexts.
 
Research specifically concerning musculoskeletal conditions is growing; Davies and Goodwin (2024) found that people with non-specific low back pain who possessed more positive Health Styles were more likely to engage in rehabilitation and health-promoting behaviours. However, no studies have explored how these health-related behavioural patterns affect the prevalence of knee pain specifically in university students.
 
By determining prevalence of PFP in the University population, this study could identify unmet health needs at Manchester Met, and help guide support or services to students affected by PFP. Identifying associations between activity, heath styles and other key variables may also generate hypotheses for future longitudinal studies into incidence, prediction and prognosis of PFP and development of potential strategies to manage PFP.

title: Human learning from predictive AI
description: We examined the effects of predictive AI deployment on the immediate performance and learning of medical novices. In two pre-registered field experiments, we varied whether AI input was provided during the training or practice of lung cancer diagnoses, or both. Our results show that different AI deployments have distinct implications for learning: AI input during training or practice independently improves individuals’ diagnostic accuracy, whereas deployment across both phases yields gains that exceed either approach alone. Furthermore, AI input in both training and earlier practice can improve the accuracy of individuals’ subsequent independent diagnoses. Beyond individual accuracy, AI deployment affects the diversity of errors across individuals, with consequences for the accuracy of group decisions (e.g. when getting a second or third opinion on a diagnosis).

title: Diagnostic Performance of AI-assisted Digital Chest Radiography Interpretation for Pulmonary Nodule Detection in Adults: A Scoping Review
description:
Background: Lung cancer requires early nodule detection to improve patient prognosis. Although chest radiography (CXR) is the primary imaging modality used in primary healthcare, its sensitivity is limited by the superimposition of anatomical structures and inter-reader variability in radiographic interpretation. Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a diagnostic support tool capable of reducing errors and optimizing diagnostic accuracy. The objective of this study is to map the available evidence on the diagnostic performance of AI applied to the interpretation of digital CXR for pulmonary nodule detection in adults.

Methodology: A scoping review was conducted in accordance with the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) guidelines and the PRISMA-ScR statement. For the systematic search, full-text primary studies published between 2016 and 2026 were identified in PubMed, LILACS, Scopus, IEEE Xplore, Scopus, Embase, ProQuest and Google Scholar.

title: Clinical diagnosis of pulp condition in pediatric dentistry: a scoping review
description: The clinical diagnosis of pulpal conditions in pediatric dentistry presents a significant challenge due to the complexity of clinical manifestations and the variability in children's responses to sensitivity tests. Studies indicate that factors such as the immaturity of the child's nervous system, limited communication, and lack of collaboration during clinical examination make diagnosis even more challenging. The difficulty in distinguishing between different conditions and their respective etiologies can lead to inapropriate interventions, compromising the success of treatment and long-term oral health. In this sense, histological analysis would allow the identification of characteristics such as hyperemia, inflammatory infiltration, and necrosis, which are essential for determining the apropriate treatment, confirming the pulpal condition. However, histological diagnosis cannot be performed before treatment, highlighting the need for improved clinical testing. Thus, a careful and systematic approach, combined with the use of apropriate diagnostic technologies, is essential to improve clinical diagnostic accuracy in pediatric dentistry.

title: Diagnostic performance and feasibility of bowel elastography in the pediatric population: a systematic review
description:
This systematic review evaluates the diagnostic performance and feasibility of bowel elastography in the pediatric population (≤18 years). Ultrasound elastography (strain and shear wave) and MR elastography quantify bowel-wall stiffness and may non-invasively characterize inflammatory versus fibrotic change, but existing syntheses are limited to adults or to Crohn disease. We will systematically review elastography of the bowel wall and appendix across pediatric pathologies — inflammatory bowel disease, celiac disease, acute appendicitis and intussusception — and in healthy children (normative/feasibility studies).

PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science and Cochrane CENTRAL will be searched from inception, supplemented by hand-searching of reference lists. Two reviewers will independently screen, extract data, and assess risk of bias (QUADAS-2; JBI for case series). Primary outcomes are diagnostic accuracy (sensitivity, specificity, AUC, correlation with reference standards) and normative values with feasibility/reproducibility. Evidence will be synthesized narratively (SWiM), with quantitative meta-analysis attempted only where studies are sufficiently homogeneous in modality, unit and outcome. Certainty will be graded with GRADE.

Reporting follows PRISMA 2020 and PRISMA-DTA.

title: SCOPING REVIEW OF THE EVOLUTION OF DELIRIUM DETECTION, DIAGNOSTIC, AND SEVERITY ASSESSMENT SCALES
description:
The morbidity and mortality associated with delirium, or acute confusional syndrome, and the significant burden it represents at clinical, administrative, and family levels, have been well-documented. Early detection of delirium is critical to enabling timely intervention in its underlying causes and establishing appropriate treatment, which has driven numerous researchers over the past 70 years to develop and refine specific diagnostic tools. This work has resulted in a wide array of assessment methods that have evolved significantly over time in response to the inherent complexities of this syndrome.
In its early stages, diagnostic evaluations involved complex and lengthy batteries, whose application was limited to psychiatry specialists, who could establish a diagnosis through prolonged processes. However, these methodologies proved insufficient to address the growing population affected by delirium. Two main factors underlie this insufficiency: the high incidence of the syndrome, as highlighted by recent studies showing its presence across hospital settings, nursing homes, and home care, and the fluctuating nature of delirium, which complicates the continuous identification of symptoms without constant monitoring by psychiatrists.
The combination of these factors has driven the creation of various diagnostic tools that allow delirium identification by other healthcare professionals and even caregivers and family members. Additionally, the variability of clinical settings in which these patients present has led to the adaptation of these tools for specific populations, such as pediatric patients, patients in critical care units (including those intubated or on mechanical ventilation), and in emergency services, thereby optimizing the sensitivity and specificity of diagnostic methods within these contexts. The high workload faced by healthcare professionals has necessitated the simplification of these tools, promoting the development of faster and shorter screening scales.
The considerable number and diversity of diagnostic instruments developed underscore the need for an in-depth analysis to identify and contextualize the primary studies, gathering the original psychometric data of each tool and establishing a timeline that clarifies the evolution of delirium diagnosis. This analysis will provide a solid foundation for comparing and validating new detection instruments, offering a reference framework to evaluate their accuracy and clinical relevance in diagnosing delirium.

title: Performance of Federated Learning in Health Services Research: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
description:
Protocol for Rapid Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
1. Title and Registration Title: Performance of Federated Learning in Health Services Research: A Rapid Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
Registration: This protocol will be registered with the Open Science Framework (OSF).
2. Background
Federated learning (FL) is a decentralized machine learning (ML) approach that enables multi-institutional model development without sharing patient-level data. It has emerged as a promising strategy for clinical modeling in health services research (HSR), particularly under data governance constraints. However, the comparative performance of FL models relative to local and centralized models and the consistency of reporting and implementation practices in HSR remain incompletely summarized.
3. Objectives
To evaluate the performance of FL models in HSR relative to local and centralized models and to assess the transparency of reporting, model sharing practices, and methodological consistency.
4. Methods
4.1 Eligibility Criteria
We will include original peer-reviewed studies applying FL to clinical prediction tasks in HSR, including diagnosis, prognosis, segmentation, and resource allocation. Studies must compare FL models to local and/or centralized models and report at least one model performance metric (e.g., sensitivity, specificity, AUC, F1 score). We will exclude reviews, editorials, commentaries, protocols, and studies not involving human clinical data.
4.2 Information Sources and Search Strategy
We will systematically search Ovid MEDLINE and PubMed from inception to June 10, 2025. Search terms will include: “federated learning,” “machine learning,” “health services research,” “clinical prediction,” and related synonyms. No language restrictions will be applied.
4.3 Study Selection
Two reviewers will independently screen titles, abstracts, and full texts. Disagreements will be resolved by consensus.
4.4 Data Extraction and Risk of Bias Assessment
Two reviewers will extract data on study design, country, care setting, FL architecture (e.g., FedAvg, FedSGD), number of participating sites, sample size, type of clinical task, and model performance metrics (e.g., sensitivity, specificity, AUC, F1). Due to the rapid review nature, interrater reliability (e.g., kappa) and formal risk of bias assessment will not be conducted.
4.5 Data Synthesis
We will conduct a narrative synthesis and, where feasible, perform random-effects meta-analyses on pooled performance metrics. Results will be stratified by comparator model type (local vs centralized) and clinical use case (diagnosis, prognosis, segmentation).
5. Limitations
This review will follow rapid review methodology. Limitations include absence of interrater agreement measures, no formal risk of bias or publication bias assessments, and single-reviewer screening confirmation.
6. Dissemination Plans
The findings will be submitted for peer-reviewed publication and shared at relevant academic conferences and via professional networks. The full dataset and extraction code will be made publicly available to promote reproducibility.
7. Funding and Conflicts of Interest
This review is unfunded. The authors declare no conflicts of interest.
8. Ethics Approval
Not applicable; this review does not involve primary data collection.

title: Real-time detection of eating behavior and meal consumption by commercial wrist-worn smartwatches: protocol for a systematic review and meta-analysis
description: Accurate assessment of dietary consumption and eating behavior is essential for understanding nutrition-health relationships, yet traditional dietary assessment methods are subject to recall bias, social desirability bias, and high participant burden. Commercial wrist-worn smartwatches provide a promising, unobtrusive platform for real-time detection of eating behavior by capturing hand-to-mouth movements and related intake gestures through embedded sensors in naturalistic settings. This systematic review protocol aims to synthesize the existing evidence on the diagnostic accuracy, analytical performance, and feasibility of commercial wrist-worn smartwatches for real-time detection of eating behavior and meal consumption. The review will be conducted in accordance with PRISMA 2020 guidelines, with additional adherence to PRISMA-DTA for diagnostic accuracy studies and PRISMA-P for protocol reporting. Findings will inform the translational potential of smartwatch-based approaches for applications in clinical nutrition, behavioral interventions, and public health monitoring.

title: Medical competence, diagnostic accuracy and treatment accuracy among health workers in Africa: A systematic review protocol
description:
The shortage, both quantitative and qualitative, of the health workforce in Africa has been widely reported. Recent regional reports (Organization, 2021; Asamani et al., 2024) have shown an increasing number of the stock of health workers in Africa as a result of increasing production capacity. Paradoxically, the fiscal space constraints of the respective member countries do not allow for the recruitment of all the qualified health professionals, creating high-health worker unemployment in Africa. As such, there are critical gaps in the health workforce needed for universal health coverage. Additionally, recent discourse has reported inconsistencies in the quality of the recruited health workforce across member countries, health professions, diseases, and assessment methods. Thus, this review sought to synthesize the competencies, diagnostic accuracy and treatment accuracy of the health workforce in the African region.
The primary synthesis will be structured around competence construct, clinical domain, geography, cadre and measurement method. Studies will first be grouped by outcome type: clinical knowledge or vignette competence; diagnostic accuracy; treatment accuracy or correct management; guideline adherence and prescribing; observed practice or standardised-patient performance; and intervention-related change. Within each group, results will be summarised by clinical domain, country, cadre and study design. Large representative studies will be distinguished from small facility-level or programme studies because their inferential value differs.
Meta-analysis will be considered only when at least three studies report sufficiently comparable outcome definitions, denominators and populations. For binary outcomes, proportions or risk ratios may be pooled using random-effects models after variance stabilisation where appropriate. For continuous competence scores, standardised mean differences may be considered if instruments are conceptually comparable. Statistical heterogeneity will be assessed using I2, prediction intervals where useful and visual inspection of forest plots. If pooling would obscure more than clarify, results will be reported narratively with structured tables and descriptive visualisations.
Where meta-analysis is not appropriate, SWiM-informed synthesis will describe the grouping logic, report study-level results transparently, avoid vote counting by statistical significance alone and explain how study size, representativeness, risk of bias, directness and consistency influence interpretation (Campbell et al., 2020). Quantitative findings will be reported with denominators, percentages, confidence intervals and effect estimates as available. The final review will avoid producing a single continental competence estimate unless the underlying evidence supports that inference.
Planned Subgroup and Sensitivity Analyses
• Cadre: physicians, nurses, midwives, clinical officers, non-physician clinicians, community health workers and mixed cadres.
• Clinical domain: maternal and child health, malaria, HIV and infectious diseases, cervical cancer screening, emergency care, general primary care and other domains.
• Measurement method: vignette, written test, standardised patient, direct observation, record review, surveillance data and diagnostic reference standard.
• Setting: country, region, facility level, facility ownership, urban or rural location and public or private sector where reported.
• Risk of bias: primary interpretation including all eligible studies, with sensitivity analyses excluding high-risk studies and separating large, representative studies from smaller, selected samples.

title: Deep Learning-Enhanced PET Imaging for Intelligent Medical Diagnosis
description:
Abstract
Positron Emission Tomography (PET) is widely used in modern healthcare to analyze metabolic and biochemical processes within the human body. It is particularly valuable for the early detection and diagnosis of diseases such as cancer, neurological disorders, and cardiovascular conditions. However, PET imaging is often affected by challenges like image noise, low spatial resolution, and high computational demands, which can limit its diagnostic effectiveness. These limitations highlight the need for more advanced and efficient computational techniques to improve image quality and interpretation.
To overcome these challenges, this study proposes a deep learning-based approach for enhancing PET image analysis. The framework combines multiple advanced models to improve feature extraction and learning efficiency. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) are used to capture important spatial features from PET images, while Residual Networks (ResNet) enable deeper model training without performance degradation. In addition, Transformer-based models are incorporated to understand global patterns and long-range dependencies within the images. The integration of PET with complementary imaging techniques such as PET/CT and PET/MRI further strengthens diagnostic accuracy by combining functional and structural information.
The proposed method demonstrates improved performance in key clinical applications, including tumor detection, neurological disorder analysis, and cardiac assessment. It enhances image clarity, increases diagnostic accuracy, and reduces computational limitations compared to traditional approaches. Overall, this work highlights the potential of deep learning to make PET imaging more reliable and efficient. Future research will focus on real-time implementation, minimizing radiation exposure, and improving model transparency through explainable artificial intelligence techniques.

Computational methods for analysis of medical imaging or imaging reports hold potential to improve the clinical management of IPMNs by providing quality control and improving the diagnostic accuracy of imaging methods for IPMN assessment. title: Exploring the effectiveness of intimate partner violence screening tools in pregnant women: a mixed method systematic review protocol
description:
In this mixed method systematic review, we explore the effectiveness of intimate partner violence (IPV) screening tools used to screen pregnant women. Despite clinical guidelines supporting IPV screening in prenatal care, the effectiveness of the tools currently in use and the experiences of those being screened are poorly understood.

The main objective of this review is to explore the effectiveness of current screening tools used to assess IPV in women throughout their pregnancy journey. The pregnancy journey encompasses the period from preconception (actively trying to get pregnant) to the perinatal period (the period you become pregnant and up to one year after giving birth). 

To examine the effectiveness of these tools, we will explore the reported psychometric properties, such as tool sensitivity and specificity, in pregnant women who have undergone IPV screening in healthcare settings. To explore the topic, we will use a targeted search strategy in which studies will be sourced from CINAHL, MEDLINE, PsycINFO, CENTRAL, and Google Scholar. Only studies published between 2015 and 2025 in English will be included. Qualitative, quantitative, and mixed-methods research will be considered. All studies will be screened on the Covidence with 10% of studies requiring two independent reviewers. All conflicts will require a consensus from the entire research team. Data extraction will also take place on Covidence, which will require 10% of studies to be reviewed by two independent reviewers. The data extracted from both reviewers must be identical and will need consensus to move on to the data analysis phase. 

Once the screening and data extraction processes are completed, findings will be synthesized using inductive and thematic analysis to identify patterns in patient experiences and reported psychometric properties regarding screening tools and their effectiveness. The results of this review will add to the evidence about trauma-informed and effective IPV screening practices and support future research, clinical decision-making, and policy development.

title: Diagnostic Accuracy of Soft Tissue Cytology and Risk of Malignancy Across the IAC–IARC–WHO Six-Tier Reporting System: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis with Retrospective Category Mapping
description:
• Background: Soft tissue tumours present a major diagnostic challenge due to their morphological heterogeneity and cytomorphological overlap between benign and malignant lesions. Fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) is a minimally invasive, cost-effective technique used for the preliminary assessment of soft-tissue masses; however, its clinical utility has historically been limited by the lack of a standardised reporting framework.
• Context: The IAC–IARC–WHO Cytopathology Reporting System for Soft Tissue Lesions, published in 2025, introduces a six-tier diagnostic framework (Insufficient/Nondiagnostic/Inadequate, Benign, Atypical, Soft Tissue Neoplasm of Uncertain Malignant Potential [STNUMP], Suspicious for Malignancy, and Malignant) aligned with the WHO Classification of Tumours.
• Objectives: This systematic review and meta-analysis aims to (1) evaluate the overall diagnostic accuracy (sensitivity, specificity, likelihood ratios, diagnostic odds ratio) of soft tissue cytology using a bivariate random-effects model; (2) determine the pooled risk of malignancy (ROM) for each of the six IAC–IARC–WHO categories through retrospective category mapping of published studies; and (3) assess the clinical utility of this reporting system as a risk-stratified decision-support framework in the preoperative management of soft tissue lesions.
• Methods: A systematic literature search was conducted in PubMed and additional electronic databases up to February 2026, with no date restrictions, following PRISMA-DTA guidelines. Studies reporting soft tissue cytology cases with histopathological confirmation and sufficient categorical detail for mapping to the IAC–IARC–WHO six-tier system were eligible. Two independent reviewers performed data extraction, retrospective category mapping, and quality assessment using the QUADAS-3 tool. Pooled diagnostic accuracy estimates were derived using a bivariate random-effects model, and hierarchical summary ROC (HSROC) curves were generated. Heterogeneity was assessed using I² statistics. Subgroup analyses and meta-regression were conducted. Pooled ROM for each WHO category was calculated using a random-effects proportion meta-analysis. The certainty of the evidence was assessed using the GRADE framework.
• Expected Outcomes: This study is expected to provide the most comprehensive meta-analytic evaluation of the diagnostic accuracy of soft tissue cytology, including pooled ROM estimates for all six WHO categories and an assessment of the reporting system’s validity as a risk-stratification tool.

title: Artificial Intelligence for Obstructive Sleep Apnea: A Bibliometric and Translational Mapping of Diagnostic Modalities (2015–2025)
description:
This project is a bibliometric performance analysis combined with a descriptive translational mapping of the indexed research literature on artificial intelligence (AI) for obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), focused on diagnostic modalities and published between 2015 and 2025. Its purpose is to characterize how research attention is distributed and how the scientific focus has evolved across the field, and to relate diagnostic modality families to plausible clinical use cases while maintaining a clear distinction between research activity and demonstrated clinical performance. OSA remains substantially underdiagnosed because access to attended polysomnography (PSG) and expert scoring is constrained; AI may support sleep-laboratory workflows (automated sleep staging, respiratory-event scoring, signal-quality assessment) and expand detection through simplified biosignals (oximetry, single-lead ECG, wearable PPG/multisensor systems, audio/snore analysis).
The review will draw on two multidisciplinary databases, Scopus and the Web of Science Core Collection (WoS-CC). Because the abbreviation "OSA" and broad computational terminology retrieve substantial unrelated technical literature, the intentionally sensitive merged retrieval will not be used directly; instead, a conservative explicit-OSA specificity screen (records retained only when an explicit OSA-related phrase appears in the title, abstract, or indexed keywords) will define the single analytic denominator. Bibliometric performance indicators (annual production, sources and source concentration, author productivity, citations, country participation by full counting with SCP/MCP, and normalized author-keyword frequency) will be computed in Bibliometrix/Biblioshiny. The thematic landscape will be characterized through normalized author keywords and a VOSviewer temporal overlay. Modality-linked mapping will assign records to five predefined, non-mutually-exclusive signal families (automated PSG/PSG-adjacent; single-channel oximetry/SpO₂; single-lead ECG; wearable PPG/multisensor; audio/snore) using transparent, locked term dictionaries, and a descriptive translational interpretation overlay will relate these families to four use-case categories (supervised workflow augmentation; screening/triage; remote monitoring/case finding; exploratory development). Reporting follows the BIBLIO guideline, PRISMA-S, a PRISMA 2020-style flow diagram, and the Donthu et al. (2021) framework. The unit of analysis is the indexed bibliographic record; the study analyzes no patient-level data and requires no ethics approval.
The study addresses scientometric research questions on the evolution of production and source structure, the distribution of research attention across modality families, the thematic landscape, and the descriptive translational positioning of each modality family with its principal remaining evidence requirement. Expected outcomes are a transparent, reproducible field-level map and a structured translational overlay intended to contextualize where research attention concentrates and how it has shifted (broadly, from automated PSG scoring toward simplified-signal triage and wearable/consumer-facing applications). No formal or validated readiness score is assigned. All findings will be interpreted as patterns of research attention and apparent positioning, never as evidence of diagnostic accuracy, comparative effectiveness, or implementation readiness, which require external validation and prospective clinical-impact studies.
This registration is hybrid: the search strategy was developed retrospectively through preliminary and exploratory equations up to the final locked equations, while all subsequent phases (corpus extraction, de-duplication, metadata eligibility cleaning, the explicit-OSA specificity screen, performance analysis, keyword overlay mapping, modality-linked mapping, and the translational overlay) are registered prospectively and have not been executed at the time of registration.

title: Reporting and Interpretation of Respiratory Metagenomic Results in Clinical Practice: A Systematic Review from the UK NHS Respiratory Metagenomics Network.
description:
This project aims to synthesise current evidence and practice on the reporting and clinical interpretation of respiratory metagenomic sequencing, and to develop expert consensus guidance for laboratories and clinicians. Metagenomic next generation sequencing is increasingly used for the diagnosis of severe respiratory infections, but approaches vary widely between centres. There are currently no society level guidelines specific to respiratory metagenomics, and local practice is often based on informal rules or single centre experience. This work addresses that gap.

The project has two main components. First, we are conducting a systematic review of primary studies that use metagenomic sequencing of respiratory samples for clinical reporting or decision making. Eligible studies include validation and diagnostic accuracy studies, case series, and implementation studies across a range of technologies and analytical pipelines. From each study we extract data on analytical thresholds and decision rules for reporting pathogens, use of negative controls and background contamination, handling of organisms that may represent colonisation as well as infection, strategies for reporting genotypic antimicrobial resistance, and the structure and content of laboratory reports. 

Second, we are using these findings to inform a structured Delphi consensus process within the United Kingdom National Health Service Respiratory Metagenomics Network (https://metagenomics.nhs.uk). A multidisciplinary panel of clinical microbiologists, virologists, infectious diseases physicians, and clinical scientists participate.

The expected outputs are: (i) a comprehensive narrative synthesis of current reporting and interpretation practices for respiratory metagenomic diagnostics, highlighting key methodological and implementation challenges; (ii) a set of consensus guidance statements and a practical framework for laboratory reporting, including suggested approaches to thresholds, negative controls, colonisation prone organisms and antimicrobial resistance reporting; and (iii) identification of priority areas for future research and validation. The guidance is primarily intended for use in health systems similar to the UK NHS but will be written so that it can be adapted to other settings through local validation and governance.

title: Serotonergic system alterations in schizophrenia: a systematic review
description:
Abstract
Schizophrenia is a psychiatric disorder characterized by symptoms that significantly impair an individual’s social and functional life, including psychosis, hallucinations, anhedonia, as well as alterations and distortions in thought and speech organization. It affects about 1% of the population, with the first symptoms usually emerging during adolescence or early adulthood. Men and women are affected in similar proportions, although onset tends to occur earlier in men, which is also associated with a worse prognosis in this group. Its origin is mainly related to dysregulation of the mesocorticolimbic dopaminergic pathway and abnormal synaptic pruning during neurodevelopment. However, there is a growing consensus that schizophrenia has a multifactorial nature, combining multiple genetic and environmental factors that influence its onset. Despite its high heritability, disease progression is also strongly influenced by alterations in other neuromodulator systems, stress, inflammatory processes, and neurodevelopmental abnormalities. Serotonin (5-HT), a neuromodulator widely distributed in the central nervous system, plays an important role in regulating mood, cognition, and perception—functions frequently impaired in individuals with schizophrenia. Evidence suggests that dysfunctions in serotonergic receptors, particularly the 5-HT2A and 5-HT1A subtypes, may contribute to both positive and negative symptoms. Nevertheless, their role remains insufficiently defined, as studies on the topic are heterogeneous and tend to focus on different receptor subtypes, highlighting the need for broader investigations involving other receptors. We plan to carry out a systematic review of the literature on alterations in serotonergic pathways and their involvement in different stages and manifestations of schizophrenia. The focus will be on studies assessing receptor modifications in patients with schizophrenia compared with healthy controls, in order to identify patterns, the most affected brain regions, and their relationship with serotonin’s neurobiological functioning. We will include original studies using molecular imaging techniques such as PET and PET-CT to analyze receptor density, distribution, and activation in living patients, as well as postmortem studies assessing the same outcomes through histological methods. Searches will be conducted on PubMed, Embase, and Web of Science – Core collection. We hope this review will gather evidence capable of guiding future investigations into the relationship between schizophrenia and the serotonergic system, as well as other potentially associated factors, with the ultimate aim of broadening perspectives on the disorder’s pathophysiology and contribute to the development of more effective therapeutic strategies.
Key-words: Schizophrenia; Serotonin; Neuromodulators; Sistematic Review



INTRODUCTION
Background
Schizophrenia is a chronic brain disorder characterized by delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, thought disturbances, and lack of motivation (American Psychiatric Association, 2013). It affects approximately 1% of the global population and is one of the leading causes of disability worldwide (Yoon et al., 2016). The disorder can significantly impair an individual’s ability to perform daily activities, with variability in the degree of functional impairment (American Psychiatric Association, 2013). In the United States, the average life years lost among people with schizophrenia is estimated at nearly three decades (Velligan, 2023).
Diagnosis is based on the presence of at least two core symptoms, including positive symptoms such as delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, grossly disorganized behavior, or negative symptoms such as avolition and reduced emotional expression, persisting for at least one month. Additional diagnostic criteria include a decline in functioning since onset, continuous disturbance for at least six months, and exclusion of medical or substance-related causes (American Psychiatric Association, 2013).
Psychotic symptoms typically emerge between late adolescence and early adulthood, most commonly between 20 and 30 years of age. Onset tends to occur earlier and be more severe in men. While the condition can develop abruptly, it usually follows a gradual and progressive course. Prognosis remains uncertain: approximately one-fifth of patients achieve favorable outcomes, full recovery is rare, and the majority require long-term support (American Psychiatric Association, 2013).
Rationale
Treatment of schizophrenia is still primarily based on antipsychotic medications combined with multiprofessional care. However, this approach faces limitations related to medication availability, side effects, and patient adherence (American Psychiatric Association, 2020). Despite decades of use, few significant advances have been made in therapeutic strategies, underscoring the need for new approaches (American Psychiatric Association, 2024).
The disorder has been classically associated with abnormal dopaminergic activity across different brain regions (Araripe Neto; Bressan; Busatto Filho, 2007). Nevertheless, evidence also highlights the involvement of other neurotmodulatory systems, particularly the serotonergic system. Serotonin plays a broad role in brain function, affecting anything from synaptic communication to cellular integrity in a variety of brain regions, without a clear functional logic uniting its disparate functions (Cools; Nakamura; Daw, 2011; Cummings; Arias; Stahl, 2025). Its interaction with dopamine is especially relevant, as it could, potentially, both attenuate and exacerbate dopaminergic dysfunction (Cools; Nakamura; Daw, 2011). Additionally, several effective antipsychotics exert their therapeutic effects in part through serotonergic modulation, suggesting that this system may play a central role in the pathophysiology of schizophrenia (Reynolds, 2022).
Although this topic has already been addressed in previous systematic reviews, such as that of Selvaraj et al. (2014), which the present study aims to update, those analyses often presented significant limitations, including a restricted focus on specific receptor subtypes or the lack of clear conclusions regarding the causal relationship between serotonergic alterations and clinical symptoms. Moreover, the advancement of neuroimaging techniques and the publication of new studies during this period further justify a comprehensive update of the available literature.
Objective
This study aims to systematically review the literature about alterations on the serotonergic system in schizophrenia. Specifically, it seeks to determine whether there are differences in serotonergic receptor expression between healthy patients and those with schizophrenia, and is so, to characterize their nature, identify the most affected receptor subtypes, and map the brain regions most consistently involved.
 
 METHODS
Study Design
This study consists of a systematic literature review, which will be conducted according to the methodological principles described by Gough, Oliver, Thomas (2012), Cooper (1982), and the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews (Higgins et al., 2019). The reporting of the review will follow the PRISMA 2020 guidelines whenever applicable (Page et al., 2021).
Guiding Question
The framing of the review question will be organized around the following elements: the population, comparison, and outcome of interest, all of which are further detailed below:
• Population refers to patients diagnosed with schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder.
• The outcomes of interest are the receptor density, distribution, and/or activation patterns of different serotonergic receptor subtypes in different brain regions, as assessed in living patients through molecular imaging methods or postmortem through histological methods.
• The comparison of the outcome should be made against healthy individuals without schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder, who will also undergo receptor analysis through molecular imaging.

Search Strategy
The searches will be conducted on the PubMed, Web of Science, and EMBASE databases, with no restrictions regarding publication date or language. The search terms, specified for each database, will be as follows:
PubMed ("Serotonin"[Mesh] OR 5-HT* OR Serotonin* OR 5-Hydroxytryptamine OR "5 Hydroxytryptamine" OR Enteramine OR Hippophaine OR Hydroxytryptamine) AND ("Schizophrenia"[Mesh] OR Schizo*) AND ("Autopsy"[Mesh] OR Post-mortem OR Postmortem OR autopsy OR necropsy OR "Positron Emission Tomography Computed Tomography"[Mesh] OR PET OR PET-CT OR SPECT OR SPET OR Positron OR "Emission tomography")
Web of Science (5-HT* OR Serotonin* OR 5-Hydroxytryptamine OR "5 Hydroxytryptamine" OR Enteramine OR Hippophaine OR Hydroxytryptamine) AND (Schizo*) AND (Post-mortem OR Postmortem OR autopsy OR necropsy OR PET OR PET-CT OR SPECT OR SPET OR Positron OR "Emission tomography")
EMBASE ('serotonin'/exp OR '5-ht*' OR 'serotonin*' OR '5-hydroxytryptamine' OR '5 hydroxytryptamine' OR 'enteramine' OR 'hippophaine' OR 'hydroxytryptamine') AND ('schizophrenia'/exp OR 'schizo*') AND ('autopsy'/exp OR 'post-mortem' OR 'postmortem' OR 'autopsy' OR 'necropsy' OR 'positron emission tomography-computed tomography'/exp OR 'pet' OR 'pet-ct' OR 'spect' OR 'spet' OR 'positron' OR 'emission tomography')


The development of the search terms was based on the search string used by [orginal paper citation], with some revisions. New terms and their variations were added based on an initial screening of the literature and on the use of thesaurus terms from PubMed. 

Inclusion criteria
The inclusion criteria will be organized into the following categories: study design, population of interest, outcome, and comparison.
1. Study Design: Empirical studies.
2. Population: Patients diagnosed with schizophrenia or any clinical subtype of the disorder.
3. Outcome: Analysis of serotonin receptor density, distribution, and/or acitivty using molecular imaging methods in living patients or histological methods in postmortem samples.
4. Comparison: Outcomes must be reported in comparison to a control group composed of healthy participants/samples.
Variables such as the presence of antipsychotic treatment, type of medication used, or cause of death will not be considered exclusion criteria, as they will be evaluated independently at a later stage. Any study not meeting these criteria will be excluded.
Article selection will be performed independently by two reviewers. In case of disagreement, a third reviewer will evaluate the study.
Data Collection
Data will be collected from the previously selected articles using a standardized form and will be transferred and stored in a spreadsheet. To characterize the sample and assess the clinical and methodological profile of the included studies, the following variables will be considered:
• PANSS Score (Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale): Used as a measure of the severity of psychotic symptoms, allowing comparison across different symptom levels in the analyzed groups.
• Duration of Illness: Defined as the time from the onset of psychotic symptoms to the time of evaluation, important for distinguishing possible receptor alterations related to disease course.
• Presence of Antipsychotic Treatment: A central variable in the analysis, categorized as “treated” or “untreated.” It will be considered the primary independent variable of this review, aiming to evaluate its effects on receptor binding.
• Type of Analysis (in vivo or post-mortem): Allows differentiation of data acquisition methods, with potential implications for accuracy, feasibility, and interpretation of findings.
• Suicide as Cause of Death: In post-mortem studies, this variable will be included to control for potential biases related to clinical outcomes and neurobiology associated with suicide.
• Receptor Analysis Method: Refers to the techniques used for receptor–ligand binding quantification, such as PET, SPECT, autoradiography, among others, which are essential for evaluating methodological comparability across studies.
• Radiotracer Used: Identifies the radiopharmaceutical employed in each study, allowing assessment of specificity and sensitivity in detecting the receptor subtype under investigation.
• Receptor Subtype Analyzed: Defines the specific neurochemical target. Given the wide variety of serotonin receptors, this is fundamental for analyzing the heterogeneity of findings.
• Region of Interest (ROI): Refers to the specific brain areas selected for receptor binding analysis, according to each study’s hypothesis.
• Reference Region: Used as a comparative baseline for calculating specific binding in the ROI, important for standardization and interpretation of results.
In addition to these variables, the number of participants in the experimental and control groups (N experimental group; N control group) will also be collected, in order to assess the statistical power and methodological quality of the included studies.
Finally, comparative findings across samples will be systematically extracted and synthesized, focusing on differences in receptor binding between individuals with and without antipsychotic treatment, as well as potential interactions with other clinical, demographic, and methodological variables.
Risk of Bias Assessment
The studies included in this review will undergo a risk of bias assessment using the Critical Appraisal Checklist for Systematic Reviews and Research Syntheses, developed by the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI), as described by Aromataris et al. (2015). This tool consists of 11 questions that cover different aspects of the methodology of systematic reviews, including formulation of research questions, inclusion criteria, search strategies, resources used, assessment of publication bias, and support for final recommendations. Details and specific guidance on the use of the checklist are available in the publication by Aromataris et al. (2015), produced by the Joanna Briggs Institute.
Statistical Analysis
A meta-analysis will be conducted if there is a sufficient number of comparable and homogeneous studies. Analyses will be performed using R software (R Core Team, 2024). When possible, a random-effects model will be applied, and the effect size will be calculated using the standardized mean difference, estimated by Hedges’ g (Hedges & Olkin, 1985).
Heterogeneity will be assessed using Cochran’s Q test and the I² statistic (Verestein et al., 2014). In addition, meta-regression will be applied to explore potential sources of heterogeneity, and a funnel plot will be used to evaluate the risk of publication bias.

title: Diagnostic Accuracy of the Neck Circumference–to–Thyromental Distance Ratio Versus the Modified Mallampati Score for Predicting Difficult Tracheal Intubation in Adult Surgical Patients: A Systematic Review and Diagnostic Meta-Analysis
description:
Background: Difficult tracheal intubation remains a major challenge in anesthesia practice and can lead to serious complications. Preoperative airway assessment tools such as the Modified Mallampati Score (MMS) are commonly used, but their predictive accuracy is variable. Recently, the Neck Circumference–to–Thyromental Distance Ratio (NC/TMD) has been proposed as a potentially more reliable predictor.

Objective: This systematic review and diagnostic meta-analysis aims to compare the diagnostic accuracy of the NC/TMD ratio versus the Modified Mallampati Score in predicting difficult tracheal intubation in adult surgical patients.

Methods: A comprehensive literature search will be conducted in databases including PubMed, Scopus, and Cochrane Library. Studies evaluating NC/TMD ratio and/or Modified Mallampati Score against a reference standard for difficult intubation will be included. Data will be extracted to construct 2×2 contingency tables. Pooled sensitivity, specificity, diagnostic odds ratio, and summary receiver operating characteristic (SROC) curves will be analyzed.

Significance: This study will help determine the most reliable bedside screening tool for predicting difficult airway, improving patient safety and perioperative outcomes.

title: **Title:** Artificial intelligence and the public health workforce in sub-Saharan Africa: a scoping review of anticipated impacts on job roles, skill requirements, and worker wellbeing
description:
This scoping review maps the anticipated impacts of artificial intelligence (AI) decision-support tools—spanning surveillance, contact-tracing, and resource-allocation applications—on job roles, skill requirements, and worker wellbeing within the public health workforce of sub-Saharan Africa (SSA). The public health workforce is defined broadly to include epidemiologists, surveillance officers, and community health workers, distinct from hospital-based clinical cadres. As AI-assisted tools are increasingly piloted and deployed across SSA health systems, concerns have emerged that these technologies may reshape task composition, alter required competencies, and affect professional identity and psychological wellbeing among public health workers—yet no synthesis currently exists mapping this evidence base for the region.

The review follows Arksey and O'Malley's scoping review methodology as advanced by Levac et al., with reporting according to PRISMA-ScR guidelines. Eligible sources include empirical studies and conceptual/narrative literature published in SSA settings that address AI's anticipated or observed effects on public health workforce roles, skills, or wellbeing. Sources addressing digital health tools without an AI or machine-learning component, or addressing AI diagnostic accuracy without workforce-relevant outcomes, are excluded. Findings will be charted against an integrated conceptual framework combining the automation-augmentation paradox (Raisch & Krakowski, 2021), Job Demands-Resources theory (Bakker & Demerouti, 2017), and the WHO Health Labour Market Framework (Sousa et al., 2013), situating task-level and wellbeing-level findings within the broader workforce pipeline of education, entry, performance, retention, and exit.

Purpose: to synthesize the current state of evidence on how AI decision-support tools are anticipated to affect public health workforce roles, required skills, and wellbeing in SSA, and to identify gaps in the evidence base relevant to workforce planning and resilience.

Expected outcomes: a peer-reviewed manuscript presenting a systematically charted map of the existing SSA-specific literature; identification of the evidence base's current composition (predominantly conceptual/narrative work with limited empirical grounding); articulation of gaps—particularly the near-absence of empirical measurement of task change, professional identity, or wellbeing outcomes attributable to AI deployment in this population; and policy-relevant recommendations to inform workforce development, training pipeline design, and psychological support strategies as AI tools are scaled across SSA public health systems.

title: Biomarkers used for the diagnosis, monitoring or prognosis of patients with mucopolysaccharidosis type IVA: a scoping review protocol

title: Determining the Minimally Clinically Important Difference of the 2-Minute Walk Test in Individuals with Subacute Stroke: A Multicenter Cohort Study
description:
Background: Stroke impairs mobility in up to 80% of survivors, and the 2-Minute Walk Test (2MWT) is used to measure walking capacity in subacute stroke rehabilitation.
Aim: To establish the minimally clinically significant difference (MCID) for the 2MWT in individuals with subacute stroke.
Methods: We enrolled 150 participants (<180 days post-stroke) from 07 Pakistani rehabilitation centres. Participants received standard rehabilitation (6–8 weeks) and were assessed using the 2MWT, Activities-specific Balance Confidence (ABC) scale (gait subscale, ABC_Gait), Global Perceived Effect (GPE) scale, and Modified Barthel Index (MBI). An anchor-based approach (ABC_Gait ≥10% improvement) determined the MCID.
Results: The 2MWT MCID was 33 meters (80% CI: 30–36 meters), with 87% sensitivity and 82% specificity. 2MWT and ABC_Gait change scores correlated strongly (r = 0.68, p < 0.001).
Conclusions: The 33-meter MCID enhances clinical assessment of rehabilitation outcomes. Further validation in chronic stroke is needed.

title: Iodine maps from photon-counting detector CT in contrast-enhanced thoracic imaging: a scoping review of clinical applications
description: This scoping review maps the early clinical evidence on iodine maps generated by photon-counting detector computed tomography (PCD-CT) in adult thoracic imaging. PCD-CT represents a fundamental technological shift from conventional detectors, as it directly converts individual photons into electrical signals and inherently acquires spectral data at any acquisition protocol, without requiring dedicated dual-energy tube-voltage switching. Iodine maps derived from this system quantitatively visualize the regional distribution of iodinated contrast material, enabling simultaneous functional and morphologic assessment in a single scan. The review identified 10 original studies (832 patients, published 2022–2025), all single-center, distributed across four clinical domains. In pulmonary vasculature, PCD-CT iodine maps enable perfusion assessment from ultra-high-pitch CT pulmonary angiography — a combination technically impossible with conventional dual-energy energy-integrating detectors. In chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension, they demonstrated diagnostic accuracy comparable to perfusion SPECT/CT at approximately five times lower radiation dose. In parenchymal lung disease, iodine maps improved radiologist diagnostic confidence when differentiating morphologically overlapping attenuation patterns such as consolidation, ground-glass opacity, and reticular disease. In pleural empyema, they enhanced diagnostic accuracy in combination with virtual monoenergetic images at high energy levels. In cardiac applications, PCD-CT iodine maps quantified myocardial extracellular volume and detected late iodine enhancement with strong correlation to cardiac MRI, positioning the technique as a potential alternative for patients with contraindications to MRI. Collectively, the review concludes that early evidence is consistently promising across all four domains but insufficient to support clinical adoption recommendations, as it derives exclusively from small single-center retrospective series at European academic institutions, without multicenter prospective data or standardized acquisition protocols.

title: Large Language Models in Cardiology Education, Training, and Assessment: Protocol and Supplementary Materials
description:
This project is a scoping review and evidence map of large language models (LLMs) in cardiology-related education, training, and assessment. The review aims to map how LLMs and generative artificial intelligence systems have been studied in learner-centered cardiovascular education, including knowledge assessment, board or certification examinations, case-based learning, feedback, simulation, multimodal interpretation, and other training or assessment applications. 

The review focuses on health professions learners, clinicians, educators, and assessment settings related to cardiovascular medicine. Eligible contexts include general cardiology and relevant subspecialty or training areas. Studies focused solely on patient education, patient-facing communication, clinical decision support, diagnostic accuracy, or general cardiovascular clinical applications without an explicit education, training, or assessment purpose are outside the scope of this review. 

The review was designed in accordance with JBI guidance for scoping reviews and is reported using PRISMA-ScR. The planned information sources include PubMed, Scopus, Embase, and Web of Science, with English-language records since January 1, 2022. Study selection, data charting, and synthesis focus on the characteristics of included studies, cardiology domains, learner groups, LLM systems, model versions, task formats, comparators, outcomes, reporting transparency, methodological limitations, and evidence gaps. Because the included studies are expected to be heterogeneous in models, tasks, educational settings, and outcomes, results are synthesized descriptively rather than by meta-analysis. 

The expected outcomes of this project are to clarify the current evidence base for LLMs in cardiology education, training, and assessment; identify areas where evidence is concentrated, such as examination or question-bank performance; and highlight gaps related to learner-centered outcomes, assessment validity, multimodal and simulation-based tasks, reproducibility, and responsible implementation. The findings are intended to inform future research design, transparent reporting, and cautious educational use of LLMs in cardiovascular training contexts.

Title

Diagnostic Accuracy of Oral Health Literacy (OHL) Assessment Tools in Adults: A Systematic Review

Purpose of the Research

The primary purpose of this research is to systematically evaluate the diagnostic accuracy and psychometric validity of oral health literacy (OHL) assessment tools used among adults. Oral health literacy—defined as an individual's ability to obtain, process, and understand basic oral health information—plays a critical role in shaping oral health behaviors, self-care practices, and treatment adherence.

Despite the availability of multiple OHL instruments, such as the Rapid Estimate of Adult Literacy in Dentistry (REALD-30), Health Literacy in Dentistry Scale (HeLD-14), and Oral Health Literacy Adult Questionnaire (OHL-AQ), the comparative diagnostic performance of these tools against well-established reference instruments (e.g., REALD-99, HeLD-29) remains unclear.

This systematic review seeks to consolidate and critically appraise the existing evidence to determine which OHL tools most accurately identify adults with low oral health literacy, thereby supporting effective screening, intervention planning, and research standardization.

Diagnostic Variability in Symptoms and Risk Factors of Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder (PMDD): A Scoping Review
description:
Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder (PMDD) is a severe, cyclical mood disorder characterized by affective, behavioral and somatic symptoms occurring during the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle (O'Brien et al., 2011). It is formally recognized in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition (DSM-5), with diagnostic criteria requiring the presence of at least five symptoms, including one core mood symptom and confirmation through prospective daily symptom ratings across at least two menstrual cycles (American Psychiatric Association, 2013).

Despite its formal classification, PMDD remains underdiagnosed and inconsistently identified in both clinical and research contexts (Islas-Preciado et al., 2024). One major challenge lies in the variability of diagnostic approaches. While prospective tools such as the Daily Record of Severity of Problems (DRSP) are considered the gold standard, many studies and clinical settings rely on retrospective self-report measures, which are associated with recall bias and reduced diagnostic accuracy (Reilly et al., 2024).

Furthermore, symptom presentation in PMDD is heterogeneous, with considerable variation in how symptoms are defined, measured and interpreted across studies (Reilly et al., 2024). Similarly, a range of biological, psychological and social risk factors have been proposed, including hormonal sensitivity, stress exposure and psychiatric comorbidities, yet there is no harmony on how these factors are assessed or their relative contribution to diagnosis (Jadhav et al., 2022; Reilly et al., 2024; Roy et al., 2025).

This inconsistency limits comparability across studies, contributes to variability in prevalence estimates and may hinder effective clinical recognition and management (Reilly et al., 2024). Additionally, there is evidence suggesting that healthcare professionals may lack adequate training and awareness regarding PMDD diagnostic criteria and tools (Islas-Preciado et al., 2024).

To date, no comprehensive synthesis has systematically mapped the diagnostic tools, symptom definitions and risk factor assessments used in PMDD research and practice. Given the methodological diversity and lack of standardisation, a scoping review is warranted to explore the breadth of existing evidence, identify patterns in diagnostic approaches and highlight gaps in the literature.

Understanding diagnostic variability is essential for improving clinical practice, informing guideline development and addressing educational needs among healthcare professionals.

title: Applications of Verbal Autopsy in Maternal, Neonatal and Child Mortality Surveillance in Ghana - A Scoping Review
description:
Accurate causes of death (CoD) are crucial for guiding health policies and enhancing health system responsiveness. however, many low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) lack complete civil registration and vital statistics (CRVS) systems. According to the latest estimation by the WHO, nearly 40% of all medically certified deaths around the globe are not identified with a CoD, while the majority of them occur in LMICs.1 In Ghana, this data gap contributes to the underreporting of maternal, neonatal and child deaths, especially in rural and underserved areas. Verbal autopsy (VA) has been widely adopted as a method to determine probable CoDs in such settings, utilizing structured questionnaires to conduct interviews with caregivers to reconstruct events prior to death. Both physician-certified VA (PCVA) and computer-coded VA (CCVA) approaches have been used in Ghana in national surveys and community-based longitudinal studies to strengthen maternal, neonatal and child mortality surveillance, however, the consistent integration of VA into mortality monitoring remains limited. 

Objectives: This scoping review explores the application of VA in maternal, neonatal and child mortality surveillance in Ghana, focusing on implementation practices, diagnostic accuracy, and system-level implications.
