title: Social Attention and Communication Checklist for identifying autism spectrum disorder in infants and children: a systematic review and meta-analysis
description:
Preterm birth is associated with a 3-fold increased likelihood of a diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder (ASD). This increassed likelihood of autism is believed to stem from a combination of biological and environmental factors. Premature birth often results in disrupted brain development during a critical period of neurogenesis and synaptogenesis. Neonatal complications such as intraventricular haemorrhage, hypoxia, and infections further exacerbate the risk by affecting brain regions involved in social communication and sensory processing. Additionally, prolonged hospitalization and reduced parental bonding during early life may contribute to atypical developmental trajectories.
Furthermore, the association between preterm birth and ASD appears to be consistent across sexes, although some studies report slightly higher prevalence ratios in boys. These findings remained robust even after adjusting for familial genetic and environmental factors, supporting a potential causal relationship between gestational age and ASD risk.
Clinically, these insights underscore the importance of early monitoring and intervention for preterm infants. Paediatricians and developmental specialists should be vigilant in screening for autism-related behaviours in this population, especially during the first few years of life when early intervention can significantly improve outcomes due to underlying neuroplasticity. Tailored support services, including speech therapy, occupational therapy, and behavioural interventions, are crucial for optimizing developmental trajectories.
The Social Attention and Communication Surveillance (SACS) tool is a validated, evidence-based checklist designed for the early identification of ASD in infants and young children.
It evaluates a child’s social attention and communication behaviors, including eye contact, response to name, imitation, joint attention, and use of gestures. These behaviors are known to be atypical in children with autism and can be reliably observed in naturalistic settings.
The SACS has undergone extensive validation and has demonstrated high diagnostic accuracy. In a large-scale study involving over 13,500 children Barbaro et al reported that the SACS-Revised (SACS-R) and SACS-Preschool (SACS-PR) tools had a sensitivity of 82% and specificity of 99% when used together. This makes it one of the most effective early autism screening tools globally. Importantly, children identified as high likelihood for autism through SACS are referred for formal diagnostic assessments, enabling earlier intervention and support.
The tool has been widely implemented across Australia, including in Victoria and Tasmania, where over 45,000 children have been monitored using the SACS approach. It has also been adapted for use in more than 15 countries and translated into multiple languages. In China alone, over one million infants have been screened using the SACS as part of a national health initiative.
We aim to systematically review the SACS-R tool in detecting ASD in infants and young children.

title: Diagnostic Accuracy of Artificial Intelligence in Radiographic Detection of Impacted Maxillary Canines: A Systematic Review of Human Studies
description:
Purpose of the Study:
This systematic review aims to evaluate the diagnostic performance of artificial intelligence (AI) algorithms in detecting impacted maxillary canines using dental radiographic imaging. Impacted canines are among the most common dental anomalies, with early and accurate detection being critical for preventing complications such as malocclusion, root resorption, and aesthetic issues. Traditional imaging interpretation is often time-consuming and prone to variability among practitioners. AI-driven tools, especially those utilizing deep learning (e.g., convolutional neural networks or CNNs), have shown potential to improve diagnostic accuracy and efficiency. However, the performance and reliability of these systems vary across studies.

Objectives:

To assess the diagnostic accuracy (e.g., sensitivity, specificity, AUC) of AI algorithms in detecting impacted maxillary canines on dental radiographic images.

To compare the performance of different AI architectures and imaging modalities (e.g., CBCT vs. panoramic radiographs).

To evaluate the strengths, limitations, and methodological quality of existing studies applying AI to this diagnostic task.

To identify current research gaps and propose recommendations for future development and clinical integration of AI systems in dental diagnostics.

Methods Overview:
A systematic literature search was conducted in PubMed, Web of Science, Science Direct, and Google Scholar. Eligible studies include original research involving human subjects, applying AI models for the diagnosis of impacted maxillary canines through radiographic imaging, and reporting quantitative performance outcomes. Study selection, data extraction, and risk of bias assessment will be conducted by two independent reviewers. Quality will be assessed using the QUADAS-2 tool (for diagnostic accuracy) and the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (for observational studies).

Where appropriate, a meta-analysis using a bivariate random-effects model will be performed to generate pooled estimates of diagnostic accuracy. Narrative synthesis will supplement the quantitative analysis, especially where heterogeneity is high or meta-analysis is not feasible.

Expected Outcomes:

Comprehensive synthesis of current evidence on the diagnostic performance of AI for detecting impacted maxillary canines

Identification of high-performing AI models and preferred imaging modalities

Evaluation of methodological strengths and weaknesses in the literature

Recommendations for future studies including the need for standardized datasets, model validation, and integration strategies for clinical practice

The findings will guide dental researchers, clinicians, and technology developers in improving and implementing AI-based diagnostic tools in clinical settings.

title: The Limits of AI in Medical Imaging: A Systematic Review of Accuracy, Bias, and the Irreplaceable Role of the Radiologist
description:
This study examines the reliability and equity of artificial intelligence in medical imaging by testing the hypothesis that AI diagnostic performance is less consistent in real-world and diverse patient populations than in controlled benchmark settings. A structured review and meta-analysis of 30 peer-reviewed studies (2018–2024) was conducted, with quantitative synthesis of sensitivity and specificity in diabetic retinopathy screening and pneumonia detection.

The results show that while AI systems achieve high diagnostic accuracy overall, performance varies significantly across clinical settings, with substantial heterogeneity between studies. Evidence across the literature also reveals consistent patterns of demographic bias, with higher error rates in underserved populations. These findings suggest that current AI systems are better suited to support rather than replace radiologists. This study highlights the importance of evaluating AI not only by accuracy, but by reliability and fairness in real-world healthcare environments.

title: Thoracoscopy versus closed pleural biopsy with Cope needle in undiagnosed exudative pleural effusions: systematic review
description: This systematic review aims to compare thoracoscopy with closed pleural biopsy using a Cope needle in adults with undiagnosed exudative pleural effusions following thoracentesis and initial pleural fluid analysis. Pleural effusion is a common clinical condition associated with diverse pulmonary and systemic diseases, and accurate etiological diagnosis is essential for appropriate management and prognosis. When initial investigations are inconclusive, pleural biopsy becomes a critical diagnostic step. Closed pleural biopsy with a Cope needle remains widely used, particularly in resource-limited settings, due to its low cost and accessibility, although its diagnostic yield is variable. In contrast, medical thoracoscopy (pleuroscopy) enables direct visualization and targeted biopsies, offering higher diagnostic accuracy, especially for malignant pleural disease, albeit with greater infrastructure requirements. This review will systematically evaluate and synthesize available evidence on the overall diagnostic yield and safety profile of these procedures. Secondary outcomes will include diagnostic yield by etiology (malignancy and tuberculosis), complication rates, need for additional diagnostic procedures, and length of hospital stay. The study will follow PRISMA 2020 guidelines, assess methodological quality using validated tools, and evaluate the certainty of evidence using the GRADE approach. By providing a comprehensive and methodologically rigorous comparison, this review aims to inform clinical decision-making and optimize diagnostic strategies, particularly in diverse healthcare settings, including low- and middle-income countries.

description:
This research project is part of a doctoral investigation conducted in the Eastern Amazon and focuses on advancing the understanding of postpartum uterine health in buffaloes (Bubalus bubalis). The work is supervised by Prof. Dr. Rinaldo Batista Viana, a leading expert in clinical medicine and reproductive physiology of ruminants, particularly within Amazonian buffalo production systems. The project is executed by veterinarian Anderson Silva Coelho, who is responsible for the clinical, ultrasonographic and microbiological components, and supported by veterinarian Raysa Brenda Marques Maia, a collaborating researcher with expertise in ruminant medicine, evidence-based veterinary medicine, systematic reviews and meta-analysis. Together, the team integrates field-based clinical research with rigorous methodological and analytical approaches.
The overarching purpose of the doctoral project is to generate new knowledge regarding the reproductive health of postpartum buffaloes kept under different ecosystems and levels of technification in the Amazon. The study combines clinical evaluations, advanced reproductive ultrasonography and microbiological profiling of the uterus to investigate how environmental and management factors influence uterine disorders and reproductive efficiency.
As part of this broader research effort, a systematic review and meta-analysis will be conducted to assess the diagnostic accuracy of reproductive ultrasonography, including B-mode, color Doppler and power Doppler, for detecting metritis and endometritis in buffaloes. This review follows PRISMA-DTA and PRISMA-P guidelines and incorporates predefined eligibility criteria, comprehensive search strategies, risk-of-bias assessment using the QUADAS-2 tool and statistical synthesis through bivariate random-effects models. The expected outcomes include pooled estimates of sensitivity, specificity, likelihood ratios, diagnostic accuracy indices and the summary receiver operating characteristic (SROC) curve. These results will support the development of reliable ultrasonographic parameters for early diagnosis of uterine diseases and improve clinical decision-making in buffalo reproductive management.
Overall, the project aims to contribute to scientific, technological and practical advancements in buffalo reproduction in the Amazon. The expected outcomes include a deeper understanding of the uterine microbiome, validated diagnostic parameters for reproductive ultrasonography and evidence-based strategies for improving postpartum reproductive health, ultimately supporting the sustainability and productivity of buffalo farming in the region.

title: Establishment of Hematological and Coagulation Reference Intervals in Healthy Yemeni Adults
description:
Project Description

This project aims to establish comprehensive hematological and coagulation reference intervals for healthy Yemeni adults living in Al-Dhale’ Governorate, Yemen. Accurate reference intervals are essential for clinical decision-making, disease diagnosis, and laboratory quality assurance. However, most currently used intervals in Yemen are extrapolated from Western or other regional populations, which may not reflect local genetic, nutritional, and environmental factors.

Objectives

1. To generate population-specific reference intervals for complete blood count (CBC) parameters in healthy Yemeni adults.


2. To determine reference ranges for key coagulation tests (PT, aPTT, INR, fibrinogen).


3. To assess sex- and age-related differences in hematological and coagulation markers.


4. To provide open-access supplementary datasets and R scripts for reproducibility and secondary analyses.



Methodology

Design: Cross-sectional study.

Participants: 258 apparently healthy Yemeni adults (174 males, 84 females), aged 18–50 years.

Exclusion Criteria: History of chronic illness, acute infection, medication affecting blood parameters.

Data Collection: Sociodemographic data, venous blood samples, standardized laboratory procedures.

Laboratory Analysis: CBC performed using automated hematology analyzers; coagulation tests performed manually with inter-operator reliability analysis.

Statistical Analysis: Outlier detection (Tukey/Boxplot), calculation of 2.5th–97.5th percentiles, bootstrapped confidence intervals, and sensitivity analyses excluding endemic-infection regions.


Outputs on OSF

Main dataset (CSV, de-identified).

R scripts for statistical analysis and figure generation.

Supplementary tables (Word/PDF) covering demographic data, QC metrics, and inter-operator reliability.

Figures (TIFF/PNG) illustrating distributions, reference limits, and sex/age differences.


Significance

This study provides the first locally-derived hematological and coagulation reference intervals for Yemeni adults. The open-access dataset and analysis scripts will support:

Improved diagnostic accuracy in Yemeni hospitals and laboratories.

Regional and global comparative hematology research.

Transparency, reproducibility, and secondary analyses by other researchers.

title: Diagnostic performance of TFOS DEWS III confirmatory signs: a systematic review and meta-analysis
description:
Dry eye disease (DED) is one of the most common ocular surface disorders worldwide, affecting between 5% and 50% of the population and placing a substantial burden on visual function, quality of life, and healthcare utilisation. Historically, its diagnosis has been inconsistent, with different studies and clinics relying on diverse questionnaires, thresholds, and clinical signs.

In 2025, the Tear Film & Ocular Surface Society (TFOS) released the DEWS III Diagnostic Methodology report, which standardised the definition of DED as the presence of symptoms, preferably measured with the OSDI-6 (cut-off ≥4), together with at least one of three confirmatory signs: tear film instability (non-invasive breakup time <10 seconds), tear hyperosmolarity (≥308 mOsm/L or inter-eye difference >8 mOsm/L), or ocular surface staining of the cornea or conjunctiva. This framework was designed to harmonise both clinical practice and research.

Although narrative reviews and individual studies, such as Papas et al. (2023), have reported diagnostic accuracy for specific signs, the relative diagnostic performance of the three DEWS III confirmatory signs has not yet been systematically pooled or standardised across studies. A quantitative comparison is important because it can provide evidence to support or refine the DEWS III framework, clarify how historical studies align with current standards, and establish benchmarks for future diagnostic and epidemiological research.

Most existing diagnostic accuracy studies predate DEWS III and were conducted under the TFOS DEWS II framework (2017). DEWS II recommended the use of validated symptom questionnaires, particularly the full Ocular Surface Disease Index (OSDI, cut-off ≥13) and the Dry Eye Questionnaire-5 (DEQ-5, cut-off ≥6), in combination with at least one abnormal clinical sign. For this review, studies applying these symptom thresholds together with one of the three DEWS III confirmatory signs are considered “near-DEWS III” criteria. Both direct DEWS III and near-DEWS III studies therefore provide relevant evidence for synthesis.

Previous reviews of dry eye diagnostics have largely been narrative or restricted to single tests, with heterogeneous thresholds limiting comparability. To address this, the present review applies a novel approach using Hedges’ g, a bias-corrected standardised effect size, together with effect-size–to–ROC transformations. This method allows findings from studies using different measurement scales to be expressed on a common axis of diagnostic accuracy, yielding pooled AUROC estimates that are clinically interpretable and directly comparable across signs.

The aim of this review is to quantify and compare the diagnostic performance of the three TFOS DEWS III confirmatory signs in symptomatic DED, using studies that define DED and non-DED according to DEWS III or near-DEWS III criteria.

"Intelligent Networks: AI's Role in Healthcare Information Systems" by Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, published in 2021 by Telehealth and Medicine Today Publishing in Evanston, explores the transformative impact of Artificial Intelligence (AI) on healthcare information systems. The book addresses the increasing integration of AI into health data management, diagnostics, and personalized care, providing insights into how AI enhances efficiency and effectiveness in medical institutions.
Definition and Basic Concepts
The book begins by introducing health information systems and the integration of AI, outlining key concepts and definitions. AI in healthcare refers to the use of advanced algorithms and machine learning models to process health data, support clinical decisions, and improve patient outcomes. The chapter provides an overview of the evolution and development of AI in the healthcare sector.
Underlying Phenomena
The motivation behind this book is the rapid advancement of AI technologies and their growing application in healthcare information systems. The author emphasizes the increasing volume of healthcare data, the need for accurate and timely decision-making, and the demand for personalized patient care as driving forces behind AI integration. The book explores how these technologies can address contemporary healthcare challenges and improve patient outcomes.
Problem Statement
The central problem addressed by the book is the effective integration of AI into healthcare information systems to enhance data management, diagnostics, and personalized care. It examines the challenges and opportunities associated with leveraging AI in healthcare settings, aiming to understand how these technologies can be implemented to improve healthcare delivery while ensuring data security and privacy.
Research Objectives
The book aims to provide a comprehensive analysis of the role of AI in healthcare information systems. It explores the applications, benefits, and challenges of integrating AI into health data management, diagnostics, and personalized care. title: Large language models for conducting risk of bias assessments during systematic reviews
description:
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being explored as tools to support systematic reviews, including the assessment of risk of bias (RoB), a critical but time-consuming step in evidence synthesis. Although several studies suggest that LLMs may assist or partially automate RoB assessments, the existing evidence is fragmented, methodologically heterogeneous, and limited by small sample sizes and inconsistent reporting. As a result, it remains unclear how accurately and reliably LLMs perform, how they should be integrated into review workflows, and what risks they may pose, such as hallucinations or lack of transparency.

This project is a systematic review of evaluation studies examining the use of LLMs for RoB assessment in health-related systematic reviews. We will include studies that use LLMs alone, compare LLM-generated judgments with those of human reviewers, or apply hybrid human–AI workflows. The primary outcomes are accuracy and reliability, assessed through agreement with reference judgments and diagnostic accuracy metrics. Secondary outcomes include efficiency (e.g., time savings), usability and acceptability, and quality-of-output issues such as hallucinations and incomplete outputs.

Searches will be conducted across major bibliographic databases, preprint servers, and additional sources without language or date restrictions. Two reviewers will independently screen studies, extract data, and assess methodological quality using QUADAS-2 or QUADAS-C, supplemented with LLM-specific signalling questions. Where appropriate, quantitative synthesis will be performed using hierarchical models; otherwise, findings will be summarised narratively.

The review will provide a comprehensive overview of current evidence on LLMs for RoB assessment, identify methodological gaps, and inform future research and responsible implementation of AI-supported approaches in systematic review workflows.

title: Application of bleeding assessment tools in rare inherited bleeding disorders: a scoping review
description:
This project is a scoping review on the application of bleeding assessment tools in rare inherited bleeding disorders. The purpose of the review is to map the existing evidence on how these tools have been used in patients with rare inherited bleeding disorders or in individuals suspected of having such disorders. Specifically, this review will summarize the main types of bleeding assessment tools, their contents and dimensions, their application settings, and the outcomes reported in the literature, such as reliability, validity, sensitivity, and specificity when available.
The review will systematically search major Chinese and English databases, screen eligible studies according to predefined criteria, and extract key information using a standardized data charting form. The findings will be synthesized descriptively and presented in tables and narrative form.
The expected outcomes of this project are to provide a clear overview of the current research landscape, identify which tools have been most commonly applied, clarify the strengths and limitations of existing evidence, and highlight research gaps that need further attention. This review is expected to support future research on tool development, validation, and clinical application, and to provide a reference for healthcare professionals involved in the assessment and identification of rare inherited bleeding disorders.

title: Estimating the accuracy of early life predictors of 11-year language outcome: A replication study
description:
Background: Early identification of language disorders can help provide support to children who need it most to improve development and quality of life outcomes. A previous study identified 6 preschool indicators that predict 11-year language outcome with 75% sensitivity and 81% specificity using data from the Early Language in Victoria Study (ELVS). These items relate to sentence complexity, vocabulary and gross motor skills. This study aims to replicate these methods in the Longitudinal Study of Australian Children (LSAC) birth cohort.
Method: Between 0-3 years of age, LSAC collected parent surveys, direct assessments and investigator observations relating to the child. At 11 years the children completed the sentence recall task of the Clinical Evaluation of Language Fundamentals, 4th Edition as a potential indicator of Language Disorder. Here we use SuperLearner to estimate the accuracy of the set of 6 questions identified by the previous ELVS study in predicting 11-year language outcome (dichotomised as sentence recall score >1.5SD below the mean). We also use random forests to identify whether any additional variables relating to families’ socioeconomic status, parents’ or children’s general health and development arise as predictive of language outcome.
Expected results: We expect that the accuracy of the 6 items will attenuate in comparison to the results of the previous study. We may find that the items relating to children’s morphosyntax, vocabulary and motor skills predict with “fair” (>70%) accuracy which children will have language difficulties in late childhood, replicated across two population-based cohorts.

title: A Comparison of Contrast Enhanced Spectral Mammography (CESM) and Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) in the Diagnosis of Breast Cancer in Women.
description: Contrast-enhanced breast MRI is widely regarded as the imaging gold standard for breast lesion characterisation due to its high sensitivity and specificity. It is also utilised as a supplementary screening tool for specific cohorts such as those with increased breast cancer risk or with dense breasts. Contrast-Enhanced Spectral Mammography (CESM) is a relatively new breast imaging technique that combines Full-field digital mammography (FFDM) with the administration of an iodine-based contrast agent to improve lesion detection. The aim of this study is to evaluate the existing literature in a structured and methodical manner to assess whether CESM has the potential to play a significant role in breast tumour investigation as a breast MRI substitution. Results from this scoping review will provide a clearer understanding of the technique and identify gaps in knowledge, thus mapping regions requiring further research.

title: Machine learning based detection of EGFR mutation and HER2 over expression in metastatic brain adenocarcimoma:a systematic review and meta-analysis
description: This systematic review and meta-analysis explores the innovative application of machine learning techniques in the detection of Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor (EGFR) mutations and Human Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor 2 (HER2) overexpression in metastatic brain adenocarcinoma. As these biomarkers play a crucial role in the prognosis and targeted therapy of brain tumors, the study aims to evaluate the efficacy and accuracy of machine learning algorithms in identifying these genetic alterations compared to traditional diagnostic methods. The review synthesizes data from multiple studies, assessing the performance of various machine learning models, including supervised and unsupervised learning approaches. Key metrics such as sensitivity, specificity, and overall accuracy are analyzed to provide insights into the potential of these technologies in clinical settings. Additionally, the meta-analysis aims to highlight trends, challenges, and future directions for integrating machine learning into routine diagnostics for brain adenocarcinoma. By collating evidence from diverse research efforts, this study seeks to establish a comprehensive understanding of how machine learning can enhance the detection of critical biomarkers, thereby improving patient outcomes through personalized treatment strategies. The findings are expected to contribute significantly to the fields of oncology, neuro-oncology, and computational medicine, paving the way for more effective diagnostic tools in the fight against metastatic brain tumors

title: The Comparison of Accuracy and Practicability between Ultrasound and Spiral CT in the Diagnosis of Intestinal Obstruction：A protocol for systematic review and meta-analysis
description:
Abstract: 
background: Acute abdominal pain is often caused by intestinal obstruction, with high morbidity and mortality, so that the early diagnosis is particularly important. Currently, both spiral CT and ultrasound are common imaging diagnostic methods. However, the accuracy and practicality of the diagnosis are controversial. Therefore, the purpose of this study is to systematically evaluate the accuracy and practicality of spiral CT and ultrasound in the diagnosis of intestinal obstruction.
Methods：Retrieval of English database（PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, the Cochrane Library）and Chinese database （CNKI, WAN FANG, VIP, CBMDISC) by computers. From the establishment of the database to October 2020, a diagnostic experimental study on the diagnosis of intestinal obstruction by ultrasound and spiral CT was conducted. Two researchers independently conducted data extraction and quality evaluation of literature on the included studies, and Meta Disc1.4 and RevMan5.3 were used for Meta-analysis on the included literature.

Conclusion: This study is aimed at providing an evidence-based basis for clinicians to choose an appropriate or optimal diagnostic method by comparison of the accuracy and practicality between spiral CT and ultrasound in the diagnosis of intestinal obstruction.

title: Comparative diagnostic accuracy of ophthalmic artery Doppler indices for prediction of preeclampsia: a Bayesian network meta-analysis
description:
This network meta-analysis (NMA) compares the diagnostic accuracy of distinct ophthalmic artery (OA) Doppler indices — including peak systolic velocity (PSV) ratio, second systolic peak velocity (S2V), pulsatility index (PI), resistance index (RI), and first diastolic peak velocity (PD1) — for the prediction of preeclampsia (PE) across pregnancy trimesters. We use a Bayesian network meta-analysis of diagnostic test accuracy (NMA-DTA) framework (Owen et al. 2018) to allow head-to-head comparison both via direct (multi-index paired) evidence and indirect (single-index anchored to PE outcome) evidence. The protocol follows PRISMA 2020, PRISMA-NMA (Hutton 2015), and PRISMA-DTA (McInnes 2018)
reporting standards; risk of bias is assessed via QUADAS-C (Yang 2021). Companion to the bivariate Reitsma+HSROC meta-analysis prospectively registered on OSF 2026-05-28 (DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/NWVYS).

title: A Framework for Safe, Ethical, and Trustworthy AI Deployment and Integration in U.S. Hospitals A Systematic Review and Regulatory Gap Analysis
description:
This systematic review and regulatory gap analysis addresses the critical policy gap surrounding AI governance in American hospitals through three interconnected objectives: (1) to describe the current state of AI governance in U.S. hospitals, synthesizing federal regulations, agency guidance, and peer-reviewed evidence published between 2018 and 2026; (2) to assess the most significant gaps between existing regulatory requirements and the governance needs of modern hospital AI; and (3) to propose a comprehensive Framework for Safe, Ethical, and Trustworthy AI Deployment that is both practically feasible and ethically grounded.

The deployment and integration of artificial intelligence technologies into hospital operations represents one of the most consequential technological transformations in contemporary medicine. Deep learning models now process radiological images with diagnostic accuracy comparable to expert radiologists, predict sepsis onset hours before clinical detection, and inform oncology treatment decisions through precision genomic analysis. By the end of 2025, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) had cumulatively authorized over 1,451 AI and machine learning-enabled medical devices, while hospitals and health systems are investing billions in these technologies. Despite this rapid proliferation, the legal and regulatory frameworks governing hospital AI remain fragmented, reactive, and ill-equipped to address the unique challenges posed by these dynamic technologies.

This systematic review was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 guidelines. Four electronic databases (PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, and Google Scholar) were systematically searched for peer-reviewed articles published between database inception and 2026. The PICOS framework was used to structure inclusion and exclusion criteria. Methodological quality was assessed using the Critical Appraisal Skills Programme (CASP) checklist, the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS), and QUADAS-2 criteria. A narrative synthesis approach was employed given the heterogeneity of included studies.

Among 1,065 studies identified through systematic searching, 24 studies fulfilled the eligibility criteria and were included in the final analysis, encompassing a total of 6,314 study participants across multiple stakeholder groups. The results highlighted that current regulatory standards, especially those developed by the FDA, the Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology (ONC), and the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), were inconsistent and poorly tailored to address the evolving capabilities of AI algorithms. Four critical regulatory gaps were identified: post-market surveillance deficiencies, equity protection and bias mitigation failures, accountability clarification shortcomings, and governance capacity disparities. Evidence indicated poor consistency between pre-market approval and real-world implementation performance, underutilization of continuous surveillance methods, and failure to conduct subgroup analysis for detecting biases.

This review emphasizes the necessity of a collaborative framework with a lifecycle approach to the governance of artificial intelligence within U.S. hospitals. The framework incorporates continuous monitoring, transparency assurance, equity safeguards, accountability mechanisms, and scalable governance structures to ensure the safe, ethical, and trustworthy deployment of AI technologies in healthcare settings. Without such an integrated approach, the ongoing expansion of AI deployment risks exacerbating existing health inequities and exposing patients to inadequately governed technologies.

The urgency of this analysis is underscored by industry projections indicating that AI-enabled technologies will influence decision-making in most major U.S. health systems within the coming decade. In the absence of an effective national governance framework, the risks of patient harm, exacerbation of existing health inequities, erosion of clinical trust, and liability exposure will expand commensurately with technology proliferation. This article therefore seeks not merely to catalog regulatory deficiencies but to articulate a concrete vision for AI governance - one that fosters innovation while ensuring that AI deployment in U.S. hospitals adheres to the foundational medical principle of primum non nocere: first, do no harm.

Assessment of the sensitivity and specificity of the revised shorter version of Sound Scouts Hearing Screening App
description: The Sound Scouts app (Dillon et al. 2018) utilises mobile technology to screen an individual’s ability to listen in quiet and noisy environments with the test elements embedded in a game. The app consists of three test activities which assess speech perception in quiet, speech perception in noise and detection of tones in noise. Age-based scores are calculated by the app for each of these activities. Each player receives a report with their score, and when a “fail” or “borderline” evaluation result is received the ‘likely cause’ is suggested (i.e. conductive or sensorineural hearing loss or difficulties listening in noise). The test can be completed without clinical supervision, increasing access to a test and thereby assisting with the early identification of hearing loss and other listening disorders, such as auditory processing disorder (APD). In addition to promoting awareness on the importance of checking hearing regularly, the app directs users to appropriate hearing healthcare pathways (i.e. general practitioner, audiologist or speech pathologist). This project will assess, for the first time, the sensitivity and specificity of the new (7-minute) version of Sound Scouts in the general child population, young adult population, and in children with known hearing loss. The project will also assess whether the short version, which contains technical enhancements designed to improve its ability to determine the type of hearing loss, is accurate at making that determination.

title: "Exploring Extended Reality in Orthodontics: Trends, Challenges, and Opportunities – A Scoping Review"

XR enables immersive, interactive experiences that enhance clinical training, patient education, and treatment planning, particularly in orthodontics. Studies have demonstrated its potential to improve manual dexterity, diagnostic accuracy, and procedural efficiency while reducing patient anxiety and managing pain during dental treatments. Additionally, XR has been widely explored in education, offering realistic simulations that address limitations in traditional training methods, such as limited access to real-world cases and expert supervision. Despite its promising applications, challenges remain regarding cost, accessibility, ethical considerations, and integration into standardized curricula and clinical practice. Given the increasing digitalization of orthodontics and the need for innovative educational and patient-centered approaches, this study aims to map XR's current applications and future potential in orthodontics, identifying gaps in knowledge and areas for further development.

title: Pre-Service Teachers' Diagnostic Process Profiles in Learning Simulation: A Between-Subjects Study Using Eye-Tracking and Log Data
description: This study investigates process profiles of pre-service teachers when diagnosing virtual student errors on the mathematical topic of functions and graphs in a web-based learning simulation and examines whether these profiles are causally influenced by a pedagogical content knowledge (PCK) intervention. Using a between-subjects design (N = 100), participants are randomly assigned to either an intervention group (PCK related lecture prior to the learning simulation) or a control group (learning simulation first). Eye-tracking (Tobii Pro Fusion) and log data are used to derive and validate diagnostic process profiles. Based on prior theoretical and empirical work four profiles are expected: an efficient profile (large proportion of tasks with high diagnostic potential, a comparatively lower absolute number of tasks selected, and a large proportion of fixations on relevant areas); an active profile (similarly large proportion of tasks with high potential, but less efficient processing of relevant areas an inefficient profile (low proportion of tasks with high potential and inefficient processing of visual cues); and a passive profile (overall low activity). Outcome quality is assessed via log-data (diagnostic hypothesis accuracy) and text responses (justification quality, intervention quality).

title: Diagnostic Accuracy of Nonbronchoscopic Bronchoalveolar Lavage for Diagnosing Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia in Term and Preterm Newborns, Infants, and Children: A Systematic Review
description:
Background: Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) is a serious complication of mechanical ventilation, especially in term and preterm newborns, infants, and children. Early and accurate diagnosis of VAP is essential for optimal treatment outcomes. Nonbronchoscopic bronchoalveolar lavage (NB-BAL) is a minimally invasive procedure that can be used to obtain samples of lower respiratory tract secretions for microbiological analysis. However, the diagnostic accuracy of NB-BAL for VAP in this population is not well established.
Objective: The objective of this systematic review is to assess the diagnostic accuracy of NB-BAL for VAP in term and preterm newborns, infants, and children.
Methods:
• Search strategy: We will search the following electronic databases for relevant studies: Pubmed , MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), and CINAHL. We will also search the reference lists of included studies and relevant review articles.
• Inclusion criteria: Studies will be included if they meet the following criteria:
o Study design: Prospective or retrospective observational studies or randomized controlled trials
o Population: Term and preterm newborns, infants, and children with suspected VAP
o Intervention: NB-BAL
o Reference standard: Bronchoscopic bronchoalveolar lavage (BB-BAL), lung biopsy, or clinical diagnosis of VAP
o Outcome measure: Diagnostic accuracy of NB-BAL for VAP
• Data extraction: Two independent reviewers will extract data from included studies using a standardized data extraction form. The following data will be extracted:
o Study characteristics: Author, year of publication, study design, population, intervention, reference standard, and outcome measure
o Results: Sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), and accuracy of NB-BAL for VAP
• Data analysis: We will conduct a meta-analysis of the data to calculate pooled estimates of sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, and accuracy of NB-BAL for VAP. We will also assess for heterogeneity between studies and perform subgroup analyses to investigate the potential effects of study characteristics on the diagnostic accuracy of NB-BAL.

title: p16 immunohistochemistry for melanocytic neoplasia: A meta-analysis of diagnostic accuracy studies
description:
The gold standard for diagnosis of melanoma is histopathology. However, diagnosis by histopathology can be challenging. Interobserver discordance on benign versus malignant classification of melanocytic lesions by histopathology is not infrequent, even among expert pathologists. The underdiagnosis of melanoma has serious medical and legal consequences. Dermatopathologists increasingly resort to ancillary testing beyond conventional hematoxylin-eosin stained histology slides both to improve diagnostic accuracy and to mitigate liability. 

Ancillary tests for melanoma include immunohistochemistry, fluorescence in situ hybridization, comparative genomic hybridization, gene expression profiling, and next generation sequencing. Immunohistochemistry (IHC) is the most accessible and inexpensive of these testing platforms. p16, PRAME, Ki-67, and HMB-45 are the most commonly used ancillary IHC tests for melanoma. The current scientific literature suggests PRAME is the most robust of these tests and that Ki-67 and HMB-45 are of low value for diagnosis of melanoma in most settings. 

The diagnostic accuracy of p16 IHC testing for melanoma is unknown. A systematic review in 2018 concluded that p16 IHC testing was of limited use in differentiating benign from malignant melanocytic lesions. The existing literature at that time was limited by heterogeneous reporting of expression patterns and cut-off levels. Many dermatopathologists continue to use p16 IHC testing and published articles suggest diagnostic value in specific diagnostic settings. The goal of this study is to perform a meta-analysis of diagnostic accuracy studies on p16 IHC testing for melanoma. The specific aims are to answer the following questions:

1. What is the accuracy of p16 loss by immunohistochemistry for diagnosis of melanoma?
2. What is the optimum cut-off level of p16 loss?
3. Is diagnostic accuracy for p16 loss higher in different subtypes of melanoma and nevus?

title: Comparative Accuracy of Delirium Screening Tools for Critically Ill Children and Adolescents: A Bayesian Diagnostic Network Meta-analysis
description: Pediatric delirium is a common, severe neuro-psychiatric complication in the PICU associated with increased mortality, prolonged stay, and long-term neurodevelopmental adversity. Although routine screening is recommended, existing guidelines lack a purpose-specific hierarchy for tool selection. Diagnostic accuracy evidence remains fragmented, lacking head-to-head comparisons or frameworks considering developmental stages, diagnostic thresholds, and baseline prevalence. Therefore, we conducted a systematic review and Bayesian diagnostic network meta-analysis to evaluate and compare the diagnostic performance of validated pediatric delirium screening instruments—including observational tools (CAPD), feature-based approaches (pCAM-ICU/psCAM-ICU), anesthesia-related scales (PAED), and symptom-based assessments (SOS-PD)—against standard reference criteria (DSM-5/DSM-IV) in critically ill children. The primary outcomes are pooled sensitivity and specificity across different functional assessment domains and developmental age groups. A Bayesian framework will be utilized to compare threshold-dependent performance, rank instruments through hierarchical modeling, and estimate post-test probabilities across clinically relevant baseline prevalence ranges (from general PICU to high-risk populations). Ultimately, this study aims to provide a comparative, purpose-specific framework to guide clinicians in selecting optimal screening instruments based on the clinical context (e.g., high-sensitivity rule-out screening vs. high-specificity confirmatory assessment), bridging the gap between empirical evidence and bedside clinical decision-making in child psychiatry and critical care medicine.

title: Transcranial Doppler for the diagnosis of intracranial hypertension: an updated systematic review and meta-analysis.
description:
Intracranial hypertension (ICH) is a frequent and potentially lethal complication in patients with acute brain injury, including traumatic brain injury (TBI), subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH), and stroke. Intracranial pressure (ICP) levels >20 mmHg are consistently associated with higher mortality rates and worse neurological outcomes, as demonstrated by classic cohorts and recent analyses of critically ill patients (1–3).
Invasive ICP monitoring remains the gold standard. However, it is not universally available, involves risks (hemorrhage, infection), and has contraindications in specific scenarios. Thus, non-invasive methods have been explored for screening, patient selection, serial bedside assessment, and support for transfer decisions, especially in resource-limited settings.
Transcranial Doppler (TCD) is an increasingly available method for bedside assessment of the neurocritically ill patient. Spectral wave-derived indices — such as the pulsatility index (PI) and mathematical estimates of intracranial pressure such as estimated Perfusion Pressure (ePPC) and Doppler-estimated Intracranial Pressure (ICPtcd) — have been evaluated as potential predictors of ICH (3).
Despite being the most accepted index in various studies on the subject, the main systematic review published to date (4) identified low accuracy of isolated PI as a diagnostic tool for ICH, although the evidence has been hampered by methodological heterogeneity, technical difficulties with acoustic windows and lack of standardization among studies.
More recent studies, such as IMPRESSIT-II(3), evaluated methodologies based on ePPC/ICPtcd formulas and demonstrated high negative predictive value in excluding ICH — reaching NPV close to 95% for ICP >22 mmHg. Meta-analyses conducted in low- and middle-income countries also suggest that DTC may play a promising role as a screening tool for ICH, with sensitivity greater than 90% in some scenarios (5).
However, no current meta-analysis simultaneously brings together studies with DTC measurement performed up to 1 hour after ICP measurement (essential criterion for diagnostic accuracy) in patients with acute brain injury (TBI, SAH, stroke) with concomitant use of invasive ICP as the gold standard (with ICP >20 mmHg). In addition, none of them constructed a separate analysis of the different methods derived from DTC (IP, PPCe, ICPtcd) and assessment of the risk of bias according to QUADAS-2. Thus, an updated meta-analysis is needed to determine the real performance of DTC in detecting intracranial hypertension.

title: Assessment of Artificial Intelligence Algorithms for ROTEM
description:
This retrospective observational validation study aims to evaluate the accuracy and clinical decision-making performance of artificial intelligence (AI)-based language models in interpreting rotational thromboelastometry (ROTEM) findings. ROTEM is a point-of-care viscoelastic testing modality widely used in high-risk surgical settings, including cardiac surgery and liver transplantation, to assess hemostatic function and guide transfusion decisions. Although ROTEM-guided algorithms such as Görlinger’s protocol have contributed to improved clinical outcomes, the interpretation of ROTEM results remains complex and highly dependent on clinical expertise.

In this study, de-identified ROTEM datasets previously obtained from adult patients (≥18 years) who underwent elective cardiac surgery or liver transplantation will be retrospectively collected and converted into structured clinical vignettes. Only cases with complete, technically valid ROTEM results will be included. Each case vignette will be assessed by at least three experienced clinicians, forming an expert consensus that serves as the reference standard. Parallelly, the same ROTEM cases will be interpreted by one or more large language models (LLMs) developed for clinical reasoning tasks.

Each AI model will be presented with standardized prompts containing ROTEM parameters and relevant clinical context, including Görlinger’s ROTEM interpretation algorithm, and asked to answer a set of 14 structured clinical questions. These questions aim to identify the presence and type of coagulopathy and to recommend appropriate treatments, such as antifibrinolytics, protamine, fibrinogen, platelets, or coagulation factor replacement. Responses will be limited to binary (“Yes” or “No”) format for consistency across evaluators.

The primary outcome is the agreement between the AI models and the expert panel regarding the decision to initiate treatment. Secondary outcomes include the diagnostic classification of coagulopathies, concordance in specific treatment recommendations, and standard diagnostic accuracy metrics (sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, negative predictive value, overall accuracy, and Cohen’s Kappa).

As this study involves secondary use of previously collected clinical data, no direct patient interaction or modification of clinical care is involved. All data will be anonymized prior to analysis, and appropriate ethical approvals and waivers will be obtained for retrospective chart review.

The expected outcome of this study is to determine whether large language models can accurately interpret ROTEM findings and make clinically sound transfusion recommendations. These findings may support future integration of AI-assisted decision support tools in perioperative bleeding management.

title: Diagnostic Accuracy of Point-of-Care Ultrasound (POCUS) for Non-Traumatic Chest Pain in the Emergency Department: A Scoping Review Protocol
description:
Background
Non-traumatic chest pain is a common presentation in emergency departments (EDs), accounting for 5-10% of visits and encompassing life-threatening conditions such as acute coronary syndrome, pulmonary embolism, cardiac tamponade, pneumonia, and aortic dissection. Point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) offers rapid, bedside evaluation with potential high diagnostic accuracy. However, the evidence is fragmented across applications. A scoping review is needed to map the literature on POCUS diagnostic accuracy for this symptom.

Objectives
To map the extent, range, and nature of evidence on the diagnostic accuracy of POCUS for non-traumatic chest pain in EDs, identify gaps, and inform future research.

Methods
This scoping review will follow the Arksey and O'Malley framework, enhanced by Levac et al., and report using the PRISMA extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR). We will search PubMed, MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, Cochrane, and grey literature from inception to December 2025. Eligibility criteria include studies reporting diagnostic accuracy metrics (e.g., sensitivity, specificity) of POCUS for non-traumatic chest pain in ED settings. Two reviewers will independently screen titles, abstracts and full texts, chart data using a standardized form, and synthesize findings thematically and quantitatively where appropriate. No formal quality appraisal will be conducted, consistent with scoping review methodology.

Inclusion Criteria
Participants/Population: All patients presenting with non-traumatic chest pain in ED settings.
Concept: Studies evaluating the diagnostic accuracy of POCUS (e.g., sensitivity, specificity, positive/negative predictive values, area under the curve) compared to reference standards (e.g., CT, echocardiography, final diagnosis, clinical outcomes).
Context: ED or equivalent acute care environments such as Urgent care centres .
Types of evidence sources: Primary research such as observational studies, RCTs, cohort studies, case series with ≥10 cases, and grey literature.
Time Period: From database inception to December 2025.
Language: English literature only will be considered due to lack of funding for translation services.

title: The Visual Revolution in Anal Fistula Management: Mapping the Evolving Role of MRI and Ultrasound in Diagnosis and Prognosis – A Scoping Review
description:
Anal fistula is a chronic, debilitating inflammatory condition characterized by an anomalous tract connecting the anal canal to the perianal skin, or occasionally other pelvic structures. Its prevalence is significant, negatively impacting patients' quality of life with symptoms like persistent pain, purulent discharge, pruritus, and recurrent infections. While predominantly cryptoglandular, a challenging subgroup manifests in patients with fistulizing perianal Crohn's disease (FPC), where underlying intestinal inflammation exacerbates the complexity and recalcitrance of the fistulous disease.

Accurate diagnosis and precise characterization of anal fistulas are intrinsically linked to successful treatment. However, evaluation is notoriously difficult due to the complex three-dimensional anatomy of the anorectal region, involving the delicate sphincter system and the potential for multiple fistulous tracts, secondary ramifications, and occult abscess collections. Physical examination, though fundamental, often underestimates the true extent of the disease, leading to incomplete surgical interventions and high recurrence rates. Thus, an accurate understanding of the main tract, its extensions, the location of internal openings, and its relationship with the sphincters is indispensable for guiding therapeutic decisions and monitoring treatment response.

In recent years, diagnostic imaging has witnessed remarkable advancements, with new techniques and optimization of existing modalities, such as magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and various ultrasound (US) technologies, including 3D and contrast-enhanced approaches. Given the rapid evolution and diversity of these tools, and the need to understand their comparative performance and ideal applications, this scoping review is justified.


This scoping review aims to:

Map and correlate the most recent findings (published between 2020-2026) from studies evaluating imaging modalities for anal fistula and FPC.
Analyze the diagnostic accuracy, prognostic value, and clinical impact of MRI and various US modalities in this context.
Provide an updated synthesis of evidence to support evidence-based clinical practice and identify current research trends and gaps.


A scoping review methodology will be employed, following the guidelines of the PRISMA Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR).

Search Strategy: A systematic search will be conducted in three main electronic databases: PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, and Scopus. The search strategy will be developed with the assistance of a specialized librarian and adapted for each database. The last search will be conducted in [Preencher com a data da sua última busca].
Eligibility Criteria: Studies published from January 2020 to December 2024 focusing on emerging imaging methods for anal fistula diagnosis and characterization will be included. Exclusion criteria will comprise animal/in vitro studies, conventional methods in isolation, case reports/series with <10 patients, editorials, letters, and non-peer-reviewed literature.
Study Selection: A two-stage selection process will be carried out by two independent reviewers (title/abstract screening followed by full-text evaluation), with discrepancies resolved by consensus or a third reviewer. Rayyan software will be used for selection and blinding.
Data Extraction: Data will be extracted by two independent reviewers using a standardized form developed a priori. Categories for extraction include study identification, characteristics, population, diagnostic method details, reference standard, primary/secondary outcomes, statistical analysis, risk of bias, certainty of evidence (where applicable), clinical applicability, and conflicts of interest.
Quality Assessment: Methodological quality and risk of bias of included studies will be assessed independently by two reviewers. QUADAS-2 will be used for diagnostic accuracy studies, ROBINS-I for observational studies, and ROB 2 for randomized clinical trials. For consensus studies, narrative evaluation of methodology will be performed.
Data Synthesis: Data will be synthesized narratively due to expected heterogeneity across studies. Results will be organized by imaging modality, presenting study characteristics, diagnostic accuracy measures, and identified limitations. Evidence tables will be constructed where appropriate.


This project expects to:

Identify dominant imaging modalities (MRI, US) and their specific strengths in anal fistula and FPC diagnosis.
Highlight the high diagnostic accuracy of MRI for complex anatomical characterization and its prognostic value.
Demonstrate the competitive accuracy and cost-effectiveness of advanced US techniques, particularly for superficial lesions and initial assessments.
Map the current landscape of research, including geographical distribution, study designs, and the predominant use of surgical findings as a gold standard.
Conclude that while significant advancements have been made, the overall certainty of evidence remains predominantly low to moderate, urging for more prospective, multicenter studies.
Ultimately, the findings will provide a current synthesis to guide clinical decision-making, optimize therapeutic planning, and improve patient outcomes by informing the selection of appropriate imaging strategies.

title: Accuracy of Intraoperative Surgical Margin Assessment Techniques in Veterinary Oncology
description:
Accurate determination of surgical margin status is fundamental for detecting residual microscopic residual cancer in patients, predicting clinical outcomes, and optimizing treatment planning. Postoperative histopathology following surgical tumor resection is considered the gold standard for margin evaluation; however, this process typically takes one or two weeks to obtain results and only a limited sample of the surgical margins are assessed. Consequently, this delay results in a missed opportunity to evaluate surgical margins in real time and to utilize that information for immediate intraoperative decision-making, which could improve patient outcomes. Several techniques are available for intraoperative surgical margin assessment, each with different levels of accuracy, including frozen tissue section biopsy, imprint cytology margin, near-infrared fluorescence imaging, and optical coherence tomography (OCT) which has the potential to guide surgical-decision making in real-time.

This review aims to compare the diagnostic accuracy of intraoperative surgical margin evaluation techniques as individual studies focus on the reporting of accuracy of one technique in comparison to histopathology. Only studies on canine cutaneous or subcutaneous tumors will be included in the review. 
The primary outcome of the review is comparison of diagnostic accuracy for detection of positive surgical margins in cutaneous and subcutaneous tumors across techniques.

title: Self-sampling for HPV detection in cervical screening in women aged 25 to 65 years – Scoping Review
description:
Introduction: 
Cervical cancer is one of the leading causes of morbimortality in women worldwide, with human papillomavirus (HPV) infection as its main etiological factor. Although traditional screening tests are essential for early diagnosis, their use has been affected by accessibility barriers and sociocultural factors. In response to this, self-sampling for HPV detection has emerged as an alternative, with a primary care approach to address equity and social determinants, strengthening individual capacities and facilitating access to screening. Therefore, a scoping review is needed to synthesize the evidence and guide the strengthening of cervical screening programs by integrating this self-sampling tool with high potential for impact on public health. 

Methodology: A scoping review will be conducted following the methodology of the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) and the PRISMA-ScR guidelines. Qualitative, quantitative, and mixed studies, reviews, and gray literature with empirical evidence published between 2015 and 2025 in Spanish or English will be included. Searches will be conducted in PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and BIREME, using MeSH/DeCs descriptors and Boolean operators. The selection will be carried out in three phases: elimination of duplicates, review of titles/abstracts, and reading of full texts, documenting said results using the PRISMA-ScR diagram. The data will be extracted into a standardized template and synthesized using narrative analysis and thematic categorization.

Expected results: This review is expected to gather and synthesize the most recent evidence on self-sampling for HPV detection as a cervical screening strategy, identifying the different methods and devices available, describing their diagnostic accuracy compared to sampling performed by healthcare personnel, and analyzing parameters such as sensitivity, specificity, and coherence. It will also evaluate women's acceptability, perception, and adherence, as well as the barriers and facilitators associated with the use of self-sampling, especially in populations with low access to traditional screening.

title: Barriers and Enablers to the integration of Non-Invasive Diagnostic Approaches for patients with Endometriosis within clinical Diagnostic Pathways: A Scoping Review.
description:
Introduction 
Endometriosis affects approximately 10% of women of reproductive age worldwide, with 
prevalence estimates ranging from 6% to 13%(Moradi et al., 2025; World Health 
Organization, 2025) . As a leading cause of chronic pelvic pain, the disorder significantly 
impairs daily functioning, mental health, and fertility; affected individuals demonstrate 3.3
fold higher odds of infertility compared to controls (Eisenberg et al., 2022; Wang et al., 
2025). Beyond the profound physical and psychological toll, endometriosis imposes a 
substantial economic burden, with lifetime per-person losses estimated to exceed INT $1.9 
million—driven largely by productivity loss (Armour et al., 2022; Tewhaiti-Smith & Armour, 
2026). These findings underscore the urgency of timely management to mitigate long-term 
patient and systemic outcomes. 

In response to this clinical burden, there has been a paradigm shift toward non-invasive 
diagnostic approaches. Advanced imaging, such as specialist transvaginal ultrasound and 
high-resolution MRI, now demonstrates sensitivities and specificities of approximately 90% 
for deep endometriosis (Avery et al., 2024). Concurrently, biomarker research—including 
circulating inflammatory signatures and BCL6 expression—offers potential laboratory-based 
complements to imaging (Khoyloo et al., 2026). Guideline bodies, including NICE and 
ESHRE, increasingly recommend these non-invasive investigations as first-line tools, 
reserving laparoscopy for therapeutic purposes or inconclusive cases (Kennedy et al., 2005; 
Mondelaers, 2024). 

Despite technological advancements, diagnostic delays remain a persistent global challenge. 
Large-scale reviews report mean intervals of 6–8 years between symptom onset and 
confirmed diagnosis (Fryer et al., 2024, 2025). Delays are pervasive across varied healthcare 
systems, including cohorts in the United Kingdom, France, and the United States (De Corte et 
al., 2025; Hadfield et al., 1996) . While patient-level factors like pain normalization 
contribute to these delays, provider-level barriers—such as insufficient training, lack of 
standardized reporting, and persistent perceptions that laparoscopy is required for definitive 
diagnosis—frequently inhibit the transition from guideline recommendation to real-world 
practice (Condous et al., 2024; Nisenblat et al., n.d.). 

While individual diagnostic modalities have been extensively researched, there is limited 
synthesis regarding the integration of these tools into clinical pathways. Broader 
organisational and systemic factors—such as equipment availability, clinician training, 
medico-legal concerns, and geographic access—create a complex landscape of barriers and 
enablers (VanBuren et al., 2024; Young et al., 2024). Although implementation science 
frameworks like NASSS and CFIR have been applied to other healthcare innovations (Abell 
et al., 2023; Meunier et al., 2023), no comprehensive synthesis has specifically examined the 
determinants influencing the integration of non-invasive endometriosis diagnostics into 
routine care. 

The evidence base in this field is highly heterogeneous, encompassing qualitative patient
experience studies, quantitative diagnostic accuracy trials, clinical guidelines, and policy 
literature. Traditional systematic reviews focused on narrowly defined interventions are 
unsuitable for this diverse, emerging field. A scoping review is therefore the appropriate 
methodology to systematically map this broad range of evidence, clarify key concepts, 
identify systemic barriers, and highlight gaps in current research. Guided by the JBI 
methodology for scoping reviews (Campbell et al., 2023), this review aims to map the 
available evidence regarding the use and integration of non-invasive diagnostic approaches 
within clinical diagnostic pathways for endometriosis. Consequently, this review addresses 
the following research question: What evidence exists on the use and integration of non
invasive techniques by healthcare professionals in the diagnostic process of endometriosis? A 
preliminary search of MEDLINE, the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, Embase, 
and JBI Evidence Synthesis confirmed no current or underway reviews addressing this 
integration, further justifying the necessity of this work (Armour et al., 2022; Saunders & 
Horne, 2025).

title: Validation of a deliberative multi-LLM Delphi panel for safe automated title/abstract screening in systematic reviews: a study protocol
description: This pre-registration introduces Delph-AI — a deliberative multi-LLM Delphi panel — and pre-registers a retrospective, multi-dataset diagnostic accuracy study evaluating its capacity for autonomous, safe exclusion of records during title and abstract screening in systematic reviews. Performance is assessed against published human screening decisions from completed systematic reviews used as the reference standard. Unlike active-learning tools that prioritize records for human inspection, Delph-AI is evaluated for autonomous classification against pre-specified safety thresholds, with mandatory human review restricted to irrecoverable technical failures. The pipeline operates on atomized eligibility criteria across a panel of three large language models from distinct architectural families. Primary validation requires the simultaneous satisfaction of three pre-specified thresholds, evaluated as the median across confirmatory systematic reviews: a safe auto-exclusion rate of ≥40% of records, a sensitivity of ≥95.0%, and a negative predictive value lower bound of ≥99.0%. Pre-specified component ablations isolate the contributions of multi-round deliberation (versus single-round majority voting) and criterion atomization (versus monolithic record-level evaluation). The protocol follows PRISMA-P 2015, STARD-AI 2025, and TRIPOD+AI 2024 reporting guidance, and proposes the Delphi-LLM Validation Extension (Appendix A; DL-1 to DL-20) as a complementary reporting checklist for deliberative multi-LLM screening systems. Pre-registered via OSF Open-Ended Registration. Protocol v1.0, April 2026. A Freeze Date amendment will be filed upon dataset, model, and prompt finalization.

title: Robotics Applications in Traditional East Asian Medicine: A Scoping Review
description:
This scoping review aims to systematically map and analyze the current landscape of robotics applications in Traditional East Asian Medicine (TEAM), including Traditional Chinese Medicine, Korean Medicine, and other oriental medicine practices. As the Fourth Industrial Revolution transforms healthcare delivery, there is growing interest in integrating robotic technologies with traditional medicine approaches to enhance diagnostic accuracy, treatment precision, and therapeutic standardization.
The primary purpose of this study is to comprehensively examine how robotic systems have been developed, implemented, and evaluated within various TEAM domains, including acupuncture, moxibustion, pulse diagnosis, tongue diagnosis, cupping therapy, herbal medicine preparation, and manual therapies. We will systematically search four major databases (PubMed/MEDLINE, EMBASE, CNKI, and RISS) to identify relevant literature published from 1990 onwards.
Our research will categorize robotics applications by both TEAM specialty areas and robot functionality (diagnostic, therapeutic, educational, or assistive robots). We will analyze technological characteristics, clinical validation status, commercialization levels, and research trends across different regions and time periods.
Expected outcomes include: (1) a comprehensive mapping of the current state of TEAM-robotics integration, (2) identification of research gaps and future opportunities, (3) analysis of technological advancement patterns and clinical adoption barriers, and (4) recommendations for future research directions and policy considerations. This work will serve as a foundational resource for researchers, technology developers, clinicians, and policymakers interested in the convergence of traditional medicine and modern robotics, potentially facilitating evidence-based decision-making for technology adoption and research investment in this emerging field.

However, limited specialized equipment and ENT-specific training in family medicine often result in high rates of unnecessary referrals to tertiary hospitals.
Tele-Otolaryngology (Tele-ENT) has emerged as a transformative solution, utilizing digital otoscopes, smartphone-integrated imaging, and asynchronous "store-and-forward" platforms to bridge this gap. By enabling remote specialist consultation or enhancing the diagnostic accuracy of PCPs through digital tools, Tele-ENT has the potential to streamline patient triaging, reduce travel burdens, and lower healthcare costs. Understanding the current efficacy and diagnostic reliability of these technologies within the primary care setting is essential for their integration into routine clinical practice. This review seeks to map the evidence regarding the implementation of Tele-ENT tools and their impact on clinical decision-making at the frontline of medicine.

title: Systematic Review of Non-invasive Ultrasound and Laboratory Predictors for the Diagnosis and Risk Stratification of Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis
description:
Purpose and Rationale
Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) is a life-threatening complication of liver cirrhosis that requires rapid diagnosis to reduce high morbidity and mortality rates. While diagnostic paracentesis remains the gold standard, it is often delayed by procedural challenges or resource limitations. This research project is a systematic review designed to evaluate non-invasive alternatives- specifically laboratory biomarkers and ultrasound (USG) findings as early predictors of SBP.
The primary purpose of this study is to move beyond simple diagnostic identification and investigate the "Risk Stratification" potential of these markers. By bridging the gap between traditional ascitic fluid analysis and modern bedside technology, this work aims to establish a more objective, rapid, and reproducible diagnostic framework.
Methodology and Scope
This systematic review follows the PRISMA 2020 guidelines and utilizes a multi-database search strategy (PubMed, Cochrane CENTRAL, and ClinicalTrials.gov) updated through April 2026.
The study integrates data from 38 included records, categorized into:
Laboratory Predictors (32 studies): Evaluating high-accuracy biomarkers such as IP-10 (Serum/Ascitic), Calprotectin, and 2026-current prognostic markers like INR and Child-Pugh Class C.
Ultrasound Predictors (6 studies): Evaluating localized fluid characteristics (echogenicity, debris) and systemic hemodynamic markers, including novel modalities such as VExUS (Venous Excess Ultrasound) and Lung POCUS.
Comparative Analysis
A core component of this research is the head-to-head comparison between laboratory and ultrasound modalities. We seek to determine if the immediate "bedside" utility of ultrasound can match or supplement the analytical precision of laboratory-based biomarkers. Due to the inherent methodological and clinical heterogeneity of the evidence, specifically regarding varying biomarker cut-offs and the operator-dependent nature of USG, a qualitative narrative synthesis will be employed instead of a meta-analysis.
Expected Outcomes
Identification of Superior Markers: To pinpoint the specific non-invasive predictors with the highest diagnostic accuracy (AUC, Sensitivity, and Specificity).
Prognostic Framework: To establish which markers (e.g., Intrarenal Doppler Resistive Index >0.83) most accurately predict SBP-related complications like renal failure.
Integrated Diagnostic Algorithm: The final outcome will be a proposed multimodal workflow that combines bedside imaging with systemic laboratory triage to provide a faster, safer, and more accurate diagnostic path for patients with suspected SBP.
Dissemination
The findings will be synthesized to provide a comprehensive overview of the current evidence base as of April 2026 and will be submitted for publication in a high-impact, peer-reviewed medical journal.

title: Autofluorescence-Based Devices for Screening of Oral Potentially Malignant Diseases and Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma Screening: A Scoping Review on GOCCLES and OralID
description: This scoping review will systematically map and synthesize the existing primary literature on GOCCLES and OralID, two autofluorescence-based adjunctive devices used for the detection and assessment of oral potentially malignant disorders (OPMDs) and oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC). The review is motivated by the substantial global burden of oral cancer, the persistence of late-stage diagnoses, and the limitations of conventional oral examination, which relies on operator experience, subjective visual inspection and palpation under white light. GOCCLES and OralID exploit tissue autofluorescence to enhance visualization of mucosal changes, yet current evidence is scattered across small, methodologically diverse studies with heterogeneous outcomes, making it difficult to draw clear clinical conclusions. The primary purpose of this project is therefore to chart the breadth, nature, and characteristics of studies evaluating these devices, summarize their reported diagnostic and clinical performance, and describe the contexts and populations in which they have been used. Expected outcomes include a descriptive map of study designs and settings, a structured synthesis of diagnostic accuracy and feasibility data, and identification of key evidence gaps to inform future clinical research and potential integration of autofluorescence-based tools into practice and guidelines.

title: Utility of fecal elastase-1 in estimating pancreatic function in cystic fibrosis – A scoping review
description:
Scoping Review

Background and Rationale 
In people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF), approximately 85% have exocrine pancreatic insufficiency (EPI). The gold standard test for evaluating EPI is direct pancreatic function testing using endoscopic pancreatic stimulation test. Even though it is the standard test, it is obsolete in clinical practice due to its invasiveness. The commonly used indirect tests include coefficient of fat absorption (CFA) and quantitative fecal elastase-1 (FE-1) estimation (1). CFA is nonspecific for pancreatic function as the results could be affected in other causes of malabsorption or maldigestion. Further, it is cumbersome as the stool collection involves for 72 hours and dietary intake of fat also should be tightly controlled. FE-1 is commonly used noninvasive test commonly utilized to estimate the pancreatic status (function) in pwCF. The cut-off values utilized widely ranges between 100-200 ug/gm of stool with lower cut off provide higher specificity for EPI. However, there is limited literature regarding its diagnostic accuracy in CF and multiple challenges in addressing several questions such as when to estimate the pancreatic function, what cut-off value to use and the diagnostic accuracy of the test. 

Here in, we intend to explore the diagnostic accuracy of FE-1 using a scoping review methodology, and also will compare the utility of FE-1 with other methods of EPI such as the coefficient of fat absorption (CFA), endoscopic pancreatic stimulation test, stool chymotrypsin, etc. Due to the variabilities in the cut off, wide range of patient population (neonates, infants, children and adults), and also the availability of different diagnostic methods to compare, we intend to carry out a scoping review. Again, given these limitations, a formal quality assessment will not be done here (unlike in systematic review) (2-3).

title: The German version of the WHO ASSIST: Evaluating its validity for assessing alcohol and tobacco consumption in an outpatient psychotherapy setting
description: Excessive alcohol and nicotine use significantly impact both individuals and society, with heightened risks among those with comorbid mental disorders. Despite the urgent need for accurate identification and treatment of risky and dependent substance use, these efforts remain insufficiently implemented within the German healthcare system. The World Health Organization "Alcohol, Smoking, and Substance Involvement Screening Test" (ASSIST) questionnaire offers a promising solution to current challenges by efficiently assessing multiple substance classes simultaneously, enabling both comprehensive evaluation of substance use and monitoring of treatment-related changes. This study aims to test the validity and diagnostic accuracy of the German self-report version of the ASSIST for alcohol and tobacco subscales within an outpatient psychotherapy setting.
