title: MRI in the Management of Pediatric Head and Neck Emergencies: A Scoping Review Protocol
description: This scoping review aims to map the existing evidence on the use of Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) in the management for acute pediatric head and neck emergencies. While Computed tomography (CT) is commonly used, children are particularly vulnerable to its ionizing radiation. MRI is a radiation-free alternative, but its use is often limited by longer scan times and the need for sedation or anesthesia. Recent advances, such as rapid-sequence MRI and non-pharmacological strategies, may improve feasibility of MRI in acute care settings. The review will summarize evidence on the diagnostic accuracy, feasibility, and implementation of MRI for pediatric patients with non-abusive traumatic brain injury, neck infections, mastoiditis, and periorbital or orbital cellulitis. Particular emphasis will be placed on strategies to perform MRI without general anesthesia or sedation. The review follows the scoping review framework and PRISMA-ScR guidelines. Searches will be conducted in PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, and selected trial registries. Results will be synthesized narratively to map current evidence, identify implementation strategies, and highlight research gaps. Findings are intended to support clinicians and healthcare decision-makers in optimizing imaging pathways for acutely ill children while minimizing radiation exposure and anesthesia-related risks.

title: The Efficacy of AI-Assisted Triage Systems in Primary Care: A Systematic Review
description:
Study Protocol: The Efficacy of AI-Assisted Triage Systems in Primary Care: A Systematic Review
Principal Investigator: Dr. Waqar Ahmed Khan, Specialist in Family Medicine Affiliation: Monir Clinic, Al-Sharaya District, Makkah, Saudi Arabia Date: January 17, 2026

1. Background
The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in primary care is rapidly evolving. Triage, the process of determining the priority of patients' treatments based on the severity of their condition, is a critical bottleneck in family medicine. AI-assisted triage systems, including symptom checkers and clinical decision support tools, offer the potential to improve clinical efficiency and patient outcomes. However, a synthesized evidence base specifically focused on the family medicine setting remains necessary to validate these tools for clinical practice.

2. Objective
The primary objective of this systematic review is to evaluate the clinical efficacy, diagnostic accuracy, and operational efficiency of AI-assisted triage systems compared to traditional human-led triage within primary care and family medicine settings.

3. Review Questions
How does the diagnostic accuracy of AI triage tools compare to standard clinical assessment by primary care providers?

What impact does AI-led triage have on patient wait times and clinic workflow efficiency?

What are the safety profiles (rate of under-triage or over-triage) of currently available AI systems in ambulatory care?

4. Methodology
This review will follow the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) guidelines.

4.1 Inclusion Criteria
Population: Patients presenting to primary care, family medicine clinics, or general practice settings.

Intervention: Use of AI-based algorithms, chatbots, or symptom checkers for the purpose of triage.

Comparison: Human-led triage (nurses, physicians, or administrative staff) or standard-of-care protocols.

Outcomes: Sensitivity, specificity, triage accuracy, time-to-consultation, and patient/provider satisfaction.

Study Design: Randomized controlled trials (RCTs), prospective and retrospective cohort studies, and cross-sectional studies published between 2019 and 2026.

4.2 Search Strategy
We will search major electronic databases including PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and Google Scholar. The search string will incorporate terms related to "Artificial Intelligence," "Triage," and "Primary Care."

5. Data Extraction and Synthesis
Data will be extracted using a standardized form. Quality assessment of the included studies will be performed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool for RCTs or the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale for observational studies. A narrative synthesis of the findings will be provided, and where data allow, a meta-analysis will be conducted.

title: Bridging the Pediatric Neurology Gap: Teleneurology for Screening, Referral, and Diagnostic Workup of Global Developmental Delay and Epilepsy in Children in LMICs — A Scoping Review
description:
Study Type: Scoping Review (PRISMA-ScR / JBI Methodology)
Target Journal: Frontiers in Pediatrics, Special Issue: Global Child Health: Innovations Within Our Reach (Topic ID: 80206)
Search Window: 2016– 2026
Language: English only
Reporting Standard: PRISMA-ScR (Tricco et al., 2018); JBI Scoping Review Methodology (Peters et al., 2020)

Background
In many low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), a significant proportion of children with global developmental delay (GDD) and epilepsy go undiagnosed or receive delayed diagnoses due to a scarcity of pediatric neurologists and severely restricted access to specialist neurological services. Globally, 8.4% (95% UI 7.7–9.1) of children under five years have developmental disabilities — a category encompassing epilepsy, intellectual disability, autism spectrum disorder, and hearing and vision loss — with approximately 95% of affected children residing in LMICs.[1] GDD specifically, defined as significant delay in two or more developmental domains in children under five years, affects 1–3% of children globally.[1] The period from ages 2–5 represents a critical but frequently missed window for neurodevelopmental detection and intervention — yet only 25.4% of children in LMICs receive adequate nurturing care during this period, and fewer than one in three attend early childhood care and education programmes.[2]
Childhood epilepsy incidence in LMICs is approximately threefold higher than in high-income countries, driven by birth asphyxia, CNS infections, neonatal encephalopathy, and malaria.[3] Both conditions share a common structural barrier: in Africa, there are only 0.007 child neurologists per 100,000 population in the lowest-resourced settings — with a continental median of 0.01 per 100,000 and 73% of low-income countries having no access to child neurologists whatsoever — compared to a median of 0.59 per 100,000 across high-income countries.[4] Both conditions are time-sensitive — early detection and intervention during the neuroplastic window of the first five years of life directly alters long-term neurological outcomes.
Telemedicine, portable diagnostic tools, and task-shifting to non-specialist providers offer a pathway to extend specialist neurological reach. However, three relevant bodies of evidence — tele-neurology for pediatric conditions, task-shifting for neurodevelopmental screening, and digital tools for GDD and epilepsy detection — exist in isolation from each other and have not been synthesised. No review has mapped the critical transition from community-level clinical suspicion to neurologist-confirmed diagnosis and structured workup via telemedicine in LMIC settings.

Objectives
This scoping review aims to:
 1. Map existing evidence on the use of telemedicine and tele-neurology for the identification, referral, and diagnostic workup of GDD and epilepsy in children aged 0–18 years in LMICs and analogous low-resource settings from 2015–2025.
 2. Characterise provider roles and task-shifting models within telemedicine-supported pediatric neurology pathways.
 3. Identify the specific evidence gap at the transition from community detection to specialist neurological diagnosis and workup, and to propose a structured research agenda and a conceptual implementation framework for pediatric tele-neurology referral pathways in LMICs.

Methods
This scoping review follows JBI scoping review methodology (Peters et al., 2020) and will be reported according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) checklist (Tricco et al., 2018).
Search Strategy
JBI recommends a three-step search strategy. Step 1 involves a limited preliminary search of PubMed and Embase to identify relevant keywords and index terms from the titles and abstracts of retrieved articles, which will then inform the full search string. Step 2 consists of a full systematic search across PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, Web of Science, and Global Health (CAB Abstracts), using all identified keywords and index terms. Step 3 involves reference list scanning of all included studies to identify additional relevant sources. Grey literature will be searched through WHO IRIS, UNICEF publications, World Bank reports, and ILAE resources. The search period covers January 2015 to May 2025.
Eligibility Criteria — PCC Framework
Population: Children aged 0–18 years with confirmed or suspected GDD or epilepsy.
Concept: Any telemedicine, tele-neurology, or digital health intervention used for screening, referral, diagnosis, workup, or follow-up of GDD or epilepsy.
Context: LMIC settings as defined by the World Bank income classification at the time of publication. Studies from rural or remote low-resource settings in high-income countries will be considered where the telemedicine model is explicitly designed for specialist-scarce, low-connectivity environments analogous to LMIC peripheral health systems. Studies conducted in well-resourced high-income settings without relevance to resource-constrained environments will be excluded.

Exclusion Criteria
Studies exclusively in adults without pediatric subgroup data will be excluded. Studies set exclusively in well-resourced high-income settings without relevance to access gaps will be excluded. Studies without a telemedicine or digital health component will be excluded. Single case reports (n < 5) will be excluded. Conference abstracts without extractable data will be excluded. Studies published before January 2015 will be excluded. Studies not published in English will be excluded. This language restriction is acknowledged as a potential source of selection bias, particularly given the volume of relevant research published in Portuguese, French, and Spanish from LMIC settings in Latin America, West Africa, and Southeast Asia.
Evidence Domains
Three domains will be mapped simultaneously. Domain 1 covers tele-neurology delivery models for pediatric epilepsy and GDD in low-resource settings, including delivery model type, outcomes, equity data, and scalability. Domain 2 covers task-shifting and community health worker roles in neurodevelopmental screening and epilepsy detection, including competencies, training models, and supervision structures. Domain 3 covers digital and portable tools for GDD and epilepsy detection and diagnostic workup in low-resource settings, including tele-EEG, AI-assisted diagnosis, and neurodevelopmental assessment platforms.
Study Selection
Screening of titles/abstracts and full texts will be performed by the principal investigator using Rayyan systematic review software. A random subset of 20% of records will be independently screened by a second reviewer to assess reliability, with inter-rater agreement reported as percent agreement or Cohen’s kappa statistic. A PRISMA-ScR flow diagram will document all records identified, screened, assessed for eligibility, and included at each stage, with reasons for exclusion recorded at the full-text review stage.
Data Charting and Synthesis
A standardised data charting form will capture study characteristics including author, year, country, World Bank income group at time of publication, study design, and sample size. It will also capture setting (urban, rural, or mixed), telemedicine model type (synchronous, asynchronous, mHealth, AI-assisted, or hybrid), provider roles (community health worker, nurse, clinical officer, primary care physician, or pediatric neurologist), diagnostic workup access (EEG modality, neuroimaging, metabolic and genetic testing — whether accessible via telemedicine or requiring in-person attendance), outcomes reported (diagnostic accuracy, feasibility, acceptability, cost, time to diagnosis, equity indicators), and equity data where reported.
Narrative synthesis will be organised thematically across five implementation domains: burden and unmet need; telemedicine delivery model; provider roles and task-shifting; diagnostic workup access; and equity and scalability.
No meta-analysis is planned. Consistent with JBI scoping review methodology, formal critical appraisal of included sources will not be performed; however, study designs and methodological characteristics will be charted to contextualise findings. Results will be presented using tables, figures, and a conceptual evidence map aligned with the three evidence domains.
Expected Outcomes
Based on preliminary searches, a substantive evidence base is anticipated for tele-epilepsy follow-up predominantly from high-income settings, emerging evidence on portable EEG and AI-assisted epilepsy diagnosis in LMICs, sparse evidence on tele-neurodevelopmental assessment for GDD in low-resource settings, and a critical absence of integrated models linking community screening to pediatric neurologist-guided diagnostic workup.
The review will produce a synthesised evidence map across the three domains and identify priorities for a research agenda and conceptual implementation framework for tele-neurology referral pathways targeting children with GDD and epilepsy in LMICs. The framework will be developed inductively from synthesised evidence, structured around five implementation pillars: burden and unmet need, telemedicine delivery model, provider roles and task-shifting, diagnostic workup access, and equity and scalability.

Language Restriction
Only studies published in English will be included due to resource constraints on translation. This constitutes a potential source of selection bias and will be explicitly acknowledged as a limitation of this review, particularly given the volume of relevant research published in Portuguese, French, and Spanish from LMIC settings.

AI Use Disclosure
Claude Sonnet 4.6 (Anthropic, 2025), and OpenEvidence were used for ideation, literature finding and structural drafting during protocol development. All content has been independently verified, critically evaluated, and rewritten by the author. All cited statistics have been confirmed against primary peer-reviewed sources. Disclosed per Frontiers in Pediatrics author guidelines, to be stated in both the Acknowledgements and Methods sections of the final manuscript according to the Publisher rules.

title: Sensitivity and Specificity of Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL) Algorithms in the Diagnosis of Thoracolumbar Injuries Resulting in Vertebral Fractures: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
description: Spinal injuries, often due to high-energy trauma like accidents and falls, are most frequent at the thoracic-to-lumbar transition. Thoracolumbar fractures are more common in males aged 20 to 40. Flexion, often combined with compression, causes primary injury forces, while extension injuries are rare but life-threatening. Globally, traumatic spinal injuries occur at a rate of 10.5 per 100,000 persons annually, with 37.3% involving spinal cord injuries. Men are 3.37 times more affected than women, and the cervical spine is most frequently injured. Common injury mechanisms include traffic accidents and falls. Thoracolumbar spine fractures, accounting for 10% of skeletal injuries, often occur at the thoracic-to-cruciate transition. Timely diagnosis challenges have led to the integration of AI and ML technologies in clinical practice. Machine Learning, especially Deep Learning with neural networks, holds promise in assessing spinal conditions, aiding personalized medicine and improving diagnoses, treatment forecasts, and cost calculations. Despite recognized benefits, studies are limited due to the lack of efficient ML algorithms. This review explores ML and deep learning for prompt thoracolumbar spine injury diagnosis, highlighting potential clinical benefits, including enhanced diagnosis, personalized care, reduced long-term disability, and accurate cost calculations.

title: Effectiveness of educational interventions to improve diagnostic accuracy: A Systematic Review
description: Diagnostic errors represent a significant global concern, with an estimated 10-15% of diagnostic hypotheses made by physicians proving to be incorrect. These misdiagnoses can lead to adverse events for patients and are a major cause of malpractice claims. Several strategies can be used to improve diagnostic performance and reduce cognitive diagnostic errors, which can be divided into two general categories: educational interventions and workplace interventions. Previous reviews of strategies to improve diagnostic reasoning and decision-making have combined both educational and workplace interventions. However, a systematic review focused specifically on educational interventions for improving diagnostic accuracy is still lacking. This study aims to answer the following question: What is the effectiveness of educational interventions to improve medical students’ and physicians’ diagnostic accuracy? The review will follow the PRISMA and Cochrane Handbook guidelines. A comprehensive search will be conducted in the following databases: Cochrane Library; National Library of Medicine (PubMed); PsycInfo; EMBASE; Educational Resource Information Center (ERIC); CINAHL; SCOPUS; Web of Science, GreySource and Grey Literature. For bias analysis, the Cochrane Risk of Bias Scale RoB 2 will be used for randomized studies and ROBINS-I for non-randomized studies. All articles will be assessed by the risk of bias and the medical education research study quality instrument (MERSQI). The collected data will be stored and extracted in an electronic spreadsheet application for analysis. Sensitivity analyses will be performed on the primary outcomes. The GRADEpro GDT will be used to assess the quality of the evidence.

title: Prevalence of anal intraepithelial neoplasia in patients with high-grade intraepithelial lesions of the lower genital tract.
description: High-risk HPV (hrHPV) infection is strongly associated with high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions (HSILs) of the cervix, vagina, vulva, and anus, and with cancer (Moscicki et al., 2006; Crawford et al., 2011; Rietbergen et al., 2018). The prevalence of hrHPV in anal cancer is 85–91% (Plummer et al., 2016; Ebisch et al., 2017). Anal cancer is a disease in which malignant cells develop in the epithelial tissue of the anus. The incidence of anal squamous cell carcinoma (ASCC) has increased in many countries, in both sexes, a phenomenon mainly attributed to the increased sexual transmission of human papillomavirus (HPV) at the population level. Recent studies show that the prevalence of high-grade anal intraepithelial neoplasia (HSIL-AIN) reaches 13.4% in this specific group, while the detection of high-risk HPV in anal samples reaches 73%, with the HPV-16 genotype being the most frequent (Monti et al., 2023). Some systematic reviews corroborate that women with genital HSIL have a higher prevalence of anal HPV and dysplasia, even in non-immunosuppressed populations (Stier et al., 2015). It is also observed that HSIL-AIN are precursor lesions to anal cancer and, moreover, that patients undergoing treatment for anal HSIL have a progression rate to anal cancer almost 60% lower than those who underwent active monitoring and did not receive treatment, emphasizing the need for strong efforts in early detection of these lesions, prevention, and treatment. A second aspect of great relevance is the fact that the risk of anal canal neoplasia is higher in patients with high-grade vulvar, vaginal, and cervical neoplasia. Currently, studies on anal HPV infection, anal lesions, and SCCA have focused primarily on men, especially men who have sex with men (MSM), due to their high absolute risk of SCCA. Few studies have been conducted in women with anal intraepithelial neoplasia, and most have focused on HIV-infected women. Therefore, the effectiveness of different anal cancer screening methods in these patients needs to be determined. We have multiple screening techniques available in our setting with varying costs, accessibility, sensitivity, and specificity, including the use of high-resolution anoscopy (HRA) and anal cytology. This project investigates the prevalence of high-grade anal intraepithelial neoplasia (AIN2/3) and the detection of high-risk HPV in anal sites in patients with HSIL of the lower genital tract, as well as evaluating the sensitivity of anal HPV genotyping, anal cytology, and high-resolution anoscopy in the diagnosis of AIN. Furthermore, the implementation of “patient navigation,” that is, support geared towards efficient referral and reduction of barriers to diagnosis, has proven effective in cancer screening programs—especially for cervical and breast cancer—increasing screening rates by up to 64.5 percentage points (Community Preventive Services Task Force, 2024; Women’s Preventive Services Initiative, 2024). Although still incipient in the anal context, this approach shows strong potential to promote equity in access to HRA (high-resolution anoscopy) when indicated. Finally, the global scenario disrupts this priority: anal cancer is a neoplasm on the rise, with increasing incidence (Ebrahimi et al., 2024). In addition, anal cancer has shown a global increase in incidence, as evidenced by recent epidemiological data, approximately 90% of anal cancer cases are related to HPV (Ebrahimi, 2024; English, 2024).

title: Diagnostic Accuracy of Biomarkers for Microaspiration in Mechanically Ventilated Patients: A Systematic Review
description:
This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluates the diagnostic accuracy of biomarkers for detecting microaspiration and predicting Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia (VAP) in mechanically ventilated adults. While microaspiration is a key pathogenic mechanism, identifying reliable diagnostic markers remains challenging due to heterogeneity in study designs and reference standards.

To address these methodological limitations, this study adopts a conditional synthesis strategy:

Quantitative Synthesis (Meta-Analysis): A meta-analysis will be performed for biomarkers where sufficient homogenous data are available to support statistical pooling (e.g., Airway Amylase). For these analyses, inclusion will be strictly restricted to studies utilizing a confirmed clinical VAP reference standard to ensure prognostic validity. Subgroup analyses will be conducted to investigate the impact of specimen matrix (e.g., Mini-BAL vs. Tracheal Aspirate) on diagnostic accuracy and heterogeneity.

Qualitative Synthesis (Systematic Review): For biomarkers where data are insufficient for pooling, or where studies rely on physiological proxies (e.g., Pepsin, Blue Dye tests, FEES) rather than clinical outcomes, a comprehensive narrative synthesis will be conducted. These studies will be critically appraised for biological plausibility but excluded from meta-analysis to avoid incorporation bias and ensure clinical homogeneity.

This review aims to provide an updated, rigorously stratified assessment of microaspiration biomarkers, determining which candidates offer robust diagnostic utility for clinical practice.

title: A scoping review to explore what is known about midwives working to support the delivery of high risk care (HRC)
description:

Abstract 
Background
Midwives are essential to global maternal health, providing woman-centred and culturally sensitive care. While their expertise in low-risk pregnancies is well documented, the increase in global pregnancy complexity has increased midwives’ working to support high-risk care delivery (HRC), often in obstetric-led models. In the UK, these shifts coincide with workforce strain and declining maternal outcomes. However, little is known internationally about how changes in midwifery may impact on how they experience their role.
Methods
This protocol outlines a scoping review conducted in accordance with JBI methodology and reported following the PRISMA-ScR checklist. Searches will be undertaken in PubMed, CINAHL, Web of Science, OVID, JSTOR, and ScienceDirect, supplemented with Google Scholar and grey literature sources. The search strategy draws on terms used by professional and regulatory bodies and includes conditions associated with high-risk pregnancy. Two reviewers will independently screen records in Rayyan, extract data using a standardised tool, and conduct inductive thematic analysis using NVivo.
Expected Outcomes
The review will map and synthesise international evidence on midwives’ experiences, attitudes, and perceptions of supporting the delivery of HRC. Findings will highlight common themes, context-specific insights, and gaps in knowledge, informing future research, education, and practice to strengthen midwifery contributions within obstetric-led care.






















Introduction 
Midwives are indispensable for achieving equitable, effective, and comprehensive sexual, reproductive, maternal, and adolescent health services globally. Their care not only improves maternal and infant health outcomes but also influences broader health and social determinants, a benefit linked to midwifery’s unique, woman-centred philosophy (Nove et al., 2021). While there is substantial evidence on midwives’ role in low-risk maternity care, less is known about their experiences when providing high-risk care (HRC).

Internationally, the scope of midwifery practice varies widely. In many low- and middle-income countries, midwives take on broad responsibilities, adapting to community needs. This adaptability is critical as the complexity of pregnancies increases due to increasing numbers of preexisting conditions and other factors (Nove et al., 2021). Maternal morbidity and mortality remain largely preventable with skilled care yet continue to disproportionately affect women (Bar-Zeev et al., 2021; Nove et al., 2021).

In high-income settings such as the UK, midwives’ scope may be more restricted in comparison to international colleagues. Tasks considered routine elsewhere are sometimes classified as advanced practice. Restrictive policies can limit midwives’ autonomy, affecting women’s experiences and outcomes. By contrast, when midwives are fully integrated into multidisciplinary teams and supported to practise to the full extent of their training, care is safer, higher-quality, and more respectful (Nove et al., 2021). Expanding midwife-led interventions could prevent maternal and newborn deaths globally (Lancet Midwifery Series Steering Group, 2014).

Women are also presenting with increasingly complex pregnancies. In the UK, this shift has led to more obstetric-led models of care, where midwives follow doctor-directed care plans rather than working autonomously. These changes coincide with workforce attrition, rising maternal and perinatal deaths, and mounting pressure on maternity services, demonstrated by the proposed review of UK maternity services to be conducted by the UK Secretary for Health in 2025 (Royal College of Midwives, 2023). 

Models of Care
Midwives are trained to provide autonomous care for women with uncomplicated pregnancies, supporting the natural processes of pregnancy, labour, and the postnatal period, often referred to as low-risk care (Pelak, Dahlen & Keedle, 2023). The International Confederation of Midwives defines midwifery as skilled, knowledgeable, and compassionate care across the reproductive continuum, with core characteristics including prevention and management of complications, timely referral, and partnership with women (International Confederation of Midwives, 2022). In most settings, women with low-risk pregnancies are cared for primarily by midwives throughout their childbearing journey (Toll et al., 2023).

High-risk care refers to pregnancies where factors increase the likelihood of poor maternal or fetal outcomes. These may include complications of pregnancy (e.g., preeclampsia, haemorrhage), pre-existing conditions (e.g., diabetes, heart disease), or fetal anomalies (Isaacs & Andipatin, 2020). HRC is usually led by an obstetrician, with midwives providing ongoing support and clinical care within a multidisciplinary team. Worldwide declining maternal health (World Health Organisation, 2019) has increased demand for obstetric input, limiting opportunities for autonomous midwifery-led practice (International Confederation of Midwives, 2022).

Maternity Services in the UK
The UK has a long history of midwifery-led care. Women report valuing midwives’ support, particularly during high-risk pregnancies (Nursing and Midwifery Council, 2019; Pelak, Dahlen & Keedle, 2023). However, the profession faces rising attrition and service pressures. UK maternity care is now considered to be in crisis, with concerning upward trends in maternal and perinatal mortality (Royal College of Midwives, 2023). How these systemic shifts impact midwives’ experiences remains poorly understood.

Framing the Issue
Women with multiple adversities and co-morbidities are over represented in reports such as the UK maternal deaths reported by Mothers and Babies: Reducing Risk through Audits and Confidential Enquiries across the UK (MBBRACE) and (International Stillbirth Alliance Stillbirth Advocacy Working Group., 2023). Much research focuses on midwives delivering high quality care for women who require a routine pathway and normal birth. However, as women become more complex, midwives are increasingly involved in the delivery of HRC as part of wider teams providing complex medical and obstetric care. This review seeks to map what is currently known about midwives’ experiences in these contexts. 
Review Question
What is known about the experience of Midwives supporting the delivery of high risk care (HRC)?

Eligibility Criteria
Participants
This review will include studies focusing on midwives and midwifery professionals who have received formal education in maternity care that meets the standards recognised by the International Confederation of Midwives (ICM). This ensures comparability across health systems in more than 120 countries where ICM-recognised training is in place.
To ensure inclusivity, search terms are aligned with the SRMNAH (Sexual, Reproductive, Maternal, Newborn, and Adolescent Health) workforce definitions (Nove et al., 2021) and will include:
• Midwifery professionals
• Nursing professionals with midwifery training
• Midwifery associate professionals
• Nursing associate professionals with midwifery training
Studies where midwives are clearly identifiable as participants, either as autonomous practitioners or as part of multidisciplinary teams, will be considered eligible.

Concept
The review will consider studies that explore midwives’ experiences, perceptions, or attitudes when providing care for women identified as requiring high-risk maternity care (HRC). For the purposes of this review, HRC is defined as care provided outside the typical scope of low-risk, midwife-led practice, where obstetric input is required due to known or emergent complications.

This includes contexts where midwives deliver care under obstetric-led decision-making or in partnership with obstetricians, rather than acting solely as autonomous providers. The review will exclude studies focused exclusively on low-risk models of care, or those where midwives have undertaken advanced practice training beyond standard midwifery education.

Context
This review will consider studies from any international setting where midwives contribute to the delivery of maternity care for women requiring obstetric-led input. To maintain comparability, studies must be situated within health systems that provide midwifery education recognised by the ICM.
Studies published from 2014 onwards will be included. The date range was selected to align with two key milestones in global maternal health: the Lancet Midwifery Series (2014), which highlighted the potential of midwifery to transform outcomes, and the international adoption of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (2015), which prioritised maternal and newborn health worldwide. Restricting the timeframe ensures the review captures contemporary models of practice making findings more relevant to today’s workforce and policy environment.

Only studies published in English will be included. The decision is consistent with scoping review methodology, which prioritises breadth of evidence mapping within feasible boundaries. This restriction is due to resource limitations, as translation services are beyond the scope of this review. While this may exclude some evidence from non-English-speaking contexts, the focus on ICM-recognised midwifery training (represented across more than 120 countries, including many with English-language publication practices) is expected to mitigate the impact. 

Types of studies to be included 
This scoping review will consider quantitative, qualitative, and mixed methods study designs for inclusion. In addition, systematic reviews, text and opinion papers will be considered for inclusion in the proposed scoping review

Inclusion Criteria: Exclusion Criteria:
Studies exploring midwives' experience, attitudes and perceptions of their role in supporting HRC delivery. Studies that do not focus on midwives' experiences or perceptions or, where midwives’ voices are not clearly defined if other colleagues have also been included in the study.
Studies conducted in healthcare systems comparable to the UK’s National Health Service (NHS). Studies originating in countries where midwives are not receiving an education recognised by the ICM (International Confederation of Midwives., 2022).

Studies involving autonomously practicing midwives. Studies focusing on low-risk care models.
Studies published in English. Studies within healthcare systems which significantly differ from the NHS.
Peer-reviewed articles, grey literature (blogs, editorials, opinion pieces), and other academic works. Studies where midwives are delivering HRC because there is minimal or no obstetric support.
Studies in which midwives are working of part of the MDT where they would usually be working as experts in low risk care but are delivering HRC as part of an obstetrically decided care plan. Studies which focus on midwives’ perception of a specific intervention or screening tool.
Studies exploring midwives' experience, attitudes and perceptions of their role in supporting HRC delivery. Studies which focus on midwives who have undertaken additional training to provide additional care or services to women (advanced practitioners).




Methods
The proposed scoping review will be conducted in accordance with the JBI methodology for scoping reviews (Peters et al., 2024) and be reported in line with PRISMA-ScR.

Search Approach
Database Selection
The search strategy will combine academic databases and grey literature sources to maximise coverage. Searches will be undertaken in PubMed, CINAHL, Web of Science, OVID, JSTOR, and ScienceDirect. In addition, Google Scholar will be used to capture grey literature and less formally published work. To ensure feasibility and relevance, only the first 200 results from Google Scholar, ordered by relevance, will be screened, this is consistent with intentions for the review to remain broad but feasible. Reference lists of included studies will also be searched to identify additional relevant publications.

The search strategy has been developed using keywords and MeSH terms informed by professional and regulatory bodies as the term “high risk care” is not used universally to describe the care provision for women who require obstetric input. It will be adapted for each database to ensure maximum retrieval. 
The search terms used in the search strategy were generated from terms identified by the following organisations:
• Nursing and Midwifery Council, UK (NMC)
• Royal College of Midwives, UK (RCM)
• National Health Service, UK (NHS)
• Health Education England (HSE)
National Institute for Clinical Excellence, UK (NICE)
• Royal College of Obstetrics and Gynaecology, UK (RCoG)
International Confederation of Midwives (ICM)








Terminology of Risk
The term high-risk care (HRC) is used deliberately in this review. Initial work completed to identify key terms for the scoping review reveal the inconsistency of classification language within the UK and internationally. Whilst alternative terms such as ‘complex care’ or ‘additional needs’ are increasingly promoted by some midwifery bodies to emphasise nuance beyond binary risk classification and to reduce stigma associated with the use of it as a label, the use of these alternative phrases does not accurately reflect the phenomenon under exploration. Additionally, preliminary scoping work undertaken for this review indicates that alternative terms are not used consistently in the international literature and, in some cases, return results unrelated to maternity care.
This review is not focused on reframing the language of complexity and risk within a midwifery-led philosophical model, but with examining the current context of how midwives practise within obstetric-led systems of care. These systems are explicitly structured around medically defined thresholds of risk, surveillance, and escalation and the search terms and subsequent discourse should reflect this. Internationally, ‘high risk’ remains the dominant terminology used across professional, regulatory, and policy frameworks to describe pregnancies requiring obstetric oversight, including those produced by bodies such as the International Confederation of Midwives, the World Health Organization, and UK national regulators. 
The choice to use high risk terminology aims to ensure conceptual clarity, the support of comprehensive literature retrieval, and to accurately reflect the clinical and organisational realities shaping midwives’ work. The use of high risk is thus appropriate to the methodological intent of the review and to making visible the structural and experiential consequences of this shift for midwives.

Search Terms and Keywords
A combination of keywords and MeSH terms have been used to capture the full range of relevant literature. (Full list in appendix 1).

High-risk care “high risk*” OR complication* OR “complex need*” OR “increased risk” OR “risk factor*” OR “pre-existing condition*” Include MeSH terms: Pregnancy, High-Risk; adapt to database thesaurus

Search Strategy
The search strategy is designed to capture both published and unpublished evidence, including primary studies, reviews, and text or opinion papers. A preliminary (“soft”) search will first be conducted in PubMed to scope the range of available literature and to identify key papers. 

Key papers will be used to validate the effectiveness of the search terms and confirm that the chosen keywords and MeSH terms are returning relevant results. Revisions of the keyword list will be made if deemed appropriate by the first and second authors. Additional search strings will be developed by analysing the text words in the titles and abstracts of relevant articles and the index terms used to describe them. The strategy, including all identified keywords and MeSH terms, will then be adapted for each database to ensure maximum sensitivity and specificity. Reference lists of all included studies will be hand searched to identify additional relevant publications. 

Following the initial searches all identifiable records will be collated and uploaded into Rayyan (Ouzzani et al., 2016). This software will be used to remove duplicates and to perform initially screening of titles and abstracts. A second, independent reviewer will screen against the inclusion criteria. This systematic approach is intended to ensure comprehensive coverage of diverse study designs and perspectives, capturing midwives’ experiences of supporting the delivery of high-risk care within obstetric-led contexts. Reasons for exclusion will be noted and recorded for transparency. Any lack on consensus between the first and second author will be mediated by a third reviewer. 
The results of the search will be reported via a PRISMA flow diagram. References for the review will be managed in a reference manager tool.

Data Extraction
Data will be extracted from eligible studies using a standardised form, adapted from the JBI data extraction tool (see Appendix 2). Extracted information will include: study characteristics (author, year, country, design), population (midwives and context), concept (experience of high-risk care), methodology, and key findings relevant to the review question.

Two reviewers will independently extract data, with discrepancies resolved through discussion or referral to a third reviewer. NVivo software will be used to support the organisation of extracted data and facilitate coding for thematic analysis.

Data Analysis and Presentation
A systematic thematic analysis of the papers will be conducted in order to identify, analyse and identify recurrent patterns/ themes. This approach will ensure a comprehensive exploration of the literature available (Braun & Clarke, 2006; Clarke & Braun, 2017). 

Data will be analysed thematically to identify and synthesise recurrent patterns across studies (Braun & Clarke, 2006; Clarke & Braun, 2017). Analysis will proceed in stages:
• Familiarisation: Full-text reading to ensure a comprehensive understanding of each study.
• Initial coding: Identification of key concepts and experiences relevant to midwives’ roles in high-risk care.
• Theme development: Organisation of codes into broader themes and sub-themes, using an inductive approach that allows themes to emerge from the data (Fereday & Muir-Cochrane, 2006).
• Review and refinement: Iterative checking to ensure themes accurately reflect the source material, are distinct from one another, and capture the breadth of findings (Nowell et al., 2017).

Rigour will be enhanced by the involvement of two independent reviewers at each stage, with disagreements resolved through discussion or by a third reviewer where necessary.

Remaining consistent with the JBI standards for a scoping review, findings will be presented in both narrative and tabular form (draft example Appendix 3). The synthesis will highlight recurrent themes, context-specific insights, and gaps in the evidence, providing a comprehensive overview of midwives’ experiences in supporting the delivery of high-risk care.

Strengths and Limitations
Conducting the study in line with the JBI methodology for scoping reviews and reported according to the PRISMA-ScR checklist, ensuring methodological transparency and reproducibility is a cealr strength. The search strategy is comprehensive, combining multiple academic databases with grey literature sources, and is informed by internationally recognised terminology from professional and regulatory bodies. By focusing on midwives educated to standards recognised by the International Confederation of Midwives (ICM), the review will provide insights that are broadly comparable across more than 120 countries. In addition, the use of independent reviewers at each stage, along with systematic data extraction and thematic analysis, will enhance rigour.

The review also has limitations. Restricting the search to 2014 onwards may exclude earlier studies; however, this timeframe was chosen to reflect contemporary midwifery practice following the Lancet Midwifery Series (2014) and the Sustainable Development Goals (2015), both of which shifted global attention toward the midwifery workforce. Limiting the review to studies published in English is necessary due to resource constraints. Finally, as is standard in scoping reviews, no formal quality appraisal of included studies will be undertaken. This means the review will map the breadth and nature of available evidence rather than assess its methodological robustness.

title: Multimodal Artificial Intelligence for the Diagnosis of Depression and Anxiety: A Systematic Review
description:
Overview:
This systematic review aims to comprehensively evaluate the current landscape of multimodal artificial intelligence (AI) frameworks designed for the screening and differential diagnosis of depression and anxiety. Traditionally, psychiatric diagnosis has relied on subjective self-reports, which are susceptible to recall bias and social stigma. While AI has introduced objective, data-driven biomarkers, most existing models rely on unimodal data, which often lacks the capacity to capture the complex and overlapping symptoms of co-occurring mental health disorders.

Purpose:
The primary purpose of this study is to analyze how the integration of diverse data streams—specifically the fusion of behavioral signals (e.g., speech, facial expressions, and physical activity) and physiological signals (e.g., EEG, ECG, and heart rate variability)—enhances diagnostic precision. By applying the PICO framework, we systematically investigate:

The prevalence and effectiveness of various data fusion strategies (early, late, and hybrid fusion).

The performance of advanced computational architectures (ranging from traditional machine learning to deep learning models like Transformers and GNNs) in achieving differential diagnosis.

The methodological consistency and clinical validity of AI-driven biomarkers compared to traditional gold standards.

Expected Outcomes:
We expect this review to provide a definitive mapping of current multimodal AI methodologies in mental healthcare. The outcomes will include:

A comparative analysis of diagnostic accuracy across different modality combinations and algorithms.

Identification of critical methodological gaps, such as data scarcity, lack of interpretability (XAI), and domain adaptation challenges.

A strategic roadmap for developing next-generation, objective, and individualized diagnostic support systems that can be integrated into real-world clinical workflows.

title: Magnetic resonance imaging of the lumbar spine: assessing clinical impact and potential harm from overuse in a Swedish setting.
description:
Globaly imaging for lower back pain has increased over the last decades, especially the use of MRI. This trend is true for Sweden as well. A previous study by Wnuk et. al. found that 13% percent of outpatient MRI´s of the lower back had actionable findings. With a rather high rate of false positive findings. The rate of actionable findings in a Swedish context is unkown thus we intend to replicate the study done by Wnuk et al. but in a Swedish setting.

Methods
This study is a retrospective cohort study of lumbar spine MR imaging. The study is descriptive in nature. Simple descriptive statistics will be used to summarize data. Two reviewers will independently go through radiological reports and patient journals manually to note findings and whether they led to a change of treatment or new diagnoses. In the case of disagreement a third senior reviewer will be used to settle the case. Independent manual assessment will be used instead of automatic text search engine in order to mitigate risk of over or under-assessing any of the study endpoints. The outcomes of the study are "actionable exams", "potentially harmful findings" and appropiateness as descriped below. 


Actionable exams: Examinations will be classified as either “actionable,” or “non-actionable” using the definitions created by Wnuk et. al. An examination could satisfy more than one set of criteria but would contribute only once to the overall total of actionable examinations.
An actionable examination is one which either:

1. Contributes to planning of an anatomically specific treatment;
2. Contributes to a new diagnosis of fracture, cancer or infection;
3. Is performed to follow known lumbar spine pathology (other than degenerative conditions).

Examinations that do not meet any of the three criteria are classified as non-actionable.

Anatomically specific treatment: An examination is classified as actionable if a spine procedure occurred within 12 months following the examination, without an intervening lumbar spine MRI, for which the anatomical imaging information might be used in planning. Procedures considered included laminectomy, foraminotomy, resection, drainage, decompression, discectomy, vertebral fusion, vertebroplasty and radiation therapy performed at spinal levels from T12 through S1, inclusive.
Furthermore we will also note less invasive treatments (nerve root block, facet joint injection,) and of more doubtful efficacy. They will be presented in aggregate and separate.

Contribution to a new diagnosis: New diagnoses of cancer, infection, acute fracture of the spine or other clinically significant disease requiring treatment. For all positive reports, clinical notes will be examined up to one year following the examination. A finding will be considered a “true positive” if confirmed by subsequent imaging, blood tests or biopsy, or if treatment was initiated based on the imaging findings. Treatment might include surgery, chemotherapy or radiation therapy for cancer, and treatment with antibiotics or drainage for infection. A finding will also considered a true positive if accepted as real by the clinician as indicated in the clinical chart. False positives (see below) were considered as harmful.

Following a known condition: Examinations are classified as actionable if they are used to follow known condition (other than degenerative disease).

Potentially harmful: When the suggestion of cancer or infection raised in the report is not substantiated by subsequent events the finding was considered a “false positive,” and the examination is classified as potentially harmful since it may lead to further evaluations, incorrect treatment and/or patient anxiety. 

Appropriateness: While not formally used in our setting we asses this in a smaller random sample in order to benchmark our referrals to the findings in the previous study by Wnuk et al. Appropriateness scores, based on ACR criteria, from 1-9 will be assessed based on information given in the referrals.

Study population: Outpatient adult lumbar spine MRI performed in Skane county between 20220101 and 20230101. Imaging protocols vary to some extent but generally include sagittal T1 and T2 weighted images covering the lower thoracic spine through the sacrum. Usually there is also a coronal T2 TIRM sequence covering the whole abdomen and pelvis. 
Exams were performed on either 1.5 or 3.0 Tesla and interpreted by radiologists of varying training and subspecialty, some by musculoskeletal radiologists or neuroradiologists. Exams were read at non-academic institutions. Demographic information, indications for the study, and appropriateness scores will be obtained from the radiology information system(PACS). Examinations will be excluded if they were incomplete or if the patient is younger than 18 years of age.

title: Comparative Diagnostic Performance of Psychometric, Machine Learning, and Hybrid Approaches in Detecting Cheating on Educational Tests: A PRISMA 2020-Compliant Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
description:
Cheating on educational tests threatens the validity, reliability, and fairness of measurement. Three method families have evolved historically to detect such behavior: (i) psychometric forensic analysis (person-fit statistics, answer-copying indices, response time models), (ii) machine learning (ML) approaches (supervised classifiers, anomaly detection, deep learning), and (iii) hybrid/ensemble approaches that combine psychometric features with ML algorithms. The literature is fragmented across cheating types, data modalities, ground-truth quality, and reporting metrics — preventing direct comparison.

This systematic review and multi-tier meta-analysis aims to: (a) synthesize the comparative diagnostic performance of these three families, (b) test the "reliability illusion" hypothesis that simulation studies systematically inflate performance, and (c) examine how ground-truth quality moderates method-family comparisons.

Following PRISMA 2020 reporting guidelines and PRISMA-P 2015 protocol standards, the study uses a six-axis conceptual framework (E1: cheating type × E2: data modality × E3: method family × E4: ground-truth quality × E5: testing context × E6: design/validation) and a three-tier synthesis architecture (Tier A: diagnostic test accuracy / bivariate-HSROC; Tier B: classification metrics / multilevel rma.mv with RVE; Tier C: simulation-based Type I and detection rates with meta-regression).

Primary research questions test (i) whether method families differ in pooled diagnostic performance, (ii) whether hybrid approaches outperform single-family methods, (iii) whether simulation studies systematically inflate performance, (iv) how method-family effects depend on cheating-type × data-modality interactions, and (v) how ground-truth quality moderates method-family comparisons. Six moderator questions and four exploratory questions complete the analytical framework.

title: Content-routed hybrid extraction from free-text pathology reports in Brazilian Portuguese: a human-anchored internal and external validation study
description:
STUDY DESIGN:
Diagnostic accuracy study (STARD-AI compliant). Retrospective analysis of free-text pathology reports in Brazilian Portuguese.

SOURCE COHORT:
848,987 pathology reports (2015-2025) from a private pathology laboratory (Lâmina Lab) in Brasília, Brazil. Reports include anatomopathological (AP), immunohistochemistry (IHC), cytology, and molecular biology exams across breast, gastric, thyroid, cervical, and other domains.

SYSTEM UNDER VALIDATION:
Hybrid AI extraction system with 4 components:
1. Content-based routing (validates IHC reports by conclusion content, not specimen metadata — addressing 27% misrouting rate found in development)
2. Domain-selective extraction: regex + LLM for breast AP/IHC; regex-only for gastric; regex + LLM-subtypes for thyroid; regex-first for cervical
3. Ontological canonicalization (behavior_class replacing benign/malignant; dual HER2/Ki-67 representation)
4. Reconciliation with discordance flagging

Models: Claude Sonnet 4 (primary extractor), Claude Opus 4 (secondary dual reader — does not correct primary output).

DATASETS:
- Development set: 145 reports (used for prompt iteration)
- Internal benchmark: 656 reports (used for pipeline decisions — NOT test data)
- Frozen holdout: 980 reports (seed=51, zero overlap with above) — PRIMARY EVALUATION
- Challenge set: 100 reports (separate stress test, not included in success thresholds)
- External validation: ~400 reports from independent laboratory (Diagnose)

HOLDOUT COMPOSITION:
- Breast AP: 200 (80 biopsy carcinoma, 60 surgical, 60 benign)
- Breast IHC: 200 (20 HER2 3+, 30 HER2 2+, 30 triple-negative, 80 luminal, 40 non-breast IHC)
- Gastric: 180 (60 OLGA 0, 50 OLGA I, 40 OLGA II, 15 H.pylori+, 15 dysplasia)
- Thyroid Bethesda: 200 (25 Cat I, 25 Cat II, 40 Cat III, 40 Cat IV, 35 Cat V, 35 Cat VI)
- Cervical: 200 (80 NILM, 40 ASC-US, 20 ASC-H, 25 LSIL, 25 HSIL, 10 AGC)

REFERENCE STANDARD:
- Primary: Pathologist 1 (P1) — blinded annotation of ALL 980 holdout reports
- Reliability: Pathologist 2 (P2) — blinded annotation of 150 reports (30 per domain, stratified)
- Adjudication: Pathologist 3 (P3) — resolves P1↔P2 discordances in the 150 subsample
- External: P1 reviews 100% of ~400 Diagnose reports

PRIMARY ENDPOINTS (per domain):
- Breast AP: behavior_class, tipo_hist_canonical, margem_status, invasive_malignancy
- Breast IHC: re_status, rp_status, her2_status
- Gastric: h_pylori, olga, displasia
- Thyroid: bethesda_category
- Cervical: resultado_bethesda, adequabilidade

SUCCESS THRESHOLDS:
- F1/macro-F1 ≥ 0.90 for primary categorical/binary variables per domain
- Weighted kappa ≥ 0.85 for ordinal variables
- ICC ≥ 0.85 for numeric variables
- Inter-rater reliability (P1↔P2) kappa ≥ 0.80
- Study passes if ≥ 4 of 5 domains meet all primary thresholds

ANALYSIS PLAN:
- Metrics computed after ontological canonicalization; raw agreement reported in supplement
- CIs via stratified bootstrap (2,000 iterations)
- Secondary analyses: inter-AI agreement (Sonnet↔Opus), performance by pathologist/period, challenge set

FROZEN PIPELINE:
Version v5.2.1 — No further tuning of prompts, regex, routing, ontology, or canonicalization rules after this registration. Any post-hoc deviations will be documented and reported.

ETHICS:
Protocol submitted to CEP/FEPECS (12/02/2026). Broad scope. Waiver of informed consent.

DATA AVAILABILITY:
Raw reports contain PHI and cannot be shared. Will provide: prompts, regex code, canonicalization rules, anonymized outputs, analysis code.

title: Defining the minimal important difference in the treatment of early-onset schizophrenia using antipsychotic drugs
description:
Background
Early onset schizophrenia (EOS) can be a highly disabling condition and is associated with cognitive impairment, hospitalization, and poor long-term outcomes.(1, 2) The Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS) is the gold-standard instrument for assessing symptom severity in individuals with schizophrenia, but the threshold for clinically relevant improvement in EOS is unknown. 

A way of defining the minimal important difference (MID) in symptoms, is to compare the PANSS with an overall impression of patient illness related wellbeing. The Clinical Global Impression Improvement (CGI-I) is often used in clinical trials, with a CGI of 3 (‘minimally improved’) as a benchmark for MID. The aim of this study is to define the MID in children and adolescents with EOS treated with antipsychotic drugs. 

Methods
This study will obtain individual participant data from short-term, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trials on antipsychotic drugs submitted to the Dutch Medicines Evaluation Board (MEB) for registration purposes. All studies involving children and adolescents (18 years and under) that used both Clinical Global Impression-Improvement (CGI-I) and the Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS) will be included. All trials were approved by the original ethical committee and participants and caregivers signed informed consent. Weekly measurements of the CGI-I were used from week 1 to 4. 

The PANSS is a 30-item interview that rates positive and negative symptoms, and general psychopathology from 1 (absent) to 7 (extreme). The total score varies between 30 (no symptoms) and 210 (most severe symptoms).(5) 

The CGI-I captures the assessor’s impression of change/ global improvement or worsening with the following scores: 1 = very much improved, 2 = much improved, 3 = minimally improved, 4 = no change, 5 = minimally worse, 6 = much worse, and 7 = very much worse.

Primary outcome
The primary outcome is defined as the change in PANSS score (PANSS score at follow-up minus PANSS at baseline) that will be linked to a CGI-I score of 3 on global impression (“minimally improved”).

Secondary outcomes
Secondary outcomes will be a CGI-I of 3 linked to the percentage of PANSS reduction. An analysis calculating the MID for patients with severe symptoms (PANSS >95), moderate symptoms (76-95) and mild symptoms (PANSS 58-75), will be performed using established severity benchmarks.(6)

As an alternative method to define the minimal important difference, Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) analyses will be conducted and the Area Under the Curve (AUC) will be calculated. Participants will be categorized as being at least slightly improved (CGI-I score 3 or lower), or unchanged/worsened (CGI-I score 4 or higher) after 4 weeks

Data analysis
Pooled analysis of the CGI-I and PANSS for weeks 1, 2, 3 and 4 will be conducted. For each week, list-wise deletion will be used to exclude participants with missing outcome data. The correlation of outcomes will be assessed, a Spearman's rank correlation coefficient of 0.5 or higher is predefined as a sufficient correlation. If this condition is met, equipercentile linking with log-linear smoothing will be applied, using a bootstrap approach to generate 95% confidence intervals (CIs). A single average linking score will be presented, representing the collective outcomes across all time points. For variables that are normally distributed, the Pearson correlation coefficient will be used. Not normally distributed data will be analyzed using the Spearman correlation coefficient.

As an alternative method to calculate the MID scores, participants will be categorized as being at least slightly improved (CGI-I score 3 or lower) or unchanged/worsened (CGI-I score 4 or higher) at follow up. Both the actual score and the percentage PANSS change score will be used as MID variables. To identify the optimal MID values, a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses will be conducted and the area under the curve (AUC) will be calculated with 95% CI. The Youden index will be used to identify the optimal MID value, as it maximizes sensitivity and specificity simultaneously and is less sensitive to imbalanced groups. Both the actual score and the percentage PANSS change score will be used as MID variables.

Analyses will be performed using R version 4.2 and the equate package.

title: From “hands up” to “pencils down”: An investigation of student academic performance in the wake of a fatal police shooting
description:
This project examines associations between a nearby fatal police shooting and the academic performance of public-school students in the district in which the shooting occurred. We draw on a rich dataset from an education technology provider that includes information about daily lessons students complete (including lesson duration and pass rate) as well as their performance on thrice-yearly standardized (“diagnostic”) assessments. Temporal and geographic distance from the shooting are examined as moderators, as are student age and ethnoracial group and school subject (math or reading).

Assessing impacts within one academic year and one school district, this study examines the acute effects of nearby police violence. We identify students as treated or exposed to this violence if their schools are proximate to the shooting (as described below) and ask whether their academic performance suffers in the immediate aftermath (days to weeks) of the incident. We note that this acute focus differs somewhat from existing work that has examined impacts in the academic year that followed a high-profile killing (Gershenson & Hayes, 2018) and from studies that have identified impacts on adult mental health among Black adults living in the same state in which an unarmed Black individual was killed by police (Bor, Venkataramani, Williams, & Tsai, 2018).

School distance from shooting events will be an important measure for determining which schools were “treated.” We anticipate that residing or going to school in the same neighborhood as a fatal police shooting would be even more disruptive to a child than residing in the same city as the incident or hearing about it on the news. However, the definitions of proximity included in some prior work on exposure to neighborhood violence (i.e., distance from a child’s home) suggest that neighborhood may be quite small: within 1,000 feet (Sharkey, Tirado-Strayer, Papachristos, & Raver, 2012) or less than half of a mile (2,640 ft) (Heissel, Sharkey, Torrats-Espinosa, Grant, & Adam, 2017). According to the US Department of Transportation, the majority of children living in urban areas travel one mile or more to school (2008). This statistic has at least two implications for our study design: First, there may be few, if any, schools within half a mile of a fatal police shooting. Additionally, the students who live closest to the shooting may go to school several miles from their home. In other words, a child's home and school may, or may not, share the same immediate neighborhood context. This phenomenon brings us to a classic situation of balancing between sensitivity and specificity: we want to draw neighborhood boundaries large enough that they contain the students whose home or school environments were most directly impacted by a fatal police shooting, but not so large that it dilutes the true effect of this exposure.

Importantly, Black Americans are at disproportionate risk of experiencing violence during police encounters (by some estimates over three times more likely to be killed than whites; Schwartz & Jahn, 2020). Among the fatal police shootings we examine, all victims were Black. For this reason, while we imagine proximity to such an event could be distressing for any young person, we anticipate these incidents would be particularly upsetting for Black students.

title: “Non-Infectious Causes of Rash Mimicking Infectious Diseases: A Clinical Review for Undergraduate Medical Training “
description:
Background: Rashes are a frequent clinical presentation in both ambulatory and hospital settings. While infectious diseases are often presumed to be the primary cause, numerous non-infectious conditions mimic infectious exanthems, leading to diagnostic errors, unnecessary antibiotic use, and delayed management of the true underlying disorder.
Objective: To provide an evidence-based, undergraduate-level clinical review of the major non-infectious causes of rash that resemble infectious diseases, and highlight key differentiating features that aid accurate diagnosis.
Methods: A comprehensive review of established dermatology and internal medicine literature was conducted, focusing on conditions commonly presenting with exanthematous or infection-like rashes. Key data from standard textbooks, clinical guidelines, and peer-reviewed sources were synthesized. Conditions were categorized into drug reactions, autoimmune diseases, allergic disorders, systemic diseases, dermatologic disorders, environmental causes, and nutritional deficiencies. Diagnostic clues distinguishing non-infectious rashes from infectious counterparts were summarized.
Results: The analysis identified several high-yield non-infectious mimickers—including drug eruptions, autoimmune vasculitides, Kawasaki disease, contact dermatitis, erythema multiforme, psoriasis variants, photodermatitis, and nutritional deficiencies. Distinguishing clinical clues include onset relative to drug exposure, distribution patterns, pruritus, mucosal involvement, presence or absence of fever, systemic symptoms, and exposure history. A consolidated comparison table between infectious and non-infectious rashes enhances diagnostic clarity.
Conclusion: Non-infectious rashes frequently resemble infectious exanthems, posing a diagnostic challenge for clinicians and trainees. Understanding their characteristic patterns and key differentiating features can significantly reduce misdiagnosis, prevent unwarranted antimicrobial therapy, and improve patient outcomes. This review provides a concise, structured framework to support undergraduate medical students in developing diagnostic accuracy in dermatologic presentations.

title: Does AI Improve Cancer Detection or Reduce Interval Cancers in Breast Screening? Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
description: This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluates whether artificial intelligence (AI)-supported mammography reading improves clinically meaningful outcomes in population breast cancer screening. Unlike prior reviews based on retrospective reader studies and historical cohorts, eligibility is restricted to prospective deployments of AI in live screen-reading against a concurrent non-AI comparator, including randomized trials and prospective cohorts.The review distinguishes the effect of AI on cancer detection from its effect on the interval and advanced cancers that serve as surrogates for screening benefit and mortality. Primary outcomes are the cancer detection rate and the interval cancer rate; secondary outcomes include recall, false positives, positive predictive value, advanced cancer rates, and screen-reading workload. Diagnostic accuracy is reported only as a supplemental upper bound, given the partial-verification and incorporation bias inherent to single-round screening data.Risk of bias is assessed with design-matched tools (RoB 2, ROBINS-I, and QUADAS-3), with certainty of evidence rated using GRADE. Effect estimates are synthesized using random-effects models with estimand-matched handling of paired within-woman studies, prediction intervals, and outcomes that cannot be pooled summarized following SWiM guidance. The review follows PRISMA, PRISMA-DTA, and PRISMA-S reporting standards.The expected outcome is a clarified evidence base distinguishing what AI-supported screening has been shown to achieve (cancer detection) from what remains unproven (reduction in interval and advanced cancers, and improvement in screening effectiveness), with implications for screening policy and the design of future trials.

title: Virtual Healings: Virtual Reality and Augmented Reality Innovations in Modern Medicine
description:
Rachmad, Yoesoep Edhie. 2021. Virtual Healings: Virtual Reality and Augmented Reality Innovations in Modern Medicine. Perspectives in Health Information Management Publishing, Chicago Book Special Issue, 2021. https://doi.org/10.17605/osf.io/ryz6q
"Virtual Healings: Virtual Reality and Augmented Reality Innovations in Modern Medicine" by Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, published in 2021 by Perspectives in Health Information Management Publishing in Chicago, examines the transformative impact of Virtual Reality (VR) and Augmented Reality (AR) technologies on modern medicine. This book was written in response to the growing interest and significant advancements in VR and AR technologies, emphasizing their potential to revolutionize healthcare practices and patient outcomes.
Definition and Basic Concepts
The book provides a foundational understanding of VR and AR technologies, tracing their historical development and technological evolution. VR is defined as a simulated experience that can mimic or differ from the real world, while AR overlays digital information onto the real world. Both technologies are explored within the medical context, highlighting their capabilities to enhance healthcare delivery.
Underlying Phenomena
The driving force behind this book is the rapid development and adoption of VR and AR technologies in healthcare. The increasing need for advanced training tools, accurate diagnostic methods, and innovative therapeutic solutions are key phenomena that underscore the significance of VR and AR in modern medicine. The author highlights the potential of these technologies to address critical healthcare challenges and improve patient care.
Problem Statement
The primary issue addressed by the book is the integration of VR and AR into healthcare practices. It seeks to understand how these technologies can be effectively utilized to enhance medical training, diagnostics, surgical procedures, rehabilitation, and patient care, while also considering the potential social and psychological impacts.
Research Objectives
The book aims to explore the various applications of VR and AR in healthcare, providing a comprehensive analysis of their benefits, challenges, and future potential. It seeks to offer insights into how these technologies can be implemented to improve healthcare outcomes and to provide recommendations for their ethical and effective use.
Indicators
Key indicators of successful VR and AR integration in healthcare, as identified in the book, include enhanced medical training outcomes, improved diagnostic accuracy, safer and more efficient surgical procedures, and more effective rehabilitation therapies. The book also emphasizes the importance of understanding the social and psychological impacts of these technologies on patients.
Operational Variables
Operational variables discussed in the book include VR and AR hardware and software, medical training programs, diagnostic tools, surgical aids, and rehabilitation protocols. The book also considers variables related to patient outcomes, such as recovery rates, psychological well-being, and overall treatment efficacy.
Determining Factors
Several factors are crucial for the successful implementation of VR and AR in healthcare, including technological advancements, healthcare professionals' willingness to adopt new tools, regulatory support, and patient acceptance. The book highlights the importance of interdisciplinary collaboration and continuous innovation to overcome challenges and maximize the benefits of these technologies.
Implementation and Strategy
The book outlines strategies for integrating VR and AR into healthcare, such as developing robust training programs for healthcare professionals, investing in cutting-edge VR and AR technologies, and fostering collaborations between technology developers and medical practitioners. It also emphasizes the need for regulatory frameworks and ethical guidelines to ensure responsible use.
Challenges and Supportive Factors
The book identifies several challenges, including the high cost of VR and AR technologies, potential technical issues, and the need for comprehensive training for healthcare professionals. Supportive factors include ongoing technological innovations, supportive policies and regulations, and positive patient outcomes. The author calls for a balanced approach to leverage supportive factors while addressing challenges effectively.
Determining Factors of the Book
The relevance and impact of the book are determined by its timely exploration of emerging technologies, its comprehensive analysis, and its practical recommendations for healthcare professionals and policymakers. The book’s ability to address ethical considerations and propose actionable strategies contributes significantly to its importance.
Research Findings
The book presents numerous case studies demonstrating successful applications of VR and AR in healthcare. These include enhanced surgical training through virtual simulations, improved diagnostic accuracy using 3D visualizations, and effective rehabilitation therapies in controlled virtual environments. These findings highlight the tangible benefits of VR and AR in transforming healthcare delivery.
Conclusion and Recommendations
In conclusion, the book emphasizes the vital role of VR and AR in modernizing healthcare. It advocates for their ethical and responsible adoption, emphasizing the need for continuous education and adaptation among healthcare professionals. The author recommends fostering interdisciplinary collaborations, investing in technological innovations, and developing comprehensive regulatory frameworks to ensure the successful integration of VR and AR in healthcare.
"Virtual Healings: Virtual Reality and Augmented Reality Innovations in Modern Medicine" offers a detailed exploration of how VR and AR can enhance traditional medical practices and pave the way for new approaches in healthcare. It underscores the importance of innovation, ethical responsibility, and strategic implementation to harness the full potential of these transformative technologies.
