title: An exploratory cross-sectional study of the association between characteristics, physical activity and perceived health motivation and the prevalence of patellofemoral pain in students aged 18-40 in a UK university.
description:
Patellofemoral pain (PFP) is considered one of the most prevalent musculoskeletal (MSK) conditions facing primary healthcare (Crossley et al., 2016). Characterised by pain in the anterior aspect of the knee along the patella, it is usually aggravated by movements that load the patellofemoral joint, such as squatting, running, climbing stairs, and sitting for prolonged periods (Gaitonde et al., 2019). Given the chronic trajectory of this condition with 50%-57% of individuals reporting persistent symptoms 5-8 years after the incidence (Lankhorst et al., 2016), it creates a considerable financial burden on healthcare systems (Willy et al., 2019). In the United Kingdom, it is estimated that PFP accounts for 100,000 visits per year, representing a significant economic challenge for the National Health Service (Garza-Borjón et al., 2024).
 
A systematic review by Smith et al. (2018) demonstrated that the prevalence of PFP in the general population is approximately 22.7%, rising to 28.9% in young adults aged 15–24. The majority of epidemiological studies focus on adolescents, military personnel, or the general active population, meaning the university student population, both active and sedentary, is under-represented in the literature.
 
Despite these high estimates, research describing PFP’s longitudinal pattern in university cohorts remains scarce, particularly in the UK. This is important, as the university student population is a uniquely high-risk cohort. The academic lifestyle is inherently sedentary, often requiring prolonged periods of sitting for lectures and study that frequently exceed the 10-hour daily threshold associated with increased risk of chronic knee pain (Hanna et al., 2019; Lee et al., 2019). The link between prolonged sitting and PFP is well established, with Collins et al. (2016) finding that 80% of the PFP population experience anterior knee pain when sitting for a long time. While Bhatti et al. (2022) discovered an association between prolonged sitting and PFP in a university environment, their cohort included staff over the age of 40. This inclusion introduces diagnostic confounding, as PFP symptoms often overlap with patellofemoral osteoarthritis (PFOA) in older cohorts Crossley et al., 2016). By limiting this study to students typically below 40, a more homogenous sample is ensured, reducing the risk of degenerative changes skewing results.
 
A significant limitation in existing literature is the implementation of non-validated measurement instruments, mainly relying on subjective history (Smith et al., 2018), leading to the potential over or underestimation of prevalence. To address this, recent studies have implemented the Survey Instrument for Natural History, Aetiology and Prevalence of Patellofemoral Pain Studies (SNAPPS). Developed by Dey et al. (2016), the SNAPPS utilises a knee pain map and clinical feature questions to differentiate PFP from other injuries with high sensitivity (92%) and specificity (94%).
 
The SNAPPS has been successfully utilised in various global contexts. Xu et al. (2018) found a PFP prevalence of 20.7% in a Chinese community sample, while Akodu and Nwakalor (2018) observed a 45.3% prevalence among amateur runners in Nigeria. 
Only once has the SNAPPS been used in the general university setting by Ibeachu et al. (2019). However, the study looked at general knee pain and not PFP specifically. Furthermore, Yusuf et al. (2021) validated an electronic version (eSNAPPS), demonstrating excellent agreement with the paper version (ICC: 0.99 95% CI 0.99 — 1.00, p < 0.0001). This study will utilise the eSNAPPS to provide a standardised methodology. The benefit of using a validated tool in research to diagnose PFP is providing a standardised methodology to minimise heterogeneity. This will provide more accurate results and allow data from different studies to be pooled and compare the prevalence from different studies (Migliavaca et al., 2020). The use of such tools enhances the reliability of meta-analyses, especially when addressing the complexities of prevalence studies and their inherent heterogeneity (Migliavaca et al., 2022). However, it is noted that as a retrospective self-reported questionnaire, recall bias remains a limitation.
 
While PFP limits physical activity, with 74% of sufferers reducing or stopping sports participation (Heintjes et al., 2003), evidence also suggests that activity behaviours themselves impact knee symptoms. Ibeachu et al. (2019) linked knee symptoms to activity behaviours in UK students, suggesting that both sedentary and highly active lifestyles may influence joint loading and symptom development.
 
To categorise these levels, the International Physical Activity Questionnaire (IPAQ) is widely used in epidemiological studies. Craig et al. (2003) established the IPAQ as a reliable and valid tool for large-scale population studies. Although recent validation studies point out limitations in agreement with device-based measurements in some clinical groups, its usefulness in adult populations remains generally supported for observational cohort studies.
 
A cross-sectional study was done by Varela-Mato, Victor et al. [A10] (2012) in Spain to investigate the lifestyle habits and physical activity levels of university students. The search involved undergraduate students across various academic fields. The data were gathered using the International Physical Activity Questionnaire to evaluate physical activity, recording weekly engagement in vigorous activity, moderate exercise, and walking. This questionnaire enabled the researchers to determine physical activity levels in Metabolic Equivalent in Task (MET)- minutes per week and categorise participants into low, moderate, or high physical activity levels based on IPAQ scoring guidelines. The findings revealed that a significant number of students failed to meet the recommended physical activity levels, with lifestyle behaviour differences identified between male and female students (Varela-Mato, Víctor et al., 2012).
 
It is important to understand how patients feel about their health and what motivates them to take care of it, which may be associated with physical activity and PFP "Health styles" describe how people interact with their health through choices, actions, and motivations. Davies and Goodwin (2024) stressed the need to assess these traits, as they affect how people respond to treatment, comply with rehabilitation, and deal with symptoms over time.
 
Population segmentation methods have been employed to classify individuals into distinct health profiles based on patterns such as diet, smoking, mental health, and alcohol consumption (Bareham et al., 2012). Wolff et al. (2010) validated a model for health consumer segmentation, revealing that these behavioural profiles were linked to preventive health practices. In the UK, La Placa et al. (2014) categorised individuals into five behavioural segments, emphasising that health behaviours are significantly affected by personal motivations and social contexts.
 
Research specifically concerning musculoskeletal conditions is growing; Davies and Goodwin (2024) found that people with non-specific low back pain who possessed more positive Health Styles were more likely to engage in rehabilitation and health-promoting behaviours. However, no studies have explored how these health-related behavioural patterns affect the prevalence of knee pain specifically in university students.
 
By determining prevalence of PFP in the University population, this study could identify unmet health needs at Manchester Met, and help guide support or services to students affected by PFP. Identifying associations between activity, heath styles and other key variables may also generate hypotheses for future longitudinal studies into incidence, prediction and prognosis of PFP and development of potential strategies to manage PFP.

title: SOURCES OF INFORMATION AND SEARCH STRATEGIES
description:
In Scopus, the search was conducted in the title, abstract, and keyword fields, using the following expression: TITLE-ABS-KEY(("cross-dataset" OR "cross dataset" OR "multi-dataset" OR "multi dataset") AND ("hybrid system" OR "hybrid approach" OR "ensemble approach" OR ensemble) AND ("anomaly detection" OR "intrusion detection") AND ("computer network" OR "network traffic" OR "network security" OR SDN OR "wireless network" OR "cloud network") AND (evaluation OR experiment OR benchmark OR accuracy OR precision OR recall OR "F1-score")) AND NOT TITLE-ABS-KEY(review OR survey OR "systematic review" OR "meta-analysis" OR conceptual OR theoretical). This formulation prioritizes thematic specificity by restricting the search to the most informative metadata and by excluding, even in the initial retrieval, secondary studies and works of a non-empirical nature.

In IEEE Xplore, the strategy maintained the conceptual core, since the database shows strong adherence to the domain of networks, security, and applied computing. The expression used was: ("cross-dataset" OR "cross dataset" OR "multi-dataset" OR "multi dataset") AND ("hybrid system" OR "hybrid approach" OR "ensemble approach" OR ensemble) AND ("anomaly detection" OR "intrusion detection") AND ("computer network" OR "network traffic" OR "network security" OR SDN OR "wireless network" OR "cloud network") AND (evaluation OR experiment OR benchmark OR accuracy OR precision OR recall OR "F1-score") NOT (review OR survey OR "systematic review" OR "meta-analysis"). In this database, subsequent refinement by year, language, and publication type contributes to reducing the presence of ineligible materials without compromising sensitivity.

In the ACM Digital Library, an equivalent formulation was adopted, adjusted to the platform's text search logic: ("cross-dataset" OR "cross dataset" OR "multi-dataset" OR "multi dataset") AND ("hybrid system" OR "hybrid approach" OR "ensemble approach" OR ensemble) AND ("anomaly detection" OR "intrusion detection") AND ("computer network" OR "network traffic" OR "network security" OR SDN OR "wireless network" OR "cloud network") AND (evaluation OR experiment OR benchmark OR accuracy OR precision OR recall OR "F1-score") NOT (review OR survey). This adaptation sought to balance comprehensiveness and precision, preserving the essential concepts of the review without excessively expanding the retrieval of tangential studies.
In SpringerLink, the strategy was more controlled, due to the greater tendency of this database to retrieve occurrences distributed throughout the full text. The expression used was: ("cross-dataset" OR "cross dataset" OR "multi-dataset" OR "multi dataset") AND ("hybrid system" OR "hybrid approach" OR "ensemble approach" OR ensemble) AND ("anomaly detection" OR "intrusion detection") AND ("computer network" OR "network traffic" OR "network security" OR SDN OR "wireless network" OR "cloud network") AND (evaluation OR experiment OR benchmark OR accuracy OR precision OR recall OR "F1-score") NOT (review OR survey OR "systematic review" OR "meta-analysis"). This version maintains conceptual consistency with the other databases, but sought to contain the noise resulting from the broader indexing characteristic of SpringerLink.
In ScienceDirect, the search expression was simplified due to the platform's limitation to a maximum of eight Boolean operators and the lack of support for wildcard characters. For this reason, a condensed version was used: ("cross-dataset" OR "multi-dataset") AND (hybrid OR ensemble) AND ("anomaly detection" OR "intrusion detection") AND ("computer network" OR "network traffic") AND evaluation. Based on this, the other eligibility criteria, such as exclusion of revisions, time limits, language, and document type, were handled by native filters and manual screening of the retrieved records.

title: Gluteal Tendinopathy in Postmenopausal Women: A Scoping Review of Epidemiology, Pathophysiology, Diagnosis, and Nonoperative Management
description:
Background:
Gluteal tendinopathy is the most common cause of lateral hip pain, disproportionately affecting postmenopausal women. Prevalence estimates suggest that up to 23-35% of postmenopausal women may be affected, with hormonal changes, particularly estrogen decline, implicated in tendon degeneration, altered collagen metabolism, and reduced tendon healing capacity. Despite its high prevalence and significant impact on function, sleep, and quality of life, the condition remains underdiagnosed and inconsistently managed. The existing literature spans multiple disciplines including sports medicine, rheumatology, orthopedics, and women's health, but no comprehensive scoping review has mapped the breadth of evidence specific to the postmenopausal population.

Purpose:
The purpose of this scoping review is to systematically map and synthesize the available evidence on gluteal tendinopathy in postmenopausal women across four domains: (1) epidemiology and prevalence, (2) pathophysiology including hormonal influences on tendon biology, (3) diagnostic approaches including clinical examination and imaging, and (4) nonoperative management strategies including exercise-based rehabilitation, corticosteroid, NSAID, and platelet-rich plasma injections, shockwave therapy, ultrasound guided percutaneous tenotomy, and emerging therapies. This review will also examine the role of proximal iliotibial band pathology as a commonly coexisting or overlapping condition in this population.

Research Questions:
What is the reported epidemiology and prevalence of gluteal tendinopathy in postmenopausal women?
What pathophysiological mechanisms, including hormonal influences, contribute to gluteal tendinopathy in this population?
What diagnostic methods are described for evaluating gluteal tendinopathy in postmenopausal women?
What nonoperative management strategies have been studied, and what is the evidence for their effectiveness in this population?

Design:
This scoping review will follow the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology for scoping reviews and adhere to the PRISMA Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) reporting guidelines. The protocol has been developed in accordance with the Arksey and O'Malley framework as refined by Levac, Colquhoun, and O'Brien (2010) and Peters et al. (2020).

Search Strategy:
A comprehensive search will be conducted across PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, SPORTDiscus, and the Cochrane Library. The search strategy will combine terms related to three concept blocks: (1) gluteal tendinopathy and related conditions (e.g., greater trochanteric pain syndrome, proximal iliotibial band syndrome), (2) postmenopausal women and hormonal factors, and (3) epidemiology, pathophysiology, diagnosis, and nonoperative treatment. The search will be limited to English-language publications from January 2015 to May 2026. Grey literature will be searched via Google Scholar, OpenGrey, and conference abstracts from AMSSM, ACSM, and BJSM. The search strategy will be peer-reviewed by a medical librarian using the PRESS checklist prior to execution.

Eligibility Criteria:
Population: Postmenopausal women (natural or surgical menopause) or mixed populations where postmenopausal subgroup data can be extracted. Studies of women aged ≥45 years will be included if menopause is implied or likely.
Concept: Gluteal tendinopathy, greater trochanteric pain syndrome, proximal iliotibial band syndrome, or lateral hip pain attributed to soft tissue pathology.
Context: Any clinical setting (primary care, sports medicine, orthopedics, rheumatology, rehabilitation).
Study types: Randomized controlled trials, cohort studies, case-control studies, cross-sectional studies, case series, and qualitative studies.
Exclusions: Systematic reviews, narrative reviews, meta-analyses, editorials, commentaries, and opinion pieces; surgical intervention studies, isolated trochanteric bursitis without tendon involvement, pediatric or adolescent populations, non-English publications, and animal studies. However, reference lists of relevant reviews identified during screening will be hand-searched to identify additional primary studies for inclusion.

Screening and Selection:
All retrieved records will be imported into Covidence for deduplication and screening. Two independent reviewers will screen titles and abstracts, followed by full-text review of eligible studies. A calibration exercise will be performed to ensure inter-rater agreement (target ≥80%). Discrepancies will be resolved by discussion or adjudication by a third reviewer.

Data Extraction:
Data will be extracted using a standardized charting form. Extracted variables will include: author(s), year, country, study design, sample size, population characteristics (age, menopausal status, BMI, comorbidities), definition of gluteal tendinopathy used, diagnostic method(s), intervention(s) studied, outcome measures, key findings, and reported limitations.

Data Synthesis:
Results will be synthesized narratively and presented in tabular and graphical formats organized by the four review domains. A PRISMA-ScR flow diagram will document the study selection process. Evidence gaps and areas requiring future primary research will be explicitly identified.

Expected Outcomes:
This review is expected to provide the first comprehensive map of the evidence on gluteal tendinopathy specific to postmenopausal women. Anticipated outcomes include: identification of the most effective nonoperative management strategies for this population, clarification of the role of hormonal factors in tendon pathophysiology, evaluation of the diagnostic accuracy of clinical and imaging modalities, and identification of critical evidence gaps to guide future research priorities. The findings are intended to inform clinical practice for sports medicine, primary care, and rehabilitation providers managing this common and often undertreated condition.

Funding: None.

Conflicts of Interest: None declared.

AI Disclosure: An AI-assisted knowledge tool (OpenEvidence) was used to help draft the initial protocol framework. All content was independently reviewed, verified, and modified by the author team. The authors take full responsibility for the accuracy and intellectual content of this protocol.

title: Prevalence of Stroke and Vascular Risk Factors in the Rural Highlands of Benguet, Philippines: A Population-Based Study
description:
Stroke remains a leading cause of death and long-term disability worldwide, contributing significantly to the global burden of disease. Low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), including the Philippines, bear a disproportionate share of this burden, with a substantial concentration of stroke-related death and disability. Despite advances in stroke prevention and acute care, LMICs continue to face substantial gaps in reliable epidemiologic evidence. This is particularly true in the Philippines, where existing stroke data derive primarily from hospital-based studies concentrated in urban centers, limiting the development of targeted public health strategies and equitable resource allocation.

The rural highlands of Benguet is formed by 13 landlocked mountainous municipalities situated at the southern tip of the Cordillera mountain range in northern Luzon. The area has been continuously inhabited since at least the 14th century by indigenous populations of Ibaloi and Kankana-ey descent, both belonging to the larger Igorot ethnolinguistic group native to the Cordillera region [5,6]. Recent in-migration from adjacent lowland provinces has remained limited. Its cultural, lifestyle, and dietary characteristics, shaped by an agrarian livelihood centered on manual farming and the consumption of locally produced crops and livestock, are relatively homogenous yet distinct from those of other regions in the Philippines. These differences are partly attributable to Benguet’s high elevation and temperate to subtropical climate, which contrast with the lowland tropical conditions that characterize much of the country. Access to healthcare is constrained by rugged terrain, dispersed settlements, and limited infrastructure.

The burden of stroke in Benguet has not yet been systematically characterized. This study aims to determine the prevalence of stroke and vascular risk factors among adults residing in its municipalities through a population-based survey. In doing so, it addresses a major evidence gap in a largely underrepresented region and provides a unique opportunity to examine stroke burden in a relatively isolated indigenous population with environmental, ethnic, and sociocultural characteristics distinct from the rest of the Philippines.

A planned substudy will aim to evaluate the reliability and diagnostic accuracy of the PSSQ, using assessments by a board-certified vascular neurologist as the reference standard.

title: Artificial Intelligence Enhanced Prehospital Stroke Recognition and Emergency Response in Resource-Limited Settings: A Scoping Review.
description:
Background: Stroke is a leading cause of mortality and long-term disability worldwide, with the prehospital phase being critical to survival and functional recovery. In resource-limited settings, delayed recognition of symptoms, inadequate emergency response, and infrastructural challenges exacerbate morbidity and mortality. Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a promising strategy to enhance prehospital stroke recognition, triage, and decision-making, yet its implementation in under-resourced environments remains underexplored.
Objective: This scoping review aims to systematically map current evidence on AI-enabled prehospital stroke recognition and emergency response in resource-limited settings. The review seeks to identify the types of AI tools employed, the operational contexts in which they are applied, reported outcomes, barriers to implementation, and gaps in knowledge.
Methods: Following Arksey and O’Malley’s framework and PRISMA-ScR reporting guidelines, a comprehensive search of electronic databases (MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, PsycINFO) and grey literature sources (Google Scholar, ProQuest, preprint servers) will be conducted. Studies involving suspected or confirmed prehospital stroke patients, emergency personnel, or AI-based decision-support systems will be included. Data extraction will capture study characteristics, AI interventions, prehospital context, outcomes (diagnostic accuracy, feasibility, usability), and implementation challenges. Narrative and tabular synthesis will summarize findings, highlighting opportunities and limitations of AI application in constrained health systems.
Results: It is anticipated that the review will identify a growing but uneven evidence base, with most AI applications emerging from high-income settings and limited studies from resource-constrained environments. AI-enabled tools are expected to demonstrate improved triage accuracy, faster stroke recognition, and operational feasibility, though challenges including infrastructure deficits, data gaps, algorithmic bias, and limited digital literacy among responders are likely to constrain adoption. Evidence on context-sensitive adaptation, user interaction, and longitudinal outcomes is anticipated to be sparse.
Conclusion: AI has significant potential to transform prehospital stroke care in resource-limited settings, offering improved early recognition, triage efficiency, and emergency coordination. This review will provide a comprehensive synthesis of current evidence, identify key gaps, and inform future research, policy, and system-level interventions to promote equitable and context-appropriate integration of AI in prehospital stroke management.

title: Diagnostic accuracy of MTAP immunohistochemistry for CDKN2A homozygous deletion and for distinguishing mesothelioma from reactive mesothelial proliferations: a systematic review and bivariate meta-analysis
description:
This registration documents a systematic review and bivariate / HSROC meta-analysis of the diagnostic accuracy of MTAP immunohistochemistry in mesothelioma pathology. The review was conducted to PRISMA-DTA 2018 standards. The synthesis was executed against a locked v12 dataset between 3 and 4 June 2026, and the present OSF registration follows completion of the synthesis prior to journal submission, in the absence of an active PROSPERO Diagnostic Test Accuracy template at the time of synthesis completion. The full locked protocol, search strategy, locked dataset, analysis code, and analysis-output files are deposited as project files.

REVIEW QUESTIONS

(a) Primary question: What is the diagnostic accuracy of MTAP immunohistochemistry, used alone, for detecting CDKN2A homozygous deletion in pleural and peritoneal mesothelioma, taking dual-colour CDKN2A FISH (or equivalent CNV / NGS reference) as the gold standard?

(b) Secondary question: What is the diagnostic accuracy of MTAP immunohistochemistry for distinguishing histologically or cytologically confirmed mesothelioma from reactive mesothelial proliferations, taking the integrated clinical-radiological-pathological diagnosis as the reference?

POPULATION AND SPECIMENS

Adult patients with suspected mesothelioma (pleural primary; peritoneal as a pre-specified subgroup) undergoing diagnostic biopsy or pleural / peritoneal effusion cytology, in whom MTAP IHC has been applied as part of the ancillary diagnostic workup.

INDEX TEST

MTAP immunohistochemistry on formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tissue or cell block. Pre-specified primary loss definition: complete cytoplasmic loss with positive internal control. Pre-specified sensitivity-analysis convention: each study's own threshold including broader patterns (nuclear loss, focal loss, ≥30% cells lost). Antibody clone recorded as a pre-specified subgroup variable (2G4 reference clone; mAb1813; EPR6893; 2B1G6; polyclonal / unspecified).

REFERENCE STANDARD

Primary: CDKN2A homozygous deletion by dual-colour FISH (Vysis LSI CDKN2A/CEP9 most common; ≥10% nuclei threshold standard). CNV array and targeted NGS panels with explicit CDKN2A copy-number calls are accepted equivalents.

Secondary: integrated clinical-radiological-pathological diagnosis per IMIG 2017 / WHO 2021 with at least 12 months follow-up for benign controls. Incorporation bias acknowledged and addressed in QUADAS-2 D3.

OUTCOMES

Primary: pooled sensitivity, specificity, positive and negative likelihood ratios, diagnostic odds ratio (all with 95% CI); summary HSROC curve with 95% confidence + prediction regions.

Secondary: between-study heterogeneity (τ², I²); pre-specified subgroup pooled estimates by antibody clone, specimen format, MTAP loss threshold, anatomic site, time period; pooled proportion of uninterpretable MTAP IHC results.

SEARCH

PubMed and Embase from inception to 2 June 2026. Two-strand strategy: (1) core ("MTAP" OR "methylthioadenosine phosphorylase") AND ("mesothelioma" OR "mesothelial") AND (immunohistoch* OR IHC), 149 records; (2) sensitivity expansion same intersection without IHC term, 104 records. Full strategy with date stamps deposited in MTAP_search_strategy.md.

DATA EXTRACTION AND DUAL-REVIEWER VERIFICATION

Two independent reviewers (V. Tayade, Grant Government Medical College, Mumbai; G. Singh, All India Institute of Medical Sciences, Rajkot). First-reviewer extraction across twelve audit iterations (v1 to v12) into the structured workbook MTAP_locked_dataset_v12.xlsx. Second-reviewer independent re-extraction returned 100% cell-level agreement across all four data sheets (948 of 948 cells). Agreement pathway: text confirmation between the two reviewers followed by mechanical mirroring of the locked first-reviewer dataset into the second-reviewer workbook artefact, in lieu of independent direct population of a blanked template. This procedural deviation from the standard direct-population workflow is disclosed in full in agreement_provenance.md and is acknowledged in the manuscript Limitations section.

RISK OF BIAS

QUADAS-2 (Whiting 2011), four domains (patient selection, index test, reference standard, flow and timing), each scored for risk of bias and applicability.

DATA SYNTHESIS

Bivariate random-effects meta-analysis (Reitsma 2005 / Rutter-Gatsonis HSROC) using the mada package in R. Logit-transformed sensitivity and specificity jointly modelled. Step-6 uninterpretable-proportion synthesis via metaprop (meta package), logit transformation, continuity correction. Reproducible analysis code deposited as MTAP_analysis_code.R; analysis-output files deposited as MTAP_pooled_estimates.csv and the six forest / SROC PDFs.

Primary pool composition (pleural HD, MTAP-alone, k=6): Chapel 2020, Chapel 2021, Vrugt 2023, Febres-Aldana 2024 (mAb1813 arm), Şeker 2024 (broad threshold), Broggi 2024. Aoe 2025 primary subset in pre-specified sensitivity-only pool.

Secondary pool composition (MM vs RMP, MTAP-alone, k=6): Lynggård 2022 (histology + cytology arms), Berg 2020, Quaranta 2025 peritoneal cyst cohort, Aoe 2025, Şeker 2024. Fukuoka cluster in sensitivity-only pools.

PRE-SPECIFIED SENSITIVITY ANALYSES

(i) Exclude Şeker 2024 from secondary main pool. (ii) Stratify by specimen (tissue versus cytology). (iii) Stratify by clone (2G4 versus other). (iv) Primary-pool sensitivity with each study's own threshold. (v) Sa-Ngiamwibool ID-handling variant. (vi) Lynggård 2022 cytology-only sensitivity to bound the effect of the shared TN=20 reactive mesothelial controls used in both Lynggård arms.

SUBGROUP ANALYSES

Specimen (tissue versus cell block versus effusion); histologic subtype (epithelioid versus sarcomatoid including desmoplastic versus biphasic versus mixed); anatomic site (pleural versus peritoneal); MTAP clone; MTAP loss threshold (strict cytoplasmic versus broader); reference standard modality; time period (pre-2020 versus 2020 onward).

STAGE AT REGISTRATION

Data acquisition complete; second-reviewer dual extraction complete with 100% cell-level agreement; risk-of-bias assessment complete; LOCK declaration effective 4 June 2026 on joint reviewer ratification (G. Singh WhatsApp confirmation on briefing v3); synthesis complete; manuscript v1 drafted. Journal submission pending OSF registration.

FUNDING AND CONFLICTS

No external project funding. The reviewers declare no conflicts of interest. No relationship with manufacturers of any antibody clone or FISH probe vendor.

title: DEEP LEARNING MODELS FOR THE DETECTION OF CLEFT PALATE ON PANORAMIC RADIOGRAPHS: A SCOPING REVIEW
description:
Background: Cleft lip and palate (CLP) is a congenital craniofacial anomaly that requires continuous dental follow-up from birth. Panoramic radiography (PR) is widely used in the monitoring of these patients due to its accessibility, low cost, and reduced radiation exposure, allowing the identification of alterations such as alveolar clefts (AC). However, image interpretation may be impaired by the superimposition of anatomical structures and by radiologists’ workload, which may lead to visual fatigue and potential diagnostic errors. In this context, deep learning (DL) models, particularly convolutional neural networks (CNNs), have emerged as promising tools to support diagnostic decision-making.
Objective: This scoping review aims To evaluate the effectiveness of deep learning models applied to panoramic radiography for the detection of cleft palate.
Methods: The protocol will be registered on the Open Science Framework (OSF). The search strategy will include the descriptors “cleft palate,” “panoramic radiography,” and “deep learning,” combined using Boolean operators in the PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, LILACS, EMBASE, and Google Scholar databases. Observational studies that applied supervised DL models to detect CLP on PRs and directly compared their performance with human professionals will be included. Two calibrated reviewers will independently perform study selection and data extraction, including methodological characteristics, cleft type, model architecture, image acquisition parameters, and diagnostic accuracy metrics.
Conclusion: The results are expected to support the clinical use of artificial intelligence, contributing to more accurate diagnoses and a reduction in errors related to human limitations.

title: Validation of Large Language Model-Based Extraction of NIH Stroke Scale Scores from Clinical Narratives: A Diagnostic Accuracy Study
description:
The NIH Stroke Scale (NIHSS) is a standardized clinical instrument for quantifying neurological deficit severity in acute ischemic stroke. Developed in the late 1980s by the Stroke Research Group of the National Institutes of Health, the scale was designed to provide a rapid, objective, and reproducible bedside assessment. In the original validation study, Brott et al. (1989) demonstrated good to excellent interrater reliability, with weighted kappa values exceeding 0.60 for most individual items and high agreement for the total score. Subsequent studies consistently confirmed high interrater reliability across different professional groups and clinical settings, with intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC) for the total NIHSS score typically ranging from 0.82 to 0.95, particularly following standardized training (Lyden et al., 1994; Goldstein & Samsa, 1997; Dewey et al., 1999). These findings established the NIHSS as a reliable and reproducible severity measure and supported its widespread adoption in stroke trials, registries, and clinical guidelines. 

 

The objective of this study is to determine the validity and reliability of large language model–based extraction of NIHSS scores from routine clinical documentation. We hypothesize that LLM-derived NIHSS scores demonstrate high agreement with expert-rated reference standards and may serve as a scalable method for structured secondary use of unstructured stroke documentation. 

 

Primary objective 

To evaluate the overall agreement between NIHSS item scores extracted by a large language model (LLM) using two different prompt strategies (simple and refined prompts) and those assigned by two NIHSS-certified physicians serving as the reference standard, across all NIHSS items. 

The primary analysis will quantify overall item-level agreement between the LLM and the physician-derived reference ratings separately for each prompt strategy. 

 

Secondary study objective 

Item-specific agreement: To assess the agreement between the LLM and the physician reference standard for each individual NIHSS item, separately for the simple and refined prompt strategies. 

Interrater reliability between physician: To evaluate the agreement between the two NIHSS-certified physicians in order to quantify the human reference variability. 

Agreement of total NIHSS score: Agreement between the LLM-derived total NIHSS score and the physician-derived reference total NIHSS score, quantified using the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC), separately for each prompt strategy. 
This comparison will be performed separately for each prompt strategy. 

Stratified analysis by stroke severity: To assess the primary endpoint (overall item-level agreement between LLM and physicians) stratified by stroke severity categories (mild, moderate, severe) and analyzed separately for both prompt strategies. 

Stroke severity categories will be defined according to established NIHSS thresholds (mild: 0–4, moderate: 5–14, severe: ≥15). 

Comparative performance of prompt strategies: To directly compare agreement metrics between the simple and refined prompt strategies to determine whether prompt refinement improves extraction accuracy.

title: Diagnostic accuracy of cone-beam computed tomography in detecting root perforations: a systematic review
description:
Background and Rationale
Endodontic root perforations represent a severe iatrogenic or pathological complication characterized by an unnatural communication between the aseptic root canal system and the highly vascularized periodontal apparatus. If not immediately diagnosed and repaired, these defects rapidly precipitate microbial colonization, localized inflammatory responses, and crestal bone loss, ultimately jeopardizing the survival of the tooth. While conventional two-dimensional (2D) periapical radiography is the standard frontline diagnostic tool, it is intrinsically constrained by anatomical superimposition, often rendering perforations on the buccal or lingual root surfaces imperceptible. Although Cone-Beam Computed Tomography (CBCT) has revolutionized three-dimensional maxillofacial imaging, its specific diagnostic test accuracy (DTA) for detecting root perforations remains inconsistently reported in the literature, particularly regarding the profound confounding variables of spatial resolution and beam-hardening artifacts caused by intracanal radiopacities.

Purpose and Objectives
The primary objective of this systematic review is to comprehensively aggregate, synthesize, and critically evaluate the diagnostic test accuracy (Sensitivity and Specificity) of CBCT specifically for the detection of endodontic root perforations.

The secondary objectives are to determine how diagnostic accuracy is modulated by specific technical and clinical parameters, namely:

The obturation status of the root canal system (evaluating the detrimental impact of photon starvation and beam-hardening artifacts caused by gutta-percha, heavy-metal sealers, and metallic posts).

The spatial resolution of the CBCT scan (comparing high-resolution versus low-resolution voxel sizes).

The anatomical localization of the defect (e.g., furcal, lateral, strip, or apical perforations).

The comparative accuracy of CBCT against alternative diagnostic modalities, specifically Electronic Apex Locators (EALs) and digital periapical radiography.

Methodological Scope
To ensure strict statistical homogeneity, this review utilizes a specialized PIRD (Population, Index test, Reference standard, Diagnosis of interest) framework. The analysis will be strictly limited to primary diagnostic accuracy studies utilizing extracted permanent human teeth (in vitro and ex vivo laboratory models) validated by an absolute, independent physical reference standard (e.g., digital calipers or stereomicroscopy). Continuous linear measurement studies and animal models are explicitly excluded. The methodological quality and external applicability of the included literature will be independently appraised utilizing the QUADAS-2 (Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies) framework.

Expected Outcomes and Clinical Significance
The anticipated outcome of this systematic review is the establishment of the first definitive, evidence-based clinical imaging guidelines for the detection of root perforations.

This project is expected to demonstrate that while CBCT significantly outperforms 2D radiography in anatomical "blind spots," its application must be highly strategic. We anticipate the data will formulate the following clinical directives:

For non-obturated teeth: Low-resolution CBCT is highly efficacious and should be utilized to strictly adhere to the ALARA (As Low As Reasonably Achievable) radiation dosimetry principle.

For obturated teeth: The expected data will likely prove that CBCT accuracy is severely compromised by artifact scatter, necessitating either high-resolution scanning protocols to mitigate partial volume averaging, or a multimodal diagnostic approach prioritizing radiation-free Electronic Apex Locators (EALs) and eccentric multi-angle periapical radiography during active retreatment procedures.

title: Biomarkers for the prediction of hemorrhagic transformation in adult patients with ischemic stroke treated with reperfusion: a scoping review
description:
Stroke remains one of the leading causes of death and acquired long-term disability worldwide, and ischemic stroke accounts for the large majority of all cases. The cornerstone of acute treatment is timely reperfusion of the ischemic territory, achieved through intravenous thrombolysis with recombinant tissue plasminogen activator (alteplase) or tenecteplase, mechanical thrombectomy or endovascular therapy in cases of large vessel occlusion, or a combination of both approaches (bridging therapy). Although reperfusion has substantially improved functional outcomes and survival, it also carries a significant risk of complications, the most feared of which is hemorrhagic transformation.
Hemorrhagic transformation refers to bleeding into infarcted brain tissue and represents a spectrum that ranges from asymptomatic petechial hemorrhagic infarction to parenchymal hematoma. When it produces clinical worsening, it is classified as symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage (sICH), an event consistently associated with early neurological deterioration, increased mortality, and poor long-term functional prognosis. Its pathophysiology is multifactorial and involves blood–brain barrier disruption, oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, activation of matrix metalloproteinases, and reperfusion injury. Because hemorrhagic transformation can offset the benefits of reperfusion therapy, the ability to identify, before or shortly after treatment, which patients are at highest risk has become a clinically relevant priority for individualized risk stratification and decision-making.
In this context, biomarkers have emerged as promising tools for risk prediction. A biomarker is a measurable indicator of a biological state or process, and blood-based biomarkers (serum, plasma) are particularly attractive because they are minimally invasive, reproducible, and potentially rapid to obtain. A growing body of research has evaluated diverse molecular, biochemical, inflammatory, coagulation-related, and other candidate biomarkers as predictors of hemorrhagic transformation in patients undergoing reperfusion therapy. However, this evidence is highly heterogeneous, with variability in the populations studied, treatment modalities, biomarker definitions, timing of measurement, outcome definitions, and the statistical measures of association reported. To date, there is no consolidated overview that maps which biomarkers have been investigated, in what clinical contexts, and with what predictive value.
The purpose of this scoping review is to systematically map and characterize the available evidence on biomarkers used to predict hemorrhagic transformation in adult patients (over 18 years of age) with confirmed ischemic stroke treated with reperfusion therapy, whether by intravenous thrombolysis, mechanical thrombectomy, or both. Rather than estimating a single pooled effect, the review aims to clarify the breadth and nature of existing research, identify the most frequently studied and most promising biomarkers, describe the reported measures of association (odds ratio, relative risk, hazard ratio, likelihood ratio, sensitivity, and specificity), and highlight gaps and inconsistencies in the current literature.
This review will be conducted in accordance with the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology for scoping reviews and will be reported following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR). A structured search will be performed in PubMed, Scopus, and ScienceDirect, covering original human studies published between 2016 and 2026 in English, Spanish, or Portuguese, using predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria.
The expected outcome is a comprehensive evidence map that summarizes the biomarkers studied for the prediction of hemorrhagic transformation, the clinical and treatment contexts in which they have been assessed, and their reported predictive performance. By consolidating this fragmented body of evidence, the review is expected to support clinical risk stratification, inform the design of future confirmatory and prognostic studies, and provide a foundation for the potential development of predictive tools and subsequent systematic reviews in this field.

title: Role of AI in the Detection of Dental caries in Pediatric Dentistry
description:
Early identification of dental caries in children is essential for preventive care and minimally invasive treatment. Detecting carious lesions at an early stage allows clinicians to intervene before extensive damage occurs. Conventional diagnostic methods, including visual-tactile examination and radiographs, are reliable but often require clinical expertise, specialized equipment, and in-person visits. These limitations may delay timely diagnosis, especially in rural or underserved communities where access to pediatric dental care is restricted.
Recent progress in artificial intelligence and mobile health technologies offers innovative alternatives for screening and early detection. AI-enabled mobile applications use smartphone cameras to capture intraoral photographs, which are then analysed with trained algorithms to identify early carious changes. These tools can support parents, caregivers, and community health workers in recognizing suspicious lesions outside the dental clinic, ensuring prompt referral to pediatric dentists. Beyond detection, such applications can provide preventive advice, caries risk assessment, and follow-up reminders, promoting better oral health practices and patient engagement.
However, challenges remain before clinical adaptation. Variability in image quality, lighting conditions, and differences in children’s oral anatomy can affect diagnostic accuracy. Concerns about data privacy, ethical use of AI, and the need for regulatory approval also present barriers. Integration into healthcare systems will require user compliance and interdisciplinary collaboration.
AI-powered mobile applications have strong potential to complement conventional diagnostic methods. With further research, validation, and policy support, these tools could significantly enhance access to early caries detection in pediatric dentistry.

title: Using Implementation Science to Improve Autism Assessment in Healthcare: A Rapid Review
description:
Timely and accurate autism assessment supports early access to appropriate services, yet assessment pathways in many health systems remain fragmented, delayed and inequitable. In Australia, the mean age of diagnosis has been estimated at 46.5 months, well beyond the 18 to 36 month window associated with better school-age developmental outcomes. Implementation science offers a structured approach to improving the uptake, fidelity and sustainability of evidence-based practice in real-world settings, but its application to autism assessment remains underexplored.
This rapid review examines how implementation science has been used to understand or improve autism assessment in health system settings, including primary care, specialist services, allied health, community services and hospital-based tertiary care. Assessment is defined broadly to include screening, referral, diagnostic evaluation and post-diagnostic support planning. The review has four objectives: to describe the context, structure and content of implementation science-based strategies applied to autism assessment, to identify the frameworks and models used, to describe the reported impact of these strategies on assessment processes and outcomes such as timeliness, equity and diagnostic accuracy, and to synthesise perceived barriers and enablers.
We will search Medline, Embase, PsycINFO and Web of Science Core Collection for peer-reviewed empirical studies published in English from 1 January 2015, conducted in a health system setting and describing an implementation science-based strategy applied to autism assessment. Screening and extraction will follow Cochrane Rapid Review guidance. Findings will be synthesised descriptively, with barriers and enablers analysed using inductive content analysis. Meta-analysis is not anticipated given expected heterogeneity.

title: Attitudes Towards Profiling Survey - Study 3
description:
This is an experimental moral psychological study on people's attitudes towards "pre-crime" profiling and pre-crime police work (that is, using profiling or other information to prevent people who may be about to commit a crime from doing so). The study has a 3 (between-subjects) x 4 (within-subjects) x 2 (within-subjects) mixed design using the contrastive vignettes method.

This study expands from the previous studies in this project by introducing different types of crimes as targets of prevention. In the previous studies, the vignettes always concerned an individual that was suspected of planning to start cultivating cannabis plants; in this study, we include this specific crime in addition to other crimes not related to illegal drugs. Based on the pilot study, people may consider pre-crime profiling more or less acceptable based on the type of the target crime: for example, participants found it more acceptable to use profiling to prevent murder or credit fraud than to use profiling to prevent drug-related crimes. The motivation for including other crimes as targets is simply to examine whether the effects observed in prior studies replicate for more or less "serious" crimes.

In Studies 2a (https://osf.io/nhgc2/?view_only=f053c361e0fb4adc877ee7c427cfa73e) and 2b (https://osf.io/qhbd4/?view_only=25af6cdd494846ffa9bd7c5835ff7f3e), we found evidence of outcome biases: moral judgments of pre-crime profiling and/or the police's decision to investigate were more positive when the information about the suspect turned out to be correct (true positive) than when there was an error (false positive). However, in those prior studies, the outcome of the investigation was a between-subjects manipulation, and thus it is unclear whether such an outcome bias would still hold for individuals judging both outcomes. In order to test the robustness of the outcome bias effect, we included the outcome of the investigation as a within-subjects manipulation in this study.

title: The Impact of Interruptions on Clinical Decision Making in the Emergency Department: A Scoping Review
description:
Interruptions are a routine part of emergency medicine, reflecting the fast-paced, dynamic nature of the emergency department (ED). However, the high frequency and unpredictable nature of these interruptions pose significant challenges to clinical decision-making, cognitive performance, and workflow efficiency. While existing literature extensively quantifies the frequency and sources of interruptions in the ED, less is known about their cognitive impact on physicians and how they influence diagnostic accuracy and patient care outcomes.

Previous reviews have predominantly focused on interruptions among nursing staff or have examined general workplace interruptions without specifically addressing their clinical implications in emergency medicine. Few have synthesised evidence relating to how these interruptions affect physicians’ reasoning processes or explored the effectiveness of interventions aimed at mitigating their impact.

This scoping review aims to bridge this gap by:
- Mapping current literature on the nature and impact of ED interruptions
- Focusing specifically on how interruptions influence physician decision-making
- Reviewing strategies used to prevent or minimise interruptions
- Highlighting areas requiring further research

By consolidating this information, the review will provide a clearer understanding of the cognitive burden interruptions place on emergency physicians and guide the development of more targeted interventions.

title: Clinical utility of cardiac MRI in the diagnostic work-up of patients with suspected or known ischemic heart disease.
description: This systematic review evaluates the diagnostic, functional, and prognostic role of cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMR) in patients with suspected or confirmed ischemic heart disease, synthesizing peer-reviewed evidence published between January 2021 and January 2026. Conducted in accordance with PRISMA 2020 guidelines, the literature search was independently performed by three reviewers across PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus using structured Boolean search strategies, with study selection, data extraction, and quality assessment carried out using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale, AMSTAR 2, and the GRADE framework. The review addresses three main clinical dimensions: the diagnostic accuracy of CMR in suspected or known coronary artery disease, including its role in MINOCA diagnosis and reclassification; its prognostic value after acute myocardial infarction through parameters such as infarct size, microvascular obstruction, global longitudinal strain, and AI-derived markers; and its utility in guiding revascularization decisions through myocardial viability assessment. Expected outcomes include a comprehensive synthesis of the added clinical value of CMR over standard care, identification of its strongest evidence-supported indications, and a critical appraisal of current limitations including protocol heterogeneity, patient selection bias, and restricted access to the technology.

title: Role of Artificial Intelligence in Veterinary Preventive Medicine: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
description:
This systematic review and meta-analysis aims to comprehensively evaluate the current role and effectiveness of artificial intelligence (AI) applications in veterinary preventive medicine across different animal species. The review will focus on original research articles that report the use of AI technologies such as machine learning, deep learning, expert systems, and computer vision in disease prediction, surveillance, early diagnosis, and foodborne disease monitoring in animals including cattle, poultry, swine, sheep, goats, and companion animals (e.g., dogs).
Veterinary preventive medicine is a rapidly evolving field that emphasizes proactive measures to ensure animal health, minimize disease transmission, and enhance food safety. With growing interest in AI technologies globally, the veterinary sector is beginning to embrace data-driven solutions to optimize preventive strategies. However, evidence remains fragmented and lacks a unified synthesis of outcomes, methodologies, and species-specific applications. This systematic review addresses this gap by assessing the diagnostic accuracy, surveillance efficiency, and overall effectiveness of AI tools used in preventive veterinary practice.
This review will be conducted following PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Articles will be screened based on PECO eligibility criteria: Population – any animal species; Exposure – use of AI models for preventive purposes; Comparison – not mandatory but may include traditional methods; Outcome – diagnostic performance (accuracy, sensitivity), and surveillance effectiveness. Only peer-reviewed original research articles published between January 2021 and May 10, 2025 will be included. Reviews, conference proceedings, and non-peer-reviewed literature will be excluded. There will be no language restrictions.

Electronic databases including Google Scholar, PubMed, Elsevier, and Wiley will be searched. Data will be managed using Zotero, and risk of bias will be assessed using QUADAS-2. A meta-analysis will be conducted where data allow; otherwise, a narrative synthesis will be presented.
This protocol has been registered to ensure transparency and minimize bias. The review is expected to be completed within 6 months. No funding was received, and the authors declare no conflicts of interest.

title: Diagnostic Performance of Imaging for Scaphoid Proximal Pole Osteonecrosis: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
description:
This study is a systematic review and meta-analysis evaluating the diagnostic performance of imaging modalities for detecting osteonecrosis of the proximal pole of the scaphoid. Osteonecrosis of the scaphoid, particularly involving the proximal pole, is a clinically significant condition associated with impaired vascular supply, delayed union, and poor functional outcomes. Accurate and early diagnosis is critical for guiding treatment decisions and improving patient prognosis.

The objective of this review is to synthesize the available evidence on the diagnostic accuracy of imaging techniques, particularly criteria, including magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), computed tomography (CT), radiography, and other advanced imaging modalities, in identifying proximal pole scaphoid osteonecrosis. The study will assess key diagnostic performance metrics such as sensitivity, specificity. 

Eligible studies will include those that evaluate imaging modalities against an appropriate reference standard, intraoperative findings, histopathology. A systematic literature search will be conducted across multiple databases, and study selection, data extraction, and risk of bias assessment will be performed in accordance with established methodological guidelines.

Where appropriate, quantitative synthesis will be conducted using meta-analytic techniques to pool diagnostic accuracy estimates. Heterogeneity will be explored through subgroup and sensitivity analyses, and the methodological quality of included studies will be assessed using validated tools.

This registration is retrospective. Data collection and/or analysis had commenced prior to registration, and this protocol is intended to transparently document the study objectives, methods, and analytic approach.

title: Hemodynamic Significance of Carotid Artery Ultrasound Predictors in Assessing Volume Status in Critically Ill Patients: A Scoping Review
description:
Abstract

Background: Accurate, timely, and non-invasive assessment of volume status in critically ill patients, including those on mechanical ventilation (MV) or in shock, is crucial for effective hemodynamic management and the prevention of multiorgan failure. Traditional static markers of preload, such as central venous pressure (CVP), have definitively demonstrated their pathophysiological and clinical inadequacy in predicting fluid responsiveness. Meanwhile, classic dynamic parameters based on heart-lung interaction, such as pulse pressure variability (PPV) and stroke volume variability (SVV), require invasive arterial monitoring and are subject to strict physiological limitations. In recent years, point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) of the carotid artery (CA) has gained significant popularity as an innovative, accessible, and non-invasive method for predicting fluid responsiveness.

Objectives: To conduct a comprehensive scoping review to map existing evidence regarding the diagnostic accuracy, physiological limitations, "grey zone" sizes, and reproducibility (both intra- and inter-operator) of various carotid artery ultrasound parameters in patients within the intensive care unit (ICU).

Methods: In accordance with the PRISMA-ScR methodology, a systematic search will be conducted across the MEDLINE, Embase, and Cochrane Library databases. The analysis will include studies evaluating corrected flow time (FTc), respiratory variability of peak systolic velocity, carotid blood flow (CBF), velocity-time integral (VTI), and carotid artery diameter variability in combination with dynamic tests, such as the passive leg raise (PLR) test, end-expiratory occlusion test (EEOt), and fluid bolus.Expected Results: The review is expected to synthesize data demonstrating that carotid artery Doppler indices possess moderate to high predictive value. It is anticipated that parameters based on flow time (FTc) and relative peak velocity variation ($\Delta$Vpeak) will outperform absolute carotid blood flow (CBF) calculations due to their lower dependence on the insonation angle and reduced mathematical errors associated with vessel diameter measurement. The issue of "grey zones," which can reach 61% for certain parameters, will be described in detail, as this critically limits their isolated use at the bedside.

Conclusions: Ultrasound assessment of the carotid artery is a promising tool in the intensive care armamentarium. Nevertheless, high inter-operator variability among novice specialists, the impact of vascular compliance in geriatric patients, and the presence of broad zones of diagnostic uncertainty necessitate the standardization of scanning protocols and cautious interpretation of data within the context of comprehensive multimodal hemodynamic monitoring.

title: Diagnostic methods and criteria for ventilator-induced diaphragm dysfunction in critically ill adult patients: a scoping review
description:
What diagnostic methods, measurement parameters, and criteria have been used to identify ventilator-induced diaphragm dysfunction (VIDD) in critically ill adult patients receiving mechanical ventilation, and how do these vary across studies in terms of:
1.The type of diagnostic method employed (e.g., ultrasound, transdiaphragmatic pressure, diaphragm electromyography, airway occlusion pressure, maximum inspiratory pressure, phrenic nerve stimulation)?
2.The specific measurement parameters and cut-off values used to define diaphragm dysfunction?
3.The timing of diagnostic assessment relative to mechanical ventilation (e.g., at ICU admission, during spontaneous breathing trials, prior to extubation, post-extubation)?
4.The diagnostic performance (sensitivity, specificity, area under the curve) of each method when reported?
5.The degree of standardization or consensus across studies regarding the definition of VIDD?
3. Objective(s)
To systematically map and synthesize the existing literature on diagnostic approaches for VIDD in critically ill adult patients, with the specific aims of:
Cataloguing all diagnostic methods used to assess diaphragm function in mechanically ventilated patients;
Extracting and comparing cut-off values, thresholds, and diagnostic criteria across studies;
Identifying the timing and clinical context of diagnostic assessments;
Assessing the degree of heterogeneity in VIDD definitions across the literature;
Identifying gaps in the current evidence base to inform future research and guideline development.
4. PCC framework
Element Definition
Population (P) Critically ill adult patients (≥18 years) receiving invasive mechanical ventilation in the intensive care unit (ICU)
Concept (C) Diagnostic methods, measurement parameters, cut-off values, and criteria used to identify diaphragm dysfunction attributable to mechanical ventilation
Context (C) ICU settings (medical, surgical, mixed, cardiac, neurocritical care); any duration of mechanical ventilation; any phase of the ventilation-weaning trajectory
5. Eligibility criteria
5.1 Inclusion criteria
Population: Adult patients (≥18 years) receiving invasive mechanical ventilation in ICU settings
Concept: Studies that report on at least one method of assessing diaphragm function (including but not limited to: diaphragm ultrasound [thickness, thickening fraction, excursion], transdiaphragmatic pressure [Pdi], esophageal pressure [Pes], diaphragm electrical activity [EAdi], airway occlusion pressure [P0.1], maximum inspiratory pressure [PImax/MIP], phrenic nerve magnetic stimulation, sniff nasal inspiratory pressure [SNIP], or biomarkers of diaphragm injury)
Context: Studies conducted in ICU settings (including medical, surgical, mixed, cardiac, neurocritical care, and postoperative ICUs)
Study design: Observational studies (prospective, retrospective, cross-sectional), diagnostic accuracy studies, randomized controlled trials (where diagnostic assessment is reported), systematic reviews and meta-analyses (for reference mining), narrative reviews (for background context only, not for data extraction), clinical guidelines, and consensus statements
Language: English and Chinese
Time frame: January 1, 1994 (the year of the first experimental VIDD study by Le Bourdelles et al.) to the date of the final search
5.2 Exclusion criteria
Studies exclusively involving pediatric (<18 years) or neonatal populations
Studies exclusively involving animal or in vitro models (these will be addressed in Paper 2)
Studies focusing on diaphragm dysfunction due to non-ventilation causes (e.g., phrenic nerve injury during cardiac surgery, spinal cord injury, neuromuscular disease) without reference to mechanical ventilation effects
Studies on non-invasive ventilation or high-flow nasal cannula without invasive mechanical ventilation
Editorials, letters, commentaries, and conference abstracts (unless providing unique diagnostic data not available in full publications)
Studies that mention diaphragm assessment but do not report any diagnostic parameters, thresholds, or criteria
6. Information sources
The following electronic databases will be searched from inception to the search date:
1.PubMed/MEDLINE (via NCBI)
2.Embase (via Elsevier)
3.Web of Science Core Collection (via Clarivate)
4.Cochrane Library (Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials and Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews)
5.CNKI (China National Knowledge Infrastructure) — for Chinese-language literature
6.Wanfang Data — for Chinese-language literature
Additional sources:
Reference lists of included studies (citation tracking / snowballing)
Reference lists of relevant systematic reviews and meta-analyses identified during screening
ClinicalTrials.gov for ongoing studies
Google Scholar (first 200 results) for grey literature
7. Search strategy
The search strategy will be developed in consultation with a medical librarian and piloted in PubMed before translation to other databases. The search will combine three concept blocks using Boolean operators:
Block 1 (Population/Condition): ventilator-induced diaphragm dysfunction, VIDD, diaphragm dysfunction, diaphragm weakness, diaphragm atrophy, respiratory muscle weakness
Block 2 (Diagnostic methods): ultrasound, sonography, thickening fraction, excursion, transdiaphragmatic pressure, esophageal pressure, diaphragm electrical activity, EAdi, airway occlusion pressure, P0.1, maximum inspiratory pressure, MIP, PImax, phrenic nerve stimulation, magnetic stimulation, sniff nasal inspiratory pressure, biomarker
Block 3 (Context): mechanical ventilation, artificial respiration, positive-pressure ventilation, intensive care, critical care, critical illness, ventilator weaning, extubation, spontaneous breathing trial
The full search strategies for each database are provided in a separate document (Search_Strategy_Paper1.md).
No date or language restrictions will be applied during the initial search. Language restriction (English and Chinese) will be applied during screening.
8. Study selection
8.1 Screening process
Level 1 (Title/Abstract screening): Two independent reviewers will screen all titles and abstracts against the inclusion/exclusion criteria. Studies marked as "include" or "uncertain" by either reviewer will proceed to full-text screening.
Level 2 (Full-text screening): Two independent reviewers will independently assess full texts of potentially eligible studies. Disagreements will be resolved by discussion and, if necessary, consultation with a third reviewer.
Level 3 (Citation tracking): Reference lists of included studies will be hand-searched to identify additional relevant studies not captured by the electronic search.
8.2 Tools
Rayyan QCRI (or Covidence) for title/abstract screening
Standardized full-text screening form
PRISMA flow diagram to document the selection process
8.3 Inter-rater reliability
A pilot screening of 50 randomly selected titles/abstracts will be conducted by both reviewers to calibrate the screening criteria. Cohen's kappa will be calculated, and if κ < 0.70, the screening criteria will be refined before proceeding.
9. Data extraction
9.1 Data charting form
A standardized data charting form will be developed and piloted on 10 randomly selected included studies before full extraction. The following data items will be extracted:
A. Study characteristics
Field Description
Author First author et al.
Year Publication year
Country Country where study was conducted
Study design Prospective, retrospective, cross-sectional, RCT, etc.
Setting ICU type (medical/surgical/mixed/cardiac/neuro)
Single/Multi-center Single-center or multi-center
Sample size Number of patients assessed
Duration Study period (months/years)
B. Patient characteristics
Field Description
Age Mean/median age (years)
Sex Male %
BMI Mean/median BMI
Primary diagnosis Reason for ICU admission / MV
MV duration Duration of MV before assessment (hours/days)
Ventilation mode Control, assisted, spontaneous, mixed
SAPS II / APACHE II Severity scores if reported
C. Diagnostic method details
Field Description
Method type Ultrasound / Pdi / EAdi / P0.1 / PImax / phrenic stimulation / other
Method subtype For ultrasound: thickness / thickening fraction / excursion; For Pdi: sniff / magnetic stimulation / voluntary
Measurement site For ultrasound: zone of apposition / subcostal; For pressure: airway / esophageal / gastric
Equipment Device and probe specifications
Timing At ICU admission / during SBT / pre-extubation / post-extubation
Frequency Single measurement / serial measurements
Operator Physician / sonographer / respiratory therapist
Blinding Blinded to outcome?
D. Diagnostic parameters and criteria
Field Description
Parameter measured Tdi,ee / Tdi,pi / DTF / DE / Pdi / P0.1 / PImax / EAdi / etc.
Cut-off value Threshold used to define dysfunction
Definition of VIDD/dysfunction Author's explicit definition (verbatim quote)
Sensitivity If reported (%)
Specificity If reported (%)
AUC If reported
PPV / NPV If reported
Reference standard What was the gold standard used for comparison?
E. Key findings
Field Description
Main finding Primary result of the study
Association with outcome Association between diagnostic finding and clinical outcome (weaning success, MV duration, mortality)
Author conclusions Author-stated conclusions
F. Quality assessment
Field Description
Tool used QUADAS-2 (for diagnostic accuracy studies) / JBI critical appraisal (for other designs)
Risk of bias Low / Unclear / High
Applicability concerns Low / Unclear / High
9.2 Extraction process
Two reviewers will independently extract data from all included studies
A third reviewer will verify a random 20% sample
Disagreements will be resolved by consensus
10. Quality appraisal
The methodological quality of included studies will be assessed using:
QUADAS-2 (Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies) for studies reporting diagnostic accuracy metrics (sensitivity/specificity/AUC)
JBI Critical Appraisal Tools for observational studies not reporting diagnostic accuracy
Quality assessment will be conducted by two independent reviewers. Results will be presented narratively and in summary tables. Studies will not be excluded based on quality assessment results, as is standard for scoping reviews; however, quality findings will inform the interpretation of results and identification of evidence gaps.
11. Synthesis and presentation of results
Results will be presented according to the PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews) guidelines. The synthesis will include:
1.PRISMA flow diagram: Documenting the study selection process
2.Study characteristics table: Summarizing all included studies (tabular format)
3.Narrative synthesis organized by diagnostic method:
Section per diagnostic method (ultrasound, Pdi, EAdi, P0.1, PImax, phrenic stimulation, etc.)
Within each section: parameters used, cut-off values, timing, diagnostic performance
4.Cross-method comparison table: Comparing cut-off values and diagnostic performance across methods
5.Mapping of VIDD definitions: A summary table or figure showing how VIDD/diaphragm dysfunction was defined across all studies
6.Identification of evidence gaps: Areas where diagnostic standardization is lacking
7.Visual summary: A figure summarizing the current state of VIDD diagnostic approaches (e.g., a mind map or conceptual framework diagram)
No meta-analysis will be performed, as this is a scoping review. However, descriptive statistics (frequencies, proportions, ranges) will be used to summarize the data.
12. Registration and reporting
This scoping review protocol is registered with PROSPERO (registration number: [to be obtained])
The review will be reported following the PRISMA-ScR checklist
Any deviations from the protocol will be reported and justified in the final manuscript

title: Use and appropriateness of Reporting Guidelines in physical therapy research: a protocol for a meta-research study
description:
INTRODUCTION: Problems about reporting of a scientific study can affect dissemination of research in different manners. It is known that study methods are frequently not described in adequate detail and that results are presented ambiguously or selectively. To overcome these problems, reporting guidelines (e.g. CONSORT, PRISMA, STARD and STROBE statements) have been developed to increase the transparency of research. While recent evidence suggested that these guidelines are frequently used inappropriately in studies published in the major medical journals, the extent and appropriateness of use in physical therapy research has not been systematically evaluated. The aim of this meta-research study will be to evaluate the frequency of using reporting guidelines and their appropriate use in physical therapy published research.
METHODS: A cross-sectional analysis is planned on a random sample of 200 studies published in the last ten years (2010-2019) in the five generic rehabilitation journals with the highest 5-year impact factor. Randomization will be stratified for publication date to include an equal number of studies from 2010 to 2014 (n=100), and from 2015 to 2019 (n=100). Randomised controlled trials, systematic reviews, diagnostic accuracy studies and observational studies will be included. Crude prevalence estimates with 95% confidence intervals of using and appropriateness of using will be estimated. A bivariate analysis will assess the relationship between the use of reporting guidelines and the year of publication.
DISSEMINATION PLANS: Several studies have shown the positive influence of reporting guidelines on the completeness of research reporting but no one investigated the use and the appropriateness of reporting guidelines in physical therapy research. Therefore, this study will add relevant knowledge that may contribute to improve further the reporting of rehabilitation research. The results of this research will be published in a peer-reviewed journal and will be presented at relevant (inter)national scientific events.
