title: Comparative Diagnostic Accuracy of Large Language Models and Human Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery Specialists Using Balanced Clinical Vignettes
description:
Title:
Comparative Diagnostic Accuracy of Large Language Models and Human Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery Specialists Using Balanced Clinical Vignettes
1. Overview
This preregistration describes a two-part study designed to evaluate diagnostic performance in Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery (OMFS) using standardized, expert-validated clinical vignettes.
Both parts will use the same vignette dataset, gold standard criteria, and scoring methodology to ensure comparability.
Part 1 – Model-to-Model Evaluation: Head-to-head comparison of multiple large language models (LLMs), including ChatGPT-4, ChatGPT-3.5, and Google Gemini, for diagnostic accuracy.
Part 2 – Human-to-AI Evaluation: Comparative diagnostic accuracy of ChatGPT-4 versus independent OMFS specialists (≥5 years post-qualification) under blinded conditions.
2. Background and Rationale
Accurate diagnosis of OMFS lesions is critical for effective patient management. While large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated potential in various medical domains, systematic benchmarking against both competing AI models and human experts in OMFS is limited.
A balanced vignette design minimizes selection bias and allows robust cross-category comparison.
The two complementary parts of this study will together provide a comprehensive performance benchmark for AI in OMFS diagnostics.
3. Objectives
Part 1: Compare the diagnostic accuracy and reasoning clarity of multiple LLMs on a standardized OMFS vignette dataset.
Part 2: Compare the diagnostic accuracy of ChatGPT-4 with that of independent OMFS specialists.
Identify recurring diagnostic error patterns across both AI and human participants.
Explore differences in performance across lesion categories.
4. Methods
4.1 Study Design
Cross-sectional diagnostic performance study using balanced, expert-validated clinical vignettes.
Each vignette represents one OMFS lesion and is text-based, containing essential clinical information but no images.
Equal number of vignettes per diagnostic category to reduce selection bias.
4.2 Vignette Development
Six diagnostic categories:
Odontogenic infections
Inflammatory bone lesions
Odontogenic cysts/tumors
Salivary gland disorders
Oral mucosal lesions
Malignant neoplasms
10 vignettes per category (total = 60 vignettes).
Developed and validated by 3 OMFS specialists (not participating in Part 2 comparisons).
Gold standard diagnosis established by consensus.
4.3 Participants and Comparators
Part 1:
ChatGPT-4 (OpenAI), ChatGPT-3.5 (OpenAI), Google Gemini (Google).
All models accessed in the same month to minimize version drift.
Part 2:
Three independent OMFS specialists (≥5 years post-qualification), blinded to gold standards, not involved in vignette development.
4.4 Prompting and Response Capture
Standardized zero-shot prompt: “Based on the following clinical information, provide the most likely diagnosis.”
AI outputs recorded verbatim; human responses collected via structured Google Form.
4.5 Outcome Measures
Primary Outcome: Diagnostic accuracy (% correct vs. gold standard).
Secondary Outcomes:
Cohen’s κ for inter-rater agreement (humans) and AI–human agreement.
Qualitative analysis of reasoning clarity in AI outputs.
Error pattern classification (overgeneralization, underspecificity, underestimation of malignancy, etc.).
4.6 Statistical Analysis
Accuracy comparisons: McNemar’s test for paired comparisons.
Agreement: Cohen’s κ with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals.
Between-model/human differences: Chi-square or Fisher’s exact as appropriate.
Error pattern frequencies summarized descriptively.
5. Ethics
The study protocol was reviewed by the Institutional Ethics Committee, Dr. Hedgewar Smruti Rugna Sewa Mandal's Dental College and Hospital, Hingoli, Maharashtra, which granted exemption on 15 March 2025.
No identifiable patient information is used.
6. Sample Size Justification
For a 95% confidence level, ±10% margin of error, and expected accuracy of 70%, the minimum sample size is 81 vignettes.
We will use 60 vignettes (10 per category) for feasibility in this phase, with future expansion planned.
7. Data Management and Availability
All vignette text and gold standard diagnoses will be uploaded as supplementary material upon study acceptance.
Raw anonymized outputs from AI models and human raters will be made publicly available on OSF post-publication.
8. Timeline
March–April 2025: Vignette development and validation.
May 2025: AI and human evaluation.
June 2025: Data analysis.
July–August 2025: Manuscript drafting (Part 1).
August–September 2025: Manuscript drafting (Part 2).
9. Planned Publications
Part 1 – Model-to-Model Evaluation: Comparative Diagnostic Accuracy of Large Language Models in Oral and Maxillofacial Lesions: Balanced Vignette Study (Part 1 – Model-to-Model Evaluation)
Part 2 – Human-to-AI Evaluation: Comparative Diagnostic Accuracy of ChatGPT-4 and Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery Specialists: Balanced Vignette Study (Part 2 – Human-to-AI Evaluation)
Both will reference this OSF registration.

title: Integrating Rapid Serology, Portable ECG, and Point-of-Care Ultrasound for Chagas Disease Screening: A Scoping Review Protocol

title: Combining genetic and behavioral predictors of 11-year language outcome: A multi cohort study
description:
Background: Early identification of language disorders ensures children in need receive support to improve development and quality of life outcomes. Two previous studies identified six parent-reported survey items that predicted a comparable 11-year language outcome with ≥71% sensitivity and specificity. One used data from the Early Language in Victoria Study (ELVS) and the other from the Longitudinal Study of Australian Children (LSAC) birth cohort. This study will combine data from these two cohorts and add polygenic scores (PGS) of 24-38-month vocabulary. We will assess whether predictive accuracy of 11-year language outcome improves when adding PGS to a set of parent-reported behavioral predictors.

Method: ELVS and LSAC collected six parent-reported measures about the child’s development between 24-36 months of age and a language outcome at 11 years. Both studies also collected genetic data at 7 (ELVS) or 11-12 (LSAC) years of age from which we derived PGS of 24-38-month vocabulary. We will use an ensemble machine-learning approach (SuperLearner) to estimate the accuracy of the six survey items and the PGS in predicting low 11-year language outcome (>1.5SD below the mean).

Expected results: Predictive accuracy may improve when combining the parent-reported survey items with PGS. This will inform the extent to which future studies should prioritize collecting genetic data to help predict language outcomes.

title: Data Visualisation Methods Used to Compare Diagnostic Test Accuracy in Systematic Reviews: Protocol
description:
This project addresses a key methodological gap in the synthesis and communication of comparative diagnostic test accuracy (DTA) evidence. While multiple diagnostic tests are often available for a given condition, and robust statistical methods such as network meta-analysis (NMA) are increasingly used to compare their accuracy, far less attention has been given to how comparative results are visualised and interpreted. This is a critical issue, as data visualisation underpins both the understanding of evidence structures and the communication of findings to a wide range of stakeholders, including clinicians, guideline developers, and patients.

The project comprises two components. First, a targeted review of methodological guidance will identify recommendations on the visualisation and interpretation of comparative DTA results from key organisations and methodological literature. Second, a systematic review of published DTA reviews will examine how comparative accuracy data are currently visualised in practice, including the types of data presented, graphical methods used, and how visualisations are interpreted to support conclusions.

Findings will be synthesised descriptively and narratively, with the development of a taxonomy of visualisation approaches and an assessment of alignment between recommended and observed practice. The project will also incorporate input from a Patient Advisory Group and key stakeholders to evaluate the interpretability and usability of common visualisations.

Overall, this work will provide the first comprehensive evaluation of how comparative DTA evidence is visualised and interpreted, with the aim of improving the clarity, transparency, and reliability of evidence communication to support clinical decision-making and guideline development.

title: Validation of the UK English Oxford Cognitive Screen-Plus in Sub-Acute and Chronic Stroke Survivors.
description:
Stroke survivors are routinely screened for cognitive impairment with tools that often fail to detect subtle impairments. The Oxford Cognitive Screen-Plus (OCS-Plus) is a brief tablet-based screen designed to detect subtle post-stroke cognitive impairments. We examined its psychometric properties in two stroke cohorts (subacute: <3 months post-stroke, chronic: >6 months post-stroke).
Patients and Methods
This study included 347 stroke survivors (mean age = 73 years; mean education = 13 years; 43.06% female presenting; 74.42% ischaemic stroke). The OCS-Plus was completed by 181 sub-acute stroke survivors and 166 chronic stroke survivors. All participants also completed the Oxford Cognitive Screen (OCS) and a subset completed the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) and further neuropsychological tests. 
Results
First, convergent construct validity of all OCS-Plus tasks against task-matched standardized neuropsychological tests was confirmed. Second, we evaluated divergent construct validity of all OCS-Plus subtasks. Third, we report the sensitivity and specificity of each OCS-Plus subtask compared to neuropsychological test performance. Fourth, we found that OCS-Plus detected cognitive impairments in a large proportion of those classed as unimpaired on MoCA and OCS.
Discussion and Conclusion
The OCS-Plus provides a valid screening tool for sensitive detection of subtle cognitive impairment in stroke patients. Indeed, the OCS-Plus detected subtle cognitive impairment at a similar level to validated neuropsychological assessments and exceeded detection of cognitive impairment compared to standard clinical screening tools.

title: From African Genomes to Function: A Systematic Review and Evidence Map of Disease Models in Africa, with Meta-analysis of Patient-Derived Organoid Treatment-Response Prediction
description:
This is a retrospective registration of the protocol and analytical framework for a systematic review, evidence map, and diagnostic-accuracy meta-analysis examining functional disease-modelling research relevant to African genomics. The review addresses two complementary evidence streams. The first systematically identifies and maps peer-reviewed primary studies using human cell and induced pluripotent stem cell systems, patient-derived organoids, Drosophila, Caenorhabditis elegans, zebrafish, and related functional genomic approaches where there is substantive African institutional participation or African-derived biological material. The second evaluates the clinical validity of patient-derived tumour organoids as predictors of treatment response using matched patient-organoid studies with clinically interpretable treatment-response outcomes.
The review evaluates the geographic and experimental distribution of functional disease-model research in Africa, methodological and reporting characteristics of the included studies, and opportunities for cross-platform functional validation. Quantitative synthesis is restricted to clinically coherent patient-derived organoid treatment-response studies rather than combining biologically incompatible experimental outcomes across different model systems. Diagnostic performance is assessed using sensitivity, specificity, diagnostic odds ratios, random-effects models, and sensitivity analyses. Risk of bias for the organoid clinical-validity studies is assessed using QUADAS-2, while model-specific methodological domains informed by SYRCLE principles are used for the broader African evidence map.
The protocol was finalised before final eligibility coding and quantitative synthesis but was not prospectively registered. This OSF registration therefore documents the review retrospectively for transparency and reproducibility. Search strategies, eligibility criteria, extraction fields, risk-of-bias assessments, analysis scripts, and supporting data will be deposited with the registration and/or associated research materials. Any database-search updates or resulting amendments made before final journal submission will be documented transparently.

title: Attitudes Towards Profiling Survey Study 4
description:
This is an experimental moral psychological study on people's attitudes towards the use of profiling to catch criminals. This study is a continuation of prior studies within this project. In each prior study thus far, the content of the study has only concerned "pre-crime" police work: using profiling or other information to prevent people who may be about to commit a crime from doing so. The primary purpose of the present study is to examine whether the effects observed in those prior studies replicate for more typical "post-crime" arrests; that is, arresting someone based on the suspicion that they have committed a crime. 

The study uses the contrastive vignettes method, and has a 2 (time: pre-crime, post-crime; between-subjects) x 3 (information source: AI profiler, expert group, anonymous source; between-subjects) x 4 (type of crime: murder, credit fraud, cannabis growing, graffiti; within-subjects) x 2 (outcome: true positive, false positive; within-subjects) mixed design. The design and vignette content in this study is very similar to that of Study 3B (https://osf.io/7r3dx/?view_only=38ffadb92b2f46ea9cedd943cf402b9f), except for the addition of the post-crime condition. 

In prior studies, we have observed relatively consistent information source effects: judgments about the overall process leading to an arrest and about the arrest decision itself tended to be more negative when the arrest was made based on profiling, compared to when the arrest was made based on an anonymous tip. Outcome effects were also consistent for both within-subjects and between-subjects designs: judgments were more positive when the arrested suspect was in fact planning to commit a crime. In Studies 3 and 3B, the type of crime also mattered: preventing more serious crimes (murder, credit fraud) led to more positive judgments. We have also observed interactions between information source and outcome (larger outcome effect for the anonymous source condition) and crime and outcome (larger outcome effects for more serious crimes). In this study, we will examine these effects and compare them between the pre-crime and post-crime conditions.

title: FMMI: An Innovative, Comparative, and Integrated Protocol to Unravel Integral
description:
Objective: This protocol article outlines the theoretical development and prospective clinical validation plan for the Functional Mandibular Movement Index (FMMI), a composite and objective metric designed to overcome the limitations of subjective and single-parameter assessments in the evaluation of Temporomandibular Disorders (TMD).
Methods: The FMMI quantitatively integrates functional maximal mouth opening (MMO_F), protrusive and lateral excursions, and an innovative Multiplicative Symmetry Factor (Φ). The proposed validation protocol involves a two-phase prospective cohort study: 1) a cross-sectional analysis comparing TMD patients (DC/TMD criteria) to asymptomatic controls to establish diagnostic cut-off points via ROC analysis and to correlate the FMMI with biopsychosocial measures (pain intensity, Jaw Functional Limitation Scale, PHQ-9); and 2) a longitudinal arm, following a subset of patients over six months to assess the FMMI's sensitivity to therapeutic changes, comparing it with the standard maximum mouth opening (MMO) measure using mixed linear models. Computational simulations were performed to illustrate the expected behavior of the index and to underpin sample size calculations.
Anticipated Results: Based on simulations, the FMMI is projected to demonstrate high diagnostic accuracy (area under the ROC curve >0.90) for discriminating TMD patients from controls and for differentiating TMD subtypes (e.g., arthrogenic vs. myogenous). It is also expected to exhibit strong negative correlations with pain and functional limitation scores, alongside greater sensitivity as a therapeutic outcome measure when compared to MMO alone.
Conclusion: This protocol aims to establish the theoretical and methodological foundation for the validation of the FMMI, a proposed integrative indicator designed to bridge biomechanical assessment with the biopsychosocial model of TMD. The prospective validation study seeks to determine its clinical utility for differential diagnosis, treatment planning, and longitudinal monitoring in TMD-related research and clinical practice.

title: Iodine maps from photon-counting detector CT in contrast-enhanced thoracic imaging: a scoping review of clinical applications
description: This scoping review maps the early clinical evidence on iodine maps generated by photon-counting detector computed tomography (PCD-CT) in adult thoracic imaging. PCD-CT represents a fundamental technological shift from conventional detectors, as it directly converts individual photons into electrical signals and inherently acquires spectral data at any acquisition protocol, without requiring dedicated dual-energy tube-voltage switching. Iodine maps derived from this system quantitatively visualize the regional distribution of iodinated contrast material, enabling simultaneous functional and morphologic assessment in a single scan. The review identified 10 original studies (832 patients, published 2022–2025), all single-center, distributed across four clinical domains. In pulmonary vasculature, PCD-CT iodine maps enable perfusion assessment from ultra-high-pitch CT pulmonary angiography — a combination technically impossible with conventional dual-energy energy-integrating detectors. In chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension, they demonstrated diagnostic accuracy comparable to perfusion SPECT/CT at approximately five times lower radiation dose. In parenchymal lung disease, iodine maps improved radiologist diagnostic confidence when differentiating morphologically overlapping attenuation patterns such as consolidation, ground-glass opacity, and reticular disease. In pleural empyema, they enhanced diagnostic accuracy in combination with virtual monoenergetic images at high energy levels. In cardiac applications, PCD-CT iodine maps quantified myocardial extracellular volume and detected late iodine enhancement with strong correlation to cardiac MRI, positioning the technique as a potential alternative for patients with contraindications to MRI. Collectively, the review concludes that early evidence is consistently promising across all four domains but insufficient to support clinical adoption recommendations, as it derives exclusively from small single-center retrospective series at European academic institutions, without multicenter prospective data or standardized acquisition protocols.

title: The Validity of the Tool “statcheck” in Discovering Statistical Reporting Inconsistencies
description: The R package “statcheck” (Epskamp & Nuijten, 2016)  is a tool to extract statistical results from articles and check whether the reported p-value matches the accompanying test statistic and degrees of freedom. A previous study showed high interrater reliabilities (between .76 and .89) between statcheck and manual coding of inconsistencies (.76 - .89; Nuijten, Hartgerink, Van Assen, Epskamp, & Wicherts, 2016). Here we present an additional, detailed study of the validity of statcheck. In Study 1, we calculated its sensitivity and specificity. We found that statcheck’s sensitivity (true positive rate) and specificity (true negative rate) were high: between 85.3% and 100%, and between 96.0% and 100%, respectively, depending on the assumptions and settings. The overall accuracy of statcheck ranged from 96.2% to 99.9%. In Study 2, we investigated statcheck’s ability to deal with statistical corrections for multiple testing or violations of assumptions in articles. We found that the prevalence of corrections for multiple testing or violations of assumptions in psychology was higher than we initially estimated in Nuijten et al. (2016). Although we found numerous reporting inconsistencies in results corrected for violations of the sphericity assumption, we demonstrate that inconsistencies associated with statistical corrections are not what is causing the high estimates of the prevalence of statistical reporting inconsistencies in psychology.

title: Effectiveness, Safety, and Cost-Effectiveness of Therapeutic Drug Monitoring for Adults: A Scoping Review Protocol
description:
Therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) is the measurement of drug concentrations in patients for the purpose of predicting medication-related benefit or harm. In clinical practice, TDM allows clinicians to titrate drug dosages based on measured concentrations at set times in relation to dose, compared to a pre-established reference range. The goal of this process is to optimize benefit, avoid toxicity, and prevent adverse drug events (ADEs). Moreover, TDM has been used as a low quality indicator of patient adherence and has postulated to potentially identify malabsorption or drug clearance variance.

TDM is thought to be especially helpful for medications with narrow therapeutic windows and those whose therapeutic effects cannot be directly observed or measured. For instance, TDM is frequently used with antibiotics such as vancomycin due to its narrow therapeutic window and potential for nephrotoxicity, for psychotropics such as lithium, and for antiepileptics such as phenytoin because of risks of neurotoxicity. Warfarin remains a unique example of a commonly used medication for which monitoring does not need to rely on drug levels since there exists a pharmacodynamic measure that can predict both benefits and harm. Dosing for warfarin is adjusted based on routinely measured international normalized ratios (INRs) which correlate with both clotting and bleeding.
 
The premise of TDM assumes that there is a predictable relationship between serum concentration, medication dose, medication effectiveness, or medication harm. Additionally, TDM assumes that there is an accurate correlation between the established therapeutic window reference ranges and the benefit or toxicity of medication. In practice however, inter-patient variability, serum sample collection timing errors, diagnostic test accuracy variation, variable adherence, and poorly validated reference ranges (i.e., not based on ability to predict patient clinical outcomes), have brought into question the true value of TDM.

A 2018 review highlighted the limited evidence upon which reference ranges were developed. The majority of ranges focused on toxicity and were based upon case reports, anecdotal evidence, and small trials with limited external validity.4 Several studies recognized the paucity of randomized controlled trials (RCTs), sufficient sample sizes, and studies that examine concentration relationship to clinical outcome (efficacy and toxicity). Only a few of these medications, such as antivirals for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and immunosuppressants for kidney transplants (e.g., cyclosporine, everolimus), have been further investigated with larger sample sizes, RCTs, and have updated guidelines for their ability to predict outcomes. A contributing factor to the dearth of research on the benefits and harms of TDM of existing medications is thought to be research funding. Current research efforts and resources, especially from pharmaceutical companies, are more likely to be directed towards newer and patent-protected drugs.
 
TDM is ubiquitous in health care in wealthy countries, but the imperative for evidence-based care based on important patient outcomes, health care budget pressures, and resource stewardship concerns have made TDM a target for review. As such, the objective of this study is to undertake a scoping review of the high-quality literature to determine the benefits, harms, and cost-effectiveness of TDM in improving patient outcomes.

title: Bioelectrical Impedance Analysis Technologies for Skeletal Muscle Assessment in Older Adults: A Scoping Review
description:
This project aims to conduct a scoping review to systematically map the technological approaches of bioelectrical impedance analysis used for skeletal muscle mass assessment in older adults. Although bioelectrical impedance analysis has been widely applied in this population because of its non-invasive nature, portability, and feasibility in both clinical and community settings, substantial heterogeneity exists in the way the technology is implemented across studies. Differences in frequency strategies, measurement configurations, and definitions of muscle-related outcomes indicate that studies addressing similar research questions may rely on markedly different technical designs.

Most existing reviews in this field have focused on evaluating diagnostic accuracy or the predictive performance of bioelectrical impedance–based equations. In contrast, the present scoping review is designed to examine the technological and methodological characteristics that underpin these applications. The review will identify and classify the frequency strategies used for measurement, the configurations adopted for data acquisition, and the muscle-related outcomes reported in studies involving older adults.

By systematically charting and synthesizing these technological features, this review seeks to provide a structured overview of how bioelectrical impedance analysis is currently applied for skeletal muscle assessment in older populations, rather than to compare the relative accuracy or effectiveness of different approaches. The expected outcome is a comprehensive mapping of technological pathways and their research contexts, highlighting prevailing patterns of use, methodological diversity, and areas in which reporting practices and standardization remain limited. This work is intended to inform future study design, support clearer interpretation of existing evidence, and contribute to more consistent and transparent application of bioelectrical impedance analysis in research and practice involving older adults.

title: The Use of AI-Assisted Digital Otoscopes for Evaluating Pediatric Patients in Rural Settings: A Scoping Review
description:
Introduction: Otitis media (OM) is one of the most prevalent infectious diseases in childhood and represents a significant public health problem due to its association with hearing loss, developmental complications, and frequent antibiotic use. In this context, Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative technology for evaluating the tympanic membrane using digital otoscopes, showing great potential for improving diagnostic accuracy and expanding access to specialized care in rural settings. However, the implications of these technologies extend beyond their diagnostic performance and include aspects related to their implementation, feasibility, acceptance, and applicability in resource-limited settings. Therefore, the objective of this project is to map the available evidence on the use of AI-assisted digital otoscopes for the evaluation of the tympanic membrane in pediatric patients, identifying their applications, benefits, limitations, challenges, and future opportunities.
Objective: To map and synthesize the available evidence on the use of AI-assisted digital otoscopes for evaluating the tympanic membrane in pediatric patients in rural settings
Methodology: A scoping review will be conducted following the methodology of the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) and the PRISMA-ScR guidelines. Databases such as PubMed, 


Scopus, Web of Science, LILACS, and BIREME will be searched using MeSH and DeCS terms related to AI, digital otoscopy, and middle ear pathology in pediatrics. Scientific articles, reviews, and technical and institutional reports published between 2015 and 2025 will be included.
Expected results: The study aims to generate a comprehensive mapping of the available evidence on the characteristics and diagnostic performance of AI-assisted digital otoscopes in the pediatric population; the types of devices and AI systems used; the reported diagnostic performance indicators; the contexts of use and the feasibility of implementation in rural settings; as well as the advantages, barriers, and challenges to their adoption. The results will provide relevant evidence for educators, clinicians, health policy makers, and researchers interested in the digital transformation of pediatric care in rural areas.

title: DIAGNOSTIC ACCURACY AND REPRODUCIBILITY OF GPT-4o VERSUS CLINICIAN OF GRADED EXPERTISE IN IDENTIFYING INCREASED OVERJET AND OTHER COMMON MALOCCLUSION TRAITS FROM STANDARDIZED CLINICAL PHOTOGRAPHS : A COMPARATIVE CROSS-SECTIONAL DIAGNOSTIC ACCURACY STUDY
description:
This study aims to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy and reproducibility of GPT-4o for orthodontic diagnosis using standardized clinical photographs. Recent advances in large language models with multimodal capabilities have created opportunities for artificial intelligence to assist clinicians in interpreting clinical images. However, evidence regarding the diagnostic performance, consistency, and clinical applicability of GPT-4o in orthodontic diagnosis remains limited.

This prospective, comparative, cross-sectional diagnostic accuracy study will compare GPT-4o with three groups of human evaluators—expert orthodontists, orthodontic postgraduate residents, and general dental practitioners—using standardized eight-view orthodontic photographic records. The reference standard will be the consensus diagnosis established by senior orthodontists based on complete clinical records, including clinical examination, study models or digital scans, and radiographs where indicated.

The primary objective is to determine the diagnostic accuracy of GPT-4o in identifying increased overjet (>4 mm). Secondary objectives include evaluating GPT-4o performance for additional orthodontic diagnostic traits, including overbite, crowding, spacing, anterior open bite, anterior crossbite, posterior crossbite, Angle's molar relationship, canine relationship, midline deviation, and gingival display. The study will also assess the reproducibility of GPT-4o through repeated assessments of the same cases and compare its performance with that of human clinicians.

The findings are expected to provide robust evidence regarding the strengths and limitations of GPT-4o as a clinical decision-support tool in orthodontics. If GPT-4o demonstrates high diagnostic accuracy and reproducibility comparable with expert clinicians, it may have potential applications in orthodontic screening, education, teleorthodontics, and clinical decision support. Conversely, identification of diagnostic limitations will help define areas where expert clinical judgment remains essential and guide the responsible integration of artificial intelligence into orthodontic practice.

title: Ultrasound Diagnosis of Inflammatory Breast Cancer In Pregnancy and Lactation: Challenges and Emerging Strategies; A Scoping Review
description:
This scoping review, titled “Ultrasound Diagnosis of Inflammatory Breast Cancer in Pregnancy and Lactation: Challenges and Emerging Strategies”, aims to map existing literature on the diagnostic complexities associated with identifying inflammatory breast cancer (IBC) in pregnant and lactating women using ultrasound. The project seeks to clarify how physiological breast changes during these periods such as increased vascularity, glandular density, and lactational alterations can obscure or mimic malignancy, leading to delayed or missed diagnoses.

The purpose of this review is to identify and synthesize reported diagnostic challenges, imaging limitations, and evidence gaps in the use of ultrasound for IBC detection within this unique population. It will also explore emerging strategies and technological advancements such as elastography, contrast-enhanced ultrasound, and AI-assisted interpretation that may improve diagnostic accuracy and clinical decision-making.

By collating and analyzing findings from peer-reviewed studies published between 2010 and 2026, this review will provide a comprehensive overview of current evidence and highlight areas requiring further research

title: Use of the Keratograph® 5M for the Diagnosis of Dry Eye Disease: A Scoping Review
description:
Dry Eye Disease (DED) is a multifactorial disorder of the ocular surface characterized by tear film instability and associated ocular symptoms. Objective assessment of tear film parameters and meibomian gland function is essential for accurate diagnosis and subtype classification. In recent years, non-invasive imaging technologies have been increasingly incorporated into clinical practice to enhance diagnostic precision and reduce variability associated with traditional tests.

The Keratograph® 5M (Oculus Optikgeräte GmbH, Germany) is a Placido-disc–based corneal topographer that integrates automated, non-contact measurements of tear film stability and ocular surface parameters. The device provides non-invasive break-up time (NIBUT), tear meniscus height (TMH), meibography, ocular redness quantification, and additional surface analyses. Although widely used in ophthalmology and optometry settings, the scope, consistency, and characteristics of the published evidence regarding its diagnostic application in DED have not been comprehensively mapped.

The purpose of this scoping review is to systematically identify, describe, and synthesize the available scientific literature evaluating the use of the Keratograph® 5M in the diagnosis of Dry Eye Disease. Specifically, this review aims to: (1) map the clinical contexts in which the device has been studied; (2) describe the tear film and glandular parameters assessed; (3) summarize reported measurement properties (e.g., repeatability, reproducibility); and (4) identify research gaps related to diagnostic performance and clinical implementation.

This review will follow established methodological guidance for scoping reviews and will include peer-reviewed primary studies evaluating the Keratograph® 5M in adult or mixed populations undergoing assessment for DED or related ocular surface conditions. Data extraction will focus on study design, population characteristics, diagnostic parameters evaluated, reference standards (when applicable), and key findings. No formal meta-analysis is planned, as the objective is evidence mapping rather than quantitative synthesis.

Expected outcomes include a structured overview of the current evidence landscape, identification of methodological heterogeneity in diagnostic assessment, and clarification of how the Keratograph® 5M is positioned within the diagnostic pathway of DED. The findings may inform future diagnostic accuracy studies, health technology assessments, and clinical guideline development.

title: Beyond the Total Score: Investigating Depression Dimensions and Item-Level Analyses in Adolescents with Autism Spectrum Disorder
description: Depression is highly prevalent among adolescents with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), yet its clinical presentation may differ from that of neurotypical peers. This study examines depressive symptom expression in adolescents with and without ASD using the Beck Depression Inventory-II (BDI-II). Specifically, we compare groups across affective, cognitive, and somatic subdomains of depression and at the individual item level. Clinical data from approximately 220 adolescents in treatment (50% ASD) will be analyzed using one-way ANOVAs and independent-samples t-tests. The expectation is that adolescents with ASD will show higher somatic and cognitive symptom scores and distinct item-level endorsement patterns, such as greater fatigue and pessimism. Findings will clarify whether depressive symptom structures differ between ASD and non-ASD adolescents, improving diagnostic accuracy and informing tailored clinical assessment.

title: Biomarkers in Pediatric Neuropsychiatric Systemic Lupus Erythematosus: A Systematic Review
description:
This is the protocol for a systematic review aiming To evaluate and synthesize current evidence on the diagnostic, predictive, or disease-monitoring value of biomarkers in pediatric patients with neuropsychiatric systemic lupus erythematosus (pNPSLE).
Inclusion criteria

Population: Children and adolescents (≤18 years old) diagnosed with SLE and presenting neuropsychiatric symptoms.
Study Types: Original peer-reviewed studies (cohort, case-control, cross-sectional).
Intervention/Exposure: Measurement of biomarkers related to neuropsychiatric involvement in SLE.
Outcomes: Diagnostic accuracy, association with NP symptoms, or prognostic relevance of biomarkers.
Exclusion criteria

Case reports, case series, review articles.
Studies without separate pediatric data.
Animal studies or non-human participants.
Studies without data on relevant biomarkers.
Databases and Search Strategy

Databases searched: We followed the PRISMA guidelines to perform a systematic literature search of articles relevant to pediatric NPSLE and biomarkers in four databases

PubMed (n=24)
EMBASE (n=24)
Scopus (n=7)
Google Scholar (n=48)
A total of 29 studies were selected for data extraction and narrative synthesis.Data were extracted manually from full texts and supplementary materials. Extracted information included: author, year, country, study design, population size, NP symptomatology, biomarker type and measurement method, sensitivity/specificity, and association with NP outcomes.The Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS) adapted for cohort, case-control, and cross-sectional studies was used. Quality grading followed the AHRQ thresholds. Most studies were of poor quality due to small samples and lack of control for confounding.A qualitative synthesis was performed. No meta-analysis was conducted due to high heterogeneity in study designs, biomarkers, and outcome measures.

Generative AI in systematic reviews of the biomedical literature (regenAIrate): Protocol for a living systematic review
description:
Background: Generative AI (genAI) tools have been used for different stages of the systematic review process but the evidence on their performance has been inconclusive so far. 

Objective: This living review aims to systematically collect and synthesize evidence on how genAI tools perform when used to automate different types of SR tasks in comparison with human reviewers. 

Methods: We will systematically search the biomedical literature for comparative studies of genAI tools for any SR task (from development of the search strategy to data extraction and grading of the evidence), as compared with human reviewers. A team of researchers will screen the identified studies and will extract data in duplicate on the following outcomes: recall (sensitivity), specificity, precision (positive predictive value), F1 score, and kappa statistics, as well as workload to task completion. We will present the study-specific results and synthesise the performance of tools in subgroups by SR task, using the bivariate model for diagnostic test accuracy studies meta-analysis. We will adapt the QUADAS 2 tool to our context to assess the risk of bias in the included studies, and we will assess the certainty of evidence using the principles of GRADE. We will continually monitor the literature for new studies and update the review every 6 months. 

Conclusions: This living systematic review will offer evidence-based assessments of different genAI tools for SR tasks and their performance compared with human reviewers. It will act as a basis for forming recommendations for practice.

title: Optic Nerve Sheath Diameter as a Diagnostic Marker for Post-Dural Puncture Headache: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
description:
This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluates the diagnostic accuracy of optic nerve sheath diameter (ONSD) measurement for post-dural puncture headache (PDPH) following lumbar puncture or spinal anesthesia. The study aims to quantify the magnitude of ONSD differences between PDPH patients and controls, determine diagnostic accuracy through pooled sensitivity, specificity, and area under the curve (AUC), identify optimal ONSD cut-off values, and assess evidence quality using GRADE criteria.
The review follows PRISMA 2020 guidelines and includes four studies (70 PDPH patients, 285 controls) reporting ONSD measurements at 24 hours post-procedure. Primary outcome is the pooled effect size (Hedges' g) using Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman (HKSJ) random-effects meta-analysis. Secondary outcomes include pooled AUC for diagnostic accuracy with logit transformation, optimal cut-off values, and GRADE evidence assessment.
Expected outcomes include quantitative estimates of ONSD discriminatory power for PDPH diagnosis and a comprehensive evidence quality rating. The findings will inform whether ONSD measurement can serve as a non-invasive surrogate marker for intracranial hypotension associated with PDPH.

title: Individual Differences and Design Features in Simulation-based Learning
description:
This Master’s thesis uses secondary data collected within the COSIMA Research Unit (Collaborative Simulation-Based Learning in Higher Education; COSIMA Research Unit, n.d.). The thesis aims to advance understanding of how simulation-based learning in higher education can be designed and adapted to learners’ characteristics and needs. Using a person-centered approach grounded in expectancy-value theory (EVT), it identifies motivational profiles of learners based on three indicators: expectancy of success, utility value and interest value. The profiles are then examined in their relation to diagnostic performance and, more broadly, in how they interact with the instructional support built into the simulation design. 

This preregistration covers two confirmatory hypotheses: one regarding the stability of motivational profiles, and one regarding profile differences in diagnostic accuracy. The remaining research questions concerning motivational profiles, simulation design features, and extraneous cognitive load are not preregistered and will be reported as exploratory.

title: Quantifying AI Anchoring Bias in Gleason Grading: A Blinded, Gamified Study of Pathologists and Medical Students
description: This single-blind randomized study examines whether AI-suggested Gleason grades systematically shift pathologists' and medical students' grading decisions through cognitive anchoring bias. Fifty participants (25 board-certified pathologists, 25 medical students) will each grade 60 gland-level prostate biopsy images using GleasonArena, a web-based gamified grading platform. Three experimental variables are randomized at the trial level within a single session: AI suggestion timing (shown before participant commits, shown after with revision option, or not shown), AI accuracy (correct, deliberately off by one grade, or off by two grades), and time pressure (self-paced, 30-second limit, 15-second limit). Participants are blinded to the AI manipulation — they are told they are completing a Gleason grading quiz. The AI suggestions are scripted experimental variables, not actual model outputs, with direction of bias (overgrading vs undergrading) balanced. Primary outcomes are grade shift rate toward AI suggestions, resistance threshold as a function of AI error magnitude, and directional asymmetry of bias. Secondary outcomes include diagnostic accuracy, completion time, expertise-dependent susceptibility, and discrepancy between self-reported and objectively measured AI influence. Results will inform evidence-based design guidelines for AI-assisted diagnostic tools in clinical pathology.

title: The impact of content feedback and performance feedback on diagnostic performance
description:
Diagnostic errors, defined as failures to establish an accurate and timely diagnosis or to communicate the diagnosis with the patient (1), are a major patient safety concern (2). Overconfidence among physicians is seen as an important factor contributing to these errors (2,3). Overconfident physicians tend to underestimate their chances of being wrong and consequently, they fail to use available resources to support their diagnostic processes (4). 
It is hypothesized that this overconfidence is the result of bad calibration between the physician’s confidence in the accuracy of their diagnosis and the actual accuracy of their diagnosis (3,5,6). For instance, as a case gets more difficult, physicians tend to overestimate their ability to solve it (4): their accuracy does not align with their confidence (4). Since physicians do not always receive feedback in clinical practice (6), they have few opportunities to calibrate and remain overconfident.
Previous research has suggested that improving the calibration between one’s confidence and objective accuracy may decrease the likelihood of diagnostic errors (4-6). As known from studies in the field of applied psychology (7,8), calibration can be achieved through feedback (5). There are two main types: feedback can be directive or facilitative (9). Directive feedback only informs the recipient of what is incorrect and indicates how they performed (9). This is alternatively called performance feedback. On the other hand, facilitative feedback provides suggestions to help the recipient in their learning (9). This is also known as information feedback, as it explains how the recipient can reach the correct answer. Research has shown that performance feedback can improve calibration (7,10). It is suggested that this effect occurs by raising awareness for the mismatch between estimated performance and actual performance (8). Existing studies have shown that information feedback can enhance learning outcomes (9), however, to our knowledge, the effect of information feedback on calibration has not been studied yet.
Although previous literature indicates that feedback can be an effective tool to reduce errors, whether feedback can also benefit physicians might depend on several factors (9), such as level of expertise, acceptability, and openness to learning. These factors all moderate the effectiveness of feedback (9). It is especially important to understand how physicians of different levels of expertise can benefit from feedback. Psychological research indicates that even though specialists are generally better calibrated than students (10), both can benefit when they receive feedback (10). Therefore, it is valuable to examine the effects of feedback in both novices and experts. 
Since, outside of medical education, little feedback is given (6), evidence of the effect of feedback on diagnostic performance from clinical settings is missing (5). In this study, we aim to determine whether feedback improves the diagnostic performance of medical students and medical professionals. We will also explore whether the type of feedback (i.e., performance feedback or information feedback) differentially affects performance. Based on previous psychological research (7), we hypothesize that improving calibration via feedback will not only reduce overconfidence, but will also improve reasoning accuracy.

(2) Berner ES, Graber ML. Overconfidence as a cause of diagnostic error in medicine. Am J Med 2008 May;121(5 Suppl):2.
(3) Cassam Q. Diagnostic error, overconfidence and self-knowledge. Palgrave Communications 2017;3(1):17025.
(4) Meyer AN, Payne VL, Meeks DW, Rao R, Singh H. Physicians' diagnostic accuracy, confidence, and resource requests: a vignette study. JAMA Intern Med 2013 Nov 25;173(21):1952-1958.
(5) Meyer AND, Singh H. The Path to Diagnostic Excellence Includes Feedback to Calibrate How Clinicians Think. JAMA 2019 Feb 26;321(8):737-738.
(6) Zwaan L, Hautz WE. Bridging the gap between uncertainty, confidence and diagnostic accuracy: calibration is key. BMJ Qual Saf 2019 May;28(5):352-355.
(7) Dunlosky J, Rawson KA. Overconfidence produces underachievement: Inaccurate self evaluations undermine students’ learning and retention. Learning and instruction 2012 Aug;22(4):271-280.
(8) Rawson KA, Dunlosky J. Improving students' self-evaluation of learning for key concepts in textbook materials. European journal of cognitive psychology 2007 Jul 1;19(4-5):559-579.
(9) Archer JC. State of the science in health professional education: effective feedback. Medical education 2010 Jan;44(1):101-108.
(10) Nederhand ML, Tabbers HK, Splinter TAW, Rikers RMJP. The Effect of Performance Standards and Medical Experience on Diagnostic Calibration Accuracy. Health professions education 2018 Dec;4(4):300-307.

title: Role of 7 Tesla MRI in surgical planning for patients with pharmacoresistant epilepsy: systematic review and meta-analysis
description:
Pharmacoresistant epilepsy affects approximately one-third of individuals with epilepsy and is associated with significant disability, reduced quality of life, and increased morbidity. For patients with pharmacoresistant epilepsy, surgery remains the most effective treatment option. Successful surgical intervention requires precise localization of the epileptogenic zone, where neuroimaging plays a crucial role. While lower-strength magnetic fields such as 1.5 Tesla (T) or 3T MRI are widely used, the majority of patients remain “MRI-negative,” which complicates surgical decision‑making and planning.

Ultra-high-field 7T MRI has emerged as a promising imaging modality due to its improved spatial resolution, higher signal‑to‑noise ratio, and increased sensitivity for detecting subtle structural lesions. With 7T MRI, the lesion‑detection rate increases by roughly 30% compared with lower‑field MRIs, and as 7T MRI becomes more accessible in clinical centers, understanding its added value in pre‑surgical evaluation is increasingly relevant.

This systematic review aims to comprehensively evaluate the role of 7T MRI in surgical planning for patients with pharmacoresistant epilepsy. Specifically, the review will assess the diagnostic yield of 7T MRI, its ability to detect previously unseen lesions compared with 1.5T and 3T MRI, its impact on surgical decision‑making, and its association with postsurgical outcomes, including seizure control. By synthesizing evidence from clinical trials, cohort studies, diagnostic accuracy studies, and case series, this review will provide a detailed summary of how 7T MRI influences the pre‑surgical workflow and overall patient management.

Expected outcomes of this review include:

- A clear understanding of the diagnostic advantages of 7T MRI relative to conventional MRI. 
- Insight into how frequently 7T findings change patient eligibility and surgical strategies.
- Evaluation of whether improved lesion detection correlates with better postoperative seizure outcomes.

By consolidating current evidence, this review aims to inform clinicians, imaging specialists, and surgical teams about the practical utility and clinical implications of integrating 7T MRI into the pre‑surgical evaluation of patients with pharmacoresistant epilepsy.

title: Diagnostic Methods for Rotator Cuff-Related Shoulder Pain in Clinical Trials: Protocol for Scoping Review
description:
Background
A significant portion of the world’s population will experience shoulder pain during their lifetime, with a median community prevalence of 16% (range 0.67 to 55.2%) (Lucas, van Doorn, Hegedus, Lewis, & van der Windt, 2022). Shoulder pain is the third leading cause of musculoskeletal pain presentations in primary healthcare settings (Urwin et al., 1998) with yearly incidence rates of pain ranging from 7.7 to 62 (median 37.8) per 1000 person (Lucas et al., 2022). Mismanagement of shoulder pain and broader musculoskeletal disorders can result in chronic conditions becoming costly for the patient and healthcare system (Eubank et al., 2016; Kuijpers, van Tulder, van der Heijden, Bouter, & van der Windt, 2006; Mäntyselkä, Kumpusalo, Ahonen, & Takala, 2002), potentially leading to unnecessary surgeries, delays in rehabilitation, and loss of function. 

 

Rotator cuff related shoulder pain (RCRSP) has the highest prevalence among all diagnoses of shoulder pain (Hodgetts & Walker, 2021). RCRSP is a non-specific term used to describe shoulder pain and impairment typically with shoulder abduction and external rotation (Lewis, 2016). The term is used after excluding specific pathologies of the shoulder such as sinister pathologies, referred pain, stiff shoulder or unstable shoulder. Recent evidence has stated structural changes such as acromiohumeral distance, acromial shape, scapular dyskinesis and rotator interval tendon thickness, are not associated with shoulder pain and functional deficit experienced by patients (Lo, van Griensven, & Lewis, 2022; S. Navarro-Ledesma, Struyf, Falla, & Luque-Suarez, 2019; Santiago Navarro-Ledesma et al., 2017). Without definitive structural changes, it is challenging to diagnose patients with RCRSP and to identify the cause of shoulder pain. 

 

Currently there are no universally recognised diagnostic standards for RCRSP (Dinnes, Loveman, McIntyre, & Waugh, 2003). The lack of standardised diagnostic criteria could lead to non-evidence-based diagnosis and intervention (Desmeules et al., 2025). There is a high percentage of disagreement on interpretation of special orthopaedic tests and imaging between experienced professionals, revealing poor inter-rater reliability (Barreto, Braman, Ludewig, Ribeiro, & Camargo, 2019; Cadogan, Laslett, Hing, McNair, & Williams, 2011). Poor specificity and anatomical validity of special orthopaedic tests also contribute to nonconsensual diagnosis of RCRSP, mainly due to the complexity of shoulder structures (Boettcher, Ginn, & Cathers, 2009). A systematic review concluded that the diagnostic accuracy of special orthopaedic tests for shoulder pain was limited, and questioned the utility in differentially diagnosing pathologies of the shoulder (Hegedus et al., 2008). Salamh and Lewis (2020) have since argued that if special orthopaedic tests are unable to identify pathological structures, their primary role becomes provocation of shoulder symptoms during physiological movement testing, functional testing, or activity testing. In such case, special orthopaedic tests do not add any further value to the clinical picture, rendering them pain provocation tests. However, researchers and clinicians continue to use and recommend special orthopaedic tests to diagnose RCRSP (Desmeules et al., 2025; Green, Keren, F., & and Perrott, 2008; Lädermann et al., 2021). A clinical practice guideline released in 2025 lists several special orthopaedic tests that can be performed to rule in or out rotator cuff tendinopathy (Desmeules et al., 2025). Additionally, a recent Delphi study has proposed 18 clinical descriptors to be used as a standardised approach to diagnosing RCRSP, which does not include special orthopaedic tests (Requejo-Salinas et al., 2022). This adds to the confusion and complexity of diagnosing shoulder pain pathologies. Overall, concerns remain on the clinical utility of diagnostic methods of RCRSP, leading to a lack of agreement in clinical practice and guidelines. 

Significance of the Review 
Diagnosis plays an important role in making treatment decisions for RCRSP. Missed or inaccurate diagnosis can result in delayed treatment and poorer prognosis, which increases the economic burden for each patient up to AUD $56.92/day (Marks, Comans, Bisset, & Scuffham, 2016). Therefore, an accurate and early diagnosis of RCRSP is crucial for providing high-value care. However, a consensus on standardised criteria to confirm a diagnosis of RCRSP has not been met. There continues to be variability within the literature of what clinical tests and/or symptoms descriptors should be used, or whether imaging can play a role in confirming a diagnosis of RCRSP. To contribute to the existing literature on the topic, this proposed scoping review will map and summarise the criteria used to confirm a diagnosis of RCRSP in existing clinical trials.

title: Artificial intelligence for sports and musculoskeletal injury self-triage: a scoping review
description:
Artificial intelligence (AI) tools, including large language models such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini, as well as AI-powered symptom checkers, are increasingly accessible to the public through smartphones and web browsers. Recreational and amateur athletes, and physically active individuals, may use these tools for first-response injury advice, self-triage, or to inform decisions about whether to seek urgent medical assessment. The safety implications of such use depend partly on whether AI tools can reliably identify serious musculoskeletal (MSK) and sports injury presentations containing clinical red flags, such as suspected compartment syndrome, cauda equina syndrome, septic joint, fracture, or vascular compromise. Preliminary searching suggests that no scoping review has specifically mapped the evidence relating to AI use for sports and MSK injury self-triage, AI triage performance in this context, and AI recognition of red-flag MSK and sports injury presentations.

The objective of this scoping review is to map and characterise the existing evidence on the use, performance, and patient safety implications of user-facing AI tools for sports and MSK injury self-triage. Specifically, the review will examine which types of AI tools have been studied, what user behaviours and levels of trust have been reported, what is known about the accuracy and safety of AI-generated triage advice, how effectively AI tools recognise clinical red flags in MSK presentations, and what patient safety concerns or implementation recommendations have been described.

This scoping review will follow JBI methodology and will be reported in accordance with PRISMA-ScR. The PCC framework is defined as follows: Population — recreational and amateur athletes, physically active individuals, and simulated sports or MSK injury vignette studies relevant to non-professional users; Concept — user-facing AI tools for injury advice, self-triage, triage performance, red-flag recognition, and patient safety; Context — sports medicine, MSK injury, digital health, and community or university sport settings. Eligible sources will include empirical studies, vignette-based evaluations, surveys, qualitative studies, mixed-methods studies, diagnostic or triage accuracy studies, and relevant evidence syntheses evaluating user-facing AI tools for sports or MSK injury advice, self-triage, triage performance, red-flag recognition, or patient safety. Opinion pieces, editorials, commentaries, commercial webpages, and studies without primary or synthesised evidence will be excluded.

Six databases will be searched from inception to the date of final search: PubMed, EMBASE, CINAHL, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, and Scopus. Reference lists of included studies will also be screened. Two reviewers will independently screen titles/abstracts and full texts against predefined eligibility criteria, with disagreements resolved through discussion and, where necessary, consultation with a third reviewer. Data will be charted using a piloted standardised form covering study characteristics, AI tool characteristics, population or vignette type, injury domain, triage or safety outcomes, red-flag recognition, and key findings relevant to the review question. Findings will be synthesised descriptively and presented in narrative, tabular, and/or diagrammatic formats. Formal critical appraisal will not be undertaken, as the aim is to map the extent, range, and nature of the evidence rather than to produce pooled estimates of effectiveness or diagnostic accuracy. The review is expected to provide a structured map of the current evidence base, identify key research gaps, and inform subsequent empirical work on athlete use of AI and AI red-flag recognition in sports injury presentations.

title: In-Vivo Confocal Microscopy in the Diagnosis and Management of Ocular Surface Squamous Neoplasia: A Scoping Review
description:
Purpose:
Ocular Surface Squamous Neoplasia (OSSN) encompasses a spectrum of premalignant and malignant epithelial lesions of the conjunctiva and cornea. Early and accurate diagnosis is essential for effective management and prevention of recurrence. In-vivo confocal microscopy (IVCM) has emerged as a promising, noninvasive imaging tool that provides real-time, high-resolution visualization of the ocular surface at the cellular level. Despite growing interest, the literature on IVCM’s diagnostic accuracy, characteristic imaging features, and clinical utility in OSSN remains fragmented.

This scoping review aims to systematically identify, chart, and synthesize the existing evidence on the application of IVCM in OSSN. It will examine how IVCM has been used to detect, characterize, and monitor OSSN lesions; assess correlations between IVCM and histopathology; and explore its integration with complementary imaging modalities such as optical coherence tomography (OCT) and ultrasound biomicroscopy (UBM). The review will also map methodological limitations and research gaps to inform future clinical and technological advancements in ocular oncology imaging.

Expected Outcomes:
The review will produce a comprehensive summary of current knowledge on the diagnostic and monitoring role of IVCM in OSSN. It will:

Identify characteristic IVCM features associated with various OSSN grades.

Evaluate the strengths, limitations, and diagnostic accuracy of IVCM compared to standard histopathology.

Highlight how IVCM has been applied in monitoring treatment response and disease recurrence.

Identify knowledge gaps and propose directions for future studies, including the potential role of artificial intelligence in automating IVCM image analysis.

Overall, this review will serve as a foundational reference for clinicians and researchers, clarifying the present and potential roles of IVCM in OSSN diagnosis and management, and guiding the development of noninvasive, multimodal imaging approaches in ocular surface oncology.

title: Diagnostic performance of urinary biomarkers in reducing unnecessary prostate biopsies in men with suspected prostate cancer: a scoping review
description:
: Prostate cancer (PCa) is the second most common malignancy in men worldwide and one of the leading causes of male cancer-related morbidity and mortality. Prostate-specific antigen (PSA) remains the principal initial screening tool, but its low specificity leads to a high number of prostate biopsies in men without clinically significant disease, with the consequent risk of procedure-related complications (infection, sepsis, bleeding). Given this scenario, various complementary risk-stratification strategies have emerged, including multiparametric magnetic resonance imaging and, more accessibly, non-invasive urinary biomarkers such as prostate cancer antigen 3 (PCA3), the ExoDx Prostate IntelliScore (EPI), and SelectMDx, aimed at reducing unnecessary biopsies without compromising the detection of clinically relevant disease.
Objective: To map and synthesise the available scientific evidence on the diagnostic performance, clinical utility and limitations of urinary biomarkers (PCA3, ExoDx/IntelliScore, SelectMDx and the Michigan Prostate Score (MiPS)) in reducing unnecessary prostate biopsies in adult men with suspected prostate cancer.
Methodology: A scoping review of original articles, diagnostic accuracy studies, clinical utility studies and systematic reviews published in databases such as PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science and Bireme. The search strategy will use MeSH/DeCS terms and keywords associated with urinary biomarkers, prostate cancer and prostate biopsy.

title: Diagnostic accuracy of chest X-ray for lung cancer in symptomatic adults > 40 years
description:
Chest X-ray remains the most commonly ordered imaging test for adults who present with respiratory symptoms in primary and secondary care. Despite its availability and low radiation dose, concerns persist that CXR misses early lung cancers leading to diagnostic delay and poorer outcomes. Conversely, over-reliance on CXR abnormalities can cause unnecessary CT scanning. Therefore, a clear and up-to-date estimate of CXR diagnostic accuracy is therefore essential for clinicians and guideline developers.

Purpose:
To determine the accuracy of chest X-ray for detecting lung cancer in symptomatic adults > 40 years, using CT or CT-confirmed histology as the reference standard.

Methods:
MEDLINE, Embase and Scopus will be searched from inception to 3 Jun 2025. Two reviewers will independently screen titles and abstracts, assess full texts, and extract data. Risk of bias will be appraised with QUADAS-2. If four or more homogeneous studies are identified, a bivariate random-effects meta-analysis will estimate pooled sensitivity and specificity; otherwise findings will be synthesized narratively.

Expected outcomes:
The review will provide pooled or best available accuracy estimates.

title: Diagnostic Accuracy of Generative and Multimodal Artificial Intelligence Models in Chest Radiograph Interpretation: A Systematic Review and Exploratory Bivariate Hierarchical Meta-analysis
description:
This registration covers the systematic review and meta-analysis of the diagnostic performance of Generative AI (Large Language Models) and Multimodal AI (Vision-Language Models) in interpreting chest radiographs.

Purpose:
The primary goal is to evaluate the sensitivity and specificity of these models compared to human radiologists or clinical reference standards. We focus on common thoracic pathologies, including pneumonia, pneumothorax, and tuberculosis, providing an evidence-based synthesis of current GenAI capabilities in medical imaging.

Methodology:
Following PRISMA-DTA guidelines, we searched major medical databases (PubMed, SciELO, BVS) to identify relevant diagnostic studies. Data extraction focused on raw 2x2 contingency tables. We employed a bivariate hierarchical random-effects model (Reitsma et al.) estimated by Restricted Maximum Likelihood (REML) to calculate summary estimates and generate SROC curves, accounting for the correlation between sensitivity and specificity.

Expected Outcomes:
The study provides a comprehensive overview of the current diagnostic accuracy of LLMs and VLMs in radiology, identifying strengths in specific diagnostic tasks and highlighting methodological gaps for future research. All source code, raw data, and analytical pipelines used for these findings are hosted in our GitHub repository (https://github.com/Borghi2000/metaanalysis) to ensure full transparency and scientific reproducibility.

title: Evaluating the Diagnostic Accuracy and Integration Potential of Multiple Artificial Intelligence Models in Medicine Ward Patients: A Multi-Hospital Pilot Study in Pakistan

title: Diagnostic Accuracy of Clinical Assessment, Imaging, and Diagnostic Procedures for Injuries Requiring Repair After Penetrating Abdominal Trauma: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
description:
This project will be a systematic review and meta-analysis of diagnostic test accuracy studies evaluating clinical assessment, imaging, and diagnostic procedures for penetrating abdominal trauma. The purpose will be to estimate how accurately commonly used diagnostic approaches identify injuries requiring therapeutic surgical or endovascular repair, a clinically relevant target condition that is distinct from peritoneal violation, radiographic injury, any organ injury, or non-therapeutic laparotomy.

Eligible studies will include patients with penetrating abdominal, thoracoabdominal, flank, or back trauma and will need to provide sufficient data to construct 2 × 2 diagnostic accuracy tables for at least one eligible index test. Index tests will include initial clinical assessment, individual clinical findings, serial clinical examination, FAST or ultrasonography, plain radiography, CT, local wound exploration, diagnostic laparoscopy, and diagnostic peritoneal lavage.

MEDLINE, Embase, and CENTRAL will be searched from inception to present date. Two reviewers will independently screen studies, extract study characteristics and diagnostic accuracy data, and assess risk of bias using QUADAS-2. The reference standard will be injury requiring therapeutic surgical or endovascular repair, determined by operative findings, endovascular intervention, therapeutic laparoscopy, or uneventful clinical observation or follow-up among patients managed nonoperatively.

For each index test, sensitivity, specificity, likelihood ratios, and diagnostic odds ratios will be calculated when data permit. Pooled sensitivity and specificity will be estimated using bivariate random-effects models when studies are sufficiently comparable. Subgroup analyses and meta-regression will explore variation by injury mechanism, particularly stab wounds versus gunshot wounds, where data permit. Certainty of evidence for key comparisons will be assessed using GRADE for diagnostic tests and strategies.

The expected outcome will be a clinically interpretable synthesis of the diagnostic evidence supporting selective management of penetrating abdominal trauma. The review will clarify which tests and findings are most useful for identifying repair-requiring injury, which approaches may support safe nonoperative management in selected patients, and where important uncertainty remains.

title: Neuropsychologycal Assessment Through Videoconferencing
description: With the emergence of COVID-19, significant changes have occurred in the day-to-day functioning of society around the world. Psychologists had to adapt their interventions to a new format, using web-based videoconferencing to assess and intervene with their patients. title: Diagnostic accuracy of cone-beam computed tomography in detecting root perforations: a systematic review and meta analysis
description:
Background and Rationale
Endodontic root perforations represent a severe iatrogenic or pathological complication characterized by an unnatural communication between the aseptic root canal system and the highly vascularized periodontal apparatus. If not immediately diagnosed and repaired, these defects rapidly precipitate microbial colonization, localized inflammatory responses, and crestal bone loss, ultimately jeopardizing the survival of the tooth. While conventional two-dimensional (2D) periapical radiography is the standard frontline diagnostic tool, it is intrinsically constrained by anatomical superimposition, often rendering perforations on the buccal or lingual root surfaces imperceptible. Although Cone-Beam Computed Tomography (CBCT) has revolutionized three-dimensional maxillofacial imaging, its specific diagnostic test accuracy (DTA) for detecting root perforations remains inconsistently reported in the literature, particularly regarding the profound confounding variables of spatial resolution and beam-hardening artifacts caused by intracanal radiopacities.

Purpose and Objectives
The primary objective of this systematic review is to comprehensively aggregate, synthesize, and critically evaluate the diagnostic test accuracy (Sensitivity and Specificity) of CBCT specifically for the detection of endodontic root perforations.

The secondary objectives are to determine how diagnostic accuracy is modulated by specific technical and clinical parameters, namely:

The obturation status of the root canal system (evaluating the detrimental impact of photon starvation and beam-hardening artifacts caused by gutta-percha, heavy-metal sealers, and metallic posts).

The spatial resolution of the CBCT scan (comparing high-resolution versus low-resolution voxel sizes).

The anatomical localization of the defect (e.g., furcal, lateral, strip, or apical perforations).

The comparative accuracy of CBCT against alternative diagnostic modalities, specifically Electronic Apex Locators (EALs) and digital periapical radiography.

Methodological Scope
To ensure strict statistical homogeneity, this review utilizes a specialized PIRD (Population, Index test, Reference standard, Diagnosis of interest) framework. The analysis will be strictly limited to primary diagnostic accuracy studies utilizing extracted permanent human teeth (in vitro and ex vivo laboratory models) validated by an absolute, independent physical reference standard (e.g., digital calipers or stereomicroscopy). Continuous linear measurement studies and animal models are explicitly excluded. The methodological quality and external applicability of the included literature will be independently appraised utilizing the QUADAS-2 (Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies) framework.

Expected Outcomes and Clinical Significance
The anticipated outcome of this systematic review is the establishment of the first definitive, evidence-based clinical imaging guidelines for the detection of root perforations.

This project is expected to demonstrate that while CBCT significantly outperforms 2D radiography in anatomical "blind spots," its application must be highly strategic. We anticipate the data will formulate the following clinical directives:

For non-obturated teeth: Low-resolution CBCT is highly efficacious and should be utilized to strictly adhere to the ALARA (As Low As Reasonably Achievable) radiation dosimetry principle.

For obturated teeth: The expected data will likely prove that CBCT accuracy is severely compromised by artifact scatter, necessitating either high-resolution scanning protocols to mitigate partial volume averaging, or a multimodal diagnostic approach prioritizing radiation-free Electronic Apex Locators (EALs) and eccentric multi-angle periapical radiography during active retreatment procedures.

title: Characterization of strategies for teaching Nursing Diagnoses: a scoping review
description:
Purpose: To map the characteristics of strategies employed in teaching nursing diagnoses within undergraduate nursing programs
Methods: A scoping review was conducted following JBI methodology. The literature search was in March 2025, across seven data bases. Twenty-nine studies published between 1993 and 2024 were included. Results were systematically presented in tables and narratively.
Findings: The strategies identified include simulation (n=7), virtual tools (n=6), educational programs (n=6), group work (n=3), case studies (n=3), and other methods (n=4) such as board game, outcome present state test model, guided visual metaphorical strategy and arch method. Simulation and virtual tools showed consistent positive results in diagnostic reasoning, documentation, and student engagement.
Conclusions: The findings highlight the predominance of active, student-centred methodologies that foster critical thinking and reflective practice. These strategies enhance diagnostic competence and better prepare students for clinical decision-making. The review underscores the need for standardized evaluation tools and longitudinal research to assess the sustainability and scalability of these approaches across diverse educational contexts.
Implications for nursing practice: Incorporating these strategies into undergraduate curricula can better prepare nursing students for clinical decision-making, improve diagnostic accuracy, enhance patient safety, and foster reflective, evidence-based practice.
