title: Protocol: ChatGPT as the New Second Opinion? Patient Use of General-Purpose AI to Interpret Raw Radiology Images and Its Legal Implications — A Scoping Review
description:
Purpose: This research project aims to map and synthesise the emerging evidence on how patients and healthcare consumers use ChatGPT and other multimodal large language models (LLMs) to interpret raw radiology images such as X-rays, CT, or MRI scans. While clinicians have long used AI-enabled software for image analysis under regulated “Software as a Medical Device” (SaMD) frameworks, the recent release of consumer-facing vision-enabled models has enabled patients to upload their own images and seek informal second opinions outside of clinical supervision.
This development introduces both opportunities (greater accessibility, patient empowerment, potential for early health-seeking) and risks (misdiagnosis, false reassurance, unnecessary alarm, data privacy breaches, and regulatory non-compliance). Moreover, it raises unresolved questions about liability and regulation: if patients act on AI-generated interpretations, who is responsible—the patient, the clinician, the AI developer, or the platform? A scoping review is therefore timely to clarify what is known, identify research gaps, and examine the evolving medico-legal frameworks that govern patient use of such tools.

Objectives: To identify and categorise all published and grey literature on patient or consumer use of general-purpose AI for raw radiology image interpretation. To describe the range of tasks and modalities studied (e.g., chest radiography, CT brain, MRI spine, mammography). To assess outcomes reported, including diagnostic accuracy, failure modes, safety concerns, and patient experiences (trust, anxiety, behaviour change). To examine the legal and regulatory implications, including medical device classification, malpractice and product liability, and data protection requirements (HIPAA, GDPR, EU AI Act, MHRA). To generate a conceptual framework linking clinical outcomes with regulatory risk and to highlight gaps in research, policy, and practice.

Methods: The review will follow the PRISMA-ScR and Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology for scoping reviews. Searches will be conducted across biomedical, technical, and legal databases (PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, HeinOnline, SSRN, LexisNexis), as well as grey literature sources (preprints, regulator white papers, conference abstracts).
Two reviewers will independently screen, extract, and chart data. Extracted variables will include study design, imaging modality, AI model/version, input format (e.g., DICOM vs screenshot), diagnostic performance, safety signals, patient outcomes, and legal/regulatory considerations. Findings will be synthesised narratively, with evidence maps and comparative legal tables.

Expected Outcomes: 1. Evidence Map: A comprehensive overview of empirical studies and reports on patient-facing raw-image interpretation using ChatGPT/LLMs. 2. Performance and Risk Profile: Summary of diagnostic accuracy, common error types, and safety concerns relevant to patient use. 3. Regulatory Synthesis: Comparative analysis of liability, privacy, and device regulation frameworks in the UK, EU, and US. 4. Conceptual Framework: An integrated map linking clinical benefits/risks with regulatory responsibilities and liability allocation. 5. Policy Agenda: Practical recommendations for future empirical research, clinician guidance when patients present AI outputs, and policy directions for regulators and healthcare organisations.

Significance: This will be the first scoping review to focus on patient use of multimodal LLMs for raw radiology image interpretation, situating technical performance within a legal and regulatory context. By bridging the clinical, technical, and legal perspectives, the project will provide a foundational reference for radiologists, policymakers, ethicists, and AI developers. Its outputs will help shape safe, equitable, and legally robust approaches to integrating generative AI into patient interactions with medical imaging.

title: Serum LDH in preeclampsia: is it a useful biomarker? A meta-analysis
description:
Protocol and registration
The present meta-analysis will be designed according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. The study will be based in aggregated data that have been already published in the international literature. Patient consent and institutional review board approval will not be retrieved as they are not required in this type of studies. 
Types of studies and patients
The eligibility criteria for the inclusion of studies will be predetermined. Observational studies that assess differences in serum LDH levels among women with hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (gestational hypertension, preeclampsia, eclampsia, HELLP syndrome) and healthy controls will be considered eligible for inclusion. Small case series (<10 patients), case reports, conference proceedings and animal studies will be excluded from the present systematic review. Studies that involve pregnant women with comorbidities will be excluded from the present systematic review. The control group will consist of healthy pregnant women, without evidence of any gestational complication. Studies will not be excluded based on preeclampsia definition, since no date restrictions are applied.
Information sources and search methods
We will use the Medline (1966–2021), Scopus (2004–2021), Clinicaltrials.gov (2008–2021), EMBASE (1980-2021), Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials CENTRAL (1999-2021) and Google Scholar (2004-2021) databases in our primary search along with the reference lists of electronically retrieved full-text papers. The date of our last search will be set at March 18, 2021. Our search strategy included the text words “lactate dehydrogenase; LDH; preeclampsia; gestational hypertension; HELLP”.
Studies will be selected in three consecutive stages. Following deduplication, the titles and abstracts of all electronic articles will be screened independently by three authors (MP, VP and SS) to assess their eligibility. The decision for inclusion of studies in the present meta-analysis will be taken after retrieving and reviewing the full version of articles that will be considered as potentially eligible. Discrepancies that will arise in this latter stage will be resolved by consensus from all authors.
Predefined outcomes
Outcome measures will be predefined during the design of the present systematic review. Data extraction will be performed using a modified data form that was based in Cochrane`s data collection form for intervention reviews for RCTs and non-RCTs 16. Investigated outcomes will be predetermined based in our previous systematic review that examined the role of serum uric acid as a predictive factor of preeclampsia. Briefly, the main outcome of interest will be the comparison of serum uric acid levels among preeclamptic and healthy pregnant women in all gestational trimesters. 
The prognostic role of uric acid isplanned to be evaluated by comparing its levels among women with mild and severe preeclampsia, as well as with eclampsia and HELLP (hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes and low platelet count) syndrome. The diagnostic accuracy of serum uric acid in terms of predicting adverse perinatal outcomes (rate of cesarean section, fetal growth restriction, low birth weight, preterm birth, 5’ Apgar score <7, fetal or neonatal death) will be also evaluated. 
Assessment of risk of bias and quality of evidence
The methodological quality of the included studies will be assessed by two independent reviewers (V.P and S.S.) using the Newcastle Ottawa scale. The scale incorporates domains that include assessment of selection of study groups, comparability of groups and methods ascertainment of the outcome of interest. A point is awarded in a 9-point based system. For the purposes of the present systematic review the two points that are awarded for comparability of groups will refer to differences in baseline gestational age at assessment of serum LDH and in maternal age.
Quality of evidence will be evaluated under the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) framework, ranging from very low to high. More specifically, credibility of evidence will be assessed by taking into account the following domains: study limitations, directness, consistency, precision and publication bias. In particular, study limitations will be evaluated based on risk of bias assessments (NOS score), while directness will be judged using the PICOS (population, intervention, comparison, outcome, study type) approach. To assess consistency and precision, clinically important effects will be defined after determining the 95% CI of individual studies. In this context, consistency will refer to the agreement of 95% confidence and prediction intervals for each outcome in relation to clinically relevant effects, while precision assessment will be made by taking into account whether 95% CI extended into the range of equivalence.
Statistical analysis
Statistical meta-analysis will be performed with RStudio using the meta and metafor functions (RStudio Team (2015). RStudio: Integrated Development for R. RStudio, Inc., Boston, MA URL http://www.rstudio.com/). Statistical heterogeneity will not be considered during the evaluation of the appropriate model of statistical analysis as the anticipated methodological heterogeneity of included studies is anticipated to not leave space for assumption of comparable effect sizes among studies included in the meta-analysis. Confidence intervals will be set at 95%. We will calculate pooled risk ratios mean differences (MD) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) with the Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman instead of the traditional Dersimonian-Laird random effects model analysis (REM). The decision to proceed with this type of analysis was taken after taking into consideration recent reports that support its superiority compared to the Dersimonian-Laird model when comparing studies of varying sample sizes and between-study heterogeneity. 
Subgroup analysis will be conducted on the basis of pregnancy trimester (1st, 2nd or 3rd), preeclampsia onset (early or late), severity (mild or severe) and complications (eclampsia and HELLP syndrome). Residual heterogeneity will be explored by conducting meta-regression analysis taking into account the following parameters: year of publication, sample size (using a cut-off of 100 patients in at least one arm of the analysis), region (stratified in North America, Europe and other countries), Newcastle-Ottawa Scale score, study design, type of sample and definition of preeclampsia. Meta-regression will not be performed for covariate levels with <3 studies. Publication bias will be assessed by examining the possibility of small-study effects through the visual inspection of funnel plots. The asymmetry of funnel plots will be statistically evaluated using the Egger’s regression and Begg-Mazumdar’s rank correlation tests. Publication bias will be evaluated by examining the potential presence of small-study effects through the visual inspection of funnel plots.
Prediction intervals
Prediction intervals (PI) wll be calculated as well, using the meta function in RStudio, to evaluate the estimated effect that is expected to be seen by future studies in the field. The estimation of prediction intervals takes into account the inter-study variation of the results and express the existing heterogeneity at the same scale as the examined outcome. 
Trial sequential analysis
To evaluate the information size, we will perform trial sequential analysis (TSA) which permits investigation of the type I error in the aggregated result of meta-analyses performed for primary outcomes that were predefined in the present meta-analysis. A minimum of 3 studies will be considered as appropriate to perform the analysis. Repeated significance testing increases the risk of type I error in meta-analyses and TSA has the ability to re-adjust the desired significance level by using the O` Brien-Flemming a-spending function. Therefore, during TSA sequential interim analyses are performed that permit investigation of the impact of each study in the overall findings of the meta-analysis. The risk for type I errors was set at 5% and for type II errors at 20%. The TSA analysis was performed using the TSA v. 0.9.5.10 Beta software (http://www.ctu.dk/tsa/).

title: Diagnostic accuracy of D-dimer testing for splanchnic vein thrombosis: a systematic review
description: D-dimer testing is integral to the diagnostic algorithm for deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism. title: Protocol for Systematic Review of Rehabilitation Management for Ankle Impingement Syndrome: Evidence Synthesis and Clinical Implications from Diagnosis to Prevention
description:
Ankle Impingement Syndrome (AIS) affects approximately 40% of individuals after ankle sprain and often leads to chronic pain and functional limitation, while evidence-based rehabilitation pathways for AIS remain fragmented in clinical practice. This systematic review aims to systematically synthesize the latest clinical evidence and establish an evidence-based rehabilitation framework for AIS from diagnosis to prevention.
Review Objective and Research Questions
Primary Objective: To systematically evaluate the latest evidence on AIS rehabilitation management from diagnosis to prevention.
Secondary Objectives:
To assess the diagnostic accuracy of different imaging modalities for various AIS subtypes (anterior/posterior/lateral).
To compare the short-term and long-term efficacy of non-operative rehabilitation interventions (e.g., exercise therapy, PRP injection, balance training) for AIS in terms of pain relief, functional improvement and recurrence reduction.
To establish population-tailored rehabilitation protocols for AIS high-risk groups (e.g., elite athletes, ballet dancers, elderly adults).
To evaluate the public health value and application potential of AIS prevention strategies in different populations.
Expected Outcomes
A comprehensive evidence synthesis of AIS rehabilitation management, clarifying the diagnostic performance of advanced imaging techniques (AI-assisted MRI, dynamic ultrasound) and the efficacy of core non-operative interventions.
An evidence-based three-pillar framework for AIS management (precision diagnosis, effective intervention, population-tailored protocols) to guide clinical practice.
Population-specific rehabilitation and prevention recommendations for AIS, providing evidence-based tools for public health chronic pain control and sports-related injury prevention.
Identification of existing evidence gaps in AIS rehabilitation research, and proposal of key directions for future high-quality clinical studies.

title: The EVIDENCE Framework: A Pre‑registered Protocol for Detecting and Preventing Evidence Recycling in AI‑Assisted Systematic Reviews and Meta‑Analyses
description:
Purpose: The EVIDENCE Framework is an eight domain editorial checklist (Evaluation of originality, Verification of sources, Integrity in synthesis, Diversity of data, Ethical AI use, Novel contribution, Contextual relevance, Editorial responsibility) designed to detect evidence recycling – the AI driven paraphrasing of existing research findings that creates an illusion of novel evidence without new data. This pre registered protocol outlines the prospective validation of the framework.
Methods: We will conduct a diagnostic accuracy study using 100 systematic reviews or meta analyses that declared use of generative AI. Two independent reviewers will apply the EVIDENCE Framework (index test) blinded to a reference standard. The reference standard consists of a three expert panel manually auditing all sources for evidence recycling using semantic similarity tools. Primary outcomes are sensitivity, specificity and inter rater reliability (Cohen’s κ). Secondary outcomes include feasibility (median completion time) and positive/negative predictive values.
Expected outcomes: We anticipate that the EVIDENCE Framework will demonstrate high sensitivity (>80%) and substantial inter rater reliability (κ > 0.7) for detecting evidence recycling. The protocol includes pre specified editorial action thresholds (e.g., any “Not met” on Verification of sources triggers mandatory dependency matrix submission). Results will inform journal policies on AI assisted evidence synthesis.
Data sharing: De identified dependency matrices, EVIDENCE scores and reference standard judgments will be deposited on OSF with a CC BY license upon publication.

title: Objective assessment of motor competence in developmental coordination disorder: A systematic review of wearable technologies
description:
1. Background and Rationale
Developmental Coordination Disorder (DCD) is a highly prevalent neurodevelopmental condition characterized by persistent deficits in the execution and acquisition of coordinated motor skills. While traditionally viewed through a pediatric lens, mounting clinical evidence recognizes DCD as a lifelong condition. The motor control deficits observed in early childhood frequently persist into adolescence and adulthood, acting as a primary catalyst for a negative, lifelong trajectory of physical inactivity, cardiometabolic risk, and secondary psychosocial issues.

Despite the critical need for accurate identification and monitoring across the lifespan, current assessments of DCD rely heavily on standardized behavioral tests (e.g., the MABC-2 for children) or subjective self-report questionnaires (for adults). While clinically established, these tools are inherently restricted by subjective observer bias, episodic clinic-based testing, and a lack of resolution required to detect subtle, underlying neuromuscular control deficits. Consequently, many individuals with marginal or "invisible" DCD—both children missing early intervention windows and adults passing unacknowledged genetic risks to their children—remain underdiagnosed.

With the rapid advancement of micro-electro-mechanical systems (MEMS) and machine learning, wearable technologies (e.g., triaxial accelerometers, IMUs) present a transformative opportunity to shift from subjective observation to objective quantification. By capturing high-frequency physical time-series data in both structured and natural environments, researchers can extract advanced kinematic and non-linear dynamic features to precisely quantify motor chaos, complexity, and competence. However, the application of these "digital phenotypes" in DCD research remains highly fragmented across age groups and scientific disciplines.

2. Purpose of the Review
The primary purpose of this systematic review is to comprehensively map, synthesize, and evaluate the current landscape of wearable technology applications for the objective assessment of motor competence in individuals with DCD and related motor deficits across the lifespan.

Specifically, this review aims to:
(1) Synthesize Methodological Approaches: Detail the types of wearable hardware utilized, anatomical placement strategies, and the specific motor tasks assessed (ranging from structured clinical assessments to unconstrained free-living monitoring) across different age cohorts.
(2) Evaluate Feature Extraction Techniques: Investigate how raw sensor signals are processed to quantify motor competence, transitioning from traditional macro-level activity metrics to advanced micro-kinematic and non-linear dynamic algorithms.
(3) Assess Clinical Validity and Diagnostic Efficacy: Determine the concurrent validity between sensor-derived digital biomarkers and traditional clinical gold standards, and evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of these technologies in differentiating individuals with motor deficits from typically developing peers or healthy adults.

3. Methodology 
Following PRISMA guidelines, a systematic search will be conducted across major electronic databases encompassing medicine, sports science, and engineering (e.g., PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, IEEE Xplore, SPORTDiscus). The review will include empirical studies that utilize wearable sensors to capture objective motor data in individuals—including children, adolescents, and adults—formally diagnosed with DCD, probable DCD (pDCD), or presenting with idiopathic motor coordination deficits. To ensure pathological specificity, studies focusing on motor deficits secondary to clear neurological lesions, progressive structural anomalies, or profound intellectual disabilities (e.g., Cerebral Palsy, acquired brain injury, Parkinson's disease) will be strictly excluded.

4. Expected outcomes and significance
This systematic review is expected to yield several critical outcomes that will drive future research and clinical practice:
(1) Establishment of Lifespan "Digital Biomarkers": The review will identify which specific kinematic or non-linear dynamic features derived from wearables are the most sensitive and robust indicators of motor competence deficits across different developmental stages.
(2) Standardization of Protocols: By highlighting current methodological discrepancies, the review will provide evidence-based recommendations for optimal sensor placement, sampling frequencies, and algorithmic pipelines tailored to both pediatric and adult populations.
(3) Paradigm Shift in Assessment: The findings will provide the theoretical and technological foundation for transitioning DCD screening from a subjective, clinic-based model to an objective, continuous, and highly scalable "digital diagnosis" framework suitable for real-world environments.

Ultimately, this review will consolidate the existing evidence base, justifying the integration of digital phenotyping into the standard assessment of motor competence, and directly informing the development of next-generation digital therapeutics and familial/lifespan screening systems for motor development.

title: Testing Human Anxiety Associations of Genes Previously Implicated by Mouse Anxiety Models
description:
Anxiety disorders are some of the most common mental health disorders in the United States, with an estimated 31.1% of the population experiencing an anxiety disorder at some point in their life (National Institute of Mental Health, 2017). Some anxiety disorders, particularly generalized anxiety disorder (GAD), have been associated with the overuse of primary care medical services (Peter P. Roy-Byrne & Wayne Katon, 1997), but low rates of professional treatment, with only approximately half receiving professional help (Wang et al., 2005). 

Anxiety disorders are moderately heritable with an estimated 30-40% of phenotypic variance being caused by additive genetic variance based on twin studies (Hettema et al., 2001). However, genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have reported SNP heritabilities between 8% and 10% and identified numerous genome-wide significant associations with small effect sizes (Levey et al., 2020; Otowa et al., 2016), indicating that anxiety disorders are highly polygenic and genetic variance is made up of many common variants with small phenotypic effects. A more complete understanding of the genetics of anxiety disorders is needed in order to improve diagnostic accuracy, develop novel treatments, and clarify causes of these disorders.

Mouse models of anxiety-like behaviors have implicated hundreds of genes potentially related to different aspects of human anxiety, and are an appealing study system because of the well-characterized mouse genome, controlled experimental settings, and established paradigms of anxiety-like behaviors. Established behavioral paradigms used to model anxiety-like behavior in mice include the light-dark box, elevated plus-maze, open-field test, and the zero maze, among others. These tests have been used to evaluate the effectiveness of anti-anxiety drugs (anxiolytics) and to identify genes that are associated with anxiety-like behaviors (Fonken et al., 2016, Henderson et al., 2004, Heredia et al., 2013, Hovatta et al., 2005). Research by Philip et al. (2010) evaluated anxiety phenotypes across 63 BXD recombinant inbred strains and found that no strain consistently exhibited high or low anxiety-like behavior across a range of behavioral paradigms, raising questions about how different behavioral paradigms reflect genetic factors of anxiety.

We aim to investigate whether human orthologs of genes previously implicated in mouse anxiety-like behaviors also contribute to human anxiety phenotypes, and whether this relationship is affected by the human phenotype considered, or mouse behavior test or analysis conducted.

title: Post-traumatic stress disorder diagnostic accuracy rates in clinical settings: a systematic review and meta-analysis
description:
This project involves a completed systematic review and meta-analysis examining the diagnostic accuracy of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) in real-world clinical settings. Despite the availability of validated diagnostic instruments (e.g., CAPS-5, SCID-5, PCL-5), PTSD remains widely underdiagnosed or misdiagnosed across both primary care and specialized mental healthcare. This review synthesizes evidence from a broad range of peer-reviewed studies to evaluate how often PTSD is correctly identified by clinicians, what diagnostic tools are used or omitted, and how clinician-level factors (such as training, bias, and time constraints) and contextual barriers (such as comorbidities or limited access to mental health services) impact diagnostic outcomes.

The review follows PRISMA 2020 guidelines and includes both qualitative synthesis and a quantitative meta-analysis of diagnostic accuracy metrics using a random-effects model. Studies were identified through structured searches across major academic databases and AI-assisted search tools. Risk of bias was assessed using ROBINS-I, QUADAS-2, JBI, and GRADE, and all procedures were transparently documented and independently conducted by the author.

The expected outcome of this review is to provide clinicians, researchers, and policymakers with a clearer understanding of how PTSD is identified in everyday practice, where diagnostic gaps occur, and what systemic changes may improve diagnostic accuracy. The results aim to inform better clinical training, diagnostic protocols, and policy decisions surrounding trauma-informed care.

Upon publication of the final manuscript, all materials (including the protocol, data, and analysis code) will be shared openly via OSF in alignment with FAIR data principles.

title: Teledentistry for older adults in institutional and domestic care: A scoping review
description:
To map the evidence on teledentistry for older adults in institutional and domestic care and identify knowledge gaps for future research.
Older adults in long-term care often have limited access to dental services. Teledentistry, the remote delivery of oral healthcare through digital technologies, may address this gap, but evidence for geriatric populations remains fragmented.
Materials and methods: Following the Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and PRISMA-ScR guidelines, MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL and the Cochrane Library were searched, with grey literature (medRxiv) and manual screening. Eligible studies were empirical research of any design involving adults aged 60 years and older in long-term care. Data were synthesised descriptively, and study quality was appraised with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT).
Results: Of 6,577 records, 18 studies (published 2014–2025) were included. Most were small-scale pilot or descriptive studies, with one randomised controlled trial. Asynchronous methods (e.g. photographs) were more practical and less costly, synchronous approaches (video consultation) diagnostically stronger. Diagnostic accuracy was moderate to excellent, though studies reported problems such as poor lighting, lack of suction and inconsistent operator training. Barriers were equipment and training costs, unreliable connectivity, varying digital literacy among participants, and the need for trained on-site personnel; facilitators were mainly staff engagement and caregiver support. MMAT ratings were mostly positive.
Conclusion: Teledentistry is a feasible complementary model of care, but current evidence is limited and uneven. Synchronous and asynchronous approaches have complementary strengths. Evidence for domestic care remains scarce, and standardised outcomes are needed before firmer conclusions.

title: The role of artificial intelligence in neurodegenerative disorders detection and diagnosis: a systematic review
description:
Dementia represents a healthcare challenge, as pathological changes often emerge years before overt symptoms. Early manifestations such as Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) and Subjective Cognitive Decline (SCD) are critical transitional stages between normal aging and dementia. 
Thus, distinguishing these conditions (i.e. MCI, SCD) and whether they could evolve to dementia remains crucial. However, to date, the clinical tools available, chiefly among them neuroimaging and the neuropsychological assessment remain not always clearly interpretable and resource intensive as well. 
In recent years, Artificial Intelligence (AI), including Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL), has shown promising capabilities in enhancing early detection, predicting progression, and supporting differential diagnosis across neurodegenerative disorders.
This systematic review aims at synthesizing the current evidence on the extent to which AI-based approaches are being applied to improve diagnostic accuracy and prognostic assessment in dementia. A comprehensive literature search of studies published between 2015 and 2025 was carried out across major scientific databases following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, and studies were evaluated with respect to data modality, methodological rigor, performance metrics, and clinical applicability. 
The results highlight that AI models, particularly DL architectures applied to neuroimaging, electrophysiological signals, speech and language features, biomarker profiles, and digital behavioral data, consistently achieve high diagnostic accuracy for distinguishing MCI, Alzheimer’s disease, and healthy aging. Moreover, predictive models demonstrate potential in predicting conversion from MCI to dementia and in monitoring real-world cognitive and functional trajectories using wearable or smart-home technologies. However, the evidence also reveals substantial heterogeneity, limited external validation, and methodological inconsistencies that constrain clinical translation. 
In conclusion, this review highlights that AI is a rapidly evolving and promising tool for the early detection and monitoring of neurodegenerative disorders. Binding together the studies reported in this review, underscore the need for standardized pipelines, larger multicenter datasets, and explainable AI frameworks to support a real clinical implementation of this technology.

title: Advancing Cervical Cancer Screening: A Systematic Review of Traditional and Novel Screening Methods
description: This systematized review aims to evaluate the diagnostic performance, feasibility, and implementation potential of non-HPV-based screening methods for detecting precancerous cervical lesions (specifically cervical intraepithelial neoplasia, CIN) and cervical cancer. While HPV testing is the current primary screening method recommended in many guidelines, it is not universally accessible or effective in all populations, especially in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). Additionally, a subset of cervical cancers are HPV-negative, highlighting the need to evaluate complementary or alternative screening approaches. To address these gaps, this review focuses on alternative methods that do not rely on HPV detection. These include cytology-based methods (conventional and liquid-based), visual inspection techniques (e.g., VIA and VILI), protein biomarkers, host DNA methylation and miRNA markers, serum biomarkers, and AI-assisted or smartphone-based tools. The purpose of this review is to systematically compare non-HPV-based screening approaches by evaluating their diagnostic performance (e.g., sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, negative predictive value, and other reported accuracy measures), feasibility, and implementation across different healthcare settings, particularly in LMICs. Expected outcomes include a comprehensive synthesis of existing evidence, identification of knowledge gaps, and comparison of the strengths and limitations of each screening approach. The methodological quality of included studies will be assessed using the Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies-2 (QUADAS-2) tool. A meta-analysis may be conducted depending on the homogeneity of the included data. The findings are intended to support future research, clinical practice, and implementation strategies focused on improving early detection of cervical precancer, especially in under-resourced settings.

title: Novel Retinal Imaging Techniques in the Diagnosis and Clinical Management of Vitreoretinal Lymphoma: A Scoping Review
description:
NOTE ON REGISTRATION TIMING: This registration was created after the literature search and screening had already been conducted. It is registered not as a prospective pre-registration but as a transparency measure, to publicly document the eligibility criteria, search strategy, and data-charting plan actually used, consistent with open-science practice. All methodological decisions recorded here reflect those applied during the review; no criteria were altered retrospectively to match results obtained.

ABSTRACT: Vitreoretinal lymphoma (VRL) is a rare intraocular malignancy that frequently masquerades as chronic uveitis, delaying diagnosis and worsening prognosis given its strong association with primary CNS lymphoma. While multimodal imaging (conventional OCT, fundus photography, fluorescein/indocyanine green angiography, fundus autofluorescence) has a well-established, previously reviewed role in raising diagnostic suspicion, a newer generation of imaging and computational techniques — OCT angiography (OCTA), swept-source OCT, ultra-widefield imaging, adaptive optics, and AI/deep-learning-assisted image analysis — is increasingly being applied to VRL, without a systematic map of this evidence base. This scoping review systematically maps the extent, range, study designs, and reported clinical utility of these novel imaging techniques in VRL, following JBI scoping review methodology and PRISMA-ScR reporting standards.

RESEARCH QUESTION (PCC FRAMEWORK): What is the clinical utility and current research landscape of novel retinal imaging techniques for the diagnosis and management of vitreoretinal lymphoma?
- Population: Patients (any age) with confirmed or clinically suspected vitreoretinal lymphoma (primary or secondary; B-cell or T-cell subtype).
- Concept: Application of novel/emerging retinal imaging modalities (OCTA, swept-source OCT, ultra-widefield imaging, adaptive optics, AI/deep-learning-assisted analysis), distinct from established modalities (conventional OCT, fundus photography, FA, ICGA, FAF) used alone.
- Context: Diagnosis, differential diagnosis from uveitis mimickers, disease-activity monitoring, or treatment-response assessment, in any country, any year, with emphasis on recent research trends.

OBJECTIVES (scoping reviews are exploratory and do not test hypotheses):
1. Map the extent and type of evidence on novel retinal imaging techniques in VRL (by modality, year, country, study design, sample size).
2. Summarize reported diagnostic/clinical utility of each modality.
3. Identify how these techniques are used to differentiate VRL from uveitis mimickers and to monitor treatment response.
4. Identify evidence gaps to inform future primary research.

STUDY DESIGN: Scoping review, conducted per JBI methodology and reported per PRISMA-ScR. Not applicable: randomization, blinding, control groups (this is a literature-mapping exercise, not a primary study).

ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA:
Include — Human studies (case reports, case series, cohort, cross-sectional) reporting novel-modality (OCTA/SS-OCT/UWF/adaptive optics/AI-assisted) imaging findings in confirmed or suspected VRL, in English, any publication year.
Exclude — Animal/in-vitro studies; studies reporting only conventional OCT/FA/ICGA/FAF/fundus photography with no novel-modality component; studies focused solely on cytology/molecular diagnostics without an imaging component; conference abstracts without full text (excluded from primary charting and listed separately as grey literature).
(Full eligibility table is in the companion protocol document.)

INFORMATION SOURCES / SAMPLING PLAN: Databases searched — PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science Core Collection, Cochrane Library (CENTRAL). Supplementary sources — Google Scholar (first 200 results) and reference-list hand-searching of included studies and relevant narrative reviews. Three-step JBI search process: (1) initial limited search to identify key terms, (2) full search of all databases with the complete term set, (3) reference-list hand-searching of included studies and reviews. No date restriction was applied.

DATA CHARTING PLAN: A standardized charting form (piloted on 5 studies, refined iteratively) extracted: study identification (author, year, country, journal, funding); study design and sample size; population characteristics (VRL subtype, CNS involvement, prior treatment); imaging modality and device details; key reported findings and, where available, diagnostic accuracy metrics; clinical application (diagnosis / differential diagnosis / monitoring); author-reported limitations.

ANALYSIS PLAN: Descriptive, non-inferential synthesis — frequency counts of studies by modality, year, country, and study design; PRISMA-ScR flow diagram of search and selection; summary table mapping each modality to its reported clinical applications; narrative synthesis organized by modality, highlighting evidence depth and gaps. No formal critical appraisal (risk-of-bias) or meta-analysis was planned, consistent with scoping review methodology; this is stated explicitly as a limitation.

SCREENING AND SELECTION PROCESS: Search results were de-duplicated in a reference manager. Title/abstract screening and full-text review were performed by a single reviewer against the eligibility criteria. Independent second-reviewer verification of all screened records, with third-reviewer arbitration of disagreements, is planned before journal submission to calculate inter-rater agreement — this had not yet been completed at the time of this registration. Results are reported via a PRISMA-ScR flow diagram including reasons for full-text exclusion.

RESULTS SUMMARY (completed at time of registration): 153 records identified (PubMed 10, Embase 92, Web of Science 50, Cochrane CENTRAL 0, other sources 1) → 45 duplicates removed → 108 records screened at title/abstract → 83 excluded at that stage → 11 full-text articles assessed for eligibility → 6 excluded at full-text stage (wrong concept/no novel modality, n=5; wrong study type, n=1) → 19 studies included. Included studies spanned AI/deep-learning-assisted OCT classification (n=3), OCT angiography/swept-source OCTA (n=8), ultra-widefield imaging (n=6), and en face OCT/Retromode imaging (n=2). Full results are reported in the companion manuscript draft and PRISMA-ScR flow diagram.

REPORTING STANDARD: JBI Manual for Evidence Synthesis (scoping review chapter) + PRISMA-ScR checklist.

CONFLICTS OF INTEREST: The authors declare no conflicts of interest.

FUNDING: This study was funded by the Ministry of Health and Welfare, Republic of Korea (grant number: RS-2025-25465506), through a grant from the Korea Health Technology R&D Project via the Korea Health Industry Development Institute (KHIDI).

REGISTRATION NOTE: This registration was created on August 10, 2026, after search and screening were complete, as a transparency measure documenting the eligibility criteria, search strategy, and data-charting plan used. Companion files (full protocol, data-charting form, manuscript draft) are available from the authors upon request.

title: Tuberculosis (TB) Research Signals from the Union Conference 2025: A Map Toward End TB 2035 Using Transparent Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Synthesis
description:
Project overview

This project aims to develop and evaluate a structured, transparent and human-supervised artificial intelligence framework for synthesising scientific evidence presented at the Union World Conference on Lung Health 2025. The conference contains a large and diverse body of emerging tuberculosis research, including clinical trials, diagnostic studies, implementation research, epidemiology, mathematical modelling, health-systems research, community and lived-experience evidence, policy discussions, and early-stage scientific innovations.

Conference evidence is highly valuable because it often includes new findings before they are fully published. However, the volume and heterogeneity of conference presentations make it difficult for researchers, clinicians, policymakers, funders and affected communities to identify the most reliable findings, distinguish mature evidence from preliminary claims, and understand which developments could realistically contribute to ending tuberculosis.

The project therefore uses a multi-stage, AI-assisted evidence-synthesis workflow to convert conference presentations and transcripts into a structured and auditable evidence map. The objective is not to replace scientific reviewers or conduct a conventional systematic review of published literature. Rather, the project will assess whether artificial intelligence can support a rapid, reproducible and evidence-weighted synthesis of an entire major scientific conference while maintaining explicit human oversight.

Purpose and research objectives

The primary purpose is to identify the most credible, decision-relevant and potentially scalable tuberculosis evidence signals presented at the conference and assess their relevance to global End TB priorities.

The specific objectives are to:

Create a structured dataset of individual conference presentations and their principal scientific claims.
Classify each presentation by study design, intervention, population, setting, evidence maturity and thematic area.
Assess each presentation using a predefined six-domain evidence-scoring framework.
Distinguish reliable evidence from promising but immature findings, contextual information and claims requiring human adjudication.
Map conference findings to the WHO End TB Strategy, the 2023 United Nations High-Level Meeting commitments and the current global tuberculosis progress gaps described by WHO.
Identify areas in which scientific innovation is advancing faster than implementation, policy adoption or equitable access.
Identify populations and research questions that remain underrepresented, including children, pregnant and lactating women, people with HIV, people with drug-resistant or extrapulmonary TB, migrants, refugees, incarcerated populations and other underserved groups.
Produce a transparent conference-to-evidence synthesis framework that could be adapted for future tuberculosis conferences and other global health fields.
Evidence sources

The primary evidence source is the scientific content presented at the Union World Conference on Lung Health 2025. The source corpus includes cleaned conference transcripts, session information and structured extraction tables covering symposia, plenaries, TBScience sessions, late-breaker presentations and spotlight sessions.

The current combined dataset contains approximately 247 individual presentations. Each row represents a presentation or evidence unit and may contain:

session and talk identifiers;
presentation title;
speaker and institutional affiliation;
collaborating organisations or research networks;
country or geographical setting;
study design and research question;
intervention or exposure;
study phase or evidence maturity;
population and sample size;
main findings;
statistical results;
limitations and uncertainties;
relevance to End TB goals; and
AI-generated and human-reviewed evidence scores.

The conference evidence will be interpreted against three principal normative sources:

the WHO Global Tuberculosis Report 2025;
the 2023 Political Declaration of the United Nations High-Level Meeting on the Fight Against Tuberculosis; and
WHO documentation summarising the commitments and targets arising from the 2023 High-Level Meeting.

These documents provide the reference framework for assessing whether conference findings address major gaps in tuberculosis prevention, diagnosis, treatment, research, financing, equity, social protection and implementation.

AI-assisted evidence-synthesis workflow

The project uses generative artificial intelligence as a structured research-assistance tool rather than as an autonomous decision-maker.

Stage 1: Transcript preparation and evidence extraction

Conference transcripts are cleaned and organised by session and presentation. A large language model is used to extract structured information from each presentation, including the research question, study design, population, intervention, outcomes, numerical findings, statistical methods, limitations and End TB relevance.

The extraction prompt requires the model to preserve uncertainty, identify unclear terminology, flag speaker or study-name ambiguities and avoid inventing information not present in the source material.

Stage 2: Presentation-level evidence scoring

Each presentation is scored independently across six domains from 1 to 5:

A. Leadership and institutional credibility

Assesses whether the accountable institutions have relevant tuberculosis expertise, research infrastructure, operational capability and an established record of delivering research, policy or implementation work.

B. Collaboration breadth and implementation reach

Assesses the geographical and institutional breadth of the collaboration, including involvement of high-burden settings, national programmes, community organisations, implementation partners and multicentre networks.

C. Potential near-term impact and decision relevance

Assesses the likelihood that the finding could influence policy, clinical practice, product development, programme delivery or research decisions within approximately five years.

D. Methodological robustness

Assesses alignment between the research question and design, appropriateness of comparators, sampling, outcome definitions, bias control, confounding adjustment and transparency of limitations.

E. Data and statistical adequacy

Assesses sample size, denominators, uncertainty estimates, analytical methods, prespecification, handling of missing data and whether the reported effect is clinically or programmatically interpretable.

F. External validation, generalisability and reproducibility

Assesses replication across datasets or settings, external validation, transferability, consistency with prior evidence and whether the methods could be reproduced.

Institutional prominence and collaboration breadth are treated as contextual confidence modifiers. They are not permitted to compensate for weak methodology, inadequate statistical support or lack of validation.

Stage 3: Evidence-quality guardrails and tier classification

The following quantities are calculated:

context and reach subtotal: A + B;
decision-impact score: C;
evidence-quality subtotal: D + E + F; and
total score: A + B + C + D + E + F.

Presentations are classified as:

Tier 1 — Must capture

Total score of at least 24, with C, D and E each at least 4, F at least 3, and an evidence-quality subtotal of at least 12.

Tier 2 — Capture and verify carefully

Total score of 18–23, or a higher total that fails one of the evidence-quality guardrails. This category can include high-impact early-stage work with strong methodology but insufficient external validation.

Tier 3 — Usually exclude from principal claims

Total score of 17 or below, or C, D or E of 2 or below.

Within each tier, evidence is ranked first by the evidence-quality subtotal, followed by near-term impact, collaboration breadth and institutional credibility. This prevents institutional prestige from outranking stronger empirical evidence.

Stage 4: Independent audit and conservative rescoring

The initial AI-generated evidence table is independently reviewed using a second analytical stage. The audit checks:

row matching and duplicated presentations;
missing or inconsistent fields;
scoring and spreadsheet formula accuracy;
study-design classification;
whether the main claim exceeds the available data;
whether observational associations are incorrectly expressed as causal effects;
whether exploratory, interim or post-hoc analyses are overstated;
whether preclinical findings are framed as clinically actionable;
whether modelled impact is confused with observed impact;
whether diagnostic accuracy is incorrectly equated with improved patient outcomes; and
whether weak or absent external validation is sufficiently acknowledged.

Conservative score caps are applied where the source material consists of expert commentary, advocacy, protocols without results, incomplete transcripts, preclinical evidence, interim analyses or claims without adequate numerical support.

Stage 5: Claim-level signal classification

The presentations are converted into claim-level evidence signals and classified as:

Core evidence signal: mature, methodologically robust and quantitatively supported evidence;
Probable evidence signal: credible and decision-relevant evidence requiring limited verification;
Promising but immature signal: potentially important early-phase, preclinical, exploratory or modelled evidence;
Controversial or human-adjudication signal: an important claim with unresolved methodological, statistical, safety, generalisability or interpretive concerns; or
Low-confidence or contextual finding: information insufficient to support a principal scientific or policy claim.

Presentations arising from the same trial, dataset or research programme are consolidated to avoid double counting.

Thematic framework

Evidence is organised into six major End TB themes:

Diagnostics and screening
Treatment and regimen optimisation
Prevention, tuberculosis preventive treatment and infection control
Vaccines and immunology
Implementation, community engagement, equity and health systems
Surveillance, modelling, epidemiology and financing

Each signal is mapped to one primary theme and, where necessary, one secondary theme.

Mapping to End TB goals

Each evidence signal is mapped to the End TB Strategy pillars and to specific WHO and UN commitments, including:

reductions in tuberculosis incidence and mortality;
at least 90% treatment coverage;
at least 90% tuberculosis preventive treatment coverage among eligible populations;
universal initial testing with WHO-recommended rapid molecular diagnostics;
improved diagnosis and treatment of drug-resistant tuberculosis;
development and equitable access to a new tuberculosis vaccine;
universal health and social-benefit coverage;
elimination of catastrophic costs;
meaningful engagement of affected communities;
increased annual financing for tuberculosis services;
increased annual investment in tuberculosis research; and
stronger surveillance, accountability and multisectoral action.

Signals are additionally classified according to their likely contribution:

direct acceleration of an End TB target;
enabling health-system or policy change;
contribution to the research and product-development pipeline; or
contextual or descriptive contribution.

Implementation readiness is categorised as immediate, medium term, long term or uncertain.

Human oversight and adjudication

Human review is retained as an essential component of the project.

High-priority human adjudication is required for:

all Tier 1 evidence;
all signals proposed for the final Top 10;
safety or non-inferiority findings;
incomplete or technically compromised transcripts;
influential mathematical or economic models;
claims that could materially affect clinical or programme decisions;
evidence with conflicting denominators or statistical interpretations;
exploratory subgroup analyses; and
claims that appear inconsistent with current WHO recommendations.

For each flagged signal, the framework generates a specific adjudication question identifying what must be checked in the original abstract, presentation slides, trial registration, publication or dataset before inclusion in the manuscript.

Expected outputs

The planned outputs are:

A complete scoring and audit dataset

A structured table containing all included conference presentations, extracted evidence, original and audited scores, evidence tiers, maturity classifications, cautions and human-review priorities.

A theme-level evidence map

A claim-level synthesis of the strongest evidence across the six End TB themes, including evidence type, quantitative findings, evidence strength, limitations, implementation readiness and End TB relevance.

A consolidated Top 10 evidence-signal list

A ranked set of the most reliable and strategically important findings, with overlapping presentations consolidated by trial or research programme.

A human-adjudication queue

A prioritised list of claims requiring expert review before manuscript inclusion, together with explicit verification questions and the potential consequences of overstatement.

An End TB target-gap matrix

A comparison between official global commitments, current progress, conference evidence, remaining evidence gaps and recommended actions for 2026–2027, 2028–2030 and 2031–2035.

A manuscript-ready scientific synthesis

A structured Results and Discussion synthesis describing the strongest areas of convergence, the most important unresolved gaps, the balance between innovation and implementation, underrepresented populations and a strategic roadmap towards 2035.

A methodological framework

A reusable and adaptable framework for AI-assisted conference evidence synthesis, including prompts, extraction fields, scoring rules, audit procedures and human-review safeguards.

Open-science materials

Where conference permissions and intellectual-property restrictions allow, the project will share the protocol, scoring rubric, analysis prompts, data dictionary, decision rules, audit templates and de-identified derived evidence tables. Full transcripts or copyrighted conference materials will not be publicly redistributed without permission.

Expected contribution and significance

The project addresses a gap between conventional conference reporting and formal evidence synthesis. Conference summaries commonly describe selected highlights but rarely assess all presentations using explicit methodological and statistical criteria. Conventional systematic reviews, in contrast, generally rely on published studies and may not capture emerging conference evidence for months or years.

This project tests a middle approach: a rapid but conservative conference-scale evidence synthesis that identifies emerging signals without treating unpublished conference findings as definitive evidence.

The project is expected to contribute in three areas.

First, it will provide a broad picture of the direction of global tuberculosis research and implementation at a major international conference.

Second, it will identify which findings are sufficiently mature to inform near-term decisions and which require further validation, replication or implementation research.

Third, it will evaluate a reproducible model for responsible use of generative AI in scientific synthesis, with explicit attention to transparency, auditability, uncertainty and human accountability.

The project may represent one of the first tuberculosis-specific attempts to combine conference-wide transcript analysis, claim-level evidence grading, multi-stage AI review, policy-target mapping and structured human adjudication in a single workflow.

Limitations

The project has several anticipated limitations.

Conference presentations are not equivalent to peer-reviewed full publications. Important information on study design, denominators, statistical uncertainty, missing data, adverse events and subgroup definitions may be absent from transcripts or slides.

Transcript quality may vary, and automated transcription can introduce errors in speaker names, terminology, study names and numerical values.

The scoring framework is designed for evidence triage and prioritisation. It is not a validated replacement for formal risk-of-bias tools.

The corpus contains heterogeneous evidence types. Clinical trials, diagnostic studies, modelling, qualitative research, community evidence and policy discussions cannot be evaluated identically. Scores will therefore be interpreted according to the type and purpose of the evidence.

Large language models may produce extraction errors, inconsistent scores or unsupported interpretations. For this reason, AI outputs will be retained as auditable intermediate products rather than accepted as final judgements.

Evidence presented at the conference may later change following peer review, final data analysis, regulatory review or publication.

Implementation readiness estimates are judgement-based and depend on factors not always captured in scientific presentations, including manufacturing, affordability, regulatory approval, health-system capacity, financing, political commitment and community acceptability.

Overall anticipated outcome

The anticipated final outcome is an evidence-weighted roadmap showing what the Union 2025 conference indicates about progress towards ending tuberculosis, which innovations could realistically influence practice before 2030, which developments may contribute closer to 2035, and where major scientific, implementation, equity and financing gaps remain.

The project will not present artificial intelligence as a replacement for tuberculosis expertise. Its intended contribution is a scalable and transparent first-pass synthesis system that helps experts focus their limited time on the findings with the greatest potential impact and the greatest risk of misinterpretation.

title: Diagnostic role of abdominal ultrasound (point-of-care ultrasonography) in confirming nasogastric tube position: a living systematic review
description:
Purpose: The primary objective of this research is to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of ultrasonography as a bedside tool for confirming the correct placement of nasogastric and orogastric tubes in clinical practice. While chest radiography remains the "gold standard," it involves exposure to ionizing radiation, creates delays in starting nutrition or medication, and increases healthcare costs.
This project seeks to synthesize the available evidence to determine if abdominal and cervical ultrasound can safely and accurately replace or complement radiography. Given the rapid emergence of new studies in the field of Point-of-Care Ultrasound (POCUS), this study is designed as a Living Systematic Review. This methodology ensures that the findings are updated every six months, maintaining the clinical relevance and currency of the evidence for decision-making in emergency and critical care settings.

Methodology Overview: Following the PRISMA guidelines and Cochrane methodology, we will include observational studies (prospective cohorts, cross-sectional, and case-control) that compare ultrasonography against radiography. The risk of bias will be assessed using the QUADAS-2 tool, and the certainty of the evidence will be evaluated using the GRADE approach. We will utilize bivariate random-effects models for the meta-analysis to account for the inherent correlation between sensitivity and specificity.

Expected Outcomes:
Diagnostic Accuracy Metrics: We expect to define a pooled sensitivity and specificity for ultrasound. Based on previous evidence, we anticipate a specificity near 100%, which is critical for preventing pulmonary aspiration.
Safety and Efficiency: We aim to demonstrate that ultrasound significantly reduces the "time-to-confirmation" compared to X-rays, facilitating faster clinical interventions.
Subgroup Insights: The review expects to identify factors that influence accuracy, such as the anatomical "acoustic window" (cervical vs. abdominal), the use of dynamic techniques (air/saline bolus), and patient characteristics (BMI and sedation status).
Living Evidence Map: A major outcome will be a continuously updated evidence synthesis that provides clinicians with a reliable, evidence-based protocol for the bedside use of ultrasound in gastric tube verification.

title: The Expertize in Question Formulation: Homogeneity and Discriminability of Questions in the Concealed Information Test
description:
Factors related to questions that affect the accuracy (sensitivity and specificity) of CIT and the expertise in formulating a set of questions have become important topics. 
In CIT, it is essential for maintaining the specificity of CIT to choose the non-critical items so that the critical item is not made salient in question sets (i.e., homogeneity of items) because an outstanding critical item may bias an innocent examinee and increase their physiological response to the critical item (Ogawa et al., 2015). This could potentially cause false arrest or even prosecution. In fact, Japanese practitioners have been trained to formulate homogeneous questions for cases with different backgrounds to avoid the risk of such bias. Nevertheless, the relationship between homogeneity in question sets and the expertise in formulating questions has never been tested.
Another aspect, that may affect the sensitivity of CIT, is the selection of items that are likely to be recognized by examinees who encoded these critical items during crime commission (i.e., discriminability of items). The concreteness of items presented to examinees (Geven et al., 2019) has been identified as a factor in discriminability. For instance, a robber may encode that they used scissors in a broken-into house to threaten a victim but may not encode the type of scissors (e.g., kitchen scissors, fabric shears, and garden shears). In addition, even if the offender encoded a specific type of scissors, the retention and retrieval of that detail may become more difficult as a function of time. Therefore, it is ideal to formulate question sets using a higher level of category to achieve optimal discriminability of items.
Another factor related to the discriminability of question sets is to formulate them with few elements. When it comes to, for example, the cash being stolen from a velcro purse, the velcro purse can be used as a critical item consisting of two elements: "velcro," which is a type of opening and closing of a purse, and "purse," which is a type of container. In this case, since it is not necessary to discriminate all items by one type of element (e.g., the container of stolen money), it is possible to share the same cue (e.g., purse) among items by selecting an item such as “zipper purse” as a non-critical item. The sharing of the same element increases the probability that multiple elements ("purse" and "velcro") will be required to identify the critical item (i.e., the examinee needs to remember multiple elements to detect the critical item). It is more challenging for the examinees to remember more elements, and the difficulty of the retention and retrieval may increase over time similar to the items with a lower level of category. In the meantime, the above issue does not occur when formulating a set of questions with one type of element, such as "wallet" and "envelope." Formulating a set of questions with fewer elements encourages choosing items of higher category levels (e.g., the container of stolen money). Therefore, the number of elements can be considered as a factor of the discriminability of items closely related to the category level. However, the factors related to questions that affect the discriminability in CIT has just started being tested, and their relationship with expertise in formulating a set of questions has not been examined.
Therefore, we will compare question sets formulated by university students and CIT examiners by measuring the factors of the homogeneity and discriminability of these sets. In addition, we will examine if the expertise in question formulation makes a difference in perceived homogeneity evaluated by a sample that is not aware of the critical items (study 1) and in discriminability measured by a recognition test using a sample that encodes the critical items (study 2).

title: Diagnostic Accuracy of Artificial Intelligence for Differentiating Ameloblastoma from Odontogenic Cysts on Radiographic Imaging: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
description:
Ameloblastoma is the most common clinically significant odontogenic tumor of the jaws, characterized by locally aggressive behavior and a high rate of recurrence, requiring wide surgical resection. Odontogenic cysts, including dentigerous cysts, odontogenic keratocysts, and radicular cysts, frequently present as radiolucent jaw lesions that closely mimic ameloblastoma on conventional imaging, creating a significant diagnostic challenge for clinicians. While histopathological examination remains the definitive gold standard, it is invasive and only available post-biopsy or post-surgery, meaning preoperative imaging plays a critical role in treatment planning.
Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI), particularly deep learning architectures such as convolutional neural networks (CNNs), ResNet, and YOLO, have shown promise in automating and improving the interpretation of dental and maxillofacial radiographic images. Several primary studies have evaluated AI models for distinguishing ameloblastoma from odontogenic cysts using panoramic radiographs (OPG), cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT), CT, and MRI, but findings vary across studies in terms of diagnostic accuracy, model architecture, and imaging modality.
This systematic review and meta-analysis will synthesize the existing evidence on the diagnostic accuracy of AI-based radiographic analysis for differentiating ameloblastoma from odontogenic cysts, using histopathological diagnosis as the reference standard. Pooled estimates of sensitivity, specificity, area under the curve (AUC), diagnostic accuracy, and diagnostic odds ratio (DOR) will be calculated using bivariate random-effects meta-analytic methods. Secondary analyses will explore performance differences by imaging modality (OPG vs. CBCT vs. CT vs. MRI) and by AI model type (CNN-based vs. non-CNN architectures). The expected outcome is a quantitative, evidence-based summary of how accurately AI can perform this specific differential diagnosis, identification of which imaging modalities and AI architectures yield the highest diagnostic performance, and identification of gaps and methodological weaknesses (via QUADAS-2 risk-of-bias assessment) in the current literature to guide future research and inform the potential clinical integration of AI-assisted diagnostic tools in oral and maxillofacial radiology.

title: Artificial intelligence for detecting periapical lesions in dental imaging: a scoping review protocol (PRISMA-ScR, JBI) — Retrospective OSF registration
description:
Project overview

Title: Artificial intelligence for detecting periapical lesions in dental imaging: a scoping review (PRISMA-ScR, JBI)
Modalities: intra-oral periapical radiographs (IOPA), panoramic radiographs (OPG), cone-beam CT (CBCT).
Purpose: Map and synthesize the evidence on AI methods for detecting periapical lesions across dental imaging modalities; summarize performance and evaluation practices; assess reporting transparency; and identify gaps that affect clinical translation.

Rationale

Research on AI for periapical pathology is growing but highly heterogeneous in tasks, datasets, reference standards, units of analysis, and metrics. This variability hinders comparison and practical adoption. A structured scoping review will organize the field and provide actionable guidance for future studies and clinical pathways.

Methods (summary)

Scoping review per PRISMA-ScR and JBI (PCC); PRISMA-S for search reporting.
Inclusion: English-language, human, primary AI studies (2010–present) that develop, fine-tune, or evaluate AI for periapical lesion tasks (classification/detection/segmentation) on IOPA/OPG/CBCT.
Process: Dual independent screening and data charting (e.g., Rayyan) with consensus/third reviewer.
Data items: modality; task; dataset/source; unit of analysis (tooth/region/patient); reference standard (e.g., expert consensus, histology, CBCT confirmation); sample sizes/splits (patient-level where applicable); external validation/multicenter; augmentation; model family; transparency (code/data).
Synthesis: Descriptive (no meta-analysis). We will report sensitivity/specificity, AUC, accuracy, F1 (and Dice/IoU for segmentation), and map reporting completeness against key CLAIM/MI-CLAIM concepts.

Timeframe & six-week plan (actual timeline)

Coverage: 2010 → present.

Week 1 — 1–7 Aug 2025: Preparation (define PCC, eligibility, draft protocol outline; select databases).

Week 2 — 8–14 Aug 2025: Protocol drafting; PRISMA-S strategy drafting (v0.9); small sanity-check queries.

Week 3 — 15–21 Aug 2025: Pilot search (~100 records) + pilot screening; refine eligibility; finalize strategies (v1.0).

Week 4 — 22–28 Aug 2025: Full multi-database search and cross-database deduplication; create Rayyan project.

Week 5 — 29 Aug–4 Sep 2025: Title/abstract screening; full-text retrieval; pilot extraction (10 sources); lock data-charting template (4 Sep).

Week 6 — 5–11 Sep 2025: Full extraction (data charting) and initial descriptive synthesis; draft PRISMA-ScR flow.
Finalization & registration: 12–15 Sep 2025 — verify counts; re-run update search (15 Sep 2025) for currency; register on OSF.

Expected outcomes

Narrative synthesis with evidence tables/figures by modality and task.

PRISMA-ScR flow diagram.

Comparative view of performance metrics and evaluation rigor (patient-level splits, external validation, multicenter use).

Gap analysis + a minimum-practice checklist to improve reproducibility and clinical relevance.

Practical recommendations for dataset reporting and reference standards in dental imaging AI.

Registration & timeline

Retrospectively registered on OSF. Initiation: 1 Aug 2025 (protocol drafting and early preparation). OSF registration: 15 Sep 2025. Planned manuscript submission: 18 Sep 2025.

Data/materials availability

Search strategies (with exact run dates), anonymized screening logs, the data-charting template, and the PRISMA-ScR flow will be deposited on OSF; the charted dataset will be shared subject to publisher policy.

Ethics, funding, conflicts

No human/animal intervention; ethics approval not required. No specific funding; authors declare no conflicts of interest.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Dermatology: A Scoping Review of Clinical Effectiveness, Patient-Clinician Relationship, and Ethical Considerations in Clinical Practice
description:
This scoping review maps and synthesizes peer-reviewed evidence on artificial intelligence (AI) in dermatology across three domains: clinical effectiveness, the patient-clinician relationship, and ethical considerations in clinical practice. The review is being conducted to support a chapter commissioned by Springer Nature for the Handbook of Tissue Reconstruction and Regeneration, titled "A Dermatologist's Perspective on the Effectiveness of AI: From Patient-Clinical Relationship to Ethical Considerations in Clinical Practice."
The clinical effectiveness domain covers AI modalities including image-based convolutional neural networks (CNNs), large language models (LLMs), teledermatology platforms, mobile health applications, clinical decision support systems, dermatopathology AI, and administrative workflow tools, applied across dermatologic conditions including skin cancer, inflammatory skin disease, wound care, hair loss, and cosmetic conditions. The patient-clinician relationship domain synthesizes evidence on patient trust and acceptance of AI, communication and consultation experience, access to care, and informed consent. The ethical considerations domain covers algorithmic bias and performance disparities across Fitzpatrick skin tones, data privacy, informed consent, explainability, accountability, and regulatory frameworks including the FDA, EU AI Act, and international standards.
Four databases will be searched (PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Cochrane). The search covers January 2018 to present. Two independent reviewers will screen titles, abstracts, and full texts using Covidence or Rayyan. Data will be synthesized narratively and organized by the three primary domains, with summary tables for diagnostic accuracy studies, patient trust studies, and ethical considerations. The review will be reported in accordance with PRISMA-ScR guidelines.
The expected outcome will be a comprehensive evidence map of AI in dermatology suitable for a clinical reference handbook audience of dermatologists, clinicians, graduate students, and researchers. This study will identify evidence gaps to inform future primary research.

title: What are the most frequently reported clinical signs and symptoms in individuals diagnosed with motor neurone disease? A scoping review
description:
Overview
Motor Neurone Disease (MND) is a progressive and incurable neurodegenerative disorder that results in the degeneration of upper and lower motor neurons, leading to debilitating loss of muscle function, mobility, speech, and ultimately prematurely ending life. Although MND encompasses a spectrum of subtypes including amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), progressive muscular atrophy (PMA), primary lateral sclerosis (PLS), progressive bulbar palsy (PBP), and flail limb variants each presents with variable clinical signs and symptoms, leading to significant delays in diagnosis and overall condition management.
Despite existing guidelines from NICE (2016) highlighting the importance of early recognition and referral, diagnostic delays persist, averaging 12 months from initial symptom onset. Misdiagnosis is common due to the overlap of MND symptoms with those of other neuromuscular and neurological disorders. Recognising the full range of signs and symptoms associated with MND is essential to improving diagnostic accuracy, enhancing care pathways, and potentially providing earlier access to supportive treatments and clinical trials.
Purpose
The purpose of this scoping review is to systematically identify, describe, and map the range of clinical signs and symptoms reported in individuals diagnosed with MND. This includes an exploration of motor, bulbar, respiratory, cognitive, and any atypical or under-recognized symptoms documented across MND subtypes. The review aims to clarify these symptoms and consolidate the evidence with the aim of informing future clinical guidelines.
Research Objectives
1. To explore how the current literature describes the clinical signs and symptoms of MND.
2. To map which specific signs and symptoms aid healthcare professionals in recognising patients with MND.
Methodology

This review will follow the Joanna Briggs Institute methodology for scoping reviews and adhere to the PRISMA-ScR reporting guidelines. The five-stage framework by Arksey & O’Malley (2005) will be employed, including identifying the research question, searching and selecting studies, charting the data, and summarising the results.
A comprehensive search using MEDLINE, APA PsycInfo, CINAHL Ultimate, Academic Search Ultimate, and SPORTDiscus, followed by hand-searching reference lists and Google Scholar will be carried out. Eligible studies included peer-reviewed literature that reported numerical data on clinical signs and symptoms in individuals with a confirmed MND diagnosis, using clinical-epidemiological or descriptive study designs.
Expected Outcomes
• A comprehensive map of signs and symptoms across MND subtypes.
• A clearer understanding of symptom prevalence.
• Identification of knowledge gaps to guide future research and inform clinical training materials.
Significance
This scoping review will support earlier and more accurate recognition of MND by consolidating evidence on its signs and symptoms. It will also contribute to refining diagnostic criteria, educating clinicians, and ensuring timely access to multidisciplinary care, supportive services, and clinical trials for people living with MND.

title: Machine Learning- and Deep Learning-Based Gait and Movement Analysis versus Standard Clinical Bedside Scales for Predicting Falls in Older Adults: A Systematic Review with Synthesis Without Meta-analysis (SWiM)
description: This systematic review and meta-analysis aims to evaluate and directly compare the prognostic accuracy of machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) based gait and movement analysis systems against standard clinical bedside balance and mobility scales for predicting future fall risks in older adults. The expected outcome is to deliver definitive empirical evidence regarding the incremental diagnostic value, sensitivity, and specificity of advanced technological assessments in geriatric physical therapy and rehabilitation workflows.
