title: A Prospective Cohort Study on the Development and Validation of a Novel Pressure Injury Risk Assessment Scale for Hepatobiliary Surgery Patients
description:
Background: The widely used Braden Scale is a universal tool for predicting pressure injury (PI) risk, but it lacks specificity for patients undergoing hepatobiliary surgery. These patients frequently present with severe jaundice (hyperbilirubinemia) and hypoalbuminemia, which lead to skin barrier disruption, pruritus, severe generalized edema, and significantly reduced tissue tolerance to pressure. Consequently, traditional assessment scales may underestimate their actual PI risk.


Purpose: This research project aims to develop and clinically validate a novel, hepatobiliary-specific pressure injury risk assessment scale by incorporating key indicators of liver dysfunction (e.g., serum bilirubin levels, albumin/prealbumin levels, and degree of ascites/edema) into conventional risk factors.


Methods: The study utilizes a two-stage design.

Phase 1 (Scale Development): A preliminary item pool will be constructed through literature review. Subsequently, 2-3 rounds of Delphi expert consultations involving a multidisciplinary team (MDT)—including surgeons, anesthesiologists, intensivists, and wound/ostomy nurses—will be conducted to finalize the scale items and assign appropriate weights.

Phase 2 (Clinical Validation): A prospective cohort study will be conducted on patients undergoing major hepatobiliary surgery. Patients will be assessed using both the traditional Braden Scale and the newly developed scale concurrently at critical time points (e.g., admission, immediately post-op, and specific postoperative days). Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curves and Area Under the Curve (AUC) will be calculated to compare the predictive validity of the two scales.


Expected Outcomes: We hypothesize that the newly developed hepatobiliary-specific scale will demonstrate superior predictive validity (higher AUC, sensitivity, and specificity) compared to the standard Braden Scale. Ultimately, this tool is expected to provide clinical nurses with a more accurate assessment instrument, facilitating precise preventive interventions and reducing PI incidence in this vulnerable population.

title: The Diagnostic Utility of Glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) in the Early Detection of Cancer: A Systematic Review
description:
In the field of oncology, there is a growing demand for accurate and reliable diagnostic tests that can detect cancers at an early stage. Non-invasive liquid biopsies are promising for enhancing prognosis and improving patient outcomes. However, most liquid biopsies rely on genomic biomarkers, which have limited sensitivity for early-stage tumors and certain cancer types such as genitourinary or brain tumors.
One potential approach that has become of growing interest is using glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) as a multi-cancer early detection (MCED) metabolic biomarker. GAGs are a family of polysaccharides found abundantly in the extracellular matrix (ECM) of tissues. Research has indicated that the dysregulation of ECM, including changes and disruptions in GAGs, contributes to various cancer hallmarks such as metabolic reprogramming, persistent growth signals, immunosuppression, angiogenesis, tumor invasion, and metastasis. However, the diagnostic potential of using glycosaminoglycan (GAGs) profiles as biomarkers in early cancer detection has not been thoroughly investigated. To address this knowledge gap, the proposed systematic review will evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of GAGs in the early detection of cancers.

title: Episodic Memory Encoding and Retrieval in Face-Name Paired Paradigm: An fNIRS Study
description:
Background. Early detection of process-specific episodic memory (EM) impairment can facilitate diagnostic accuracy and early intervention for aging and pathology related neurocognitive decline. Despite a high sensitivity of behavioral paradigms such as the paired-associate learning (PAL) paradigm, the determination of the underlying neurobiological dysregulations remains challenging. The present study was a first attempt to combine the PAL paradigm with functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) to offer a method suitable to investigate Central and Autonomous Nervous System in more ecological and clinically contexts. 

Methods. Twenty-two male students (age: mean = 20.55, SD = 1.62) were included in this study and were asked to complete a PAL paradigm using faces. A 40-channel fNIRS system was used to measure relative changes in oxygenated hemoglobin in the bilateral prefrontal, superior parietal, inferior parietal, and middle occipital cortices. Changes were associated to different aspects of the paradigm, including memory phases, novelty, and difficulty level in face-name pairs.

Results. Broad regions encompassing the bilateral frontal cortex (Brodmann area 1, 9, 11, 45, 46) were deactivated during encoding (FDR corrected p-values = 0.048, 0.012, 0.048, 0.048, 0.029), whereas a regional specific increase in the left orbitofrontal cortex (Brodmann area 11) was observed during retrieval (FDR corrected p-value = 0.048). The opposite brain responses of superior (increased HbO concentration compared to baseline) and inferior (decreased HbO concentration) parietal cortices were observed during encoding and the dominant activation of left PFC during retrieval. The higher paradigm difficult level was associated to greater beta value and HbO concentration in the bilateral prefrontal cortices; the higher novelty was found to generate greater occipital activation. Significant neurobio-behavioural correlations between the magnitude of brain activation (the right PFC) and behavioral performance (i.e., accuracy) during the retrieval process were also observed.

Conclusion. The combination of a paired-associate learning paradigm with fNIRS provided the means to differentiate the two EM phases. Hence, fNIRS presents a promising technique to determine process-specific brain processes engaged in EM. This approach may provide a method for an early detection of EM deficits which, in turn, may allow for a timely onset of intervention counteracting EM decline.

title: Under-diagnosis of Dementia in Nursing Home Residents: A scoping Review
description:
As per the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders-5 (DSM-5), dementia is diagnosed when there is evidence of decline in activities of daily living (ADL) as well as decline in cognitive ability in one or more of the following domains: complex attention, executive ability, learning and memory, language, perceptual - motor - visual perception, praxis and social cognition (1). Progression of these deficits to the extent one’s ability to conduct activities of daily living is impaired is one of the major reasons for older individuals transition to residential aged care facilities (RACF) or nursing homes (2,3,4,5). 
Dementia is a significant public health issue in Australia and a health condition that is highly prevalent amongst residents of RACF (6,7). Under-diagnosis of dementia may affect the quality of care provided to the RACF residents, eventually impacting their health-related outcomes (8). Overarching this issue is the fact that funding allocation to RACF for the care of residents is dependent on whether the diagnosis of dementia is present or not (9). 
 It is estimated that three quarters of people living with dementia globally are living without the diagnosis made (7,8). More than 50% of residents living with dementia in RACF are said to have not been diagnosed as living with dementia (8,9,10,11). The issue of under-diagnosis likely begins before entry into the RACF given that a 2017 meta-analysis of 23 studies found that more than 63% of people living with dementia in the community had not been diagnosed with dementia (12). The same study also revealed that the true prevalence of dementia in RACF was double that reported, meaning that half of the residents were not diagnosed (12). Similar results were also reported by another study focusing on diagnosis of dementia in RACF residents (13). 
Findings from Australian studies have identified similar gaps in the diagnosis of dementia. The South Australian Longitudinal Frailty In Residential Sector over Time [FIRST] Study of RACF residents speculated that dementia might not have been diagnosed in almost half of the residents given that 75.6% of residents were identified as possibly living with dementia when using the Dementia Severity Rating Scale (DSRS), whilst a diagnosis of dementia was recorded in the medical records for only 37.1% residents (14). In another Australian study, 83% of residents scored 4 or more on the Psychogeriatric Assessment Scale (PAS-cog) suggesting the presence of dementia but only 65% had a recorded diagnosis of dementia (15). Clearly, the degree of under-diagnosis reported varies according to the method used to identify dementia (16). Methods that are used to make the diagnosis of dementia in RACF can range from a diagnosis recorded in medical records, to scales used to screen for dementia risk and all the way up to a more definitive diagnosis by clinical experts (e.g., geriatricians, neurologists or expert panels). 
It is important to be cognizant of the fact that screening tools such as the DSRS and PAS-cog only identify the risk of dementia and that too with varying performance. The DSRS for example, was able to differentiate between mild cognitive impairment and dementia with a sensitivity of 41% and specificity of 79% or a post-test probability of 74% (16). Additionally, the study design can also influence the reported prevalence for dementia with prevalence varying depending on if the prevalence was estimated at the time of admission to RACF or cross-sectionally, where the prevalence of dementia was determined for all residents at the time the study was conducted (16).
Ensuring that those living with dementia are diagnosed in a timely manner is important (15,16) as a missed diagnosis could result in the resident missing out on funding allocations (e.g., dementia supplement) that would enable the resident to receive increased care hours (17,18,19,20). A timely diagnosis also facilitates conversations regarding the medical management of residents including future care planning (21). It is no surprise therefore that timely diagnosis has been identified as an essential care requirement as per the National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC) guidelines (21). Timely dementia diagnosis has also been highlighted as a priority area for action in the National Framework for Action on Dementia (22).

title: Verbal Classifiers and the Post-Identification Feedback Effect
description:
Imagine that you are a witness to a crime. A police officer shows you a photo spread of six individuals, and asks whether you remember seeing anyone in the lineup, noting that the true perpetrator may or may not be present. One of the faces looks vaguely familiar, so you point at the photo. The officer exclaims, “Good job, you identified the suspect!” and then queries you about how confident you were at the time of the identification. What would you say?
 Research shows that post-identification feedback can influence eyewitnesses’ numeric confidence ratings (e.g., Wells & Bradfield, 1998). When a lineup administrator hints that the suspect has been identified in a lineup (e.g., “Good job, you identified the suspect!”), witnesses tend to provide greater numeric confidence in their identifications, as compared to when no feedback is given. Similarly, disconfirming feedback (e.g., “actually, the suspect was somebody else”) typically results in lower numeric confidence, though the effect is generally smaller (Steblay et al., 2014). Importantly, because feedback is provided after the witness makes a lineup decision, the accuracy of the decision remains constant, thus changing the relationship between numeric confidence and accuracy.
Beyond influencing witnesses’ confidence in their identification, post-identification feedback also disrupts the ability of human evaluators (e.g., jurors) to distinguish accurate from inaccurate identifications. For example, Smalarz and Wells (2014) video-taped testimony from a group of mock-witnesses who received either confirmatory feedback or no-feedback after a six-person lineup identification. A second group of participants viewed the mock-witness testimony videos, and then were asked whether they believed the witnesses’ identifications were likely to be accurate or inaccurate. When judging testimony from mock witnesses in the no-feedback condition, results showed that evaluators were generally able to distinguish accurate from inaccurate identifications (70.3% vs. 35.9% believed accurate, respectively). Yet, when judging testimony from mock-witnesses who received confirmatory feedback, the same evaluators could not distinguish between accurate and inaccurate identifications (64.1% vs. 62.5% believed accurate, respectively). 
Recommendations that police collect verbal confidence hinge on the assumption that these statements are properly interpreted. Recent developments in machine-learning technology may help us better understand verbal expressions of confidence. Researchers have built machine-learning classifiers that quantify the diagnostic value of natural language in a word recognition task (e.g., Dobbins & Kantner, 2019), and eyewitness lineup tasks (e.g., Seale-Carlisle et al., in press). For example, language classifiers might interpret the phrase, “I’m fairly certain” as though the person is 75% likely to be accurate. In this experiment we address two questions. First, we ask if verbal classifiers’ predictions are more robust to the effects of confirmatory feedback than numeric confidence ratings. Second, of profound applied importance, is whether classifiers’ predictions are more diagnostic of accuracy than human evaluators’ assessments. 
Dobbins and Kantner (2019) proposed that language classifiers trained on episodic memory data are sensitive to the presence and absence of language that refers to recollection. Based on this recollection sensitivity account, we hypothesize that verbal classifiers applied to mock witness statements should be more resistant than numeric confidence to the effects of confirmatory feedback. Whereas mock witnesses may express greater numeric confidence in their decisions after receiving confirmatory feedback, we surmise this will not cause them to spontaneously use language associated with recollection. In contrast, we expect humans evaluating the same statements will be considerably worse at distinguishing correct from incorrect identifications in the confirmatory feedback condition than in the no-feedback condition, because they are either less sensitive to the presence or absence of recollective language than classifiers or more sensitive to general expressions of certainty (e.g., ‘I’m pretty certain’, ‘I’m fairly confident’, etc.). This will result in the verbal classifier showing a diagnostic advantage over human evaluators – particularly in the confirmatory feedback condition.

title: Abstract
description:
Introduction: Oral cancer, the sixteenth most common cancer worldwide, presents a significant health burden, particularly in regions like South Asia and Europe, due to risk factors such as tobacco use, betel quid, and alcohol consumption. VELscope, a diagnostic device, aids in early detection by identifying abnormal fluorescence in oral tissues. This scoping review will evaluate the clinical and cost-effectiveness of VELscope in detecting oral premalignant and malignant lesions, identify research gaps, and provide insights into its utility in clinical practice.The objective of this scoping review is to comprehensively assess the available evidence regarding the clinical and cost-effectiveness of VELscope for detecting oral premalignant lesions, and oral cancer. 
Method & Analysis: Adhering to JBI Scoping Review Methodology and PRISMA-ScR guidelines, we will systematically map evidence from peer-reviewed studies in English published until January 2025. Key outcomes include diagnostic accuracy (sensitivity, specificity) and cost-effectiveness. Databases such as MEDLINE (PubMed), Scopus, Embase, and Cochrane will be searched, with screening and data extraction conducted independently by two reviewers by using appropriate software (e.g. Rayyan and Microsoft Excel). Findings will be synthesized using tables, figures, and a PRISMA flow diagram to highlight gaps and inform future research and clinical practice.
Ethics and Dissemination: This scoping review does not involve primary data collection; therefore, ethics approval is not required. The findings will be disseminated through peer-reviewed journals, presentations at national and international conferences, and workshops aimed at healthcare professionals and policymakers.

title: Artificial intelligence for automatic detection of diabetic retinopathy: Scoping review.
description:
Introduction: Diabetic retinopathy (DR) is one of the most prevalent complications of diabetes mellitus (DM) and one of the leading causes of blindness worldwide. Its high epidemiological burden emphasizes the need to improve early detection and diagnosis strategies to mitigate the onset of irreversible changes. The limitations of the current approach to DM in identifying complications such as DR in a timely manner reinforce the importance of incorporating innovative detection strategies. In this context, artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a promising tool, demonstrating high levels of early diagnostic accuracy to optimize the quality of health services, mainly in developing countries. 

Methodology: Through a scoping review, scientific articles, reviews, technical literature, and gray literature published between 2019 and 2025 will be analyzed, covering the available evidence on artificial intelligence modalities in the automatic detection of diabetic retinopathy in adults worldwide. The PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and BIREME databases will be included, using MeSH and DeCS descriptors. 

Expected results: We expect to provide a comprehensive overview of the main types of artificial intelligence used for the automatic detection of diabetic retinopathy in adults worldwide, identifying benefits, limitations, and future opportunities. The findings will generate useful evidence for healthcare professionals and service planners, facilitating the design of strategies and interventions aimed at contributing scientific knowledge in this area, opening up horizons for improvement in healthcare.

The results of this review will be complemented by a series of cases from our institution, which will provide real-life examples of how imaging findings alter clinical management and patient survival. This work will provide valuable information to optimize the diagnostic approach to cardiac metastases in patients with NETs and improve patient care.

title: Diagnostic Accuracy of Ultrasound Optic Nerve Sheath Diameter for Identifying Cerebral Involvement in Preeclampsia and Eclampsia: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
description:
Preeclampsia and eclampsia are major hypertensive disorders of pregnancy associated with significant maternal and fetal morbidity and mortality. Neurological manifestations, including headache, visual disturbances, seizures, cerebral edema, and elevated intracranial pressure, represent some of the most serious complications of these conditions. Optic nerve sheath diameter (ONSD) measured using transorbital ultrasonography has emerged as a noninvasive bedside surrogate marker of elevated intracranial pressure. Numerous observational studies have investigated ONSD in women with preeclampsia and eclampsia and compared measurements with those obtained from normotensive pregnant women. However, reported effect sizes and diagnostic thresholds vary across studies.

The purpose of this systematic review and meta-analysis is to synthesize available evidence regarding the association between hypertensive disorders of pregnancy and ONSD enlargement and to evaluate the diagnostic performance of ONSD for identifying cerebral involvement in preeclampsia and eclampsia. The primary outcome will be the pooled difference in ONSD measurements between women with preeclampsia/eclampsia and normotensive pregnant controls. Secondary outcomes will include pooled sensitivity, specificity, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, and reported diagnostic cut-off values where sufficient data are available. The findings are expected to clarify the clinical utility of ONSD ultrasonography as a rapid and noninvasive screening tool for neurological complications in hypertensive disorders of pregnancy.

title: Diagnostic accuracy of routine assessed inflammatory biomarkers for early infection after cardiac surgery
description:
Inflammatory biomarkers, such as CRP and leucocytes, are often routinely assessed after surgery to determine whether patients are at risk of early postoperative infection. Increased levels means infection is more likely, while decreased levels indicate that early infection is less likely. This way inflammatory biomarkers can be used to scale up diagnostics (e.g. chest x-ray, sputum cultures) or for reassurance. 
In recent years, increasing attention is paid to other inflammatory biomarkers such as PCT, IL-6 and NRL.
Currently it is unclear what their diagnostic value for early postoperative infection is and how this compares to the biomarkers that are usually used in postoperative care.

title: Exploration of Differentially Expressed circulating microRNAs as Diagnostic Biomarkers for Primary Aldosteronism
description:
Primary Aldosteronism (PA) is the most common cause of secondary hypertension and is associated with significant cardiovascular morbidity when left undiagnosed. Despite its clinical importance, the condition remains underdiagnosed due to the lack of reliable, minimally invasive biomarkers that can effectively distinguish PA from primary (essential) hypertension (PH). The current diagnostic pathway relies on screening with aldosterone-to-renin ratio, confirmatory tests, and adrenal vein sampling, which are invasive, costly, and not widely available.

This project aims to explore circulating microRNAs (miRNAs) as potential diagnostic biomarkers for PA. miRNAs are small, non-coding RNAs that regulate gene expression and are increasingly recognized for their stability in blood and disease-specific expression patterns. Leveraging machine learning and bioinformatics approaches, we will analyze miRNA expression profiles obtained from plasma/serum samples of patients with confirmed PA compared to those with PH. Differential expression analysis will identify candidate miRNAs that show significant and reproducible differences between the two groups.

We will then employ supervised machine learning models (e.g., Random Forest, Gradient Boosting) to evaluate the discriminatory power of these candidate miRNAs. Feature selection methods will be used to derive a parsimonious diagnostic signature with optimal sensitivity and specificity. Cross-validation and independent validation subsets will be applied to minimize overfitting and assess generalizability.

The expected outcome of this research is the identification of a panel of circulating miRNAs that can serve as non-invasive biomarkers for distinguishing PA from PH. Such a biomarker panel could improve early diagnosis, reduce dependence on invasive procedures, and ultimately guide more targeted and effective management of patients with hypertension. Beyond diagnostic utility, this study may also provide insights into the molecular pathways underlying aldosterone excess and its cardiovascular consequences.

title: Accuracy of diagnostic tests for microaspiration in ICU patients: a systematic review and methodological critique
description:
Background: Microaspiration is a key pathogenetic factor for ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) in intensive care unit (ICU) patients. However, its diagnosis is challenging due to the lack of a gold standard, leading to significant heterogeneity in the primary literature regarding the accuracy of various diagnostic tests.   
This heterogeneity makes traditional quantitative meta-analysis inappropriate and potentially misleading.   
Objectives: This project outlines a systematic review that shifts its strategic focus from summarizing diagnostic accuracy to conducting a systematic methodological critique of the existing evidence base. The primary goal is to deconstruct the sources of heterogeneity in studies evaluating diagnostic tests for microaspiration in mechanically ventilated ICU patients and to provide guidance for future research.   
Methods: This systematic review will follow the PRISMA-DTA guidelines. We will perform a comprehensive search in major databases (e.g., PubMed, Embase) using a validated search strategy.   
Instead of a meta-analysis, we will conduct a structured narrative synthesis. The analysis will be framed around a pre-defined hierarchy of reference standards and will critically appraise studies using the QUADAS-2 tool, with a special focus on methodological flaws such as incorporation bias and the inappropriate use of downstream clinical outcomes (e.g., VAP) as reference standards.   
The study will address distinct clinical sub-questions based on the origin of aspirate (gastric vs. oropharyngeal).

title: Diagnostic performance of radiomics-based machine learning models for differentiating primary central nervous system lymphoma from glioblastoma: a systematic review and meta-analysis
description:
Accurate preoperative differentiation between primary central nervous system lymphoma (PCNSL) and glioblastoma (GBM) remains a major clinical challenge, as these two highly aggressive brain tumors require distinct therapeutic strategies. While GBM typically necessitates maximal resection followed by chemoradiotherapy, PCNSL is managed primarily with high-dose methotrexate–based chemotherapy. Conventional MRI often shows overlapping features, leading to diagnostic uncertainty and risks of suboptimal treatment.

This project systematically reviewed and meta-analyzed the diagnostic performance of radiomics-based machine learning (ML) models in distinguishing PCNSL from GBM. Radiomics extracts quantitative imaging features that capture tumor heterogeneity beyond visual assessment, while ML algorithms convert these features into predictive diagnostic tools. A comprehensive search of PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, and ClinicalTrials.gov up to August 2025 identified 18 eligible studies including 2,963 patients.

The pooled results demonstrated excellent diagnostic accuracy (AUC = 0.94, 95% CI 0.92–0.97), confirming the promise of radiomics-based ML. However, substantial heterogeneity and methodological limitations, such as limited external validation and potential overfitting, were identified.

Expected outcomes include: (1) a rigorous evidence-based synthesis of radiomics ML performance; (2) clear identification of methodological gaps; and (3) recommendations for standardized imaging protocols and robust validation to enable clinical translation. This work will advance AI-driven neuro-oncology diagnostics, supporting more precise, noninvasive decision-making and improved patient outcomes.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Robotics in Glaucoma: A Scoping Review
description:
Glaucoma is the second leading cause of irreversible blindness worldwide, affecting an estimated 80 million people globally and projected to exceed 111 million by 2040. Despite the availability of effective treatments, a substantial proportion of patients continue to experience preventable visual impairment due to delayed diagnosis, suboptimal monitoring, and the technical demands of surgical intervention. These challenges are particularly acute in low- and middle-income countries, where access to trained ophthalmologists and specialized diagnostic infrastructure remains limited.
Over the past decade, artificial intelligence and surgical robotics have each independently demonstrated transformative potential in medicine. In ophthalmology, deep learning algorithms have achieved diagnostic accuracy comparable to fellowship-trained specialists in tasks such as optic disc segmentation, retinal nerve fiber layer analysis, and visual field interpretation. Robotic platforms, meanwhile, have been introduced in vitreoretinal and anterior segment surgery to compensate for physiological hand tremor and to enable micromanipulations at a scale and precision beyond unaided human capability. What has not been formally mapped or synthesized is the literature addressing the functional integration of both technologies within the glaucoma care continuum, specifically systems in which AI-driven perception or decision support is coupled with physical robotic actuation for diagnostic, monitoring, or surgical purposes.
This scoping review aims to fill that gap. Using the JBI scoping review methodology and the PCC framework (Population, Concept, Context), the review will systematically search nine bibliographic databases and registries: PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, the Cochrane Library, LILACS/BVS, ClinicalTrials.gov, and OSF Preprints. The search covers publications from 2010 to the present and is not restricted by geography. Study selection and data extraction will be conducted independently by two reviewers, with disagreements resolved by a third. Reporting will follow the PRISMA extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR).
The review addresses the following PCC question: What evidence exists regarding the integration of artificial intelligence and robotics in the diagnosis, monitoring, and treatment of glaucoma in adults, across clinical or preclinical settings?

title: ENSURE-AI: Independent Evaluation of AI tools for Prostate Cancer in Pathology
description:
Background
Increasing uptake of digital pathology has opened the door for the introduction of novel AI-based tools to support the diagnostic workflow.(1,2) These technologies have the potential to streamline workflow efficiency, alleviate workload pressures, reduce costs, enhance diagnostic accuracy, and improve patient outcomes.(3-5) One necessary step in proving clinical benefit is to demonstrate high levels of accuracy and generalisability for each tool. 
 
At present, there are at least 26 AI-based tools for analysing Haematoxylin and Eosin (H&E) digital pathology images that have received regulatory approval as medical devices to be placed on the UK market.(6) However, there is limited information available on the performance of devices approved for clinical use, and the quality of evaluation studies used to test their performance is variable.(6) Additionally, whilst a product may perform well on some data sources, this may change when utilised on different data in a different setting.(7) Evaluation on UK NHS data is important prior to widespread deployment of such tools. 
 
One of the most mature areas of the commercial market for AI-based products in digital pathology is in the prostate cancer field. There are currently multiple products with regulatory approval for placement on the EEA/GB market that interpret H&E images of prostate core needle biopsies and predict cancer location and Gleason grade. 

Study aims
1. To develop a framework and recommendations for performing retrospective evaluations using hidden datasets for AI products for diagnostic tasks in digital pathology 
2. To develop the technical infrastructure and processes for performing evaluations of multiple AI products within NPIC 
3. To engage with industry to perform balanced assessments of AI products and ensure their participation, whilst maintaining independence in the evaluations. 
4. To design an output report to describe evaluations and results for individual products 

Study summary
Obtaining the full benefit of AI for patients, whilst ensuring safe adoption into busy clinical laboratories is of great importance in pathology. There are many challenges to be faced by healthcare providers when deciding whether to purchase products with existing regulatory approvals and to introduce these to the clinical workflow. 
 
At the time of writing, the authors are not aware of a standardised accepted framework for the evaluation of AI for adoption into a clinical pathology laboratory. External validation studies of such AI products so far are variable in terms of their approach, whether they include UK NHS data and are often not conducted in a way that is independent from the vendor.(6) 
 
This is an evaluation study of prostate cancer AI products on a multicentre retrospective dataset of prostate biopsies. This project aims to evaluate the performance of multiple AI products with existing regulatory approval for prostate cancer diagnosis in pathology. A further aim is to develop an evaluation framework that could be replicable in other disease areas and within different laboratories. 
 
This work is broken down into six workpackages to perform the project set up, data curation, evaluation across multiple centres and a usability assessment. The final assessment will be summarised and made publicly available, along with details of the evaluation framework that is developed.

Lay summary
To diagnose cancer, samples of tissue are often taken from patients. This tissue is processed in a laboratory to fit on a glass slide. New digital scanning technology means that glass slides can now be "digitised" to become an electronic image. A pathologist can then view the tissue as a detailed image on a computer screen, instead of using a microscope. Increasing availability of these digital images of tissue has created more opportunities to develop and use artificial intelligence (AI) to help with a diagnosis, because AI tools can analyse these images automatically. 
 
In the UK, 97% of pathology laboratories do not have enough staff to meet the demand for quick and accurate diagnoses.(8) AI could help by providing key information in a diagnosis. It could also automate tasks to assist a pathologist when examining a case. The potential of AI to improve cancer diagnosis is very exciting. However, before use in routine patient care, this technology must be tested and evaluated to ensure it is safe, accurate and useful. 
 
This project aims to evaluate the performance and usefulness of existing prostate cancer AI products with regulatory approval and to develop a framework for evaluating AI products in pathology in general.

This is a hospital-based study coordinated by the National Pathology Imaging Co-operative (NPIC) at Leeds Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust, in collaboration with other hospitals within the NPIC network. www.npic.ac.uk

title: Effect of checklists on diagnosing normal and abnormal EKGs
description: Many interventions have been developed to reduce diagnostic errors and a promising intervention is the use of checklists (e.g. Nedorost, 2018; Shimizu et al., 2013; Sibbald et al., 2013a; 2014; 2019). title: Thoracoscopy versus closed pleural biopsy with Cope needle in undiagnosed exudative pleural effusions: systematic review
description: This systematic review aims to compare thoracoscopy with closed pleural biopsy using a Cope needle in adults with undiagnosed exudative pleural effusions following thoracentesis and initial pleural fluid analysis. Pleural effusion is a common clinical condition associated with diverse pulmonary and systemic diseases, and accurate etiological diagnosis is essential for appropriate management and prognosis. When initial investigations are inconclusive, pleural biopsy becomes a critical diagnostic step. Closed pleural biopsy with a Cope needle remains widely used, particularly in resource-limited settings, due to its low cost and accessibility, although its diagnostic yield is variable. In contrast, medical thoracoscopy (pleuroscopy) enables direct visualization and targeted biopsies, offering higher diagnostic accuracy, especially for malignant pleural disease, albeit with greater infrastructure requirements. This review will systematically evaluate and synthesize available evidence on the overall diagnostic yield and safety profile of these procedures. Secondary outcomes will include diagnostic yield by etiology (malignancy and tuberculosis), complication rates, need for additional diagnostic procedures, and length of hospital stay. The study will follow PRISMA 2020 guidelines, assess methodological quality using validated tools, and evaluate the certainty of evidence using the GRADE approach. By providing a comprehensive and methodologically rigorous comparison, this review aims to inform clinical decision-making and optimize diagnostic strategies, particularly in diverse healthcare settings, including low- and middle-income countries.

title: Intraoperative IDH Detection for Molecular Margin Delineation in Diffuse Glioma Surgery: Scoping review
description:
Diffuse gliomas are infiltrative brain tumours where achieving maximal safe resection is limited by difficulty identifying tumour margins intraoperatively. Mutations in isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH1/2), which result in accumulation of the oncometabolite D-2-hydroxyglutarate (2-HG), are highly prevalent in adult-type lower-grade gliomas and represent a practical molecular marker for delineating the “molecular margin.” Conventional methods for IDH detection, such as immunohistochemistry or sequencing require fixed tissue and multi-day processing and are therefore unsuitable for guiding surgical decision intraoperatively. Rapid intraoperative assays are emerging, but no synthesis exists mapping their methods, turnaround times, diagnostic accuracy, and feasibility. This scoping review will map intraoperative or intraoperatively-feasible IDH detection approaches in diffuse gliomas.
Objective:
To map the landscape of rapid, intraoperatively feasible assays for detecting IDH1/2 mutations (directly) or their surrogate metabolite 2-HG (indirectly) in diffuse gliomas. Additionally, to characterize each assay’s potential to delineate the molecular margin and identify key research gaps in their methods, diagnostic accuracy, and clinical application.
Methods and Analysis:
The review will follow PRISMA-ScR, informed by Arksey and O’Malley and JBI methodological guidance. Ovid MEDLINE, Embase, and Web of Science will be searched, and the results will be limited to English-language studies, including human and non-human preclinical research. Reference lists will be screened. Two reviewers will independently and in duplicate conduct title/abstract and full-text screening. Data will be extracted by a single reviewer using a piloted form, with a second reviewer verifying a portion of the extracted data to ensure accuracy. Extracted variables will include measured outputs (turnaround time and diagnostic accuracy), workflow feasibility, and clinical utility (margin application and intraoperative impact). Findings will be synthesised narratively and presented in tables grouped by assay category (e.g., PCR, mass spectrometry, biosensors, rapid IHC) and their salient surgical workflow variables (turnaround time, accuracy, clinical utility).

title: A Scoping Review of Applications of Machine Learning for the Diagnosis and Classification of Multiple Myeloma
description:
This review systematically maps how machine learning (ML) has been applied to improve the diagnosis of multiple myeloma through serum protein electrophoresis (SPE) and immunofixation electrophoresis (IFE), two tests that remain central but heavily dependent on expert interpretation. By reviewing ML applications ranging from early neural-network models to modern deep learning systems, the study captures the full landscape of automated M-protein detection, band classification, and electrophoretic pattern recognition. Through rigorous scoping review methodology, it synthesizes evidence from diverse datasets, model architectures, diagnostic objectives, and performance outcomes, offering the first comprehensive overview of this rapidly evolving field.

Early and accurate detection of multiple myeloma is often limited by human interpretation, variable expertise, and resource constraints, particularly in settings with uneven access to trained laboratory personnel. ML models consistently demonstrate high diagnostic accuracy—sometimes surpassing expert readers—yet their clinical readiness, generalizability, and integration remain unclear without a consolidated evidence base. Understanding where these models excel, where they fail, and what methodological gaps persist is essential for guiding responsible adoption of AI in diagnostic laboratories. This review is therefore crucial for identifying strengths, limitations, and unrealized opportunities such as explainable AI, multi-centre validation, workflow integration, and multimodal diagnostic approaches.

The review establishes that ML has strong potential to enhance or even automate components of electrophoresis-based myeloma diagnostics, but real-world impact depends on addressing key gaps in generalizability, transparency, and clinical deployment. It delivers an evidence map, highlights methodological weaknesses, and outlines a clear research roadmap to support future development of trustworthy, scalable AI tools. Ultimately, this project provides essential groundwork for improving diagnostic equity and accelerating early detection of multiple myeloma, especially in resource-limited healthcare systems, while informing laboratories, clinicians, and policymakers considering AI adoption

title: Comparison of the practicability of ultrasound and spiral CT in the diagnosis of colon cancer: A protocol for systematic review and meta-analysis
description:
Abstract
Background: Colon cancer is a common malignant tumor of the gastrointestinal tract. Therefore, a clear diagnosis is particularly important for the treatment of colon cancer. Ultrasound and spiral CT can both be used in the diagnosis, but each has its own advantages and disadvantages, which could cause confusion in clinical choice. The purpose of this study was to systematically evaluate the practicability of spiral CT and ultrasound in the diagnosis of colon cancer.
Methods: A systematic search was performed by retrieving on English databases (PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, the Cochrane Library) and Chinese databases (CNKI, Wanfang, Weipu (VIP), CBM). Besides, manually search for Google and Baidu academic of diagnostic experimental study of ultrasound and spiral CT in the diagnosis of Colon Cancer. The retrieval time limit was from the establishment of the database to October 2020. Two researchers independently extracted and evaluated the quality of the data in the included study. A meta-analysis was performed using Meta Disc1.4 and RevMan5.3 software.
Results: Sensitivity, specificity, po-sitive Likelihood ratio, NE-gative likelihood ratio, and diagnostic odds ratio were used to determine the diagnostic efficacy of ultrasonography and helical CT in colorectal cancer.
Conclusions: This study will compare the practicability of CT and ultrasound in the diagnosis of colon cancer and provide reliable evidence-based basis for clinicians to choose the appropriate or best evidence-based basis.

title: A Meta-Analysis of the Associations Between Social Class and Social Cognition
description:
This project is a preregistered meta-analysis investigating the relationship between socioeconomic status (SES) and social cognitive abilities, specifically empathy and Theory of Mind (ToM). Prior research has yielded contradictory findings: some studies suggest lower-SES individuals exhibit heightened sensitivity to others' mental and emotional states, while others associate low SES with poorer performance on social cognitive tasks. 

To resolve these inconsistencies, this project aims to quantitatively synthesize the existing literature to determine the overall effect size and identify key moderators. Potential moderators include the type of SES measure (subjective vs. objective), the nature of the social cognition task (e.g., facial emotion recognition, perspective-taking) and sample characteristics (e.g., age, gender, culture).

The study adheres to PRISMA guidelines and employs a three-level meta-analytic model to account for effect size dependence. We expect our findings to clarify the generalizability of SES effects on social cognition and contribute to theoretical debates on class-based cognitive patterns, domain specificity, and cultural variation.

title: Aural language skills and the emergence of reading in bilingual children: A follow-up
description:
This pre-registered study uses a longitudinal design that aims to investigate the relationship between bilingual English-Chinese (Mandarin) children’s language environment and the contribution of auditory skills to later literacy (reading and spelling) outcomes. The overarching aim is to clarify how early auditory speech perception relates to the reading development in bilingual children, and to determine how early readers’ developing reading neural networks may differ from the brain networks of adults who speak the same languages. This study will determine how these factors assessed at or prior to primary school entry relate to reading skills at later primary school (grade 2-3). Investigation of the effects on reading neural networks using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) is contained in a separate pre-registration document (Viñas-Guasch, Tan & Chen, 2023).

This pre-registration concerns the follow-up in the longitudinal study, taking a prospective approach to examine early skills prior to reading acquisition and their relation to developed reading skills. The study concerns data from two timepoints: T1 - the end of Kindergarten year 2 (K2) to beginning of Primary grade 1 (P1); and T2 - the end of Primary grade 2 (P2) to the beginning of Primary grade 3 (P3). Data collected from this timepoint (T2) will be compared against those from Timepoint 1 to achieve greater understanding in how early perceptual and learning skills relate to the literacy outcomes. A target sample of 168 final-year kindergarteners and early first graders (K2/P1s) studying in Singapore were recruited in T1 (O’Brien, Chen, Styles, Ke & Lim, 2019). At T2, the researchers follow up on the same participants at primary school (P2/P3), where information on their reading skills are collected through the administration of age-appropriate language, and cognitive behavioral tasks. In addition, perceptual and reading skills are also assessed for these bilingual children in Chinese at T2. A comparison of English and Chinese auditory perceptual skills is investigated in a separate pre-registration (Pan & Styles, 2023).

Data collected from T1 are included in the analyses, along with the new data collected with the same children from language, cognitive and literacy assessments. Additional information is is collected with a parent-report survey. Building on the language background information (input, output, proficiency, and literacy habits) collected from T1, the same parents will be invited to complete a second part of the Language Background Questionnaire comprising questions regarding their literacy beliefs.

In this study, we aim to address research questions pertaining to the relation of speech perception to literacy for English and for Chinese in this bilingual sample. We will also investigate the sensitivity and specificity of audio speech perception relative to other predictors in identifying children with poor reading (relative to peer-norms).

title: Replication of the consequences of stereotype threat on the academic performance of white and non-white lower income college students
description: Harrison et al. Examined the effects of socioeconomic stereotypes on college students from different income backgrounds. They essentially wanted to expand their understanding of stereotype threat on participants with varying income backgrounds and determine whether it influences academic performance of white and non-white college students and additionally the influence on test anxiety, academic identification, and state self-esteem. In order to do this Harrison et al. Recruited 269 participants who were randomly assigned to either math or verbal test first and then randomly assigned to the diagnostic or non-diagnostic condition. The diagnostic condition was the control group where stereotype threat was placed and assessed. Participants completed various assessments after math and verbal tests to determine effort, identification, test anxiety, self-esteem, and demographic (SES, gender, ethnicity). Overall, the results suggest lower income students performed worse when stereotype threat was activated, had higher test anxiety scores, and experienced less academic identification with either math or English compared to middle and upper income students. However, lower income students self-esteem was not effected by the stereotype threat. Middle income students performance, test anxiety, and identification were not affected by stereotype threat in anyway. While upper income students performed better with the stereotype threat in math and verbal tests and academic identification. These results have led me to want to replicate stereotype threat on lower and upper income college students, specifically wanting to examine how it affects their math performance and test anxiety scores. title: Does early non-improvement predict for treatment failure in pharmacotherapy for OCD? A diagnostic test meta-analysis
description:
Preregistration of a protocol for determining the predictive accuracy of early non-improvement in the treatmnet of OCD.

Rationale 
Standalone treatment with selective serotonin inhibitors (SSRI’s) is the first choice for pharmacotherapy of obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), and, in case of initial non-response, switching to another SSRI or to clomipramine are the preferable treatment options (1, 2). However, despite common use of these compounds, non-response, defined as a decrease of symptoms (measured by the Yale-Brown obsessive compulsive scale, YBOCS) of less than 35 percent, appears in forty to sixty percent of patients (3). Whether or not patients with OCD respond to SSRI’s or clomipramine is typically evaluated after 12 weeks of treatment, which is considerably longer compared to other psychiatric illnesses (e.g. 6-8 weeks in case of major depressive disorder and 4-6 weeks in case of acute psychosis) (4-6). Recent evidence from an aggregate data meta-analysis of randomized-controlled trials in OCD suggests, however, that most short-term improvement is evident by week 6 (7). This raises the question if patients who do not show any noticeable symptom improvement in the first weeks of treatment, should continue their medication until week 12 before deciding to discontinue and switch, or if this decision could be made earlier. There have indeed been studies investigating if symptom change at 4 weeks predicts eventual response in OCD pharmacotherapy, albeit with small sample sizes and heterogenous methodologies (8, 9). 
Using such a predictor, clear stopping criteria could be developed which can aid shared-decision making. Clear stopping criteria may help early identification of ineffective treatments and shorten the time for patients before receiving a treatment which does benefit them. Importantly, it might also lower the threshold for patients to commence pharmacotherapeutic treatment, as a decision regarding cessation can be made earlier and more easily. 
In this study, we will use individual participant data of randomized-controlled trials of SSRI’s, some using clomipramine as a comparator, in order to create a meta-analysis of diagnostic accuracy. Our aim is to investigate if early lack of symptom improvement can predict subsequent non-response, in pharmacological treatment of OCD.

title: On the Equivalency of Factor and Network Loadings
description: Recent research has demonstrated that the network measure node strength or sum of a node’s connections is roughly equivalent to confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) loadings. A key finding of this research is that node strength represents a combination of different latent causes. In the present study, we sought to circumvent this issue by formulating a network equivalent called network loadings. In two simulations, we evaluated the extent to which network loadings could effectively (1) separate the effects of multiple latent causes and (2) estimate the population or true factor loading matrix of factor models. We demonstrate that the network loadings could effectively separate multiple latent causes and estimate the population factor loadings. We also leveraged the second simulation to derive effect size guidelines for network loadings. In a third simulation, we evaluated the similarities and differences between factor and network loadings when the data generating model was a random or network model. We found sufficient differences between the loadings, which allowed us to develop an algorithm called Loadings Comparison Test (LCT). The LCT had high sensitivity and specificity when predicting the true data generating model. In sum, our results suggest that network loadings can provide similar information to factor loadings when the data are generated from a factor model and therefore can be used in a similar way (e.g., item selection, measurement invariance, factor scores). Moreover, we found that network loadings may be a general case that can be effectively applied to any data generating model.

title: Exhaled Breath Biomarkers in the Diagnosis of Cardiovascular Disease: A Scoping Review
description:
Research Project Description Overview This research project is a scoping review titled *Exhaled Breath Biomarkers in the Diagnosis of Cardiovascular Disease*, designed to systematically map, summarize, and synthesize the existing body of literature on the use of exhaled breath biomarkers for the diagnosis of cardiovascular diseases (CVDs). Guided by the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology for scoping reviews and reported in accordance with the PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews) guidelines, the review aims to address critical gaps in understanding the current state of research on noninvasive breath-based diagnostic tools for CVDs. The project was pre-registered on the Open Science Framework (OSF) on November 5, 2025 , to ensure transparency and methodological rigor. Purpose & Rationale CVDs—including coronary artery disease, myocardial infarction, heart failure, arrhythmias (e.g., atrial fibrillation), valvular heart disease, and cardiomyopathies—remain a leading cause of global morbidity and mortality. Early and accurate diagnosis is essential for improving patient prognosis, enabling timely intervention, and reducing the long-term burden on healthcare systems. However, current diagnostic approaches for detecting CVDs (e.g., coronary angiography, blood-based biomarkers) often have limitations: they may be invasive, costly, require specialized equipment or clinical settings, or lack sensitivity for early-stage disease. This creates a pressing need for noninvasive, accessible tools to improve early detection, screening, and differential diagnosis of CVDs. 
Exhaled breath biomarkers have emerged as a promising solution. These biomarkers—including volatile organic compounds (VOCs), nitric oxide (NO), and carbon monoxide (CO) ect.—are endogenously produced by metabolic and pathophysiological processes in the cardiovascular system and released into exhaled breath. Despite growing interest and an expanding volume of primary studies in this area, several key challenges hinder the clinical adoption of breath biomarkers for CVD diagnosis. First, the specific VOCs associated with cardiovascular pathology remain heterogeneous across studies, and no clear consensus has been established regarding their diagnostic validity or clinical applicability. Second, methodological inconsistencies—including differences in breath collection procedures, storage protocols, and analytical techniques such as gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS) or electronic noses—limit the comparability of findings and preclude standardization.Given these gaps, a comprehensive synthesis of the current evidence base is urgently needed to clarify the state of research, evaluate diagnostic performance metrics (e.g., sensitivity, specificity), and identify methodological barriers to clinical translation. This scoping review seeks to map the landscape of studies investigating exhaled breath biomarkers for the diagnosis of CVD. Through a systematic and structured synthesis, we aim to: (1) Identify VOCs and other exhaled breath biomarkers that have been investigated in association with cardiovascular diseases; (2) Evaluate the reported diagnostic performance of these biomarkers, including metrics such as sensitivity, specificity, and overall discriminatory ability in differentiating individuals with and without CVD; (3) Examine the methodologies employed for breath sample collection, processing, and analytical detection, highlighting variations or inconsistencies that may affect data comparability and validity; and (4) Summarize the current state of research on breath-based diagnostics for CVD, identify key knowledge gaps, and propose directions for future research and potential clinical translation. Methodology To achieve these objectives, the review will employ a rigorous, systematic approach: 1. Literature Search A comprehensive search strategy, developed in consultation with an experienced medical librarian, will be applied to seven databases: Medline (via PubMed), Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, ProQuest, CINAHL, and the Cochrane Library. 
1、The search will cover literature from database inception to May 2025, using combinations of MeSH terms and keywords related to three core concepts: (1) CVDs (e.g., “coronary artery disease,” “heart failure,” “arrhythmia”), (2) exhaled breath biomarkers (e.g., “volatile organic compound,” “exhaled nitric oxide,” “breath biomarker”), and (3) diagnosis (e.g., “early detection,” “screening,” “noninvasive diagnosis”). No restrictions on geographic region or study design will be imposed during the initial search phase.
 2. Study Eligibility Studies will be included if they: (1) involve adult participants (≥18 years old) with suspected or confirmed CVD; (2) evaluate any exhaled breath biomarker for diagnostic purposes; (3) use eligible study designs (observational studies, diagnostic accuracy studies, or interventional studies reporting baseline diagnostic performance); and (4) are peer-reviewed and published in English. Studies will be excluded if they focus on animals, are review articles/editorials/conference abstracts without full text, or prioritize treatment monitoring/prognosis over diagnosis.
 3. Study Selection & Data Extraction Duplicates will be removed using EndNote, followed by two independent reviewers screening titles/abstracts and full texts for eligibility. Discrepancies will be resolved via discussion or adjudication by a third reviewer, with the process documented in a PRISMA flow diagram. Data will be extracted independently by two reviewers using a pilot-tested form, capturing variables such as author, year, country, study design, CVD subtype, biomarker type, detection method, reference standard, and diagnostic performance. 
4. Data Synthesis Extracted data will be synthesized descriptively (no formal meta-analysis, given the scope of the review). Findings will be presented in tables and narrative summaries, stratified by CVD subtype (e.g., heart failure vs. coronary artery disease) and biomarker category (e.g., VOCs vs. NO) to clarify disease-specific patterns. 
Expected Outcomes 
This scoping review is expected to generate several key outputs: 1. Comprehensive Mapping of the Field: A structured overview of which exhaled breath biomarkers have been studied for each CVD subtype, the detection methods employed, and the geographic/chronological distribution of research. This will highlight understudied areas (e.g., biomarkers for arrhythmias or congenital heart disease) and emerging trends (e.g., portable electronic nose technology). 2. Summary of Diagnostic Performance: A synthesis of available evidence on the diagnostic utility of breath biomarkers, including consistent findings (e.g., acetone as a marker for acute heart failure) and inconsistencies (e.g., variable NO levels across CVD subtypes). This will help prioritize biomarkers with the strongest preliminary diagnostic potential. 3. Methodological Insights: A critical appraisal of detection methods, identifying which technologies (e.g., GC-MS, e-nose, spectroscopy) are most widely used, validated, or accessible for clinical translation. This will inform recommendations for standardized protocols to reduce methodological heterogeneity. 4. Research Gaps & Future Directions: Clear identification of unmet needs, such as the lack of large-scale multicenter studies, limited validation of biomarkers against gold-standard diagnostics, or insufficient data on comorbidity-related confounders (e.g., diabetes affecting breath acetone). These gaps will guide future research agendas for translating breath biomarkers to clinical practice. 5. Clinical & Public Health Implications: A discussion of how the review’s findings can inform the development of noninvasive screening tools for CVDs—particularly in low-resource settings or for at-risk populations where traditional diagnostics are unavailable. This has the potential to improve early detection, reduce healthcare costs, and enhance patient access to timely care. Significance By consolidating fragmented literature on exhaled breath biomarkers for CVD diagnosis, this scoping review will serve as a foundational resource for researchers, clinicians, and policymakers. It will advance understanding of a promising noninvasive diagnostic approach, accelerate translation of basic research to clinical practice, and ultimately contribute to reducing the global burden of CVDs through improved early detection and screening.

title: Interaction of potentiation and fatigue on skeletal muscle twitch torque and displacement
description:
Tensiomyography (TMG) is a non-invasive method to assess the contractile properties of skeletal muscles. TMG measures the displacement of a single muscle belly during an electrically stimulated twitch and has been frequently used to evaluate muscular fatigue. Muscular fatigue is associated with a reversible decrease in force production and shortening velocity. Conversely, post-activation potentiation causes a temporary increase in force production and shortening velocity following a conditioning activity, such as a maximum voluntary contraction. As fatigue and post-activation potentiation can co-exist, skeletal muscle contractile properties generally reflect the net balance of the two phenomena.
The effects of fatigue and post-activation potentiation on the muscle force production capacity during electrically stimulated twitches have been previously investigated in many studies. However, a direct comparison of muscle force production capacity and muscular displacement under these physiological conditions is scarce. Therefore, the purpose of this study is to investigate the relationship between the simultaneously developed torque and displacement during electrically stimulated twitch contractions of a single muscle belly under potentiated and fatigued conditions. Further, this study aims to investigate the diagnostic accuracy of tensiomyographic parameters with regard to the peak twitch torque under these physiological conditions.

title: Hemodynamic Significance of Carotid Artery Ultrasound Predictors in Assessing Volume Status in Critically Ill Patients: A Scoping Review
description:
Abstract

Background: Accurate, timely, and non-invasive assessment of volume status in critically ill patients, including those on mechanical ventilation (MV) or in shock, is crucial for effective hemodynamic management and the prevention of multiorgan failure. Traditional static markers of preload, such as central venous pressure (CVP), have definitively demonstrated their pathophysiological and clinical inadequacy in predicting fluid responsiveness. Meanwhile, classic dynamic parameters based on heart-lung interaction, such as pulse pressure variability (PPV) and stroke volume variability (SVV), require invasive arterial monitoring and are subject to strict physiological limitations. In recent years, point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) of the carotid artery (CA) has gained significant popularity as an innovative, accessible, and non-invasive method for predicting fluid responsiveness.

Objectives: To conduct a comprehensive scoping review to map existing evidence regarding the diagnostic accuracy, physiological limitations, "grey zone" sizes, and reproducibility (both intra- and inter-operator) of various carotid artery ultrasound parameters in patients within the intensive care unit (ICU).

Methods: In accordance with the PRISMA-ScR methodology, a systematic search will be conducted across the MEDLINE, Embase, and Cochrane Library databases. The analysis will include studies evaluating corrected flow time (FTc), respiratory variability of peak systolic velocity, carotid blood flow (CBF), velocity-time integral (VTI), and carotid artery diameter variability in combination with dynamic tests, such as the passive leg raise (PLR) test, end-expiratory occlusion test (EEOt), and fluid bolus.Expected Results: The review is expected to synthesize data demonstrating that carotid artery Doppler indices possess moderate to high predictive value. It is anticipated that parameters based on flow time (FTc) and relative peak velocity variation ($\Delta$Vpeak) will outperform absolute carotid blood flow (CBF) calculations due to their lower dependence on the insonation angle and reduced mathematical errors associated with vessel diameter measurement. The issue of "grey zones," which can reach 61% for certain parameters, will be described in detail, as this critically limits their isolated use at the bedside.

Conclusions: Ultrasound assessment of the carotid artery is a promising tool in the intensive care armamentarium. Nevertheless, high inter-operator variability among novice specialists, the impact of vascular compliance in geriatric patients, and the presence of broad zones of diagnostic uncertainty necessitate the standardization of scanning protocols and cautious interpretation of data within the context of comprehensive multimodal hemodynamic monitoring.

title: Understanding the Role of Anxiety in Planfulness Across the Lifespan
description: Previous studies indicate that adolescents with higher levels of anxiety create fewer and vaguer future-oriented goals (Dickson and Macleod, 2004). Furthermore, children who are more reactive, as opposed to forward-thinking and proactive, were projected to have higher levels of anxiety (Troller-Renfree, 2019). While these studies imply a negative correlation between anxiety and forward thinking in children and adolescents, there is limited knowledge in emerging adults and beyond. Furthermore, there are conflicting results about the correlation of age and anxiety, with some studies claiming anxiety is less prevalent in older adults (Flint, et al 2012), and others predicting the risk of anxiety and depression increases upon aging (Gao, et al 2023). Therefore, this project aims to explore if planfulness moderates the relationship between anxiety across the adult lifespan using a general linear model. As the mental health field is constantly developing, these findings can help differentiate how certain symptoms present themselves in different age groups, which may improve quality of care, diagnostic accuracy, and treatment.

title: Fundus Camera Use in the Emergency Department: A Scoping Review of Current Evidence and Clinical Applications
description:
Presentations involving ocular complaints account for approximately 1.5% to 6% of all emergency department (ED) visits, representing a wide spectrum of acuity from benign conditions to vision- and life-threatening emergencies. Direct visualization of the posterior segment through funduscopy is a crucial element of the physical examination for evaluating critical pathologies such as papilledema secondary to elevated intracranial pressure, retinal detachment, or life-threatening systemic vascular crises like malignant hypertension. However, traditional direct ophthalmoscopy is severely underutilized in acute care owing to its narrow field of view, steep learning curve, technical difficulty, and low diagnostic yield when performed by non-specialist clinicians, leading to high rates of missed findings in emergency settings. 

Modern digital fundus cameras, including handheld, non-mydriatic tabletop, and smartphone-based tools, have emerged as a practical solution to overcome these challenges. These devices allow ED providers to capture wide-field digital fundus photographs in seconds, typically without requiring pupillary dilation. These high-resolution images can be reviewed immediately, stored in electronic health records, or transmitted off-site to support tele-ophthalmology consultation networks. While studies demonstrate that integrating fundus photography into the ED significantly improves examination rates and clinician diagnostic accuracy, the existing body of literature remains heterogeneous, spread across disparate specialties, and varied in device designs, indications, and workflow implementation strategies. 

To address this evidence gap, the purpose of this scoping review is to systematically map the extent, range, and nature of research concerning fundus camera use in emergency care settings. Following established scoping review frameworks, this study will map the types of imaging devices studied, summarize clinical indications for fundus evaluation, synthesize diagnostic yield and management outcomes, and document implementation barriers, facilitators, and training protocols. The expected outcome is a comprehensive evidence map that will inform emergency clinical workflow design, elucidate barriers to adoption, and highlight critical research gaps to guide future primary studies and acute care practice guidelines.

title: Artificial intelligence as a training tool in the interpretation of images for abdominal trauma: a scoping review
description:
Abdominal trauma is a leading cause of morbidity and mortality in emergency departments worldwide, requiring rapid and accurate diagnostic methods for clinical decision-making. Proper interpretation of studies such as FAST ultrasound and computed tomography is essential for identifying critical injuries, but mastering these techniques presents a significant challenge for students and physicians in training due to the complexity of the clinical setting and the variability of clinical presentations (1,2,3).

The importance of artificial intelligence has been steadily growing, due to its diverse applications and the ability to maximize its potential. This has meant that, in recent years, artificial intelligence has emerged as a promising tool in the clinical and educational fields.
Its ability to analyze large volumes of data, identify subtle patterns, and provide immediate feedback positions it as a valuable alternative to support the teaching of image interpretation. Algorithms such as convolutional neural networks and supervised learning models have demonstrated comparable, and even superior, performance to that of human experts in various diagnostic tasks. (4,5,6) 
This potential extends to the field of medical training, where AI could facilitate autonomous learning, standardize teaching, and reduce diagnostic errors during clinical training. (7,8)
Health education has undergone a significant transformation in recent decades, driven by the need to train professionals capable of responding to complex and high-demand clinical scenarios. 
The interpretation of diagnostic images, particularly in critical situations such as abdominal trauma, has become a core competency in medical training programs. The World Health Organization (WHO) emphasizes that strengthening early diagnostic skills in healthcare professionals is essential to improving the quality of care and reducing preventable mortality, especially in emergency and acute care settings (9). In this regard, educational programs must integrate innovative pedagogical tools that promote the acquisition of these competencies in a safe, reproducible, and evidence-based manner.

The incorporation of emerging technologies in health education, such as simulation,
computer-assisted learning, and, more recently, artificial intelligence, has been shown to improve clinical performance and knowledge retention. Several studies have documented that traditional lecture-based methods have limited effectiveness compared to active learning models, especially when it comes to highly complex technical and cognitive skills, such as the interpretation of FAST, ultrasound, POCUS, or CT scans in trauma (10,11). 

The literature indicates that the use of active methodologies increases diagnostic accuracy in students by 20% to 40% when simulators or digital tools that allow for immediate feedback are integrated (12).

The importance of strengthening training in image interpretation in trauma settings is evident when considering global epidemiological data. Trauma is responsible for approximately 4.4 million deaths annually, with abdominal injuries being a frequent cause of preventable mortality when not identified promptly (13). Despite this, multiple studies report that students and residents perform suboptimally in detecting key findings on FAST or abdominal CT scans compared to specialists, with error rates reaching up to 30% in the early stages of training (14). This underscores the need for innovative educational strategies, where AI emerges as a resource with the potential to improve training through automated analysis, objective feedback, and self-directed learning opportunities.

title: Evaluation architecture and reported discrimination of chest radiography AI for tuberculosis: a systematic review and meta-epidemiological analysis
description:
This project is a systematic review and exploratory meta-epidemiological analysis of reported diagnostic discrimination (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, AUC) for artificial intelligence applied to chest radiography (CXR-AI) for tuberculosis. The study reconstructs the evidence architecture linking published reports, result sets, extractable AUC effects, and independent study clusters, accounting for within-cluster dependence between correlated effect estimates.

The primary objectives are: (1) to estimate the pooled reported AUC and between-study prediction interval across CXR-AI evaluations for tuberculosis; and (2) to assess whether binary study-level classifications — including data collection direction (retrospective vs. prospective), evaluation structure (single-site vs. multisite-pooled), screening vs. non-screening intended use, threshold provenance reporting, and exclusively symptomatic vs. mixed populations — are associated with AUC heterogeneity.

The initial protocol proposed multivariable meta-regression and publication-bias assessment, but evidence reconstruction revealed insufficient independent clusters and moderator overlap for reliable multivariable estimation. Given correlated effects, substantial heterogeneity, and incomplete diagnostic 2×2 data, conventional asymmetry testing was not considered interpretable. The analytic scope was narrowed before model fitting, and five moderators were evaluated separately using multilevel random-effects meta-regression with cluster-robust variance estimation (CR2) and Satterthwaite degrees of freedom.

The expected outcome is a characterization of the current published evidence base for CXR-AI discrimination in tuberculosis, quantifying average reported performance, the range of uncertainty across evaluation settings, and the explanatory ability (or lack thereof) of commonly used binary design classifications. This analysis does not establish deployment criteria for specific products or settings; rather, it provides an evidence-appraisal framework for researchers, regulators, and tuberculosis programmes evaluating the robustness and transferability of published CXR-AI performance estimates.

title: Artificial intelligence applications in fundus photograph image analysis for diagnosis and screening of brain tumours: A Systematic Review
description:
This systematic review aims to evaluate the utility and diagnostic accuracy of artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), and deep learning algorithms applied to fundus and retinal imaging for the detection, diagnosis, and screening of brain tumours and related intracranial pathologies. Brain tumours, including gliomas, pituitary neoplasms, and other intracranial neoplasms, often present with ocular signs such as papilloedema and other optic nerve head abnormalities that can be detected through fundus photography. Early identification of these signs via non-invasive retinal imaging has the potential to facilitate timely diagnosis and improve patient outcomes.

The primary purpose of this review is to synthesise current evidence on the performance of AI-based diagnostic tools in analysing retinal images to identify brain tumours and their associated ocular manifestations. Specifically, the review will assess the diagnostic accuracy of AI algorithms - measured by sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve - in diverse clinical and screening settings. It will also examine the potential of these technologies to improve early detection, screening processes, and clinical decision-making compared to conventional methods, such as clinical examination and neuroimaging.

The review will include original research studies, including diagnostic accuracy studies, cohort studies, case-control studies, and observational reports, that have evaluated AI/ML models applied to fundus or retinal photographs. The studies will be scrutinised for quality and bias using the QUADAS-2 tool to ensure robustness of findings.

Expected outcomes include a comprehensive synthesis of evidence regarding the effectiveness of AI in this context, identification of knowledge gaps, and recommendations for future research and clinical practice. Ultimately, this review aims to inform stakeholders - including clinicians, researchers, and healthcare policymakers - about the feasibility and accuracy of integrating AI-based retinal image analysis into routine screening and diagnostic pathways for brain tumours.
