title: Use of extracellular vesicles as biomarkers for the diagnosis of Rheumatoid Arthritis: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
description: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a multifactorial autoimmune inflammatory disease with a polyarticular pattern, characterized by joint stiffness, chronic pain, and synovitis mainly affecting the small proximal synovial joints. The repercussions of this disease are systemic, and there may be extra-articular and constitutional manifestations. Regarding the diagnosis of RA, clinical biomarkers are currently used which have limitations, mainly regarding sensitivity and specificity. Therefore, exosomes are being studied as promising biomarkers for more efficient diagnosis and monitoring of RA. Exosomes are extracellular vesicles (EVs) secreted by almost all cell types physiologically and pathologically, playing a major role in RA. Therefore, this research aims to evaluate, by a systematic review, the effectiveness of EVs as a biomarker for the diagnosis of RA. To this end, the study will be conducted based on the recommendations of the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA). The electronic literature search will be carried out using the PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Cochrane Library databases, which will be carried out until March 2025 to answer the PICO question: “Would the use of extracellular vesicles as a biomarker be more efficient than the markers used currently used for the diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis?” Efficacy in diagnosis will be considered the primary outcome. The biological material used as the source of EVs and the method for biomarkers will be included in the secondary outcomes. After selecting the articles and extracting the data, they will be subjected to bias analysis and meta-analysis. It is expected to determine the effectiveness of EVs as a biomarker for the diagnosis of RA.

title: Point-of-Care Lung Ultrasound Versus Chest CT in Adults with Acute Pulmonary Disorders: A Systematic Review
description:
Computed tomography (CT) is widely regarded as the gold standard for diagnosing various acute pulmonary conditions, including pneumonia, pneumothorax, pleural effusion, atelectasis, pulmonary embolism, and pulmonary congestion. However, CT scans expose patients to ionizing radiation, which has been associated with an increased long-term risk of cancer (CHAVEZ MA,et al 2014). Recent studies estimate that CT scans may account for up to 5% of all annual cancer cases in the United States, with approximately 103,000 future cancer diagnoses linked to the 93 million CT scans performed in 2023 alone (SMITH-BINDMAN R,et al, 2025). The cumulative effect of repeated imaging is particularly concerning in hospital settings such as emergency departments and intensive care units, where critically ill patients often undergo multiple scans during a single hospitalization (CAO CF et al, 2022).
Point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) has emerged as a rapid, non-invasive, and radiation-free imaging modality that can be performed at the bedside by clinicians. It has demonstrated high diagnostic accuracy for various pulmonary pathologies ( HANSELL L, et al 2021). For instance, studies have shown that POCUS has a sensitivity of 97% and specificity of 94% for diagnosing pneumonia (CHAVEZ MA,et al 2014) and a sensitivity of 87,2% for detecting pulmonary manifestations of COVID-19 (FRATIANNI G et al, 2022; MATTHIES A, et al 2023) . Despite these promising results, the diagnostic performance of POCUS compared to CT varies across the literature, and its reliability as an alternative or adjunct to CT in clinical decision-making remains under evaluation (HANSELL L, et al 2021).
Therefore, a systematic review of the diagnostic accuracy of lung POCUS compared to chest CT is crucial to clarify its clinical utility, identify contexts in which it may serve as a safer alternative, and ultimately contribute to reducing unnecessary radiation exposure without compromising diagnostic quality.

title: CT-Based Radiomics and Deep Learning for Classifying the Invasiveness of Ground-Glass Lung Adenocarcinoma: A Systematic Review and Diagnostic Test Accuracy Meta-analysis of AIS, MIA, and IAC
description:
This project is a systematic review and diagnostic test accuracy (DTA) meta-analysis evaluating the performance of computed tomography (CT)-based radiomics, deep learning, artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning, quantitative imaging, and hybrid models for classifying the invasiveness of ground-glass lung adenocarcinoma.

The review focuses on differentiating adenocarcinoma in situ (AIS), minimally invasive adenocarcinoma (MIA), invasive adenocarcinoma (IAC), and invasive-spectrum lesions presenting as ground-glass, part-solid, or subsolid pulmonary nodules. The primary objective is to synthesize evidence regarding the diagnostic accuracy of imaging-based AI models and to compare their performance across different target conditions and model categories.

A comprehensive literature search was conducted across Embase, Europe PMC, OpenAlex, PubMed, Scopus, Semantic Scholar, and Web of Science. Eligible studies evaluated CT, HRCT, or LDCT-based radiomics, deep learning, machine learning, AI-assisted quantitative imaging, or hybrid approaches and reported sufficient data to calculate diagnostic accuracy metrics.

The primary outcomes include pooled sensitivity, specificity, positive likelihood ratio (LR+), negative likelihood ratio (LR−), diagnostic odds ratio (DOR), and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). Diagnostic performance is synthesized using random-effects models and bivariate DTA meta-analytic methods. Risk of bias and applicability concerns are assessed using the QUADAS-2 tool.

The findings are intended to provide an evidence-based assessment of the current capabilities and limitations of AI-assisted imaging technologies for preoperative invasiveness assessment of lung adenocarcinoma presenting as ground-glass nodules, identify methodological gaps in the literature, and inform future research and clinical translation. Based on the included evidence, CT-based AI and radiomics models demonstrate good performance for identifying invasive adenocarcinoma, although substantial heterogeneity and validation challenges remain for reliable subclassification of AIS and MIA.

This registration documents the review methodology, eligibility criteria, data extraction framework, statistical analysis plan, and risk-of-bias assessment procedures prior to dissemination of the final results.

title: Identifying Existing Critical Appraisal Tools to Evaluate the Methodological Quality of SRs in Special Education——A Cross-sectional Study
description:
1 Background
A systematic review (SR) is characterized by a clearly defined question, a predetermined method for identifying and selecting primary studies, and an approach to assessing and synthesizing all relevant evidence to minimize bias1, thereby providing reliable scientific evidence for decision-making2. Although systematic reviews have been launched in healthcare3, they are now implemented across various academic disciplines4. The volume of systematic reviews is expanding at an exponential pace, exceeding the number of primary trials within the healthcare domain5,6. Umbrella review (UR), is a systematic collection and assessment of multiple systematic reviews and meta-analyses on a specific research topic, whose validity depends on the coverage and quality of both the primary studies and the available systematic reviews and meta-analyses7. At the same meta-level of evidence as the umbrella review, the reviews’ nomenclature is also identified as “overview of reviews”8, “systematic review of systematic reviews”9, “meta-meta-analysis”10, and systematic meta-review11.
Critical appraisal is a transparent examination of potential methodological biases in research12. As a key component in conducting an umbrella review, critical appraisal should be employed to assess the methodological quality of the included systematic reviews. In the field of education, systematic reviews are used to synthesize extensive educational primary studies and serve as an essential foundation for evidence-based practice13,14. Moreover, the demand for evidence-based decision-making in education is steadily increasing15,16. The distinctiveness of special education lies in its interdisciplinary nature17: children or adolescents with special educational needs require interventions from the health sector to meet health needs, alongside educational interventions to support developmental needs. As such, evidence in this field spans multiple disciplines. Failure to rigorously apply existing scientific evidence can result in management decisions that are less likely to the outcome variables (thus failing to optimize the use of limited resources) or may even cause harm4.
Despite the growing number of systematic reviews in the field of education, clear guidance on how to critically assess systematic reviews specific to educational topics remains lacking. Critical appraisal tools for systematic reviews are designed to detect important potential biases in the included reviews, allowing us to consider these biases when interpreting research results and providing recommendations for decision-making18. Although critical appraisal tools are widely used in other fields, they were mostly developed within the context of healthcare and may not be directly applicable to the field of education. From a methodological perspective, while there are overlaps between the standards of education and medicine13—such as consistency in research questions and methods, quality assessment of included studies, and the scientific rigor of evidence synthesis19—the detection of potential key biases in systematic reviews of educational interventions remains distinct. For example, the implementation context of educational interventions, including the country and setting, significantly influences how applicable the results of synthesized evidence are to educational decision-makers20. These factors have not yet been adequately captured in the existing critical appraisal tools.
In this article, we clarify the critical appraisal tools available in the field of special education and examine the commonalities and specificities of the appraisal areas the tools focus on.

1.1Critical appraisal for systematic reviews in education
Ensuring the methodological quality of systematic reviews in education, similar to the healthcare field, begins with controlling the inclusion of different types of primary studies, as the potential biases inherent in these studies may vary21. The higher the level of evidence in primary studies may indicate the lower the risk of bias, and the greater the certainty of the results22. Campbell and Stanley pioneered the concept of evidence hierarchy, assigning the highest quality to randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and introducing the concepts of internal validity and external validity23. The widely accepted evidence hierarchy in research includes Systematic reviews and meta-analyses of randomized controlled trials, Randomized controlled trials (RCT), Non-randomized intervention studies, Observational studies, Non-experimental studies, and Expert opinion24. It is undeniably true that conducting RCT poses greater challenges in many areas of education compared to certain aspects of healthcare13. Consequently, researchers evaluating educational methods often rely on controlled comparisons of matched schools, classrooms, or communities and model the impact of external variables13, which marks nuances from primary studies in healthcare.
Another approach to ensuring the methodological quality of systematic reviews is to guarantee that all critical steps of the systematic review process are conducted. According to the WWC (What Works Clearinghouse) standards, systematic reviews (SRs) in education include the following key steps: developing the review protocol, identifying relevant literature, screening studies, reviewing studies, and reporting findings19. However, the WWC standards do not offer a critical appraisal tool for assessing the methodological quality of systematic reviews at a meta-level, namely, the level of conducting an umbrella review.

1.2Critical appraisal tools
As for assessing the methodological quality of the effectiveness of SRs, the Risk of Bias in Systematic Reviews (ROBIS)25, the Assessing the Methodological Quality of Systematic Reviews 2 (AMSTAR-2)12 and the JBI Checklist for Systematic Review and Research Synthesis26 are the tools previously heavily cited. The ROBIS aims to provide a thorough and robust assessment of the level of bias within the intervention effectiveness systematic review in healthcare25. Modifying items from AMSTAR to the assessment of SRs that include randomized or non-randomized studies of healthcare interventions, or both, the AMSTAR 2 was developed and proven to be good at assessing methodological quality for SRs in healthcare27. The purpose of JBI checklist for SRs is to evaluate the methodological rigor of a study and to determine the extent to which it has systematically addressed potential biases in its design, conduct, and analysis26. These tools are widely utilized; however, none explicitly indicate their applicability for assessing the methodological quality of systematic reviews in the field of education. More data-driven evidence is needed to confirm whether the methodological requirements for systematic reviews in education are consistent with those in healthcare.
Different item responses and scoring methods can significantly impact the discrimination of the quality assessment tools in the systematic review25,28. A study of diagnostic accuracy was marked by QUADAS (A quality assessment tool for diagnostic accuracy studies)29 as the best quality using the scoring method of “weighting based on the evidence” and “appraiser subjective scoring”. However, the same study was considered as average quality using “equal weighting”, “equal weighting accounting for unclear”, and “weighting according to item type” scoring approaches28. This highlights the importance of reporting key item scores individually rather than relying solely on a summarizing score. Confidence ratings based on AMSTAR-2 do not differentiate among systematic reviews of healthcare interventions, except for Cochrane SRs that meet the criteria for high confidence ratings5. This suggests the presence of a floor effect when assessing the methodological quality of non-Cochrane systematic reviews. The above research proposes assessment of intervention effectiveness systematic reviews in the field of education by CATs, to our knowledge, have yet to be verified.
Methodological quality assessment tools differ from reporting quality assessment tools, such as PRISMA 202030. Methodological quality tools evaluate whether the steps undertaken during the process of conducting an SR are sufficient to minimize bias. In contrast, reporting quality assessment tools aim to address reporting bias in SRs30,31. This distinction is particularly relevant to CATs in determining whether it is necessary for a scale or checklist to include item response options such as "unclear" or "no information." On one hand, marking a key criterion as "unclear" implies that the step might have been conducted during the SR process but was not reported, which is fundamentally different from explicitly indicating that the step was "not conducted." On the other hand, based on practical experience from authors, assessors often find it challenging to distinguish between when to select "no" versus "unclear" while using the tools. Whether it is necessary to consider the specificity of item response options in tools for evaluating systematic reviews in the field of education remains an open question that warrants further investigation.
The current study aims to describe how the methodological quality of intervention effectiveness of SRs in special education was assessed in an umbrella review or overview of SRs and to identify existing critical appraisal tools and the key domains that these tools valued.

title: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis on Diagnostic Accuracy of Near Infrared Spectroscopy for Brain Tumor Detection
description:

title: Tracking Diagnostic Performance Drift Across the Reasoning-Model Generation: A Multi-Provider Longitudinal Evaluation of Large Language Models on Medical Question-Answering
description:
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly evaluated for clinical decision support, yet most benchmarking studies treat models as static: querying a single version at a single point in time. Chen, Zaharia, and Zou (2023) demonstrated that this assumption is unsafe, documenting GPT-4 accuracy shifts of up to 33 percentage points within three months. However, their study predated the reasoning-model era and compared only two snapshots.

This project systematically tracks diagnostic accuracy across date-stamped model snapshots from four major providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, DeepSeek) spanning 2024–2026. We evaluate up to 21 model versions, including both conventional and reasoning-class models (e.g., OpenAI o-series, Claude extended thinking, Gemini thinking, DeepSeek-R1), on fixed evaluation sets of 500 MedQA-USMLE and 200 DiagnosisArena items. Each model is queried three times per item at temperature 0.2 to separate temporal drift from stochastic variation.

We quantify drift using accuracy deltas, question-level flip rates, Cohen's kappa, Jaccard similarity, and KL divergence between consecutive snapshots. A mixed-effects model decomposes variance across providers, snapshots, and questions. We test three pre-registered hypotheses: (1) that at least one snapshot pair shows >10% absolute accuracy change, (2) that reasoning models are more temporally stable than pre-reasoning models, and (3) that question-level flip rates exceed aggregate accuracy changes, indicating hidden instability beneath stable top-line numbers.

All evaluation items, prompts, analysis code, and raw API responses are released in full. The study informs regulatory frameworks, particularly the FDA's Predetermined Change Control Plan (PCCP) guidance, by providing empirical evidence on whether current model versioning practices are sufficient for safe deployment in clinical settings.

title: Diagnostic Accuracy of Consensus Guidelines for Clinical Management of Pancreatic Intraductal Papillary Mucinous Neoplams
description:
Intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasms (IPMNs) represent a clinically significant category of pancreatic cystic lesions with well-established malignant potential. Two major international consensus guidelines used to stratify resection risk and guide clinical decision-making: the 2017 International Association of Pancreatology (IAP) Fukuoka guidelines and the updated 2024 Kyoto guidelines. Both frameworks rely on morphological and clinical features to classify lesions as low-risk (surveillance) or high-risk (resection-warranted), yet their real-world diagnostic accuracy and rates of overtreatment and undertreatment remain incompletely characterised across heterogeneous patient populations. 

This systematic review and meta-analysis aims to:
1. Identify the primary studies reporting the diagnostic accuracy of the 2017 Fukuoka and/or 2024 Kyoto consensus guidelines in patients with IPMN.
2. Compute pooled estimates of sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), and diagnostic odds ratios (DOR) for each guideline against a reference standard.
3. Quantify rates of overtreatment (unnecessary resection in benign disease) and undertreatment (missed high-grade dysplasia or invasive carcinoma under surveillance).
4. Compare diagnostic performance between the Fukuoka 2017 and Kyoto 2024 guidelines, including any changes in sensitivity-specificity trade-offs introduced by the revised criteria.

title: Diagnostic Accuracy of Wearable Technologies for Atrial Fibrillation Detection: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
description:
Abstract 
Background: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most common sustained cardiac arrhythmia and a major cause of stroke, heart failure, and mortality. Due to its often paroxysmal and asymptomatic nature, AF frequently remains undiagnosed using conventional short-term monitoring strategies. Wearable technologies have emerged as scalable tools for AF detection, but their overall diagnostic accuracy across platforms remains uncertain.
Objective: To systematically evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of wearable devices for detecting AF using a diagnostic test accuracy meta-analysis.
Methods: A systematic review was conducted following PRISMA-DTA guidelines. PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane Library databases were searched from inception to February 2026. Prospective and retrospective diagnostic accuracy studies assessing wearable AF detection devices in adults. Eligible studies used electrocardiographic reference standards and reported sufficient data to estimate sensitivity and specificity. Devices were categorized into handheld ECG-based devices, smartphone-based photoplethysmography (PPG) applications, passive smartwatch monitoring systems, and prolonged monitoring devices. Pooled sensitivity and specificity were estimated using bivariate random-effects models.
Results: A total of 51 studies comprising 33,374 participants were included. Wearable devices demonstrated high diagnostic accuracy across all categories. Pooled sensitivity ranged from 92.5% to 96.8%, while specificity ranged from 93.6% to 98.0%. Smartphone-based PPG applications showed the highest sensitivity (96.8%), whereas passive smartwatch monitoring demonstrated the highest specificity (98.0%). Handheld ECG devices also showed strong performance with high sensitivity and low negative likelihood ratios. Moderate heterogeneity was observed across studies.
Conclusion: Wearable technologies demonstrate high diagnostic accuracy for atrial fibrillation detection, particularly in controlled and selected populations, and show promise for large-scale screening and monitoring.

description:
This project evaluates pre-biopsy diagnostic pathways for clinically significant prostate cancer in the MRI era. Its purpose is to identify which strategies can safely reduce unnecessary prostate biopsies while maintaining very high sensitivity for clinically significant cancer, primarily defined as ISUP Grade Group 2 or higher.

title: Biomarkers for mood disorders: a scoping review of research from India
description:
Introduction:
Mood disorders are a major global health concern that pose significant diagnostic and therapeutic challenges. Biomarker research offers the potential to improve diagnostic accuracy and facilitate personalized treatment approaches. However, geographic validation of biomarkers remains limited. This scoping review aimed to synthesize evidence from biomarker studies on mood disorders conducted in India, identify methodological trends, and highlight research gaps to inform future investigations.
Methodology:
A systematic literature search was conducted across PubMed and Scopus for studies published between January 2000 and December 2024. Studies conducted in India that evaluated biomarkers in individuals with major depressive disorder (MDD) or bipolar disorder (BD), diagnosed according to ICD-10 or DSM-IV/DSM-5 criteria, were included. Study quality was assessed using the AXIS tool, and findings were synthesized narratively.
Results:
A total of 56 studies met the inclusion criteria. In MDD, elevated levels of interleukin-6 (IL-6) and cortisol were consistently reported. IL-6 and tumour necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) levels decreased and brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) levels increased following treatment. C-reactive protein (CRP), neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio, malondialdehyde, and cortisol levels were associated with depression severity. Neuroimaging and electroencephalography (EEG) studies demonstrated fronto-limbic circuit involvement in both MDD and BD. In BD, cognitive studies consistently reported impairments in executive function, learning, and memory. Additional novel findings included abnormalities in retinal arteriolar tortuosity and deficits in eye movement.
Discussion:
Biomarker findings from Indian studies largely align with evidence reported in Western populations. However, considerable heterogeneity across studies suggests that biological alterations may not be universally consistent. Methodological differences and clinical heterogeneity further limit interpretation and comparability of findings. Future research should emphasize standardized methodologies, larger multicentric cohorts, and multimodal biomarker approaches, as combining biological markers may offer greater diagnostic, predictive, and prognostic utility than individual biomarkers.

title: Risk of Bias and Limitations
description:
Risk of bias and applicability
Risk of bias and applicability will be assessed using QUADAS-2, tailored to this review question. The four domains will be patient selection, index test, reference standard, and flow/timing. Applicability concerns will be assessed for patient selection, index test and reference standard.
For this review, particular attention will be given to whether studies included a representative adult IBD population, whether nutritional screening tool thresholds were clearly reported, whether GLIM, ESPEN criteria or SGA were clearly defined and applied to the relevant population, whether the same participants received both the screening tool and comparator, and whether assessments were performed within an appropriate timeframe.
Studies will be rated as low, high or unclear risk of bias for each domain. Abstract-only studies will usually be rated as unclear where insufficient methodological detail is available. Applicability concerns will be described where studies involve selected populations, such as surgical or remission-predominant cohorts.
Certainty and limitations of evidence
The overall strength of evidence will be discussed narratively, considering risk of bias, applicability to the review question, consistency of findings across studies, precision of diagnostic accuracy estimates, and completeness of reporting.
Type 1 studies with complete or reconstructable 2 x 2 data will be considered separately from Type 2 studies that provide supportive evidence only.

title: Diagnostic Utility of Intraoperative Neuromonitoring in Carotid Revascularization: A Systematic Review
description:
This project is a systematic review evaluating the diagnostic accuracy and clinical utility of intraoperative neuromonitoring (IONM) during carotid revascularization procedures, with particular emphasis on transcarotid artery revascularization (TCAR). IONM modalities such as electroencephalography (EEG), somatosensory evoked potentials (SSEP), transcranial Doppler (TCD), near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS), and bispectral index (BIS) are increasingly used to detect intraoperative cerebral hypoperfusion or embolic events; however, their routine use remains controversial due to limited and heterogeneous evidence. This review aims to synthesize existing data to clarify the diagnostic performance, clinical relevance, and safety implications of IONM in carotid interventions.

A systematic literature search was conducted in PubMed and Scopus following PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Eligible studies included observational studies and randomized trials reporting the use of any IONM modality during carotid revascularization, including TCAR, carotid endarterectomy (CEA), and transfemoral carotid artery stenting (TF-CAS). Data extraction focused on monitoring modalities, alert rates, correlations with neurological outcomes (stroke or transient ischemic attack), intraoperative interventions prompted by neuromonitoring, and diagnostic accuracy measures (sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, and negative predictive value). Risk of bias was assessed using the Newcastle–Ottawa Scale for observational studies.

The expected outcomes of this review include a comprehensive assessment of the diagnostic performance of IONM modalities, identification of circumstances in which neuromonitoring may meaningfully influence intraoperative decision-making, and clarification of the potential value of multimodal monitoring strategies. By consolidating current evidence, this study aims to inform clinical practice, highlight gaps in the literature, and guide future prospective studies evaluating standardized neuromonitoring protocols in carotid revascularization, particularly TCAR.

title: Beyond Boundaries: Integrating Artificial Intelligence into Society 5.0’s Healthcare
description:
Rachmad, Yoesoep Edhie. 2021. Beyond Boundaries: Integrating Artificial Intelligence into Society 5.0’s Healthcare. Australian Health Book Publishing, Collingwood Special Issue, 2021. https://doi.org/10.17605/osf.io/xs459



"Beyond Boundaries: Integrating Artificial Intelligence into Society 5.0’s Healthcare" by Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, published in 2021 by Australian Health Book Publishing in Collingwood, explores the intersection of advanced technologies and healthcare within the framework of Society 5.0. This book emerges from the need to address the evolving landscape of healthcare, driven by technological advancements and the concept of Society 5.0, which envisions a society deeply integrated with sophisticated technologies to improve the quality of life.
Definition and Basic Concepts
The book introduces Society 5.0, a paradigm where digital transformation, particularly Artificial Intelligence (AI), plays a crucial role in enhancing various sectors, including healthcare. It defines AI as a set of algorithms and computational models designed to perform tasks that typically require human intelligence. The core concept revolves around leveraging AI to enhance diagnostic accuracy, treatment efficiency, and overall healthcare management.
Underlying Phenomena
The motivation for this book stems from the rapid advancements in AI and its potential to revolutionize healthcare. The increasing volume of healthcare data, the need for personalized medicine, and the global demand for accessible and efficient healthcare services are key phenomena driving this exploration. The author underscores the urgency to integrate AI into healthcare systems to address these contemporary challenges.
Problem Statement
The central problem addressed by the book is the integration of AI into healthcare within the Society 5.0 framework. It examines the challenges and opportunities of incorporating AI technologies in healthcare settings, aiming to understand how these technologies can be effectively utilized to improve healthcare outcomes while navigating ethical, legal, and practical considerations.
Research Objectives
The book aims to provide a comprehensive analysis of how AI can be integrated into healthcare, exploring its applications, benefits, and challenges. It seeks to outline strategies for successful implementation, emphasizing the importance of ethical guidelines and regulatory frameworks to ensure the responsible use of AI in healthcare.
Indicators
The book identifies several key indicators of successful AI integration in healthcare, including improved diagnostic accuracy, enhanced treatment efficacy, efficient healthcare data management, and broader access to healthcare services. It also considers the development of robust ethical and legal frameworks as critical indicators.
Operational Variables
Operational variables in the book include AI technologies such as machine learning algorithms, neural networks, and natural language processing tools. The book also explores variables related to healthcare outcomes, data management practices, and regulatory compliance.
Determining Factors
The determining factors for the successful implementation of AI in healthcare, as discussed in the book, include technological advancements, data availability and quality, regulatory environments, and societal readiness to embrace AI-driven healthcare solutions. The author emphasizes the role of interdisciplinary collaboration in overcoming technical and ethical challenges.
Implementation and Strategy
The book outlines various strategies for integrating AI into healthcare, such as investing in AI research and development, fostering collaboration between technology developers and healthcare professionals, and establishing comprehensive training programs for healthcare workers. It also highlights the need for continuous monitoring and evaluation to adapt to evolving technologies and healthcare needs.
Challenges and Supportive Factors
The book identifies several challenges, including data privacy concerns, algorithmic biases, and the potential for job displacement within the healthcare sector. Supportive factors include technological innovations, supportive regulatory policies, and public acceptance of AI in healthcare. The author calls for a balanced approach to address these challenges while leveraging supportive factors to maximize the benefits of AI.
Determining Factors of the Book
The factors determining the relevance and impact of the book include the timeliness of its publication amidst the growing interest in AI, the comprehensiveness of its analysis, and its practical recommendations for healthcare professionals and policymakers. The book’s ability to address ethical considerations and propose actionable strategies also contributes to its significance.
Research Findings
The book presents several case studies demonstrating successful AI applications in healthcare, such as improved diagnostic processes, effective telemedicine solutions, and enhanced data management systems. These findings illustrate the tangible benefits of AI integration, providing evidence of its potential to transform healthcare delivery.
Conclusion and Recommendations
In conclusion, the book reaffirms the vital role of AI in shaping the future of healthcare under the Society 5.0 paradigm. It advocates for responsible and ethical adoption of AI technologies, emphasizing the need for regulatory frameworks and continuous evaluation. The author recommends fostering collaboration across disciplines, investing in education and training, and promoting public awareness to ensure the successful integration of AI into healthcare.
"Beyond Boundaries: Integrating Artificial Intelligence into Society 5.0’s Healthcare" offers a detailed roadmap for leveraging AI to enhance healthcare, underscoring the importance of innovation, ethical responsibility, and strategic implementation.

Risk of bias and methodological quality will be assessed using the QUADAS-2 tool. If the identified studies are sufficiently homogeneous, a quantitative meta-analysis will be conducted. Statistical analyses will be performed to assess clinical utility and potential sources of heterogeneity among the included studies.

title: The diagnostic accuracy of SARS-CoV-2 nasal rapid antigen self- test: a systematic review and meta-analysis
description:
Introduction: Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) is
the cause of corona virus disease (COVID-19), a disease that quickly spread into a
pandemic. So, reliable diagnostic tests for SARS-CoV-2 are vital for the management of
COVID-19 pandemic. The gold standard for the diagnosis of SARS-CoV-2 is the
molecular detection test using the reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction
technique (rt-PCR), which is characterized by various disadvantages in contrast to the
self-taken nasal rapid antigen tests which give results faster, have lower costs and do not
require specialized personnel. Therefore, the usefulness of self-taken rapid antigen tests
is indisputable in disease management, facilitating both the health system and the
examinees. Our systematic review aims to access the diagnostic accuracy of the self-
taken nasal rapid antigen tests.
Methods: This systematic review conducted following the PRISMA guidelines and the
Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies 2 (QUADAS-2) tool was used to
assess risk of bias in the included studies. All the studies included in this systematic
review were found after searching the 2 databases Scopus and PubΜed. Anything but
original articles were excluded from this systematic review while all the studies
concerning self-taken rapid antigen tests with a nasal sample and using rt-PCR as a
reference test were included. Meta-analysis results and plots were obtained using
RevMan software and the MetaDTA website.
Results: All 22 studies included in this meta-analysis demonstrated a specificity of self-
taken rapid antigen tests greater than 98%, which exceeds the minimum required yield
for the diagnosis of SARS-CoV-2, according to WHO. However, the sensitivity varies
(from 40% to 98.7%), which makes them in some cases unsuitable for the diagnosis of
positive cases. In the majority of the studies, the minimum required performance set by
the WHO, is achieved, which is 80% compared to the rt-PCR. In this meta-analysis the
pooled sensitivity of self-taken nasal rapid antigen test was calculated 91,1% and the
pooled specificity 99,5%.
Conclusion: In conclusion, self-taken nasal rapid antigen tests have many advantages
over rt-PCR, such as those related to the rapid reading of the results and their cheap cost.
They also have considerable specificity and some self-taken rapid antigen tests kits also
have remarkable sensitivity. Consequently, self-taken rapid antigen tests have a wide
range of utility, but are not able to completely replace rt-PCR tests.

title: “Family History of Premature Coronary Artery Disease and Its Influence on Age of Onset and Disease Severity in Middle-Aged Adults in India: A Systematic Review with Narrative Synthesis”
description:
Title
“Family History of Premature Coronary Artery Disease and Its Influence on Age of Onset and Disease Severity in Middle-Aged Adults in India: A Systematic Review with Narrative Synthesis”
________________________________________
Review type
Systematic review with primary narrative synthesis; conditional meta-analysis if data are sufficiently homogeneous.
Review question / primary objective
Among Indian adults aged 30–60 years, how does a family history (FHx) of premature coronary artery disease (CAD) influence:
1. Age at CAD onset, and________________________________________
Rationale / Background (brief)
Familial predisposition is a recognised risk factor for premature CAD, but there is no focused synthesis of evidence on how FHx modifies age of presentation and angiographic severity in middle-aged Indian adults. This review will collate, appraise, and synthesise observational evidence to inform clinicians and researchers and identify gaps for future study. 
________________________________________
Eligibility criteria
• Population: Indian adults aged 30–60 years with angiographically confirmed CAD.
• Exposure: Positive family history of premature CAD (first-degree relative <55 years for men; <65 years for women).
• Comparator: FHx-negative (no family history of premature CAD).
• Outcomes:
o Primary: Age at first CAD diagnosis (mean ± SD or median).
o Secondary: CAD severity metrics (Gensini score, SYNTAX score, number of diseased vessels) if available.
• Study designs: Observational studies — cross-sectional, case-control, cohort studies.
• Language: English.
• Dates: 2000 to present.
• Exclusions: Case reports, editorials, reviews, and studies lacking separate FHx analysis.
________________________________________
Information sources & search strategy
• Databases: PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, IndMed.
• Supplementary sources: Reference lists of key articles, conference proceedings, theses, and grey literature.
• Search terms (examples): “coronary artery disease” OR “CAD” AND “family history” OR “familial” AND “premature” AND “India” AND “age of onset” OR “severity” OR “Gensini” OR “SYNTAX”.
• Date of planned database search: May 2025 (see timeline). 
________________________________________
Screening and selection
• Platform: Rayyan for deduplication and screening.
• Process: Two independent reviewers will screen titles/abstracts, then full texts, against eligibility criteria. Disagreements resolved by consensus or a third reviewer. A PRISMA 2020 flow diagram will record numbers at each stage.
________________________________________
Data extraction
• Tool: Standardised Excel extraction form.
• Items to extract: Study ID, year, journal, location, design, sample size, sex distribution, FHx definition and ascertainment method, age metrics by FHx status, severity scores, statistical tests and effect estimates (mean differences, ORs/RRs), confounder adjustments, and key study limitations.
• Procedure: Two reviewers extract independently; discrepancies reconciled by discussion.
________________________________________
Risk of bias / quality assessment
• Tool: Newcastle–Ottawa Scale (NOS) for observational studies.
• Reporting: Studies graded as low, moderate, or high risk of bias and results considered in synthesis and sensitivity analyses.
________________________________________
Data synthesis & analysis plan
• Primary approach: Narrative synthesis structured around study design, population characteristics, FHx definitions, and outcomes. Descriptive tables will summarise characteristics and main findings. 
• Quantitative synthesis (conditional): If studies reporting the same outcome (e.g., mean age at diagnosis) are sufficiently homogeneous (comparable populations, consistent FHx definitions, similar outcome metrics), pooled mean differences (FHx-positive vs FHx-negative) will be calculated using random-effects meta-analysis. For proportions or effect measures (OR/RR) of premature presentation, pooled estimates may be computed if appropriate.
• Heterogeneity assessment: Clinical and methodological heterogeneity will be evaluated qualitatively; statistical heterogeneity (I²) reported if meta-analysis performed.
• Subgroup analyses (if data permit): By sex, and by key comorbidities (e.g., diabetes).
• Sensitivity analyses: Excluding high risk-of-bias studies; varying FHx definitions.
• Publication bias: If ≥10 studies contribute to a meta-analysis, funnel plots and Egger’s test will be considered.
• Visuals: Forest-style plots (for pooled or study-level mean differences), bar charts of severity distributions, and summary tables.
________________________________________
Handling missing data
Investigators will be contacted for missing or unclear data. Where necessary and justifiable, reported medians may be converted to means using established methods; sensitivity analyses will assess the impact of such conversions.
________________________________________
Reporting & guidelines
• The review will adhere to PRISMA 2020 and guidance for narrative syntheses. Reporting will include full methods, risk-of-bias results, and transparent presentation of strengths/limitations.
________________________________________
Registration & dissemination
• Intended registry: OSF (this submission).
• Planned outputs: OSF project with final report, submission to a peer-reviewed journal, and sharing of extracted datasets and code used for any meta-analyses. 
________________________________________
Timeline
• Protocol submission: (completed)
• Database search: May 2025
• Screening & selection: June 2025
• Data extraction & risk-of-bias: July–August 2025
• Synthesis & write-up: August–September 2025
• Submission to journal: September 2025. 
________________________________________
Conflicts of interest & funding
• Conflicts: None declared.
• Funding: No external funding.
________________________________________
Notes / additional methodological points
• FHx thresholds use sex-specific ages for “premature” CAD (male relative <55 years; female relative <65 years).
• The review focuses on angiographically confirmed CAD to increase clinical specificity of outcomes.
• All methodological details and extraction templates are available in the protocol document referenced above.

Family history; premature coronary artery disease; age of onset; India; middle-aged adults; systematic review; narrative synthesis.

title: Low-Value Abdominal X-Ray Use in Emergency Department Patients: a Scoping Review.
description:
Introduction. Abdominal X‑rays remain commonly ordered in emergency departments despite growing evidence that their diagnostic utility is limited for many clinical indications. For conditions such as non‑specific abdominal pain, constipation, renal colic, and suspected bowel obstruction, AXRs often have low sensitivity and specificity and rarely alter patient management when compared with alternative imaging modalities or clinical assessment alone. The aim of this literature review is to map the extent, range and nature of the literature on the clinical utility, diagnostic yield, and appropriateness of abdominal X-rays in emergency department (ED) settings, including how low-value AXR use is defined and quantified.

Methods and analysis. This scoping review will be conducted in accordance with the JBI methodology for scoping reviews and reported per the PRISMA extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR). MEDLINE (Ovid), Emcare (Ovid), Scopus (Elsevier), CINAHL (EBSCOhost), and Web of Science (Clarivate) will be searched, supplemented by backward and forward citation chaining. Eligible sources will be primary research studies (quantitative, qualitative, or mixed-methods) reporting AXR-specific data on use in ED settings, published in English. Title/abstract, full-text screening and data charting will be performed in duplicate by two independent reviewers, with disagreements resolved by a third reviewer. Results will be synthesised narratively by clinical indication and presented in tabular and diagrammatic form.

Ethics and dissemination. Ethics approval is not required for this scoping review. The findings of this review are expected to contribute to the growing evidence base about the clinical utility of abdominal X-rays (AXRs) as well as inform emergency medicine practitioners about potential low-value imaging practices. Findings will directly inform a planned retrospective cohort study of low-value AXR at Townsville University Hospital Emergency Department (TUH-ED).

description: Background: Sepsis-associated encephalopathy (SAE) is a common and severe complication of sepsis, associated with increased mortality and long-term cognitive dysfunction. Early diagnosis remains challenging due to the lack of specific diagnostic biomarkers. Several blood-based biomarkers have been investigated for SAE diagnosis, but their clinical utility remains unclear.Objective: To systematically evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of blood biomarkers for sepsis-associated encephalopathy through a meta-analysis of diagnostic test accuracy (DTA) studies.Methods: We will systematically search PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, CNKI, Wanfang, and VIP databases. We will use the bivariate random-effects model to calculate pooled sensitivity, specificity, diagnostic odds ratio, and area under the SROC curve. Threshold effect analysis and subgroup analyses will be performed to explore heterogeneity. Methodological quality will be assessed using the QUADAS-2 tool.Expected outcomes: This study will provide a comprehensive evaluation of the diagnostic accuracy of major blood biomarkers for SAE, identify the most promising candidates, and highlight gaps in current evidence. The findings may inform clinical practice and guide the design of future biomarker validation studies.

description: Evaluating the impact of new technology on populations at smaller scale is crucial before full-fledged implementation for all. This research aimed at examining the impact of EchoGo Pro, an artificial intelligence driven stress echocardiography analysis system designed to support diagnosis of cardiac conditions including cardiac ischaemia and potential coronary artery disease. EchoGo Pro provides clinicians with decision support system by generating diagnostic recommendations for the identification of coronary heart disease and risk of heart failure, etc. The potential impacts of the technology in public health settings are (i) the autonomous nature of the system increases medical decision consistency between providers, (ii) improved diagnostic accuracy, (iii) support of earlier intervention and (iv) increased confidence to less experienced clinicians in making diagnostic decisions. These in turn increase speed and capacity to process tests, identify at-risk patients, and provide more preventive treatment and ultimately have fewer acute cardiac events amongst screened patients. This technology may also boosts the confidence of clinicians, especially junior doctors. These improvements in turn should benefit public in terms of good value and affordable health gains and, potentially, reducing health inequity. Relying on a combination of interviews and focus groups and comparisons of quantitative health outcomes, our research intends to answer four questions; a) Is EchoGo Pro acceptable to patients and providers? Q2: Is EchoGo Pro safe and does it reduce health inequality? Q3: Does EchoGo Pro positively impact health problems through early or more frequent detection and intervention? Q4: Does the expenditure to implement EchoGo Pro can be justified by the improvements in health care decision making and ultimately patient outcomes and patient experience? Using financial metrics as a proxy for ‘value’ -what would an EchoGo Pro service be worth from the perspective of a patient, service manager/ or member of staff working in cardiac services?

title: Validation of an expert system of an app-based exercise recommendation for musculoskeletal pain patients – analysis of risk, sensitivity, and specificity
description:
Lee et al. (2018) showed that mobile app-based interventions could be useful to improve various health-promoting behaviors such as diet and physical activity for the general healthy population. Most of the app interventions studied focused on monitoring health status and behavior change and providing feedback or health-related information. App programs may be more effective if social support is advocated and if they include entertainment or visualization features. Future research should address the effectiveness of mobile apps for health promotion in developing countries. In a clinical trial by Balk-Møller et al. (2017), an app-based intervention was shown to reduce body weight, body fat percentage, and waist circumference among social and health care workers, particularly among those specifically motivated to lose weight. When used to recommend exercises for patients suffering from musculoskeletal pain an app could be a helpful resource to enhance exercise frequency and thereby promote pain reduction. 
The current market shows that most applications rely on standardized exercise plans. In these applications, for example, it is not possible to combine several areas of complaint, nor do the exercise plans adapt to the individual needs of the user/patient regarding types of sport, physical strain within the working day, etc. The user/patient is not able to choose between different types of exercise. To process this complex information, an expert system is needed. An expert system contains knowledge from experts, which has been digitized and thus made applicable in algorithms. Both factual knowledge and procedural knowledge are entered into the expert system by the experts. After knowledge acquisition and system verification, the expert system can then solve problems independently based on the experts' knowledge. To treat pain patients with exercise recommendations the medicalmotion GmbH developed an expert system. 
This expert system recommends exercises, which are presented to the end user within an app and the user can perform them with the help of videos. Before the user can start performing exercises, he must first fill out a questionnaire on pain quality, sporting activity and workload. After-wards, exercises are recommended to the user, which can be adapted daily in response to the course of pain and well-being. Due to the constant changes in pain progression and well-being, it must be ensured that the expert system no longer recommends any exercises if the pain progression or other pain data contradict this. So, the implementation of an expert system for treatment of musculoskeletal pain patients may involve risks, as e.g., wrong exercises or ongoing treatment caused of misinterpreted informations by the expert system. 

For the reasons stated above, the objective of this study is firstly to evaluate the risk in performing the exercise recommendations of the expert system. Secondary, the evaluation of the specificity and sensitivity of the expert system while treatment is to be performed.

title: Diagnostic performance of multitarget stool DNA test for advanced colorectal neoplasia: a systematic review and meta-analysis
description:
Colorectal cancer (CRC), the third most common cancer and a leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide, emphasizes the critical need for effective early detection strategies. Advanced colorectal neoplasia (ACN), encompassing high-grade adenomas and CRC, is a pivotal target for screening due to its association with improved outcomes when detected preclinically. Multitarget stool DNA (mt-sDNA) tests have emerged as noninvasive alternatives to colonoscopy, leveraging molecular markers (e.g., mutations in KRAS, APC, TP53, and methylated DNA sequences like NDRG4, BMP3) to identify neoplastic cells shed into the gastrointestinal tract. Despite growing clinical adoption, substantial heterogeneity exists in reported diagnostic performance across studies, attributed to variations in study populations, reference standards (e.g., colonoscopy with pathological confirmation), detection thresholds, and comparator tests (e.g., fecal immunochemical test [FIT]).
This systematic review and meta-analysis aims to synthesize current evidence on the diagnostic accuracy of mt-sDNA tests for ACN, providing a comprehensive assessment of their sensitivity, specificity, and predictive values. Specifically, we will evaluate how performance metrics differ across key subgroups, including test types (e.g., Cologuard®, Epi proColon™), study design (prospective vs. retrospective), population demographics (average-risk vs. high-risk individuals), and ACN definitions (advanced adenomas vs. CRC). By addressing methodological inconsistencies and pooling data from eligible studies, we seek to clarify the clinical utility of mt-sDNA tests in real-world screening scenarios.
Expected outcomes include robust estimates of diagnostic accuracy for ACN, identification of sources of heterogeneity, and insights into optimal patient populations for mt-sDNA testing. These findings may inform evidence-based guidelines for colorectal cancer screening, facilitate comparisons with established methods like FIT and colonoscopy, and highlight areas for future research—such as refining marker panels or improving risk stratification. Ultimately, this project aims to strengthen the evidence base supporting mt-sDNA tests as a viable component of colorectal screening programs, potentially enhancing accessibility and adherence to early detection initiatives globally.

title: Comparison of different methods for the meta-analysis of diagnostic test accuracy studies – a simulation study
description: Meta-analysis of diagnostic test accuracy (DTA) studies is, due to its co-primary endpoint of sensitivity and specificity, methodologically more challenging than its univariate counterpart in intervention studies. In medical practice, methods for the meta-analysis of DTA studies often do not distinguish between diagnostic thresholds in the primary studies and only use information from a single threshold per study. In contrast, more recent approaches incorporate all available information by considering all diagnostic thresholds and can express summary estimates depending on the threshold. We will systematically compare eleven methods for the meta-analysis of DTA studies, five of which consider a single diagnostic threshold per study, while the other six consider all available thresholds. Using simulation scenarios that resemble realistic meta-analysis datasets, we will investigate the methods’ bias, empirical coverage and convergence behavior for diagnostic tests on both the continuous and ordinal scale. Our aim is to detect situations in which certain methods are superior or inferior to others and thus aiding practitioners in an adequate choice of method when performing meta-analysis in a specific setting.

title: Scoping review protocol: Psychometric evidence of instruments for assessing mental health in older adults from Latin America and the Caribbean
description:
This scoping review aims to systematically identify, summarize, and evaluate the psychometric properties of mental health assessment tools used with adults aged 60 years and older in Latin America and the Caribbean (LAC). Valid and reliable instruments are essential for geriatric care; however, evidence supporting an instrument’s validity in one context does not guarantee applicability across diverse cultural and linguistic populations.

The review addresses the question: What is the evidence on reliability, validity, and diagnostic accuracy of instruments assessing mental health in older adults in LAC?

Following the PRISMA-ScR guidelines and Arksey and O’Malley’s five-step framework, we will conduct a systematic search across eight databases (including PubMed, SciELO, and PsycINFO) for studies published between 1990 and 2024. Data will be mapped by country, mental health domain (e.g., cognition, depression, anxiety), and type of psychometric analysis. Findings will be evaluated considering internal structure, relations to other variables, and reliability to determine clinical applicability.

Expected Outcomes:

Identification of geographic and thematic gaps in psychometric evidence across LAC.

Evaluation of the sufficiency of current validation practices, highlighting over-reliance on single-metric analyses.

Development of a charting data and decision-support guide for clinicians to select context-sensitive tools validated in specific LAC countries.

This protocol will provide a foundation for improving the assessment and care of mental health in older adults across the region and support future research and collaborative initiatives.

title: Evaluation of Imaging Research Adherence to the STARD 2015 Reporting Guideline: Update 8 Years After Implementation and Baseline Assessment
description:
Abstract:
Background: The adherence of articles of diagnostic accuracy imaging research to STARD 2015 was assessed at 'baseline' in 2016-reporting was incomplete with only 55% of items reported in a sample of 142 imaging studies. Since this baseline assessment, several knowledge translation (KT) strategies have been implemented by the STARD group. However, the impact of these has not been assessed. 

Purpose: The purpose of this study is to evaluate the adherence to STARD 2015 of diagnostic accuracy studies recently published in imaging journals in order to determine if there has been an improvement since 2016. The STARD group will use this work to inform further targeted KT strategies. 

Methods: Diagnostic accuracy studies from a select group of radiology journals will be assessed over the previous ~12 months; the time span will be modulated to reach a sample size of 100-150 included studies. Two reviewers will independently extract (disagreements resolved through discussion) the following data: Study author, country of corresponding author's institution, journal, journal impact factor, year of publication, subspecialty area, diagnostic test used (imaging modality), study design and adherence to the 30 STARD 2015 reporting requirements. Analysis will evaluate overall adherence to STARD 2015 (out of 30 items), adherence on a per item basis, association with journal, country, impact factor, modality, study design and subspecialty area. Comparison to the baseline completeness of reporting observed in 2016 will be done.

title: Medical decision-making and confidence in Ghana
description:
Overconfidence among medical decision makers has been linked to diagnostic and treatment errors, which are associated with increased mortality and morbidity in a variety of contexts. While a number of interventions have been tested to directly address overconfidence among medical experts, these interventions have shown only modest success in improving diagnostic quality. Furthermore, we lack a systematic understanding of the prevalence and drivers of overconfidence in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). Our study aims to fill this gap. We propose to conduct a cross-sectional survey with 1,000 medical decision-makers in Ghana. More specifically our sample will be comprised of medical doctors and physician assistants practicing at GHS health care facilities across Ghana. Further, we include medical students who are enrolled in a medical program in Ghana and who are participating in their 2-year residency training at a teaching hospital. Our study will focus on three aspects:
(1) The drivers of overconfidence, discerning between self-image and social image concerns, (2) the real-world implications of overconfidence for patient treatment decisions, and (3) the extent to which existing institutional structures can filter and mitigate the effects of overconfidence on medical decision-making. 
Through this study, we aim to provide valuable insights that can inform targeted interventions and policy frameworks aimed at mitigating the risks associated with overconfidence in medical practice in LMICs such as Ghana. By understanding the dynamics underlying overconfidence and its consequences, we aim to contribute to improving diagnostic accuracy, treatment effectiveness, and ultimately patient outcomes in these health care contexts.

title: Saliva as a diagnostic specimen for emerging and pandemic-prone infections: a scoping review protocol
description:
Objective: To map the extent and nature of evidence on saliva-based diagnostics for emerging and pandemic-prone pathogens, and to identify gaps in this evidence, to inform prioritisation of prospective studies. 

Introduction: Saliva is an attractive diagnostic sample for surveillance, outbreak response, and detecting dangerous pathogens, because it is accessible, non-invasive, scalable, and requires minimal training and equipment. Evidence suggests promise for some pathogens, such as SARS-CoV-2 and measles, but studies are limited for most pathogens, and few rigorous evaluations have been reported. Further work is required to adequately assess its utility, which should be informed by a systematic mapping of the extent and types of evidence available. 

Inclusion criteria: Systematic reviews and studies assessing the use of saliva or similar specimens, including oral fluid, for diagnosis of infections in humans, caused by pathogens which are emerging, or have the potential to cause pandemics, prioritised in a multidisciplinary international roundtable meting in March 2026. 

Methods: We will apply a tiered approach to pathogen inclusion, with tier 1 being of highest priority: Middle-East respiratory syndrome coronavirus (MERS-CoV), dengue virus, Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever (CCHF) virus, avian influenza virus, and chikungunya virus. Tier 2 comprises Nipah virus, enterovirus, human metapneumovirus, and West Nile virus. In tier 3 are Lassa, Ebola, Sudan, Marburg, monkeypox clade 1, and severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS) viruses. The scoping review team will screen results and extract data for tier 1 viruses, followed by tier 2 and tier 3, if feasible. 

Using guidance from the Joanna Briggs Institute, we will search multiple databases and grey literature, screen results, and extract data from included reports. We will employ a hierarchical approach to enrich for evidence of the highest-certainty, including proof-of-concept studies and case series only for pathogens for which systematic reviews and diagnostic test accuracy studies/trials are not found. 

We will present our findings using tables, a narrative summary, and visualisation using a map of the evidence and its gaps, displaying study designs, outcomes assessed, and results for each pathogen.

title: Classification performance of machine learning algorithms in predicting job burnout: A systematic review and meta-analysis
description:
This preregistration outlines the protocol for a systematic review and diagnostic test accuracy (DTA) meta-analysis evaluating the classification performance of machine learning (ML) algorithms for job burnout detection.
1. Research Question
What is the overall diagnostic performance of ML algorithms in predicting job burnout, and how do algorithm type, data modality, and validation method influence model performance?
2. Eligibility Criteria
Inclusion: Original studies using ML algorithms to classify job burnout; reporting at least one performance metric (accuracy, AUC, sensitivity, specificity); sample size ≥50; published in English or Chinese.
Exclusion: Studies using only traditional statistical methods; reviews, case studies, conference abstracts; duplicate datasets; studies focusing on non-working populations.
3. Outcome Measures
Primary outcomes: pooled classification accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC).
4. Statistical Analysis Plan
Single-group proportion meta-analysis (Freeman-Tukey transformation, random-effects model) for accuracy.
Bivariate random-effects DTA meta-analysis for joint synthesis of sensitivity and specificity.
Subgroup analyses by algorithm type, data modality, validation method, and occupation.
Sensitivity analysis by leave-one-out method.
Publication bias assessed via Egger's test and trim-and-fill method.
All analyses will be conducted in R using the meta and mada packages.
5. Quality Assessment
Methodological quality of included studies will be evaluated using the QUADAS-2 tool.

title: DISCERN: coupled disease-variant inference in inherited bleeding and platelet disorders
description:
DISCERN computes a single coupled posterior over disease and variant, P(D,V|E), for use in inherited bleeding and platelet disorders. Its per-code partition and variant-intrinsic layer are already validated on open data and are not the subject of this registration. The purpose of this protocol is to test, in advance and with a fixed analysis plan, whether the coupling itself adds value: specifically, whether a calibrated phenotype likelihood driving PP4, the disease to variant link, improves reclassification of variants of uncertain significance beyond what a variant-intrinsic-only model achieves.

The primary hypothesis, H6, will be evaluated on paired phenotype and variant data using paired bootstrap net reclassification improvement against ClinVar or VCEP 2-star+ truth labels, with a circularity guard ensuring each ACMG code enters exactly one factor. A superiority margin and a falsification condition are both fixed before any paired-cohort data is examined, and the analysis will run once, after registration, on the locked dataset. Secondary work addresses misdiagnosis rescue on documented mislabelled cases, a confident-and-wrong safety rate that must be reported regardless of outcome, and per-class conformal coverage. A companion reader study measures whether the DISCERN output changes non-specialist diagnostic accuracy and time-to-decision on a locked vignette bank.

Expected outcomes are reported symmetrically: the protocol commits to publishing the result whether the coupling improves reclassification or not, with pre-drawn negative-result figures and tables and no optional stopping. A public-data precursor proof-of-concept, run before this registration and not claimed as prospective, found a working set too small to power its binary endpoint, motivating the confirmatory cohort study specified here. No claim that the coupling improves reclassification will be made until that confirmatory primary endpoint is reported on real paired data.

Although traditionally taught within dermatology residency and continuing medical education, dermoscopy is increasingly incorporated into undergraduate medical education. title: Laboratory Manual on Primer Design, PCR Technologies, and Bioinformatics Applications
description:
Molecular biology has revolutionized biological research, diagnostics, agriculture, biotechnology, forensic science, and personalized medicine. Among the various molecular techniques developed over the past few decades, the Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) remains one of the most powerful and widely used tools for nucleic acid amplification. Since its invention by Kary Mullis in 1983, PCR has transformed the ability of researchers to detect, characterize, and quantify genetic material with unprecedented sensitivity and specificity.
The success of PCR-based applications depends largely on appropriate primer design, reaction optimization, and accurate interpretation of results. Advances in bioinformatics have further enhanced primer design capabilities through computational tools capable of predicting primer specificity, thermodynamic stability, and potential secondary structures. Consequently, modern molecular biology laboratories require students and researchers to possess both theoretical knowledge and practical skills in primer design, PCR optimization, and data interpretation.
This laboratory manual has been developed for undergraduate and postgraduate students in Biotechnology, Molecular Biology, Genetics, Bioinformatics, and related disciplines. The manual integrates theoretical concepts with hands-on laboratory exercises and bioinformatics tutorials to provide a comprehensive understanding of primer design and PCR methodologies. Particular emphasis is placed on evidence-based troubleshooting, experimental design, and the use of freely accessible computational tools including Primer3, Primer-BLAST, OligoCalc, BLAST, and the UCSC Genome Browser.
The exercises included in this manual are designed to promote critical thinking, experimental planning, and analytical skills required in modern molecular biology laboratories. Furthermore, each protocol is supported by peer-reviewed literature to ensure scientific accuracy and reproducibility.

title: NyameriNet
description: The development of "Nyameri," a hypothetical next-generation mobile application for diabetic retinopathy (DR) image analysis, represents a synthesis of cutting-edge academic research and commercial product features into a cohesive, plausible technology. The core of the Nyameri system is its custom-designed Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), named NyameriNet. This architecture is engineered to deliver high diagnostic accuracy while operating efficiently on mobile devices without constant reliance on cloud connectivity. While specific architectural details like the exact number of layers are not provided in the source materials, the design philosophy aligns with state-of-the-art models known for their balance of performance and efficiency. For instance, NyameriNet's estimated size of approximately 40 MB is comparable to DRNet13, which was reported to be 35 MB. This suggests an architecture that may incorporate techniques such as depthwise separable convolutions or other forms of model optimization to maintain a small footprint. The primary function of NyameriNet is a five-class classification task: No DR, Mild, Moderate, Severe, and Proliferative DR. This multi-stage grading is a standard benchmark in the field, reflecting the clinical need for precise disease staging. The simulated performance of NyameriNet is projected to exceed current clinical standards, positioning it as a highly advanced tool. The model is expected to achieve an accuracy rate between 96% and 98%, a figure supported by numerous studies on complex CNN architectures. For example, a DenseNet-121 model using CLAHE and ESRGAN preprocessing on the APTOS 2019 dataset achieved 98.36% accuracy , while a hybrid Inception v3 model reached 98.7% accuracy on the same dataset. Similarly, a modified VGGNet-based transfer learning model trained on the Kaggle EyePACS dataset achieved 96.6% accuracy after extensive data augmentation. Sensitivity and specificity are critical metrics for any screening tool, and NyameriNet's projected values aim to surpass established benchmarks. An estimated sensitivity of 97-98% significantly outperforms the minimum requirements set by bodies like the British Diabetic Association (BDA) of 80%. This level of performance is consistent with top-tier models; for instance, a study on the Messidor-2 dataset achieved a sensitivity of 97.63% , and another model reached 99.21% on the Kaggle test dataset. Specificity is projected to be in the range of 95-97%, also exceeding the BDA's 95% minimum requirement. Models like DeB5-XNet have demonstrated 97.1% specificity on the DDR dataset , and a WFDLN model achieved 98.0% specificity on the Messidor dataset. These figures underscore the potential of modern deep learning to provide highly reliable screening results. The model's precision and F1-score are also projected to be very high, at 0.96-0.98, indicating a low rate of false positives and a strong balance between precision and recall.

title: AI-Assisted Detection of High-Grade Histologic Patterns in Lung Adenocarcinoma on Digital Pathology Slides: A Systematic Review and Diagnostic Test Accuracy Meta-analysis
description:
**Description**

Lung adenocarcinoma demonstrates substantial histologic heterogeneity, and the presence of high-grade growth patterns, particularly micropapillary and solid components, is strongly associated with recurrence, metastasis, therapeutic resistance, and poor survival outcomes. Accurate identification of these patterns on hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained pathology slides is therefore essential for prognostic stratification and clinical decision-making. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI), deep learning (DL), machine learning (ML), and computational pathology have enabled automated detection and classification of histologic patterns from digitized whole-slide images (WSIs). However, the diagnostic accuracy, reproducibility, and clinical readiness of these AI-based systems remain incompletely synthesized.

This study is a systematic review and diagnostic test accuracy (DTA) meta-analysis evaluating the performance of AI-assisted approaches for detecting high-grade histologic patterns in lung adenocarcinoma on digital pathology slides. The review focuses on AI models designed to identify micropapillary, solid, and other aggressive histologic components using H&E-stained WSIs, tissue microarrays, or digitized histopathologic images.

The review was conducted according to PRISMA-DTA guidelines. Multiple electronic databases were systematically searched, including PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, Cochrane Library, Europe PMC, and additional sources where applicable. Eligible studies included original investigations that developed, validated, or externally tested AI/DL/ML algorithms for high-grade pattern detection in lung adenocarcinoma and reported sufficient diagnostic accuracy data.

Primary pooled outcomes include sensitivity, specificity, positive likelihood ratio (LR+), negative likelihood ratio (LR−), diagnostic odds ratio (DOR), and summary receiver operating characteristic (SROC) analysis. Study quality and risk of bias are assessed using the QUADAS-2 tool. Heterogeneity, threshold effects, publication bias, and subgroup analyses are also evaluated where feasible.

This review aims to provide a comprehensive evidence synthesis regarding the diagnostic performance, methodological quality, and translational potential of AI-assisted digital pathology systems for identifying clinically aggressive histologic patterns in lung adenocarcinoma. The findings may support future integration of computational pathology tools into precision oncology workflows and routine thoracic pathology practice.

title: From Clinic to Referral: A Scoping Review of First-Contact Diagnostic Pathways and Imaging Stewardship for Atraumatic Adult Shoulder Pain in Primary Care
description:
Atraumatic shoulder pain is one of the most common musculoskeletal complaints encountered in primary care, yet first-contact diagnostic workups vary considerably across providers and settings. This variability contributes to inconsistent diagnostic accuracy, unnecessary imaging, and delayed referral to specialty care. Evidence and society guidelines relevant to this topic are dispersed across primary care, orthopedics, sports medicine, and radiology, making it difficult for first-contact clinicians to follow a unified approach.

This scoping review maps the available literature on first-contact diagnostic pathways for atraumatic adult shoulder pain in primary care, including history and ROM patterns, physical exam tests and clusters, imaging stewardship strategies, and referral triggers. Conditions of focus include rotator cuff disease and adhesive capsulitis. Searches will be conducted across MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, Cochrane, and Scopus, with additional guideline portal and grey literature searches. Screening and data charting will follow PRISMA-ScR guidance.

Expected outputs include a first-contact diagnostic pathway algorithm, an imaging stewardship pathway, and a summary of evidence gaps specific to primary care implementation.

title: Living Evidence Network: Comprehensive Insights on POCUS in Adult and Pediatric Healthcare
description: The Living Evidence Network: Comprehensive Insights on POCUS in Adult and Pediatric Healthcare is a collaborative initiative designed to generate and sustain high-quality, continuously updated evidence on the clinical use of point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) across adult and pediatric populations. This project will be built upon two living systematic reviews (LSRs) that address the evolving landscape of POCUS applications in different healthcare settings. The first review, Shaping the Future of Adult Healthcare, will synthesize and maintain up-to-date evidence on the use of POCUS in adult patients, with emphasis on its diagnostic and procedural value in emergency medicine, critical care, anesthesiology, and other key specialties. The second review, Shaping the Future of Pediatric Healthcare, will focus on the pediatric population, highlighting the growing utility of POCUS in neonatology, pediatric intensive care, and ambulatory care environments. Both reviews will classify the evidence into six main domains: Clinical applications Education and training Technological innovations Safety and diagnostic accuracy Impact on health outcomes Guidelines and clinical protocols This living evidence platform will support real-time integration of new findings to guide clinical decision-making, enhance patient safety, and promote evidence-informed practices. The project will be led by a multidisciplinary team of clinicians, methodologists, and academic researchers, and will contribute to the global effort to optimize the implementation of POCUS through accessible, rigorously maintained, and clinically relevant evidence.

description:
